en: Ekottarika Āgama, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kipin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: Introduction. Introduction. Chapter One.
I take refuge in the Benevolent One, the Seventh Sage, who proclaims the unsurpassed path of the noble ones;
forever adrift in the long-flowing river of birth and death, the World-Honored One now delivers the common people.
The venerable Kāśyapa and the assembly of monks, the wise Ānanda of immeasurable learning;
having made offerings to the relics of the Sugata’s parinirvāṇa, they traveled from Kauśāmbī to Magadha.
Kāśyapa contemplated with focused mind the practice of the four immeasurables; these classes of sentient beings fall into the five realms.
Now that the Perfectly Awakened One has manifested the Way and departed from the world, I remember the Honored One’s skillful instructions and weep with compassion.
Kāśyapa contemplates the root of the True Dharma: how may it be disseminated and long remain in the world?
The Most Honored One has uttered various verbal teachings; he holds them all in his grasp, never letting them be lost.
Who possesses this power to assemble all dharmas, the fundamental causes and conditions found everywhere?
Among this assembly now is a man of wisdom, the virtuous and excellent Ānanda of immeasurable learning.
He immediately struck the *gandī* to assemble the fourfold assembly;
eighty-four thousand bhikṣus were all Arhats whose minds were liberated, having been freed from bondage and attachment—the field of merit.
Out of compassion for the world, Kāśyapa has recalled the World-Honored One’s kindness from the past;
since the World-Honored One entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda, may he propagate and expound the Dharma so that it endures long in the world.
How is it that the sequence does not lose its thread?

Through the accumulation of the Dharma-treasure over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the four classes of followers are enabled to hear the Dharma; having heard it, they immediately attain liberation from all sufferings.
Ānanda then declined, saying: "I am not capable; the various dharmas are exceedingly profound.
How could I dare to discern the Tathāgata’s teaching—the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddha-dharma’s merit!"
Now the Honored Kāśyapa is capable and fit; the Hero of the World has entrusted the Dharma to this elder.
Great Kāśyapa now acts for the sake of all people; while the Tathāgata was in the world, he invited him to share half his seat.
Kāśyapa replied: "Though such things exist, my years have declined and I am old, prone to forgetfulness;
you now possess the karma of dhāraṇī and wisdom, able to cause the root of the Dharma to abide forever in the world."
I now possess three kinds of pure eyes, And am likewise able to know the minds of others;
Among all the various classes of sentient beings, None can surpass the Venerable Ānanda.
Brahmā descended along with Śakra, the four world-protecting kings and all the devas;
Maitreya from Tuṣita soon arrived, accompanied by incalculable billions of bodhisattvas.
Maitreya, Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Kings all joined their palms and addressed him:
"All dharmas are sealed by the Buddha; Ānanda is the vessel for our Dharma."
If you were to wish for the Dharma not to endure, you would be destroying the teachings of the Tathāgata;
may you preserve the fundamental essentials for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may be rescued from peril and delivered across all hardships!
The Teacher Śākyamuni has appeared in the world with an exceedingly short lifespan; though his physical body has passed away, his Dharma-body remains.
You must ensure that the root of the Dharma is not severed; Ānanda, do not decline, but preach the Dharma at this time!
Kāśyapa, most honored among the noble assembly, Maitreya, Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Kings, entreated Ānanda with compassion at that time, saying:
"Ensure that the teachings of the Tathāgata shall not perish."
Ānanda, endowed with benevolence, gentleness, and the four immeasurables, turned his mind toward the subtle lion’s roar;
looking back at the fourfold assembly and gazing into the void, he wept with such grief that he could not restrain himself.
He then manifested radiant light and a serene countenance, Universally illuminating all sentient beings like the rising sun;
Maitreya beheld this light as well as Śakra and Brahmā, And gathering his mind to listen, he awaited the Unsurpassed Dharma.
The four assemblies were tranquil and focused their minds, desiring to hear the Dharma with undistracted intent;
the venerable Kāśyapa and the noble assembly gazed directly at his countenance with unblinking eyes.
At that time, Ānanda had preached immeasurable sūtras; who could have compiled them all into a single collection?
I shall now divide them into three parts and compose ten sūtras into a single verse.
One part of the Sūtras, two parts of the Vinaya, and three parts of the Abhidharma;
the Buddhas of the past all possessed these three divisions:
the Sūtra, the Vinaya, and the Dharma constitute the Tripiṭaka.

The Sūtras shall now be divided into four sections: first is named Aṅguttara (Increasing by One), second is Majjhima (Middle-length), third is called Dīgha (Long) and Saṃyukta-āgama (Connected Garland), and the miscellaneous sūtras (Kṣudraka) shall constitute the fourth division at the end.
The Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is indestructible; it shall endure forever in the world without interruption, so that devas and humans may hear it and attain the fruit of the Path."
There may be a certain teaching whose meaning is profound, difficult to maintain, difficult to recite, and impossible to remember;
I shall now collect the meaning of that one teaching, following each aspect in sequence so that the thread is not lost.
There are also two dharmas that correspond to two; three dharmas correspond to three like a string of pearls.
Four dharmas correspond to four, and five likewise to five; five dharmas follow six, and six follows seven.
The meaning of eight dharmas is broad, nine follow in sequence, and ten dharmas extend from ten to eleven.
Thus this Dharma-treasure shall never be forgotten, and it shall remain long-enduring as it constantly abides in the world;
having gathered this Dharma amidst the great assembly, Ānanda immediately ascended the seat.
Maitreya praised him, saying, "Excellent! Well-spoken indeed! for he has appropriately matched the meanings of all dharmas.
Furthermore, there are various dharmas that should be categorized, as the World-Honored One has taught them each differently;
when Bodhisattvas resolve their minds toward the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgata explains these various distinctions.
The Honored One among Men has taught the six perfections:
generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditation, and the power of wisdom; like the waxing moon, they reach the ultimate perfections and perceive all phenomena.
Those who possess courage and give away their heads and eyes, Who do not begrudge their own bodies, blood, or flesh, And who renounce their wives,
concubines, kingdoms, wealth, and children— This is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) and should not be abandoned.
The perfection of ethical discipline is like a vajra; it is indestructible, unviolated, and free from loss.
One should hold the mind and guard the precepts as one would a fragile clay vessel; this is called the perfection of ethical discipline and should not be abandoned.
Should someone come to sever one's hands and feet, one does not give rise to anger, for the power of patience is strong;
like the ocean that contains all without increase or decrease, this is called the perfection of patience and should not be abandoned.
Those who perform various deeds of good and evil, never wearying of the three actions of body, speech, and mind—
though these hinder others' practices and prevent them from reaching the Way— this is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), which should not be abandoned.

All those who sit in meditation on the inhalation and exhalation, Whose minds are firm and free from distracted thoughts, Even if the earth should shake, their bodies do not waver; This is called the perfection of dhyāna, which one should not abandon.
Through the power of wisdom, one knows the number of atoms, And the number of kalpas, which are beyond measure in their millions and billions;
The accumulation of writings and commentaries does not disturb the mind— This is called the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), which should not be abandoned.
The profound discourse on all phenomena explains the principle of emptiness; it is difficult to clarify, difficult to comprehend, and cannot be perceived.
Those who come later will harbor doubts; therefore, one should not abandon the virtues of this bodhisattva.
Ānanda himself confessed this thought:
"The conduct of a bodhisattva is something the foolish do not believe; only those arhats who have attained faith and liberation can have such faith without hesitation."
The fourfold assembly has resolved their minds upon the Way, as have all classes of sentient beings;
possessing firm faith and free from doubt, they gather these various dharmas as a single portion.
Maitreya praised this, saying, "Excellent! How well spoken! The resolve to set out upon the Mahāyāna is most vast;
some dharmas sever the fetters and afflictions, while other dharmas bring about the fruit of the Path."
Ānanda said: "What does this mean?
I have seen the Tathāgata expound this Dharma, yet there are aspects of it that I have not heard from the Tathāgata directly. Is it not the case that one should have doubts regarding this Dharma?"
If I were to say that this meaning is incorrect, there would be falsehood regarding the assembly of the future;

therefore, I now cite the various sūtras which state: "Thus have I heard"—that the Buddha resided in such cities and kingdoms, preaching the Dharma for the first time in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, and subduing the three Kāśyapas in the kingdom of Magadha.
The kingdoms of Śrāvastī, Kauśāmbī, and Kāśi; Campā, Kauśāmbī, and Vaiśālī;

the palaces of the devas, the nāgas, and the asuras, as well as the gandharvas and others in the city of Kuśinagara—even if one cannot speak of the place where the sūtra was preached, one should state that its origin lies in Śrāvastī.

That which I have heard concerning a single event: The Buddha was in Śrāvastī with his disciples at the Jetavana Monastery, cultivating wholesome deeds in the garden offered by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, the Buddha was among them and addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should cultivate one dharma with single-minded focus, contemplating one dharma without negligence.
What is this one dharma?"
Mindfulness of the Dharma, the Sangha, and the precepts; Mindfulness of generosity, followed by the removal of signs and the devas;
Mindfulness of cessation, ānāpāna, and the body; And mindfulness of death—these ten are called the ten recollections that eliminate distraction.
These are called the ten recollections; furthermore, there are ten more, Who shall subsequently be named the Honored Disciples:
The first converted was Kauṇḍinya, a true son of the Buddha, And the last, the youngest, was named Subhadra.
By means of this expedient, one realizes the single dharma; from two comes the second dharma, and from three the third;
through four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and up to the eleventh dharma, there is nothing that is not understood.
From one increasing by one up to all dharmas, The meaning is abundant and wisdom vast, inexhaustible;
Each and every sūtra’s meaning is likewise profound, Therefore it is named the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
Now I seek a single dharma that is difficult to comprehend, difficult to uphold, difficult to understand, and impossible to clarify;
yet this bhikṣu himself proclaims his own meritorious deeds, and now he claims to be the most honored and foremost.
Just as a potter fashions vessels, Creating them at will without hesitation;
So too is this Ekottarika Āgama Dharma, Teaching the Three Vehicles without distinction.
The Buddha’s sutras are subtle and most profound, Able to eliminate the fetters like a flowing river;
Yet this *Ekottarika* is supreme among them, Able to purify the three eyes and remove the three defilements.
Whoever single-mindedly upholds the *Ekottarika-āgama* thereby possesses the dhāraṇī of the Tathāgatagarbha;
even if their present body does not exhaust all fetters, they shall attain lofty wisdom and talent in future lives.
If there are those who transcribe this sutra into volumes, And offer it with silk banners, flowers, and canopies,
Their merit shall be immeasurable and beyond reckoning, For this treasure of the Dharma is difficult to encounter.
When these words were spoken, the great earth shook, and celestial flowers and incense rained down as high as the knees;
the devas in the sky exclaimed, "Excellent!"—
what the Most Honored One has said is entirely appropriate and fitting.
The Sūtra-piṭaka is the first treasury, the Vinaya-piṭaka the second, and the Abhidharma-sūtra the third treasury;
the profound and subtle meaning of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna, along with various other sūtras, constitutes the Miscellaneous Treasury (Kṣudraka-piṭaka).
The Buddha’s words are established and shall never change; the causes, conditions, beginning, and end all accord with them.
Maitreya and the devas all praise this as excellent; the Sūtra of Śākyamuni shall endure for a long time.
Maitreya immediately reached out his hand and took a flower; with joy, he held it and scattered it over Ānanda.
"This sutra is the true teaching spoken by the Tathāgata," he said, "to cause Ānanda to quickly realize the fruit of the Path."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda and the Brahmā, leading all the Brahmakāyika devas, all came to assemble;
the Paranirmitavaśavartin devas, leading their retinues, all came to gather together;
and the Nirmāṇarati devas, leading their retinues, all came to the assembly.
The Heavenly King Tuṣita led the hosts of devas, all of whom came to assemble;
the King of the Yāma Heaven led his retinue, all of whom came to assemble;
Śakra Devānām Indra led the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, all of whom came to gather together.
The Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra led the gandharvas and others, all of whom gathered there;
the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka led the various yakṣas, all of whom gathered there;
the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa led the hosts of nāgas, all of whom gathered there.
The Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa led the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, and they all assembled there.
At that time, the Great Being Maitreya addressed the bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa:
"You should exhort the sons and daughters of good family to recite, uphold, and extensively propagate this *Ekottarika-dharmaparyāya*, so that devas and humans may practice it."
When these words were spoken, the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, mahoragas, kinnaras, and others each addressed him, saying:
"We shall all together protect these good men and good women who recite, uphold, and widely propagate this *Ekottarika-dharma*, ensuring that it never comes to an end."
Then, the Venerable Ānanda said to Udāyin:
"I now entrust this Aṅguttara Nikāya to you; recite and study it well so that it does not diminish or fall away. Why is this?"
Whoever treats this sublime sutra with contempt shall fall away and engage in the conduct of an ordinary person.
Why is this so? O Uttara, from this *Ekottarika Āgama* emerge the teachings on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and all dharmas arise from it.
Then, Mahākāśyapa asked Ānanda: "How is it, Ānanda?
Is it that the *Ekottarika-āgama* is able to give birth to the teachings on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and that all dharmas arise from this?"
Ānanda replied: "So it is, so it is, Venerable Kāśyapa!
The *Ekottarika Āgama* gives birth to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and all dharmas likewise arise from it."
"Setting aside the *Ekottarika Āgama* for a moment, even within a single verse, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all dharmas are produced.
Kāśyapa asked: "In what kind of verse are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all dharmas produced?"
Then, the Venerable Ānanda spoke this verse:
"Commit no evil; Practice all that is good; Purify your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas."
"The reason for this is that 'committing no evil' is the foundation of all dharmas, from which all wholesome dharmas arise;
by giving rise to wholesome dharmas, the mind becomes pure."
"Therefore, Kāśyapa, the bodily, verbal,
and mental actions of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are always cultivated in purity. Kāśyapa asked:
"What do you think, Ānanda?
Does only the *Ekottarika-āgama* give rise to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all other dharmas, or do the other four *āgamas* also give rise to them?"
Ānanda replied, "Let it be for now, Kāśyapa!"
Within a single verse of the meaning of the Four Āgamas, the teachings of all Buddhas, as well as those of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas, are fully contained.
This is because: "Commit no evil" is the prohibition for the fulfillment of precepts;
"Practice all that is good" is the conduct of purity.
With a pure mind, one purifies one's own intent;
to eliminate false and inverted views is the teaching of all Buddhas, for it removes deluded and confused conceptions.
What do you think, Kāśyapa?
If the precepts are pure, how could the mind not be pure?
When the mind is pure, one is free from inversion;
through the absence of inversion, deluded perceptions are extinguished, and the fruits of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are thereby accomplished.
"Since the fruit of the Way is accomplished, is it not, indeed,
through all dharmas? Kāśyapa asked, "How is this so, Ānanda?"
"In this way, did you entrust the *Ekottarika Āgama* to Udāyin, but not entrust all other dharmas to the other bhikṣus?
Ānanda replied, "The *Ekottarika Āgama* is itself all dharmas, and all dharmas are themselves the *Ekottarika Āgama*; they are one and not two."
Kāśyapa asked: "For what reason was this *Ekottarika Āgama* entrusted to Udāyin, and not entrusted to other bhikṣus?"
Ānanda replied: "Kāśyapa, you should know that ninety-one kalpas ago, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin appeared in the world."
At that time, this bhikṣu Udāra was named Ikṣvāku-udāra; at that time, that Buddha entrusted him with the *Ekottarika-dharma*, instructing him to recite, chant, and study it.
From this point forward, after thirty-one kalpas, there shall again be a Buddha named Śikhi Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, this bhikṣu Udāra shall be named Maudgalyāyana.
Śikṣaṇī Tathāgata further entrusted this Dharma to that person, commanding them to recite, chant, and read it.
Then, within those thirty-one kalpas, Viśvabhū Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, appeared again in the world.
At that time, this bhikṣu Udāra was named Nāgudāra; he further entrusted this Dharma to that person, instructing him to recite, chant, and read it:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that within this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Udāra, also known as Vidyud-Udāra, who further entrusted this Dharma to that person, causing him to recite, chant, and read it.
Subsequently, in this Bhadrakalpa, another Buddha appeared in the world, named Kanakamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the bhikṣu Udāra, named Deva-Udāra, further entrusted this Dharma to that person, causing them to recite, chant, and read it.
Subsequently, within this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared another Buddha in the world, named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, the bhikṣu named Udāra, also known as Brahmodyāra, further entrusted this Dharma to that person, commanding him to recite, chant, and read it:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni has now appeared in the world."
This bhikṣu is named Udāra; although the Buddha Śākyamuni has entered parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣu Ānanda still remains in the world.
The World-Honored One entrusted the Dharma entirely to me, and I now, in turn, transmit this Dharma to Udāra.
Why is this? One should observe the vessel and examine its original nature before bestowing the Dharma.
For what reason?

In the past, during this Bhadrakalpa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat Krakucchanda appeared in the world.

At that time, there was a king named Mahādeva who ruled and transformed the world according to the Dharma, never acting with crookedness. His lifespan was exceedingly long; he was peerlessly handsome and rare in the world. For eighty-four thousand years he sported as a youth; for eighty-four thousand years he ruled and transformed the world as a crown prince according to the Dharma; and for eighty-four thousand years he further ruled the world as a sovereign king according to the Dharma.

“Kāśyapa, you should know that at that time the World-Honored One was wandering within the Amalaka Grove. After his meal, following his usual custom, he was walking back and forth in the central courtyard. At that moment, I and my attendant were there; the World-Honored One then smiled, and from his mouth issued light of five colors.”
Having seen this, I knelt before him with my right knee on the ground and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; I pray that you will explain its origin and conclusion.
A Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyak-saṃbuddha never smiles in vain."
"At that time, Kāśyapa!
The Buddha said to me:

'In a past age, during this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Tathāgata named Krakucchanda, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world and extensively preached the Dharma for his disciples at this very place.'"
Furthermore, within this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni; at that time, that Buddha also extensively preached the Dharma in this very place.
Furthermore, next, during this Bhadrakalpa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world; that Tathāgata Kāśyapa also extensively preached the Dharma at this very place.
“At that time, Kāśyapa! I knelt before the Buddha and said to him:

‘I pray that the future Śākyamuni Buddha shall also, at this very place, preach the Dharma in its entirety for his disciples, so that this place may become the adamantine seat of four Tathāgatas, forever uninterrupted.’”
"At that time, Kāśyapa! Śākyamuni Buddha, while seated there, addressed me, saying: 'Ānanda!'"
Long ago, while seated here, there was a king born into the world during this Bhadrakalpa named Mahādeva.
He ruled for eighty-four thousand years, governing by the laws of kings and instructing his people through virtue. As the years passed, he addressed Kapphiṇa, saying:
"If you see white hairs upon my head, inform me at once."

At that time, having heard the king’s command, after several more years had passed, the man saw white hairs growing upon the king’s head. He then knelt before him and addressed the Great King, saying:
“Great King, you should know that white hairs have already grown upon your head.”
Then the king said to that man,
"Take a pair of golden tweezers, pluck out my white hairs, and place them in my hand. At that time, the man,
receiving the king's command, took up the golden tweezers and stepped forward to pluck the white hairs.
"At that time, having seen the white hair, the Great King spoke this verse:
'Now upon my head, The hair of decay has already grown;
The messenger of the gods has arrived— It is fitting that I renounce the world this very moment.'"

"I have now already enjoyed the blessings of the human realm; it is fitting that I should exert myself to cultivate the virtues for ascending to heaven. Having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the three dharma robes, I shall, with firm faith, leave the household life to study the Way and be free from all suffering."
"At that time, King Mahādeva addressed his eldest son, named Jīvadatta: 'Do you know, my son?
White hairs have already grown upon my head.
I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and with firm faith, leave the home life to study the Way and depart from all suffering.'"
"You shall succeed to my position and govern according to the Dharma; do not allow any failure or transgression of my teachings by engaging in the conduct of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Why is this so? If there should be such a person who violates my words, they will indeed be practicing the conduct of an ordinary person."
"Ordinary worldlings dwell perpetually within the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions.

At that time, King Mahādeva, having entrusted the royal throne to the crown prince and bestowed wealth and treasures upon Kapphiṇa, shaved off his hair and beard right there, donned the three dharma robes, and with firm faith left the household life to study the Way, thereby departing from all suffering.

For eighty-four thousand years he practiced the holy life with excellence, cultivating the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
"At that time, King Dīrghāyu remembered his father king’s instruction and never abandoned it for even a moment.

He governed and transformed the people according to the Dharma, without any crookedness. Before even ten days had passed, he once again became a Wheel-Turning Sage King, fully endowed with the seven treasures."

As for what are called the seven treasures: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward treasure, and the military commander treasure—these are known as the seven treasures.
Furthermore, he had a thousand sons, valiant and wise, capable of eliminating all suffering and governing the four quarters.
At that time, King Long-life (Dīrghāyus), following the laws of former kings, composed a verse as follows:
"Revere the Dharma and honor those worthy of respect; Do not forget the fundamental kindness, but repay it."
"Furthermore, one who can honor the three types of action is what the wise hold in high esteem!
"Having contemplated this meaning, I bestowed this *Ekottarika Āgama* upon the bhikṣu Udāra."
"Why is this? Because all phenomena have their causes.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda said to Udāyin:

"When you were previously a Wheel-Turning Sage King, you did not fail to carry out the king's instructions; now I again entrust you with this Dharma so that you shall not fail the true teaching. Do not engage in the conduct of an ordinary person."
You should now know this: if anyone violates or neglects the Tathāgata’s excellent teachings, they will fall into the stage of ordinary worldlings. Why is this?
At that time, King Mahādeva was unable to reach the ground of ultimate liberation; he had not yet attained liberation to the place of peace and security.
Although one may receive the karmic rewards of Brahmā, these do not yet constitute the ultimate;
the wholesome karma of a Tathāgata, however, is called the place of ultimate peace and security, where bliss is infinite, and which is honored by gods and humans, ensuring the attainment of nirvāṇa.
For this reason, Udāyin, you should uphold this Dharma,
reciting, chanting, reading, and reflecting upon it,
so that it remains without deficiency or omission.
At that time, Ānanda spoke these verses:
"Because of mindfulness of the Dharma, the Tathāgata was born;
From the arising of the Dharma, the path of the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats is perfected."
The Dharma can eliminate all sufferings and can also bring forth the fruits of fruition;
If one keeps the Dharma in mind without departing from it, one will receive its reward both now and hereafter.
Should you wish to attain Buddhahood, just like Śākyamuni, [you must practice this].
Uphold and maintain the Dharma of the Tripiṭaka, with its phrases and clauses unconfused.
Though the Tripiṭaka is difficult to uphold, its principles and meanings are inexhaustible;
one should recite the Four Āgamas, thereby cutting off the path for devas and humans.
Though the Āgamas are difficult to recite, the meaning of the sūtras is inexhaustible;
do not let the precepts be lost—this is the treasure of the Tathāgata.
The prohibitions and rules are likewise difficult to maintain, and the Āgamas are the same.
Firmly uphold the Abhidharma, and you shall subdue the arts of the non-Buddhists.
Proclaim and spread the Abhidharma, for its meaning is likewise difficult to maintain;
you should recite the three Āgamas, not losing a single word or phrase of the sūtras.
The Sūtras and the Abhidharma, and the Vinaya, have spread throughout the world;

When the Venerable Ānanda had spoken these words, heaven and earth shook in six ways. The various honored devas in the void of space took celestial flowers in their hands and scattered them over the Venerable Ānanda, as well as over the fourfold assembly.

Excellent, Venerable Ānanda!

As it has been said, among gods and humans, there are none who do not achieve accomplishment through the Dharma.
If one commits evil deeds, one will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda let out a lion’s roar amidst the fourfold assembly, exhorting all people to practice this Dharma.
At that moment, thirty thousand devas and humans present in the assembly attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, the devas, and the people of the world, having heard what the Venerable One had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

"One should practice one dharma and one should propagate one dharma;
thereby one will achieve supernormal powers, eliminate all distracted thoughts, attain the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally realize nirvāṇa."
What is this one dharma?

It is the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). One should practice it skillfully and propagate it widely; thereby one will accomplish supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), eliminate all distracted thoughts, attain the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally realize nirvāṇa.
Therefore, monks, you should practice one dharma and propagate one dharma. Thus it is, monks!

"I have now already enjoyed the blessings of humanity; it is fitting that I should exert myself to cultivate the virtues for ascending to heaven. Chapter Three: The Chapter on Extensive Exposition (3) (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One dharma should be practiced; one dharma should be widely disseminated.

Having practiced this one dharma, one will attain renown, achieve great fruit and retribution, and all virtues will universally arrive. One will obtain the taste of the Deathless, reach the state of the unconditioned, and thereby accomplish supernormal powers, eliminate all distracted thoughts, attain the fruits of śrāmaṇya, and personally realize nirvāṇa.”
"What is this one dharma?
It is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"How does one practice the recollection of the Buddha so as to gain renown, achieve great karmic fruition, have all virtues arrive universally, obtain the taste of the nectar of immortality, reach the state of the unconditioned, attain supernormal powers, eliminate all distracted thoughts, realize the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally attain nirvāṇa?"
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Tathāgata has spoken of the root of all dharmas.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this wondrous meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard it from the Tathāgata, the bhikṣus shall receive and uphold it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail. He replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Having received the instruction from before, the bhikṣus said this.
The World-Honored One then addressed them, saying:

"If there is a bhikṣu who straightens his body and composes his mind, sits cross-legged, binds his mindfulness to the object before him, harbors no other thoughts, and single-mindedly contemplates the Buddha."
One contemplates the form of the Tathāgata, never departing from one's sight;
having not departed from one's sight, one then recollects the merits of the Tathāgata:
the body of the Tathāgata is composed of vajra, fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, courageous and powerful amidst the assembly.
The Tathāgata’s countenance is upright and peerless; one never tires of gazing upon it.
His accomplishment in the virtue of the precepts is like a diamond, indestructible; he is pure and flawless, like lapis lazuli.
The Tathāgata’s samādhi has never diminished; it is eternally quiescent and free from other thoughts.
Arrogance, stubbornness, and all turbulent emotions have subsided; the mind of desire, thoughts of malice, the deluded heart, and the knots of hesitation have all been completely eliminated.
The Tathāgata’s body of wisdom is boundless and unfathomable, free from all obstructions.

The body of the Tathāgata is the perfection of liberation; having exhausted all realms of existence, there is no further portion of rebirth, such that one could say, "I shall fall again into birth and death."

The body of the Tathāgata has crossed over the city of knowledge and vision; he knows the faculties of others, whether they are ready for deliverance or not, and where one dies here to be born there. He fully knows all who wander to and fro at the threshold of birth and death—those who possess liberation and those who do not.

This is called the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha; thereby one gains renown, achieves great karmic fruition, and all virtues arrive universally. One attains the taste of the Deathless (amṛta), reaches the state of the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and manifests supernormal powers (abhijñā). With all distracted thoughts eliminated, one obtains the fruits of the śramaṇa and personally realizes nirvāṇa.
Therefore, monks, you should always reflect and never be parted from mindfulness of the Buddha; then you shall obtain these various wholesome merits. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
