This gift I now bestow is the supreme among gifts; it is forever free from regret and devoid of any thought of seeking recompense, whereby I have swiftly attained wholesome benefit.
If someone reviles me, I shall never retaliate;

even if someone harms me—whether by striking me with their fists, attacking me with swords and staves, or hurling tiles and stones at me—I shall give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and not arouse anger.
"Whatever I give, my intention to give is never interrupted.
This, O bhikṣus, is called the 'Great Gift.

It brings about great fruit and reward; all virtues arrive universally; one attains the flavor of the Deathless (amṛta); one reaches the state of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); one then achieves supernormal powers (abhijñā), eliminates all distracted thoughts, obtains the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally realizes nirvāṇa."
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should always reflect and never be separated from the mindfulness of giving; then you shall obtain these various wholesome merits. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One dharma should be practiced; one dharma should be widely disseminated.”

Having practiced this one dharma, one immediately gains renown, achieves great fruition, and all virtues arrive universally. One attains the Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta), reaches the state of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and thereby accomplishes supernormal powers (abhijñā). With all distracted thoughts eliminated, one attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya and personally realizes nirvāṇa.
"What is this one dharma?
It is mindfulness of the devas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“How does one practice the mindfulness of the devas so as to gain renown, achieve great fruit and retribution, have all virtues universally arrive, obtain the taste of the Deathless, reach the state of the Unconditioned, attain supernormal powers, eliminate all distracted thoughts, realize the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally reach Nirvāṇa?”
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Tathāgata has spoken of the root of all dharmas.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this sublime meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard it from the Tathāgata, the bhikṣus shall receive and uphold it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail. The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Having received the instruction from before, the bhikṣus said this.
The World-Honored One then told them:

“If there is a bhikṣu who straightens his body and composes his mind, sits cross-legged, binds his mindfulness before him, has no other thoughts, and with single-minded diligence recollects the heavens.
With body, speech, and mind purified, one refrains from defiled conduct; by practicing the precepts, one perfects the physical body.
The body emits radiance that illuminates all things, thereby perfecting that celestial body;
through the ripening of wholesome fruits, one perfects that celestial body.
When all practices are fully perfected, one attains a celestial body.
Thus, monks, this is called "mindfulness of the devas" (devatānussati);

when it is fully accomplished, it brings about great fruit and reward, all virtues arrive, one attains the taste of the Deathless (amṛta), reaches the state of the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), achieves supernormal powers (abhijñā), eliminates all distracted thoughts, attains the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally realizes Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, monks, you should always reflect and never be separated from mindfulness of the devas; then you shall obtain these various wholesome merits. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One dharma should be practiced; one dharma should be widely disseminated.”

Having practiced this one dharma, one immediately gains renown, achieves great fruition, and all virtues arrive universally. One attains the taste of the Deathless, reaches the state of the Unconditioned, and thereby accomplishes supernormal powers, eliminates all distracted thoughts, realizes the fruits of asceticism, and personally attains Nirvana.
"What is that one dharma?
It is the mindfulness of cessation.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"How does one practice mindfulness of rest so as to attain renown, achieve great fruit and retribution, have all manner of goodness arrive universally, obtain the taste of the Deathless, reach the state of the Unconditioned, manifest supernormal powers, eliminate all distracted thoughts, realize the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally attain Nirvāṇa?"
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
“The root of all dharmas is as taught by the Tathāgata.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this sublime meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard it from the Tathāgata, the bhikṣus shall receive and uphold it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail. The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Having received the instruction from before, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, who said to them:
“If there is a bhikṣu who straightens his body and composes his mind, sits cross-legged, binds his mindfulness before him, has no other thoughts, and with single-minded diligence contemplates rest.

What is called "rest" means that the mind and thoughts are at rest, the disposition is calm and discerning, and there is no sudden agitation; one is constantly single-minded, delights in dwelling in seclusion, always seeks skillful means, and enters the concentration of samādhi.
"Constantly maintain mindfulness of non-greed; its supreme radiance reaches upward. Thus, O bhikṣus!

This is called the 'resting of mindfulness. When it is fully perfected, it brings about great fruit and reward; all virtues arrive universally, one attains the taste of the Deathless (amṛta), and reaches the state of the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). Thereupon, one accomplishes supernormal powers (abhijñā), eliminates all distracted thoughts, attains the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally realizes Nirvāṇa."
Therefore, monks, you should always reflect and never be parted from the mindfulness of rest; then you shall obtain these various wholesome merits. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One dharma should be practiced; one dharma should be widely propagated.”

Having practiced this one dharma, one immediately gains renown, achieves great fruition and retribution, becomes fully endowed with all virtues, attains the taste of the Deathless, reaches the state of the Unconditioned, acquires supernormal powers, eliminates all distracted thoughts, realizes the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally attains nirvāṇa.
"What is that one dharma?
It is mindfulness of ānāpāna.
Thus the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"How does one practice mindfulness of *ānāpāna* so as to gain renown, achieve great fruit and reward, be universally endowed with all virtues, attain the taste of the Deathless (*amṛta*), reach the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), eliminate all distracted thoughts, obtain the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), and personally realize *nirvāṇa*?"
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"The root of all dharmas is that which has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this wondrous meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard it from the Tathāgata, the bhikṣus shall receive and uphold it."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail. The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Having received the instruction from the Buddha, the bhikṣus stood before him.
The World-Honored One addressed them, saying:

"If there is a bhikṣu who straightens his body and composes his mind, sits cross-legged, binds his mindfulness before him, has no other thoughts, and single-mindedly applies himself to the mindfulness of ānāpāna."
Regarding what is called *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing):
when the breath is long, one should observe and know, "My breath is now long";
when the breath is short, one should likewise observe and know, "My breath is now short."
If the breath is extremely cold, one should likewise observe and know: "My breath is now cold.
If the breath is hot, one should likewise observe and know: "My breath is now hot.
One should fully observe the body, observing and knowing it from head to foot.

Furthermore, if the breaths are long or short, one should likewise observe that the breaths are long or short; maintaining the body with focused attention, one knows the length of the breaths and understands them all completely, following the inhalation and exhalation and discerning them with clear comprehension.
If the mind maintains the body and knows the length of the breath, one also knows it; one counts the length of the breath, discerning and clearly understanding it.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!

This is called mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breath); by practicing it, one attains fulfillment, achieves great karmic fruition, and all virtues arrive universally. One obtains the taste of the Deathless (*amṛta*), reaches the state of the Unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and thereby accomplishes supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Having eliminated all distracted thoughts, one attains the fruits of the śramaṇa and personally realizes Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, monks, you should always reflect and never be separated from mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), and you shall then obtain these various wholesome merits. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One dharma should be practiced; one dharma should be widely disseminated.”

Having practiced this one dharma, one immediately gains renown, achieves great fruition, and all virtues arrive universally. One attains the taste of the nectar of immortality, reaches the path of the unconditioned, and thereby accomplishes supernormal powers. With all distracted thoughts eliminated, one realizes the fruits of the śramaṇa and personally attains nirvāṇa.
"What is that one dharma?
It is mindfulness of the body.
Thus the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus.

"How does one practice mindfulness of the body so as to gain renown, achieve great fruit and retribution, have all virtues arrive, attain the taste of the nectar of immortality, reach the state of the unconditioned, accomplish supernormal powers, eliminate all distracted thoughts, obtain the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally realize nirvāṇa?"
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The root of all dharmas has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound this sublime Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata, the bhikṣus shall then receive and uphold it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail. The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Having received the instruction from the World-Honored One, the bhikṣus stood before him.
The World-Honored One then addressed them, saying:

"If there is a bhikṣu who straightens his body and composes his mind, sits cross-legged, binds his mindfulness to the object before him, has no other thoughts, and with single-minded diligence contemplates the body."

What is called "mindfulness of the body" refers to: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, gallbladder, liver, lungs, heart, spleen, kidneys, large intestine, small intestine, mesentery, bladder, feces, urine, stomach, intestines, spleen, bubbles, tears, saliva, nasal mucus, pus, blood, fat, grease, marrow, and skull-brain.
What constitutes this body?
Is it the earth element?
Is it the water element?
Is it produced from the element of fire?
Is it produced from the element of wind?
Or is it created by the elements of the father and mother?
From where do they come?
By whom were they created?
As for the eye, ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind—where will they ultimately be reborn?
Thus it is, monks!

That which is called "mindfulness of the body" (kāyagatāsati), when fully perfected, yields great fruit and reward; all virtues arrive therein, one attains the taste of the Deathless (amṛta), reaches the state of the Unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), achieves supernormal powers (abhijñā), eliminates all distracted thoughts, attains the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally realizes Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, monks, you should always practice reflection and remain undivided from mindfulness of the body; then you shall obtain these various wholesome merits. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One dharma should be practiced; one dharma should be widely disseminated.”

Having practiced this one dharma, one immediately gains renown, achieves great fruit and retribution, and all virtues arrive universally. One attains the taste of the nectar of immortality, reaches the state of the unconditioned, and thereby accomplishes supernormal powers. With all distracted thoughts eliminated, one attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya and personally realizes nirvāṇa.
"What is that one dharma?
It is mindfulness of death.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"How does one practice the mindfulness of death so as to attain renown, achieve great fruit and retribution, have all virtues arrive universally, obtain the taste of the nectar of immortality, reach the state of the unconditioned, attain supernormal powers, eliminate all distracted thoughts, realize the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally attain nirvāṇa?"
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
“The root of all dharmas has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound this sublime Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata, the bhikṣus shall then receive and uphold it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail. The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Having received the instruction from before, the bhikṣus said this.
The World-Honored One then addressed them, saying:
"If there is a bhikṣu who straightens his body and composes his mind, sits cross-legged, binds his mindfulness before him, has no other thoughts, and with single-minded diligence contemplates death."

What is called "death" means passing away from here and being born there, wandering through the various realms of existence; life flows on without ceasing, yet the sense faculties disperse and perish like rotten wood. The life-faculty is severed, kinsmen are parted, and there is no form, no sound, and no appearance whatsoever.
Thus, monks, that which is called mindfulness of death is fully perfected;

it brings about great fruit and reward, all virtues arrive therein, one attains the taste of the Deathless, reaches the unconditioned state, achieves supernormal powers, eliminates all distracted thoughts, realizes the fruits of the śramaṇa, and personally attains nirvāṇa.
Therefore, monks, you should always reflect and never be separated from the mindfulness of death; then you shall obtain these various wholesome merits. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[They cultivated] mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha, up until the point of death.
Although they share the same names as those above, their meanings are each distinct and different.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya*, Volume II; *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, Volume III.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Four: Disciples. Section One. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Among my śrāvakas, there is a foremost bhikṣu who is broad-minded and benevolent, widely learned, skilled in exhortation and transformation, and who nurtures the noble assembly while never losing his dignified deportment; he is none other than the bhikṣu Ajñātakauṇḍinya.”
The one who first tasted the flavor of the Dharma and contemplated the Four Noble Truths was the bhikṣu Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
The one who was skilled at exhorting and guiding others, bringing merit and deliverance to the people, was the bhikṣu Udāyin.
The one who swiftly attained supernormal powers without receiving instruction midway was the bhikṣu Mahānāman.
The one who constantly flies through the void without his feet ever touching the ground was the bhikṣu Śobhita.
One who travels through the void to teach and transform others, with no desire for honor or gain, is the bhikṣu called Pāva.
One who dwells in delight in the heavens and does not remain among humans is the bhikṣu called Goṣpada.
The bhikṣu Śubhavyūha is the one who constantly contemplates the perception of the impurity of foul secretions.
The one who nurtures the noble assembly with the fourfold offerings is the bhikṣu Uruvilvākāśyapa.
One whose mind is tranquil and who has subdued all fetters is the bhikṣu Gaṅgā-Kāśyapa.
One who contemplates and fully understands all dharmas, remaining entirely unattached, is the bhikṣu Nāga-Kāśyapa.
(1) Kolita, Upatiṣya, and Māṭhara; (2) Svastika, Pañcaśikha, Gośṛṅga, and Bhadrajit; (3) the three brothers Kāśyapa.
(2) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu in majestic appearance and upright demeanor, walking with measured and dignified steps, is the bhikṣu Aśvajit."
One whose wisdom is inexhaustible and who resolves all doubts is the bhikṣu Śāriputra;
one whose supernormal powers allow for light-footed flight to the ten directions is the bhikṣu Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
He who is courageous and diligent, capable of enduring ascetic practices, is the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
He who possesses the twelve dhūta practices, deeds difficult to attain, is the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa.
The foremost in the divine eye, who perceives the realms of the ten directions, is the bhikṣu Aniruddha.
The one who sits in meditation and enters samādhi with an undistracted mind is the bhikṣu Revata.
The one who was able to widely exhort and lead others to establish fast-day assemblies and lectures was the bhikṣu Dharmamitra.
The one who built monasteries and established the *caitya* for the Saṃgha was the so-called Lesser Dharmamitra Bhikṣu.
One of noble and wealthy lineage who left the household life to study the Way is the bhikṣu Rāṭha-bala.
One who skillfully discerns meanings and expounds the teachings of the Buddha is the bhikṣu Mahākātyāyana.
(3) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu who is capable of receiving the tally and does not transgress the prohibitive rules is the bhikṣu Kuṇḍadhāna.
Aśvajit, Śāriputra, Kauṣṭhila, Kātyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Revata, Maudgalyāyana, Pūrṇa, and Kātyāyana.
(3) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu who is capable of receiving the tally and does not transgress the prohibitive rules is the bhikṣu Kuṇḍadhāna."
The one who subdues non-Buddhists and practices the True Dharma is the bhikṣu Piṇḍola.
The one who attends to the sick and provides them with medicine is the bhikṣu Śrī.
One who provides the four requisites of robes, food, drink, and bedding,
and is also a bhikṣu who is capable of composing verses to praise the virtues of the Tathāgata, is the bhikṣu Paṅkṣaśa.
The one whose speech is eloquent and free from doubt or obstruction is also the bhikṣu Śāradvatīputra.
The one who has attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is able to respond to any challenge is the bhikṣu Mahākauṣṭhila.
One who dwells in pure seclusion and finds no pleasure among people is the bhikṣu Dṛḍha.
One who begs for alms, endures insults, and avoids neither cold nor heat is the bhikṣu Nanda.
Dwelling alone in quietude and sitting in meditation with single-minded devotion to the Way refers to the bhikṣu Vīra;
eating but one meal a day and not moving from his place refers to the bhikṣu Śaila.
One who maintains the three robes and does not part from them even for a meal or a breath—
this is the bhikṣu Bhumija. Muṇḍa, Piṇḍola, Bhāradvāja, Kapphiṇa, Sāḷha, Nanda, and now Upavīta, Śaila, and Māluṅkyaputra.
(4) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu who sits in meditation under a tree with an unshakable mind is the bhikṣu named Vītaśoka."
The one who torments his body by sitting in the open air, avoiding neither wind nor rain—this is the bhikṣu Vatsa.
The one who delights in solitude and dwells in empty, quiet places, focusing his mind on contemplation—this is the bhikṣu Dhvasu.
One who wears the fivefold patched robe and does not wear ornamental finery is the bhikṣu Nīpa.
One who always delights in dwelling among burial mounds and does not stay among people is the bhikṣu Uttara.
He who constantly sat upon grass mats and daily brought blessings and salvation to others was the bhikṣu Rohiṇī;
he who did not speak with others and walked while gazing at the ground was the bhikṣu Ujjvamaniyaṅga.
The one who remains constantly in samādhi whether sitting, rising, walking, or moving about is the bhikṣu named Sandhāna.
The one who delights in traveling to distant lands to instruct the people is the bhikṣu named Dharmaruci.
He who delights in gathering the assembly of noble ones and discussing the flavor of the Dharma is the bhikṣu Kāli.
Also: Kātyāyana, Vatsagotra, Udāyin, Subhūti, Udralomaka, Upagupta, Śikṣānanda, Dharmaruci, and Kāla.
(5) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu in having an extremely long life who never meets an untimely death is the bhikṣu Vakkula."
One who always delights in dwelling in seclusion and does not remain among the crowds is the bhikṣu Bakula.
One who is able to expound the Dharma extensively and analyze its principles and meanings is the bhikṣu Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
The one who upholds the precepts without transgressing them is the bhikṣu Upāli.
The one who has attained liberation through faith, with a mind free from hesitation, is the so-called bhikṣu Vakkali.
One whose physical form is upright and distinct from that of the world is the bhikṣu Nanda;
one whose faculties are tranquil and whose mind is unchanging is also the bhikṣu Nanda.
The one whose eloquence suddenly bursts forth, resolving the doubts and obstructions of others, is the bhikṣu Vātsīputra.
The one who can extensively expound upon meanings without contradicting principle is the bhikṣu Sthavira.
The one who delighted in wearing fine robes and whose conduct was fundamentally pure was the bhikṣu Deva-Subhūti.
The one who always took pleasure in instructing later students was the bhikṣu Nandaka.
The one who skillfully instructs the community of bhikṣuṇīs regarding the prohibitions and precepts is the bhikṣu Sumana. [Also] Bakula,
Pūrṇa, Upāli, Vakkali, Nanda, Ānanda, Subhūti, Nanda, and Sumana.
(6) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu, whose merit is full and complete, who is without deficiency in whatever he undertakes, is the bhikṣu Śivara."
The one who is fully endowed with the dharmas of the various practices and paths is the bhikṣu Upasena Kākaṇḍaputra.
The one whose speech is harmonious and pleasing, never wounding the minds of others, is the bhikṣu Vatsa.
The one who practiced *ānāpāna* and contemplated the foulness of the body was the bhikṣu Mahākātyāyana.
The one who reckoned the self as impermanent and whose mind was free from conceptualization was the bhikṣu Upatissa.
The one who is able to engage in various discourses and gladden the mind and consciousness is the bhikṣu Kumāra-Kāśyapa.
The one who wears tattered and foul garments without any sense of shame is the bhikṣu Mukharāja.
He who does not violate the prohibitions and precepts and recites them without slackening is the bhikṣu Rāhula.
He who, by means of his supernormal power, can make himself invisible is the bhikṣu Panthaka.
Those who are able to transform their physical forms and manifest various transformations are,
namely, the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka; Śiva, Upasena, Vatsa,
Kātyāyanīputra, Udāyin, the King, Kāśyapa, Rāhula, and the two Panthakas.
(7) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu who is of noble and wealthy lineage and naturally gentle by nature is the bhikṣu Śaila."
He who is insatiable in seeking alms and inexhaustible in teaching and transforming others is the bhikṣu Bhaṭṭipāla.
He who possesses powerful vigor and is free from fear or difficulty is also the bhikṣu Bhaṭṭipāla.
The one whose voice was pure and resonant, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven, was the bhikṣu Rāvaṇavati.
The one whose body was fragrant and pure, perfuming the four quarters, was the bhikṣu Aṅgaja.

Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu is one who knows the proper time, understands things clearly, moves without hesitation, possesses an unforgetting memory, has heard much and extensively, and is capable of receiving and honoring [the teachings]; he is the bhikṣu Ānanda.
The one who was adorned with finery and whose gait was such that he would look back at his own reflection is the bhikṣu Kāṣṭhila.
The one whom all kings honored and whom the ministers revered is the bhikṣu Candraprabha.
He who is honored by gods and men, whom they constantly attend and serve in audience, is the bhikṣu Śuddhipanthaka.
Because he has cast off his human form and bears a countenance like that of a deva, he is also the bhikṣu Śuddhipanthaka.
The one who serves as the guide for the various devas and imparts the sublime Dharma is the so-called Devaputra Bhikṣu.
The one who remembers his own past lives throughout incalculable kalpas is the so-called Phaladaśāka Bhikṣu.
Śreṇika, Vādi-bhadraka, Rāva, Aṅgaja, Ānanda, Candraprabha, Śuddhipanthaka, Deva, and Bhadrika (8).
“Among my śrāvaka bhikṣus, the foremost is the bhikṣu Aṅgulimāla; his nature is of sharp faculties, and his wisdom is profound and far-reaching.”
He who is able to subdue the Māras, the non-Buddhists, and their evil karmas is the bhikṣu Saṃghama.
He who enters the water-samādhi without regarding it as difficult is the bhikṣu Citta-Śāriputra.
The one who possessed vast discernment and was revered by all people was the bhikṣu Citta-Śāriputra.
The one who entered the fire-samādhi and universally illuminated the ten directions was the so-called Bhikṣu Svāgata.
The one who was able to subdue the dragons and cause them to revere the Triple Gem is the bhikṣu Nārada.
The one who subdued the ghosts and spirits, leading them to abandon evil and cultivate goodness, is the bhikṣu Ghaṭa.
The one who has subdued the gandharvas and diligently practices wholesome conduct is the bhikṣu Vairocana.
The one who constantly delights in the concentration on emptiness and discerns the meaning of emptiness is the bhikṣu Subhūti.
One whose resolve is set upon emptiness and stillness, and who possesses subtle and wondrous virtues, is also the bhikṣu Subhūti.
One who practices the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and eliminates all discursive thoughts is the bhikṣu Giri-māla-na.
He who enters the concentration of wishlessness and whose mind does not give rise to distraction is the bhikṣu named Jvalita.
Aṅgulimāla, Saṃghama, Citra, Vatsa, Nālandā, Puḷuṣa, Kalyāṇakārin, and Mānava.
(9) "Among my śrāvakas, the bhikṣu foremost in entering the samādhi of loving-kindness with a mind free from anger is the bhikṣu Brahmāda."
He who entered the samādhi of compassion and accomplished his original practice is the bhikṣu named Susīma.
He who attained the virtue of joyful conduct and was free from manifold perceptions is the bhikṣu named Samita.
He who constantly guards his mind and never abandons it is the bhikṣu called Yebhaka.
He who practices the Samādhi of Blazing Flames and never attains liberation is the bhikṣu called Dhammika.
One whose speech is coarse and who shows no deference to those of noble status is the bhikṣu Bhallika.
One who enters the Golden Light Samādhi is also the bhikṣu Bhallika.
He who has entered the vajra-samādhi and cannot be destroyed is the bhikṣu Abhaya.
He whose speech is definitive and resolute, and who harbors no timidity or weakness, is the bhikṣu Sunetra.
He who constantly delights in stillness and solitude, whose mind does not dwell in distraction—this is the bhikṣu Dhama.
He whose meaning is unsurpassable and whom none can ever subdue—this is the bhikṣu Surata.
Brahmadatta, Susīma, Samitiya, Lakkhaṇa, Tārukkha, Pāṭaliya, Abhaya, Sunīta, and Sūra. (10) “Among my śrāvakas,
the foremost bhikṣu who understands the constellations and foreknows good and ill fortune is the bhikṣu Nāgasamāla.”
The monk Vāsiṣṭha is one who dwells in the *samādhi* of Constant Joy and takes the delight of meditation as his food.
The monk Sunakṣatra is one who constantly takes joy as his food.
He who constantly practices patience and does not give rise to anger even when provoked is the bhikṣu Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
He who cultivates the Sūryaprabha-samādhi is the bhikṣu Makhali.
The one who is proficient in the methods of arithmetic without any error is the bhikṣu Nikhila;
the one who distinguishes equal wisdom and never forgets it is the bhikṣu Mṛgaśīrṣa.
The one who has attained the Vajra-thunder Samādhi and harbors no fear is the bhikṣu named Dīpa.
The one who contemplates and realizes the fundamental nature of the body is the bhikṣu named Dhūmrasagotra.
Finally, he attained the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows;
this was the bhikṣu Subhadra. Nāga, Ṭaśana, Mikhinikula, Mṛgadanta, Dṛḍha, and Dhūna—Subhadra was the very last.
These hundred noble ones should all be extensively expounded upon.

**The Chapter on Bhikṣuṇīs, the Fifth of the Ekottarika Āgama.** (1) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī, who has long practiced the life of renunciation and is revered by kings, is the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī."
The one of wisdom and intelligence is the bhikṣuṇī Caṃpā;
the one foremost in supernormal powers, who can summon all the spirits, is the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā.
The one who practices the dhūta-dharmas with eleven restrictions is the bhikṣuṇī Kiṭāśagautamī.
The one foremost in the divine eye, whose vision is unimpeded, is the bhikṣuṇī Śakulī.
She who sits in meditation and enters samādhi with a mind undistracted is the bhikṣuṇī Śamathā.
She who discriminates the meanings and principles and extensively expounds the Way and its teachings is the bhikṣuṇī Pāṭalāñjanā.
She who upholds the Vinaya teachings without committing any transgression is the bhikṣuṇī Pāracana.
She who has attained faith-liberation and shall never regress is the bhikṣuṇī Kātyāyanī.
She who has attained the four analytical knowledges and harbors no timidity is this most excellent bhikṣuṇī.
Mahāprajāpatī, Kṣemā, Utpalavarṇā, Khaṇḍā, Mādrī, Kuṭī, Śakulā, Lāḍhā, Nandā, Kātyāyanī, and Bhadrā.
2. (Second) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī who personally remembers the events of countless kalpas of past lives is the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilī."
The one of upright countenance whom all people revere and love is the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā.
The one who subdued the non-Buddhists and established them in the True Teaching is the bhikṣuṇī Śūṇā.
She who extensively explains the divisions of the teachings by discerning their meanings and purports is the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinā.
She who wears coarse clothing without feeling any shame is the bhikṣuṇī Uttarā.
She whose faculties are tranquil and who is always as if in single-minded concentration is the bhikṣuṇī named Prabhāvatī.
She whose robes are neatly arranged and who always conforms to the Dharma teachings is the bhikṣuṇī named Dhyāyinī.
She who is able to engage in various forms of discourse without hesitation or impediment is the bhikṣuṇī Tāndya.
She who is capable of composing verses to praise the virtues of the Tathāgata is the bhikṣuṇī Devadattā.
One who is widely learned, possessed of vast knowledge, and gracious in wisdom toward those below is the bhikṣuṇī Gopā. Bhadrā, Śrī, Śūna,
Dharmā, Udakaprabhā, Dhyānā, Dantā, Devadattā, and Gopā.
(3) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī is the one who constantly dwells in seclusion and does not reside among people; she is the bhikṣuṇī Abhayā."
The one who practices the ascetic discipline of begging for food without discriminating between the noble and the lowly is the bhikṣuṇī Viśākhā.
The one who remains seated in a single place until the end of her life without ever shifting is the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrāpālā.
She who went about begging for alms to widely deliver the people was the bhikṣuṇī Maṅgūśrī.
She who swiftly attained the fruit of the Path without lingering in the interim was the bhikṣuṇī Dharmā.
She who always maintained the three robes and never parted from them was the bhikṣuṇī Sūdharmā.
She who sat constantly beneath trees with an unwavering mind was the bhikṣuṇī Lakuṇṭaka-Bhadrā.
She who constantly dwells in the open air, never thinking of a roof-cover, is the bhikṣuṇī Śraddhā.
She who delights in secluded places and does not remain among the laity is the bhikṣuṇī Ugrā.
She who sits perpetually upon a grass mat and wears no ornaments is the bhikṣuṇī known as Nanda.
She who wears the fivefold patched robe and distributes it in turn is the bhikṣuṇī known as Anupamā.
Abhaya, Tāpissī, Bhaddekarattā, Anupamā, Sundarīnandā, Sīsupacālā, and Uppalavaṇṇā.
(4) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī who delights in dwelling in empty cemeteries is the bhikṣuṇī Uppalavaṇṇā."
She who frequently dwells in loving-kindness and compassionately regards all living beings is the bhikṣuṇī Qingming.
She who pities sentient beings and laments those who have not yet attained the Way is the bhikṣuṇī Soma.
She who joyfully attained the Way and vowed that her merit extend to all beings is the bhikṣuṇī Mādrī.
She who guarded and maintained all practices with a mind never wavering is the bhikṣuṇī Kālīkā.
Guarding emptiness and clinging to the void, yet realizing that nothing exists therein—this refers to the bhikṣuṇī Devaśū.
Her mind delights in non-conceptualization and she has eliminated all attachments—this refers to the bhikṣuṇī Sūryaprabhā.
She who cultivates the wishless (*apraṇihita*), whose mind is ever intent on universal salvation—she is the bhikṣuṇī Manāpā.
She who is free from doubt regarding all dharmas and saves beings without limit—she is the bhikṣuṇī Vimadā.
She who is able to expound the meaning extensively and analyze the profound Dharma is the bhikṣuṇī Samantaprabhā.
These are: Utkaca, Prabhā, Sumatī, Mātā, Kā, Devasūryaprabhā, Manava, Vimada, and Samantaprabhā.
(5) "Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī, who possesses a mind of patience that receives all like the earth, is the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā."
The one who was able to teach and transform others, causing them to establish assemblies for giving (dāna), was the bhikṣuṇī Sunetra.
The one who prepared the seats and couches was also the bhikṣuṇī Sunetra.
She whose mind has attained eternal stillness and no longer gives rise to distracted thoughts is the bhikṣuṇī Indrasenā.
She who contemplates all phenomena with insatiable diligence is the bhikṣuṇī Nāgā.
She whose will is strong and courageous, free from all defilement and attachment, is the bhikṣuṇī Kuṇāla.
She who enters the samādhi of water and universally moistens all beings is the bhikṣuṇī Vasu.
She who entered the Samādhi of Flaming Light and illuminated all classes of sentient beings was the bhikṣuṇī Khaṇḍā.
She who contemplated the impurity of foul secretions and discerned dependent origination was the bhikṣuṇī Cchāpā.
The bhikṣuṇī who nurtures and supports the multitude and bestows upon them what they lack is Kāśyapī.
The bhikṣuṇī among my śrāvakas who is foremost in being the very last [to attain parinirvāṇa] is Bhadrā-kāpilānī.
Dharmā, Suyāmā, Indrā, Nāgā, Kunāpā, Vasu, Varā, Cāpā, Śaucikā, and Bhadrā—
these fifty bhikṣuṇīs shall be explained in detail as above.

Chapter Six: On the Lay Disciples (*Upāsaka-varga*). *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter Six on the Lay Disciples, Sūtra 1. (1) "Among my disciples, those who first heard the medicine of the Dharma and attained the realization of a noble one (*ārya*) are these three merchants who have reached the third fruit."
The foremost in wisdom is the Elder Citta;
the foremost in spiritual power is the one known as Kātyāyanīputra;
the one who subdues non-Buddhists is the Elder Kokālika.
The one capable of expounding the profound Dharma is the Elder Upagupta.
The one who constantly sits in meditative contemplation and censures arrogance is Kāśyapa Ārāḍa.
The one who has subdued the palace of Māra is the Elder Śūra.
As for one whose merit is full and abundant, it is the Elder Śāriputra.
As for the great patron and lord of donors, it is the Elder Sudatta.
As for one who has perfected his lineage and clan, it is the Elder Mṛgāra.
Trayaphala, Citta, Ghaṭīkāra; Kukkuṭa, Vajjiya, Bāvarī, Soṇa, Sāriputta, Sudatta; Mendaka—these are called the ten.
(2) "The foremost among my disciples, lay followers who delight in inquiring into the meaning and purpose [of the Dharma], is the brahmin Jāti-Āḷavaka."
The one of sharp faculties who was universally enlightened was Vāmadeva.
The messenger of faith for all Buddhas was the young brahmin Aśvajit.
The one who reckoned the body as selfless and delighted in hearing the Dharma was the brahmin Śreṇika.
The one who is invincible in debate is the Brahmin Viśvāmitra;
the one capable of composing and reciting verses is the Elder Upāli;
and the one whose speech is swift and rapid is likewise the Elder Upāli.
One who delights in giving precious things and possesses no stinginess is the Elder Sudatta.
One who establishes the roots of goodness is Ugga of Vesālī.
The one capable of preaching the sublime Dharma is the foremost, fearless Upāsaka.
The one who preaches fearlessness by skillfully examining the faculties of others is the General Tama, who leads Vaiśālī.
Jātiśroṇa, Brahmāyu, Aśvajit, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, Upāli, Sudatta, Uttara, Bhaya-bhīru, and Māgandiya.
(3) "Among my disciples, the foremost among laymen (*upāsaka*) who delight in giving is King Viśākha."
He who gave but little in alms was King Prabhāsa.
He who established the roots of goodness was King Prasenajit.
He who attained rootless faith and gave rise to a heart of joy was King Ajātaśatru.
The one who with a sincere heart turned toward the Buddha, his mind unchanging, was King Udayana.
The one who served the True Dharma was Prince Candraprabha.
One who serves the noble assembly with a mind always impartial is the Prince of Jetavana.
One who constantly delights in rescuing others and does not act for his own sake is the Prince Siṃha.
The one who was exceptionally respectful toward others, without distinction between high and low, was Prince Abhaya.
The one whose countenance was upright and superior to all others was Prince Kukkuta.
Vaiśravaṇa, Prabhāsa, Prasenajit, King Śreṇika, Jeta, Udayana, Siṃha, Bhīma, and Kukkuta.
(4) "The foremost among my disciples, laymen who constantly practice loving-kindness, is the householder Citta."
He whose mind is constantly filled with compassion for all classes of beings is the Śākya named Mahānāman.
He who always practices a mind of joy is the Śākya named Bhadrika.
One who constantly practices guarding the mind and does not lose virtuous conduct is the upāsaka Viśākha.
One who is capable of practicing patience is the general Siṃha.
The one capable of engaging in various discourses is the lay follower Viśākha.
The one who remains in noble silence is the lay follower Nandipāla.
The one who diligently cultivates wholesome conduct without ceasing is the lay follower Uttara.
He whose faculties are tranquil is the upāsaka named Dhammika;
he who is the last among my disciples to realize the fruit is Kūṭadanta.
Upāli, Mahānāma, Bhadda, Uttaraseṇi, Vīra, Lāḷudāyi, Deva, and Māluṅkyaputta—
these forty lay followers (upāsakas) are all fully explained as above.

Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Faithful Laywomen (*Upāsikā*) from the *Ekottarika Āgama*. (1) "Among my disciples, the foremost among upāsikās who have first received the path and attained realization is the upāsikā Nandā-Nandapālā."
The foremost in wisdom is the upāsikā Jīvā Tārā;
she who constantly delights in sitting in meditation is the upāsikā Subhadrā;
she whose faculty of wisdom is lucid is the upāsikā Vibhū.
The one capable of preaching the Dharma is the female lay disciple Aṅgajātā;
the one who skillfully expounds the meaning of the sūtras is the female lay disciple Bhadrā Śrīyamā.
She who subdues non-Buddhists is the female lay follower (upāsikā) Vāsudā;
she whose voice is clear and penetrating is the female lay follower Anupamā;
she who is capable in various forms of debate is the female lay follower Bhāradvājī.
She who is courageous and diligent is the upāsikā Sthūlanandā. Nanda, Āyuṣmatī, Sthūlā, Viśākhā, and Aṅgajā.
(2) "Sujātā and Anupamā, Pāṭalī and Sujātā.
"Among my disciples, the foremost among upāsikās in making offerings to the Tathāgata is the lady Mallikā."
She who served the True Dharma was the lady Sulasa;
she who made offerings to the noble assembly was the lady Viśākhā;
and she who looked after the worthy ones of the past and future was the lady Candraprabhā.
The foremost among donors was Lady Vajrāśani.
She who constantly practiced the samādhi of loving-kindness was the upāsikā Mahāprabhā.
She who practiced compassion and pity was the upāsikā Bhadrikā.
She whose joyful mind never ceases is the upāsikā Utpalā.
She who practices the karma of protection is the upāsikā Mātṛ-Nandā.
She who has attained liberation through faith is the upāsikā Prabhāvatī.
Mali, Surādha, Śāmi, Prabhācandra, Garjita-mahāprabha, Vidiśa, Dhara, Nanda, and Ālokakāra.
(3) “Among my disciples, this is the foremost who constantly practices patience: namely, the upāsikā named Uruvilvā.”
She who practices the samādhi of emptiness is the upāsikā Viśākha;
she who practices the samādhi of signlessness is the upāsikā Upananda.
The one who practices the samādhi of wishlessness is the upāsikā Vimalā.
The one who delights in instructing others is the upāsikā Śrīmatī.
The one who is well-able to maintain the precepts is the upāsikā Aṅgikā.
She of upright appearance is the upāsikā Vidyutprabhā;
she of tranquil faculties is the upāsikā Varā;
she of vast learning and wide knowledge is the upāsikā Nīlā.
The one capable of composing verses and hymns is the courtesan Sundarī.
The one who is free from all timidity is also the courtesan Sundarī.
Among my śrāvakas, the last to attain realization as an upāsikā is the upāsikā Uruvilvā.
There are also Upacālā, Viśākhā, Puṇṇā, Vimalā, Śyāmāvatī, Ghosilā, Bhadrā, Mṛgī, and Uruvilvā-mātā.
These thirty *upāsikās* are explained in detail as above.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on Asuras *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter Eight: The Chapter on Asuras (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among those who have received a physical form, none is greater than the King of the Asuras.
Bhikṣus, you should know that the body of the Asura is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height and breadth, and his mouth is one thousand yojanas in length and width."

"Monks, you should know that there may be a time when the Asura King, wishing to assail the sun, transforms his body to a height of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas and proceeds before the sun and moon."
When King Candrasūrya saw this, he was filled with terror in each case and could not remain at ease in his place.
This was because the form of the asura was exceedingly fearsome.
Because that King Sun and Moon, being filled with fear, no longer possess radiance;
yet the asuras do not dare to come forward and seize the sun and moon. Why is this?
The Sun and Moon possess majestic virtue and great supernormal powers; their lifespans are exceedingly long, their countenances are upright and handsome, and they enjoy inexhaustible bliss.
If one wishes to know the length of their lifespan, it lasts for one kalpa.
Furthermore, it is due to the merit and blessings of the sentient beings here that the Sun and Moon Kings are not troubled or harassed by the asuras.
At that time, the asuras became filled with sorrow and anxiety, and immediately vanished from that place.
"Thus it is, bhikṣus!
Māra Pāpīyān constantly follows behind you, seeking opportunities to destroy your roots of goodness."
Pāpīyān then manifested extremely wondrous and extraordinary phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and tactile sensation, intending to delude and distract the minds of the bhikṣus.
Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"I shall encounter the opportunity to gain access through the bhikṣus' eyes; likewise, I shall gain access through their ears, noses, mouths, bodies, and minds."
At that time, although the bhikṣu beheld the most exquisite objects of the six sense-faculties, his mind was not stained by attachment.
Thereupon, the evil Māra Pāpīyān became filled with sorrow and anxiety, and immediately withdrew and departed.
The reason for this is due to the majestic power of the Tathāgata, the Arhat. Why is this so?
Because these bhikṣus do not draw near to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles.

At that time, a bhikṣu should constantly train himself in this way: "Receiving the faithful offerings of others is extremely difficult; they are hard to digest and will cause one to fall into the five realms of existence, preventing one from attaining the unsurpassed, true, and right path."

"You must apply yourselves with single-minded devotion so that what has not been attained may be attained, what has not been acquired may be acquired, those who have not crossed over may cross over, and those who have not realized the fruit may be taught to achieve realization. Therefore, O bhikṣus!"
When there is no gift of faith, no conceptualization arises;
because there is a gift of faith, one is able to digest it and does not give rise to defiled attachment.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there should appear in the world a certain person who brings great benefit to others, who brings peace and security to sentient beings, who has compassion for the multitudes of the world, and who desires to cause devas and humans to obtain their blessings and protection.”
Who is this one person? It is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

This is called the one person who appears in the world to bring great benefit to humanity, to bring peace and security to all sentient beings, to have compassion for the multitudes of living beings in the world, and to cause gods and humans alike to obtain his blessings and protection.
Therefore, monks, you should always cultivate reverence toward the Tathāgata. Therefore, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If one person appears in the world, then there is one person who enters the Path within the world; likewise, the two truths, the three gates of liberation, the true Dharma of the four truths, the five faculties, the cessation of the six wrong views, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the nine abodes of sentient beings, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eleventh, the liberation through a mind of loving-kindness—all these appear in the world.”
Who is this one person? It is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. This is called the one person who appears in the world;

with his appearance, there is one person who enters the Way and abides in the world. Furthermore, there appear in the world the two truths, the three gates of liberation, the true Dharma of the four truths, the five faculties, the cessation of the six false views, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, the nine abodes of sentient beings, the ten powers of the Tathāgata, and the eleventh, the liberation through a mind of loving-kindness. These all appear in the world.
"Therefore, monks, you should always cultivate reverence toward the Tathāgata, and you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If one person appears in the world, then the light of wisdom appears in the world.
Who is this one person? It is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
This is called the appearance of one person in the world, whereby the light of wisdom appears in the world.
Therefore, monks, you should place your faith in the Buddha with an undeviating mind.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is one person who appears in the world, the great darkness of ignorance naturally vanishes.

At that time, ordinary and foolish people, bound and entangled by this ignorance, do not know as it truly is the destination of birth and death; they wander to and fro between this life and the next, from eon to eon, without ever finding release.
When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, the great darkness of ignorance naturally vanishes.”
Therefore, monks, you should mindfully attend upon the Buddhas. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If one person appears in the world, then thirty-seven factors appear in the world.”
What are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment?

They are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; these have appeared in the world.
Who is this one person?
It is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
"One should always serve the Buddha and likewise train in this manner.

The reason for this is that these are their limits and these are their measures.
Among the disciples of the World-Honored One who have received his certification, there are the householder Citta and the youth Hatthaka.

Focus your mind on wholesome thoughts; that which you have not attained, you shall attain; that which you have not acquired, you shall acquire; and that which you have not yet realized, you shall now realize.

3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The mind is also like this; that which distinguishes the preceding thought from the succeeding thought is that the mind revolves with such speed that it cannot be grasped by means of skillful methods. Therefore, O bhikṣus!

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One dharma should be practiced; one dharma should be widely disseminated.”
Having practiced one dharma and widely disseminated one dharma, one then attains supernormal powers, the tranquility of all formations, the fruits of the śramaṇa, and reaches the realm of nirvāṇa.
What is this one dharma?
It is the practice of heedfulness.
What is the practice of heedfulness?
This is what is called guarding the mind.
How does one guard the mind? In this regard, O bhikṣus!

One should constantly guard the mind regarding outflows (*āsrava*) and phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*). When one thus guards the mind regarding outflows and phenomena associated with outflows, one will find joy in those phenomena associated with outflows; furthermore, one will possess faith and delight, remaining steadfast without wavering, always concentrating the mind, and exerting oneself through personal effort.
"So it is, bhikkhus! He practices with heedfulness and is always self-restrained."
The outflow of sensual desire that has not yet arisen does not arise;
the outflow of sensual desire that has already arisen can be brought to cessation;
the outflow of existence that has not yet arisen does not arise.
One can cause the arisen taints of existence to cease;
one can prevent the unarisen taint of ignorance from arising;
and one can cause the arisen taint of ignorance to cease.

When a bhikṣu practices without negligence therein, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, constantly maintaining self-awareness and sporting within himself, his mind is liberated from the outflow of desire; his mind is liberated from the outflow of existence and the outflow of ignorance.

Having attained liberation, he then attains the knowledge of liberation; he knows as it truly is: "Birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence to be experienced."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The trace of ambrosia is freedom from pride; negligence is the path to death.
One who is without arrogance does not die; for the arrogant, there is death."
"Therefore, monks, you should practice with mindfulness and heedfulness. Thus, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:

At that time, seeing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted his invitation, the elder circumambulated the Buddha three times, returned to his residence, and upon arriving at his house, prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink that very night. Having spread out seats extensively, he announced:
"The time has come; the meal is prepared. I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to visit us."

At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by the assembly of bhikṣus, donned his robes and took up his bowl, proceeding to the city of Śrāvastī. Upon arriving at the house of the elder, he and the others each took their seats; the community of bhikṣus also sat down one after another in order.
At that time, seeing that the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus were seated, the elder personally served and distributed various kinds of food and drink.
When they had finished eating and each had withdrawn their bowl and sat down, he took a lower seat and sat before the Tathāgata, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Excellent, Tathāgata!

I permit the bhikṣus to take from the households of their disciples whatever items they require—namely, the three robes, the alms bowl, the needle case, the sitting mat, the waistband, the ritual water flask, and all other miscellaneous articles of a śramaṇa. All such things are permitted to be taken.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If you require robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, ritual water jars, or any other miscellaneous requisites of a śramaṇa, I permit you to take these from him; do not harbor doubts or difficulties, nor give rise to thoughts of attachment."
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wonderful Dharma to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Having finished preaching the sublime Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada again practiced extensive acts of charity at the four city gates; furthermore, at the fifth location, the marketplace, and the sixth, his own home, he gave food to those who needed food, drink to those who needed drink, and provided carriages, music, incense, and necklaces to all who required them.

At that time, the World-Honored One heard that the elder Anāthapiṇḍada was extensively practicing charity at the four city gates, further bestowing gifts upon the poor and destitute in the great marketplace, and moreover giving boundlessly within his own home.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the foremost upāsaka who delights in giving is the elder Sudatta."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The Blessed One said to him:
“How is it, householder?”
"Does your noble family constantly practice almsgiving to the poor? The elder replied, "It is so."
"Bhagavān! He constantly gives alms to the poor and destitute, practicing extensive giving at the four city gates, and furthermore, he provides whatever is needed within his own home. Bhagavān!
At times I have had this thought: "I wish to give alms to wild animals, birds, pigs, dogs, and their like.
Yet I have no such thought as, "This one should be given to, and that one should not be given to."
Furthermore, he has no such thought as, "This should be given much; this should be given little.
He constantly maintains this thought: "All sentient beings sustain their lives by means of food; with food they survive, and without food they perish."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Householder!
You have, with the mind of a bodhisattva, single-mindedly and with focused diligence bestowed vast gifts.
Yet these sentient beings are sustained by food; without food, they perish."
"Householder!
You shall obtain a great fruit, attain great renown, and receive a great karmic reward; your fame shall reach the ten directions, and you shall obtain the flavor of the nectar-like Dharma."

The reason for this is that when a bodhisattva dwells in the world, they always practice giving with a mind of equanimity, single-mindedly and with focused intent, mindful that all classes of sentient beings subsist through food: where there is food, they are sustained; where there is no food, they perish.
"This is what is meant, householder!
It is that the Bodhisattva’s mind dwells in peace while bestowing extensive gifts.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One should practice universal giving, never harboring a heart of stinginess or regret;
one will surely encounter a virtuous friend and attain salvation to reach the other shore. Therefore, O Householder!"
One should practice extensive giving with an impartial mind.
In this way, householder,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the elder rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Just as I today clearly know the origins and destinies of the faculties of sentient beings, I likewise know the retribution for giving.”
When there was nothing left but the very last morsel, he did not eat it himself but bestowed it upon others; at that time, he did not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of resentment or envy.
Because these sentient beings do not know the fruit of giving, whereas I know it all completely:
the fruit of giving is an impartial retribution, and my mind toward it is without distinction.

"For this reason, sentient beings are unable to practice impartial giving and thus fall into ruin; they are constantly possessed of a mind of stinginess and envy, which entangles and envelops their thoughts.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Sentient beings do not realize for themselves The teachings of the Tathāgata;"
One should always practice universal and impartial giving, directing it solely toward those who are true persons (*satpuruṣa*).
With a mind and nature purified, the merit obtained will be manifold;
by sharing that merit equally with others, one shall later attain a great fruition.
This gift is now most excellent; with a mind directed toward the vast field of merit, one who passes away from this human world will surely be reborn in the heavens.
Having reached that auspicious place, one shall enjoy happiness and delight oneself.
Auspicious and exceedingly joyful, with nothing lacking or deficient,
through the power of celestial majesty and karma, jade maidens serve as his retinue;
because of the reward for impartial giving, he has thus obtained this blessed fortune.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should not fear the retribution of merit. Why is this? For this is the appropriate result of experiencing happiness, and it is most worthy of love and respect."
That which is called "merit" (puṇya) is so named because it possesses this great retribution.
You all should fear the absence of merit.

Why is this? Because this is the very root of suffering; its sorrows, anxieties, and afflictions are beyond reckoning, and there is no joy or delight in it—this is what is called the absence of merit.

"Monks! In the past, I reflected that by practicing loving-kindness for seven years, I did not return to this world for another seven kalpas; for another seven kalpas, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; for another seven kalpas, I was born in the realm of the Brahmā of Emptiness as Mahābrahmā, peerless and sovereign over a hundred thousand worlds; thirty-six times I took the form of Śakra, Lord of Devas; and for incalculable lifetimes, I was a Wheel-turning King."
Therefore, bhikṣus! Do not grow weary in the performance of merit. Why is this?
Because this is called the appropriate response for receiving happiness; it is most worthy of affection and respect, and thus it is termed "merit."
You all should fear the lack of merit.
Why is this so? The root of suffering consists of grief, anxiety, and affliction beyond measure; this is what is called the lack of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"How joyful is the retribution of merit! Whatever one aspires to is attained; One swiftly reaches extinction And arrives at the state of the unconditioned."
Even if there were hundreds of millions of Māras, the Wicked One, they could not disturb one who performs meritorious deeds.
Such a person constantly seeks the path of the noble ones; thus they exhaust all suffering and thereafter have no more sorrow.
"Therefore, monks, do not grow weary of performing meritorious deeds. Therefore, monks..."
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is one who upholds and follows a single dharma and does not depart from it, Māra Pāpīyas will be unable to find an opportunity against him, nor will he be able to come and disturb or harass such a person."
What is this one dharma?
It is merit, virtue, and karmic action.

Why is this so? I recall that in the past, while I was beneath the Bodhi tree, I gathered together with the various bodhisattvas in one place. At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān led a host of soldiers numbering in the tens of billions, with various forms and appearances—countless beings with animal heads and human bodies—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and mahoragas, all of whom came and assembled there.
"At that time, Māra Pāpīyān spoke to me, saying:
'Śramaṇa, quickly cast yourself to the ground!

The Buddha, by means of the great power of his merit, subdued the demonic adversaries; all defilements were eliminated, and being free from all impurities, he immediately attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path."

"O Bhikṣus! You should contemplate this meaning: if there is a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with meritorious qualities, the evil Māra Pāpīyān will be unable to find an opportunity to destroy those qualities."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Those with merit experience happiness; those without merit suffer. In this life and in lives to come, one experiences joy through the cultivation of merit.”
"Therefore, monks, do not grow weary in the performance of meritorious deeds.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is a bhikṣu who practices one dharma, he will not be ruined by the evil destinies; this one [dharma] leads to the good destination and the other leads to nirvāṇa.
What is the practice of that one dharma by which one cannot be ruined by the evil destinies?"
What is meant by "the mind lacking firm conviction"? This refers to practicing this one dharma so as not to fall into the evil destinies.
What is the practice of this one dharma that leads to the happy realms?
What is called "firm faith in mental conduct" is said to be the cultivation of this one dharma by which one attains rebirth in a good destination.
How does one practice one dharma to reach nirvāṇa?
What is called "constant single-minded mindfulness" is said to be the cultivation of this dharma by which one reaches nirvāṇa.
Therefore, monks, concentrate your minds and be mindful of the roots of all that is wholesome. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there is one person who appears in the world, this class of sentient beings will have their lifespans increased and their years extended; their complexions will become radiant and lustrous, their physical strength will flourish, their happiness will be boundless, and their voices will be harmonious and elegant."
Who is this one person? It is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

When this one person appears in the world, these classes of beings increase in lifespan and years, their complexions become radiant and moist, their physical strength becomes flourishing, their happiness becomes boundless, and their voices become harmonious and elegant.
Therefore, monks, you should always be single-mindedly and diligently mindful of the Buddha. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
