Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Entering the Path Ekottarika Āgama (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“There is a single entrance to the Path that purifies the conduct of sentient beings, removes sorrow and grief, eliminates all afflictions, attains great wisdom, and realizes the realization of Nirvāṇa.”
That is to say, one should extinguish the five hindrances and contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness.
What is called "one entrance"?
It refers to single-minded concentration; this is what is meant by "one entrance."
What is the Path? It is the Noble Eightfold Path:

first, right view; second, right resolve; third, right action; fourth, right livelihood; fifth, right effort; sixth, right speech; seventh, right mindfulness; and eighth, right concentration. This is called the Path; this is called the single entrance to the Path.
"How should one extinguish the five hindrances?

Namely, the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, and the hindrance of doubt—these are what should be extinguished."
"How does one contemplate the four foundations of mindfulness?
In this regard, a bhikṣu contemplates his own body internally, removing evil thoughts and being free from sorrow and anxiety;
he contemplates his own body externally, removing evil thoughts and being free from sorrow and anxiety."
Contemplating the body internally and externally, one eliminates evil thoughts and remains free from sorrow and anxiety.
One contemplates feelings internally as feelings, and externally as feelings, and both internally and externally as feelings;
one contemplates the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally, thereby finding joy therein.
"One contemplates the internal phenomena, contemplates the external phenomena, and contemplates both the internal and external phenomena, thereby finding delight therein.
How does a bhikkhu contemplate the body internally and find delight therein?"

Thereupon, the bhikṣu contemplates this body according to its nature and course: from head to foot, and from foot to head, he observes that within this body there is nothing but impurity, and nothing at all to be craved.

Furthermore, one contemplates this body as consisting of hair, head-hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, fat, grease, intestines, stomach, heart, liver, spleen, kidneys, and so forth, observing and knowing them all completely.
One should observe and understand that feces, urine, the two receptacles of the raw and cooked, tears, saliva, nasal mucus, blood vessels, fat, and bile are all devoid of anything worth desiring.
"In this way, monks, you should contemplate the body as something for your own enjoyment, removing evil thoughts and being free from sorrow and anxiety. Furthermore, monks,"
Furthermore, he contemplates this body: "Is there an earth element in it?
Are there water, fire, or wind elements?
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates this body.
Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Contemplate this body by analyzing its various elements. This body consists of four elements, just as a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having dissected a cow joint by joint, observes for himself: "This is the leg, this is the heart, this is the joint, and this is the head."
In this way, that bhikṣu analyzes this realm and observes within his own body the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
In this manner, the bhikṣu contemplates the body and finds delight therein.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! Contemplate this body as having various apertures from which impurities flow out,
just as that person contemplates a bamboo grove or a thicket of reeds."
In this way, monks, one contemplates this body as having various apertures from which various impurities flow out. "Furthermore, monks,
one contemplates a corpse that has been dead for one night, or two nights, or three, four, five, six, or seven nights, its body bloated, foul-smelling, and impure."
Furthermore, he observes his own body as no different from that [corpse], thinking: "My own body cannot escape this affliction.
Again, if a bhikṣu contemplates a corpse being devoured by crows, magpies, and owls;
or being devoured by tigers, wolves, dogs, and various other kinds of insects and beasts.
Furthermore, he observes his own body as no different from theirs, thinking, "My own body is not exempt from this affliction.
This is called a bhikṣu observing the body for his own delight. "Furthermore, bhikṣu!
One contemplates a corpse that is half-eaten and scattered upon the ground, foul-smelling and impure.
One further observes one's own body as no different from it, thinking: "My body is not exempt from this nature."
Furthermore, one contemplates a corpse whose flesh has completely decayed, leaving only bones stained with blood.
One then observes that this body and that body are no different from one another.
In this way, bhikṣus, one contemplates this body. Furthermore, bhikṣus,
one contemplates a corpse bound together with sinews like a bundle of firewood, and then contemplates one's own body as no different from it.
In this way, bhikṣu, you contemplate this body. Furthermore, bhikṣu,
you contemplate a corpse whose bones and joints are scattered and dispersed in various places, such that the hand-bones and foot-bones each lie in a different location.
Or the shoulder blade bone, or the pelvic bone, or the hip bone, or the arm bone, or the shoulder bone, or the rib bone, or the spinal bone, or the neck bone, or the skull.
Furthermore, this body is no different from that; I cannot escape this law, for my own body too shall perish.
In this way, bhikṣus, one contemplates the body and finds joy therein.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!
Observe a corpse that is white, the color of white jade.
Then observe your own body as no different from it, thinking: 'I am not exempt from this condition. This is called a bhikṣu observing his own body."

"Furthermore, bhikṣu! If one sees a corpse that is blue-black and discolored, such that there is nothing in it to be craved; or if it has become the same color as ash or dust, indistinguishable from them.
In this way, bhikṣus!
Observe your own bodies, eliminate evil thoughts, and be free from sorrow and anxiety;
this body is impermanent and subject to dissolution.
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally, contemplates the body externally, and contemplates the body both internally and externally, understanding that there is nothing whatsoever.
How does a bhikṣu contemplate feelings internally as feelings?
Thereupon, when a bhikṣu experiences a pleasant feeling, he immediately knows for himself: "I experience a pleasant feeling";
when he experiences a painful feeling, he immediately knows for himself: "I experience a painful feeling";
and when he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he immediately knows for himself: "I experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
When experiencing a pleasant feeling born of contact, one clearly knows: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling born of contact";
when experiencing a painful feeling born of contact, one clearly knows: "I am experiencing a painful feeling born of contact";
and when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of contact, one also clearly knows: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of contact."
When he experiences a pleasant sensation born of fasting, he clearly knows to himself: "I am experiencing a pleasant sensation born of fasting";
when he experiences a painful sensation born of fasting, he also clearly knows to himself: "I am experiencing a painful sensation born of fasting";

and when he experiences a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant born of fasting, he also clearly knows to himself: "I am experiencing a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant born of fasting."
In this way, a bhikṣu observes feelings within himself.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time he does not experience a painful feeling; at that time, he clearly knows for himself: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling."
When one experiences painful feeling, at that time one does not experience pleasant feeling; one clearly knows for oneself: "I am experiencing painful feeling.
When one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time there is neither pain nor pleasure; one clearly knows for oneself: "I am experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
He practices the dharma of origination and finds delight therein; he also contemplates the dharma of cessation, and further contemplates the dharma of both origination and cessation.

Or again, there may be feelings that manifest before him, which can be known and seen; by contemplating their original source and finding no basis upon which to rely, he finds delight within himself and does not give rise to worldly thoughts.
Within this state, he is neither startled nor terrified; because he is neither startled nor terrified, he attains nirvāṇa.
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—thus he knows it as it truly is.
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates feelings within himself, removing distracted thoughts and being free from sorrow;
he contemplates feelings externally, and contemplates feelings both internally and externally, removing distracted thoughts and being free from sorrow."
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates feelings both internally and externally.
How does a bhikṣu contemplate the mind and mental factors and find delight therein?
In this regard, when a bhikṣu has a mind possessed by desire, he immediately recognizes that he has a mind possessed by desire.
When there is no mind of sensual desire, he knows within himself that there is no mind of sensual desire.
When there is a mind of ill will, he knows within himself that there is a mind of ill will;
when there is no mind of ill will, he also knows within himself that there is no mind of ill will.
When there is a mind of delusion, one knows within oneself that there is a mind of delusion;
when there is no mind of delusion, one knows within oneself that there is no mind of delusion.
When there is a mind of affectionate attachment, one knows within oneself that there is a mind of affectionate attachment.
When there is no mind of affection, he knows within himself that there is no mind of affection.
When there is a mind of attachment, he knows within himself that there is a mind of attachment;
when there is no mind of attachment, he knows within himself that there is no mind of attachment.
When there is a distracted mind, one immediately knows that there is a distracted mind;
when there is no distracted mind, one immediately knows that there is no distracted mind.
When there is a scattered mind, one likewise immediately knows that there is a scattered mind.
When there is no distracted mind, he knows within himself that there is no distracted mind;
when there is a concentrated mind, he knows within himself that there is a concentrated mind;
when there is no concentrated mind, he knows within himself that there is no concentrated mind.
When there is the great mind, one immediately knows within oneself that there is the great mind;
when there is no great mind, one immediately knows within oneself that there is no great mind.
When there is the immeasurable mind, one immediately knows within oneself that there is the immeasurable mind.
When there is no immeasurable mind, he knows by himself that there is no immeasurable mind;
when there is a mind of samādhi, he knows by himself that there is a mind of samādhi;
when there is no mind of samādhi, he knows by himself that there is no mind of samādhi.
When the mind is not yet liberated, he knows within himself that the mind is not yet liberated;
when the mind is already liberated, he knows within himself that the mind is already liberated.
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells with mindfulness established upon the contemplation of the nature of the mind.

"Contemplating the dharma of origination, contemplating the dharma of cessation, and contemplating the dharma of both origination and cessation, one delights in the contemplation of dharmas through reflection.

That which can be known, that which can be seen, that which can be reflected upon, and that which cannot be reflected upon—being without dependence and not giving rise to worldly perceptions; having not given rise to such perceptions, there is no fear;
having no fear, there is no remainder."
With nothing remaining, he attained parinirvāṇa:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knew this as it truly is.
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells with the mind as an object of internal contemplation, establishing mindfulness of the mind; he removes distracted thoughts and is free from sorrow.
He contemplates the mind externally, and he dwells with the mind as an object of both internal and external contemplation, establishing mindfulness of the mind.
In this way, bhikṣus, one dwells with mindfulness as the foundation by contemplating the mind in the mind.
How does a bhikṣu dwell with mindfulness as the foundation by contemplating phenomena in phenomena?
In this regard, a bhikṣu cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and relinquishing all unwholesome states.

One cultivates the awakening factor of dharma-discernment, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity; relying on contemplation, relying on dispassion, and relying on cessation, one abandons all unwholesome states.
In this way, bhikṣu, one dwells with mindfulness by contemplating the mind in relation to phenomena (dharma-dharmānupaśyanā-smṛtyupasthāna).

"Furthermore, bhikṣu, liberated from sensual desires, having removed evil and unwholesome states, with directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapturous joy (prīti) and ease (sukha), one enjoys the first dhyāna as one's own delight."
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells with mindfulness established by contemplating the mental states of phenomena as phenomena. "Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Having abandoned applied thought and sustained thought, with internal joy born of concentration and one-pointedness of mind, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied thought or sustained thought, and possesses mindfulness, equanimity, joy, and bliss, delighting therein."
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells with mindfulness established by contemplating the mental object as a mental object. "Furthermore, bhikṣus!

Having relinquished applied thought, he cultivates sustained attention; he experiences within himself that joy of which the noble ones declare, 'Tranquil and mindful, one dwells in happiness,' and thus practices the third dhyāna, possessing the purity of mindfulness through equanimity."
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells with mindfulness established by contemplating the mind in accordance with phenomena. "Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Having relinquished both pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of elation and dejection, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity through equanimity and mindfulness."
In this way, bhikṣu, one dwells with attention directed toward the mental object of phenomena by contemplating phenomena as phenomena.

Practicing the dharma of arising and practicing the dharma of cessation, and further delighting in the practice of both arising and cessation, one then attains the application of mindfulness to phenomena, which becomes manifest before one.
That which can be known and seen, when one eliminates discursive thoughts and has nothing upon which to rely, the perception of the world does not arise;
once such perceptions do not arise, there is no fear;
once there is no fear, birth and death come to an end.
"The holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further undergoing of existence—thus he knows it as it truly is. Monks!

By relying on this single entrance to the path, sentient beings attain purity, distance themselves from sorrow and grief, are free from further thoughts of delight, and thereby reach wisdom and realize the attainment of Nirvana."
"This is what is meant by extinguishing the five hindrances and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Among all things, I do not see a single dharma that perishes as swiftly as malice toward those who practice the holy life.”
Therefore, monks, you should practice loving-kindness and patience;
act with loving-kindness in body, act with loving-kindness in speech, and act with loving-kindness in mind. Thus, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“When a certain person appears in the world, he is the most honored and supreme among devas, humans, Māras and their followers, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; there is no one equal to him. He is the foremost field of merit, worthy of service and veneration.”
Who is this one person? It is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

This is called the one person who appears in the world, surpassing all devas, humans, asuras, māras and their celestial hosts, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas; he is the most honored and supreme, with no equal, the foremost field of merit, worthy of service and reverence.
In this way, monks, you should always make offerings to the Tathāgata. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Whoever tends to the sick, they thereby tend to me.”
"Whoever tends to the sick, they tend to me. Why is this so?
Because I myself now wish to personally attend to those who are ill. Monks!"
I do not see a single person among the devas, the world, the śramaṇas, or the brāhmaṇas whose giving is superior to this gift. Only when one practices such giving is it truly a gift;
it yields great fruit and reward, brings forth great merit, causes one's fame to spread everywhere, and allows one to attain the flavor of the nectar of the Dharma.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows that among all forms of giving, there is no gift superior to this.
When one practices this giving, it is only then considered true giving; it yields great karmic fruit and brings about great merit.
For this reason, I now say:
"To attend to the sick is no different from attending to me; you shall obtain great merit and blessings throughout the long night."
“In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. (Five) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Whoever praises those who dwell in the forest retreats (āraṇyaka) praises me;
for this reason, I myself now constantly praise the practice of dwelling in forest retreats.
Whoever slanders those who dwell in forest retreats slanders me."
If anyone praises and speaks in commendation of begging for alms, they are praising me.
This is because I always praise those who are able to beg for alms;
if anyone slanders and disparages begging for alms, they are disparaging me.
Whoever praises those who sit in solitude, they praise me;
for this reason, I always praise those who are able to sit in solitude.
Whoever disparages those who sit in solitude, they disparage me.
Whoever praises the practice of eating in a single sitting and eating only once a day, they praise me;
for this is because I always praise those who eat in a single sitting and eat only once a day.
Whoever disparages it, they disparage me.
If anyone praises those who sit beneath a tree, they are praising me without distinction.
This is because I always praise those who dwell beneath trees;
if anyone disparages those who sit beneath a tree, they are disparaging me.
Whoever praises and speaks in praise of sitting in the open air, they are praising and speaking in praise of me. Why is this?
Because I constantly praise those who sit in the open air.
Whoever disparages one who sits exposed to the elements, disparages me;
whoever praises the life of seclusion, praises me.
Why is this? Because I have always praised and spoken in praise of those who dwell in secluded places;
therefore, whoever insults or disparages those who dwell in secluded places, they insult and disparage me.
Whoever praises and speaks in praise of the five-fold rag-robe robe is praising and speaking in praise of me.
Why is this? Because I constantly praise and speak in praise of those who wear the five-fold rag-robe.
"Whoever disparages those who wear the five-layered rag-robes, they disparage me.
Whoever praises those who maintain the three robes, they praise me."
Why is this? I constantly praise and speak in commendation of those who maintain the three robes;
whoever insults or disparages one who maintains the three robes, they thereby insult and disparage me.
Whoever praises and speaks in commendation of those who sit among the burial mounds, they praise and speak in commendation of me.
Why is this? Because I constantly praise and speak in commendation of those who sit among the burial mounds.
Whoever insults or disparages one who sits among the tombs, they insult and disparage me.
Whoever praises the practice of eating but one meal a day, they praise and speak in praise of me.
Why is this? For I constantly praise and speak in favor of those who eat but one meal;
whoever insults or disparages those who eat but one meal, they thereby insult and disparage me.
Whoever praises eating at midday is praising me. Why is this?
Because I always praise those who eat at midday.
"Whoever disparages or insults those who eat at the proper time is insulting me.
Whoever praises and speaks in praise of the various dhūta practices is praising and speaking in praise of me."
The reason for this is that I constantly praise and speak of the various dhūta practices;
whoever disparages or insults those who practice the dhūtas, they thereby disparage and insult me.
I now instruct all you bhikṣus:
you should act as Mahākāśyapa has acted, so that there shall be no lapses or omissions.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa possesses these various practices.
Therefore, O bhikṣus! You should always train yourselves in the manner of Mahākāśyapa. Thus, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa dwelt in the forest hermitages (*āraṇya*). When it was time for alms, he went to beg for food without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy. He would sit in a single place and never move to another; he sat beneath trees, in the open air, or in secluded spots. He wore the five-layered rag-robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) or carried the three robes (*tricīvara*). He stayed among burial mounds, sometimes ate only one meal a day, sometimes ate only at midday, and practiced the dhūta ascetic virtues. He was advanced in years and of great stature.
At that time, after his meal, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa went to sit in meditative concentration beneath a tree.
Having finished his meditation, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw Kāśyapa coming from afar and said to him,
"Welcome, Kāśyapa! Then Kāśyapa approached the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat down to one side.
The World-Honored One said:
“Kāśyapa! You are now advanced in years and great in stature; your will has become worn out and decrepit.”
"You may now abandon begging for alms, as well as all the dhūta practices; you may also accept invitations from householders and receive robes.
Kāśyapa replied, "I shall not now follow the Tathāgata’s instruction."
The reason for this is that had the Tathāgata not attained unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, I would have become a pratyekabuddha.

Such a pratyekabuddha practices entirely in the forest hermitages (āraṇya), begging for food at the proper time without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy; he sits alone in one place and never shifts his position, dwelling beneath trees, in the open air, or in secluded places; he wears the five-layered rag-robe or maintains only the three robes; he stays among burial mounds; he eats only once a day, or eats only at midday; and he practices the dhūta ascetic virtues.
"Now I dare not abandon what I have originally practiced to further study other paths.
The World-Honored One told him, "Excellent!"
Excellent, Kāśyapa!
You have brought great benefit, delivering immeasurable people and extending widely to all— both devas and humans— who have attained liberation.
The reason for this is as follows, Kāśyapa:
if these dhūta practices remain in the world, my Dharma shall likewise endure for a long time in the world.

Should the Dharma remain in the world, it will further increase the heavenly realms and cause the three evil paths to diminish; furthermore, the paths of the three vehicles—srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, and anāgāmin—will all be preserved in the world.
"O bhikṣus! All that you learn should be practiced exactly as Kāśyapa has practiced.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Gain and offerings are extremely heavy; they prevent a person from reaching the unsurpassed, truly correct path."
The reason for this, monks,
is that the foolish Devadatta took those five hundred pots of food belonging to Prince Brahmadatta and offered them as alms.
If Devadatta, that foolish man, had not been given [the food], he would never have committed such evil;

because Prince Brahmadatta came daily to provide offerings of five hundred cauldrons of food, Devadatta gave rise to the five heinous crimes, and upon the dissolution of his body at the end of life, he was reborn in the Great Avīci Hell.
By this expedient means, one should know that gain and profit are extremely heavy; they prevent a person from reaching the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
If a mind for gain and profit has not yet arisen, it should not arise; if it has already arisen, it should be extinguished.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, Devadatta caused dissension among the Sangha, injured the Tathāgata’s feet, incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father the King, and further killed an Arhat bhikṣuṇī; then, in the midst of the great assembly, he spoke thus:
"Where is there any evil?"
From where does evil arise?
Who commits this evil that one must receive its retribution?
I have not committed this evil, nor shall I receive its retribution.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms and heard these words being spoken by the foolish Devadatta in the midst of the great assembly:
"Where is there any evil?"
"From where does evil arise?
Who commits this evil and undergoes its retribution?

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having finished their meal, took up their robes and bowls, placed their sitting mats over their right shoulders, and went to where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads to the ground and sat down to one side.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"Devadatta, a fool, has made this statement in the midst of the great assembly:
'How can there be no calamity for evil deeds, and no retribution for performing merit? There is no receiving of the retribution for good or evil.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is evil and there is fault; all deeds, whether good or evil, have their retribution.
If that foolish Devadatta had known that there is retribution for good and evil, he would have withered away, filled with grief and sorrow, finding no joy."
Boiling blood then gushed from his face; because Devadatta did not understand the retribution of good and evil, he made this statement in the midst of the great assembly:
"There is no retribution for good or evil; committing evil brings no calamity, and performing good brings no blessing."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The fool clearly perceives himself, Thinking that evil deeds bring blessings;
But I now already understand beforehand The retribution for both good and evil."
"In this way, monks! You should distance yourselves from evil and cultivate merit without weariness. Monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (Nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Receiving offerings and sustenance from others is extremely heavy and difficult; it prevents people from reaching the state of unconditioned liberation.”
The reason for this is that the retribution for gain and offerings penetrates to the person's skin; having penetrated the skin, it then penetrates the flesh;
having penetrated the flesh, it then penetrates the bone;
and having penetrated the bone, it reaches the very marrow.
"O bhikṣus! By this means you should know that gain and offerings are extremely heavy.
If the mind for gain has not yet arisen, do not let it arise; if it has already arisen, seek to extinguish it."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is extremely difficult to receive offerings from others, for it prevents one from reaching the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).

This is because, had that teacher, the bhikṣu Śīlila, not been greedy for gain and offerings, he would not have committed such immeasurable acts of killing; thus, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in hell."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When one receives heavy offerings and sustenance from others, It ruins their pure and white conduct.
Therefore, one should restrain the mind And not greedily cling to flavors."
"Śāriputra, having attained meditative concentration, even reached the palace of the Lord of Devas;
yet he subsequently regressed from his supernormal powers and fell among the slaughterers. O Bhikṣus!"
By this means, one should know that it is extremely difficult to receive offerings and sustenance from others.

Thus, a bhikṣu should train himself in this way: he shall restrain the unarisen thought of seeking gain so that it does not arise, and he shall seek skillful means to extinguish such thoughts once they have arisen.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Five; Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: On Gain and Honor (Liyangpin) (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Receiving offerings from others is extremely difficult; it prevents people from reaching the state of non-action."
The reason for this is that if the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had not been greedy for gain and offerings, he would never have abandoned the three dharma robes within the Dharma to become a householder.
“The bhikṣu Śūradatta practices the great forest-dwelling (āraṇyaka);

he goes for alms at the proper time, eats in one sitting at a single location, or eats only at midday; he dwells under trees or in the open air, delights in secluded places, wears the five-fold patched robe or carries only the three robes, frequents cemeteries, and diligently performs ascetic practices—thus he practices these dhūta austerities.”
At that time, the bhikṣu Śūradatta constantly received the offerings of King Puḥu, who daily provided him with food of a hundred flavors.
At that time, the bhikṣu’s mind became stained by this food, and he gradually abandoned the practice of the āraṇyaka:

he no longer went for alms at the proper time, nor did he sit in one place, nor eat only at midday, nor dwell under trees or in the open air, nor reside in secluded places, nor wear the five-fold patched robe, nor maintain the three robes, nor take pleasure in dwelling among tombs, nor exert his body and mortify his flesh.

Having completely abandoned these [vows] and cast off his three Dharma robes, he returned to being a layman; he slaughtered oxen and took life in incalculable numbers, and when his body perished at the end of his life, he was reborn in hell.
"O bhikṣus! By this means, you should know that gain and honor are extremely heavy, causing people to be unable to reach the unsurpassed, truly right path.
If gain and honor have not yet arisen, you must restrain yourselves so they do not arise; if they have already arisen, seek skillful means to cause them to cease."
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. At that time,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When one dharma is extinguished, I declare that you have realized the fruit of supernatural power and that all taints have been exhausted.
What is this one dharma?
It is called sensual craving."
"Therefore, monks, you should extinguish this craving for flavors;
I testify that you shall achieve the fruit of supernatural powers and that all taints will be exhausted.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Sentient beings, attached to this taste, fall into the evil realms at death;
now you should abandon this desire, and you shall become arhats. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
One should always abandon this perception of attachment to flavors. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who had recently lost a son whom he cherished and revered so deeply that he could never bear to let him go.
Upon seeing his son’s death, he fell into a state of madness and delusion, wandering back and forth without staying in one place for even a moment.
Whenever he saw someone, he would say: "Have you seen my son?
At that time, the man gradually made his way to the Jeta Grove Monastery, arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, and stood to one side.
At that time, the man addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! Have you perhaps seen my son?"
The World-Honored One said to the householder,
"For what reason is your countenance displeased and your faculties so disordered?
At that time, the householder replied to Gautama:
"How could it not be so? The reason is this:
I now have but one son, who has abandoned me to pass away.
I cherished and revered him deeply, never for a moment having been out of my sight."
Out of compassion for that son, I have been driven to madness.
I now ask the Śramaṇa: have you seen my child?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Thus it is, householder!
As you have asked, birth, old age, sickness, and death are the constant laws of the world;
the suffering of separation from those one loves, the suffering of encountering those one hates, and the impermanence of a son leaving his father—how could these not be contemplated?"
At that time, having heard what the World-Honored One had said, that person did not take it to heart; he then abandoned him and withdrew.
As he walked on, he saw another man and spoke to him again, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has declared:..."
"When affectionate attachments are analyzed, there is indeed happiness. Is it as the śramaṇa has said?
The person before him replied:
"What joy is there in the separation from those one loves?
At that time, not far from the city of Śrāvastī, there were many people gathered together playing at dice.
At that time, that man thought to himself:
"These men are clever and wise; there is nothing they do not know. I shall now question these men regarding this matter."
At that time, he went immediately to a place where people were gambling and asked the crowd,
"The śramaṇa Gautama said to me:
'The suffering of separation from those one loves and the suffering of meeting with those one hates— these are happiness.'"
"What do you all think now? At that time, the gamblers replied to that person,
"In the separation from those one loves, what joy can there be?"
"As for what you say regarding 'happiness,' this meaning is not so.
At that time, that person thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata’s words are indeed true; they are never false."
"How can there be happiness in the separation from those one loves?
This principle is not so.
At that time, that man entered the city of Śrāvastī and, having reached the outer gate of the palace, proclaimed:
"The ascetic Gautama teaches that 'the separation from those one loves and the meeting with those one hates— this is happiness.
At that time, this report spread throughout the city of Śrāvastī and the inner palace, reaching everywhere without exception.
At that time, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā were together upon a high terrace, amusing themselves in play.
Then, King Prasenajit said to Queen Mallikā:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has indeed spoken these words:"
"Separation from those one loves and meeting with those one hates—these are all sources of happiness.
The lady replied, "I have not heard such a teaching from the Tathāgata; yet, if the Tathāgata had indeed given such an instruction, it would not be false."
King Prasenajit said: "It is just as a teacher instructs a disciple:
'Do this; abandon that.'"
The disciple replied, "So it is, Great Master!
You, Māluṅkyāputta, are just like that; although that śramaṇa Gautama speaks thus, you should speak as follows:
"Thus it is not otherwise; there is no falsehood.
"However, you must depart at once; you need not stand before me.
At that time, Lady Mālikā said to the brahmin Veṇudhārin:
"Go now to the Jeta Grove Monastery, approach the Tathāgata, and prostrating at his feet, speak these words in my name:

'In the city of Śrāvastī and within the inner palace, there is this discussion: "The śramaṇa Gautama says that the separation from those one loves and the meeting with those one hates are both forms of happiness. "
"I wonder if the World-Honored One has such a teaching?
Whatever the World-Honored One may say, you should receive it well and report it back to me.
At that time, the Brahmin Naḍagola, having received the lady's instructions, immediately went to the Jeta Grove Monastery.
Having approached the Blessed One, they exchanged greetings with one another.
When the greetings were concluded, they sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“Lady Māri paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and inquired after the Tathāgata’s well-being: ‘Are you light and at ease in your daily life? Is your movement strong and healthy?
In training and transforming those who are blind and ignorant, do you not find it wearying?’”
He further spoke these words:
"Throughout this city of Śrāvastī, this report has spread everywhere:
'The śramaṇa Gautama gives such an instruction:'"
"To be separated from those one loves and to encounter those one hates—how joyful and pleasant this is!
I do not know if the World-Honored One has ever spoken such a teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin Bamboo-Arm:
"In this city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who lost a son; grieving for him, he became deranged and lost his senses, running hither and thither, and whenever he saw someone, he would ask:
'Who has seen my son?'"
"Furthermore, O Brahmin!
The suffering of separation from those one loves and the suffering of encountering those one hates—these are all devoid of joy.
Previously, in this city of Śrāvastī, there was another old woman who passed away; she too became deranged and lost her sense of direction."
Furthermore, there was an old father who passed away;
likewise, there were brothers and sisters who all met their end.
Witnessing these transformations of impermanence, he became deranged and lost his senses, no longer recognizing east from west.
"Brahmin! Long ago, in this city of Śrāvastī, there was a man who had recently taken a wife; she was peerlessly beautiful.
At that time, before long, that man fell into poverty."
At that time, the parents of the woman, seeing that this man was poor, conceived this thought:
"I shall take my daughter away and marry her to another.
The man overheard that his wife's parents intended to take him away and marry her to another family.
At that time, that man, carrying a sharp blade within his garment, went to the woman’s house; at that very moment, the woman was spinning outside the wall.
At that time, the man went to his wife’s parents’ house and asked, "Where is my wife now?
His mother-in-law replied:
"Your wife is spinning in the shade outside the wall.
At that time, the man went to where his wife was.
Having arrived, he asked her:
The husband asked, "Does your father wish to take you away to marry someone else?
The wife replied,
"It is true that such words have been spoken, yet I find no pleasure in hearing them."
At that time, the man immediately drew his sharp sword, seized his wife, and stabbed her to death; he then took the sharp sword again and pierced his own belly, saying further:
"The two of us shall both die together."

"O Brāhmaṇa! By this means, you should know that the suffering of separation from those one loves and the suffering of encountering those one hates are entirely grief and anxiety, truly beyond words."
At that time, the brahmin Veṇudhāra addressed the Blessed One, saying: “So it is,
Blessed One!”
Having these various afflictions is truly suffering and not joy.
The reason for this is that in the past I had a son who abandoned me and passed away.
Day and night I have pursued his memory, never letting him leave my heart.
At that time, as I thought of my son, my mind became frantic and deluded; I ran hither and thither, and whenever I saw someone, I would ask: "Who has seen my son?
What the śramaṇa Gautama now says is indeed exactly as he has spoken.
"The affairs of state are many and pressing; I wish to return to my quarters.
The World-Honored One replied, "Now is precisely the right time."
The brahmin Vaṃśa rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed.
He went to the lady Mallikā and reported the matter to her in full detail.
At that time, Lady Māllikā went again to King Prasenajit; having arrived, she said to the Great King:
"I now wish to ask something; I only pray that the Great King will grant me an answer for each matter!"
"What do you think, Great King? Do you remember Prince Vairāṭya?
The king replied:
"How deeply you care!
Your compassion never leaves the forefront of your mind. The lady asked:
"If the prince were to undergo change and transformation, Great King,
would you have cause for sorrow?
The king replied again:
"It is so, my lady! It is as you have said. The lady asked:
"Great King, you should know that the separation from those one loves gives rise to sorrowful thoughts.
What do you think, Great King? Do you still remember Prince Eḷa?"
The king replied,
"I hold him in great love and respect. The lady asked:
“Great King! If a prince were to undergo change and transformation, would he experience sorrow and distress?
The king replied:
"I am filled with great sorrow and anxiety. The lady replied,
"By this very circumstance you should know that there is no joy in the separation from those one loves."
"What do you think, Great King?
Do you remember the Sālavatī Kṣatriya clan?
The King replied:
“I love and revere him deeply.
The lady said, “How so, Great King?”
"If Lady Sālā were to undergo change and death, Great King, would you feel sorrow?
The King replied, "I would indeed feel grief and anxiety."
The lady said, "Great King!
You should know that the separation from those one loves is entirely suffering."
The lady said, "Does Your Majesty think of me?
The king replied:
"I love and cherish you. The lady said,
"If my body were to undergo change, would Your Majesty feel sorrow?"
The king said: "If your body were subject to change, you would surely experience sorrow.
"Great King! [he replied.]
"You should know through this expedient means that there is no heart of joy in the separation from those one loves and the meeting with those one hates.
The lady said, "How so, Great King?"
"Do you think of the people of Kāśī and Kośala?
The King replied,
"I hold the people of Kāśī and Kośala very dear."
The queen said, "If the people of Kāśi and Kosala were to undergo change and perish, would Your Majesty feel sorrow?
The king replied:
"The people of Kāśī and Kosala are subject to change; since my own life cannot endure, how much less can I speak of sorrow?
For it is because of the strength of the people of the kingdoms of Kāśī and Kosala that I am able to survive."
"By this expedient means, one knows that even life itself does not endure; how much more so, then, can sorrow and anxiety not arise?
The lady said, "From this I know that in the separation from those we love, there is always this suffering; there is no joy."
At that time, King Prasenajit knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence toward the World-Honored One,
and spoke thus: “How extraordinary!
"How extraordinary!
That Blessed One has taught this Dharma.
If that śramaṇa Gautama were to come here, only then could we engage in discussion with him."
He spoke again to the lady:
"From this day forward, I shall look upon you even more favorably than on ordinary days; the garments and ornaments you wear shall be no different from my own."
At that time, having heard that Lady Mallikā had established this fundamental discourse with the Great King, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Lady Mallikā is exceedingly intelligent. Had King Prasenajit questioned me regarding these words, I would have explained the meaning to that king in exactly the same way as Lady Mallikā has just spoken to him; there would have been no difference."
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost upāsikā who has attained realization and possesses firm, steadfast faith is this Lady Māli."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Vaiśālī, at the Deer Park in the Haunt of Ghosts on Mount Śiṃśumāra.
At that time, the householder Nāḷijaṅgha went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
After a short while, he withdrew slightly from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“I am now advanced in years and further afflicted by illness; I am beset by many anxieties and distresses. I only pray that the World-Honored One will provide me with timely instruction, so that all classes of sentient beings may attain peace and security throughout the long night.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the householder:
"As you have said, this body is full of fear and pain; what can it rely upon?
It is merely covered over by a thin layer of skin."
Householder, you should know that for those who rely upon this body, there can be but a momentary pleasure;
this is the mind of a fool, not what the wise hold in esteem.
Therefore, householder! Although the mind may be afflicted by illness, one should cause the mind to be free from illness.
Thus it is, householder!
"You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, having heard these words, the elder rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew.
At that time, the householder again thought to himself:
"I should now go to the Venerable Śāriputra and inquire about this matter.
Śāriputra was not far from him, sitting beneath a tree.
At that time, the householder Naulāra went to where Śāriputra was, prostrated with his head at his feet, and sat to one side. Then, Śāriputra asked the elder:
"Your countenance is serene and your faculties are tranquil; surely there must be a cause for this."
"Elder! Should you not, therefore, hear the Dharma from the Buddha?
At that time, the elder addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"How is it, Venerable Śāriputra, that your countenance is not serene and joyful? For what reason is this?
Just now, the World-Honored One has drenched your heart with the Dharma of the Deathless."
Śāriputra said: "How is it, householder?
With the Dharma of ambrosia, you irrigate your heart and mind?"
The householder replied:
"In this regard, Śāriputra!
I went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated myself at his feet with my head, and sat to one side."
At that time, I addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I am aged and advanced in years, constantly afflicted by illness and suffering from countless pains beyond measure. I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze this body for me, so that all sentient beings may universally attain this peace and security!"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed me, saying:
"It is so, householder! This body is full of various decays and sufferings, covered over only by a thin skin."
Householder, you should know that those who rely upon this body may indeed experience a momentary pleasure, yet they do not realize that they will suffer immeasurably throughout the long night.
Therefore, householder!
Although this body is subject to affliction, you should ensure that the mind remains free from affliction.
Thus it is, householder!
"One should train in this way.
Thus, the World-Honored One has sprinkled me with this Dharma of the Deathless. Śāriputra said:
"How is it, householder?
Do you not ask the Tathāgata again about this matter:
how is it that the body may have affliction while the mind has no affliction?"
"What is it to have a diseased body but a healthy mind?
The elder said to Śāriputra, "I truly lack the eloquence for this;
let me ask the World-Honored One again: what is it to have both body and mind afflicted by illness, and what is it to have a body afflicted by illness but a mind free from affliction?"
"Venerable Śāriputra must certainly possess this eloquence; we pray that you will explain it in detail.
Śāriputra said, "Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall expound its meaning to you in detail. He replied:
"So it is, Śāriputra! Having received this instruction from him, [he replied].
Śāriputra said to the householder:
"In this regard, householder,
an ordinary person does not see the noble ones, does not receive the noble teaching, and does not follow their instructions."
Furthermore, they do not perceive a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and do not associate with a spiritual friend.
They reckon form (rūpa) as the self, form as belonging to the self, and the self as belonging to form;
they hold that the self is within form and form is within the self, such that form and the self, or form and my-self, are conjoined in one place.
When that form and my own form are gathered together in one place, the form then decays and perishes, shifting without ceasing; therein, moreover, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress arise.

Regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, one contemplates them all as: "I have consciousness," "consciousness is within me," and "I am within consciousness," such that that consciousness and my consciousness meet and merge in a single place.

When that consciousness and the self-consciousness meet in one place, consciousness then perishes; it shifts and passes away without ceasing, and therein further arises sorrow, lamentation, and affliction.
"In this way, householder,
the body also has its afflictions, and the mind also has its afflictions.
The householder asked Śāriputra:
"What is meant by 'the body has affliction, but the mind has no affliction'?
Śāriputra replied, "In this regard, householder!"
The noble disciple serves the noble ones and practices the prohibitive precepts;
he associates with virtuous friends and draws near to virtuous friends.
Furthermore, he does not contemplate that "I have form."
One does not perceive a self within form, nor form within a self;
one does not perceive form as belonging to a self, nor a self as belonging to form.
Since that form is subject to change and instability, and since that form undergoes transformation, one gives rise to no sorrow, affliction, or the distress of a dejected countenance.
Furthermore, one does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not perceive a self within consciousness, nor consciousness within a self;
one does not perceive consciousness as belonging to a self, nor a self as belonging to consciousness.
When that consciousness and the notion of "my consciousness" meet in one place, consciousness then perishes; therein, no sorrow, lamentation, or distress arises.
Thus it is, householder!
"The body may have afflictions, but the mind has no afflictions.
Therefore, householder, you should practice in this way:
leave behind the body and depart from the mind, remaining free from attachment."
"Householder!
You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, the householder Naulāra, having heard what Śāriputra had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by several tens of millions of followers, who attended him before and behind as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, a brahmin from the riverbank, carrying a heavy burden upon his back, went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he set down his burden and stood silently to one side in the presence of the World-Honored One.
At that time, that brahmin thought to himself:
"Today, the śramaṇa Gautama, surrounded before and behind by a multitude of many tens of millions, is preaching the Dharma."
"I am now pure, no different from the śramaṇa Gautama. Why is this so?
The śramaṇa Gautama eats fine non-glutinous rice and various delicacies, whereas I now sustain my life by eating fruits and gourds."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the brahmin’s mind, addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there are sentient beings whose minds are defiled and attached by twenty-one fetters, you should observe that such persons will certainly fall into the evil realms and will not be born in a good destination.”
What are the twenty-one fetters? They are:

the fetter of a mind of anger, the fetter of a mind of malice and harm, the fetter of a mind of sleepiness, the fetter of a mind of restlessness, the fetter of a mind of doubt, the fetter of a mind of resentment, the fetter of a mind of jealousy, the fetter of a mind of vexation, the fetter of a mind of haste, the fetter of a mind of hatred, the fetter of a mind lacking shame, the fetter of a mind lacking remorse, the fetter of a mind of illusion, the fetter of a mind of deceit, the fetter of a mind of hypocrisy, the fetter of a mind of contention, the fetter of a mind of arrogance, the fetter of a mind of pride, the fetter of a mind of envy, the fetter of a mind of overweening pride, and the fetter of a mind of greed. Monks!
If there is a person whose mind is defiled by these twenty-one fetters, one should observe that such a person will certainly fall into the evil realms and not be reborn in a good destination.

It is like a new garment of white cotton cloth that has become old and worn over time and is covered with much dust and grime; even if one intends to dye it into colors such as blue, yellow, red, or black, they can never be achieved.
Why is this? Because there are defilements.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
If there is anyone whose mind is stained and attached by these twenty-one fetters, one should know that such a person will certainly fall into the evil realms and not be born in a wholesome place.
Furthermore, if there is someone whose mind is not stained or attached by these twenty-one fetters, one should know that this person will certainly be born in the heavens and will not fall into hell.
It is like a piece of fresh, clean white cotton cloth: whatever color one wishes to make it—blue, yellow, red, or black—it will certainly take on that color and will never spoil.
The reason for this is that they are pure. This case is likewise:

if there are those whose minds are free from these twenty-one fetters and defilements, one should observe that such persons will certainly be reborn in the heavens and will not fall into the evil realms.

"If that noble disciple gives rise to the fetter of a mind of ill will, having observed it, he is able to still it. He may give rise to the fetter of a mind of malice; the fetter of a mind of sloth and torpor; the fetter of a mind of restlessness and remorse;

the fetter of a mind of doubt; the fetter of a mind of anger; the fetter of a mind of resentment; the fetter of a mind of vexation; the fetter of a mind of impatience; the fetter of a mind of hatred; the fetter of a mind lacking shame; the fetter of a mind lacking dread; the fetter of a mind of delusion; the fetter of a mind of deceit; the fetter of a mind of hypocrisy; the fetter of a mind of contention; the fetter of a mind of arrogance; the fetter of a mind of pride; the fetter of a mind of envy; the fetter of a mind of overweening pride; or the fetter of a mind of greed."

"If that noble disciple is without ill will, without malice, and without delusion, with a mind full of harmony and joy, he dwells pervading one direction with a heart of loving-kindness, finding delight therein; and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions."

In the four intermediate directions, above, and below, among all things, everything is also everything; throughout the entire world, which is infinite, immeasurable, and beyond calculation, he sports freely with a mind free from anger.
With this mind of loving-kindness, he pervades all within it; having attained joy, his mind becomes upright.

Furthermore, with a mind of compassion, he universally fills one direction and finds delight therein; he does the same for the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the four intermediate points, the zenith, and the nadir. Throughout all things—wherein everything is everything—he sports with a mind free from malice toward the entire world, which is immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable.
With this mind of compassion, he pervades all within it; having attained joy, his mind becomes upright.

Furthermore, with a mind of sympathetic joy, he universally fills one direction and finds delight therein; he does likewise for the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the four intermediate points, the zenith, and the nadir. Throughout everything, in every way, and for everyone, throughout the entire world, he sports with a mind that is immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable, free from ill will and anger.
With this mind of joy, he pervades it entirely; having attained such joy, his mind becomes upright.

Furthermore, with a mind of equanimity, he fills one direction and finds delight therein; he does likewise for the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the four intermediate points, the zenith, and the nadir. Throughout all things, in every way, and for everyone, throughout the entire world—immeasurable, limitless, and incalculable—he sports with a mind free from anger.
With this mind of protection, he pervades it entirely; having attained joy, his mind becomes upright.
Thus, regarding the Tathāgata, he establishes the faculty of faith, its root unshakable, raising high the banner of victory so that it cannot be moved.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as the people of the world, will find joy therein, and their minds will become upright.

This is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the one perfected in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One; finding joy therein, his mind becomes upright, and he likewise achieves realization in the Dharma.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is exceedingly pure, immovable, and beloved and revered by all people.
A wise person should contemplate it in this way; thereby they shall attain joy within it and also bring benefit to the multitude.

The noble assembly of the Tathāgata is exceedingly pure; their nature and conduct are purely harmonious, and they have achieved perfection in every dharma: perfection in ethical discipline, perfection in meditative concentration, perfection in wisdom, perfection in liberation, and perfection in the vision and knowledge of liberation.
The Noble Assembly consists of the four pairs and eight classes; this is the Noble Assembly of the Tathāgata, which is lovely and precious, truly worthy of service.
By finding joy therein, one's mind becomes upright.

"Furthermore, by means of this samādhi, his mind becomes pure and free from defilement; all fetters are exhausted and he is no longer stained. His nature and conduct become supple, and having attained supernormal powers, he is able to personally know immeasurable past lives, knowing everything regarding the places from which he has come."

Whether one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; through eons of formation and destruction, eons of non-formation and non-destruction, eons of both formation and destruction and non-formation and non-destruction, or countless eons of formation and destruction and countless eons of non-formation and non-destruction—I have existed therein, with such a name, such a designation, and such a clan; such was my birth, such was my food, such were the sufferings and pleasures I experienced, and such was the length of my life. From there I passed away and was born in that other place; from there I passed away and was born here.
In this way, he personally recollects countless matters of his past lives.
Furthermore, by means of this samādhi, with a mind pure and free from blemish, he knows the thoughts and intentions within the minds of sentient beings.

Furthermore, with his divine eye, he observes the various classes of sentient beings—those who are born and those who pass away; those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance; those in happy destinies and those in miserable destinies; whether they are handsome or unattractive—he knows all of this according to the karmic fruits produced by the conduct of each sentient being.

There may be sentient beings who commit evil through body, speech, and mind; they revile the noble ones and hold wrong views, performing actions based on those wrong views. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the three evil realms and fall into the mire of suffering.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who practice virtue in body, speech, and mind; they do not revile the noble ones, possess right view and are free from wrong view, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination in the heavenly realms.
This is called the pure divine eye with which one observes the various classes of sentient beings:

those who are born and those who pass away; those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance; those in happy realms and those in miserable realms; whether they are handsome or unattractive—one knows all this according to the karmic fruits produced by the conduct of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, by means of this samādhi, his mind becomes pure and free from blemish; being devoid of fetters and afflictions, his mental nature becomes supple, and he attains the supernormal powers."
Furthermore, he finds delight through the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
He contemplates this suffering and knows it as it truly is;
he further contemplates the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the transcendence of suffering, knowing each as it truly is.

Having performed this contemplation, his mind was liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), and his mind was liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhavāsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).
Having attained liberation, he realized the knowledge of liberation:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence"—he knew this as it truly is.
In this way, bhikṣus,
when a noble disciple’s mind has attained liberation, even if he were to eat fine rice and various exquisite delicacies in quantities as vast as Mount Sumeru, he would ultimately incur no fault.

The reason for this is that because he is without desire and has exhausted all craving, because he is without hatred and has exhausted all resentment, and because he is without delusion and has exhausted all ignorance—he is called a bhikkhu among bhikkhus!
"Then, having finished bathing thoroughly within.
At that time, a brahmin by the riverbank said to the World-Honored One: "Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"You may go to the banks of the Sunda River to bathe.
The World-Honored One said,
"What do you think, brahmin?"
"Why is it called the Sunda River?
The brahmin replied, "The Sunda River is a deep abyss of merit and the light of the world. Any person or being who bathes in that river has all their evils completely eliminated."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"This body, throughout incalculable eons, Has passed through and bathed in those rivers;
As for all the small ponds and pools, There is none it has not completely traversed."
The fool always delights in that which is dark and impure;
with past transgressions filling his inner being, how could that river save him?
The pure person is always happy, and the purity of the precepts is likewise blissful.
The pure perform pure deeds, and their aspirations will surely be fulfilled.
If one refrains from taking what is not given, practices loving-kindness and abstains from killing;
maintains integrity and avoids false speech, with a mind of equanimity free from increase or decrease.
"If you bathe here now, you will surely attain a state of peace and security;
as for that river, where does it lead? It is like a blind man casting himself into the darkness.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Stop! Stop, Gautama!"

It is like a hunchbacked person gaining the ability to straighten up, a person in darkness seeing the light, a lost person being shown the way, lighting a lamp in a dark room, or providing eyes for one who has none.
"Thus it is, Śramaṇa Gautama!
You have taught this sublime Dharma through countless skillful means; we pray that you will allow us to follow the Path.
At that time, the Brahmins by the river immediately attained the state of the Path and received full ordination.
Therefore, sons of noble family, having left the household life to study the Way and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life, they know according to reality:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further undergoing of existence."
At that time, the Venerable Sundarika immediately attained arhatship.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Venerable Sundarika rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, as the day had passed and evening approached, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Tathāgata with a verse concerning this meaning:
“Capable of speaking and proclaiming, You have crossed the stream and attained the state of outflowlessness;
Having crossed the abyss of birth and death, I now ask you, Gautama, about this meaning.”
As I observe these sentient beings, And the meritorious deeds they have performed;
Among the various kinds of practices they have cultivated, To whom does the most supreme merit belong?
O Honored One, now upon this Vulture Peak, I only pray that you will expound this meaning.
Knowing the intent of the Śākya’s purpose, he likewise proclaimed it for the sake of the donor:
that by performing merit in the four realms of existence, one may fully accomplish the four fruits;
those who are trainees attaining the tracks [of the path] should faithfully believe and honor this Dharma.
Free from desire and free from hatred, the fool becomes one without outflows;
having crossed over all abysses, he bestows [merit] upon others to achieve great fruit.
Whatever meritorious deeds these various classes of sentient beings perform—
Performing various kinds of practices, one gains great merit by giving to the Saṅgha.
This assembly delivers immeasurable beings, like the ocean producing precious gems;
the noble assembly is likewise, expounding the Dharma of the light of wisdom.
"O Gautama, that virtuous person who is able to give to the Sangha obtains incalculable merit; this is what the Most Victorious One has taught.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and then withdrew from that place.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti was also at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, staying in a separate hut where he was practicing meditation.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti’s body was afflicted by a severe and heavy illness, and he thought to himself:
"From what does this pain of mine arise?"
"Furthermore, from what do they cease,
and where do they go? At that time,

the Venerable Subhūti spread his sitting mat upon the open ground, sat with his body straight and his mind upright, focusing his attention with single-minded concentration in the full lotus posture, contemplating the sense bases (*āyatana*) in order to eliminate suffering.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing the thoughts of the Venerable Subhūti, addressed Pāñcika with these verses:
“The one of virtuous deeds, liberated from all bonds, Dwells upon Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
Now afflicted by a most grievous ailment, He delights in emptiness and the concentration of the sense-faculties.”
"Come quickly to inquire after his illness and to behold the countenance of the Honored One;
having thus obtained great merit, there is no way to plant virtue that surpasses this.
At that time, Pāñcika replied:
"So be it, Venerable One!

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with five hundred devas and Pāñcika, vanished from the Heaven of the Thirty-three as quickly as a man might bend or stretch his arm, and arrived at Vulture Peak Mountain. Not far from the Venerable Subhūti, he addressed Pāñcika with this verse:
“You have now awakened to wholesome karma; you delight in the samādhi of dhyāna.
With your gentle and pure voice, you now cause me to rise from my meditative seat. Pācārṣa replied:
"So be it. At that time, having heard these words from Śakra Devānām Indra, Pāñcaśikha tuned his lapis lazuli lute and approached Subhūti, praising him with this verse:
"All fetters are exhausted without remainder; / All thoughts are free from confusion."
All defilements are utterly exhausted; may you swiftly awaken from dhyāna.
With a tranquil mind, you have crossed the river of existence; having subdued Māra, you have transcended all fetters.
Your merit is like the great ocean; may you swiftly arise from samādhi.
The eye is pure like a lotus flower, with no defilements ever clinging to it;
providing a refuge for those without refuge, one swiftly arises from the concentration on emptiness.
Having crossed the four floods into the unconditioned, one is well-versed in the absence of old age and sickness.
Having escaped the calamities of conditioned existence, the Honored One alone has awakened to the certainty of the time.
Five hundred devas above and the Śākyas themselves have come;
desiring to behold the countenance of the Holy Honored One, they arise swiftly to understand emptiness.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat and again addressed Pāpīyān, saying:
“Excellent, Pāpīyān! Excellent!”
Now your voice and the lute are in harmony, and the lute and your voice are in harmony, such that there is no difference between them.

Yet the sound of the lute does not depart from the sound of the song, nor does the sound of the song depart from the sound of the lute; these two things combine together to produce this wondrous sound.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra went to the place where the Venerable Subhūti was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra addressed Subhūti, saying: "How is it?
Has the suffering and pain with which you are afflicted from your past wholesome karma increased or decreased?"
Now, from what does this bodily illness arise?
Does it arise from the body,
or does it arise from the mind?
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śakra,
Lord of the Devas: “Excellent, Kauśika!
Phenomena arise from themselves, and phenomena cease from themselves;
phenomena move one another, and phenomena rest of their own accord.
It is just so, Kauśika!
There are poisonous drugs, and there are also harmful poisonous drugs.
O Śakra, Lord of Devas!
It is the same with this: dharmas disturb one another, yet dharmas also naturally subside by themselves.
Dharmas can give rise to dharmas: dark dharmas are treated with white dharmas, and white dharmas are treated with dark dharmas.
Śakra, Lord of Devas!
One treats the disease of greed with the contemplation of impurity; one treats the disease of hatred with a mind of loving-kindness; and one treats the disease of delusion with wisdom.
Thus it is, Śakra Devānām Indra!
All that exists returns to emptiness; there is no self, no person, no life-span, no vital principle, no individual, no man, no form, no image, and neither male nor female.
It is just as, Śakra Devānām-Indra!
when the wind destroys a great tree, its branches and leaves wither and fall;
or when thunder and hail destroy the seedlings, their flowers and fruits, though once flourishing, wither away for lack of water.
"When the heavens send down timely rain, the sprouts are able to survive.
In this same way, O Śakra, Lord of Devas!

Though dharmas may be in mutual disorder, each dharma naturally finds its own stability. The ailments, pains, and afflictions that I originally suffered have today been eliminated; I no longer have any suffering."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to Subhūti:
"I too have had sorrow, grief, and affliction; now that I have heard this Dharma, I no longer have any sorrow."
"Affairs are so numerous and complex that I wish to return to the heavens.
I have my own business as well as the business of the various devas, all of which are exceedingly manifold.
At that time, Subhūti said:
"Now is precisely the right time; you should depart at once.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra rose from his seat, went forward to prostrate at the feet of Subhūti, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti spoke these verses:
“The Capable One has spoken these words, In which the root is fully complete;
The wise attain peace and security, And by hearing the Dharma, all ailments are stilled.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra, having heard what the Venerable Subhūti had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
