Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on the Five Precepts (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this assembly, I do not see a single dharma which, when cultivated and practiced extensively, results in the conduct of hell-beings, the conduct of animals, or the conduct of hungry ghosts."
If one is born among humans, one’s lifespan will be extremely short; this refers to those who take life.
Monks! If there is a person whose mind delights in killing, they will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
If one is born among humans, one’s lifespan will be extremely short; this is because one has taken the lives of others.
Therefore, one should train oneself not to kill living beings.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Within this assembly, I do not see a single dharma that, when practiced and extensively cultivated, brings such human blessings, celestial blessings, and the realization of Nirvana as does the abstention from taking life."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is a person who does not commit killing, nor even entertain thoughts of killing, their lifespan will be exceedingly long.
Why is this? It is because they do not cause harm or disturbance."
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in non-killing. Thus, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“In this assembly, I do not see a single dharma which, when practiced and extensively cultivated, results in conduct leading to hell, or conduct leading to the realms of hungry ghosts and animals.”
If born among humans, one will be extremely impoverished, with clothing that does not cover the body and food that does not fill the mouth;
this is what is called being a thief. O bhikṣus!
If there is someone whose mind delights in robbery and who takes the property of others, they will fall among the hungry ghosts or the animals.
If they are born among humans, they will be extremely impoverished.
The reason for this is that it severs the karma of future births.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves to avoid taking what is not given.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Within this assembly, I do not see a single dharma that, when practiced and practiced extensively, brings such human blessings, celestial blessings, and the realization of Nirvana as the so-called 'generous giving'."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there is someone who extensively practices giving, they will obtain physical beauty and strength in this present life, and their various faculties will be fully perfected; they will enjoy immeasurable merit among both gods and humans."
Therefore, monks, you should practice giving; do not harbor a mind of stinginess. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Within this assembly, I do not see a single dharma which, when practiced and extensively cultivated, results in the conduct of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.”
If one is born among humans, they will live as a householder with lewd and licentious conduct, lacking pure behavior, being censured by others and constantly subjected to slander.
What is this single dharma?
"This is what is called sexual misconduct.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is someone who is licentious and unrestrained, delighting in violating the wives of others, they will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals."
If one is born among humans, one's household will be characterized by sexual licentiousness.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should always maintain right mindfulness; do not give rise to lustful thoughts, and be careful not to commit adultery.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Within this assembly, I do not see a single dharma that, when practiced and frequently cultivated, brings such human blessings, celestial blessings, and the realization of Nirvana as this: namely, refraining from sexual misconduct, whereby one’s body becomes fragrant and pure, and no depraved thoughts arise.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there is anyone who is chaste and free from lust, they shall receive the blessings of the heavens and among humans. Therefore, bhikṣus!"
"Do not commit sexual misconduct by giving rise to lustful intentions. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this assembly, I do not see a single dharma which, when practiced and extensively practiced, results in conduct leading to hell, or conduct leading to the realms of hungry ghosts and animals."
If one is born among humans, their breath will be foul and offensive, and they will be detested by others; this is what is called false speech. O bhikṣus!
If there are those who speak falsely, engage in frivolous chatter, or incite strife and discord, they shall fall into the realms of animals or hungry ghosts.
Why is this? It is because of false speech.
Therefore, one should be sincere and must not speak falsely.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

As for those who do not speak falsely, their breath is fragrant and their fame and virtue are heard far and wide.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Within this assembly, I do not see a single dharma which, when practiced or extensively practiced, leads to the retribution of animals, hungry ghosts, or hell-beings."
If one is born among humans, one will be insane, foolish, deluded, and unable to distinguish the true from the false; this is what is meant by drinking alcohol. O Bhikṣus!
If there is a person whose mind delights in drinking alcohol, in whatever place they are born, they will lack wisdom and will constantly harbor folly.
Thus, monks, you must be careful never to drink alcohol. Thus, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:

"What is this one dharma?

If there is someone who does not drink alcohol, they will be intelligent from birth, free from delusion, widely learned in the scriptures, and their mind will not be confused.

"You should train yourselves in this way.

Chapter Fifteen: On Existence and Non-existence, from the *Ekottarika Āgama*. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know that there are these two views. What are the two?
These are the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
Any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have studied and recited these two views, yet ultimately do not follow their teaching and do not know them as they truly are—they are neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas.
Regarding śramaṇas, they violate the dharma of śramaṇas;
regarding brahmins, they violate the dharma of brahmins; these śramaṇas and brahmins ultimately do not take bodily realization as their own play.

Whosoever among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas recites, chants, and contemplates these two views, knowing how to relinquish them and knowing them as they truly are—these are indeed śramaṇas who maintain the practice of a śramaṇa, and brāhmaṇas who know the practice of a brāhmaṇa; they personally realize and dwell therein, knowing according to reality:
"Birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence."
Therefore, monks, you should not practice these two views, nor should you recite them; you must abandon them entirely. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these two views.”
What are the two views? They are the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
What is meant by the view of existence?
These are the views regarding existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What is meant by the view regarding existence in the realm of desire?
It refers to the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
What are the five desires? They are as follows:
when the eye sees forms, one feels intense love, respect, and mindfulness, never abandoning them, and worldly people revere them.
When the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the mouth perceives flavors, the body perceives smoothness and softness, and the mind cognizes all phenomena—this is called "having views."
What is meant by "non-view"?

It refers to the view of permanence, the view of impermanence, the view of annihilation, the view of non-annihilation, the view of finitude, the view of infinity, the view of self-existence, the view of non-self-existence, the view of a life-principle, the view of no life-principle, the view of the body being one thing and the life-principle another, and the view of the body being one thing and the life-principle another. These sixty-two views are called "non-view"; they are not true vision. This is what is meant by "non-view."
Therefore, monks, you should abandon these two views. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these two kinds of giving."
What are these two?
They are the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth. O bhikṣus!
Among all forms of giving, none surpasses the gift of the Dharma.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should always train yourselves in the gift of the Dharma.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these two types of action.
What are the two types of action? There is the action of phenomena (dharma-karman) and there is the action of material things (āmiṣa-karman).”
Among all types of karmic action, none is superior to the karma of the Dharma.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in the karma of the Dharma, and not in the karma of material wealth.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these two kinds of kindness.
What are the two? They are the kindness of the Dharma and the kindness of material wealth.”
The highest among all forms of gratitude is none other than the gratitude for the Dharma.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should practice gratitude for the Dharma.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The fool possesses these two characteristics. What are the two?

"Thus it is said, monks:
the fool possesses these two characteristics.
Furthermore, monks:"
The wise person has two characteristics. What are these two?
In this regard, the wise person does not attempt to accomplish what cannot be accomplished, nor do they abandon a task that is nearly finished.
Therefore, monks! You should abandon the two characteristics of the fool and should mindfully practice the two characteristics of the wise person. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:

you should train yourselves.

16. Chapter on the Extinction of Fire, *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter Sixteen, Part One. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda was staying in the Elephant Park (Hastigṛha) at Śrāvastī.
Then, while the Venerable Nanda was in a secluded place, this thought arose in him:

"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare; he appears only once in hundreds of millions of eons and is truly difficult to behold. Only after a long night of vast antiquity does a Tathāgata appear."
Just as the udumbara flower appears only at rare intervals, so it is with this:

the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; he appears only once in billions of kalpas and is truly not easily seen. This place, too, is difficult to encounter; it is where all conditioned formations have completely ceased and stilled, where craving is exhausted without remainder, where there is no further defilement, and which is the extinction of Nirvāṇa.

At that time, there was a certain Māracāriṇī devaputra who, knowing the thoughts in the Venerable Nanda’s mind, went to the Śākya woman Sundarī and, hovering in the air, praised her with these verses:
“Now arouse your joy, Adorn yourself and prepare the five kinds of music;
Nanda is now casting off his robes— He shall come to delight you.”

At that time, having heard the words of the deva, Sundarī, the daughter of the Śākya clan, was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself. She immediately adorned herself, renovated her quarters, spread out fine seats, and prepared musical performances, just as when Nanda remained at home.
At that time, King Prasenajit was assembled in the Hall of Universal Assembly when he heard that the bhikṣu Nanda had returned to lay life, discarding his dharma robes to resume his household duties.
The reason for this was that a deva in the sky had said to his wife: [Nanda has returned to the world].
At that time, having heard these words, King Prasenajit was filled with sorrow and anxiety; he immediately mounted his white elephant and proceeded to that garden.
Upon arrival, he entered the Lotus Elephant Pond and saw the Venerable Nanda from afar. He then approached Nanda, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda said to King Prasenajit: "Great King,
for what reason have you come here with such a changed countenance?"
"Furthermore, for what reason have you come to my place?
Pārśvanika replied, "Venerable sir,
you should know that earlier at the Universal Assembly Hall, I heard that you had discarded your dharma-robes and returned to being a layman."
Having heard these words, I have come here specifically; I do not know what the Venerable One intends to command or inform me.
At that time, Nanda smiled and slowly said to the King:
“If you have neither seen nor heard [of this], Great King, why do you speak such words?”
"Great King! Have you not heard from the Tathāgata: 'My various fetters have been removed;

birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall no longer receive a womb-birth,' knowing this as it truly is, and having now become an Arhat with a mind liberated?"
King Prasenajit said,
"I have not heard from the Tathāgata that the bhikṣu Nanda has exhausted birth and death, attained arhatship, and achieved liberation of mind."
The reason for this was that a deity came to inform Sundarī, the daughter of the Śākya clan, saying:
"At that time, having heard these words, Lady Sundarī prepared music and song, adorned herself with finery, and spread out various seats."
"Having heard these words, I have come to the presence of the Venerable One.
Nanda replied, "The King neither knows nor hears; for what reason, Great King, do you speak such words?"

There are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not delight in this pleasure of rest, this pleasure of the Sugata, this pleasure of the śramaṇa, and this pleasure of nirvāṇa, yet they do not examine for themselves this pit of the fire of lust.

Furthermore, as for those who would pursue this matter, it is not so: the bones are like a chain and the flesh is like a heap of stones; it is like a knife smeared with honey—to sit and covet a small profit without considering future calamities.

It is like a branch weighed down by an abundance of fruit; it is like a loan that must soon be returned; it is like a thicket of sword-trees, like a poisonous tree, like a harmful poison, like a toxic drug, and like a poisonous flower or fruit—to contemplate sensual desire is likewise thus.

For one whose mind is stained by attachment, this is not possible; from the desire for a pit of fire to that for poisonous fruit, if one does not contemplate these things, it is impossible for such a person to cross over the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.

It is impossible that one who has not crossed over the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance should enter the realm of nirvana without remainder and attain parinirvāṇa; such a thing cannot be.
"Great King, you should know that when any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas observe this pleasure of rest, the pleasure of the Sugata, the pleasure of the śramaṇa, or the pleasure of nirvāṇa, it is not so."

By means of such observation, he understands that the fire of the pit of lust is like a skeleton, a mass of flesh, a sharp blade smeared with honey, a branch heavy with fruit that must soon be broken, or a borrowed object that cannot last; it is also like a sword-tree, a poisonous tree, or a harmful poison. He perceives and fully comprehends all these as being merely provisional states.

Once one has understood and realized how the fire of lust arises, one will certainly be able to cross over the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance; this is inevitable.
It is certain that he has already crossed over the flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
How so, Great King? Based on what vision and what knowledge do you make this statement?
"Now, Great King! I have become an Arhat;
birth and death are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I shall no longer enter a mother's womb, for my mind has attained liberation."
At that time, King Prasenajit felt great joy and a virtuous mind arose within him. He addressed the Venerable Nanda, saying:
"I no longer have even a hair’s breadth of doubt; I now know that you, Venerable One, have attained Arhatship. I now take my leave to return, for my state affairs are many."
Nanda replied, "Please know that now is the time. Thereupon,
King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and withdrew.
Not long after King Prasenajit had departed, the Māra-deva came to the Venerable Nanda and, standing in mid-air, addressed him with this verse:
“The lady’s face is like the moon, Her body adorned with gold and silver necklaces;
Remembering her lovely countenance, May you always delight yourself in the five pleasures.”
"Striking the lute and plucking the strings, singing with sounds most gentle and soft,
able to dispel all sorrows and anxieties— I find joy in dwelling within this forest.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda had this thought:
"This is the conduct of Māra and his celestial beings.
Having realized this, he replied with a verse:
"In the past, I possessed such a mind; / I was lewd and dissolute, never satisfied."
Enveloped by desire, one does not perceive old age, sickness, and death.
I have crossed the abyss of craving; I am undefiled and unstained.
All glory and status are but suffering; I alone delight in the Dharma of True Suchness (Tathatā).
"I am now free from all fetters; lust, anger, and delusion are entirely exhausted.
I shall no longer practice these ways; let the foolish take note!
At that time, having heard these words, Māra, the celestial being who wanders among men, was filled with sorrow and immediately vanished from that place, no longer appearing.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"As for physical beauty among bhikṣus, none surpasses the bhikṣu Nanda."
That his faculties are serene is also the case with the bhikṣu Nanda;
that he is free from desire is also the case with the bhikṣu Nanda;
that he is free from ill will is also the case with the bhikṣu Nanda.
The one who was free from delusion was also the bhikṣu Nanda;
the one who attained arhatship was also the bhikṣu Nanda.
This is because the bhikṣu Nanda was handsome and his sense faculties were tranquil.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvaka disciples, the one who is most handsome is the bhikṣu Nanda.
He whose faculties are tranquil is also the bhikṣu Nanda."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these two dharmas of the realm of nirvāṇa. What are the two?
There is the realm of nirvana with remainder and the realm of nirvana without remainder.
What is called the realm of nirvana with remainder?
In this regard, a bhikṣu extinguishes the five lower fetters and attains parinirvāṇa right there, not returning again to this world; this is called the realm of nirvana with remainder.
What is called the realm of nirvana without remainder?

In this regard, a bhikṣu exhausts all taints and becomes free from outflows; his mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated. Having realized this for himself and dwelling therein, he knows as it truly is:
"Birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence. This is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Regarding these two realms of nirvāṇa, you should seek skillful means to reach the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the parable of the crow and also the parable of the pig; reflect upon them well, and I shall expound them."
He replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"In what way is that person said to be like a crow?"

It is like a person who, while dwelling in a secluded place, constantly indulges in sexual desire and commits various evil deeds; later, feeling shame and repenting of his transgressions, he speaks of them to others, recounting the actions he has committed.
The reason for this is that he may be censured by his fellow practitioners of the holy life, who say:
"This person indulges in sensual desires and commits various evil deeds.

Having committed such evil deeds, he repents before others and feels shame within himself; it is just like that crow who, constantly suffering from hunger, eats filth and immediately wipes its beak, fearing that other birds might see him and speak of it.
"Just as one might say, 'This crow eats impurity,' so it is with this case.

Suppose there is a person who, dwelling in a secluded place, indulges in sexual desire and commits unwholesome deeds; later, feeling shame and remorse for his own transgression, he proclaims and recounts what he has done to others."

The reason for this is that he may be observed and recognized by his fellow practitioners of the holy life as one who is habituated to sensual desires and commits various evil deeds; such a person is said to be like a crow.
"How is it that a person is said to be like a pig?

It is when a certain person dwells in a secluded place, habitually indulges in sexual desire, commits various evil deeds, feels no shame, does not repent, yet boasts of himself to others with arrogance and self-will, saying:
'I am able to obtain the five desires for my own enjoyment, whereas these other people cannot obtain the five desires.'"
Having committed evil, he feels no shame; such a person is like a pig that constantly eats filth, lies in filth, and then leaps about toward other pigs.
This case is also like that.

Suppose there is a person who indulges in sexual desire and commits various evil deeds, yet feels no shame and does not repent; instead, he boasts to others and acts with arrogant self-importance, saying:
"I am able to obtain the five sensual pleasures for my own enjoyment, whereas these other people cannot obtain the five sensual pleasures for their own enjoyment."
"Such a person is called a human being who is like a pig.
Therefore, monks, you should abandon and stay far away from this."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of those persons who resemble donkeys and those who resemble oxen; listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well."
The bhikṣus replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"What kind of person is called 'a human figure with a donkey's nature'?"
Suppose there is a person who shaves off his hair and beard, dons the three dharma robes, and out of firm faith leaves the household life to study the Path.

At that time, if that person’s faculties are not settled, and upon seeing forms with the eye, he gives rise to perceptions of form that race in ten thousand directions, then the faculty of the eye is not pure; various distracted thoughts arise, and being unable to restrain or maintain them, all manner of evils arrive in abundance, and he likewise cannot guard the faculty of the eye.

When the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue perceives tastes, the body perceives textures, and the mind perceives mental objects (*dharma*), consciousness arises accordingly, racing toward ten thousand directions. At that time, the faculty of the mind (*manendriya*) is not pure; it gives rise to various distracted thoughts and cannot maintain self-restraint. Consequently, manifold evils arrive everywhere, and one is likewise unable to guard the faculty of the mind.

Lacking any propriety in dignified deportment, whether in walking or stopping, bending or stretching, looking down or up, or in holding his robes and bowl, he violates all the prohibitions and precepts. Consequently, he is censured by those who practice the holy life:
"Alas! This foolish man—who is he that resembles a śramaṇa?"
He then took up his lute and said:
"If you are indeed a śramaṇa, you ought not to act in this manner. He spoke these words:
"I too am a bhikṣu! I too am a bhikṣu!
It is just like a donkey entering a herd of oxen and declaring of itself: [“I too am an ox!”]
"I am also an ox! I am also an ox!
However, when one examines its two ears, they do not resemble those of an ox; its horns do not resemble them either, nor does its tail. Their voices are each different.
At that time, the herd of oxen may butt with their horns, trample with their hooves, or bite with their mouths.

This bhikṣu is just like this: his faculties are not settled; when the eye sees a form, it gives rise to perceptions of form, racing toward ten thousand directions. At that time, the faculty of the eye is not pure; various distracted thoughts arise, and he cannot restrain or maintain them. All manner of evils arrive from every side, and he likewise cannot protect the faculty of the eye.

When the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue perceives tastes, the body experiences tactile sensations, and the mind cognizes dharmas, consciousness arises accordingly and flows toward ten thousand directions. At that time, the faculty of the mind is not pure; it gives rise to various distracted thoughts and cannot maintain self-control. Consequently, all manner of evils arrive in abundance, and one is likewise unable to guard and protect the faculty of the mind.

Lacking the propriety of dignified conduct and ritual decorum—in their walking, stopping, advancing, retreating, bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up—and failing to maintain the prohibitive precepts, they are rebuked and censured by those who practice the Brahma-faring:
"Alas! This foolish person looks like a śramaṇa, yet he is not one."
He then drew his bow and said:
"If he is indeed a śramaṇa, he ought not to act in such a manner.
At that time, he spoke these words:
"I am a śramaṇa"—this is like a donkey entering a herd of oxen; this is what is meant by a person who resembles a donkey.
"How does that person resemble an ox?"
Suppose there is a person who shaves off his hair and beard, dons the three dharma-robes, and with firm faith leaves the household life to study the Way.

At that time, that person’s faculties are tranquil and settled; he knows moderation in food and drinks and practices walking meditation throughout the day, never departing from the mental cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

If, when seeing forms with the eye, one does not give rise to perceptions of form, nor harbors thoughts of restless pursuit, then at that time the faculty of the eye shall be pure; it will give rise to various wholesome perceptions and be able to maintain self-restraint, free from further evils, and constantly protect the faculty of the eye.

When no afflicted consciousness arises regarding sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tactile sensations felt by the body, or mental phenomena perceived by the mind, at that time the faculty of the mind becomes purified.
That person then approaches the fellow practitioners of the holy life; seeing him coming from afar, those fellow practitioners each raise their voices, saying:
"Welcome, fellow student!"
"Providing offerings at all times without deficiency, he is like a fine bull entering a herd of cattle and declaring of himself:
'I am now this bull!'"
"However, its hair, tail, ears, horns, and voice were entirely those of an ox; when the other oxen saw it, they each came to lick its body.
This case is also like that: having shaved off beard and hair and donned the three dharma robes, one leaves the household life with firm faith to study the Way."

At that time, that person’s faculties were tranquil and composed; he knew moderation in eating and spent the entire day walking in meditation, never departing from his mental engagement with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

If, when seeing forms with the eye, one does not give rise to perceptions of form, nor harbors thoughts of restless pursuit, then at that time the faculty of the eye attains purity; it gives rise to various wholesome perceptions and is able to maintain self-restraint, such that there are no longer any evils, and one constantly protects the faculty of the eye.

When no afflictions of consciousness arise regarding ear-sounds, nose-odors, tongue-flavors, body-tactiles, or mind-phenomena, at that time the faculty of the mind becomes fully perfected; this is what is meant by saying that such a person is like an ox.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves to be like oxen, and not to be like donkeys. Thus, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of wholesome and unwholesome actions; listen attentively!”
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well. The bhikṣus replied:
“So be it, World-Honored One! The World-Honored One said to him:
"What is called unwholesome? What is called wholesome?
That which is killing is unwholesome; that which is non-killing is wholesome."
Taking what is not given is unwholesome; taking what is given is wholesome.
Sexual misconduct is unwholesome; abstaining from sexual misconduct is wholesome.
False speech is unwholesome; abstaining from false speech is wholesome.
Frivolous speech is unwholesome; abstaining from frivolous speech is wholesome.
Divisive speech is unwholesome; abstaining from divisive speech is wholesome.
Sowing discord between this party and that is unwholesome; not sowing discord between this party and that is wholesome.
Coveting others is unwholesome; not coveting others is wholesome.
Giving rise to anger is unwholesome; not giving rise to anger is wholesome.
Wrong view is unwholesome; right view is wholesome.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
Having committed such evil, one falls into the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and hells.
If, however, one practices goodness, one will be born among humans, in the heavens, or in the various happy destinies among the asuras.
Therefore, one should distance oneself from unwholesome conduct and cultivate wholesome conduct. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall explain to you the subtle and wondrous Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it possesses meaning and flavor, and is the method for fully cultivating the holy life—namely, the two dharmas."
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in full detail.
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them: "What are those two dharmas?

That which is called wrong view and right view; wrong conduct and right conduct; wrong speech and right speech; wrong action and right action; wrong livelihood and right livelihood; wrong effort and right effort; wrong mindfulness and right mindfulness; wrong concentration and right concentration—these, monks, are called the two dharmas.
I have now fully explained these two dharmas to you; that which the Tathāgata ought to do is now complete.
Maintain wholesome mindfulness and contemplate them with recitation; do not be indolent. If you do not practice now, it will be too late for regret later.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the Dharma of the lamp’s illumination, and I shall also speak of the karma by which one proceeds from the lamp toward the Path."
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
The bhikṣus replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What is meant by 'the light of a lamp'?
It refers to the total exhaustion of lust, hatred, and delusion."
What is meant by "the karma of proceeding toward the path by means of a lamp"?

It refers to right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is called the karma of proceeding toward the path by means of a lamp.
By this, I have already explained the lamp of illumination, as well as the karma by which one proceeds toward the Path through that lamp. That which the Tathāgata ought to do is now complete.
Practice mindfulness and recitation without indolence; if you do not practice now, it will be too late for regret.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these two powers. What are the two powers?

What are called the power of patience and the power of contemplation: had I not possessed these two powers, I would ultimately never have attained unexcelled, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, had I not possessed these two powers, I would never have performed the six years of ascetic practice at Uruvilvā, nor could I have subdued the demonic adversaries to achieve the path of unexcelled, perfect, true enlightenment and sit upon the site of awakening.
"Because I possess the power of patience and the power of contemplation, I am able to subdue the hosts of Māra, achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and sit at the site of enlightenment."

Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to cultivate these two powers— the power of patience and the power of reflection— and thereby achieve the path of the stream-enterer, the path of the once-returner, the path of the non-returner, and the path of the arhat, attaining parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Thus it is, monks! You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was in Kuśinagara, at his own place of birth.
At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, five hundred devas, and twenty-eight great ghost-king spirits went together to where the Venerable Aniruddha was staying.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet and stood to one side.
He then praised Anuruddha with this verse:
"I take refuge in the Supreme among Men, Who is venerated by all people."
"We do not know now upon what kind of meditation we are relying.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Śabala, who was a disciple of Brahmayu.
He then went to the Venerable Aniruddha, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the brahmin asked Aniruddha:
"I was born in the royal palace, yet I have never before smelled such a natural fragrance. Who has come here? Is it a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a human, or a non-human?"
At that time, Aniruddha replied to the brahmin, saying:

"Just now, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, five hundred devas, and twenty-eight great ghost-king spirits came to my place; they prostrated themselves with their heads at my feet and stood to one side."
Furthermore, he praised me with this verse:
"We take refuge in the Supreme among Men, whom all people revere and honor;
yet we do not know now upon what kind of dhyāna you rely."
The brahmin asked: "For what reason do I not see their forms now?
Where are Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings?"
Aniruddha replied: “It is because you lack the divine eye that you do not see Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the five hundred devas, and the twenty-eight great kṣetrapāla spirits.”
The brahmin asked:
"If I were able to obtain the divine eye, would I see these Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the twenty-eight great ghost-king spirits?"
Aniruddha replied, "If one were to possess the divine eye,
one would be able to see Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, five hundred devas, as well as the twenty-eight great kṣetrapāla kings."
Furthermore, brahmin!
What is so remarkable about this divine eye?
There is a Brahmā named Thousand-Eyed who perceives these thousand worlds as clearly as a man with sight might examine a jeweled crown upon his own palm.
This Brahmā is likewise; he perceives this thousandfold world-system without any obstruction, yet this Brahmā does not perceive the garment he himself is wearing.
The brahmin asked:
"For what reason does the thousand-eyed Brahmā not see the form of his own body or the garments he wears?"
Aniruddha said: "Because those devas lack the unsurpassed eye of wisdom, they do not see for themselves the garments and ornaments they wear."
The brahmin asked,
"If I were to attain the unsurpassed eye of wisdom, would I see the garments and ornaments worn upon this body? Anuruddha replied:
"If one can obtain the unsurpassed eye of wisdom, then one will be able to see the forms of the garments and ornaments one wears.
The brahmin asked, "I pray that the Honored One will explain to me the most sublime Dharma, so that I may attain the unsurpassed eye of wisdom."
Anuruddha asked, "Do you possess the precepts?
The brahmin then questioned him, saying:
"What is meant by 'precepts'? Anuruddha replied,
"To refrain from all evils and not to transgress what is unrighteous."
The brahmin replied,
"Regarding such precepts as these, I am capable of upholding them. Anuruddha said:
“Now, brahmin! You should uphold the precepts without missing even a hair’s breadth; you should also eliminate the fetter of pride and must not harbor thoughts of self-attachment or clinging.”
Then, the brahmin again asked Anuruddha: "What is this 'mine'? What is this 'I'?"
“What is the fetter of pride?
Anuruddha replied, “The ‘I’ is the conscious spirit; the ‘me’ is the collection of physical forms.”
The arising of consciousness therein that gives rise to the notions of "I" and "mine" is called the fetter of conceit (*māna*). Therefore, O Brahmin,
you should seek skillful means to eliminate these fetters.
"It is so, brahmin! You should train yourself in this way.
The brahmin then rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of Anuruddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Before he had reached his destination, while reflecting on this meaning along the way, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

At that time, there was a deva who had previously been a close friend of this brahmin; knowing that the brahmin’s mind had exhausted all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, [the deva rejoiced].
At that time, that deva went again to the Venerable Aniruddha, prostrated with his head at his feet, and stood to one side.
He then praised Aniruddha with this verse:
“The brahmin, before reaching home, Attained the tracks of the Path midway.”
"With defilements exhausted, the Dharma-eye is purified; there is no doubt and no hesitation.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha again addressed the deva in verse:
"I previously observed his mind, and he was on the path to the tracks of the noble ones."
"That person, under Kāśyapa Buddha, once heard this teaching of the Dharma.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha immediately departed from that place and traveled among the people; gradually arriving at Śrāvastī, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One fully instructed Ānanda with words of the Dharma; having received the Buddha’s teaching, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and then withdrew.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvaka disciples, the one who has attained preeminence in the divine eye is the bhikṣu Aniruddha."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was devotedly practicing the precepts without transgressing them; he avoided even minor offenses, let alone major ones, yet he had not attained liberation of the mind through the destruction of the outflows.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads to the ground, and sat to one side.
Then, those many bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The bhikṣu Rāhula faithfully observes the prohibitive precepts and commits no transgressions; yet, his mind remains defiled by outflows and is not liberated."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Fully endowed with the laws of the precepts, And having perfected the sense faculties,
One shall gradually attain The exhaustion of all fetters.”
"Therefore, monks, you should always mindfully cultivate and maintain the True Dharma so that it suffers no loss or decay. Thus, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Nanda, Nirvāṇa, and the two unwholesome [states] of the donkey.
Candle and Patience Contemplation; The Brahmin and Rāhula.
Chapter Seventeen: Ānāpāna (Mindfulness of Breathing), Part One. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms together with Rāhula.
Then, turning his gaze to the right, the World-Honored One said to Rāhula:
"You should now contemplate that form is impermanent."
Rāhula replied: “So it is, World-Honored One!
Form is impermanent.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Rāhula! Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent."
Rāhula replied: “So it is, World-Honored One!
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent.”
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula again had this thought:
"What is the cause and condition for this? Just as I am now heading toward the city to beg for alms on the road, why does the World-Honored One address and instruct me face-to-face?"
"Now it is fitting that I should return to my own dwelling; I ought not to enter the city to beg for food.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula immediately turned back on his way and returned to the Jetavana Monastery. Taking his robes and bowl, he went beneath a tree, straightened his body and composed his mind, and sat down cross-legged. With single-minded concentration, he contemplated the impermanence of form, and contemplated the impermanence of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his almsround in Śrāvastī, walked in meditation after his meal within the Jetavana Monastery, gradually approaching Rāhula.
Having arrived, he addressed Rāhula, saying:
"You should practice the method of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing). By practicing this method, all thoughts of sorrow and anxiety shall be completely eliminated."
You should now further cultivate the perception of the impurity of foulness; all lustful desires shall be completely extinguished. Now, Rāhula!
You should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; once you have cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, all ill will shall be entirely eliminated.
Now, Rāhula! You should practice compassion; having practiced compassion, all harmful intentions shall be completely eliminated. Now, Rāhula!
One should practice the mind of sympathetic joy; having practiced the mind of sympathetic joy, all envy shall be completely eliminated.
Now, Rāhula! You should practice the mind of equanimity; having practiced the mind of equanimity, all arrogance shall be completely eliminated.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Rāhula:
"Do not repeatedly give rise to thoughts of attachment; You should always accord with the Dharma yourself.
A wise person such as this Will have their fame spread far and wide."
"Holding a bright torch for others, he destroys the great darkness;
gods and dragons bear him with reverence, honoring the venerable Teacher.
At that time, the bhikṣu Rāhula again addressed the World-Honored One with this verse:
“I do not give rise to conceptual attachments, but always remain in accordance with the Dharma;
such a wise person is one who can truly honor their teachers.
Having given this instruction, the World-Honored One then departed and returned to his quiet chamber.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula again had this thought:
"How now should I practice ānāpāna so as to eliminate sorrow and grief, and to be free from all conceptualizations?"
At that time, Rāhula rose from his seat and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.
After a short while, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How does one practice *ānāpāna* so as to eliminate sorrow and grief, become free from all discursive thoughts, obtain the great fruit of retribution, and attain the taste of the Deathless?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Rāhula! You are indeed able to roar the lion’s roar before the Tathāgata, asking about such a matter as this:
"How does one practice ānāpāna so as to eliminate sorrow and grief, become free from all perceptions, obtain the great fruit of retribution, and attain the taste of the Deathless?"
"Listen attentively now, Rāhula! Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well;
I shall explain it to you in full detail. He replied:
"So be it, Blessed One! At that time, the Venerable Rāhula received the instruction from the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"In this regard, Rāhula!

If there is a bhikṣu who delights in a secluded and solitary place, he straightens his body and composes his mind, sits cross-legged, and without other distracting thoughts, fixes his attention on the tip of the nose. He knows when the out-breath is long that the out-breath is long; he also knows when the in-breath is long that the in-breath is long.
He knows when the out-breath is short that the out-breath is short; he also knows when the in-breath is short that the in-breath is short."
When the exhaled breath is cold, he knows the exhaled breath is cold; when the inhaled breath is cold, he knows the inhaled breath is cold.
When the exhaled breath is warm, he knows the exhaled breath is warm; when the inhaled breath is warm, he knows the inhaled breath is warm.
He observes the inhalation and exhalation throughout the entire body and knows them all completely.
When there is breath, he knows that there is; when there is no breath, he also knows that there is none.
If the breath goes out from the heart, one likewise knows it goes out from the heart;
if the breath comes in from the heart, one likewise knows it comes in from the heart.
In this way, Rāhula, one who can practice ānāpānasati will be free from thoughts of sorrow, grief, and agitation; they will obtain a great fruit and attain the taste of the Deathless.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had fully expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to Rāhula, Rāhula rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

He went to the Andhavana grove and, beneath a tree, straightened his body and composed his mind, sitting cross-legged. Without any other thoughts, he fixed his attention on the tip of the nose: when breathing out long, he knew he was breathing out long; when breathing in long, he knew he was breathing in long.
When breathing out short, he knew he was breathing out short; when breathing in short, he knew he was breathing in short.
When breathing out cold, he knew he was breathing out cold; when breathing in cold, he knew he was breathing in cold.
When breathing out warm breath, he knows the warmth of the exhaled breath; when breathing in warm breath, he knows the warmth of the inhaled breath.
He observes the entire body throughout both inhalation and exhalation, knowing them all completely.
Sometimes there is breath and he knows that there is; sometimes there is no breath and he knows that there is none.
If the breath issues from the mind, he also knows that it issues from the mind.
If the breath enters through the heart, he likewise knows it enters through the heart.
At that time, Rāhula reflected thus, and his mind of desire attained liberation, with no further evil remaining.
With directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one dwells in the first dhyāna, maintaining mindfulness, joy, and tranquility.

With the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, inwardly joyful and focused with a single mind, free from directed and sustained thought, one dwells in the second dhyāna, possessing samādhi, mindfulness, and joy.
Free from thoughts of joy, he dwells in the mindful awareness of bodily bliss—the state constantly sought and protected by the noble ones—and thus dwells in the third dhyāna.
With the extinction of both suffering and pleasure, free from sorrow and joy, and with equanimity and mindfulness purified, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna.

By means of this samādhi, his mind becomes pure and free from defilement; his body becomes supple, he knows his origins, remembers his past deeds, and personally recognizes the events of countless kalpas of his former existences.

He also knows one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, ten thousand births, hundreds of thousands of births; he knows eons of formation, eons of destruction, and countless eons of formation and destruction, for billions of years beyond calculation—thinking, "I was born there, with such a name and such a surname, eating such food, experiencing such suffering and pleasure, with such a lifespan; when that life ended, I was born here; and when this life ends, I shall be born there."
By means of this samādhi, his mind is pure, free from blemish, and devoid of all fetters.
He also knows the thoughts that arise in sentient beings. Furthermore, with the divine eye—pure and free from blemish—he observes the various classes of sentient beings:

those being born and those passing away; those of beautiful form and those of ugly form; those in fortunate realms and those in unfortunate realms; whether they are handsome or hideous; and he knows, as it truly is, their conduct and their deeds.

There are some sentient beings who commit evil through body, evil through speech, and evil through mind; they revile the noble ones, practice wrong views, and perform actions based on wrong views; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they enter into hell.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who practice virtue in body, speech, and mind; they do not revile the noble ones, but constantly maintain right view and act in accordance with right view. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in a favorable state, in the heavens above.
This is called the pure and stainless divine eye, by which one observes the various classes of sentient beings:

those who are born and those who pass away; those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance; those in fortunate realms and those in unfortunate realms; whether they are handsome or unattractive, one knows truly their conduct and their deeds.
Furthermore, he further applies his mind to achieve the state of a mind free from outflows; he contemplates this suffering and knows it as it truly is.
He further contemplates the origin of suffering, knows its cessation, and knows the path leading to its transcendence, knowing them all as they truly are.

By means of this contemplation, his mind was liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), and his mind was liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhavāsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyāsrava*). Having attained liberation, he realized the knowledge of liberation:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence"—he knew this as it truly is.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula attained arhatship.

Having become an arhat, the Venerable Rāhula rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"That which was sought has been attained; all outflows have been extinguished."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among all those who have attained arhatship, there is none equal to Rāhula.
Regarding the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya), it is likewise the bhikṣu Rāhula."
Regarding those who uphold the prohibitive precepts, they are likewise the bhikṣu Rāhula.
Why is this so? Because among all the Tathāgatas, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, there was also this very bhikṣu Rāhula.
"If one wishes to speak of a 'Son of the Buddha,' it is also the bhikṣu Rāhula, who was born directly from the Buddha and is the foremost among those of the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost disciple capable of upholding the prohibitive precepts is the bhikṣu Rāhula."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Fulfilling the laws of the prohibitive precepts, And likewise perfecting the faculties;
Gradually one shall attain The total extinction of all fetters.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll Seven. *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter on Ānāpāna, Part Two (2). (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The appearance of two kinds of persons in the world is extremely rare.”
Who are these two persons?
They are as follows: it is extremely rare for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha to appear in the world;
it is also extremely rare for a Wheel-turning Sage King (Cakravartin) to appear in the world.
"The appearance of these two individuals in the world is extremely rare.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Two individuals appear in the world who are exceedingly rare to encounter. Who are these two? They are:
a Pratyekabuddha appearing in the world, who is exceedingly rare to encounter;”
It is extremely rare for a disciple of the Tathāgata, an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, to appear in the world.
Thus it is said, O Bhikṣu:
these two types of persons appearing in the world are exceedingly rare.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (IV) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these two things in the world that are extremely vexing.
What are these two things?"
That which is said to be the root of all evil deeds, giving rise to various resentments and animosities, and furthermore failing to cultivate wholesome conduct— the very foundation of all virtues.
This, O Bhikṣu, is called the second dharma that is exceedingly afflictive.
Therefore, monks, you should clearly understand these phenomena of affliction, and you should also clearly understand the phenomena that are not afflictions.
Regarding all phenomena of affliction, you should bring them to mind for the purpose of abandoning them.
One should practice with mindfulness those dharmas that are free from affliction. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The thoughts, inclinations, and other various formations of sentient beings with wrong views are entirely devoid of anything worthy of esteem; they are not what the people of the world crave or delight in."
The reason for this is that their views are wrong and unwholesome.

It is just as if there were seeds of bitter fruits—namely, seeds of the bitter fruit, the bitter *kaṇṭakārī*, the mustard seed, the *bṛhatī*, and other such bitter seeds—and one were to plant these seeds in fertile soil; subsequently, the sprouts that emerge would still be bitter as before.
The reason for this is that their very nature is fundamentally suffering.

It is the same with these sentient beings of wrong views: whatever physical, verbal, and mental actions they perform, whatever their inclinations, thoughts, and various evil deeds may be, none of them are worthy of esteem; they are not what the people of the world desire or delight in.
The reason for this is that such views are false, evil, and unwholesome.
Therefore, monks, you should eliminate wrong view and practice right view.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The thoughts, inclinations, and all other conducts of sentient beings with right view are entirely worthy of esteem and respect, and are what the people of the world desire and delight in.”
Why is this? It is because their right view is sublime.

It is just as if there were various sweet fruits—such as sugarcane, grapes, or any other sweet and delicious fruit—and someone were to cultivate fertile ground and plant them; subsequently, the seeds that sprout would all be sweet and delicious, such that people would delight in them.

The reason for this is that because the fruit is inherently sweet and delicious, so too it is with these beings of right view; whatever they contemplate, whatever they pursue, and all their other activities are entirely worthy of being craved and delighted in, such that there is no person in the world who does not rejoice in them.
Why is this? Because right view is sublime. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
"One should practice right view. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was in a secluded place, reflecting alone, when this thought arose in him:
"All living beings give rise to thoughts of sensual desire, which then produce craving for sense-pleasures; they practice them day and night, never reaching satiety."
At that time, as evening approached, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes and straightened his garments, and proceeded to where the Blessed One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Just now, while in a quiet and secluded place, this thought arose in me:
'All sentient beings who give rise to thoughts of sensual desire produce that sensual desire; they practice it through the long night without ever reaching satiety.'"
The World-Honored One said: "So it is, Ānanda!"
As you have said, whenever people give rise to thoughts of sensual desire, they increase their longing for such desires; practicing them through the long night, they never reach satiety.

Why is this so? Long ago, Ānanda, in a past age, there was a Wheel-turning Sage King named Mūrdhaja, who ruled and transformed the world according to the Dharma; he was free from deceit and guile, and the seven treasures were perfected.
The so-called seven treasures are:

the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure; these are called the seven treasures.
Furthermore, he had a thousand sons who were brave, powerful, and strong, capable of subduing all evils and ruling over the four continents without the use of weapons or staffs.
Ānanda, you should know that at that time, King Mūrdhaja the Holy conceived this thought:
"I now possess this land of Jambudvīpa, where the population is flourishing and there are many precious treasures. I have also heard from the elders and seniors:"
"In the west lies the land of Aparagoyānī, where the people are flourishing and many rare treasures abound.
I shall now go there to govern that kingdom. At that time, Ānanda!
As soon as Mūrdhagata had this thought, he led his fourfold army and vanished from this Jambudvīpa, proceeding directly to the land of Aparagoyānī.

At that time, when the people of that land saw the Holy King approaching, they all came forward to welcome him, prostrating themselves in greeting and inquiring after his welfare: "Welcome, Great King!"

Now, this country of Aparagoyānī is teeming with a flourishing population; we only pray that the Holy King shall govern and transform its people here, causing them to follow the teachings of the Dharma!
“At that time, Ānanda, King Mūrdhaja immediately ruled over the people of Aparagoyānī for several hundred thousand years.
Then, at another time, King Mūrdhaja conceived this thought:”
"I possess Jambudvīpa, where the population is flourishing and precious treasures abound; even the rain of the seven kinds of jewels falls as high as the knees.
Now I also possess this Aparagoyānī, where the population is flourishing and precious treasures abound."
I have also heard from the elders that there is further the land of Pūrvavideha, where the population is flourishing and many rare treasures abound.
I shall now go to govern that territory, transforming it through the rule of Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda!
As soon as King Śakra-janman gave rise to this thought, he led his fourfold army, vanished from Aparagoyānī, and proceeded directly to Pūrvavideha.

"At that time, when the people of that land saw the holy king approaching, they all came forward to welcome him; they prostrated, knelt, and inquired after his well-being, speaking with one voice in these words:
'Welcome, Great King!'"

"Now this Pūrvavideha is populous and abounds in many precious treasures; we pray only that Your Majesty shall govern and transform its people here, causing them to follow the teachings of the Dharma!"
“At that time, Ānanda, King Mūrdhaja immediately ruled over the people of Pūrvavideha for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
Then, at another time, King Mūrdhaja conceived this thought:”
"In Jambudvīpa, the population is flourishing and there are many precious treasures; it even rains the seven kinds of jewels up to the knees.
Now there is likewise this Aparagoyānī, where the population is flourishing and there are many precious treasures.
Now there is likewise this Pūrvavideha country, where the population is flourishing and there are many precious treasures."
I have also heard from the venerable elders:
"Furthermore, there is Uttarakuru, where the population is flourishing, precious treasures abound, people act with complete freedom, and no one holds fast to possessions."
Their lifespan shall not be cut short by untimely death; they will live for a full thousand years.

When their life there ends, they will surely be reborn in the heavens and never fall into other realms of existence. They will wear garments of karpāsa silk and eat naturally grown non-glutinous rice.
"I shall now go to govern that kingdom and transform it through the Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda, as soon as King Śakra-vartī conceived this thought, he led his fourfold army, vanished from Pūrvavideha, and proceeded to Uttarakuru.
From afar he saw that land appearing a deep, vibrant blue; having seen it, he asked his ministers at his side, "Do you all see this land appearing as a deep, vibrant blue?"
He replied, "Indeed, I have seen them.
The King then addressed his ministers, saying:
"This is soft grass, as supple as celestial garments and no different from them.
O worthy ones, you should sit upon this.
Having proceeded a short distance further, he saw from afar that the land was a brilliant yellow, and he addressed his ministers, saying:
"Do you all see this land shining with a pervasive yellow light? They replied, "We all see it."
The Great King said:
"This is called 'naturally grown non-glutinous rice. These worthy ones always eat this food.
Just as you do now, you too shall eat this non-glutinous rice."

At that time, the holy king proceeded forward a little further and again saw that the land was entirely level and even. Seeing from afar a high terrace of extraordinary splendor, he spoke again to his ministers:
"Do you all see how this land is everywhere level and even?"
He replied, "It is so;
I have seen them all. The Great King said in response:
"This is called the Kārpāsika-tree garment; you all shall likewise wear these tree garments. At that time, Ānanda!
When the people of that land saw the Great King approaching, they all rose to meet him, prostrated themselves, knelt, and inquired after his welfare, speaking with one voice in this way:

"Welcome, Holy King! This Uttarakuru is prosperous with many inhabitants and abounds in rare treasures; we pray that Your Majesty will govern the people here and cause them to follow the teachings of the Dharma!"
“At that time, Ānanda, King Māndhātṛ reigned over the people of Uttarakuru for hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
Then, at another time, King Māndhātṛ conceived this thought:”
"I now possess Jambudvīpa, where the population is flourishing and there are many precious treasures; even the rain of the seven jewels falls as high as the knees.
Now I also possess Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and this Uttarakuru, where the populations are flourishing and there are many precious treasures."
I have also heard from the venerable elders:

"There are the Thirty-three Heavens, whose happiness is beyond compare, whose lifespan is exceedingly long, where food and clothing appear spontaneously, and where celestial maidens attend in service beyond all calculation."
"I shall now go to take charge of that celestial palace and govern it with the Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda, as soon as King Śakra-vartī conceived this thought, he led his fourfold army, vanished from Uttarakuru, and proceeded to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing King Māndhātṛ approaching from afar, spoke thus:
"Welcome, Great King!
Please be seated here."
"At that time, Ānanda!
King Śrīghoṣa sat down together with Śakra Devānām Indra.
When the two sat together, they could not be distinguished; their countenances, gestures, speech, and voices were identical and no different."
At that time, Ānanda!
After King Mūrdhaja had resided there for several thousand years, he conceived this thought:
"I now possess this Jambudvīpa, with its teeming population and abundance of precious treasures; even the seven kinds of jewels rain down here until they reach the knees."
There is also Aparagoyānī, as well as Pūrvavideha, and likewise Uttarakuru; their populations are flourishing and they abound in many rare treasures.
"I have now arrived here in the Heaven of the Thirty-three; I should now slay this Śakra, Lord of the Devas, so that I alone may reign as king over all the gods in this place. At that time, Ānanda!
As soon as King Mūrdhagata conceived this thought, he immediately fell from his seat; he descended to the land of Jambudvīpa, and his fourfold army fell along with him.

At that time, the wheel-treasure was also lost, and its whereabouts remained unknown; the elephant-treasure and the horse-treasure both died at the same time; the jewel-treasure extinguished itself; and the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure all likewise passed away.
"At that time, King Mūrdhaja fell gravely ill. All his kinsmen and relatives gathered together to inquire after the king's illness, asking:
'How are you, Great King?'"
If, after Your Majesty has passed away, someone should come and ask about this matter:
"What were the final instructions of Great King Mandhātu at the time of his death?"
"If such a question were asked, how should I respond? King Śrīṃjaya replied:
"If my life should come to an end, and someone should ask me after my death, I would answer them thus:"

"King Māndhātṛ ruled over these four continents yet remained insatiable; he further ascended to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and dwelt there for several hundred thousand years, yet his mind still gave rise to greed and he desired to harm the Lord of Devas. Consequently, he fell from that realm and immediately met his end."
"Ānanda, do not harbor any doubt now! Was that King Mūrdhaja at that time anyone other than this very person?"
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? King Mūrdhaja at that time was none other than myself.
At that time, I ruled over these four continents and even reached the Heaven of the Thirty-three, yet I found no satiety amidst the five sensual pleasures.
Ānanda! You should understand through this skillful means that those who give rise to a mind of lust increase their conceptualizations, finding no satiety amidst sensual desires.
If you seek such satiety, you must seek it within the wisdom of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in the midst of the great assembly, spoke these verses:
“Lustful desire is like seasonal rain; one can never have enough of it.
Pleasure is slight while suffering is vast; it is something the wise abandon.”
Even if one were to enjoy celestial desires, delighting oneself in the five pleasures;
it would not equal the disciple of the Perfectly Awakened One who has severed the heart of craving.
Greed and desire prolong [suffering] for billions of eons; when merit is exhausted, one returns to the hells.
"How long can one enjoy pleasure before suddenly suffering the pains of hell? Therefore, Ānanda,
by this means you should know that one must abandon desire through desire, never again giving rise to thoughts of it."
"You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-Āsrava went to where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-śroṇa addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"How should one regard a person who is a bad friend?
The Blessed One replied:
"One should contemplate them as one contemplates the moon. The Brahmin asked,
"How should one contemplate a virtuous friend?"
The Blessed One said:
“One should contemplate it as one contemplates the moon. The brahmin asked:
“Regarding what the śramaṇa Gautama has now spoken, you have briefly stated its essential points but have not explained the broad meaning.
We only pray that Gautama will explain the meaning extensively and universally, so that those who do not yet understand may come to understand.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin, listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall expound its meaning to you in detail.
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"So be it, Gautama," replied the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇī, receiving the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"It is just as, O Brahmin, with the waning moon at the end of the month: as day and night pass, it only diminishes and never increases.
Because of this diminution, there are times when the moon does not appear, and no one can see it."
It is the same in this case, O Brahmin!

If one associates with evil friends, then throughout day and night they gradually come to lack faith, lack ethical discipline, lack learning, lack generosity, and lack wisdom. Because they lack faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom, at that time those evil friends, upon the breakup of the body after death, enter into hell.
Therefore, O brāhmaṇa! When I now speak of this evil friend, it is like the final day of the month. It is just so, O brāhmaṇa!

When the moon first arises, its radiance gradually increases throughout the days and nights it passes; it slowly becomes full until, on the fifteenth day, it is completely and perfectly full, such that there is no sentient being who does not see it.
In this way, brahmin!
