If one has a virtuous friend, throughout the days and nights, they will increase their faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom.

Because he had increased his faith, ethical discipline, generosity, learning, and wisdom, at that time, when the spiritual friend passed away and his body perished, he was reborn in a good place in the heavens.
"Therefore, O Brahmin, I now describe the destination of such a spiritual friend as being like the full moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person possesses greed, and their hatred and delusion are not exhausted;
their goodness will gradually diminish, like the moon approaching its end.
If a person is without greed, and their hatred and delusion are likewise exhausted;"
"In wholesome qualities there is gradual increase, just like the waxing moon.
Therefore, O Brahmin, you should train yourself to be like the new moon."
At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Excellent, Gautama!"
It is as if one who was bent has been straightened, one in darkness sees light, or a wanderer finds the path; it is like obtaining illumination within profound obscurity. It is even so for me:

the Śramaṇa Gautama, through countless skillful means, has preached the Dharma for my sake. I now take refuge in the World-Honored One, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. From this day forward, I request to be accepted as an upāsaka; for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life.
At that time, Jāti-srota, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak on the dharma of good spiritual friends and also speak on the dharma of evil spiritual friends; listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well. The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, Blessed One. At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"What, monks, are those things called the qualities of a bad friend?
In this regard, monks:"
A person of evil association gives rise to this thought:
"I have left the household life to study the Path from a noble family, whereas these other bhikṣus have left the household life from lowly and base families.
Relying on his own lineage and status, he disparages others; this is called the dharma of an evil associate.
"Furthermore, an evil companion may give rise to this thought:
'I am extremely diligent in upholding the true Dharma, whereas other bhikṣus are not diligent in maintaining the precepts. "
Furthermore, by means of this same principle, one disparages others while being conceited oneself;
this is called the dharma of an evil friend. Moreover, an evil friend further thinks:
"I have accomplished samādhi, whereas other bhikṣus lack samādhi; their minds are distracted and not concentrated."
Relying on this samādhi, he constantly becomes arrogant and disparages others; this is called the dharma of an evil spiritual friend (*pāpamitra*).
Furthermore, the evil spiritual friend thinks again:
"My wisdom is foremost, while these other bhikṣus possess no wisdom."
"Relying on this wisdom, he becomes arrogant and disparages others; this is called the quality of an evil friend (pāpamitra).
Furthermore, an evil friend thinks to himself:
'I now constantly receive food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for illness, whereas these other bhikṣus cannot obtain such articles of support.'"
"Relying on these objects of gain and profit, he becomes arrogant and disparages others; this is called the quality of a bad friend.
This, monks, is what is meant."
"Evil associates practice such perverse deeds.
What, then, is the dharma of a virtuous associate?
In this regard, bhikṣu!"
A person who is a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) does not think:
"I was born into a noble family, whereas these other bhikṣus were not born into noble families.
He regards himself as no different from them; this is called the dharma of a true spiritual friend.
"Furthermore, a person who is a good friend does not think:
'I now maintain the precepts, whereas these other bhikṣus do not maintain the practice of the precepts.
His own self and those others are neither increased nor diminished; relying on these precepts, he is neither conceited nor does he disparage others. This, O bhikṣu, is called [a good friend]."
This is called the Dharma of spiritual friends.
Furthermore, monks, a person who is a spiritual friend does not think in this way:
"I have attained mastery in samādhi, whereas these other bhikṣus have distracted and unsettled minds.

Yet, there is neither increase nor decrease between his own person and theirs; relying on this samādhi, he does not become conceited, nor does he disparage others. This, O bhikṣu, is called [true samādhi].
This is called the Dharma of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). "Furthermore, monks!
A person who is a spiritual friend does not harbor such thoughts as these:"

"I have accomplished wisdom, whereas these other bhikṣus possess no wisdom"—in this regard, there is neither increase nor decrease between oneself and others. When one relies on this wisdom, one does not become conceited, nor does one disparage others. This, O bhikṣu, is called [true wisdom].
This is called the Dharma of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). Furthermore, monks,
a person who is a spiritual friend does not entertain such thoughts:
"I am able to obtain robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and medicine for the sick, whereas these other bhikṣus are unable to obtain robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and medicine for the sick."
"Neither for oneself nor for others does there arise any increase or decrease; relying on these gains and offerings, one neither becomes conceited nor disparages others. This, O bhikṣu, is called..."
This is called the teaching on spiritual friends.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now distinguish for you the teaching on evil associates, and I shall also speak to you regarding the teaching on spiritual friends.”
Therefore, monks, you should together distance yourselves from the qualities of bad associates and practice together with mindfulness the qualities of good associates. Thus it is, monks.
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Śrāvastī together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, more than five hundred eminent and noble members of the Śākya clan from the kingdom, wishing to engage in discussion, gathered at the Viśvārtha Lecture Hall.
At that time, the world-renowned Brahmin went to where those Śākyas were and said to them: "What do you say, sirs!
Is there among you any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, or worldly person who is able to engage in debate with me?"
At that time, the many Śākyas replied to the brahmin Śaikha:
"In this place, there are currently two men of high talent and vast learning who reside in the kingdom of Kapilavastu."
Who are these two persons?
One is the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, and the second is Gautama, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha of the Śākya clan.
Among the multitude, there are those who know little and have heard nothing, who lack wisdom, whose speech is coarse and ugly, and who cannot discern where to go or stay—such as Pāṇḍaka and his like.

Furthermore, within this single kingdom of Kapilavastu, there are those who are ignorant and unlearned, lacking in cleverness and wisdom, who are physically unsightly and full of various impurities—such as Gautama and his like.
"You may now engage in debate with him.

If you, O Brāhmaṇa, are able to defeat those two in debate, we, the five hundred or so of us, shall provide for your every need as required, and we shall also bestow upon you a thousand measures of pure gold."
At that time, the brahmin conceived this thought:
"These Śākyas of Kapilavastu are all clever and possess many technical skills, yet they are treacherous, hypocritical, and devoid of upright conduct."

If I were to debate with those two men and emerge victorious, what would be so remarkable about that? Or, if they were to find my weakness and overcome me, it would merely mean I have been defeated by fools.
Reflecting on these two principles, he thought, "I am not fit to engage in debate with him.
Having said this, he withdrew and departed.
At that time, Cūḍapanthaka, having reached the proper hour, took his bowl and entered Kapilavastu to beg for alms.
At that time, the world-renowned brahmin saw Cūḍapanthaka approaching from afar and thought to himself:
"I shall now go and question that man regarding the meaning [of these verses]."
Then, the world-renowned brahmin went to where the bhikṣu was and said to Cūḍapanthaka,
"Śramaṇa! What is your name?"
Cūḍapanthaka said: "Stop, brahmin!"
"Why need you ask for the characters?
Since you have come here wishing to inquire about the meaning, you may ask at this time. The Brahmin said:
“Śramaṇa! Can you engage in debate with me? Cūḍapanthaka replied:
"I am now even capable of debating with Brahmā; how much more so with you, a blind man without eyes?
The brāhmaṇa said, "Is not a blind man indeed one who lacks eyes?"
"If one has no eyes, is one not blind?
This is one meaning; how could it not be redundant?
At that moment, Cūḍapanthaka ascended into the air and performed the eighteen transformations.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses only supernormal powers; he does not understand debate.
If he were to explain this meaning to me, I would then become his disciple."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra heard these words with his divine ear:
"Cūḍapanthaka is engaged in this discussion with the brahmin Lokāyata."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra immediately transformed his body into the form of Pāṇṭaka; he concealed the form of Pāṇṭaka so that it was no longer visible, and said to the brāhmaṇa: "O brāhmaṇa!..."
If you think: "This śramaṇa possesses only supernatural powers (ṛddhi) and is incapable of debate," listen now attentively;
I shall explain it for you to answer your previous argument. Based on this fundamental treatise, I shall further provide an analogy.
"Brahmin, what is your name now? The brahmin replied:
"I am named Brahmā. Cūḷapanthaka asked, "Are you a man?"
The Brahmin said, "I am a man. He asked again:
"Is this a human being?
The brāhmaṇa replied, "This is a human being."
Cūḍapanthaka asked: "How so, Brahmin?
A man is also a human being, and a human being is also a man; these are one and the same meaning—is this not redundant?"
"However, O Brahmin! There is a difference in meaning between being blind and having no eyes. The Brahmin said:
“What do you mean, śramaṇa? Why is he called ‘blind’? Cūḍapanthaka replied:

"Just as one who does not see this world or the world beyond, nor birth or cessation, nor beautiful or ugly forms, nor the good or bad deeds performed by sentient beings—failing to know them as they truly are and never perceiving them at all—is therefore called 'blind.'"
The brahmin asked, "In what way is one 'without eyes'? Cūḍapanthaka replied:
"The eye is the eye of unsurpassed wisdom.
Because that person lacks this eye of wisdom, they are called 'blind. The brāhmaṇa said:
"Stop! Stop! Śramaṇa!"
Setting aside this digression, I now wish to ask about a profound matter.
How is it, Śramaṇa? Is it possible to attain nirvāṇa without relying on the Dharma?
Cūḍapanthaka replied,
“One attains nirvāṇa without relying on the five aggregates of clinging. The brāhmaṇa said:
"What do you say, ascetic?
Are these five aggregates of clinging produced with conditions,
or are they produced without conditions?"
Cūḍapanthaka replied, "These five aggregates of clinging arise with conditions; they do not arise without conditions. The brahmin said:
"What is the condition for these five aggregates of clinging?
The bhikṣu replied,
"Craving is the condition."
The brahmin asked, "What is craving? The bhikṣu replied:
"This is birth. The brāhmaṇa asked, "What is meant by 'birth'?"
The bhikṣu said: "It is precisely craving. The brāhmaṇa said:
"What is the path for craving?
The śramaṇa replied,
"It is the Noble Eightfold Path."
That which is called right view, right action, right speech, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this is termed the Noble Eightfold Path.

At that time, after Cūḍapanthaka had extensively expounded the Dharma, the brahmin, having heard such instruction from the bhikṣu, was cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; he then passed away on the spot, as a wind-sword arose within his body.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra restored his original form, flew into the air, and returned to his dwelling.
At that same time, the Venerable Bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka went to the Mahāvana Lecture Hall where many members of the Śākya clan were gathered.
Having arrived, he said to those Śākyas,
"Quickly prepare ghee and firewood, and go to cremate the brahmin Śāṇakavāsin. Thereupon,
the Śākyas immediately prepared the ghee and oil and went to cremate the brahmin Śāṇakavāsin.
They erected stūpas at the four crossroads, each leading the others, and proceeded together to the place where the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka was staying.
Upon arrival, they prostrated themselves at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Śākyas addressed the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka with this verse: “Yāva-jīvaṃ upāsakaṃ dhāretu no bhante;
We have gained great benefit, having encountered such auspicious grace.”
At that time, the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka replied to Śakra with this verse:
"Now you turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma, Subduing all those of external paths;
With wisdom like the great ocean, You have come here to subdue the brahmins."
"Whatever deeds of good or evil one has performed— In the past, future, or present— They are not forgotten for billions of eons; Therefore, one should cultivate merit.
At that time, after the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka had extensively preached the Dharma to those Śākyas, the Śākyas addressed Cūḍapanthaka, saying:

"If the Venerable One requires robes, food and drink, bedding, mats, or medicine for illness, we shall provide for all these needs; we only pray that you will accept our invitation and not reject this humble request."
At that time, the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka silently assented.
Then, the Śākyas, having heard what the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
11 (Eleven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the wicked man Devadatta went to the prince Brahmadatta and said to him:
"In the past, the lifespan of the common people was extremely long; nowadays, the human lifespan does not exceed a hundred years."
"Prince, you should know that human life is impermanent; it may be that you do not ascend the throne before your life ends prematurely—would that not be a great tragedy!
Prince, you should now take the life of your father, the King, and rule over the people."
"I shall now slay the śramaṇa Gautama!
Having become the Unsurpassed, Truly Realized, and Perfectly Awakened One, what joy it would be to have both a new king and a new Buddha within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha!"
"Like the sun piercing through the clouds, there is nowhere it does not illuminate; like the moon when the clouds have dispersed, it is the most brilliant among the stars.
At that time, Prince Brahmadatta immediately seized his father the king and placed him in an iron prison, then established new ministers and officials to govern the people.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms and heard that Devadatta had instructed the prince to seize his father, the king, and place him in an iron prison, while establishing his own ministers and aides.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having returned from their alms-round to their respective lodgings, put away their robes and bowls and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Prostrating themselves at his feet, they said to the World-Honored One:

"This morning we entered the city for alms and heard that the fool Devadatta has instructed the prince to arrest the King, our father, and cast him into prison, while establishing new ministers and officials."
He further commanded the prince, saying:
"You have killed the father-king, and I shall harm the Tathāgata; in this realm of Magadha, with a new king and a new Buddha, will it not be most gratifying!"
“At that time, the ministers and assistants also practiced what is not the Dharma;
when the ministers and assistants had already practiced what is not the Dharma, at that time the prince also practiced what is not the Dharma;
when the prince had already practiced what is not the Dharma, at that time the various ministers and high officials also practiced what is not the Dharma.”
When the ministers and high officials have already practiced unrighteousness, at that time the people within the realm will also practice unrighteousness;
when the people within the realm have already practiced unrighteousness, at that time the populace and the military will also practice unrighteousness;
when the military forces have already practiced unrighteousness, at that time the sun and moon will move in reverse order and lose their proper seasons.
Once the sun and moon have lost their proper timing, there will be no regular years;
once there are no regular years, the days and months will deviate and err, and they will no longer possess their refined radiance.
When the sun and moon no longer possess their refined radiance, at that time the constellations will manifest anomalies.
When the constellations have already manifested strange portents, violent winds arise;
once violent winds have arisen, the deities become incensed;
when the deities are incensed, at that time wind and rain do not fall according to the seasons.

At that time, the grains upon the earth will no longer grow; the various classes of people and all crawling and flying creatures will have their complexions altered and their lifespans become exceedingly short.
"Furthermore, when there is a time when the king governs according to the True Dharma, at that time the ministers also practice the True Dharma;
when the ministers have practiced the True Dharma, then the crown prince also practices the True Dharma;
when the crown prince has practiced the True Dharma, at that time the high officials also practice the True Dharma."
Once the high officials have practiced the True Dharma, the people within the realm will likewise practice the True Dharma;

the sun and moon will follow their regular courses, wind and rain will arrive at their proper seasons, calamities and anomalies will not appear, the spirits and deities will rejoice, and the five grains will flourish in abundance.
The ruler and his ministers will be harmonious and respectful toward one another, regarding each other as elder and younger brothers, never causing increase or decrease [in their mutual regard].

Among all beings with form, their complexions were radiant and lustrous; food digested itself spontaneously, they suffered no calamities, their lifespans were exceedingly long, and they were loved and revered by others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as when oxen cross a river, If the leader does not go straight, All will likewise go astray; This is because of the original leader."
Sentient beings are likewise thus: among the multitude there must be a leader;
yet if the leader practices what is contrary to the Dharma, how much more so for those of inferior and petty character!
All classes of beings suffer because the king’s laws are unjust.
Because one knows what constitutes unrighteous conduct, all people likewise follow suit.
It is like cattle crossing a river: if the leader walks correctly, those following also walk correctly; this is due to the original leader.
So it is with sentient beings: within the multitude there must be a guide;
if the guide practices the True Dharma, how much more so the common people!
All living creatures receive happiness because the king’s laws and teachings are correct.
"By knowing the practice of the True Dharma, all people shall likewise do so.
Therefore, O bhikṣus! You should abandon what is not the Dharma and practice the True Dharma."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume VIII and Volume IX.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 18: On Shame and Remorse (Hrī-vyapatrāpya) (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two sublime dharmas that protect the world.
What are these two dharmas?"
This refers to having a sense of shame (*hrī*) and a sense of dread (*apatrāpya*). Monks!

If these two qualities did not exist, there would be no distinction in the world between father and mother, elder and younger brother, wife and children, friends and acquaintances, or those of high and low station; one would then be exactly the same as the six domestic animals—pigs, chickens, dogs, oxen, sheep, and so forth.

Because this world possesses these two dharmas that protect the world, there exist separately fathers and mothers, brothers, wives and children, elders, and those of high or low status; furthermore, one does not share [these distinctions] with the six domestic animals.
Therefore, monks, you should cultivate a sense of shame and a sense of dread. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are two kinds of people in the world who pass away without having attained contentment.”
Who are these two persons? They are:
one who, upon obtaining wealth or goods, always hides and stores them away;
and another who, upon obtaining goods, rejoices in giving them to others.
"These are called the two types of persons who pass away without having attained contentment.
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"World-Honored One, we..."
Not understanding the meaning of this brief explanation:
how does one receive an object for storage?
How does one receive an object to give to another?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively expound its meaning.
The World-Honored One told him:
“Listen attentively!”
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall analyze its meaning for you. He replied:
"So it is. At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In this regard, there are sons of noble family who study various arts and crafts—some practice agriculture, some practice calligraphy and correspondence, some practice calculation, some practice astronomy, some practice geography, some practice divination and physiognomy, some learn long-distance diplomacy, or serve as royal ministers. They do not avoid cold or heat, hunger or thirst, nor do they shirk diligent toil, as they strive to provide for themselves."

Though he exerts such effort to acquire wealth, that person is unable to consume it; nor does he give it to his wife or children, nor to his slaves, servants, or circle of kinsmen—he gives nothing to any of them at all.

The wealth and goods he has acquired may be plundered by kings, seized by bandits, or destroyed by fire or swept away by water; scattered to various places, he fails to reap their benefits. Furthermore, within his own household, there may be those who disperse these possessions, so that they cannot remain intact.
This, bhikkhus, is called one who has acquired wealth and stores it away.
"How does one acquire wealth and distribute it? [The Buddha said:]..."

There are sons of noble family who study various arts and crafts: some practice agriculture, some practice calligraphy and record-keeping, some practice calculation, some practice astronomy and geography, some practice divination and physiognomy, some learn to serve as envoys to distant lands, and some act as royal ministers; they do not avoid cold or heat, hunger or poverty, nor do they shrink from toil and hardship, as they strive to provide for themselves.

Having acquired wealth through such exertion of effort, that person bestows it as alms upon sentient beings, providing for their parents, slaves, servants, wives, and children; furthermore, he extends it widely to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, performing various meritorious deeds and planting the seeds of heavenly blessings.
This, bhikkhu, is called giving a gift after having acquired it.
This, bhikkhu, is called [giving].
The two individuals are insatiable.
Just as the first person who acquires wealth and hoards it should contemplate relinquishing it,
so the second person who acquires it and distributes it widely should train in this practice.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should always practice the gift of Dharma and not habituate yourselves to the gift of food.
Why is this? Because you now possess the protection of karmic fruition, which enables my disciples to revere the Dharma and not crave gain and offerings."
If one is greedy for gain and offerings, they commit a great transgression against the Tathāgata. Why is this?
It is because such beings do not discern the Dharma and thereby disparage the teaching of the World-Honored One.
Having already violated the teaching of the World-Honored One, they will henceforth no longer be able to reach the path to Nirvāṇa; this brings me shame.

Why is this so? It is because the disciples of the Tathāgata are greedily attached to gain and offerings, do not practice the Dharma, do not discern the Dharma, violate the teaching of the World-Honored One, and do not accord with the True Dharma;
having thus violated the teaching of the World-Honored One, they further fail to reach the path to Nirvāṇa.

"O bhikṣu, you should now mindfully practice the gift of Dharma; do not think of the gift of sensual desires, for by doing so you will obtain renown far and wide, be honored for the Dharma, and not covet material wealth—this shall leave you free from shame."
The reason for this is that the disciples of the Tathāgata give the gift of the Dharma with joy, not out of a craving for the gift of material wealth.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should mindfully practice the gift of the Dharma and not emulate the gift of material wealth.
"O bhikṣus, for what purpose have I taught this doctrine, and on account of what meaning have I explained this causal connection?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain each point in detail."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a man who invited me for a meal offering; however, at that time, I had certain residual dharmas that ought to have been discarded."
Two bhikṣus came from afar, their bodies exhausted and their complexions altered.
At that time, I spoke to those bhikṣus, saying:
"There are remaining dharmas that may be set aside; whatever you require at this time, you may take it and provide for yourselves."
At that time, a certain bhikṣu had this thought:
"The World-Honored One today has left behind some residual teachings that may be set aside; whatever is required at any given time may then be taken from them."
"Furthermore, if we do not take this food, we shall simply discard it on clean ground or cast it into the water.
However, we ought now to take this food to satisfy our hunger and exhaustion, so that we may gain strength."
At that time, that bhikṣu further trains himself thus:
“The Buddha has also said this:
‘One should practice the gift of Dharma; do not practice the gift of desire.’”
"The reason for this is that among all forms of giving, there is none superior to the gift of material wealth; yet, among these, the gift of the Dharma is the most honored.
"I am now capable of sustaining myself even without eating for the entire day; therefore, I have no need to accept the merit of that faithful offering."

At that time, that bhikṣu immediately stilled his mind and did not accept the offering; his physical condition became so severely distressed that he no longer looked to his own life. Then, the second bhikṣu thought again:
"The World-Honored One has also left behind a method for removal; if we do not take this food, we shall surely become severely distressed."
"Now, by using this food to satisfy my hunger and deficiency, I have gained strength and am peaceful day and night.
At that time, that bhikṣu took and ate it; he became peaceful day and night, and his strength was fully restored.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Although that bhikṣu accepted those offerings, thereby removing his hunger and exhaustion and becoming fully restored in strength, he is not as worthy of veneration, as noble, or as highly respectable as the bhikṣu mentioned previously."
That bhikṣu has long been renowned for his fame; he is content with the Vinaya, easily satisfied and easily fulfilled.
All bhikṣus should practice the gift of Dharma; do not practice the gift of desire.
"What I have previously stated was for this reason.
When the World-Honored One had finished speaking these words, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus again thought to themselves:
"Previously, the World-Honored One briefly stated the essential points but did not elaborate upon them at length, and then rose from his seat and entered a quiet chamber.
Now, who among this assembly is capable of taking these brief meanings and expounding their significance in full detail?"
At that time, many bhikṣus again had this thought:
"Now the Venerable Śāriputra is praised by the World-Honored One; we should all go together to where that Śāriputra is."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to the place where the Venerable Śāriputra was, paid their respects to him, and sat down to one side.
Having sat down to one side, they [addressed him].
At that time, the many bhikṣus recounted to Śāriputra everything they had heard from the World-Honored One.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"How is it that the disciples of the World-Honored One are so attached to gain and offerings that they do not practice the Dharma?"
"How is it that the disciples of the World-Honored One delight in practicing the Dharma, yet do not delight in gain and offerings?
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus said to Śāriputra:
"We have come from afar to inquire about this meaning so that we may practice it."
"Venerable Śāriputra, you are capable; please expound its meaning in detail for us. Śāriputra replied:
"Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall expound its meaning to you in detail.
At that time, the many bhikṣus replied:
"So it is," Śāriputra replied. "The disciples of the World-Honored One train in tranquility, mindfulness, and serenity; the śrāvaka disciples do not train in this way."
Regarding the dharmas that ought to be abandoned as taught by the Blessed One, the bhikṣus do not abandon them;
therein they become indolent and give rise to various distracted thoughts, being unwilling to perform what should be done while instead practicing what should not be done.
At that time, the venerable elder bhikṣus felt shame regarding three matters.
What are these three?
The World-Honored One always delights in places of tranquility; if at that time the śrāvakas do not train accordingly, the elder bhikṣus feel shame.
The Blessed One has taught that people should extinguish these phenomena; yet when a bhikṣu does not extinguish them, the elder bhikṣu feels shame.
When, amidst this, he gives rise to thoughts of distracted ideation and his mind is not single-minded, the elder bhikṣu feels shame.
“Virtuous ones, you should know that a middle-rank bhikṣu feels shame in three respects.
What are these three?
The World-Honored One always delights in places of tranquility; if at such times a śrāvaka does not train accordingly, the middle-rank bhikṣu feels shame.
The World-Honored One has taught that people should extinguish this dharma; yet that bhikṣu does not extinguish it, and thus the middle-ranking bhikṣu feels shame.
Within this, he gives rise to thoughts of distracted conceptualization, and his mind is not single-minded; thus the middle-ranking bhikṣu feels shame.
“Virtuous ones, you should know that a young bhikṣu feels shame regarding three matters.
What are these three?
The disciples of the World-Honored One always delight in places of tranquility; if at such a time a śrāvaka does not train accordingly, the young bhikṣu feels shame.
The World-Honored One teaches people that they should extinguish this dharma; yet when those bhikṣus do not extinguish it, the young bhikṣus feel shame.
Furthermore, if within that state they give rise to thoughts of distraction and their minds are not single-minded, the young bhikṣus again feel shame.
"This is what is meant, O virtuous ones!
One is attached to wealth, not attached to the Dharma.
The bhikṣus said to Śāriputra:
“How is it that a bhikṣu is attached to the Dharma but not attached to material wealth?
Śāriputra replied: “In this regard, bhikṣu!”
The World-Honored One delights in places of tranquility, and the śrāvakas likewise train to delight in places of tranquility as the Tathāgata does.
Regarding that which the World-Honored One has taught should be abandoned, the bhikṣus then abandon it;
they are neither indolent nor distracted, practicing what ought to be practiced and refraining from what ought not to be practiced.
Venerable friends, you should know that an elder bhikṣu gains renown through three things.
What are these three?
The World-Honored One delights in places of tranquility; the śrāvakas also delight in places of tranquility; thus, the elder bhikṣu gains renown.
The World-Honored One taught that people should extinguish these phenomena; when the bhikṣus then extinguished these phenomena, the elder bhikṣus gained a reputation for themselves.
Within this state, they did not give rise to thoughts of distraction, their minds were always single-pointed, and thus the elder bhikṣus gained a reputation for themselves.
"Virtuous ones, you should know that a middle-ranking bhikkhu gains renown in three respects.
What are these three?
The Blessed One delights in places of solitude; the disciples also delight in places of solitude; thus, the middle-ranking bhikkhu gains renown."
The World-Honored One taught that people should extinguish these dharmas; at that time, the bhikṣu extinguished these dharmas, and thus the middle-ranking bhikṣu gained a reputation.
Because he did not give rise to thoughts of distraction therein, his mind was always single-minded, and the middle-ranking bhikṣu thereby obtained renown.
“Virtuous ones, you should know that a young bhikṣu gains renown in three respects.
What are these three?
In this regard, bhikṣus!”
The Blessed One delights in places of solitude, and the young bhikṣu also delights in places of solitude; thus the young bhikṣu acquires a reputation.
The Blessed One teaches people that they should extinguish this dharma, and at that time the bhikṣu extinguishes this dharma; thus the young bhikṣu acquires a reputation.
Within this state, he does not give rise to thoughts of distraction; his mind is always single-minded. Thus, the young bhikṣu soon gains a reputation:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that greed is a disease, a truly great calamity; the same is true of hatred."
When lust and hatred are extinguished, one attains the Middle Way; vision arises and wisdom arises, all fetters are stilled, and one reaches Nirvana.
Avarice and envy are diseases that are likewise extremely grave; they burn and cook one with afflictions, and pride is also profound.
Deceptive and false, lacking shame and a sense of propriety, one is unable to relinquish them; lust ruins what is right, and arrogance and overweening pride are likewise not abandoned.
"When these two forms of conceit are extinguished, one attains the Middle Way; vision arises, wisdom arises, all fetters are stilled, and one reaches Nirvana.
The bhikṣu said: "How is this so, Venerable Śāriputra?"
"The Middle Way gives rise to vision and gives rise to knowledge; it brings rest to all fetters and leads to the attainment of Nirvana.
Śāriputra said, "Virtuous ones, you should know that this is what is called the Noble Eightfold Path."
That is to say: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This, O worthy ones, is what is meant.
"The Middle Way gives rise to vision, gives rise to knowledge, brings rest to all fetters, and leads to the attainment of Nirvana.
At that time, the many bhikṣus, having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food, arriving at a certain street.

At that moment, there was a brahmin woman in that lane who wished to provide a meal for a brahmin; she stepped out of her door and saw the World-Honored One from afar. She then went to where the World-Honored One was and asked him:
"Have you seen a brahmin by any chance?"
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was already in the street.
The World-Honored One then raised his hand and pointed, saying, "This is the brahmin."
At that time, the brahmin’s wife gazed intently at the face of the Tathāgata, remaining silent and saying nothing.
Then, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“One who is without desire and without anger, Who has abandoned folly and is free from delusion;”
The Arhat whose outflows are exhausted—this one is called a brahmin.
One who is without desire and without hatred, who has abandoned folly and is free from delusion;
having relinquished the mass of fetters—this one is called a brahmin.
One who is without desire and without anger, who has abandoned folly and is free from delusion,
and who has severed the conceit of "I" and "mine"— such a person is called a brahmin.
If you wish to know the Dharma, it is that which was taught by the Three Buddhas.
"With utmost sincerity they take refuge in him, the Most Honored One, who has no superior.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"You should go to this brahmin woman and manifest yourself before her; she shall thereby be freed from her past transgressions."
At that time, Kāśyapa, having received the instruction from the Buddha, went to the house of the brahmin woman and sat down upon the seat.
Then, that brahmin woman prepared various kinds of fine foods and drinks and offered them to Kāśyapa.
At that time, Kāśyapa accepted the food and drink; wishing to deliver those people, he recited this verse of dedication for them:
"Fire is supreme among sacrifices; Verses are foremost among all books;
The king is the most honored among men; And the ocean is supreme among all flowing waters."
Among the stars, the moon is foremost; for illumination, the sun is first.
Throughout the four quarters, the zenith, and the nadir—in all regions and realms—the Buddha is the most honored and supreme among both gods and the people of the world.
"Those who seek such merit should take refuge in the Three Buddhas.
At that time, having heard these words, the brahmin’s wife was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself;
she stepped forward and said to Mahākāśyapa, "I pray only that the brahmin may always accept my invitation to eat at this house."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa accepted her invitation and partook of the food there.
When the brahmin woman saw that Kāśyapa had finished eating, she took another low seat and sat before him.
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke to him in due order concerning the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

That is to say, he discoursed on generosity, on ethical discipline, and on rebirth in the heavens; he taught that sensual desire is impure, that the severing of outflows is supreme, and that renunciation is essential.
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa, knowing that the mind of the brahmin woman had opened and her thoughts were liberated, was filled with great joy.
The Dharma that all Buddhas constantly teach consists of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

At that time, while the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was preaching for the brahmin woman, she immediately, while still on her seat, had all dust and defilement cleansed away and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Just as a fresh, clean white cloth, free from dust and grime, is easily dyed with color, so it was with the brahmin’s wife;
she likewise attained the purity of the Dharma-eye right there on her seat. Having attained the Dharma and seen the Dharma, she discerned its nature and was free from doubt.
Having reached fearlessness, she took refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha—and undertook the five precepts.
At that time, after the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had again preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the brahmin woman, he rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after Kāśyapa had left, the husband returned home.
The brahmin saw that his wife’s countenance was exceedingly joyful, unlike that of an ordinary person.
At that time, the brahmin immediately questioned his wife, and she then related the circumstances in full to her husband.
At that time, having heard these words, the brahmin took his wife and together they went to the vihāra.
Upon arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, the brahmin exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and sat down to one side.
The Brahmin’s wife bowed her head at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
Then, the Brahmin said to the World-Honored One:
"A while ago, a certain Brahmin came to my home; where is he now?"
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was not far from the World-Honored One; sitting cross-legged with his body upright and his mind composed, he contemplated the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One pointed from afar toward Mahākāśyapa and said,
"This is the venerable elder, the brāhmaṇa. The brāhmaṇa said:
“How is it, Gautama? Is a śramaṇa the same as a brāhmaṇa?
Are a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa not indeed different?”
The World-Honored One said:
"If one wishes to speak of a śramaṇa, it is I myself. Why is this so? Because I am indeed a śramaṇa."
"Whatever śramaṇa precepts and disciplines there are that are upheld, I have already attained them all.
Now, as for those who would discuss the brāhmaṇas, I am they myself. Why is this so? Because I am indeed a brāhmaṇa."
I have fully understood all the dharmas and practices maintained by the brahmins of the past.
As for those who would discuss the śramaṇas, it is Mahākāśyapa.
This is because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa has encompassed all the vinayas of the śramaṇas.
If one wishes to discuss the brāhmaṇas, they are likewise the bhikṣu Kāśyapa.
Why is this so? Because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa fully understands all those brāhmaṇas who uphold the prohibitive precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I do not call one a brahmin merely because he knows incantations;
one who proclaims, 'I am born in the Brahma-heaven,' is still not free from bondage."
"Without bondage and without rebirth, able to liberate oneself from all fetters;
no longer praising celestial blessings—such a one is a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Regarding what you call 'bondage,' what is meant by 'fetter'?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Sensual desire is a fetter; ill will is a fetter; delusion is a fetter."
The Tathāgata is free from this craving and desire, which has been extinguished forever without remainder; it is the same for hatred and delusion.
The Tathāgata no longer possesses these fetters.
The brāhmaṇa said, “I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound the profound and wondrous Dharma, so that there may no longer be these various fetters, bonds, and attachments.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually delivered a subtle and sublime discourse to that brāhmaṇa.
As for what is called discourse:
discourse on giving, discourse on morality, and discourse on rebirth in heaven; [the teaching that] sensual desire is impure, the severing of outflows is supreme, and renunciation is essential.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the mind of that brahmin had opened and his understanding was resolved, and seeing that he was filled with great joy, taught him at that moment the Dharma always taught by the Buddhas of antiquity:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Thus, the World-Honored One explained them all to the brahmin.
At that moment, all defilements and impurities were cleansed from the brahmin as he sat upon his seat, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
It was just like a fresh, clean white cloth, free of dust and grime, which easily takes on whatever color it is dyed.

At that time, the brahmin was likewise; he immediately attained the purity of the Dharma-eye while still upon his seat. Having attained the Dharma and seen the Dharma, he discerned its principles and was free from doubt.

Having reached fearlessness, he took refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha—and received the five precepts, becoming a true son of the Tathāgata, never again to regress.
At that time, the Brahmin couple, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru had an elephant named Nālāgiri, who was extremely fierce, cruel, and violent; yet he was so brave and powerful that he could subdue external enemies, and by virtue of that elephant’s strength, there was no one in the kingdom of Magadha who did not submit.
At that time, Devadatta went to King Ajātaśatru.
Upon arrival, he spoke as follows:
"Great King, you should know that this elephant is fierce and capable of subduing all enemies; you may give him strong liquor to drink so that he becomes intoxicated."
"At dawn tomorrow, the śramaṇa Gautama will surely enter the city to beg for alms; we shall release this intoxicated elephant to trample and kill him.
Then, King Ajātaśatru, having heard Devadatta’s instruction, immediately issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:
"Tomorrow at dawn, an intoxicated elephant shall be released; let no people wander through the streets and alleys."
At that time, Devadatta said to King Ajātaśatru:
"If that śramaṇa Gautama possesses all-knowledge and knows future events, he will certainly not enter the city to beg for alms tomorrow."
King Ajātaśatru said, "I shall follow your instructions;
even if there were one who possessed all-encompassing wisdom, he would not enter the city to beg for alms tomorrow at dawn."

At that time, the men and women, young and old, within the city of Rājagṛha who were followers of the Buddha, heard that King Ajātaśatru intended to release a drunken elephant in the early morning to harm the Tathāgata. Having heard this, they were each filled with grief and anxiety; they immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In the early morning of tomorrow, we pray that the World-Honored One will not enter the city again!"
The reason for this is that King Ajātaśatru now has issued a command, decreeing to the people within the city:
"Tomorrow, do not move about in the streets and alleys again; I intend to release a drunken elephant to harm the śramaṇa Gautama."
"If the śramaṇa possesses omniscience, he will not enter the city to beg for alms tomorrow at dawn.

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will not enter the city again; it would cause injury to the Tathāgata, and the people of the world would lose their eyes, leaving them without further protection."
The World-Honored One said: "Stop! Stop!"
"O upāsakas! Do not harbor grief or distress.
For what reason? The body of the Tathāgata is not an ordinary, mundane body; it cannot be harmed by others, and such a thing shall never happen."
"O upāsakas, you should know that Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas wide from east to west and twenty-one thousand yojanas long from south to north;
Aparagoyānī is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, shaped like a half-moon;
and Pūrvavideha is nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with its land being square."
Uttarakuru is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its land is as circular as the full moon.

Even if these four continents were filled with intoxicated elephants as densely as fields of rice, hemp, or thickets of forest—were their number such as this—they still could not move even a single hair of the Tathāgata, much less cause him any harm.
"Such a thing can never be!

[If one were to] abandon the four continents, and furthermore possess a thousand such sets of continents—namely, a thousand suns and moons, a thousand Mount Sumerus, a thousand oceans of the four seas, a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānīs, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand [realms of] the Four Heavenly Kings, a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens—this is called a 'thousandfold world system' (sahasracakravāḍa).
Even up to two thousand such worlds, this is called a 'middle thousandfold world system' (dvisāhasramadhyama-lokadhātu)."
Even if the entire trichiliocosm were filled with the nāga king Elāpattra, he could not move a single hair of the Tathāgata, let alone this elephant wishing to harm the Tathāgata.
This is absolutely impossible.
Why is this so? Because the supernatural power of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; once the Tathāgata has appeared in the world, he can never be harmed by anyone.
"Each of you should return to your respective abodes; the Tathāgata himself shall know the course of these transformations.
At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
At that time, having heard the True Dharma, the upāsakas and upāsikās each rose from their seats, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and then withdrew.
Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed in his robes, took up his alms bowl, and intended to enter the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, leading the gandharvas and their retinues, came from the east to attend upon the World-Honored One.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka, leading the kumbhāṇḍas, attended upon the Tathāgata.
In the west, Virūpākṣa leads the hosts of nāgas as attendants of the Tathāgata.
In the north, the Heavenly King Kubera leads the hosts of rākṣasa demons as attendants of the Tathāgata.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, leading a multitude of several tens of millions of devas, vanished from the Tuṣita Heaven and came to where the World-Honored One was. At that same time, Brahmā-devarāja, leading a multitude of several tens of millions of Brahmā-devas, came from the Brahma Heaven to where the World-Honored One was.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the deities of the twenty-eight heavens, along with the great kings of the ghost spirits, each said to one another:
"Today we shall observe these two deities as the dragon and the elephant battle; who shall be victorious and who shall be defeated?"

At that time, the fourfold assembly of Rājagṛha saw from afar the World-Honored One entering the city with his bhikṣus to beg for alms; then the people within the city all raised their voices and called out.
King Ajātaśatru again heard this sound and asked his attendants,
"What kind of noise is this that reaches even here?
The ministers replied:
"This is the Tathāgata entering the city to beg for alms; when the people saw him, they made this sound.
Ajātaśatru said, "The śramaṇa Gautama possesses no noble path, nor does he know the signs of the changes that come upon the human mind."
King Ajātaśatru immediately commanded the elephant trainer:
"Quickly bring the elephant and feed it strong liquor; fasten a sharp sword to its trunk, then release it to run loose."
At that time, the World-Honored One led the bhikṣus toward the city gate;
as soon as he raised his foot to enter it, heaven and earth shook violently, and the honored devas in the midst of the void scattered various kinds of flowers.
At that time, when the five hundred bhikṣus saw the intoxicated elephant approaching, they each fled in haste, not knowing where to go.
Then, seeing the Tathāgata from afar, that violent elephant charged straight toward him.
Seeing the intoxicated elephant approaching, the attendant Ānanda, standing behind the World-Honored One, could not remain at ease and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This elephant is fierce and evil; it may cause you harm, so you should keep your distance from it."
The World-Honored One said:
"Do not be afraid, Ānanda!"
"I shall now, with the divine hand of a Tathāgata, subdue this elephant.

The Tathāgata observed the violent elephant from a distance that was neither too near nor too far, and he immediately manifested lions, kings of beasts, on his left and right, and created a great pit of fire behind the elephant.

At that time, seeing the lion kings on his left and right and the pit of fire, the wild elephant immediately lost control of its bladder and excrement; finding no place to flee or charge, it then moved forward toward the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Do not harm the nāga; it is very difficult for a nāga to appear.
By harming a nāga, one shall not be born in a good realm."

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the World-Honored One, the wild elephant—as if consumed by fire—immediately unfastened his sword, knelt with both knees before the Tathāgata, and prostrated himself on the ground, licking the Tathāgata’s feet with his trunk.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right hand and stroked the elephant’s head, speaking these words:
“Hatred gives birth to the hells, And also produces the forms of snakes and vipers;
Therefore, one should abandon anger, So as never again to receive such a body.”
At that time, the divine lords and devas in the void scattered hundreds of thousands of varieties of flowers over the Tathāgata.
Then, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the fourfold assembly, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits.

At that time, more than sixty thousand men and women who had witnessed the taming of the elephant were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; eighty thousand devas and humans likewise attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, a "sword-wind" arose within the body of that intoxicated elephant; his body perished and his life ended, and he was reborn in the palace of the Four Great Kings.
Then, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, having heard what the World-Honored One had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Nanda, wearing robes of exquisite beauty that dazzled the eyes of men, and wearing sandals inlaid with gold, having also applied ointment to his two eyes, took up his alms-bowl and intended to enter the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus saw from afar the Venerable Nanda entering the city of Śrāvastī for alms, wearing robes of exquisite beauty.

Then those many bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side. After sitting there for a short while, they withdrew and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Just now, the bhikṣu Nanda entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms, wearing robes of such exquisite beauty that their colors dazzled the eyes of men.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go quickly to the place where the bhikṣu Nanda is and say:
'The Tathāgata calls for you!'"
He replied, “So it is, World-Honored One.”
Then, that bhikṣu, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet and departed.
He went to where the bhikṣu Nanda was, and upon arrival, he said to Nanda:
"The World-Honored One calls for you."

At that time, having heard the words of the bhikṣu, Nanda immediately went to where the World-Honored One was; having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda, saying:
"For what reason do you now wear these most exquisite robes and put on sandals to enter the city of Śrāvastī for alms?"
At that time, the Venerable Nanda remained silent and said nothing.
The World-Honored One spoke to him again, saying:
"What do you think, Nanda?"
"Do you not, indeed, have firm faith in leaving the household life to study the Path? Nanda replied, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:

“Son of good family, you who have now left the household life to study the Way with firm faith ought not to act contrary to the Vinaya. For what reason do you again wear such exquisite garments and groom your appearance and robes, intending to enter the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms?”
"What difference is there between him and those who wear white robes?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"On what day shall I see Nanda Capable of practicing the conduct of an araṇya-dweller?"
Delighting in the dharma of the śramaṇa is the dhūta-pāramitā. "Nanda,
you must no longer perform such practices as these!"
At that time, the Venerable Nanda and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda was unable to continue practicing the holy life; he wished to cast off his dharma robes and adopt the conduct of a layman.
Then, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and sat to one side.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
“The bhikṣu Nanda is unable to practice the holy life; he wishes to cast off his dharma robes and adopt the conduct of a householder.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu: "Go to Nanda and say:
'The Tathāgata summons you.'"
He replied, “It is so, World-Honored One.”
Then, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, that bhikṣu rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One,
and withdrew. He went to where the bhikṣu Nanda was and said,
"The World-Honored One summons you."
Nanda replied, “So be it. Thereupon,
the bhikṣu Nanda followed that bhikṣu to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Nanda: "What is this, Nanda?
Do you take no pleasure in practicing the holy life, and wish instead to cast off the dharma robes to practice the conduct of a layperson?"
Nanda replied, “So it is, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One said:
"For what reason, Nanda? "
Nanda replied, "My lustful mind is burning fiercely; I am unable to restrain it myself.
The World-Honored One said to him:
"Nanda, what do you think?
Are you not a son of noble family who has gone forth to study the Way? Nanda replied:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
I am a son of noble family who has gone forth to study the Way with firm faith.”
The World-Honored One said:
"O son of noble family!
This is not appropriate for you who have left the household life to study the Way and cultivate pure conduct."
How does one abandon the desire for the true Dharma and cultivate defilement?
Nanda, you should know that there are two things for which one can never have enough; if a person practices these things, they will never reach satiety.
What are the two things?
They are sensual desire and drinking alcohol.
These are called the two things for which there is no satiety.

If there is anyone who practices these two dharmas, they will never reach satiety; because they take the fruits of such conduct as their condition, they will likewise be unable to attain the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, Nanda!
You should contemplate abandoning these two dharmas; thereafter, you will certainly achieve the fruition of outflow-free retribution. Now, Nanda!
Cultivate the holy life well; there is no path to the fruit of the Way that does not proceed by means of this.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a roof is not sealed tight, The rain will leak through;
If a person does not reflect upon their conduct, Leakage of lust, anger, and delusion will follow."
"When a roof is well-sealed, the rain does not leak;
when a person practices with mindfulness, there is no lust, anger, or delusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"This son of good family has excessive sensual desire; I should now extinguish fire with fire.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, took Nanda in his hand and, like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, brought Nanda to Mount Gandhamādana.
At that time, there was a rocky cave on the mountain where a blind monkey lived.
Then the World-Honored One took Nanda by his right hand and said to him: "Nanda! You, Nanda!"
"Do you see this blind monkey? He replied, "I do."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:
“What is it that is excellent?”
"Is it the beautiful Sundarī of the Śākya clan who is superior,
or is this blind monkey superior? Nanda replied:
"It is just as if someone were to wound the nose of an extremely vicious dog and further smear it with poison; that dog would become even more malicious.
This case is exactly like that.

To compare the Śākya woman Sundarī to this blind monkey is an inadequate analogy; it is like a great conflagration burning through mountains and forests, which becomes even more fiercely blazing when dry firewood is added—this case is exactly like that."
"I remember that Śākya maiden; she does not leave my heart.
At that moment, in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, the World-Honored One vanished from that mountain and arrived in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven gathered together in the Sudharmā Hall. Not far from the Sudharmā Hall, there was another palace where five hundred jade maidens entertained themselves; it was inhabited solely by women, with no men present.
At that time, Nanda saw from afar five hundred celestial maidens performing music and dance, amusing themselves together. Having seen this, he asked the World-Honored One:
"What are these? Why are five hundred celestial maidens performing music and dance, amusing themselves together?"
The Blessed One said, "Nanda, you go yourself and ask him.

At that time, the Venerable Nanda went to where the five hundred celestial maidens were; he saw their palace with hundreds of kinds of fine seats spread out, consisting entirely of women and no men at all.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda asked those goddesses:
"Who are you goddesses who take such delight together and experience such happiness?"
The goddesses replied, "We are five hundred in number, all of us pure and without husbands.

We have heard that there is a disciple of the World-Honored One named Nanda, who is the son of the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Having practiced the pure holy life under the Tathāgata, he shall be reborn hereafter in this realm to become our husband, with whom we shall enjoy ourselves."
At that time, the Venerable Nanda was filled with such immense joy that he could not contain himself, and he thought to himself:
"I am now a disciple of the World-Honored One, and furthermore, I am the son of my aunt; these celestial maidens shall all become my wives."
At that time, Nanda withdrew and went to where the World-Honored One was.
The World-Honored One addressed him, saying: "How is it, Nanda?"
"What did those jade maidens say? Nanda replied,
"Those jade maidens each said this:"
"We each have no husbands, and we have heard that there are disciples of the World-Honored One who practice the holy life well; after their lives end, they shall come to be reborn here.
The World-Honored One said to him:
"Nanda, what do you think?"
"Nanda! What do you think? Nanda replied:
At that time, he immediately thought to himself:
"I am a disciple of the World-Honored One, and furthermore, I am the son of the Buddha’s maternal aunt; all these celestial maidens shall become my wives."
The World-Honored One said:
"How excellent, Nanda! You have well cultivated the holy life; I shall bear witness for you, so that these five hundred women shall all become your attendants."
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"What do you think, Nanda?
Is Sundarī, the daughter of the Śākyas, beautiful?"
"Are these five hundred celestial maidens beautiful?
Nanda replied, "They are like blind monkeys on a mountain peak compared to Sundarī; they possess neither luster nor beauty."
"This case is also like that.
When Sundarī stands before the celestial maidens of other heavens, she likewise possesses no radiance.
The World-Honored One said:
“You have well cultivated the holy life; I shall bear witness that you have attained these five hundred devas.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
“I shall now extinguish Nanda’s fire with my own fire.”
Just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, the World-Honored One took Nanda by the arm with his right hand and led him into the hells.
At that time, the sentient beings in the hells were undergoing various forms of suffering and affliction.
At that time, within that hell there was a great cauldron, empty and devoid of anyone.
Having seen this, he was struck with fear and his hair stood on end; he stepped forward and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"All these sentient beings here are undergoing suffering and pain, yet this cauldron alone is empty and without a person."
The World-Honored One replied, "This is called the Avīci Hell.
At that time, Nanda became even more terrified; the hair on his body stood on end, and he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This is the Avīci Hell, yet it is entirely empty and there are no sinners here?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Nanda, you should go there yourself and ask."
At that time, the Venerable Nanda asked himself:
"What is this, warder? What kind of hell is this?"
"What kind of hell is this, empty and devoid of people?

The warder replied, "Bhikṣu, you should know that there was a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha named Nanda. Having practiced the pure holy life under the Tathāgata, upon the dissolution of his body at the end of his life, he was reborn in a good destination, in the heavens, where he has lived for a thousand years, enjoying himself to his heart's content."
"Furthermore, after passing away from that life, one is born here within this Avīci Hell; these empty cauldrons are none other than its chambers.
When the Venerable Nanda heard these words, he was seized with terror and his hair stood on end. He immediately thought to himself:
"These empty cauldrons are surely for me alone."
He approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I pray that you will accept my repentance. Due to the conditions of my own transgressions, I failed to cultivate the holy life and have thus disturbed the Tathāgata.”
At that time, the Venerable Nanda spoke this verse:
"Human life is not to be prized; even celestial longevity ends in loss.
The pains and agonies of hell are unbearable; only Nirvana brings true bliss."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Nanda:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as you have said: Nirvana is indeed the ultimate bliss. Nanda!
I accept your confession; you were foolish and deluded, and you yourself recognized your fault before the Tathāgata."
"Now I accept your confession; henceforth, do not commit such offenses again.

At that moment, in the time it takes to extend and contract one's arm, the World-Honored One took Nanda by the hand and vanished from the hell, arriving directly at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in the Jeta Grove of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda, saying: "Now, Nanda,
you should cultivate two dharmas."
What are these two dharmas?
They are namely śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Furthermore, one should further cultivate two more dharmas.
What are the two dharmas?
That birth and death are not to be delighted in, and that one knows nirvana to be bliss—these are called the two dharmas.
Furthermore, one should cultivate another two dharmas.
"What are these two dharmas?
They are wisdom and eloquence.
At that time, the World-Honored One explained these various dharmas to Nanda.

At that time, having received the instruction from the World-Honored One, the Venerable Nanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew to go to the Andhavana Grove.
Having arrived, he sat cross-legged beneath a tree, straightening his body and composing his mind, fixing his mindfulness before him as he contemplated such teachings of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Venerable One remained in a secluded place, constantly contemplating the teachings of the Tathāgata without departing from them for even a moment.

For this reason, the son of noble family, having gone forth with firm faith to study the Path and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya), realized according to reality: "Birth and death are ended; the holy life is established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence to be received."
At that time, the Venerable Nanda attained arhatship.
Having become an arhat, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One, regarding those five hundred celestial maidens whom you previously promised me as disciples, I now renounce them all."
The World-Honored One said:
"Now your cycle of birth and death is ended, and the holy life has been established; I shall now let you go.
At that time, he spoke this verse:
“I now see Nanda practicing the dharma of a śramaṇa;
all evils have been stilled, and he is without fail in his dhūta austerities.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“The one who has attained arhatship is the bhikṣu Nanda here.
He who is free from lust, anger, and delusion is also the bhikṣu Nanda.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park of the Śākyas, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"May the World-Honored One continue long to transform those who are ignorant and deluded, and may you always protect all living beings."
The World-Honored One said:
"Gautamī, you should not speak these words to the Tathāgata."
“The Tathāgata’s life span is infinite; he shall eternally protect your life.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī spoke this verse:
“How should one pay homage to the Most Victorious One, Whom none in the world can equal?”
"Able to sever all doubts, for this reason these words were spoken.
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied to Gautamī in verse:
"Her diligence is such that her resolve is difficult to break; she always possesses a courageous mind."
"To regard the śrāvakas with equanimity—this is to pay homage to the Tathāgata.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī said to the World-Honored One:
"From this day forward, I shall pay homage to the World-Honored One; for the Tathāgata now commands that one pay homage to all sentient beings, his mind being without increase or decrease."
"Among those in the heavens, among humans, and among the asuras, the Tathāgata is the most supreme.
At that time, the World-Honored One approved of what Mahāprajāpatī had said.
She immediately rose from her seat, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and then withdrew.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost disciple in broad acquaintance and vast knowledge is Mahāprajāpatī."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of people who give rise to slander against the assembly of the Tathāgata.
Who are these two? [They are:]..."
That is to say, to claim what is not the Dharma is the Dharma, and to claim what is the Dharma is not the Dharma—these are called the two types of people who slander the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are two other types of people who do not slander the Tathāgata.
What are these two? They are:
that which is non-Dharma is indeed non-Dharma, and that which is true Dharma is indeed true Dharma. These are called the two persons who do not slander the Tathāgata.
Therefore, monks! That which is not the Dharma should be called "not the Dharma," and that which is the true Dharma should be called "the true Dharma. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these two kinds of people who obtain immeasurable merit."
What are these two?
They are those who praise those who deserve praise and do not praise those who do not deserve praise; these are called the two persons who obtain immeasurable merit.
Furthermore, there are two types of people who undergo immeasurable suffering for their offenses. Who are these two?
They are those who revile those who are worthy of praise, and those who praise those who do not deserve praise.
"O bhikṣus! Do not train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Nine; Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nineteen: Exhortation and Entreaty (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had attained the Way, he had this thought:

"This Dharma of mine is now extremely profound, difficult to comprehend and difficult to understand; it is hard to awaken to, inconceivable, subtle and exquisite, to be realized only by the wise. Those who can discern its principles and cultivate it without weariness will immediately attain joy."
If I were to preach the sublime Dharma to others, and they neither believed and accepted it nor practiced it, my labor would be in vain and I would suffer loss.
"I should now remain silent; what need is there for me to preach the Dharma?

At that time, Brahmā, dwelling in the Brahma Heaven, perceived from afar the thoughts of the Tathāgata. Like a man extending or contracting his arm, he vanished from the Brahma Heaven and appeared before the World-Honored One. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“This Jambudvīpa will surely fall into ruin, and the Three Realms will lose their eyes.

Since the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world, he ought to expound the Jewel of the Dharma; yet now, you do not further proclaim the flavor of the Dharma. We only pray that the Tathāgata will extensively expound the profound Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings!”
Furthermore, the roots and origins of these beings are such that they are easily delivered.
If they do not hear [the Dharma], they will forever lose the Eye of the Dharma.

These should be considered the remaining children of the Dharma, like the *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, which, though emerging from the earth, have not yet risen above the water, nor have they yet blossomed.

At that time, as those flowers were gradually about to emerge, they had not yet risen above the water; sometimes these flowers did emerge above the surface of the water, and sometimes these flowers were not adhered to by the water.

These classes of sentient beings are also like this: they are pressed and hurried by birth, old age, sickness, and death; their faculties should have matured, yet those who pass away without hearing the Dharma—how bitter that is!
"Now is precisely the right time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the mind of the Brahmā and out of compassion for all sentient beings, spoke this verse:
"The Brahmā has now come to exhort me; The Tathāgata shall open the gate of the Dharma."
Those who hear it shall attain firm faith and discern the profound essentials of the Dharma.
Like one standing atop a high mountain, surveying all classes of sentient beings;
I now possess this Dharma and ascend the hall to manifest the Eye of the Dharma.
At that time, Brahmā thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata will surely preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Overjoyed and leaping for joy beyond measure, he prostrated his head at [the Buddha's] feet and immediately returned to the heavens.
