At that time, Brahmā, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Sages.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these two things which those training in the Path should not associate with.
What are these two things?

That which is called attachment to desire and the pursuit of pleasure is a base, lowly, and vulgar teaching; furthermore, these various sufferings and manifold afflictions are of a hundred kinds. These two matters are what those training in the Path should not associate with.

Thus, having abandoned these two matters, I myself attained the essential path to perfect enlightenment; vision arose, wisdom arose, my mind found rest, I attained the various supernormal powers, realized the fruits of the śramaṇa, and reached nirvāṇa.

What is the essential path for attaining perfect enlightenment, so that vision arises, wisdom arises, the mind finds rest, the various supernormal powers are attained, the fruits of the śramaṇa are realized, and one reaches nirvāṇa?
This is what is called the Noble Eightfold Path. Namely:
right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is known as the essential path.

Now that I have attained perfect enlightenment, vision has arisen and wisdom has arisen; my mind has found rest, I have attained the various supernormal powers, realized the fruits of the śramaṇa, and reached nirvāṇa.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves to abandon these two former matters and practice the path that is the ultimate essential. Thus, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[So too did] Rāhula, Kāśyapa, Nanda and Upananda, and Mahāprajāpatī.
Slander and non-Brahmin conduct—these two matters are the very last.
(3) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“How does a bhikṣu sever craving and desire, so that his mind attains liberation, even reaching the ultimate state of peace and security, free from all afflictions, and revered by gods and humans?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śakra-devānām-indra, saying:
"In this regard, Kauśika!
If a bhikṣu hears this teaching on emptiness and understands non-existence, he will then attain the complete understanding of all dharmas and know them as they truly are."

Regarding the phenomena of suffering and pleasure perceived by the body, as well as those phenomena that are neither painful nor pleasant, one contemplates this very body as entirely impermanent and sees that all things ultimately return to emptiness.
Having thus observed this transformation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, he does not give rise to perception; because there is no perception, there is no fear;
because there is no fear, he attains parinirvāṇa, knowing as it truly is:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"Thus it is said, Śakra Devānām Indra!
A bhikṣu who has severed craving and desire attains liberation of mind, reaching even the ultimate state of peace and security, free from all calamity, and revered by gods and humans."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times and withdrew.
At that moment, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was seated cross-legged not far from the World-Honored One; he straightened his body and composed his mind, binding his mindfulness before him.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Did Śakra, who has attained the tracks of the path, ask these questions?
Or did he ask about these meanings without having attained the tracks of the path?"
"I shall now test him.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, by means of his supernormal power, reached the Heaven of the Thirty-three in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra saw Mahāmaudgalyāyana approaching from afar; he immediately rose to welcome him and spoke these words:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
It has been a very long time since you last came here.
I wish to discuss the meaning of the Dharma with you; please sit here.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana asked Śakra Devendra:
“The World-Honored One has taught you the Dharma for severing craving and desire; I wish to hear it. Now is the very time for him to explain it to me.”
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed him, saying:
"I am currently burdened with many affairs among the devas—whether they be my own personal matters or the affairs of the devas—and what I have heard I immediately forget."
In the past, Maudgalyāyana, you fought with the asuras; on the day of that battle, the devas were victorious and the asuras retreated.
At that time, I went there in person to fight, and having soon led the devas back to the celestial palace, I sat in the Hall of Supreme Victory.

Because it was won through victory in battle, it is named the Hall of Supreme Victory. Its stairways and alleys are arranged in rows, with each path intersecting the next; at the head of each staircase are seven hundred pavilions, and upon each pavilion dwell seven jade maidens, and each jade maiden has seven attendants. I pray that the Venerable Maudgalyāyana will go there to observe them.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra and King Vaiśravaṇa followed behind the Venerable Maudgalyāyana as they proceeded to the Hall of Supreme Excellence.
Then, Śakra Devānām Indra and King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the Great Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"This is the Hall of Supreme Excellence; you may wander through and view it all."
Maudgalyāyana said: "O Heavenly King! This place is exceedingly subtle and wondrous;

it is entirely due to the meritorious blessings performed in previous lives that this natural jeweled hall has come to be. It is just like a small place of pleasure in the human world where people each celebrate their own joy, no different from a celestial palace—all of which is brought about by the merit performed in previous lives."

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra’s attendant jade maidens each fled in haste, not knowing where to go; they were like people in the human world who have encountered a taboo, all filled with shame and remorse.
At that time, the jade maidens brought by Śakra Devānām Indra did likewise.
Seeing Mahāmaudgalyāyana approaching from afar, they each fled in haste, not knowing where to go.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"This Śakra Devānām Indra is exceedingly heedless; I should now cause him to feel fear."
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana pressed the ground with his right toe, and that palace shook in six ways.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa were both seized with terror; their hair stood on end, and they thought to themselves:
"This Mahāmaudgalyāyana possesses great supernormal power (ṛddhi), for he can cause this palace to shake six times! How extraordinary!"
"How extraordinary!
This has never happened before!
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Now this Śākyan body is filled with fear; I should now inquire about its profound meaning.
"How so, Kauśika? Regarding the Sūtra on the Elimination of Craving taught by the Tathāgata, now is precisely the time; we pray that you will explain it to us."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied:
“Maudgalyāyana!
Previously, I went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated my head at his feet, and stood to one side.”
At that time, I addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"How does a bhikṣu sever craving and desire so that his mind attains liberation, even reaching ultimately the state of the unconditioned, free from affliction and suffering, and honored by devas and humans?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed me, saying:
"In this regard, Kauśika!
After the bhikṣus have heard the Dharma, they are entirely without attachment; they do not cling to form, for they fully understand all dharmas as being ultimately non-existent."

Having known all phenomena—whether suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—one contemplates and realizes their impermanence; they are extinguished without remainder, yet without annihilation or destruction.
Observing this, he became entirely free from attachment; having ceased to give rise to worldly perceptions, he was further without fear.
Being without fear, he attained parinirvāṇa, knowing as it truly is:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence to be received."
Thus it is said, Śakra Devānām Indra!
A bhikṣu who has severed desire attains liberation of mind, even reaching the ultimate state of the unconditioned, free from affliction and suffering, and revered by gods and humans.
At that time, having heard these words, I prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times, and then withdrew and departed, returning to the heavens.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, with words concerning the profound Dharma, explained and analyzed the matter in detail for Śakra Devānām Indra and Vaiśravaṇa.

At that time, after Maudgalyāyana had finished preaching the Dharma, he vanished from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as quickly as a strong man might bend or extend his arm and arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. He approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the World-Honored One from his seat, saying:
"The Tathāgata previously taught the Dharma for the elimination of desire to Śakra Devendra; I only pray that the World-Honored One will now teach it to me."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"You should know this: Śakra Devānām Indra has come to where I am, prostrated with his head at my feet, and stands to one side."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra asked me about this matter:
"How is it, World-Honored One,
that a bhikṣu severs craving and desire, and his mind attains liberation?"
At that time, I said to Śakra Devānām-indra: "Kauśika!

If there is a bhikṣu who understands that all dharmas are empty and non-existent, and has no attachments; who fully understands that all dharmas are ultimately non-existent; and who, knowing that all dharmas are impermanent, realizes they are extinguished without remainder and are neither annihilated nor destroyed."
Having observed this, he is entirely without attachment, no longer gives rise to worldly perceptions, and is free from fear.
Being free from fear, he attains parinirvāṇa:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
"Thus it is said, Śakra Devānām Indra, that a bhikṣu who has severed desire attains liberation of mind.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra rose from his seat, bowed his head at my feet in salutation, and then withdrew.
"Return to the heavens.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“In this world, there are two kinds of people who feel no fear when they see lightning and thunderbolts.”
Who are these two persons?
The lion, the king of beasts, and the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted.
These, O bhikṣu, are called the two.
When these two persons exist in the world, they do not harbor fear even when seeing lightning and thunderbolts.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves to become Arhats whose outflows are exhausted.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these two qualities that cause a person to lack wisdom.
What are these two qualities?
Not delighting in questioning superior persons, and being merely fond of sleep without the intent for diligence.”
"Monks, it is said that there are these two qualities that cause a person to lack wisdom.
Furthermore, there are two other qualities that cause a person to achieve great wisdom."
"What are these two things? They are: taking pleasure in inquiring about the meaning of the Dharma from others, and not being greedy for sleep but possessing a mind of diligence.
These, O bhikṣu, are called the two things that cause a person to possess wisdom; one should train in distancing oneself from unwholesome dharmas."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these two things that cause a person to be poor and lowly, lacking in wealth and goods.
What are these two things?
If, upon seeing another giving, one restrains them, and furthermore, refuses to give oneself.
"Monks, these are the two things that cause a person to be poor and lowly, lacking wealth and treasures. Monks!"
Furthermore, there are two dharmas that cause a person to become wealthy and noble.
What are these two dharmas?
If, when seeing someone giving things to others, one rejoices in their joy and personally delights in practicing generosity.
"Thus it is said, monks:
there are these two qualities that make a person wealthy and noble. It is so, monks!"
"One should practice generous giving and harbor no greedy thoughts.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these two dharmas that cause a person to be born into a poor and lowly family.”
What are the two dharmas?
They are being unfilial toward one's parents and various venerable elders, and likewise failing to serve those who are superior to oneself.
These, O bhikṣu, are called [the two dharmas].
There are these two things that cause a person to be born into a poor and lowly family.
Monks! Furthermore, there are two things that lead to birth into a noble family.
What are these two?
To show reverence to one’s parents, brothers, and kinsmen, to bring them to one’s own home, and to bestow all that one possesses upon them.
This, O bhikṣus, is what is meant.
Possessing these two qualities, one is born into a noble family. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a brahmin girl named Susīma who went to the place where the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila was.
Having arrived, she prostrated with her head at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin girl Susīma said to Cūḷa Koṭṭhita:
"Udaka Rāmaputta and Sāḷha Moggalliputta did not ultimately receive transformation through this profound Dharma; each met his end, and the World-Honored One declared of these two men:
'One was born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, and one was born in the Sphere of Nothingness.'"
When these two individuals had lived out their full lifespans and each passed away, one was to become a king of a frontier land who would inflict incalculable harm upon the people;
the other was to become a winged, malevolent wildcat, from which no flying or running creature could escape.
After their lives ended, they were both reborn within the hells.
"Furthermore, why does the Blessed One not declare when that person shall reach the end of suffering? Why does the Blessed One not predict that this person shall reach the end of suffering?
At that time, the Venerable Koṭṭhita said to the woman Suja:
"The reason the Blessed One does not speak on this matter is that no one has asked about its meaning; therefore, the Blessed One has not predicted when that person shall reach the end of suffering."
The woman Susīma said,
"Since the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa here, it is not possible to question him;
had he still been in the world, I would have gone to ask about this meaning."
"Now that the Venerable Kūṭadanta has explained this to me, when will that person reach the end of suffering?
Then, the Venerable Kūṭadanta spoke this verse:
"The various fruits are not the same, And so it is with the destinies of sentient beings."
Regarding self-awakening and awakening others, I have no such eloquence to speak of it.
Regarding the eloquence of meditative wisdom and liberation, and the recollection of past lives and the divine eye—
abilities that can exhaust the very root of suffering— I have no such eloquence to speak of them.
At that time, the woman Susīma spoke these verses:
“The Sugata possesses this wisdom; He is upright and free from blemish.
Courageous and subduing all that must be subdued, He seeks the practice of the Mahāyāna.”
At that time, the Venerable Kauṣṭhila further spoke these verses:
"This mind is exceedingly difficult to attain; It can acquire the essentials of the extraordinary Dharma.
That which is difficult to accomplish is now being achieved, As it turns toward things most marvelous."
At that time, the Venerable One expounded the essentials of the Dharma to the woman Suśīma, who thereupon conceived a heart of joy.
Then, the woman rose from her seat, prostrated with her head at his feet, and withdrew.
At that time, the woman Susīma, having heard what the Venerable Koṭṭhila had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (Nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana was staying in the country of Vāṇijagāma by the side of the Deep Pool, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana had such a reputation that it spread far and wide.
The Venerable Elder Caṅkī, a brāhmaṇa, was traveling and teaching there.

At that time, the brahmin heard that the Venerable Kātyāyana was staying by the side of this pond to wander and teach, accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus—the Venerable Elder who was fully endowed with merit. [He thought: "I should now go to pay my respects to him."
At that time, the brahmin Suvarṇavarṇa, leading five hundred disciples, went to the place where the Venerable Kātyāyana was; they exchanged greetings with one another and sat down to one side.
At that time, that brahmin asked the Venerable Kātyāyana:
"According to the conduct of Kātyāyana, this is contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya, that a young bhikṣu does not pay homage to us, the highly venerable brahmins."
Kātyāyana said: "Brahmin, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taught these two stages.
What are these two stages?
"The first is called the stage of old age; the second is called the stage of youth. The brahmin asked:
"Which one is the stage of old age?"
"What constitutes being in one's prime? Kātyāyana replied,

"Even if a brahmin is eighty or ninety years of age, if that person does not cease from lustful desires and continues to commit various evil deeds, it is said that although this brahmin may be called old, he is actually in his prime."
The brāhmaṇa asked, “Who is it that,
though young in years, dwells in the state of old age? Kātyāyana replied:

“Brahmin! If there is a bhikkhu who is twenty years old, or thirty, forty, or fifty, and he neither indulges in sexual desire nor commits unwholesome deeds, this, Brahmin, is called being ‘in the stage of old age while still in the prime of youth.’”
The brahmin asked, "In this great assembly,
is there perhaps even a single bhikṣu who does not engage in sexual conduct or commit evil deeds? Kātyāyana replied:
"In my great assembly, there is not a single bhikṣu who indulges in sensual desires or commits evil.
At that time, the brahmin rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣus, and spoke these words:
"You are young in years yet abide in the state of the aged; I am old in years yet abide in the state of the youthful."
At that time, the brahmin went again to where Kātyāyana was, prostrated with his head at his feet, and declared:
"I now take refuge in Kātyāyana and the community of monks; for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill."
Kātyāyana said: "Do not take refuge in me now;
you should instead go toward those in whom I myself have taken refuge. The brāhmaṇa said:
“Venerable Kātyāyana, to whom do you take refuge?
At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana knelt upright toward the place where the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa and said:
“There is one born of the Śākya clan who left home to study the Path; I have always taken refuge in him, for he is my teacher.”
The brahmin said, "Where is this śramaṇa Gautama?
I wish to see him now."
Kātyāyana said, "That Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa. The brāhmaṇa said:
"If the Tathāgata were still in the world, I would travel hundreds of thousands of yojanas to inquire after his well-being.

Although that Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, I now once again take refuge in and pay homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; for as long as my life lasts, I shall no longer kill living beings."
At that time, the Brahmin of Superior Appearance, having heard what the Venerable Kātyāyana had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two persons who appear in the world, whom it is extremely difficult to encounter.
Who are these two persons?
It is extremely rare to encounter a person capable of expounding the Dharma appearing in the world;
it is extremely rare to encounter a person capable of hearing the Dharma, receiving and upholding it, and practicing it accordingly.
This is what is meant, O Bhikṣus!
The appearance of these two types of persons in the world is extremely rare to encounter. Therefore,
monks, you should train yourselves in the teaching of the Dharma,
and you should train yourselves in the hearing of the Dharma.
"In this way, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
11 (Eleven). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the realm of Magadha and gradually arrived at the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, he was staying in the Āmrapālī Garden to the north of Vaiśālī, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the daughter Ambapālī heard that the World-Honored One had arrived at the grove together with five hundred great bhikṣus.

Thereupon, she mounted a carriage adorned with precious feathers and departed from the city of Vaiśālī. Reaching the entrance of the narrow pass, she proceeded to where the World-Honored One was; having alighted from her carriage, she went on foot to his presence.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw the woman approaching from afar and addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you, be single-mindedly diligent; do not give rise to improper thoughts.
Then the woman approached the World-Honored One, prostrated herself at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the most sublime Dharma.
Having finished preaching the most sublime Dharma, the woman addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"Please accept my invitation, as well as that of the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the woman's invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted her invitation, the woman rose from her seat, prostrated herself at his feet with her head and face, and returned home by the same path.
At that time, the men and women, the old and the young, of the city of Vaiśālī heard that the World-Honored One was in the Āmrapālī Garden together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, there were five hundred billion youths in the city, riding various chariots adorned with feathers and jewels—some riding white chariots and white horses, with their robes, canopies, banners, and attendants all white;
some riding red chariots and red horses, with their robes, canopies, banners, and attendants all red;
and others riding blue chariots and blue horses, with their robes, canopies, banners, and attendants all blue.

Or, riding in a yellow carriage drawn by yellow horses, with clothing, parasols, banners, and attendants all yellow—his majestic appearance solemnly adorned according to the custom of kings—he departed from the city of Vaiśālī and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was. Before he had yet arrived, he encountered that woman on the road; she ran and struck the oxen of his carriage, then galloped toward the interior of the city.
At that time, the youths asked the girl: "You are a woman;
you ought to feel ashamed. Why did you beat the oxen and drive the cart, racing toward the city?"
Then the woman replied, "Virtuous sirs, you should know that I have invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for tomorrow; that is why I am driving the carriage.
The youth replied:
"I also wish to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; I now give you a thousand taels of pure gold so that you may prepare it for us tomorrow.
At that time, the woman replied, "Stop!
"Stop! Son of good family!
I do not permit it."
The youth replied again:

"I will give you two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, five thousand, even up to one hundred thousand pieces of gold, yet you still do not grant permission; tomorrow, let us provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
The woman replied:
"I do not grant permission.
The reason for this is that the World-Honored One constantly says: "
"There are two kinds of hope that worldly people are unable to abandon.
What are these two?
The hope for gain and the hope for life."
"Who can guarantee that I shall live until tomorrow? I have already invited the Tathāgata; now I must prepare the offerings.
At that time, the youths each shook their hands and said, "We, so many in number, are not like this woman!"
Having spoken these words, they each departed for their respective homes.
Then, the youths went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing the youths approaching, addressed the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus, observe the majestic bearing and attire of these youths; they are no different from those of Śakra, Lord of Devas, when he comes forth for a tour of inspection."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth, saying:
"There are two things in the world that are most impossible to obtain. What are these two?"
There are those who are grateful and who never forget even a small kindness, let alone a great one.
Thus it is said, young men:
there are these two things that are most difficult to find.
"Young man, you should know that one must be mindful of kindness and recognize those who have done even a small favor, let alone a great one.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Knowing kindness and recognizing favors, One should always be mindful of those who instruct and guide."
"He is honored and served by the wise, and his fame is heard by gods and men.
"So it is, young men!"
"You should know that you must train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One fully expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the youths.
Having heard it, they each rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and then withdrew.
At that time, during that very night, the woman prepared various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink, and spread out many seats; then at dawn, she said:
"The time has come; now is precisely the right moment. I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to visit my humble home."
At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robe, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the bhikṣus who followed before and behind him, went to the city of Vaiśālī and arrived at the woman's house.
At that time, seeing that the World-Honored One was seated, the woman personally took up food with her own hands and offered it to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
After she had fed the Buddha and the bhikṣu-saṃgha and served them pure water, she took another small seat inlaid with gold and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, the woman addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I offer this Āmrapālī Garden to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus, so that the Saṃgha of the future, the past, and the present may have a place to dwell within it. I pray that the World-Honored One will accept this garden."
At that time, for her sake, the World-Honored One accepted this garden.
The World-Honored One then uttered this benediction:
"The gift of garden fruits brings coolness; bridges enable people to cross."
By building latrines near the path, people find rest;
day and night they obtain peace and security, and their merit is beyond measure.
Having perfected the precepts of all dharmas, they will surely be reborn in the heavens after death.
At that time, having spoken this prophecy, the World-Honored One rose and departed.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, the woman rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll Ten: The Severing of Craving and the Lion;
Ignorance, the Poor Householder with Little Wealth, and the Woman Suśīlā;
Kātyāyana, the Dharma-Preacher, and the Woman.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Eleven, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kipin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty: On Good Friends (Sukalyāṇamitra-varga). Chapter Twenty: On Good Friends.
1. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should associate with spiritual friends and not practice evil deeds or place faith in unwholesome karma. Why is this so, monks?
Having associated with spiritual friends, one’s faith increases; likewise, learning, generosity, and wisdom all increase universally."
If a bhikṣu associates with virtuous friends, he should not practice evil conduct.
Why is this? Because if one associates with evil friends, one will lack faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
Therefore, monks, you should draw near to virtuous friends and not draw near to evil friends. Thus it is, monks.
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Karanda Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
Surrounded by them before and behind, he preached the Dharma for them.
At that time, Devadatta was passing by not far from the Tathāgata with five hundred bhikṣus.
Seeing Devadatta leading his own disciples from afar, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Do not associate with evil friends, Nor follow after fools; ... (the rest of the verse follows)"
One should draw near to virtuous friends, those who are most excellent among men.
Originally, humans possess no inherent evil; yet by associating with evil friends, one will surely plant the roots of evil thereafter and remain forever in the midst of darkness.

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the World-Honored One, Devadatta’s five hundred disciples came to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and sat down to one side.
After withdrawing for a moment, they sat down and repented before the World-Honored One, saying:
"We were foolish and deluded, possessing no true understanding; we only pray that the World-Honored One will accept our repentance."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the repentance of those five hundred bhikṣus and preached the Dharma for them, causing them to attain the faculty of faith.
Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus dwelt in a secluded place, contemplating the profound Dharma.
The reason for this is that these sons of noble family have left the household life to study the Way, practicing the unsurpassed holy life with firm faith.
At that time, those five hundred bhikṣus became arhats:
birth and death were ended, what was to be done had been accomplished, the holy life was established, and they knew as it truly is that they would no longer undergo rebirth in a womb.
At that time, five hundred people became arhats.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a boundless multitude as he preached the Dharma.

At that time, Dharmaruci was in a quiet chamber, contemplating alone; he entered the samādhi of dhyāna and perceived his previous existence as a fish in the great ocean, with a body seven hundred yojanas long.
He immediately rose from his quiet chamber and, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, went to the great ocean and walked back and forth upon the remains of a long-dead corpse.
At that time, Dharmaruci spoke this verse:
"Through countless kalpas of birth and death, Transmigrations have been beyond measure; The body is like a house of suffering, A vessel for the accumulation of impurities."
Each seeks their own security, yet repeatedly undergoes suffering and affliction.
Even if they were to see their own bodies again and desire to build a dwelling for them,
all their limbs and joints would be ruined, and their physical form could not remain whole.
"The mind has already detached from all conditioned formations, and craving is forever extinguished without remainder;
no longer receiving this physical form, one dwells eternally in bliss within Nirvāṇa.

At that time, after the Venerable Dharmaruci had spoken these verses, he immediately vanished from that place and arrived at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, proceeding to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing Dharmaruci approaching,
spoke to him thus: "Excellent, Dharmaruci!"
"I have been here for a long time.
Dharmaruci addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
We have been here for a long time.
At that moment, the Elder and the various bhikṣus each gave rise to this thought:
"This Dharmaruci has always remained by the World-Honored One's side; yet now the World-Honored One says:
'Excellent, Dharmaruci!'"
"He has been here for a long time.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the minds of the bhikṣus and wishing to sever their doubts, addressed the bhikṣus:
"It was not because Dharmaruci had been here for a long time that I spoke this meaning."

The reason for this is that in the past, incalculable eons ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat, named Dīpaṃkara. He resided in the great kingdom of Padma, together with a great assembly of one hundred and forty-eight thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was beyond reckoning; kings, ministers, officials, and the common people all came to make offerings and provide for whatever they required.

"At that time, there was a brahmin named Yaññadatta who lived on the slopes of the Himalayas. He had mastered all secret prophecies, astronomy, and geography, possessing profound and extensive knowledge of them; he was also fully conversant with scripts, commentaries, and written characters. Furthermore, he understood the recitation of a single verse of five hundred words concerning the marks of a Great Man, and he served the fire-gods, the sun, the moon, and the constellations, teaching five hundred disciples day and night without weariness."
The brahmin Yajñadatta had a disciple named Meghadundubhi, whose countenance was so upright and handsome as to be rare in the world, and whose hair was a deep blue-black.

This brahmin Meghadundubhi was intelligent and possessed vast knowledge; there was no subject he did not master. He was constantly loved and respected by Yajñadatta, never leaving his side for even a moment.
At that time, the spells and incantations practiced by the brahmin were all fully mastered.
Then, the brahmacārin Meghadundubhi thought to himself:
"That which I ought to learn has now been entirely completed."
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"According to what is recorded in the scriptures, those students among the brahmins who have mastered the arts ought to repay their teacher's kindness.
Moreover, I now know all that is to be learned; it is fitting for me now to repay my teacher's kindness."
"However, I am poor and destitute, possessing nothing at all with which to make offerings to my teacher;
it would be best for me to go to other lands to seek what is required.
At that time, the brahmin Meghadundubhi went to his teacher's place and said to him:
"The technical arts studied by a brahmin have now all been mastered; furthermore, as recorded in the scriptures, one who excels in any field of learning ought to repay their teacher's kindness."

However, we are poor and destitute, possessing no gold, silver, or precious jewels with which to make offerings; we now wish to travel throughout the realm to seek wealth and goods in order to provide for our teacher.
At that time, the Brahmin Yajñadatta thought to himself:
"This brahmacārin Meghadundubhi is dear to me; he does not leave my mind."
"If even when I am dead we cannot part, how much less so today when you wish to abandon me and depart?
What means should I now employ to ensure that you remain and stay?"
At that time, the brahmin Yajñadatta said to Meghadundubhi: "O brahmin!
There are still things that a brāhmaṇa ought to learn which you do not yet know."
At that time, the brahmin Meghadundubhi came forward and said to his teacher, "I pray you will instruct me: what is it that I have not yet recited?
Thereupon, the brahmin Yajñadatta reflected upon composing five hundred words for recitation and told Meghadundubhi:
"Now there is this scripture called the 'Recitation of Five Hundred Words'; you may receive it.
Yunlei replied, "I pray that the Master will grant it to me; I wish to recite it!"
"Monks, you should know that at that time, Yaññadatta then bestowed this five-hundred-word recitation upon his disciple.
Before many days had passed, the disciple had mastered it all with complete fluency."
At that time, the brahmin Yajñadatta said to his five hundred disciples:
"This brahmacārin Meghadundubhi is fully equipped with all technical skills; there is nothing he does not master. Therefore, let us establish a name for him and call him Atiśaya."
"This Brahmin Ulūka is of exceptionally high talent; there is nothing in astronomy or geography that he has not studied extensively, and he is fully proficient in all scripts and written characters.
Then, after several more days had passed, the Brahmin Ulūka again addressed his teacher, saying:

"I have now mastered all the technical arts and methods learned by a Brahmin. Furthermore, regarding those who possess scholarship exceeding what is recorded in the books, one ought to repay the teacher's kindness."

Furthermore, being destitute, I have no gold, silver, or precious jewels with which to make offerings to my teacher. I now wish to travel through the kingdom to seek wealth and goods for the purpose of making offerings to my teacher; I only pray that you will grant me permission!
At that time, the brahmin Yajñadatta said,
"You know the proper time.
The brahmin Atimātra prostrated at his teacher's feet and then withdrew.

"At that time, not far from the city of the great kingdom of Padma, there was a gathering of many brahmins assembled in one place, desiring to perform a grand sacrifice together and also wishing to engage in debate."
At that time, eighty-four thousand brahmins gathered together.

The foremost elder among them was likewise one who recited the treatises of the non-Buddhist paths; there was nothing he did not master, for he fully understood astronomy, geography, and the portents of the stars and constellations.

When each was about to depart, they presented five hundred units of gold, a golden staff, a golden water pitcher, and one thousand oxen as offerings to their teacher, bestowing them upon the foremost senior monk.

At that time, the brahmin Atimuktaka heard that not far from the great kingdom of Padma, eighty-four thousand brahmins had gathered in one place; it was announced that to anyone who excelled in the trial of skills, they would grant five hundred measures of gold, a golden staff, a golden water-pitcher, and a thousand large oxen.
At that time, the brahmin Atreya thought to himself:
"Why should I now go from house to house begging?
It would be better to go to that great assembly and compete with them in our respective skills."
At that time, the brahmin Atidhṛti went to where the great assembly was.
Then, seeing the brahmin Atidhṛti from afar, the many brahmins each called out in loud voices, saying:
"Excellent! Good!"
"The master of this shrine has now attained great benefit, for he has caused the Great Brahmā himself to descend.
At that time, eighty-four thousand brahmins each rose together to welcome him, speaking with one voice:
"Welcome, Great Brahmā Deva!"
At that time, the brahmin Atimuktaka had this thought:
"These brahmins claim that I am Brahmā, yet I am not Brahmā."
At that time, the brahmin Atidhīra said to the other brahmins:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Venerable friends!
Do not address me as 'Brahmā.
Have you not heard it said?"
"To the north of the Snowy Mountains, there is a great brahmin master named Yajñadatta, who is thoroughly versed in all matters of astronomy and geography.
The brahmins said, "We have heard of him, but we have not seen him."
The brahmin Ulūka said, "I am his disciple; my name is Ulūka.
At that time, the brahmin Ulūka addressed the foremost elder seated at the head of that assembly, saying:
“If there is one who knows this craft, let him explain it to me.
At that time, the foremost elder among that assembly recited the three baskets of the craft to the brahmin Uttara without any omission or error.
Then, the brahmin Atula spoke again to that senior monk, saying:
"A single verse consists of five hundred words; you may now recite it.
At that time, the senior monk said:
"I do not understand this meaning: what is this 'one sentence of five hundred words'?
At that time, the brahmin Uttara replied, "Venerable sirs!..."
"In silence, listen to this one phrase of five hundred words concerning the marks of a Great Man.
"Monks, you should know that at that time, the brahmin Atreya recited the arts of the Three Piṭakas as well as this one phrase of five hundred words concerning the marks of a Great Man."
At that time, eighty-four thousand brahmins marveled at what they had never before experienced, exclaiming:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
"From the beginning, we have not heard a single word or five hundred phrases regarding the marks of a Great Man; now, Venerable One, it is fitting that you occupy the foremost seat at the head.
At that time, the brahmin Atula moved the other person from that head seat and sat down himself in the foremost seat at the head.
At that time, the senior monk of that assembly, harboring intense anger, made this vow:
"Now this man has displaced me from my seat and taken its place for himself."
"Whatever merit may arise from the scriptures I now recite, my observance of the precepts, and my ascetic practices, I hereby pledge it all:
'In whatever place this person is born, and whatever deeds they wish to accomplish, I shall constantly ruin their success.'"

At that time, the patron of the offering immediately brought forth five hundred measures of gold, a golden staff, a golden water-pitcher, one thousand head of cattle, and a beautiful woman, presenting them to the presiding elder to offer as a blessing.
At that time, the Elder addressed the host, saying:
"I shall now accept these five hundred ounces of gold, along with the golden staff and the golden water-pitcher, to use for making offerings to my teacher."
"This woman, along with the thousand oxen, shall be returned to their owner.
The reason for this is that I do not practice desire, nor do I accumulate wealth.
At that time, the brahmin Uttara, having accepted this golden staff and water jar, proceeded to the great kingdom of Padma.
The king’s name was Prabhāsa.
At that time, the king invited the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and the assembly of bhikṣus to provide them with offerings of food, clothing, and other necessities.
Then, the king issued a proclamation throughout the city:
"Should there be among the people any fragrant flowers, none shall be sold; should any sell them, they shall be severely punished.
I myself will go out to purchase them; you need not resell them."
He further commanded the people to sweep and sprinkle the ground until it was pure, ensuring there were no traces of dust, sand, or filth;
they hung silk banners and canopies, smeared the ground with fragrant liquid, and performed music and dance in numbers beyond reckoning.
At that time, having seen this, the brahmin asked a traveler on the road:
"What day is this? Why have the roads been swept and sprinkled, the impurities cleared away, and banners, streamers, and canopies hung in such incalculable numbers?"
"Could it be that the king or the crown prince has taken a bride? The traveler replied,
"Does the brahmin not know?"

The King of the great kingdom of Padma has now invited the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara; because he is providing offerings of food, clothing, and other necessities, he has leveled and smoothed the roads and hung up silken banners and canopies.
"Moreover, the secret records of the brahmins also contain this statement:

'The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; he appears only from time to time and is truly not easily seen, just like the udumbara flower, which appears only from time to time.'"
"This is also like that: the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare to encounter.
Furthermore, there is a saying in the Brahmin scriptures:
'There are two persons who appear in the world and are very difficult to encounter.'"
Who are these two persons?
They are the Tathāgata and the Wheel-turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
It is extremely difficult for these two persons to appear and to encounter them.
At that time, he again had this thought:
"I should now swiftly repay the Buddha's kindness; for now, I shall offer these five hundred ounces of gold to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara."
He further thought to himself:
"According to what is recorded in the scriptures, the Tathāgata does not accept gold, silver, or precious jewels;
I shall take these five hundred taels of gold to purchase flowers and incense to scatter upon the Tathāgata."
At that time, the brahmin immediately entered the city to seek the purchase of flowers and incense.
Then, a passerby in the city informed him, saying:
"Does the brahmin not know?
"The king has issued a decree that anyone who sells fragrant flowers shall be severely punished.
At that time, the brahmin Uttara thought to himself:
"I am unfortunate; I seek flowers but cannot obtain them. What shall I do?"
He then returned and went out of the city, standing outside the gate.
At that time, there was a Brahmin girl named Sumaṅgalā who was carrying a water jar to fetch water, holding five flowers in her hand.
Having seen this, the brahmin said to the woman:
"Sister! I now require flowers; I pray that you will sell them to me."
The brahmin girl said: "When was I ever your sister?
Do you even know my parents?"
At that time, the brahmin Atimuktaka again had this thought:
"This woman’s character is broad and expansive; her intent lies in jest.
He then spoke to her again:
“Worthy lady! I shall give you the price; do not offer me these flowers as a gift.
The Brahmin girl said:
"Have you not heard that the Great King has issued a strict decree that flowers may not be sold?
The Brahmin said, "Virtuous lady!"
"This matter is not painful; the King cannot do anything to you!
I must have these five flowers immediately. If I obtain these flowers, you shall receive a high price."
The brahmin girl said, "You are in urgent need of flowers; what do you intend to do with them?
The brahmin replied:
"I have now seen a fertile ground where I wish to plant these flowers," the Brahmin woman said.
"These flowers have already been severed from their roots; they can never grow again."
"How can you say that I wish to plant it?
The brahmin replied, "According to what I have observed today regarding fertile fields, even if one plants dead ashes there, they will still sprout; how much more so this flower?"
The Brahmin woman asked,
"What kind of fertile field is it where seeds sown in dead ashes nevertheless sprout?
The Brahmin replied:
“O virtuous woman!
There is a Buddha, a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha named Dīpaṃkara, who has appeared in the world.
The brahmin girl said:
"What kind of person was the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara?
The brahmin then replied to the girl:
"The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara possessed such virtues, such precepts, and had perfected all meritorious qualities."
The brahmin girl asked,
"If one possesses merit, what kind of blessing does one seek?
The brahmin replied:
“‘I vow that in my future lives I shall be like the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara; may my prohibitive precepts and merits also be thus.
The Brahmin girl said: ‘If you promise me that we shall be husband and wife in every life, I will give you these flowers.’”
The brahmin said,
"In what I now practice, my mind is not attached to desire.
The brahmin’s daughter said:
"Just as my present body does not seek to be your wife, may I become your wife in a future life.
The brahmin Atimuktaka said, "In the conduct of a Bodhisattva, there is no sense of attachment or possessiveness; if you were to become my wife, it would surely destroy my mind."
The Brahmin’s daughter said:
"I shall never frustrate your intention to give; even if you were to offer my own body to others, I would never allow it to hinder your mind of generosity."
At that time, he took five hundred gold coins and used them to purchase five flowers, which he gave to the woman; they made a vow together and then went their separate ways.

"At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, having reached the proper hour, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the great kingdom of Padma, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him."

At that time, the brahmin Suprabuddha saw from afar the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, whose countenance was upright and majestic; all who saw him were filled with joy. His faculties were tranquil, his gait was unhindered, and he possessed the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
It was like clear water, free from turbidity, its radiance shining through without any obstruction.
It was also like a mountain of jewels, rising above all other mountains.
Having seen this, he conceived a heart of joy; taking these five stalks of flowers from the Tathāgata, he went to the presence of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
Having arrived, he stood to one side.
Then, the brahmin Atidhīra addressed the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, saying:
"I pray that you will accept me; if the World-Honored One does not grant me a prediction of enlightenment now, I shall take my own life right here and do not wish for this birth to continue."
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin! These five stalks of flowers cannot be offered to one who has attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
The brahmin addressed him, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain to me the dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva!
Dīpaṃkara Buddha replied:
"The conduct of a bodhisattva is such that there is nothing held back or cherished.
At that time, the brahmin spoke in verse:
"I would not dare to take my parents And give them as a gift to another."
The Buddhas, the True Persons, and one's parents—these too one does not dare to give away.
The sun and moon as they traverse the world—these two cannot be given;
all else may be given, for when the mind is resolved, there is no difficulty.
At that time, Dīpaṃkara Buddha again addressed the brahmin with these verses:
"The giving you have described Is not as the Tathāgata has taught.
You must endure suffering for billions of eons To give away your head, body, ears, and eyes."
"Wife, children, kingdom, and treasures; Chariots, horses, and servants— If you are able to grant these, I shall now bestow upon you my prediction.
At that time, the young brahmin (maṇava) spoke again in verse:
"Even if a great mountain blazes like fire, I could bear it upon my head for billions of kalpas;
yet I cannot destroy my resolve for the Way—only pray that you grant me the prediction of enlightenment at this time."
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara remained silent and said nothing.
Then, the brahmin took five stalks of flowers in his hand, knelt with his right knee on the ground, scattered them over the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, and spoke these words:
"By this merit and blessing, may I in a future age become like the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—without any difference!"
He then immediately disheveled his hair and stood upon the mud,
saying, "If the Tathāgata will grant me a prediction of enlightenment, let him then step over my hair with his feet.
Bhikṣus, you should know:
At that time, Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, observing the thoughts in the mind of the brahmin, addressed him, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become Śākyamuni Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

“At that time, the brahmin Supraṇidhi had a fellow student named Dharmaruci who was standing beside the Tathāgata. He saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowing the prophecy upon the brahmin Supraṇidhi, and he also saw [the Buddha] tread upon his hair with his foot.”
Having seen this, he spoke thus:
"How can these shaven-headed śramaṇas bear to lift their feet and tread upon the hair of such pure brahmins?
This is not the conduct of human beings!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"As for that brahmin Yajñadatta at that time, could he have been anyone else?
Do not view it in this way."
The reason for this is that he who was Yaññadatta at that time is now King Śuddhodana;
and he who was the foremost of the eighty-four thousand brahmins at that time is now Devadatta himself.
The brahmin named Atiśaya at that time was none other than myself.
The brahmin girl who sold flowers then is now Gopī.
The master of the sacrifice at that time is now the brahmin Daṇḍapāṇi.
At that time, Dharmaruci produced unwholesome sounds through his speech; he is this very Dharmaruci of today.

Furthermore, throughout incalculable kalpas, Dharmaruci constantly took birth as an animal, until finally receiving a body as a fish in the great ocean, seven hundred yojanas in length. Having died there, he was reborn in this world, where he associated with virtuous friends, remained constantly in their proximity, practiced all wholesome dharmas, and attained sharp faculties.
For these reasons, I said: "I have been here for a long time.
Dharmaruci also made this same declaration:
"So it is, World-Honored One! I have been here for a long time. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
"One should always cultivate the conduct of body, speech, and mind. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of those who resemble lions and those who resemble sheep; listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well.
The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"How is it that such a person resembles a lion?
In this regard, bhikṣus,
there may be someone who receives offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick."

Having received it, he ate it himself without giving rise to a mind of attachment, nor did he have any desire; he gave rise to no conceptualizations and had no such thoughts at all, for he knew for himself the Dharma of transcendence.
Even if one does not obtain gain or offerings, one should not give rise to distracted thoughts, nor harbor a mind of increase or decrease.
It is like a lion king devouring small animals; at that time, the king of beasts does not think, "This one is good" or "This one is not good.
He gives rise to no mind of attachment, has no desire, and does not produce any conceptualizations.

This person is also like this: if they receive offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, or medicine for the sick and weak, having received them, they consume them without giving rise to thoughts of attachment;
even if they do not receive them, they likewise have no such thoughts.

"It is just as if there were a person who receives from others offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick; having received them, he immediately consumes them for himself, giving rise to a mind of attachment and a sense of craving, and failing to know the path to liberation.
Even if he does not receive them, he constantly gives rise to such thoughts."
Having received such offerings, that person becomes arrogant toward the bhikṣus and disparages others, saying:
"The robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick that I am able to obtain, these bhikṣus are unable to obtain."

"It is just as if there were a single sheep among a great flock; having left the flock, it went to a large heap of dung. After this sheep had eaten its fill of excrement, it returned to the flock and became arrogant, saying:
'I am able to obtain fine food, whereas these other sheep cannot obtain any.'"

"It is just like this: if there is a person who, having obtained gains, robes, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick, gives rise to various distracted thoughts and a mind of defiled attachment, he then approaches the bhikṣus and becomes arrogant, saying:
'I am able to obtain offerings, whereas these bhikṣus are not able to obtain offerings.'"
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves to be like the lion king, and not like sheep. Thus, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there are sentient beings who know how to repay kindness, such persons are worthy of veneration; they do not forget even a small favor, let alone a great one!”
Even if one were to be separated from this place by a thousand yojanas or a hundred thousand yojanas, it would not be considered far; such a person is no different from being close to me.
Why is this so? Monks, you should know that I always praise those who possess a sense of reciprocity and gratitude.
Those sentient beings who do not know how to repay kindness do not even remember great favors, let alone small ones!
Such persons do not draw near to me, nor do I draw near to them; even if they were wearing a saṃghāṭī robe at my side, such a person would still be far away.
The reason for this is that I never speak of those who lack reciprocity.
Therefore, monks, you should be mindful of reciprocity; do not learn to be ungrateful.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is someone who is indolent and plants unwholesome deeds, they will suffer loss in their endeavors.
If one can be diligent and not indolent, this is most excellent; for then there will be an increase in all wholesome qualities."

The reason for this is that although Maitreya Bodhisattva was destined to become a Buddha, a Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha after thirty kalpas, I have used the power of my diligence and my courageous mind to place Maitreya behind me.
All the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all attained Buddhahood through valor and diligence.
By this expedient means, you should know that indolence is suffering; it leads to the commission of various evil deeds and causes harm in all matters.
If one can be diligent, courageous, and firm of mind, all wholesome merits will increase. Therefore, monks,
you should be mindful of diligence and not be indolent.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7 (Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“An araṇya-dwelling bhikṣu should practice two dharmas.
What are these two dharmas?
They are namely śamatha and vipaśyanā.”

If a forest-dwelling bhikṣu attains rest and tranquility, he will then achieve perfection in the precepts, maintain his dignified deportment, refrain from violating prohibitions, and cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues.
Furthermore, when a forest-dwelling bhikṣu has attained this contemplation, he then contemplates this suffering and knows it as it truly is.
He contemplates the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering, knowing them as they truly are.

Having observed in this way, his mind was liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsava*), and his mind was liberated from the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avijjā-āsava*). He then attained the knowledge of liberation:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further state of existence"—he knew this as it truly is.
"All the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas attained their realization through these two dharmas.
This is because, when a Bodhisattva sat beneath the King of Trees, he first contemplated these two dharmas: śamatha and vipaśyanā."
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains śamatha, they are then able to subdue the maras and their adversaries;

if, moreover, a bodhisattva attains vipaśyanā, they immediately achieve the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā) and realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Therefore, monks, a monk who dwells in the forest should seek skillful means and practice these two dharmas. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is an araṇyaka bhikṣu dwelling in a secluded place, not among the assembly, he should always maintain reverence and give rise to a heart of joy.”

Furthermore, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu stays in a secluded and quiet place, yet lacks reverence and does not give rise to a joyful heart, even if he is among a great assembly and is criticized by others for not knowing the dharma of forest-dwellers, they will say:
"This forest-dwelling bhikṣu has no heart of reverence and does not give rise to joy!"

"Furthermore, bhikṣus! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who stays in a secluded and quiet place, not among the crowds, should always be diligent and never indolent; he must fully comprehend the essentials of all dharmas."

Furthermore, if a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who stays in a secluded place develops a mind of indolence and commits various evil deeds, he will be criticized by others in the midst of the assembly, saying:
"This forest-dwelling bhikṣu is lazy; he possesses no diligence."

"Therefore, bhikṣus! A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who stays in a secluded place rather than among the multitude should always humble his mind and give rise to a heart of joy. He must not be indolent or arrogant, nor lacking in reverence; he should practice mindfulness and diligence, with a mind that does not waver, so as to fully perfect all wholesome dharmas."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are two kinds of people who cannot skillfully preach the Dharma. Who are these two?
It is extremely difficult to preach the Dharma of faith to one who lacks faith;”
To preach the Dharma of giving to those who are stingy and greedy is also extremely difficult.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!

If one preaches the Dharma of faith to a person devoid of faith, they will immediately give rise to anger and a mind of malice; it is just like a dog that, when its nose is further injured, becomes all the more enraged.
"O bhikṣus! It is just the same in this case:
when one who lacks faith is told the Dharma of faith, they immediately give rise to anger and conceive a mind of malice.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!"

When a person who is stingy and greedy is taught the Dharma of giving, they immediately give rise to anger and a mind of malice; it is like a festering ulcer that has not yet ripened, which is further subjected to the cutting of a blade—the pain being unbearable.
This is also like that: when a person who is stingy and greedy is taught the Dharma of giving, they become even more angry and give rise to a mind of malice and harm.
This, O bhikṣus, is what is meant.
"These two types of persons are difficult to teach the Dharma.
Furthermore, bhikṣu, there are two other types of persons who are easy to teach the Dharma."
What are these two?
To those who possess faith, one teaches the Dharma of faith; to those who are not stingy or greedy, one teaches the Dharma of giving. If, O bhikṣu!
When one who possesses faith is taught the Dharma of faith, they immediately attain joy, and their mind does not waver or regret.
It is just as when a sick person is told of the medicine that eliminates illness; they immediately recover.
It is the same in this case: when a person of faith is taught the Dharma of faith, they immediately attain joy and their mind does not waver.
Furthermore, when a person free from greed is taught the Dharma of giving, they immediately attain joy and have no sense of regret.
It is just as when there is a man or woman who is handsome and upright, taking pleasure in bathing their body, hands, and face;
then another person comes and presents them with fine flowers, whereupon their complexion becomes even more radiant;
furthermore, one presents that person with fine garments and ornaments, and having received them, that person feels all the more joy in their heart.
"This is also like that: when one who is free from stinginess and greed is taught the Dharma of giving, they immediately attain joy and have no sense of regret.
This is what is meant, O Bhikṣu!"
"These two types of people are easy to teach the Dharma.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in faith, and you should also train yourselves in generosity; do not harbor stinginess or greed."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“There are two dharmas which, when practiced by an ordinary person, lead to great merit, bring about a great karmic fruition, result in the taste of the Deathless, and lead to the state of the Unconditioned.
What are these two dharmas?
To make offerings to one's parents is called the two persons who obtain great merit and achieve a great karmic fruition.
Furthermore, if one makes offerings to a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood, one obtains great merit and attains a great fruition.
"Monks, it is said that giving to these two persons yields great merit, brings about a great reward, attains the taste of the Deathless, and leads to the state of the Unconditioned."
Therefore, monks, always mindfully practice filial piety and provide for your parents. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 11 (11) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“It is impossible to repay the kindness of two people who have taught you to do good.”
What are these two?
They are one’s father and mother.
Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Suppose there were someone who placed their father on their left shoulder and their mother on their right shoulder, carrying them for ten million years, providing them with clothing, food, bedding, and medicine for their illnesses; even if they were to discharge excrement and urine upon their shoulders, they still could not repay their debt of gratitude.

"Monks, you should know that the kindness of parents is profound: they embrace and nourish their child, protecting them at all times and never missing the proper seasons, so that the child may behold the sun and the moon."
By this expedient means, one knows that this debt of gratitude is difficult to repay. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
You should make offerings to your parents and always be filial and obedient, never missing the proper occasion.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
12. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Paṇḍita addressed his younger brother Cūḍapanthaka, saying:
"If you cannot maintain the precepts, you shall return to being a layperson.
When Cūḍapanthaka heard these words, he went to the gate of the Jetavana Monastery and stood there weeping.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his purified divine eye, beheld the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka standing outside the gate, weeping piteously and unable to restrain himself.
Then, the World-Honored One rose from his quiet chamber and, as if walking for exercise, went to the gate of the Jeta Grove Monastery and addressed Cūḍapanthaka, saying: "Bhikṣu!"
"For what reason are you weeping here? Cūḍapanthaka replied,
"World-Honored One!"
Her elder brother saw her being driven away and said, "If you cannot maintain the precepts, return to being a layperson; you need not remain here.
For this reason, she weeps in sorrow.
The World-Honored One said, "Bhikṣu!
Do not harbor fear. My attainment of supreme, perfect enlightenment was not dependent upon your brother, Paṇḍita, for me to have realized the Way."
At that time, the World-Honored One took Cūḍapanthaka by the hand, led him to a quiet room, and instructed him to take a seat. The World-Honored One further instructed him to take up a broom, saying:
"Recite these characters; what do these characters mean?"
At that time, Cūḍapanthaka could recite "sweep" (saṃmārj), but he forgot "broom" (saṃkāra);
if he recited "broom," he would forget "sweep.
Thus, the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka spent several days reciting these two words, "sweep" and "broom."
Furthermore, this sweeping is also called "removing defilement. Cūḍapanthaka then thought to himself:
"What is that which is removed?
What is that which is the defilement?"
"Dirt" refers to ashes, soil, tiles, and stones; "removing" refers to purification.
He further thought: "For what reason does the World-Honored One instruct and admonish me with this?"
"I shall now contemplate this meaning.
As he contemplated this meaning, he further thought:
"Now there is also dust and grime upon my own body; I shall use myself as an analogy. What is it that removes them?"
"What is defilement? He further thought: "The fetters and bonds are defilement;
wisdom is their removal. I can now use the broom of wisdom to sweep away these fetters and bonds."
At that time, the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka contemplated the five aggregates of clinging as they arise and pass away:
namely, this form, the origin of form, and the cessation of form; and likewise feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as they arise and pass away.

At that time, having reflected upon these five aggregates of clinging, his mind was liberated from the outflow of sensual desire; his mind was liberated from the outflow of existence and the outflow of ignorance.
Having attained liberation, he then attains the knowledge of liberation:

"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further undergoing of existence in a womb"—he knows this as it truly is.
The Venerable Cūḍapanthaka then became an arhat.
Having become an arhat, he immediately rose from his seat, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
He said to the Blessed One:
"Now I possess knowledge; now I possess wisdom; now I have understood the broom.
The Blessed One told him:
“Bhikṣu! How do you understand this? Cūḍapanthaka replied:
"To remove is called wisdom; defilement is called fetters.
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent!"
“Monk! As you have said, that which is removed is wisdom, and that which is defiled is the fetter.
At that time, the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka addressed these verses to the World-Honored One:
"Now this recitation is sufficient, just as the Venerable One has taught;
wisdom can eliminate the fetters, not by means of any other practice.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Bhikkhus! It is as you have said: it is by means of wisdom, and not by any other means.
At that time, the Venerable One, having heard what the Blessed One had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
13 (13) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these two things that should not be honored or attended to, nor are they worthy of attachment; they are cast aside by the world.
What are these two things?
The meeting with those one hates and loathes is something that should not be honored or attended to, nor is it worthy of attachment; it is cast aside by the world.”
The separation from those one loves cannot be honored or welcomed, nor is it worthy of attachment; it is that which is discarded by the world.
Thus, bhikṣus, there are these two things which the world does not delight in and which cannot be honored or welcomed.
“Monks! Furthermore, there are two things that the people of the world do not abandon.
What are these two things?
Separation from those one hates and dislikes is what people of the world delight in;
the gathering together of those one loves and cherishes is deeply beloved and respected, and is what people of the world delight in.
This is what is meant, O Bhikṣu!
"There are these two things that the world delights in:
'I shall now speak of the meeting with those one hates and the separation from those one loves;
and further, I shall speak of the separation from those one hates and the meeting with those one loves. What is the meaning of this?"
"What is the reason for this? The bhikṣus replied:
"The World-Honored One is the King of All Dharmas; we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it to us. Having heard it, the bhikṣus shall together practice it accordingly."
The World-Honored One said:
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well."
I shall explain this to you in detail.
Monks! These two dharmas arise from craving, are born from craving, are accomplished by craving, and originate from craving.
"You should train yourselves to eliminate craving so that it does not arise. In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 11. *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 12.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-one: The Three Jewels (Triratna). Section One. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three virtues of taking refuge.”
What are the three? They are:
taking refuge in the Buddha as the foremost virtue, taking refuge in the Dharma as the second virtue, and taking refuge in the Sangha as the third virtue.
What is meant by "taking refuge in the Buddha as a virtue"?

Among all sentient beings—whether bipeds, quadrupeds, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; whether with perception or without perception; up to the Niṣyanda heaven above—all of whom the Tathāgata surpasses as the most honored and supreme, such that none can equal him.
From the cow one obtains milk; from milk, curd; from curd, butter; and from butter, clarified butter (ghṛta).
Yet, among these, clarified butter is the most honored and supreme, with nothing that can equal it.
