It is likewise here: among all sentient beings—whether two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; whether with perception or without perception—up to the heavens of the Nimi-devas, the Tathāgata is the most honored and the most supreme, with none able to equal him.
All sentient beings who serve the Buddha are said to be serving the foremost virtue.
By attaining this foremost virtue, they receive the blessings of the heavens and among humans; this is called the foremost virtue.
"What is meant by taking refuge in the Dharma?
It refers to all dharmas:
those with outflows and those without outflows; conditioned and unconditioned; desireless and undefiled; cessation and nirvana."
However, among all phenomena, the dharma of nirvāṇa is the most honored and supreme, with nothing that can equal it.
From the cow one obtains milk; from milk one obtains curd; from curd one obtains butter; and from butter one obtains clarified butter (ghṛta).
Yet, within these, clarified butter is the most honored and supreme, with nothing that can equal it.
This is also like this regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*):

whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), free from desire (*vītarāga*) or unstained (*asaṃkliṣṭa*), or cessation (*kṣaya*) and nirvana (*nirvāṇa*).
Yet among all these phenomena, the dharma of nirvana is the most honored and supreme, such that nothing can equal it.

Any sentient beings who serve the Dharma are said to be serving the foremost virtue; by attaining this foremost virtue, they receive the blessings of the heavens and among humans—this is called the foremost virtue.
"What is meant by taking refuge in the Noble Sangha?
That which is called the 'Noble Sangha' refers to the great assembly, the great multitude of sentient beings with form.
Among all living beings, the Tathāgata’s Saṅgha is the most honored and supreme within this assembly; none can equal it."
From the cow one obtains milk; from milk, curd; from curd, butter; and from butter, clarified butter (ghṛta).
Yet among these, clarified butter is the most honored and supreme, with nothing able to surpass it.

This is also like that: what is called the "Noble Assembly" or the "Great Gathering" is such that, among all sentient beings who possess form, the Tathāgata’s Saṃgha is the most honored and supreme within this assembly, with none able to equal it.
This is called the foremost virtue of service; by attaining this foremost virtue, one receives the blessings of the heavens and among humans—this is termed the foremost virtue.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"First, serve the Buddha, The most honored, beyond whom there is none;
Next, serve the Dharma, Free from desire and without attachment."
To reverently serve the assembly of noble sages is the most excellent field of merit;
such a person possesses the foremost wisdom and receives blessings before all others.
Whether among gods or humans, they shall stand as the true guide for the multitude.
They shall also obtain the most sublime seat, naturally partaking of the nectar of immortality;
their bodies shall be clothed in robes of the seven treasures, and they shall be revered by all people;
their precepts shall be perfectly complete, and their faculties shall be without deficiency or leakage.
One also attains the ocean of wisdom, gradually reaching the realm of Nirvāṇa;
for those who possess these three refuges, proceeding toward the Path is not difficult.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these three types of meritorious action. What are the three?
Generosity is a meritorious action; equanimity is a meritorious action; and reflection is a meritorious action.”
"What is meant by 'the meritorious deed of giving'?

Suppose there is a person who, with an open heart, practices generosity toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the extremely destitute, the solitary, and those who have no one to turn to; providing food to those in need of food, drink to those in need of drink, clothing, meals, bedding and furniture, medicinal requisites for the sick, incense and flowers, and lodging—giving whatever they require according to their needs without any sense of stinginess—this is called the meritorious deed of giving."
"What is meant by 'equanimity as a meritorious action'?
It is when a person refrains from killing and refrains from stealing, always possesses a sense of shame and remorse, and does not give rise to evil thoughts."
He neither steals nor pilfers; he delights in giving to others and is free from greed or stinginess. His speech is harmonious and elegant, never wounding the hearts of others.
He does not commit adultery with others; he personally cultivates pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), being fully content with his own appearance.
Furthermore, he does not speak falsely, but always maintains utmost sincerity and refrains from deceitful speech; thus he is respected by the people of the world, with neither praise nor blame.
He also does not drink alcohol and always knows how to avoid disorder.

Furthermore, with a mind of loving-kindness, he pervades one direction; he does the same for the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the eight cardinal points and the zenith and nadir, filling them all to the extent that it is immeasurable, limitless, boundless, and incalculable.
With this mind of loving-kindness, he universally covers all beings, causing them to attain peace and security.

Furthermore, with the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, he fills one direction; he does the same for the second, third, and fourth directions. He completely fills the eight directions, as well as above and below, immeasurably, boundlessly, and beyond calculation.
To completely fill [the world] with this mind of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity is called the meritorious karma of impartiality.
What is that dharma called "meritorious karma through reflection"?
In this regard, monks!
One cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on dispassion, relying on non-observation, relying on cessation, and relying on renunciation.

One cultivates the awakening factor of dharma-discernment, cultivates the awakening factor of energy, cultivates the awakening factor of rapture, cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility, cultivates the awakening factor of concentration, and cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity, relying on dispassion, relying on non-observation, relying on cessation, and relying on renunciation.
This is what is called reflecting upon meritorious action. "Thus it is, bhikṣu!"
"There are these three meritorious karmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Generosity and equanimity, The compassionate mind, and protective reflection;"
There are these three states which the wise should cultivate;
they receive their retribution here in this world, and likewise in the heavens.
Because these three states exist, one will certainly be born in heaven—of this there is no doubt.
"Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to investigate these three bases. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three causes and conditions by which consciousness comes to enter a womb.”
What are the three? In this regard, bhikṣus,
when the mother has desire and the parents come together in one place and dwell there overnight, yet the external consciousness does not descend to enter, then conception does not take place.
Furthermore, if the consciousness seeking rebirth arrives but the parents do not unite, conception does not occur.
Moreover, if the mother lacks desire while the parents are together, and at that time the father’s desire is intense while the mother is not very ardent, conception does not occur.
Furthermore, if the father and mother come together, but the mother’s desire is intense while the father is not ardent, conception does not occur.
Moreover, if the father and mother come together, but the father has a wind disorder (*vāta*) and the mother has a cold disorder (*śīta*), conception does not occur.
Furthermore, if the father and mother come together in one place, but the mother has a wind-disorder (*vāta*) while the father has a cold-disorder (*śīta*), then conception does not occur.

Again, if at some time the father and mother come together in one place, but the father’s body is excessively dominated by water-humors (*ap-dhātu*) while the mother has no such affliction, then conception does not occur.

"Furthermore, if at some time the father and mother come together in one place, but the father possesses the signs for a son while the mother lacks the signs for a son, then conception does not occur.
If at some time the father and mother come together in one place, but the mother possesses the signs for a son while the father lacks the signs for a son, then conception does not occur."
Furthermore, if at any time both parents are mutually without the conditions for procreation, conception does not occur.
Moreover, if at any time the consciousness-principle (*vijñāna*) enters the womb but the father is away on a journey, conception does not occur.
Furthermore, there may be times when the father and mother ought to come together, yet the mother has traveled far away and is not present; in such a case, conception does not occur.

Again, there may be times when the father and mother ought to come together, yet the father’s body is afflicted by a grave illness; even if the consciousness descends at that time, conception will not take place.

Furthermore, there may be times when the father and mother are gathered in one place and the consciousness descends, yet because the mother’s body suffers from a grave illness, conception does not occur.
Again, there may be times when the father and mother are gathered in one place and the consciousness descends, yet because both the father and mother suffer from illness, conception does not occur.

"Furthermore, monks! When the father and mother come together in one place, and the parents are free from illness, and the consciousness-element (vijñāna) descends, and furthermore, the parents are both capable of procreating a child—then conception occurs."
These are called the three causes and conditions by which one enters the womb.
Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to sever these three causes and conditions. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and possess a heart of profound faith, and who serve and attend upon their parents, brothers, kinsmen, family members, friends, and acquaintances, they should establish them in three states so that they do not waver.”
What are the three?

One should give rise to joy and remain unmoving in mind toward the Tathāgata—him who is the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
“Furthermore, one should resolve to apply oneself to the True Dharma.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is well-expounded and unimpeded; it is most subtle and wondrous, and by means of this, one achieves the fruit.”
Thus should the wise person train to understand this!
"One should also direct one's intention toward the Noble Assembly.
The Noble Assembly of the Tathāgata is entirely harmonious, free from confusion, and fully accomplished in every dharma."
The accomplishment of morality, the accomplishment of concentration, the accomplishment of wisdom, the accomplishment of liberation, and the accomplishment of the vision and knowledge of liberation.

What is called the Noble Assembly consists of the four pairs and eight classes, the twelve types of noble ones; this is the Tathāgata’s Noble Assembly, worthy of honor and esteem, and it is the unsurpassed field of merit in the world.
Any bhikṣus who train in these three bases will achieve great fruit and reward.
Thus, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kokālika went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, that bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The conduct of these bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana is extremely wicked; they have committed various evil deeds."
The World-Honored One said:
"Do not speak such words.
You have given rise to a heart of joy toward the Tathāgata; the conduct of the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana is purely virtuous and free from all evil."
At that time, the bhikṣu Kokālika addressed the World-Honored One a second and a third time, saying:
“What the Tathāgata has spoken is truly without falsehood;
yet the conduct of the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana is exceedingly evil, and they possess no roots of goodness.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Are you a fool, that you do not believe what the Tathāgata has spoken? You say:..."
"Śāriputra and the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana have committed most grievous acts.
You too have now performed these evil deeds; before long, you shall receive their retribution.

At that moment, on his very seat, the bhikṣu developed malignant sores upon his body: at first as large as mustard seeds, then like soybeans, gradually like *āmala* fruits, then like walnuts, and finally like joined palms. Pus and blood flowed forth, and when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Padma Hell.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having heard that Kokālika had passed away, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
After a short while, he withdrew to sit down and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Where has the bhikṣu Kokālika been reborn?
The World-Honored One replied:
"That person who has passed away has been reborn in the Lotus Hell.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to the World-Honored One:
"I now wish to go to that hell to convert that person."
The World-Honored One said:
"Maudgalyāyana,
there is no need to go there."
Maudgalyāyana again addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I wish to go to that hell to convert those people.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not reply.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, like a strong man bending or stretching his arm, vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared no more, arriving instead within the Padma Great Hell.
At that time, the body of the bhikṣu Kokālika was ablaze with fire, and furthermore, a hundred oxen were plowing his tongue with a plow.
At that moment, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana sat cross-legged in mid-air and snapped his fingers to address the bhikṣu.
That bhikṣu looked up and asked,
"Who are you? Maudgalyāyana replied:
“Kūṭadanta! I am a disciple of the Buddha Śākyamuni; my name is Maudgalyāyana and my clan is Kautika.
At that time, having seen Maudgalyāyana, the bhikṣu uttered these evil words:
"Having now fallen into this evil destiny, shall I still not escape you?
Having spoken these words, at that very moment, a thousand-headed ox appeared to plow his tongue.

Having seen this, Maudgalyāyana’s sorrow and distress redoubled; feeling deep remorse, he vanished from that place and returned to Śrāvastī to the presence of the World-Honored One. There, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"I told you before that you need not go there to see such an evil person."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“When a man is born, an axe is in his mouth; it is by means of evil speech that he cuts himself.”
His breath and my breath—these two are both good.
Having committed evil deeds, one falls into the evil realms; this is the most evil.
Whether finite or infinite, to direct malice toward the Tathāgata—this is the gravest of all.
"Thirteen thousand, six-one are the ash-hells; those who slander the Noble Ones fall there, having created [evil] through body and speech.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should train in three dharmas to bring their practice to fulfillment.
What are these three?
Good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind."
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes three qualities, he will well obtain happiness in this present life, and through courageous diligence, he will bring an end to the outflows (āsrava).
What are these three?
"In this regard, monks!
One whose faculties are tranquil, who knows moderation in eating, and does not neglect walking meditation—
how is it that a monk’s faculties are tranquil?

Thus, when a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he does not give rise to conceptual attachment or formative thoughts, nor does he harbor conscious recollections; he attains purity regarding the faculty of the eye and, seeking liberation through that, constantly guards the faculty of the eye.

If, when hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tactile sensations with the body, or cognizing mental objects with the mind, one does not give rise to conceptual attachment or discursive thought, but attains purity within the faculty of the mind, then by seeking liberation through that, one constantly guards the faculty of the mind.
In this way, bhikṣus, the sense faculties are tranquil.
"How does a bhikṣu know moderation in eating?
In this regard, a bhikṣu reflects on the origin of food; he does not seek it for the sake of plumpness or beauty, but only to sustain the body and maintain the four great elements."
I shall now eliminate old pains so that new ones do not arise, enabling my body to have strength to practice the Way and ensuring that the holy life (brahmacarya) is not interrupted.
It is just as when men or women develop a malignant ulcer on their bodies and apply medicinal ointments or fats to the wound.
The reason one applies ointment to a wound is to cause it to heal in due time;
this case is likewise. Monks!

One should know moderation in food and drink. In this regard, a monk reflects on the origin of his food and drink, not seeking physical plumpness or beauty, but merely desiring to sustain the body, maintain the four great elements, eliminate old pains, prevent new ones from arising, provide strength for the body so that he may practice the Way, and ensure that the holy life (brahmacarya) does not come to an end.
It is just as one greases the hubs of a heavily laden cart so that it may reach its destination with its heavy burden.

So too is it for a bhikṣu: he knows moderation in food and drink, reflecting on the origin from which it comes; he does not seek fatness or whiteness, but desires only to sustain the body, to maintain the integrity of the four great elements. "I shall now eliminate old pains and prevent new ones from arising; I shall give strength to this body so that I may practice the Way and ensure that the holy life (brahmacarya) is never interrupted."
In this way, a bhikṣu knows moderation in eating.
How does a bhikṣu not lose the practice of walking meditation?

In this regard, a bhikṣu, during both the first and last watches of the night, constantly maintains mindfulness for walking meditation; he does not miss the proper time, and always keeps his mind tied to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā).
Whether walking or sitting during the day, he contemplates the sublime Dharma and removes the hindrances.
Furthermore, during the first watch of the night, whether walking or sitting, he contemplates the sublime Dharma and removes the hindrances.
Furthermore, during the middle watch of the night, he lies on his right side and contemplates with his mind fixed upon light.
He then rises again during the final watch of the night, practices contemplation on the profound Dharma, and removes the hindrances and coverings.
In this way, a bhikṣu does not neglect walking meditation.

If there is a bhikṣu whose faculties are tranquil, who knows moderation in eating, who does not neglect walking meditation, and who constantly maintains mindfulness and fixes his attention upon the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā), this bhikṣu will attain two fruits; he will realize the state of an Anāgāmin in this very life.
It is like a skilled charioteer driving a four-horse carriage upon a level and straight road; there is no obstruction, and wherever he wishes to go, he will surely arrive without doubt.

This bhikṣu is also like this: if his faculties are tranquil, he knows moderation in eating, does not neglect walking meditation, and constantly maintains mindfulness and binds his attention to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā), then this bhikṣu attains two fruits; having exhausted the outflows (āsrava) in this present life, he becomes a non-returner (anāgāmin).
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three great afflictions. What are the three?
It is said, monks, that wind is a great affliction, phlegm is a great affliction, and cold is a great affliction.
These, monks, are called the three great afflictions; yet these three great afflictions have three excellent medicines.
What are the three?
For one suffering from wind disorders, ghee is the excellent medicine, as well as food prepared with ghee.
For one suffering from phlegm disorders, honey is the excellent medicine, as well as food prepared with honey.
For those suffering from cold, oil is an excellent medicine,
as are foods prepared with oil. Thus, bhikṣus,
these three great afflictions have these three remedies.
"In this way, monks, there are also these three great afflictions. What are the three?
Namely, greed, hatred, and delusion."
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus:
there are these three great afflictions.
Furthermore, for these three great afflictions, there are three excellent medicines."
What are the three?
When sensual desire arises, one counters it with the contemplation of impurity and cultivates the path of impurity.
When the great affliction of hatred arises, one counters it with a mind of loving-kindness and cultivates the path of loving-kindness.
The great affliction of ignorance is treated by means of wisdom, as well as by the path arising from causes and conditions.
Thus it is said, O Bhikṣu:
these three afflictions have these three medicines.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should seek skillful means to obtain these three medicines. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three types of unwholesome conduct.”
What are the three?
They are, namely, misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
These, O bhikṣus, are called [the three].
There are three types of unwholesome conduct.
One should seek skillful means to cultivate the three types of wholesome conduct. What are these three?
One who engages in misconduct of body should cultivate good conduct of body;
one who engages in misconduct of speech should cultivate good conduct of speech;
one who engages in misconduct of mind should cultivate good conduct of mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One should guard against evil conduct of the body, Cultivate good conduct of the body;
Mindful of abandoning evil conduct of the body, One should train in good conduct of the body."
One should guard against verbal misconduct, cultivate verbal good conduct, and mindfully abandon verbal misconduct; one should train in verbal good conduct.
One should guard against mental misconduct and cultivate mental good conduct.
Mindful of abandoning unwholesome conduct of mind, one should train in wholesome conduct of mind.
Wholesome is the conduct of body; so too is the conduct of speech.
Wholesome is the conduct of mind; all [conduct] is likewise thus.
Guarding speech and purifying the mind, Not committing evil deeds with the body—
By purifying these three tracks of action, One reaches the state of the Sages,
the unconditioned. "Thus it is, O bhikṣus!"
One should abandon the three unwholesome courses of action and cultivate the three wholesome courses of action. Thus,
bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, when the hour arrived, donned their robes and took up their bowls to enter the city for alms.
At that moment, the many bhikṣus had this thought:
"We have entered the city for alms, but it is still early in the day; we should now lead one another to the dwellings of the non-Buddhist brahmins."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the heterodox brahmins were.
Having arrived, they exchanged greetings with them and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin asked the śramaṇa:
"Gautama, you constantly discourse on desire, form, sensation, and perception; what is the distinction between these various discourses?"
"What we discuss is also what the śramaṇas speak; what the śramaṇas speak is also what we discuss.
Their exposition of the Dharma is the same as my exposition of the Dharma; their instruction is the same as my instruction."
At that time, having heard those words, the many bhikṣus neither praised them as good nor criticized them as evil; they immediately rose from their seats and departed.
They then thought to themselves:
"We should go and ask the World-Honored One about this matter.
At that time, a great many bhikṣus went to the place where the World-Honored One was after their meal.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, many bhikṣus went to the brahmin and asked about the causes, conditions, and the beginning and end of the matter, reporting everything in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If that brahmin were to ask such a question, you should answer his inquiry with this meaning:
'What flavor do you desire?'"
Furthermore, what fault is there?
One should abandon desire for form.
What is the gratification of form?
Furthermore, what fault is there?
One should abandon and depart from form (*rūpa*).
What is the gratification (*āsvāda*) in feeling (*vedanā*)?
"Furthermore, what fault would there be?
One should abandon and leave behind suffering.
When you respond to their questions with these words, those brahmins will remain silent and offer no reply.
Even if they were to speak, they would be unable to understand this profound meaning; consequently, their ignorance and delusion would increase, and they would fall into extreme views.
This is because it is not within their sphere of experience.
Furthermore, monks!

As for Māra and the gods of Māra, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, and non-humans—who could understand this profound meaning? This does not even need to be discussed, with the exception of the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and those among the noble assembly of the Tathāgata who have received my teaching.
"What is the flavor of desire?
It is what is called the five sensual pleasures. What are these five?"
When the eye sees forms, it gives rise to visual consciousness; one conceives intense affection and reverence for them, which is what worldly people delight in.

If the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the tongue perceives tastes, or the body perceives tactile sensations, one conceives intense affection and reverence for them, which is what worldly people delight in.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to thoughts of suffering or pleasure regarding these five desires, this is called the "taste of desire.
What are the faults of desire?
Suppose there is a son of noble family who studies various arts and crafts to provide for himself.

Some study agriculture; some study calligraphy and commentary; some study hired labor; some study arithmetic; some study stratagems and deception; some study engraving and carving; some study correspondence, traveling from there to here.

Or, one may study by serving the person of a king, avoiding neither cold nor heat; burdened by toil and hardship, lacking self-autonomy, one undergoes such arduous labor to acquire wealth and property—this constitutes the great fault of desire.
The sufferings and afflictions of the present life arise from this affection, all of which stem from craving.

Furthermore, if that son of noble family exerts such diligent effort yet fails to obtain wealth and treasures, he will then harbor sorrow and anxiety, experiencing an incalculable amount of suffering and affliction.
He then reflected to himself:
"I have exerted such labor and employed every possible stratagem, yet I have not obtained wealth.
One who is in such a situation should resolve to renounce it."
"This is what is meant by abandoning desire.

Furthermore, that son of good family may at times employ various schemes to acquire wealth; having acquired such wealth, he extensively employs expedient means to constantly protect it himself, fearing it might be confiscated by royal decree, stolen by thieves, swept away by water, or consumed by fire."
Again, he thought to himself:
"If I wish to bury it in a pit, I fear it will later be lost; if I wish to draw interest from it, I fear I shall not succeed.
Or perhaps a wicked son may be born into my household and squander my wealth."
"Thus, desire is a great affliction; all these calamities arise from the very root of desire.
Furthermore, son of good family, one constantly gives rise to this thought: 'I wish to protect my wealth and goods.'"
Later, it was again seized by kings, plundered by bandits, swept away by floods, or consumed by fire;
even the treasures buried in pits could not be recovered,
and though he invested his capital at high interest, he still failed to gain anything.

When one lives at home and fathers wicked sons who squander wealth and goods such that not even one ten-thousandth is recovered, they become filled with sorrow, grief, and affliction, beating their breasts and crying out:
"The wealth and goods I originally obtained have now all been lost!"

"Thus they become deluded and confused, their minds and intentions disordered; this is called desire being a great affliction, for by taking this desire as a root, one does not reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, by taking this desire as a root, people don armor and take up weapons to attack and subdue one another."

They attack one another, sometimes before an elephant division, sometimes before a cavalry division, sometimes before an infantry division, or sometimes before a chariot division; they see horses fighting with horses, elephants fighting with elephants, chariots fighting with chariots, and infantry fighting with infantry; they hack and shoot at one another, and strike and stab one another with spears.
In this manner, desire is a great affliction.
With desire as its root, these calamities and transformations arise.

Furthermore, because of this root of desire, they don armor and take up weapons; whether at the city gates or atop the city walls, they hack and shoot at one another, or pierce each other with spears, or crush each other’s heads with iron wheels, or drench one another with molten iron.
Suffering from these afflictions, many die.
Furthermore, desire is likewise impermanent; it is all subject to succession and transformation, never remaining still nor coming to rest.
This desire, which is subject to transformation and impermanence, is what is called the great affliction of desire.
"How should one abandon desire? If one can practice the removal of greedy desire, this is called abandoning desire."

It refers to those ascetics and brahmins who do not know the great peril of desire, nor do they know the source of abandoning desire; they do not know, as it truly is, what constitutes an ascetic or the deportment of an ascetic, and they do not know what constitutes a brahmin or the deportment of a brahmin. These are neither ascetics nor brahmins, and furthermore, they are unable to realize it with their own bodies as a direct witness and dwell therein.
This refers to those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who thoroughly understand that desire is a great affliction and are able to abandon it, in accordance with reality and without falsehood.

They know that a śramaṇa possesses the deportment of a śramaṇa, and they know that a brāhmaṇa possesses the deportment of a brāhmaṇa; having personally realized this through direct experience, they dwell therein. This is what is meant by abandoning desire.
"What is the gratification of form?

Suppose one sees a daughter of the Kṣatriya caste, the Brāhmaṇa caste, or the Gṛhapati caste, fourteen, fifteen, or sixteen years of age—neither tall nor short, neither fat nor thin, neither too fair nor too dark, peerlessly beautiful, and rare in the world."
When one first sees that color and gives rise to the perception of joy and pleasure, this is called the gratification of form (*rūpa-svāda*).
"What is the great danger of form?
Furthermore..."

If later he sees that woman at eighty, ninety, or even a hundred years of age, her complexion having changed and her youth long past; her teeth fallen out, her hair white as snow, her body soiled and grimy, her skin sagging and her face wrinkled, her back bent and groaning with pain, her body like an old cart, her limbs trembling as she walks leaning on a staff.
"What do you think, bhikṣus?
When one first sees a beautiful form, which later undergoes change and decay—is this not indeed a great affliction? The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is what is called form being a great affliction.
Furthermore, if one sees that woman suffering from a grave illness, lying upon her bed and bedding, having lost control of her excrement and urine, and unable to rise or move."
"What do you think, bhikṣus?
Having previously seen exquisite forms, one now encounters this affliction;
is this not indeed a great affliction? The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One! The World-Honored One said:
“Monks, this is called form as a great affliction. Furthermore, monks:”
If one sees that woman’s body destroyed and her life ended, being carried to the cemetery—what do you think, bhikṣu?
That which was once seen as beautiful has now changed; to perceive notions of suffering or pleasure therein—is this not a great affliction?
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called form being a great affliction.

Furthermore, if one sees that woman after she has been dead for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, or even seven days, her body bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling, scattered in one place."
"What do you think, bhikṣus?
That which formerly possessed exquisite beauty has now undergone this transformation;
is this not indeed a great affliction? The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One! The World-Honored One said:
"This is what is called form being a great affliction.

Furthermore, if one sees that woman being vied for and devoured by crows, magpies, owls, and vultures; or being devoured by foxes, dogs, wolves, and tigers; or being devoured by crawling insects, wriggling creatures, and even the most minute worms."
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
That which once possessed exquisite beauty has now undergone this transformation; to give rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure within it—is this not a great affliction?"
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called form being a great affliction.
Furthermore, if one sees that woman's body with half of it devoured by worms and birds, its intestines, stomach, flesh, and blood being foul and impure."
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
That which once possessed exquisite beauty has now undergone this transformation; that one gives rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure therein—is this not a great affliction?"
The bhikṣus replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called form being a great affliction.
Furthermore, if one sees that woman’s body with its flesh and blood exhausted, and only the skeletal remains connected together."
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
That which once possessed exquisite beauty has now undergone this transformation; that one gives rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure therein—is this not indeed a great affliction?"
The bhikṣus replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called the great affliction of form.
Furthermore, if one sees that woman’s body with its flesh and blood exhausted, remaining only as sinews binding together a bundle of firewood."
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Originally possessing exquisite beauty, it has now undergone this transformation; that one gives rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure therein—is this not a great affliction?"
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called form being a great affliction.

Furthermore, if one again sees that woman’s body with the skeletal remains scattered, each in a different place—perhaps the bones of the feet in one place, the bones of the upper arms in another, the bones of the thighs in another, the bones of the hips in another, the ribs in another, the bones of the shoulders and arms in another, the neck bones in another, or the skull in another."
"What do you think, monks?
That which once possessed exquisite beauty has now undergone this transformation; to give rise to perceptions of suffering or pleasure therein—is this not indeed a great affliction?"
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called form being a great affliction.
Furthermore, if one sees that woman’s body as white as bone, or perhaps the color of a pigeon."
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Previously there was exquisite beauty, yet now it has undergone this transformation; to give rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure therein—is this not indeed a great affliction?"
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called form being a great affliction.
Furthermore, if one sees that woman’s skeleton after countless years have passed, perhaps decayed and ruined until it is the same color as the earth."
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
That which once possessed exquisite beauty has now undergone this transformation; to give rise to perceptions of suffering or pleasure within it—is this not a great affliction?"
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"This is called form being a great affliction.
Furthermore, this form is impermanent and subject to change; it cannot endure for long, and there is no distinction between old and young. This is called form being a great affliction."
"What is the escape from form? If one can relinquish form and eliminate all distracted thoughts, this is called relinquishing form.

As for those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are attached to form and enamored by form, who do not know it to be a great affliction and do not relinquish it—failing to know it as it truly is—they are neither śramaṇas nor brāhmaṇas. They do not know the deportment of a śramaṇa, nor do they know the deportment of a brāhmaṇa; they are unable to realize it for themselves through direct experience and dwell therein."

This refers to those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not cling to form, who deeply understand it to be a great affliction, and are able to know how to relinquish it. This is called knowing the deportment of a śramaṇa among śramaṇas, and knowing the deportment of a brāhmaṇa among brāhmaṇas; having realized this for oneself and dwelling therein, this is called relinquishing form.
"What is the gratification of feeling?
In this regard, monks, when one experiences a pleasant feeling, one knows: 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling';"
When experiencing painful feeling, one knows: "I am experiencing painful feeling";
when experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one knows: "I am experiencing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
When experiencing a pleasant feeling born of contact, one knows: "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling born of contact";
when experiencing a painful feeling born of contact, one knows: "I am experiencing a painful feeling born of contact";
when experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of contact, one knows: "I am experiencing a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of contact."
When he does not experience painful feeling, he knows for himself: "I do not experience painful feeling";
when he does not experience pleasant feeling, he knows for himself: "I do not experience pleasant feeling";
when he does not experience neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows for himself: "I do not experience neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."

"Furthermore, bhikṣu! When one experiences a pleasant sensation, at that time one does not experience a painful sensation, nor does one experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation; at that time, I have only a pleasant sensation."
When one experiences a painful sensation, at that time there is no pleasant sensation, nor is there a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant;
there is only a painful sensation. Furthermore, monks!
When one experiences neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, at that time there is no pleasant sensation nor painful sensation; there is only neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
Furthermore, sensation is impermanent and subject to change; because one knows that sensation is impermanent and subject to change, this is called the great affliction of sensation.
“What is the escape from feeling? If one can relinquish feeling regarding feeling and eliminate all distracted thoughts, this is called relinquishing feeling.

Any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are attached to feeling regarding feeling do not know it to be a great affliction, nor do they relinquish it; they do not know it as it truly is. These are not śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; they do not know the deportment of a śramaṇa, nor do they know the deportment of a brāhmaṇa, and they are unable to realize it for themselves through bodily witness and dwell therein.”

Whosoever among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas does not cling to feeling, deeply understands it to be a great affliction, and is able to know how to relinquish it—this is called a śramaṇa who knows the deportment of a śramaṇa, and a brāhmaṇa who knows the deportment of a brāhmaṇa; one who personally realizes this through bodily witness and dwells therein is said to have relinquished feeling.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not know painful feeling, pleasant feeling, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as they truly are, yet still teach and exhort others to practice accordingly, this is not appropriate for them."

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are able to abandon and detach from suffering, knowing it as it truly is, and further exhorting and instructing others to distance themselves from it—this is what is appropriate; this is called the abandonment and detachment from suffering.

“Monks, I have now taught the speaking of the faults of sensual desire and the gratification of sensual desire, and that desire is a great affliction; furthermore, I have taught how one who is able to relinquish it may do so.
I have also taught the speaking of the faults of form and the gratification of form, and that form is a great affliction; one should be able to abandon and depart from form.”

I have already explained that feeling is suffering and that the taste of feeling is suffering; that feeling is a great affliction, and that one who can relinquish feeling performs what all Tathāgatas ought to do—namely, that which is designated as such—and this, I have now completed.
"You should always keep in mind to stay beneath trees or in secluded places, practicing meditation and contemplation without any indolence; this is my instruction.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three things that are not secure. What are the three?
The body is not secure, life is not secure, and wealth is not secure.”
"Monks, these are called the three things that are not firm or reliable.
In this regard, monks..."
Among the three things that are not secure, one should seek skillful means to achieve the three things that are secure.
What are these three? Regarding the body that is not secure, one seeks that which is secure; [and likewise for the other two].
One does not seek what is secure in that which is insecure regarding life,
nor does one seek what is secure in that which is insecure regarding wealth.
"What is it to seek what is secure in that which is insecure regarding the body?"
This refers to practicing humility, reverence, and prostration, and inquiring after others' well-being at appropriate times.
This is called not seeking a secure body, but seeking what is secure.
What is meant by "not seeking a secure life, but seeking what is secure"?

Thereupon, if there be sons or daughters of good family who, for as long as life lasts, refrain from killing living beings, do not employ blades or staves, always possess a sense of shame and remorse, maintain a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, and universally keep all sentient beings in mind;
who, for as long as life lasts, refrain from stealing, constantly contemplate giving, and have no thought of stinginess in their hearts;
and who, for as long as life lasts, refrain from sexual misconduct and do not engage in illicit sexual acts with others;
For as long as life lasts, one shall not speak falsely, always maintaining sincerity and never deceiving the people of the world;
for as long as life lasts, one shall not drink alcohol, so that the mind remains undisturbed and one upholds the prohibitions and precepts of the Buddha.
This is called: "Life is not secure; seek that which is secure.
What is meant by "wealth is not secure; seek that which is secure"?

If there are sons or daughters of good family who constantly contemplate practicing generosity toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those who are impoverished—giving food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink, clothing, bedding, seats, dwellings, medicine for the sick, houses, cities, and all necessary requisites—they give them all.
In this way, wealth is not secure; one should seek what is secure.
"This is called, O bhikṣu, seeking these three securities by means of these three insecurities."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Knowing that the body is not secure, And that life likewise is not firm,
That wealth is subject to decay and loss— One should seek that which is secure."
"A human body is extremely difficult to obtain; life, too, does not remain for long.
Wealth and goods are subject to decay; therefore, with joy, one should contemplate giving.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three kinds of persons who should be venerated by the people of the world.”
What are these three?
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is worthy of being venerated by the world;
and the disciples of the Tathāgata, the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, who are worthy of being venerated by the world.
"A Wheel-Turning Sage King is one whom the people of the world ought to honor.
By what causes and conditions, then, is the Tathāgata one whom the people of the world ought to honor?

Indeed, the Tathāgata subdues those who are unsubdued, brings low those who are unbrought low, and delivers those who are undelivered. He causes those who have not attained liberation to attain liberation, and leads those who have not entered parinirvāṇa to achieve nirvāṇa. To those without protection, he acts as a protector; to the blind, he acts as eyes; and to the sick, he acts as their refuge."

The Most Honored and Foremost One; among Māras, Māra-devas, devas, and human beings, he is the most honored field of merit, worthy of reverence and esteem. He acts as a guide for humanity, causing them to know the right path; to those who have not yet found the way, he expounds the teachings that lead the way. For these reasons, the Tathāgata is one whom the world should honor and provide for.
“Furthermore, for what reason and by what causes are the Tathāgata’s disciples, the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, worthy of the world’s offerings?

Bhikṣus, you should know that the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted have crossed over the source of birth and death and will no longer undergo further existence. Having attained the unsurpassed Dharma, their lust, anger, and delusion are exhausted; they can never again be fully bound. They are the field of merit for the world.”
By virtue of these causes and conditions, from beginning to end, the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted is one whom the people of the world should honor and provide for.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is the Wheel-Turning Sage King one whom the people of the world should honor and provide for?
"Monks, you should know that a Wheel-Turning Sage King governs by means of the Dharma; he never takes life, and furthermore, he teaches and transforms others so that they do not take life;
he himself does not steal, and likewise teaches others so that they do not commit theft;
he himself does not engage in sexual misconduct, and furthermore teaches others so that they do not engage in sexual misconduct."
One refrains from false speech oneself and also teaches others to refrain from false speech;
one refrains from divisive speech that causes strife between this party and that, and also teaches others to refrain from divisive speech;
one refrains from envy, malice, and delusion oneself, and also teaches others not to practice these things.
Practicing right view oneself and further teaching others so that they do not hold wrong views—
by these causes and conditions, by this beginning and end, one causes the Wheel-Turning Sage King to become worthy of the offerings of the people of the world.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"There are three roots of goodness that are inexhaustible and lead gradually to the realm of nirvāṇa.
What are these three?"
That is to say, the merit planted in the presence of the Tathāgata—this root of goodness is inexhaustible.
The merit planted in the True Dharma—this root of goodness is inexhaustible.
When one plants roots of merit within the noble Saṃgha, these roots of goodness are inexhaustible.
Thus it is said, Ānanda:
these three roots of goodness are inexhaustible and lead to the realm of Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should seek skillful means to obtain this inexhaustible merit. Thus it is, Ānanda!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these three kinds of feeling.”
What are the three?
They are pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Monks, you should know that pleasant feeling is the underlying tendency of sensual desire.
That painful sensation is driven by hatred;
that neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation is driven by delusion. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
One should train in skillful means to seek the cessation of these underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Why is this so? Because one should be self-illuminating, practice the Dharma for oneself, and attain the incomparable Dharma.

"Monks, you should know that after my parinirvāṇa, there will be monks who are mindful of self-illumination, who cultivate their practice of the Dharma, and who attain the peerless Dharma; these shall be the foremost śrāvakas."
"How is it, bhikkhu? You should be self-luminous, you should practice for yourself, attain the Dhamma of practice, and obtain the incomparable Dhamma.
In this regard, bhikkhu..."
Internally observing the body, externally observing the body, and internally and externally observing the body, one dwells in playful mastery;
internally observing feelings, externally observing feelings, and internally and externally observing feelings;
internally observing the mind, externally observing the mind, and internally and externally observing the mind.
Contemplating phenomena internally, contemplating phenomena externally, and contemplating phenomena both internally and externally, one sports therein. Thus, bhikṣu!
You should make yourself a beacon, diligently practice the Dharma, and attain the peerless Dharma.
"Those bhikṣus who practice this Dharma shall be the foremost disciples among the śrāvakas. Thus, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three things that are excellent when concealed, but not excellent when exposed.
What are these three?"
First, a woman is excellent when concealed but not excellent when exposed;
the incantations of a Brahmin are excellent when concealed but not excellent when exposed;
and the karma of wrong views is excellent when concealed but not excellent when exposed.
"Monks, these are the three things that are excellent when concealed but not excellent when exposed.
Furthermore, there are three things that are excellent when exposed but not excellent when concealed."
What are these three?
The sun and the moon are excellent when exposed but not excellent when covered;
likewise, the Tathāgata’s Dharma discourse is excellent when exposed but not excellent when covered.
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus:
there are these three things which are excellent when exposed, but not excellent when concealed.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“Women, sorcery, and wrong views leading to unwholesome conduct—
these three things in the world are most excellent when kept concealed.
Yet the broad radiance of the sun and moon, and the true Dharma-teachings of the Tathāgata, [shine forth openly].”
"These are the dharmas of the three periods of time; their manifestation is the foremost excellence.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should manifest the Dharma of the Tathāgata and not allow it to be concealed."
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These three are the conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. What are the three?
Knowing from whence they arise, knowing that they shall undergo transformation, and knowing that they shall perish."
How does one know that from which it arises?

It is what is called birth, growing up, and the formation of the five aggregates (skandhas), as well as the acquisition of the bases (āyatanas) and elements (dhātus); this is what is meant by "that from which it arises."
What is meant by "cessation"? It refers to death:

the passing away of life, the non-abiding of existence, impermanence, the dissolution and disintegration of the aggregates (*skandhas*), separation from one's kin, and the severance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). This is called cessation.
What is this transformation?
The loss of teeth, the graying of hair, the exhaustion of physical strength, the gradual decline of years, and the dissolution of the body—this is called the nature of transformation.
"These, monks, are the three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned; you should know these three conditioned characteristics and discern them well. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Fools have three characteristics and three qualities upon which they cannot rely.”
What are the three?
In this regard, the fool reflects upon that which should not be reflected upon;
he speaks of that which should not be spoken of.
One practices that which is not to be practiced.
"How is it that the fool contemplates what should not be contemplated?
In this regard, the fool brings to mind and recollects the three types of mental conduct."
What are these three?
In this regard, the fool gives rise to envy; regarding the wealth and property of others, as well as their female companions, he harbors malicious thoughts and arouses envy in his heart, thinking:
"May all that they possess be mine."
"In this way, the fool reflects upon that which should not be reflected upon.
How does the fool discourse upon that which should not be discoursed upon?
In this regard, the fool commits the four verbal transgressions."
What are the four?
In this regard, the fool constantly delights in false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, and inciting strife between others.
Thus, the fool commits these four transgressions of speech.
"How does a fool engage in unwholesome conduct?
In this regard, a fool engages in bodily misconduct, constantly thinking of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct."
In this way, the fool performs unwholesome deeds.
Thus, bhikṣus, the fool possesses these three modes of conduct; the deluded person practices these three things.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!
There are three things that the wise should mindfully practice.
What are these three?
Thereupon, the wise person should contemplate that which is to be contemplated,
discourse upon that which is to be discoursed upon,
and practice virtue in that which is to be practiced as virtuous.
"What are the things that a wise person should contemplate and then contemplates?
In this regard, the wise person contemplates the three mental activities.
What are these three?"
Thus, the wise person is free from envy, anger, and delusion; they always practice right view and do not give rise to covetous thoughts upon seeing the wealth and goods of others.
In this way, the wise person reflects upon whatever is worthy of reflection.
"How should a wise person discourse upon this?
In this regard, a wise person accomplishes four modes of verbal conduct. What are these four?"

Thus, the wise person does not engage in false speech, nor do they instruct others to speak falsely; seeing others speaking falsely, their mind finds no pleasure therein. This is called the wise person guarding their speech.

Furthermore, the wise person does not engage in frivolous speech, harsh speech, or inciting discord between others; nor do they instruct others to engage in frivolous speech, harsh speech, or inciting discord.
In this way, the wise person accomplishes the four modes of verbal conduct.
How does the wise person accomplish the three modes of bodily conduct?
In this regard, the wise person reflects upon bodily conduct and refrains from committing any transgression.
Furthermore, the wise person does not kill living beings themselves, nor do they instruct others to kill; seeing someone killing, their heart finds no pleasure in it.
They do not steal themselves, nor do they instruct others to commit theft; seeing someone stealing, their heart finds no pleasure in it.
He is neither licentious nor dissolute; upon seeing the form of another's wife, no thoughts of desire arise in his mind, nor does he instruct others to engage in sexual misconduct.

Should he see an elderly woman, he regards her as his own mother; one of middle age, as his elder sister; and one younger, as his younger sister—his mind free from any sense of superiority or inferiority.
In this way, the wise person accomplishes three practices in the body; this is called the conduct of the wise.
Thus, bhikṣus, there are these three characteristics of the conditioned.
Therefore, monks, the wise should always abandon the three characteristics of the fool; these three are practiced by the wise and are not manifested even for a moment. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“There are these three things that cannot be perceived; they are neither seen nor heard. Throughout the cycle of birth and death, they have never been beheld; neither I nor you have ever seen or heard of them.”
What are these three?

They are the precepts of the noble ones (ārya-śīla), which cannot be perceived, nor seen, nor heard; throughout the cycle of birth and death, they have never been beheld, for neither I nor you have ever seen or heard of them.

The noble samādhi and the noble wisdom are beyond conceptual cognition; they are neither seen nor heard. Yet now, my own body as well as yours have all fully cognized the noble precepts, the noble samādhi, and the noble wisdom; we have achieved them all, shall no longer undergo further existence, and have severed the very root of birth and death.
Therefore, monks, you should mindfully practice these three dharmas. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three things that are most worthy of veneration and affection, which people of the world crave.”
What are the three? They are:
youth, which is exceedingly dear and respected, and coveted by the world;
and freedom from illness, which is exceedingly dear and respected, and coveted by the world.
Longevity is deeply cherished and respected, and is what the people of the world crave.
Thus it is said, bhikṣu:
there are these three things that are deeply cherished and respected, and craved by the people of the world.
"Furthermore, bhikkhus!
Although these three qualities are very dear and respected, and are what the world covets, there are yet another three qualities that are not dear or respected, and are not what the world covets.
What are these three?
Although one may be young and strong, one will inevitably grow old; this is not to be cherished or revered, nor is it what worldly people crave.
Bhikṣus, you should know that although one may be free from illness, one will inevitably fall ill; this is not to be cherished or revered, nor is it what worldly people crave.
"Monks, you should know that although there is life, one must inevitably die; it is not to be cherished or revered, nor is it something the world craves. Therefore, monks!"
Though one may possess youth and vigor, one should seek the state of agelessness, reaching the realm of Nirvana;
though one may be free from illness, one should seek skillful means so as not to fall ill;
though one possesses a lifespan, one should seek skillful means so as not to meet one's end.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is just as when great hail falls from the heavens in springtime; even if a Tathāgata were not to appear in the world, sentient beings would still enter hell in this same manner.
At that time, women will enter hell in greater numbers than men."
The reason for this, bhikṣus, you should know, is that due to three things, beings—upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life—enter the three evil destinies.
What are these three? They are namely:
sensual desire, sloth and torpor, and restlessness. When one is bound by these three things to the mind, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one enters the three evil destinies.
“Women spend the entire day practicing and indulging in three things for their own amusement.
What are these three?

In the early morning, they bind themselves with a mind of jealousy; at midday, they further wrap themselves in the fetter of sleep; and toward evening, they bind themselves with a mind of sensual craving.”
By reason of this cause and condition, that woman, upon the dissolution of the body after death,
will be reborn in the three evil destinies. Therefore, monks,
you should be mindful of remaining free from these three things.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Envy, sloth, and restlessness, And covetousness are evil dharmas;
They drag people into hell, Where there is ultimately no liberation.”
"Therefore, you should abandon jealousy and sloth, as well as desire; do not commit those evil deeds.
For this reason, O bhikṣus!"

One should constantly reflect on abandoning envy and being free from a stingy mind, always practicing generosity, not clinging to sleep, practicing non-attachment, and remaining unattached to sensual desire.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these three things which, when practiced and cultivated, lead to no sense of satiety and do not allow one to reach the place of rest.
What are the three?
This refers to sensual desire.
If there is a person who practices this dharma, they have no sense of satiety from the beginning.
Furthermore, if there is a person who practices drinking alcohol, they likewise have no sense of satiety from the beginning.
Furthermore, if there is a person who cultivates the habit of sleep and is never satisfied from the outset,
this, O bhikṣu, is called one who practices these three dharmas and is never satisfied from the outset; such a person will likewise be unable to reach the state of cessation.
Therefore, monks, you should always abandon these three things and not associate with them. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. [The verses:
Offerings, the three roots of goodness, the three types of sensation, and the three coverings and exposures.
Marks, Dharmas, and the Three Non-Awakenings; Affection and Reverence, Spring, and Insatiability.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Volume Twelve; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Three: The Chapter on the Lord of the Earth (Bhūmipati-varga). (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed his ministers, saying:
"You all, hasten to prepare the precious royal chariot; I wish to go to the place where the World-Honored One resides to pay my respects and inquire after his well-being."
At that time, the attendants received the king’s command and immediately prepared the carriage adorned with peacock-feather jewels;
they then addressed the king, saying, “The carriage is ready; now is the very moment.”

At that time, King Prasenajit mounted a precious feathered chariot and, surrounded by several thousand infantry and cavalry in front and behind, departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jetavana Monastery to visit the World-Honored One.

In accordance with the custom of kings, he removed his five ornaments—namely, the parasol, the celestial crown, the sword, the sandals, and the golden fly-whisk—and setting them aside to one side, he approached the World-Honored One.
He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the profound Dharma to him, exhorting, encouraging, and gladdening him.
Having heard this teaching of the Dharma, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation for three months, together with the community of bhikṣus, and not stay elsewhere.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted King Prasenajit’s invitation by remaining silent.

At that time, King Prasenajit, seeing that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head, and withdrew.
Returning to the city of Śrāvastī, he commanded his ministers, saying:
“I wish to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for three months as an act of worship, supplying all their necessary provisions.”
"You should also give rise to a heart of joy regarding robes, food and drink, bedding and seats,
and medicinal requisites for the sick. The ministers replied, "So be it."

At that time, King Prasenajit immediately constructed a great lecture hall outside the palace gates; it was exceedingly exquisite, adorned with suspended silken banners and canopies, and provided with an incalculable number of performers and musical entertainments.
He provided various bathing pools, prepared oil lamps, and arranged diverse kinds of food and drink of a hundred flavors.
At that time, King Prasenajit said: "The time has come;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to visit this place."

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the hour had come, donned his robes and took up his bowl; surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, he entered the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the lecture hall.
Having arrived, he took his seat, and the community of bhikṣus each sat down according to their rank.

At that time, King Prasenajit, accompanied by his palace attendants, personally served the food and provided all necessities for three months, leaving nothing lacking; he supplied them with robes, meals, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

Seeing that the World-Honored One had finished eating, he took various kinds of flowers and scattered them over the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus. He then took a small seat and sat before the Tathāgata, addressing the World-Honored One:
"I have previously heard from the Buddha the full account of causes and conditions:
one who gives food to an animal obtains a hundredfold merit;..."
If one gives food to a person who has violated the precepts, one obtains a thousandfold merit;
if one gives food to a person who upholds the precepts, one obtains a ten-thousandfold merit;
if one gives food to a rishi who has severed desire, one obtains a hundred-millionfold merit.
If one gives food to those who are progressing toward the stage of *srotāpanna*, the merit obtained is incalculable;
how much more so for those who have already become *srotāpannas*?
How much more so for those progressing toward the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin* or those who have attained the path of *sakṛdāgāmin*!
How much more so for those who are heading toward the stage of non-returner and have attained the path of a non-returner!
How much more so for those who are heading toward arhatship and have attained the path of an arhat!
How much more so for those who are heading toward pratyekabuddhahood and have attained the state of a pratyekabuddha!
How much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha!
How much more so for the attainment of Buddhahood and the Bhikṣu-saṅgha!
The merit and virtue thereof are beyond measure and calculation; the merit I have now performed has been accomplished this very day.
The World-Honored One said:
"Great King! Do not speak such words; one should never tire of performing meritorious deeds."
For what reason do you say today that what was to be done has been accomplished?
It is because birth and death are long and far-reaching, beyond calculation or record.
"In the distant past, there was a king named Bhūmipati who ruled over this land of Jambudvīpa."
That king had a minister named Shanming (Sunlight), who had been his companion since childhood and with whom he felt no fear or difficulty.
At that time, the king divided half of Jambudvīpa and entrusted it to that minister to govern.
At that time, the minor king Śubhaprabha built a city for himself, twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas wide; its land was fertile and abundant, and its population was vast.

"At that time, there was a city named Dūraprabhā. The chief queen of King Suprabha was named Sūryacandrā; she was neither tall nor short, neither fat nor thin, neither too fair nor too dark, and her countenance was so upright and beautiful as to be rare in the world."
Her mouth emitted the fragrance of *utpala* flowers, and her body exuded the scent of *candana*.
Before many days had passed, she became pregnant.
The lady then went to inform the king:
"I am now pregnant. Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself;
he immediately commanded his attendants to prepare further seating arrangements, and his happiness was beyond compare.
When the lady’s months of pregnancy were fully completed, she gave birth to a son.

At the moment of his birth, the interior of Jambudvīpa was brilliantly illuminated with a golden light; his countenance was upright and handsome, endowed with the thirty-two marks, and his body was golden in color.

When Great King Sunming saw this prince, he leaped for joy with immeasurable celebration. He then summoned his various masters—the Brahmins and Daoist practitioners—and personally cradled the prince, instructing them to examine his features:
"Now that I have fathered this son, you shall examine his marks for me and bestow upon him a name."
Then, the physiognomists, having received the king’s command, each took hold of him and observed his features, after which they all addressed the king:
"O Holy King!..."
The Crown Prince is upright and peerless, his faculties are unimpaired, and he possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Now this prince shall have two possible destinies:
if he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, fully endowed with the seven treasures.

What are called the seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure; these are the seven.

He shall have a thousand sons, valiant, fierce, and resolute, capable of repelling all enemies; throughout these four seas, they shall bring others to submission naturally, without the use of weapons or force.
"If this prince leaves the household life to study the Way, he will attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment, and his name and virtue will spread far and wide, filling the world.
On the very day this prince was born, a great radiance shone afar; therefore, we shall now name the prince Dīpamkara (Lamp-Light)."
Then, the physiognomists established his name and each withdrew to their seats and departed.
At that time, the king cradled this prince all day long, never taking his eyes off him.

At that time, the king established three lecture halls for this prince, suited to the appropriate conditions for each season—autumn, winter, and summer—and filled the palace with court ladies and maidservants, so that my son might sport and play therein.
"At that time, the Prince was twenty-nine years old; with firm faith, he left the household life to study the Way.
On the very day he left home, that same night he attained Buddhahood."
At that time, throughout the land of Jambudvīpa, everyone heard and knew:
"The crown prince has left home to study the Way and has attained Buddhahood this very day.
When the father king heard at dawn that his son had left home to study the Way and had attained Buddhahood that very night, he was moved.
At that time, the Father King thought to himself:
"Last night, I heard all the devas in the sky together praising me as 'well done. This must surely be a favorable omen and not an ill portent; I should now go there to meet him."
At that time, the king, surrounded by a retinue of four billion people—both men and women—proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata Pradīpadhvaja was.
