Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side;
the four billion people likewise each prostrated at his feet and sat to one side.

At that time, the Tathāgata gradually expounded a sublime discourse to the Father King and an assembly of four billion beings. This discourse concerned generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in the heavens; it taught that sensual desire is defiling and its outflows are impure, and that renunciation is essential for attaining pure retribution.
At that time, the Tathāgata observed the minds and dispositions of the assembly; their natures were gentle and pliant.

The Tathāgatas, Buddhas of all times, constantly teach the Dharma of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. He then extensively expounded the meaning of these truths to those four billion beings. Thereupon, while still seated, their defilements were completely exhausted, and they attained the pure Dharma-eye.
"At that time, an assembly of four billion beings said to the Tathāgata Pradīparāja:
'We wish to shave off our hair and beards, leave the household life, and study the Way.
Great King, you should know this."
At that time, the assembly of four billion beings all attained renunciation and studied the Way, becoming Arhats on that very day.
Then, the Tathāgata Dīpamkara, together with those four billion beings—all of whom were free from attachment—traveled through the realms of that land.
The people of that land provided the four requisites for his support—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick—with no lack whatsoever.

At that time, the Great King Dharaṇīndra, hearing that his son Dīpamkara had attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, led a retinue of four billion beings, all of whom were free from attachment, to travel to that realm.
"I shall now dispatch a messenger to invite the Tathāgata to come and dwell here to transform and guide beings;
if he comes, my original vow will be fulfilled;
if he does not come, I shall go in person to pay homage, kneel, and inquire after his well-being."
He then commanded a minister:
"Go to him and inquire after the Tathāgata’s well-being; convey my name, prostrate yourself at his feet, and ask whether he is light and agile in his daily life and strong in his movements."
"King Meghadatta sends his greetings to the Tathāgata, inquiring whether you are at ease in your daily life and whether your movements are healthy and strong.
We pray only that the World-Honored One will deign to visit this land.
At that time, the man received the king's command and proceeded to that kingdom.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and spoke thus:

“The Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra pays homage at the Tathāgata’s feet. Having completed his inquiries and salutations, he asks whether you are dwelling in ease and comfort and whether your movements are vigorous and strong. He prays only that the World-Honored One will deign to visit his kingdom.”
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted his invitation by remaining silent.
Then, the Tathāgata Pradīpa, together with a great assembly and accompanied by a community of four billion great bhikṣus, gradually traveled through the human world.

"Wherever he went, there was no one who did not show him reverence; they all offered him robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick and infirm. Gradually, he arrived at the realm of the lord of the land. At that time, the Great King, the Lord of the Land, heard that the Tathāgata Dīpāṅkara had reached this realm and was staying in the Northern Brahman Garden with a great assembly of four billion bhikṣus, and thought:
'I should now go in person to welcome him.'"
Then, the Great King Dharaṇīndra again led a multitude of four billion beings to the place where the Tathāgata Pradīpa was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
After the assembly of four billion people had prostrated at his feet, they sat to one side.

At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpamkara gradually engaged the king and the assembly of four billion in a sublime discourse, namely: a discourse on generosity, a discourse on ethical discipline, and a discourse on rebirth in the heavens; [he spoke of] how sensual desires are defiling, how outflows lead to impure conduct, and how renunciation is essential for attaining pure retribution.

At that time, the Tathāgata, observing the inclinations of the assembly’s minds and seeing that their natures were gentle and pliant, extensively expounded for those four billion beings the meaning of the Dharma always taught by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Thereupon, while still seated, they were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
"At that time, a multitude of four billion beings said to the Tathāgata Prabhāsa-pradīpa:
'We wish to shave off our hair and beards, leave the household life, and study the Way.
Great King, you should know this."
At that time, the assembly of four billion people all attained renunciation and studied the Way, becoming Arhats on that very day.
Then, the King, Lord of the Earth, rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and withdrew.

"At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpamkara, accompanied by a multitude of eight billion beings—all of whom were arhats—traveled through that realm. The people of that land provided them with the four types of offerings:
clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick; they supplied everything so that there was no lack or deficiency."

At that time, on another occasion, the sovereign king, accompanied by his various ministers, went to the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpamkara taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to that king. The Great King Bhūmipati addressed the Tathāgata, saying:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, will accept my offerings for as long as I live. I shall provide robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick; I shall provide all these necessities."
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara accepted the king’s invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation through silence, the king addressed the World-Honored One once more:
“I now seek a boon from the World-Honored One; may you deign to grant me your permission!”
The World-Honored One replied,
"The Dharma of the Tathāgata transcends such vows.
The King addressed the World-Honored One:
"The aspiration I now seek is exceedingly pure and sublime.
The World-Honored One said,
"In what way is the aspiration you seek pure and sublime?"
The King addressed the World-Honored One:
"In my mind, I think that today the assembly of monks eats from one vessel, and tomorrow they eat from another vessel;
today the assembly of monks wears one kind of robe, and tomorrow they change to different robes."
Today the community of monks sits upon one kind of seat, and tomorrow they sit again upon other seats;
today a certain person is sent by the community of monks to perform service, and tomorrow another person is sent in his stead.
"That which I seek and pray for is precisely this.
The Tathāgata Dīpapradyota replied,
"In accordance with your wish, now is the very time."
King Mahārāja Bhūmipati, filled with joy and leaping for gladness beyond measure, rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet, and then withdrew.
Returning to the palace, once he had arrived, he addressed his ministers:

"I now desire, for as long as my life lasts, to provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara and the community of bhikṣus. You all should likewise encourage one another and assist me in preparing these offerings."
The ministers replied, “As the Great King commands.

Within one *yojana* of the city, they constructed halls and residences, adorned with carvings and engravings in the five colors—black, yellow, red, white, and green. They hung silk banners and canopies, performed music and dance, sprinkled fragrant liquids upon the ground, prepared bathing pools, and provided lamps, sweet delicacies, food and drink, as well as seating arrangements.
He then announced:
"The time has come; now is precisely the right moment. We pray that the World-Honored One will deign to visit us!

At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpamkara, knowing the hour had arrived, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, proceeded to the lecture hall and sat down upon each of their respective seats.

At that time, King Mahārāja Bhūmipati, seeing that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, led his palace ladies, court beauties, and various ministers; with his own hands, he served and distributed various foods and drinks, each consisting of a hundred different flavors.

Great King, you should know that at that time, for seventy thousand years, the King, Lord of the Earth, made offerings to the Tathāgata Pradīpadhvaja and his assembly of eight billion arhats, never once becoming weary or negligent.
At that time, when that Tathāgata had finished his work of teaching and transforming beings, he entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.

Then, the Great King Dharaṇīndra made offerings of various hundreds of kinds of incense and flowers; at the crossroads, he erected four temples and monasteries, each constructed of the seven treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and hung them with silken banners and canopies. Furthermore, eighty billion beings each gradually entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.

At that time, the Great King took eighty billion followers, gathered the śarīra relics, and each erected a divine temple, adorning them all with suspended silken banners and canopies, and making offerings of incense and flowers.

Great King, you should know that at that time, the Great King Dharaṇīndra again made offerings to the temple of the Tathāgata Pradīpadhvaja and to the temples of eight billion arhats. For seventy thousand years, he continued to provide seasonal offerings, lighting lamps, scattering flowers, and hanging silken banners and canopies.
"Great King, you should know that only after the remaining teachings of the Tathāgata Dīpaprakāśa have completely vanished will that king finally pass into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, was the Great King Bhūmipati anyone other than this person?"
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? The Great King, the Lord of the Earth at that time, was none other than myself.

During those seventy thousand years, I made offerings to that Buddha with robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick and infirm, ensuring that these provisions never diminished.

After his parinirvāṇa, for another seventy thousand years, they made offerings to his physical remains and relics, burning incense, lighting lamps, and hanging silken banners and canopies, never lacking for anything.
At that time, by means of these merits, I sought to obtain such blessings while remaining within the cycle of birth and death, rather than seeking liberation.
Great King, you should know: do any remnants of all those merits from that time still exist today?
Do not hold such a view!
As I observe his wealth today, there is not even a hair’s breadth of it remaining.
This is because birth and death are long and vast, beyond reckoning; within that cycle, all his merit has been consumed until nothing remains, not even a single hair's breadth.
Therefore, Great King,
do not speak thus, saying:
"The merit and blessings I have performed are now fully accomplished."
"Great King! You should speak thus:

'All the various actions performed by me now through body, speech, and mind are solely for the sake of seeking liberation; I do not seek the karmic merit of remaining in saṃsāra, whereby I shall abide in immeasurable peace and security throughout the long night.'"
At that time, King Prasenajit was seized with fear; his hair stood on end and he was overcome with weeping.
Wiping away his tears with his hand, he prostrated himself before the World-Honored One’s feet and confessed his transgressions:
"I have been like a fool and like one who is senseless, lacking all discernment. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance!"

"Now, prostrating myself with my five limbs touching the ground, I repent for my past transgressions and vow never again to produce such words or teachings. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my confession.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
The World-Honored One said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Great King!
Now, before the Tathāgata, you repent for your unrighteousness, reforming the past and cultivating the future. I now accept your confession; do not commit such acts again."
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī in the great assembly named Kātyāyanī. She rose from her seat, prostrated herself with her head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What the World-Honored One has now spoken is most subtle and wonderful.”
Furthermore, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit with these words:

"Great King, you should know that all the various practices performed by body, speech, and mind should be directed solely toward seeking liberation; do not seek to remain within birth and death to enjoy the fruits of such meritorious karma, for only thus will you attain immeasurable peace and security throughout the long night."

The reason for this is that I recall from my own memory thirty-one eons ago, when the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śiṅgha-ketu appeared in the world—a being perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Bhagavat—who was dwelling in the world of Yama.
"At that time, when it was the proper hour, that Buddha put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Hayamukha to beg for food.
At that moment, there was a messenger within the city named Pure Black."
At that time, the messenger saw the Tathāgata entering the city with his alms bowl to beg for food.
Having seen him, he thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata must surely require food and drink now that he has entered the city."
He immediately entered his home, brought out food to offer to the Tathāgata, and made this aspiration:
"By means of this merit, may I not fall into the three evil realms;
may I, in a future life, likewise encounter such a Holy Honored One."
"I must also cause that Holy Honored One to preach the Dharma for me, so that I may attain liberation at that time.
The World-Honored One and King Prasenajit both knew this fully.
At that time, was the messenger Pure-Black anyone else? No, he was not. It was none other than myself.
Do not hold such a view.
For what reason? That messenger of pure black karma at that time was none other than myself.
At that time, after I had offered a meal to the Tathāgata Śikhi, I made this vow:
"May I, in future ages, encounter such a Holy Honored One who shall preach the Dharma to me, so that I may attain liberation at that time.

For thirty-one kalpas, I did not fall into the three evil realms, but was born among devas and humans; finally, today, having received this physical body, I have encountered the Holy Honored One, left the household life to study the Path, exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), and become an Arhat.
The World-Honored One, speaking with supreme subtlety, addressed King Prasenajit:
"Regarding all actions performed by body, speech, and mind, seek liberation from them all; do not remain within birth and death to consume these karmic merits."
"If I see bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās whose minds are filled with joy and directed toward the Tathāgata, I then form this thought:
'Why do these worthy ones not yet apply their minds to love, revere, and make offerings to the Tathāgata?'"
"If I were to see the fourfold assembly, I would immediately go and say to them:
'Virtuous ones, what do you require? Is it robes and alms bowls, or a sitting mat?'"
"Whether it be a needle-case, a water-pot,
or any other requisites of a śramaṇa, I shall provide them all."
"I have already given my consent, so I shall go begging from place to place.
If I obtain it, that will be a great fortune;
if I do not obtain it, I shall go to Uttarakuru, Aparagoyānī, and Pūrvavideha to seek it out and bring it here."
"The reason for this is that all these four assemblies have attained the path to Nirvāṇa through her.
At that time, the World-Honored One observed the mind of the bhikṣuṇī Kātyāyanī and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see anyone among you who possesses such faith and liberation as the bhikṣuṇī Kātyāyanī?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“We do not see it, World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said:
“Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī who has attained liberation through faith is the bhikṣuṇī Kātyāyanī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kātyāyanī, King Prasenajit, and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Bakula was in a mountain cleft mending old robes.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra, seeing from afar the Venerable Bakula in the mountain cleft mending old robes, thought to himself: "This Venerable Bakula has already become an Arhat;

his fetters are all untied. He is long-lived and immeasurable, ever self-subdued, contemplating impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. He does not attach himself to worldly affairs, nor does he preach the Dharma to others, practicing in silent seclusion like a follower of an external heterodox school."
"I wonder whether this venerable one is able to preach the Dharma to others,
or if he is incapable?
I shall now put him to the test."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, vanished from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and appeared on Vulture Peak, standing before the Venerable Bakula with his head bowed at the elder’s feet, and remained there to one side.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra spoke these verses:
"What is praised and spoken by the wise—why do you not teach the Dharma?
To destroy the fetters and accomplish the noble practice—why do you remain in silent stillness?"
At that time, the Venerable Bakula replied to Śakra, Lord of the Devas, with these verses: “The Buddha,
Śāriputra, Ānanda, Kuṇḍadhāna, And likewise the other elders—
They are well able to preach the sublime Dharma.”
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Venerable Bakula, saying:

"The faculties of sentient beings are of many kinds; yet, Venerable Sir, you should know that the Blessed One has also said that the varieties of sentient beings are more numerous than the particles of dust upon the earth. For what reason, Venerable Bakula, do you not preach the Dharma to others?"
Vakula replied: "The various classes of sentient beings are difficult to awaken; the worlds are manifold and the lands are diverse, yet all are attached to 'mine' and 'not mine'."
"Having now contemplated this meaning, I do not preach the Dharma to others.
Śakra Devānām-indra said,
"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain to me the meaning of 'what belongs to a self' and 'what does not belong to a self.'"
The Venerable Bakula said:
"Whether they be men or women, whether they be husbands or wives—beings such as these all exist by depending entirely upon this life."
Furthermore, Kauśika!
The World-Honored One has also said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that you must be self-illuminating, not give rise to unwholesome dharmas, and remain in noble silence."
"Having contemplated this meaning, I remained silent.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, from afar, joined his palms toward the World-Honored One and spoke this verse:
"I take refuge in the Honored One of Ten Powers, Whose perfect radiance is free from all defilement."
"For the sake of all people, this is truly most extraordinary. Venerable Bakula replied:
"For what reason did Śakra make such a statement?"
"This is most extraordinary!
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"I recall that in the past I went to the presence of the World-Honored One; having arrived, I prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and asked about this meaning:"
"What are the conceptions of the classes of devas and humans?
At that time, the World-Honored One said to me:
"This world consists of various kinds, each distinct and different, with diverse origins."
Having heard these words, I immediately replied: "It is so, World-Honored One.

The worlds spoken of by the World-Honored One are of various kinds, each different from the others; yet if one were to preach the Dharma to those sentient beings, they would all receive and uphold it together, and there would be those who achieve results."
"For this reason, I said:
'This is most extraordinary!
Yet what the Venerable Bakula has said is likewise so."
"The worlds are of various kinds, each being different.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"This Honored One is capable of preaching the Dharma to people; it is not that he is unable."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra rose from his seat and departed.
Having heard what the Venerable Bakula had said, Śakra Devānām Indra rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(3) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying by the side of the Ghoṣitārāma Lake in the kingdom of Campā.

At that time, the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was in a secluded place, practicing the foundations of the Dharma for himself. He did not abandon the twelve dhūta ascetic practices and practiced walking meditation day and night, never departing from the teachings of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. Whether sitting or walking, he constantly cultivated the True Dharma; through the first, middle, and last watches of the night, he was always self-exerting and diligent, not ceasing for even a moment. Yet, he was still unable to attain liberation of mind regarding the outflows of desire.

At that time, at the place where the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was practicing walking meditation, his feet were so wounded that blood flowed and filled the sides of the path, like a place where oxen are slaughtered and crows and magpies feed on the blood; yet even so, he was still unable to attain liberation of mind from the outflows of desire.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra (Viśākha) had this thought:
"Among the disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha who practice asceticism and diligence, I am the foremost; yet today my mind remains defiled and has not attained liberation.

Furthermore, my family estate is wealthy with abundant treasures; it would be fitting for me to renounce the robes, return to the life of a layman, and use my wealth to practice extensive acts of charity."
"However, to become a śramaṇa now is extremely difficult and not easy!

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing from afar what Ervāvaṭika was thinking in his mind, ascended into the air and went to the place where he was walking to and fro; there he spread out a seat and sat down.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet with his head, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One asked Śāriputra:
"Why did you just now have this thought?"
"Among the disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha who practice asceticism with diligence, I am the foremost; yet today my mind remains defiled and has not attained liberation.

Furthermore, my family estate is abundant in wealth and treasures; it would be fitting for me to cast off these robes, return to the life of a layman, and use my riches to give extensively in charity."
"However, to now become a śramaṇa is extremely difficult and not easy. Vītaśoka replied, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said:
“I shall now question you in return; answer me as you see fit.”
"What do you think, Śāriputra!
When you were formerly living at home, were you skilled at playing the lute? Śāriputra replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
When I was formerly a householder, I was skilled at playing the lute."
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa?
If the strings are tuned too tightly, so that the tones are uneven, can the sound of the lute then be appreciated?"
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One said:
“What do you think, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa!
If the strings of a lute were again too loose, would the sound of that lute be worth listening to?”
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa replied, “No,
World-Honored One! The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Śāriputra! If the strings of a lute are neither too tight nor too loose, can the sound of that lute then be heard and appreciated? Śāriputra replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
If the strings of a lute are neither too loose nor too tight, then the sound of that lute can be heard and appreciated."
The World-Honored One said:
"It is just like this.
Even one who exerts extreme diligence is like a person engaged in play."
If one is indolent, this constitutes falling into false views;
if one can remain within this [middle way], this is the superior practice.
In this manner, before long, one shall become a person free from outflows (anāsrava).
At that time, after the Blessed One had taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, he returned to the side of the Ghoṣavatī Lake.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, reflecting upon the Blessed One’s instructions, practiced that Dharma in a secluded place without ceasing for even a moment.
Therefore, sons of noble family leave the household life to study the Way, shaving off their hair and beards to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life:
they know according to reality that birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
The Venerable Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa then became an arhat.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Among my śrāvakas, this bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa is the foremost disciple in diligent ascetic practice.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (IV) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Bhaddiya in the city of Śrāvastī fell ill and passed away; however, as that householder had no sons or heirs, all his wealth and treasures were confiscated by the state.
At that time, King Prasenajit, his body covered in dust, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One asked the king: "Great King!"
"For what reason have you come to me with your body covered in dust?
King Prasenajit replied to the World-Honored One:

"In this city of Śrāvastī there is an elder named Bhadra who has passed away today. As he left no offspring, I went in person to collect his wealth and treasures to ensure they were properly transferred to the royal treasury."
There were eighty thousand *kārṣāpaṇas* of pure gold, let alone other miscellaneous goods!

Yet, during that elder’s lifetime, the food he consumed was exceedingly coarse and inferior; he did not eat anything refined. The clothes he wore were soiled and impure, and the carriage and horse he rode were extremely emaciated and weak.
The World-Honored One said:
“So it is, Great King! It is just as you have said.”

"Those who are stingy and greedy, upon obtaining such wealth and goods, are unable to consume them; they do not give them to their parents, wives, children, servants, or slaves, nor do they give them to friends or acquaintances, nor even to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or various venerable elders."

If a wise person obtains such wealth and treasures, they are able to practice generous giving for the sake of universal relief, cherishing nothing at all, and provide for śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those of high virtue.
At that time, King Prasenajit asked,
"When this householder Bhaddiya passed away, where was he reborn?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This householder Vādi, at the end of his life, has been reborn in the Tāpana Great Hell.
This is because this person who has severed the roots of virtue, upon the dissolution of the body after death, is reborn in the Tāpana Hell."
King Prasenajit asked, "Has the householder Bhadrika severed his roots of goodness?
The World-Honored One replied:
"So it is, Great King! As you have said, that householder has severed his roots of goodness; however, that householder's former merit was already exhausted, and he did not create any new."
King Prasenajit asked,
"Does that householder possess any remaining merit?
The World-Honored One replied:
"No, Great King! There is not even a hair's breadth of existence remaining. It is like that farmer who only harvests and does not sow; later he becomes destitute and eventually passes away."
The reason for this is that he merely consumes his past karma and creates no new karma.
This householder is just like that: he merely consumes his past merit and creates no new merit; therefore, this householder shall dwell tonight in the Tih-k'u (Weeping) Hell.

At that time, King Prasenajit was seized with fear; he wiped away his tears and said, "What meritorious deeds and roots of virtue did this elder perform in the past to be born into such a wealthy family?"
"What unwholesome root did he further cultivate that he does not obtain this wealth of extreme abundance, nor take delight in the midst of the five pleasures?
At that time, the World-Honored One told King Prasenajit:
"In the distant past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this elder was a son of a farmer in this city of Śrāvastī."
At that time, after the Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, a pratyekabuddha appeared in the world and went to the house of this elder.
When the elder saw the pratyekabuddha standing outside his gate, he thought to himself:
"It is extremely rare for such a venerable one to appear in the world; I should now offer food and drink to this person."
At that time, the elder gave food to the pratyekabuddha; having received the food, the pratyekabuddha flew into the air and departed.
When the elder saw the pratyekabuddha performing such supernormal power, he made this vow:
"By the merit of this root of goodness, may I never fall into the three evil realms in whatever place I am born in successive lifetimes, and may I always possess abundant wealth and treasures."
Later, he felt regret, thinking:
"The food I had previously possessed should have been given to my servants; I should not have given it to this shaven-headed mendicant to eat.
At that time, was the householder of the field anyone else? [It was none other than myself.]
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?
The householder who was the head of the field at that time is none other than this present Vaddha.

Having made that offering, he then uttered this vow: "By virtue of this merit, may I never fall into the evil realms in whatever place I am born; may I always possess abundant wealth and jewels, be born into a family of great prosperity, and never suffer from lack."
Having already given the gift, he later felt regret, thinking:
"I would rather have given this food to my slaves and servants than to these shaven-headed mendicants.

Due to these causes and conditions, from beginning to end, he was unable to enjoy this most excellent wealth, nor did he delight in the five kinds of sensual pleasures, nor did he provide for himself.

Furthermore, he does not share with his parents, brothers, wife, children, servants, friends, or acquaintances; nor does he give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or various venerable elders. He merely consumes his past karma and creates no new karma.
Therefore, Great King!
If a wise person obtains such wealth, they should practice extensive giving without any sense of stinginess; in this way, they shall further attain inexhaustible riches.
"In this way, Great King,
you should train yourself.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"From this day forward, I shall extensively practice giving to the fourfold assembly of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; however, I cannot bear to give to those who come as beggars from among the various non-Buddhists and heterodox teachers."
The World-Honored One said:
"Great King, do not harbor such a thought."
"The reason for this is that all sentient beings subsist by means of food; without food, they perish.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One should contemplate practicing extensive giving, And never allow the mind of generosity to cease."
"One shall surely encounter the worthy sages and cross over this source of birth and death.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now feel redoubled joy toward the Tathāgata. The reason for this is that all sentient beings exist by means of food; without food, none can survive."
At that time, King Prasenajit said, "From this day forward,
I shall practice extensive giving and have no sense of stinginess. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the king.
Then the king rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet with his head, and withdrew.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, while in a secluded place, had this thought:
“Is there perhaps such a fragrance in the world that wafts against the wind, with the wind, and both against and with the wind?
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"While I was in a secluded place, this thought arose in me:
'Is there perhaps such a fragrance in the world that wafts both against the wind, with the wind, and both against and with the wind?'"
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"There is this wondrous fragrance; it is a fragrance that travels against the wind, a fragrance that travels with the wind, and a fragrance that travels both against and with the wind."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What kind of incense is this?
It wafts against the wind, it wafts with the wind, and it wafts both against and with the wind.”
The World-Honored One replied:
"There is such a fragrance; moreover, the power of this fragrance extends against the wind, with the wind, and both against and with the wind."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of fragrance is this, which wafts against the wind, with the wind, and both against and with the wind?
The World-Honored One replied:
"These three kinds of incense have fragrance that travels against the wind, fragrance that travels with the wind, and fragrance that travels both against and with the wind.
Ānanda asked: "What are these three?"
The Blessed One said:
“The fragrance of morality, the fragrance of learning, and the fragrance of generosity.
These, Ānanda, are what I call [the fragrances].”
There is this kind of fragrance; moreover, this fragrance wafts against the wind, with the wind, and both against and with the wind.
Of all fragrances existing in the world, these three kinds of fragrance are the most excellent, the most supreme; there is nothing equal to them, and none can surpass them.
It is just as there is curd from cow's milk, butter from curd, and ghee from butter; yet this ghee is the most excellent, the most supreme, with nothing equal to it, and nothing that can surpass it.
"This is also like that: among all the various worldly incenses, these three kinds of incense are the most excellent, the most supreme, and none can equal them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Kālānusāri and sandalwood, Utpala and all other fragrances,"
Among all various kinds of fragrances, the fragrance of morality is the most supreme.
When this morality is perfected— one who is free from desire and undefiled,
liberated through equal wisdom— the destination of such a person is unknown even to Māra.
Although these fragrances are exquisite, as are the various scents of sandalwood and honey,
the fragrance of the precepts is most sublime, for it is heard throughout the ten directions.
Though sandalwood possesses scent, as do the utpala lotus and other perfumes, [none compare to the fragrance of the precepts].
Among all these various fragrances, the fragrance of hearing is foremost.
Though sandalwood possesses fragrance, as do the utpala and other scents,
among all these various fragrances, the fragrance of giving is foremost.
"These are called the three kinds of incense that waft against the wind, with the wind, and both against and with the wind. Therefore, Ānanda!"
"You should seek skillful means to accomplish these three fragrances. Thus, Ānanda,
you should train yourself."
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms-bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
At that same time, Devadatta also entered the city for alms.
At that time, as Devadatta entered a certain alleyway, the Buddha also went there; however, seeing Devadatta approaching from afar, the Buddha wished to withdraw and depart.
At that time, Ānanda said to the World-Honored One,
"For what reason do you wish to leave this alley?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Devadatta is now in this lane; therefore, let us avoid him.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!”
"Are you afraid of Devadatta?
The World-Honored One replied, "I am not afraid of Devadatta; however, this evil person should not be allowed to meet with me."
Ānanda said: "Indeed, World-Honored One!
It may be that this Devadatta could be sent to another realm."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I never harbor such a thought: 'Let him go elsewhere;
let him create his own karma, and let him dwell wherever he pleases.'"
Ānanda said to the World-Honored One:
"Indeed, Devadatta has committed an offense against the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One replied:
"One should not associate with a foolish and deluded person.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda with this verse:
"One should not look upon the fool; One should not engage in affairs with the fool."
"Nor should you engage them in debate, nor speak of matters of right and wrong.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the World-Honored One with this verse:
"What is it that the fool is capable of? What is the fault of the fool?"
"Even if we were to engage in conversation together, what kind of fault would there ultimately be?
At that time, the World-Honored One further replied to Ānanda with these verses:
"The fool creates his own actions; that which he performs is contrary to the Dharma."
Right view opposes the heterodox rules, yet false views increase day by day. "Therefore, Ānanda!
Do not associate with evil friends."

The reason for this is that if one associates with foolish people who lack faith, precepts, learning, and wisdom, one will not progress; however, if one associates with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), one increases all merits and achieves the perfection of the precepts.
"In this way, Ānanda,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7 (Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove together with five hundred people.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru regularly provided Devadatta with food from five hundred cauldrons.

At that time, Devadatta’s fame spread far and wide; he was fully endowed with the virtue of the precepts and possessed a complete reputation, such that he was even able to cause the king to come daily to provide him with offerings.
At that time, having obtained these gains and offerings, the bhikṣus heard of it and said to the World-Honored One:
"The people of the country praise Devadatta, and his fame has spread so far as to cause King Ajātaśatru to come constantly to provide him with offerings."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus, do not harbor such thoughts as to covet the offerings and gains of Devadatta."

The reason for this is that the foolish Devadatta committed these three acts through his body, speech, and mind, yet he felt no alarm or fear, nor did he experience any dread. Just as with the foolish Devadatta today, he shall eventually exhaust all these roots of wholesome merit; it will be like taking a wicked dog and breaking its nose, making it twice as fierce and malevolent.
The foolish Devadatta was likewise; having received these offerings and gains, he consequently gave rise to arrogance.
Therefore, monks, do not allow your minds to become attached to gain and offerings.
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who is attached to gain and profit, yet does not attain three dharmas.
What are these three?
They are the noble precepts, the noble samādhi, and the noble wisdom, which he fails to accomplish.
If there is a bhikṣu who does not cling to gain and honor, he will obtain three dharmas.
What are these three?
They are the noble precepts, noble samādhi, and noble wisdom.
If you wish to accomplish these three dharmas, you should give rise to a virtuous mind and remain unattached to gain and honor.
Thus, O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these three unwholesome roots.
What are the three? They are as follows:"
The unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
If a bhikṣu possesses these three unwholesome roots, he will fall into the three evil destinies.
What are the three?
They are the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"If one possesses these three unwholesome roots, there are then the three evil destinies.
Bhikṣus, you should know that there are these three wholesome roots. What are the three? "
The root of goodness of non-greed, the root of goodness of non-hatred, and the root of goodness of non-delusion—these are called the three roots of goodness possessed by a bhikṣu.
If one possesses these three roots of goodness, there are two wholesome destinations, with nirvāṇa as the third.
What are the two destinies?
They are namely the human and the celestial realms.
Thus, it is said that a bhikṣu who possesses these three virtues will be born in these auspicious places.
Therefore, monks, you should abandon the three unwholesome roots and cultivate the three wholesome roots. Thus it is, monks.
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these three groups.”

What are the three? They are the group of those destined for correctness (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi), the group of those destined for error (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi), and the group of those who are undetermined (aniyata-rāśi).
What is meant by the group of those destined for correctness?
That which is called right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this is termed the aggregate of the right.
What is called the "wrong category"?
It refers to wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration; this is called the wrong category.
What is meant by the "indeterminate group"?

It refers to those who do not know suffering, do not know its origin, do not know its cessation, do not know the path, do not know the right group, and do not know the wrong group; this is called the indeterminate group.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are further three groups.
What are the three?
They are the group of the wholesome, the group of the indeterminate, and the group of the fixed.”
What is called the "good accumulation"?
It refers to the three roots of goodness.
What are these roots of goodness?
What are called the roots of goodness of non-greed, the roots of goodness of non-anger, and the roots of goodness of non-delusion—these are termed the "heap of goodness.
What is termed the "heap of the equal"?

It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are termed the "heap of the equal."
What is meant by the "determined group" (niyata-rāśi)?

It refers to knowing suffering, knowing its origin, knowing its cessation, knowing the path, knowing the accumulation of merit, knowing the evil destinies, and knowing the determined group; this is what is called the determined group.
Therefore, monks! Among these three groups, you should distance yourselves from the group of the wrong and the group of the undetermined; you should practice and follow this group of the right.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these three perceptions. What are the three?
They are the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of cruelty.”
This is called the bhikṣu possessing these three perceptions.
A bhikṣu should know that if one contemplates perceptions of desire, at the time of death one will fall into hell;
if one contemplates perceptions of ill-will, at the time of death one will be born among animals.
That is to say, those belonging to the species of chickens and dogs, or the class of snakes and vipers, are born therein.
Furthermore, those who die while contemplating harmful thoughts are reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); their bodies are ablaze, and their suffering is difficult to describe.
"Monks, these are called the three perceptions that lead to birth in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, and among the animals.
Furthermore, there are three other perceptions; what are the three?
These are the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-harming, and the perception of non-ill will.
If there is a person who possesses the perception of renunciation, at the time of death they will be reborn among these people.
If there is one who possesses the perception of non-harming, at the time of death they will naturally be reborn in the heavens.
If there is a person who has no intent to kill, at the time of death they will sever the five fetters and attain parinirvāṇa right there.
"Monks, this is what is meant:
there are these three perceptions which one should constantly keep in mind and practice; these three unwholesome perceptions should be abandoned. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[The names of the bhikṣus were: Dharaṇīmdhara, Bakula, Karṇa, Vādi, Anulomaviloma, and Gandha.
Folly, the world, the three unwholesome [roots], and the three aggregates;
the contemplation follows later. *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 13 and Scroll 14.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The High Banner (Ucchaya-dhvaja).
Part One. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, spoke to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven:"

"O you all, when you enter the midst of a great battle, if there should arise in you any heart of terror or fear, you must look back at my tall and broad banner; once you have seen my banner, you shall be free from fear."
If you do not remember my banner, you should remember the banner of the Heavenly King Īśvara;
by remembering that banner, all fear and dread shall naturally be extinguished.
If you do not recollect my banner, nor the banner of Īśāna, then at that time you should recollect the banner of the Heavenly King Varuṇa;
by recollecting that banner, all fears and terrors will naturally be extinguished.

"I now likewise declare to you all: if there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who experience fear such that their hair stands on end, they should at that time mindfully recollect my body—this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Worthy, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the One Blessed by the Multitudes—who has appeared in the world."
Should there be any fear that causes the hair on one's body to stand on end, it shall immediately vanish.
If you do not yet think of me, then at that time you should think of the Dharma.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is exceedingly subtle and wondrous; it is that which the wise study.
For one who recollects the Dharma, all fears and terrors will naturally vanish.
"If you do not recollect me, nor do you recollect the Dharma, then at that time you should recollect the Noble Saṅgha."
The noble assembly of the Tathāgata is exceedingly harmonious, having achieved perfection in every dharma:
perfection in ethical discipline, perfection in meditative concentration, perfection in wisdom, perfection in liberation, and perfection in the knowledge and vision of liberation.

What are called the four pairs and eight classes constitute the noble assembly of the Tathāgata; they are worthy of honor and service, the field of merit for the world—this is what is meant by the noble assembly of the Tathāgata.
At that time, once one has recollected the Sangha, all fear and dread will naturally vanish.

"Bhikṣus, you should know this: even Śakra Devānām Indra possesses lust, anger, and delusion; yet when the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three recollect their lord, they are free from fear and dread.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, who is entirely without desire, anger, or delusion—could he ever have fear or dread when recollected?"
If any bhikṣu experiences fear, it shall be extinguished of its own accord.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should keep the Triple Gem in mind:
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a spirit in the realm of the Vṛji country named Viśa.

Within that kingdom, he was extremely fierce and violent, killing immeasurable people; every day he would kill one person, or sometimes two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty people.
At that time, various spirits and rākṣasas filled that country.
Then, the people of Vaiśālī all gathered together and spoke thus:
"We should be able to avoid this country and go to the borders of another kingdom; we need not remain here."
At that time, the evil spirit Viśāla, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those people, spoke to them, saying:
"Do not leave this place to go to other lands."
"The reason for this is that you shall ultimately not escape my hands.
You all must offer one person each day as a sacrifice to me; I shall certainly not trouble you otherwise.
At that time, the people of Vārāṇasī took one person every day to sacrifice to that evil spirit.
At that time, after that ghost had devoured the man, it took his bones and cast them away into the mountains of another region; thus, the bones filled the streams and valleys of those mountains.

At that time, there was an elder named Sujāta living there, possessing abundant wealth and many treasures, with accumulated riches amounting to a thousand koṭis. His mules, donkeys, and camels were beyond counting, and his gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, pearls, and amber were likewise beyond measure.
At that time, that elder had a son named Nāyula; being his only child, he cherished and revered him deeply, never letting him out of his sight.
At that time, there was this restriction: it was next the turn of the boy Naula to make offerings to the spirits.
Then, the parents of Naula bathed the boy, dressed him in fine clothes, and led him to the cemetery, arriving at the abode of those spirits.
Having arrived, they wept and wailed beyond measure, all saying:
"O gods, O earth-gods, may you all bear witness together:
this is our only son; we pray that the divine beings will bear witness to this."

Furthermore, the twenty-eight great ghost-king deities shall together protect this child, ensuring that no lack shall occur; the Four Heavenly Kings shall all take refuge together, vowing to provide protection for this child so that they may be delivered from danger;
Śakra-devānām-indra shall likewise take refuge, vowing to save this child’s life;
and Brahmā-devānām-indra shall also take refuge, vowing to deliver this child from death.
All the spirits and deities who protect the world also turn toward me in refuge, so that I may be delivered from this calamity;
all the disciples of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, I now likewise take refuge in, so that I may be delivered from this calamity;
and all the Pratyekabuddhas who have awakened by themselves without a teacher also take refuge in me, so that I may be delivered from this calamity.

That Tathāgata now likewise takes refuge in himself: he subdues those not yet subdued, delivers those not yet delivered, enables those not yet attained to attain, and liberates those not yet liberated; he causes those who have not entered parinirvāṇa to enter parinirvāṇa. To those without protection, he provides protection; to the blind, he becomes their eyes; to the sick, he becomes a great King of Physicians. Among devas, nāgas, spirits, all people, māras, and mārakāyikas, he is the most honored and supreme, with none able to equal him. He is worthy of reverence and esteem, serving as a field of merit and a source of blessing for humanity; there is no one who surpasses the Tathāgata.
"Nevertheless, may the Tathāgata examine this; we pray that the Tathāgata will behold this utmost sincerity.
At that time, Nandīpāla’s parents, having entrusted their son to the spirit, withdrew and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his purified divine eye and his far-reaching divine ear, heard these words: "The parents of Naulāra are weeping beyond measure."
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, went to the mountain where the malevolent spirits resided.
At that moment, those malevolent spirits had gathered at the abode of the ghosts and spirits to the north of the Snowy Mountains.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the abode of the spirits and sat down, straightening his body and composing his mind in the full lotus posture.
At that same time, the boy Naula gradually arrived at the dwelling place of those malevolent spirits.

At that time, the boy Naula saw from afar the Tathāgata in the abode of the malevolent spirits, his radiance brilliant and glowing; with body upright and mind composed, he maintained mindfulness before him; his countenance was dignified and peerless in the world; his faculties were tranquil, and he had attained all merits, having subdued all Māras—such virtues as these were beyond measure or calculation.

He is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics that grace his body; like Mount Sumeru rising above all other peaks, his face is like the sun and moon, and also like a mountain of gold, its radiance shining afar.
Having seen him, he immediately gave rise to a heart of joy toward the Tathāgata and thought to himself:
"This must certainly not be the evil Piśāca demon.
For this reason, as I behold him now, I feel an extreme sense of joy; had he been an evil demon, he would have devoured me at his will."
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Naulā! It is as you have said;
I am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and have therefore come to rescue you and to subdue this evil spirit."

At that time, having heard these words, Nāula was filled with joy and exultation beyond measure; he then went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded for them the sublime Dharma.

That is to say, he spoke on the discourse of giving, the discourse of morality, and the discourse of rebirth in heaven; he taught that sensual desires are defiled and impure, that the outflows are unwholesome, and that leaving the household life is essential for removing all distracted thoughts.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the boy Naulā’s mind was joyful and his disposition was supple, taught him in full the Dharma that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly preach: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Right there on his seat, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, having mastered and internalized all phenomena, he was free from doubt; understanding the teaching of the Tathāgata, he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and received the five precepts.
At that time, the evil ghost Viśāla returned to his original dwelling place.
Thereupon, the evil ghost saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting upright in contemplation, his body unmoving.
Upon seeing this, he immediately gave rise to wrath and anger, raining down thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts toward the place where the Tathāgata was, or raining down swords and blades;
yet before they had even fallen to the ground, they were transformed into *utpala* lotuses.
At that time, the ghost became even more enraged and rained down mountains, rivers, and rocky cliffs;
yet before they could reach the ground, these were transformed into various kinds of food and drink.
At that time, the ghost again transformed himself into a great elephant and roared as he approached the place where the Tathāgata was.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One again transformed himself into a lion king.
At that time, the ghost further transformed himself into the form of a lion and approached the place where the Tathāgata was.
Then, the World-Honored One manifested a great mass of fire.
At that moment, the ghost became even more enraged and transformed himself into a great seven-headed dragon.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested as a great garuḍa. Then, the ghost thought to himself:
"I shall now manifest all my supernatural powers; yet this śramaṇa’s hair and feathers do not stir. I should now go and inquire about his profound meaning."
At that time, the ghost asked the World-Honored One:
"I, Vaiśravaṇa, now wish to inquire about a profound matter; if you cannot answer me, I shall seize your two feet and hurl you across the southern sea."
The World-Honored One said:

"Evil spirit, you should know that I have personally observed that there is no deva, nor human, nor śramaṇa, nor brāhmaṇa, nor any person or non-person capable of seizing my two feet and hurling me across the southern ocean."
"But if you now wish to inquire about a matter, you may do so.
At that time, the evil spirit asked: "Śramaṇa!..."
What is past practice? What is new practice?
What is the cessation of practice?
The World-Honored One said:
"Evil spirit, you should know that the eye is a conditioned formation produced in the past; it is a conditioned formation brought about by conditions and suffering.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these are also conditioned formations produced in the past; they are conditioned formations brought about by conditions and suffering."
"This, O evil spirit, is called 'past action.
The Piśāca spirit said: "O Śramaṇa!"
"What is this 'new practice'?
The World-Honored One replied:
"The three actions of body, four of speech, and three of mind performed by one's current self—this, O evil spirit, is what it is called."
"This is new practice.
Then the evil spirit asked:
"What is the cessation of practice?"
The World-Honored One said:

"Evil spirit, you should know that when volitional formations (saṃskāra) have been extinguished and do not arise again, and one no longer creates them—being able to grasp this state so that they are forever unborn, forever exhausted without remainder—this is called the cessation of volitional formations."
At that time, the ghost said to the World-Honored One:
"I am now extremely hungry; for what reason do you deprive me of my food?
This child is my prey, O Śramaṇa!"
"You may take this child back to me.

The World-Honored One said, "In the past, before I had attained the Way, when I was still a bodhisattva, a dove flew to me; I did not begrudge my own body or life in order to rescue that dove from its peril."
How much more so now that I have become a Tathāgata—could I ever abandon this child for you to devour?
You evil spirit, though you exhaust all your supernatural powers, I shall never give this child to you.
"How is it, evil spirit? In the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you once became a śramaṇa and practiced the holy life; later, however, you violated the precepts and were reborn as this evil spirit."
At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the evil spirit recalled the various deeds he had committed in the past.
Thereupon, the evil spirit went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke thus:

“I am now deluded and ignorant, failing to distinguish the true from the false, and have even conceived such thoughts toward the Tathāgata. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance.”
Thus he repeated this three or four times.
The World-Honored One said to him:
"I grant you absolution from your transgression; do not commit it again."
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the Piśāca spirit, exhorting him to rejoice.
Then, that evil spirit held up several thousand taels of gold in his hands and offered them to the World-Honored One, saying to him:
"I now offer these mountain valleys to the Saṃgha of the four quarters; I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept them from me, as well as these several thousand taels of gold."
Thus he requested a second and a third time.
Then the World-Honored One accepted this mountain valley and spoke these verses:
"By giving orchards and fruits for cool refreshment, And by constructing waterways, bridges, and causeways,"
If one can construct a great ship, along with all the necessities for sustaining life,
without ceasing day or night, the merit obtained will be immeasurable.
Through the accomplishment of the Dharma, its meaning, and the precepts, one will be reborn in the heavens after death.
At that time, the ghost addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "I do not know,
World-Honored One, what further instructions you may have?
The World-Honored One replied:

"Now, you should cast off your original form, don the three robes, become a śramaṇa, and enter the city of Vārāṇasī. At every place you go, issue this proclamation: 'Virtuous ones, you should know that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world.

He subdues those who are unsubdued; he delivers those who are undelivered; he brings to liberation those who are not liberated; he provides protection for those who have no protector; he acts as eyes for the blind. Among gods, humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, māras, mārakāyikas, humans, and non-humans, he is the most honored and supreme, with none equal to him. He is worthy of reverence and esteem, serving as a field of merit and a source of blessing for all people.'"
"Today I have ordained the youth Naula and subdued the evil spirit Piśāca; you all should go there to receive his transformation. They replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the Piśāca demon assumed the form of a śramaṇa, donned the three dharma robes, and entered the streets and alleys, issuing this command:
“Today the World-Honored One has delivered the boy Naūla and subdued the evil Piśāca demon; you all should go there to receive his instruction.”
At that time, the realm of the kingdom of Vaiśālī was flourishing with a vast population.

Upon hearing these words, the elder Sujāta was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he took eighty-four thousand people and beings and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, among the people of Vārāṇasī, some prostrated themselves at his feet, while others joined their palms in reverence.
At that time, the assembly of eighty-four thousand people were already seated to one side.
Then, the World-Honored One gradually preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to them.

That discourse consisted of a discussion on giving, a discussion on ethical discipline, and a discussion on rebirth in the heavens; it further addressed the impurity of sensual desires and how the outflows (āsrava) constitute a great affliction.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed those eighty-four thousand assemblies, their minds filled with joy.

The Dharma that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly teach—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—he preached this Dharma universally to those eighty-four thousand assemblies. Thereupon, while still seated, the various defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Just as a clean, white cloth is easily dyed with color, so it was with these eighty-four thousand followers:

all their defilements were exhausted, and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; they attained the Dharma, saw the Dharma, and discerned all phenomena. Free from doubt and having attained fearlessness, they took refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha—and received the five precepts.
At that time, the householder Nāḷijaṅgha’s father addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“I pray only that the Blessed One will accept my invitation.
Then, the Blessed One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

At that time, seeing that the World-Honored One had accepted by remaining silent, the elder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to his residence. There he prepared various kinds of food and drink of many flavors, and at dawn, he personally announced:
"The time has come."

At that time, when it was time for the meal, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Vaiśālī. He proceeded to the house of the elder and sat down upon the prepared seat.

When the elder saw that the World-Honored One was seated, he personally served various kinds of food and drink. Having seen that the World-Honored One had finished eating and had been provided with pure water, the elder took a seat and sat before the Tathāgata, addressing the World-Honored One:
“Excellent! [...]”
"Blessed One!
If the fourfold assembly requires robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicine for the sick and infirm, let them all take these from my home."
The Blessed One said: "So it is, householder!
It is just as you have said."
The World-Honored One then expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the elder. Having finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that moment, in the time it takes to bend or extend one’s arm, the World-Honored One vanished from Vṛji and returned to the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If the fourfold assembly requires clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicine for the sick and infirm, you should take them from the house of Nandipāla’s father."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my upāsakas today, the foremost disciple who has nothing he begrudges is this one, namely, the father Nāula."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Kapilavastu together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, several thousand members of the prominent Śākya clans went to where the World-Honored One was; having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the Śākyas said to the World-Honored One:
"Today you shall become king and govern this realm; thus our lineage will remain imperishable, and the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King shall not be extinguished in you."

If the World-Honored One had not left the household life, he would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King over the world, ruling over the four continents with a full thousand sons; our family name and title would have spread far and wide, for a Wheel-Turning Sage King has emerged from the Śākya clan.
"For this reason, World-Honored One,
you should exercise royal governance so that the royal lineage shall not be severed.
The World-Honored One replied:
"I am now truly in the body of a king, and my name is Dharmarāja (Dharma King).
Why is this so? I shall now ask you, O Śākyas: 'What do you think?'"
"You speak of the Wheel-Turning Sage King being fully endowed with the seven treasures and having a thousand valiant sons;

yet I am now, within this trichiliocosm, the most honored and supreme, with none able to equal me. I have accomplished the treasure of the seven factors of enlightenment and am attended by countless thousands of sons who are śrāvakas."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"What is the use of this position?
Having attained it, one loses it again."
This state is most supreme; it has no end and no beginning.
Because it is supreme, nothing can take it away; this supremacy is the most supreme.
Yet, regarding the Buddha’s immeasurable conduct—being traceless, who could follow his traces?
"Therefore, O Gautamas! You should seek skillful means to govern as righteous Dharma-kings.
Thus it is, O Śākyas!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the Śākyas, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, that bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Is there such a form that remains eternally without change?
That endures for a long time in the world without ever shifting?"
“Is there perhaps any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that remains eternally without change,
that persists for a long time in the world, and does not shift?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Monks! There is no such form that remains constant, unchanging, and endures for a long time in the world; nor is there any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that remains constant, unchanging, and endures for a long time in the world.”
Furthermore, monks!
If this form were to exist eternally, unchanging, and persisting for a long time in the world, then those who practice the holy life would be unable to discern it.

If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were to endure in the world for a long time without changing or decaying, then those who practice the holy life could not achieve discernment. Therefore, bhikṣus!

Because form cannot be differentiated and does not endure long in the world, those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) are able to differentiate it and exhaust the root of suffering; likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not endure long in the world, and therefore the holy life can differentiate them and exhaust the root of suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of dust, placed it upon his fingernail, and said to that bhikṣu:
"What do you think, bhikṣu?
Do you see this dust on my nail?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“Indeed, I have seen them, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“If such a vast amount of form were to exist eternally in the world, then those who practice the holy life would be unable to discern the end of suffering.
For this reason, bhikṣus!”
Since there is no such form remaining, one is able to practice the holy life and bring an end to the root of suffering.
Why is this so? Monks, you should know that in the past, I was once a great king!
He ruled over the four continents, transforming them through the Dharma, governing the people, and possessing the seven treasures.

These so-called seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, when I was this Wheel-Turning Sage King ruling over the four continents, I had eighty-four thousand divine elephants, and the name of these elephants was Puhū.”

Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand chariots adorned with feathered jewels; some were covered with lion skins, while others were covered with wolf or dog skins, all of which were equipped with suspended banners and lofty canopies.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand high and broad terraces, resembling the abodes of the Lord of Devas.
There were also eighty-four thousand lecture halls, comparable to the Hall of Dharma.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand assemblies of jade maidens, whose appearance was like that of celestial nymphs.
There were also eighty-four thousand high and broad seats, all inlaid with gold, silver, and the seven precious gems.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand garments and ornaments, all embroidered with patterns and soft to the touch.
Additionally, there were eighty-four thousand vessels for food and drink, containing various kinds of flavors.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time I was riding a great elephant of exquisite white color, with six tusks from its mouth, adorned with gold and silver. Its body could fly through the air and could also become invisible; it could grow large or small. The name of this elephant was Puhuo.”

At that time, I rode a divine horse whose hair and tail were crimson in color; it moved without the body shifting, was adorned with gold and silver, could fly through the air, and could also make itself invisible or change its size at will—large or small. This horse was named Mowwang (King of Hair).
At that time, among eighty-four thousand high and wide terraces, I dwelt upon one terrace named Sunima, which was made entirely of pure gold.
At that time, I was staying overnight in a lecture hall named Dharmadeśanā, which was made entirely of pure gold.
At that time, I rode in a precious feathered carriage named Jyeṣṭha, which was also made entirely of pure gold.
At that time, I took a jade maiden as my attendant, whom I treated like a sister.
At that time, among eighty-four thousand high and wide seats, I sat upon one seat adorned with gold, silver, and necklaces beyond measure.
At that time, I wore a single exquisite garment, resembling celestial raiment.
The food I consumed tasted like nectar.

During that period, I was a Wheel-Turning Sage King; at that time, eighty-four thousand divine elephants came every morning, and those injured outside the gates were so numerous as to be beyond calculation.
At that time, I thought to myself:
"These eighty-four thousand divine elephants come every morning, and those injured outside my gate are so numerous as to be beyond counting."
"I now intend to divide [them] into two parts, so that forty-two thousand may come every morning to offer their congratulations. At that time,
O Bhikṣu, I had this thought:
"What merit did you perform in the past?
What virtue did you cultivate,
that you have now attained such power as this?"
Again, he thought: "It is due to three causes and conditions that I have obtained this merit and blessing.
What are these three?"
That is to say: generosity, loving-kindness, and self-restraint.
A bhikṣu should observe that at that time all conditioned phenomena are extinguished without remainder, yet at that time one still wanders within the realm of desire, never reaching satiety.
What is called "satiety" refers to satiety regarding the precepts of the noble ones.
What do you think, bhikṣu:
is this form permanent?
"Is it impermanent?
The bhikṣu replied, "It is impermanent."
“World-Honored One!
If, moreover, it were impermanent and subject to change, could you give rise to this thought: ‘This is mine; I belong to that’?”
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent?
The bhikṣu replied:
“It is impermanent, World-Honored One.
“If it is impermanent and subject to change, you might give rise to this thought: ‘This is mine; I am this; this is my self.’”
He replied: "No, World-Honored One."
"Therefore, bhikṣus! Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present;
whether great or small."
Whether beautiful or ugly, whether distant or near, this form is not mine, nor am I its; this is what the wise study.
Whatever feelings there are—whether past, future, or present; whether distant or near—these feelings are not mine, nor am I theirs.
This is what the wise perceive and understand.

A bhikṣu should contemplate in this way: if a śrāvaka feels weary of the eye, weary of forms, and weary of eye-consciousness, he should likewise feel weary of the suffering and pleasure that arise conditioned by the eye.
He also feels weary of the ear, weary of sounds, and weary of ear-consciousness; if suffering or pleasure arises dependent upon ear-consciousness, he likewise feels weary of that.
