He also feels weary of the nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as mental objects; if suffering or pleasure arises dependent upon the mind, he likewise feels weary of that.
Having become weary [of existence], one is liberated;
being liberated, one attains the knowledge of liberation:
"Birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—one knows this as it truly is.

At that time, having received such instruction from the World-Honored One, that bhikṣu dwelt in a secluded place, reflecting and practicing for himself. Thus, the son of noble family who had shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, and left the home life to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life, came to know it as it truly is:
"Birth and death are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence to be undergone."
That bhikṣu then became an arhat.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 51 (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was at the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha, having just attained Buddhahood.
At that moment, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"I have now attained this most profound Dharma, which is difficult to understand, difficult to comprehend, difficult to discern, and difficult to know; it is realized only by the most subtle and wondrous wisdom. With whom should I first preach this Dharma?"
"Who is it that can understand my Dharma?
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Rāḍha and Uruvelakassapa have fully matured faculties; they should be the first to attain liberation, yet they must wait for me to possess the Dharma."
Having formed this thought, a deva in the sky addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Rāṣṭrapāla has been dead for seven days.
At that time, the World-Honored One again reflected:
"How bitter it is that they have met their end without hearing my Dharma;
had they heard my Dharma, they would have attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought to himself:
"To whom shall I first preach the Dharma so that they may attain liberation?
Now, Udraka Rāmaputra should be the first to be delivered; I shall preach it to him, for having heard my Dharma, he will be the first to attain liberation."
The Blessed One had this thought, when a deva in the sky spoke these words:
"In the middle of last night, he passed away.
At that time, the Blessed One then had this thought:
"How tragic it is for Udraka Rāmaputra!
He has passed away without hearing my Dharma;
had he been able to hear my Dharma, he would have attained liberation."
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"Who shall be the first to hear the Dharma and attain liberation?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One reflected once more.
“The five bhikṣus have been of great benefit to me; when I was first born, they followed after me.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought to himself:
“Where, now, are those five bhikṣus?”
He then observed with his divine eye that the five bhikṣus were staying at the Deer Park of the Sages in Vārāṇasī.
"I shall now go there first to teach the Dharma to the five bhikṣus; having heard my Dharma, they shall attain liberation."
At that time, for seven days, the World-Honored One gazed intently at the Bodhi tree without blinking his eyes.
Then, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"In this place where I now sit, I have endured the sufferings of birth and death."
Grasping the axe of wisdom, he has forever severed the roots and the sprouts.
When the Heavenly King arrived here, along with all his hosts of māras and enemies,
he further subdued them through skillful means, causing them to don the crown of liberation.
Now, beneath this tree, seated upon the diamond throne,
I have attained all-knowledge and reached unimpeded wisdom.
Sitting here beneath this tree, I behold the suffering of birth and death.
"The root source of death has been cast aside; old age and sickness shall forever be no more.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed, intending to go toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, the brahmin Upika saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s radiance was brilliant, eclipsing the light of the sun and moon; having seen this, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Gautama!..."
Where does the Master currently reside?
Under whom has he gone forth to study the Way?
And what teachings and doctrines does he always delight in expounding?
"From where have you come?
Where do you intend to go?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin and spoke this verse:
“I have attained arhatship; I am peerless in the world. Among gods and humans, I am now supreme.
I have no teacher or protector, nor is there anyone equal to me.”
The Sole Honored One, beyond reproach, Who was cold and no longer warm, shall now turn the Wheel of Dharma. He will go to the land of Kāśī;
Now, with the medicine of ambrosia, he shall open the eyes of those who are blind and in darkness.
In the realm of Vārāṇasī, within the kingdom of Kāśi,
at the dwelling place of the five bhikṣus, I wish to proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma,
so that they may quickly attain the Way and achieve the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows.
"Because it eradicates the root of unwholesome dharmas, it is therefore the most supreme.
At that time, the brahmin sighed in admiration; with his head bowed and hands joined in reverence, he snapped his fingers and smiled as he took the path and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded toward Vārāṇasī.
When the five bhikṣus saw the World-Honored One coming from afar, they consulted one another, saying:
"This is the śramaṇa Gautama coming from the distance; his temperament is disordered and his mind is not focused."
"We shall no longer speak with him, nor shall we rise to greet him, nor invite him to sit.
At that time, the five men spoke this verse:
"This man is not worthy of respect; nor should he be looked upon with intimacy."
"Do not address him again as 'Welcome,' nor invite him to sit.
When the five men had spoken this verse, they all remained silent.
At that time, the World-Honored One approached the place where the five bhikṣus were;
as he drew near, the five bhikṣus gradually rose to meet him, some preparing a seat for him and others fetching water.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat down before him and reflected thus:
"This is a foolish person who has ultimately failed to fulfill his original commitment."
At that time, the five bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One by the familiar term "you. Thereupon, the World-Honored One said to the five bhikṣus:
"Do not address the Unsurpassed, Truly Realized, and Perfectly Enlightened One as 'you'."
The reason for this is that I have now attained supreme, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and have secured the nectar of the Dharma.
Attend closely and listen to my discourse on the Dharma.
At that time, the five bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:

“Gautama! When you formerly practiced asceticism, you were still unable to attain the state of a superior person; how much less can you claim to have attained the Way now, when your mind and emotions are so disordered?”
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, five men!
Have you ever heard me speak falsely?"
The five bhikṣus said, “No, Gautama!”
The World-Honored One said:
"The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has already attained the Deathless; you all should listen with single-minded attention as I preach the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"I am now capable of subduing these five men.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus:
“You should know that there are these Four Noble Truths. What are the four?
They are the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the path leading to the transcendence of suffering.”
What is called the Truth of Suffering?

It refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of grief, lamentation, distress, and despair—sorrows and pains beyond measure or description.

The suffering of association with the loathed, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and not obtaining what one desires—these, too, are suffering. To speak in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*): this is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
"What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
It refers to the pursuit of the objects of craving, practicing this without weariness, and the mind’s constant attachment; this is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering."
"What is the truth of the cessation of suffering?
That which causes this craving to be extinguished without remainder and not to arise again—this is called the truth of the cessation of suffering.
What is called the truth of the way leading out of suffering?"
This is called the Noble Eightfold Path;
namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
This is what is called the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
"Furthermore, O five bhikṣus!

Regarding this Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, as for the Truth of Suffering, the eye arose, knowledge arose, clarity arose, awakening arose, light arose, and wisdom arose, concerning a Dharma never heard before."
Furthermore, the Truth of Suffering is real, certain, not false, and not deceptive; it will never be otherwise.
Because it was spoken by the World-Honored One, it is called the Truth of Suffering.

Regarding the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (*duḥkhasamudayasatya*): for one who has not previously heard the Dharma, there arises the eye, there arises knowledge, there arises clarity, there arises awakening, there arises light, and there arises wisdom.
Furthermore, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering is real, fixed, not false, and not deceptive; it will never be otherwise.
Because it is what the World-Honored One has taught, it is called the Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

Regarding the truth of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodhasatya*): for me, who had never before heard this Dharma, there arose the eye, there arose knowledge, there arose clarity, there arose awakening, there arose wisdom, and there arose light.
Furthermore, the truth of the cessation of suffering is real, certain, not false, not deceptive, and will never be otherwise;
because it was spoken by the Blessed One, it is called the truth of the cessation of suffering.

Regarding the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha-gāminī-pratipad-āryasatya*): for me, who had not heard this Dharma before, there arose the eye, knowledge (*jñāna*), insight (*vidyā*), awakening (*buddhi*), light (*āloka*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering is real, fixed, not false, not deceptive, and will never be otherwise;
because it was spoken by the Blessed One, it is called the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

"O five bhikṣus, you should know that regarding these Four Noble Truths, if one does not understand them as they truly are through their three turnings and twelve aspects, then one does not achieve unsurpassed, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment."

Because I have discerned these Four Noble Truths through their three turnings and twelve aspects, knowing them as they truly are, I have therefore attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, as this Dharma was being taught, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was cleansed of all dust and defilements, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Kauṇḍinya, saying:
"Have you now reached the Dharma and attained the Dharma?"
Kauṇḍinya replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"Because he has attained the Dharma and reached the Dharma.
At that time, having heard these words, the Earth Deity proclaimed:
"Now the Tathāgata, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, turns the Wheel of Dharma."

That which cannot be turned back by gods, worldlings, Māras, or those who belong to the realm of Māra, nor by humans or non-humans—the Tathāgata today turns this wheel of Dharma, and Ājñātakauṇḍinya has already attained the Dharma of the Deathless.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings heard the proclamation from the earth deities and further announced:
"Ājñātakauṇḍinya has attained the Dharma of the Deathless."

At that time, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three heard it from the Four Great Kings; the Yāma gods heard it from the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three; and so on, until the sound was heard in succession up to the Tuṣita Heaven, and even as far as the Brahmā Heaven:

"The Tathāgata is turning the Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī—a wheel that has never been turned by gods, worldlings, Māras, or those belonging to the realm of Māra, whether humans or non-humans—and today the Tathāgata turns this Wheel of Dharma."
At that moment, he was named Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus:
"Two of you remain here to receive my instructions, while three go out for alms. Of the food obtained by those three, all six of us shall share it together."
"Three of you shall remain to receive instruction, while two go out to beg for food; the food obtained by those two shall be shared and eaten by all six.
At that time, this instruction became the Dharma of unarisen *nirvāṇa*, and it also became unarisen, free from illness, free from old age, and free from death.
At that time, the five bhikṣus all became arhats.
At that time, there were five arhats in the trichiliocosm, with the Buddha as the sixth.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus:
"All of you should go together to the human world for alms; be careful not to travel alone.

Furthermore, there are among the classes of sentient beings those whose faculties are fully matured and who are ready to be delivered; I shall now go to the village of Uruvilvā and preach the Dharma there."
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the village of Uruvilvā.

At that time, there was Kāśyapa dwelling on the banks of the Nairañjanā River; he was learned in the celestial and terrestrial sciences, possessing universal and profound mastery, and he understood the calculation of the number of leaves upon every tree, leading five hundred disciples whom he instructed daily.
Not far from Kāśyapa’s dwelling was a stone cave, within which a venomous dragon resided.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where Kāśyapa was.
Having arrived, he spoke to Kāśyapa, saying:
"I wish to stay overnight in a stone cave;
if you grant me permission, I shall go there to reside."
Kāśyapa replied, "I do not begrudge it;
however, there is a venomous dragon there, and I fear it might harm you.
The World-Honored One said:
“Kāśyapa! Do not worry!
The dragon will not harm me; I have merely requested permission to stay for one night.”
Kāśyapa replied, "If you wish to stay, go and dwell there as you please.

At that time, the World-Honored One went to the stone cave, spread out his seat, and stayed overnight; he sat cross-legged, straightening his body and composing his mind, binding his mindfulness before him.
At that time, seeing the World-Honored One seated, the venomous dragon spat forth fiery poison.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi of loving-kindness; emerging from that samādhi of loving-kindness, he entered the samādhi of blazing light.
At that time, the dragon-fire and the Buddha’s radiance appeared simultaneously.
Then, Kāśyapa rose in the night and, observing the stars, saw a great mass of fire within the stone cave.
Having seen this, he said to his disciples:
"This Śramaṇa Gautama was of handsome appearance; that he has now been harmed by a dragon is truly pitiable!"
"I have already said this before:
'There is an evil dragon there; one must not stay overnight.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed his five hundred disciples:
"Take your water jar and the high ladder; go and extinguish that fire so that the śramaṇa may be delivered from this calamity.
At that time, Kāśyapa, leading five hundred disciples, went to the stone chamber to extinguish the fire;
some carried water to sprinkle it, while others provided ladders, yet they were unable to extinguish the fire at once—all this was due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi of loving-kindness, gradually causing that dragon to be free from anger.
Then, that evil dragon, harboring fear in his heart, ran hither and thither, seeking to escape the stone chamber, yet he was unable to leave it.
At that time, that evil nāga came toward the Tathāgata and entered the World-Honored One’s almsbowl to dwell there.
Then, the World-Honored One stroked the body of the evil nāga with his right hand and spoke this verse:
“Extremely difficult it is for a nāga to emerge; A nāga gathering together with other nāgas.”
Nāga, do not give rise to a harmful mind; it is extremely difficult for a nāga to emerge from its realm.
Though countless Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have entered parinirvāṇa in the past, you have never encountered them; all this is due to the fire of your anger.
With a virtuous mind directed toward the Tathāgata, quickly abandon this poison of anger;
having eliminated the poison of hatred, one shall then be reborn in the heavens.
— *Ekottarika Āgama*, Volume XIV.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The High Banner (Uccadhvaja), Part Two.
At that time, that evil dragon extended its tongue, licked the Tathāgata’s hand, and gazed intently at the Tathāgata’s face.
Then, on the following morning at dawn, the World-Honored One took this evil dragon in his hands and went to visit Kāśyapa, saying to him:
"This is an evil dragon, extremely fierce and violent; I have now subdued it."
At that time, having seen the evil dragon, Kāśyapa was struck with terror and said to the World-Honored One:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Śramaṇa! Do not come forward again; the dragon is prepared to harm you.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Kāśyapa! Do not fear; I have now subdued it, and it will never cause you harm.
This is because this dragon has already received my teaching.”
At that time, Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples marveled at what they had never before experienced, exclaiming:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
"This śramaṇa Gautama possesses immense majestic power; he was able to subdue this evil dragon and prevent it from doing harm.
Nevertheless, even so, he is still not equal to me in attaining the true Way."
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “Great Śramaṇa!
Please accept my invitation for ninety days; whatever you require—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicines for illness—I shall provide it all.”
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted Kāśyapa’s invitation.

Then, the World-Honored One placed this divine nāga into the great ocean; subsequently, according to the length of its lifespan, that evil nāga, after its life ended, was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
At that time, the Tathāgata returned to stay in the stone cave.
After Kāśyapa had prepared various kinds of food and drink, he went to inform the World-Honored One:
"The meal is ready; you may go to take your meal."
The World-Honored One said, "Kāśyapa shall go on ahead; I shall follow shortly.
After Kāśyapa had departed, he proceeded to the border of Jambudvīpa and, beneath a jambu tree, took a jambu fruit.
Returning, he arrived first and sat within the stone cell of Kāśyapa.
At that time, seeing the World-Honored One in the stone cell, Kāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Śramaṇa!..."
"By which path did you come to reach this stone chamber?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After you had departed, I went to the realm of Jambudvīpa, gathered jambu fruits, and returned here to sit."
"Kāśyapa, you should know that these fruits are exceedingly fragrant and delicious;
you may take them and eat them. Kāśyapa replied, "I have no need for them."
"The śramaṇa has taken some for himself and is eating it.
At that time, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses extraordinary supernormal powers and great majesty; he was even able to go to the top of Jambudvīpa and take these delicious fruits."
"Even so, it is still not as true as my Way.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating, he returned to stay overnight at that place.
At dawn the next morning, Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was; having arrived, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The time for the meal has arrived; you may go and take your seat.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow later."
After Kāśyapa had departed, [the Buddha] went to the border of Jambudvīpa, took some āmalaka fruits,
and returned, arriving first at Kāśyapa’s stone cave where he sat down.
Kāśyapa addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Śramaṇa!
By which path have you come to this place?"
The World-Honored One said, "After you have departed, go to the realm of Jambudvīpa and bring back these fruits; they are exceedingly fragrant and delicious.
If you require them, simply take and eat them."
Kāśyapa replied, “I have no need for this; let the śramaṇa take it and eat it himself.
At that time, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses extraordinary supernormal power and great majestic authority; after I left, he came here to fetch these fruits.
Nevertheless, even so, he is not my equal, for I have already attained the Way."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, returned to his lodging for the night.
On the following day, Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was and said:
"The time for the meal has arrived; you may go to take your meal."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, “You go on ahead; I shall follow later.
After Kāśyapa had departed, the World-Honored One went to Uttarakuru in the north, took some naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and returned to Kāśyapa’s stone cave.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha:
"Śramaṇa! By what path did you come to sit here?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Kāśyapa, you should know that after you had departed, I went to Uttarakuru and gathered naturally grown non-glutinous rice, which was exceedingly fragrant and fine."
“Kāśyapa! If you need it, take and eat it. Kāśyapa replied:
"I have no need for this;
let the śramaṇa take it and eat it himself.
Kāśyapa then thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses supreme supernormal powers and great spiritual might.
Nevertheless, he is still not equal to the true attainment of the Way as I have achieved it.
At that time, having finished his meal, the World-Honored One returned to his lodgings for the night.
The next day, Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was and said, "The time for the meal has arrived; you may go to take your meal.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You go on ahead; I shall follow later.
After Kāśyapa had departed, the World-Honored One went to Aparagoyānī, took some harītakī fruits, and arrived first at Kāśyapa’s stone cave to sit there.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha,
"Śramaṇa! By what path have you come to sit here?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After you had departed, I went to Aparagoyānī and brought back these fruits; they are exceedingly fragrant and delicious. Kāśyapa!"
"If you need it, you may take and eat it.
Kāśyapa replied, "I have no need for this."
"The śramaṇa took it himself and ate it.
Kāśyapa then thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses extraordinary supernormal power and great majestic authority."
"Even so, it is still not as good as my attaining the true Way.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating, he returned to his lodging for the night.
The next day, Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was and said:
"The time has come; you may go to take your meal.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow later."
After Kāśyapa had departed, the World-Honored One went to Pūrvavideha, took a viṣṇulaka fruit, and arrived first at Kāśyapa’s stone cave where he sat down.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha, “Śramaṇa!...”
"By which path did you come to reach this seat?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After you had departed, I went to Pūrvavideha and brought back these fruits; they are exceedingly fragrant and fine."
“Kāśyapa! If you wish, you may take it and eat it. Kāśyapa replied:
"I have no need for this; you, Śramaṇa, may take it and eat it yourself.
Kāśyapa then thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses extraordinary spiritual power and great supernormal faculties."
"Even so, it is still not equal to my attaining the true Way.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he returned to that place to stay overnight.
At that moment, Kāśyapa was about to perform a great sacrifice; five hundred disciples were holding axes to split firewood, yet though they held the axes in their hands, the blades would not descend.
At that time, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This must surely have been done by the śramaṇa.
Then, Kāśyapa asked the World-Honored One:
"I now wish to split firewood; why does the axe not descend?
The World-Honored One replied, "Do you desire for the axe to descend?"
He said, "I wish for it to go down.
The axe immediately went down.
At that time, once the axe had been brought down, it could not be lifted again.
Kāśyapa spoke to the Buddha once more, saying:
"For what reason can the axe not be lifted?"
The World-Honored One asked,
"Do you wish for the axe to be lifted up?
He replied:
"I wish to lift it up.
The axe was immediately lifted.
At that time, Kāśyapa’s disciples wished to kindle a fire, but the fire would not ignite.
At that time, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This must surely have been done by the śramaṇa Gautama.
Kāśyapa then addressed the Buddha:
"Why does the fire not burn?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do you wish for the fire to burn?"
He said, "I wish to make it burn.
The fire immediately ignited.
At that time, he intended to extinguish the fire, but the fire would not go out.
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
"For what reason does the fire not go out?"
The Buddha asked Kāśyapa,
"Do you wish for the fire to be extinguished? He replied:
"I wish for it to be extinguished.
At that very moment, the fire was extinguished.
Kāśyapa then thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa Gautama has a countenance so upright and handsome that he is a rarity in the world.
Tomorrow I intend to perform a great sacrifice, and the king, the people, and all others will gather there. If they should see this śramaṇa, I shall no longer be able to provide for his offerings."
"If this śramaṇa does not come tomorrow, it would be a great blessing.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew what was in Kāśyapa’s mind:
at dawn the following day, he went to Uttarakuru to gather naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and to Aparagoyānī to take milk, then proceeded to the Anavatapta Spring to eat.
Having stayed there all day, he returned toward evening to his stone cave to lodge for the night.
On the following morning, Kāśyapa went to the World-Honored One and asked: "Śramaṇa!..."
"Why did you not come yesterday?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Yesterday you had this thought:"
"This Gautama is exceedingly handsome, a rarity in this world.
If the king and his subjects see him at my great sacrifice tomorrow, they will surely cut off my offerings."
"If you do not come, it would be a great blessing.

I immediately knew what was on your mind; I went as far as Uttarakuru to fetch naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and from Aparagoyānī to fetch milk, and then proceeded to the Anavatapta Spring to eat.
He remained there all day, and as evening fell, he returned to stay the night in the stone cave.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa possesses extraordinary supernormal powers; he truly has majestic spiritual power."
"Even so, it is still not equal to my attaining the true Way.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating, he returned to the stone chamber to stay the night.

That very night, the Four Heavenly Kings came to where the World-Honored One was to listen to the Dharma; the Four Heavenly Kings also possessed radiance, and the Buddha likewise emitted a great light that illuminated the mountains and valleys, making them all one uniform color of brilliant brightness.
At that time, Kāśyapa saw a brilliant light during the night.
At dawn the following day, he went to where the World-Honored One was, and having arrived, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What was that light last night that illuminated these mountains and forests?"
The World-Honored One replied, "Last night, the Four Heavenly Kings came to my dwelling to listen to the Dharma; it was their radiance.
At that time, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa possesses extraordinary supernatural power, such that he can cause the Four Heavenly Kings to come and listen to the Dharma.
Although he has such power, it is still not equal to the true realization of the Path attained by me."
At that time, having finished his meal, the World-Honored One returned to stay there for the night.
At midnight, Śakra Devānām Indra came to where the World-Honored One was to listen to the Dharma; the radiance of the Heavenly Emperor again illuminated that mountain.
Then, at night, Kāśyapa rose and observed the stars, seeing this radiance.
At dawn the next morning, Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was and asked: "Gautama!..."
"Last night the radiance was exceedingly extraordinary; what is the cause and condition for this light?
The World-Honored One replied, "Last night Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came here to listen to the sutra; it is for this reason that there was this light."
At that time, Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"This śramaṇa Gautama possesses supreme supernormal power and great majestic authority, such that he can cause Śakra, the Lord of Devas, to come and listen to the Dharma."
"Even so, it is still not equal to my attainment of the true Way.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating, he returned to stay overnight there.
At midnight, Brahmā, King of Devas, emitted a great radiance that illuminated the mountain, approaching the place where the World-Honored One was to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, Kāśyapa rose in the night and saw a brilliant light. On the following day, he went to the World-Honored One and asked:
"Last night there was a brilliance that shone with double the intensity, surpassing the radiance of the sun and moon. What causes and conditions have brought about such a light?"
The World-Honored One said,
"Kāśyapa, you should know that last night the Great Brahmā King came to my place to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"This śramaṇa Gautama possesses extraordinary supernatural power, for he was able to cause my grandfather to come here to this śramaṇa’s presence to listen to the Dharma.
Nevertheless, even so, it is still not equal to my own attainment of the true Way."
At that time, the World-Honored One obtained five tattered rags from a dust-heap and, wishing to wash them, had this thought:
"In what place shall I wash these robes?"
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what was in the World-Honored One’s mind, immediately manifested a bathing pool and said to the World-Honored One:
"You may wash your robes here."
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"In what place shall I tread and wash these robes?
Then, the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing the thought in the World-Honored One's mind, lifted a large square stone and placed it by the water's edge, saying to the World-Honored One:
"One may spread out one's robes here.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"Where shall I dry these robes?"
At that time, the tree deity, knowing what was in the World-Honored One’s mind, lowered a branch of the tree and said to the World-Honored One:
“I only wish that you would dry your robes here.”
The next morning at dawn, Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was and asked the World-Honored One:
"Originally there was no such pond, yet now there is this pond;
originally there was no such tree, yet now there is this tree."
"Originally there was no such stone, yet now there is this stone.
By what causes and conditions has this transformation occurred?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This was made by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, last night when he knew that I wished to wash my robes;
thus he created this bathing pool. I then thought to myself:
'In what place shall I tread upon and wash these robes?'"
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing what was in my mind, brought this stone here.
I then thought again: "In what place shall I spread out these robes?"
At that time, the tree deity, knowing the thoughts within my mind, simply bent down this branch of the tree.
Then, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
“Although this śramaṇa Gautama possesses such supernatural powers, he is still not equal to me in having attained the true Way.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, returned there to stay for the night.
Then, at midnight, a great black cloud arose and sent down heavy rain; it flowed like a great river, overflowing to an extreme degree.
At that time, Kāśyapa again thought to himself:
"This river is overflowing; the śramaṇa will surely be swept away by the water. I shall now go and watch him."
At that time, Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples went to the riverbank; meanwhile, the World-Honored One was walking upon the water, his feet remaining unsullied by the water.
At that time, Kāśyapa saw from afar the World-Honored One walking upon the water.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
"How extraordinary!
The śramaṇa Gautama is indeed able to walk upon the water; I too am able to walk upon the water, though I cannot prevent my feet from becoming soiled."
"Although this śramaṇa possesses supernatural powers, he is still not equal to me in attaining the true Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kāśyapa:
"You are not an arhat yourself, nor do you know the path of an arhat; you do not even recognize the name 'arhat,' much less have attained the Way."
"You are blind; your eyes see nothing. Although the Tathāgata has manifested such transformations as these, you said:
'It is not equal to the reality of the Path attained by me.
Yet now you speak these words:"
"I am able to walk upon the water.
Now is precisely the time; may we walk upon the water together?
You should now abandon this mind of false views, lest you suffer such affliction for a long night.
At that time, having heard the words of the World-Honored One, Kāśyapa came forward and prostrated himself at his feet, saying:
"I now repent my transgression; I deeply realize it was contrary to the Dharma that I have thus offended the Tathāgata. I only pray that you will accept my repentance."
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
The World-Honored One said to him:
"I grant you leave to amend your error; you have now come to realize yourself that you have disturbed the Tathāgata."
At that time, Kāśyapa said to his five hundred disciples:
"Each of you should follow what is appropriate for you; as for me, I now take refuge in the Śramaṇa Gautama."
At that time, the five hundred disciples said to Kāśyapa:
"We too previously had our hearts set upon the śramaṇa Gautama; when he subdued the dragon, we were immediately about to take refuge in him."
"If our teacher himself has taken refuge in Gautama, then we five hundred disciples shall all likewise take refuge in Gautama. Kāśyapa replied:
"Now is indeed the right time; yet my mind clings to this delusion, and even after seeing such transformations, my thoughts remain unconvinced; therefore, I have spoken thus."
"My Way is truly authentic.

At that time, Kāśyapa, surrounded by five hundred disciples before and behind him, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will allow us to become śramaṇas!"
"Practice pure conduct.
This is the constant law of all Buddhas.
If one recites:
“Welcome, bhikṣu! and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! This Dharma is subtle and profound; practice the holy life well.

At that moment, the robes worn by Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples were all transformed into saffron-colored monastic garments (kāṣāya), and their hair fell off of its own accord as if they had been shaved, appearing as though seven days had passed since the tonsure.
At that time, Kāśyapa cast all his scholarly implements and incantations into the water.
Then, five hundred disciples addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will allow us to become śramaṇas."
The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣus!
At that moment, the five hundred disciples immediately became śramaṇas; the saṃghāṭī robes appeared upon their bodies and their hair fell away of its own accord.
At that time, as they were drifting downstream with the current, there was a brahmin named Uruvelā-Kāśyapa who lived by the riverbank.
Seeing the implements for his incantations all being swept away by the water, he thought to himself:
"Alas! What a pity!"
"Has my eldest brother been drowned by the water?
At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa, leading three hundred disciples, followed the river upstream in search of his brother's remains.
From afar he saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree, surrounded by Mahākāśyapa and five hundred disciples before and behind him as he preached the Dharma.
Having seen this, he went forward to where Kāśyapa was and spoke these words:
"Is this matter truly excellent?"
"Originally you were a teacher of men, yet now you are a disciple.
Elder brother, for what reason have you become a disciple of a śramaṇa? Kāśyapa replied:
"This place is excellent; there is nothing superior to this place.
At that time, Upaka-Kāśyapa spoke this verse to Nadi-Kāśyapa:
"This Master is honored by gods and men; I now take him as my teacher."
“The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is extremely difficult to encounter.
At that time, when Nadi-Kāśyapa heard the name of the Buddha, he was filled with great joy; leaping for joy, he could not contain himself, and went before the World-Honored One, saying:
“I pray that you will allow me to follow the Path.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! Cultivate the holy life well and bring an end to suffering."
At that time, Nadi-Kāśyapa and his three hundred disciples immediately became śramaṇas; the saṃghāṭī robes appeared upon their bodies and their hair fell away of its own accord.
Thereupon, Nadi-Kāśyapa and his three hundred disciples cast all their implements for incantations into the water.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Gayākāśyapa living downstream by the riverbank.
Seeing from afar the implements for incantations being carried away by the water, he thought to himself:
"I have two elder brothers who are practicing the Way upstream."
"Now that the implements for our incantations have all been swept away by the water, the two Mahākāśyapas will surely be harmed by it.
He then led his two hundred disciples up the river against the current until they reached the place where he had studied. Seeing his two elder brothers from afar as śramaṇas, he spoke these words:
"Is this a pleasant place?"
"Formerly you were honored among men; now you are a disciple of a śramaṇa.
Kāśyapa replied, "This place is most sublime; nothing surpasses this place."
At that time, Gayākāśyapa had this thought:
"Now my two elder brothers are widely learned and possess great knowledge; this place must surely be a favorable ground for them to study the Way. I, too, may now study the Way here."
At that time, Gayākāśyapa came forward and addressed the World-Honored One:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to become a śramaṇa.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! Cultivate the holy life well and reach the end of suffering.
At that moment, Gayākāśyapa immediately became a śramaṇa; the saffron robe was upon his body and his hair fell away of its own accord, as if he had been shaved for seven days.

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying by the side of that river, beneath a nyagrodha tree, not long after attaining Buddhahood, accompanied by a thousand disciples, all of whom were venerable elders of great seniority.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught by means of three methods.
What are these three? They are:
teaching through supernormal powers, teaching through verbal instruction, and teaching through admonition and exhortation.
What is meant by "conversion through the supernormal powers" (*ṛddhipāda*)?
At that time, the World-Honored One may manifest various forms and then merge them back into one; he may become invisible, or he may appear.

They passed through stone walls without any obstruction; they emerged from the earth or entered into it as freely as flowing water, encountering no resistance. They sat cross-legged, filling the entirety of space, like birds flying through the air without hindrance.
It is also like a great volcanic mountain from which immeasurable smoke issues forth.
These sun and moon possess great supernormal power that is beyond measure; one could reach out and seize them with the hand, and the body would extend as far as the Brahma Heaven.
In this manner, the World-Honored One manifested his supernormal powers.
What, then, is meant by "teaching and transforming through verbal instruction"?
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed the bhikṣus:
"One should abandon this, set aside this.
One should approach this, distance oneself from this.
One should attend to this, cast off this."
"One should contemplate this, and not contemplate that.
As for how one should cultivate this and not cultivate that: one should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment to extinguish the three fetters.
How should one contemplate and how should one not contemplate?
One should contemplate the three fetters as being wholesome for a śramaṇa:
namely, the joy of renunciation, the joy of non-ill will, and the joy of non-anger.
How does he fail to contemplate?
It refers to the three kinds of suffering of a śramaṇa. What are the three?
That is to say: the contemplation of desire, the contemplation of ill-will, and the contemplation of anger.
What should one attend to, and what should one not attend to?
At that time, one should attend to the Truth of Suffering, one should attend to the Truth of Origination, one should attend to the Truth of Cessation, and one should attend to the Truth of the Path.
Do not harbor thoughts of false truths:

such as the view of permanence or the view of impermanence; the view of finitude or the view of infinity; that the soul is the same as the body or that the soul is different from the body; that the Tathāgata exists after death, that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, that he both exists and does not exist after death, or that he neither exists nor does not exist after death.
Do not entertain such thoughts.
What is meant by "instructing and transforming"?
Furthermore, one should go in this way and not go in that way; one should come in this way and not come in that way; one should remain silent or speak in this manner:
"One should wear such robes and not wear such robes; one should enter a village in this manner and not enter a village in that manner.
This is what is called instruction and admonition.
At that time, the World-Honored One used these three matters to instruct the thousand bhikṣus.
Having received the Buddha’s teaching, those thousand bhikṣus all became arhats.

At that time, when the World-Honored One saw that the thousand bhikṣus had attained arhatship, there were then one thousand arhats and five bhikṣus on the land of Jambudvīpa; with the Buddha as the sixth teacher, he turned his seat toward Kapilavastu.
At that time, Upika Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"For what reason has the World-Honored One sat facing toward Kapilavastu?
Thereupon, Upika Kāśyapa immediately knelt before him with his right knee on the ground and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I do not understand why the Tathāgata is seated facing Kapilavastu.
The World-Honored One replied:
"When a Tathāgata dwells in the world, he should perform five things."

What are the five? First, he shall turn the wheel of Dharma; second, he shall preach the Dharma to his father; third, he shall preach the Dharma to his mother; fourth, he shall guide ordinary persons to establish themselves in the bodhisattva practice; and fifth, he shall bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon bodhisattvas.
"Kāśyapa, this is what is meant by the five dharmas that a Tathāgata, appearing in the world,
should practice. At that time, Upaka Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"The Tathāgata remembers his kinsmen and his native land; it is for this reason that he is seated facing in that direction.

At that time, the five bhikṣus gradually approached the banks of the Nairañjanā River, arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin saw from afar the Blessed One sitting facing Kapilavastu; having seen him, he thought to himself:
"The Blessed One surely intends to go to Kapilavastu to see his kinsmen."
At that time, Udāyin immediately knelt before him and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am now capable of wishing to ask a question; I only pray that you will expound upon it."
The World-Honored One said,
"Ask whatever you wish to ask.
Udāyin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Observing the Tathāgata’s intention, he wishes to go toward Kapilavastu.
The World-Honored One said, "It is so; it is as you have said."
"Udayin, you should know that you must go first to King Śuddhodana’s palace, and I shall go later.
This is because a member of the Kṣatriya caste should first be informed by a messenger before the Tathāgata goes."
"When you arrive, say to the king:
'Seven days from now, the Tathāgata shall come to see the king. Udāyin replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!

At that time, Udāyin rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and vanished before him. He proceeded to Kapilavastu and arrived at the residence of King Śuddhodana.
Having arrived, he stood before the king.
At that time, King Śuddhodana was seated upon the great terrace together with his court ladies.
Then, Udāyin flew up into the air.
At that time, King Śuddhodana saw Udāyin standing before him holding a bowl and carrying a staff; having seen him, he was seized with fear and said:
"Who is this person?"
Is it a human?
Is it a non-human?
Is it a deva?
"Is he a ghost?
Or a yakṣa, a rākṣasa, a deva, a nāga, or a spirit?
At that time, King Śuddhodana asked Udāyin:
"Who are you? He then addressed Udāyin with this verse:
"Are you a deva, or are you a ghost?"
Are you a Gandharva or one of his kind?
What is your name now? I wish to know it.
At that time, Udāyin again addressed the king with these verses:
“I am not a deva, nor am I a gandharva; I am a man of this land of Kapilavastu, within the realm of the Great King.”
"In the past, he destroyed eighteen billion of the wicked Māra Pāpīyas’s hosts;
my teacher Śākyamuni is his true disciple.
Then, King Śuddhodana again spoke this verse to Udāyin:
"Who has destroyed the eighteen billion followers of the evil Māra Pāpīyān?
Who is named Śākyamuni?
You should now praise and proclaim this."
At that time, Udāyin spoke again in verse:
"When the Tathāgata was first born, heaven and earth shook throughout;
his vows were all fulfilled, and today he is named Siddhārtha!"
He has subdued eighteen billion of the wicked Māra Pāpīyas;
his name is Śākyamuni, and today he has attained the Way of the Buddha!
That man, the Lion of the Śākyas, is the foremost disciple of Gautama.
"Today he has become a śramaṇa; his original name was Udaya!
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having heard these words, was filled with such joy that he could not contain himself, and he said to Udaya: "How is this, Udaya?"
"Is Prince Siddhārtha still alive? Udāyin replied,
"The Buddha Śākyamuni is present today."
Then the king asked,
"Has he now already attained Buddhahood? Udāyin replied:
"He has now already attained Buddhahood.
The king asked again, "Where,
then, is the Tathāgata located today?"
Udayin replied, "The Tathāgata is currently in the kingdom of Magadha, beneath a nyagrodha tree.
Then the king replied:
"Who are these disciples who follow him?
Udāyin replied, "Myriads of devas,
thousands of bhikṣus, and the Four Heavenly Kings are always at his side."
Then the king asked,
"As for the clothing he wears, what kind does it resemble? Udāyin replied:
“The garment worn by the Tathāgata is called a kāṣāya.
Then the king asked,
“What kind of food does he eat?”
Udaya replied, "The body of the Tathāgata takes the Dharma as its food.
The king asked again:
“How is it, Udāyin? Can the Tathāgata be seen? Udāyin replied:
"O King, do not be distressed; seven days from now, the Tathāgata shall enter the city.
At that time, the king was filled with such extreme joy that he could not contain himself; he personally served and made offerings to Udāyin.

At that time, King Śuddhodana beat the great sounding drum and commanded the people throughout the realm to level and repair the roads, remove all impurities, sprinkle the ground with fragrant liquid, hang silken banners and canopies, and perform musical performances beyond measure.
He further commanded that all those in the kingdom who were deaf, blind, or mute be made to disappear; after seven days had passed, Siddhārtha would enter the city.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, hearing that the Buddha was about to enter the city, did not sleep for seven days.
When the seventh day arrived, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"It is now appropriate for me to travel by means of my supernormal power to the kingdom of Kapilavastu."
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the bhikṣus before and behind him, proceeded toward the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Having arrived, he went to the Sālavana grove to the north of the city.
At that time, King Śuddhodana heard that the World-Honored One had already arrived at the Sāl Grove to the north of Kapilavastu.
Thereupon, King Śuddhodana, accompanied by the assembly of Śākyas, went to the place where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought to himself:
"If King Śuddhodana were to come here in person, it would not be appropriate for me; I should now go there to meet him."
"The reason for this is that the kindness of parents is profound, and the sentiment of their nurturing is most intense.
At that time, the World-Honored One, leading the assembly of bhikṣus, went toward the city gate and flew into the air at a height of seven *ren* above the ground.

At that time, King Śuddhodana beheld the World-Honored One, whose countenance was peerlessly upright and rare in the world; his faculties were tranquil and free from manifold thoughts, and his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Filled with a heart of joy, he immediately prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these words:
“I am a king of the Kṣatriya caste, named King Śuddhodana.”
The World-Honored One said:
“May the Great King enjoy an inexhaustible lifespan. Therefore, Great King!”
One should govern and transform others by means of the True Dharma, and not employ false dharmas.

Great King, you should know that those who govern and transform others by means of the True Dharma, upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens above.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded through the air and arrived at the palace of King Śuddhodana.
Having arrived, he took his seat.

When the king saw that the World-Honored One was seated, he personally served various kinds of food and drink. Seeing that the World-Honored One had finished eating, he offered pure water, then took another small seat to listen to the sutra.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually expounded the sublime teachings to King Suddhodana, namely:
discourse on generosity, discourse on morality, and discourse on rebirth in the heavens; [he explained that] sensual desires are impure, and that the way out of them is true happiness.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the king’s mind was opened and his understanding attained, fully expounded to the king the Dharma that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly teach: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, while still upon his seat, was cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having thus preached the Dharma to the king, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, King Śuddhodana assembled the Śākya clan and spoke thus:
"These śramaṇas have most unsightly countenances; it is not fitting for the Kṣatriya caste to lead a multitude of brahmins.
It would be far better if the Kṣatriya Śākyas were to join with the Kṣatriya host."
The Śākyas replied, "So be it,
Great King! As Your Majesty commands,
that a Kṣatriya should regain his place among the Kṣatriya assembly is indeed excellent."
At that time, the king announced throughout the kingdom:
"Among all those who have two brothers, one must take one to become a practitioner of the Way; those who do not shall be severely punished."
At that time, the Śākya assembly heard the king’s command:
“Among all those who have two brothers, one shall be taken to enter the religious life; whoever does not comply with this order shall be severely punished.”
At that time, Devadatta of the Śākya clan said to Ānanda of the Śākyas:
"Today King Śuddhodana has issued this command:
'Among all brothers, two shall divide one to become a seeker of the Way.'"
"Now that you have left the household life to study the Way, I shall remain at home to manage our family affairs.
At that time, Ānanda, the Śākya, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, replying:
"I shall do as my elder brother instructs."
At that time, Nanda the Śākya said to Anuruddha the Śākya:
"King Śuddhodana has issued a command:
'If there are two brothers, one must be ordained as a monk; those who do not do so shall be severely punished.'"
"You have now gone forth into homelessness; I shall remain at home.
At that time, having heard these words, Anuruddha of the Śākya clan was filled with joy and exultation beyond measure, and he replied: "So be it."
"I shall follow your instructions, elder brother.
At that time, King Śuddhodana took Mahānāma Śākya and Aṃgulaśālī Śākya to the place where the World-Honored One was.
Then, he mounted a carriage drawn by four white horses, with a white canopy and harnessed to white steeds.
The second Śākyan rode a blue chariot with a blue canopy, drawn by blue horses;
the third Śākyan rode a yellow chariot with a yellow canopy, drawn by yellow horses;
the fourth Śākyan rode a red chariot with a red canopy, drawn by red horses.
At that time, among the Śākyas, some were riding elephants and some were riding horses; they all assembled together.
Then, seeing King Śuddhodana approaching with the multitude of Śākyas from afar, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should observe this assembly of Śākyas, and you should also observe the assembly of King Śuddhodana."
“Bhikṣus, you should know that when the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three go out to their parks and pleasure groves, it is also according to this same law; there is no difference.
At that time, Ānanda was riding upon a great white elephant, dressed in white robes and with a white parasol.
Having seen this, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this Ānanda Śākyan riding a white elephant and dressed in white garments?
The bhikṣus replied:
“Yes, World-Honored One! We have seen it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This man shall leave the household life to study the Path; he will be foremost in great learning and capable of attending upon me.
Do you all see this Anuruddha? The bhikṣus replied:
“Yes, I have seen him. The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“This person shall leave the household life to study the Path and become foremost in the divine eye.”

At that time, King Śuddhodana, along with his four brothers, as well as Nanda and Ānanda, all proceeded forward on foot; having removed their five ornaments, they approached the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, King Śuddhodana said to the Buddha:
"Last night, this thought arose in me:
'The assembly of Kṣatriyas should not lead the assembly of Brahmins; rather, they should lead the assembly of Kṣatriyas—this is what is appropriate.'"
I then issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:
"Among all those who have two brothers, let one of them be taken to leave the household life and study the Path.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant permission for him to leave the household life and study the Path.
The World-Honored One said: "Excellent,
Great King!"
It brings great benefit, and gods and humans attain peace. Why is this so?

Because these spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are excellent and auspicious fields of merit; it is by relying on spiritual friends that I have been able to escape this cycle of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
At that time, the Śākyas attained the path.
Then, King Śuddhodana addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One would instruct these new bhikṣus, just as you instructed Udāyin!"
The reason for this is that this bhikṣu Udāyin possesses supreme supernormal powers.
We pray that bhikṣu Udāyin will remain constantly within the palace to teach and transform, so that all classes of sentient beings may attain peace and security throughout the long night.
The reason for this is that this bhikṣu possesses supreme supernormal power; as soon as I first saw the bhikṣu Udāyin, I felt a heart of joy. I then thought:
"If even a disciple possesses such supernormal power, how much more so must the Tathāgata possess it?"
The World-Honored One said:
"So it is, Great King! Just as Your Majesty has taught, this bhikṣu Udāyin possesses supreme supernormal power and great majestic virtue."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The foremost disciple, who is widely learned and possesses great knowledge, and whom kings hold in high esteem, is the bhikṣu Ājñātakauṇḍinya."
The one who is able to exhort and transform the people is the bhikṣu Udāyin.
The one who possesses swift wisdom is the bhikṣu Mahānāman.
The one who constantly delights in flying is the bhikṣu Subhūti.
The one who travels back and forth through the air is the bhikṣu Pāva.
The one with many disciples is the bhikṣu Upakaśyapa.
The one who has attained the contemplation of emptiness in his mind is the bhikṣu Gaṅgā-Kāśyapa.
"He who has attained tranquility and insight is the bhikṣu Kāśyapa. At that time,
the World-Honored One extensively expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for King Śuddhodana.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the king rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and withdrew.
Then, the bhikṣus and King Śuddhodana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Fifteen; Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The High Banner, Part Three (6). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"On the fifteenth day, there are three observances of the fast-day (upoṣadha). What are the three?
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days.

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there may be times when, on the eighth-day fast day, the Four Great Kings dispatch their subordinate ministers to observe the world: 'Who among them is performing good deeds, and who is performing evil deeds?'"
What kind of sentient beings possess compassion and filial piety toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders?

Are there any sentient beings who delight in practicing generosity, cultivating precepts, patience, diligence, and samādhi, who expound and disseminate the meaning of the sūtras, and who observe the eightfold fast?
He discerns this fully.
Suppose there were no sentient beings who were filial toward their parents, nor toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or elders; at that time, the ministers would say to the Four Heavenly Kings:

"In this world today, there are no sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, nor toward śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way, who practice the four immeasurable minds and show compassion for sentient beings."
When the Four Heavenly Kings heard this, they were filled with sorrow and distress, feeling dejected and unhappy.
Thereupon, the Four Heavenly Kings went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and assembled in the Sudharma Hall, where they reported the matter in detail to Śakra:
"O Lord of Devas, you should know that in this world today there are no sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, nor toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or elders."

At that time, having heard these words, Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were all filled with sorrow and distress; they were despondent and displeased, as the ranks of the devas diminished and the ranks of the asuras increased.

"Furthermore, suppose there is a time when among the various classes of beings in the world, there are those who are filial and obedient toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders; who observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), cultivate pure virtue, and do not violate even the smallest prohibitions, such as those as fine as a hair."
At that time, the messenger was filled with joy and exultation, unable to contain himself, and he said to the Four Kings:
"In this world today, there are many sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all their elders."
Upon hearing this, the Heavenly King was filled with great joy and immediately went to where Śakra Devānām Indra was, reporting the matter in detail to him:
"O Lord of Devas, you should know that there are currently many sentient beings in this world who are filial toward their parents, and respectful toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and their elders."

At that time, Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven were all filled with such joy that they could not contain themselves; the hosts of devas increased while the hosts of asuras diminished. The tortures of hell naturally ceased, and agonizing pains no longer occurred.

"If on the fourteenth day, the day of the fast, you dispatch the Crown Prince to descend and tour the world, observing the people and examining their conduct regarding good and evil: whether there are any sentient beings who believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; who are filial toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders; who delight in giving; who observe the eightfold fast; who restrain the six sense-faculties; and who guard against the five desires."
If there were no sentient beings who practiced these five dharmas— filial piety toward one's parents, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—
at that time, the prince addressed the Four Great Heavenly Kings.

Upon hearing this, the Four Heavenly Kings were filled with sorrow and distress; their countenances were gloomy and displeased. They went to where Śakra Devānām-indra was and reported the matter in detail to the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should know that in this world today there are no sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, nor toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or elders."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were filled with sorrow and distress; they were gloomy and displeased, as the host of devas diminished while the host of asuras increased.
"Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders, and observe the eightfold precepts of the fast,
at that time the Prince will leap for joy, unable to contain himself, and shall immediately go to inform the Four Heavenly Kings: 'Great Kings,
you should know that in this world today there are many sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all their elders.'"

At that time, having heard these words, the Four Heavenly Kings were filled with great joy. They immediately went to where Śakra Devānām-indra was and reported this matter in detail to the Lord of Devas:

"O Holy King, you should know that in this world today there are many sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and their elders; who receive the three refuges; who offer counsel with a compassionate heart; and who are sincere, trustworthy, and free from deceit."

At that time, Śakra, the Four Great Kings, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were all filled with such joy that they could not contain themselves; the hosts of devas increased, while the hosts of asuras diminished.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that on the fifteenth day when the precepts are recited, the Four Great Kings personally descend from heaven to travel throughout the world and observe the conduct of its people.”
What kind of sentient beings are filial toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders; who delight in giving and uphold the eightfold fast, the fast-dharma of the Tathāgata?

If there are no sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, or who show respect toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders, then the Four Great Kings will become sorrowful and depressed; they will go to the abode of Śakra and report this matter in detail to the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Great King, you should know that in this world today there are no sentient beings who are filial toward their parents, nor those who show respect toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and various elders."

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven were all filled with sorrow and distress; they were dejected and unhappy, as the hosts of devas diminished while the hosts of asuras increased.

"Furthermore, at such a time, if there are among the classes of sentient beings those who are filial and obedient toward their parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and other elders, and who observe the eightfold precepts of the fast;

At that time, the Four Great Kings were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, unable to contain themselves. They immediately went to the abode of Śakra and, for this reason, addressed the Lord of Devas in full detail:
"Great King, you should know that in this world today there are many sentient beings who are filial toward their parents and respectful toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and their elders."

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the Four Heavenly Kings were all filled with joy; they leaped for joy beyond measure, increasing the hosts of devas and diminishing the hosts of asuras.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“How is the eightfold precept fast observed on the fifteenth day?
Thereupon, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
“The Tathāgata is the king of all dharmas and the seal of all dharmas.
We pray that the World-Honored One will expound this meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall respectfully put it into practice.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in full detail.

Therefore, bhikṣus! If there be a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the month during the recitation of the precepts and the observance of the fast, goes among the fourfold assembly and should speak these words:
"I am now on a fast day and wish to observe the eightfold precepts of the *poṣadha*.
I only pray that the Venerable One will explain them to me!
At that time, the fourfold assembly shall instruct and preach the eightfold precepts of the *poṣadha* for him.
First, instruct them to say these words:
"Good son, you should state your own name.
Once they have stated their name, you should then explain the Eightfold Precepts of the Uposatha to them.
At that time, the instructor should teach the person before him to speak these words:
"I now uphold the fasting dharma of the Tathāgata; until the clear dawn of tomorrow, I shall cultivate pure precepts and eliminate unwholesome dharmas."

If I have committed evil deeds of body, uttered evil words of mouth, or conceived evil thoughts of mind—whether these three types of bodily, four types of verbal, or three types of mental misdeeds were already done or yet to be done; whether they were created through greed, hatred, or delusion; whether they were created because of noble lineage, or due to the influence of evil associates; whether they occurred in this life, future lives, or countless lifetimes; whether they arose from ignorance of the Buddha or the Dharma, or from causing strife within the Saṃgha, or from killing one’s parents, elders, or teachers—I now confess them all myself and shall not conceal them. Relying upon the precepts and the Dharma, I shall perfect my practice of the precepts and receive the Eightfold Restraint (Aṣṭāṅga) of the Tathāgata’s fasting rite.
"What is the method for the Eightfold Precepts of Fasting?

One should maintain the mind as that of a true person (*satpuruṣa*): for the duration of one's life, one shall not kill, harbor no intent to harm, and maintain thoughts of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings."
"I am now [name], observing the fast until the clear dawn of tomorrow; I shall not kill, harbor no harmful intent, and maintain a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings."
"Just as an Arhat is free from wrong thoughts and, for as long as life lasts, refrains from stealing and delights in giving,
so too am I, [name], from this day until tomorrow, shall refrain from stealing for as long as life lasts and maintain my mind in this way."

“‘Such a true person as I shall now, for as long as life lasts, refrain from sexual misconduct; free from depraved thoughts, I shall constantly cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya). My body shall be fragrant and pure. Today I uphold the precept against lust, neither thinking of my own wife nor entertaining thoughts of other women, until the clear dawn of tomorrow, without committing any transgression.’”

"Just as an Arhat, for as long as life lasts, does not speak falsely, always knowing the ultimate truth and not deceiving others, so from now until tomorrow I shall not speak falsely; from this day forward, I shall no longer speak falsely."

"Just as an Arhat does not drink alcohol, his mind is undisturbed, and he upholds the Buddha’s prohibitions without transgressing them, so shall I now likewise act: from this day until tomorrow morning, I shall no longer drink alcohol, but shall uphold the Buddha’s prohibitions without transgressing them."
"Just as an Arhat, for as long as life lasts, does not violate the rules of the fast, always eats at the proper time, eats little with contentment, and does not become attached to flavors."

I shall now do likewise: for as long as life lasts, I will not violate the rules of the fast; I will always eat only at the proper time, eating little and knowing contentment, without attachment to flavors, from this day until tomorrow morning.
"Just as an Arhat never sits upon a high or wide bed—namely, a high or wide bed made of gold, silver, or ivory;
or a bed of horn; or the seat of a Buddha, the seat of a Pratyekabuddha, the seat of an Arhat, or the seat of a venerable teacher."
At that time, an Arhat does not sit upon these eight kinds of seats; nor do I sit upon them, yet I do not violate the rules regarding such seating.
"Just as an Arhat does not attach himself to the adornments of incense, flowers, unguents, or powders."
"I, too, shall now act in this same way: for as long as my life lasts, I shall not indulge in the pleasures of incense, flowers, ointments, or powders.
"I, who am now called [Name], shall distance myself from these eight matters and uphold the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast, so that I do not fall into the three evil realms."

By upholding these merits, one shall not enter the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal realm, or the eight difficult conditions; one will constantly encounter virtuous friends and never associate with evil companions; one will always be born into families with excellent parents and never be born in borderlands where the Buddha-Dharma does not exist; one shall not be reborn among the long-lived devas, nor become a slave to others, nor become a Brahmā, nor take the form of Śakra, nor become a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King, but shall instead be constantly born in the presence of the Buddhas.
"By personally seeing the Buddha and personally hearing the Dharma, they cause their faculties not to be distracted.
If I vow to practice toward the three vehicles, may I swiftly attain the fruit of the Way.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that if there are upāsakas or upāsikās who maintain this Eightfold Precept of Abstinence, those sons and daughters of good family shall proceed toward the three paths:"
"Or they will be born among humans, or born in the heavens, or attain parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Not killing, nor stealing, Not committing adultery, nor speaking falsehoods,"
Avoiding wine and staying far from incense and flowers, those who indulge in flavors and violate the fast;
those who perform songs, dances, and theatrical displays—may they learn to renounce these like an Arhat.
Now observing the Eight Precepts, may one not forget them day or night.
May there be no suffering of birth and death, and no cycle of wandering;
may there be no gathering with those one loves, nor meeting with those one hates.
May the suffering of the five aggregates be extinguished, along with all pains and the afflictions of birth and death.
“Nirvāṇa is free from all afflictions; I now take refuge in it.

Therefore, monks, if there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) to leave behind all suffering, to attain a favorable rebirth, or to exhaust all outflows (āsrava) and enter the city of Nirvāṇa, they should seek skillful means to perfect this dharma of the eightfold fast.”
The reason for this is that the honorable positions among humans are not worthy of being considered noble, and the bliss in the heavens is beyond measure.
If good sons or good daughters wish to seek unsurpassed merit, they should seek skillful means and accomplish this method of the fast.

"I now solemnly charge you once more: if there are good men or good women who observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), they shall also attain their wish if they desire to be reborn above the Four Heavenly Kings."
One who upholds the precepts obtains whatever they wish for; it is for this reason that I have explained this meaning.
The positions of honor among humans are not to be considered noble.

If good men or good women observe the eightfold fast of abstinence, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will be reborn in a favorable place among the heavens; they will be born in the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven—this shall never fail to come to pass.
The reason for this is that those who uphold the precepts obtain whatever they wish for.
"O Bhikṣus! I now tell you again:

if there are men or women who observe the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), whether they are reborn in the heavens of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu), their wishes shall likewise be fulfilled."
Why is this so? Because those who uphold the precepts obtain whatever they wish for.

Furthermore, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family upholds the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) with the desire to be reborn in the formless heavens (ārūpyadhātu), their wish shall likewise be fulfilled.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family observes the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), they shall likewise be reborn into the families of the four castes if they so desire.”

Furthermore, if good men or good women who observe the eight precepts of the fast wish to become a deva-king of one quarter of the world, or a deva-king of two quarters, three quarters, or all four quarters, they shall likewise obtain their wish.
Those who wish to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King shall likewise obtain their aspiration.
This is because for one who upholds the precepts, whatever they aspire to is attained.
If good sons or good daughters desire to seek the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha-vehicle, all their vows shall be fulfilled.
That I have now attained Buddhahood is due to my observance of the precepts—the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions—through which there is no vow that is not obtained. O bhikṣus!
"If you wish to accomplish that Way, you should train yourself in this manner.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When three things are present before one, at that time a son of good family or a daughter of good family obtains immeasurable merit."
What are the three?
When faith manifests before them, good sons and good daughters obtain immeasurable merit.
If material wealth manifests before them, at that time, good sons and good daughters obtain immeasurable merit.
Furthermore, if one brings the holy life (*brahmacarya*) into presence, at that time a son or daughter of good family obtains immeasurable merit. Thus, O Bhikṣu,
when these three things are brought into presence, one obtains immeasurable merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The wealth of faith is difficult for Brahmā to obtain; The recipient is one who upholds the precepts.
Having realized these three matters, The wise give at the appropriate time."
"Throughout the long night they obtain peace and security; the various devas constantly support and escort them.
Therein they enjoy themselves, never satiated with the five desires.
For this reason, O bhikṣus!"
