If good sons or good daughters should seek skillful means, they shall accomplish these three dharmas.
Thus, O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in the city of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the bhikṣu Kuśin was constantly fond of quarreling and litigating; he committed various evil deeds, engaging in face-to-face disputes, and at times even attacking one another with knives and staves.
Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One went to where that bhikṣu was.
Having arrived, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"You bhikṣus, be careful not to engage in quarrels or disputes; do not find fault with one another. O bhikṣus!"
"When we are united and harmonious, sharing the same teacher and companions, like water and milk blended as one, why do we engage in strife and litigation?
At that time, the bhikṣu Kuśin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will not worry about this matter!"
"I shall consider this matter for myself;
regarding such transgressions, I shall recognize my own fault.
The World-Honored One said:
“What do you think? Do you practice the path for the sake of becoming a member of the royal lineage? Or do you practice the path out of fear?
Or do you practice the path because the world is impoverished? The bhikṣus replied, “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said:
“What do you think, bhikṣu?”
"Is it not the case that you have set out upon the path because you wish to leave birth and death behind and seek the unconditioned Way?
Yet, this body of the five aggregates is truly not something that can be preserved. The bhikṣus replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!

Just as the World-Honored One has taught, the reason we sons of good family have left the household life to study the Way is to seek the unconditioned path and to extinguish the body of the five aggregates; for this purpose, we study the Way."
The World-Honored One said: "O bhikṣus!
You should not engage in strife while on the path, clashing with fists, disputing face-to-face, or addressing one another with harsh words."
You all should accomplish this practice:

sharing one Dharma and receiving it from one teacher, you should also practice these six kinds of dharmas, you should also practice these actions of body, speech, and mind, and you should also practice this offering to those who lead the holy life.
The bhikṣus replied, "This is our concern;
may the World-Honored One not worry about this matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣu Kuśin:
"How is this, you fools! Do you not believe the words of the Tathāgata?
You have just told the Tathāgata not to worry about this matter, yet you yourselves shall surely undergo the retribution for these wrong views."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed those bhikṣus, saying:
"In the distant past, there was a king in this city of Śrāvastī named King Dīrghāyu. He was clever and wise, and there was nothing he did not know."

However, although he is well-versed in the arts of the sword and blade, he lacks precious objects and his treasuries are not filled; his wealth and goods have diminished, his fourfold army is no longer numerous, and his ministers and attendants have also decreased.

At that time, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. He was valiant and robust, subduing all whom he encountered; his treasuries were filled with wealth and the seven precious jewels, his fourfold army was never lacking, and he was fully provided with ministers and attendants.
At that time, King Brahmadatta thought to himself:
"This King Dīrghāyu has no ministers or assistants, lacks wealth and goods, and possesses no precious treasures; I should now go and attack and punish his kingdom."
At that time, King Brahmadatta immediately raised an army and went to punish his kingdom.
When King Dīrghāyu heard that an army had been raised to attack and punish his kingdom, he devised a stratagem:

"Although I currently lack the wealth of the seven treasures, my ministers and the four divisions of my troops—though that king possesses many soldiers—my strength as a single man today is sufficient to destroy his hundreds of thousands of hosts. I must not slaughter countless sentient beings for the sake of the glory of a single lifetime, thereby committing an eternal sin."
"I should now leave this city and go to another kingdom so that there will be no more strife.
At that time, King Dīrghāyu did not speak to his ministers or officials; taking his chief consort and a single attendant, he departed from the city of Śrāvastī and entered the deep mountains.
At that time, the ministers and the people of Śrāvastī, not having seen King Dīrghāyu, dispatched messengers to King Brahmadatta with these words:
"We pray that Your Majesty will come to this land; we do not know where King Dīrghāyu has gone."
At that time, King Brahmadatta came to the kingdom of Kāśī and governed it himself.
Now, King Dīrghāyu had two queens, both of whom were pregnant and were about to give birth.

At that time, the lady dreamed that she was giving birth in the marketplace while the sun was just rising; four divisions of troops, each holding five-foot swords, surrounded her on all sides, yet she gave birth alone without any assistant.
Having seen this, she was startled awake and reported these circumstances to King Dīrghāyu.
The king said to his queen:
"I am currently here in the midst of these deep mountains; for what reason would I be giving birth within the city of Śrāvastī, in the middle of a marketplace?"
"If you now wish to give birth, you must do so like a deer.
At that time, the lady said,
"If I am not permitted to give birth in this manner, I shall simply die right here."
At that time, having heard these words, King Dīrghāyu immediately changed his clothes that very night and entered the city of Śrāvastī without bringing any followers.
At that time, King Dīrghāyu had a chief minister named Supuṣpa, whom he held in great affection.
On a minor errand, he went out of the city and saw King Dīrghāyu entering it.
At that time, the minister Subhūṣita gazed intently at the king, then departed; sighing and shedding tears, he retraced his steps.
King Dīrghāyu pursued the minister and, leading him to a secluded place, spoke to him, saying:
"Be careful not to let this out."
The minister replied, "As Your Majesty commands;
we do not yet know what instructions the Illustrious King has given. King Dīrghāyu said:
"Remembering my old kindness, I shall surely repay it.
At that time, the minister replied:
"As the Great King commands, I shall see to its fulfillment."
King Dīrghāyu said:
"My queen dreamed last night that she gave birth in the marketplace while surrounded by the four divisions of the army; she gave birth to a son who was exceedingly handsome."
"If she does not give birth as in a dream, she shall meet her end within seven days.
The minister replied, "I am capable of accomplishing this matter; I shall act according to Your Majesty's command."
Having spoken these words, they each departed.
At that time, the minister went to King Brahmadatta.
Upon arrival, he spoke as follows:
"During these seven days, I wish to observe the Great King's military forces—
the elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry— to see exactly how many there are."
At that time, Brahmadatta commanded his attendants, saying:
"Mobilize the elite troops immediately, just as Subhaddha has requested.
Thereupon, within seven days, the minister Subhaddha assembled the military forces in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, for seven days, the lady came to the marketplace.
Then, the minister Suvakṣa saw the lady approaching from afar and spoke thus: "Welcome, noble lady!"
"Now is precisely the right time.
At that moment, having seen the fourfold army, the lady was filled with joy and commanded her attendants to set up a great canopy.
At that time, when the sun first rose, the lady gave birth to a son who was peerlessly handsome and rare in the world.
Thereupon, the lady took the child in her arms and returned to the mountains.
At that time, King Dīrghāyu saw the queen approaching from afar carrying her child, and he spoke these words:
"May the child live long; may his life-span be infinite."
The lady said to the king,
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant her a name!
Thereupon, the king immediately bestowed a name upon her, calling her Changsheng (Long Life).
At that time, Prince Jīvaka was nearly eight years old.
His father, King Dīrghāyu, entered the city of Śrāvastī on a minor errand.
At that moment, the former minister of King Dīrghāyu, named Kapphiṇa, saw the king entering the city and gazed at him intently from head to foot.
Having seen this, he went to King Brahmadatta.
Upon arrival, he spoke as follows:
"Great King!"
"He is extremely heedless; King Dīrghāyu is currently in this city.
At that time, the king became enraged and commanded his attendants to swiftly arrest King Dīrghāyu.
"At that time, the ministers on his left and right led this Kapphiṇa and searched for him from east to west.
Then, seeing King Dīrghāyu from afar, Kapphiṇa pointed him out with his eyes and said to the ministers,
'This is King Dīrghāyu.'"
He immediately went forward to arrest him and brought him before King Brahmadatta.
Having arrived, he addressed the king, saying: "Great King!"
"The person who is King Dīrghāyu is this very man.

When the people of the kingdom all heard and learned that they had captured the body of King Dīrghāyu, the queen also heard that King Dīrghāyu had been seized by Brahmadatta. Having heard this, she thought to herself:
"What use have I for living any longer?
It would be better to share my life with the Great King at this very moment.
Thereupon, the lady immediately led the Prince into the city of Śrāvastī.
The lady said to the crown prince,
"You must now seek another place to live.
Upon hearing this, the crown prince Changsheng remained silent and did not speak.
Then, the lady went straight to King Brahmadatta. Seeing her approaching from afar, the king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself;
he immediately commanded his ministers: "Take this lady and King Jīvaka to the crossroads and divide them into four parts."

Then, the ministers, having received the king’s command, took King Dīrghāyu and his consort, bound them both from behind, and paraded them around the city of Śrāvastī so that the common people might see them.
At that time, among the people, there was none whose heart was not pierced with grief!
Then, Prince Changsheng, amidst the great multitude, saw his parents being led to the marketplace to be executed, yet his countenance remained unchanged.
Then, King Dīrghāyu turned back and said to Jīvaka:
"Do not look at what is long, nor look at what is short.
At that moment, he spoke this verse:
“Hatred never ceases through hatred; this has been the law from of old.
Only by overcoming hatred with non-hatred does one bring it to an end; this law is eternal.”
At that time, the ministers said to one another:
"This King Cīrṇadīrgha is utterly foolish and deluded. Who is this Prince Jīvaka, who dares to recite such verses before us?"
At that time, King Dīrghāyu addressed his ministers, saying:
"I am not deluded; only those among you who possess wisdom can clearly understand my words.
You worthy ones should know that by the strength of my single person, I am fully capable of destroying these hundreds of thousands of troops."
Nevertheless, I further reflected:
"The number of deaths among these classes of sentient beings is difficult to count; for the sake of my single body, I must not undergo suffering through successive lifetimes."
"Enmity never ceases through enmity; this has been the law from of old. Only by being free of enmity can one overcome enmity; this law remains forever undecaying.
At that time, those ministers took King Dīrghāyu and the queen’s bodies to a crossroads, divided them into four parts, and immediately departed, each returning to their respective places.
At that time, Prince Jīvaka gathered firewood toward evening and performed the cremation of his parents before departing.
At that moment, King Brahmadatta was atop a high tower and saw from afar a young boy performing the cremation of King Dīrghāyu and his queen. Having seen this, he commanded his attendants, saying:
"This must be a kinsman of King Dīrghāyu; you must go quickly and arrest him."
At that time, the ministers and citizens immediately went to him; however, before they had even arrived, the boy had already fled.
Then, Prince Jīvaka thought to himself:
"This King Brahmadatta has killed my parents and yet continues to dwell within my kingdom; I must now take vengeance for my parents."
At that time, Prince Jīvaka went to the lute player’s place.
Having arrived, he spoke thus:
"I now wish to learn how to play the lute."
Then the lute master asked,
"What is your surname now?
Where are your parents?"
The boy replied, "I have no parents;
I originally lived in this city of Śrāvastī, but my parents died long ago.
The lute player responded:
"Whoever wishes to learn may do so.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, Prince Jīvaka began to study the lute and vocal music.
Since Prince Jīvaka was naturally intelligent, within a few days he was able to play the lute and sing songs, knowing nothing that he did not master."

At that time, Prince Changsheng took his lute and went to the place where King Brahmadatta was; staying within the elephant stable, he played the lute alone at an unseasonable hour and sang with pure melody.
At that time, King Brahmadatta was atop a high tower when he heard the sound of lute-playing and singing. He then asked his attendants, saying:
"Who is this person in the elephant stable, playing the lute and singing songs alone?"
The ministers and attendants replied,
"In this city of Śrāvastī, there is a young boy who plays the lute and sings songs alone.
At that time, the king said to his attendant:
"You may command this young boy to come here and play; I wish to see him.
At that time, the messenger summoned the boy, who came into the presence of the king.
At that time, King Brahmadatta asked the boy,
"Were you playing the lute in the elephant stable last night? He replied:
"So be it, Great King! said Brahmāda.
"You may now remain by my side, playing the lute and singing and dancing; I shall provide you with clothing, bedding, food, and drink."
"Monks, you should know that at that time, Prince Jīvaka performed before King Brahmadatta, playing the lute, singing, and dancing with the utmost refinement and skill."
At that time, King Brahmadatta, hearing the sound of this lute, was filled with extreme joy and said to Prince Jīvaka:
"You shall guard my precious treasures for me."

At that time, Prince Changsheng received the King’s instructions and never failed to follow them; he always acted in accordance with the King’s wishes, smiling before speaking and constantly discerning the King’s intentions.
At that time, King Brahmadatta again issued this command:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You are now a person of extreme intelligence; I now command you to determine what is permissible within the palace—you must understand this.

At that time, Prince Changsheng was within the inner palace, teaching the various court ladies with the sound of this lute, and also instructing them in elephant-riding, horsemanship, and the arts of performance, such that there was nothing he did not know.

At that time, King Brahmadatta desired to go out for an excursion to the gardens and pavilions to enjoy himself; he immediately commanded Jīvaka to hasten the preparation of the precious feathered chariot.

At that time, Prince Changsheng immediately received the King’s command and ordered the carriage with precious feathers to be prepared, as well as the elephant to be fitted with its silver and gold saddle and bridle. He then returned and informed the King:
"The carriage is ready; may Your Majesty know that it is now the proper time."
King Brahmadatta mounted a chariot of precious feathers and appointed Changsheng (Jīvaka) to drive it, leading a fourfold army.
At that time, Prince Changsheng drove the chariot as a guide, always keeping himself apart from the main body of troops.
At that time, King Brahmadatta asked Prince Jīvaka, "Where are the troops today? Jīvaka replied:
"Your servant also does not know where the army is located.
Then the king said to him, "You may stay here for a short while; my body is utterly exhausted, and I wish to rest for a moment."
At that time, Prince Jīvaka immediately halted his advance to allow the King to rest.
During this interval, the army had not yet arrived.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that at that moment, King Brahmadatta leaned his head upon Prince Jīvaka’s lap and fell asleep."
At that time, Prince Changsheng, seeing that the king was asleep, thought to himself:
"This king is my greatest enemy; he has killed my parents and now dwells within the borders of my kingdom. If I do not take revenge now, when shall I ever have the chance to do so?"
"I shall now sever his life-root.
At that time, Prince Jīvaka drew his sword with his right hand and grasped the King’s hair with his left, yet he further thought to himself:
"When my father was on the verge of death, he spoke these words to me:"
"Changsheng, you should know:
do not see things as long, nor do you see them as short.
He then spoke this verse:
"Enmity never ceases through enmity; this has been the law since ancient times.
Only by being free from enmity can one overcome enmity; this law is eternal and indestructible."
"I now renounce this enmity," he said,
and immediately withdrew his sword.
This he did three times, and then he thought again:
"This king is my greatest enemy; he has even seized and killed my parents. Since he now dwells within my own realm, if I do not take revenge, when ever will I be able to strike him down?"
"I shall now, at this very moment, sever this life-faculty; only then can it be called 'retribution for enmity.
At that time, he further reflected:
"O Long-Life, you should neither see me as long nor see me as short."
The Father King gave this instruction:
"Hatred does not cease through hatred; this has been the law since antiquity. Only by being without hatred can one overcome hatred; this law remains forever undecaying."
"I should now abandon this enmity.
He then withdrew his sword back inside.
At that time, King Brahmadatta saw in a dream that Prince Jīvaka, the son of King Dīrghāyu, was about to seize and kill him; he became terrified and immediately woke up.
At that time, Prince Changsheng said: "Great King!
For what reason have you risen in such alarm as this?"
Brahmadatta said, "Just now I was asleep and dreamed that Prince Jīvaka, the son of King Jīvaka, drew his sword and intended to kill me; for this reason I am startled."
At that time, Prince Changsheng (Long-life) thought to himself:
"Now this king already knows that I am Prince Changsheng.
He immediately drew his sword with his right hand, seized [the king's] hair with his left hand, and said to the king:

"I am indeed the Crown Prince Changsheng, son of King Changshou. Yet the King is my great enemy; he seized and killed my parents and now dwells within my own realm. If I do not take revenge now, on what day shall I ever succeed?"
At that time, King Brahmadatta immediately addressed Jīvaka, saying:
"My life now rests in your hands; I pray you grant me your pardon and spare me, so that my life may be preserved!"
Jīvaka replied, "I can restore the King to life, but the King cannot spare my own life.
The King replied to Jīvaka:
"I only pray that you will grant me your protection; I shall never take your life!
At that time, Prince Changsheng and the king made a mutual oath:
"As for those whose lives we have saved together, we shall never harm one another."
"Monks, you should know that at that time, Prince Jīvaka restored the King’s life.
Then, King Brahmadatta said to Prince Jīvaka:
'I pray that you, Prince, will return and provide me with my magnificent chariot adorned with precious feathers, so that we may return to our kingdom.'"
At that time, the prince immediately prepared his precious feathered chariot, and the two of them rode together directly to the city of Śrāvastī.
Then, King Brahmadatta assembled his ministers and spoke thus:
"Suppose you were to see the son of King Dīrghāyu; what would you wish to do with him?"
Among them, some ministers spoke thus:
"His hands and feet should be severed. Others said:
"One should divide him into three parts," some said; others said,
"One should seize and kill him."
At that time, Prince Jīvaka was seated beside the king; with body upright and mind composed, he contemplated the words spoken.
Then, King Brahmadatta took Prince Jīvaka by the hand with his own hands and said to the people:
"This is Prince Jīvaka, the son of King Dīrghāyu; this person is he."
"You all must not speak further or dare to say anything more.
Why is this? Because Prince Changsheng saved my life, I shall likewise save this man's life."
At that time, when the various ministers had heard these words, they marveled at what they had never before experienced:
"This king and his crown prince are truly marvelous!
Truly extraordinary!"
"And furthermore, one is able not to retaliate against an enemy.
At that time, King Brahmadatta asked Jīvaka:
"You ought to have taken my life; for what reason were you released, and why did you not kill me?"
"What causes and conditions will there be?
I now wish to hear of them.
Changsheng replied:
"Great King! Listen well. When my father, the King, was on the verge of passing away, he spoke these words:
'You must now neither see the long nor see the short.'"
He further spoke these words:
"Hatred never ceases through hatred; this has been the law since antiquity. Only by overcoming hatred with non-hatred does one triumph; this law endures forever."
At that time, when the ministers heard these words of the Father King, they all said to one another:
"This man is deluded and speaks much; who, after all, is this person named Changsheng?"
King Dīrghāyu replied: "You should know that among you there is a wise person who understands these words.
Having recalled this speech of his father the king, he thereby preserved the life-force of the king.

Upon hearing these words, King Brahmadatta marveled at what had been done; he sighed in wonder at such an unprecedented feat, for [the prince] was indeed able to uphold his deceased father’s instructions without falling away from them.
"At that time, King Brahmadatta said to the crown prince:
'The meaning of what you have just spoken, I still do not understand; you should now explain its meaning to me so that I may attain comprehension.'"
At that time, Prince Changsheng replied:
"Great King! Listen well!"
I shall explain this to you.

King Brahmadatta took King Dīghāvu and killed him; even if Dīghāvu’s own ministers and closest kinsmen had taken the king and killed him, and even if Brahmadatta’s own ministers and assistants had in turn taken Dīghāvu’s ministers and assistants and killed them—this is what is called a cycle of enmity that never ceases.
‘If one wishes to sever enmity, there is only one way: by not retaliating against others.
Having now contemplated this principle, I have therefore not harmed the king.

At that time, King Brahmadatta, having heard these words, was filled with such great joy that he could not contain himself; this prince was exceedingly clever, for he was able to expound upon the meaning so extensively.”
At that time, King Brahmadatta immediately offered a confession:
"It was my transgression that I seized and killed King Dīrghāyu.

He then personally removed his celestial crown and gave it to the envoy of Dīrghāyu to wear; furthermore, he bestowed his daughter upon him and returned the kingdom of Śrāvastī along with its people, entrusting them to the envoy of Dīrghāyu to govern, while the king himself returned to Vārāṇasī to rule.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that although this was the constant custom of kings in ancient times—
that despite such laws for warring between nations, they still exercised mutual forbearance and did not inflict harm upon one another— ”

How much more so for you, bhikṣus, who have left the household life to study the Path with firm faith, having abandoned the minds of greed, hatred, and delusion; yet now you again engage in strife and contention, lacking mutual harmony, failing to endure one another, and refusing to repent and reform.
"O bhikṣus! By this cause and condition, you should know that fighting is not appropriate.
Being fellow disciples under the same teacher, sharing as one water and milk, do not engage in mutual strife or litigation."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Without strife and without contention, With a heart of loving-kindness pitying all,
Free from harm toward any being— This is what all Buddhas praise."
"Therefore, monks, you should practice patience. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kuśin spoke to the World-Honored One, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One need not concern himself with this matter; we ourselves shall clarify this Dharma."
“World-Honored One!
Although these words have been spoken, the matter is not as they say.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed and went to the country of Vṛji.
At that time, there were three sons of noble family in the Vṛji country: Aniruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.
Those sons of noble family together established a regulation:
Whenever there were those who went out to beg for alms, those remaining behind would sweep and sprinkle the ground to make it clean, ensuring that no necessity was lacking.
When the food was brought back, they would share it with them so they might eat; if it was sufficient, that was well; if it was insufficient, they were free to go wherever they pleased.
If there is any remainder, he pours it into a vessel and departs.
If another comes for alms last, if the food is sufficient, that is well; if it is not sufficient, he takes the food from the vessel and puts it into his own bowl.

At that time, he took his water jar and placed it in another spot; he then spent the day sweeping the dwelling, and subsequently, in a secluded place, sat with body upright and mind composed, fixing his mindfulness before him and contemplating the sublime Dharma. Furthermore, that person never spoke with him, and each remained in silent stillness.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha contemplated the perception of the impurity of sensual desire; mindful of joy and bliss, he dwelt in the first dhyāna.

At that moment, Nandiya and Kimbila, knowing what was in Anuruddha’s mind, likewise contemplated the perception of the impurity of sensual desire; mindful of joy and bliss, they too dwelt in the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, when the Venerable Aniruddha contemplates the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, at that time the Venerables Nandiya and Kimbila likewise contemplate the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

Furthermore, when the Venerable Aniruddha contemplates the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, at that time the Venerable Nandiya likewise contemplates the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, when the Venerable Aniruddha contemplates the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), at that time the Venerable Nandiya also contemplates the attainment of cessation.
Such are these dharmas; thus do the worthy ones contemplate these dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled to the kingdom of Siṃhala.
Then, as the guardians of the country saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar, they spoke thus:
"Śramaṇa, do not come to enter our country."
The reason for this is that there are three sons of noble family in this country named Aniruddha, Nandi, and Kumbhīra; take care not to provoke or harass them.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha, with his purified divine eye and through the supernormal power of the divine ear, heard the city guards speaking thus to the World-Honored One, seeking to prevent the World-Honored One from entering the city.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha went out and said to the gatekeeper:
"Do not stop him; the World-Honored One is coming now, wishing to come here to look."
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha immediately went in and informed Kumbhīra, saying:
"Come quickly; the World-Honored One is now outside the gate.
Thereupon, the three Venerables arose from their samādhi and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet and stood to one side, each addressing him:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
Venerable Aniruddha stepped forward to take the World-Honored One’s bowl; Venerable Nandika spread out a seat; and Venerable Kumbhīra brought water for the World-Honored One to wash his feet.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aniruddha, saying:
"You three have been together here in harmony, free from other thoughts; has your alms-round been successful?"
Anuruddha said: “It is so, World-Honored One.”
I do not consider begging for alms to be a hardship.
Why is this? When I contemplate the first dhyāna, at that time Nandika and Kimbila likewise contemplate the first dhyāna.

If I contemplate the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the samādhi of cessation, at that time Nandiya and Kimbila likewise contemplate the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the attainment of cessation.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
We have reflected upon this Dharma.
The World-Honored One told them:
"Excellent! Excellent, Aniruddha!"
"Is there any time when you have further attained the qualities of a superior person? Ānanda replied, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
We have further attained the qualities of a superior person.
The World-Honored One replied:
“What is this Dharma of the superior person? Aniruddha replied: “There is this wondrous Dharma that transcends the Dharma of the superior person.

Furthermore, if we, with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), pervade one direction, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions; if we likewise pervade the four intermediate directions, the zenith, and the nadir—in all things, everywhere—pervading them all with a mind of loving-kindness, immeasurable, limitless, and beyond calculation, and thus sport therein.”

Furthermore, with a mind of compassion, a mind of joy, and a mind of equanimity, he pervades one direction; he does the same for the second, third, and fourth directions, as well as the four intermediate points, the zenith, and the nadir, thus sporting therein.
“This is what we call, World-Honored One,
further attaining this state of a superior person.
At that time, the Venerable Nandiya and Kimbila said to Anuruddha:
"When did we ever come to you to ask about this matter?
Now, in the presence of the World-Honored One, you speak of it yourself. Anuruddha said:
“None of you have ever come to me to ask about this matter;
rather, it was the devas who came to my presence and spoke of this matter.
Therefore, they spoke of this matter before the Blessed One.”

However, throughout the long night, I have known the minds of you venerable ones; it is because you venerable ones have attained this samādhi that you speak these words in the presence of the World-Honored One.
At that time, as this Dharma was being taught, the General Jīvaka arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then, the General Jīvaka addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One, are you teaching the Dharma today to these people?"
At that time, the World-Honored One related this matter in detail to the General Dīrghanakha.
Then the General addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The great kingdom of Vṛji has truly attained a great benefit, for these three sons of noble family come here to wander and teach."
"Aniruddha, Nandiya, and Kimphila.
The World-Honored One told him: "So it is, General!"
As you have said, the great kingdom of the Vṛjis has gained a most excellent benefit.
Setting aside the great kingdom of the Vṛjis for a moment, even the great kingdom of Magadha has gained a most excellent benefit, in that there are these three sons of noble family.
If the people of the great kingdom of Magadha were to keep these three sons of noble family in mind, they would obtain peace and security for a long night.
Great General, you should know that if there are these three sons of noble family within any district, town, or city, the people therein will obtain peace and security for a long night.

The families from which these three sons of noble lineage were born have also attained great benefit, for they were able to give birth to such exalted persons; furthermore, if their parents and five kinds of relatives should keep these three men in mind, they too will attain great benefit.
Furthermore, if devas, nāgas, or spirits should recollect these three sons of noble family, they too will obtain great benefit.
If anyone praises the arhats, they should likewise praise these three men.
If there is anyone who praises those who are without greed, without delusion, and without hatred, one should likewise praise these three persons.
If there is anyone who praises this field of merit, one should likewise praise these three persons.
Just as I have practiced with diligent austerity for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas to achieve the Unsurpassed Way, so shall I cause these three men to accomplish this Dharma-meaning. Therefore, General!
"You should give rise to a heart of joy toward these three sons of noble family. Thus, General,
you should train yourself."
At that time, the Great General, having heard what the World-Honored One had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are three fetters that bind sentient beings, preventing them from crossing from this shore to the other shore."
"What are the three? They are namely:
bodily wrong view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). What is meant by 'bodily wrong view'?"

What is called the fetter of the false view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) refers to calculating that the body possesses a self, giving rise to the notion of "I" and "mine," having the notion of a sentient being, having a life-force, having longevity, having a person, having a human being, having conditions, and having attachments; this is what is termed the fetter of the false view of self.
"What is called the fetter of doubt?
It refers to such [hesitations] as: 'Is there a self? Is there no self?'"
Is there birth? Is there no birth?
Is there a self, a person, or a life-span?
Is there no self, no person, and no life-span? Are there parents,
or are there no parents?
Is there this world and a future world?
Is there no this world and no future world?
Are there śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?
Are there no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas?
Is there an arhat in the world,
or is there no arhat in the world?
Is there one who attains realization?
Or is there none who attains realization?
This is called the fetter of doubt.
"What is called the fetter of the clinging to precepts?

That which is known as the clinging to precepts is: 'By means of these precepts, I shall be born into a great clan, or into the family of a householder, or into the family of a brahmin; or I shall be born among the devas and various spirits. This is what is called the fetter of the clinging to precepts."

“Monks, it is said that there are these three fetters which bind sentient beings, preventing them from going from this shore to the other shore, just as two oxen yoked to the same pole remain forever inseparable.”
These classes of sentient beings are also like this: bound by the three fetters, they are unable to go from this shore to the other shore. What is "this shore"?
What is the "other shore"?
That which is called "this shore" is the perversion of the body; that which is called the "other shore" is the cessation of the perversion of the body.
This, O bhikṣu, is what it means.
The three fetters bind sentient beings, preventing them from crossing from this shore to the other shore. Therefore, O bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to extinguish these three fetters.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These three samādhis— what are the three?
They are the emptiness samādhi, the wishlessness samādhi, and the signlessness samādhi."
"What is called the emptiness samādhi?
That which is called 'emptiness' refers to contemplating all dharmas as entirely empty and void; this is what is termed the emptiness samādhi."
"What is called the samādhi of non-conception?

That which is termed 'non-conception' refers to the total absence of any conceptualization regarding all dharmas, such that they cannot even be perceived; this is what is called the samādhi of non-conception."
"What is called the wishless samādhi?
That which is called 'wishless' refers to not seeking or aspiring toward any phenomena whatsoever; this is what is called the wishless samādhi."
"In this way, bhikṣus! There are those who do not attain these three samādhis; they remain long in saṃsāra and are unable to awaken by themselves. Thus it is, bhikṣus!"
"You should seek skillful means to attain these three samādhis. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Dhvaja, Vaiśravaṇa, Dharmarāja; Gautama, Ṛddhivikurvaṇa, Upavāsa; Pratyutpanna, Dīrghāyu, Saṃyojana, Samādhi.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Sixteen and Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 25: The Four Noble Truths, Part One. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should practice the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. What are these four?
What is called the first Truth of Suffering has inexhaustible meaning; its meaning cannot be exhausted, and the teaching of it is endless.
The second, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, has inexhaustible meaning; its meaning cannot be exhausted, and the teaching of it is endless.
The third is the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering; its meaning is inexhaustible, its meaning is unfathomable, and the teaching of it is endless.
The fourth is the Truth of the Path Leading to the Escape from Suffering; its meaning is inexhaustible, its meaning is unfathomable, and the teaching of it is endless.
"What is called the Truth of Suffering? That which is called the Truth of Suffering consists of:

the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair; the suffering of association with the disliked; the suffering of separation from the beloved; the suffering of not obtaining what one desires; and, to state it in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). This is what is called the Truth of Suffering."
"What is called the Truth of the Origin of Suffering?
That which is called the Truth of the Origin refers to craving accompanied by desire, with the mind constantly stained and attached; this is what is called the Truth of the Origin of Suffering."
"What is called the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering?

That which is called the Truth of Cessation refers to the eternal exhaustion of craving for sensual desire without remainder, such that one no longer creates further [karma]; this is what is called the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering."
"What is called the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering?

The Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering refers to the Eightfold Noble Path, namely: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is what is called the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering."
"In this way, bhikṣus! There are these Four Noble Truths, which are real and not false; they are taught by the World-Honored One, and are therefore called 'truths.

Among all sentient beings—whether two-footed, three-footed, or four-footed; those of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; those with perception or without perception—the Tathāgata is supreme."
However, because these four truths are established, they are called the Four Truths.
Thus it is said, "O Bhikṣus!
These four truths exist."
Yet, being unaware [of this], I have long dwelt in birth and death, transmigrating through the five realms.

Now that I have attained these Four Truths, I have gone from this shore to the other shore; having accomplished this purpose, I have severed the root of birth and death and shall no longer undergo further existence, knowing this as it truly is.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Now there are the Four Noble Truths; If one does not know them as they truly are, One will revolve within birth and death, And never attain liberation."
"Now there are the Four Noble Truths; through awakening and clear understanding, one cuts off the root of birth and death and shall no longer undergo further existence.
If there are members of the fourfold assembly who do not attain these truths, and remain unawakened and ignorant, they will follow along the five destinies."
Therefore, monks, you should apply yourselves with skillful means to realize these Four Noble Truths. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four dharmas that bring great benefit to people."

What are the four? First, one should associate with spiritual friends; second, one should hear the Dharma; third, one should understand the Dharma; fourth, one should clearly comprehend the characteristics of each phenomenon.
"Monks, these are called the four qualities that are of great benefit to people. Therefore, monks!"
"You should seek skillful means to accomplish these four dharmas. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, four unprecedented phenomena appear in the world."

What are the four? These classes of sentient beings have many attachments; yet when the Dharma of non-attachment is taught, they likewise receive it, practice it with mindfulness, and their minds do not stray from it.
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, these four unprecedented qualities appear in the world; this is called the first unprecedented quality that appears in the world.

"Furthermore, Ānanda! Revolving without ceasing, they constantly dwell within the five realms of existence; even when one wishes to preach the Dharma, they likewise receive it, their minds never departing from it."
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, these two unprecedented qualities appear in the world.

Furthermore, Ānanda, these classes of sentient beings constantly harbor pride, which does not depart from the forefront of their minds; yet, if he were to preach the Dharma, they would receive it and their minds would not turn away from it.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

These classes of sentient beings constantly harbor arrogance and do not depart for even a moment; even when the Dharma is being preached, they receive it with acceptance. This is called the third unprecedented phenomenon appearing in the world.
"Furthermore, Ānanda! These classes of sentient beings, though covered by ignorance, will nevertheless receive and not forget the teaching of the Dharma of clarity when it is proclaimed.
Furthermore, Ānanda,
when this teaching on the phenomena of light and darkness is being expounded, if one’s mind becomes gentle and supple, and one constantly delights in practice—
this, Ānanda, is called [the mark of a noble disciple].
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, these four unprecedented qualities appear in the world.
When a Tathāgata is present in the world, these four unprecedented qualities appear in the world.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should give rise to a heart of joy toward the Tathāgata. Thus it is, Ānanda!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall now speak of the burden, and I shall also speak of the bearer of the burden; I shall speak of the causes and conditions of the burden, and I shall also speak of the laying down of the burden.”
"You bhikṣus, listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall now speak."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"What is that which is called 'the burden'?"
These are what are called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*). What are the five?
They are the aggregates of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); these are what are called the burden.
"What is meant by the 'bearer of the burden'? The bearer of the burden refers to the human person.
Having such a surname and such a name, born in such a manner, eating such food, experiencing such suffering and pleasure, and having such a lifespan—this is what is called the bearer of the burden."
"What is meant by the 'condition for the burden'?
The so-called condition for the burden is the condition of craving and attachment.
To be accompanied by desire, with the mind not remaining detached—this is what is called the condition for the burden."
“What, monks, is called ‘the laying down of the burden’?
It refers to being able to bring that craving to an end forever without remainder, having already removed it and vomited it out.
This, monks, is called [the laying down of the burden].”
This is called "the laying down of the burden.

"In this way, bhikṣus, I have now explained the burden, explained the cause of the burden, explained the bearer of the burden, and explained the laying down of the burden; that which ought to be done by all Tathāgatas, I have now accomplished."
"If you sit beneath trees, in open spaces, or in the open air, always mindfully practice seated meditation; do not act with negligence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"One should mindfully lay down the heavy burden, And never again create a new burden."
Carrying this burden is the sickness of the world; laying down the burden is the supreme bliss.
One should likewise eliminate the fetters of craving and abandon unrighteous conduct;
having completely relinquished these, one shall no longer undergo further existence through craving.
"Therefore, monks, you should apply yourselves with skillful means to cast off the burden. Thus, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are these four modes of birth.”
What are the four? They are namely:
birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation.
What is meant by "birth from an egg"?
Regarding those born from eggs: chickens, sparrows, crows, magpies, peacocks, snakes, fish, ants, and their like—all these are born from eggs.
This is what is called birth from an egg. What is meant by birth from a womb?
It refers to humans and animals, up to and including two-legged insects; this is what is called birth from a womb.
"What is meant by 'arising through causes and conditions'?
It refers to such things as worms in rotting flesh, worms in latrines, and worms in corpses.
All such categories are said to arise through causes and conditions."
"What is meant by 'birth by transformation' (upapāduka)?
It refers to the various devas, those in the great hells, hungry ghosts, humans, and animals; these are called birth by transformation."
"Monks, these are called the four modes of birth. Monks,
having abandoned these four modes of birth, you should seek the means to realize the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Maudgalyāyana were staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa, the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of persons in the world. What are these four?"
It is said that there is one person who is accompanied by fetters, yet being internally possessed of fetters, he does not know it.
Alternatively, there is another person who is accompanied by fetters, yet being internally possessed of fetters, he knows it as it truly is.
There may be a person who is not accompanied by fetters, yet does not know, as it truly is, that there are no fetters within.
There may be a person who is not accompanied by fetters, and knows, as it truly is, that there are no fetters within.

"Virtuous ones, you should know this: the first person is accompanied by fetters; yet, though there are fetters within him, he does not know it. Among these two persons who possess fetters, this person is the most base."
Regarding those two types of persons: the second person is accompanied by fetters; he knows as it truly is that there are fetters within him, and such a person is most excellent.

The third person is not accompanied by fetters, yet he does not know as it truly is that there are no fetters within him; among these two types of persons who are without fetters, this person is the most base.
Regarding that fourth person, who does not associate with fetters and knows as it truly is that there are no fetters within, this person is the foremost among those who are free from fetters.
"Virtuous ones, you should know that there are these four kinds of persons in the world.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana asked Śāriputra:
"By what causes and conditions is it that among those persons who follow along with their fetters (*saṃyojana*), one is base and lowly while another is most excellent?"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do these two persons free from fetters travel together, yet one is lowly while the other is most excellent?
Śāriputra replied, "The other travels with fetters;
though he has fetters within, he does not know them as they truly are."
That person thinks: "I shall cultivate the perception of purity.
He then reflects and cultivates the perception of purity.
When he forms the perception of purity, a mind of desire arises; having given rise to a mind of desire, he dies with a mind of lust, hatred, and delusion.
At that time, failing to employ skillful means to extinguish this lustful mind, one passes away with a mind of anger and delusion.
Maudgalyāyana, you should know it is like a person who goes to the market and buys a copper vessel that is covered in dust and grime, being utterly impure.
If that person does not wipe it at the proper time and does not wash it clean at the proper time, the copper vessel will become even more fouled with grime and become extremely impure.
This first type of person is just like this: accompanied by defilements, they do not know as it truly is the fetters within; they then think to themselves:
"I shall cultivate perceptions of purity."

Having contemplated pure perceptions, he gives rise to a mind of desire; once the mind of desire has arisen, he dies possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion, failing to seek skillful means to extinguish this mind of desire.
“That second person, accompanied by fetters, knows as it truly is that there are fetters within him:
‘I should now abandon the perception of the pure and cultivate the perception of the impure.’”

Having abandoned the perception of purity, he contemplates the perception of impurity. By contemplating the perception of impurity, he no longer gives rise to a mind of desire; he seeks skillful means, and that which was not obtained he obtains, that which was not acquired he acquires, and that which was not reached he reaches. Thus, he is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, and likewise passes away without fetters.

It is just as if someone were to purchase a copper vessel from the marketplace that was stained with dust and grime; that person would, at the appropriate time, repair it and wash it until it was clean.
This person is also like this.
Accompanied by fetters, he knows as it truly is that there are fetters within him.

That person then abandons the perception of purity and contemplates the perception of impurity. As he contemplates the perception of impurity, he further seeks skillful means; what he had not attained he attains, what he had not acquired he acquires, and what he had not realized he is taught to realize. Having thus become free from desire, free from ill will, and free from delusion, he passes away.
"This is what I mean, Maudgalyāyana!
These two types of people are accompanied by their fetters; one is base and lowly, while the other is most sublime.
Maudgalyāyana said:
“Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do these two persons not associate with the fetters, yet one is lowly and base while the other is most excellent?
Śāriputra replied, “That third person does not associate with the fetters, yet internally he does not know the fetters as they truly are.”
He then reflects: "I have not sought out the means of reflection to attain what has not been attained, to obtain what has not been obtained, or to realize what has not been realized."
That person dies bound by desire, hatred, and delusion.

It is just as if someone were to go to the market to buy a copper vessel that is stained with dust and grime, yet they do not wash or clean it at the proper time, nor do they repair it at the proper time;

this third type of person is also like this. Defilements (saṃyojana) do not accompany him, yet he does not truly know that there are no defilements within, nor does he train himself thus: "I shall seek skillful means to extinguish these various defilements."
Yet they pass away with minds still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion.
As for that fourth person, he does not dwell together with the fetters; he knows, as it truly is, that within him there are no fetters.
He then reflects in this way and seeks a means, so that what he has not attained he may attain, what he has not acquired he may acquire, and what he has not realized he may realize;
thus, free from these fetters, he passes away.
It is just as if a person were to go to the market and obtain a fine copper vessel that is extremely clean and bright, which they then further refine and polish at the appropriate time.

At that moment, the vessel becomes even more pure and beautiful. This fourth person is also like this: he does not associate with the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and knowing truly that there are no fetters within, he reflects thus: "I shall seek skillful means so that what has not been attained may be attained, what has not been acquired may be acquired, and what has not been realized may be realized. Thereupon, being free from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed, hatred, and delusion, when his body breaks up and his life ends, [he attains final liberation].
"Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
These two persons do not associate with the fetters; they know as it truly is that there are no fetters within them. One is superior, and the other is base."
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana asked Śāriputra:
"For what reason is it called a 'fetter' (saṃyojana)? Śāriputra replied:
“Maudgalyāyana, you should know that unwholesome and evil dharmas give rise to various false views; therefore, they are called fetters (saṃyojana).
Furthermore, some people may think:

‘The Tathāgata questioned me about the meaning [of the Dharma] and subsequently taught the Dharma to the bhikṣus; he did not question other bhikṣus about the meaning, yet the Tathāgata taught the Dharma to those bhikṣus.’”
"Or again, there may be a time when the World-Honored One speaks the Dharma to other bhikṣus, yet does not speak the Dharma to that bhikṣu,
[thinking], 'The Tathāgata is not speaking the Dharma to me and the bhikṣus.'"
"Or there may be unwholesomeness, or there may be lust.
Since there is both unwholesomeness and lust, these two are both unwholesome.
Or again, at times, a bhikṣu might think:
"I always enter the village for alms at the head of the bhikṣus, not allowing any other bhikṣu to enter the village for alms ahead of me.
There may be times, however, when another bhikṣu enters the village for alms ahead of me, and I do not allow that bhikṣu to enter the village for alms ahead of the rest.
"I do not enter a village to beg for alms while remaining behind the bhikṣus.
This is unwholesome; furthermore, there is greed—these two are both unwholesome.
“Maudgalyāyana, you should know that there may be a time when a bhikṣu thinks to himself:
‘I shall sit before the other bhikṣus; I shall receive water first and receive food first, so that no other bhikṣu sits before me, receives water before me, or receives food before me.’”

Furthermore, there may be times when another bhikṣu sits before a bhikṣu, receiving water first and receiving food first; [the latter] does not allow that bhikṣu to sit before him, receive water first, or receive food first.
"I do not sit before the bhikṣus; I receive water first and obtain food first.
Since there is both unwholesomeness and greed, these two are both unwholesome.
"Furthermore, there may be a time when a bhikṣu thinks:
'I shall preach the Dharma to the donor after I have finished eating, so that other bhikṣus do not finish eating and then preach the Dharma to the donor.'"

Furthermore, there may be times when other bhikṣus, having finished their meal, preach the Dharma to the donor, rather than allowing that bhikṣu to preach the Dharma to the donor after he has finished his meal.
“May he not give me the Dharma teaching after I have finished eating;
thus, there is both unwholesomeness and greed, and these two are both unwholesome.
“Furthermore, at times, a bhikṣu may think:”
"I shall go to the park myself to teach the Dharma to the elder and the brahmin, so that no other bhikṣu goes to the park to teach the Dharma to the elder and the brahmin."

Furthermore, there may be times when other bhikṣus go to the park and teach the Dharma to householders and brahmins, yet they do not allow other bhikṣus to go to the park to teach the Dharma to those householders and brahmins.
“May he not allow me to go into his garden to teach the Dharma to the elder and the brahmin.
This is unwholesome; furthermore, there is greed—these two are both unwholesome.
"Furthermore, there may be a time when a bhikṣu thinks:
'I have now violated the precepts; let the other bhikṣus not know that I have violated the precepts.

Or again, there may be a time when that bhikṣu violates the precepts and the other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has violated the precepts. Since there is already unwholesomeness, and furthermore there is greed, these two are both unwholesome."
"Furthermore, there may be a time when a bhikṣu thinks:
'I have now transgressed the precepts, yet I do not let other bhikṣus tell me that I have transgressed.
Or again, there may be a time when that bhikṣu has transgressed the precepts, and other bhikṣus tell him that he has transgressed."
Since there is both unwholesomeness and greed, these two are both unwholesome.
"Furthermore, at times that bhikṣu may think:
'I have now transgressed the precepts; let a pure bhikṣu inform me of it, not an impure bhikṣu.'"
Furthermore, there may be a time when an impure bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu,
"That bhikṣu has violated the precepts.
Since this involves both unwholesomeness and covetousness, these two are both unwholesome.
"Furthermore, there may be a time when a bhikṣu thinks:
'I have now committed an offense.
If there is a bhikṣu who informs me of it, I shall do so in a private place, not in the midst of the great assembly.'"
"Furthermore, there may be a time when that bhikṣu has transgressed the precepts and is publicly reproached by the assembly rather than in private. That bhikṣu then thinks:
'These bhikṣus are reproaching me in the midst of the assembly, not in private.'"
"Since there is unwholesomeness and furthermore there is craving, these two together are unwholesome.
Maudgalyāyana, you should know that this is the root of all dharmas; the arising of these practices is called 'fetter' (saṃyojana)."
Maudgalyāyana!
Furthermore, you should know that when members of the fourfold assembly commit such transgressions, they all hear and know of them together.

Although one may say, "I practice in the āraṇya, dwelling in a secluded place; even though I wear the five-fold patched robe and constantly go on alms-round, choosing neither between the poor and the wealthy; my conduct is not violent or abrupt; whether coming or going, staying or sitting, moving or remaining still, speaking or remaining silent," that bhikṣu nevertheless harbors these thoughts:
"May these practitioners of the holy life—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—constantly come to make offerings to me.
Although that monk harbors such a thought, the fourfold assembly does not make offerings to him at all times.
The reason for this is that because those bhikṣus have not eliminated their evil and unwholesome conduct, they continue to see, hear, perceive, and know it.

It is just as if there were a person who had a copper vessel that was extremely clean, yet he placed impurities inside that copper vessel, covered its opening with another vessel, and carried it along to travel through the kingdom.
Having seen this, the crowd asked the man,
"What is that which you are carrying? We wish to see it."
At that time, as the people had long been accustomed to hunger and scarcity,
they cried out, "This is excellent food!
They immediately lifted the lids of the vessels, only to see that it was indeed impure, which everyone witnessed together.
This bhikṣu is also like this.

Although he practices in the forest (āraṇyaka), begs for food at the proper time, wears the fivefold patched robe, and maintains an upright body and mind with mindfulness fixed before him, he nevertheless gives rise to this thought:
"I wish to cause those who practice the holy life (brahmacārin) to come and provide offerings to me at the proper time."
"Furthermore, fellow practitioners of the holy life do not provide him with timely offerings.
This is because that bhikṣu has not yet exhausted his evil, unwholesome dharmas and fetters."

"Maudgalyāyana, you should know that there are bhikṣus who are free from these evil and unwholesome dharmas, whose fetters are exhausted, and who perceive, hear, recollect, and know [the truth]; even if they dwell and travel near a city, they are still persons who uphold the Dharma."
Whether receiving an invitation from others or being provided for by the offerings of elders, that bhikṣu harbors no thoughts of craving.
At that time, the fourfold assembly and all fellow practitioners of the holy life come to make offerings.
The reason for this is that because those bhikṣus practice purity, all see, hear, recollect, and know it.

It is just as if there were a person with a fine bronze vessel filled with excellent food and drink, its aroma being exceedingly fragrant; having covered it with a lid, he carries it along and enters a kingdom.
When the people see it, they ask that person, "What is this? We wish to behold it."
Then, they immediately went to look and saw that it was food and drink, so they all took and ate it together.

It is just the same in this case: although a bhikṣu sees, hears, remembers, and knows [the offerings], and even while living near a city and receiving the hospitality of a householder, he does not form this thought:
"May those fellow practitioners of the holy life come to provide for me."
"Furthermore, all fellow practitioners of the holy life come to make offerings to him.
This is because that bhikṣu has completely eliminated his evil and unwholesome conduct."
"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana!
Because of these various formations, they are called fetters and latent tendencies.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”

The reason for this is that in the past, while I was traveling here to the Karanda Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, I dressed myself, took my bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. Upon reaching the house of that chariot-maker, I stood silently outside his door.
At that time, the carpenter was holding an axe in his hand and cutting timber.
At that moment, another elder carpenter, having some minor business, came to this carpenter’s house.
At that time, the carpenter was working on the timber planks.
Then, the elderly carpenter had this thought:
"Does this young apprentice saw the timber according to my intention?"
"I shall now examine it.
At that time, the carpenter took all those parts he had disliked and cut them away.
Then, the old carpenter was filled with great joy and thought to himself:
"Excellent! Excellent!
The timber you have cut is exactly as I intended."

"This is also like that: there are bhikṣus whose minds are not gentle and harmonious, who abandon the conduct of a śramaṇa, whose hearts harbor guile and deceit, who do not follow the dharma of a śramaṇa, whose nature and behavior are coarse and negligent, who lack a sense of shame and remorse, who force a smile while enduring humiliation, who engage in base and ignoble actions, and who possess no courage or vigor."

Some are prone to much forgetfulness, failing to remember what they have done; their minds are unsettled, their actions are confused, and their faculties are unstable. Yet now, the Venerable Śāriputra, having observed their dispositions and conduct, disciplines and reforms them.

“Any sons of noble family who, with firm faith, leave the household life to study the Way, who deeply revere the precepts, do not abandon the sublime and holy Dharma of the śramaṇas, are free from deceit and hypocrisy, do not act with violence, possess gentle minds, always smile when speaking, do not wound the feelings of others, maintain constant mental concentration, are free from notions of right and wrong, and have their faculties undisturbed—[they shall attain this].”
Having heard the words of the Venerable Śāriputra, he accepted them and did not forget them.
It was as if a man or a woman, peerlessly handsome, having bathed thoroughly and put on fine new clothes, were to anoint their bodies with fragrant perfumes.
If there were another person who further offered an *utpala* flower to him, and upon receiving it, that person placed it upon his head and leaped for joy, unable to contain himself.

It is the same in this case: if there is a son of noble family who, with firm faith, leaves the household life to study the Way, reveres the precepts, does not lose the dharma of a śramaṇa, is free from illusion and hypocrisy, does not act with violence, has a gentle mind, always smiles when speaking, does not wound the feelings of others, maintains constant mental concentration, is free from notions of right and wrong, and has his faculties undisturbed.
Having heard these words from the Venerable Śāriputra, he was filled with such great joy that he could not contain himself, and he accepted his instruction.
In this manner, these sons of noble family expounded this Dharma teaching.
At that time, the venerable ones each heard what was said, and with joy they practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these four fruits. What are the four?
There are fruits that are raw yet appear ripe; there are fruits that are ripe yet appear raw; there are fruits that are ripe and appear ripe; and there are fruits that are raw and appear raw.
"Thus it is said, bhikkhus:
there are these four fruits in the world.
There are likewise these four kinds of persons in the world."

What are the four? There are those who are ripe but appear unripe; there are those who are unripe but appear ripe; there are those who are unripe and appear unripe; and there are those who are ripe and appear ripe.
“What kind of person is one who appears mature at birth?

There may be someone whose coming and going and walking are not impetuous; whose gaze is always in accordance with the Dharma; who puts on robes and carries an alms bowl in accordance with the Dharma as he walks, looking at the ground and not glancing left or right.

Yet, he violates the precepts and does not follow right conduct; though not truly a śramaṇa, he resembles a śramaṇa, and though he does not practice the holy life, he claims to practice the holy life. He utterly destroys and ruins the True Dharma, being like a seed that has rotted at its root. This is called a person who is born appearing to be mature.”
"How is it that a person is ripe yet appears raw?
There may be a bhikṣu whose natural conduct seems coarse, whose gaze is not upright, and who does not practice in accordance with the Dharma, often looking about to the left and right;

yet he is diligent and learned, practices wholesome dharmas, constantly upholds the precepts, does not lose his dignified demeanor, and upon seeing even a slight instance of what is contrary to the Dharma, he feels fear. This is called a person who is ripe yet appears raw."
"What is meant by a person being born resembling one who is not truly born?

There may be a bhikṣu who does not maintain the prohibitive precepts, who does not know the etiquette of walking, nor how to come and go, nor how to wear his robes or hold his bowl; whose faculties are disordered, and whose mind is attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile objects. Such a person violates the prohibitive precepts and does not practice the True Dharma; he is not a śramaṇa yet resembles a śramaṇa, and does not practice the holy life (brahmacarya) yet resembles one who practices it. Being a person of ruined faculties, he cannot be refined or adorned. This is called a person who is born resembling one who is not truly born."
"What is meant by a person who is mature yet appears to be immature?

There may be a bhikṣu who maintains the precepts and prohibitions; his coming and going, walking and stepping do not lose their proper timing, and his observation of others does not lose its dignified decorum.

He is exceedingly diligent in practicing wholesome dharmas, and he fully accomplishes all dignified conduct and etiquette. Upon seeing even a minor unrighteous act, he feels fear and trepidation, let alone a major one. This is called a person who is mature yet appears to be immature."
“Monks, these are the four kinds of persons found in the world; you should train yourselves to become those who are like ripe fruit. Thus, monks!”
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Today there is a *vilambaka* wind in the sky. Should any flying birds reach that place—whether they be crows, magpies, geese, or cranes—if they encounter that wind, their heads and brains and their wings will each be scattered in different places."
A bhikṣu here is just like this:

having abandoned the precepts and engaged in the conduct of a layperson, at that time his three robes, alms bowl, needle case, and the other six articles each remain in one place, just as the vāta-śaraṇa wind blew away and killed those birds.
Therefore, monks, you should practice the holy life. Thus, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (Nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there are these four kinds of birds.”

What are the four? There are birds whose voices are beautiful but whose forms are ugly; there are birds whose forms are beautiful but whose voices are ugly; there are birds whose voices are ugly and whose forms are also ugly; and there are birds whose forms are beautiful and whose voices are also beautiful.
"What is it that has a beautiful voice but an ugly form?
It is the kokila bird. This is what is meant by having a beautiful voice but an ugly form."
What is it that has a beautiful form but an ugly voice?
It is the bird of prey. This is what is meant by having a beautiful form but an ugly voice.
What kind of bird has both an ugly voice and an ugly form?
It is the hare-owl (*śaśagṛdhra*).
This is what is meant by a bird that has an ugly voice and an ugly form.
Furthermore, what bird has both a beautiful voice and a beautiful form?
It is the peacock. This is what is meant by a bird that has both a beautiful voice and a beautiful form.
"Monks, these are called the four birds that one should recognize together. It is just so;
there are likewise four persons in the world who resemble birds, whom one should recognize together."
What are the four?

In this regard, there may be a bhikṣu whose physical appearance is upright and handsome; whether entering or leaving, coming or going, putting on his robes or carrying his bowl, bending, stretching, looking down or looking up, he is perfected in dignified deportment.

Yet he is unable to recite any of the teachings—the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—and he cannot uphold the instructions of the Dharma, nor can he skillfully recite or study them.
This is called a person whose physical form is handsome but whose voice is not.
Furthermore, what kind of person has a beautiful voice but an ugly form?

There may be a certain bhikṣu who, in his coming and going, advancing and retreating, bending and stretching, bowing and looking up, in putting on his robes and holding his bowl, does not achieve mastery in dignified deportment; yet he always delights in speaking at length.

Furthermore, that person is diligent and observant of the precepts; having heard the Dharma, they are able to understand what is to be learned. They have heard much of all the teachings—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with profound meaning and logic, fully cultivating the holy life (brahmacarya). Moreover, they properly uphold and properly recite those teachings.
This is called a person whose voice is pleasant but whose form is ugly.
Furthermore, what kind of person is there whose voice is ugly and whose form is also ugly?
There may be a person who violates the precepts, lacks diligence, and has not heard much; having heard [the teachings], they immediately lose them.
Regarding these teachings, he ought to fully practice the holy life, yet he is unwilling to accept it.
This is called a person whose voice is ugly and whose form is also ugly.
"What kind of person has both a beautiful voice and a beautiful form?
There may be a bhikṣu whose appearance is upright and handsome; whether entering or exiting, coming or going, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl, he does not look to the left or right;
yet he further applies himself with diligence to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, though he is fully endowed with the precepts, he still harbors fear upon seeing even a minor instance of what is not the Dharma, let alone a major one!

Moreover, he is widely learned and does not forget what he has received; regarding all dharmas that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, he cultivates their wholesome practices and skillfully recites and studies such teachings.
This is called a person whose voice is excellent and whose form is also excellent.
These are the four types of persons found in the world whom those living in the world should recognize together.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves to have both a beautiful voice and a beautiful form.
Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of clouds."

What are the four? There may be clouds and thunder but no rain; there may be clouds and rain but no thunder; there may be both clouds, rain, and thunder; or there may be neither clouds, nor rain, nor thunder. These are called the four kinds of clouds.
There are four kinds of people in the world who resemble clouds.

What are these four? There may be a bhikṣu who thunders but does not rain; there may be a bhikṣu who rains but does not thunder; there may be a bhikṣu who neither rains nor thunders; and there may be a bhikṣu who both rains and thunders.
"What is meant by a bhikṣu who thunders but does not rain?
