It refers to a certain bhikṣu who recites aloud with a loud voice the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas."
If one thus recites and studies these various teachings well, grasping their meaning without loss,
yet does not extensively expound the Dharma for others—
this is called the person who thunders but does not rain.
"What kind of person is like rain falling without thunder? It is a bhikṣu who possesses a handsome and upright countenance;

whether entering or exiting, coming or going, his every movement and posture is perfectly appropriate. He cultivates all wholesome dharmas without the slightest lapse. Yet, he is not widely learned, nor does he recite them aloud;

furthermore, he does not practice the sūtras, nidānas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulya-s, adbhuta-dharma-s, or upadeśa-s. Nevertheless, having received these from others, he does not forget them; he delights in associating with virtuous friends and also delights in preaching the Dharma to others."
This is called a person who has rain but no thunder.
What kind of person is neither raining nor thundering?

There may be a person whose appearance is not handsome, whose deportment in coming and going, advancing and stopping is entirely lacking in propriety, and who does not cultivate various wholesome dharmas.

Yet they do not possess extensive learning, nor do they recite, practice, or read with a loud voice; furthermore, they do not cultivate the sūtras from the Āgamas up to the Vaipulya, nor do they preach the Dharma to others.
This is called a person who neither rains nor thunders.
Furthermore, what kind of person both rains and thunders?

There may be a person whose countenance is upright and handsome; in coming and going, advancing and retreating, he fully understands the propriety of his movements; he delights in learning, and what he has received he does not lose.
Furthermore, he delights in preaching the Dharma to others, exhorting and encouraging them so that they may receive and uphold it.
This person is said to be both like thunder and like rain.
Thus it is said, O Bhikṣu!
"There are these four types of persons in the world. Therefore, bhikkhus,
you should train yourselves thus."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Truths, Benefit, Ānanda; The Heavy Burden, the Four Births, the Fetters, the Four Fruits, the Vāta-vāyu wind; The Four Birds, Thunder behind.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Seventeen; Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Eighteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Six: The Four Right Efforts (Catvāri-samyakprahāṇa), Part One. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just as mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, the hundred grasses, and the five grains all depend upon the earth to grow and flourish, yet this earth is the most honored and supreme."
This is also like that: by abiding in the ground of heedfulness, one causes all the factors conducive to wholesome states to grow and increase.
A monk who is heedful cultivates the four right efforts and frequently practices the four right efforts.
What are the four? In this regard, bhikṣu!
Regarding unarisen evil and unwholesome states, one seeks skillful means to prevent their arising; the mind does not turn away from them, but constantly desires their cessation.

Regarding unwholesome states that have already arisen, one seeks skillful means to prevent them from arising again; with a mind that does not turn away from this, one constantly desires to extinguish them.
Regarding wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one seeks skillful means to cause them to arise.

Regarding wholesome states that have already arisen, one seeks skillful means to increase and expand them, ensuring they are not lost or forgotten, and practicing them fully with a mind that never forgets.
In this way, monks, one cultivates the four right efforts. Therefore, monks,
you should seek skillful means and cultivate the four right efforts.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that all the minor kings and great kings come to attend upon the wheel-turning monarch; the wheel-turning monarch is the most honored and supreme among them.”
It is the same here: among all the wholesome dharmas of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the dharma of heedfulness is the foremost.
"A heedful bhikṣu cultivates the four right efforts."
In this regard, monks!
Regarding unarisen evil and unwholesome states, one seeks the means to prevent their arising; with the mind not turning away, one constantly desires their cessation.
Regarding arisen evil and unwholesome states, one seeks the means to prevent their future arising; with the mind not turning away, one constantly desires their cessation.
Regarding wholesome states not yet arisen, one seeks skillful means to cause them to arise;
regarding wholesome states already arisen, one causes them to increase further, never forgetting them, fully practicing them, and keeping them in mind without forgetfulness.
In this way, monks, you should cultivate the four right efforts. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among all the lights of the constellations, the light of the moon is the foremost.
It is the same in this case: among all wholesome merits and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the practice of heedfulness is the foremost, the most honored, and the most noble."
“The heedful bhikṣu cultivates the four right efforts.
What are the four? In this regard, bhikṣu:”
If unwholesome and evil states have not yet arisen, one seeks skillful means to prevent their arising;
if unwholesome and evil states have already arisen, one seeks skillful means to eliminate them;
if wholesome states have not yet arisen, one seeks skillful means to bring them into being.
If wholesome states have already arisen, one seeks skillful means to cause them to increase further, never allowing them to be lost, practicing them fully, and maintaining mindfulness in the mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu cultivates the four right efforts.
Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means and cultivate the four right efforts. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among all varieties of flowers—such as the campaka flower and the sumana flower—among those in the heavens and among humans, the vārṣika flower is the foremost."
It is the same in this case: among all wholesome merits and the dharmas of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, non-negligence is foremost.
"If a bhikṣu who is non-negligent cultivates the four right efforts..."
What are the four? In this regard, bhikṣus!
If unwholesome and evil states have not yet arisen, one seeks skillful means to prevent them from arising;
Regarding unwholesome states that have already arisen, one seeks the means to eliminate them;
regarding wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one seeks the means to cause them to arise;
regarding wholesome states that have already arisen, one seeks the means to increase them, ensuring they are never lost, practicing them fully, and maintaining them in the mind without forgetfulness.
In this way, bhikṣus, you cultivate the four right efforts. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means and cultivate the four right efforts.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, riding in a precious feathered carriage, departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jetavana Monastery, wishing to pay homage to the World-Honored One.

It is the constant custom of kings to possess five marks of majesty; setting these aside, he approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great King, saying:
"Great King, you should know that four kinds of persons appear in the world.
What are these four?
There may be a person who was first in darkness and later becomes bright;
there may be a person who was first bright and later becomes dark;
and there may be a person who was first in darkness and remains in darkness.
There may be a person who was first in darkness and later becomes enlightened.
How is it that such a person was first in darkness and later becomes enlightened?

In this regard, there may be a person born into a low and despised family—perhaps of the Caṇḍāla caste, or the Pukkusaka caste, or the Kārava caste, or born into a family of lechers; or one who is blind, or lacks hands and feet, or is sometimes naked and barefoot, or has disordered faculties.
Furthermore, he practices wholesome dharmas through body and speech, and maintains wholesome thoughts in his mind.

Whenever he sees śramaṇas, brahmins, or other venerable elders, he constantly remembers to pay them homage without missing the proper occasion; he rises to greet them upon their arrival and escorts them when they depart, speaks with a smile before speaking words, and provides for them according to the season.

Furthermore, whenever he sees a beggar—whether a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, a traveler on the road, or one who is destitute—if he possesses wealth, he takes it and gives it as a gift; if he has no goods, he goes to the house of a wealthy man to beg for and give as a gift.
Furthermore, if one sees that donor and feels joy and exultation such that one cannot contain oneself,

practicing wholesome dharmas through body, cultivating wholesome dharmas through speech, and intending wholesome dharmas through mind, then at the breaking up of the body after death, one will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens.

It is just as if there were a person who went from the ground to a bed, from the bed onto a horse, from the horse onto an elephant, and from the elephant into a lecture hall; for this reason, I now say that this person was first in darkness and later in light.
In this way, Great King,
such a person is said to be "first in darkness and later in light.
How is it that a person is "first in light and later in darkness"?

Thereupon, there may be a person born into a great family—whether of the Kṣatriya caste, the householder (gṛhapati) caste, or the Brāhmaṇa caste—who possesses abundant wealth and many treasures: gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, crystal, and lapis lazuli; whose servants and slaves are beyond counting; and who is fully provided with elephants, horses, pigs, and sheep.

Furthermore, although this person’s countenance is handsome and fair as the color of a peach blossom, he constantly harbors wrong views associated with extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). He holds such a view:

"There is no giving, no receiving, nor is there anyone to whom a gift is given; there is no conduct of good or evil, nor is there this world or a future world; there are no attainers of the Path, and there are no Arhats in this world or a future world who may be venerated or who can provide realization."
If he sees a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, he immediately gives rise to anger and lacks a mind of reverence.

If he sees someone practicing generosity, his heart finds no joy; the actions of his body, speech, and mind are uneven, and because he practices unrighteous conduct, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in hell.
It is just as if there were a person who went from the lecture hall to an elephant, from the elephant to a horse, from the horse to a bed, and from the bed to the ground.
For this reason, O Great King, I now speak of this person in such a manner.
This refers to one who was previously bright and later becomes dark.
What is meant by "a person going from darkness to darkness"?

It is when a person is born into a lowly family—whether a family of *caṇḍālas*, or a family of meat-eaters, or an extremely impoverished family—and is necessarily born therein; furthermore, at times their faculties are incomplete and their appearance is coarse and ugly.
Furthermore, that person constantly harbors wrong views; he holds this view:

"There is no present world nor a future world; there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor anyone who has attained the Path; there are no arhats worthy of veneration, nor anything in the present or future world that can be realized through direct experience."
If they see śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, they immediately give rise to anger and lack a heart of reverence.
If they see someone coming to offer gifts, their mind finds no joy; the actions they perform through body, speech, and mind are uneven, as they slander the sages and revile the Triple Gem.

Having failed to practice giving himself, he further witnessed others practicing it and harbored intense malice; because of this practice of malice, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in hell.
It is just as if someone were to go from darkness to darkness, or from one flame to another flame, abandoning wisdom and resorting to folly.
For this reason, such a person may be said to have been dark before and dark afterward; Great King, you should know that it is for this reason he is called "one who goes from darkness to darkness."
"What kind of person is said to go from light to light?
There is one who is born into a noble family—whether of the Kṣatriya caste, or a royal family, or a great minister's family—possessing abundant wealth and immeasurable treasures."
Furthermore, that person’s complexion is handsome, like the color of a peach blossom.
That person always possesses right view, and their mind is never confused.
They possess this right view:
There is giving, there is merit, and there is one who receives; there is the retribution of good and evil; there are this world and the next world; and there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.

Furthermore, if that person, upon seeing śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, gives rise to a mind of reverence with a gentle countenance and pleasant expression; if they themselves always delight in giving and also exhort others to practice giving; and on the day of giving, their heart is filled with such exuberance that they cannot contain it; and if they practice virtue of body, speech, and mind—then at the dissolution of the body after death, they will be reborn in a favorable realm.
It is just as if there were a person who went from lecture hall to lecture hall, from palace to palace;
in this sense, I say that such a person goes from light to light.
"These, Great King, are the four kinds of persons found in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"O King, you should know that even a poor man who possesses faith and delights in giving,
upon seeing śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and other worthy recipients of gifts,
is able to rise and greet them respectfully, and teaches them the right view."
When giving, one is filled with supreme joy; one does not oppose the requests of others.
Such a person is a true friend, who never commits evil deeds, always delights in practicing right view, and constantly keeps in mind the pursuit of wholesome dharmas.
Great King, like that man who, at the time of death,
has a destination where he will surely be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven— first in darkness and later in light;
like a person of extreme wealth who lacks faith and is prone to anger.
With a mind of stinginess and greed, timid and weak, they hold wrong views and do not reform them.
Upon seeing śramaṇas, brahmins, and various seekers, they always delight in reviling and abusing them; with their wrong views, they say that nothing exists.
Seeing a gift given, they give rise to anger and do not allow the donor to have it;
that person’s conduct is extremely base, creating the very root of all evils.
Such a person, when their life is about to end, [will suffer].
When one is born into the hells, it is first light and then dark.
Like a person who is poor and lowly, lacking faith and prone to anger,
who performs various unwholesome deeds and holds wrong views while disbelieving the truth.
Even upon seeing a śramaṇa or anyone worthy of service, they treat them with contempt and derision; being stingy and greedy, they lack faith.
They feel no joy when giving themselves, and likewise when seeing others give.
The deeds performed by that person find no place of rest.
Such a person as this will surely meet their end and be reborn in hell— first in darkness, and then in further darkness.
Like a person who possesses great wealth, Who has faith and delights in giving,
Whose right view is free from other thoughts, And who always joyfully seeks the wholesome Dharma;
Should they encounter various practitioners Or those worthy of receiving gifts,
Rising with reverent welcome and respect, one trains in right view.
Being exceedingly harmonious and joyful with the times, one constantly maintains impartiality;
bestowing gifts without stinginess, one does not act contrary to the hearts of others.
That person who has received the certainty of the teaching and does not commit any unrighteous acts—
know that when such a person approaches the end of life,
they will surely be reborn in a favorable and virtuous realm; first luminous, and then luminous.
"Therefore, Great King, you should train in being bright first and bright later; do not train in being bright first and dark later.
Thus it is, Great King."
"You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side. After a short while, he again rubbed the Tathāgata’s feet with both hands and then kissed the tops of the Tathāgata’s feet, saying:
“Why is the body of the World-Honored One in such a state?”
"The body has become extremely slack; the Tathāgata’s body is no longer as it was.
The World-Honored One replied, "It is so."
Ānanda! As you have said, the skin and flesh of the Tathāgata’s body are now slack; his present body is not as it was before.
This is because one who has received a physical form is inevitably beset by illness.
If there are sentient beings who should be healed but are beset by illness;
or sentient beings who should pass away but are pressed by death;
today the Tathāgata has already reached a state of decline, being over eighty years of age.
At that time, having heard these words, Ānanda wept with such sobbing and distress that he could not restrain himself, and spoke thus:
"Alas! Old age has come upon me to such an extent."
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
As he proceeded gradually through the city begging for food, he arrived at the residence of King Prasenajit.
At that time, there were several dozen dilapidated old carts abandoned to one side in front of King Prasenajit’s palace.
Seeing the carts cast aside to one side, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"These are King Prasenajit’s carts. In the past, when they were first made, they were exceedingly exquisite; yet as we look at them today, their color is no different from that of tiles and stones."
The World-Honored One said:
"It is so, Ānanda! Just as you have said, consider all these chariots: though they were once exceedingly exquisite, fashioned from gold and silver, today they are ruined and can no longer be used."
"If even such external things are subject to decay and ruin, how much more so those that are internal?
Then the World-Honored One spoke this verse: "Alas!
This old age, sickness, and death Destroy the most flourishing beauty of man."
In the beginning, one’s mind was full of delight; now one is pursued by the messenger of death.
Though one may live for a hundred years, all must return to death;
none can escape this suffering, for all shall ultimately follow this path.
Just as all that exists within the internal body is driven toward death,
so too do all external elements of the four great constituents return to their original non-existence.
Therefore, in seeking the deathless, there is only nirvāṇa.
"He is without death and without birth; he is entirely devoid of these conditioned phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat down upon the seat prepared for King Prasenajit.
Then, King Prasenajit provided the World-Honored One with various kinds of food and drink.
Observing that the World-Honored One had finished his meal, the king took another small seat, sat before the Tathāgata, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One?"
"Are the physical forms of all Buddhas composed of vajra, and do they likewise undergo old age, sickness, and death?
The World-Honored One replied, "It is so, Great King."
"As the Great King has said, so too shall the Tathāgata be subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death.
I am now likewise among the ranks of men; my father’s name is Śuddhodana and my mother’s name is Māyā, and I have emerged from the lineage of the Cakravartin Universal Monarchs."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas appear among humanity; His father’s name is True Purity, And his mother’s name is Utmost Subtlety; He is of the noble Kṣatriya clan."
"The path of death is utterly confining; it makes no distinction between the noble and the base.
Even the Buddhas cannot escape it, let alone other ordinary worldly beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse to King Prasenajit:
"In sacrificial rites, fire is supreme; among the *śāstras*, the *Sūtras* are most honored.
Among humans, the king is noblest; among all streams, the ocean is foremost.
Among the stars, the moon is highest; in brilliance, the sun is first."
Throughout the eight directions, above, below, and in the center, within all that the world contains—
gods and the people of the world— the Tathāgata is the most honored.
Those who seek fortune and prosperity should make offerings to the Three Buddhas.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed, returning to the Jeta Grove Monastery where he took his seat.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four qualities by which one is loved and respected by people in the world."
What are the four? Being in the prime of youth is loved and respected by the people of the world;
being free from illness and pain is loved and respected by others.
Longevity is loved and respected by people;
the accumulation of affection is loved and respected by people.
This is what is meant, O bhikṣus!
"There are these four qualities by which people of the world are loved and respected.
Furthermore, monks, there are another four qualities by which people of the world are not loved or respected."
What are the four? Bhikṣus, you should know: when one is in the prime of youth, it is disliked by the world when one becomes old and sick;
if one is free from illness, it is disliked by the world when one subsequently falls ill.
If one who has attained a lifespan should then meet their end, it is not what the people of the world desire;
that those gathered through affection and love should later be separated is likewise not what the people of the world desire.
"Monks, these are called the four dharmas that revolve with the world; they are shared by gods and humans, even by universal monarchs and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. This, monks, is so."
"In this world there are these four dharmas that revolve with the world.
When one does not awaken to these four dharmas, one wanders through birth and death, circling through the five destinies."
What are the four?
They are the noble and holy precepts, the noble and holy concentration, the noble and holy wisdom, and the noble and holy liberation.
These, bhikṣu, are they.
Those who possess these four dharmas yet do not realize them will undergo the aforementioned four states.
Now, both I and you, by realizing these four noble dharmas, have severed the root of birth and death and shall no longer undergo further existence.
Now, the Tathāgata’s physical form has grown old and must undergo this retribution of decay. Therefore, O bhikṣus!

You should seek this eternal quiescence of nirvāṇa—where there is no birth, no aging, no illness, and no death—and where there is no separation from those you love; always remain mindful of the transformations of impermanence.
"In this way, monks, you should reflect.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit immediately commanded his ministers and officials to prepare the precious feathered chariot, intending to depart from the city of Śrāvastī to visit the Earth Hall for a lecture.

At that time, King Prasenajit’s mother passed away; she was extremely advanced in years, nearly a hundred years old, and the king held her in such high esteem that his thoughts of her never left his sight.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a high minister named Asvaghosa, whose talent surpassed all others and whom the people of the world revered.
Then, the minister thought to himself:
"The mother of this King Prasenajit is nearly a hundred years old; today her life has come to an end."
"If he were to hear this, the king would become deeply distressed and anxious; unable to eat or drink, he would fall gravely ill.
I must now devise a skillful means to ensure that the king does not grieve and remains free from sickness."

At that time, the minister immediately prepared five hundred white elephants, likewise prepared five hundred horses, and further prepared five hundred infantrymen; he also prepared five hundred courtesans, five hundred elderly women, five hundred Brahmins, and five hundred śramaṇas; furthermore, he prepared five hundred garments and five hundred precious jewels. Having constructed a magnificent coffin for the deceased, adorned it with exquisite painted designs, and suspended silk banners and canopies, he provided an incalculable array of musical performances and went out from the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit returned to the city.
Having some minor business, the King saw the deceased from afar and asked his attendants:
"Who is this person, for whom such offerings have been made as these?"
Then Asvaghosa said, "In this city of Śrāvastī, there was a matron who passed away; these are her belongings.
The king then spoke again, saying:
"What further use are these elephants, horses,
and carriages? The minister replied,
"These five hundred old women are to be presented to King Yama as a ransom for their lives."
At that time, the king smiled and said:
"This is the way of fools; life is difficult to preserve, so what can be accomplished?
It is like a person who has fallen into the mouth of a makara fish; to wish to escape is truly difficult to achieve."
"This is also like that: having fallen into the presence of King Yama, it is truly difficult to obtain release.
"These five hundred courtesans shall also be used to redeem my life."
The king replied, "This,
too, is difficult to obtain.
Then the minister said:
"If this courtesan cannot be obtained, we shall use another to ransom her.
The king said,
"This one is also difficult to obtain."
The minister said,
"If this cannot be obtained, we shall redeem him with five hundred precious treasures.
The king replied:
"This too is difficult to obtain," the minister said.
"As for that which cannot be obtained, we shall ransom it with five hundred garments."
The king said,
"This too is difficult to obtain.
The minister said:
"If these garments cannot be obtained, we shall employ the incantations of these five hundred brahmins to take them through magic.
The king said,
"This too will be difficult to achieve."
The minister said,
"If these five hundred brahmins cannot be obtained, we shall instead take this śramaṇa of high talent who preaches the Dharma and use him as a ransom for them."
The king said,
"This cannot be obtained.
The minister said:
"If the Dharma cannot be obtained, we shall assemble our troops and engage in a great battle to seize it.
At that time, King Prasenajit laughed loudly and said, "This is the way of fools;
having fallen into the mouth of a makara fish, one will never emerge."
Then the king said, "You should know this: is there anyone who is born and yet does not die?
At that time, the minister replied:
"This is truly unattainable. Then the Great King replied, "It is indeed unattainable;
all Buddhas have also said this: birth is followed by death, and life is likewise difficult to obtain."
At that time, Asvamedha knelt and addressed the king, saying:
"Therefore, Great King, do not grieve so deeply; all sentient beings must return to death."
Then the king asked,
"For what reason am I sorrowful?
At that time, the minister addressed the king:
“Your Majesty, you should know that the Great King’s mother has died this very day.
When King Prasenajit heard these words, he sighed eight or nine times and said to his ministers, “Excellent! Excellent!”
"What you have said shows that you truly understand skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).
At that time, King Prasenajit returned to the city and prepared various kinds of incense and flowers to make offerings to his deceased mother.
Having made offerings for his deceased mother, he returned by carriage to the place where the World-Honored One was.
Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked:
“Great King! Why is your body covered in dust?
The king replied to the World-Honored One:
"The Mother of the Gods has passed away and was sent out beyond the city walls.
She has now come to the presence of the World-Honored One to inquire about the cause of her death.

While she was alive, she maintained the precepts with diligence and constantly cultivated wholesome dharmas; she was nearly a hundred years old, and having passed away today, she has therefore come to the presence of the World-Honored One."
If my life could be ransomed by holding back an elephant, I would likewise ransom it with an elephant;
if my life could be ransomed by a horse, I would ransom it with a horse;
if my life could be ransomed by a carriage, I would then ransom it with a carriage.
If my life could be saved by ransoming it with gold, silver, or precious jewels, I would ransom it with gold, silver, and precious jewels;
if my life could be saved by ransoming it with slaves, servants, cities, or territories, I would ransom my life with cities and territories;
if my life could be saved by ransoming it with the people of the kingdom of Kāśi, I would ransom it with the people of Kāśi—do not let my mother, my heavenly parent, come to her end.
The World-Honored One said:
"Therefore, Great King, do not grieve so deeply; all sentient beings must return to death."
Regarding all things subject to change, it is ultimately impossible to prevent them from changing.
Your Majesty should know that the nature of the human body is like a ball of snow; it must inevitably crumble away.
It is also like a clay pot; likewise, it returns to destruction and cannot be preserved for long.
It is also like a mirage or a magical illusion—deceptive and unreal;
it is also like an empty fist used to deceive a small child.
Therefore, Great King!
Do not harbor sorrow or anxiety, nor rely upon this body.

Great King, you should know that there are these four great terrors which come upon this body; they cannot be warded off or protected against, nor can they be eliminated by means of speech, incantations, medicinal herbs, or talismans.
What are the four? First is called aging, which destroys youthfulness and deprives one of a healthy complexion;
second is called the exhaustion of illness, which destroys health.
Third is called the exhaustion of death, which destroys the life-faculty;
fourth is that all things which possess permanence return to impermanence.
These, Great King, are what is meant.
"There are these four things that cannot be obstructed or guarded against, nor can they be overcome by power.
Great King, you should know that it is like four great mountains from the four directions coming toward living beings to crush them; they cannot be repelled by force."
Therefore, Great King!
That which is not a solid substance cannot be relied upon.
For this reason, Great King!
"You should govern by means of the Dharma, and not by what is contrary to the Dharma.
Your Majesty, you too will not remain long; you shall reach the ocean of birth and death.
Your Majesty should also know that those who govern by means of the Dharma, when their bodies perish and their lives end, are reborn in a good destination, in the heavens."
If, moreover, one governs and transforms others through what is not the Dharma, at the dissolution of the body after death,
one will be reborn in hell. Therefore, Great King,
you should govern and transform through the Dharma, and not through what is not the Dharma.
"In this way, Great King,
you should train yourself.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is the name of this Dharma?
How should it be practiced?
The World-Honored One replied:
“This teaching is called ‘the removal of the thorn of sorrow.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying,
“It is indeed so, World-Honored One!”
The reason for this is that having heard this Dharma, all the thorns of my sorrow have been removed today.
However, World-Honored One, the affairs of my kingdom are many; I wish to return to my dwelling place.
The World-Honored One said,
"Know that now is the time.
King Prasenajit immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I am not only the most honored among the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; I am the sole supreme one even among the people of the world. Now there are four fundamental dharmas, from beginning to end, which I have personally realized and of which I bear witness before the fourfold assembly, the devas, and humans."
What are the four? First, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; I have now realized this and bear witness to it before the fourfold assembly, among the devas, and among humans.
Second, all conditioned phenomena are suffering (*duḥkha*);...
Third, all conditioned phenomena are without self;
fourth, nirvana is cessation.
I now know this, and I bear witness to it among the fourfold assembly, as well as among gods and humans.
“Monks, these are called the four foundations of the Dharma; for this reason, one alone attains preeminence among gods and humans.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One wished to go to Rājagṛha for the summer retreat; Śāriputra also wished to go to Rājagṛha for the summer retreat, as did all one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples. However, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were to enter parinirvāṇa at the conclusion of their summer retreat.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, traveled to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove near the city of Rājagṛha and observed the summer retreat there.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"These one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples are here for the summer retreat with you; however, the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana shall enter parinirvāṇa."
"How is it, Śāriputra? Are you capable of preaching the sublime Dharma to the bhikṣus?
My back now aches, and I wish to rest for a short while."
Śāriputra replied, “So it is, World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One personally folded his saṃghāṭī robe, lay on his right side upon the ground with one foot叠叠 (placed) upon the other, and fixed his mind upon clarity.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"When I first received the precepts, after half a month had passed, I attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) as a realization, fully endowed with their principles and meanings."
I shall now explain it, analyzing its meaning so that you may understand; I will reveal and analyze it for you.
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
The bhikṣus replied, “So be it.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from Śāriputra.
Śāriputra said: "What are the four analytical knowledges?
That which I have realized is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid);..."
By means of this, I have realized what is called the analytical knowledge of the Dharma;
by means of this, I have realized what is called the analytical knowledge of eloquence;
by means of this, I have realized what is called the analytical knowledge of self.
I shall now extensively analyze its meaning.
If there are those among the fourfold assembly who harbor doubts, they may inquire about that meaning while I am still present here.
Furthermore, worthy ones!
If you have any doubt regarding the four dhyānas, or furthermore, worthy ones!
if you have any doubt regarding the four immeasurable states of mind, you may question me; I shall now explain them to you.
Furthermore, worthy ones!
If you have any doubts regarding the four right efforts (*catur-samyakprahāṇa*), you may ask me about their meaning, and I shall now explain them.

If you have any doubts regarding the four bases of power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), or the four truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*), come and ask me about their meaning, and I shall now explain them.
"If you do not ask now, it will be of no avail for your future regrets!

I now possess only the profound Dharma, the various practices, and the meanings of the teachings of the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; you should also question me on these matters, and I shall explain them to you, so that you may have no regrets later."
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having dressed and taken his bowl at the proper hour, was about to enter the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
Then, the brahmins carrying staffs saw Maudgalyāyana coming from afar;
they approached one another and said, "Among the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama, there is none who surpasses this man. Let us all surround him together and beat him to death."

At that time, those brahmins surrounded and seized him, each striking him with tiles and stones until they killed him and then departed. There was no part of his body that was not struck; his flesh and bones were completely mangled, and his suffering and agony were beyond measure.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"These brahmins have surrounded me and beaten me until my flesh and bones were completely worn away, and then they abandoned me and departed."
"My body now has no part that does not ache; I am so afflicted by pain that I have no strength to return to the park on foot. I shall now return to the vihāra by means of my supernormal power."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately returned to the monastery by means of his supernormal powers. Arriving at where Śāriputra was, he sat down to one side.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said to Śāriputra:

"This brahmin Daṇḍapāṇi surrounded me and beat me until my flesh and bones were completely mangled. My body is in such pain that it is truly unbearable; I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa, and have therefore come to take my leave of you."

Then Śāriputra said: “Among the disciples of the World-Honored One, you are foremost in supernormal powers and possess great majestic might; for what reason do you not use your supernormal powers to avoid this?”

Maudgalyāyana replied, "The karmic actions I originally committed were extremely grave; they must necessarily result in retribution that can never be avoided. It is not as if this retribution is being experienced in empty space."
"However, today my body is afflicted with extreme pain; therefore, I have come to bid you farewell and enter parinirvāṇa.

Śāriputra said, "If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have cultivated the four bases of psychic power and extensively expounded their meaning, and if such persons wish in their minds to remain for an eon, or beyond an eon, or even until they do not pass into extinction, why do they not remain and instead enter extinction?"
Maudgalyāyana replied, "So it is,
Śāriputra! Thus has the Tathāgata spoken:"
"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī cultivates the four bases of psychic power (catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ) and wishes to remain for the duration of a kalpa, they may indeed do so.
However, as for the Tathāgata remaining for a kalpa, I too shall remain.
However, today the World-Honored One will soon enter parinirvāṇa; the lifespan of sentient beings is extremely short, and furthermore, I cannot bear to see the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa.
"However, my body is in extreme pain, and I wish to enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Maudgalyāyana:
"You wait a moment; I shall first attain extinction."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana remained silent and did not respond.
Then Śāriputra went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa; I only pray that you will grant me permission.
At that moment, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not reply.
Then Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One a second and a third time, saying:
"Now is precisely the right time for me to enter parinirvāṇa.
At that moment, the World-Honored One said to Śāriputra:
"Why do you not remain for one kalpa, but instead pass beyond one kalpa?
Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I have personally heard from the World-Honored One and have personally received his teaching: the lifespan of sentient beings is extremely short; their maximum life does not exceed a hundred years. Because the lives of sentient beings are so short, the lifespan of the Tathāgata is likewise short."
"If the Tathāgata were to remain for the duration of one kalpa, I too would remain for the duration of one kalpa.
The World-Honored One said, "As Śāriputra has spoken, because the lives of sentient beings are short, the lifespan of the Tathāgata is likewise short; however, this matter is also beyond discussion."
The reason for this is that in the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Sunaṭhasaṃkalpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years and no one died prematurely, that Tathāgata Praṇidhānasumanas, upon attaining Buddhahood, immediately manifested as immeasurable Buddhas on that very day. He established immeasurable sentient beings in the practices of the Three Vehicles, some dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression;
furthermore, he established immeasurable sentient beings within the four castes.

Furthermore, he established immeasurable sentient beings in the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the heavens of desire, the heavens of form, and the formless heavens; and on that same day, they also entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Now, Śāriputra, you say:
"Because the lifespan of sentient beings is short, the lifespan of the Tathāgata is also short.
What do you think, Śāriputra?
And he made this statement:
"The Tathāgata shall remain for one kalpa, until the end of that kalpa; I too shall remain for one kalpa, until the end of that kalpa.
Nevertheless, sentient beings were unable to know the length of the Tathāgata’s lifespan.

What are the four? A stūpa should be erected for a Wheel-Turning Sage King; a stūpa should be erected for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted; a stūpa should be erected for a Pratyekabuddha; and a stūpa should be erected for a Tathāgata.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“By what causes and conditions should a stūpa be erected for a Tathāgata?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions should stūpas be erected for a Pratyekabuddha, an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted, and a Wheel-Turning Sage King?”
The World-Honored One said:

"You should now know that a Wheel-Turning Sage King practices the ten wholesome actions as his preparatory application, cultivates the ten meritorious virtues, and likewise teaches others to practice these ten wholesome meritorious virtues."
What are the ten? One does not kill living beings oneself and further teaches others not to kill.
One does not steal oneself and further teaches others not to steal.
One refrains from sexual misconduct oneself and further teaches others to refrain from sexual misconduct.
One refrains from false speech oneself and further teaches others to refrain from false speech.
One refrains from frivolous speech oneself and further teaches others to refrain from frivolous speech.
One does not harbor envy oneself and further teaches others not to harbor envy.
One does not engage in strife or litigation oneself and further teaches others not to engage in strife or litigation.
One’s own mind is upright, and one further teaches others so that their minds do not become disordered.
One’s own view is correct, and one further teaches others so that they practice correct view.
Bhikṣus, you should know that a wheel-turning sage king possesses these ten merits; for this reason, a stūpa should be erected for him.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

When the multitude saw this, they were filled with supreme joy.
Therefore, Ānanda, it is said that a stūpa should be erected for the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"Gather all the bhikṣus residing in Śrāvastī in one place; I have instructions to give.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the World-Honored One’s instruction, immediately assembled the bhikṣus at the Sahasravarga Hall and returned to inform the World-Honored One:
"Today the bhikṣus have assembled in one place.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, went to the vihāra of the bhikṣu Bakula.

At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān desired to know where the consciousness of the Venerable Bakkula was located; he wished to know in what place it resided—whether it remained within a human being or not.
Are you a non-human being?
A deva, nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, asura, garuḍa, kinnara, or mahoraga?
"Now, as for this divine consciousness, where exactly does it reside? In what place does it arise and roam?

I do not see it in the east, west, south, or north, nor in the four intermediate directions or above and below; though I have searched everywhere, I do not know the location of this divine consciousness."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān’s body was utterly exhausted, and he did not know where he was.
Then, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, arrived at that vihāra.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that Māra Pāpīyas wished to know the location of the consciousness,
addressed the bhikṣus: "Have you heard a great sound within this vihāra?"
"Furthermore, were there any strange lights? The bhikṣus replied, "It was so."
“World-Honored One!
We have already seen it.
The World-Honored One told them:
“This evil Māra Pāpīyān wishes to know where the consciousness of Vakkali is located.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“I pray that the Blessed One will explain where the consciousness of the bhikṣu Vakkali is located.”
The World-Honored One said:
"The consciousness of the bhikṣu Vakkali is forever without attachment.
That son of good family has attained parinirvāṇa; you should maintain this understanding."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"On what day did this bhikṣu Bakula attain these Four Noble Truths?
The Blessed One replied:
"Today, in the midst of this day, he has attained these Four Noble Truths.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "This bhikṣu has been afflicted by illness for a long time; originally, he was but an ordinary person."
The Blessed One said: “It is so, Ānanda! It is as you have said.

However, that bhikkhu has practiced with great austerity for a very long time; among all the disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, he is the most preeminent in terms of liberation through faith, yet his mind with outflows (āsrava) has not yet attained liberation.”
"I should now seek a blade to stab myself.
At that time, as the bhikṣu was about to stab himself, he immediately contemplated the merits of the Tathāgata;
on the day he relinquished his life, he contemplated the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādānaskandha).
"This is the arising of this form; this is the cessation of this form.
At that time, having reflected upon this, the monk causes all conditioned phenomena to be completely extinguished; this monk has attained parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

27. Chapter on Equally Approaching the Four Noble Truths, *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter Twenty-Seven, Part One. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, this is what we have always taught:
the so-called Four Noble Truths. By means of countless skillful expedients, we have examined this Dharma, analyzed its meaning, and expounded it extensively for others.”
What are the four? They are as follows:
regarding the Dharma of the Truth of Suffering, one observes this Dharma through countless skillful means, analyzes its meaning, and expounds it extensively for others;

likewise, regarding the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path, one explains them through countless skillful means, observes these Dharmas, analyzes their meanings, and expounds them extensively for others.
“Monks, you should draw near to the bhikṣu Śāriputra, serve him, and make offerings to him. Why is this?
Because that bhikṣu Śāriputra, by means of countless skillful methods, has proclaimed these Four Noble Truths and expounded them extensively for others.”

When the bhikṣu Śāriputra analyzed its meaning for all sentient beings and the fourfold assembly, and expounded it extensively to others, at that time immeasurable sentient beings were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
“O bhikṣus, you should draw near to the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, serving and making offerings to them.
Why is this so? It is because of the bhikṣu Śāriputra!”
They are the parents of sentient beings, for they give birth to them, nourish them, and cause them to grow. As for the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana:
it is because the bhikṣu Śāriputra teaches the essential Dharma to others, establishing them in the Four Noble Truths;
whereas the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana teaches the essential Dharma to others, establishing them in the Ultimate Meaning and in untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*).
"You all should draw near to the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
After the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he returned to his private chamber.
Not long after the World-Honored One had departed, at that time Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Whoever is able to attain the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths has gained a most excellent benefit. What are these four?
They are the Truth of Suffering, whose meaning is extensively expounded through countless skillful means."
What is the Truth of Suffering?

It refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; in brief, it is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging—this is called the Truth of Suffering.
What is the truth of the origin of suffering?
It is what is called the fetter of craving.
What is the truth of cessation?
That which is called the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) refers to the eternal exhaustion of the fetters of craving without remainder;
this is called the truth of cessation.
What is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*)? It is the noble eightfold path.
Right view, right resolve, right speech, right effort, right livelihood, right action, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are called the Truth of the Path.
"Those sentient beings have gained a great and wholesome benefit, for they are able to hear this Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.

At that time, as the Venerable Śāriputra was preaching this Dharma, immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, upon hearing this teaching, were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
"We, too, have gained a most excellent benefit; the World-Honored One has taught us the Dharma and established us in a ground of merit.
"Therefore, the fourfold assembly should seek skillful means and practice these Four Noble Truths."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus entered the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, many bhikṣus had this thought:
"It is still early for us to go on our almsround; we should go to the village of the non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners and engage them in debate."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to the village of the non-Buddhists.
Having arrived, they exchanged greetings with one another and sat down to one side. Once seated to one side, they remained there.
At that time, a wanderer asked the ascetic, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama teaches this Dharma to his disciples, saying:
'You, bhikṣus, must all study this Dharma; you must all fully understand it; having fully understood it, you should together practice it.'"
We, too, shall preach this Dharma to our disciples, saying:
"You all must study this Dharma thoroughly; you must fully understand it, and having understood it, you must practice it together."
"What difference is there between the śramaṇa Gautama and us?
What is his superiority or inferiority? For what he teaches, we also teach; what he instructs, we also instruct."
At that time, having heard these words, many bhikṣus neither affirmed nor denied them, but immediately rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus said to one another, "We should go and inform the World-Honored One of this matter.

Then, those many bhikṣus entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms; having finished eating, they gathered up their robes and bowls, placed their sitting mats (niṣīdana) over their left shoulders, and went to where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If those non-Buddhists should ask such a question, you should reply to them with these words:"
"Is there one ultimate goal,
or are there many ultimate goals?
One who is able to speak with impartiality regarding those brahmins should say this:
"This is the single ultimate, not a plurality of ultimates.
Regarding that ultimate, is it the ultimate of one who possesses desire,
or is it the ultimate of one who is free from desire?
What is called "that ultimate" refers to the ultimate state of desirelessness.
As for that which is called "the ultimate," is it the ultimate state of having ill will,
or is it the ultimate state of being without ill will?
Regarding what is called "that which is ultimate": it is the ultimate state of non-aversion, not the ultimate state of aversion.
What is the ultimate state of delusion? What is the ultimate state of non-delusion?
Regarding what is called "that ultimate": it is the ultimate freedom from delusion.
As for that ultimate, is it the ultimate of one who possesses craving, or is it the ultimate of one who is free from craving?
Regarding what is called "that ultimate": it is the ultimate of non-craving.
How is it that for that ultimate there is the ultimate of sensation, or is it the ultimate of non-sensation?
That which is called "ultimate" is the ultimate of non-apprehension.
As for this ultimate, is it the state of one who possesses wisdom, or is it not?
What is called "the ultimate reached by the wise"—
is this ultimate reached by those who are angry,
or is it reached by those who are not angry?
Regarding what is called "this ultimate," it should be explained as follows: it is not the ultimate for one who is angry.
"Monks! There are these two views. What are the two views? [They are: 'The world is eternal' and 'the world is not eternal.'"
These are the view of existence and the view of non-existence.

Any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who do not understand the beginning and end of these two views will possess a mind of desire, a mind of hatred, a mind of delusion, a mind of attachment, and a mind of grasping; they are thus ignorant.

That person possesses a mind of anger and does not act in accordance with the practice; such a person is not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, and is not freed from the myriad forms of bitterness and pain.

Whosoever among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas knows this as it truly is, they will then be free from delusion and ill-will; being constantly in accord with practice, they shall attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
I shall now explain the root source of suffering.
Thus, bhikṣus, there is this sublime Dharma; this is called the Dharma of equality.
Those who do not practice the Dharma of equality fall into the five views.
Now I shall explain the four graspings. What are the four graspings?
They are the grasping of desire, the grasping of views, the grasping of precepts and rituals, and the grasping of self; these are called the four graspings.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who fully know the names of the various types of grasping (*upādāna*), even though they know the names of these types of grasping, they do not apply themselves accordingly; they fully analyze the names of all graspings, first analyzing the name of the grasping for sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*), yet they do not analyze the names of the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), the grasping for precepts and vows (*śīlavratopādāna*), or the grasping for a self (*ātmopādāna*).
The reason for this is that those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are unable to distinguish between these three types of feeling.

Therefore, some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while fully distinguishing all these feelings, distinguish the feeling of desire and the feeling of views, yet do not distinguish the feeling of precepts and the feeling of self.
The reason for this is that those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are unable to distinguish between these two types of feeling.

If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas were able to fully distinguish all feelings—or even if they were only partially able to do so—they would be able to distinguish the feeling of desire, the feeling of views, and the feeling of precepts, yet they fail to distinguish the feeling of self.
The reason for this is that those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are unable to discern my feelings.
Therefore, there are further śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who exhaustively discern all feelings, yet even among them, some are incomplete.
"What is the meaning of these four types of feeling?
How are they distinguished?
These so-called four feelings arise from craving."
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
There is this sublime Dharma which ought to be analyzed.
If one does not practice these various feelings in this way, this is not called equanimity.
The reason for this is that the meaning of all dharmas is difficult to comprehend and difficult to understand.
Such a meaning that is contrary to the Dharma was not spoken by the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

"Monks, you should know that the Tathāgata is fully able to discern all feelings (*vedanā*). Because he is able to discern all feelings, he is in accord with them, and thus he is able to discern the feeling of desire (*kāma-vedanā*), the feeling of views (*dṛṣṭi-vedanā*), the feeling of self (*ātma-vedanā*), and the feeling of precepts (*śīla-vedanā*)."
Therefore, when the Tathāgata fully discriminates all sensations, they are in perfect accord with the Dharma and there is no contradiction.
"From what do these four sensations arise?"

However, these four feelings arise from craving and grow through craving. Once one has accomplished these feelings, one is no longer able to give rise to further feelings; because one does not give rise to further feelings, one is without fear; and because one is without fear, one attains parinirvāṇa: Thus it is said: "When a bhikṣu has abandoned all feelings, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, so that they are no longer subject to future arising, he is called one who has reached the end of suffering. This is what was taught. This is because this Dharma is most subtle and wondrous, spoken by all Buddhas, and thus possesses no deficiency or omission regarding any practices.

"Therefore, monks! There is the first śramaṇa, the second śramaṇa, the third śramaṇa, and the fourth śramaṇa; there is no other śramaṇa who exists beyond these, nor any who can surpass them, as they utter this lion’s roar."

3 (III) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One asked the householder: “How is it, householder?”
"Do you constantly practice giving in your home?
The elder addressed the Buddha:
"Our poor family constantly practices giving; however, our food and drink are coarse and inferior, not the same as those of others."
The World-Honored One replied:

"If, at the time of giving, whether the gift be fine or coarse, much or little, one does so without mental intention, without making a vow, and without faith, then as a result of such action, in whatever place one is born, one will not obtain good food."

The mind does not crave pleasure; the mind likewise does not delight in fine clothing, nor does it delight in excellent fields and estates; the heart does not cling to the midst of the five desires. Even if one has servants and slaves, one does not accept their instructions.
The reason for this is precisely that he did not apply his mind during the act; therefore, he receives such retribution.

If, when a householder gives alms—whether the gift be fine or coarse, much or little—one should apply the heart with utmost sincerity and not allow it to fluctuate, lest one destroy the bridge for future generations.

Wherever they may be born, food and drink will appear spontaneously, and they will be fully endowed with the seven riches; their minds will always delight in the midst of the five desires, and even if they have servants or laborers, these will constantly obey their instructions.
The reason for this is that he gave rise to a heart of joy from within.

"Householder, you should know that in the distant past there was a brahmin named Vīrama, who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures—pearls, amber, musaragalva, agate, crystal, and lapis lazuli—and who delighted in giving alms."

At that time, when practicing generosity, he used eighty-four thousand silver bowls filled with crushed gold, and furthermore, eighty-four thousand gold bowls filled with crushed silver, making such offerings.
Furthermore, he gave eighty-four thousand silver and gold bathing jars as offerings.
He also gave eighty-four thousand oxen, all with their horns covered in gold and silver; he performed such acts of giving in this manner.
Furthermore, he gave away eighty-four thousand jade maidens, covering them with his own garments.
He also gave away eighty-four thousand bedding sets, all covered with woolen rugs, embroidered fabrics, and fine carpets.
Furthermore, he bestowed eighty-four thousand garments as alms.
He also bestowed eighty-four thousand dragon-elephants, all adorned with gold and silver.
He further bestowed eighty-four thousand horses, each equipped with its own saddle and bridle made of gold and silver.
Furthermore, he gave away eighty-four thousand chariots as alms, performing such great acts of giving.

He also gave away eighty-four thousand houses as alms at the four city gates; to those who needed food, he gave food; to those who needed clothing, he gave clothing. He provided robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick and infirm—all of these he gave to them.

“Householder, you should know that although Vīrama performs such acts of giving, they do not equal the merit of constructing a single dwelling and offering it as a gift to the Saṃgha of the four quarters; this merit is immeasurable.”

Even if one were to perform such acts of giving as constructing and offering dwellings to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, it would not equal the merit of taking the three refuges in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṃgha; this latter merit is beyond measure.

Even if that person were to perform such acts of giving, construct dwellings, and further receive the three refuges, although they would possess such merit, it would still not equal the merit of upholding the five precepts.

Even if that person were to perform such acts of giving, construct dwellings, take the three refuges, and uphold the five precepts—though they possess such merit, it is not equal to the compassion shown toward sentient beings for even the duration of a finger-snap; the merit and virtue of this latter act is beyond measure.

"Even if that person were to perform such acts of giving as building monasteries, taking the three refuges, upholding the five precepts, and extending compassion toward sentient beings for even the duration of a finger-snap—though they possess such merit, it is not equal to the merit of giving rise, for even a brief moment, to the perception that the world is not to be relished; the merit of this latter cannot be measured."
However, regarding the meritorious deeds they have performed, I fully testify to them: I also know the merit of constructing monastic dwellings;
I also know the merit of receiving the three refuges;
and I also know the merit of upholding the five precepts.
In the space of a finger-snap, out of compassion for sentient beings, I also know this merit;
in a mere moment, giving rise to the perception that the world is not to be relished, I also know this merit.
"At that time, was that brahmin who performed such a great act of giving anyone else? Do not view it so.
Why is this? The donor at that time was none other than myself."
Householder, you should know that for a long time in the past, you have cultivated meritorious deeds with uninterrupted faith, never giving rise to thoughts of attachment.
Therefore, householder!

When you wish to practice giving—whether the gift be much or little, fine or coarse—bestow it with joy and do not give rise to conceptual attachments. Give with your own hands and do not employ others; resolve to seek no reward and subsequently seek to receive no merit for yourself. Elder, in this way you shall obtain inexhaustible merit.
"In this way, householder,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the householder rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When the sun first rises, the people all go forth together to their labors in the fields; the hundred birds cry out in sorrow, and infants and women wail in grief.
Now, bhikṣus, you should know that this is a parable; you must understand its meaning."
How should this meaning be understood?
When the sun first rises, it is likened to the appearance of the Tathāgata in the world.

The various classes of people collectively engaging in agricultural work are likened to the donors and patrons who, according to the season, provide clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick and infirm.
The hundred birds crying out in grief is a metaphor for this Dharma Master of High Virtue, who is able to preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
The infants and children wailing and calling out is a metaphor for the evil Māra Pāpīyān.
Therefore, monks! Just as when the sun first rises, so does the Tathāgata appear in the world, removing the darkness and illuminating all that is not yet lit. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice the dāna-pāramitā, fulfill the six pāramitās, and swiftly attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices four fundamental dharmas and fulfills the six pāramitās, they will swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment."

What are the four? In this regard, a bodhisattva bestows gifts upon Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and even down to ordinary people, treating all with impartiality and without discrimination. He constantly maintains this thought:
"All beings exist because of food; without food, they perish."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of this first dharma, whereby he fulfills the six perfections.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva practices giving, whether it be his head, eyes, marrow, or brain, or his kingdom, wealth, wife, or children, he gives with joy and does not give rise to thoughts of attachment.
Just as a person facing death might suddenly return to life and leap for joy, unable to contain their exultation, so too is the Bodhisattva’s heart at the moment of generating the resolve;
likewise, they practice giving without giving rise to conceptual attachments.
"Furthermore, Maitreya!

When a bodhisattva practices giving, he extends it universally to all beings and does not do so for his own sake, but rather to bring about the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment. This is called accomplishing these three dharmas and fulfilling the six perfections."
"Furthermore, Maitreya!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving, they reflect thus:
'Among all classes of sentient beings, the bodhisattva is the foremost; he is fully endowed with the six perfections and has realized the fundamental nature of all phenomena.'"

Why is this? Having eaten, their faculties become tranquil; they contemplate the prohibitions and precepts, give rise to no anger, and practice a mind of loving-kindness. With courageous diligence, they increase wholesome dharmas and eliminate unwholesome dharmas. Constantly remaining single-minded, their intellects are not confused; they possess eloquence and never transgress the sequence of the Dharma gates, thereby causing these various acts of giving to fulfill the six perfections and achieve the *dānapāramitā*.
“If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices these four dharmas, they will swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, Maitreya!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to practice giving, they should make this vow and fulfill all practices.”
"In this way, Maitreya,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Maitreya rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, there are four kinds of fearlessness. Having attained these four fearlessnesses, the Tathāgata is unattached to anything in the world; amidst the great assembly, he roars the lion's roar and turns the Brahma-wheel."
“What are the four? I have now fully accomplished this Dharma;

even if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māra, or the devas of Māra, or any crawling and flying creatures were to stand amidst this great assembly and say that I have not accomplished this Dharma, such a thing would not be possible.”
To attain fearlessness therein is the first fearlessness:
"As I am today, all outflows are exhausted, and I shall no longer receive a womb."
If there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or any class of sentient beings, who declare within a great assembly that their outflows are not yet exhausted, this is not so.
This is called the second fearlessness:
"I have now departed from the states of ignorance and darkness; it is absolutely impossible that I would ever again resort to such states of ignorance and darkness."

Furthermore, if any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, or a deity of Māra among the classes of sentient beings were to say in the midst of a great assembly, "I shall return to the dharma of ignorance and darkness," this would not be possible.
This is called the Tathāgata’s three kinds of fearlessness.

Regarding the noble and holy dharmas that constitute the definitive path out [of suffering] and bring an end to the limits of suffering, it is impossible for anyone who desires them not to emerge from that path.

If there should be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, Māra, or a deity of Māra among the classes of sentient beings who, in the midst of a great assembly, should say that the Tathāgata has not reached the end of suffering, this would not be so.
These are called the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses.
"In this way, bhikṣus, with these four fearlessnesses, the Tathāgata is able to roar the lion's roar and turn the Brahma-wheel amidst the great assembly."
"In this way, monks! You should seek skillful means to accomplish the four fearlessnesses. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are now four kinds of persons who are intelligent and courageous, erudite in antiquity and clear-sighted regarding the present, and accomplished in every dharma.”
What are the four? There is the bhikṣu who is learned, well-versed in the ancient and clear about the present, and is foremost among the great assembly.

There is the bhikṣuṇī who is learned, well-versed in the ancient and clear about the present, and is foremost among the great assembly. There is the upāsaka who is learned, well-versed in the ancient and clear about the present, and is foremost among the great assembly. There is the upāsikā who is learned, well-versed in the ancient and clear about the present, and is foremost among the great assembly.
"Monks, these are the four persons who are foremost among the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“Courageous and fearless, learned and able to preach the Dharma,
acting as a lion among the assembly, he can eliminate the dharma of timidity.
A bhikṣu accomplished in the precepts, a bhikṣuṇī of great learning,”
The upāsaka possesses faith, and the upāsikā is likewise;
among the assembly they are foremost, provided they can harmonize with the group.
One who wishes to understand this meaning is like the sun when it first rises.
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves to be learned in antiquity and clear-sighted regarding the present,
achieving mastery in each and every dharma. Thus, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four kinds of garuḍas.”
What are the four?
There are golden-winged garuḍas born from eggs, those born from a womb, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation; these are the four kinds of golden-winged garuḍas.
In this way, bhikṣus, there are four kinds of nāgas. What are the four?
There are dragons born from eggs, dragons born from wombs, dragons born from moisture, and dragons born by transformation.
These, monks, are called the four kinds of dragons.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that when a garuḍa born from an egg wishes to eat a nāga, it ascends the Iron Fork Tree and throws itself into the ocean.

That ocean is two hundred and eighty thousand *li* in length and breadth, and beneath it lie four kinds of nāga palaces: those of nāgas born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, and those born by transformation.”
