At that time, the egg-born garuḍa strikes the water with its great wings, splitting it in two directions to seize and eat the egg-born nāgas;
however, should it happen to face a womb-born nāga, the body of the garuḍa will immediately perish.
At that time, the garuḍa seizes a nāga from the water; before the water has even closed over him, he returns to the top of the Iron Fork Tree.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that when a garuḍa born from a womb wishes to eat a nāga, he ascends the Iron Fork Tree and throws himself into the ocean.
Although that ocean is two million eight hundred thousand li in length and breadth, he strikes the water and dives down until he encounters a nāga of the womb-born class."
If it encounters an egg-born dragon, it can also seize it and carry it out from the sea;
however, if it encounters a moisture-born dragon, the bird’s body dies immediately.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that when a moisture-born garuḍa wishes to eat a dragon, it ascends a tree of iron forks and throws itself into the sea."
If it encounters a dragon born from an egg, one born from a womb, or one born from moisture, it can capture them all;
however, if it should encounter a dragon born by transformation, its avian body will immediately perish.
“Monks, when a garuḍa born by transformation wishes to eat a nāga, it flies up to the Iron Fork Tree and plunges itself into the ocean.

Although that ocean is two hundred and eighty thousand li in length and breadth, it strikes the water and descends until it encounters a nāga born from an egg, one born from a womb, one born from moisture, or one born by transformation; it can seize any of them. Before the waters have closed over it, it returns to the Iron Fork Tree.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know that if a dragon king serves the Buddha, at that time the garuḍa will be unable to devour him. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata constantly practices the four immeasurable minds; for this reason, the bird cannot eat the dragon.”
"What are the four immeasurables?
The Tathāgata constantly practices loving-kindness, constantly practices compassion, constantly practices sympathetic joy, and constantly practices equanimity.
These, O bhikṣus, are called [the four immeasurables]."
The Tathāgata constantly possesses these four kinds of equanimous mind; he has great strength and great valor that cannot be thwarted or destroyed.
For this reason, the garuḍa cannot devour the nāga.
Therefore, monks, you should practice the four immeasurable minds. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (Nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“When a virtuous friend practices giving, there are four kinds of meritorious qualities.”
What are the four? Giving at the proper time, rather than at an improper time;
giving with one's own hands, rather than having others do so;
Generosity is always pure and never impure;
the gift is supremely subtle and never defiled.
When a spiritual friend practices giving, there are these four merits.
"Therefore, monks, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices giving, they should be endowed with these four merits.
By being endowed with these merits, they obtain great karmic fruitfulness and attain the extinction of ambrosia (nirvāṇa)."
However, this merit is beyond measure; it would be impossible even for space to contain it were one to say that there is such-and-such an amount of meritorious karma.

It is like the water of the great ocean, which cannot be calculated by the names used for counting—such as one *hu*, half a *hu*, one *he*, or half a *he*—for its meritorious karma cannot be fully described.

In this way, the merit performed by good sons and good daughters is beyond measure; they shall obtain great karmic blessings, attain the extinction of ambrosia (nirvāṇa), and it can be said that their merit shall be as vast as this.
Therefore, monks, a son of good family or a daughter of good family should be endowed with these four qualities. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are now four kinds of persons who are worthy of veneration and esteem, the fields of merit for the world.
What are these four?"

These are known as those who uphold faith, those who revere the Dharma, those who have realized it through their own bodies, and those who have attained vision. What is meant by a person who upholds faith?

It refers to a certain individual who, having received instruction from others, possesses firm faith and no doubt or hesitation; they have faith in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Trainer of Beings, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
One who believes the words of the Tathāgata, believes the words of the brahmins, and constantly believes the words of others, rather than relying on their own wisdom—
such a person is called one who "upholds faith."
"What is meant by one who honors the Dharma?
In this regard, there is a person who discriminates regarding the Dharma, does not rely on others, and examines the Dharma: 'Does it exist? "
Is it non-existent? Is it real?
Or is it illusory?
He then thinks: "This is the word of the Tathāgata; this is the word of the brahmin.
Knowing thus that these are the various teachings of the Tathāgata, he upholds them.
Those who distance themselves from all proponents of external paths are called practitioners who honor the Dharma. What, then,
is meant by a person who has realized through bodily witness?

Thereupon, there is one who has realized this for himself through direct experience, yet does not believe others, nor does he believe the words of the Tathāgata, nor does he believe the teachings spoken by the Venerable Ones; he merely wanders according to his own nature.
This is called a person who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
"What is meant by a person who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)?

In this regard, there is a person who has severed the three fetters, becoming a *srotāpanna* established in the dharma of non-retrogression. He possesses this view: 'There is giving; there are recipients; there is the retribution for good and evil; there are this world and the world beyond; there is father and mother; and there are those such as Arhats who have received the teachings. Having personally realized this with faith, he wanders and transforms others."
This is called a person who has attained vision.
"Monks, these are the four types of persons;
you should keep in mind that one should abandon the first three and keep in mind the practice for realizing the cultivation of the body."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Nineteen; Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Twenty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Disciples (Śrāvaka-varga) 1. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the four great śrāvakas gathered in one place and spoke thus:

"Let us together observe within this city of Rājagṛha who are those that do not make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha to perform meritorious deeds, and who have been without faith from the beginning; we shall exhort them to place their faith in the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Kāśyapa, the Venerable Aniruddha, and the Venerable Piṇḍola.
At that time, there was a householder named Bhaddiya, who possessed immense wealth and many treasures beyond measure:
gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, pearls, amber, elephants, horses, carriages, and vehicles, as well as male and female slaves and attendants—all were fully provided.

Furthermore, being stingy and greedy, they were unwilling to practice giving; they possessed not even a hair’s breadth of merit toward the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, nor did they have sincere faith. Consequently, their merit was exhausted and they created no new merit. They constantly harbored wrong views, thinking: "There is no giving, no merit, and no recipient;

there is no present life or future life, nor is there retribution for good or evil deeds; there are no parents, nor are there those who have attained Arhatship, nor indeed anyone who has realized such realization."

That householder had seven successive gates, each with its own gatekeeper, so as not to allow beggars to reach the doors; furthermore, he covered the central courtyard with an iron cage, fearing that birds might fly into the courtyard.

The elder had an elder sister named Nanda, who was likewise stingy and greedy, unwilling to practice generosity. She did not plant the roots of merit; thus, what was old had perished, yet she created nothing new. Furthermore, she harbored false views, thinking: "There is no giving, no merit, and no recipient;
there is no present life nor future life, nor the retribution for good and evil deeds; there are no parents, no Arhats, and furthermore, there is no one who attains realization."
Nanda’s residence also had sevenfold gates and gatekeepers who prevented anyone from coming to beg; furthermore, it was covered with iron grates so that birds could not enter the house.
"Today we shall cause Nanda’s mother to develop firm faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
At that time, the householder Badrika was eating cakes in the early morning.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the Venerable Aniruddha put on his robes, took up his bowl, and sprang forth from the ground within the elder’s house, extending his bowl toward the elder.
At that time, the elder was filled with profound sorrow and gave a small portion of cakes to Aniruddha.
Having received the cakes, Aniruddha then returned to his dwelling place.
At that time, the elder became incensed and said to the gatekeeper:
"I have given this command:
'Let no one enter within the gates.'"
"Why did you allow these people to enter?
At that time, the gatekeeper replied, "The gates and chambers were firmly secured; I do not know from where this practitioner came."
At that time, the householder remained silent.
When the householder had finished eating the cakes, he proceeded to eat the fish and meat.
Then the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, went to the householder’s home; he emerged from the midst of the earth and held out his bowl toward the householder.
At that time, the elder was deeply distressed with grief and gave him a small amount of fish and meat.
Having received the meat, Kāśyapa then vanished from that place and returned to his own abode.
At that time, the elder became even more enraged and said to the gatekeeper:
"I previously gave this command:
'Do not let anyone enter the house.'"
"Why, then, have you allowed these two śramaṇas to enter the house to beg for alms?
At that time, the gatekeeper replied,
"We did not see from where these śramaṇas came as they entered."
The elder replied, "This shaven-headed śramaṇa is skilled in illusionary arts; he deludes the people of the world and possesses no upright conduct.
At that time, the elder’s wife sat not far from the elder, watching him.
Now, this wife of the householder was the sister of the householder Citta, whom he had taken from Mount Māśika.
At that time, the wife said to the householder:
"You should guard your speech; do not speak these words, saying:"
"The śramaṇas study the arts of illusion.
Why is this so? Because these śramaṇas possess great majestic power; thus, their coming to the house of the elder brings much benefit.
"Elder! Do you recognize that bhikṣu from before? The elder replied:
"I do not know him," the woman replied at that time,
"O Householder!"

"Have you heard that in the kingdom of Kapilavastu there was a prince of the Ikṣvāku clan named Aniruddha, at whose birth this earth shook in six ways and hidden treasures spontaneously emerged within a distance of one yojana around his residence?"
The householder replied,
"I have heard that there is one named Aniruddha, but I have not seen him.
Then, the wife said to the householder:

"This son of a noble family, having renounced the household life to go forth and study the Way, has cultivated the holy life and attained the path of Arhatship; he is foremost in the divine eye, with none surpassing him."
However, the Tathāgata has also said:
"Among my disciples, the foremost in the divine eye is the bhikṣu Aniruddha.
Do you recognize the second bhikṣu who has come here to beg?
The elder replied, “I do not know him. His wife said:

“Householder! Have you heard that within this city of Rājagṛha there is a great brahmin named Kapila, who possesses immeasurable wealth and treasures beyond counting, and who owns nine hundred and ninety-nine oxen for his farming?”
The householder replied,
"I have personally seen this brahmin with my own eyes. His wife replied:

“Householder! Have you heard that the brahmin’s son named Vipula-yajña has a body of golden hue and a wife named Bhadrā, the most excellent among women; that even if one were to place polished purple-gold before her, it would appear black by comparison to her whiteness?”
The elder replied, "I have heard that this brahmin has a son named Vipulaśraddhāna,
yet I have not seen him. His wife replied:
"The monk who arrived later is that very person.

Having renounced this treasure of a jade maiden, he left the household life to study the Path and has now attained Arhatship. He constantly practices the dhūta austerities; among all those who possess the complete dharmas of the dhūta practices, none surpasses the Venerable Kāśyapa."
The World-Honored One has also said:
"Among my disciples, the foremost bhikṣu in the practice of dhūta is Mahākāśyapa.
Now this householder has gained excellent benefit, for he has caused a noble and holy person to come here to beg for alms.
Having contemplated this meaning, I have therefore said:
"Guard your own speech well; do not slander the noble and holy ones by claiming they are mere illusions."
"These disciples of Śākyamuni all possess divine powers; they must have spoken these words.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana put on his robes, took up his bowl, and soared through the air to the house of the elder. He shattered the iron cage, causing it to fall into mid-air, and sat down cross-legged.
At that time, the householder Bhadrika saw Maudgalyāyana sitting in mid-air; seized with fear, he spoke these words: "Are you a deva?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"I am not a deva. The householder asked:
"Are you a gandharva? Maudgalyāyana replied, "I am not a gandharva."
The elder asked, "Are you a ghost? Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I am not a ghost. The elder asked,
"Are you a rākṣasa, a ghost that devours humans?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I am not a rākṣasa, a ghost that devours humans.
At that time, the elder Bhadrika spoke this verse:
"Are you a deva, a gandharva,
or a rākṣasa spirit? Or do you say that you are neither a deva nor a rākṣasa spirit?"
You do not resemble the Gandharvas, nor are you one who wanders through the various realms;
what is your name now? I wish to know it.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana replied with a verse:
“Neither devas nor gandharvas, Neither ghosts nor rākṣasas;
Having attained liberation throughout the three times, I am now a human being.”
"He who has subdued the Māras and accomplished the Unsurpassed Way is the Teacher named Śākyamuni; my name is Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
At that time, the elder Bhadrika said to Maudgalyāyana:
“Bhikṣu! What are your instructions?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I now wish to preach the Dharma to you; reflect upon it well.
At that time, the householder again thought to himself:
"These ascetics have long been attached to food and drink; what they now wish to discuss must surely be food and drink itself."
"If he were to ask me for food, I would say that there is none.
Nevertheless, he further thought:
"I shall now listen to what this person has to say for a short while."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, knowing what was in the elder’s mind, spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata speaks of two kinds of giving: The gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth.
Now I shall speak of the gift of Dharma; Listen with single-minded attention.”
At that time, when the elder heard that there would be a gift of the Dharma, he was filled with joy and said to Maudgalyāyana:
"I pray you, expound it now; having heard it, I shall understand."
Maudgalyāyana replied, "Householder, you should know that the Tathāgata has taught five great acts of giving; for as long as life lasts, you should keep them in mind and practice them.
At that time, the householder again thought to himself:
"Previously, Maudgalyāyana intended to teach the Dharma and its practice, yet now you speak again of the five great gifts.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, knowing what was in the elder’s mind, spoke again to the elder, saying:
"The Tathāgata has taught that there are two great gifts."
"There are what are called the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth.
I shall now speak of the gift of Dharma, not the gift of material wealth.
The householder replied:
"What are the five great gifts?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "The first is that one must not kill living beings; this is called a great gift, O Householder!"
One should practice these for as long as one lives.
Second, refraining from stealing is called the "Great Gift," which one should practice for as long as one lives.
One should refrain from sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants, practicing them for as long as one lives.
"Householder, these are called the five great gifts; you should reflect upon them and practice them.
At that time, having heard these words, the householder Bhadrika was filled with extreme joy and thought to himself:
"What the Buddha Śākyamuni has taught is most wonderful; what he now proclaims requires no precious objects. Just as I am currently unable to take life, this can be practiced and followed."
Furthermore, my family is abundant in wealth and treasures, and we never engage in theft; this too is my practice.
Moreover, my family possesses women of the highest excellence, and I never commit adultery with others; this is my practice.
Furthermore, I do not favor those who speak falsely, much less would I myself speak falsely; this too is my practice.
Just as today my mind does not think of wine, much less would I taste it myself; this too is my practice.
At that time, the householder said to Maudgalyāyana:
"I am able to practice these five kinds of giving.
At that moment, the householder had this thought in his mind:
"I shall now provide a meal for this Maudgalyāyana.
The elder raised his head and said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Please deign to lower your divine presence and take a seat here."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana descended from his seat upon hearing the voice.

Then, the elder Bhadrika personally prepared various kinds of food and drink for Maudgalyāyana. When Maudgalyāyana had finished eating and the ritual water had been offered, the elder thought to himself:
"I should offer a piece of fine cotton cloth to Maudgalyāyana."

At that time, he entered the storehouse to select white cotton cloth; wishing to take one of poor quality, he instead obtained one of good quality, whereupon he immediately set it aside and took up another piece of cloth. Yet it was again of such good quality, so he set that aside as well and took up yet another.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, knowing what was in the elder’s mind, spoke this verse:
“Giving while the mind is in conflict—this merit is abandoned by the wise.
When it is time to give, it is not time for conflict; one should give according to the heart at the proper time.”
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"Now Maudgalyāyana knows what is in my mind.
He then took a piece of white cotton cloth and offered it to Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately offered a prayer of blessing:
"To observe and give is foremost; To know there are noble and holy ones Is the highest among all acts of giving, Like a fertile field that produces fruit."
Then, after Maudgalyāyana had offered his benediction, he accepted the white cotton cloth so that the elder might receive inexhaustible merit.
At that time, the elder sat to one side, and Maudgalyāyana gradually delivered to him a sublime discourse on the Dharma, namely:
a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, and a discourse on rebirth in heaven; [he spoke of] the impurity of sensual desires and how renunciation is bliss.
The Dharma taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, consists of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana explained these to him in their entirety.

Just as an extremely clean cloth easily takes on dye, so it was with this householder Bhaddiya; he too, while still upon his seat, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having attained the Dharma and seen the Dharma, free from doubt, he received the five precepts and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha.
At that time, having seen that the elder had attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, Maudgalyāyana spoke this verse:
“The sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata are complete in their fundamental source;
the eye is pure and free from defilement, without doubt and without hesitation.”
At that time, the elder Bhadrika said to Maudgalyāyana:

"From this day forward, may you and the fourfold assembly always accept my invitations; I shall provide robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick, without any sense of stinginess."
At that time, after Maudgalyāyana had taught the Dharma to the elder, he rose from his seat and departed.
The other great śrāvakas—Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Venerable Aniruddha—said to Venerable Piṇḍola:
"We have already converted the elder Bhadrika; you may now go to subdue that old woman Nandā."
Piṇḍola replied, "This matter is most excellent. At that time,
the old woman Nanda personally prepared the *sarpis-pūpa* (butter cakes).

At that time, when it was time for the meal, the Venerable Piṇḍola put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. Gradually arriving at the house of the old woman Nanda, he rose up from the ground, extended his hand holding his bowl, and begged for alms from the old woman Nanda.
At that time, having seen Piṇḍola, the old woman was filled with extreme anger and spoke these evil words:
"Bhikṣu, you should know that even if your eyes were to fall out, I would never beg for food from you."
At that time, Piṇḍola immediately entered into samādhi and caused his two eyes to protrude.
Then, Mātā Nandā became even more incensed and spoke these evil words:
"Even if this śramaṇa were to hang upside down in mid-air, I would never give you food."
At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola, by the power of samādhi, suspended himself upside down in the air.
Then, Mātā Nandā became even more enraged and uttered these evil words:
"Even if this śramaṇa were to emit smoke from his entire body, I would never give you food."
At that time, Piṇḍola again used the power of samādhi to emit smoke from his entire body.
When the old woman saw this, her anger redoubled, and she spoke these words:
"Even if this śramaṇa were to set his whole body ablaze, I would never give you food!"
At that time, Piṇḍola immediately used his samādhi to cause his entire body to blaze with fire.
When the old woman saw this, she spoke these words again:
"Even if this śramaṇa were to draw water from his whole body, I would never give you food."
At that time, Piṇḍola, by the power of his samādhi, caused water to flow from his entire body.
When the old woman saw this, she spoke these words again:
"Even if this śramaṇa were to die right before me, I would never give you food."
At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola immediately entered the samādhi of cessation; with his inhalation and exhalation suspended, he passed away before the old woman.
Because she could no longer perceive his breath, the old woman was seized with terror and her hair stood on end as she spoke these words:

"This śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, is widely renowned and honored by the king. If it were heard that he has died in my home, I would surely face legal trouble from the authorities and fear I could not escape it."
They all spoke these words:
"If the śramaṇa returns to life, we shall give food to the śramaṇa.
At that moment, Piṇḍola immediately arose from samādhi.
Then, Mother Nanda again thought to herself:
"This cake is far too large; I shall make a smaller one and give it to him.
At that time, the old woman took a small amount of flour to make a cake, but the cake grew larger and larger.
When the old mother saw this, she thought again:
"This cake is far too large; I should make smaller ones.
However, since the cake has already grown so large, I shall take what was made first and give it to him."
He then stepped forward to take it, but the cakes were all joined together.
At that time, Mother Nanda said to Piṇḍola: "Bhikṣu!"
"If you need food, take it yourself; why do you trouble me so much?
Piṇḍola replied, "Sister, you should know that I have no need for food; I only wish to say something to my mother."
The mother Nandā replied,
"Bhikṣu! What instructions do you have?"
Piṇḍola said: "Old mother, you should know now that we shall take these cakes and go to where the World-Honored One is.
If the World-Honored One has any instructions or exhortations, we shall together carry them out."
The old woman replied,
"This matter is most excellent. At that time,
the old woman personally carried these cakes behind the Venerable Piṇḍola and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Piṇḍola addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“This Mother Nandā is the elder sister of the householder Bhaddiya; she is stingy and greedy, eating alone and refusing to give to others.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for me the Dharma of steadfast faith, so that I may attain understanding.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mātṛ Nandā:
"You have now brought these cakes to offer to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus."
At that time, Mātṛnanda immediately offered [the food] to the Tathāgata and the rest of the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
Because some cakes remained, Mātṛnanda said to the World-Honored One,
“There are still some leftover cakes.”
The World-Honored One said,
"Serve more food to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
Mother Nanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, again took this cake and offered it to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
Thereupon, there was still a cake remaining as before.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mātṛ Nandā:
"You should now take this cake and give it to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the upāsakas, and the upāsikās."
Nevertheless, some cakes remained. The World-Honored One said, "Take these cakes and give them to the poor.
Nevertheless, some cakes still remained. The World-Honored One said:
"You may take these cakes and discard them in a clean place, or cast them into extremely pure water.
The reason for this is that I do not see any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, or human being who could digest these cakes, except for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
He replied, “So it is, World-Honored One.”
At that time, Mātṛnanda immediately cast this cake into pure water, whereupon flames instantly burst forth.
Having seen this, Mātṛnanda was seized with fear; he went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught him the Dharma, namely:
discourse on giving, discourse on morality, and discourse on rebirth in heaven; he spoke of sensual desire as impure, of the outflows as defilements, and of renunciation as essential.

At that time, seeing that Mātṛ-nandā’s mind was opened and understood, the World-Honored One taught her the Dharma that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly preach—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and at that moment, the World-Honored One explained them all to Mātṛ-nandā.
At that moment, the old woman attained the purity of the Dharma-eye upon her seat, just as white cotton cloth is easily dyed with color.
It was even so for Mātā Nandā; all defilements were exhausted, and she attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.

Having attained the Dharma and perfected the Dharma, he was free from doubt; having transcended hesitation, he attained fearlessness and served the Three Honored Ones while upholding the five precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One again preached the Dharma for him, causing him to give rise to joy.
Then Nanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"From this day forward, let the fourfold assembly come to my home to receive offerings; from now on, I shall constantly practice giving, cultivate all manner of merit, and serve the worthy and holy ones."
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha’s] feet with his head, and then withdrew.
At that time, the elder Bhadrika and his mother Nanda had a younger brother named Upaka, who was a childhood friend of King Ajātaśatru and held him in the highest affection.

At that time, the householder Upakaṇi was engaged in agricultural work. Having heard that his elder brother Bhadrika and his sister Nandā had received the transformative teaching of the Tathāgata, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; for seven days he neither slept nor took food or drink.
At that time, having finished his field work, the elder was returning toward the city of Rājagṛha when he thought to himself:
"I shall first go to the place where the World-Honored One is, and only then return home."
At that time, the elder went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Has my elder brother Baddhika and my sister Nandā received the transformative teaching of the Tathāgata?"
The World-Honored One said: "It is so, householder!
Now, Bhadrika and Nanda have seen the Four Truths and are practicing all wholesome dharmas."
At that time, the householder Upakaṇi addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“We who dwell at this gate have obtained a most great benefit.
The Blessed One replied:
"So it is, householder! Just as you have said, your parents have now gained a most excellent benefit and planted the seeds of merit for future lives.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the householder. Having heard the Dharma, the householder immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet with his head and face, and then withdrew.
He went to King Ajātaśatru and sat to one side.
At that time, the king asked the elder:
"Have your brother and sister been transformed by the Tathāgata?"
He replied: "So it is, Great King!"

Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately struck the bells and beat the drums, issuing a proclamation throughout the city:
"From this day forward, let no household that serves the Buddha be burdened with taxes or levies, and let those who serve the Buddha be provided with escorts for their arrivals and departures."
"The reason for this is that they are all my brothers in the Dharma.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru brought forth various kinds of food and drink and presented them to the elder. Then, the elder thought to himself:
"I have never yet heard the World-Honored One explain the dharma for a lay follower (*upāsaka*) regarding what kind of food one ought to eat."
"What kind of beverage should I drink?
I shall first go to the World-Honored One to inquire about this matter, and only then will I eat.
At that time, the householder said to one of his attendants:
“Go to where the World-Honored One is.
Upon arrival, prostrate yourself at his feet and, conveying my words, address the World-Honored One thus:
‘The householder Upakaṇi says to the World-Honored One:’”
"Now, according to the Dharma of the virtuous, how many precepts should one uphold?
Furthermore, by violating how many precepts does one cease to be a lay follower of pure faith (*upāsaka*)?
And what kind of food should one consume?"
"What kind of beverage should he drink?
At that time, the man, having received the elder's instruction, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, that man, bearing the name of the elder, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"According to the Dharma for a pure-faith layman (*upāsaka*), how many precepts should he observe?
By violating how many precepts does one cease to be an *upāsaka*?"
"Furthermore, what kind of food should one eat?
What kind of beverage should one drink?
The World-Honored One replied:
"You should now know that there are two kinds of food: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated. What are these two?
If, when consuming food, unwholesome states arise and wholesome states diminish, this food is not to be cultivated."
When obtaining food, if wholesome qualities increase and unwholesome qualities diminish, this food may be approached.
Regarding drinks, there are likewise two cases: if, upon obtaining a drink, unwholesome qualities arise and wholesome qualities diminish, this should not be approached;
if, upon obtaining a drink, unwholesome qualities diminish and wholesome qualities increase, this may be approached.

Now, according to the dharma for lay followers of pure faith, there are five precepts as limits; among these, whether one can uphold one precept, two precepts, three precepts, four precepts, or even all five precepts, one should maintain them all.
When asked repeatedly, those who are able to uphold them should be made to do so;
if a lay follower (*upāsaka*) violates even a single precept, at the dissolution of the body after death, he will be reborn in hell.
"If even a lay follower of pure faith who upholds a single precept is reborn in a good place, in the heavens, how much more so for those who uphold two, three, four, or five?
At that time, having received this instruction from the Buddha, the man prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet and then withdrew.
Not long after that person had departed, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize the bestowing of the five precepts and the three refuges upon upāsakas."

When a bhikṣu wishes to confer the precepts upon a male or female lay follower (upāsaka/upāsikā), he instructs them to bare their arms, join their palms with hands crossed, and recite their own names while taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Having instructed them to recite their names and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha two or three times, he further instructs them to declare for themselves:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Bhikṣu Saṅgha."

"Just as when the Buddha Śākyamuni first accepted the five hundred merchants, they took the three refuges and for the duration of their lives refrained from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking alcohol."
If one upholds a single precept, the remaining four are sealed;
if one receives two precepts, the remaining three are sealed;
if one receives three precepts, the remaining two are sealed.
"If you receive four precepts, you must seal them with the remaining one;
if you receive five precepts, you should maintain them all in their entirety.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Today the sun and moon have fourfold obscurations that prevent them from emitting their radiance.
What are these four? First is the cloud; second is wind-blown dust; third is smoke; and fourth is the asura, which covers the sun and moon so they cannot emit their radiance."
"Monks, these are the four obscurations of the sun and moon that prevent them from emitting great radiance.
It is the same, monks, in this case."
There are four fetters that shroud the human mind, preventing it from attaining liberation. What are these four?
First is the fetter of sensual desire, which shrouds the human mind, preventing it from attaining liberation.
Second is malice, third is delusion, and fourth is gain; these obscure the human mind so that it cannot attain liberation.
This, monks, is what is meant.
These four fetters shroud and obscure the human mind, preventing it from attaining liberation; you should seek skillful means to extinguish these four fetters.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying near the Āravī shrine.
At that time, it was the height of winter, and the trees were withered and fallen.
Then, the householder’s son, Hatthāroha, emerged from that city and, while walking for exercise in the open air, gradually approached the place where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the son of the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I wonder if you slept well during the night?”
The World-Honored One said: "It is so, young man;
you sleep well indeed."
At that time, the son of the householder addressed the Buddha:

“It is now a day of intense cold, and all things have withered and fallen; yet the World-Honored One sits upon a bed of grass and wears clothing that is exceedingly thin. How can the World-Honored One say:
‘I sleep a most pleasant and sound sleep’?”
The World-Honored One said: "Young man!"
Listen attentively!
I shall now question you again; answer as you see fit.

Suppose there were a householder who had well-constructed his dwelling, free from wind and dust, and within that house there were couches, rugs, woolen blankets, and fine furs, with everything fully provided. Furthermore, there were four jade-like maidens of exquisite beauty, their faces like peach blossoms—rare in this world and such that one could never tire of gazing upon them—and they delighted in bright lamps. Would that householder sleep soundly?
The son of the householder replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
"There is a fine bed for lying upon; one can sleep soundly and pleasantly.
The World-Honored One said, "What do you think, son of a householder?"
"If that person has slept soundly, but then a desire arises, would they be unable to sleep because of that desire?
The householder's son replied, "It would be so."
“World-Honored One!
If that person’s sensual desire arises, they will not be able to sleep.
The World-Honored One said:
"Just as that intense desire has now been forever exhausted by the Tathāgata without remainder, with no further root remaining and never to arise again—
what do you think, son of a householder?"
"If thoughts of anger or delusion arise, how can one sleep well?
The youth replied, "One cannot sleep well."
"The reason for this is that they possess the mind of the three poisons.
The World-Honored One replied, "The Tathāgata no longer possesses such a mind today; it is forever exhausted without remainder, nor does it have any root."
"Young man, you should know that I shall now explain four kinds of sitting.
What are these four?
There is the low seat, the celestial seat, the Brahma seat, and the Buddha seat."
"Young man, you should know that the low seat is the seat of a wheel-turning sage king;
the celestial seat is the seat of Śakra-devānām-indra;
and the Brahma seat is the seat of the Brahmā-rāja."
The Buddha’s seat is the seat of the Four Noble Truths.
The low seat is the seat directed toward the stage of Srotāpanna.
The celestial seat is the seat attained by one who has become a Srotāpanna.
The Brahmā-seat is the seat of the *sakṛdāgāmin*.
The Buddha-seat is the seat of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The low seat is the seat attained by the *sakṛdāgāmin*.
The "Heavenly Seat" (devāsana) is the seat directed toward the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin).
The "Brahma Seat" (brahmāsana) is the seat attained upon realizing the fruit of non-returner.
The "Buddha Seat" (buddhāsana) is the seat of the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni).
The low seat is the seat of the desire realm;
the celestial seat is the seat of the form realm;
the Brahma seat is the seat of the formless realm.
"The Buddha’s sitting is the sitting of the four bases of psychic power.

Therefore, young man, because the Tathāgata sits upon the sitting of the four bases of psychic power, he sleeps soundly and well; therein he does not give rise to lust, anger, or delusion. Because he does not give rise to these three poisons, he enters parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence—this I know as it truly is.
Therefore, son of a householder, having contemplated this meaning, I say that the Tathāgata sleeps in peace."
At that time, the son of the householder spoke these verses:
"We have seen each other for a very long time; The Brahmin has attained parinirvāṇa.
Having reached the power of the Tathāgata, He with the clear eye has entered extinction."
The humble seat, the celestial seat, the Brahma seat, and the Buddha seat—the Tathāgata discerns them all; therefore, he attains peaceful sleep.
I take refuge in the Honored One among men, and I also take refuge in the Supreme among men.
"I am currently unable to know upon what kind of dhyāna you rely.
After the son of the householder had spoken these words, the World-Honored One gave his assent.
At that time, the son of the householder then thought to himself:
“The World-Honored One has granted his assent; I am filled with such extreme joy that I cannot contain myself.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the youth rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his quiet chamber, descended from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and together with the brahmin Mṛgaśiras, gradually traveled on until he reached the Great Fear Cemetery.
At that time, the World-Honored One took a human skull and gave it to the brahmin, saying: "Now, brahmin!

You are skilled in the stars and constellations, and you are also proficient in medicine, able to treat all manner of ailments. You understand all realms of existence and can likewise know the causes and conditions of a person's death."
I now ask you: whose skull is this? Is it that of a man or a woman?
Furthermore, by what illness did they meet their end?
At that time, the brahmin took up the skull and examined it from every side; he then struck it with his hand and said to the World-Honored One, "This is the skull of a man, not a woman."
The World-Honored One said:
“It is so, brahmin! As you have said, this is a man, not a woman.”
The World-Honored One asked,
"By what means did you pass away?
The brahmin again grasped him by the hand and struck him, saying to the World-Honored One:
"Because these various ailments have converged and the hundred joints ache with pain, it brings about the end of life.
The World-Honored One asked,
"By what means should this be treated?"
The brahmin Mṛgaśiras said to the Buddha:
"One should take a harītakī fruit and mix it with honey; then, by consuming this, the illness will be cured."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! It is as you have said; had this person obtained this medicine, he likewise would not have died."
"This person has ended their life today; where have they been reborn?
Having heard this, the brahmin again took hold of the skull and struck it, saying to the World-Honored One:
"This person, having ended their life, has been reborn in the three evil realms and not in a good place."
The Blessed One said: "So it is, brahmin!"
"As you have said, they were born in the three evil realms and not in a good place.
At that time, the World-Honored One again took up another skull and handed it to the brahmin, asking him:
"Whose was this? Was it a man?"
"A woman? At that time,
the brahmin struck it again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"This skull is the body of a woman."
The World-Honored One asked,
"By what ailment did he meet his end? At that time,
the brahmin Mṛgaśiras struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This woman has met her end because she was pregnant.
The Blessed One asked,
"By what cause did this woman meet her end?"
The brahmin said to the Buddha,
"This woman’s months of pregnancy were not yet complete when she met her end because of giving birth to a child.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Excellent! Excellent, brahmin!”
"It is as you have said.
Furthermore, by what method do they treat her while she is pregnant?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
“For such a patient, excellent ghee and clarified butter are required; if he takes them, he will recover.
The World-Honored One told him, “So it is, so it is, just as you have said.”
"Now that this woman has passed away, where has she been reborn?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha,
saying, "This woman, having passed away, has been reborn among the animals."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Brahmin! It is as you have said.
At that time, the World-Honored One again took another skull and handed it to the brahmin, asking him:
"Is it a man? Or a woman?
At that moment, the brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This skull is the body of a man.
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent!"
Excellent! It is as you have said.
By what ailment did this end of life come about?
The brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This man met his end because he had overindulged in food and drink and subsequently suffered from a violent diarrhea."
The World-Honored One asked:
"By what method do you treat this illness?
The brahmin replied to the Buddha:
"If one abstains from food for three days, one will be cured.
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent!"
Excellent! It is as you have said.
Where will this person be reborn after the end of his life?
At that time, the brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This person, at the end of his life, was reborn among the hungry ghosts.
This is because his thoughts were attached to water."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as you have said.
At that time, the World-Honored One again took up another skull and gave it to the brahmin, asking him:
"Is this a male?"
"A woman? At that time,
the brahmin struck it again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"This skull is the body of a woman."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as you have said.
By what illness did this man die?
The brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"At the time of giving birth, she meets her end.
The Blessed One asked,
"In what way does she meet her end at the time of giving birth?"
The brahmin struck her again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This woman’s body is utterly exhausted in strength; furthermore, she has died of hunger."
The World-Honored One asked,
"When this man’s life has ended, where will he be reborn?
At that time, the brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This person, at the end of his life, will be reborn in the human realm.

The World-Honored One replied, "As for one who has died of starvation, it is impossible that they would be reborn in a good destination; rather, it is only logical that they would be reborn in one of the three evil realms."
At that time, the brahmin struck her again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This woman has maintained her precepts in their entirety until the end of her life."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
As you have said, that woman’s body was fully endowed with the observance of the precepts when she met her end.
This is because, for any man or woman who has maintained the prohibitive precepts in their entirety, at the time of death they shall fall into one of two destinies:
either among the devas or among human beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One again took up a skull and handed it to the brahmin, asking:
"Is this a male or a female?"
At that time, the brahmin struck it again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One,
saying, “This skull belongs to a male body.
The World-Honored One told him:
"Excellent! Excellent!
As you have said, by what affliction did this person meet their end?"
The brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying, “This man was not ill;
he met his end because he was harmed by another.
The World-Honored One told him:
“Excellent! Excellent!
It is as you have said: because he was harmed by others, his life came to an end.”
The World-Honored One asked,
"When this man's life ends, where will he be reborn?
At that time, the brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This person, at the end of his life, has been reborn in a good destination, in the heavens.
The World-Honored One said:
"What you have said is inconsistent with both the preceding and the subsequent discourse."
The brahmin said to the Buddha,
"By what causal basis are they not in accord?
The World-Honored One replied:
"All those men and women who are harmed by others and meet their end are reborn entirely in the three evil realms; how can you say they are reborn in the good places of the heavens?"
The brahmin struck him again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This man upheld the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome actions; therefore, at the end of his life, he attained rebirth in a good destination, the heavens."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"As you have said, one who upholds the precepts without transgression will be reborn in a good place, in the heavens.
The World-Honored One spoke again, saying:
"How many precepts did this person uphold when he met his end?"
At that time, the brahmin again concentrated his mind single-pointedly without any other thoughts, struck him with his hand, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Do you maintain a single precept?"
Is it not so? Is it two, three, four, or five? Is it not so?
"However, this person observed the eightfold precepts of the fast when they passed away.
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent!"
"Excellent!
It is as you have said; he took his final rebirth while observing the eightfold fast.
At that time, in the southern part of the Universal Fragrant Mountain within the eastern realm, there was a bhikṣu named Udayana, who entered parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At that time, in the mere twinkling of an eye as the World-Honored One extended and withdrew his arm, he went and brought back that skull, handing it to the brahmin and asking him:
"Is this a male?"
"A woman? At that time, the brahmin struck it again with his hand and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"As I observe this skull, its original nature is neither male nor female."
The reason for this is that when I observe this skull, I see neither birth nor cessation, nor do I see it circling or coming and going.
The reason for this is that when I observe the eight directions, above, and below, there is absolutely no sound or resonance.
“World-Honored One,
I do not yet know whose skull this is.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Stop! Stop! Brahmin!”
Do you not know whose skull this is?

You should know that this skull has no end and no beginning, nor does it have birth or death; it has no destination in the eight directions, above or below. This is the skull of the Arhat, the Bhikṣu Udāyin, who attained parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder within the domain of the Universal Fragrance Mountain in the eastern quarter.
At that time, having heard these words, the brahmin marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I can now observe these ants and know entirely where they have come from; I can distinguish the calls of birds and beasts, knowing which is male and which is female."
Yet when I observe this Arhat, he perceives nothing at all; neither does he see a place from which he comes, nor a place to which he goes. How truly extraordinary is the True Dharma of the Tathāgata!
The reason for this is that while the root of all dharmas issues from the divine mouth of the Tathāgata, the Arhat issues from the root of the sūtras and the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said: “So it is, brahmin!”
As you have said, the root of all dharmas issues from the mouth of the Tathāgata; even the devas, worldlings, Māras, or the Mārakāyikas can never know the destination of an Arhat.
At that time, the brahmin prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I am able to fully know the destinations of the ninety-six kinds of paths; I know them all.
Yet, regarding the destination of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, I cannot discern it. I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow me to enter the ranks of those on the Path.”
The World-Honored One said: "Excellent, brahmin!"
"Quickly practice the holy life (brahmacarya); furthermore, there is no one who knows the destination to which you are headed.
At that time, the brahmin immediately left the household life to study the Way, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place to contemplate the methods of the Path.

What is meant by a son of good family who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and—having exhausted birth and death, established the holy life, and accomplished what was to be done—truly knows that he will no longer undergo rebirth in a womb.
At that time, the brahmin immediately became an arhat.
Then, the Venerable Mṛgaśiras addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have now come to know the Dharma practiced in the conduct of an arhat."
The World-Honored One said:
"How do you know the conduct of an Arhat?
Mṛgaśiras replied to the Buddha:
"Now there are four elements. What are the four?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element."
"Thus it is, O Tathāgata!
There are these four elements.

When a person’s life comes to an end at that time, earth returns to its own nature as earth, water returns to its own nature as water, fire returns to its own nature as fire, and wind returns to its own nature as wind."
The Blessed One said:
"How is it, bhikkhu? How many elements are there now?"
Mṛgaśīrṣa said to the Buddha:
"In reality there are four elements, but in terms of their meaning, there are eight elements.
The World-Honored One replied:
“What are the four elements, and how can their meaning comprise eight elements?
Mṛgaśiras replied to the Buddha:
“There are now four elements.”
What are the four elements?
Earth, water, fire, and wind—these are called the four elements.
In what sense are there eight elements?
The earth element is of two kinds: either the internal earth element or the external earth element.
What is called the internal earth element?
Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, the body, skin, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, intestines, stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, and kidneys—these are called the internal earth element.
What is the external earth element?
Whatever is solid and firm is called the external earth element.
These are known as the two types of earth elements.
"What is the water element? There are two kinds of the water element: either the internal water element or the external water element.
As for the internal water element:"
Saliva, spittle, tears, urine, blood, and marrow—these are called the internal water element.
All external soft and moist things are called the external water element.
These are called the two kinds of water elements. What are called the fire elements?
There are two kinds of fire elements: either internal fire or external fire.
What is called "internal fire"?
That which causes all consumed food to be digested without remainder—this is called internal fire.
What is called "external fire"?
All external objects that are intensely hot are called the external fire element.
What is called the wind element?
Furthermore, there are two kinds of wind element: either internal wind or external wind.

That which is called the wind within the lips, the wind of the eyes, the wind of the head, the wind of exhalation, the wind of inhalation, and the winds within all the joints—this is termed internal wind.
What is meant by external wind?
That which is light, flickering, oscillating, and swift-moving—this is called external wind.
This, World-Honored One, is what is meant [by external wind].
"There are two kinds, yet in reality there are four, numbering eight.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!
Observing this principle, I see that when a person's life comes to an end, these four types each return to their respective origins."
The World-Honored One said:
"The nature of impermanence does not coexist with permanence.
Why is this so? The element of earth is twofold: either internal or external."
At that time, the internal earth element is an impermanent phenomenon, a phenomenon subject to change;
the external earth element, however, remains constant and does not change.
Thus, there are two kinds of earth, neither of which corresponds to permanence or impermanence.
The other three great elements are likewise thus; they do not correspond with either permanence or impermanence.
Therefore, Mṛgaśiras, although there are eight kinds, in reality there are only four.
"In this way, Mṛgaśiras, you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Mṛgaśiras rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are now four great and extensive teachings.”
What are the four? They are the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and the Precepts; these are called the four.
A bhikṣu should know that if a bhikṣu comes from the east, reciting the sūtras, upholding the Dharma, and practicing the prohibitive precepts, he might speak as follows:
‘I am able to recite the sūtras and uphold the Dharma; I observe the prohibitions and precepts, and I am extensively learned and well-versed.
Even if such a bhikṣu has something to say, one should not accept it nor place firm trust in it. One should instead engage that bhikṣu in discussion and debate with him according to the Dharma.
"What is meant by discussing together in accordance with the Dharma?

What is called 'discussing in accordance with the Dharma' refers to this extensive exposition of the four great elements; that is to say, the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and the Precepts. One should speak to that bhikṣu regarding the Sūtras, manifest the Vinaya, and analyze the Dharma."

Even when the sūtras are being expounded, or when the vinaya is displayed and the dharma is analyzed, if what is displayed therein corresponds to the sūtras and corresponds to the vinaya and the dharma, one should then receive and uphold it.
If it does not accord with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, you should reply to that person with these words:
"You should know this: this was not spoken by the Tathāgata."
However, what you have stated is not the basis of the authentic scriptures.
Why is this so? Because what I am now teaching—namely the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—is entirely inconsistent with it.
Since it is inconsistent with [the Dharma], one should inquire about their conduct regarding the precepts; if they do not accord with the practice of the precepts, one should say to that person:
"This is not the Tathāgata-garbha."
One should immediately dispatch the messenger; this is called the first exposition of the fundamental meaning of the Great Dharma.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! Suppose there is a bhikṣu who comes from the south and speaks as follows:"
"I can recite the sūtras, uphold the Dharma, observe the prohibitions and precepts, and possess extensive learning and great erudition.
Even if such a bhikṣu has something to say, one should not accept it, nor should one place firm faith in it; rather, one should engage that bhikṣu in debate.
Even if a bhikṣu should have something to say that does not correspond to the meaning, it should be set aside.
If, however, it does correspond to the meaning, one should reply to that person, saying:
"This is an exposition of the meaning, but it is not the original text of the True Sūtra."
At that time, one should grasp that meaning and not cling to the literal text of the sūtra.
Why is this so? Because meaning is the source for interpreting the sūtra; this is called the second fundamental principle for expounding the Great Meaning.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus! Suppose there is a bhikṣu who comes from the western direction, one who recites the sūtras, upholds the Dharma, observes the prohibitions and precepts, and is extensively learned and well-versed in the teachings.

When you are explaining the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma to that bhikṣu, yet that bhikṣu correctly understands the phrasing (*vyañjana*) but does not understand the meaning (*artha*), you should say to that bhikṣu:
"We do not clearly know whether these words were spoken by the Tathāgata."
"Is it not wrong?

Even when he preaches the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, if he understands the phrasing but not the meaning, although one hears what that bhikṣu has said, it is neither sufficient to praise as good nor sufficient to criticize as bad.
Furthermore, he questioned him regarding his conduct in the precepts; if [the disciple's response] corresponded [to the truth], he was mindful to accept it.

The reason for this is that when conduct in the precepts corresponds to the flavor [of the Dharma], its meaning cannot be fully clarified [through mere words]. This is called the third exposition of the meaning.
"Furthermore, monks! Suppose there is a monk who comes from the north, one who recites the discourses, upholds the Dharma, and practices the precepts:
'Virtuous ones, if you have any doubts or difficulties, come and ask about their meaning; I shall explain them to you.'"

"Even if that bhikṣu has something to say, it is not worth receiving nor worth reciting; however, one should question that bhikṣu regarding the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and the Precepts, and whatever corresponds to these, one should then inquire about its meaning."
If, moreover, it is consistent with the meaning, one should then praise that bhikṣu, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Worthy sir! This is truly what the Tathāgata has spoken.
Its meaning is not confused; it is entirely consistent with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and the precepts.
"One should seek that bhikṣu through the offering of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata reveres the Dharma; therefore, whoever makes an offering to the Dharma has already paid reverence to me."
As for the contemplation of dharmas, one contemplates that because there are dharmas, there is a self;

because there are dharmas, there is the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; because there are dharmas, there are the fourfold assemblies; and because there are dharmas, there are the four castes existing in the world.
The reason for this is that as long as the Dharma remains in the world, there will appear in the Bhadrakalpa a Great Majestic King; from that time onward, the four castes have existed in the world.
If the Dharma remains in the world, then the four castes remain in the world:
the Kṣatriyas, the Brāhmaṇas, the artisans, and the householders.
If the Dharma remains in the world, then the position of the Wheel-Turning Sage King will not be interrupted.

If this Dharma remains in the world, then the lineage of the Four Great Kings, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven shall likewise remain in the world.
If this Dharma remains in the world, then the devas of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm will likewise remain in the world.

If this Dharma remains in the world, then the fruit of the srotāpanna, the fruit of the sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of the anāgāmin, the fruit of the arhat, the fruit of the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-vehicle will all manifest in the world.

Therefore, bhikṣus! You should properly revere the Dharma. When that bhikṣu makes offerings at the appropriate time and provides what he requires, you should speak to that bhikṣu, saying: "Excellent!"
"Excellent!
What you have said today is truly what has been spoken by the Tathāgata.
Thus it was said, O bhikṣus!
There is this meaning of the extensive exposition of these four great elements.
"Therefore, monks, you should maintain the mind and fix the intention to practice these four matters, without allowing them to leak away or be lost."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit assembled the fourfold army early in the morning, mounted his precious feathered chariot, and went to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the Great King, saying: "Great King!
From where have you come?"
"Furthermore, why is it that your body is covered in dust and you have assembled the fourfold army? What is the cause for this?
King Prasenajit replied to the World-Honored One:
"In this kingdom, a great bandit has arisen; last night at midnight, I raised my troops and captured him."
However, his body being weary, he wished to return to the palace; yet on the way, he again thought to himself:
"I ought first to go to where the Tathāgata is, and only then enter the palace."
"Because of these matters, I have been restless both in sleep and waking;

now, as the merit of destroying the bandits is established, I am so filled with joy and exultation that I cannot contain myself, and have therefore come here to pay my respects and seek your audience."
"If I had not mobilized the army last night, I would not have captured the bandit.
At that time, the World-Honored One said, "It is so."
"Great King! It is as Your Majesty has said.
Your Majesty should know that there are four conditions which are fundamentally characterized by initial suffering followed by subsequent happiness."
What are the four? Rising early at dawn involves initial suffering followed by later happiness;
likewise, consuming oil and clarified butter involves initial suffering followed by later happiness.
If, when taking medicine, there is first suffering followed by happiness;
or if in one's household affairs and marriage, there is first suffering followed by happiness—
this, Great King, is what is meant.
"Based on these four conditions, there is first suffering and subsequently happiness.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What the World-Honored One has spoken is truly appropriate; based on these four conditions, there is first suffering and subsequently happiness."
"The reason for this is that as I observe these four matters today, they are like looking at jewels in the palm of one's hand; all of them follow the principle of suffering first and happiness later.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to King Prasenajit, causing his heart to give rise to joy.
Having heard the Dharma, the king addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"State affairs are numerous and pressing; I wish to return to my domain.
The World-Honored One told him:
"It is time to know that this is the moment.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew.
Not long after the king had departed, at that time the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are now these four causal bases which are painful at first but pleasant in the end. What are the four?"
Cultivating the holy life is first difficult and later joyful;
reciting and studying the scriptures is first difficult and later joyful;
practicing seated meditation and mindfulness-concentration is first difficult and later joyful.
Counting the inhalations and exhalations is initially painful but later becomes pleasant. This, monks,
is what is meant by practicing these four things which are initially painful but later become pleasant.
If there are bhikṣus who practice this dharma of initial suffering followed by subsequent happiness, they will surely attain the bliss of the fruit of retribution as a śramaṇa later on.
"What are the four? [They are:]..."

If there is a bhikṣu who applies himself diligently to this Dharma, free from desire and unwholesome states, maintaining mindfulness, joy, and tranquility, he dwells with his mind in the first dhyāna and attains the bliss of a śramaṇa.

Furthermore, when initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) have ceased, and with a mind full of joy within, one becomes focused and single-minded; being without initial application or sustained application, one dwells in the second dhyāna, maintaining mindfulness of joy and tranquility. This is called attaining the second happiness of a śramaṇa.

Furthermore, with non-thought, one dwells the mind in equanimity (*upekṣā*), constantly maintaining self-awareness; one perceives the body as possessing bliss, that which is cherished and hoped for by the noble ones (*ārya*). Dwelling in the joy of mindful equanimity, one roams the mind in the third dhyāna. This is called attaining the third happiness of a śramaṇa.

Furthermore, when suffering and pleasure have already ceased, and there is no longer the affliction of sorrow or grief, one dwells in neither-suffering-nor-pleasure with pure mindfulness and awareness, the mind roaming in the fourth dhyāna; this is called possessing these four joys of the śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

If there is a bhikṣu who practices this—first undergoing hardship and later obtaining the four kinds of śramaṇa bliss as its retribution—he severs the net of the three fetters, becomes a srotāpanna established in the dharma of non-retrogression, and will certainly reach nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, bhikṣus!
If one severs these three fetters and attenuates lust, anger, and delusion, one becomes a sakṛdāgāmin; returning once more to this world, one will surely bring an end to suffering.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!
If there is a bhikṣu who has severed the five lower fetters and become a non-returner (anāgāmin), he attains parinirvāṇa there and does not return to this world.

"Furthermore, bhikṣus! If there is a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, who has attained the untainted liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself through direct experience in this very life and dwelling therein:
'Birth and death have been ended; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further taking of a womb,' he knows this as it truly is."
By practicing this method of initial suffering, that bhikṣu subsequently attains the bliss of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
"Therefore, O bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means to accomplish this state of initial suffering followed by subsequent bliss."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Four types of persons appear in the world. What are the four?
There is the śramaṇa who resembles the flower of the *utpala* (blue lotus).”
There is the śramaṇa who resembles the pāṭali flower;
there is the śramaṇa who resembles the soft;
and there is the śramaṇa who is the softest among the soft.
"What is meant by a śramaṇa who resembles the *utpala* flower?

There is a certain person who has severed the three fetters, become a *srotāpanna*, and entered the state of non-retrogression; he is destined for *nirvāṇa*, though at the very slowest, he will undergo seven deaths and seven births.

Or again, there are those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*) or attain the state of being 'born only once more' (*ekavīcika*), who are like the *utpala* flower that blooms in the morning and grows in the evening."

This bhikṣu is also like this: having exhausted the three fetters, he becomes a srotāpanna, established in the dharma of non-retrogression and destined for nirvāṇa. At the very slowest, he will undergo seven deaths and seven births; however, if he seeks skillful means with a courageous mind, he may attain the stage of "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula) or "one with only one more interval" (ekavīcika), thereby entering the path to enlightenment. This is called the saṃgha-member who is like the *yūthikā* flower.
"What is meant by a śramaṇa who is like a *pāṭalī* flower?

There is a certain person whose three fetters (*saṃyojana*) are exhausted, whose lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated; having become a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), he returns to this world only once more to bring an end to suffering."
If one is somewhat slow, they will reach the end of suffering upon arriving in this world;
if one is courageous, they will reach the end of suffering right here and now.
It is like the *pāṭalī* flower, which opens at dawn and withers by evening; such is called a *pāṭalī* flower ascetic.

“What is a gentle śramaṇa? There is a certain person who has severed the five lower fetters, become a non-returner (anāgāmin), and attains parinirvāṇa right there, not returning to this world; he is called a gentle śramaṇa.”
“What is a śramaṇa who is the softest among the soft?

There is a person whose outflows are exhausted, who has attained the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and who, having realized this for himself through direct experience in the present life, dwells therein, knowing as it truly is:
‘Birth and death have been ended; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further undergoing of rebirth.’”
This is called the most supple among the supple śramaṇas. "These, bhikṣus,
are the four types of persons who appear in the world."
Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to be gentle śramaṇas amidst gentleness. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Sudatta, Sumaṅgala, Piṇḍola, Reṇu, Andhaka, and Hasta.
The Deer Head Chapter: Extensive Exposition of Meaning;
The Chapter on Subsequent Joy and the Sūtra on Gentleness.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll Twenty; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll Twenty-One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-nine: On Suffering and Pleasure (Duḥkha-sukha-varga). (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are now four types of persons who appear in the world.”
What are the four?
Some people are first in suffering and later in happiness;
some people are first in happiness and later in suffering.
Some people are first in suffering and later in suffering;
some people are first in happiness and later in happiness.
"What kind of person is first in suffering and later in happiness?"

There may be a person born into a low and humble family—perhaps among the caste of executioners, the caste of craftsmen, or the caste of heretics—or born into other families that are destitute and lacking in food and clothing; such a person is born into that kind of household.
Furthermore, that person is free from wrong views and holds this view:

there is giving and there are recipients; there is this world and there is the next world; there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; there are fathers and mothers; there are arhats and others in the world who have received the teachings; and there are also the karmic fruits and retributions of good and evil.
If there is a family of extreme wealth, they do so because they recognize the retribution for the merit of their past giving and the retribution for their non-negligence.
If they further see those who lack food and clothing, they know that such people failed to practice the virtue of giving and thus constantly encounter poverty and low status.

That I have now encountered poverty and low status, lacking both food and clothing, is entirely due to my failure to cultivate merit in the past; by deceiving the people of the world and practicing ways of heedlessness, I have reaped the retribution for these evil deeds, and thus now encounter poverty and low status, with food and clothing insufficient.
Furthermore, if one sees śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who practice wholesome dharmas, one should immediately confess before them and reform one's past actions;
moreover, whatever remains should be shared equally with others.
When his body breaks up and his life ends, he is reborn in a happy destination;
if he is reborn among humans, he possesses abundant wealth and many treasures, lacking nothing.
This is called the case of one who first experiences suffering and later experiences happiness.
"Who are those people who first experience pleasure and later experience suffering?
