In this regard, there is a certain person born into a noble family—whether of the Kṣatriya caste, the Vaiśya caste, a great clan, or a wealthy and influential household—where food and clothing are abundant, and he is thus born into such a family."
However, that person constantly harbors wrong views and is associated with extreme views; he then holds this view:

"There is no giving, there is no recipient, nor is there retribution for deeds in this world or the next; there are no parents, there are no arhats in the world, nor are there any who have attained realization, and furthermore, there is no retribution for good or evil."
That person holds such a false view; furthermore, when they see a family of great wealth and status, they think:
"This person has possessed these riches for a long time."
The male has long been male, the female has long been female, and the animal has long been an animal.
They do not delight in giving alms, nor do they uphold the precepts.
If they see a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who upholds the precepts and give rise to a mind of anger, thinking:
"This person is hypocritical; how could there ever be a response of karmic reward for him?"
After that person’s body perishes and their life ends, they will be reborn in hell;
if they should obtain human birth, they will be born into a poor household, lacking food and clothing, with their bodies exposed and without sufficient sustenance.
This is called the person who first experiences pleasure and later experiences suffering.
What kind of person first experiences suffering and later experiences suffering?

In this regard, there is a person born into a poor and lowly family—perhaps a family of executioners, or artisans, or other such inferior families—who lacks food and clothing; such a person is born into that kind of household.
Furthermore, that person harbors wrong views and is associated with extreme views; such a person holds this view:
"There is no giving, there is no recipient, nor is there any retribution for good or evil in this world or the next; there are no parents, and there are no arhats in the world."
They do not delight in giving, nor do they uphold the precepts.
Furthermore, when they see śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, they immediately give rise to anger toward these noble and holy persons;
when such people see the poor, they say, "This has been so for a long time."
Seeing a wealthy person, one says, "They have had this for a long time";
seeing one's father, one thinks, "He was my father in the past"; seeing one's mother, one thinks, "She was my mother in the past.
When such a person’s body breaks up and their life ends, they are reborn in hell.
If one is born among humans, being extremely poor and lowly, with food and clothing insufficient, this is called a person who was miserable before and is miserable after.
"What kind of person is one who is happy before and happy after?

There may be a person born into a wealthy and noble family—whether of the Kṣatriya caste, the Brāhmaṇa caste, the royal lineage, or the merchant lineage—or born into a household with abundant wealth and many treasures; in whatever place they are born, there is no lack or deficiency, and such a person is thus born into this family.
Thereupon, that person possesses right view and is free from wrong view; he then holds this view: there is giving and there is one who receives;

there is this world and the world beyond; there are recluses and brahmins in the world, as well as the retribution for good and evil deeds; there is a father and there is a mother; and there are arhats in the world.
If that person again sees a wealthy and noble family possessing abundant riches and many treasures, they will then think:
"This was brought about by the generosity of this person in former days."
Furthermore, if one sees a poor and lowly family, [one should think]: "This person was formerly such because they did not practice giving.
Therefore, I should now give according to the occasion, lest I be reborn again into a poor and lowly family; thus, I shall always delight in bestowing gifts and favors upon others."

If that person sees a śramaṇa or a practitioner of the Way, they should inquire after their well-being at the appropriate time according to propriety, and provide them with clothing, bedding, food and drink, seats and bedding, and medicine for illness and weakness, giving all these as acts of charity.
Furthermore, after the end of life, if one is reborn in a good destination among the devas,
or among humans in a wealthy and noble family with abundant riches and many treasures, this is called "one who was happy first and is happy later."
At that time, a certain bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“I observe that among the beings of this present world, some experience suffering first and happiness later; some experience happiness first and suffering later; some experience suffering first and suffering later; and some experience happiness first and happiness later.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:

"There are these conditions by which certain classes of sentient beings experience suffering first and happiness later; there are likewise those sentient beings who experience happiness first and suffering later; there are likewise those sentient beings who experience suffering first and suffering later; and there are likewise those sentient beings who experience happiness first and happiness later."
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“By what causes and conditions does one first experience pleasure and later suffering?
And by what causes and conditions does one first experience suffering and later pleasure?”
“Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is there suffering first and suffering later?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is there happiness first and happiness later?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Monks, you should know that even if a person lives for a hundred years, it is merely ten decades.
Even if one’s life were to last through the entirety of winter, summer, spring, and autumn.”
Furthermore, monks!

Suppose one were to perform various meritorious deeds for a hundred years, yet during those same hundred years were to commit various evil karmas and hold various wrong views; at another time, he might experience pleasure in winter and suffering in summer.
If, throughout a hundred years, one’s merit is complete and never deficient;

or if, within those same hundred years, one has held various wrong views and committed unwholesome deeds, one will first undergo the retribution for those sins and subsequently receive the blessings of one's merit.
Furthermore, if one performs merit for a short time but commits offenses for a long time,
then at the time of rebirth, one will experience merit for a short time but experience suffering for a long time.

If, moreover, one commits offenses for a short time and continues to commit offenses for a long time, that person will experience suffering first and suffer even more afterward at the time of rebirth.
Furthermore, if one performs various meritorious deeds and practices the giving of alms for even a short time, one will experience happiness first and happiness later in future lives.
This, monks, is what is meant.

By these causes and conditions, there is first suffering and later happiness; by these causes and conditions, there is first happiness and later suffering; by these causes and conditions, there is first suffering and later suffering; and by these causes and conditions, there is first happiness and later happiness.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only this, World-Honored One:
if there are sentient beings who desire initial happiness followed by subsequent happiness, they should practice giving to seek this initial happiness followed by subsequent happiness."
The World-Honored One said:

“It is so, bhikṣu! As you have said, if there are sentient beings who wish to attain nirvāṇa, the path of an arhat, or even the path of a buddha, they should practice giving within that state and cultivate all manner of meritorious deeds.”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Four types of persons appear in the world. What are the four?
There is the person whose body is at ease but whose mind is not at ease;”
There are some whose minds are delighted but whose bodies are not;
there are some whose minds are not delighted and whose bodies are also not delighted;
and there are some whose bodies are delighted and whose minds are also delighted.
“What kind of person is one whose body is happy but whose mind is not?

In this regard, there is an ordinary person who performs meritorious deeds and provides the four requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick—with nothing lacking; yet they cannot avoid the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell, nor can they escape the miserable destinies.”
This is called a person whose body is at ease but whose mind is not at ease.
What kind of person has a mind at ease but a body that is not at ease?

It refers to an Arhat who does not perform meritorious deeds; among these four kinds of offerings, he cannot provide for himself and ultimately fails to obtain them, yet he merely avoids the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—just as an Arhat is merely a metaphor for a bhikṣu.
This is called a person whose mind finds joy while the body does not find joy.
What kind of person is one whose body does not find joy and whose mind also does not find joy?

It refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who does not perform meritorious deeds and is unable to obtain the four requisites of robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick; such a person constantly fails to escape the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
This is called a person whose body is not at ease and whose mind is not at ease.
What kind of person has both body and mind at ease?

It refers to an Arhat who performs meritorious deeds and is provided with the four requisites without any deficiency—namely, robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick—and who is further liberated from the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
This refers to the bhikṣu who is a mere corpse.
These, monks, are called the four types of persons found in the world.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means; you should be like the bhikṣu Śīlavanta. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of the four merits of the Brahmā realm.”
What are the four?
If there is a faithful son or daughter of good family who, where no stūpa has previously been erected, erects one therein, this is called the first Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, when a faithful son or daughter of good family repairs an old monastery, this is called the second merit of receiving Brahma-like bliss.
Furthermore, when a faithful son or daughter of good family brings the noble Saṃgha into harmony, this is called the third merit of receiving Brahma-like bliss.

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata first turned the wheel of Dharma, the devas and people of the world exhorted him to turn the wheel of Dharma; this is called the fourth reception of Brahma’s merit. These are the four receptions of Brahma’s merit.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"How much, in total, is the merit of Brahmā?
The Blessed One replied:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall now speak."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is. The World-Honored One said:

“The land of Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas from east to west and twenty-one thousand yojanas from south to north; its shape is like a chariot. All the merit possessed by the sentient beings therein is equal to the merit of a single wheel-turning monarch.”
“Goyānī is thirty-two thousand *li* in length and breadth, and its terrain is shaped like a half-moon.
Bhikṣus, you should know that the people of Jambudvīpa, together with the merit of a single wheel-turning monarch, are equal in merit to a single person there.”
"Furthermore, monks!

The land of Pūrvavideha is thirty-six hundred thousand *li* in length and breadth, and its terrain is square. Even if one were to calculate the merit of both Jambudvīpa and Aparagoyānī together, it would not equal the merit of a single person in that Pūrvavideha."

“Bhikṣus, you should know that Uttarakuru is forty thousand *li* in length and breadth, and its terrain is like the full moon. Even if one were to calculate the merit of the people of the other three continents, it would not equal the merit of a single person in Uttarakuru.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know: the merit of all the people of the four continents does not equal the virtue of the Four Heavenly Kings;
the merit of the people of the four continents together with that of the Four Heavenly Kings does not equal the merit of the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
and the merit of the four continents, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Heaven of the Thirty-three together does not equal the merit of Śakra Devānām Indra alone.”
If one were to calculate the merit of the four continents, the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and Śakra Devānām Indra, it would not equal the merit of a single Yāma Heaven deity;

if one were to calculate the merit of the four continents, the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Śakra Devānām Indra, and the Yāma Heaven, it would not equal the merit of a single Tuṣita Heaven deity;
and if one were to calculate the merit from the four continents up to the Tuṣita Heaven, it would not equal the merit of a single Nirmāṇarati Heaven deity.

If one were to calculate the merit from the four continents up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, it would not equal the merit of a single being in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations;
if one were to calculate the merit from the four continents up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, it would not equal the merit of a single Brahmā King.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that this is the merit of Brahmā.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who seek such merit, this is its measure.”
Therefore, bhikṣus! Those who desire to seek the merit of Brahmā should seek skillful means to accomplish that merit.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four kinds of nutriment for the various classes of sentient beings that sustain and nourish them.”
What are the four? They are:
edible food, whether gross or subtle; contact as food; mental volition as food; and consciousness as food. These are called the four nutriments.
"What is called 'edible food' (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra)?
That which is edible food is, for example, that which is eaten by people today—whatever items enter the mouth that are fit to be chewed and consumed; this is what is called edible food."
"What is called the nutriment of contact?

That which is called the nutriment of contact refers to clothing, parasols, various fragrant flowers, incense, fire, and scented oils; gathering with women and whatever else the body comes into contact with—this is what is called the nutriment of contact."
"What is meant by 'nutriment of mindfulness' (smṛty-āhāra)?

Whatever is mentally recollected, conceived, or contemplated within the mind—whether expressed through speech, experienced through physical contact, or comprised of the dharmas one upholds—is called the nutriment of mindfulness."
"What is the nutriment of consciousness?

That which is perceived by consciousness and known by the mind—beginning from the Brahmā heavens up to the heavens of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—takes consciousness as its nutriment; this is called the nutriment of consciousness."
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus:
there are these four nutriments; by means of these four nutriments, the classes of sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death, from this world to future worlds."
Therefore, monks, you should together abandon these four kinds of nutriment. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).”

What are the four? They are the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhānapratisaṃvid).
What is meant by the analytical knowledge of meaning?

What is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (arthapratisaṃvid) is this: regarding whatever is spoken by various beings—whether spoken by devas, nāgas, or spirits—one is able to discern their meaning; this is what is termed the analytical knowledge of meaning.
"What is meant by 'discrimination of the Dharma' (dharmapratisaṃvid)?

It refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures spoken by the Tathāgata—namely, the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, upadeśas, and the unshared teachings—as well as all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, and all outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas. That which is the indestructible reality of all dharmas, capable of being fully retained through dhāraṇī, is called discrimination of the Dharma."
"What is meant by eloquence of speech (*pratibhāna*)?

If, regarding the long and short utterances of previous beings—whether the speech of men, the speech of women, the speech of Buddhas, or the speech of brahmins, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—one preaches the Dharma to them in accordance with their respective origins, this is called eloquence of speech."
"What is meant by 'appropriate eloquence'?
When preaching the Dharma, one is without timidity and without fear, and is able to gladden the fourfold assembly; this is called appropriate eloquence."
"I shall now instruct you; you should become like Mahākauṣṭhila. Why is this?
Kauṣṭhila possesses these four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), by which he is able to provide extensive and detailed explanations for the fourfold assembly."
As I observe those among the assembly today, none surpasses Kauṣṭhila in attaining the four types of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
Since these four types of eloquence are possessed by the Tathāgata, you should therefore seek skillful means to achieve the four types of analytical eloquence.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four things that can never be conceived. What are these four?
Sentient beings are inconceivable;”
The world is inconceivable; the realm of the nāgas is inconceivable;
the sphere of the Buddha-land is inconceivable.
The reason for this is that one cannot attain the extinction of *nirvāṇa* by means of this place.
"In what way are sentient beings inconceivable?
From where do these sentient beings come?"
"From where do they go?
From what do they arise? Upon passing away from here, where will they be born?
In this way, sentient beings are inconceivable."
"What is meant by the inconceivability of the world?

There are those with false views who hold that the world is annihilated or that the world is not annihilated; that the world is finite or that the world is infinite; that this life is the same as the body, or that the life is one thing and the body another; or that the world was created by Brahmā, or by various great spirits and ghosts."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Brahmā created human beings; The world was created by spirits, or perhaps it was made by various ghosts— Who can definitively settle this claim?"
Enveloped by desire and ill will, these three are all equal;
the mind finds no autonomy, and worldly calamities arise. "Thus it is, bhikṣu!"
The world is inconceivable.
"In what way is the realm of the nāgas inconceivable?
From where does this rain issue—is it from the mouths of the nāgas?"
The reason for this is that the drops of rain do not issue from the dragon’s mouth.
Do they issue from its eyes, ears, or nose? This, too, is inconceivable.

The reason for this is that the drops of rain do not issue from the eyes, ears, or nose; rather, they depend solely on what the dragon’s mind intends. If it thinks of evil, it rains; if it thinks of good, it also rains. Furthermore, this rain is produced according to the fundamental nature of its past actions.

The reason for this is that within the belly of Mount Sumeru there is a deity named Mahābala, who knows the thoughts in the minds of sentient beings and is also able to produce rain; yet the rain does not issue from that deity’s mouth, but rather from his eyes, ears, and nose.
It is entirely because those devas possess supernatural power that they are able to produce rain.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
The realm of the nāgas is inconceivable.
"How is it that the realm of the Buddha-land is inconceivable?
Is the body of the Tathāgata created by his father and mother?
This, too, is inconceivable."
The reason for this is that the body of the Tathāgata is pure and free from defilement, receiving the vital breath of all beings.
Is it created by such persons?
This, too, is inconceivable.
The reason for this is that it transcends the conduct of ordinary beings.
The body of the Tathāgata is a great body, and this too is inconceivable.
The reason for this is that the body of the Tathāgata cannot be fabricated; it is beyond the reach of all devas.
Is the lifespan of the Tathāgata short?
This too is inconceivable. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata possesses the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Is the Tathāgata long-lived?
This, too, is inconceivable. Why is this so?
It is because the Tathāgata appears in the world and circulates therein, acting in accordance with skillful means and expedient devices.
The body of the Tathāgata cannot be measured; it cannot be described as long or short.
His voice likewise cannot be quantified; the Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice, his wisdom, and his eloquence are inconceivable, beyond the reach of worldly beings.
"In this way, the realm of the Buddha is inconceivable. Thus it is, bhikṣu!"
There are these four inconceivable matters, which are beyond the deliberation of ordinary people.

Yet these four things lack any root of goodness; they do not lead to the cultivation of the holy life, nor to the place of rest, nor even to the state of Nirvana. They merely cause people to become deluded and confused, their minds to go astray, and various knots of doubt to arise.
"The reason for this, bhikṣus, you should know, is that in the distant past, there was an ordinary person in this city of Śrāvastī who thought to himself:
'I shall now contemplate the world.'"
At that time, the man left the city of Śrāvastī and sat cross-legged by the side of a flower pond, contemplating the world:
"How was this world formed?"
What is its destruction?
Who created this world?
From where do these classes of sentient beings come?
"From where do they emerge?
At what time are they born?
At that moment, as the man pondered this, he saw four kinds of troops entering and exiting from within the pond water.
At that time, that person again thought to himself:
"I am now deluded and my mind is disordered; I am seeing here what does not exist in the world."
Then that man returned to the city of Śrāvastī and, while in the midst of the streets and alleys, spoke thus:
"Worthy sirs, you should know: that which does not exist in the world, I have now seen it."
At that time, the multitude of people replied to that person, saying:
"How can you see now that which does not exist in the world?
Then, that person replied to the multitude of people, saying:
"I previously had this thought:
'From what does the world arise?
Thereupon, I left the city of Śrāvastī and went to the side of a flower pond, where I reflected thus:"
"From where does the world come? Who created this world?
From where do these classes of sentient beings arise?"
"By whom was he born?
If his life has ended, where will he be reborn?
As I contemplated this, I then saw four kinds of troops entering and exiting from within the pond water—things that do not exist in this world, which I now behold.
At that time, the great multitude replied to that person, saying:
"If you are truly as mad and foolish as you claim, how could there be a fourfold army within the waters of a pond?
Among all those who are mad and foolish in the various worlds, you are the foremost!"
"Therefore, bhikṣus! Having contemplated this meaning, I have told you this. For what reason?
This is not a root of goodness or merit; one cannot cultivate the holy life through it, nor can one reach the state of nirvāṇa."
However, for one who attempts to conceive of this through discursive thought, it would cause madness and derangement of the mind.
Yet, bhikṣus, you should know that those people truly saw the fourfold army.
The reason for this is that in the past, when the devas and the asuras fought together, at the time of their combat, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.
At that time, the asura became terrified and transformed his body to be extremely small, passing through the hole in the lotus root.
This was seen by the Buddha’s eye, beyond the reach of others.
"Therefore, monks, you should contemplate the Four Noble Truths. Why is this?
Because these Four Noble Truths possess meaning and principle; they enable one to practice the holy life, to fulfill the dharma of a śramaṇa, and to attain nirvāṇa."
Therefore, monks! Abandoning these worldly phenomena, you should seek skillful means and contemplate the Four Noble Truths. Know this, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four bases of spiritual power (ṛddhipāda)."

What are the four? They are the supernormal power of the exhaustion of the practice of mastery-concentration; the supernormal power of the exhaustion of the practice of mind-concentration; [the supernormal power of the exhaustion of the practice of vow-concentration; and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of the practice of discernment-concentration].
The basis of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration through diligence;
the basis of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration through reflection.
What, then, is the basis of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration through mastery?

What is called the various samādhis, wherein one has mastery over what the mind desires and what the heart delights in, causing the body to become light and agile, able to conceal its form and become extremely subtle—this is called the first supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
"What is the supernormal power of the mastery of the mind through concentration?

It refers to the phenomena known by the mind pervading the ten directions, passing through stone walls without any obstruction; this is called the supernormal power of the mastery of the mind through concentration."
"What is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of formations through the samādhi of diligence?

It refers to this samādhi being free from weariness, free from fear, and possessing a courageous mind; this is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of formations through the samādhi of diligence."
"What is meant by his 'samādhi-conduct that exhausts the bases of psychic power through admonition'?
There are various samādhis by which he knows the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings, knowing them all at the moment they arise and the moment they cease."

To fully comprehend all states of mind—whether with desire or free from desire, with hatred or free from hatred, with delusion or free from delusion, with sluggishness or free from sluggishness, with distraction or free from distraction, narrow or not narrow, great or not great, limited or immeasurable, concentrated or unconcentrated, and liberated or unliberated—is what is called the supernormal power of the exhaustion of the practice of the *samādhi* of admonition.
"In this way, bhikṣus!
There are these four bases of psychic power; one who wishes to know the thoughts within the minds of all sentient beings should practice these four bases of psychic power."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four things that give rise to craving.
When craving arises in a bhikkhu, it arises because of these. What are the four?
A bhikṣu gives rise to craving because of robes;
he gives rise to craving because of alms-food;
he gives rise to craving because of bedding and seats.
"Because of medicine, a bhikṣu gives rise to craving. Thus, bhikṣu,
these are the four things that give rise to craving, by which one becomes stained and attached."
“Regarding those bhikṣus who are attached to clothing, I do not speak of them as such.
Why is this? Because even before they have obtained the robes, they give rise to anger and harbor thoughts of attachment.”
If there is a bhikṣu who is attached to such food, I do not speak of that person. Why is this?
Because even before he has obtained alms-food, he gives rise to anger and gives rise to conceptual attachments and thoughts.
As for those bhikṣus who are attached to beds and seats, I do not speak of them.
Why is this? Because even before they have obtained a bed or seat, they give rise to anger and harbor thoughts of attachment.
As for those bhikṣus who are attached to medicine and requisites, I do not speak of them as such.
Why is this? Because even before they have obtained the medicine, they give rise to anger and harbor thoughts of attachment.
“Bhikkhus, you should know that I shall now speak of two matters concerning robes: those which should be cultivated and those which should not be cultivated.
What is it that should be cultivated?
What is meant by "not associating"?
If one obtains clothing and, being excessively attached to wearing it, gives rise to unwholesome states, this is not to be associated with;
if, however, upon obtaining clothing one gives rise to wholesome states and is without attachment, this is to be associated with.
If unwholesome states arise when begging for alms, this is not to be approached;
if wholesome states arise when begging for alms, this is to be approached.
If unwholesome states arise when obtaining a seat, this is not to be approached.
"If, upon obtaining a seat, wholesome qualities arise, this may be cultivated; the same applies to medicine.
Therefore, monks, you should cultivate wholesome qualities and eliminate unwholesome qualities."
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves in this way:
desiring that the donors and benefactors obtain their merit, receive inexhaustible blessings, and attain the extinction of ambrosia (nirvāṇa).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Regarding the giving of clothing, food and drink, and bedding and seats—do not give rise to attachment therein; do not be reborn in any world."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are now four great rivers that flow from the Anavatapta Spring. What are these four? [The text continues with the names of the four rivers and their respective directions.]"
These are the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Vakṣu, and Śītā.

The waters of the Gaṅgā issue from the mouth of an ox-head and flow toward the east; the Sindhu flows south, issuing from the mouth of a lion; the Śītā flows west, issuing from the mouth of an elephant; and the Vakṣu flows north, issuing from the mouth of a horse.

At that time, after the four great rivers had circled the Anavatapta Spring, the Gaṅgā entered the eastern ocean, the Sindhu entered the southern ocean, the Vakṣu entered the western ocean, and the Sītā entered the northern ocean.
"At that time, once the four great rivers have entered the ocean, they no longer retain their original names, but are simply called 'the ocean.
This is also the case here.
There are four castes."
What are these four?

They are those of the kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, gṛhapati, and vaiśya castes who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, shave off their hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to study the Path, and no longer possess their original surnames, being called only "śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya."

The reason for this is that the assembly of the Tathāgata is like the great ocean; the Four Noble Truths are like the four great rivers, which, having removed the fetters and afflictions, lead one into the city of fearless Nirvāṇa.

"Therefore, monks, those of the four castes who shave off their hair and beard and, with firm faith, go forth from home to study the Path, they shall abandon their original names and call themselves disciples of the Śākyas."
The reason for this is that I am now truly a son of the Śākyas, having gone forth from among the Śākya clan to study the Path.
Bhikṣus, you should know that if one were to discuss the true meaning of being "born of a son," it is precisely the śramaṇa, the son of the Śākya clan, who should be so named.
Why is this? Birth arises from me;
it originates from phenomena and is accomplished through phenomena. Therefore, bhikṣus!
"You should seek skillful means so as to become a son of the Śākyas. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four immeasurable states of mind. What are the four?
Regarding loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*): for what reason are these called the "Brahma Palace"?

A bhikṣu should know that there is a Brahmā, a Great Brahmā, named *Sahasra*, to whom none are equal and who surpasses all others; he governs a thousand world-systems, and this is his palace. Therefore, it is called the "Brahma Palace."
“Monks! By the power and majesty inherent in these four Brahma-abodes, one is able to perceive this thousandfold world system;
therefore, they are called ‘Brahma-abodes. For this reason, monks!”

If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to transcend the heavens of the desire realm and dwell in a state free from desire, that assembly of the fourfold community should seek skillful means to accomplish these four Brahma-vihāras.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Twenty-one and Volume Twenty-two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 30: On the Srotāpanna, Number Thirty-One (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Mount Paṃsukūla in the kingdom of Magadha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his quiet chamber early in the morning and was walking in meditation outside.
At that moment, the novice Śuddha was walking in meditation behind the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One turned back and addressed the śrāmaṇera, saying:
"I now wish to question you on a matter of principle; listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well."
The śrāmaṇera Sudarśana replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"The permanent form and the impermanent form— do they constitute a single meaning,
or do they possess various distinct aspects?"
The novice Sudarśana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for the existence of both permanent form and impermanent form, these meanings are manifold; they do not constitute a single meaning."
The reason for this is that that which possesses permanent form is internal, while that which lacks permanent form is external; for this reason, the meanings are manifold rather than being singular.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Sudatta! As you have said, you have eloquently explained this meaning: that there is both permanent form and impermanent form; this meaning is manifold, not a single meaning."
"What do you think, Sūta!
Are the meaning of 'with outflows' (sāsrava) and the meaning of 'without outflows' (anāsrava) one and the same meaning,
or are they different meanings?"
The śrāmaṇera Sudāsa replied:
"The meaning of 'with outflows' (sāsrava) and the meaning of 'without outflows' (anāsrava) are distinct; they are not a single meaning.
Why is this so? The meaning of 'with outflows' refers to the fetters (saṃyojana) of birth and death."
"The meaning of 'outflow-free' (anāsrava) is the dharma of nirvāṇa.
For this reason, its meanings are manifold; it is not a single meaning.
Thus spoke the World-Honored One.
“Excellent! Excellent, Sūda!
"As you have said, that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is nirvāṇa.
The World-Honored One replied:
"The phenomenon of aggregation and the phenomenon of dispersion—do these have the same meaning?"
"Is this because there are several meanings?
The novice Sudatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The form of aggregated phenomena and the form of dispersed phenomena—these meanings are manifold; they are not a single meaning."
The reason for this is that "the form of the aggregated dharmas" refers to the physical forms of the four great elements;
"the form of the dispersed dharmas" refers to the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering.
Speaking from this perspective, the meanings are manifold and not of a single meaning.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Sudatta! As you have said, the matter of "aggregated form" and "dispersed form" has several meanings;
it is not a single meaning. How so, Sudatta?
“Are the meaning of ‘appropriation’ (upādāna) and the meaning of ‘aggregate’ (skandha) one and the same, or are they many?
The novice Śuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The meaning of 'feeling' (vedanā) and 'aggregate' (skandha) differs; they do not have the same meaning.
Why is this so? Feeling is formless and invisible, whereas the aggregates possess form and are visible. For this reason, their meanings differ; they do not have the same meaning."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Śūta! As you have said, the meaning of 'feeling' (vedanā) has many aspects; it is not of a single meaning.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Regarding the words ‘existence’ and ‘non-existence,’ how many meanings do they have?
Are they one and the same meaning?
The śrāmaṇera addressed the Buddha, saying:
“There are words and there are wordlessness; their meanings are manifold, not of a single meaning.
Why is this so? That which has words refers to the fetters of birth and death;
that which is wordless refers to nirvana.”
"Speaking from this perspective, the meanings are manifold; they are not of a single meaning.
The World-Honored One said: "Excellent!"
Excellent, Sūda!
As you have said, that which possesses letters is birth-and-death;
"That which is without words is nirvana.
The World-Honored One said,
"What do you think, Sūta?"
"Why is it that having names and letters is called birth-and-death, while being without names and letters is called nirvāṇa?
The śrāmaṇera addressed the Buddha, saying:
"That which has names and letters has birth and death, and has end and beginning; that which is without names and letters has no birth and no death, and no end and no beginning."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Suḍata! As you have said, that which has words is the dharma of birth and death;
that which is wordless is the dharma of nirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the śrāmaṇera, “You have spoken these words well; I now grant you the status of a great bhikṣu.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One returned to the Sahasravarga Lecture Hall and addressed the bhikṣus:

"The realm of Magadha has gained a great and excellent benefit by allowing the śrāmaṇera Sudatta to wander within its borders. Furthermore, those who provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick will also gain excellent benefit.
Even his parents who gave him birth have gained excellent benefit, for they were able to give birth to this bhikṣu Sudatta."
If the family into which a bhikṣu like Sūta is born attains great fortune, I now tell you, monks:
you should train yourselves to be like the bhikṣu Sūta.
Why is this? This bhikṣu Sudatta is extremely intelligent; he expounds the Dharma without obstruction and without any timidity. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves to be like the bhikṣu Sūta! This, monks,
is how you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude before and behind as he preached the Dharma.
At that moment, there was an elder bhikṣu among the assembly who, facing the World-Honored One, lay down with his legs extended and fell asleep.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera Sumana, about eight years of age, sat cross-legged not far from the World-Honored One, his mind focused on the practice before him.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar the elder bhikṣu sleeping with his legs outstretched, and he also saw the śrāmaṇera sitting upright in contemplation.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"One who is called an 'elder' Is not necessarily one whose hair and beard are shaved."
Though one may be advanced in years, If one does not escape foolish conduct,
But if one perceives the Dharma of the Truths, And brings no harm to living beings,
Having abandoned all defiled and evil deeds— Such a person is called an elder.
I now say, O Elder, that one need not necessarily have gone forth first to be considered foremost;
rather, it is by cultivating the roots of wholesome action and discerning right practice that one excels.
Even if one is young in years, if their faculties are complete and without deficiency, they shall be preeminent.
"This is what is called being an elder who discerns the practice of the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this elder sleeping with his legs stretched out?"
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
“We all see this. The World-Honored One told them:
“For five hundred lifetimes, this elder bhikṣu has constantly been in the form of a nāga; if he were to die now, he would surely be reborn among the nāgas.”
The reason for this is that they lack a heart of reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
If there are sentient beings who lack a heart of reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they shall all be born among the nāgas.
“Do you see the novice Śramaṇa Sumana, who is nearly eight years old, sitting upright in meditation not far from me?
The bhikṣus replied, “We do.”
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Seven days from now, this śrāmaṇera shall attain the four bases of psychic power and the Dharma of the Four Truths; he shall attain mastery over the four dhyānas and skillfully cultivate the four right efforts.”
The reason for this is that this śrāmaṇera Sumana possesses a heart of reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
For this cause, O bhikṣus!
"You should always diligently cultivate reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was an elder named Anāthapiṇḍada, who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures:
gold, silver, rare jewels, musāragalva, agate, pearls, amber, crystal, lapis lazuli, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, male and female slaves, and servants beyond measure.
At that time, in the city of Pūrṇabhadda, there was an elder named Pūrṇabhadra, who was also exceedingly wealthy and possessed many treasures:

*śukti*, *musāragalva*, pearls, amber, crystal, lapis lazuli, as well as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, male and female slaves, and laborers beyond measure. Furthermore, he had been a close friend of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada since their youth; they held mutual affection and respect for one another, never forgetting or forsaking each other.

Furthermore, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada always possessed many tens of millions of precious treasures and goods for sale in the city of Pūrṇavardhana, entrusting the elder Pūrṇa to manage and oversee them;
likewise, the elder Pūrṇa also possessed many tens of millions of precious treasures and goods for sale in the city of Śrāvastī, entrusting the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to manage and oversee them.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada had a daughter named Sujātā, whose countenance was upright and beautiful, with a complexion like the color of a peach blossom, rare in the world.
At that moment, the elder Pūrṇa, having some minor business, arrived at the city of Śrāvastī; he went to the house of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, and having arrived, took his seat.

At that time, the maiden Sumati emerged from her private chamber; she first prostrated herself before her parents, and afterwards prostrated herself before the elder Pūrṇa, before returning to her private chamber.

At that time, the householder Pūrṇa, seeing that the maiden Sumati was of upright countenance and the color of a peach blossom—rare in this world—asked the householder Anāthapiṇḍada: "Whose daughter is she?"
Anāthapiṇḍada replied, "The girl mentioned earlier was my own daughter. The elder Pūrṇa said:
"I have a young son who has not yet been married; could he be given in marriage to your humble family?
At that time, the elder Anāthapiṇḍika replied, "That would not be appropriate."
The householder Pūrṇa said,
"For what reason would it be improper?
Is it because of our family lineage?"
"Is it because of wealth? The householder Anāthapiṇḍada replied, "As for lineage and wealth, we are perfectly matched.
However, the deity you serve is different from mine; this girl serves the Buddha, a disciple of Śākya, whereas you serve heterodox teachers. For this reason, I have not acceded to your request."
Then the elder Pūrṇa said, "We shall naturally perform our own separate sacrifices for those we serve, and we shall separately provide offerings for those whom this girl serves.
The elder Anāthapiṇḍada said:

"If my daughter were to marry into your family, the wealth and treasures she would bring would be beyond measure; likewise, you, O Elder, would also have to provide wealth and treasures beyond measure."
The householder Pūrṇa said,
"How much wealth and treasure do you now demand?
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada replied:
"I now require sixty thousand measures of gold.
At that time, the householder immediately gave him sixty thousand measures of gold.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada again had this thought:
"I have tried to delay her by various means, yet I am still unable to stop it.
He said to the elder:
"If I were to give my daughter in marriage, I would go to consult the Buddha; whatever instructions the World-Honored One may give, I shall carry them out."

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada made an excuse for his business, as if it were a minor matter, and immediately went out to the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The daughter Sumati has been sought by the householder Pūrṇa of the city of Pūrṇavardhana; may she be given to him?"
"Is it not possible to give her?
The World-Honored One replied,
"If the maiden Śrīmālā were to marry into that kingdom, she would bring great benefit and deliver immeasurable numbers of people."
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada again thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One, through his wisdom of skillful means, will surely act in accordance with the needs of that land.

Thereupon, the householder prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew. Returning to his home, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink for the householder Pūrṇa.
The elder Pūrṇa said, "What shall I do with this food?
Will you simply give your daughter in marriage to me?"
Anāthapiṇḍada said, "If you desire it so, you may follow my advice.
Fifteen days from now, have your son come here."
Having spoken these words, he withdrew and departed.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇa, having prepared all that was required, arrived from within a distance of eighty yojanas riding in a precious feathered chariot;

meanwhile, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, having adorned his daughter, bathed her, and perfumed her with incense, set out in a precious feathered chariot to go and meet the son of the elder Pūrṇa, and they encountered one another midway.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇadhana took his daughter and brought her to the city of Pūrṇavasu.
At that moment, the people of the city of Pūrṇavasu had established a regulation:
"If any woman in this city marries into another country, she shall be severely punished."
"Furthermore, if anyone from another country takes a wife and brings her into the kingdom, they shall also be subject to severe punishment.
At that time, there were six thousand brahmins in that country who were honored by the people.
There was a restriction that stated:
"Should one violate this rule, one must provide a meal for six thousand brahmins.
At that time, the householder, realizing he had violated the rule, immediately provided a meal for six thousand brahmins.
As for the food consumed by the brahmins, they eat pork and pork broth, along with heavily fermented wine.
Furthermore, as for the clothing worn by the brahmins, they wear either white cotton cloth or garments of coarse wool.
Now, according to the custom of those brahmins, when entering a kingdom, they wear their robes draped over the right shoulder, leaving half the body exposed.
At that time, the householder said:
"The time has come; the food and drink are ready."
At that time, six thousand brahmins, all wearing their robes draped over one shoulder so as to leave half their bodies exposed, entered the householder’s home.

When the householder saw the brahmins approaching, he crawled forward on his knees to meet them, paying them respectful homage. The senior brahmin raised his hand in greeting, saying, "Excellent! He then went forward to embrace the householder around the neck and led him to his seat; the other brahmins each sat down in order according to their rank.
At that time, when the six thousand brahmins had finished taking their seats,
the elder said to the maiden Sumati:
"Adorn yourself and pay homage to our teachers."
The woman Sumati replied: "Stop! Stop!"
"Venerable sirs, I am unable to pay homage to those who go naked.
The elder said, "These are not naked people; they are not without a sense of shame."
"As for the garments they wear, those are their 'Dharma robes.
The woman Sumati said, "These shameless people all expose their bodies in public; what use do they have for Dharma robes?"
"Householder, please listen!
The World-Honored One has also spoken of two causes and conditions that are esteemed by the people of the world:
namely, having a sense of shame and having a sense of dread."

If these two matters did not exist, then it would be impossible to distinguish between parents, brothers, and the five types of kinsmen, nor could one differentiate between the honorable and the humble, or the high and the low.
Nowadays, there are fowl, dogs, pigs, sheep, donkeys, mules, and their like; all belong to the same category and possess no distinction of noble or base.
It is because these two principles exist in the world that one knows there is a difference between the noble and the base.

However, such persons, being devoid of these two qualities, are like chickens, dogs, pigs, sheep, donkeys, and mules kept together in a herd; they are truly unfit to be the object of one's prostrations.
Then, Sumati’s husband said to his wife, "You should now rise and pay homage to our teachers; these people are all the deities whom we serve."
The maiden Sumati replied: "Stop,
son of good family!"
"I cannot bring myself to pay homage to these shameless, naked people;
I am now a human being paying homage to donkeys and dogs.
Then the husband spoke again, saying:
"Stop! Stop! Noble lady!"
Do not speak such words; guard your own mouth and do not commit any transgression.
This is neither a donkey nor a deceptive delusion; the garment he wears is indeed the Dharma-robe.
At that time, the maiden Sumati wept and wailed with tears streaming down her face; her complexion changed, and she spoke thus:
"My parents and kinsmen would rather have their bodies mutilated or have their life-faculties severed for five watches than ever fall into such wrong views."
At that time, six thousand brahmins each raised their voices together and spoke thus:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Householder!
Why did you cause this maidservant to revile you so?
If she were invited, she would have prepared and served food and drink at the proper time."
At that time, the elder and his wife, Sumati, immediately prepared pork, pork soup, and heavily fermented wine, feeding six thousand brahmins until they were all fully satisfied.
After the brahmins had finished eating, they engaged in some discussion and then rose to depart.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇa was sitting alone on his high tower, distressed and lamenting in grief as he reflected:
"My taking these people here has brought ruin upon my household; it is no different from bringing disgrace upon my family."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Subhadra who had attained the five supernormal powers and also mastered the various dhyānas; he was highly esteemed by the elder Pūrṇa.
At that time, the brahmin Sūbhūti had this thought:
"It has been a long time since I parted from the householder; I should now go to see him.
Thereupon, the brahmin entered the city of Pūrṇa and went to the householder's residence, asking the gatekeeper:
“Where is the elder now? The gatekeeper replied, “The elder is on the upper floor;
he is in extreme distress and grief, beyond description.”
Then the brahmin went straight up to the upper story and met with the householder. The brahmin asked the householder:
"For what reason are you so distressed as this? Are you not being oppressed by officials, thieves, water, fire, or any other calamities?"
"Furthermore, is there no discord within your household?
The elder replied, "There have been no calamities from government officials or thieves; it is simply that minor domestic affairs have not gone as desired."
The brahmin asked, "I must hear the details; what were the circumstances?
The householder replied:
"Yesterday, I married off my son and thereby violated the national prohibition;

furthermore, my five close relatives were insulted. I invited the various masters to my home and intended to take my daughter-in-law there to pay them homage, yet they did not comply with my request."
The brahmin Subhadra replied, "In which country does this girl's family reside? Is it near or far for us to go and request her hand in marriage? The elder said:
"This woman is Anāthapiṇḍada’s daughter from the city of Śrāvastī.
When the brahmin Subhadra heard these words, he was struck with astonishment and alarm; covering his ears with both hands, he spoke thus:
"Alas! Alas!"
"Ha! Householder, how extraordinary!"
"How extraordinary!
That this woman was able to remain here, neither taking her own life nor throwing herself from the tower below—this is truly a great fortune.
For the reason being, the masters she serves are all practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya) who are present right now; how marvelous!"
"How extraordinary! The elder said,
"Having heard your words, I wished to mock you further."
The reason for this is that you are a follower of external paths and heterodox teachings; why then do you praise the conduct of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya?
What kind of majestic power and virtue does the teacher whom this woman serves possess?
"What kind of supernatural transformation is this? The brahmin replied, "Householder!"
"Do you wish to hear of this woman teacher’s divine virtue?
I shall now briefly explain its origins. The elder said:
"I wish to hear its explanation.
The brahmin replied:
"In the past, I went among the people north of the Snowy Mountains to beg for food; having obtained food, I flew to the Anavatapta Spring."
At that time, those devas, nāgas, and spirits saw me coming from afar; they all came toward me brandishing swords and shields, and spoke to me together, saying:
"O Seer Subhadra, do not come to stay by this spring, and do not defile it!
If you do not follow our words, your life-force shall be severed right now!"
Upon hearing these words, I immediately went to eat not far from that spring.

"Householder, you should know that the youngest disciple of this woman’s teacher is a novice named Kṣullaka; this novice also went to the north of the Snowy Mountains to beg for food, flying to the Anavatapta Spring, where he stood with palms joined holding a shroud from a corpse between the tombs, stained with blood and grime."
At that time, the great devas, nāgas, and spirits of Lake Anavatapta all rose to meet him, greeting him with reverence and asking after his well-being:
"Welcome, Teacher of Men; please be seated here."
Then, the novice Saṃtu went to the place where the spring was located.
Furthermore, at the center of the spring, there was a table made of pure gold.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera took the clothes of this deceased person and soaked them in water;

afterwards, he sat down to eat. Having finished his meal, he rinsed his bowl and sat cross-legged upon a golden table, straightening his body and composing his mind, fixing his mindfulness before him, and immediately entered the first dhyāna. Rising from the first dhyāna, he entered the second dhyāna;
rising from the second dhyāna, he entered the third dhyāna.
Emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Arising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness;
arising from the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the samādhi of cessation.

Emerging from the Samādhi of Cessation, he entered the Samādhi of Fiery Radiance; emerging from the Samādhi of Fiery Radiance, he entered the Samādhi of Watery Vapor; emerging from the Samādhi of Watery Vapor, he entered the Samādhi of Fiery Radiance.

Next, he again entered the Samādhi of Cessation; next, he entered the Samādhi of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; next, he entered the Samādhi of the Sphere of Nothingness; next, he entered the Samādhi of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness; next, he entered the Samādhi of the Sphere of Infinite Space; next, he entered the Fourth Dhyāna; next, he entered the Third Dhyāna; next, he entered the Second Dhyāna; next, he entered the First Dhyāna. Emerging from the First Dhyāna, he washed the clothes of the deceased.
At that time, devas, nāgas, and spirits would either tread upon the robes, or wash them, or take water from them to drink.
Then, having finished washing the robes, he lifted them up into the air to dry them.
At that time, having gathered his robes, the śrāmaṇera flew into the air and returned to his dwelling.
"Householder, you should know that at that time I saw him from afar but was unable to approach."
If even the youngest disciple of this woman’s teacher possesses such supernatural power, how much more so must it be for the eldest disciple?
And how could anyone possibly equal his teacher—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
Having contemplated this meaning, he spoke these words:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
"This girl was indeed capable of taking her own life, yet she did not sever the life-faculty.
At that time, the elder said to the brahmin,
"May we be permitted to see the teacher whom this girl serves?"
The brahmin replied, "You may ask this girl.
Thereupon, the elder questioned the maiden Sumati.
"I now wish to see the teacher you serve; can you cause him to come?
At that time, having heard this, the woman was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself, and she said:
"Please prepare food and drink at once; tomorrow the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus shall come here."
The elder replied, "You may now request it yourself; I do not understand the Dharma.
At that time, the elder’s daughter bathed her body, took a censer in her hand, ascended to the upper story of the high tower, joined her palms toward the Tathāgata, and spoke these words:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion; for although none are able to see the crown of Your head, there is nothing the World-Honored One does not know and nothing You do not perceive. This woman now stands here in distress; I only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon her with compassion."
Furthermore, he praised him with this verse:
"Beholding the world without exception, That which the Buddha-eye surveys,
He subdues the various ghost-kings and spirits, And likewise subdues Hārītī."
Just as that man-eating demon, who took human fingers to make garlands and later sought to harm his own mother, was nevertheless subdued by the Buddha;
and again, when a fierce elephant in the city of Rājagṛha was about to come and do him harm—
Furthermore, when he took refuge and offered his life, the various devas exclaimed, "Excellent!
He then traveled to the kingdom of Mātikā, where he encountered an evil dragon king;
upon seeing the Vajrapāṇi Mārṣa, the dragon himself took refuge and offered his life.
The various transformations are incalculable, yet you cause all to establish themselves in the Right Path;
now that I have encountered this calamity, I pray only that the Honored One will deign to bend his divine power.
At that time, fragrances like clouds hung darkly in the void of space.
Pervading the Jeta Grove and dwelling before the Tathāgata,
the Śākyas in the air paid homage with joy;
they also saw the incense before them, which had been requested by Sumati.
A rain of various kinds of flowers fell, beyond all measure,
completely filling the Jeta Grove, as the Tathāgata smiled and emitted light.
At that time, Ānanda perceived this wondrous fragrance within the Jeta Grove.
Having seen him, he went to where the World-Honored One was.
Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“May the World-Honored One deign to tell us:
what kind of fragrance is this that pervades the entire Jeta Grove Monastery?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This incense is sent by the Buddha; it was requested by the woman Sumati in the city of Pūrṇa.
You must now summon all the bhikṣus!
Have them assemble in one place and cast lots, and issue this command:”

"Monks, there are Arhats among you whose outflows are exhausted and who have attained the supernormal powers; they shall take up their bowls, for tomorrow we shall go to the city of Pūrṇa to accept the invitation of Sumati."
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction,
Ānanda immediately assembled the bhikṣus in the Hall of Universal Assembly and formed this thought:
"Let all those who are arhats who have attained the Way take up their robes and bowls."
At that time, the senior monk of the assembly was named Kūṭadanta; he had attained the stage of Srotāpanna, yet his fetters were not yet exhausted, and he had not attained the supernormal powers.
At that time, the Elder thought to himself: "Among this great assembly, I am the most senior elder;
yet my fetters are not yet exhausted, nor have I attained the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Therefore, I shall not be able to reach the city of Pūrṇa for the meal tomorrow.

However, among the Tathāgata’s followers, the one of the lowest rank is the novice Śrāmaṇera Nanda; he possesses supernormal powers and great majesty, and is capable of going there to accept the invitation. I, too, should now go to accept that invitation."
At that time, the Elder, with a mind of purity, while still abiding on the stage of training, received the voting tally (*śalākā*).

Then, the World-Honored One, with his purified divine eye, saw that Kuṇḍopadhānīya, who was abiding on the stage of training and receiving the tally, had immediately attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the one foremost in receiving śalākās is the bhikṣu Kuṇḍopadhānīya."

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus endowed with supernormal powers—Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Revata, Subhūti, Upagupta, Mahākapphiṇa, the Venerable Rāhula, Kuṇḍalapanthaka, and the novice Kuṇḍadhāna:
"By means of your supernormal powers, you should go ahead to that city."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the monk of the Sangha named Gaṇḍa, at the clear dawn of the following day, personally carried a large cauldron and flew through the air until he reached that city.
At that time, the elder and the people, having ascended to the high terrace desiring to behold the World-Honored One, saw from afar a messenger coming while carrying a cauldron on his back.
Then, the elder and his daughter spoke this verse:
“Clad in white robes with long hair, His body exposed like a swift wind.”
"Furthermore, she carries a large cauldron upon her back; is this your teacher?
At that time, the woman replied with a verse:
"This is not a noble disciple, but a messenger of the Tathāgata."
"One who possesses the three trainings and the five supernormal powers is called a *khaṇḍa*.
At that time, the messenger of Khaṇḍa circumambulated the city three times and went to the house of the elder.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera Sundara manifested five hundred flowering trees of various colors, all of them lush and flourishing; their colors were as exquisite as those of the utpala lotus.
Such flowers were beyond measure, and he proceeded toward that city.
At that time, the elder saw the śrāmaṇera approaching from afar and again questioned him with this verse:
"These many kinds of flowers, All suspended in the void;
And there is a person with supernormal powers— Is he perhaps your teacher?"
At that time, the woman replied with a verse:
"Regarding Subhadra’s previous statement about the foremost śrāmaṇera, his teacher is named Śāriputra; he is that man’s disciple."
At that time, the novice Saṃgharakṣita circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same time, the Venerable Pindola Bhāradvāja manifested five hundred oxen, all with blue coats and hair;
he sat cross-legged atop the oxen and traveled toward that city.
At that time, the elder saw her from afar and again asked the girl in verse:
"These great herds of cattle, their coats all blue-black;
sitting alone upon them— is this your teacher?"
The woman replied with a verse:
“He who can transform a thousand bhikṣus, Who dwells within the Jīvaka Grove,
Whose mind and spirit are exceedingly lucid— This one is named Paṇḍita.”
At that time, the Venerable Cūḍapanthaka, having circumambulated that city three times, went to the house of the elder.
At that same time, Rāhula again manifested five hundred peacocks of various colors;
sitting cross-legged upon them, he proceeded toward that city.
Having seen this, the elder again addressed the girl with these verses:
"These five hundred peacocks, Their colors are most wondrous;
Like those great generals of an army, Are these your teachers?"
Then the girl replied with these verses:
“The Tathāgata has taught the prohibitive precepts, In which there is nothing whatsoever to transgress;
One who can guard the precepts within the precepts Is the Buddha’s son, Rāhula.”
At that time, Rāhula circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same time, the Venerable Kapphiṇa manifested five hundred garuḍas of extreme ferocity;
sitting cross-legged upon them, he went toward that city.
At that time, having seen them from afar, the elder again questioned the girl with this verse:
"Five hundred garuḍas, Extremely powerful and courageous,
Fearless as they soar above— Are these your teachers?"
Then the woman replied with a verse:
“One who can practice the inhalation and exhalation, Who turns the mind toward wholesome conduct,
And whose power of wisdom is exceedingly vigorous— This one is called Kappina.”
Then, the Venerable Kapphiṇa circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the householder.
At that time, Upaka-Kāśyapa manifested five hundred nāgas, each with seven heads;
he sat upon them in the full lotus posture and went toward that city.
Having seen her from afar, the elder again questioned the girl in verse:
"These seven-headed nāgas, Their majestic countenances are most fearsome;
Those who come are beyond counting— Are these your teachers?"
Then the woman replied:
"He who always has a thousand disciples, who transforms Vaiśravaṇa through his supernormal powers,
and who is Upakaśyapa— he can indeed be called this man."
Then, Upika-Kāśyapa circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti manifested a mountain of lapis lazuli;
entering it, he sat cross-legged and proceeded toward that city.
At that time, having seen her from afar, the elder questioned the girl with a verse:
"This mountain is most wondrous, Entirely the color of lapis lazuli;
Now sitting within this cave— Is this your teacher?"
Then the woman replied with this verse:
"By virtue of the fruit of my past giving, I have now obtained this merit;
Thus I have become a fertile field of blessings, Like Subhūti, who understands emptiness."
At that time, Subhūti circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
Then, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana again manifested five hundred cranes, all pure white in color, and went toward that city.
At that time, having seen them from afar, the elder questioned the girl with this verse:
"These five hundred cranes, All their colors pure white,
Filling the entirety of space— Are these your teachers?"
Then the woman replied with these verses:
“The one who explains the teachings spoken in the Buddha’s sūtras, Who analyzes their meanings and phrases,
And further expounds upon the collection of fetters— This is named Kātyāyana.”
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana circumambulated that city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same time, Revata manifested five hundred tigers;
sitting upon them, he went toward that city.
Having seen this, the elder questioned the girl with these verses:
"These five hundred tigers, whose fur is so lustrous and sleek—
And he who sits upon them, is he your teacher?"
Then the woman replied with a verse:
"All are at the Jetavana Monastery, For six years they have not moved;
In meditative concentration they are foremost— This one is named Revata."
At that time, the Venerable Revata circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the householder.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha manifested five hundred lions, exceedingly fierce;
he sat upon them and went toward that city.
At that time, having seen this, the elder questioned the girl with a verse:
"These five hundred lions, Brave and most fearsome— Is he who sits upon them Your teacher?"
Then the woman replied with a verse:
"At the time of his birth, heaven and earth shook, and precious jewels emerged from the ground.
With pure eyes free from defilement— this is Aniruddha, the younger brother of the Buddha."
At that time, Aniruddha circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that same time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa manifested five hundred horses, all with vermilion manes and tails, adorned with gold and silver;
he sat upon them, and as celestial flowers rained down from the sky, he proceeded toward that city.
The elder saw them from afar and asked the girl in verse:
“Five hundred golden horses with vermilion manes and tails—
Are these the Universal Monarch, or are they your teacher?”
The woman replied with a verse:
"Foremost in the practice of dhūta, always compassionate toward the poor and destitute,
he to whom the Tathāgata gave half his seat— this is Mahākāśyapa."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana manifested five hundred white elephants, each with six tusks, seven parts of their bodies perfectly proportioned, and adorned with gold and silver;
he sat upon them and approached, emitting a great radiance that filled the entire world.
They proceeded toward the city, and while suspended in mid-air, they performed music and dance in incalculable variety, raining down all kinds of diverse flowers.
Furthermore, within the void, silken streamers, banners, and canopies were hung, most wonderfully marvelous.
At that time, having seen him from afar, the elder questioned the girl with a verse:
"A white elephant with six tusks, Seated above like a celestial king;
Now hearing the sound of music, Is this Śākyamuni?"
Then the woman replied with a verse:
"On that great mountain, he who has subdued the Nanda Dragon and is foremost in supernormal powers is named Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"My Teacher has not yet arrived; these are his disciples.
The Holy Teacher shall now come, and there is no place his radiance does not illuminate.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana circumambulated the city three times and proceeded to the house of the elder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the hour had come, donned his saṃghāṭī robe and ascended into the air to a height of seven fathoms above the ground.
At that moment, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya stood to the right of the Tathāgata, and Śāriputra stood to his left.
At that time, Ānanda, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, stood behind the Tathāgata holding a fly-whisk.
He was surrounded in front and behind by twelve hundred disciples, with the Tathāgata positioned most centrally among them.
Furthermore, among the disciples possessed of supernatural powers, Ājñātakauṇḍinya transformed himself into the Moon Deva-son, and Śāriputra transformed himself into the Sun.
"O Son of Heaven, among the other bhikṣus possessing supernormal powers, some may manifest as Śakra-devānām-indra, or manifest as Brahmā;
some may manifest as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, or take the form of Virūḍhaka, or Virūpākṣa, or take the form of Vaiśravaṇa, leading all the spirits and ghosts; or there may be others..."
Those who had assumed the form of a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) king manifested various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*):
some entered the fire-light samādhi, some entered the water-crystal samādhi, some emitted light, and some emitted smoke.

At that time, Brahmā Śakra stood to the right of the Tathāgata, and Śakra-devānām-indra stood to his left, holding a fly-whisk in his hand. Guhyaka Vajrapāṇi stood behind the Tathāgata, holding a vajra in his hand. Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, stood in the midst of the void above the Tathāgata, holding a canopy made of the seven treasures, fearing that dust or soil might fall upon the Tathāgata’s body.

At that time, Pañcaśikha held a lapis lazuli lute in his hand and extolled the merits of the Tathāgata; meanwhile, all the celestial deities remained in the midst of the void, performing tens of millions of kinds of music and scattering various heavenly flowers upon the Tathāgata.

King Prasenajit, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and the people of Śrāvastī all saw the Tathāgata in the air, seven fathoms above the ground; having seen him, they were all filled with joy, leaping for gladness beyond their own control.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada spoke this verse:
“The Tathāgata is truly divine and wondrous; He loves the people as his own infants.
How joyful is Sumati! He shall receive the Dharma of the Tathāgata.”
At that time, King Prasenajit and the householder Anāthapiṇḍada scattered various kinds of named incenses and mixed flowers.

Then the World-Honored One, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind, as well as by innumerable devas and spirits, proceeded toward that city like a king of peacocks soaring through the void.
At that time, Pañcaśikha praised the Buddha in verse:
"All fetters of birth are forever exhausted; The mind’s intentions are no longer confused.
