Being free from the hindrance of dust and defilement, He has entered that ancient realm."
The nature of the mind is utterly pure, having severed all demonic and evil thoughts;
with merit like the great ocean, you now enter that land.
Your countenance is most extraordinary, and no afflictions shall ever arise again.
Because he does not abide for himself, he has now entered that realm;
having crossed the abyss of the four floods, he has escaped birth, old age, and death;
having severed the root-source of existence, he has now entered that realm.

At that time, the elder Pūrṇa saw from afar the World-Honored One approaching; his faculties were serene and tranquil, a rarity in the world, as pure as celestial gold. Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his body was magnificent, like Mount Sumeru rising above all other mountains, or like a mass of gold emitting great radiance.
At that time, the elder questioned Sumati with a verse:
"Is this the light of the sun?
Never before have I seen such a countenance. Amidst these many thousands of millions of rays, I do not dare look upon it closely."
At that time, the maiden Sumati knelt with palms joined toward the Tathāgata and replied to the elder in verse:
"He is neither sun nor non-sun, yet he emits a thousand kinds of light;
for the sake of all sentient beings, he is likewise my teacher."
"All together they praise the Tathāgata, as previously described;
now we shall surely obtain the great fruit—let us diligently increase our offerings.
At that time, the elder Pūrṇadhana knelt with his right knee on the ground and again praised the Tathāgata in verse, saying:
“I take refuge in the Honored One of Ten Powers, whose golden-hued body is encircled by a halo, and whom gods and humans alike praise and revere; today I take refuge in his life.
The Honored One is now the King of the Day, as radiant as the moon among the stars.”
Having delivered those not yet delivered, today I take refuge in you.
Like the image of the Lord of Devas, like one who practices the Brahma-conduct with a compassionate heart,
liberated yourself and delivering all sentient beings— today I take refuge in you.
"Honored One among gods and men, supreme above all ghost kings,
you who have subdued all non-Buddhists— to you I now take refuge. At that time,
the maiden Sumati knelt with palms joined and praised the World-Honored One, saying:
"One who has subdued oneself can subdue others; one who is self-corrected can correct others.
By means of deliverance, one delivers the people; having attained liberation oneself, one further liberates others.
Having crossed over defilement, one enables others to cross over defilement; having illuminated oneself, one illuminates the multitude of living beings."
There is nothing that lacks measure; removing strife, there is no contention or dispute.
Abiding in ultimate purity, the mind does not waver.
Out of compassion for the world, the One of Ten Powers—him I reverently prostrate with my head.

“Possessing a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; endowed with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; most honored and foremost within the desire realm; supreme among the gods; fully possessing the seven riches; naturally born as Brahmā among devas and humans; peerless and beyond all comparison or likeness—I now take refuge in you.”
At that time, when the six thousand brahmins saw the World-Honored One perform such a supernatural manifestation, they each said to one another:
"We should leave this country and go to other lands; for this śramaṇa Gautama has brought the people of this kingdom under his influence."
These six thousand brahmins immediately departed from the kingdom and never entered it again.

They were like the lion, king of beasts, who emerges from the mountain valleys, surveys the four quarters, and lets out three roars; only then does he proceed toward his prey, while all other beasts and insects scatter in every direction, not knowing where to go, some fleeing through the air and others sinking into the earth.
Furthermore, if powerful divine elephants hear the roar of a lion, they each flee toward their respective destinations, unable to remain at ease.
This is because the Lion, the King of Beasts, possesses supreme majesty and spiritual power.
It was just like this: when those six thousand brahmins heard the sound of the World-Honored One’s voice, they each fled in haste, unable to find peace.
This was because the śramaṇa Gautama possessed such great majestic power.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers and entered the city of Pūrṇavardhana according to his usual custom.
As the World-Honored One stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the earth and heavens shook violently, and the various honored devas scattered flowers as an offering.
At that time, the people beheld the World-Honored One’s countenance; his faculties were serene and tranquil, and he was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
The people then spoke this verse:
"The Two-legged Honored One is most sublime; The brahmin does not dare to equal him.
There is no need to serve the brahmin; We have lost this Honored One among Men."
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the house of the elder and sat upon the prepared seat.
At that moment, the people of that country were extremely numerous.
Then, eighty-four thousand members of the elder’s household all gathered together, desiring to demolish the elder’s residence in order to see the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"These people will surely suffer some loss; I should exercise my supernormal powers so that all the people of the entire kingdom may see my body and the community of bhikṣus."

At that time, the World-Honored One transformed the house of the elder into the color of lapis lazuli, such that the interior and exterior could be seen of each other as clearly as looking at a jewel in the palm of one's hand.
Then, the girl Sumati approached the World-Honored One, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and with a heart filled with both sorrow and joy, she spoke this verse:
"Endowed with all wisdom, You have fully transcended all phenomena."
Furthermore, having severed the fetters of sensual desire, I now take refuge in myself.
It would be better for my parents to destroy both my eyes than for me to come to this place among those of wrong views and the five heinous crimes.
"What evil conditions did I create in my past lives, that I have come to this place, like a bird caught in a net? I pray you, sever this knot of doubt.
Then, the World-Honored One replied to the woman in verse:
"Do not now worry at all; let your mind be tranquil and open.
Do not give rise to conceptual attachments, for the Tathāgata shall now expound [the Dharma].
Originally you had no karmic conditions for transgression that led you to this place."
By the fruit of the vow I have made, I wish to deliver these sentient beings.
Now I shall uproot their very source so that they do not fall into the three evil realms;
thousands of classes of sentient beings shall attain liberation before you.
"Today you shall purify yourself, so that wisdom may become bright;
may the gods and the people alike behold you as one gazes upon a precious gem.
At that time, having heard these words, the maiden Sumati was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself.

At that time, the elder took his own servants and attendants and provided them with food and drink of various sweet delicacies. Seeing that the World-Honored One had finished eating, he offered pure water and took another small seat to sit before the Tathāgata;
the various attendants and the assembly of eighty-four thousand people each sat down in order, some sitting while announcing their own names.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually delivered a sublime discourse to the elder and the eighty-four thousand people of his kind. The discourse consisted of:

a teaching on ethical discipline, a teaching on generosity, and a teaching on rebirth in the heavens; it further explained that sensual desires are impure, that outflows are defilements and evils, and that renunciation is the essential path.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the mind of the elder, the girl Sumati, and the eighty-four thousand classes of people had been opened and their intentions liberated, preached to all these sentient beings the Dharma constantly taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Each of them, while still in their seats, was cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, just as an extremely pure white cotton cloth is easily dyed with color.

It was even so for the elder Pūrṇa, the maiden Sumati, and the eighty-four thousand people; their defilements were exhausted, they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, were freed from doubt, and attained fearlessness. They all took refuge in the Triple Gem and received and upheld the five precepts.
At that time, the maiden Sumati spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"The Tathāgata’s ears are pure and clear; Hearing that I have encountered this suffering, He has descended his spirit to arrive here, So that all people may attain the Dharma-eye."
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and returned to his dwelling.
Then, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions did the girl Sumati originally come to be born into a wealthy and noble family?"
By what causes and conditions did he fall into a family of such wrong views?
By what wholesome merits did he now attain the purity of the Dharma-eye?
And by what merits did he cause eighty-four thousand people to all attain the purity of the Dharma-eye?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa—a teacher perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One—who was wandering and teaching within the borders of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, together with a great assembly of twenty thousand bhikṣus."
At that time, there was a king named Karuṇā and a daughter named Sumana.

At that time, this girl possessed a heart of profound reverence; she upheld the prohibitive precepts before the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, constantly delighted in practicing generosity, and furthermore provided him with the four types of offerings.
What are the four? First, giving; second, affectionate respect; third, benefiting others; and fourth, impartial benefit.
At the abode of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, he recited the Dharma-verses from atop a high tower, chanting them aloud and making this universal vow:

"I have constantly maintained these four dharmas of receiving [the teachings], and have further recited the Dharma-verses before the Tathāgata. If there is even a hair’s breadth of merit therein, may I not fall into the three evil realms in whatever place I am born, nor fall into a poor household; in future lives, may I again encounter such a Honored One as this, cause me never again to turn back into a woman's body, and attain the purity of the Dharma-eye."
At that time, the people of the city, hearing that the princess had made such a vow, all gathered together and went to where the princess was, saying:
"Today the princess is most profoundly faithful; she performs various meritorious deeds, lacking nothing in the four requisites—generosity, loving-kindness, benefiting others, and impartial benefit."
He further made this vow:
"May I encounter such a Honored One in a future age.
If he should preach the Dharma for me, may I immediately attain the pure Dharma-eye."
"Today, by the power of this vow and oath made by the princess, may she and all the people of our kingdom and lands attain deliverance simultaneously.
At that time, the princess replied, "I take this merit and bestow it upon you all;
should we encounter a Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, may we all attain deliverance together."
"O bhikṣus, do you have any doubt?
Do not hold such a view.
The King Kāruṇika of that time was none other than the present Elder Sudatta."
The princess at that time was the present daughter Sumati;
the people of that kingdom at that time were the present assembly of eighty-four thousand.

By virtue of that vow, they have now encountered my person, heard the Dharma, and attained the Way; furthermore, all those among the populace have attained the pure Dharma-eye. This is its significance; you should bear it in mind and practice accordingly.
The reason for this is that these four things are the supreme fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
If there is a bhikṣu who draws near to these four things, he will attain the Four Noble Truths; he should seek skillful means to accomplish the dharma of these four things.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Twenty-two and Volume Twenty-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
31. The Thirty-First Chapter on the Superior-Superior Class (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī went to where the Blessed One was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
Then the brahmin said to the Blessed One:
"To dwell in a secluded cave is truly a hardship!"
"To dwell alone and walk by oneself, it is extremely difficult to apply the mind.
The World-Honored One told him: "It is so."
"O Brahmin! As you have said:
'To dwell in seclusion and live in caves is truly a great hardship! "
"To dwell alone and walk solitary is extremely difficult for the mind!
This is why: in the past, before I had attained the Way of the Buddha, while practicing as a bodhisattva, I constantly thought:
"To stay in a secluded and quiet cave is truly bitter; to dwell alone and walk solitary is extremely difficult for the mind."
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there is a son of noble family who, with firm faith, leaves the household life to study the Way, the śramaṇa Gautama is now the foremost among them; he brings great benefit and acts as a guide for those living beings."
The Blessed One said: "It is so, brahmin."
As you have said:
"Among all those sons of noble family who, with firm faith, leave the household life to study the Path, I am the foremost; I bring great benefit and act as a guide for my fellow beings."
"If they were to see me, they would all feel shame and remorse, and go to dwell in the mountains, marshes, or secluded caves. At that time, I would think:
'Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose bodily conduct is impure yet who frequent secluded places where no people dwell;
though their bodily conduct is impure, they labor in vain, for this is not true practice, as they fear unwholesome and evil states.'"
However, my bodily conduct today is not impure, as I draw near to places of seclusion;
those whose bodily conduct is impure yet draw near to places of quietude—this is not mine.
The reason for this is that my bodily conduct is now pure; among all those Arhats whose bodily conduct is pure, who delight in dwelling in seclusion and in caves, I am the foremost.
"In this way, brahmin! Observing for myself that my conduct was pure and that I delighted in dwelling in seclusion, I felt even greater joy.
At that time, I had this thought:"

"Whosoever among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas has impure mental conduct and impure livelihood, even if they resort to dwelling in seclusion in uninhabited places, though they possess such practices, they are still not genuine; they are fully possessed of evil and unwholesome dharmas—this is not my teaching."
The reason for this is that the conduct of my body, speech, mind, and livelihood is now pure.
There are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose body, speech, mind, and livelihood are pure, who delight in dwelling in secluded and pure places; they are what belongs to me.

The reason for this is that my current conduct of body, speech, mind, and livelihood is pure; among all those Arhats whose body, speech, mind, and livelihood are pure, I am the foremost in delighting in secluded and quiet places.
"In this way, brahmin, when my body, speech, mind, and livelihood were pure, and I dwelt in a secluded place, my joy increased all the more."
"At that time, I thought to myself:
'These śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are full of fear; though they dwell in secluded and quiet places, they are nevertheless afraid of evil and unwholesome states.

But today I have no fear whatsoever. While dwelling in a secluded and quiet place where there is no one, I say that the fearful minds of those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who dwell in secluded places do not belong to me.'"
The reason for this is that I am now forever free from fear and dwell in solitude, sporting at my ease;
those who dwell in seclusion while still harboring a fearful heart are not I.
"The reason for this is that I have now departed from suffering and affliction;
I am not the same as them. Thus, brahmin, having contemplated this meaning, I was without fear and my joy increased.
“‘There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who disparage others and praise themselves; even though they dwell in secluded places, they still harbor impure thoughts.
However, I, O Brāhmaṇa!’”
Nor do I disparage others, nor do I praise myself.
Those who boast of themselves while disparaging others—such people are not my followers.
Why is this? Because I am now free from pride; among all the noble ones who are without pride, I am the foremost.
Having contemplated this meaning, I was all the more filled with joy:
"While there are śramaṇas who seek gain and honor and cannot rest themselves, today I have no seeking for gain and honor."
The reason for this is that I now seek nothing from others and am likewise content;
yet, among those who are content, I am the foremost.
Having contemplated this meaning, I was filled with even greater joy.
"Any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who harbor indolence in their hearts, who do not apply themselves with diligence, and who do not draw near to secluded places—they do not belong to me."

The reason for this is that I now possess a courageous mind, and therefore I do not grow weary or slacken in the midst of my efforts; among all those who possess the courageous mind of the worthy and noble ones, I am the foremost.
Having personally contemplated this meaning, my joy increased all the more.
At that time, I further thought:
"There are many śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are prone to forgetfulness; though they dwell in secluded places and practice such conduct, they still possess evil and unwholesome dharmas."
However, today I am free from all forgetfulness.
Furthermore, Brahmin!
As for those people who are forgetful, they do not belong to me; among all those noble and holy ones who are free from forgetfulness, I am the foremost.
"Having now contemplated this meaning, I dwell in seclusion with redoubled joy.
At that time, I further thought:
'Whosoever among the śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas has a distracted and unsettled mind, they will possess evil and unwholesome states, which coexist with evil conduct.'"
However, today my mind is ultimately undisturbed and remains constantly one-pointed;
those who possess distracted minds and lack mental stability do not belong to me.
This is because I am always one-pointed, and if there were any noble ones with a concentrated mind, I would be their foremost leader.
"Having now observed this, although I dwell in a secluded and quiet place, my joy increases all the more.
At that time, I further thought:
'Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be who are foolish and shrouded in darkness like a flock of sheep—they possess evil and unwholesome dharmas; those are not mine.'"
"However, today I am always possessed of wisdom and free from delusion, dwelling in seclusion.
If there be anyone who practices in such a manner, they belong to me; for I have now achieved wisdom, and among all those noble ones who have achieved wisdom, I am the foremost."
Having now contemplated this meaning, even though I dwell in seclusion, my joy increases all the more.
While I am in this state of seclusion, should trees be broken and birds and beasts flee, at that time I think to myself:
"This is a forest of great fear."
At that time, he further thought:
"If fear should arise, I must seek skillful means so that it does not come again.
If fear arose while I was walking in meditation, at that time I would neither sit nor lie down; I would only sit once the fear had been eliminated.
If, while I am staying, fear and dread should arise, at that time I shall neither walk nor sit; I will ensure that their fear and dread are dispelled before I sit down.
If fear should arise while I am sitting, I shall not practice walking meditation; I must first eliminate that fear before I sit again.
If fear should arise while I am lying down, at that time I shall neither practice walking meditation nor sit; I must ensure that the fear is eliminated before I lie down.
“Brahmin, you should know that among all those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who do not understand the Dharma day and night, I declare such people to be utterly deluded.”
However, O Brahmin!

Day and night I have understood the Dharma of the Path; moreover, with a mind of vigor and without falsehood, my thoughts undisturbed and always as if one-pointed, free from perceptions of sensual desire, with directed thought and sustained thought, mindful of joy and bliss, I dwell in the first dhyāna.
This, brahmin, is called my first experience of delight within the present life: having removed directed thought and evaluation,
with internal joy and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, dwelling in the second dhyāna, which is characterized by concentration, mindfulness, and joy.
"This, brahmin, is called the second mind that attains happiness in the present life.

Observing within myself that there is no thought of sensual desire, I experience bodily bliss— the state desired by the noble ones— which is protected by mindfulness and joy, as I dwell in the third dhyāna."
This, brahmin, is called the third mind. Furthermore,

when suffering and pleasure have been eliminated, and there is neither sorrow nor joy, but a state of neither suffering nor pleasure, with mindfulness purified through equanimity, one dwells in the fourth dhyāna.
"O Brahmin! This is called the fourth higher mind, through which one personally realizes and dwells within the sphere of the mind:

'While I was dwelling in seclusion, I possessed these four higher minds; by means of this samādhi-mind—pure, stainless, and free from fetters—I attained fearlessness and personally recognized the events of countless past kalpas.'"

At that time, I recollected my past lives—one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, and a thousand births; I discerned all the kalpas of their formation and destruction:
"I was born there, with such a surname and such a given name, eating such food and experiencing such suffering and pleasure; passing away from there, I was born here; dying here, I was born there."
"The causes and conditions, from beginning to end, are all clearly understood.

'Brahmin, you should know that during the first watch of the night, I attained the first illumination; having eliminated ignorance, there was no longer any darkness, and my mind, delighting in solitary dwelling, attained self-awakening.'"
Furthermore, with a mind of samādhi free from defilement and devoid of fetters, his heart remains in meditative concentration, attaining fearlessness.

He also knows those among the multitude of beings who are born and those who die; moreover, with the divine eye he observes the various classes of beings—those born and those dying, those of beautiful form and those of ugly form, those in happy realms and those in miserable realms, whether handsome or unattractive—and he discerns them all according to their good and evil deeds.

There are sentient beings who commit evil through their bodily actions, evil through their verbal actions, and evil through their mental actions; they slander the noble ones, constantly harbor wrong views, and are associated with such wrong views. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.

Whosoever among sentient beings practice wholesome conduct of body, cultivate wholesome conduct of speech, and cultivate wholesome conduct of mind; who do not revile the noble ones, constantly maintain right view, and are endowed with right view—upon the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly realms.

Furthermore, with the pure and stainless divine eye, he observes all classes of sentient beings—those who are born and those who die, those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance, those in happy destinies and those in miserable destinies, whether handsome or hideous—and knows them all according to the roots of their past conduct.

“Brahmin, you should know that when one attains the second illumination during the middle watch of the night, there is no longer any darkness, and one personally realizes the joy of dwelling in seclusion.

Furthermore, with a mind of samādhi that is pure and free from blemish, devoid of fetters and afflictions, having attained concentration of mind, fearlessness, and the exhaustion of outflows, one knows this suffering as it truly is, not falsely. When I attained such a state of mind, my mind was liberated from the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance. Having attained liberation, I immediately attained the knowledge of liberation:
‘Birth and death have ended; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not again receive a womb. Thus I knew it as it truly is.”
“This is what I call, brahmin,
attaining the third knowledge in the latter part of the night, so that there is no longer any darkness.
What do you think, brahmin?”
"O Brahmin, do you harbor such a thought:
that the Tathāgata possesses a mind of desire, a mind of hatred, or a mind of delusion, and has not yet exhausted these while dwelling in seclusion?"
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?

Although the Tathāgata has today forever eliminated all outflows (*āsrava*) and constantly delights in dwelling in seclusion, no longer remaining among humans, it is because I have today contemplated this meaning that I delight in the place of secluded dwelling.
"What are these two?
Furthermore, you personally dwell in secluded retreats while simultaneously delivering sentient beings beyond all measure.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-āsrava addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Out of compassion for sentient beings, he intends to deliver them all.
The brahmin spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "Stop!
"Stop! World-Honored One!
What you have said is so much more than enough; it is like a hunchback finding extension, a lost person finding the path, a blind person gaining eyes, or one in darkness seeing light."

"In this way, the Śramaṇa Gautama has taught the Dharma through countless skillful means. I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; from this day forward, I shall observe the five precepts and refrain from taking life, becoming a lay follower (upāsaka)."
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-śroṇa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Gosiṅga Grove, a place where four past Buddhas had resided.
At that time, King Udayana, along with five hundred women, Queen Śrīmālā, and others, wished to go to the park to sightsee and enjoy themselves.
At that moment, there was a bhikṣu in the city of Śrāvastī who thought to himself:
"It has been a long time since I last saw the World-Honored One; I wish to go to pay my respects, receive his teachings, and inquire after his well-being."
Then, at the proper time, that bhikṣu dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
After his meal, he set aside his robe, bowl, and sitting mat, and by means of his supernormal power, flew into the air to go to the Kośamba Garden.

At that time, that bhikṣu withdrew his supernormal powers and went into the forest; there, in a secluded place, he sat cross-legged, straightening his body and composing his mind, fixing his mindfulness before him.
At that time, Lady Śyāmā, accompanied by five hundred women, came to this grove.

Thereupon, Lady Śyāmā saw from afar the bhikṣu sitting beneath a tree, having attained spiritual power through the Way. Having seen him, she approached the bhikṣu, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and stood before him with palms joined. The five hundred ladies likewise all prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and also stood surrounding him with palms joined.
At that time, King Udayana saw from afar five hundred women with palms joined, standing around this bhikṣu; having seen them, he thought to himself:
"There must surely be a herd of deer here."
"If there were indeed wild beasts, it would certainly not be doubted.
At that time, the king mounted his horse and galloped swiftly toward the assembly of women.
Then, Lady Śyāmā saw the king approaching from afar and thought to herself:
"This King Udayana is extremely fierce and cruel; he will surely seize this bhikṣu and kill him.
At that time, the queen raised her right hand and said to the king, "Great King, you should know that this is a bhikṣu; do not be afraid anymore."
At that time, the king immediately dismounted from his horse, laid aside his bow, and approached the bhikṣu, saying to him: "Bhikṣu!
Teach me the Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣu raised his eyes, looked up at the king, and remained silent without speaking.
Then the king spoke again to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Quickly teach me the Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣu again raised his eyes to gaze up at the king, remaining silent and saying nothing. Then the king thought to himself:

“I should now ask about the matters concerning the intermediate stages of dhyāna; if he should explain them to me, I shall provide him with offerings for as long as my life lasts, bestowing upon him robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the treatment of illness.”
"If you do not grant my request, I shall have you executed!
At that time, the king spoke again to the bhikṣu, saying: "Bhikṣu!..."
"Preach the Dharma to me.
At that time, the bhikṣu remained silent and did not respond.
Then, the tree deity, knowing his thoughts, immediately manifested a herd of deer from afar, intending to distract the king’s ears and eyes and cause him to give rise to other thoughts.
At that time, when the king saw the deer from afar, he thought to himself:
"Let me set this śramaṇa aside for now!
Where, after all, will this śramaṇa go?"
He immediately mounted his horse and went to shoot at the herd of deer.
At that time, the lady said to the practitioner: "Bhikṣu!..."
"Where are you going now?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I wish to go to the abode of the four Buddhas to pay my respects to the World-Honored One!"
The lady said: "Bhikṣu!
Now is precisely the right time; go quickly to your destination and do not remain here any longer. If you are harmed by the king, his guilt will be exceedingly grave."
At that time, the bhikṣu rose from his seat, gathered his robes and bowl, and flew into the air, departing for a distant place.
When the lady saw the practitioner soaring high in the sky, she spoke to the king from afar:
"I pray the Great King observe this bhikṣu’s great supernormal powers; he now moves freely, leaping and diving within the void."
"If even this bhikṣu still possesses such power, how much more so the Buddha Śākyamuni—how could anyone possibly equal him?

At that time, the bhikṣu arrived at the Ghoṣita Garden; he then relinquished his supernormal powers and proceeded to the World-Honored One by ordinary means. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "How is it, bhikṣus?
Were you weary during the summer retreat in Śrāvastī?"
"Is it not also wearying to beg for food at all times?
The bhikṣu replied,
"While I was in Śrāvastī, I truly felt no weariness."
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"For what reason have you come here today?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
"Therefore, I have come to visit your holiness and inquire after your well-being.
The World-Honored One said,
"Do you now see me and these four abodes of the Buddhas?"
"It is truly most marvelous that you have now escaped the king's hand; why did you not preach the Dharma for the king?
Furthermore, King Udayana spoke these words: "O Bhikṣu!"
"Now you should preach the Dharma for me.
For what reason do you not preach the Dharma for me now?

If a bhikṣu were to preach the Dharma to the king, King Udayana would feel the utmost joy; having felt such joy, he would provide offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick throughout the remainder of his life.
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At that time, the king wished to inquire about matters concerning the intermediate stages of dhyāna; for this reason, he did not respond to this teaching.
The World-Honored One told him:
“O bhikṣu! Why did you not speak to the king about the intermediate matters of dhyāna?
The bhikṣu replied:
"What use has King Udayana for this dhyāna? By nature he was violent and devoid of compassion;

he slaughtered sentient beings beyond counting. Bound by desire, his three poisons were ablaze, and he was submerged in a deep abyss. He did not behold the True Dharma, but practiced delusions and ignorance; all manner of evils accumulated within him. He acted with arrogance, relying on the power and influence of his kingship to covet wealth and treasures, treating the people of the world with contempt. Blind and without eyes, what use does this man have for dhyāna?"

Now, the dharma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the most subtle among all dharmas; it is difficult to perceive, devoid of form or characteristics, and beyond the scope of the mind. This is not within the reach of ordinary people, but is known only by the wise.
"For this reason, I shall not preach the Dharma to the King.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"If there is old or worn clothing, it must first be washed before it becomes clean."
When the mind of desire is extremely intense, one must contemplate the perception of impurity; only then will it be eliminated.
If hatred is intense, one should eliminate it with a mind of loving-kindness.
The darkness of ignorance is only completely eliminated through the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Bhikṣu!
For what reason did you not preach the Dharma to King Udayana?
"If he were to preach the Dharma for me, the King would be filled with supreme joy; even a most raging fire could be extinguished, let alone a mere man.
At that time, the bhikṣu remained silent and said nothing.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“The Tathāgata’s dwelling in the world is most marvelous!
Most extraordinary!”
If devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, or gandharvas should come to inquire about the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teachings, I shall explain them to them;
if kings, ministers, or members of the common people should come to inquire about the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teachings, I shall likewise explain them to them;
and if kṣatriyas or those of the four castes should come to inquire about the meaning, I shall likewise explain them to them.
The reason for this is that today the Tathāgata has attained the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and thus in preaching the Dharma he is without any timidity;

he has also attained the four dhyānas, exercising mastery within them, and furthermore has attained the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) in incalculable measure. He practices the four immeasurable minds (*brahmavihāra*); therefore, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he is without any timidity, a state which neither Arhats nor Pratyekabuddhas can attain.
For this reason, the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is also without difficulty.
"Now, monks, you should seek skillful means and practice the four immeasurable minds: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.

Why is this? Because whatever sentient beings a bhikṣu encounters as spiritual friends, as well as all his parents and kinsmen, he should instruct them in all matters through the four bases of sympathy so that they may come to know the Dharma."
What are the four?

First, one should revere the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata is the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who delivers immeasurable beings.
One should seek the Dharma and practice the true and correct Dharma, eliminating defiled and evil conduct; this is what the wise practice.

Furthermore, one should skillfully provide offerings to the Saṃgha. The assembly of the Tathāgata is always in harmony and free from dispute; they are accomplished in the Dharma, accomplished in precepts, accomplished in samādhi, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation.

What are known as the four pairs and eight classes, the twelve noble persons—these constitute the Sangha of the Tathāgata’s disciples, worthy of honor and esteem, the unsurpassed field of merit in the world.
Furthermore, one should encourage and assist others to practice the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones—untainted, undefiled, tranquil, and unconditioned.
If there are bhikṣus who wish to practice the Way, they should all together practice these four dharmas.
The reason for this is that among offerings made to the Triple Gem, the offering of the Dharma is the most honored and supreme;
none can surpass it. Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four types of practice.”
What are the four? There is the practice of the pleasant path where progress is slow and deluded; this is called the first path.
Furthermore, there is the practice of the pleasant path where progress is swift.
Furthermore, there is the practice of the path of asceticism that is characterized by delusion;
and there is the practice of the path of asceticism that is characterized by rapid progress.
What, then, is called the practice of the path of pleasure that is characterized by delusion?

There may be a person whose greed is intense, and whose hatred and delusion are intense; their conduct is extremely painful and does not correspond with the root of practice. Such a person’s five faculties are dull and dark, and neither swift nor sharp.
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, and the faculty of concentration.
If one seeks the exhaustion of all outflows through samādhi with a deluded mind, this is called the path of practice for those of dull faculties who attain the Way through delight.
"What is meant by 'one who practices the path of the faculty of pleasure with speed'?
It refers to a person who is free from desire and free from lust;

yet regarding sensual craving, they are naturally and consistently deficient and not diligent in it, while their anger and delusion are extremely diminished, and their five faculties are swift and alert without negligence."
What are the five? They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; these are called the five faculties.
By attaining these five faculties, one accomplishes samādhi, exhausts all outflows, and realizes the state beyond outflows; this is called "one of sharp faculties practicing the path."
"How is it that one practices the path of asceticism while wandering in delusion?
There may be a person whose lustful intent is excessive, and whose anger and ignorance are blazing."
He delights in these dharmas, exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*), and realizes the state of being without outflows; this is called the practitioner of the path of asceticism with dull faculties.
"What is the practitioner of the path of asceticism who proceeds with swiftness?"
Thereupon, suppose there is a person who has few desires and little lust, who is without ill will and does not give rise to conceptual thoughts, practicing these three dharmas.
At that time, he possesses these five faculties without deficiency or impairment.
What are the five? They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; these are called the five.
By means of these dharmas, one attains samādhi, exhausts the outflows, and realizes the state of being without outflows; this is called the path of practice for those of sharp faculties.
"It is said that a bhikkhu who possesses these four modes of conduct should seek skillful means to abandon the first three modes of conduct and should together practice the latter one mode."
The reason for this is that the samādhi of the traces of ascetic practice is difficult to attain; once it is attained, one immediately achieves the Way and remains long in the world.
This is because one cannot seek happiness through happiness; it is only by means of suffering that one subsequently achieves the Way.
Therefore, monks, always employ skillful means to accomplish this course of practice. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, four brahmins who had all attained the five supernormal powers and practiced wholesome dharmas gathered together in one place and held this discussion:
"When the Lord of Death comes, he spares neither the powerful nor the strong; let us each hide ourselves so that the Lord of Death does not know our whereabouts."
At that time, a certain brahmin flew into the air, wishing to escape death; yet he could not avoid it, and he passed away while still in mid-air.
The second brahmin entered the depths of the great ocean, desiring to escape death, but he passed away right there.
The third brahmin, likewise desiring to escape death, entered the interior of Mount Sumeru, yet he died within it as well.
That fourth brahmin entered the earth down to the adamantine base, seeking to escape death, yet he likewise passed away right there.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye, saw that each of the four brahmins had sought to avoid death, only for them all to pass away together.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Not in the sky, nor in the midst of the sea, Nor by entering into mountain clefts—
There is no place on earth Where one may dwell and escape death."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "In this regard, bhikṣus!
There were four brahmins who gathered in one place, desiring to escape death; each fled to his own refuge, yet none escaped death."
One person is in the air, one enters the sea, one enters the belly of a mountain, and one enters the earth;
they all die together. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
Those who wish to escape death should contemplate the four fundamental principles. What are these four?
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; this is called the first fundamental principle, which one should mindfully practice.
"All conditioned phenomena are suffering"—this is called the second foundation of the Dharma; you should contemplate it together.
"All phenomena are non-self"—this is the third foundation of the Dharma; you should contemplate it together.
Cessation is nirvāṇa; this is called the fourth foundation of the Dharma, which you should contemplate together.
Thus, monks, you should contemplate these four foundations of the Dharma together.
The reason for this is that one thereby becomes liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair; these are the very root of suffering.
Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to accomplish these four dharmas. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The Heaven of the Thirty-three has four pleasure groves where the devas amuse themselves and enjoy the five kinds of music.”
What are the four? They are the Nandanavana Grove, the Cūḍāmaṇi Grove, the Day-and-Night Grove, and the Miśrakāvana Grove.
Within these four groves, there are four bathing pools.
The Pool of Extreme Cold, the Fragrant Pool, the Light and Convenient Pool, and the Crystal-clear Pool.
What are these four? First is the Nanda Pool; second is the Nandottara Pool; third is the Sumana Pool; and fourth is the Rati Pool.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that within these four parks there are these four bathing pools, which make the bodies of people fragrant, clean, and free from dust and grime.
For what reason is the park named Nandanavana?

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter the Caitraratha Garden, their hearts are filled with such joy that they cannot contain themselves; they take their pleasure therein, and for this reason it is called the Caitraratha Garden.
"For what further reason is it called the Rough and Astringent Garden?

Once the gods of the Thirty-three have entered this garden, their bodies become extremely coarse, just as one's body becomes extremely coarse when scented unguents are applied during the winter; it is just like this."

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter this garden, their bodies become extremely coarse and no longer resemble their usual state; for this reason, it is called the Coarse and Rough Garden Park.
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Garden of Day and Night?

If the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three enter this garden, at that time the complexions of the various gods become diverse and they assume various forms, just as women wear various garments so that they no longer resemble their original appearances."

This is likewise: when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter this garden, they manifest various colors that differ from their original appearance; for this reason, it is called the Garden of Day and Night.
"For what reason is it called the Garden of Various Kinds?

At that time, when the most honored devas, the middle-ranking devas, and the lower-ranking devas enter this garden, they all become of one kind. Even if the lowest-ranking deva is unable to enter the other three gardens, it is just as when the park entered by a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) cannot be entered by other kings to bathe; the common people can only see it from afar."
This is likewise: when the most honored divine beings enter the park to bathe, the other minor devas may no longer enter; therefore, it is called the "Mixed Bathing Pond."
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Nanda bathing pool?
Because when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter this pool, they experience the utmost joy; therefore, it is called the Nanda bathing pool."
"For what further reason is it called the Nanda-śīrṣa bathing pool?

Once the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven have entered this pool, they take each other by the hand and bathe while massaging one another's heads; even the celestial maidens do likewise. For this reason, it is called the Nanda-śīrṣa bathing pool."
"For what further reason is it called the Soma Bathing Pond?

Once the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have entered this pond, at that time the countenances of all those gods become identical to human color, without any distinction; for this reason, it is called the Soma Bathing Pond."
"For what further reason is it called the Pool of Joyful Delight?

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enter this pool, they are entirely free from thoughts of pride or superiority and inferiority; their desires become greatly diminished, and at that time they all bathe with a single mind. Therefore, it is called the Pool of Joyful Delight."
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus:
because of these causes and conditions, this name exists.
Now, within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata it is likewise; there are four parks by name."
What are the four? First, the garden of loving-kindness; second, the garden of compassion; third, the garden of sympathetic joy; and fourth, the garden of equanimity.
These, O bhikṣu, are called [the four gardens].
Within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, there are these four gardens.
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Garden of Loving-kindness?

A bhikṣu should know that by virtue of this Garden of Loving-kindness, one is born in the Brahma Heaven; having passed away from the Brahma Heaven, one shall be born into a noble and honorable family, possessing abundant wealth and many treasures, constantly delighting in the five pleasures without ever being out of sight of them. For this reason, it is called the Garden of Loving-kindness.
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called the 'Garden of Compassion' (Karūṇāvana)?
Monks, you should know that if one can draw near to the mind of liberation through compassion, one will be reborn in the Brahmakāyika Heaven."

If one is reborn among humans, one will be born into a noble family, free from anger, and possessed of abundant wealth and many treasures; for this reason, it is called the Garden of Compassion (*karuṇā-ārāma*).
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Garden of Joy (*muditā-ārāma*)?"
If one can draw near to the Garden of Joy (Nandana), one will be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
If one returns to birth in the human realm, one will be born into a royal family and will always harbor joy; therefore, it is named the Garden of Joy.
"For what further reason is it called 'Guarding the Garden'?
If anyone draws near to this guardian, they will be reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva), where their lifespan lasts eighty-four thousand kalpas."

If they are reborn among humans, they shall be born into a central land and family; furthermore, they will be free from anger and will constantly protect all from unrighteous conduct. For this reason, they are called "Garden Protectors."

“Bhikṣus, you should know that within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata there are these four gardens, wherein all the śrāvakas may sport and play. Furthermore, within these four gardens of the Tathāgata, there are four bathing pools, wherein I have my śrāvakas bathe and sport themselves, exhausting all outflows (āsrava) to achieve the state of no-outflow (anāsrava), free once more from dust and defilement.”

What are the four? First is the bathing pool with directed thought and sustained thought; second is the bathing pool without directed thought and sustained thought; third is the bathing pool of protective mindfulness; and fourth is the bathing pool of neither suffering nor pleasure.
"For what reason is it called the bathing pool with applied thought and sustained thought?

If a bhikṣu, having attained the first dhyāna, constantly possesses applied thought and sustained thought regarding all phenomena, contemplates all phenomena, and eliminates the fetters and entanglements so that none remain, for this reason it is called 'with applied thought and sustained thought.'"
"For what further reason is it called the bathing pool of 'without applied thought and without sustained thought'?

If a bhikṣu, having attained the second dhyāna, extinguishes applied thought and sustained thought and takes that dhyāna as his sustenance, for this reason it is called 'without applied thought and without sustained thought'."
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called the 'Pool of Mindful Protection'?

If a bhikṣu, having attained the third dhyāna, extinguishes directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), and remains without directed thought or sustained thought, constantly protecting and being mindful of the third dhyāna—for this reason, it is called the Pool of Mindful Protection."
“Furthermore, for what reason is it called the ‘Pool of Neither-Pain-Nor-pleasure’?

If a bhikṣu has attained the fourth dhyāna, he neither dwells on pleasure nor dwells on pain; he does not dwell on dharmas of the past or the future, but directs his mind solely toward dharmas of the present. For this reason, it is called the Pool of Neither-Pain-Nor-pleasure.”

"Therefore, monks, within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata there are these four bathing pools, by which my śrāvakas may bathe therein, extinguish the twenty-one fetters, cross the ocean of birth and death, and enter the city of Nirvāṇa."
"O bhikṣus! Those who wish to cross this ocean of birth and death should seek skillful means to extinguish the twenty-one fetters and enter the city of nirvāṇa."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is just as if there were four great venomous snakes, extremely fierce and violent, placed together within a single box.

Suppose a person were to come from the four directions, wishing to live and not seeking death, desiring happiness and not seeking suffering, being neither foolish nor deluded, with an undisturbed mind, and free from all attachments.
At that time, whether it be the king or a royal minister, they would summon this man and say to him:

"Now there are four great venomous snakes that are exceedingly fierce and violent. You must now attend to them at the proper times, bathing them to keep them clean, and providing them with food and drink at the proper times so that they never lack for anything; now is the right moment, you should go and carry out these tasks."
At that time, the man was filled with fear and did not dare to go straight forward; he abandoned his path and fled, not knowing where to go into the depths.
Again, [the king] addressed the man with these words:
"I shall now have five men, all carrying swords and blades, follow behind you. Should any of them catch you, they shall take your life; there must be no delay."
At that time, that man, terrified of the four great venomous snakes and further fearing the five men brandishing swords and blades, fled hither and thither, not knowing what to do.
He further addressed that person, saying:
"I now command six enemies to follow behind you; whoever catches you shall take your life.
Whatever you wish to do, you must accomplish it at once."

At that time, that person, fearing the four great venomous snakes, further fearing the five men bearing swords and staves, and furthermore fearing the six enemies, fled hither and thither. When that person saw a deserted ruin, he desired to enter it to take refuge.

If he encounters an empty house, or a breach in a wall where there is no place of security, or sees an empty vessel that is entirely devoid of anything, and if there is another person who is a friend of his and wishes to rescue him, they would tell him:
"In this secluded place there are many bandits; whatever you wish to do, you may now do as you please."

At that time, that man, further fearing the four great venomous serpents, further fearing the five men bearing swords and staves, further fearing the six enemies, and further fearing the desolate village, fled hither and thither.

As that person proceeds forward, he may see a great body of water, exceedingly deep and vast, with neither people nor bridges by which he might cross to the other shore; moreover, the place where he stands is filled with many wicked bandits.
At that time, that person thought to himself:
"This water is exceedingly deep and vast, and abounds with many bandits; how shall I manage to cross to the other shore?"
"I should now gather timber and grass to construct a raft; by means of this raft, I shall be able to go from this shore to the other shore.
At that time, the man gathered wood and grass to make a raft, and having done so, he immediately reached the other shore, his resolve unshaken.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that I shall now provide a parable; you should reflect upon it so as to understand its meaning.
When this teaching is spoken, what is its significance?
That which is called ‘the four venomous snakes’ refers precisely to the four great elements.”
What are the four great elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element; these are called the four great elements.
The five men bearing swords and blades are the five aggregates of clinging.
What are these five?
They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
As for the six enemies, they are sensual desire and craving.
The "empty village" refers to the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). What are these six?
The so-called six sense bases are: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
"If one with wisdom contemplates the eye, it is entirely empty and non-existent, and moreover, not solid;
if one further contemplates the ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind, they too are entirely empty and non-existent—all are void, all are quiescent, and none are solid."
"Clouds and water" refers to the four floods (*ogha*).
What are the four? They are the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*), and the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*).
The great raft is the Noble Eightfold Path. What are the eight?
Right view, right resolve, right speech, right effort, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are called the Noble Eightfold Path.
Seeking to cross over within the water is the power of skillful means and diligent effort.
This shore is the perversion of the body;
the other shore is the cessation of the perversion of the body.
"This shore" refers to the realm of King Ajātaśatru;
"the other shore" refers to the realm of King Vaiśravaṇa.
"This shore" refers to the realm of Pāpīyān.
"The 'other shore' is the realm of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that moment, there was a lay follower (upāsaka) in the city of Śrāvastī who, having passed away, was reborn in the household of a great elder in Śrāvastī, where the principal wife was pregnant.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye—pure and free from blemish—saw that this upāsaka had been born into the family of the wealthiest elder in the city of Śrāvastī.
On that very day, there was another brahmin whose body perished and life ended, and he was reborn in hell; at that time, the World-Honored One also observed this with his divine eye.

Furthermore, on that same day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s life ended, and he was reborn in a good destination, the heavens; at that time, the World-Honored One also observed this with his divine eye.
On that very day, a certain bhikṣu passed into parinirvāṇa, which the World-Honored One also beheld with his divine eye.
At that time, having witnessed these four matters, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"If a person receives a womb, And through evil conduct enters hell,"
The virtuous are born in the heavens; those free from outflows enter nirvāṇa.
The noble one has now entered the womb; the brahmin enters hell.
Sudatta is born in the heavens; the bhikṣu attains parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his private chamber, proceeded to the Hall of Universal Assembly, and took his seat.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now there are four matters."
If a person is able to practice this, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will be reborn among human beings.
What are these four? They are:
purity of body, speech, mind, and livelihood, being free from all blemish and defilement.
If, at the time of death, one is reborn among human beings.
Furthermore, bhikṣus, there are four other dharmas which, when practiced by some people, lead them into hell.
What are the four?
They are the impurity of body, speech, mind, and livelihood.
These, O bhikṣu, are called [the four].
"There are these four things.
If anyone associates with them, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will be reborn in hell. Furthermore, monks!"
Furthermore, there are four dharmas; those who practice and cultivate them will be reborn in a good place, in the heavens. What are these four?
Generosity, loving-kindness, benefiting others, and impartiality.
"Monks, this is called one who practices this Dharma;
at the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Furthermore, monks,"

Furthermore, there are four further dharmas; if anyone practices them, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will exhaust all outflows and achieve the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom:
knowing as it truly is that birth and death have been ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further undergoing of conception.

What are the four? They are: dhyāna with directed thought and sustained examination; dhyāna without directed thought and sustained examination; dhyāna of protective mindfulness; and dhyāna of the cessation of suffering and pleasure. These, it is said, are the four dharmas of a bhikṣu.
If there is anyone who practices this, they will exhaust all outflows (āsrava) and achieve the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are free from outflows;

they will know for themselves as it truly is: "Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence after this."

"Therefore, monks! If there are sons of noble family or members of the fourfold assembly who wish to be born among humans, they should seek skillful means and practice purity of body, speech, mind, and livelihood;
if they wish to be born in the heavens, they should likewise seek skillful means and practice the four kinds of benevolence."

If one attains the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava) and achieves the liberation of mind through the outflow-free state and the liberation through wisdom, one should likewise seek skillful means and practice the four dhyānas.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in a grove outside the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, before I had attained the Way of the Buddha, I dwelt upon that Great Fear Mountain."
At that time, on that mountain, those who enter it—whether with lustful minds or without lustful minds—have their hair stand on end.
Furthermore, during times of extreme heat, when shimmering mirages stretch across the land, they sit there with their bodies exposed; at night, they then enter deep into the forests.
Furthermore, on days of extreme cold when wind and rain intermingled, I would enter the forest by day and sit out in the open at night.
At that time, I was able to recite a single verse, one never heard before and never seen before.
"Tranquil and at ease by night, yet greatly fearing the mountains, I have exposed my body; this is my vow:
'If I reach the cemetery, I shall take the garments of the dead to cover my body.'"
At that time, even if the people of Aṭṭhaka Village were to come and take pieces of wood and thrust them into my ears or my nose, or spit upon me, or urinate on me, or heap earth upon my body;
nevertheless, at that time, I would never give rise to a thought directed toward those people.
At that time, they possessed this protective mind.
At that time, wherever there were oxen, if they saw the dung of a calf, they would take it and eat it;
if there was no dung from a calf, they would take the dung of a large ox and eat it.
At that time, having eaten this food, I again thought to myself:
"What is the use of eating now?
It would be better not to eat for the rest of the day."
At that time, as soon as I gave rise to this thought, the devas came to me and spoke these words:
"Do not continue to fast any longer.
If you should persist in fasting, we shall nourish you with the essence of ambrosia so that you may preserve your life."
At that time, I again had this thought:
"Now that I have ceased eating, for what reason do the devas send me ambrosia?
My current body must be harboring some deception."
At that time, I further thought to myself:
"Now I shall eat the remains of sesame and rice.

Then, eating but one sesame seed and one grain of rice per day, my body became emaciated and weak; my bones were joined together like a skeleton, a sore grew upon my head, and my skin and flesh fell away of their own accord, like a rotten gourd that could no longer support its head.
At that time, it was likewise so: a sore grew upon my crown, and the skin and flesh fell away of their own accord; all this was due to not eating.
It was also like the reflection of the stars appearing within deep water; at that time, my eyes were just like that, all because of not eating.
Just as an old cart is dilapidated, so too is my body; it is entirely ruined and cannot be relied upon.
It is also like the footprint of a camel, and both of my buttocks are likewise so.

When I massage my abdomen with my hand, I encounter the vertebrae; when I press upon the vertebrae, I again encounter the abdominal skin. That the body has become so weak is entirely due to not eating.
"At that time, I again took a single sesame seed and a single grain of rice as my food; yet it brought no benefit whatsoever, nor did I attain the supreme, honored Dharma."
If a desire for defecation or urination arose within my mind, I would immediately fall to the ground, unable to rise or move of my own accord.
At that time, when the devas saw this, they said:
"This śramaṇa Gautama has entered parinirvāṇa."
Furthermore, some devas made this statement:
"This śramaṇa has not yet reached the end of his life, but he will surely reach the end of his life now.
Still other devas made this statement:
"This śramaṇa has not passed away; this śramaṇa is truly an arhat, for such ascetic practices are the dharma of an arhat.
At that time, I still possessed a conscious mind and was able to perceive the external signs and inclinations of others.
At that time, I again had this thought:
"Now I shall enter the meditation of no-breathing.

I then entered the meditation of no-breathing and counted the inhalations and exhalations. As I was counting the inhalations and exhalations, I perceived a breath emerging from my ears; at that moment, the sound of the wind was like the roar of thunder.
At that time, he further thought:
"I shall now close my mouth and block my ears so that the breath does not exit.

Because the breath did not exit, the internal air then issued forth from his hands and feet; even though the air was prevented from exiting through the ears, nose, and mouth, at that moment an internal sound like the roar of thunder arose, and I was likewise at that time.
At that time, the consciousness still followed the movement of the body. Then, he again thought:
"I should further enter into the meditation of breathlessness."
At that time, I completely blocked the breath through all the apertures.

Because I had blocked all the inhalations and exhalations, I immediately suffered from a pain in my head and forehead, as if someone were boring into my head with a drill; my headache was likewise extremely agonizing.
At that time, I possessed a divine consciousness, and at that time I again had this thought:
"I shall now further practice dhyāna, so that my breath may not enter or exit."
At that time, I blocked the inhalation and exhalation, and all the breaths then gathered entirely within my abdomen.
When the breaths were thus constrained, the suffering was extremely intense; it was just as when a butcher slaughters an ox with a knife—so too was I, afflicted by extreme pain.
It was also like two strong men seizing a weak man together and roasting him over a fire; he suffered such extreme pain that it was unbearable.
I, too, am thus; this painful agony cannot be fully described.
At that time, my spiritual consciousness still remained. On the day I was practicing meditation, my physical form did not bear a human complexion;
when people saw it, they would say:
"This śramaṇa’s complexion is extremely dark."
When some people saw me, they said:
"The complexion of this śramaṇa appears as if he were dead.
Bhikṣus, you should know that during those six years I practiced such asceticism, yet I did not attain the supreme, noble Dharma.
"At that time, I thought to myself:
'Today I shall eat only one fruit. Thereupon, I ate one fruit."

On the day I ate a single fruit, my body became withered and weak, such that I could not rise or move about by myself; it was as if I were one hundred and twenty years old, with my joints and bones so disjointed that I could no longer support myself.
"Monks, you should know that at that time, what was called 'one fruit' was like a small jujube today.
At that time, I further thought:
'This is not the root of my attainment of the Way; therefore, there must be another path.'"
At that time, I further had this thought:
"I recall that in the past, beneath the tree of my father the king, I was free from lust and free from desire; having removed evil and unwholesome states, I dwelt in the first dhyāna;
and with the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, I dwelt in the second dhyāna."
With pure mindfulness and free from manifold perceptions, he dwells in the third dhyāna;
with neither suffering nor pleasure, and with pure mindfulness, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna.
"This might indeed be the path; I shall now seek this path."
"For six years, I diligently and painfully sought the Way but did not achieve it;
at times I lay upon thorns and brambles;
at times I lay upon wooden planks covered with iron nails; or I suspended my body high above the ground with my two feet upward and my head toward the earth."
Some sit with their legs crossed in a squatting posture;
some grow long beards and hair, never shaving them;
and some expose themselves to the sun or roast themselves over fires.
Some sit upon ice in the depths of winter;
some immerse their bodies in water;
or some remain in silence, refraining from speech.
At times they eat once; at times twice;
at times three times, four times, or even up to seven times.
Some eat vegetables and fruits;
some eat rice and hemp;
some eat the roots of plants.
Some eat the fruits of trees;
some eat the fragrance of flowers;
some eat various kinds of fruits and gourds.
At times they were naked;
at times they wore tattered and ruined garments;
or they wore garments made of *śara* grass.
Some wear garments of woolly hair;
some at times cover their bodies with human hair;
and some at times cultivate their hair.
At times he even took the hair of others to add to his own head-dress.
In this manner, bhikṣus,
I practiced asceticism until such an extreme, yet I did not attain the root of the four dharmas.
What are the four? They are:
the noble and holy precepts are difficult to understand and difficult to know;
the noble and holy wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
The liberation of the noble ones is difficult to understand and difficult to know;
the samādhi of the noble ones is difficult to understand and difficult to know.
This is what is meant, O bhikṣus!
"Having these four dharmas, I previously practiced asceticism but did not obtain this essential point.
At that time, I again had this thought:
'I must now seek the unsurpassed Way.'"
"What is this unsurpassed path? It consists of these four dharmas:
the noble and holy precepts, the noble and holy samādhi, the noble and holy wisdom, and the noble and holy liberation."
At that time, I again had this thought:

"One cannot seek the supreme, noble path with such a weak and inferior body. I must consume a certain amount of refined and subtle essence to nourish my physical frame until my vital strength becomes abundant; only then shall I be able to practice the Way."
While he was consuming the essence of subtle vital energy, the five bhikṣus abandoned me and withdrew, saying:
"This śramaṇa Gautama’s nature and conduct have become deranged; having abandoned the true Dharma, he has turned to perverse practices."
"At that time, I immediately rose from my seat and walked back and forth facing the east.
Then, I again had this thought: 'Where are the places where the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the Way?'"
At that time, a celestial spirit dwelling in the void spoke to me from above, saying:
"Worthy sir, you should know that in the past, buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, the World-Honored Ones, sat beneath the cool shade of the Bodhi tree and attained buddhahood."
At that time, I further thought to myself:
"In what place should I sit to attain the Way of the Buddha?
Should I sit on a seat?"
"Shall I stand?
At that time, the devas came again and addressed me, saying:
"In the past, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, sat upon grass mats and only then attained Buddhahood."
At that time, not far from me, there was an auspicious brahmin mowing grass nearby. I went up to him and asked:
"Who are you? What is your name, and do you have a clan?"
The brahmin replied,
"My name is Śrī and my clan is Bhṛgu.
At that time, I said to that man:
"Excellent! Excellent! Such a name and clan are rare in the world;

One’s name shall not be in vain; it will surely fulfill its significance. It shall cause one to experience auspiciousness and benefit in the present life, and shall forever eliminate birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Your clan name is Bhṛgu, which is the same as mine.
I now have a request; please grant me a small amount of grass. Śrī replied:
"Gautama! What are you doing with this grass today?
At that time, I replied to Śiva:
"I wish to seek four dharmas beneath this king of trees. What are these four?
They are the noble and holy ethical discipline, the noble and holy concentration, the noble and holy wisdom, and the noble and holy liberation."
“Monks, you should know that at that time, Śiva personally took some grass and went to the place of the King of Trees.
I then sat upon it, straightening my body and composing my mind, sitting cross-legged with mindfulness directed before me.”
At that time, with the mind liberated from sensual desire and having eliminated all unwholesome states, he dwells with directed thought and sustained thought in the first dhyāna;
with directed and sustained thought eliminated, he dwells in the second and third dhyānas;
and with mindfulness and equanimity purified, and with the elimination of both sorrow and joy, he dwells in the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, with a pure mind, having eliminated all fetters and afflictions, I attained fearlessness and personally recognized my own past lives through countless transformations.

I then recalled innumerable worldly affairs: one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, hundreds of thousands of millions of births; eons of formation, eons of destruction, countless eons of formation, countless eons of destruction, and countless eons of both formation and destruction. I remembered how I died here and was born there, and from there, at the end of my life, came to be born here—without any fundamental beginning or end, or causal origin—from which I recalled such innumerable worldly affairs.

"Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and stainless, I observe the various classes of sentient beings—those who are born and those who pass away; those in good destinations and those of beautiful appearance, and those in evil destinations and those of ugly appearance; whether they are handsome or unattractive, I know them all according to their fundamental conduct."

There are some sentient beings who cultivate evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind; they slander the noble ones, create the roots of perverse karma, and associate with wrong views. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.

There are some classes of sentient beings who practice virtue in body, speech, and mind; they do not revile the noble ones and are endowed with right view. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among humans. This is called the case where these sentient beings have no unwholesome karma in body, speech, or mind.
With a mind of samādhi that is pure and free from blemish, my outflows are exhausted; I have attained the liberation of mind through the absence of outflows and the liberation through wisdom.
Birth and death are ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I know according to reality that I shall no longer undergo rebirth in a womb.
Thus, one attains the unsurpassed, right, and true path. "If, O Bhikṣus!

there should be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who clearly understand all realms of existence, yet these realms have no fundamental origin, and whom I have never previously failed to visit—except for those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens who do not return to this world; [it is they who possess such knowledge]."
