Furthermore, as for the places where śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas ought to be reborn, if I were not to be born there, it would be inappropriate; having already been born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, I shall no longer return to this world.
"Venerable ones, as you have attained the noble and holy precepts, so have I attained them;
as you have attained the noble and holy samādhis, so have I attained them;
as you have attained noble and holy wisdom, so have I attained it."
The noble ones’ liberation, you have attained it, and I too have attained it;
the noble ones’ knowledge and vision of liberation, you have attained it, and I too have attained it.
Having severed the root of the womb-birth, birth and death are forever ended, and we shall never again undergo birth from a womb.
"Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to accomplish these four dharmas. And why is that?"

If a bhikṣu attains these four dharmas, the realization of the Way will not be difficult; just as I have today realized the unsurpassed, right, and true Way, all of which was achieved through these four dharmas.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, Śakra Devānām Indra of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, together with his various jade maidens, went to the Caitraratha Garden for recreation.
At that time, a certain celestial being spoke this verse:
'If one does not see the Caitraratha Garden, One will not know the existence of bliss.'"
"The abodes of the various devas—none surpass these.
At that time, another deva spoke to him, saying:
"You are now without wisdom and cannot distinguish correct principles; you take what is a source of sorrow and suffering and instead call it happiness."
That which is not solid, they call solid;
that which is impermanent, they conversely call permanent;
and that which is not essential, they further call essential.
The reason for this is that have you not heard the verse spoken by the Tathāgata?
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; That which is born must surely die.
Not to be born is surely not to die; This cessation is the supreme bliss."
"Since they possess this principle and there is also this verse, how can you say that this place is the most blissful?
You should now know that the Tathāgata has also taught that there are four floods (oghāḥ)."
If all sentient beings were submerged in these currents, they would never attain the Way.
What are the four? They are the current of desire, the current of existence, the current of views, and the current of ignorance.
"What is called the flood of desire?
It refers to the five desires. What are these five?"
That is to say: when the eye sees forms, the perception of forms arises;
when the ear hears sounds, the perception of consciousness arises;
when the nose smells odors, the perception of consciousness arises.
If the tongue perceives flavors and gives rise to the perception of consciousness;
if the body perceives tactile sensations and gives rise to the perception of consciousness—this is called the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*).
"What is called the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*)?"
That which is called "existence" (bhava) refers to the three realms of existence. What are the three?
They are the existence of desire (kāma-bhava), the existence of form (rūpa-bhava), and the existence of formlessness (ārūpya-bhava); these are termed the "flood of existence" (bhava-ogha).
"What is called the flood of views? The so-called flood of views refers to:
'The world is eternal' or 'the world is non-eternal';"
In the world there are the views of finitude and infinitude;
that the body is the life-principle and that the body is not the life-principle;

that the Tathāgata exists after death, that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, and that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
This is called the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*).
"What is the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*)?
So-called ignorance means lack of knowledge, lack of faith, and lack of vision; it is the mind being constantly possessed by craving and desire, along with its five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*):"
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
Furthermore, if one does not know suffering, does not know its origin, does not know its cessation, and does not know the path, this is called the flood of ignorance.
"Son of Heaven, you should know that the Tathāgata speaks of these four floods.
If there is anyone submerged within them, they likewise cannot attain the Way.

At that time, having heard these words, that deva—like a strong man extending or contracting his arm—vanished from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and came to where I was. He prostrated with his head at my feet and stood to one side.
At that time, that deva addressed me, saying: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
Speak these words quickly!
The Tathāgata has taught the four floods (*ogha*).
If ordinary persons do not hear of these four floods, they will not attain the four joys.
What are the four?
They are the joy of rest, the joy of perfect awakening, the joy of the śramaṇa, and the joy of nirvāṇa.
If an ordinary person does not know these four streams, they shall not obtain these four joys.
After he had spoken these words, I replied to him: "So it is, O Devaputra!
Just as you have said, if one does not awaken to these four floods, then one does not awaken to these four joys."
"At that time, I gradually engaged in discourse with those devas and humans. The discourse was as follows:

a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, and a discourse on rebirth in heaven; [I spoke of] the impurity of sensual desires, how the outflows are a great affliction, and how the way of escape is true happiness."
At that time, the devas and humans gave rise to hearts of joy;
thereupon, I extensively expounded upon the Dharma of the four floods and spoke of the four pleasures.
At that time, having focused his mind one-pointedly and contemplated this Dharma, that deva was cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
I now likewise proclaim these four dharmas and four joys, whereby one attains the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"One should cultivate the perception of impermanence; one should extensively disseminate the perception of impermanence. Having cultivated the perception of impermanence and having extensively disseminated the perception of impermanence, one severs craving for the realm of desire, craving for the realm of form, and craving for the formless realm; one completely severs ignorance and completely severs conceit, just as a great conflagration burns away grasses and trees until they are entirely consumed."
This is likewise so: if one cultivates the perception of impermanence, all fetters (*saṃyojana*) are completely eliminated and severed.
Why is this? Long ago, in the distant past, there was a devaputra who, accompanied by five hundred jade maidens as his retinue, went out to play in the Nandanavana Garden;
he then proceeded beneath a *kani* tree to enjoy himself with the five sensual pleasures.

At that time, that deva-son, while climbing the tree to sport about, became mentally deranged; as he was gathering flowers, he fell from the tree and passed away, being reborn in the household of a great elder within this city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, five hundred jade maidens beat their breasts and wailed, unable to restrain themselves:

"At that time, I beheld the deva-son with my divine eye as he passed away and was reborn into the family of a great elder in the city of Śrāvastī; after eight or nine months had passed, a son was born, peerlessly handsome, with a complexion like the color of a peach blossom."
At that time, the son of the elder gradually grew up, and his parents sought a wife for him.
Not long after he had taken a wife, she also passed away and was reborn in the great ocean, taking the form of a dragon-snake.
At that time, the elder’s family members, both great and small, followed him in mourning and wailed aloud, their hearts pierced by the agony of grief.
Then, that dragon was devoured by a garuḍa; his body destroyed and his life ended, he was reborn in the hells.
At that time, the various dragon maidens pursued their longing with such intensity that it was truly beyond words.
Then, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When those goddesses gather flowers, Their minds are distracted and find no peace."
Just as a village swept away by water is completely submerged with no means of escape,
so too at this time the host of jade maidens surrounded him, weeping;
their countenances were exceedingly beautiful, yet they perished while still cherishing the flowers.
Even among humans there was weeping; having lost their beloved son, their very entrails were torn with grief.
Before long, he met his end, destroyed by impermanence.
The nāga girl followed after him in pursuit, and all the nāgas gathered together.
The seven-headed ones, though extremely fierce, are harmed by the golden-winged garuḍas.
The devas are filled with sorrow; so too it is among human beings.
The nāga maidens are filled with sorrow, and those in hell suffer agonizing pain.
Not knowing the sublime Dharma of the Four Truths as they truly are,
one undergoes birth and death, never escaping the ocean of the long-flowing stream.
Therefore, one should give rise to right thought and cultivate all pure dharmas.
"One will surely be free from suffering and affliction, and will no longer undergo the miseries of existence.

Therefore, monks, you should constantly cultivate the perception of impermanence and extensively disseminate the perception of impermanence; thus, you shall sever craving for the realm of form and craving for the formless realm, as well as sever conceit, so that ignorance is forever exhausted without remainder."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
11 (Eleven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, two disciples—one of Maudgalyāyana and one of Ānanda—were conversing together.
“Which of us two is superior when we chant the scriptures in unison?
At that time, many bhikṣus heard these two discussing this with one another; having heard it, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"Now there are two people discussing together:
'Of us two who recite the sūtras and chant the gāthās together, which one is more excellent?'"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go and summon these two bhikṣus to come. The bhikṣu replied:
"So be it, Blessed One," the bhikṣu replied, receiving the instruction from the Buddha.
He immediately went to where those two men were and said to them,
"The World-Honored One calls for you.
At that time, having heard the bhikṣu’s words, the two men went at once to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the two men, saying:
"You fools, you truly spoke these words:
'Which of us is more excellent when we recite the sutras and chant together?'"
The two replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"Have you ever heard me teach this Dharma as something for mutual contention and dispute?
How does such a teaching differ from that of the brahmins?"
The bhikṣus replied,
"We have not heard the Tathāgata teaching this Dharma.
The Blessed One said:
"I have never from the beginning taught this Dharma to the bhikṣus for the sake of contending for victory or defeat;
rather, the Dharma I teach today is intended for subduing and for edification."
If there is a bhikṣu who receives the Dharma, he should contemplate and reflect upon the principle of the four conditions: does his mind accord with the Sūtras, the Abhidharma, and the Vinaya?
"If you wish to practice in accordance with this, you should mindfully uphold it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To recite much that is of no benefit—this dharma is not sublime."
It is like calculating the number of ox heads; this is not the essential requirement for a śramaṇa.
If one recites and practices even a little, yet acts according to the Dharma within that Dharma—this Dharma is most supreme and may truly be called the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Though one may recite a thousand chapters, what benefit is there if they are not righteous?
It is better than a single phrase, hearing which one may attain the Way.
Though one may recite a thousand words, what benefit is there if they are not righteous?
It is not as good as a single principle: hearing it, one may attain the Way.
To defeat a thousand thousand enemies with a single man is not equal to conquering oneself; those who have already attained patience are supreme.
"Therefore, monks! From this day forward, do not harbor a mind of contention or a desire for victory or defeat.
Why is this? Because you should keep in mind that you must subdue all people."
Furthermore, monks, if there should be any monk who possesses a competitive mind and contends with others through a spirit of dispute, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma and the Vinaya.
Monks, for this reason, you should practice for yourselves.
"Therefore, having heard these words of the Buddha, the two bhikṣus rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and requested forgiveness for their transgression:
'From this day forward, we shall never do so again; we only pray that the World-Honored One will accept our confession.'"
The World-Honored One said:
"Within the Great Dharma, it is well to be able to reform one's errors. Since you yourself recognize that you harbored a contentious mind, I grant you permission to repent. O bhikṣus!"
Do not do so again.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Higher [Trainings], Seating, and Paths; Impermanence, Gardens, Pools, and the Outflow-free;
Cessation, Meditative Absorptions, The Four Joys, and Freedom from Dispute.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Twenty-three and Volume Twenty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kapiśā during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Two: The Chapter on the Accumulation of Goodness (32).
Section One. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the accumulation of the wholesome; you should reflect upon it well.
The bhikṣus replied: [As you command.]
“So be it, Blessed One,” the bhikṣus replied, receiving the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"What is called the 'good accumulation'?
It refers to the five faculties."
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
These, bhikṣus, are called [the five faculties].
There are these five faculties.
If a bhikṣu practices these five faculties, he becomes a srotāpanna, attains the dharma of non-retrogression, and will certainly reach the ultimate path;
progressing further in his practice, he becomes a sakṛdāgāmin and returns to this world only once more to bring an end to the limits of suffering.
Advancing further on that path, he becomes a non-returner (anāgāmin), no longer returning to this world, but instead attaining parinirvāṇa;

advancing further in his practice, his outflows are exhausted, he becomes one without outflows (anāsrava), attains liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and realizes this for himself through direct experience, sporting therein:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
"What is called the 'accumulation of goodness' refers precisely to the five faculties.
This is because they constitute the greatest accumulation and are the most sublime among all accumulations.
If one does not practice these dharmas, one will not achieve the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, nor that of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
If one attains these five faculties, there will then be the four fruits and the path of the three vehicles.
That which is called the "accumulation of goodness" has these five faculties as its preeminent basis. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
"You should seek skillful means to practice these five faculties. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the mass of unwholesomeness; you should reflect upon it well.
The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"What is called the accumulation of the unwholesome?
It refers to the five hindrances."
What are the five?

They are the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt; these are called the five hindrances.
If you wish to know what constitutes a mass of unwholesome states, it is called the five hindrances.
Why is this so? A bhikṣu should know that if these five hindrances exist, there is the prospect of rebirth among animals, hungry ghosts, or in hell; all unwholesome dharmas arise from them.

Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to eliminate the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five merits in serving and paying homage to the Buddha. What are these five? First, physical beauty;

second, a pleasant voice; third, abundant wealth and jewels; fourth, birth into the family of a householder; and fifth, upon the dissolution of the body after death, rebirth in a happy realm, the heavens."
The reason for this is that the Tathāgata has no equal.

The Tathāgata possesses faith, possesses ethical discipline, possesses learning, possesses wisdom, and possesses the perfection of excellent physical form; thus, he has accomplished these five virtues.
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one obtain an upright and handsome appearance through prostrating before the Buddha?
It is because, upon seeing the form and image of the Buddha, one gives rise to a heart of joy; by these causes and conditions, one obtains an upright and handsome appearance."
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one obtain a beautiful voice?
Having seen the image of the Tathāgata, one thrice proclaims these titles:
"Namo to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. By these causes and conditions, one obtains a beautiful voice.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one possess abundant wealth and many treasures?

It is because they saw the Tathāgata and performed great acts of giving—scattering flowers, lighting lamps, and offering other various gifts; through these causes and conditions, they obtained great wealth and treasures.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions was he born into the family of a householder?

Upon seeing the form of the Tathāgata, his mind was free from defiled attachment; he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and paid homage to the Buddha with a sincere heart. By these causes and conditions, he was born into the family of a householder.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one, upon the dissolution of the body after death, arise in a good destination, the heavens?
It is the constant law of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, that any sentient beings who pay homage to the Tathāgata through five causal factors shall be born in a good destination, the heavens.
This, monks, is called the five causes and conditions for the merit of bowing to the Buddha. Therefore, monks!
If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to pay homage to the Buddha, they should seek skillful means to accomplish these five merits.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“It is as if there were a house with two doors facing each other; suppose there is a person living inside and another person living above, who can observe and clearly see all those entering and exiting below.”
I am also like this.

With the divine eye, I observe the various classes of sentient beings—those who are born and those who pass away, those in good destinations and those in evil destinations, those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance, whether handsome or unattractive—and I know them all according to the seeds sown by their respective actions.

"Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who practice good through body, speech, and mind; who do not revile the noble ones; and who practice right view, being endowed with correct insight—when their bodies dissolve and their lives end, they are reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly realms. This is called 'sentient beings practicing good.'"
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who practice these wholesome dharmas and do not commit evil deeds, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will come to be born among humans.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who act wickedly in body, speech, and mind, committing unwholesome deeds, after their lives end, they will be born among the hungry ghosts.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who commit evil through their body, speech, and mind; they slander the noble ones and are possessed of wrong views. After the end of their lives, they are reborn among the animals.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who commit evil through their body, speech, and mind, performing unwholesome deeds and slandering the noble ones; after their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.
At that time, the hell-wardens led this sinner before King Yama and spoke thus:
"Great King, you should know that this person committed evil deeds of body and mind in a previous life; having performed various unwholesome actions, he has been born here in this hell."
"Great King!
You should consider by what offense this person is to be punished.
At that time, King Yama gradually questioned the man privately regarding his crime and said to him:

"How is it, man! When you were formerly a human being in a previous life, did you not see that there are those born as humans who, while dwelling in the womb, experience extreme hardship and suffering that is truly difficult to endure; and when they have grown up, do they not receive nourishment through nursing and bathing of their bodies?"
At that time, the sinner replied,
"I truly saw it, Great King! Yama, the King of Hell, said:
"O man! Why do you not yourself know the essential practice of the dharma of birth?
One should cultivate the dharmas of body, speech, and mind toward all wholesome realms."
The sinner replied:
"So be it, Great King! As Your Majesty commands."
"However, because you were deluded and confused, you did not distinguish between wholesome deeds.

King Yama said, "As you have stated, the matter is no different; furthermore, I know that you committed no actions of body, speech, or mind. Nevertheless, for today, I must investigate your negligent and sinful conduct."
"This was not done by one's parents, nor was it done by kings or ministers; it was originally committed by oneself, and now one receives the retribution for it oneself.
At that time, King Yama first questions them regarding their offenses and subsequently orders them to be punished.
Next, a second heavenly messenger questioned that person, saying:

"When you were formerly a human being, did you not see an old man whose physical form was extremely debilitated, whose gait was painfully exhausted, whose clothes were soiled and dusty, who trembled in his movements, whose breath was a groan, and who no longer possessed the vigor of youth?"
At that time, the sinner replied:
"It is so, Great King! I have indeed seen it."
King Yama replied: "You should know for yourself:
'I too now possess this form subject to aging; being weary of old age, I must cultivate wholesome deeds.'"
The sinner replied, "It is so,
Great King! At that time, I truly did not believe it."
King Yama replied: "I truly know this;
you have failed to practice right conduct of body, speech, and mind. Now I shall punish you for your offense so that you will not commit it again in the future."

The evil you have committed was not done by your parents, nor was it created by the king, the ministers, or the people; you have now created this transgression yourself and must receive its retribution yourself.
At that time, after King Yama had thus exhorted him with this second divine messenger, he addressed that person again with the third divine messenger, saying:
"When you were a human being in your previous life, did you not see those who were ill?"
"Lying upon excrement and urine, unable to rise or move by oneself.
The sinner replied, "It is so."
"Great King! I truly saw it. King Yama said:
"How is it, man! Do you not know for yourself:
'I too shall have this illness; I cannot escape this affliction'?"
The sinner replied: "It is indeed so, Great King!
I truly did not see him."
King Yama said: "I also know this;
you were foolish and deluded, failing to understand. I shall now inflict punishment upon you so that you may not commit such sinful deeds hereafter."
"It was not done by father or mother, nor was it created by kings or ministers.
At that time, after King Yama had given this instruction, he further addressed that person with the words of the fourth divine messenger:
"How is it, man, that your body is like a withered tree, devoid of sensation as the wind has departed and the fire has been extinguished, while your five kinsmen surround you and wail?"
The sinner replied, "It is so, Great King!"
"I have already seen it.
King Yama said, "Why did you not think this: [that you would fall into hell]?"
"I too shall not escape this death.
The sinner replied, "It is indeed so, Great King!"
"I truly was not aware of it.
King Yama said, "I also believe that you were unaware of this dharma; now I shall punish you so that you will not commit such an offense again in the future."

This unwholesome transgression was not committed by your father, nor by your mother, nor created by kings, ministers, or the people; you yourself originally committed it, and now you yourself must undergo its retribution.
At that time, King Yama again addressed that person with the fifth divine messenger, saying:

"When you were formerly a human being, did you not see thieves who broke through walls and demolished houses to take the wealth and treasures of others, or who set fires, or who hid things along the roads?"

Suppose one were captured by a king and either had one's hands and feet cut off, or was executed, or was cast into prison, or was bound back-to-back and led to the marketplace, or was made to carry sand and stones, or was hung upside down, or was shot with a volley of arrows, or had molten copper poured over one's body, or was roasted with fire, or had one's skin flayed and forced to eat it, or had one's belly ripped open and stuffed with straw, or was boiled in boiling water, or had one's head cut with a blade or crushed under a wheel, or was trampled to death by an elephant's foot, or was impaled on a stake until death?
The sinner replied, "I truly saw it. King Yama said:
"Why have you stolen another's property in secret?
Knowing full well that there was a matter at hand, why did you commit this offense? "It is so, Great King!"
"I was truly deluded and confused.
King Yama said, "I too believe what you have said;
I shall now punish you for your offense so that you will not commit it again in the future."
This offender did not have his crime committed by his parents, nor by kings, ministers, or the people; he committed the sin himself and shall receive the retribution himself.
At that time, after King Yama had finished interrogating him regarding his offenses, he commanded the wardens of hell:
"Quickly take this man and cast him into the prison!
Thereupon, the wardens, having received the king’s command, led the offender away and cast him into the prison.
The left side of the hell is intensely ablaze with fire; it consists of iron walls and iron enclosures, and the ground is likewise made of iron.

It has four city gates that are extremely foul-smelling, appearing as defiled by excrement and urine. It is surrounded on all four sides by mountains of knives and trees of swords, and its top is covered with an iron lattice cage.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Four walls and four city gates, Vast and long, truly a fortress;
Covered by an iron cage, There is no time for seeking release."
At that time, upon the iron ground, fire blazed with extreme intensity;
the walls, extending for a hundred yojanas, were glowing with a uniform color.
In the center stood four pillars, the sight of which was truly terrifying.
When they reach the Forest of Swords, where the Iron-Beaked Crows dwell, the stench makes it truly difficult to abide; beholding it, one’s hair stands on end.
There are sixteen compartments containing various instruments of terror.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, the wardens of hell will strike and beat this person with various forms of torment.
When that sinner lifts his foot and places it within the prison, his flesh and blood are completely exhausted, and only his bones remain.”
At that time, the hell-wardens take these offenders and further hack their bodies with sharp axes; the suffering is beyond calculation, and they cannot seek death.
Only after their retribution has been extinguished can they be liberated;
until the sinful karma they committed while among humans has been entirely eliminated, they cannot escape.
"At that time, the hell-wardens lead these offenders to the Sword-Blade Trees, making them climb up and down.

While they are upon the trees, the offenders are devoured by iron-beaked crows; some peck at their heads to eat the brains, while others seize their hands and feet, breaking the bones to extract the marrow."
"However, as their retribution is not yet complete—if the retribution were finished, they would then depart.
At that time, the wardens seize those offenders and force them to embrace a hot copper pillar while sitting upon it."
In a previous life, because he delighted in lewdness and debauchery, he incurred this retribution;
pursued by his transgressions, he can never escape them.
At that time, the hell-wardens pull a sinew from the heel up to the nape of the neck and drag him forward.
Some are made to ride in carts, moving forward or backward without any autonomy; the suffering endured therein is beyond measure.
Only when their offenses have been extinguished will they finally emerge.
"At that time, the hell-wardens seize those offenders and place them upon a mountain of fire, driving them up and down.
At that time, they become utterly scorched and wasted away, only then emerging."
At that time, because of these causes and conditions, the offenders are unable to seek death; they must have their offenses completely exhausted before they can emerge.
Then, the hell-wardens again seize the offenders, pull out their tongues, and cast them behind their backs, where they undergo unspeakable suffering and are unable to seek death.
At that time, the hell-wardens again take the offenders and place them upon the Mountain of Blades; they sever their feet, or sever their heads, or sever their hands.
Only when their offenses have been extinguished will they finally be released.

"At that time, the hell-wardens further cover the bodies of the offenders with hot, large iron leaves, just as one puts on clothes when alive. At that moment, the suffering and agony are difficult to endure; all this is due to the cause of greed, which leads them to commit such sins."

At that time, the hell-wardens further compelled the offenders to perform five kinds of forced labor; they drove them down to lie prostrate and took iron nails to pierce their hands and feet, and then used another nail to pierce their hearts. Within this state, they underwent such agony as is truly beyond description.
"One must cause one's sins to be extinguished before one may depart.
At that time, the wardens again seized the offenders, turned their bodies upside down, and cast them into the cauldrons.
At that time, the body reaches the lower part and is completely scorched and destroyed;
when it returns to the upper part, it is likewise scorched and destroyed.

When it reaches the four sides, it is again completely scorched and destroyed. The bitter and agonizing pain is beyond measure; whether manifest or unmanifest, it is scorched and destroyed, just like small beans being boiled in a large cauldron, rising and falling.

Now this sinner is likewise: whether manifest or unmanifest, he is decomposed; he undergoes unspeakable suffering therein, and must remain until his retribution is fully exhausted before he may finally emerge.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there may be a time when, after many years have passed within that hell, the eastern gate finally opens.
At that moment, the offenders again approach the gate, and it closes of its own accord.”
At that time, all those people fell prostrate upon the ground, suffering therein in ways beyond full description.
At times, each cried out their grievances and debts, saying:
"Because of you, I was unable to leave this door."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The fool is always full of joy, Like the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
The wise man is always filled with sorrow, Like a prisoner within a jail."
"At that time, after having passed hundreds of thousands of myriads of years within the great hell, the northern gate opens again.
At that time, the offenders proceed toward the northern gate, but the gate then closes once more; they must first extinguish their offenses before they may finally emerge."
At that time, after those offenders have again passed several million years, they finally emerge; for the offenses committed among human beings must necessarily be brought to completion.
At that time, the wardens take the offenders again and hack their bodies with iron axes, making them undergo such punishments so as to exhaust their remaining retribution.
"One must ensure that the suffering of one's offenses is completely exhausted before one may emerge.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that there may come a time when that eastern gate opens once again."
At that time, those sentient beings again go to the eastern gate, but the gate closes by itself so they cannot exit;

even if they should manage to exit, there is a great mountain outside toward which they must go. Once they have entered the mountain, they are crushed between two mountains as if sesame seeds were being pressed for oil, suffering therein in ways beyond measure.
"One must exhaust all suffering before one can finally emerge.
At that time, those sinners advance further and encounter the Hell of Hot Ashes, which is many thousands of millions of *yojanas* in length and breadth; therein they undergo suffering beyond measure.
One must exhaust the full measure of their offenses before they may depart.
Moving forward again, one encounters next the Hell of Knife Piercing.
At that time, the offender enters this Hell of Knife Piercing, whereupon a great wind arises, destroying the body, sinews, and bones of the offender, who undergoes unspeakable suffering therein.
"One must wait until one's offenses are extinguished before one may depart.
Next, there is the Great Hot Ash Hell.
At that time, the offender enters this Great Hot Ash Hell once more; their body is melted and rotted away, and they undergo immeasurable suffering.
They must cause their offenses to be extinguished before they may emerge.
At that time, although these offenders have escaped this Hell of Hot Ashes, they encounter again the Hell of Swords, which extends for many thousands of miles in both length and breadth.
At that time, the offenders enter this Hell of Swords and Blades; they undergo unspeakable suffering therein until their retribution is extinguished, after which they finally emerge.

"Next, there is the Hell of Boiling Excrement, wherein there are tiny insects that enter the bones and penetrate the marrow to devour these people; even after escaping this hell, they encounter the hell-wardens before them."
At that time, the hell-wardens asked the sinners:
"Where do you wish to go? From where have you come?"
The sinners replied:
"We do not know the place from which we have come, nor do we know where we shall go.
However, today we are extremely hungry and exhausted, and our minds desire food."
The hell-wardens replied, "We shall provide for you.

At that time, the wardens took the offender and laid him on his back; they then took a large, glowing-hot iron ball and made the offender swallow it, and thus the suffering endured by the offender was beyond measure.
At that time, glowing iron balls pass down through the mouth, completely rotting the intestines and stomach; the suffering endured is immeasurable.
Only when the retribution for their sins has been extinguished do they finally emerge.

"However, those offenders, unable to endure this agony, return once more to the Hot Excrement Hell, the Sword-and-Spear Hell, and the Great Hot Ash Hell, passing through these various hells again and again."
At that time, those beings, unable to endure the suffering, turned their heads back toward the Hot Excrement Hell.
Then, the hell-wardens said to those beings:
"Where do you wish to go?"
"From where have you come?
The offenders replied,
"We ourselves do not know from where we have come, and now we do not know where we shall go."
The hell-warden asked,
"What do you require now?
The sinner replied:
"We are extremely thirsty and wish to drink water.

At that time, the hell-wardens take the offenders and lay them on their backs, pouring molten copper into their mouths and causing it to flow down through them. They undergo unspeakable suffering therein; they must endure this until their retribution is extinguished before they may finally depart.
At that time, unable to endure this suffering, that person returns to the Hell of Boiling Excrement, the Hell of Sword-Trees, and the Hell of Hot Ashes, and enters once again into the Great Hell.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, the suffering of the offender is beyond calculation. Even if that offender sees forms with his eyes, his mind finds no pleasure in them; likewise, whether he hears sounds, smells odors, tastes flavors, feels tactile sensations, or cognizes mental phenomena with his mind, in all cases he gives rise to anger.”
The reason for this is that, due to the retribution of not having performed virtuous deeds in the past and instead constantly committing evil karma, they have incurred these offenses.
At that time, King Yama commands those offenders, saying:

"You did not obtain wholesome benefits; formerly, while among humans, you received human blessings, yet your actions of body, speech, and mind were inconsistent with them. Furthermore, you did not practice giving, benevolence, benefiting others, or impartiality. For this reason, you now undergo this suffering."
These evil deeds were not committed by one's parents, nor were they committed by kings or ministers.
Those sentient beings whose body, speech, and mind are pure and undefiled are like the Ābhāsvara devas;
those sentient beings who commit various evil deeds are like those in the hells.
"Because your bodies, speech, and minds were impure, you have incurred this retribution.
Monks, you should know that King Yama then speaks thus:
"On what day shall I be delivered from this suffering and hardship and be born among human beings?"
"Having already obtained a human body, you have further been able to leave the household life, shave off your hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and go forth to study the Way.
Even King Yama thinks thus; how much more so for you who have now obtained a human body and become śramaṇas!
Therefore, monks, you should always mindfully practice the conduct of body, speech, and mind, ensuring there is no deficiency;
you should extinguish the five fetters and cultivate the five faculties.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Eastern Grove, the Deer Mother’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the World-Honored One spread his seat upon an open space, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him. The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Now, in this open space, quickly strike the ghaṇṭā."
"The reason for this is that today, the fifteenth day of the seventh month, is the day of the *pravāraṇā* (the end of the rainy season retreat).
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and spoke this verse:
"With pure eyes beyond compare, there is no practice he has not mastered."
"Wisdom is free from attachment; what is it called that constitutes the observance of the *varṣā*?
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied to Ānanda in verse:
"The observance of the *varṣā* consists in the purification of the three karmas—those performed by body, speech, and mind."
Two bhikṣus face one another, Each confessing their own faults.
They each state their own names: "Today the assembly performs the *varṣā* (the rains retreat ceremony);
I too receive it with a pure mind. I only pray that you will forgive my transgressions."
At that time, Ānanda again asked about its meaning in verse:
“The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—
are they all the Dharma of the Buddhas?”
“Is it only Śākyamuni?
At that time, the Buddha again replied to Ānanda in verse:
“The disciples of the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, possessed pure hearts.”
These are all the dharmas of the Buddhas, not merely those of Śākyamuni today.
Pratyekabuddhas do not possess these dharmas; they have no ordained years and no disciples.
They travel alone without companions and do not preach the Dharma to others.
"In future ages, there will be Buddha-World-Honored Ones as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, beyond all calculation;
they too shall observe this year-long retreat, just as in the Dharma of Gautama today.

At that time, having heard these words, the Venerable Ānanda was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself. He immediately ascended the lecture hall, took up the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) in his hand, and spoke thus:
"I now beat this drum of the Tathāgata’s faith; all those who are disciples of the Tathāgata shall gather here in full assembly.
At that time, he further spoke these verses:
"Having subdued the enemy of the Māra-powers, He has eliminated the fetters without remainder."
When the ghaṇṭā is struck in the open air, the bhikṣus who hear it shall assemble.
All those who wish to hear the Dharma and cross the flood of the ocean of birth and death—
upon hearing this wondrous sound, they shall all gather here.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having struck the ghaṇṭā, approached the Blessed One, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Now is the right time; I pray only that the Blessed One will command what is to be done."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Sit down in order; the Tathāgata himself shall know the proper time.
Then, the World-Honored One sat upon the grass seat and addressed the bhikṣus:
"You all should sit upon grass seats.
The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣus each sat upon seats of grass.
Then, the World-Honored One, having silently observed the bhikṣus, addressed them:
"I now wish to perform the *pravāraṇā*.
Have I committed no fault toward the assembly?
Furthermore, have I not transgressed in body, speech, or mind?"
When the Tathāgata had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus remained silent and did not respond.
At that time, he addressed the bhikṣus a second and a third time:
"I now wish to observe the *varṣā* (the rains retreat)."
"Am I then without fault among the assembly?
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The assembly of bhikṣus observes that the Tathāgata has no faults of body, speech, or mind."

The reason for this is that today the World-Honored One delivers those not yet delivered, liberates those not yet liberated, and leads to parinirvāṇa those who have not attained it. He provides protection for the unprotected, serves as eyes for the blind, and acts as the Great King of Physicians for the sick. Solely honored within the triple world, there is none who can equal him; he is the most venerable and supreme. He causes those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment to give rise to the aspiration for the Way. He awakens those among the multitude who have not yet awakened, and enables those who have not heard the Dharma to hear it. For those who are lost, he provides a path, always by means of the True Dharma.
For these reasons, the Tathāgata is without fault toward the multitude, nor does he possess any transgression of body, speech, or mind.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now speak to the Tathāgata of my own accord; however, have I committed no offense against the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Now, Śāriputra, you have no non-practice whatsoever performed by body, speech, or mind."

The reason for this is that your present wisdom is unsurpassed; it is manifold wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, boundless wisdom, peerless wisdom, swift wisdom, quick wisdom, profound wisdom, and impartial wisdom. You possess few desires and are content, delighting in places of tranquility. You abound in skillful means, your mindfulness is undisturbed, and you are endowed with dhāraṇīs and samādhis.

Your faculties are fully perfected: you have achieved morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation. You are courageous and patient, your speech is free from evil, you do not engage in unrighteousness, your mind and nature are composed and orderly, and you do not act with violence.
Just as the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning Sage King is destined to succeed to the royal throne and turn the wheel of Dharma, so too is Śāriputra;

he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, which neither gods, nor humans, nor nāgas, nor ghosts, nor māras, nor the devas of Māra have ever turned before. What you have now spoken is always in accordance with the meaning of the Dharma and has never deviated from principle.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"These five hundred bhikṣus are all about to undergo the *varṣā* (rain-retreat).
Are these five hundred people entirely free from fault before the Tathāgata?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"I do not reproach these five hundred bhikṣus for their conduct of body, speech, or mind. Why is this?

Within this assembly of Śāriputra, it is exceedingly pure and free from any blemish; even the lowest-ranking member of this assembly has attained the stage of Srotāpanna and shall certainly eventually reach the stage of non-retrogression."
"For this reason, I do not resent or reproach this assembly.
At that time, Tāgisi, who was among the assembly, rose from his seat, went before the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am now capable and wish to discuss a certain matter."
The Blessed One said,
"If you wish to say something, now is the very time. Thereupon, Tāgisi,
in the presence of the Buddha, praised the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, and spoke this verse:
"On the fifteenth day of purity, five hundred bhikṣus assembled;
all fetters and bonds were completely severed, and craving no longer arose.
Like a great and holy Wheel-Turning King surrounded by his ministers,"
Pervading all worlds, both in the heavens and among men;
the Great General, the Honored One among humanity, acting as a guide for all people;
his disciples joyfully follow him, for he has mastered the three insights and the six supernormal powers.
"All are true sons of the Buddha, free from all dust and defilement;
they are able to sever the thorns of desire and craving—today I take refuge in them.
At that time, the World-Honored One approved of what the elder Kiśa had said.
At that time, Tāgisi thought to himself:
“The Tathāgata has approved what I have said today.
Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, unable to contain himself, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, withdrew, and returned to his original place.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost disciple for composing verses is the bhikṣu Tārkṣya."
"The one who spoke without hesitation was also the bhikṣu Bahudhītika.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a certain devaputra among the Trāyastriṃśa gods whose body exhibited five omens of approaching death.

What are these five? First, his flower crown withered of its own accord; second, his robes became soiled and dusty; third, sweat flowed from beneath his armpits; fourth, he took no pleasure in his own seat; and fifth, his celestial maidens turned away from him in rebellion.
At that time, that devaputra was distressed, sorrowful, and afflicted, beating his breast and sighing deeply.
When Śakra Devānām Indra heard this devaputra’s distress, sorrow, and affliction as he beat his breast and sighed, he immediately commanded another devaputra:
"What kind of sound is this that reaches even here?"
That deva replied, "O Devaputra, you should know that there is now another deva whose life is about to end, and five omens of death have appeared:

first, his flower crown withers of its own accord; second, his garments become soiled and dusty; third, sweat flows from beneath his arms; fourth, he finds no joy in his own seat; and fifth, his jade maidens turn away and desert him."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra went to where the deva who was about to die was and said to him:
"For what reason are you now so sorrowful, distressed, and afflicted as to have reached this state?"

The devaputra replied: "Venerable Indaka, how could you not be filled with grief and affliction? Your life is about to end, and there are five portents of death: your flowers wither, your garments become soiled and greasy, sweat flows from beneath your arms, you no longer take pleasure in your own place, and your celestial maidens desert you. Now these seven-jeweled palaces shall all be lost; the five hundred celestial maidens shall likewise scatter like stars, and the nectar I consume has now lost its flavor."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to that devaputra:
"Have you not heard the verse spoken by the Tathāgata?
'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; those who are born must surely die.'"
"Where there is no birth, there is no death; this cessation is the supreme bliss.
Why do you now grieve so deeply? All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; to wish for them to be permanent is impossible."
The devaputra replied: "How could it be otherwise, O Lord of Devas!
How could I not be filled with sorrow? Today my celestial body is pure and free from blemish; its radiance is like that of the sun and moon, illuminating everything without exception."
"After casting off this body, you shall be born within the womb of a pig in the city of Rājagṛha; once born, you will constantly eat excrement, and at the time of death, you will be cut by knives.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to that devaputra:
"You should now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; if you do so, you will not fall into the three evil realms."
At that time, the devaputra replied,
"Could it be that by taking refuge in the Triple Gem, one does not fall into the three evil realms?
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"In this way, O Devaputra!
Those who take refuge in the Three Jewels shall never fall into the three evil realms.
The Tathāgata has also spoken this verse:"
"Those who take refuge in the Buddha shall not fall into the three evil realms;
having exhausted their outflows among gods and humans, they shall surely reach Nirvana."
At that time, that deva asked Śakra Devānām-indra:
"Where, then, does the Tathāgata currently reside?
Śakra Devānām-indra replied:
“Now the Tathāgata is staying in Rājagṛha, in the city of Magadha, at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.”
The devaputra replied,
"I do not currently possess the power to go there and pay my respects to the Tathāgata.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
“Son of Heaven, you should know that one should place the right knee on the ground, kneel with the hands joined in prayer, and facing the realm below, speak thus:
‘I pray only that the World-Honored One will observe me well; now that I am at the point of exhaustion, I pray that you will take pity on me!’”
"Now I take refuge in the Three Honored Ones, the Tathāgata who is free from attachment.

At that time, following the words of Śakra Devānām Indra, that son of heaven knelt down toward the direction below, announced his own name, and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. For as long as his life lasted, he became a true son of the Buddha, no longer a celestial son.
When he had spoken these words three times in this manner, he was no longer to dwell in a pig’s womb, but was instead to be reborn into the family of a householder.
At that time, having witnessed these circumstances, that deva addressed Śakra Devānām Indra with this verse:
“A virtuous cause, not an evil one; For the sake of the Dharma, not for wealth.”
Guiding others by the right path—this is what the Honored One praises.
By relying on the Honored One, one does not fall into evil states; for rebirth as a pig is a most difficult condition to encounter.
One who reflects upon their own growth and development shall, by that very cause, behold the Buddha.
At that time, the devaputra, according to the length of his lifespan, was reborn into the family of a great elder in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the elder’s wife knew she was pregnant; when the ten months were nearly complete, she gave birth to a son who was peerless in his beauty, a rarity in the world.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing that this boy was approaching ten years of age, went to him repeatedly and said:
"You should remember the causal conditions you previously established, and declare:
'I shall, by means of him, behold the Buddha.'"
"Now is precisely the right time to see the World-Honored One;
if you do not go, you will surely have cause for regret later.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, when the hour arrived, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. He proceeded gradually until he reached the house of that elder and stood quietly outside the gate.

At that time, the son of a householder saw Śāriputra with his robes on and his alms bowl in hand, his appearance exceptionally distinguished. Having seen him, he went before Śāriputra and spoke these words: "Who are you now?"
"Whose disciple are you?
What Dharma do you practice? Śāriputra replied:
"My teacher is from the Śākya clan; he left the household life among them to study the Way. His name is Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and it is from him that I constantly receive the Dharma."
At that time, the young boy spoke this verse toward Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir, you now stand in stillness, Holding your bowl with a composed appearance;
What is it that you seek now?"
"With whom do you dwell here?
At that time, Śāriputra replied with a verse:
"I now seek no wealth, neither food nor clothing."
Therefore, I have come for your sake; listen well to my words.
Remember what you yourself said when you made your vow in the heavens:
"I shall see the Buddha among men. It is for this reason that I have come to inform you.
The appearance of the Buddhas is rare; the preaching of the Dharma is likewise so.
A human body is difficult to obtain, just like the udumbara flower.
Come now with me, and together behold the countenance of the Tathāgata.
"I shall certainly explain for you the essential path to the good realms.
At that time, having heard Śāriputra’s words, the son of the householder went immediately to his parents, prostrated himself at their feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the son of the householder said to his parents:
"I only pray that you will grant me permission to go to the presence of the World-Honored One to serve him, pay my respects, and inquire after his well-being."
The parents replied, "Now is precisely the right time.

The son of the householder immediately gathered fragrant flowers and fine white cotton cloth, and accompanied by the Venerable Śāriputra, proceeded together to the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"This son of a householder resides in this city of Rājagṛha, yet he does not recognize the Three Honored Ones. We only pray that the World-Honored One will skillfully preach the Dharma for him, so that he may attain liberation."

At that time, the elder’s son saw from afar that the World-Honored One was of upright and majestic countenance, with his faculties serene; his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, appearing like Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, and his face like the sun and moon, such that one could never tire of gazing upon him.
He advanced to pay homage at the Tathāgata’s feet and stood to one side.

At that time, the son of the householder scattered fragrant flowers over the Tathāgata and further offered a new white cotton cloth to the Tathāgata; he then bowed his head to the ground in prostration at the feet and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught him the Dharma, namely:

discourses on generosity, discourses on ethical discipline, and discourses on rebirth in the heavens; he explained that sensual desire is impure, that the outflows are a great affliction, and that renunciation is essential.
At that time, knowing that the young boy’s mind was opened and his intellect liberated, the World-Honored One taught him the Dharma which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly preach:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At that moment, the World-Honored One explained these in their entirety to the son of the elder.
At that moment, while still seated, the son of the householder was cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from further blemish.
Thereupon, the son of the householder rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to leave the household life and become a śramaṇa."
The World-Honored One replied, “One who would practice the Way does not take leave of his parents; such a person cannot become a śramaṇa.
At that time, the son of the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I must first obtain my parents' permission.
The World-Honored One said,
"Now is precisely the right time."
At that time, the son of the elder rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet with his head, and then withdrew.
Returning to where he was, he said to his parents:
"I only pray that you will grant me permission to become a śramaṇa."
The parents replied, "We have but this one son today;
moreover, our household business involves abundant wealth and many treasures, so it is extremely difficult to practice the way of a śramaṇa."
The son of the householder replied:
"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world occurs only once in hundreds of millions of eons; it is extremely difficult to encounter, for he appears only at rare intervals.
He is like the udumbara flower, which appears only at rare intervals."
"The Tathāgata is also like this; he appears only once in billions of kalpas.
At that time, the parents of the elder’s son each sighed and said, "Now is precisely the right time; do as you deem appropriate."
At that time, the son of the elder prostrated himself at [the elder's] feet, took his leave, and departed.
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the son of the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"My parents have granted me their permission; I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow me to enter the path.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"You should now ordain this son of a householder and cause him to become a śramaṇa. Śāriputra replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
At that time, Śāriputra received the instruction from the Buddha.
He ordained him as a śrāmaṇera and instructed him day after day.

At that time, that śrāmaṇera practiced self-discipline in a secluded place; for it is for this reason that sons of noble family leave the household life to study the Way, shave off their hair and beards, and practice the unsurpassed Brahma-faring, desiring to be free from suffering.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera immediately attained arhatship and went to where the World-Honored One was. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I have now seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma; I am entirely without doubt.”
The World-Honored One asked,
"How is it that you have seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma yet remain free from doubt?
The śrāmaṇera replied to the Buddha:

“Form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self; that which is non-self is empty; that which is empty neither exists nor does not exist, and is likewise without self.”
This is what the wise realize: feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent;

that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is without self; that which is without self is empty; that which is empty neither exists nor does not exist. This is what the wise realize: these flourishing aggregates are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self; they do not exist [as a self], they are full of manifold afflictions, incurable, a place of constant stench, and cannot be maintained for long. To perceive them all as being without self—to observe this Dharma today—is to have seen the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Śrāmaṇera! I grant that you shall become a great śramaṇa.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that śrāmaṇera rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Venerable Nārada was staying in the Bamboo Grove of the Elder at the kingdom of Pāṭaliputta.
At that time, King Muṇḍa’s chief queen passed away; the king loved and revered her deeply, and his remembrance of her never left his heart.
At that time, a certain person went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:
"Great King, you should know that the first consort has now passed away."
At that time, having heard that the queen had passed away, the king was immediately filled with grief and distress.
He said to the messenger: "Quickly carry the queen's corpse and place it in sesame oil so that I may see her."
At that time, the man, having received the king’s command, went at once to take hold of the queen’s body and placed it within sesame oil.
Then, hearing that the queen had passed away, the king was overcome with extreme grief and distress; he neither ate nor drank, ceased to practice the Dharma, and neglected his royal duties.
At that time, there was a man among the attendants named Sunian (Sumanas), who constantly held a sword for the Great King. He addressed the Great King, saying:

"Great King, you should know that within these borders there is a śramaṇa named Nārada, who has attained arhatship. He possesses great supernormal powers, is widely learned and all-knowing, and there is no matter he has not mastered. His eloquence is bold and wise, and his speech is always accompanied by a smile."
"I pray that Your Majesty will go there and listen to his preaching of the Dharma.
If Your Majesty hears the Dharma, you will no longer have sorrow, grief, or affliction.
The King replied to him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent! Well said these words.”
"Good thought! You must go now and speak first to that śramaṇa. For such is the way:
when a Wheel-turning Sage King wishes to go somewhere, he must first dispatch a messenger; it is not possible for him to arrive without having first sent a herald."
Then, Sunetra replied, "As Your Majesty commands.
Having received the king's instruction,
he went to the Bamboo Grove of the elder, approached Nārada, prostrated himself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Sunanda addressed the Venerable Nārada, saying:

"Venerable sir, you should know that the King’s consort has now passed away. Because of this affliction, the King neither eats nor drinks, nor does he attend to his royal duties or state affairs. He now wishes to come and behold your venerable countenance; we pray only that you will skillfully preach the Dharma for him, so that the King may no longer suffer from grief."
Narada replied, "If you wish to come,
now is precisely the right time. At that moment,
having heard these instructions, Sunetra prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet and then withdrew.
He went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:
"I have spoken to the śramaṇa;
Your Majesty should know this."
At that time, he immediately commanded Sunian:
"Quickly prepare the precious feathered chariot; I now wish to go and meet with the śramaṇa.
Thereupon, Sunian promptly prepared the precious feathered chariot and came forward to address the king, saying:
"The carriage is prepared; Your Majesty may know it is time.
Thereupon, the king mounted a chariot adorned with precious feathers and departed the city for Nārada’s location, proceeding on foot into the Elder’s Bamboo Grove.
According to the royal custom, the lady removed her fivefold royal regalia, bared one shoulder, and approached Nārada; she prostrated herself at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, Nārada said to the king:

"Great King, you should know that the phenomena of dreams and illusions give rise to sorrow; the phenomena of foam and bubbles, as well as masses of snow, give rise to sorrow; and furthermore, one should not allow the perception of the phenomena of flowers to give rise to sorrow."
The reason for this is that there are five things which are most impossible to obtain, as taught by the Tathāgata.
What are these five? First, when a thing is subject to exhaustion, to desire that it not be exhausted—this is impossible to obtain.
Now, as for things that are subject to extinction, to wish that they not be extinguished is impossible;
as for the law of aging, to wish that one does not age is impossible;
furthermore, regarding the law of illness, to wish that one does not fall ill is impossible.
Furthermore, Great King, it is impossible for one subject to the law of death to avoid dying. These, Great King,
are the five things that are most impossible to obtain, as taught by the Tathāgata.
At that time, Nārada spoke this verse:
"One does not obtain blessings through sorrow and distress;
if one harbors grief and anxiety, external conditions will find their opportunity."
If one who possesses wisdom does not dwell upon such thoughts,
external enemies will become distressed and find no opportunity.
Possessing perfect deportment and ritual decorum, they are fond of giving without avarice.
One should seek these skillful means so as to obtain their great benefit.
Even if they cannot be obtained, neither I nor those others will have sorrow, and thus will be free from affliction; let us see how the retribution for our actions unfolds.
"Furthermore, Great King, you should know that when one loses what ought not to be lost, one becomes sorrowful, anxious, pained, and distressed once it is lost; the suffering is beyond words."
That which I loved has been lost today; this is what is meant by losing what one has already lost. Within this, grief, sorrow, suffering, and distress arise—such pain is beyond words.
"Thus it is said, Great King:
this is the first thorn of sorrow that stains and clings to the mind; such is the nature of ordinary persons who do not know the origin from which birth, old age, sickness, and death come."
Furthermore, one hears that when noble disciples lose what ought to be lost, they do not give rise to sorrow, grief, suffering, or distress, but instead train themselves thus:
"What I have now lost is not unique to me alone; other people also possess this nature.

If I were to give rise to sorrow and grief therein, it would be inappropriate; it might cause my kinsmen to suffer sorrow and grief, bring joy to my enemies, cause my food to remain undigested and lead to illness, and result in physical fever. On account of this very cause, it may even lead to the end of life."

At that time, one is able to remove the thorns of sorrow and fear, and is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, no longer subject to the phenomena of calamity, affliction, and suffering.
"Furthermore, Great King!
When that which ought to be extinguished is extinguished, one then experiences grief, sorrow, suffering, and distress, an agony beyond words."
"That which I loved has perished today; this is called the perishing of what is perishable. Within this, grief, sorrow, suffering, and distress arise—pain that is beyond description."
"Thus it is said, Great King!
This is the second thorn of sorrow that stains and clings to the mind.
Such is the nature of ordinary people, who do not know the origin from which birth, old age, sickness, and death come."

Furthermore, one hears that when a noble disciple eliminates those things that ought to be eliminated, at that time the person does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, or distress. One should train in this way:
"What I am now eliminating is not unique to me alone; other people also possess this same nature. If I were to give rise to sorrow and lamentation regarding this, it would be inappropriate."

It may cause one's kinsmen to fall into grief and one's enemies to rejoice; it may cause food to remain undigested, thereby giving rise to illness, with the body becoming feverish and distressed, and by virtue of these causes and conditions, leading ultimately to death.

At that time, one is able to remove the thorns of sorrow and fear, and is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, no longer subject to the phenomena of calamity, affliction, and suffering.
"Furthermore, Great King!
That which is subject to aging inevitably ages; once aged, it becomes subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress—an agony beyond description."
"That which I love has today grown old; this is what is called 'that which was an object of youth has now aged,' and therein arises grief, lamentation, suffering, and distress, a pain beyond words."

"This, Great King, is called the third thorn of sorrow that stains and clings to the mind. Such is the nature of ordinary people, who do not know the origin from which birth, old age, sickness, and death come."
Furthermore, one hears that when a noble disciple encounters what is subject to aging, at that time that person does not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, or distress, but trains himself thus:
"That which I am now subject to aging is not unique to me alone; other people also possess this nature. If I were to give rise to sorrow regarding this, it would be unseemly."

Or perhaps his kinsmen will fall into grief, his enemies will rejoice, his food will not be digested and he will immediately fall ill; his body will be tormented by fever, and on account of these very causes, he will meet his end.

At that time, one is able to remove the thorns of sorrow and fear, and be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, no longer subject to the phenomena of calamity, affliction, and suffering.
"Furthermore, Great King!
That which is subject to illness becomes ill; once it is ill, it experiences grief, sorrow, suffering, and distress, such that its pain is beyond description."
That which I love is now afflicted by illness; this is what is called being ill with that which is ill, wherein grief, sorrow, suffering, and distress arise, such that the pain is beyond words.
"This, Great King, is called the fourth thorn of sorrow that stains and clings to the mind.
Such is the nature of ordinary people, who do not know the origin from which birth, old age, sickness, and death come."

Furthermore, one hears that when noble disciples fall ill with whatever ailment is appropriate to their condition, they do not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, or distress; rather, they train themselves thus:
"The illness I now suffer is not unique to me alone; other people also possess this nature. Were I to give rise to sorrow and lamentation over it, it would be unseemly."

It may cause one's kinsmen to fall into grief and one's enemies to rejoice; it may cause food to remain undigested, thereby giving rise to illness, with the body becoming feverish and distressed, and by virtue of these causes and conditions, leading ultimately to death.
At that time, one is able to remove the thorns of sorrow and fear, and cast off birth, old age, sickness, and death; there will no longer be any phenomena of calamity, affliction, or suffering.
"Furthermore, Great King!
That which is destined to die must die; once dead, it is called a 'dead thing. To give rise within that state to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair is an unspeakable pain."
This, Great King, is called the fifth thorn of sorrow that stains and clings to the mind.
Such is the nature of ordinary people, who do not know the origin from which birth, old age, sickness, and death come.
Furthermore, one hears that when a noble disciple who is subject to death dies, at that time that person does not give rise to sorrow or distress, but trains himself thus:
"I am not the only one who dies now; others also possess this nature. If I were to give rise to grief and anxiety therein, it would not be appropriate."

Or it may cause one's kinsmen to fall into grief and one's enemies to rejoice; the food consumed will not be digested, and one will immediately fall ill, with the body burning with fever. With this as its primary cause, one will eventually meet their end.
At that time, one is able to remove the thorns of sorrow and fear, and escape from birth, old age, sickness, and death, no longer subject to the phenomena of calamity, affliction, and suffering.
At that time, the Great King addressed the Venerable Nārada, saying:
"What is the name of this teaching?
How should it be practiced?"
Narada said: "This sutra is titled 'The Removal of the Affliction of Sorrow'; you should keep it in mind and practice accordingly.
At that time, the king replied:
"It is truly as you have said; my sorrow has been dispelled.
For this is why: having heard this Dharma, all my grief and suffering are now forever eliminated."
If the Venerable One has any instructions to give, please come to the palace frequently; we shall provide for you so that the people of this land may long enjoy inexhaustible blessings.

I only pray that the Venerable One will expound this Dharma extensively so that it may endure forever in the world, bringing long-term peace and security to the fourfold assembly; I now take refuge in the Venerable Nārada.
Narada said: "Great King!
Do not take refuge in me; you should instead take refuge in the Buddha."
Then the king asked,
"Where is the Buddha now? Nārada replied:

"Great King, you should know that from the Śākya clan of the Great Kingdom of Kapilavastu, the lineage of the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings has emerged. That king had a son named Siddhārtha, who left home to study the Way and has now attained Buddhahood for himself; he is titled Śākyamuni. You should take refuge in him."
The Great King asked again:
"Where is he now? How far is it from here?"
Narada replied, "The Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa.
The Great King said:
"How swift is the Tathāgata’s entry into parinirvāṇa!
Had he remained in the world, we would have traveled many tens of millions of yojanas to go and visit him.
At that moment, he rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and spoke these words:
“I take refuge in the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. For as long as life lasts, I request to be accepted as an upāsaka; I shall no longer kill living beings.
State affairs are many and pressing; I now wish to return to the palace.”
Narada said, "Now is precisely the right time.
