Thereupon, the king rose from his seat, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, King Munda, having heard what Nārada had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"A person afflicted by illness who possesses five qualities will not recover in due time, but shall remain constantly upon their bed."
What are these five?

At that time, the patient does not discriminate regarding food and drink, does not eat according to the proper seasons, does not attend to medical treatment, is full of anxiety, joy, and anger, and does not give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward those who care for him.
"Monks, it is said that a person who is ill and possesses these five qualities will not recover in a timely manner.
Furthermore, if a sick person possesses five other qualities, they shall recover in a timely manner."
What are these five?

In this regard, the patient chooses what to eat, eats at the proper times, attends to medical treatment, harbors no sorrow or anxiety, and maintains a mind of loving-kindness toward those who care for them.
"Thus it is said, bhikṣu:
when a sick person accomplishes these five qualities, they will recover in due time.
'In this way, bhikṣu!'"
The first five dharmas should be abandoned through mindfulness; the latter five dharmas should be practiced together.
Thus, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a caregiver for a sick person possesses five qualities, the patient will not recover in a timely manner and will remain constantly upon their bed."
What are these five? In this regard, the person attending to the sick does not distinguish between wholesome medicines;
they are indolent and lack a spirit of vigor; they are constantly prone to anger; and they also take pleasure in sleep.
They attend to the sick merely out of a desire for food;
they do not provide spiritual offerings, nor do they engage the sick in conversation or discourse.
This, O bhikṣus, is called...
"If a person who attends to the sick accomplishes these five qualities, they will not recover in time.
Furthermore, monks! If a person who attends to the sick accomplishes five qualities, they will recover in time and shall not remain confined to their bed."
What are the five? In this regard, the one who attends to the sick distinguishes a skilled physician;
furthermore, they do not become indolent, rising before and lying down after [the patient].
He always delights in conversation and sleeps little;
he makes offerings through the Dharma and does not crave food or drink;
he is capable of preaching the Dharma to the sick.
"Monks, it is said that one who tends to the sick and accomplishes these five qualities will recover in due time. Therefore, monks,"
When attending to a patient, one should abandon the former five qualities and adopt the latter five. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Monkey Grove at Vaiśālī together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the general Siṃha went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then the Buddha said to Siṃha: "How is it, Siṃha?"
"Do you constantly practice giving at home?
Siṃha replied to the Buddha:

"I always practice giving outside the four city gates and in the marketplace, providing alms at all times without fail. Whether it be food, clothing, incense, flowers, carriages, horses, or seats, I provide whatever they require."
The Buddha said to Siṃha: "Excellent! Excellent!"
One is thus able to practice giving without harboring thoughts of stinginess.
When a donor or patron gives at the appropriate time, there are five merits.
What are these five?
Thereupon, the fame of that donor and patron spread far and wide, and the multitude praised him, saying:
"In such-and-such a village there is a donor and patron who always delights in receiving śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; whatever he provides, he gives so that none shall lack for anything."
"This, O Siṃha, is called the first merit obtained by a donor and patron. Furthermore, O Siṃha:"

When a donor or patron enters among the assembly of śramaṇas, kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, or householders, they feel neither shame nor remorse, nor do they experience any fear—just as the lion, king of beasts, feels no dread or difficulty when amidst a herd of deer.
This, Sīha, is called the second virtue obtained by a donor, a master of charity. "Furthermore, Sīha!
A donor, a master of charity, is revered and honored by the multitude; those who see him rejoice, looking upon him with never-tiring affection, like a child beholding its father."
"Thus it is said, Siṃha, that a donor and patron obtains this third merit. Furthermore, Siṃha!
After the death of a donor and patron, they shall be reborn in one of two places: either in the heavens or among human beings."
In the heavens they are revered by the devas, and among humans they are honored and esteemed.
This, O Siṃha, is called the fourth merit obtained by a donor and patron.
"Furthermore, Siṃha! A donor, a master of giving, possesses wisdom that far surpasses that of the multitude; in this very life, he exhausts all outflows and does not undergo future rebirths.
This is what is meant, Siṃha!"
"The donor and patron obtains this fifth merit.
Indeed, there are five virtues of giving that constantly follow one's own person.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"With a mind always joyful in giving, one fulfills and perfects merit;
amidst the assembly, one is free from doubt and difficulty, and likewise possesses no fear.
The wise person should practice giving, never having a mind of regret or remorse."
"In the Heaven of the Thirty-three, he is surrounded by jade maidens.

You should know, O Siṃha, that this is because the donor and patron has been born in two auspicious realms; in his present body, he has exhausted all outflows and attained the state of the unconditioned."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Generosity is the provision for future lives; It leads inevitably to the ultimate state.
Virtuous deities will always protect such a person, And they shall likewise bring them great joy."

"Regarding why this is so, Siṃha, you should know that at the time of giving, one always harbors joy; body and mind are firm and stable, all wholesome merits are fully perfected, one attains the state of samādhi without confusion, and knows things as they truly are."
How does one know it as it truly is?
One knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading out of suffering as they truly are. Therefore, Sīha!

One should seek skillful means and bestow gifts at the appropriate time; whether one wishes to attain the path of a śrāvaka or the path of a pratyekabuddha, all shall be fulfilled according to one's wish. Thus it is, Siṃha!
"One should train in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Siṃha rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 11 (11) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“When a donor or patron bestows gifts on the day of giving, they obtain five kinds of merit.”
What are the five? First is the gift of life; second is the gift of beauty; third is the gift of peace; fourth is the gift of strength; fifth is the gift of eloquence. These are called the five.
Furthermore, when a donor or patron bestows the gift of life, they desire long life;
when bestowing the gift of physical form, they desire handsomeness;
when bestowing the gift of peace, they desire freedom from illness.
When exerting physical effort in giving, one desires to be invincible;
when exercising eloquence in giving, one desires to attain unsurpassed, true, and correct eloquence.
Bhikṣus, you should know that on the day a donor or patron bestows gifts, there are these five merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Life, form, and peace are bestowed as gifts; Strength and eloquence constitute the fifth.
When these five virtues are fully prepared, One shall later receive inexhaustible merit."
The wise should contemplate giving, And eliminate the mind of greed and desire;
In this life they will gain renown, And the same shall hold true for rebirth in heaven.
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to obtain these five merits, they should practice these five things."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
12. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five matters regarding timely giving. What are the five? First, giving to those who have come from afar;

second, giving to those who are about to depart for afar; third, giving to the sick; fourth, giving during times of scarcity; and fifth, when one first obtains new fruits, melons, or grain, one first gives them to those who observe the precepts and are diligent in practice, and only thereafter does one eat them oneself."
"Monks, this is called timely giving; it possesses these five qualities.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The wise give at the proper time, their faith remaining unbroken;
they experience joy here and are reborn in heaven, endowed with manifold virtues.
Recalling generosity according to the occasion, one receives blessings like an echo."
Forever free from lack or deficiency, one will always be born into wealth and nobility.
Generosity serves as the equipment for all practices, leading to the attainment of the unsurpassed state.
When practicing billions of acts of giving without giving rise to conceptual thoughts, joy will consequently increase.
When this thought arises within the mind, The distracted mind is forever eliminated without remainder.
Perceiving the body’s peace and bliss, The mind then attains liberation.
Therefore, a person of wisdom— Whether man or woman—does not need to inquire further.
"When practicing these five kinds of giving, one must not lose the appropriate means and suitability. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to practice these five matters, they should mindfully practice timely giving."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Wholesome and unwholesome; paying homage to the Buddha; celestial messengers; the year; the five auspicious marks;
*vācā*; relatives; attending to the sick; the five kinds of giving; giving according to the season.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Fascicle 24.
Ekottarika Āgama, Scroll Twenty-Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Three: The Chapter on the Five Kings. Chapter Thirty-Three: The Chapter on the Five Kings.
1. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, five great kings, headed by Prasenajit, had assembled in the park pavilion and were each engaged in this discussion.
Who are these five kings?
They are King Prasenajit, King Viśākhā, King Udayana, King Ajātaśatru, and King Udayibhadra.
At that time, the five kings gathered in one place and each made this discussion:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that the Tathāgata has spoken of these five sensual pleasures.
What are the five?..."
If the eye sees forms that are deeply cherished and held with reverence, which are what worldly people hope for;
if the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the tongue perceives tastes, and the body perceives subtle textures—the Tathāgata speaks of these as the five desires.
Among these five desires, which is the most excellent?
Is it the excellence of forms seen by the eye,
or is it the excellence of sounds heard by the ear?
Is it the nose that finds the fragrance exquisite?
Is it the tongue that finds the flavor exquisite?
Or is it the body that finds the subtle touch exquisite?
"Among these five things, which is the most excellent?
Among them, some kings spoke thus:
"Form is the most excellent."
Some might argue: "Sound is the most excellent. Others might argue:
"Fragrance is the most excellent. Or some may argue:
"Taste is the most sublime."
Some may hold this view: "Tactile smoothness is supreme.
At that time, those who spoke of the excellence of form were referring to what King Udayana had said.
Regarding "exquisite sound," this was discussed by King Udayana.
Regarding "exquisite fragrance," this was discussed by King Ajātaśatru.
Regarding "exquisite flavor," this was discussed by King Prasenajit.
Regarding the statement that "fine and smooth is exquisite," this was the discourse of King Vaiśravaṇa.
At that time, the five kings said to one another:
"We have all discussed these five desires together, yet we still do not know which among them is the most exquisite."
At that time, King Prasenajit said to the four kings:
"The Tathāgata is currently staying nearby at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove in Śrāvastī.
Let us all go together to the World-Honored One and inquire about this matter."
"If the World-Honored One has any instructions, we shall together carry them out.
At that time, having heard King Prasenajit’s words, the kings went together with him to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, King Prasenajit reported in full to the Tathāgata the discussion he had held regarding the five desires.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the five kings, saying:
"The discussions held by you kings were each appropriate to the occasion."

The reason for this is that those whose human nature and conduct are deeply attached to forms never tire of beholding them; such persons regard these forms as the most exquisite and supreme, with nothing surpassing them.
At that time, that person does not become attached to the phenomena of sound, fragrance, flavor, or fine touch; among the five desires, form is the most exquisite.

Furthermore, if there is another person whose nature and conduct are attached to sound, having heard that sound, they feel extreme joy and are never satiated; for this person, sound is the most exquisite and supreme, and among the five desires, sound is the most exquisite.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose nature and conduct are attached to fragrance, upon smelling it, they will feel extreme joy and never be satiated; for such a person, fragrance is the most wonderful and supreme among the five sensory desires, as fragrance is the most exquisite of all.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose nature and conduct are attached to flavors, having experienced those flavors, they feel extreme joy and are never satiated; for such a person, flavor is the most wonderful and supreme among the five desires, being the most exquisite of all tastes.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose nature and conduct are attached to fine and smooth sensations, and having obtained such fine and smooth sensations, they feel extreme joy without ever being satisfied—this person regards fine and smooth sensations as the most superior and most exquisite; among the five desires, fine and smooth sensations are the most exquisite.
"If that person's mind is attached to forms, at that time that person is not attached to sounds, odors, tastes, or the quality of tangibles;
if that person's habitual conduct is attached to sounds, at that time that person is not attached to forms, odors, tastes, or the quality of tangibles;
if that person's habitual conduct is attached to odors, at that time that person is not attached to forms, sounds, tastes, or the quality of tangibles."
Furthermore, if that person’s disposition is attached to flavors, at that time that person is not attached to the phenomena of forms, sounds, odors, or tangibles;
if, moreover, that person’s disposition is attached to tangibles, at that time that person is not attached to the phenomena of forms, sounds, odors, or flavors.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When the desire of the mind is fervent, That which is sought can surely be attained;
Having obtained it, one’s joy redoubles, And there is no doubt regarding one's wishes."
Having obtained these desires, his greedy mind finds no release;
he takes delight in them, regarding them as the most excellent of conditions.
Yet when he hears sounds, whatever he desires must inevitably be overcome.
Having heard it, his joy redoubled, and there was no doubt regarding his aspiration.
Because he had obtained this sound, his craving did not cease;
taking this as his delight, he followed after it as the most sublime.
Furthermore, when one smells a fragrance, whatever is desired can surely be attained;
having smelled it, one’s joy redoubles, and there is no doubt regarding what is sought.
Having obtained this fragrance, the mind of craving is not relieved.
Taking this as joy, it is the most excellent of all.
Furthermore, when one attains its flavor, what is desired will surely be achieved;
having attained it, one’s joy redoubles, and there is no doubt regarding what is sought.
Having obtained this flavor, his greedy mind finds no release;
he takes delight in it, regarding it as the most excellent.
When he encounters smooth and delicate sensations, his desires are inevitably fulfilled.
Having obtained it, one’s joy redoubles; there is no doubt or difficulty regarding what is desired.
Because one has obtained such fine and smooth [objects], the mind of craving is not resolved;
taking this as joy, one considers it to be the most excellent.
"Therefore, Great King!
If one says that form is wonderful, it should be discussed with impartiality.
Why is this? Because there is gratification in form."
If form were without flavor, sentient beings would never become attached to it; because it possesses flavor, among the five desires, form is the most exquisite.
Yet, form has its faults.
If form were without fault, sentient beings would have no weariness toward it; because it possesses faults, sentient beings weary of it.
Nevertheless, there is an escape from form.
If there were no escape from form, these classes of sentient beings would not be able to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
because there is this escape, sentient beings are able to reach the city of fearless nirvana.
"Among the five desires, form is the most exquisite.
However, Great King, if you say that sound is exquisite, we should discuss it with impartiality."
The reason for this is that there is flavor within sound.
If sound were without flavor, sentient beings would never become stained by or attached to it;
because it possesses flavor, among the five desires, sound is the most exquisite.
However, sound possesses defects.
If sound were without defect, sentient beings would have no weariness or aversion toward it;
because it possesses defects, sentient beings feel weary of and averse to it.
However, sounds possess an escape route.
If sounds were devoid of an escape route, these classes of sentient beings would be unable to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
because they do possess an escape route, sentient beings are able to reach the city of fearless Nirvana.
"Among the five desires, sound is the most exquisite.
Great King, you should know that if one speaks of fragrance being exquisite, it must be discussed with impartiality.
Why is this? Because within fragrance there is both odor and flavor."
If fragrance were devoid of scent, sentient beings would never become attached to it;
because it possesses scent, among the five desires, fragrance is the most exquisite.
However, incense has faults.
If incense were without faults, sentient beings would not feel weary of or distressed by it;
because it possesses faults, sentient beings grow weary of and distressed by it.
Yet incense has an escape route.
If incense had no escape route, these classes of sentient beings would not be able to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
because it has an escape route, sentient beings are able to reach the city of fearless nirvana.
"Among the five desires, fragrance is the most exquisite.
Furthermore, Great King!
If one speaks of the excellence of taste, it should be discussed with impartiality."
The reason for this is that flavor possesses a "savor" (rasa).
If flavor were devoid of savor, sentient beings would never become stained by or attached to it;
because it possesses savor, among the five desires, flavor is the most exquisite.
However, flavors possess faults.
If flavors were without faults, sentient beings would not feel weary of them;
it is because they possess faults that sentient beings grow weary of them.
However, there is an escape from sensual pleasures.
If there were no escape from sensual pleasures, these classes of sentient beings would be unable to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
because there is this escape, sentient beings are able to reach the city of fearless Nirvana.
Taste is the most exquisite.
"Furthermore, Great King, you should know that when we speak of the excellence of fine and smooth [tactile sensations], it must be discussed in comparison with others.

Why is this? Because sentient beings ultimately do not become attached to fine and smooth sensations that lack flavor; it is because they possess flavor that, among the five desires, fine and smooth sensations are the most exquisite."
However, there are faults in the smooth and supple.
If the smooth and supple were without fault, sentient beings would not feel weary of or distressed by them;
it is because they possess faults that sentient beings feel weary of and distressed by them.
However, there is an escape from the realm of the smooth and slippery.
If there were no escape from the smooth and slippery, these classes of sentient beings would not be able to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
because there is this escape, sentient beings are able to reach the city of fearless Nirvana.
Among the five desires, smoothness and softness are the most exquisite.
Therefore, Great King, wherever one finds pleasure, the mind becomes stained and attached.
"Thus it is, Great King!
You should know it in this way.
At that time, the five kings, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(2) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder named Candraprabha (Moonlight), who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures; he was fully equipped with elephants, horses, and the seven precious gems, and his gold, silver, and rare jewels were beyond measure.
However, the elder Candraprabha had no children.

At that time, because he was childless, the elder sought blessings from the celestial deities; he prayed to the gods of the sun and moon, the earth spirits, Haritī, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the twenty-eight great ghost kings, Śakra and Brahmā, the mountain spirits, the tree spirits, and the deities of the five realms, leaving no place untouched. He took refuge in all of them, entreating them to grant him a son.
At that time, after several days had passed, the wife of the elder Candraprabha became pregnant. She then said to the elder, "I am aware that I have conceived.

Upon hearing this, the elder was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately prepared a fine bed and seat for his wife, provided her with delicious food, and dressed her in fine garments.
At that time, after eight or nine months had passed, the lady gave birth to a son whose countenance was so upright and rare in the world that it was like the color of a peach blossom.
At that time, this child held a priceless maṇi jewel in both hands and immediately spoke this verse:
"This house possesses much wealth, Precious objects and grain;
I now wish to give them away as gifts, So that the poor may have no lack."
"If there were nothing at all here, yet now there is this priceless jewel; let it be constantly used to bestow gifts upon others.
At that time, having heard these words, the parents and the members of the household each fled in haste.
"How is it that you were born as this kind of ghostly spirit?
Only because her parents felt compassion for their child did they not run hither and thither.
Immediately, the mother spoke this verse to her son:
“Are you a celestial Gandharva, a malevolent spirit, or a rākṣasa?
What is your name and lineage? I now wish to know this.
At that time, the child again replied to his mother in verse:
"He is not a deva, a gandharva, a ghost, a malevolent spirit, or a rākṣasa;
he was born of my parents, so there is no need for doubt.

At that time, having heard these words, the lady was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself; for this reason, she related these words in their entirety to the elder Candraprabha.
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"What could this possibly be the cause of?
I shall now speak of this matter to the Nirgranthas."
He immediately took the child in his arms and went to the place where the Nirgrantha was; he prostrated himself at the Nirgrantha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the householder Candraprabha related this entire matter in detail to the Nirgrantha.
At that time, having heard these words, the Nirgrantha told the elder:
"This child is a person of meager merit; he is of no benefit to himself.
You should take him and kill him."
"If he is not killed, the household will suffer decline and ruin, and everyone shall eventually perish.
At that time, the Elder Candraprabha thought to himself:

"For many years past and present, I have had no offspring. For this reason, I have prayed to Heaven and Earth, leaving no place unvisited, until after so many years have passed, this son was finally born. I cannot now bear to take this child and kill him."
"I should further question other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas so that they may sever my doubts.
At that time, not long after the Tathāgata had attained Buddhahood, the multitude gave him the title "Great Śramaṇa. Then, the elder Candraprabha thought to himself:
"I shall explain this matter of mine in detail to the Great Śramaṇa."
At that time, the householder rose from his seat, took the child in his arms, and set out for the place where the World-Honored One was.
On the way, he thought again:
"Now there are elder brahmins, advanced in years, wise and intelligent, who are honored and respected by all people; yet even they do not know or see [this], how much less so this śramaṇa Gautama!"
"I have been studying the Way for but a short time as a youth; how could I possibly understand this matter?
I fear I shall not be able to resolve my doubts.
It would be best for me now to return home by way of the middle road."
At that time, there was a deva who had been an old acquaintance of the householder. Knowing what was in the householder’s mind, he spoke to him from mid-air, saying:
“Householder, you should know: advance a little further; you will surely obtain profit, attain a great fruit of retribution, and shall also reach the place of the Deathless.”
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare to encounter; a Tathāgata descends with the rain of nectar only from time to time.
Furthermore, O Householder!
There are four things that, though small, must never be disregarded. What are these four?
A king, though young, must never be disregarded;
Fire, though small, must not be disregarded;
a dragon, though small, must likewise not be disregarded;
and a person who studies the Way, though young in years, must also not be disregarded.
"Householder, these are the four things that must never be underestimated.
At that time, a deity spoke this verse:
"Though a king may be small, he executes punishments according to the law;
though a small fire has not yet blazed, it burns the grass and trees of the mountains.
Though a divine dragon may appear small, it sends down rain according to the needs of the season."
"The disciples are of tender age, yet those they have delivered are beyond measure.

At that time, the elder Candraprabha’s mind was opened and his understanding was resolved; he leaped for joy, unable to contain himself, and immediately proceeded to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
For this reason, he reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the elder:

“This boy possesses immense merit. When this boy grows up, he will come to me with a retinue of five hundred disciples, renounce the world to study the Path, and attain arhatship; among my śrāvakas, he shall be foremost in merit and virtue, such that none can equal him.”
At that time, having heard these words, the householder was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"It is as the World-Honored One has taught, and not as the words of the Nirgranthas."
At that time, the householder Candraprabha addressed the World-Honored One once more:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation, as well as that of the community of bhikṣus, and have compassion for this child.
Then, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
At that time, seeing that [the Buddha] had accepted the invitation by remaining silent, the elder rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha’s] feet with his head, and withdrew.
Returning home, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink, spread out fine seats, and at early dawn, he announced personally:
"The time has come; we pray that you will deign to descend."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the hour had come, was surrounded by the bhikṣus as they preceded and followed him; he entered the city of Śrāvastī, went to the house of the elder, and took his seat.

At that time, when the elder saw that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, he immediately prepared various kinds of food and drink. With joy and without distraction, he personally served them by hand. When he saw that they had finished eating, he removed their bowls and vessels, offered pure water, and took a small seat to sit before the Tathāgata, desiring to hear the sublime Dharma spoken by the Buddha.
At that time, the householder Candraprabha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now bestow all my household estate and fields upon this son; I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant him a name."
The World-Honored One said:
"When this child was born, everyone ran hither and thither, saying, 'This is the ghost Śivara. Therefore, let his name now be established as Śivara."
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually engaged the householder and his wife in a sublime discourse. This discourse concerned:

the teaching on giving, the teaching on morality, and the teaching on rebirth in heaven; the impurity of sensual desires, the great affliction of the outflows (*āsrava*), and the excellence of the way of escape.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the householder and his wife’s minds were opened and their intentions resolved, and that they were no longer subject to doubt, [taught] the Dharma constantly expounded by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At that moment, the World-Honored One fully explained these to the householder, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy.
At that very seat, the dust and defilements of the elder and his wife were completely cleansed, and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).

Just as a fresh, white cloth is easily dyed with color, so too did the elder and his wife, at that very seat, attain the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, they discerned all phenomena, transcended hesitation, and were no longer subject to doubt. Attaining fearlessness, they understood the profound and subtle Dharma of the Tathāgata and immediately received the five precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Sacrifice is supreme among offerings; Verse is foremost among treatises;
The king is the most honored among men; The ocean is the source of all streams."
The moon is the most luminous among the stars; the sun is the supreme among all lights.
Of all things produced throughout the eight directions and above and below, those who seek to attain merit find that the Three Buddhas are the most honored.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
Thereupon, the elder sought out five hundred youths to serve as attendants for Śivara.

At that time, Śivara was nearly twenty years old; he went to where his parents were and said to them, "I pray only that you two honored ones will permit me to leave the household life to study the Way."
At that time, the two parents immediately gave their consent.
This was because the World-Honored One had previously prophesied that they would lead five hundred youths to the World-Honored One’s presence to seek ordination as śramaṇas.
At that time, Śivara and his five hundred followers prostrated at the feet of their parents and then withdrew.
Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, they bowed their heads to his feet in salutation and stood to one side.
At that time, Śivara addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that you will grant me permission to join the ranks of those on the Path.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately granted his permission, allowing him to become a śramaṇa.
Before many days had passed, they became arhats; their six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating, and they were endowed with the eight liberations.
At that time, the five hundred youths came forward and said to the Buddha:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will grant us permission to become śramaṇas."
The World-Honored One consented by remaining silent. Not many days after his ordination, he became an arhat.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara remained in his native land at Śrāvastī; the people revered him, and he received the four requisites of support:
robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara thought to himself:
"I am currently in my native land here, which is exceedingly crowded and noisy; I should now go forth to wander and teach among the people."
At that time, when it was time for the meal, the Venerable Śivara dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having finished his almsround, he returned to his quarters, folded away his sitting mat, and, having dressed himself and taken up his bowl, departed from the Jetavana Monastery. Surrounded by five hundred bhikṣus in front and behind, he traveled through the human world to teach and transform others.
Wherever he went, there were none who did not offer him support; they all provided him with robes, food and drink, bedding and mats, and medicinal requisites for illness.
Furthermore, various devas announced to the villages:
"Now there is the Venerable Śivara, who has attained arhatship and possesses the foremost merit; leading five hundred bhikṣus, he is traveling through the human world to transform beings."
"Virtuous ones, you may go and make offerings; if you do not do so now, it will be of no avail for later regrets.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara thought to himself:
"I am now deeply weary of these offerings. Where should I go to avoid them, so that people will not know my whereabouts?"
At that time, he immediately entered deep into the mountains.
The devas, in turn, went among the villages and each announced:
"The Venerable Śivara is now here in these mountains; you should go and make offerings to him."
"If you do not act now, it will be of no avail for your regrets later.
At that time, having heard the words of the deva, the people immediately carried food and drink and went to where the Venerable Śivara was, saying:
"We pray only that the Venerable One will remain for our sake."

At that time, Śivara gradually traveled among people to teach and transform them, arriving at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha. Accompanied by five hundred great bhikṣus, he likewise received offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
At that time, Śivara again had this thought:
"Where might I now spend the summer retreat so that people will not know my location?
He then reflected further:
"I shall observe the rains retreat among the central lands, to the east of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and to the west of Mount Vipula.
He then took five hundred bhikṣus and observed the rains retreat within that mountain range.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing the thoughts in Śivara’s mind, immediately manifested a stupa within the mountains, fully equipped with gardens, fruit trees, and groves, surrounded by bathing pools. He further manifested five hundred high towers, five hundred couches, five hundred small seats, and five hundred rope beds, and provided them with celestial ambrosia for food.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara had this thought:
"The summer retreat has now concluded; it has been a very long time since I last saw the Tathāgata. I should now go to pay my respects to the World-Honored One."
He then took five hundred bhikṣus and set out for Śrāvastī; at that time, as the heat was intense, the entire assembly of bhikṣus broke into a sweat, which defiled their bodies.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara had this thought:

"Today the assembly of bhikṣus is extremely hot; it would be a most excellent thing if a small cloud were to appear above and a fine rain were to fall, providing them with a small bathing pool and a little gruel."
As soon as this thought arose, a great cloud appeared in the sky and a fine rain fell, and there was also a bathing pool.
Four non-human beings arrived carrying excellent sweet nectar, saying:
"We have been sent by King Vaiśravaṇa; we pray that the Venerable One will accept this sweet nectar and bestow it upon the community of bhikṣus."
At that time, having received this beverage, he gave it to the community of bhikṣus to drink.
Then, Śivara again had this thought:
"I should now stay and lodge here."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing the thoughts in Śivara’s mind, immediately manifested five hundred dwellings by the side of the road, complete with beds and bedding.
At that time, the devas presented him with food and drink; having finished eating, Śivara rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara’s paternal uncle was living within the city of Śrāvastī, possessing abundant wealth and many treasures, lacking nothing whatsoever.
Nevertheless, he remained stingy and greedy, refusing to practice generosity; he did not believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, nor did he cultivate merit.
At that time, his kinsmen said to this man: "O Elder!..."
"What would you do with this wealth?
Furthermore, it will not serve as provisions for the next life.
When the elder heard these words, within a single day he bestowed hundreds of thousands of taels of gold upon the heterodox brahmins, rather than directing them toward the Triple Gem.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara heard that his uncle had bestowed one hundred thousand taels of gold upon the heterodox followers of other schools, rather than bestowing it upon the Triple Gem.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara went to the Jeta Grove Monastery, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to Śivara.
Having heard the Dharma from the Tathāgata, the Venerable Śivara rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew.
At that time, on that very day, the Venerable Śivara put on his robes, took up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, and gradually made his way to his uncle’s house.
Having arrived, he stood silently outside the gate.
At that time, the householder saw the Venerable Śivara standing outside the gate seeking alms, and he said to him:
"For what reason did you not come yesterday?"
"Yesterday I gave away hundreds of thousands of taels of gold; I have a single cotton cloth which I can offer to you.
Śivara replied, "I have no need for a cloth now; I have come today specifically to beg for alms."
The householder replied, "Yesterday I gave away a hundred thousand taels of gold; I can no longer give any more.

At that time, the Venerable Śivara, wishing to bring the householder to liberation, flew into the air and manifested water and fire from his body, sitting, lying down, and walking back and forth, performing whatever he willed.
At that time, having witnessed this miraculous transformation, the householder said:
"Please come down and take your seat; I shall now bestow a gift upon you.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śivara relinquished his supernormal powers and immediately came forward to sit.
At that time, the elder provided the Venerable Śivara with food and drink that was poor, wretched, and extremely coarse and unpalatable, and urged him to eat it.

At that time, the Venerable Śivara had been raised in a noble family where he had enjoyed food and drink to his heart's content; yet, solely for the sake of that elder, he accepted this food and ate it.
At that time, after the Venerable Śivara had finished his meal, he returned to his dwelling.
That very night, a deity from the realm of space came to speak to the elder, saying:
"Your excellent giving, your most magnificent gift, was bestowed upon Śivara."
"Through desirelessness one attains liberation; by severing craving, one becomes free from doubt.
At midnight and at dawn, on these two occasions, he spoke this verse:
"Excellent is the gift, a most supreme gift, given indeed to Śivara."
"Through desirelessness one attains liberation; by severing craving, one becomes free from doubt.
At that time, having heard the words of the deva, the householder thought to himself:
"Yesterday I gave a hundred thousand pieces of gold to the heterodox teachers, yet they did not produce such a response."
"Today I gave poor, inferior food as a gift to Śivara, and this is the result that has come to pass.
When will it ever dawn?
I shall surely give Śivara a hundred thousand pieces of gold."
At that time, the householder immediately inspected his household on that very day; taking an object worth one hundred thousand pieces of gold, he went to Śivara’s place.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at Śivara’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, the householder presented Śivara with one hundred thousand pieces of gold and spoke these words:
"I pray only that you will accept these one hundred thousand pieces of gold."
At that time, the Venerable Śivara replied:
"It shall cause the householder to receive inexhaustible merit and naturally attain long life;
however, the Tathāgata does not permit bhikṣus to accept gold weighing hundreds of thousands of taels."
At that time, the householder went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
Then, that householder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow the bhikṣu Śivara to accept these one hundred thousand taels of gold, so that I may receive its merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
“Go to where the bhikṣu Śivara is and say, ‘The Master calls for you.’”
The bhikṣu replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, having received the instruction from the Buddha, that bhikṣu went to where Śivara was and informed him with the words of the Tathāgata.
Then, the Venerable Śivara, following the words of that bhikṣu, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Śivara:
"You may now accept these hundred thousand measures of gold from this elder so that he may receive its merit; this is the karma of past conditions, and you may receive its retribution."
Śivara replied: “So it is, World-Honored One.”
At that time, the Venerable Śivara immediately recited this verse of dedication:
“Having given robes and other things, desiring to seek their merit,
they shall go to the world of gods and men, and enjoy themselves with the five pleasures.”
From the heavens down to the human realm, crossing over existence without doubt or difficulty,
the state of unconditioned nirvana is that which all Buddhas delight in.
Those who bestow kindness without hindrance receive blessings and protection through this.
"One should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, performing meritorious deeds without weariness.
At that time, the Venerable Śivara said to the householder,
"You may take these one hundred thousand measures of gold and place them in my room."
At that time, the householder accepted his instruction, took these hundred thousand ounces of gold, placed them in the Venerable Śivara’s room, and then withdrew and departed.
At that time, Śivara addressed the bhikṣus:
"Whatever you may lack, come here and take it.
If you require robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, or medicine for the treatment of illness, all these are here for you to take; do not seek them elsewhere."
"Pass this word from one to another so that it may be known.
At that time, a great many bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"What merit did this Śivara perform in the past, such that he was born into a householder’s family, possessing peerless beauty with a complexion like that of a peach blossom?"
What merit did he further perform such that, grasping a jewel in both hands, he emerged from his mother’s womb?

What merit did he further perform such that, leading five hundred people, he went to the place where the Tathāgata was, left the household life to study the Way, and encountered the era of the Tathāgata?
"Furthermore, what merit did he perform such that wherever he went, food and clothing appeared spontaneously, leaving him never lacking anything, and no other bhikṣus were able to equal him?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, World-Honored One."
Having appeared in the world, he was traveling through the borders of the kingdom of Bandhumatī, accompanied by a retinue of six hundred and eighty thousand followers.
They were provided with the four requisites of support:
robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal supplies for the sick and infirm.

"At that time, there was a brahmin named Jayanta who resided in that realm; he possessed abundant wealth and many treasures—gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and amber—in incalculable quantities."
At that time, Yaññadatta departed from the borders of that kingdom and went to where the Tathāgata Vipaśyin was.
Having arrived, they exchanged greetings with one another and sat down to one side.
At that time, Vipaśyin Tathāgata gradually preached the Dharma to him, whereupon he gave rise to a heart of joy. Then Yaśoda addressed Vipaśyin Tathāgata, saying:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation; I wish to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus!"
At that time, the Tathāgata accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation through silence, the brahmin Yaññadatta rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed. He went to his home and prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink.
At that time, during the middle of the night, Yaññadatta thought to himself:
"I have now prepared various kinds of food and drink, yet I lack curds. Tomorrow at dawn, I shall go to the city gates and purchase all the curds from anyone who has them for sale."
At that time, early in the morning, Yaññadatta prepared a fine seat and immediately went to the city gate to seek curd.
At that very moment, there was a cowherd named Sivaka carrying curd who intended to go to a sacrificial offering.
At that time, the brahmin Yajñadatta said to the cowherd,
"You who sell curds, I shall give you the price. Śivara replied:
"I now wish to perform a sacrifice.
The brahmin replied, "What do you seek by performing this sacrifice to the gods?"
"Simply sell it to me, and I shall give you a generous price. The cowherd replied, "Brahmin!"
"What are you using this curd for?
The brahmin replied,
"I have now invited the Tathāgata Vipaśyin and the community of bhikṣus."
"However, although all the food and drink have been prepared,
there is none of the curd. At that time, Śivara asked the brahmin,
"What are the physical characteristics of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin?"
The brahmin replied, "The Tathāgata has no equal;
his precepts are perfectly pure, and his wisdom, concentration, and samādhi are unattainable by others. Among gods and humans, none can surpass him."
At that time, the brahmin Yaññadatta extolled the virtues of the Tathāgata; having heard this, Sivaka’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified. Then Sivaka said to the brahmin:
"I shall now personally take this curd and go to offer it to the Tathāgata; what further use is there for sacrificing it to the gods?"
At that time, the brahmin Yaññadatta took the cowherd to his home and said:
"The time has come;
now is precisely the right moment. May the Venerable One deign to visit!"

Then, the Tathāgata, knowing that the time had come, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the bhikṣus who followed him before and behind, went to the house of the brahmin Yaññadatta, where they each sat down in order.

At that time, the cowherd beheld the Tathāgata’s countenance, so rare in the world; his faculties were serene and tranquil, and his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
He was like the sun and moon, or like Mount Sumeru rising above all other mountains, its radiance shining afar, such that none failed to receive its nourishing grace.
Having seen him, he was filled with joy and proceeded toward the World-Honored One, saying:
"If the Tathāgata’s merit is indeed as the brahmin has described, let this single jar of curd suffice for the entire assembly of monks!"
At that time, Śivara addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "I pray that you will accept this curd!
Thereupon, the Tathāgata extended his bowl and received the curd, and he also gave some to the community of bhikṣus; yet there was still curd remaining.
At that time, the cowherd said to the World-Honored One,
“There is still some curd remaining.
Then, the Tathāgata told him:
"Go now and offer this curd again to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the cowherd replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the cowherd went back to prepare more curd, yet there was still some curd remaining.
The cowherd spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"There is still some leftover curd remaining.
At that time, the Tathāgata said to this person:
"You may now take this curd and give it to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the upāsakas, and the upāsikās, so that they may be fully satisfied."
"Therefore, some curd remains.
At that time, the Buddha said to the cowherd:
"Take this curd now and give it to the host, the donor."
He replied, "It is so.
Subsequently, he gave some to his host, the donor, and thus there remained some leftover curd.
He further gave it to beggars and the destitute, yet there was still some curd remaining.
He came and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"There is still some curd remaining."
Then the Buddha told him:
"Now take this curd and pour it onto clean ground, or into water.
The reason for this is that I see no one among humans, devas, or the world who can digest this curd, except for the Tathāgata."
The cowherd immediately accepted the Buddha’s instruction, took the curd, and placed it into the water.
Instantly, a great fire with blazing flames erupted from within the water, reaching a height of several dozen *ren*.

At that time, having witnessed this miraculous and extraordinary event, the cowherd marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He returned to the World-Honored One, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood with palms joined. He then made this vow: “I now offer this curd to the fourfold assembly.

If there be any merit therein, by virtue of this blessing, may I not fall into the eight difficult states, nor be born into a destitute household. In whatever place I am born, may my six sense faculties be complete and my countenance be upright and handsome. Furthermore, may I never remain a householder, and may I encounter a holy master such as this one in future lives as well.”
“Bhikṣus, you should know that thirty-one kalpas ago there was another Buddha named Śikhin Tathāgata who appeared in the world.
At that time, Śikhin Tathāgata was traveling and teaching in the world of Aśvamedha, accompanied by one hundred thousand great bhikṣus.”
At that time, when the time had come, the Tathāgata Śreṇika put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

At that moment, there was a great merchant in the city named Sudhana, who saw from afar the Tathāgata Śreṇika with his sense-faculties serene and his countenance upright; his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and his face was like the sun and the moon.
Having seen this, he immediately gave rise to a heart of joy and approached the World-Honored One. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the merchant scattered excellent precious jewels over the Tathāgata to manifest his humble sincerity and made a universal vow:

"By virtue of this merit, in whatever place I am born, may I abound in wealth and possess many treasures, never lacking for anything; may there be no moment when my hands are empty, even while within my mother’s womb."

"In this eon, there was also the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One, named Viśvabhū."

At that time, there was an elder named Sujāta, who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures; he further invited the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Viśvabhū, along with the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the elder had few servants; therefore, the elder personally prepared various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink to feed the Tathāgata, making this vow:

"By the merit I have acquired, may I always encounter the Triple Gem in whatever place I am born, never lacking for anything, and may I always have many servants. May I, in future ages, encounter a Tathāgata just as I do today."
"In this present Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Krakucchanda, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world.

At that time, there was an elder named Bahudhana who again invited the Tathāgata Krakucchanda to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for seven days, and to offer robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

He made this vow: 'May I always have abundance of wealth and many treasures in every place where I am born; may I never be born into a poor or lowly family. May I always receive the four types of offerings in every place where I am born, be honored and respected by the fourfold assembly, kings, and the people, and be welcomed by devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans.'"
“Monks, you should know this: was the brahmin Yajñadatta at that time anyone else?
Do not view it so. Why is this?
It is none other than the present Elder Candraprabha.”
The cowherd named Śivara, who at that time made an offering of curds to the Buddha, is none other than the present bhikṣu Śivara.
As for the merchant Sudhana of that time—could he have been anyone else?
Do not hold such a view; it was the bhikṣu Śivara who was then.
Do you think the householder Sudatta of that time was someone else?
Do not hold such a view; it was the bhikṣu Śivara who was then.
At that time, who was this wealthy householder?
Do not view it thus; he is none other than the bhikṣu Śivara today.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the bhikṣu Śivara made this vow: [text continues]"

"May I always be born with peerless and perfect physical beauty in every place where I am reborn; may I always be born into wealthy and noble families; and may I, in a future age, encounter the World-Honored One, so that upon his preaching the Dharma for me, I may immediately attain liberation, leave the household life, and become a śramaṇa."
"By virtue of this merit, the bhikṣu Śivara was now born into a wealthy and noble family; he is peerless in his physical beauty, and having now encountered me, he has immediately attained arhatship."

However, monks, you should know that by scattering precious jewels over the Tathāgata and holding onto this merit, he now dwells within his mother’s womb; yet, as he emerges from the womb, he holds a pair of jewels in his hands, worth as much as Jambudvīpa, and on the very day of his birth, he speaks these words.

Furthermore, he invited the Tathāgata Krakucchanda to request many followers; now, leading five hundred disciples to my place, they have left the household life to study the Path and attained arhatship.

Furthermore, during seven days, he made offerings to the Tathāgata Krakucchanda and succeeded in obtaining the four requisites for support; thus, today he lacks nothing in the way of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, or medicinal provisions for the sick and infirm.

By virtue of this merit, which other bhikṣus could not equal, Śakra Devānām Indra came in person to provide him with whatever he required; furthermore, the devas spread the news throughout the villages so that the fourfold assembly would know of Śivara—this is its significance.
"Among my disciples, the one of foremost merit is the bhikṣu Śivara.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Five types of heroic persons capable of enduring battle appear in the world. What are the five?
In this regard, there is a person who dons armor and takes up weapons to enter the army for battle; yet, seeing dust rising from afar, he becomes terrified. This is called the first type of warrior.”
"Furthermore, as for the second warrior: he dons his armor and takes up his weapons, desiring to enter the fray.
Upon seeing the dust and wind, he feels no fear;
yet, upon seeing a lofty banner, he immediately becomes terrified, unable to advance to battle. This is called the second man."
"Furthermore, as for the third warrior: he dons armor and takes up weapons, intending to enter the fray. If he sees dust rising or lofty banners, he feels no fear;
yet if he sees bows and arrows, he becomes terrified and is unable to fight. This is called the third type of person.
"Furthermore, there is a fourth type of warrior who puts on armor and takes up weapons to enter the army and fight. When he sees the dust and wind, or a high banner, or arrows, he feels no fear;
yet, as soon as he enters the ranks, he is captured by the enemy or has his life taken. This is called the fourth type of warrior."

"Furthermore, the fifth warrior puts on his armor and takes up his weapons, intending to enter the fray. Whether he sees dust and smoke, or a high banner, or an arrow, or is captured by others, even unto death, he harbors no fear.
He is able to destroy the borders of the enemy army and govern the people without external opposition; this is called the fifth warrior."
"In this way, bhikṣus! There are these five kinds of persons in the world.
Now, within this community of bhikṣus as well, there appear in the world these same five kinds of persons."
What are the five?
Suppose there is a bhikkhu traveling through another village, and he hears that in that village there is a woman of peerless beauty, whose face is like the color of a peach blossom.

Having heard this, when the time came, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food. Upon seeing that woman whose beauty was peerless, he immediately conceived thoughts of desire; he cast off his three robes, returned the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts, and became a householder. He was just like that wrestler who, upon seeing a mere speck of dust, was seized by terror—such was this bhikṣu.

"Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who hears that a woman resides in a village, peerless in her beauty. When the time comes, he puts on his robes and takes his bowl to enter the village for alms. If he sees that woman, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire;
yet he engages in mutual flirtation and converses with her back and forth.
Because of this flirtation, he abandons the dharma-robes and returns to being a layman."
Just as that second person, seeing the wind and dust, felt no fear, yet upon seeing the tall banner became filled with terror, so too it was with this bhikṣu.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who heard that in a certain village there was a woman of upright and beautiful countenance, rare in the world, with a complexion like the color of a peach blossom. When the time came, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food.
If one sees a woman and does not give rise to thoughts of desire, and even if one engages in playful dalliance with her, likewise does not give rise to thoughts of lustful intent;

yet, if by merely joining hands or pinching one another with that woman, one immediately gives rise to thoughts of desire, one abandons the three dharma robes, returns to being a white-robed layman, and resumes the affairs of a household.
Just as that third person, upon entering the ranks, feels no fear when seeing the dust raised by the wind or the high banners, yet conceives fear upon seeing the bows and arrows;

so too, there is a certain bhikṣu who hears that in a village there is a woman of upright countenance, rare in this world. When the time comes, he puts on his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village for alms. If he sees the woman, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire; even if they converse together, he still does not give rise to thoughts of desire.

However, if that woman should touch him with her fingers, he immediately gives rise to thoughts of desire; yet he does not cast off his dharma-robes to pursue the affairs of a householder. He is like that fourth person who enters the army, is captured by others, or loses his life, and is unable to escape.

"Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in dependence upon a village. He hears that there is a woman in the village; yet when the time comes for him to go on his alms-round, he puts on his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village to beg for food. Even if he sees the woman, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire. Even if they converse and laugh together, he still does not give rise to thoughts of desire. Even if they further engage in mutual touching or pinching, he likewise does not give rise to thoughts of desire."
At that time, the bhikṣu contemplates these thirty-six impure and foul substances within this body: who is it that clings to them?
From what does desire arise?
And for what purpose is this desire to be ceased?
Does it emerge from the head?
Does it issue from the physical form?
Upon examining these various things, one finds they are utterly non-existent.

From head to foot it is likewise so; that which belongs to the five viscera has no conceptual form, nor does it have a place of origin. When one contemplates the root of these conditions, one does not know from where they have come.
He further reflects: "I observe that this desire arises from causes and conditions.

Having observed this, that bhikṣu attains liberation of the mind from the outflow of desire (kāma-āsava), attains liberation of the mind from the outflow of existence (bhava-āsava), and attains liberation of the mind from the outflow of ignorance (avijjā-āsava). Thereupon, he attains the knowledge of liberation:
Birth and death are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further taking of a womb—this he knows as it truly is.
He is like that fifth combatant who roams and transforms himself without fearing the multitude of enemies.
For this reason, I now declare that this person has abandoned craving and desire, entered the state of fearlessness, and attained the city of Nirvāṇa.
This is what is meant, O bhikṣus!
"There are these five kinds of persons who appear in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"I know your origin, O Desire: The mind arises from conceptual thought."
The thought of "self" arises, yet you do not possess it. Therefore,
monks, you should contemplate the foul impurity of sexual conduct and eliminate desire for form.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five types of warriors who appear in the world. What are the five?

There is one person who puts on armor and takes up weapons to enter the army for battle; however, upon seeing the dust and wind, he becomes terrified and does not dare enter the midst of the great array. This is called the first type of person.”
"Furthermore, as for the second type of combatant: he dons armor and takes up weapons to enter the army and engage in battle;
yet, upon seeing the dust and wind, he feels no fear, but as soon as he hears the sound of the drum, he is struck with terror—this is called the second person.

"Furthermore, as for the third person: he dons armor and takes up weapons to enter the army for battle. Upon seeing the dust raised by the wind, he feels no fear; even when hearing the sound of drums and horns, he does not give rise to fear.
However, if he sees a tall banner, he immediately conceives terror and is unable to endure the battle. This is called the third person."

"Furthermore, as for the fourth type of warrior: he dons his armor and takes up his weapons, entering the fray of battle. If he sees dust and wind rising, he does not give rise to fear; if he hears the sound of drums and horns, he is not alarmed; even if he sees a tall banner, he is not terrified.
Even if he were to be seized by others or have his life-force severed, this is called the fourth person."

"Furthermore, fifthly, there is a person who dons armor and takes up weapons, enters the army to fight, and is fully capable of achieving destruction and extensively extending the borders of the kingdom; this is called the fifth kind of person appearing in the world.
“Bhikkhus, you should know that there are now five kinds of persons who appear in the world. What are the five?
There may be a bhikkhu living in a village who hears that there is a woman, peerless in beauty, with the complexion of a *pāṭali* flower.”

When that bhikṣu arrives at the proper time, he puts on his robes, takes up his bowl, and enters the village for alms. Failing to guard the doors of the sense faculties and failing to protect the dharmas of body, speech, and mind, if he sees a woman, he gives rise to lustful thoughts, abandons the prohibitive precepts, and adopts the ways of a layperson.
Just as that first man, hearing the sound of rising dust, was unable to endure the battle and became filled with terror, it is for this reason that I speak of such a person.

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in a village; hearing that there is a woman in the village of incomparable beauty, her face like the color of a peach blossom, he immediately abandons the precepts and adopts the ways of a layperson.
"Just as that second combatant, upon merely hearing the sound of drums and horns, is unable to engage in battle, so it is with this case.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu residing in a village who hears that a woman is in that village."
Having heard this, he immediately gives rise to lustful intent; yet, even when seeing a woman, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire.

He merely engages in mutual flirtation with the woman, whereupon he abandons his prohibitive precepts and adopts the ways of a layperson—just like that third man who, having seen the banner from afar, was seized by terror and became incapable of fighting.
For this reason, it is now said that this person is called the third type of warrior.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who dwells in a village; that bhikṣu hears that there is a woman in the village.

Having heard this, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food. Failing to guard his body, speech, and mind, he saw a woman of peerless beauty and immediately conceived a lustful intent toward her. He either pinched or nudged her, or exchanged fist-blows with her; thus, he abandoned the precepts and returned to being a layman.
Just as that fourth combatant, while in the midst of the great army, was seized by others and lost his life, for this reason, this person is now spoken of.
"Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who hears that in a village there is a woman who is rare in the world.

Although he hears this, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire. When it is time, that bhikṣu puts on his robes, takes his bowl, enters the village for alms, and guards his body, speech, and mind."
Although he sees women, he does not give rise to thoughts of desire, nor does he have any improper thoughts;
even if he converses back and forth with them, he still does not give rise to thoughts of desire, nor does he have any improper thoughts.

However, if he were to engage in mutual touching or the clashing of fists with a woman, at that moment he would immediately give rise to thoughts of desire, and his body, speech, and mind would become intensely inflamed.
His desire having become intensely inflamed, he returned to the grove and approached the elder bhikṣu. For this reason, he spoke to the elder bhikṣu:

"Virtuous ones, you should know that my desire is now intensely inflamed and I am unable to restrain it. I only pray that you will teach me the Dharma so that I may be liberated from the foul impurities of desire!"
At that time, the elder bhikṣu said to him:
"You should now contemplate from where this desire arises and from where it ceases."

"What the Tathāgata has taught is that one who would abandon desire does so by means of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*), as well as by practicing the path of the contemplation of impurity.
At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu spoke these verses:
"If one knows the inverted [perceptions], One applies the mind so that it blazes intensely."
"One should eliminate all fervent states of mind and allow the intentions of desire to come to rest.
"Virtuous ones, know this: desire arises from perception; by giving rise to perceptions, the intention of desire is produced."

They may bring harm upon themselves and also harm others, giving rise to various calamities and misfortunes; they will experience suffering and affliction in this present life, and furthermore, undergo immeasurable suffering in future lives.
When the intention of desire is eliminated, one neither harms oneself nor harms others, and does not undergo suffering as its retribution in the present life.
Therefore, you should now eliminate such mental conceptions.
"By means of non-conceptualization, there is no mind of desire; by means of a mind free from desire, there is no distracted conceptualization.
At that time, having received such instruction, that bhikṣu contemplated the signs of impurity.

By contemplating the perception of impurity, at that time the mind with outflows attains liberation and reaches the unconditioned state. It is like the fifth man who, donning armor and grasping weapons, enters the army to engage in battle; seeing the multitude of enemies, he feels no fear, and even if there are those who come to harm him, his mind remains unmoved. He is able to defeat external invaders and dwell within their territory.

For this reason, it is now said that this person is able to shatter the hosts of Māra, eliminate all distracted thoughts, and reach the state of unconditioned nirvāṇa; this is called the fifth person appearing in the world.
“Bhikkhus, you should know that there are these five kinds of persons who appear in the world.
Therefore, bhikkhus, you should practice with mindfulness the perception of the impurity of sensual desire.”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five things that prevent a person who sweeps the ground from gaining merit. What are these five?

In this regard, a person who sweeps the ground does not know how to sweep against the wind, does not know how to sweep with the wind, does not gather the dust into heaps, does not remove the refuse, and the place where they have swept is not made clean.”
"Monks, this is called a person who sweeps the ground: although they possess five qualities, they do not achieve great merit. Furthermore, monks,"
A person who sweeps the ground achieves five merits. What are these five?

In this regard, a person who sweeps the ground understands the principles of sweeping against the wind and with the wind; they also know how to gather [dust] and how to remove it, leaving nothing behind and making it exceedingly clean and beautiful.
This is what is called, monks!
These five things constitute great merit. Therefore, monks!
One should eliminate the first five matters and cultivate the latter five dharmas.
Thus, O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is someone who sweeps a stūpa, they may not obtain five merits. What are these five?

Thereupon, there was someone who swept the stūpa without sprinkling water on the ground, without removing shards and stones, without leveling the ground, without sweeping with a focused mind, and without clearing away filth and impurities.
"Monks, this is called a person who sweeps the ground who does not accomplish five virtues.
Monks, you should know that a person who sweeps the ground accomplishes five virtues."
What are the five?
In this regard, those who sweep the stūpa sprinkle the ground with water, remove tiles and stones, level the ground, sweep it with a focused mind, and clear away filth and impurities.
This is called, O bhikṣus,
the five things that cause a person to attain merit. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
Those who wish to seek its merit should practice these five things.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"For one who travels on long journeys, there are five hardships. What are the five?
Thereupon, those who wander constantly do not recite the Dharma teachings;
they forget the teachings they have recited;
and they fail to attain concentration of mind.
Having attained samādhi, one loses it again;
having heard the Dharma, one cannot retain it.
This is what is meant, O bhikṣu!
"One who wanders much has these five difficulties.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that one who does not wander much has five merits. What are the five?"
Attaining the Dharma where it was never before attained;
having attained it, not forgetting it;
and being able to maintain what has been heard extensively.
One is able to attain a concentrated mind;
having attained samādhi, one does not lose it again.
This, O bhikṣu, is what is meant.
Those who do not travel much possess these five merits. Therefore, monks,
do not travel much.
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves. At that time,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is a bhikṣu who constantly dwells in one place, there are five unrighteous things. What are the five?
In this case, a bhikṣu dwelling in one place becomes attached to his dwelling, fearing that others might seize it from him;”
Or their minds may be attached to property, fearing that others might seize it;
or they may accumulate many goods like laypeople, being greedily attached to their kinsmen and not wishing for others to visit the homes of their relatives,
constantly coming and going with laypeople.
"Monks, this is what is called the five unrighteous qualities found in those who dwell in a single location. Therefore, monks!"
"You should seek skillful means and not remain in one place. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five merits for a person who does not dwell in a single place. What are the five?
Not coveting dwellings, not coveting utensils, not accumulating wealth and goods in excess, not being attached to kinsmen, and not associating with laypeople—
this, O bhikṣu, is called [the practice].
