A person who does not dwell in a single place possesses these five merits. Therefore, monks,
you should seek skillful means and practice these five matters.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying by the side of the Radiant Pond in the kingdom of Magadha. At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar the great tree being consumed by fire; having seen this, the Tathāgata proceeded to another tree.
Upon arrival, he sat down beneath that tree.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think, bhikṣus?
Would you rather cast this body into this fire?"
"Would you rather associate with an upright woman?
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"We would rather associate with women than cast ourselves into this fire."
The reason for this is that the heat and toxicity of this fire are beyond measure; it severs the life-faculty, and the suffering endured is immeasurable.
The World-Honored One said:
“I now tell you all: those who practice what is not the conduct of a śramaṇa yet claim to be śramaṇas, and those who do not practice the holy life yet claim it to be the holy life;”
One who has not heard the True Dharma yet claims,
"I have heard the Dharma," and who possesses no pure and white dharmas— such a person would rather cast themselves into this fire than associate or consort with women.
The reason for this is that such a person would rather endure this suffering than enter hell because of these offenses to undergo immeasurable pain.
What do you think, bhikṣus?
"Would you rather receive the prostrations and respect of others,
or would you rather have someone take a sharp sword and cut off your hands and feet?
The bhikṣus replied:
"I would rather receive respectful salutations than have a person cut off my hands and feet with a sword.
Why is this? Because the pain of having one's hands and feet severed is beyond measure."
The World-Honored One said:
"I now tell you all: those who do not practice the conduct of a śramaṇa yet claim to be śramaṇas;
those who do not practice the holy life (brahmacarya) yet claim it is the holy life."
One who has not heard the True Dharma yet claims to have heard it,
and who lacks pure conduct while having severed their roots of goodness—
such a person would rather cast themselves down to receive this sharp sword than accept the veneration of others while lacking precepts.
The reason for this is that this pain lasts but a brief moment,
whereas the suffering of hell is beyond measure.
What do you think, bhikṣus?
"Which would you prefer: to receive garments from others, or to have your body wrapped in glowing iron plates? The bhikṣus replied:
“It would be better to receive garments from others than to undergo this suffering.
Why is this? Because this poisonous pain is beyond measure.
The World-Honored One said:
"I now tell you again: a person who lacks the precepts would rather have their body wrapped in glowing iron sheets than accept the garments of others.
Why is this? Because such pain lasts but a moment, whereas the suffering of hell is beyond measure."
What do you think, bhikṣu!
Would it be better to accept food given in faith by others,
or would it be better to swallow glowing iron balls?
The bhikṣus replied, “We would rather accept food given in faith by others than swallow hot iron balls.
Why is this? Because such pain is unbearable.”
The World-Honored One said:
“I tell you now: it would be better to swallow glowing iron balls than to receive the offerings of the faithful while lacking precepts.
Why is this? Swallowing glowing iron balls causes pain for but a moment; receiving the offerings of others while lacking precepts does not.”
"What do you think, bhikṣu!
Would you rather accept bedding and furniture from others,
or would you rather lie upon a bed of hot iron?"
The bhikṣus replied, “World-Honored One,
we would rather accept the bedding and furniture for reclining from others than lie upon iron beds.”
"The reason for this is that such poisonous suffering is beyond measure.
The World-Honored One told them:
"Those foolish people lack virtuous conduct; though not śramaṇas, they claim to be śramaṇas."
There is no holy life (brahmacarya), yet one claims to practice it; rather than lying upon an iron bed, one should never accept the faithful offerings of others without precepts.
Why is this? Lying upon an iron bed causes pain for but a moment, whereas accepting the faithful offerings of others without precepts results in suffering for a long time.

“Bhikṣus, you should know: as I observe today the destination of those who lack precepts, if they are reborn among humans, their bodies will be withered and emaciated, and boiling blood will gush from their facial orifices until they meet their end. They shall not associate or consort with women; they shall not receive the merit of others’ prostrations and respect; and they shall not receive from others robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicinal requisites for illness. Because these persons lack precepts, they do not contemplate the sins of future lives or past lives; disregarding the very root of life, they undergo such bitter suffering. Persons without precepts shall be born within the three evil realms.”
The reason for this is that it is brought about by the commission of evil deeds.

"Today, as the Tathāgata observes the destination of those who practice wholesome conduct, even if they are poisoned, wounded by a blade, or their life-faculty is severed of its own accord, [they shall attain liberation]."

Why is this? Because those who wish to cast off this body and receive heavenly blessings, and are reborn in auspicious realms, do so entirely due to the ripening of the rewards for virtuous deeds performed in previous lives.

"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should practice with mindfulness the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision and knowledge of liberation."

I wish to cause those in the present life to obtain their karmic rewards and attain the Path of Ambrosia; even while receiving from others clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for illness and debility, they shall remain free from transgression, and furthermore, I shall cause the donors to receive inexhaustible merit.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.

At that time, while this Dharma was being taught, sixty monks attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; sixty monks, however, cast off their Dharma robes and returned to the state of laymen.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Five Kings and Candraprabha; Śiva and the two types of conflict;
the two kinds of sweeping; the two modes of practice; and the two ways of departing and remaining.
The Withered Tree is at the very end. *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 25 and Scroll 26.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
34. Chapter on Right View (Samyag-dṛṣṭi-varga), Chapter Thirty-Four. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Venerable Śāriputra was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where Śāriputra was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
Then, those many bhikṣus said to Śāriputra:
"What dharmas should a bhikṣu who has accomplished the precepts contemplate?"
Śāriputra replied: "A bhikṣu who has accomplished the precepts should contemplate the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as affliction, and as full of pain and fear;
he should also contemplate them as suffering, empty, and non-self."
What are the five? They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
At that time, the bhikṣu accomplished in morality contemplates these five aggregates of clinging and thereby attains the path of the srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu said to Śāriputra: “What dharmas should a srotāpanna bhikṣu contemplate? Śāriputra replied:
“A bhikṣu who is a stream-enterer should also contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as suffering, as affliction, and as full of pain and fear;
he should also contemplate them as suffering, empty, and non-self.”
"Virtuous ones, you should know that when a bhikṣu who is a stream-enterer contemplates these five aggregates of clinging,
he then achieves the fruit of a once-returner. The bhikṣus asked:
"What dharmas should a Sakṛdāgāmin bhikṣu contemplate?

Śāriputra replied, "A Sakṛdāgāmin bhikṣu should also contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as suffering, as affliction, and as full of pain and fear; he should also contemplate them as suffering, empty, and non-self."
"At that time, when a Sakṛdāgāmin bhikṣu contemplates these five aggregates of clinging, he immediately realizes the fruit of Anāgāmin.
The bhikṣus asked: "What dharmas should an Anāgāmin bhikṣu contemplate?"
Śāriputra replied: “An ānāgāmin bhikṣu should likewise contemplate these five aggregates of clinging as suffering, as affliction, and as a source of much pain and fear;
and while contemplating these five aggregates of clinging, he shall then become an arhat.”
The bhikṣus asked, “What dharmas should an arhat bhikṣu contemplate? Śāriputra replied:
"Why is your question so excessive? The deeds of Arhat bhikṣus have already been completed;

they no longer engage in further formations. Their minds with outflows are liberated, and they do not head toward the ocean of birth and death within the five destinies, nor will they again undergo existence or perform any further conditioned actions."
Therefore, worthy ones!
A bhikṣu who maintains the precepts, as well as a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, and an anāgāmin, should contemplate these five aggregates of clinging.
"Thus it is, monks! You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what Śāriputra had said, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Ṛṣis.
At that time, not long after the Tathāgata had attained enlightenment, people of the world called him the Great Śramaṇa.
At that time, King Prasenajit had newly ascended the throne.
Then, King Prasenajit thought to himself:
"Now that I have newly ascended the throne, I should first take a maiden from the Śākya clan."
"If he grants it to me, it will suit my heart;
if he does not grant it, I shall now go and compel him by force.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed a certain minister, saying:
"Go to Kapilavastu and, upon arriving at the home of the Śākyas, convey my name and say to those Śākyas:
'King Prasenajit inquires after your welfare and asks if you are light and well, sending his greetings in abundance.'"
He further addressed those Śākyas, saying:
"I wish to take a maiden of the Śākya clan as my wife; if you grant her to me, I shall cherish your kindness forever;
if you refuse, I shall compel you by force."
At that time, the great minister, having received the king’s command, went to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, five hundred members of the Śākya clan from Kapilavastu had gathered in one place.
At that time, the minister went to where the five hundred Śākyas were and, mentioning King Prasenajit by name, spoke to those Śākyas, saying:
"King Prasenajit sends his most earnest greetings; he inquires after your well-being with great care and offers you his boundless regards."
"I wish to take a daughter of the Śākya clan; if they grant her to me, it would be a great fortune, but if they do not grant her, I shall compel them by force.
When the Śākyas heard these words, they were filled with extreme indignation.
"We are of noble lineage; for what reason should we enter into marriage with the offspring of a slave?
Among the assembly, some said they should grant their consent, while others said it was not permissible.
At that time, there was a Śākya among that assembly named Mahānāman, who spoke to the multitude, saying:
"Virtuous ones, do not be angry together.
For what reason? King Prasenajit is a man of violent and evil character; should King Prasenajit come here, he will destroy our kingdom."
"I shall now go in person to meet King Prasenajit and speak of this matter.
At that time, a maidservant in Mahānāman’s household gave birth to a daughter whose features were so beautiful and perfect as to be rare in the world.
Then Mahānāman bathed the girl, dressed her in fine garments, placed her in a precious feathered carriage, and sent her to King Prasenajit, saying further to the king:
"This is my daughter; you may take her as your wife."

At that time, King Prasenajit, having obtained this girl, was filled with extreme joy; he immediately established her as his first consort. Before many days had passed, she became pregnant, and after eight or nine months, she gave birth to a son who was peerlessly handsome and exceptionally distinguished in the world.
At that time, King Prasenajit assembled various physiognomists to bestow a name upon this crown prince.
Having heard the king’s words, the physiognomists immediately addressed the king, saying:

"Great King, you should know that when we sought a consort for him, the Śākyas all disputed the matter; some said she should be given, while others said she should not be given, causing distress and division among them."
"Now we shall establish a name for him; let his name be Vīrūḍhaka.
Having thus conferred the title, the physiognomists rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, King Prasenajit cherished this Prince Virūḍhaka so dearly that he was never out of sight.
Now, Prince Liu-li was nearly eight years old, and the King said to him:
"You are now grown; you may go to Kapilavastu to study the various arts of archery."
At that time, King Prasenajit provided several messengers and sent them on great elephants to the home of the Śākyas; arriving at the residence of Mahānāman, they said to him:
"King Prasenajit has sent us here to learn the various arts of archery; we pray only that you, our grandfather and grandmother, will instruct us in every matter."
Then Mahānāman replied, "Those who wish to study the arts may do so well. At that time,
Mahānāman of the Śākya clan gathered five hundred youths and had them study the arts together.
At that time, Prince Suddhodana was practicing archery together with five hundred youths.
At that moment, a new lecture hall had been built in the city of Kapilavastu, where devas, humans, māras, and mārakāyikas resided.
At that time, the Śākyas each said to one another:
"This lecture hall has been completed not long ago, and its murals are already finished; it is no different from a celestial palace."
"We should first invite the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus to offer them sustenance therein, so that we may receive inexhaustible merit.

At that time, the Śākyas immediately spread various kinds of seating within the hall, hung silk banners and canopies, sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground, burned many famous incenses, stored fine water, and lit numerous bright lamps.
At that time, Prince Devadatta took five hundred youths and went to the lecture hall, where he immediately ascended the lion throne.
When the Śākyas saw this, they were filled with intense indignation; they stepped forward, seized his arms, and drove him out through the door, all of them reviling him together:
"This is but the son of a slave-girl! No one among the devas or the people of the world has ever sat within this place; how dare the offspring of a slave enter and sit here?"
Again, he seized Prince Virūḍhaka and threw him to the ground.
At that moment, Prince Virūḍhaka rose from the earth, sighed deeply, and looked behind him.
At that time, there was a son of a brahmin named Bhāradvāja.
Then, Prince Devadatta said to the brahmin’s son Bhāradvāja:
"These Śākyas have humiliated me to such an extent; when I later succeed to the royal throne, you must inform me of this matter."
At that time, the son of the brahmin Bhārgava replied,
"As the Prince commands. Thereafter,
that son of the brahmin reported to the Prince three times each day.
"Remembering the humiliation inflicted by Śakra," he then spoke this verse:
"All things return to exhaustion; when fruit ripens, it must also fall."
"Whatever is gathered must inevitably disperse; wherever there is birth, there must be death.
At that time, King Prasenajit lived out his allotted lifespan and subsequently passed away. Thereupon, he installed Prince Viḍūḍabha as king.
At that time, the brahmin Bhārgava went to the king’s presence and spoke thus:
“Your Majesty, you should remember the insults and humiliations inflicted upon you by the Śākyas. Then, King Virūḍhaka replied:
“Excellent! Excellent!
You have well remembered these past events.”
At that time, King Virūḍhaka became enraged and addressed his ministers, saying,
"Who is this person who now acts as the lord of the people?
The ministers replied:
"Great King! This is what you now govern. King Virūḍhaka then said:
"Prepare the chariots with all haste and assemble the fourfold army; I wish to go and subdue the Śākyas.
The ministers replied, "So be it."
"Great King!
At that time, the ministers, having received the king's command, immediately mobilized and assembled the fourfold army.
Then, King Virūḍhaka, leading these four divisions of troops, proceeded toward Kapilavastu.

At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus, having heard that King Virūḍhaka was going forth to wage war against the Śākyas, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, stood to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One immediately went to King Udayana of Vatsa and sat cross-legged beneath a withered tree that had no branches or leaves.

At that time, King Virūḍhaka saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree; he immediately alighted from his chariot and approached the World-Honored One, prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and standing to one side.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"There are other fine trees with lush branches and leaves, such as the nyagrodha; why do you sit beneath this withered tree?"
The World-Honored One replied,
“The protection of one’s own kinsmen is superior to that of outsiders.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka thought to himself:
"Today the World-Honored One has intentionally acted for the sake of his kinsmen;
however, I should now return to my own kingdom and ought not to go and wage war against Kapilavastu.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka took his leave and withdrew.
At that time, the brahmin Bhārgava again addressed the king, saying:
"You should remember how you were humiliated by the Śākyas in the past.
Upon hearing these words, King Virūḍhaka again gave rise to intense anger.
"Quickly prepare the chariots and assemble the fourfold army; I wish to go and campaign against Kapilavastu.
At that time, the ministers immediately assembled the fourfold army, departed from the city of Śrāvastī, and went toward Kapilavastu to wage war against the Śākyas.
At that time, having heard this, a great number of bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One:
"Now King Virūḍhaka has raised a vast army and is going to attack the Śākyas.
When the World-Honored One heard these words, he immediately used his supernormal power to go to the side of the road and sit beneath a tree.

At that time, King Virūḍhaka saw the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree from afar; he immediately alighted from his chariot and approached the World-Honored One, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and standing to one side.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"There are other fine trees where one might sit; why does the World-Honored One today sit beneath this withered tree?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"The protection of one's own kinsmen is superior to that of outsiders.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“Under the cool shade of my kinsmen, the Śākya clan emerged from the Buddha;
all are my branches and leaves, therefore I sit beneath this tree.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka again thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has today emerged from the Śākya clan;
I ought not to go and wage war against him, but should instead turn back here and return to my own land.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka immediately returned to the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the brahmin Bhāradvāja spoke again to the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, you should remember the humiliations inflicted upon you by the Śākya clan.
Having heard these words, King Virūḍhaka assembled his fourfold army and departed from the city of Śrāvastī, proceeding toward Kapilavastu.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana heard that King Virūḍhaka was going to campaign against the Śākyas. Having heard this, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Today King Virūḍhaka has assembled the fourfold army to go and attack the Śākyas. I am now capable of casting King Virūḍhaka and his four divisions of troops into another world-system."
The World-Honored One said,
"Are you able to take the karmic conditions of the Śākya clan and place them in another world-system?
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly impossible for me to cause him, by means of past karmic conditions, to be reborn in another world-system.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Return to your seat."
Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am now capable of moving this Kapilavastu and placing it in the midst of space.
The World-Honored One told him:
“Are you now able to shift the karmic conditions of the Śākyas from their former lives and place them in empty space?
Maudgalyāyana replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Return now to your original seat.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May it please you to grant permission for an iron cage to be constructed as a loose covering over the city of Kapilavastu.
The World-Honored One said,
“What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?”
"Can one use an iron cage to obstruct past karmic conditions?
Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha,
"No, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Return now to your original seat. Today, the karmic conditions of the Śākya clan have matured; they shall now receive their retribution.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"To wish to turn space into earth, and again to turn earth into space—
bound as they are by their original conditions, these conditions shall not decay.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka went to Kapilavastu.
At that time, when the Śākyas heard that King Virūḍhaka was leading the fourfold army to attack them, they gathered their own fourfold host and set out for one yojana to confront King Virūḍhaka.
At that time, the Śākyas shot from a distance within a range of one yojana at King Virūḍhaka;
some arrows struck his ear canals without injuring his ears,
and others struck his topknot without injuring his head.
Some struck the bows and broke them;
some struck the bowstrings without harming the persons;
some struck the armor and weapons without injuring the persons.
Or he might shoot at a couch or seat without harming the person; or he might shoot at a chariot wheel and destroy it without injuring the person;
or he might destroy a banner or standard without harming the person.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka, having witnessed this event, was seized with terror and addressed his ministers, saying:
"Do you see from where this arrow has come?"
The ministers replied, "These Śākyas are within one yojana of here; we shall shoot arrows to summon them.
King Virūḍhaka replied:
"If they were to set their minds on harming me, they would all surely perish; it would be best for you to return home to Śrāvastī from here.
At that time, the brahmin Bhārgava came forward and said to the king:
"Great King, do not fear. These Śākyas all uphold the precepts; they do not harm even insects, much less a human being!"
"Now we should advance; we shall surely destroy the Śākyas.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka gradually advanced toward those Śākyas.
Then, the Śākyas retreated into the city.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka stood outside the city and addressed them, saying:
"Open the city gates at once!
If you do not, I shall capture and kill every one of you."

At that time, there was a Śākya youth in the city of Kapilavastu, fifteen years of age, named Śama. Hearing that King Virūḍhaka was now outside the gates, he immediately donned armor, took up weapons, and ascended the city wall to engage the King Virūḍhaka in combat alone.
At that time, the youth Śama had slain many soldiers, who fled in all directions, each saying:
"Who is this? Is he a deva?"
"Is this a ghost or a spirit?
From afar it appears like a small child.
At that moment, King Līlāvaṇa was seized with terror and immediately entered a hole in the ground to hide from him.
At that time, the Śākyas heard that King Virūḍhaka’s host had been defeated.
Thereupon, the Śākyas summoned the youth Śama and addressed him, saying:
"You are but a child; why have you brought disgrace upon our lineage?"
"Do you not know that the Śākyas practice wholesome dharmas?
We cannot even harm insects, much less take human life?
We can destroy this army; one of us can match ten thousand."
Nevertheless, we further reflect thus:
"The number of sentient beings who have been killed is beyond calculation.
The World-Honored One has also said this:"
“O lady, one who takes the life of another shall enter hell after death;
even if born among humans, their lifespan will be extremely short.
“Go quickly; do not stay here any longer.”
At that time, Prince Sudarśana immediately departed from the country and never again entered Kapilavastu.
Then, King Virūḍhaka arrived once more at the gate and said to the men there, "Open the city gates quickly; do not delay."
At that time, the Śākyas said among themselves,
"Should we open the gate, or should we not? Then, the evil Māra Pāpīyān,
being among the assembly of Śākyas, assumed the form of a Śākya and addressed them, saying:
"Open the city gates at once; do not all suffer together this day.
At that time, the Śākyas immediately opened the city gates.
Then, King Virūḍhaka addressed his ministers, saying:

"Currently, this assembly of Śākyas and the populace is extremely vast; it cannot be destroyed entirely by swords and blades. We shall take them all, bury their feet in the ground, and then have fierce elephants trample them to death."
At that time, the ministers received the king’s command and immediately had the elephant trample him to death.
Then, King Virūḍhaka commanded his ministers, saying:
"Quickly select five hundred Śākya women who are skilled in their craft."
Then, having received the king’s command, the ministers selected five hundred beautiful women and brought them to the king’s presence.
At that time, Mahānāman the Śākya went to King Virūḍhaka and spoke thus:
“You should grant my wish.”
King Liu-li said, "What kind of wish do you desire? Mahānāman replied:
"I am now submerged at the bottom of the water; let the Śākyas all escape according to my pace, whether slow or fast.
Once I emerge from the water, you may kill them as you please."
King Virūḍhaka said, "This is most excellent. At that time,
Mahānāma the Śākya immediately entered the depths of the water, tied his hair to the roots of a tree, and gave up his life.
At that time, the Śākyas of the city of Kapilavastu emerged from the eastern gate and entered through the southern gate;
some emerged from the southern gate and re-entered through the northern gate;
others emerged from the western gate and entered through the northern gate.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka said to his ministers,
"For what reason has Mahānāman’s father remained hidden within the water and does not emerge now?
Then, having heard the king's command, the ministers entered the water and brought forth Mahānāman, who had already passed away.
At that time, when King Virūḍhaka saw that Mahānāman had passed away, he felt remorse, thinking:
"Now my grandfather has met his end because of my attachment to my kinsmen."
"I did not know beforehand that my life would end here; had I known this, I certainly would not have come to attack these Śākyas.

At that time, King Virūḍhaka killed ninety-nine million nine hundred thousand people, so that the flowing blood formed rivers. He set fire to the city of Kapilavastu and proceeded to the Nyagrodha Garden.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka said to the five hundred Śākya women:
"Be careful not to grieve or worry; I am your husband and you are my wives, and we must certainly be united."
At that time, King Virūḍhaka reached out his hand, seized a Śākya woman, and intended to toy with her.
The woman then asked, "Great King, what do you intend to do?"
The king then replied,
"I wish to have intimate relations with you.
The woman answered the king:
"Why have I now had illicit relations with the offspring of a slave woman?
At that time, King Virūḍhaka was filled with intense rage and commanded his ministers, saying:
"Seize this woman immediately, maim her hands and feet, and cast her into a deep pit."
The ministers, having received the king’s command, severed his hands and feet and cast him into a pit.
Then the five hundred women all reviled the king, saying:
"Who would take this body of theirs to have sexual intercourse with the offspring of a slave woman?"
At that time, the king, consumed by rage, seized all five hundred Śākya women, mutilated their hands and feet, and cast them into a deep pit.
Having thus utterly destroyed Kapilavastu, King Virūḍhaka returned to the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, Prince Jeta was within his inner palace, enjoying himself with various female entertainers. Then, King Virūḍhaka heard the sound of musical performances and immediately asked, "What kind of sound is this, reaching even here?"
The ministers replied to the king,
saying, "This is Prince Jeta, who, within the inner palace, has provided musical performances for his own entertainment.
Thereupon, King Virūḍhaka immediately commanded his charioteer:
"Turn this elephant around and go to the residence of Prince Jeta.
At that time, the gatekeeper saw the king approaching from afar and said to him:
"Your Majesty, please proceed slowly; Prince Jeta is currently within the palace enjoying himself with the five kinds of music, so do not disturb him."
At that moment, King Virūḍhaka immediately drew his sword and killed the gatekeeper.
At that time, Prince Jeta, hearing that King Virūḍhaka was waiting outside the gate, did not take leave of his female musicians at all;
he went out to meet the king: "Welcome, Great King!"
"You may enter and halt the carriage for a short while. Then King Virūḍhaka replied,
"Do you not know that I am fighting with the Śākyas?"
Jeta replied, "I have heard it.
King Virūḍhaka then said in response:
"Why do you now dally with courtesans instead of assisting me?
Prince Jeta replied, "I am not capable of taking the lives of sentient beings."
At that time, King Virūḍhaka, filled with extreme rage, immediately drew his sword and struck down Prince Jeta.
After Prince Jeta’s life had ended, he was reborn among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, where he enjoyed himself in the company of five hundred celestial maidens.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye that Prince Jeta had reached the end of his life and been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, immediately spoke this verse:
"Receiving blessings among humans and devas— The merit of Prince Jeta,
Who receives retribution for his goodness later on, Is all due to the cause of present retribution."
One grieves here, and one grieves there; wandering through both realms, one grieves.
Having committed evil, one later receives its retribution—all this is due to the manifest results of one's actions.
One should rely upon the merit of blessings; as one acted before, so shall it be afterward.
Whether acting alone, or again, unknown to others; when one commits evil, one knows it as evil. What was done before is likewise what follows after;
whether acting alone, or again, unknown to others.
Receiving blessings among humans and devas—receiving blessings in both places—is the retribution received later for having done good;
all this is due to the nature of present retribution.
If one grieves here, one will grieve there as well; by doing evil, one grieves in both places.
"Receiving retribution for evil after the fact is entirely due to the manifestation of present retribution.
At that time, the five hundred Śākya women took refuge and invoked the name of the Tathāgata: "The Tathāgata was here;
he likewise left this very place to renounce the world and study the Way, and thereafter attained Buddhahood."
"Yet today the Buddha does not deign to remember us; we have encountered such affliction and endured such agonizing pain.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you not remember us?
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure and penetrating divine ear, heard the Śākya women voicing their grievances toward the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Come all together and behold Kapilavastu, and observe the passing away of your kinsmen."
The bhikṣu replied, "So it is,
World-Honored One!"
At that time, the World-Honored One took the bhikṣus and departed from the city of Śrāvastī, proceeding toward Kapilavastu.
Then, the five hundred Śākya women saw the World-Honored One approaching with the bhikṣus from afar; having seen him, they were all filled with shame and remorse.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-Indra and King Vaiśravaṇa were fanning the World-Honored One from behind.
Then the World-Honored One turned his gaze back and said to Śakra Devānām-Indra:
"These Śākya women are all filled with shame and modesty."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied, “So be it,
World-Honored One! Thereupon, Śakra,
Lord of the Devas, immediately covered the bodies of these five hundred women with celestial garments.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to King Vaiśravaṇa:
"These women have been hungry and thirsty for a long time; what expedient means should be employed?
King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
King Vaiśravaṇa then prepared natural celestial food and fully satisfied all the Śākya women.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the women, saying:
"It is said that all phenomena must eventually disperse; there will inevitably be parting.
You women should know that these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) shall all undergo such suffering and affliction, falling into the five realms of existence."
Now, one who has received a body composed of the five aggregates of clinging must inevitably undergo the retribution of these formative actions;
because there is the retribution of formative actions, one must then undergo conception;
having already undergone the stage of conception, one must further undergo the retribution of suffering and pleasure.
If the five aggregates of clinging did not exist, one would no longer receive a physical form;
if one does not receive a physical form, then there is no birth;
because there is no birth, there is no old age.
Because there is no aging, there is no illness;
because there is no illness, there is no death;
because there is no death, there is no affliction of meeting and parting.
Therefore, daughters, you should keep in mind these transformations of the formation and disintegration of the five aggregates.
Why is this so? Because by knowing the five aggregates, one knows the five desires.
By knowing the five desires, one knows the dharma of craving;
by knowing the dharma of craving, one knows the dharma of defiled attachment.
Having understood these various matters, one will no longer undergo rebirth in a womb.
"Because one does not undergo conception, there is no birth, aging, sickness, or death.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught this Dharma to the Śākya women, namely:
discourse on giving, discourse on morality, and discourse on rebirth in heaven; [he spoke of] the impurity of desire and the excellence of liberation as happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the minds of these women were opened and their intentions liberated, taught them the Dharma constantly expounded by all Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones— suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— and at that moment, the World-Honored One explained it all to them.
At that time, all the women were cleansed of their defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; each passed away at her respective location and was reborn in the heavens.
Then, the World-Honored One went to the eastern gate of the city and, seeing the smoke and fire blazing within the city, immediately spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; Those who are born must surely die."
"Where there is no birth, there is no death; this cessation is the supreme bliss.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you, come together and go to the Nyagrodha Grove, where you shall take your seats."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is the Nyagrodha Garden where, in the past, I dwelt and extensively expounded the Dharma to the bhikṣus; now it is empty and deserted, with no people in it."
In days of yore, many tens of millions of beings attained the Way therein, such that their Dharma-eye was purified.
From this day forward, the Tathāgata shall no longer return to this place.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had taught the Dharma to the bhikṣus, they each rose from their seats and departed, proceeding to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The King Virūḍhaka and this host of soldiers shall not remain in the world for long; seven days hence, they shall all be utterly destroyed."
At that time, King Virūḍhaka heard the World-Honored One’s prophecy:
"King Virūḍhaka and his entire host of soldiers shall all be utterly extinguished seven days from now."
Having heard this, he was struck with terror and addressed his ministers, saying:
"The Tathāgata has now prophesied regarding him, saying:
'King Virūḍhaka shall not remain in this world for long; seven days from now, he and his entire army shall utterly perish.'"
"You all observe that there are no thieves, nor calamities of water or fire coming to invade the kingdom. Why is this?
Because the words of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are without duality; what they say never differs from reality."
At that time, the brahmin Bhāradvāja addressed the king, saying:
"O King, do not be afraid; there are currently no threats from bandits or robbers in the border regions, nor are there any calamities of water or fire.
Today, may Your Majesty enjoy yourself in full delight."
King Virūḍhaka said, “Brahmin, you should know that the words of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not differ.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka sent someone to count the days; when the seventh day arrived, the Great King was so filled with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself.
Accompanied by his troops and court ladies, he went to the banks of the Ajiravatī River to enjoy himself and stayed there overnight.

At that time, at midnight, unseasonable clouds arose, bringing a violent wind and torrential rain. Consequently, King Liu-li and his entire army were swept away by the waters; they were all utterly destroyed, their bodies perished and their lives ended, as they entered the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, a celestial fire burned the inner palaces.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing with his divine eye, saw that King Liu-li and his fourfold army had been swept away by the waters; they had all met their end and entered into hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Committing evil to the utmost degree, All arises from the actions of body and speech;
In this very life one suffers affliction, And one's lifespan is likewise shortened."
"If it is kept within the home, it will be consumed by fire;
when its life comes to an end, it will surely be reborn in hell.
At that time, many bhikṣus in the assembly addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“King Virūḍhaka and his fourfold army have now met their end; where have they been reborn?
The World-Honored One replied, “King Virūḍhaka has now entered the Avīci Hell.”
The bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“By what causes and conditions did these Śākyas commit in the past that they are now being slain by King Virūḍhaka?
At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, within this city of Rājagṛha, there was a fishing village.
At that time, the world was in the midst of extreme famine; people ate the roots of plants, and one *liǎng* of gold could purchase only one *shēng* of rice."
At that time, there was a large pond in that village, which was also abundant with fish.
Then, the people of the city of Rājagṛha went to the pond to catch and eat the fish.
At that time, there were two kinds of fish in the water:
one named *Kuśu* and the other named *Dvija-hva*.
At that moment, the two fish each said to one another:

"Among these people, we have previously committed no offense; we are aquatic creatures who do not dwell on level ground. Yet this race of humans all comes to devour us. If we possessed even a small amount of merit from our past lives, we would surely use it to take revenge."
"At that time, there was a young boy in the village about eight years old. He did not catch fish, nor did he take life.
Nevertheless, all those fish that were on the shore had already died;
when the boy saw this, he felt extreme joy."
“Bhikṣus, you should know: do not hold such a view.
As for the people of the city of Rājagṛha at that time, were they anyone else?
They are none other than the Śākyas of today.”
The kṣullaka fish at that time was the King Virūḍhaka of today.
The double-tongued fish at that time was the brahmin Bhadraka of today.
The child who saw the fish on the bank and laughed at that time was my own self of today.
At that time, the Śākyas sat down and ate fish; due to this cause and condition, they entered the hells for countless kalpas and now undergo this retribution.
At that time, I sat and saw them and laughed; now I suffer from a headache as if pressed by a stone, as if carrying Mount Sumeru upon my head.
The reason for this is that the Tathāgata no longer assumes a physical form; having relinquished all conditioned activities, he has crossed over all calamities and hardships.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, it is by virtue of these causes and conditions that he now receives this retribution.
"Monks, you should guard your conduct of body, speech, and mind; you should maintain mindfulness and show reverence and service toward those who practice the holy life. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“When a devaputra is about to pass away, five unprecedented auspicious omens appear before him.”
What are the five?
First, the flowers wither;
second, the garments become soiled and dusty.
Third, the body becomes foul-smelling;
fourth, one finds no pleasure in one's own seat;
fifth, the celestial stars disperse.
"O Son of Heaven, when one is about to pass away, these five omens appear.
At that time, the son of heaven is filled with extreme sorrow and grief; he beats his breast and cries out.
Then, other sons of heaven come to where this son of heaven is and say to him:"
"Since you have come here today, you shall be born in a good realm; you have swiftly attained a good realm and swiftly attained wholesome benefit.
Having attained this wholesome benefit, you should mindfully abide in wholesome karma."
At that time, the devas instructed him thus.
Then, a certain bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"How do those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three attain birth in a good destination?"
"How does one swiftly obtain excellent benefit?
How does one dwell securely in wholesome karma?
The World-Honored One replied:

"For humans, the heavens are a favorable destination. To obtain a favorable destination and secure a favorable benefit means being born into a family with right view, associating with virtuous friends, and attaining the faculty of faith within the Dharma of the Tathāgata; this is called obtaining a truly swift and excellent benefit."
What is meant by "abiding securely in wholesome karma"?
It is when one attains the faculty of faith within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, shaves off hair and beard, and with firm faith leaves the household life to study the Path.

Through this study of the Path, one becomes fully endowed with the nature of the precepts, possesses no deficiency in the sense faculties, is moderate in eating and drinking, constantly maintains mindfulness while walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), and attains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*). This is called abiding securely in wholesome karma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"To be human is a favorable state among the heavens; A virtuous friend is a source of wholesome benefit;
To leave the home life is a wholesome deed, Leading to the exhaustion of outflows and the attainment of the outflow-free."
“Bhikṣus, you should know that the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three are attached to the five desires; they regard the human realm as a fortunate rebirth.
Having gone forth under the Tathāgata, they have attained the three types of supernormal knowledge for the sake of their excellent benefit.”
The reason for this is that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, always appears among human beings; he does not attain [enlightenment] by way of the heavens. Therefore, monks!
Having ended this life here, you shall be reborn in the heavens.
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One:
"How does a bhikṣu come to be born in a happy destination?
The Blessed One replied:
“Nirvāṇa is the bhikṣu’s happy destination. You, bhikṣu,
should now seek skillful means to reach nirvāṇa.”
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five things that bring disgrace to a renunciant who has left the household life. What are the five?
First, having long hair;”
Second, their fingernails are long;
third, their clothing is soiled with dust;
fourth, they do not know the propriety of the occasion.
Fifth, they engage in much discursive debate.
Why is this so? There are five further matters concerning the discourse of bhikṣus. What are these five?
First, people do not believe what one says;
second, they do not accept one's teachings;
third, people do not take pleasure in seeing one.
Fourth is speaking falsely;
fifth is inciting strife between parties.
These are the five matters attributed to those who engage in excessive discourse.
"Monks! You should eliminate these five and be free from wrong thoughts. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with five hundred bhikṣus.
Then, King Bimbisāra commanded his ministers:
"Quickly prepare the precious feathered chariot; I shall go to Śrāvastī to pay my respects to the World-Honored One in person.

At that time, having heard the king’s command, the ministers immediately prepared the precious feathered chariot and came forward to inform the king, saying, "The preparations are complete; Your Majesty may know it is time."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, riding in a precious feathered chariot, departed from Rājagṛha and proceeded toward Śrāvastī.

Gradually arriving at the Jetavana Monastery, he wished to enter; however, as it was the royal custom for a king to perform five dignified gestures when pouring water over his head, he set them all aside to one side. He approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to him.
Having heard the Dharma, the king addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will reside in the city of Rājagṛha for the summer retreat!"
"You should also provide robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted King Bimbisāra’s invitation.

When the king saw that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and then withdrew. He returned to the city of Rājagṛha and entered his palace.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, while in a secluded place, had this thought:

"I too am capable of providing for the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus for as long as my life lasts—with robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick—provided only that he takes pity on my lowly status."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, on that very day, addressed his ministers, saying:
"Yesterday, this thought arose in me:

'I am able, for as long as life lasts, to provide offerings to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus—robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick—and I shall likewise show compassion toward those who are lowly and inferior.'"
"Each of you should take the lead and, in succession, provide meals for the Tathāgata and the worthy ones; thus you shall receive inexhaustible blessings throughout the long night.
At that time, the King of Magadha immediately erected a great lecture hall before the palace gate and prepared various kinds of food and utensils.

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Śrāvastī and, accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus, gradually traveled through the human realm for the sake of teaching and transforming beings, until he arrived at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the World-Honored One had arrived at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, immediately mounted his carriage adorned with precious feathers and proceeded to the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"While I was in a secluded place, this thought arose in me:
'Since I am today able to provide robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick and infirm, I shall instead think of those of lowly households.'"
He then addressed his ministers:
"Each of you shall individually prepare the utensils for food and drink, and serve the Buddha in succession.
World-Honored One, what do you think?
"Is this appropriate for him,
or is it not appropriate?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Excellent! Excellent, Great King!”
"You bring great benefit and serve as a field of merit for gods and humans.
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will come to the palace for a meal tomorrow."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, seeing that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation by remaining silent,
immediately rose, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew.

At that time, on the following morning at dawn, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl, entering the city and proceeding to the royal palace, where they each sat down in order.
Then the King provided him with food of a hundred flavors, serving it with his own hands with joy and without distraction.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, seeing that the World-Honored One had finished eating and had set aside his bowl, took a low seat and sat before the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the king, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy.

Then, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the great kings and their various ministers; that is to say, he spoke on the discourse of giving, the discourse of morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven;
he taught that sensual desires are impure, that sexual lust is foul and evil, and that the way of renunciation is blissful.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the minds of those beings were opened and their intentions resolved, and that they were free from further doubt, taught them at that moment the Dharma which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly preach:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. He explained these to them in their entirety.

While seated there, more than sixty people were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; likewise, sixty great ministers and five hundred devas were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for King Bimbisāra and the multitude of people:
"Sacrifice has fire as its preeminent element; Among writings, verse is supreme;
The king is the most honored among men; Of all flowing waters, the ocean is their source."
Among the stars, the moon provides illumination; among luminous bodies, the sun is supreme.
Throughout the zenith, nadir, and the four cardinal directions, among all existing things—gods, the world, and its inhabitants—the Buddha is the most honored and supreme.
"Those who seek merit should make offerings to the Buddha.
Having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the people of the city of Rājagṛha, according to their social rank from noble to humble and the size of their households, provided meals for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One was residing in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, and there were none among the people of the kingdom who did not offer him sustenance.
At that time, it was the turn of the various brahmins in the city of Rājagṛha to prepare the meal.
Then, those brahmins gathered in one place and each made this proposal:
"Let us each contribute three or two gold coins to provide for the food."

At that time, there was a brahmin in the city of Rājagṛha named Kīṭa who was extremely impoverished; he barely managed to survive and had no money to pay his taxes, so he was driven out by the other brahmins and expelled from their midst.
At that time, the brahmin Kukkuṭa returned to his home and said to his wife:
"You should know now that the other brahmins have driven me away and will not allow me to remain among their assembly."
"The reason for this is that we have no money.
Then the wife replied, "Go back into the city and borrow from someone; you will certainly obtain it."
He further said to his master:
"Seven days hence, I shall repay you.
Should I fail to repay, both my person and my wife shall become your slaves."
At that time, the brahmin followed his wife’s words and immediately entered the city, searching everywhere, but was utterly unable to find it.
Returning to his wife, he told her:
"I have searched everywhere and been completely unable to find it; what should we do?"
Then the wife replied:
"In the east of Rājagṛha there is a great elder named Asvaghosa, who possesses abundant wealth and many treasures; you may go to him and seek a loan, saying:
'Please give me three or two gold coins, and I shall surely repay them to you after seven days.'"
"If you do not return them, I, my wife, and our children shall become your slaves.
At that time, the Brahmin took his wife’s words to Asvamedha and requested gold coins from him, saying:
"Within seven days at the most, I shall surely return them to you."
"If you do not return [the child] to me, I and my wife shall become slaves for life.
At that time, Viśvantara immediately gave him gold coins.
Then, the brahmin Kapiṅgala took these gold coins and returned to his wife's place, where he said to her:
"Having obtained this money, what would be the most appropriate course of action? The woman replied,
"You should take this money and offer it among the assembly."
At that time, the brahmin took the gold coins and went into the assembly to offer them. The other brahmins said to him, "We have already completed our preparations;
you may take these gold coins and return to your own place; there is no need for you to remain here in this assembly."
Then, that brahmin returned to his home and related these circumstances to his wife.
His wife replied, "Let us both go together to the World-Honored One and personally express our humble intentions."
At that time, the brahmin took his wife to the place where the World-Honored One was, and after exchanging greetings with him, they sat to one side.
Furthermore, his wife prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and sat to one side.
At that time, the brahmin related these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
Then, the World-Honored One said to the brahmin:
"Now, you should prepare food and drink for the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus."
At that time, the brahmin turned back and gazed intently at his wife.
Then the wife replied, "Simply follow the Buddha's teaching; there is no need for doubt or difficulty."
At that time, the brahmin rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept my invitation."
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the brahmin’s invitation.
Then, Śakra Devānām Indra stood behind the World-Honored One, attending him with his hands joined in reverence.
At that time, the World-Honored One turned back and addressed Śakra Devānām Indra:
"You may assist this brahmin in preparing the provisions for the meal.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied to the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One! At that time,
the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, not far from the Tathāgata, leading an incalculable multitude of spirits and deities, fanned the World-Honored One from afar.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to King Vaiśravaṇa:
"You, too, should assist this brahmin in preparing these provisions for the meal. Vaiśravaṇa replied:
"Excellent, Great King!

At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa went before the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then concealed his own form. He transformed himself into the likeness of a human being and, leading five hundred spirits, together prepared the utensils and provisions for the meal.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa commanded the various spirits and deities:
"Go quickly to the sandalwood grove and fetch the sandalwood.
Within the iron cauldron, five hundred spirits and deities were preparing food.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the son of the gods Īśvara, saying:
"Today Vaiśravaṇa has prepared an iron kitchen to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
"You should now manifest a lecture hall so that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus may take their meal therein.
The Devaputra Īśvara replied,
"This is most excellent."
At that time, having heard the words of Śakra Devānām-indra, the Son of the Gods Īśvara, not far from the city of Rājagṛha, manifested a lecture hall made of the seven treasures.
These so-called seven treasures were:
gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, ruby, and musaragalva.
He further manifested four stairways made of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.

Upon the golden stairway he manifested silver trees with golden roots, silver trunks, silver branches, and silver leaves; upon the silver stairway he manifested golden trees with silver roots, golden trunks, silver branches, and silver leaves.

Furthermore, upon the golden stairways and steps, silver leaves and silver branches were manifested; upon the crystal stairways, beryl trees were manifested—each of these various species being beyond measure or calculation.

Furthermore, various jewels were interspersed among them, and it was covered above with the seven precious gems; fine golden bells were suspended on all four sides, and from those bells, the eightfold sounds issued forth.
He further manifested fine couches and seats, spread with exquisite cushions, and hung with silken banners and canopies such as were rarely seen in the world.
At that time, he burned ox-head sandalwood to prepare food; for twelve *yojanas* around the city of Rājagṛha, the fragrance filled the air everywhere.
At that time, the King of Magadha addressed his ministers, saying:
"I have been raised in the depths of the palace and have never before heard of such a fragrance; for what reason do we smell this exquisite scent by the side of the city of Rājagṛha?"
The ministers said to the king, “This is the brahmin Kevaddha in the kitchen, burning celestial sandalwood incense; this is its auspicious omen.
At that time, King Bimbisāra commanded his ministers:
"Quickly prepare the carriage adorned with the finest jewels; I wish to go to the place of the World-Honored One to inquire about this matter.
At that time, the ministers replied to the king: "So be it, Great King!"
King Bimbisāra immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the king saw five hundred people preparing food within this iron kitchen; having seen this, he spoke these words:
"Whose food and drink is this being prepared?"
Then the various spirits replied in human form, saying,
"The brahmin Kikī has invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to provide them with offerings.
At that time, the various kings again saw from afar a lofty and vast lecture hall, and they asked their attendants:
"By whom was this lecture hall constructed?
It is something never seen before; for whom was it built?
The ministers replied:
“I do not know this condition.
At that time, King Bimbisāra thought to himself:
“I shall now go to the Blessed One and inquire about this matter; for the Buddha, the Blessed One, knows nothing that he does not know and sees nothing that he does not see.”
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, King Bimbisāra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In the past, I did not see this lofty and spacious lecture hall; today, I see it."
"In the past I did not see this iron kitchen, but today I see it.
What kind of object is this?
By whom has it been transformed?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"Great King, you should know that this lecture hall was constructed by the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa and the Devaputra Īśvara."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, while still seated, was overcome by a mixture of grief and weeping, unable to restrain himself.
The World-Honored One said to him: "Great King!
"For what reason do you weep so bitterly?
At that time, King Bimbisāra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I do not dare to weep out of sorrow; rather, I am mindful that future generations will not behold the arising of a Sage. People of the future will be stingy and attached to wealth and property, lacking in majestic virtue, such that they will not even hear the name of this wondrous treasure, let alone see it!"
"Now that we have encountered the Tathāgata’s marvelous and extraordinary manifestation appearing in the world, we weep with grief.
The World-Honored One told them:
"In future ages, kings and the people shall truly not behold such a manifestation."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for the king, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy.
Having heard the Dharma, the king rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the brahmin Kikī on that very day, saying:
"Stretch out your right hand.
Thereupon, Kikī stretched out his right hand, and King Vaiśravaṇa immediately gave him a gold bar and further said to him:
"Take this gold ingot yourself and cast it upon the ground.
At that moment, the brahmin immediately cast it upon the ground, whereupon it became hundreds of thousands of ounces of gold.
King Vaiśravaṇa replied, "Take this gold bar into the city and purchase various kinds of food and drink; bring them here.
At that time, the brahmin followed the king's instruction, took the gold into the city, purchased various foods and drinks, and brought them to the kitchen.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa bathed the brahmin, dressed him in various garments, held incense and a lamp in his hands, and instructed him to say:
"The time has come; now is precisely the right moment. We pray that the Venerable One will deign to visit us."
At that time, the brahmin immediately accepted his instruction; holding a censer in his hand, he said, "The time has arrived;
I only pray that you will deign to come.

Then, knowing the time had come, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and accompanied by the assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded to the lecture hall. They each sat down in order, and the assembly of bhikṣus likewise sat down in order.
At that time, the brahmin Kikī, seeing that the food and drink were extremely abundant while the assembly of monks was small, came forward and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Today the food and drink are most plentiful, yet the community of bhikṣus is few; I wonder what this means?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Now, brahmin, take a censer in your hand,
ascend to the top of a high terrace, and facing east, south, west, and north, speak these words:"
“Let all the disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha who have attained the six supernormal powers and are Arhats with outflows exhausted assemble in this lecture hall.
The brahmin replied, “So be it, World-Honored One!”
At that time, the brahmin, having received instruction from the Buddha, immediately went up to the upper story of the building and invited those Arhats who were free from outflows.
At that moment, twenty-one thousand Arhats came from the east to this lecture hall;
twenty-one thousand from the south, twenty-one thousand from the west, and twenty-one thousand Arhats from the north gathered in this lecture hall.
At that time, eighty-four thousand arhats were assembled together in one place within the lecture hall.

Then, King Bimbisāra, accompanied by his ministers, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and paid homage to the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, when the brahmin Kikī saw the community of bhikṣus, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself.
He provided the food and utensils to feed the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, personally serving them with his own hands, full of delight and never wearying of it.
However, there was still food remaining. At that time, the brahmin Kukkuṭa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have now provided a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, yet there is still leftover food remaining."
The World-Honored One said,
"You may now invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for seven days of offerings.
The brahmin replied:
"So be it, Gautama! At that time, the brahmin Kīṭāgira immediately knelt down with his right knee on the ground and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for seven days of offerings; I myself shall provide robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Then, within the great assembly, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Śakulī.
At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now had this thought arise in my mind:
'Are there any disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha who are Arhats with out-flows exhausted who have not gathered here?
Furthermore, I observed the eastern realm with the divine eye, and likewise observed the southern, western, and northern realms; there were none who did not come, as they all assembled."
"Now this great assembly is composed entirely of Arhats and True Persons who have gathered here.
The World-Honored One told him:
"So it is, Śakroli; as you have said, this great assembly consists entirely of True Persons, with none from the east, west, south, or north who has not assembled here."
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see among the bhikṣuṇīs anyone who possesses such celestial vision as these bhikṣuṇīs?"
The bhikṣus replied, “We have not seen them,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost disciple in the perfection of the divine eye (divyacakṣus) is the bhikṣuṇī Śakulī."

At that time, for seven days, the brahmin Kikī provided the noble assembly with robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick; he further scattered flowers and incense over the Tathāgata.
At that time, these flowers in the void transformed into a pavilion of seven precious jewels with latticed windows.
When the brahmin saw this pavilion, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to enter the ranks of the Way and become a śramaṇa."

At that time, the brahmin Kiki immediately attained the Way; his faculties were tranquil, and he cultivated his own resolve. He eliminated drowsiness, and even when his eyes beheld forms, he gave rise to no conceptualizations.
His faculty of sight was free from the flow of evil thoughts or wandering recollections, and thus he guarded his faculty of sight.

If the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue perceives tastes, or the body perceives tactile sensations, one does not give rise to the perception of tactile sensation; the same applies when the mind cognizes mental phenomena.
At that time, he extinguishes the five fetters and hindrances that shroud the human mind and deprive it of wisdom;

he is also free from any intent to harm, purifying his mind so that he does not kill, does not think of killing, and does not incite others to kill; he does not take up weapons such as swords or staves, but gives rise to a heart of benevolence and compassion toward all sentient beings;
he eliminates taking what is not given, does not harbor the intent to steal, and thus purifies his will.
They constantly maintain a mind of generosity toward all sentient beings and cause others not to steal.
Having themselves refrained from sexual misconduct, they likewise teach others to refrain from sexual misconduct;
they constantly cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), remaining stainless and free from defilement, purifying their minds within that holy life.
One does not speak falsely, nor does one instruct others to engage in false speech;
one constantly maintains sincerity, being free from all pretense, deception, or deluding the world, thereby purifying the mind therein.
Furthermore, one does not engage in divisive speech, nor does one incite others to do so.
If words spoken here are not transmitted there, and words spoken there are not transmitted here, one purifies the mind regarding such matters.

One should be moderate in eating, not being attached to flavors, not being attached to a fine complexion, and not being attached to a plump and fair appearance; one desires only to sustain the physical body so as to preserve its life.

To eliminate old pain and prevent new pain from arising, one attains the practice of the Path and dwells eternally in the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is like men or women who apply medicinal ointment to a wound, doing so solely with the desire to heal it.
This is also like that; therefore, one who knows moderation in food desires to cause old pains to be healed and new ones not to arise.
Furthermore, at such times, one practices the Path until dawn, not missing the proper occasion, and not failing in the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Whether sitting or walking, he removes the hindrance of drowsiness;
or during the first watch of the night, whether sitting or walking, he removes the hindrance of drowsiness;
or during the middle watch of the night, he lies on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, fixing his mind on light.
Furthermore, during the latter part of the night, he purifies his mind while either sitting or walking in meditation.

At that time, being moderate in food and drink and not missing the proper timing for walking meditation, he eliminates impure thoughts of desire and, free from all evil conduct, dwells in the first dhyāna with directed thought and sustained thought;
then, with the subsiding of thought and reflection, and possessing inner serenity and joy, he dwells in the second dhyāna.
There is no pleasure;
with pure mindfulness and awareness, he knows within himself that there is pleasure, and thus dwells in the third dhyāna, which is sought by the worthy for its pure mindfulness and awareness.

With the cessation of both suffering and pleasure, and with the disappearance of prior joy and grief, he enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by pure mindfulness and awareness.
With a mind of samādhi that is pure and free from defilement, he also attains fearlessness.
Further attaining samādhi, he recollects countless matters of past lives; he thus remembers the events of the past.

Whether it be one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or tens of millions of births; through aeons of formation, aeons of destruction, and aeons of both formation and destruction—I know them all: that I was born in such a place, with such a surname and such a given name, eating such food, experiencing such suffering and joy, and having such a lifespan; how I died there to be born here, and died here to be born there, including the causes, conditions, origins, and endings of it all.
Furthermore, with a mind purified by samādhi and free from all blemishes, he attains fearlessness and observes the various classes of sentient beings—those who are born and those who die.

Moreover, with the divine eye, he observes the various classes of sentient beings—those who are born and those who die; those in good realms and those in evil realms; those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance; whether handsome or unattractive—he knows them all exactly as they are, according to the seeds sown by their respective actions.

There are some classes of sentient beings who commit evil through body, speech, and mind, slander the noble ones, and create the roots of false karma; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds of body and speech and do not revile the noble ones; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavens.

Moreover, with the purified divine eye, he observes the classes of sentient beings—whether beautiful or ugly, in happy realms or miserable realms, of beautiful color or ugly color—and knows them all completely, attaining fearlessness. Furthermore, having applied his mind to the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*), he subsequently contemplates this suffering and knows it as it truly is.

"This is suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering"—knowing these as they truly are, and having made such an observation, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avijjā-āsava*).
Having attained liberation, he then attains the knowledge of liberation:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further taking of a womb"—he knows this as it truly is.
At that time, the brahmin Kikī immediately became an arhat.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Venerable Kikī rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five things in the world that are most impossible to obtain. What are these five?
To wish that what is destined to perish shall not perish—this is impossible to obtain;
To wish that the nature of cessation should not cease is impossible;
to wish that the nature of aging should not age is impossible; to wish that the nature of illness should not be ill is impossible;
and to wish that the nature of death should not die is impossible.
"Monks, these are the five things that are most impossible to obtain.

Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or whether a Tathāgata does not appear, this Dharma-realm remains eternally as it was, neither decaying nor perishing; yet there are sounds of loss and extinction—birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Whether they are born or pass away, all return to their origin.
This, monks, is called the five things that are difficult to obtain.
"One should seek skillful means and cultivate the five faculties. What are these five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom."
"Monks, it is said that when one has practiced these five faculties, one becomes a stream-enterer;
as a 'family-to-family' or 'one-interval' practitioner, one further progresses to become a once-returner."
Advancing further, he extinguishes the five fetters and becomes a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), attaining parinirvāṇa there without returning to this world;
