advancing further still, with the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*), he achieves the liberation of mind through the outflow-free state and the liberation by wisdom, realizing this for himself and dwelling therein, knowing as it truly is that he will never again undergo rebirth in a womb.
One should seek skillful means to eliminate the first five matters and cultivate the latter five faculties.
Thus, bhikṣu, you should train yourself in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are now five kinds of people who cannot be cured.
What are these five?"
First, those who are sycophantic and deceitful cannot be cured;
those who are treacherous and wicked cannot be cured;
those who speak with harsh words cannot be cured.
"One who is envious cannot be cured;
one who lacks gratitude and reciprocity cannot be cured.
This is what is meant, O bhikṣus!"
"These five kinds of people cannot be cured.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The person who is treacherous and evil-mouthed, Envious and devoid of gratitude,"
"This person is incurable and is abandoned by the wise. Therefore,
O bhikṣus, you should always train yourselves in right intention and eliminate envy."

One should practice dignified deportment and speak in accordance with the Dharma; one should know how to reciprocate and recognize kindness and nourishment, not forgetting even small favors, let alone great ones. One should harbor no stinginess or greed, refrain from praising oneself, and likewise avoid disparaging others.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Formerly, Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, saying:
'If, when you noble ones are fighting with the asuras, the asuras should be defeated and the gods victorious, you must seize the asura Vemacitrin and bring him here, bound in fivefold fetters.'"
At that time, Vemacitrin the asura-king again addressed the asuras, saying: "O you all!
Today we shall battle with the devas; if we achieve victory, we shall seize Śakra Devānām Indra and bind him here."
"Monks, you should know that at that time, the two families fought together; the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.

Then, the Trāyastriṃśa gods personally seized the asura king Vemacitrin, bound his body, and led him to where Śakra Devānām Indra was, placing him outside the middle gate so that he might behold his own fivefold bonds."
At that time, Vemacitrin, the King of the Asuras, thought to himself:

"The laws of these devas are orderly, whereas the conduct of the Asuras is contrary to the Dharma. I no longer take pleasure in being an Asura; I shall instead remain here in the palaces of these devas."
At that time, having given rise to this thought, he said:
"The laws of the devas are orderly, while those of the asuras are not lawful; I wish to dwell here.
Having formed this thought, he remained.
At that time, the asura king Vemacitrin suddenly realized that his body was no longer bound; he enjoyed himself with the five sensual pleasures.
Once the asura king Vemacitrin had formed this thought, he said:
"The ways of the devas are contrary to the Dharma, whereas the laws of the asuras are orderly. I have no further use for these Trāyastriṃśa Heavens; I wish to return to the asura palace."
At that time, the body of the Asura King was bound by five fetters, and the pleasures of the five desires naturally vanished.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that nothing is more urgent than this kind of entanglement;
the bondage of Māra is even more severe than this."
Even if one is bound by the Māra of the fetters (saṃyojana-māra), one who moves with the Māra is bound,
while one who does not move with the Māra is not bound. Therefore, O bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means so that the mind is not bound, and take delight in places of seclusion and tranquility.
The reason for this is that these fetters are the realm of Māra.
If a bhikṣu remains within the realm of Māra, he will never be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death, nor will he be liberated from sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
I now declare this to be the end of suffering.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu’s mind is unshakable and does not cling to the fetters, he is then liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress; I now declare this to be the end of suffering.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
to be free from the fetters and afflictions, and to transcend the realm of Māra. Thus, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Regarding what is called 'exhaustion,' of what kind of dharma does the term 'exhaustion' refer?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Ānanda! Form (rūpa) is unconditioned; it is because of causes and conditions that this name exists.
Being free from desire and unconditioned, it is called the dharma of cessation.”
That which is exhausted is called "complete extinction" (*nirodha*).

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—being unconditioned and uncreated—are all phenomena subject to wear and destruction; they are without desire and without defilement. Because that is completely extinguished, it is therefore called "complete extinction."
Ānanda, you should know that the five aggregates of clinging are without desire and without volitional activity, and are subject to the law of disintegration;
their cessation is called "complete extinction.
Because these five aggregates of clinging are forever extinguished and will never arise again, it is named "complete extinction."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “How is it, Gautama?”
By what causes and conditions, by what past actions, do these classes of people come to have an end, to perish, and to diminish?
That which was once a city wall is now ruined;
those who were once its inhabitants are now but a desolate wilderness.
The World-Honored One said: "Brahmin!

If you wish to know, it is because of the unrighteous conduct of these people that the cities and walls which once existed have today been destroyed, and the inhabitants who once lived there have today become a desolate wilderness. All this is caused by the habitual practice of the bonds of greed and stinginess among the populace, and the resulting consequences of craving and desire. Because of this, wind and rain do not come at their proper times; when the rains are untimely, the seeds and plants that are sown cannot grow, and the dead among the people fill the roads."
"O Brahmin, you should know that by these causes and conditions, the kingdom will be ruined and the people will not flourish. Furthermore, O Brahmin!

When the populace practices what is contrary to the Dharma, there arise natural portents such as thunder, lightning, and claps of thunder; the heavens send down hail and rain, which destroy the sprouting crops. At that time, the number of people who die is beyond counting."
Furthermore, brahmin!

When the people act contrary to the Dharma and engage in mutual strife and contention, they may strike one another with their hands or fists, or hurl tiles and stones at each other, until each loses his own life.
Furthermore, O Brahmin!

When those people have come to contend with one another and find no peace in their dwellings, the sovereign is not at ease; they each raise armies to attack and subdue one another, until the deaths among the great multitudes are beyond calculation.
Some were struck by swords, while others died from spears and arrows.
In this way, brahmin, due to these causes and conditions, the population diminished and no longer flourished.
Furthermore, O Brahmin!

Because the people act contrary to the Dharma, the deities do not grant them protection and find an opportunity to harm them; they may encounter misfortune and distress, or fall ill and be confined to their beds, such that those who recover are few while those who die from pestilence are many.
"This is what is meant, brahmin!
By this cause and condition, the people are diminished and no longer flourish.
At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“Gautama! What you have said is most excellent!
You have explained the meaning of this person’s original deficiency.”
The teaching of the Tathāgata is indeed such that the city-walls that once existed have today been worn away;
the people who once existed are today but desolate ruins.
This is because, through the presence of unrighteousness, stinginess and malice arise.
Because stinginess and malice arise, one consequently produces perverse karma;

because perverse karma is produced, the heavens send rain out of season, the five grains do not ripen, and the population does not flourish. Thus, it causes unrighteousness to spread, the heavens to send down calamities and transformations, and the sprouting crops to be destroyed.

Because he practiced unrighteousness and was obsessed with greed, stinginess, and malice, the sovereign of the land became restless; consequently, various military forces arose and engaged in mutual warfare, resulting in an incalculable number of deaths. Thus, the territory fell into ruin and desolation, and the people were scattered and dispersed.
What the World-Honored One has spoken today is most excellent; how wonderful!
It was due to unrighteousness that this calamity occurred.
Even if one were seized by another and their life were to be taken thereupon:
Because of unrighteousness, the mind of theft arises;
because the mind of theft has arisen, one is later executed by the king;
because of having produced such perverse karma, non-human beings find an opportunity to harm them.
Due to these causes and conditions, they met their end; as the population diminished, there were no longer any cities or settlements where people could dwell.
"Gautama! [he said.]

That which has been set forth today is for the sake of those who have transgressed excessively; it is like a hunchback finding extension, a blind person gaining eyes, one in darkness finding light, and providing eyes for those who have none.

Now the śramaṇa Gautama has taught the Dharma through countless skillful means; I now take refuge once more in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha. I pray that you will accept me as an upāsaka; for as long as life lasts, I dare not kill again.
If the śramaṇa Gautama were to see me riding an elephant or a horse, I would indeed show him respect.
Why is this? Because I am the recipient of Brahma-like merit from Kings Prasenajit, Bimbisāra, Udayana, Ajātaśatru, and Udāyana; I fear that I might lose this virtue.
"If I happen to have my right shoulder bared, may the World-Honored One accept our prostration!
If I happen to be walking and see Gautama approaching, I shall remove my sandals; may the World-Honored One accept our prostrations!"
At that time, the World-Honored One nodded his head in approval.
Then, the brahmin Jāli, filled with joy and exultation beyond measure, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now once again take refuge in the Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"I only wish that the World-Honored One would grant me permission to become an upāsaka.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to him, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy.
Having heard the Dharma, the brahmin rose from his seat and withdrew.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-Āsrava, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 26; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 27.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Five: On the Wrong Group (Mithyā-nikāya) (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is someone who belongs to the mass of wrong views, what are their characteristics?”
"What are its characteristics?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Tathāgata is the king of all dharmas, the sovereign of all dharmas."
Excellent, World-Honored One!
You should explain this meaning to the bhikṣus.
"Having heard this, we shall practice it accordingly.
The World-Honored One told them:
"Reflect upon this well; I shall analyze its meaning for you."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One told them:
"A person who belongs to the faction of the wrong (mithyā-nikāya) should be known by five matters; by seeing these five matters, one knows that this person dwells in the faction of the wrong."

What are the five? One should laugh but does not laugh; one should rejoice at a time for rejoicing but does not rejoice; one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness but does not give rise to it; one commits evil without shame; and upon hearing wholesome words, one does not take them to heart.
It should be known that such a person certainly dwells in the category of the heterodox (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi).
"If there are sentient beings who abide in the category of the heterodox (mithyātva-rāśi), they should be known by these five matters.
Furthermore, as for those sentient beings who abide in the category of the orthodox (samyaktva-rāśi), what are their characteristics?"
“What are the causes and conditions for this?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
“The Tathāgata is the king of all dharmas, the venerable one of all dharmas.”
We only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will explain this meaning to the bhikṣus.
Having heard it, we shall put it into practice.
The World-Honored One said:
"Reflect upon this well; I shall analyze its meaning for you.
The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"One who belongs to the assembly of the right should be known by five things; by seeing these five things, one knows that this person dwells in the assembly of the right."

What are these five? One should smile when it is appropriate to smile; one should rejoice when it is appropriate to rejoice; one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness when it is appropriate to do so; one should feel shame when there is cause for shame; and one should fix the mind upon hearing what is wholesome.
It should be known that such a person has already entered the assembly of the righteous.
Therefore, monks, you should abandon the assembly of the heterodox and abide in the assembly of the orthodox. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he must necessarily perform five deeds."

What are these five? First, one shall turn the wheel of the Dharma; second, one shall deliver one’s parents; third, one shall establish those without faith upon the ground of faith; fourth, one shall cause those who have not yet resolved for Bodhicitta to give rise to the Bodhisattva mind; and fifth, one shall bestow the prediction of future Buddhahood.
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he performs these five deeds. Therefore, monks,
you should arouse a mind of loving-kindness toward the Tathāgata.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five kinds of giving that do not yield merit.

What are the five? First, giving a knife to others; second, giving poison to others; third, giving a wild ox to others; fourth, giving a courtesan to others; and fifth, constructing a shrine for deities."
"Monks, these are the five kinds of giving that do not yield merit.
Monks, you should know this:"
Furthermore, there are five kinds of giving that result in great merit.

What are these five? First, the construction of gardens and parks; second, the planting of groves and trees; third, the construction of bridges; fourth, the construction of large ships; and fifth, the provision of dwellings and residences for those of the future and the past.
"Monks, it is said that there are these five things which cause one to obtain merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"By bestowing pleasure groves for cool retreats, by constructing fine bridges,
by ferrying people across at river fords, and by building excellent dwellings—
such a person shall constantly receive their merit throughout day and night."
"Through the accomplishment of virtue and concentration, this person will surely be reborn in heaven. Therefore, O bhikṣus,
you should mindfully practice these five virtues of giving."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Women possess five powers by which they treat their husbands with contempt.
What are these five? First, the power of beauty; second, the power of kinship; third, the power of landed estates; fourth, the power of sons; and fifth, the power of self-restraint.”
This is called the five powers possessed by women.
A bhikṣu should know that once a woman relies upon these five powers, she treats her husband with contempt.
Yet, even if the husband possesses but a single power, he can completely overshadow that woman.
What is the one power?
It is the power of wealth and nobility.
For when a person possesses nobility, their physical strength is inferior; likewise, their kin, their estates, their children, and even their self-possession are all inferior.
"All [of these] derive from a single power, which surpasses all those powers combined.
Now, the evil Māra Pāpīyān also possesses five powers.
What are these five?..."

These are the power of form, the power of sound, the power of fragrance, the power of flavor, and the power of tangibility. Indeed, those foolish people who are attached to the phenomena of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility cannot cross beyond the realm of Pāpīyān.
If a noble disciple accomplishes a single power, it surpasses all such powers.
What is this one power? It is the power of heedfulness.
If a noble disciple achieves heedfulness, they will not be bound by forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tactile sensations.

Because they are not bound by the five desires, they are able to discern the phenomena of birth, old age, sickness, and death; they overcome the five powers of Māra, do not fall into the realm of Māra, transcend all fears and difficulties, and reach the state of unconditioned nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Precepts are the path to the deathless; Heedlessness is the road to death.
One who is not greedy does not die; To lose the path is to bring about one’s own ruin.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should practice with mindfulness and not be negligent. Thus it is, bhikṣus!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Women have five types of sensual desires.”

What are the five perceptions of sensual desire? First, being born into a family of noble status; second, being married into a wealthy and noble family; third, causing one’s husband to follow one’s words and act according to one’s instructions; fourth, having many children; and fifth, being able to exercise independent authority within the household.
"Monks, these are the five things in which women have thoughts of desire. Thus it is."
"Monks! My monks also have five things that give rise to thoughts of desire. What are these five?
That is to say: the precepts, extensive learning, the accomplishment of samādhi, wisdom, and the liberation through wisdom.
These, O bhikṣu, are the five things that are desirable dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I was born into a noble clan, And married into a wealthy and honored family;
I could command my husband at will— Yet without merit, such things cannot be attained."
May I have many children, and may fragrant flowers adorn me naturally;
though I harbor such thoughts, they cannot be attained without merit.
Through the perfection of faith and precepts, one remains unshakable in samādhi.
Wisdom is also achieved through diligence; through indolence, one does not succeed.
If you seek to attain the fruit of the Way, it cannot be found within the abyss of birth and death;
if you wish to reach Nirvana, you will not succeed through indolence.
"In this way, monks! You should seek skillful means to practice wholesome dharmas and eliminate unwholesome dharmas, gradually advancing forward without any regret in your hearts."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are five occasions when one should not pay homage to another.

What are these five? One should not pay homage while inside a stūpa; one should not pay homage in the midst of a great assembly; furthermore, one should not pay homage while on a road; one should not pay homage when bedridden with illness; and one should not pay homage while eating or drinking."
"Monks, it is said that there are these five occasions on which one should not perform a prostration.
Furthermore, there are five occasions for a prostration that recognizes the proper time."
What are the five?
Not within a stūpa, not in the midst of the great assembly, not on a road, nor when one is ill, nor while eating or drinking—these are the occasions toward which one should pay homage.
"Therefore, monks, you should apply skillful means and know the proper timing for practice.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7 (Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Udāyin:
"Enter the city of Rājagṛha now and seek some warm water.
The reason for this is that today my back is afflicted with pain from wind."
Udāyin said to the Buddha, “It is so,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the Venerable Udāyin dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to seek hot water.
Then, the Venerable Udāyin thought to himself:
“For what reason and by what cause has the World-Honored One sent me to seek hot water?”
The Tathāgata has exhausted all fetters and all wholesome qualities are universally assembled within him.
Nevertheless, the Tathāgata further speaks these words:
"I am now afflicted by wind."
"Furthermore, since the World-Honored One has not specified a name, to whose house shall we go?
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin used his divine eye to observe the male population of Rājagṛha to see who was destined for deliverance.

At that time, he saw in the city of Rājagṛha an elder named Viśākhāputra, who had not planted roots of goodness, lacked precepts and faith, held wrong views, and was possessed by extreme views regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.

He then holds this view: "There is no giving, no offering, and no recipient; furthermore, there is no retribution for good or evil deeds; there is no present world and no future world; there is no father and no mother; and in this world there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have attained perfection, having realized it for themselves through direct experience in this life and the next, and who dwell therein."
His lifespan was extremely short; he would meet his end in no more than five days.
Furthermore, he served the Great Deity of the Five Paths.
At that time, Upatīṣya thought to himself:
“The Tathāgata surely intends to deliver this elder.
Why is this? Because after the end of this elder’s life, he shall be reborn in the Wailing Hell.”

At that time, Upatissa smiled. The Great Deity of the Five Paths saw him smiling from afar; he immediately concealed his divine form, assumed the appearance of a human being, and came to where Upatissa was to serve as his attendant.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin led the messenger to the gate of the householder’s residence and stood there in silence, saying nothing.
When the householder saw from afar a practitioner of the Way standing outside the gate, he immediately spoke this verse:
“You now stand here in silence, With shaven head and wearing the saṃghāṭī robe.”
"What do you seek to obtain, and for what reason have you come?
At that time, Upatīṣya replied with this verse:
"The Tathāgata, the Honored One free from attachment, today suffers from an onset of wind."
"If there is warm water, the Tathāgata wishes to bathe.
At that time, the elder remained silent and did not reply.
Then, the Great Deity of the Five Paths said to Viśākhā:
"The householder may favor me with hot water; you shall surely obtain immeasurable merit and receive the reward of ambrosia.
At that time, the householder replied, "I already have a great deity of the five paths; what need have I for this śramaṇa?"
"What matters can he benefit?
At that time, the Great Deity of the Five Paths spoke this verse:
"When the Tathāgata was about to be born, The Lord of Devas descended to attend him."
Who else could emerge as his equal, able to match him as a peer?
Even the deities of the five realms of existence cannot provide such salvation;
it is better to make offerings to the Teacher Śākyamuni, for one will thereby obtain a great karmic reward.
At that time, the Great Deity of the Five Paths spoke again to the elder, saying:
"You must carefully guard the actions of your body, speech, and mind. Do you not know the majestic power of the Great Deity of the Five Paths?"
At that time, the Great Deity of the Five Paths immediately manifested the form of a great spirit-ghost; holding a sword in his right hand, he spoke to the elder, saying:
"I who stand here am the Great Deity of the Five Paths. Give this śramaṇa a bath at once; do not delay."
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
"The Great Deity of the Five Paths shall then make offerings to this śramaṇa.
He immediately gave fragrant water to the practitioner and further presented rock honey to the śramaṇa.

At that time, the Great Deity of the Five Realms personally took this fragrant bath-water and, together with Upatissa, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, offering this fragrant bath-water to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One bathed his body with this fragrant water, and the wind ailment was immediately cured, never to increase in severity again.
At that moment, the elder passed away five days later and was reborn among the Four Heavenly Kings.

At that time, when the Venerable Udāyin heard that the householder had passed away, he immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, Udāyin addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"Where has this householder been reborn after his death?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This householder, having passed away, has been reborn among the Four Great Kings. Udāyin said to the Buddha,
"When this householder passes away from there, where will he be reborn?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"Having passed away there, they shall be reborn among the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and so on, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; having passed away there, they will again come to be reborn among the Four Great Kings."

This elder’s body shall not fall into the evil realms for sixty kalpas; finally, he will obtain a human body, shave off his hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to study the Path, and become a pratyekabuddha.
The reason for this is that the merit of King Tang’s benevolence resulted in such blessings.
Therefore, Upatissa! You should constantly remember to bathe the assembly of monks and listen to the exposition of the Way.
"Thus it is, Udāyin! You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who took no pleasure in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) and wished to abandon the prohibitive precepts to return to the state of a white-robed layman.
At that time, the bhikṣu went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, the bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I no longer take pleasure in practicing the holy life; I wish to relinquish the prohibitive precepts and return to being a layman."
The World-Honored One said:
"For what reason do you now find no joy in practicing the holy life, wishing to abandon the precepts and return to being a layman?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Right now my mind is ablaze and fire burns within my body.
Whenever I see a woman who is peerlessly beautiful, I then think:
'May this woman have sexual union with me.'"
Furthermore, he again thought:
"This is not the true Dharma; if I were to follow this mind, it would not be the correct principle.
At that time, I again had this thought:
"This is an evil gain, not a virtuous one;
this is an evil dharma, not a virtuous one.

I now wish to relinquish my prohibitive precepts and return to the state of a layperson (*avadātavasana*). The prohibitive precepts of a śramaṇa are truly not to be transgressed; among worldly people, I may instead practice giving through almsgiving (*dāna*).
The World-Honored One replied:
"There are five kinds of evils associated with being a woman. What are these five?
"First is foulness, second is double-tongued speech, third is envy, fourth is malice, and fifth is ingratitude.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Not for the sake of wealth or profit do they take delight; Though appearing virtuous, they harbor poison within."
"It destroys the wholesome path to the human realm, just as a hawk abandons a foul pond. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should eliminate perceptions of impurity and cultivate the contemplation of purity."
Having contemplated pure observation, the bhikṣu completely abandons sensual craving, craving for form, and craving for the formless; he completely abandons ignorance and conceit. Now, bhikṣu!
From what does desire arise?
Does it arise from the hair?
Yet the hair is a foul secretion and impure; it is entirely a phantom manifestation that deceives and deludes the people of the world.
The hands, nails, teeth, body parts, and their like have no pure place;
what among them is true? What is real?
From head to foot, it is all exactly thus.
The liver, the gallbladder, and the five viscera are material things; not one of them is worth coveting. What, then, is the truth? Now, bhikṣu, from what do you desire arise?

You must now diligently cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya); through the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, you shall surely bring an end to suffering. Human life is extremely short and does not endure long in this world; even at its longest, it does not exceed a hundred years, and yet the time spent is but a small fraction.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; hearing the Dharma is also difficult;
obtaining a physical form composed of the four great elements is likewise difficult to attain;
and having all faculties complete is also difficult to attain.”
To be born in a central land is likewise difficult to encounter;
to meet with virtuous friends is likewise difficult to obtain;
to hear the Dharma is difficult, and to discern its principles and meanings is likewise difficult to obtain.
To achieve mastery over each and every dharma is also a difficult matter. Now, bhikṣu,
if you associate with virtuous friends, you will be able to discern all dharmas and should also extensively expound their meaning to others.

Once one has heard the Dharma, one is able to discern it; having discerned the Dharma, one is able to explain its meaning. Being free from thoughts of desire, ill-will, and delusion, and having thus abandoned the three poisons, one is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death. I shall now briefly explain its meaning.
At that time, having received the instruction from the Buddha, that bhikṣu rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew.
Thereupon, in a secluded and quiet place, that bhikṣu reflected upon the Dharma.
Therefore, sons of noble family shave off their hair and beard, leave the household life to study the Way, desiring to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life:
they know according to reality that birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further taking of a womb.
At that time, that bhikṣu immediately became an arhat.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Ānanda and Tāgisi, when the time had come, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to beg for food.
At that time, in a certain alleyway, Taqisha saw a woman who was exceedingly beautiful and extraordinary compared to anyone in the world;
having seen her, his mind became disordered and was no longer as it usually was.
At that time, Tāṇḍyaśa addressed Ānanda with these verses:
"Consumed by the fire of desire, The mind is burning most fiercely.
I pray you explain the meaning of its extinction; It would be of great benefit."
At that time, Ānanda replied with this verse:
"Knowing desire to be a perverted dharma, The mind and its faculties burn most fiercely;
One should eliminate conceptual imaginings, And the mind of desire will naturally cease."
At that time, Tāgiśa replied again in verse:
"The mind is the root of the body; The eyes are the source of its perception.
When one lies down in sleep, though supported by others, The body withers like tangled grass."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda stepped forward and stroked the head of Mahākāśyapa with his right hand. He then spoke this verse:
"Mindful of the Buddha, free from desire, He has delivered Nanda from the perils of passion."
"Behold heaven and the hells; restrain the mind and leave the five destinies.
At that time, having heard the words of the Venerable Ānanda, Tāgisi spoke thus: "Stop!
"Stop! Ānanda! Having finished their almsround together, they returned to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the woman saw Dakkhiṇāyana from afar and smiled.
When Dakkhiṇāyana saw the woman smiling from afar, he conceived this thought:

"Your body now is but a skeleton bound together with skin, like a painted jar filled within with impurities; you deceive and delude the people of the world, causing them to give rise to disordered thoughts."
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa observed that woman from head to foot, [considering] what in this physical form was worth desiring;
the thirty-six components were entirely impure.
"From what do these various things arise?
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa again had this thought:
"Rather than observing the forms of others, it would be better for me now to observe my own body: from where does this desire arise?"
Is it produced from the earth element,
or is it produced from the water, fire, or wind elements?
If it were produced from the earth element, the earth element is solid and firm, and thus cannot be destroyed.
If it were born from the water element, the water element is extremely supple and cannot be grasped;
if it were born from the fire element, the fire element cannot be grasped;
if it were born from the wind element, the wind element is formless and cannot be grasped.
At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"This desire arises solely from conceptualization. Thereupon, he spoke this verse:

"O Aggivessana, [desire] is like a fire... [Note: The preceding line of the verse appears to be missing two characters; although the original texts are identical, the exact wording remains undetermined.]
“I know your origin, O desire: you arise solely from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
If I do not conceptualize you, then you shall no longer exist.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana spoke this verse; as he contemplated the perception of impurity, his mind was liberated from outflows (*āsrava*) right then and there.
Then Ānanda and Tārukkha departed from the city of Rājagṛha and went to where the World-Honored One was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, Tārukkha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have now swiftly attained a great benefit, for I have gained some realization."
The World-Honored One asked,
"How do you now perceive yourself?
Tāgisi replied to the Buddha:
"Form is not enduring and is neither solid; it cannot be truly perceived, being illusory and unreal.
Feeling is not enduring and is neither solid; it is like a bubble upon the water, illusory and unreal.
Perception is not enduring and is neither solid; it is illusory and unreal, like a mirage."
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are likewise without solidity and lack firmness; they are like the plantain tree, which has no core.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is without solidity and lacks firmness; it is illusory, false, and unreal.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"These five aggregates of clinging are without stability, nor are they firm; they are illusory, false, and not real.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke this verse:
"Form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a floating bubble, perception is like a mirage,
volitional formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is a magical illusion— this is what the Most Victorious One has taught."
Having reflected thus, one observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as entirely empty and quiescent, lacking any true reality; all this is due to this body, as taught by the Sugata.
One should extinguish three things: seeing that form is impure;
realizing that this body is likewise illusory, false, and not real—this is called the dharma of destruction;
and understanding that the five aggregates are not firm and are already unreal—one shall now return to the higher tracks.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
That which I have now awakened to is precisely this."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, Mahākośala!"
You are well able to observe the root of these five aggregates of clinging.
You should now know that a practitioner must observe the root of these five aggregates, for they are all insubstantial.

The reason for this is that when one contemplates these five aggregates of clinging, it was beneath the Bodhi tree that I attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, just as you are contemplating them today.
At that time, while this Dharma was being taught, sixty bhikṣus seated there attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind.
Then, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the elder’s son Saṃghama went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the son of the elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to enter the ranks of those on the Path.
Thereupon, the son of the elder immediately attained the state of a seeker; dwelling in a secluded place, he disciplined himself in practice and realized the fruit of the Dharma.
Therefore, sons of good family shave off their hair and beard, leave the household life to study the Path, and know according to reality:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further rebirth in a womb."
At that time, Saṃghama immediately became an arhat.
Then, while dwelling in a secluded place, he had this thought:
"The appearance of a Tathāgata is extremely difficult to encounter; a Tathāgata appears only once in a great while, just as the udumbara flower appears only once in a great while."

It is likewise in this case: the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world occurs only from time to time; the cessation of all conditioned formations is also difficult to encounter, as is the way of escape. The exhaustion of craving, dispassion, and Nirvāṇa—this is the essential goal.

At that time, when Saṃghama’s mother-in-law heard that her daughter’s husband had become a practitioner of the Way and no longer clung to desire, having abandoned his worldly burdens and even forsaken her daughter like spitting out a glob of phlegm, she was deeply moved.
At that time, the mother went to where her daughter was and said to her,
"Is it true that your husband has become a practitioner of the Way?
The daughter replied:
"Did you not also inquire whether she had practiced the Path? Her mother replied,
"You should now adorn yourself, put on fine clothes, take this boy and girl, and go to Saṃkama."
At that time, the mother and daughter went together to where Saṅghama was.
At that moment, the Venerable Saṅghama was sitting cross-legged beneath a tree.
At that time, the wife and mother stood silently before him. Then,
the old woman and her daughter gazed at Saṃghama from head to foot and said to him,
"Why do you not speak with our daughter now?"
"These children were born of you; what you have now done is truly irrational and is not permitted by others. What you are currently contemplating is not the conduct of a human being."
At that time, the Venerable Saṅghama immediately spoke this verse:
"Beyond this there is no further good; beyond this there is no further excellence;
beyond this there is nothing more true: a virtuous thought surpasses nothing."
At that time, the mother-in-law said to Saṃkama:
"What offense has my daughter committed now?
What unrighteousness has she done?"
"Why have you now abandoned it to leave the household life and study the Path?
At that time, Saṃghama spoke this verse:
"In foul places and impure conduct, In anger and a fondness for falsehood,"
"The mind of envy is unwholesome; this is what the Tathāgata has taught.
At that time, the old woman said to Saṃghama, "It is not only my daughter who possesses such a nature; all women are exactly like this."

Among the people of Śrāvastī, all who saw my daughter had their minds disturbed and desired to consort with her; like those parched with thirst seeking a drink, they gazed upon her without satiety, and all gave rise to thoughts of attachment.
Why have you now abandoned her to study the Way, only to proceed to slander and revile me?
Even if you do not take my daughter today, you must still take charge of the sons and daughters you have fathered.
At that time, Saṃghama spoke again in these verses:
"I have neither son nor daughter, Nor fields, estates, or wealth;
I have likewise no slaves, Nor kinsmen or attendants."
Walking alone without companion, delighting in secluded and tranquil places,
practicing the dharma of a śramaṇa, one seeks the true path of the Buddha.
That which men and women possess is the conduct practiced by the foolish.
"I am always without a self-body; how could there be male or female?
At that time, having heard this verse, the wife, mother, son, and daughter each thought:
"Judging by his intention as we observe it today, he will certainly not return home."
Again, he observed from head to foot; having sighed deeply, he knelt before him and spoke these words:
“Whatever unrighteousness has been committed by my body, speech, or mind, may you endure it all.”
He then circumambulated [the stupa] three times and withdrew to his dwelling.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms; seeing from afar the old woman and her daughter, he asked them:
"Did you happen to see Saṃghama earlier?"
The old woman replied,
"Though I see it, it is not seen. Ānanda replied:
“Do you converse with him?
The old woman replied,
“Although we do converse, it does not enter my heart.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke this verse:
"To wish for fire to produce water, And again for water to produce fire;
To wish for empty phenomena to exist, And to wish for the desireless to become desirous."
At that time, after the Venerable Ānanda had finished his almsround, he returned to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
He went to where Saṃkama was and sat down to one side.
He said to Saṃkama,
"Do you already know the Dharma as it truly is? Saṃkama replied:
"I have realized the Dharma as it truly is.
Ānanda replied, "In what way have you realized the Dharma as it truly is?"
Saṅgāma replied: "Form is impermanent; the meaning of this impermanence is suffering;
that which is suffering is without self."
That which is non-self is emptiness.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent; this meaning of impermanence is suffering;
and suffering is non-self.
That which is non-self is emptiness.
These five aggregates of clinging have the meaning of impermanence;
that which has the meaning of impermanence has the meaning of suffering.
"I do not belong to him, nor does he belong to me.
At that time, Saṃghama spoke this verse:
"Suffering arises from suffering, and the crossing beyond suffering is likewise so."
The Noble Eightfold Path leads even to the state of cessation;
no longer returning to this birth, one wanders among gods and humans until the very root of suffering is exhausted, forever stilled and unmoving.
"I have now seen the trace of emptiness, just as the Buddha has taught;
having now attained arhatship, I shall no longer receive a womb.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda uttered this praise:
"Excellent! You have truly and skillfully resolved the nature of reality.
At that time, Ānanda spoke this verse:
“Skillfully guarding the tracks of the holy life, and being able to practice the path well,
severing all fetters— such is a true disciple of the Buddha.
When Ānanda had spoken this verse, he rose from his seat and departed.
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Ānanda related these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one wishes to speak of those who are equal to an arhat, it should be said that the bhikṣu Saṃghama is such a person.
He who is able to subdue the hosts of Māra’s officials is also the bhikṣu Saṃghama."
The reason for this is that the bhikṣu Saṃghama went forth to subdue Māra seven times before he finally attained the Way.
From now on, it is permitted to practice the Way after seven such transformations.
"To exceed this limit would be contrary to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣu capable of subduing Māra, who has now just attained the Way, is the bhikṣu Saṃghama."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 27; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 28.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Six: Listening to the Dharma. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five merits in listening to the Dharma at the appropriate time; by receiving it at the appropriate time, one does not lose the proper sequence.”
What are the five?
That which one has never heard before, one now hears;
that which one has heard, one recites and chants repeatedly.
One sees without deviant inclinations;
being free from doubt,
one immediately understands the profoundly deep meaning.
There are five merits in listening to the Dharma at the appropriate time. Therefore, O bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to listen to the Dharma at the appropriate time.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five benefits to constructing a bathhouse. What are the five? First, it dispels wind;
second, illnesses are cured; third, dust and grime are removed; fourth, the body becomes light and agile; fifth, one attains a plump and radiant complexion.”
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus!
There are these five benefits in constructing a bathhouse. Therefore, bhikṣus!"
If there are members of the fourfold assembly who wish to seek these five merits, they should seek skillful means and construct a bathhouse.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five merits in giving tooth-sticks to others.”
What are the five? First, the elimination of wind;
second, the elimination of saliva and phlegm; third, the digestion of the contents of the stomach; fourth, the absence of foul odor from the mouth; and fifth, the attainment of clarity in the eyes.
"Monks, these are the five merits for one who gives a tooth-stick to others.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family seeks these five merits, they should mindfully practice the giving of tooth-sticks."
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you see any ox-slaughterers who, by means of this wealth and occupation, later obtain carriages,
horses, or great elephants? The bhikṣus replied, “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied, “Excellent!”
"O bhikṣus! I have neither seen nor heard of a person who slaughters oxen for a butcher, having killed them, obtaining carriage-horses or great elephants. Why is this so?
Because I have never seen a person who slaughters oxen obtain carriage-horses or great elephants; such a thing is ultimately impossible."
"What do you think, bhikṣus!

Have you ever seen those who slaughter sheep, kill pigs, or hunt deer—people who, having committed such evil deeds, subsequently acquire wealth and property and come to ride in carriages, horses, or great elephants?"
The bhikṣus replied: “No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One said: "Excellent, monks!"
I have neither seen nor heard of a person who slaughters living beings as a butcher ever obtaining carriage-horses, riding horses, or great elephants; such a thing is simply impossible.
"O bhikṣus, if you see a person who has slaughtered an ox yet travels by carriage or horse, this is due to the merit of their previous lives, not the fortune of the present life;
it is entirely brought about by their past deeds."
If you see someone who slaughters sheep yet rides in carriages and on horses, you should know that this is due to the seeds of merit planted in their past lives.
The reason for this is that, although they have slaughtered, the mind of killing has not been eradicated.
Why is this? If there is a person who associates with evil people and delights in taking life, they plant the seeds of hellish retribution.
Even if they should come among human beings, their lifespan will be extremely short.

Furthermore, if there is a person who delights in theft and plants the seeds of hellish retribution—such as that butcher of oxen who takes cheaply and sells dearly, deceiving the people of the world and failing to act according to the True Dharma.
The butcher is likewise so; because of his murderous intent, he incurs this guilt and is not permitted to ride in carriages, on horses, or upon great elephants. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
One should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
Then Śakra-devānām-indra, in the time it takes to bend or extend one’s arm, came to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Tathāgata has also said:
'When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he must necessarily perform five tasks.'"
What are the five? One shall turn the wheel of Dharma;
one shall deliver one's parents.
Those who lack faith shall be established on the ground of faith;
those who have not yet resolved to attain the mind of a bodhisattva shall be inspired to generate that bodhisattva-mind;
and in the interim, they shall receive the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment.
"By these five causes and conditions, the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world must necessarily act for their sake.

Now the mother of the Tathāgata is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, desiring to hear the Dharma; meanwhile, the Tathāgata is here within Jambudvīpa, surrounded by the fourfold assembly, with kings and commoners all gathered together.
Excellent, World-Honored One!
You may go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma to your mother.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted [the invitation] by remaining silent.
Then, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda thought to themselves:
"These shaven-headed śramaṇas are flying above us; we must employ some skillful means so that they do not treat us with such contempt."
At that time, the Dragon King gave rise to anger and unleashed a great fire and wind, causing the interior of Jambudvīpa to blaze with a brilliant conflagration.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"For what reason is there this smoke and fire within Jambudvīpa?"
The World-Honored One said:
"These two dragon kings then conceived this thought:
'This shaven-headed śramaṇa constantly flies above us; we should join together to restrain him so that he may no longer soar through the air.'"
He then gave rise to anger and released this smoke and fire; due to these causes and conditions, this calamity has occurred.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I now wish to go and engage in battle with him.”
The World-Honored One said, "These two dragon kings are extremely fierce and difficult to convert; you, sir, return to your seat.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now wish to go and subdue those evil nāgas.
The World-Honored One said, "These two evil nāgas are extremely fierce and violent; they are difficult to convert. You should return to your seat."
At that time, Revata, the Venerable Kātyāyana, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Udāyin, and the Venerable Vakula each rose from their seats and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"We now wish to go and subdue the evil dragon."
The World-Honored One said, “These two dragon kings are extremely fierce and difficult to convert; you, sir, should return to your seat.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his hands joined in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to go there to subdue the evil dragon.
The World-Honored One told him, "These two dragon kings are extremely fierce and difficult to convert; how will you now convert those dragon kings?"
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:

“I arrived there first and transformed my body into an immense form to intimidate that nāga; afterwards, I again transformed my body into one that was extremely minute, and only then subdued him by means of the ordinary method.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, Maudgalyāyana!"
"You are capable of subduing the evil dragon.
However, Maudgalyāyana, now maintain your resolve firmly and do not give rise to distracted thoughts."
"The reason for this is that those dragons are fierce and evil, and will surely harass you.
At that moment, Maudgalyāyana prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; in the time it takes to bend and stretch one's arm, he vanished from that place and arrived atop Mount Sumeru.
At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda circled Mount Sumeru seven times, giving rise to extreme anger and emitting great smoke and fire.

Then, Maudgalyāyana concealed his own form and transformed himself into a great dragon king with fourteen heads; he circled Mount Sumeru fourteen times, emitting great flames and smoke, and stationed himself directly above the two dragon kings.
At that time, the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, seeing that the Great Nāga King had fourteen heads, were seized with fear and said to one another:
"Today we must test the power of this nāga king; is he truly superior to us?"
At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda lashed their tails into the great ocean and sprayed water toward the Heaven of the Thirty-three, yet it did not even touch Maudgalyāyana’s body.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana again dipped his tail into the great ocean; the water rose as far as the Brahmakāyika heaven and also sprinkled the bodies of the two nāga kings.
At that time, the two dragon kings said to one another:
"We have exerted all our strength and power to sprinkle water upon the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
yet this great dragon king surpasses us by ascending above us. We possess exactly seven heads, whereas this dragon king now has fourteen."
"We circumambulated Mount Sumeru seven times, whereas this Dragon King now circumambulates Mount Sumeru fourteen times;
we two Dragon Kings shall now join our forces together to engage him in battle."
At that time, the two dragon kings, filled with extreme malice, unleashed thunder, lightning, and bolts of thunderbolts while emitting great flames of fire.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:

"When dragons fight, they do so by means of fire and thunderbolts. If I were to engage them in battle using fire and thunderbolts as well, the people within Jambudvīpa, as well as those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, would all be harmed."
"I shall now transform my body to be extremely small and engage in battle with you.
At that moment, Maudgalyāyana immediately transformed his body to be small and entered the dragon's mouth, emerging from its nostrils;
or he would enter through its nostrils and emerge from its ears.
Sometimes it entered his ear and emerged from his eye;
having emerged from his eye, it traveled along his brow.
At that time, the two dragon kings were seized with extreme fear and immediately thought to themselves:
"This Great Dragon King possesses such immense power that he can enter through his mouth and emerge from his nose;
enter through his nose and emerge from his eyes.
Today, we are truly inferior to him."

"We dragons of our lineage currently have four modes of birth—egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—and yet there is none who can surpass us. Now, this Dragon King possesses such power that we cannot withstand him in battle; our very lives are at stake in this instant."
They were all filled with fear, and the hair on their bodies stood on end.
At that time, seeing that the dragon kings’ hearts were filled with dread, Maudgalyāyana withdrew his manifested form, assumed his ordinary appearance, and walked upon the eyelids.
At that time, the two nāga kings, seeing Mahāmaudgalyāyana, said to one another:
"This is the śramaṇa Maudgalyāyana;
he is not a nāga king."
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!
To possess such great power as to be able to fight with us!"
At that time, the two dragon kings said to Maudgalyāyana, "Venerable One, why have you troubled us so much? What do you wish to instruct us?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"Yesterday you all had this thought:
'How is it that these shaven-headed śramaṇas always fly above us? We shall now subdue them.
" The Nāga King replied:
"So it is, Maudgalyāyana! Maudgalyāyana replied, "Nāga King, you should know that this Mount Sumeru is the thoroughfare of the devas; it is not a place for you to dwell."

The Dragon King replied, "I only pray that you will forgive me and not hold me in severe reprimand. From this day forward, I shall never again dare to cause disturbance or give rise to evil, chaotic thoughts; I only pray that you will allow me to become your disciple."
Maudgalyāyana replied, "Do not take refuge in my person; rather, take refuge in those in whom I myself have taken refuge.
The Dragon King addressed Maudgalyāyana:
"We take refuge in the Tathāgata this very day.
Maudgalyāyana told them, "You must not take refuge in the World-Honored One while remaining here upon Mount Sumeru; [you must go to him directly]."
"Now you may come with me to Śrāvastī, and there you shall find refuge.
At that moment, Maudgalyāyana took the two dragon kings and, in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, traveled from the summit of Mount Sumeru to Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to an immeasurable multitude.
Then, Maudgalyāyana addressed the two dragon kings, saying:
"You should know that today the World-Honored One is preaching the Dharma to an immeasurable multitude; you must not go before the World-Honored One in your present forms."
The Dragon King replied,
"So it is, Maudgalyāyana! At that time,
the Dragon King withdrew his dragon form and transformed himself into human form— neither tall nor short, with upright features and a complexion like that of a peach blossom.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then Maudgalyāyana said to the Dragon King:
"Now is the very moment; you should proceed."
At that time, having heard Maudgalyāyana’s words, the Dragon King immediately rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“We two sons of good family—one named Nanda and the other named Upananda—have taken refuge in the Tathāgata and received the five precepts. We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us the status of upāsakas, so that for as long as we live, we shall no longer kill living beings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One snapped his fingers in approval.
Thereupon, the two dragon kings returned to their original seats, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that moment, King Prasenajit had this thought:
"What causes and conditions are there that have made the smoke and flames within this Jambudvīpa so great?
At that time, King Prasenajit mounted a precious feathered chariot and departed from the city of Śrāvastī, proceeding to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, when the people saw the king approaching from afar, they all rose together to welcome him, saying: "Welcome, Great King!
Please be seated here."
At that time, the two dragon kings remained silent and did not rise.
Then King Prasenajit prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
Thereupon, the Great King addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now wish to ask a question; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it point by point.
The World-Honored One replied, "If you have something you wish to ask, now is precisely the right time."
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying,
“By what causes and conditions has there arisen such smoke and fire within this Jambudvīpa?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Nanda, this was created by the Dragon Kings Upananda and Nanda.
However, O Great King!
Do not harbor fear; today there shall be no further calamity of fire or smoke."
At that time, King Prasenajit thought to himself:
"I am now the great king of this country!
The people revere me, and my fame extends far and wide."
"From where have these two men come?
Seeing that I have arrived, they do not even rise to welcome me.
Had they been dwelling within my domain, I would have seized and imprisoned them."
"If anyone comes from another realm, you must seize and kill them.
At that time, the Dragon King, knowing what was in King Prasenajit’s mind, gave rise to anger.
At that time, the dragon king thought to himself:
"We have committed no offense against this king, yet he wishes to further harm our very bodies;
I must seize this king and the people of Kāśī and kill them all."
At that time, the Dragon King rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and departed immediately.
Not far from the Jeta Grove, he vanished from sight.
At that time, not long after this man had departed, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"State affairs are numerous and pressing; I wish to return to the palace."
The World-Honored One said,
“You should know that now is the time. Thereupon, King Prasenajit rose from his seat and withdrew.
He addressed his ministers, saying:
"By which path did those two depart just now?
Seize them quickly!"
At that time, having heard the king’s command, the ministers immediately galloped forth to search for him, but not knowing his whereabouts, they returned to the palace.
At that moment, the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda each had this thought:
"We have committed no offense against that king, yet he intends to seize us and harm us."
"We shall join together to harm those people until not a single one remains.
At that time, the Dragon King again thought to himself:
"What fault do the people of this land have?"
"We should harm the people of Śrāvastī.
Again, he thought further:
"What fault have the people of Śrāvastī committed against us?"
"You must seize the royal palace and its attendants and kill them all.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the dragon king's mind, addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"You must now save King Prasenajit; do not let him be harmed by the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda."
Maudgalyāyana replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, having received the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet and withdrew;
remaining above the royal palace, he sat cross-legged and made his body invisible.

At that time, the two dragon kings let out thunderous roars and crashing peals of lightning, accompanied by violent winds and torrential rain above the royal palace; they rained down tiles and stones, or swords and blades, yet before these could reach the ground, they were transformed into *utpala* lotuses suspended in mid-air.
At that time, the dragon king became even more enraged and rained down massive mountains upon his palace.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana again transformed them into various kinds of food and drink.
At that time, the dragon king’s anger flared up even more intensely, and he rained down various swords and blades.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana again transformed them into exquisite garments.

At that time, the dragon king became even more enraged and again rained down large pebbles and stones upon the palace of King Prasenajit; before they had even fallen to the ground, they were transformed into the seven precious jewels.

At that time, King Prasenajit saw various kinds of the seven treasures raining down within the palace; he was so filled with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, and he thought to himself:
"Among those of virtue within Jambudvīpa, there is none who surpasses me, save for the Tathāgata."

"The reason for this is that in my home, a single stalk of non-glutinous rice grew, from which I harvested a bushel of grain; when cooked with sugarcane juice, it was exceedingly fragrant and delicious. Now, as seven treasures rain down upon my palace, shall I not indeed become a Wheel-Turning Sage King!"
At that time, King Prasenajit led his court ladies to collect the seven treasures.
Then, the two dragon kings said to one another,
"What intention could he possibly have now?"
"When we arrived, we intended to harm King Prasenajit; today, our transformations have reached this point.
All our power and might have been fully displayed today, yet we could not move King Prasenajit even by the slightest fraction."
At that time, the Dragon King saw Mahāmaudgalyāyana sitting cross-legged upon the palace, with body erect and mind composed, his form leaning neither to the left nor to the right.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"This must surely be the doing of Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
At that moment, the two dragon kings, upon seeing Maudgalyāyana, withdrew and departed.
At that time, seeing the dragon depart, Maudgalyāyana withdrew his supernormal powers and went to the place where the World-Honored One was;
he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. Then King Prasenajit thought to himself:
"I should not eat these various kinds of food first; I must first offer them to the Tathāgata, and only then eat myself."
At that time, King Prasenajit immediately loaded precious jewels and various kinds of food and drink onto his chariot and went to where the World-Honored One was, saying:
"Yesterday, the heavens rained down the seven treasures and these foods and drinks; I only pray that you will accept them."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was not far from the Tathāgata. The Buddha said to the king:
"You should now take these vessels for food and drink made of the seven precious gems and give them to Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"The reason for this is that, through the grace of Maudgalyāyana, I have been reborn in the realm of the sages and worthies.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying,
"By what causes and conditions can it be said that I have been reborn?"
The World-Honored One said,
"Did you not come to my presence this morning wishing to hear the Dharma?
At that time, there were two other people who also came to hear the Dharma."
The king had this thought:
"In this kingdom, I am the most eminent and honored, revered by all people; yet from where have these two come?"
"Upon seeing me, he did not rise to welcome me.
Then the king said to the Buddha,
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One!"
The World-Honored One said:
"These are not humans; they are the Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda.
Knowing the King's intention, they spoke to one another:"
"We have committed no offense against this king; for what reason does he come to harm us?
We must surely find a way to destroy this kingdom.
We immediately perceived what was in the Dragon King's mind and at once commanded Maudgalyāyana:
"Now you must save King Prasenajit so that he does not suffer harm from the dragon.
He immediately accepted my instruction and, remaining above the palace, made himself invisible and manifested this transformation.

At that time, the Dragon King was filled with extreme rage; he rained down sand, gravel, and stones upon his palace, but before they could reach the ground, these were transformed into the seven treasures, garments, and utensils for food and drink.
"For this reason, Great King, today you have truly been born again.
At that moment, King Prasenajit was seized with terror; his hair stood on end as he knelt before the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow his profound grace upon me, so that I may save my life.
He then prostrated at the feet of Maudgalyāyana, bowing his head to the ground in reverence:
“By virtue of your honor’s kindness, I have been granted the saving of my life.”
At that time, the king spoke this verse: "Only the Venerable One possesses infinite life;
Throughout the long night, he protects our lives, Delivering us from suffering and dire distress; Through the Venerable One, we have escaped this peril."
At that time, King Prasenajit scattered celestial fragrant flowers over the body of the Tathāgata and spoke these words:
"I now offer these seven treasures to the Triple Gem; I only pray that you will accept them."
He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Among these fourfold assemblies, many are indolent and substitute others to listen to the Dharma."
I shall no longer seek expedient means to personally realize [the Dharma], nor shall I again seek to obtain what has not yet been obtained or to attain what has not yet been attained;
rather, I should now cause the fourfold assembly to thirst and yearn for the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One did not address the fourfold assembly, nor did he take any attendant with him; in the mere twinkling of an arm, he vanished from Jetavana and proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, seeing from afar that the World-Honored One was approaching, led the host of devas forward to welcome him. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, invited him to be seated, and spoke these words:
“Welcome, World-Honored One!”
"It has been a long time since I last paid my respects.
At that moment, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I shall now employ the power of my supernormal faculties to conceal my physical form, so that people will not see where I am."
At that time, the World-Honored One again thought to himself:
"I shall now manifest a transformation body in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, making it exceedingly vast.
At that moment, in the Sudharmā Hall of the heavens, there was a stone dais one yojana in length and breadth.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged upon the rock, his body filling it entirely.
Then, the Tathāgata’s mother, Māyā, accompanied by various celestial maidens, went to where the World-Honored One was; she prostrated herself at his feet and sat to one side.
They spoke thus:
"We have long been separated from serving you; now that we have come here, we truly receive great fortune. We have thirstily yearned to see you, and only today does the Buddha finally arrive."
At that time, Queen Māyā, having prostrated her head at his feet, sat to one side;
Śakra-devānām-indra likewise prostrated at the Tathāgata’s feet and sat to one side.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and sat to one side.
At that time, the assembly of devas saw that the Tathāgata was there increasing the host of devas and diminishing the asuras.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually delivered a sublime discourse to that assembly of devas;

that is to say, a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, and a discourse on rebirth in heaven, concerning how sensual desire is an impure perception, how sexual lust is foul and evil, and how the way of escape is true happiness.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the minds of the great assembly who had gathered and the hearts of the devas and humans were opened and their intentions resolved, taught the Dharma constantly expounded by all Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones— suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— to all the devas.
Each of them, while seated, was cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, eighteen billion hosts of celestial maidens realized the stage of the Path, and thirty-six thousand celestial beings attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, the Mother of the Tathāgata rose from her seat, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, and returned to the palace.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"With what food shall I now provide a meal for the Tathāgata?"
"Should human food be used, or natural celestial food?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Human food may be used to provide sustenance for the Tathāgata."
"The reason for this is that my body was born among humans, grew among humans, and attained Buddhahood among humans.
Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha,
saying, "So it is, World-Honored One!"
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it by means of the seasons of the heavens,
or is it by means of the seasons of the human world?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"By means of the temporal divisions of the human world. He responded:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, using human food and human seasonal meals, again served the Tathāgata.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven each said to one another,
"We have now seen the Tathāgata eating his meal throughout the entire day.
Then, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
