"I shall now enter such a samādhi that I may cause the devas to advance when I wish them to advance, and cause the devas to retreat when I wish them to retreat.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered this samādhi and, according to the requirements of the occasion, caused the devas to advance or retreat as desired.
At that time, the fourfold assembly of the human world, having not seen the Tathāgata for a long time, went to where Ānanda was and said to him:
"Where is the Tathāgata now?"
"We long with thirsty yearning to see him. Ānanda replied,
"We, too, do not know where the Tathāgata is."
At that time, King Prasenajit and King Udayana went to where Ānanda was and asked him,
"Where, finally, is the Tathāgata today?"
Ānanda replied, "Great King!
I too do not know where the Tathāgata is."
At that time, the two kings became afflicted with suffering as they gazed upon the Tathāgata.
Then, the ministers went to King Udayana and said to him,
"What is the cause of your present affliction?"
The king then replied,
"I am now afflicted by the distress of grief.
The ministers addressed the king:
"What causes one to fall into affliction through sorrow? The king replied,
"It is because I have not seen the Tathāgata."
"If I do not see the Tathāgata, I shall surely die.
At that time, the ministers thought to themselves:
"By what skillful means can we ensure that King Udayana does not pass away?"
"We should fashion an image of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the ministers said to the king:
"We wish to fashion an image so that we may also pay homage, serve, and revere it."
At that time, having heard these words, the king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he addressed his ministers, saying: "Excellent!
What you have said is most sublime."
The ministers addressed the king, saying,
"With what kind of jewels should we fashion the image of the Tathāgata?
At that time, the king immediately issued an edict to all the master craftsmen within the realm, addressing them as follows:
"I now wish to create an image.
The skilled artisan replied, "So be it."
"Great King!
At that time, King Udayana immediately fashioned an image of the Tathāgata out of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood, five feet in height.
At that time, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana had fashioned an image of the Tathāgata five feet high and was making offerings to it.
At that time, King Prasenajit again summoned the skilled artisans of the kingdom and addressed them, saying:
"I now wish to create an image of the Tathāgata; you should prepare it accordingly."
At that time, King Prasenajit had this thought:
"What kind of precious material should be used to fashion an image of the Tathāgata?
After a short while, he again had this thought:
“The physical form of the Tathāgata is as yellow as celestial gold; we should now fashion an image of the Tathāgata out of gold.
At that time, King Prasenajit fashioned an image of the Tathāgata entirely from purple-polished gold, five feet in height.
At that time, for the first time within Jambudvīpa, there appeared these two images of the Tathāgata.
Then, the fourfold assembly went to where Ānanda was and said to him:
"We thirst and yearn for the Tathāgata; we long to behold the Honored One. Where, indeed, is the Tathāgata today?"
Ānanda replied, "We, too, do not know where the Tathāgata is. However,
let us now go together to where Ānanda is and inquire about this matter."

The reason for this is that the Venerable Anuruddha is foremost in the divine eye; it is pure and free from blemish. With his divine eye, he sees a thousand worlds, two thousand worlds, and a great trichiliocosm of three thousand worlds; he is able to know and see them.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, together with Ānanda, went to where Anuruddha was and said to him:
"Now this fourfold assembly has come to me and asked me:
'Where, after all, is the Tathāgata today?'"
“I only pray that the Venerable One will use his divine eye to observe where the Tathāgata is now!
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha replied, “Cease for a moment! You all wait!”
"I now wish to observe where the Tathāgata ultimately resides.

At that time, Aniruddha straightened his body and composed his mind, fixing his mindfulness before him. With his divine eye, he surveyed Jambudvīpa but did not see him; he again surveyed Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru with his divine eye but did not see him. He further surveyed the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, even surveying up to the Brahmā Heaven, yet still did not see him.

Furthermore, he observed a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānīs, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand realms of the Four Heavenly Kings, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, a thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens, and a thousand Brahmā heavens, yet he did not see the Tathāgata.
He further surveyed the trichiliocosm, yet he did not see it.
He then rose from his seat and said to Ānanda:
"I have now surveyed the trichiliocosm, but I do not see it."
At that time, Ānanda and the fourfold assembly fell silent.
Ānanda thought to himself:
"Will the Tathāgata not enter parinirvāṇa?"
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven each said to one another:
"We have gained a most excellent benefit; we pray only that these seven Buddhas may constantly appear in the world, so that they may bring great nourishment and benefit to both devas and humans."
Some devas spoke these words:
"Setting aside the seven Buddhas for a moment, it would be most excellent even if there were six Buddhas.
Some sons of gods said:
"It is simply that there are five Buddhas," some said;
others said, "Four Buddhas."
Some said: "Three Buddhas. Others said:
"The appearance of two Buddhas in the world brings great benefit and nourishment.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the devas, saying:
"Setting aside the seven Buddhas, and even the two Buddhas, it would suffice if only Śākyamuni Buddha were to remain long in the world; then there would be much benefit and advantage."
At that time, when the Tathāgata desired for the devas to come, the devas would come; when he desired for the devas to depart, the devas would depart.
At that time, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three each said to one another,
"For what reason does the Tathāgata eat throughout the entire day?
Then Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s meal today is according to the temporal reckoning of the human world, not that of the heavens.
At that time, after three months had passed, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The fourfold assembly of Jambudvīpa has not seen me for a long time; they must feel a profound sense of longing and thirst."
"I shall now relinquish my supernormal power so that the śrāvakas may know that the Tathāgata is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that moment, the World-Honored One immediately relinquished his supernormal power.
At that time, Ānanda went to where Anuruddha was and said to him:
"Now the fourfold assembly is greatly parched with longing and wishes to see the Tathāgata."
"But will the Tathāgata not now enter parinirvāṇa?
At that time, Anuruddha said to Ānanda:
"Last night, a deva came to my place and said:"
"The Tathāgata is in the Sudharmā Hall in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
You should stop for now!
I wish to see where the Tathāgata currently resides.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha sat down cross-legged, straightening his body and composing his mind so that it remained unmoving; with his divine eye, he beheld the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and saw the World-Honored One sitting upon a stone slab one yojana square.
At that time, Aniruddha arose from samādhi and said to Ānanda:
"The Tathāgata is now in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven preaching the Dharma to his mother."
At that time, Ānanda and the fourfold assembly were filled with such joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves.
Then, Ānanda asked the fourfold assembly:
"Who among you is capable of going to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inquire after the Tathāgata’s welfare?"
Anuruddha said, "Now, Venerable Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernormal powers; we pray that you will deign to exercise your spiritual power and go to inquire after the Buddha’s health.
At that time, the fourfold assembly addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Today the Tathāgata is in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; we pray that the Venerable One will take the names of the fourfold assembly and inquire after the Tathāgata’s welfare!
Furthermore, please take this meaning and go to inform the Tathāgata:
'The World-Honored One attained the Way within the world of Jambudvīpa; we pray that you would deign to exercise your majestic spiritual power and return to the world!'"
Maudgalyāyana replied: "Excellent,
worthy ones!"

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, having received the command of the fourfold assembly, traveled to the Heaven of the Thirty-three in the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm, arriving at the place where the Tathāgata was.
Then, Śakra Devānām Indra and the gods of the Thirty-three saw Maudgalyāyana approaching from afar, and each of them had this thought:
"Is he truly a messenger of the Saṃgha?"
"Could it be that you are an envoy from these kings?
At that moment, all the devas rose and went out to meet him,
saying, "Welcome, Venerable One!"
At that time, Maudgalyāyana saw from afar the World-Honored One preaching the Dharma to a vast and countless multitude.
Having seen this, he had this thought:
"The World-Honored One is here among these devas, yet it is likewise crowded and noisy."
Maudgalyāyana went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The fourfold assembly inquires after the Tathāgata’s well-being:
whether his daily life is light and easy, and whether his movements are healthy and strong.
He further reported this matter:

"The Tathāgata was born and grew up within Jambudvīpa and attained the Way in this world; we pray only that the World-Honored One will return to this world, for the fourfold assembly is parched with longing and desires to see the World-Honored One!"
The World-Honored One said:
"Enable the fourfold assembly to advance in their practice without weariness.
What do you think, Maudgalyāyana?"
Has the community of the fourfold assembly been weary from traveling for the sake of conversion?
Are there no disputes or litigations?
Are you not being harassed by those of external paths and heterodox teachings?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“The fourfold assembly practices the Path without weariness.
[The Buddha said,] “But, Maudgalyāyana!”
As for what you previously thought, saying,
"The Tathāgata is here in a state of bustle and clamor," this is not so.
The reason for this is that when I teach the Dharma, it does not take long; furthermore, were I to form such a thought as,
"I wish to cause the devas to come," they would come,
and "I wish to cause the devas not to come," the devas would not come.
“Maudgalyāyana!
Return to the world; seven days from now, the Tathāgata shall go to the side of the great pond in the kingdom of Kauśala.

At that time, in the time it takes to bend and stretch one’s arm, Maudgalyāyana returned to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, went before the fourfold assembly, and addressed them, saying:
“Virtuous ones, you should know that seven days from now, the Tathāgata will descend to the banks of the Great Lake in the kingdom of Kāśī on Jambudvīpa.
When the fourfold assembly heard these words, they were filled with joy and exultation, unable to contain themselves.

At that time, King Prasenajit, King Udayana, King Ajātaśatru, King Udāyana, and King Bimbisāra heard that the Tathāgata would arrive at the side of the great pond in the kingdom of Aṅga seven days hence; they were filled with such immense joy that they could not contain themselves.

At that time, the multitudes of people in Vaiśālī, the Śākyas of Kapilavastu, and the multitudes of people in Kauśāmbī, hearing that the Tathāgata was about to come to Jambudvīpa, were filled with joy and exultation beyond measure.
At that time, King Prasenajit assembled the fourfold army and went to the side of the pond, desiring to see the World-Honored One.
At that moment, five kings also gathered their troops and went to where the World-Honored One was, wishing to pay their respects to the Tathāgata and the multitude of people.
The Śākyas of Kapilavastu all went to where the World-Honored One was, as did the fourfold assembly, all desiring to behold the Tathāgata.
At that time, as the seventh day approached, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the son of the gods Īśvara, saying:
"From the summit of Mount Sumeru to the waters of Lake Saṃkāśya, create three paths; observe how the Tathāgata will reach Jambudvīpa without employing supernatural powers."
The Devaputra Īśvara replied, "This is most excellent; it shall be prepared at this very moment.
Thereupon, the Devaputra Īśvara immediately manifested three paths made of gold, silver, and crystal.
At that time, the golden paths shall be situated in the center, flanking the sides of the crystal paths and the silver paths, where they will manifest as golden trees.
During those seven days, the various sublime and honored devas will all come to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a multitude of many thousands of myriads, who followed him before and behind as he preached the Dharma, saying:
"The five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
What are the five?..."
They are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
What is the aggregate of form?
It refers to this body composed of the four great elements and the matter derived from these four great elements; this is called the aggregate of form.
"What is called the aggregate of feeling?
It refers to painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; this is what is called the aggregate of feeling."
"What is called the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha)?
It refers to the coming together of the three times; this is what is called the aggregate of perception.
What is called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha)?"
What are called bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations—these are termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
What is termed the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)?
It refers to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are termed the aggregate of consciousness.
"What is that which is called form?
That which is called form includes cold as form, heat as form, hunger as form, and thirst as form."
"What is meant by 'feeling' (vedanā)?
That which is called feeling is termed 'sensation' (vijñapti).
Of what is one conscious? "
One perceives suffering, perceives pleasure, and perceives that which is neither suffering nor pleasure;
therefore, it is called "perception" (saṃjñā).
What is meant by "perception"? That which is called perception is also a form of knowing.
One who knows blue, yellow, white, and black, and knows suffering and pleasure, is therefore called "one who knows" (*jñānin*).
What is meant by "action" (*saṃskāra*)?
That which is called action is that which is capable of bringing something to completion; therefore, it is called action.
To accomplish what? It accomplishes either unwholesome conduct or wholesome conduct; therefore, it is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).
What is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)?
What is called consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which discriminates right from wrong and also discerns various flavors; this is termed consciousness.
"O sons of the gods, you should know that these five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) recognize the three evil realms, the realm of devas, and the realm of humans;
when these five aggregates of clinging are extinguished, one then knows the path to nirvāṇa."
At that time, while this Dharma was being taught, sixty thousand devas and humans attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then, having taught the Dharma to the devas and humans, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, went to the summit of Mount Sumeru, and spoke these verses:
"You all should study with diligence In the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha."
One should extinguish the path of death, as a man with a hook tames an elephant.
If one can apply oneself to this Dharma without indolence,
then one shall bring an end to birth and death, and there will be no further root of suffering.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One proceeded along the middle path.

Then, Brahmā stood on the right side of the Tathāgata by the silver path, and Śakra Devānām Indra stood by the crystal path; together with the various devas and humans, they scattered flowers and burned incense in the air, performing music and song to entertain the Tathāgata.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā heard that the Tathāgata would arrive today at the side of the Saṃkāśya lake in Jambudvīpa. Having heard this, she immediately formed this thought:
"Among the fourfold assembly, the kings, the ministers, and the people of the land, there are none who will not go."
"If I were to approach him in my usual form, it would not be appropriate.
I shall now assume the appearance of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) and go to see the World-Honored One."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā withdrew her form and assumed the appearance of a universal monarch (cakravartin), complete with the seven treasures.

These so-called seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the military commander treasure, and the steward treasure; these are called the seven treasures.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near the city of Rājagṛha, sewing garments by the side of a mountain.

At that moment, Subhūti heard that the World-Honored One would arrive today at Jambudvīpa, and that there was no one among the fourfold assembly who would not see him. He thought, "I should now go at this opportune time to pay my respects and prostrate before the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti set aside his work of sewing robes, rose from his seat, and placed his right foot on the ground.
Then he thought to himself: "Regarding this form of the Tathāgata, which one is the World-Honored One?"
Is it the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind?
Is that which goes forth to see the earth, water, fire, or wind element?
All phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent, without creation and without action, as the World-Honored One has stated in verse:
"If one wishes to pay homage to the Buddha, And to all those who are most supreme,
One should contemplate the aggregates, the bases, and the elements As being entirely impermanent."
The Buddhas of the distant past, as well as those yet to come,
and the Buddhas of the present— these are all impermanent.
If you wish to pay homage to the Buddhas, [pay homage] to those of the past and those yet to come.
It is said that within the present, one should contemplate the dharma of emptiness.
If one wishes to pay homage to the Buddhas— those of the past, those of the future,
and those of the present— one should reckon them as being without self.
"In this, there is no self, no life-principle, no person, and no agent; nor is there any form. There are teachings and those who impart them, yet all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent."
What is this "self"? This self has no master.
I now take refuge in the assembly of the True Dharma.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti returned to his seat and mended his robes.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā assumed the form of a universal monarch (cakravartin), accompanied by the seven treasures as her retinue, and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the five kings saw the Wheel-Turning Sage King approaching from afar; filled with joy and exultation beyond measure, they said to one another:
"How marvelous!"
"How extraordinary!
Two rare treasures have appeared in the world: the Tathāgata and the Wheel-Turning Sage King.
At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by tens of thousands of devas and humans, came from the summit of Mount Sumeru and arrived at the side of the pond.
At that time, when the World-Honored One lifted his foot and stepped upon the ground, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Then, the transformed Wheel-Turning Sage King gradually approached the place where the World-Honored One was, while all the minor kings and the various classes of people each made way for him.
At that time, the transformed holy king, realizing he was close to the World-Honored One, returned to his original form and paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One as a bhikṣuṇī.
When the five kings saw this, they each lamented their own misfortune and said to one another:
"Today we have suffered a great loss; we ought to have seen the Tathāgata first, yet now this bhikṣuṇī has seen him before us."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now pay homage to the Most Victorious Honored One; today I have been the first to come and see you. I, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, am a disciple of the Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to that bhikṣuṇī:
"First one pays homage with wholesome karma; That which is foremost is beyond fault.
Emptiness and the doors of liberation— This is the meaning of paying homage to the Buddha."

"If one wishes to pay homage to the Buddha, whether of the future or the past, one should contemplate that all phenomena are empty and non-existent; this is called the true meaning of paying homage to the Buddha.
At that time, five kings and an incalculable multitude of people went to where the World-Honored One was and each announced their own name.
“I am King Prasenajit of Kāśī. “I am King Udayana of Vatsa.
“I am Viḍūḍabha, lord of the people of the five cities.”
“I am the lord of the Southern Sea, named Udayana.
“I am King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha.

At that time, eleven koṭis of people gathered together, along with the fourfold assembly; the most venerable elders, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, King Udayana held an image of ox-head sandalwood in his hands and addressed the Tathāgata with these verses:
"I now wish to ask: for one who creates an image of the Buddha out of compassion to protect all beings, what kind of merit will be obtained?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Great King, listen now; I shall briefly expound its meaning.
Regarding the making of images of the Buddha, I shall now speak of it in general terms."
The faculty of the eye shall not first be impaired, And later one shall obtain the vision of the divine eye;
Black and white shall be clearly distinguished, As one cultivates the merit of the Buddha’s form and image.
The physical body shall be complete and perfect, And the mind upright, free from delusion.
One who fashions an image of the Buddha possesses power twice that of ordinary men;
they shall never fall into the evil realms, but will invariably be reborn in the heavens as a celestial king—
such is the merit of fashioning an image of the Buddha.
Other merits are beyond reckoning; those merits are inconceivable.
His fame spreads far and wide throughout the four quarters—such is the merit of creating an image of the Buddha. "Excellent!"
Excellent! Great King! You have brought great benefit, and both devas and humans receive your blessings.
At that time, King Udayana was filled with such immense joy that he could not contain himself.
Then the World-Honored One, together with the fourfold assembly and the five kings, expounded a sublime discourse. This discourse consisted of:

a teaching on generosity, a teaching on morality, and a teaching on rebirth in the heavens; [he further explained that] sensual desire is the perception of impurity, the outflows are a great affliction, and the way of transcendence is supreme.

At that time, knowing that the minds of the fourfold assembly were opened and their intentions liberated, the World-Honored One fully expounded to them the Dharma which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly teach:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that time, more than sixty thousand people among the gods and the populace seated there were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then, the five kings addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"This place is most meritorious and wondrous, a truly divine land. Since the Tathāgata first descended from Tuṣita Heaven to this spot to preach the Dharma, we now wish to establish a monument here so that it may endure forever without decay."
The World-Honored One said:
"You five kings, by establishing a shrine for the deities at this place, shall receive blessings throughout the long night; it shall never perish."
The kings replied, "How should we construct the divine temple?
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right hand, and from within the earth, the temple of Kāśyapa Tathāgata emerged. He looked upon the five kings and addressed them, saying:
“Those who wish to construct a divine temple should take this as their model.
At that time, the five kings immediately erected a great divine temple at that location.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The number of attendants of all the Tathāgatas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, was exactly like today’s and no different.
Even the number of attendants of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the future will also be exactly like today’s and no different."
This sutra is titled "The Fundamental Dharma of Wandering among the Heavens.
Thus, O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the fourfold assembly and the five kings, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 28; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 29.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Six Heavinesses (Ṣaḍ-gurutva-varga), Part One. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should reflect upon the six dharmas of respect; revere them, honor them, and hold them in your hearts so that you do not forget or lose them.”
What are the six? In this regard, bhikṣu, one practices mindfulness of loving-kindness through bodily action;
like looking at one's own reflection in a mirror, one should regard it with reverence and esteem, ensuring that it is not lost.
"Furthermore, practicing loving-kindness through verbal action and practicing loving-kindness through mental action is worthy of respect and honor; do not let it be forgotten or lost.

Furthermore, possessing the requisites for attaining the benefits of the Dharma and being able to share them with fellow practitioners of the holy life, without any thought of stinginess—this quality is worthy of respect and honor; do not let it be forgotten or lost."
"Furthermore, there are those who possess precepts that are indestructible and imperishable, perfectly complete and without flaw, which are esteemed by the wise;
they further desire to distribute these precepts to others so that all may share in their flavor,
and they hold this Dharma in reverence and esteem, ensuring it is not forgotten or lost."
"Furthermore, right view enables the noble ones to attain the way of escape;
such a view should be shared with fellow practitioners of the holy life, for it is worthy of honor and esteem, and must not be allowed to be forgotten."
“Thus it is said, monks:
there are these six bases of respect that are worthy of honor and esteem;
do not let them be forgotten. Therefore, monks!”
You should always practice the conduct of body, speech, and mind; even if you obtain the requisites for livelihood, you should think of distributing them and not give rise to thoughts of greed.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

These were all arhats who possessed the three types of supernormal knowledge, the six superknowledges, and mastery of the psychic powers; their minds were free from fear, with the sole exception of one bhikṣu, Ānanda.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon a golden lotus flower with a stem made of the seven treasures, and five hundred bhikṣus each sat upon precious lotus flowers.
Then, the Dragon King Anavatapta went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, having surveyed the assembly of noble ones, the Dragon King addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"As I now observe this assembly, it is incomplete and lacks one; the Venerable Śāriputra is not here. I only pray that the World-Honored One will dispatch a bhikṣu to summon Śāriputra so that he may come."
At that time, Śāriputra was at the Jetavana Monastery mending old robes.
Then the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana: "Go to where Śāriputra is and say to him: "
"The Dragon King Anavatapta wishes to see you.
Maudgalyāyana replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in the time it takes a person to bend and extend their arm, went to Śāriputra at the Jeta Grove Monastery and said to him:
"The Tathāgata has given this instruction:..."
"The Dragon King Anavatapta wishes to see you.
Śāriputra replied, "You go on ahead; I shall follow later."

Maudgalyāyana replied, "The entire assembly of noble ones and the Dragon King Anavatapta long for the sight of your venerable countenance and wish to meet you; we pray that you will attend at this time and do not neglect this auspicious occasion."
Śāriputra replied, "You go there first; I shall follow after you.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke again:
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Is anyone among those with supernormal powers able to surpass me?
Or have they already dispatched a messenger ahead of us?"
"If Śāriputra does not rise at once, I shall seize his arm and lead him to that spring.
At that moment, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"Maudgalyāyana is merely testing and teasing me with this skillful means."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra personally untied his saṃkakṣikā band and said to Maudgalyāyana:
"If you are indeed the foremost in supernormal powers, lift this band so that it leaves the ground, and then take me by the arm and lead me to Lake Anavatapta."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Now Śāriputra again mocks me; does he intend to test me?
He has now loosened his belt and placed it on the ground, saying:"
“Only one who can lift it may then grasp my arm and lead me to the place where the spring is.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana again thought to himself:
“There must be a cause for this; the matter cannot be so simple.”
Immediately, he reached out his hand and tried to lift the sash, yet he could not move it even by the width of a hair.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted all his strength and power to shift this sash, but he could not move it.
At that time, Śāriputra took this sash and tied it to a branch of a jambu tree.

Then, although the Venerable Maudgalyāyana exerted all his supernatural powers, wishing to lift this sash, he was ultimately unable to move it; as he attempted to lift the sash, this Jambudvīpa shook violently.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"If the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana can cause even this Jambudvīpa to tremble, how much more so this sash?"
"I shall now take this sash and fasten it to two world-systems.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana likewise lifted it;
he was able to lift it when fastened to three world-systems and four world-systems as well, just as one would lift a light garment.
At that time, Śāriputra again had this thought:
"The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is capable of lifting the four continents, yet that would not even be worth mentioning; I shall now take this sash and tie it around the waist of Mount Sumeru."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was further able to shake this Mount Sumeru as well as the palaces of the Four Great Heavenly Kings; the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven all shook and trembled.
At that time, Śāriputra again tied this sash around a thousand worlds.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was also able to move it.
Then, Śāriputra again tied this sash around the two-thousandfold world system and the three-thousandfold world system, and these too were able to be moved.
At that time, heaven and earth shook violently; yet only the Tathāgata sat by the Anavatapta Spring, unmoving, just as a strong man might play with a leaf without any difficulty.
At that time, the Dragon King Anavatapta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what reason does this heaven and earth now tremble?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One fully explained this original cause to the Dragon King, and the Dragon King said to the Buddha:
"Between these two, whose supernatural power is the most supreme?
The World-Honored One replied,
"The bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses the greatest supernatural power."
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you previously prophesied, saying:
‘Among the bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernatural powers; none surpass him.’”
The World-Honored One said:
"Nāga King, you should know that there are four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*).
What are the four? They are as follows:"
The spiritual power of the samādhi of mastery, the spiritual power of the samādhi of diligence, the spiritual power of the samādhi of mind, and the spiritual power of the samādhi of examination.
These, O Dragon King, are what they are called.
There is the power of these four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who possess these four powers of supernormality and, through close application and cultivation, do not abandon them, this constitutes the foremost power of supernormality.
The Dragon King Anavatapta addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Does the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana not possess these four bases of supernormal power?
The World-Honored One replied:
“The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana has also attained these four bases of supernormal power; he practices them closely and never abandons them.
Furthermore, if the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana wishes to remain for the duration of a kalpa, he is likewise capable of accomplishing this.”
"However, as for the samādhi entered by Śāriputra, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana does not know its name.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra again thought to himself:
"Maudgalyāyana is able to move and transport the entire trichiliocosm, yet the number of crawling insects that die thereby is beyond calculation; nevertheless, I have personally heard:"
“The seat of the Tathāgata is immovable.
I shall now fasten this sash to the place where the Tathāgata’s seat stands.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana again attempted to lift this sash with his supernormal powers, yet he was unable to move it.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana had this thought:
"Have I lost my supernormal powers?
For now I lift this belt, yet I cannot move it."
"I shall now go to the place where the World-Honored One is and inquire about this matter.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, having set aside his belt, immediately traveled by means of his supernormal power to the place where the World-Honored One was. Seeing from afar that Śāriputra was seated before the Tathāgata, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Among the disciples of the World-Honored One, there is none who excels me in supernormal power; yet am I not inferior to Śāriputra?"
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Am I not perhaps declining in my supernormal powers?
For this reason: previously, I set out from the Jeta Grove Monastery first, and Śāriputra set out after me; yet now, the bhikṣu Śāriputra is already seated before the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said:
"You have not regressed in your supernormal powers; it is simply that you do not understand the dharmas of the samādhis of supernormal power into which Śāriputra has entered."
The reason for this is that the bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses immeasurable wisdom and has attained mastery over his mind; yet he does not act according to his own will as freely as [the Buddha];
Śāriputra’s mental and spiritual faculties have attained such mastery.
"If the Dharma contemplated by the mind of the bhikṣu Śāriputra can be thus mastered," [he said].
At that moment, Mahāmaudgalyāyana remained silent.
Then, the Dragon King Anavatapta leaped for joy, unable to contain himself:
"Now, the bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses supreme supernormal power that is inconceivable; as for the samādhi he has entered, the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana does not even know its name."
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the Dragon King Anavatapta, exhorting him until he was filled with joy; he then administered the precepts there.
At dawn, leading the community of bhikṣus, he returned to Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"The World-Honored One himself declared:
'Among my śrāvakas, the foremost in supernormal powers (ṛddhi) is the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana.'"
"However, today he is not the equal of Śāriputra.
At that time, the bhikṣus conceived a sense of contempt toward Maudgalyāyana.
Then, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"These bhikṣus have conceived thoughts of contempt toward Maudgalyāyana and shall undergo incalculable suffering.
He said to Maudgalyāyana, "Manifest your supernatural powers so that this assembly may see them; do not allow the great multitude to give rise to thoughts of indolence."
Maudgalyāyana replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”

At that time, Maudgalyāyana prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and immediately vanished from before the Tathāgata. He traveled to the east, to a buddha-field as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers, where there was a Buddha named Citrābha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who had appeared in that land.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana went to that land wearing his ordinary robes and walked upon the rim of a begging bowl; furthermore, the inhabitants of that land were of immense stature.
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw Maudgalyāyana, they said to one another, "Look at this insect; it truly resembles a śramaṇa.
Then, the bhikṣus brought it and showed it to the Buddha.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
Now there is a certain insect that closely resembles a śramaṇa.
At that time, the Tathāgata Citraraśmi addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"To the west of here, beyond the sands of seven Ganges Rivers, in that world-system, there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has appeared in the world; you are his disciple, foremost in supernormal powers."
At that time, the Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"These bhikṣus have conceived thoughts of contempt; manifest your supernormal powers so that the great assembly may see them."
Maudgalyāyana replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Maudgalyāyana placed those five hundred bhikṣus in his alms-bowl netting and ascended to the Brahma Heaven.
Then, Maudgalyāyana placed his left foot upon Mount Sumeru and his right foot upon the Brahma Heaven.
At that time, he spoke these verses:
"One should always mindfully apply diligence, Cultivating the Buddha-dharma;
Subdue the hosts of Māra’s enemies, Just as a hook tames an elephant."
"If one can, regarding this Dharma, practice without negligence, one shall reach the end of the source of suffering and no longer have any further afflictions.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana caused these sounds to pervade the Jeta Grove Monastery; having heard them, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
“Where was Maudgalyāyana staying when he spoke this verse?

The World-Honored One replied, “This bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is seven *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-lands away from this buddha-field, situated directly to the east. He placed those five hundred bhikṣus in a rope net; with his left foot upon Mount Sumeru and his right foot touching the Brahma Heaven, he spoke this verse.”
At that time, the bhikṣus marveled at what they had never before experienced, exclaiming:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"

The bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana possesses great supernormal powers, yet we have become indolent and arrogant toward him; we only pray that the World-Honored One will cause the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana to bring these five hundred bhikṣus here to this place.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his power of the Way from afar to make Maudgalyāyana understand his intention.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana, leading five hundred bhikṣus, arrived at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to a multitude of many tens of millions.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, leading five hundred bhikṣus, arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was.
However, disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha looked up at that bhikṣu!
At that time, a bhikṣu from the world-system of the east prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"Bhikṣus, from where have you come?
Whose disciples are you?"
"How long has it been since you set out on this road?
Those five hundred bhikṣus addressed Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
"Our world is currently to the east; our Buddha is named Citrābha Tathāgata, and we are his disciples."
"However, we ourselves do not know from where we have come today,
nor how many days have passed.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Do you know the Buddha-world? The bhikṣus replied,
"No, World-Honored One!"
“Do you wish to go to that land today? The bhikṣus replied,
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”
"I wish to return to that land.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain to you the Dharma of the six elements; reflect upon it well."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"What is meant by the teaching of the six elements?
"Monks, you should know that a person of the six elements is born from the vital essence of the father and mother.
What are these six?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element."
"Monks, this is what is meant:
there are these six elements; the human body receives this vital energy and gives rise to the six sense bases. What are the six? "
These are what are called the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base.
Thus it is said, bhikṣu:
there are these six bases which exist by virtue of the parents; and depending upon these six bases, there arise the six groups of consciousness.
What are the six?
If based on eye-consciousness, there is the aggregate of eye-consciousness, as well as ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
"Monks, this is called the sixfold aggregate of consciousness.

If there is a monk who understands these six elements, the six sense bases, and the sixfold aggregate of consciousness, he is able to transcend the six heavens and take on further forms; even if his life there should end and he is reborn here in this world, he will be intelligent and highly talented, and in this very body, he will exhaust all fetters and attain Nirvana."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Now, take this bhikṣu back to that buddha-field.
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One! At that time,
Maudgalyāyana again placed five hundred bhikṣus in a carrying net, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew and departed.
In the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, he arrived at that buddha-field.
At that moment, Maudgalyāyana, having left this bhikṣu behind and paid homage at the feet of that Buddha, returned once more to this Sahā world-system.
At that time, when the bhikṣus of that land had heard these six elements, all their defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the foremost śrāvaka whose supernormal powers are difficult to equal is the bhikṣu Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Lion Grove in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.

There were five hundred bhikṣus of great virtue and supernormal powers, including the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Kāśyapa, the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Ānanda.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Aniruddha went to where Śāriputra was at dawn. Seeing the three great śrāvakas approaching Śāriputra from afar, Ānanda said to Revata:
"The three great śrāvakas are going to where Śāriputra is; we two should also go to where Śāriputra is."
"The reason for this is that I have heard Śāriputra preach the wondrous and marvelous Dharma.
Revata replied, "This may indeed be so."
At that time, Revata and Ānanda went to where Śāriputra was. Then Śāriputra said:
"Welcome, worthy ones!"
"Sit here. At that time, Śāriputra said to Ānanda:
"I now wish to ask something."
"This Gṛdhrakūṭa Park is exceedingly delightful; divine fragrances spread naturally throughout the four quarters. How can we ensure this park remains so joyful?

Ānanda replied, "If there are bhikṣus who have heard much and do not forget, who retain the meanings and flavors of all dharmas through dhāraṇī, who are fully accomplished in the practice of the holy life (brahmacarya), and who are endowed with all such dharmas without omission—preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly without losing the proper sequence, without abruptness, and without distracted thoughts."
"In this way, bhikṣu, you shall dwell happily here in the Gośṛṅga Park.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Revata:
"Ānanda has just now expounded this; I now wish to question you further regarding its meaning."
"The joy of the Gośṛṅga Park is such as this.
You should now speak in turn; what is its meaning? Revata replied:
"Thereupon, the bhikṣu delights in secluded places, practicing seated meditation with contemplation, in accordance with right observation.
In this way, the bhikṣu delights in the Gośīrṣa Garden."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra said to Aniruddha,
“You should now explain the meaning of ‘delight. Aniruddha replied:

"If there is a bhikṣu who, with the divine eye, sees clearly and observes the various classes of sentient beings—those who die and those who are born, those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance, those in good destinations and those in bad destinations, whether handsome or unattractive—he knows them all."
There are some sentient beings who commit evil through body, speech, and mind, and slander the noble ones; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in hell.
There are also sentient beings who perform good through body, speech, and mind, and do not slander the noble ones; they are like a person observing the sky, seeing everything without exception.
A bhikṣu possessing the divine eye is likewise; he observes the world without any doubt or difficulty.
Thus, a bhikṣu dwelling within the Gośīrṣa Garden experiences such happiness.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Kāśyapa: "I now speak to you.
Since these worthy ones have thus explained the meaning of happiness, it is now your turn to speak of it."
Kāśyapa replied: "If there is a bhikṣu who practices the forest-dwelling (āraṇyaka) life and further teaches others to practice the forest-dwelling life, praising the virtues of seclusion;
and who himself wears robes made of rags from cemeteries and further teaches others to practice the dhūta austerities;"
Personally knowing contentment while dwelling in a secluded place, he further teaches others to cultivate that practice;

his own moral virtue being complete, with the accomplishment of samādhi, the accomplishment of wisdom, the accomplishment of liberation, and the accomplishment of the vision and knowledge of liberation, he further teaches others to practice that Dharma, praising and expounding upon it so as to be able to exhort and transform them, and further teaching others to practice that Dharma;
in his instruction and admonition, he is never weary or satisfied.
"In this way, monks, one dwells in the Gosīrṣa Garden with incomparable happiness.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra said to Mahāmoggallāna:
"The noble ones have already explained the meaning of happiness; you should now explain the meaning of happiness in turn."
"The pleasure within the Gośṛṅga (Ox-Horn) Garden is peerless; how would you now describe it? Maudgalyāyana replied:

"In this regard, a bhikṣu possesses great supernormal power (ṛddhi) and has attained mastery over such powers. He can manifest countless thousands of transformations without hesitation or difficulty; he can also divide his single body into countless bodies, or again merge them back into one. He passes through stone walls as if they were open space, leaping up and diving down with complete ease."

They are like a swift river; like a bird flying through the sky leaving no trace; like a raging fire consuming mountains and forests; like the sun and moon, which there is nowhere they do not illuminate; they can raise their hands to touch and stroke the sun and moon, and they can manifest transformed bodies reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven.
"In this way, bhikṣus, one is fit for the Gośṛṅga Park.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to Śāriputra:
"Let us each speak according to our own eloquence. Let us now ask Śāriputra about this matter: the Gośṛṅga Park is exceedingly pleasant; what kind of bhikṣu is fit to dwell therein?"
Śāriputra said: "If there is a bhikṣu who can subdue his mind, yet that mind cannot subdue the bhikṣu;
and if that bhikṣu wishes to attain samādhi, he immediately attains samādhi—whatever samādhi he desires to accomplish, whether far or near, he is able to achieve it."

It is just as when a householder has fine garments stored in a chest; at that time, whatever garment the householder wishes to take according to his will, he takes it without hesitation or difficulty.

Likewise, one is able to enter samādhi according to one's will. This is also the case here: the mind can direct the bhikṣu, rather than the bhikṣu directing the mind, so that one enters samādhi according to one's will without hesitation or difficulty.
"In this way, bhikṣus, one can master the mind so that the mind does not master the bhikṣu; such a person is fit to dwell within the Gośṛṅga Garden.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the venerable ones, saying:
"We have each spoken according to our own eloquence, each explaining this meaning well in accordance with what was appropriate for our respective positions."
"Let us now go together to question the World-Honored One: how may a bhikṣu obtain happiness in this Gosīrṣa Park?
Whatever the World-Honored One may say, we shall respectfully practice it."
The bhikṣus replied, “It is so, Śāriputra!”
At that time, the great śrāvakas each took their respective companions and proceeded to where the Tathāgata was.
Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the great śrāvakas reported these circumstances in detail to the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One said: "Excellent!"
It is as Ānanda has said.
For what reason? Because the bhikṣu Ānanda is able to retain the Dharma he hears, he comprehensively gathers all dharmas, and he fully practices the holy life.
Having thus heard this Dharma well and not forgetting it, and being free from false views, he preaches the Dharma to the fourfold assembly; his words are neither confused nor abrupt.
"The words spoken by the bhikṣu Revata are indeed most excellent! For what reason?

Because he delights in secluded and quiet places, does not dwell among worldly people, constantly contemplates sitting in meditation, is free from contention, accords with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and dwells in solitude and stillness."
"How wonderful it is that the bhikṣu Aniruddha is also so!
For this reason, the bhikṣu Aniruddha is foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
With his divine eye, he beholds the trichiliocosm as clearly as a person with sight would look at a jewel in the palm of their hand."
The bhikṣu Aniruddha was likewise; with his divine eye, he surveyed this trichiliocosm without any doubt or difficulty.
"Now, how wonderful it is that the bhikṣu Kāśyapa is also thus!"
The reason for this is that the bhikṣu Kāśyapa himself practices the conduct of an araṇya-dweller and is further able to praise and speak of the practice of living in seclusion;
he himself practices alms-gathering and is further able to praise and extol the virtue of alms-gathering;
he himself wears robes of patched rags and is further able to praise and speak of the virtue of wearing robes of patched rags.
Being personally content with little, they are further able to praise and speak of the virtue of contentment;

dwelling themselves in mountain caves, they further praise and speak of the virtue of living in caves; having themselves achieved the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they are further able to teach others to achieve this fivefold body of Dharma (*pañcāṅgika-dharmakāya*); being capable of teaching through their own person, they are further able to instruct others to practice that Dharma.
“Excellent! Excellent! It is just as Maudgalyāyana has said.”

The reason for this is that the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana possesses great majestic power; he is foremost in supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and has attained mastery over his mind. Whatever he intends to accomplish, he is able to achieve it: he may manifest as a single body and then divide himself into ten billion, or merge back into one; he passes through stone walls without obstruction, leaping up and diving down with ease.

He is like a swift current that encounters no resistance, or like a bird in the sky that leaves no tracks. Just as the sun and moon shine everywhere, he can manifest his body even as far as the Brahma Heaven.
“Excellent! It is just as Śāriputra has said.
For what reason? Śāriputra is able to subdue his mind; it is not the mind that can subdue Śāriputra.”
When one wishes to enter samādhi, one is able to accomplish it without any difficulty or doubt, just as a householder takes his fine garments at will without any hesitation or difficulty.
The bhikṣu Śāriputra is also like this: he is able to subdue his mind; it is not that the mind can subdue Śāriputra. He enters samādhi at will, and all [attainments] appear before him.
“Excellent! Excellent, O bhikṣus!”
What you have said is each according to your own skillful means; however, now listen further to what I shall say.
How does a bhikṣu delight in the Gośṛṅga Park?

If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in dependence upon a village, he goes at the proper time, puts on his robes and takes his bowl, enters the village to beg for food. Having finished begging for food, he returns to his dwelling, washes his hands and face, and sits cross-legged under a tree with body erect and mind composed, binding his mindfulness before him.
That bhikṣu then thought: "Without breaking my sitting posture, I shall surely exhaust all outflows and realize the state of being without outflows.
At that moment, the bhikṣu’s mind with outflows was liberated.
In this way, bhikṣus, you should dwell in the Gośṛṅga Garden.
In this way, bhikṣus, by being constantly diligent and never indolent, there will be no place where you are not honored and followed.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the six virtues of the prayer for blessings.
Listen attentively! Reflect upon them well."
The bhikṣus replied, “So be it,
World-Honored One! At that time,
the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said: "What are those six virtues?
In this regard, a donor or patron accomplishes three dharmas."
What are the three qualities that a donor or patron fulfills?

In this regard, a donor or patron fulfills the faculty of faith, fulfills the virtue of ethical discipline, and fulfills learning; these are called the three qualities that a donor or patron fulfills.
The qualities of the gift further constitute three factors. What are these three?
They are that the object is accomplished in color, accomplished in taste, and accomplished in fragrance; these are the three factors.
"Monks, these are called the six things by which one attains great merit, becomes renowned for fame and virtue,
and receives the reward of the Deathless. Therefore, monks!"
If you wish to accomplish these six matters, you should practice giving.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to an immeasurable multitude.
At that moment, there was a bhikṣu seated in the assembly who thought to himself:
"May the Tathāgata address me with some discourse."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in the minds of the bhikṣus, addressed them:
"If there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to this thought:
'The Tathāgata is personally instructing and training me.'"
That bhikṣu, possessing the purity of precepts and free from blemish, practices śamatha and vipaśyanā, delighting in secluded and quiet places.

"If a bhikṣu desires robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicine for illness and weakness, he too should achieve the virtue of the precepts and practice by himself in a secluded place, remaining in harmony with śamatha and vipaśyanā."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu wishes to know contentment, he should be mindful of being fully endowed with the virtue of the precepts, practice by himself in a secluded place, and remain in harmony with both śamatha and vipaśyanā."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu wishes to be recognized and known by the fourfold assembly, by kings, by the people, and by all classes of sentient beings with form, he should be mindful of being fully endowed with the virtue of the precepts."
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu desires to seek the four dhyānas, without regret in his mind and without wavering, he should contemplate the accomplishment of the virtues of the precepts.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu desires to seek the four bases of psychic power, he too must be fully endowed with the virtues of the precepts."
“Furthermore, if a bhikṣu desires to seek the eight gates of liberation without obstruction, he should maintain mindfulness of the perfection of virtuous precepts.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu desires to seek the divine ear of far-reaching hearing, so as to hear the sounds of both devas and humans, he should maintain mindfulness of the perfection of virtuous precepts.”

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu desires to know the thoughts within the minds of others and their deficiencies in the faculties, he too should maintain mindfulness of the fullness of his own precepts and virtue."

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu desires to know the mental states of sentient beings—whether they have a mind of desire or a mind free from desire, a mind of hatred or a mind free from hatred, a mind of delusion or a mind free from delusion—he knows them as they truly are."
He knows as it truly is a mind with attachment and a mind without attachment; a mind with grasping and a mind without grasping. He knows as it truly is a distracted mind and an undistracted mind;

a sluggish mind and an unsluggish mind; a constricted mind and an unconstricted mind; a limited mind and an immeasurable mind; a painful mind and a painless mind; a concentrated mind and an unconcentrated mind; and a liberated mind and an unliberated mind. He knows these as they truly are.
One who desires such things should be mindful of the fullness of the virtue of the precepts.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu intends to attain immeasurable supernormal powers—dividing one body into countless forms and then recombining them into one; leaping up and sinking down with mastery; and transforming his body as far as the Brahma Heaven—he should be mindful of the fullness of the virtue of the precepts.

“Furthermore, if a bhikṣu desires to recollect his own past lives through countless kalpas—whether one birth, two births, up to a thousand births, hundreds of thousands of billions of births, or through kalpas of formation, kalpas of destruction, and kalpas of both formation and destruction beyond measure—he should recollect such immeasurable events as: ‘I died here and was born there; my name was so-and-so, my surname was so-and-so; or having passed away from there, I was born in this realm. While recollecting these events of countless kalpas, he should maintain mindfulness of the perfection of his precepts and virtue, free from other thoughts.”

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu should desire to seek the divine eye (divyacakṣus), so as to see clearly all classes of sentient beings—those in happy destinies and those in miserable destinies, those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance, whether handsome or unattractive—he knows them as they truly are."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who commit evil through body, speech, and mind, and slander the noble ones; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in hell.

Alternatively, there are sentient beings who perform good through body, speech, and mind, do not slander the noble ones, and possess right view in their minds and intentions; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in a happy place, in the heavens.
If one’s intention is such, one should be mindful of being fully endowed with the virtue of the precepts.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu intends to seek the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava), achieving the untainted liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—knowing as it truly is:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life (brahmacarya) is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further reception of a womb."
"He should be mindful of the fullness of his moral virtue (*śīla-guṇa*), reflecting within himself without distracted thoughts, dwelling in a secluded place. 'O bhikṣus!

You should be mindful of the fullness of your moral virtue; have no other thoughts. Be fully accomplished in dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*); fear even minor transgressions, let alone major ones!'"
If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to engage the Tathāgata in discussion, he should constantly be mindful of being fully endowed with the virtue of precepts;
having been fully endowed with the virtue of precepts, he should be mindful of being fully endowed with learning;
having been fully endowed with learning, he should be mindful of being fully endowed with generosity.
Having fulfilled generosity, one should further contemplate the fulfillment of wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

If a bhikṣu is complete in the aggregate of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, he will be seen, honored, and revered by devas, nāgas, and spirits; he will be venerated by both devas and humans.
Therefore, monks, you should keep in mind that one who is fully endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body is a field of merit for the world,
beyond whom none can surpass. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 29.
Ekottarika Āgama, Scroll Thirty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-seven: The Six Heavinesses (Ṣaḍ-guru-dharma), Part Two.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am currently observing the summer retreat in the city of Śrāvastī, and I wish to travel among the people to transform them through my teaching.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Now is precisely the right time.
Thereupon, Śāriputra rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet with his head, and withdrew.
Not long after Śāriputra had departed, a certain bhikṣu, harboring a mind of slander, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Śāriputra has been disputing with the bhikṣus and, refusing to repent, is now wandering among the people.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
“Go quickly and, carrying my words, summon Śāriputra.”
The bhikṣu replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda:
"You two shall summon all the bhikṣus from their respective rooms to the presence of the World-Honored One.
The reason for this is that Śāriputra has entered a samādhi and shall now deliver a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus each gathered at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, that bhikṣu, having received the World-Honored One’s instruction, went immediately to where Śāriputra was and said to him:
“The Tathāgata wishes to see you.”
At that time, Śāriputra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“Not long after you had departed, a bhikṣu of defiled conduct came to me and said to me:”
"It is said that the bhikṣu Śāriputra has been disputing with other bhikṣus and, without repenting of his transgression, is traveling and teaching among the people.
Is this indeed true?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“The Tathāgata himself shall know this.
The World-Honored One replied:
"I know it myself;
however, the great assembly now each harbors doubts.
You should now clarify and purify yourself through your own eloquence within this assembly."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Since emerging from my mother’s womb until now that I am nearly eighty years old, I have constantly reflected upon myself and have never killed a living being, nor have I ever spoken falsely—even in jest, I have not uttered a lie, nor have I ever incited discord between others.
It may be that such conduct occurred even when my mind was not focused.”
"World-Honored One, my mind is now pure;
how could I ever engage in strife or contention with those who practice the holy life?
It is just as this earth receives both the pure and the impure—it accepts excrement, urine, filth, and foulness, and it never rejects pus, blood, mucus, or saliva."
"However, this stage neither speaks of evil nor speaks of good; I am likewise so, World-Honored One!
Since my mind does not waver, how could I engage in disputes with fellow practitioners of the holy life and wander far away?"
Only those whose minds are not focused can do such a thing.
My mind is now upright; how could I engage in dispute with my fellow practitioners of the holy life and travel far away?
It is like water: it can purify fine things, and it can also purify things that are not fine.
That water does not form such thoughts as, "I shall purify this" or "I shall set this aside.
This case is likewise; since there is no such discrimination, how could one engage in quarreling with fellow practitioners of the holy life and wander far away?
Just as a blazing fire consumes mountains and forests, making no distinction between the beautiful and the ugly, and ultimately harboring no conceptual thought, so too am I;
how could I possibly have any intention to dispute with my fellow practitioners of the holy life?
It is also like sweeping and sprinkling water: one does not discriminate between the fine and the coarse, being able to remove everything without ever forming conceptual attachments.

It is like an ox that lacks its two horns; it is exceedingly gentle and kind, neither malicious nor violent, easy to lead and manage, going wherever it is directed without ever encountering doubt or difficulty.
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Such is my mind; I do not harbor thoughts of harming others, so how could I ever travel far away to engage in disputes with fellow practitioners of the holy life?"
"Just as a Caṇḍāla woman, wearing tattered and worn-out clothes, begs for alms among the people without any prohibitions, so it is with me, World-Honored One!
I am likewise without conceptual thought; why should I engage in disputes and travel afar?"
It is also like a cauldron of fat that leaks and breaks in various places; a person with eyes can see the fat leaking out from every part.
I am just like this, World-Honored One!
From among the nine orifices, impurities flow forth; how could one engage in dispute with a fellow practitioner of the holy life?
It is like a young and beautiful woman who, having a corpse tied around her neck, comes to loathe it.
World-Honored One!
I am likewise; my weariness with this body is no different from his. How could I engage in disputes with fellow practitioners of the holy life and travel afar?
"This is not so, World-Honored One!
You yourself shall know it, and that bhikṣu shall also know it.
Should such a thing truly exist, I pray that this bhikṣu accept my repentance."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"You should now repent of your transgressions yourselves.
For if you do not repent, your heads shall split into seven pieces."
At that time, the bhikṣu was seized with terror and his hair stood on end; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now recognize that I have offended Śāriputra. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance."
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣu! Confess to Śāriputra yourself; if you do not, your head shall be split into seven pieces."
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately prostrated himself at Śāriputra’s feet and said to him:
"I pray only that you accept my repentance; I was foolish and failed to distinguish the true from the false."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"You may now accept this bhikṣu’s repentance and stroke his head with your hand.
The reason for this is that had you not accepted this bhikṣu’s confession, his head would have split into seven pieces."
At that time, Śāriputra stroked his head with his hand and said to the bhikṣu, “I accept your confession!

To be foolish and deluded is human; yet within this Buddha-dharma, which is exceedingly vast and expansive, it is excellent indeed for one who is able to repent of their transgressions at the proper time!”
"I now accept your repentance; henceforth, do not commit such offenses again.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
At that moment, Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"Do not commit them again.
For there are six things that lead to hell, six things that lead to rebirth in heaven, and six things that lead to the state of Nirvana."
What are the six?
First, wishing to harm another, one gives rise to this harmful intent and feels such joy and exultation that one cannot contain oneself;
second, one instructs others to harm another, giving rise to a harmful intent therein; [and so forth].
Having succeeded in harming others, one gives rise to joy within, thinking, "I shall obtain this ill-repute";
yet before that event has even occurred, one already feels swift sorrow and anxiety.
These are called the six dharmas that cause a person to fall into the evil destinies.
"What are the six things that lead a person to a good destination? They are:

being fully endowed with bodily restraint, being fully endowed with verbal restraint, being fully endowed with mental restraint, purity of livelihood, a mind free from intent to harm, and a mind free from envy and jealousy."
It is said that by possessing these six qualities, one is born in a favorable realm.
"How does one cultivate six qualities to reach nirvana?
They are the so-called six dharmas of mindfulness."
What are the six? They are:
practicing loving-kindness with the body without blemish;
practicing loving-kindness with the mouth without blemish; [and so forth].
He practices loving-kindness with a mind free from blemish;
when obtaining requisites for livelihood, he is able to share them equally with others without any sense of stinginess;
he upholds the prohibitive precepts without flaw, as esteemed by the wise.
Such precepts are able to fully encompass all wrong views, right views, and the noble path of deliverance, and are able to bring about the exhaustion of the root of suffering.
Thus, all such views are made entirely clear.
These are called the six dharmas by which one attains nirvāṇa. Now, bhikṣu,
you should seek skillful means and practice these six dharmas.
"In this way, bhikṣu,
you should train yourself.
At that time, that bhikṣu rose again from his seat and paid homage at the feet of Śāriputra.
"I now again offer this repentance to myself: like one who is foolish and deluded, I failed to distinguish the true from the false.
I only pray, Śāriputra, that you will accept my confession of transgression, so that I shall not commit it again hereafter."
Śāriputra said: "I grant you leave to repent!
Within the Dharma of the noble ones, there is immense breadth and magnanimity; you are able to reform your past and cultivate yourself for the future—do not commit such offenses again."
At that time, having heard what Śāriputra had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7 (Seven): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the foremost and most empty dharma; you should contemplate it well.
The bhikṣus replied: [We shall do so.]
"So be it, Blessed One! At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The Blessed One said:
“What is this so-called foremost and most empty dharma?

When the eye arises, it simply arises, yet no place of origin is seen; when it ceases, it simply ceases, yet no place of cessation is seen—apart from the dharma of conventional designations and the dharma of dependent origination.”

What are conventional designations and dependent origination? They are as follows: when this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises. Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; birth conditions aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair, which are beyond calculation.
Thus is this aggregate of suffering brought about through these causes and conditions: "When this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases.

With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease; and with the cessation of aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair all utterly cease and vanish, except for the conventional designation of phenomena."

The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*): when they arise, they simply arise, yet one does not know their place of origin; when they cease, they simply cease, yet one does not know their place of cessation—except for the phenomena that are merely conventional designations.
Regarding those phenomena designated by conventional names: when this arises, it arises; when this ceases, it ceases.

These six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not created by any person; they are likewise the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense bases, which are not created by any person. There is no embryo produced by a father and mother; rather, it exists through causes and conditions. This too is a mere designation; only when there is prior sensory contact (*pratigha*) does it subsequently come to be.
It is just as when one drills wood to seek fire: because there is first the friction of the pieces against each other, fire subsequently arises;
yet the fire does not come from the wood, nor does it exist apart from the wood.
Furthermore, if someone were to split the wood in search of fire, they would still not obtain it; it is only through the coming together of causes and conditions that fire then exists.
The arising of disease through these six sense-faculties is likewise so: it all arises from the convergence of conditions within them.
When these six bases arise, they simply arise, yet their coming is not seen; when they cease, they simply cease, yet their ceasing is not seen.
Apart from this dharma of provisional designation, they exist due to the union of father and mother.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"First one receives the fetal membrane; Gradually it becomes like frozen butter, Then it further becomes like a fleshy protuberance, And finally it transforms into a shape resembling a form."
The head, neck, and shoulders form; then hands, feet, and fingers arise;
the various limbs and joints develop one by one; hair, body hair, nails, and teeth are completed.
