When the mother partakes of food and drink, of various and manifold delicacies, [the embryo likewise receives nourishment].
The vital essence is used to sustain life, serving as the original basis for conception.
The physical form is brought to full completion, and the various faculties are without deficiency;
born from the mother, such is the suffering of conception.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that it is through the conjunction of causes and conditions that this body exists.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!
Within the body of a single person, there are three hundred and sixty bones, ninety-nine thousand pores, five hundred vessels, five hundred sinews, and eighty thousand families of worms.”
"Monks, you should know that the body of the six sense bases is subject to such calamities and transformations.
Monks, you should reflect and contemplate: 'Who created these bones amidst such suffering?'"
"Who joined together these sinews and veins?
Who created these eighty thousand families of worms?
At that time, as that bhikṣu engaged in such reflection and contemplation, he immediately attained one of two fruits: either the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin) or arhatship.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Three hundred and sixty bones Are within this human body;
As expounded by the Buddhas of antiquity, I now proclaim them as well."
There are five hundred sinews, and the number of vessels is likewise;
there are eighty thousand kinds of worms and ninety-nine thousand hairs.
One should contemplate the body in this way; O bhikṣu, exert yourself with diligence!
One swiftly attains the path of Arhatship and proceeds to the realm of Nirvāṇa.
This Dharma is entirely empty and tranquil; it is craved by the foolish, yet the wise heart rejoices upon hearing this fundamental teaching of emptiness.
“Monks, this is called the first and supreme dharma of emptiness, which I have taught to you.
This is the dharma of practice taught by the Tathāgata; out of a heart of compassion, I have now fulfilled my duty.”
You should always mindfully practice this Dharma; dwelling in a secluded place, sit in meditation and contemplate, without falling into indolence.
If you do not practice now, it will be of no avail when you regret it later!
This is my instruction. Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (Eight) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went to where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
Then, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “Gautama!
"Kṣatriya, what do you seek today?
What are your practices?
To which teaching do you adhere?"
What is his ultimate goal?
What does this brahmin seek to attain?
What are his karmic activities?
To what teaching do you adhere?
What is your ultimate concern?
And what does Your Majesty seek to attain today?
What kind of conduct and practice do you follow?
To what teaching are you devoted?
And what is it that you seek to ultimately realize?
What do these thieves seek today?
What are their past deeds and practices?
To what teaching do they adhere?
For what purpose do you seek the ultimate?
What does the woman intend to seek today?
What karmic actions has she performed?
"To what teaching do you adhere?
What is it that you seek to realize?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin, saying:

“Those of the Kṣatriya caste always delight in fighting and litigation; they possess many technical skills and take pleasure in manual labor, pursuing their objectives to completion without ever ceasing midway.”
The brahmin asked: "What does the brahmin seek in his heart?
The World-Honored One replied:
“The brahmin’s mind delights in incantations; he intends to establish a household, yet he finds pleasure in secluded places, his heart set upon the Brahma Heaven.
He asked again: “What does the king seek in his heart?”
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin, you should know that the king’s desire is for the administration of the state; his intent lies in weapons and armaments, and he is greedily attached to wealth and treasures."
“What does the thief seek? The World-Honored One replied, “The thief’s intent is to steal;
his mind dwells on wickedness, desiring that human beings remain ignorant of what he has done.”
“What does a woman’s mind seek? The World-Honored One replied, “A woman’s mind seeks a man;
she is greedily attached to wealth and treasures, her heart is bound to sons and daughters, and her mind desires independence.”
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
“I know all such transformations as they truly are and not falsely.
Today, what does the bhikṣu seek?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Endowed with the full virtue of the precepts, his mind wanders through the Way and its teachings, his intent fixed upon the Four Noble Truths,
desiring to reach Nirvana— this is what a bhikṣu seeks."
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-vasa addressed the Blessed One, saying: “It is so,
Blessed One!”
The mind of a bhikṣu in its practice cannot be diverted; such is indeed the reality of its meaning, Gautama!
Nirvāṇa is the ultimate bliss.

What the Tathāgata has spoken is exceedingly profound: it is like one who was blind regaining sight, the deaf regaining hearing, or those in darkness seeing the light. What the Tathāgata has spoken today is likewise so, without any difference.
"I now have many state affairs to attend to and wish to return to my quarters.
The World-Honored One said,
"You should know that this is the right time."
At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-Āsrava went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Are there any bhikṣus here who, practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) without deficiency or flaw, cultivate the holy life in purity?"
The World-Honored One said:
“If there is a person who is fully endowed with the precepts and commits no transgressions, this is called the pure cultivation and attainment of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, O Brahmin!”

If one sees forms with the eye, yet gives rise to no conceptual attachment, gives rise to no discursive consciousness, eliminates evil perceptions, and abandons unwholesome dharmas, thereby attaining the complete purity of the eye faculty—this is called a person who purely cultivates the holy life.

If, when the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue perceives flavors, the body perceives tactile sensations, and the mind cognizes mental phenomena, one is entirely without the perception of consciousness, does not give rise to conceptual thoughts, and thus purely cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*), perfecting the faculty of the mind—such a person cultivates the holy life without any deficiency or flaw.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of person does not cultivate the holy life and is not fully endowed with pure conduct?
The World-Honored One replied:
"If there are those who associate together, this is called non-celibacy.
The brāhmaṇa said to the Buddha,
"What kind of person is one whose outflows are not complete?"
The World-Honored One said:
"If there is a person who engages in sexual intercourse with a woman, or touches her hands or feet, and harbors this in their heart without forgetting it."
"This is what is meant, brahmin:
conduct is not fulfilled, various leakages of lust flow forth, and one is associated with lust, anger, and delusion.
Furthermore, brahmin:"
Or he may engage in flirtatious dalliance with women, exchanging words with them.
This, brahmin, is called a person whose conduct is incomplete;
one who is defiled by lust, anger, and delusion, and who does not fully practice the holy life or cultivate pure conduct.
"Furthermore, brahmin!
If there is a woman who gazes with an evil eye without averting her gaze, one immediately gives rise therein to thoughts of lust, anger, and delusion, and various distracted notions arise."
"This is what is meant, brahmin:
this person's holy life is impure; he does not cultivate the holy life.
Furthermore, brahmin:"
Furthermore, if there is someone who hears from afar the sound of weeping or the sound of laughter, and therein gives rise to lust, anger, and delusion, or conceives various distracted thoughts.
"O brahmin, this is called a person who does not practice the holy life with purity; he is associated with lust, anger, and delusion, and his conduct is incomplete."
"Furthermore, brahmin!
If there is someone who has previously seen a woman, and later gives rise to perceptions, recollecting her head and eyes, and conceiving thoughts therein;
if, in a secluded place, they give rise to lust, anger, and delusion, which are associated with unwholesome conduct."
"Thus it is, brahmin!
This person does not cultivate the holy life.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-āsava addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!
This śramaṇa Gautama knows what is the holy life (brahmacarya) and also knows what is not the holy life;..."
I also know defiled conduct and I also know undefiled conduct. Why is this so?
Because I now also give rise to this thought: among all people, when men and women join their hands and feet together, they give rise to various disordered thoughts.
At that time, I immediately formed this thought:
"This person's conduct is impure; he is associated with lust, anger, and delusion.
As for the foremost object of sensory contact, it is the woman.

The first desirable thing is as follows: namely, when eyes gaze at one another, that woman may speak or smile, thereby ensnaring the man; or she may engage in conversation with him, thereby ensnaring the man.
At that time, I thought to myself:
"These six men all practice impure conduct.

What the Tathāgata has spoken today is exceedingly profound—like a blind person regaining their sight, a lost person finding the road, a fool hearing of the Way, or a person with eyes seeing forms; such is the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. From this day forward, I shall no longer kill living beings; I only pray that you will accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka).
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-śroṇa, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in a grove outside the city of Vaiśālī together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the Venerable Aśvajit dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
Then, from afar, Satyaka Nirgranthīputra saw Aśvajit approaching and went up to him, saying:
"What kind of doctrine does your teacher preach?"
"What instructions do you have?
With what admonitions do you teach the Dharma to your disciples?
The horse trainer replied:
“Brahmin! Form is impermanent;
that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self; that which is non-self is empty. That which is empty is not mine, nor do I belong to it.”
Such is that which the wise study. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent;

these five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) being impermanent are suffering; that which is suffering is non-self; that which is non-self is empty; and that which is empty is not mine, nor do I belong to it.
"If you wish to know, such is the meaning of the instruction taught by my teacher, and such is the meaning he has explained to his disciples.
At that time, Nigaṇṭha covered his ears with both hands and said:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Stop, horse trainer!
I do not wish to hear such words."
"If the ascetic Gautama were to hold such a teaching, I would truly not wish to hear it.
Why is this? According to my doctrine, form is eternal; according to the doctrine of the ascetic, it is impermanent."
"On what day shall we see the śramaṇa Gautama and engage him in debate, so that we may eliminate the śramaṇa Gautama’s perverted mind?
At that time, five hundred youths from the city of Vaiśālī gathered in one place, desiring to hold a discussion.
At that time, Nigaṇṭha went to where the five hundred youths were and said to them,
"All of you, come together and go to the place where the śramaṇa Gautama is."
The reason for this is that I wish to engage in debate with that śramaṇa Gautama, so that he may come to see the path of the True Dharma.
Regarding what the śramaṇa says—that form is impermanent—according to my doctrine, form is permanent.
It is just as when a strong man holds a long-haired sheep by its fleece; he can move it east or west according to his will without any difficulty or hesitation.
I am now likewise: when debating with that śramaṇa Gautama, I can seize or let go of him as I please, without any difficulty or hesitation.
"Just as a fierce elephant, though savage and possessing six tusks, sports in the deep mountains without any difficulty, so too am I now;
when engaging in debate with him, there shall likewise be no doubt or difficulty."
It is just as if two strong men were to seize a weakling and roast him over a fire, turning him over as they please without any hesitation or difficulty;
even so, I now engage in debate with him without any hesitation or difficulty.
"In my debates, I am even capable of harming elephants, let alone humans.
I can also command elephants to go east, west, south, or north; how could they not be like humans?"

"If even these insentient objects—the beams and pillars of this lecture hall—can be moved by me, how much more so can I prevail in debate with a human being? I shall cause his blood to gush from his face and bring about his death."
Among them, some youths spoke thus:
“The Nirgrantha will ultimately be unable to debate with the śramaṇa; rather, it is only feared that the śramaṇa Gautama will debate with the Nirgrantha.”
Some might say: "The śramaṇa does not debate with the Nigaṇṭha, but the Nigaṇṭha is able to debate with the śramaṇa.
At that time, the Nigaṇṭha thought to himself:
"Even if what the śramaṇa Gautama says were like that of the bhikṣu Aśvajit, it would be sufficient for comparison.
If there is any truth in it, we shall know upon hearing it."
At that time, Nigaṇṭha, surrounded by five hundred youths before and behind him, went to where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "How is it, Gautama?
What instruction do you have, and with what instruction do you train your disciples?"
The Buddha told Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta: "What I have taught is that form (*rūpa*) is impermanent;

that which is impermanent is suffering (*duḥkha*); that which is suffering is non-self (*anātman*); that which is non-self is empty (*śūnya*). That which is empty does not belong to me, nor do I belong to it.

Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*) are all impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self; that which is non-self is empty. That which is empty does not belong to me, nor do I belong to it."
"Such is the meaning of my instruction. Nigaṇṭha replied,
"I do not wish to hear this meaning."
"The reason for this is that, according to my understanding of the meaning, form (*rūpa*) is permanent.
The World-Honored One told him:
"For now, concentrate your mind and contemplate the subtle principle; only then should you speak."
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied, "What I have now spoken of as form is permanent; the meaning of this for these five hundred youths is likewise so.
The World-Honored One said:
"What you have now said regarding form is that it is permanent; the meaning of this for these five hundred youths is likewise so.
The World-Honored One told him, "Now, you speak with your own eloquence; why do you cite those five hundred people?"
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied:
"I now declare that form is permanent; what kind of discourse do you, O Śramaṇa, wish to have?
The Blessed One said:
"I now declare that form is impermanent and likewise without self.

This form exists through the provisional conjunction of numerical aggregates; it lacks reality, being neither firm nor solid, like a ball of snow. Such things are subject to destruction and are subject to change."
Now you say that form is permanent; I shall question you further, so answer me as you please.
What do you think, Nigaṇṭha-putra?
Does a Wheel-Turning Sage King attain sovereignty over his own kingdom?
"Furthermore, that great king should not release those who ought not to be released, nor bind those who ought not to be bound;
could such a thing be possible? Nigaṇṭha replied:
"This Holy King possesses such sovereign power that he can execute those who should not be executed, and he can bind those who should not be bound."
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Nigaṇṭha?
Would a Wheel-Turning Sage King also grow old?"
"Why is it that your head is white, your face is wrinkled, and your garments are soiled and dusty?
At that time, Nigaṇṭha remained silent and did not reply.
The World-Honored One questioned him a second and a third time, yet he likewise remained silent and did not reply a second and a third time.
At that time, the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, holding a vajra-pestle in his hand, spoke from mid-air:
"If you do not now answer this debater, I shall split your head into seven pieces before the Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Nyagrodha:
"Now, look into the sky. Then, Nyagrodha looked up into the sky and saw the Vajrapāṇi Guhyapada, and he also heard a voice from the sky:
"If you do not respond to the Tathāgata’s discourse, I shall split your head into seven pieces.
Having seen this, he was struck with terror and his hair stood on end;
he addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "I pray only that Gautama will grant me refuge; I shall now respond to your further inquiry."
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Nigaṇṭha!
Would a Wheel-Turning Sage King also grow old?"
"Will you too have your hair turn white, your teeth fall out, your skin become slack,
and your face become wrinkled? Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied, "Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Although you have spoken these words, according to my doctrine, form (*rūpa*) is eternal.
The World-Honored One said:
"Reflect well before you respond; what you have said previously and now do not correspond in meaning."
"But when it comes to the matter of the noble wheel-turning monarch, will he also grow old?
Will his hair also turn white, his teeth fall out, his skin become slack, and his face become wrinkled? Nigaṇṭha replied:
“The Wheel-Turning Sage King allows himself to grow old.
The World-Honored One said:
“The Wheel-Turning Sage King is always able to exercise sovereignty over his own kingdom; for what reason, then, can he not ward off old age, ward off illness, and ward off death?”
"I am not subject to old age, sickness, or death; I am the one who corresponds to the eternal.
If you wish for it to be so, would that principle be acceptable?
At that time, Nigaṇṭha remained silent and did not respond; he was sorrowful and unhappy, sitting quietly without speaking.
At that time, the body of Nigaṇṭha was covered in sweat; the sweat soiled his robes, permeated his seat, and even reached the ground.
The World-Honored One said to him: "Nigaṇṭha!"
"Among this great assembly, you shall let out a lion’s roar:
'You youths, come with me to the presence of Gautama to engage him in debate; he shall be subdued like a long-haired sheep, to be led wherever we wish without hesitation or difficulty.'"
It is also like a great elephant entering deep water, swimming about at will without any fear;
it is also like two strong men seizing a weak man and roasting him over a fire, turning him over as they please.
Furthermore, you said:

"I am always able to debate with great elephants; even though such beams, pillars, grasses, and trees are all insentient, when I debate with them, I can make them bend and stretch, lower and raise themselves, and even cause sweat to flow from beneath their axils."
At that time, the World-Honored One lifted his three Dharma robes and showed them to Nijianzi, saying:
"Behold how there is no sweat flowing from the Tathāgata’s armpits, whereas you today have instead produced such sweat that it even drenches the ground."
At that time, Nigaṇṭha remained silent and did not respond.
Then, a youth named Thoma was present in that assembly.
At that moment, the youth Thoma addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am now capable of performing what must be done, and I also wish to speak.
The World-Honored One told him,
"Speak as you please."
The youth Dhumaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is as if there were a fine bathing pool not far from a village, yet that bathing pool was infested with many-legged insects."

However, when the people of the village—men and women, young and old—go to the bathing pool and these insects emerge, they each take up tiles or stones to seize the insects, beating them until their hands and feet are wounded and broken; even if those insects desire to return to the water, it can never happen.
This Nigaṇṭha was just like that: though his initial resolve was fierce as he debated with the Tathāgata, his mind harbored malice and was further possessed by arrogance.
The Tathāgata has exhausted and eliminated them all, leaving nothing remaining.
This Nigaṇṭha shall never again be able to come before the Tathāgata to engage in debate.
At that time, Nigaṇṭha spoke to the youth Sāḷha, saying:
"You are now foolish and deluded, unable to distinguish the true from the false; I will not debate with you, but rather with the śramaṇa Gautama."
At that time, Nigaṇṭha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall explain it further once the principles have been asked.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Nigaṇṭha, what do you think?
Is it possible for a Wheel-Turning Sage King to prevent old age, sickness, and death from occurring?
Could such a holy great king fulfill this wish?"
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied, “This wish cannot be fulfilled. [The Buddha asked:
“If one wishes for something to have this form, or wishes for it to be without this form, can that be fulfilled?”
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta replied: "It is not so, Gautama!"
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Nigaṇṭha! Is form permanent?"
"Is this impermanent? Nigaṇṭha replied, "Form is impermanent."
"Furthermore, if it were impermanent and subject to change, would you still regard this as 'I' and acknowledge that 'I' am that which exists? He replied, "No."
"Gautama! Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent,
or are they impermanent?"
He replied, "Impermanent,
World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said:
"Furthermore, if it were impermanent and subject to change, would you ever perceive such a thing? He replied, "No."
The World-Honored One asked:
"Are these five aggregates of clinging permanent or impermanent? Nigaṇṭha replied:
"It is impermanent.
The Buddha said,
"Even if it were impermanent and subject to change, have you ever seen such a thing?"
He replied, "No. [The Buddha asked,] "How so, Nigaṇṭha?"
"Does your statement that this is permanent not contradict the underlying principle?
At that time, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am now foolish and fail to distinguish the ultimate truth; thus I harbored such a thought and engaged in debate with Gautama, claiming that form is permanent."
It is just as when a fierce beast such as a lion sees a person coming from afar;
would it have any feeling of fear?
Certainly not! Today, the Tathāgata is likewise; there is not even a hair’s breadth of [fear].
I am now deluded and have not yet clarified the profound meaning, yet I have dared to disturb you.

The errors of the śramaṇa Gautama are as numerous as the gains of sight for the blind, the restoration of hearing for the deaf, the finding of a path by the lost, or the seeing of forms by those without eyes.
The śramaṇa Gautama is likewise; he teaches the Dharma through innumerable skillful means.

I now take refuge in the śramaṇa Gautama, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I request to be accepted as an upāsaka. I shall no longer kill living beings. May Gautama and the community of bhikṣus grant me their favor!
"Please accept my invitation; I wish to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When Nigaṇṭha saw that the World-Honored One had accepted by silence, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and departed.
He went to where the Licchavi youths were; having arrived, he said to them,
"The provisions for my sustenance that you ought to provide me with, give them to me at the proper time, and not at an improper time."
"I now invite the śramaṇa Gautama and the community of bhikṣus; they shall be provided with a meal tomorrow.
At that time, each of the youths prepared the necessary utensils and implements for food and drink, which they brought and presented to him.
At that time, Nigaṇṭha prepared various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink during that very night, spread out fine seats, and said:
"The time has come; now is precisely the right moment. We only pray that you will deign to visit us."

At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and accompanied by the community of bhikṣus, entered Vaiśālī and proceeded to the house of the Nirgrantha.
Having arrived, they took their seats, and the community of bhikṣus likewise sat down in their respective order.

At that time, when Nigaṇṭha saw that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, he personally served various kinds of food and drink. Seeing that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus had finished eating, he offered pure water, then took a small seat and sat before the Tathāgata, desiring to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually spoke to him with a sublime discourse;

that is to say, a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, and a discourse on rebirth in heaven; [he explained] that sensual desires are defiled and evil, that sexual conduct is impure, and that the way of escape is bliss.

At that time, seeing that Nigaṇṭha’s mind was opened and his intellect liberated, the World-Honored One fully expounded to him the Dharma that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly teach: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that moment, while still seated upon his mat, Nigaṇṭha’s various defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Then the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“Of all sacrifices, the fire sacrifice is supreme; Among poems and books, the hymns are foremost.”
Among humans, the king is supreme; among all streams, the ocean is the source;
among stars, the moon is the most bright; and among luminaries, the sun is the most excellent.
From the zenith and nadir, as well as the four directions, whatever things are produced upon the various lands—
"Among gods and the class of human beings, the Buddha is the unsurpassed Honored One;
those who wish to seek his virtue find that the Three Buddhas are supreme.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the five hundred disciples of Nigaṇṭha heard that their teacher had accepted the Buddha’s instruction and transformation.
Having heard this, they each said to one another, "How can our great master come to take Gautama as his teacher?"
At that time, the disciples emerged from the city of Vaiśālī and stood upon the middle road.
At that moment, the Nirgrantha was on his way to the Buddha’s dwelling to listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to Nigaṇṭha, gladdening him.
Having heard the Dharma, Nigaṇṭha rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew.
At that time, when the disciples of Nigaṇṭha saw their teacher coming from afar, they said to one another:
"This disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama is now approaching on the path; each of you take up clods of earth and stones and kill him!"
At that time, having heard that Nigaṇṭha had been killed by his own disciples, the youths went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the young boys said to the World-Honored One:
"The Nigaṇṭha whom the Tathāgata was teaching has now been killed by his own disciples."
"Now that his life has ended, where has he been reborn?
The World-Honored One replied:

"That was a person of virtue who was fully endowed with the Four Noble Truths; having extinguished the three fetters, he became a Srotāpanna and will certainly reach the end of suffering. Having passed away today, he has been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. After he has seen Maitreya Buddha, he shall reach the end of suffering."
"This is its meaning; you should reflect upon it and practice accordingly.
At that time, the youths said to the World-Honored One:
"How extraordinary!
How extraordinary!
This Nigaṇṭha has come to the World-Honored One to engage in debate, yet he has instead bound himself with his own arguments and come to receive the Tathāgata’s transformation.

Indeed, one who beholds the Tathāgata will never encounter falsehood; it is just as when someone enters the sea to retrieve treasures—they will surely achieve their goal and never return empty-handed.
"It is just so with this: any sentient beings who come to the presence of the Tathāgata will surely obtain the treasure of the Dharma and shall never return empty-handed.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the youths, causing them to rejoice.
At that time, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the youths rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and then withdrew.
At that time, the youths, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 30; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 31.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Eight: On Powers (Bala-varga), Part One. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are six ordinary powers.”
What are these six? Infants take crying as their power; when they wish to say something, they must first cry.
Women take anger as their power; it is only after relying upon anger that they speak what they have to say.
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas take patience as their strength; they constantly maintain a humble mind, humbling themselves before others before speaking of themselves.
Kings take arrogance as their strength, and they speak of themselves by means of such haughty power.
However, Arhats take single-minded diligence as their strength, and thus they speak of themselves.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have perfected great compassion; with great compassion as their power, they extensively benefit sentient beings.
Thus it is said, O Bhikṣu:
there are these six powers that are ever-present in ordinary beings.
Therefore, monks! Always mindfully practice this great loving-kindness and compassion. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“You should contemplate the perception of impermanence and cultivate it extensively. Having contemplated and cultivated the perception of impermanence extensively, you will completely sever craving for the realm of desire, as well as craving for the realms of form and formlessness, and you will also sever ignorance and conceit.”
It is just as when fire burns up grass and trees until they are completely exhausted without remainder, leaving no trace behind; this is also like that.

If one cultivates the perception of impermanence, one will utterly sever craving for sense-desires, craving for form, and craving for the formless, such that ignorance and conceit are forever eliminated without remainder.
For this reason, monks: when one cultivates the perception of impermanence, the mind becomes free from desire;
with that mind free from desire, one is able to discern phenomena, contemplate their meaning, and remains without sorrow, grief, suffering, or affliction.
By contemplating the meaning of the Dharma, he is free from delusion and error in his practice.
If he sees those who are quarreling, he thinks to himself:
"These worthy gentlemen do not cultivate the perception of impermanence, nor do they widely disseminate the perception of impermanence; it is for this reason that they have come to this dispute."
Because they engage in strife and contention, they do not contemplate the true meaning;
because they do not contemplate the true meaning, their minds become deluded.
Clinging to this ignorance and confusion, at the end of their lives they enter the three evil realms: among hungry ghosts, animals, and in the hells.

"Therefore, bhikṣus! You should cultivate the perception of impermanence and disseminate the perception of impermanence; then, thoughts of ill will and delusion will cease, and you will be able to contemplate phenomena as well as their meaning."
If, after the end of life, one is born in the three good destinations— born among gods, among humans,
or on the path to nirvāṇa— it is thus, O bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on the banks of the Ukkācelā River in the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, the World-Honored One went beneath a tree, personally spread out a seat, and sat down; he straightened his body and concentrated his mind, binding his mindfulness before him.
At that time, a certain brahmin went to that place.
Thereupon, the brahmin saw that the World-Honored One’s footprints were exquisite; having seen them, he immediately had this thought:
"Whose footprints are these?"
"Are you a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a gandharva, an asura, a human, or a non-human?
Or are you my ancestor, Brahmā?"
At that time, the brahmin followed the tracks forward and saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree, with body erect and mind upright, his mindfulness fixed before him.
Having seen him, he spoke these words: "Is this a deva?"
The World-Honored One said,
"I am not a deva. [The interlocutor asked,] "Are you a gandharva?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"I am not a gandharva. [The interlocutor asked,] "Are you then a nāga prince?"
He replied, "I am not a nāga. "Are you a yakṣa?"
The Buddha replied to the brahmin:
"I am not a yakṣa; I am your grandfather."
The Buddha replied,
"I am not your grandfather.
At that time, the brahmin asked the World-Honored One:
"Who are you now? The World-Honored One replied:

"Where there is craving, there is grasping; where there is grasping, there is craving. Through the convergence of causes and conditions, they thus give rise to one another. In this way, these five aggregates of suffering continue without interruption."

"Once one has understood craving, one then understands the five desires, as well as the six external sense objects and the six internal sense bases; thus one understands the beginning and end of this mass of suffering (skandhas).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In the world there are five desires, With the mind as the sixth that arises."
"By knowing the six internal and external [bases], one should contemplate the end of suffering.
Therefore, one should seek skillful means to extinguish these six internal and external matters.
Thus it is, O Brahmin!"
"You should train yourself in this way.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, that brahmin contemplated and practiced it until it remained ever-present in his mind; immediately upon sitting there, all defilements were exhausted, and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that brahmin rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When I was originally a bodhisattva and had not yet attained the Buddha-way, I had this thought:
'This world is subject to extreme toil and suffering;'"
"There is birth, there is old age, there is sickness, and there is death; yet these five aggregates of clinging do not reach their ultimate origin.
At that time, I further thought to myself:
"By what causes and conditions do birth, old age, sickness, and death arise?"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do these calamities arise?
While reflecting on this, he further gave rise to this thought:
"Where there is birth, there is old age, sickness, and death."
At that time, while reflecting in this way, he further gave rise to this thought:
"By what cause and condition does birth arise?
This arises from existence (*bhava*).
Again, he gave rise to this thought:
"By what cause does 'existence' come to be?
While reflecting upon this, there arose in him this thought:
"This existence arises from grasping.
He further reflected:
"From what does this grasping arise?"
At that time, observing with wisdom, he saw that feeling arises from craving.
He further reflected:
"From what does this craving arise?"
He observed it again deeply and saw that from sensation (vedanā) arises craving (tṛṣṇā).
He further reflected:
"From what does this sensation arise?"
While performing this contemplation, he realized that this sensation exists because of contact.
He further reflected:
"From what does this contact arise?"
When this thought arose in me, [I realized that] this contact and pleasure exist conditioned by the six sense bases.
Then I reflected further:
"From what do these six sense bases arise?"
While observing this, I saw that from name-and-form (nāmarūpa) the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise.
Then I further thought: "By what is name-and-form brought into being?"
When he observed this, he further saw that name-and-form exists by reason of consciousness.
"By what is this consciousness produced? When he observed this, he saw that consciousness arises from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
At that time, I again had this thought:
"From what do volitional formations arise?
When I examined this, I saw that volitional formations arise from ignorance.

Ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; birth conditions aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair, beyond measure.
This is what is called the habitual accumulation of the intense aggregates of suffering. At that time, I further thought:
"By what causes and conditions do birth, old age, sickness, and death cease?"
As I observed this, there was the cessation of birth, and the cessation of old age, sickness, and death.
Then, again, this thought arose in me:
"By what means is there no birth?"
"Observing the origin of this birth, there is cessation; when there is birth, there is cessation.
He further reflected:
"By what means does it cease to exist?"
Then this thought arose in me:
"Where there is no grasping, there is no becoming.
Then this thought arose in me:
"By what is feeling extinguished?
While observing this, he saw that with the extinction of craving, feeling is extinguished.
He then gave rise to this thought:
"By what means is craving extinguished?
He observed again and saw that with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
He then reflected further:
"By what means is feeling extinguished?
While observing this, he realized that with the cessation of contact (*sparśa*), feeling ceases.
He further reflected:
"By what means is contact (sparśa) extinguished?
When he observes this, he sees that with the cessation of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact ceases.
He further observes: by what means are these six sense bases extinguished?
When observing, one sees that with the cessation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) cease. Furthermore,
observing by what cause name-and-form ceases,
one sees that with the cessation of consciousness (vijñāna), name-and-form ceases.
He further examines by what means this consciousness ceases:
with the cessation of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness ceases.
He further examines by what means these volitional formations cease.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease.
With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;
with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases.
With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases.
With the cessation of suffering, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, existence ceases.
When existence ceases, birth ceases;
when birth ceases, aging and illness cease; when aging and illness cease, death ceases. This is called the cessation of the five aggregates of clinging.
"At that time, I again gave rise to this thought:
'This consciousness is the primary source that causes humans to undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death;
yet it cannot itself know the original root from which this birth, old age, sickness, and death arise.'"
"It is just as if there were a person traveling through a mountain forest, following a narrow path.
After proceeding a short distance further, he sees an old main road where people of ancient times used to travel."

At that time, that person returned to this path and proceeded a short distance further, where he saw old city walls, gardens, and bathing pools, all of which were lush and flourishing; however, there were no inhabitants within that city.
Having seen this, the man returned to his own country and went before the king, saying:
"Yesterday, while wandering through the mountains and forests, I saw a magnificent city with lush and flourishing trees; however, there were no people within that city."
"Great King!
You may allow the people to dwell in that city.
At that time, having heard these words from the man, the king immediately settled the people there.
However, this city and its walls have returned to their former state, and the population is flourishing with incomparable happiness.

"Monks, you should know that in the past, before I had attained the state of a Bodhisattva, I was practicing the Way in the mountains. Seeing the places where the Buddhas of antiquity had traveled, I followed those paths and immediately came to know the original source from which birth, old age, sickness, and death arise. I discerned that there is arising and ceasing; I fully understood the suffering of birth, the origin of birth, the cessation of birth, and the path leading to the cessation of birth. It was the same for existence, sensation, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, volitional formations, and ignorance."

When ignorance arises, volitional formations arise; that which is produced by volitional formations further depends upon consciousness. Now, through clarity regarding consciousness, I shall explain this root to the fourfold assembly.

You should all know the origin from which this root arises: know suffering, know its accumulation, know its cessation, and know the path. Make your mindfulness distinct so as to understand the six sense bases; once you understand the six sense bases, you will understand birth, old age, sickness, and death. With the cessation of the six sense bases, birth, old age, sickness, and death cease.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means to extinguish the six sense bases. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings.
At that time, Anuruddha was seated there among the assembly.
At that moment, Anuruddha fell asleep in the midst of the crowd.
Then, seeing Anuruddha sleeping, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"One who has received the Dharma sleeps in peace; their mind is free from confusion.
This is the teaching spoken by the Noble Ones, which the wise delight in.
It is like the water of a deep abyss, clear and free from defilement."
A person who hears the Dharma in this way receives it with a pure mind and joy;
like a great square stone that the wind cannot move,
so too when encountering praise or blame, their mind remains unshaken.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Aniruddha:
"Do you practice the Way out of fear of the king's law or fear of bandits? Aniruddha replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Aniruddha:
"Why have you left the household life to study the Path?

Anuruddha replied to the Buddha, "I am weary of this old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; being tormented by such suffering, I wish to abandon it. For this reason, I have left the household life to study the Path."
The World-Honored One said:
"Now, son of good family! Your faith is firm and steadfast as you have left the household life to study the Way."
“The World-Honored One is personally preaching the Dharma today; how can one sleep amidst this?
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“From this day forward, even if my form dissolves and my body rots, I shall never again sit and sleep before the Tathāgata.”
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha remained awake throughout the night, yet he was unable to dispel his drowsiness, and consequently his faculty of sight was impaired.
Then the Blessed One said to Aniruddha:

"One who exerts himself with excessive diligence becomes subject to the hindrance of restlessness; if, on the other hand, one is indolent, one becomes subject to the fetters. You should now practice by remaining in the middle."
Aniruddha addressed the Buddha:
"I have already made a vow before the Tathāgata; I cannot now go back on my original commitment.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Jīvaka:
"I shall treat Aniruddha’s visual faculty.
Jīvaka replied, "If Aniruddha takes a brief nap, I shall treat his eyes."
The World-Honored One said to Aniruddha:
"You may sleep. For such is the case:
all phenomena subsist by means of nutriment; without nutriment, they do not subsist."

The eye has sleep as its nutriment; the ear has sound as its nutriment; the nose has fragrance as its nutriment; the tongue has flavor as its nutriment; the body has tactile sensation as its nutriment; the mind has mental objects as its nutriment; and I now declare that even Nirvana has a nutriment.
Anuruddha addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What serves as the nutriment for nirvāṇa?
The Buddha told Anuruddha:
“Nirvāṇa has heedfulness as its nutriment; by mounting upon heedfulness, one attains the unconditioned.
Anuruddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Although it is said that the eye has sleep as its nutriment, I am unable to sleep.
At that time, Aniruddha was sewing old garments.
Thereupon, his physical eyes were destroyed, yet he attained the divine eye, free from all blemish or impurity.
At that time, Ānanda was sewing his robes according to ordinary methods, yet he was unable to pass the thread through the eye of the needle.
Thereupon, Ānanda thought to himself:
"The Arhats in the world who have attained the Way should assist me in threading this needle."
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his purified divine ear, heard these words:
"All those in the world who have attained the path as arhats should provide me with needles."
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where Anuruddha was and said to him, "Bring me a needle; I shall thread it for you.
Anuruddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What you have just said means that those in the world who seek merit should give me a needle to thread.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Among those in the world who seek merit, there is none superior to me; yet the Tathāgata never grows weary of or satisfied with the six dharmas."
What are the six? First, giving;
second, instruction and admonition.
Third is patience; fourth is the teaching of the Dharma and the teaching of its meaning;
fifth is protecting sentient beings; sixth is seeking the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
These, Āniruddha, are called [the six qualities].
"The Tathāgata never tires of these six dharmas.
Aniruddha said, "The body of the Tathāgata is the body of the true Dharma; what further dharma could he possibly seek?"
“The Tathāgata has already crossed the ocean of birth and death and is further liberated from attachment and craving;
yet today he still seeks to be the foremost in performing meritorious deeds.
The World-Honored One replied:
"So it is, Anuruddha! It is as you have said;
the Tathāgata also knows that these six things lead to insatiability.
If sentient beings were to know the source of evil—the actions of body, speech, and mind—they would never fall into the three evil realms."
"Because these sentient beings do not know the source of evil and wrongdoing, they fall into the three miserable realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"All the powers possessed in the world, Wandering among devas and humans,"
"The power of merit is supreme; through merit one attains the path of Buddhahood.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should seek skillful means to acquire these six dharmas."
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. They heard that outside the palace gate of King Prasenajit there were many people, who were raising their hands and crying out, all proclaiming their grievances:

"In this kingdom there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla, who is exceedingly fierce and violent; he has slaughtered living beings beyond counting and shows no compassion for any sentient being. The people of the realm all detest him with loathing; every day he takes a person to kill and uses their fingers as a garland, which is why he is called 'Finger-Garland' (Aṅgulimāla)."
"I only pray that Your Majesty will go forth to join the battle.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having finished their almsround, returned to the Jeta Grove Monastery.

They put away their robes and bowls, placed their sitting mats (niṣīdana) over their shoulders, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads and faces touching them, and sat down to one side.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"We, many bhikṣus, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food and saw a great multitude of people outside the palace gate crying out in grievance and complaint:

'Now within the borders of this kingdom there is a thief named Aṅgulimāla, who is violent and cruel toward others and devoid of compassion. He kills all living beings; that people perish and the country becomes desolate is entirely due to this man, who also takes human fingers to make flower garlands.'"
At that time, having heard the words of that bhikṣu, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and proceeded in silence.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One arrived at that place. Those who were gathering firewood, carrying grass, or plowing, as well as those herding oxen and sheep, saw the World-Honored One approaching along that path and each addressed the Buddha, saying: "Śramaṇa!..."
"Śramaṇa! Do not take that path.
For this reason: by the side of this road dwells a bandit named Aṅgulimāla."
Any people who wished to take this path had to assemble ten, or twenty, or thirty, forty, or fifty persons, yet they could not pass beyond; they were all captured by Aṅgulimāla.
"However, the śramaṇa Gautama is alone and without a companion; he has not even noticed being harassed by Aṅgulimāla.
Although the World-Honored One heard these words, he continued forward without stopping.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla’s mother brought food and went to where Aṅgulimāla was. Then, Aṅgulimāla thought to himself:
"Is my finger-garland complete in number?"
At that time, he immediately began counting his fingers; before he had finished the count, he counted them again, yet he was still short by one finger.
Then Aṅgulimāla looked left and right, searching for a living person whom he might seize and kill;
however, though he gazed in all directions, he saw no one, and he thought to himself:
"My teacher has taught:
'If one can kill one's mother, one shall surely be reborn in heaven.
Now that my own mother has come here in person, I may simply take her life; by using her finger to complete the required number, I shall be born in the heavens."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla grasped his mother’s head with his left hand, drew his sword with his right, and said to her,
"Wait a moment, Mother! Then,
the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This Aṅgulimāla shall commit the five heinous crimes.
He then emitted a ray of light from the mark between his eyebrows, which illuminated that mountain forest everywhere.
At that time, having seen the light, Aṅgulimāla spoke again to his mother:
"What light is this that illuminates these mountains and forests?
Could it be that the king has gathered his armies to attack me?
At that time, her mother said:
“You should now know that this is not the light of the sun, the moon, or fire, nor is it the radiance of Śakra or Brahmā, the Kings of Devas.
At that time, his mother spoke these verses:
“This is not the light of fire, Nor that of the sun, moon, Śakra, or Brahmā.”
The birds do not flee in alarm, but sing with a harmony more exquisite than usual;
this light is utterly pure and brings immeasurable joy to all beings.
This must surely be the Most Exalted Honored One, the One Possessing the Ten Powers, who has arrived here.
"Among gods and men, with the divine eye he beholds the world;
therefore, desiring to deliver your person, the World-Honored One has come here.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla, hearing the sound of the Buddha's voice, was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, and he spoke these words:
"My teacher also gave me instruction and commanded me, saying:
'If you can harm your mother and also kill the śramaṇa Gautama, you will surely be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.'"
At that time, Aṅgulimāla said to his mother: "Mother!
Stay here for now; I shall first kill the śramaṇa Gautama, and only then will I eat."
At that moment, Aṅgulimāla released his mother and went to pursue the World-Honored One.
Seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, appearing like a mass of gold that illuminated everything, he laughed and spoke these words:
"This śramaṇa is surely in my hands; I shall certainly kill him without doubt."
"Whenever there are people who wish to practice this path, they assemble a great multitude and then proceed upon it;
yet this śramaṇa is alone and without companions. I shall now seize and kill him."
At that moment, Aṅgulimāla drew his sword from his waist and went to confront the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately retraced his steps and proceeded slowly, while Aṅgulimāla ran after him in pursuit, yet he could not catch up with the Tathāgata.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla said to the World-Honored One, "Stop, stop, śramaṇa!
The World-Honored One replied:
“I myself am standing still; it is you who are not standing still.
At that moment, Aṅgulimāla ran alongside him and spoke this verse from afar:
“You go, yet say you stand; you tell me that I do not stand.”
“Explain this meaning to me: who is it that abides while you do not abide?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“The World-Honored One has declared that he abides; he does no harm to any being.”
You now harbor a murderous intent, And do not depart from the source of evil.
I abide in the ground of loving-kindness, Compassionately protecting all people;
You sow the seeds of hellish suffering, And do not depart from the source of evil.
At that time, having heard this verse, Aṅgulimāla thought to himself: "Am I truly an evildoer?
Furthermore, my teacher said to me:"
"This is a great sacrifice that yields great fruit.
One who can take a thousand people and kill them to fashion a garland of fingers will achieve his wish;
such a person, after the end of life, will be reborn in a good place, in the heavens."
"If one were to kill the mother who gave birth to him and the Śramaṇa Gautama, one would be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
At that time, the Buddha exercised his majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), and the consciousness of the man was awakened; furthermore, the texts of the various Brahmins also state this:
"The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; he appears only once in many hundreds of millions of kalpas."
When he appeared in the world, he caused those who had not crossed over to cross over, and those who were not liberated to attain liberation.
He taught the Dharma for the cessation of the six views. What are these six?
To those who speak of the view of self, he teaches the method for extinguishing the six views;
to those who hold that there is no self, he likewise teaches the method for extinguishing the view of non-self;

to those who speak of both the view of self and the view of non-self, he teaches the methods regarding both the view of self and the view of non-self, and further, observing for himself, he teaches the method of observation.
I myself have taught the Dharma of non-self; it is neither a teaching spoken by me, nor is it a teaching not spoken by me.
If a Tathāgata appears in the world, he teaches this Dharma for the cessation of the six views.
"Furthermore, when I was running, I could keep pace with elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as with common people.
Yet this śramaṇa does not travel with violent speed, yet today I cannot catch up to him; he must surely be the Tathāgata."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla spoke this verse:
“Venerable One, for my sake you have now spoken these subtle and wondrous verses;
the wicked one has now recognized the truth, all through the majestic power of the Venerable One.”
"Immediately casting aside my sharp sword, I threw it into a deep pit;
now, bowing at the traces of the Śramaṇa, I seek to become a Śramaṇa.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will grant us permission to become śramaṇas.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! At that very moment, Aṅgulimāla became a śramaṇa and donned the three dharma robes.
Then, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Just as you have now shaved your head, so too shall you remove the fetters;
when the fetters are extinguished, you will attain the great fruit and no longer suffer the afflictions of grief and distress.
At that time, having heard these words, Aṅgulimāla was immediately cleansed of all dust and defilements, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One took the bhikṣu Aṅgulimāla back to the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.
At that moment, King Prasenajit assembled the fourfold army, intending to go and attack the bandit Aṅgulimāla.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"I should now go to the place where the World-Honored One is and report this matter in detail to him.
Whatever the World-Honored One may say, I shall respectfully carry it out."
At that time, King Prasenajit immediately assembled the fourfold army and went to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the king, "Great King!
Where do you intend to go today?"
“Dust has defiled my body, even to this extent.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:

“In my kingdom now there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla who is extremely fierce and violent; he has no compassion for any living being. He has caused the land to become desolate and the people to flee in all directions—all because of this thief.”
"He has now captured a person and killed them to make a garland of fingers; he is a malevolent spirit, not a human being.
I now wish to execute this man."
The World-Honored One said:
"Great King, if you were to see Aṅgulimāla with firm faith, renounce the world, and train in the Path, what would you do to him?"
The king said to the Buddha,
"What else can I know?
I shall simply serve and make offerings to him, and pay my respects at the appropriate times."
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

That person is an evil man without even a hair’s breadth of goodness; he constantly commits acts of killing and harm. How could such a person have the resolve to leave the household life and study the Way?
"Ultimately, there is no such principle.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla was not far from the World-Honored One; he sat cross-legged, straightening his body and composing his mind, binding his mindfulness before him.
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his right hand and pointed toward the king,
saying, "This is the bandit Aṅgulimāla.
Upon hearing these words, the king was seized with terror, and the hairs on his body all stood on end.
The World-Honored One told the king, "Do not harbor fear; you may go before him, and he shall naturally understand your intention.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the king immediately went before Aṅgulimāla and said to him:
"What is your clan now? Aṅgulimāla replied,
"My clan is Garga, and my mother's name is Pūrṇikā."
At that time, having prostrated at his feet, the king sat to one side.
Then the king asked:

"May you take delight in this True Dharma; do not be indolent, but cultivate the pure holy life to reach the end of suffering. For as long as I live, I shall provide you with offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for illness."
At that time, Aṅgulimāla remained silent and did not respond.

The king immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at his feet, and returned to the place where the World-Honored One was; there he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the king again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To cause those who have not submitted to submit, and those who have not been subdued to be subdued—this is most marvelous!
This is most extraordinary!"
What has never occurred before, you have now been able to accomplish by subduing these most wicked people.
We pray only that the Great Honored One may enjoy infinite longevity and sustain the people; through the grace of the World-Honored One, we shall be spared from this calamity.
"The affairs of state are numerous and pressing; I wish to return to the city.
The World-Honored One said, "The King knows the proper time."
At that time, the king rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha’s] feet with his head, and then withdrew.

At that time, Aṅgulimāla lived as a forest-dweller (araṇyaka), wearing the fivefold patched robe. When the time came, he took up his bowl and went from house to house to beg for food, returning again and again; he wore robes made of mended rags that were extremely coarse and worn-out, and he also sat in the open air, leaving his body uncovered.

At that time, Aṅgulimāla was in a secluded place, practicing his own discipline. For a son of noble family who has left the household life to study the Way desires to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*):
"Birth and death are exhausted; the holy life is established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further rebirth"—he knows this as it truly is.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla immediately became an arhat; his six supernormal powers were pure and penetrating, free from all defilement, and he had already attained the state of an arhat.
When the time arrived, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
At that time, there was a woman who was in great distress as she approached childbirth; seeing her, [the Bodhisattva] thought to himself:
"Beings of all kinds suffer extreme pain, undergoing the process of conception without end."

At that time, after his meal, Aṅgulimāla put away his robes and bowl, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet with his head, and sat to one side.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Just now, having dressed and taken my bowl, I entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food and saw a woman who was heavily pregnant."
At that time, I thought to myself:
"How is it that sentient beings undergo suffering to such an extent?
The World-Honored One said:
"Go now to that woman and say this: 'Since my birth from the noble and holy ones, I have never taken life.
By means of these words of utmost sincerity, ensure that this mother's womb remains free from harm."
Aṅgulimāla replied: “So it is, World-Honored One!”
At that time, Aṅgulimāla, on that very day, dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī. He went to where his mother was and said to her:
"Since my birth from the Noble Ones, I have never again taken life."
"By holding fast to these words of utmost sincerity, may this fetus attain liberation.
At that moment, the mother’s fetus was immediately liberated.
Then, as Aṅgulimāla went about begging for alms within the city, the men and women, both young and old, who saw him, each said to one another:
"This is Aṅgulimāla; he has killed sentient beings beyond counting, and now he is again begging for alms within the city.

At that time, the people of the city each struck him with tiles and stones, while some hacked at him with knives. His head and eyes were wounded and mangled, his robes were completely torn to shreds, and blood stained his body as he immediately left the city of Śrāvastī and went to where the Tathāgata was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar Aṅgulimāla approaching with his head and eyes wounded and broken, his robes stained with flowing blood;
having seen him, he spoke thus: "Endure this now."
"The reason for this is that this transgression must be endured for eternal kalpas.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla stood before the Tathāgata and spoke this verse:
"Be firm in listening to the words of the Dharma; be firm in practicing the Buddha's teachings;
be firm in associating with virtuous friends; and you shall attain the state of cessation."
I was once a great thief, known as Aṅgulimāla;
swept away by the current, I was rescued by your honor.
Now I contemplate my own karma of taking refuge, and I shall likewise contemplate the fundamental nature of all phenomena.
Now that I have attained the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) and accomplished the practices of a Buddha,
my former name was "Harmless," yet I had committed countless acts of killing;
now my name is "Truthful Reality," for I do no harm to any being.
Even if one’s body, speech, and mind are entirely free from any harmful consciousness, this is called non-killing; how much more so when no such thoughts arise?
A bow-maker can temper horn, and a water-man can control water.
As a skilled craftsman adjusts his wood, so does the wise man adjust himself.
Whether subdued by whip and staff, or brought to submission through words,
without ever resorting to blade or cudgel, I have now brought myself under control.
If one has committed faults and evils before others, but later ceases and does not commit them again,
this illuminates the world like the moon appearing when the clouds have vanished.
If one has committed faults and evils before others, but later ceases and does not commit them again...
This illuminates the world, like the sun appearing when the clouds have vanished.
Whether monks be old, young, or middle-aged, if they practice the path of the Buddha-dharma,
they illuminate the world, like the moon when the clouds have vanished.
Whether monks be old, young, or middle-aged, those who practice the Buddha-dharma illuminate this world like the sun when the clouds have dispersed.
I now experience little pain; I know my own measure in food and drink.
Having completely escaped all suffering, the original conditions are now exhausted.
No further traces of death shall be received, nor is there any longing for birth;
now, awaiting the proper season, he rejoices without agitation.
At that time, the Tathāgata approved what Aṅgulimāla had said.
Seeing that the Tathāgata had granted his approval, Aṅgulimāla immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"What merit did Aṅgulimāla originally cultivate such that today he is so intelligent and wise, with features so upright and handsome as to be rare in the world?"
What unwholesome deeds did he perform such that, in this present body, he has killed and harmed countless living beings?
And what meritorious deeds did he perform such that, having now encountered the Tathāgata, he has attained the path of Arhatship?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, long ago within this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world."
After the Tathāgata Kāśyapa had passed into parinirvāṇa, there was a king named Mahāphala who ruled over the realm and governed Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the king had eighty-four thousand palace ladies and handmaidens, yet none of them had any children.

At that time, King Mahāphala directed his prayers toward the tree spirits, mountain deities, the sun and moon, and the constellations, reaching out to them all without exception, seeking to obtain a son and a daughter.
At that time, the King’s principal consort conceived; after eight or nine months had passed, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was so upright and handsome as to be rare in the world.
At that time, the king thought to himself: "I originally had no offspring;
after such a long time, a son has finally been born to me. I should bestow a name upon him and enjoy myself amidst the five sensual pleasures."
At that time, the king summoned his ministers who were skilled in physiognomy and addressed them, saying:
"Now that this son has been born to me, let each of you establish a name for him."
At that time, having heard the King’s instruction, the ministers immediately addressed the King, saying:

"This crown prince is most extraordinary; his comeliness is peerless, and his face is the color of a peach blossom. He must surely possess great power and majesty; we shall now establish his name as Mahābala (Great Power)."
At that time, after the physiognomists had bestowed a name upon the prince, they each rose from their seats and departed.
At that moment, the king cherished and pitied this prince so deeply that he never allowed him out of his sight.
At that time, the prince was nearly eight years old; accompanied by his ministers and attendants, he went to his father’s presence to offer greetings and inquiries after his health.
The father-king again thought to himself:
"Now this prince is truly extraordinary."
He then said to him,
"How would it be if I were to take a wife for you now?
The Prince replied to the King:
"My son, you are still young this year; why must you marry?
At that time, the father king temporarily halted the matter and did not provide him with a wife.
Another twenty years passed, and the king spoke to him again:
"I wish to take a wife for you.
The Prince said to the King:
"There is no need to take a wife."
At that time, the father king addressed his ministers and the people, saying:
"I originally had no offspring; after a long period of time, I finally gave birth to this one son, who now refuses to take a wife, remaining pure and without blemish."
At that time, the prince changed his name to Viśuddha.
When Prince Viśuddha was nearly thirty years old, the king again addressed his ministers, saying:
"I am now advanced in years and have no further offspring."
"Now there is only the Prince Viśuddha; the high position of the king should now be conferred upon him.
However, the prince does not delight in the midst of the five desires; how then shall he manage the affairs of state?"
The ministers replied,
"We shall employ skillful means to cause him to delight in the five desires.
Thereupon, the father-king struck the bells and beat the drums, issuing a command to all within the kingdom:
"If you can cause Prince Qingjing to take pleasure in the five desires, I shall grant you a thousand pieces of gold and various precious objects.
At that time, there was a woman named Yinzhong who was fully proficient in the sixty-four arts.
That woman heard the king’s decree:
"Whoever can cause the Prince to practice the five desires shall be granted one thousand *kārṣāpaṇas* of gold and various precious objects."
He immediately went to his father the king and addressed him, saying:
"Grant me a thousand pieces of gold and various precious objects, so that I may enable the Prince to practice the five desires."
The father king replied,
"If you are truly able to do so, I shall grant you a generous reward and will not fail to keep my word.
At that time, the courtesan said to the king:
"Where does the Prince sleep? The King replied, "He is in the eastern hall;
there are no women there, and only a young boy is present to attend him."
The woman said, "I only pray that Your Majesty will command the inner palace not to restrict or block me, so that I may enter and leave at will!
At that time, the courtesan, during the second watch of that very night, stood by the side of the prince’s gate and feigned a loud cry of lamentation.
At that time, the Prince heard the sound of a woman’s weeping and commanded his attendant, saying:
"Who is this person who is weeping here?
The attendant replied:
"This is a woman weeping by the side of the gate," the Prince said.
"Go quickly and ask why she is weeping."
Then, the attendant went to her and asked the reason for her weeping.
The courtesan replied, "My husband has abandoned me; that is why I weep."
The attendant returned and informed the prince:
"This woman was abandoned by her husband and, furthermore, fears bandits; for these reasons she weeps. The prince said:
"Place this woman in the elephant stable.
Upon arriving there, she wept again;
he then took her to the horse stable, where she wept once more.
The Crown Prince again said to his attendants, "Bring him here.
They immediately led him into the hall, where he wept once more.
The Crown Prince asked in person,
"Why are you weeping again?
The courtesan replied:
"O Prince! Women are frail and weak, and they harbor extreme fear; for this reason, they weep.
The Prince replied:
"Come up onto my bed; you shall find no cause for fear.
At that time, the woman remained silent and did not speak, nor did she weep.

Then, the woman immediately removed her garments and stepped forward to grasp the Prince’s hand, lifting it onto her breast. He was instantly startled awake, and gradually the thought of desire arose within him. As this lustful mind arose, his body moved toward her.
"At that time, on the following morning at dawn, Prince Viśuddha went to his father, the king.
Then, the father king saw from afar that the prince's countenance was extraordinary compared to usual; having seen this, he spoke thus:
'Has that which you now desire been accomplished?'"
The Crown Prince replied,
"It is as the Great King has said.
At that time, the father king was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, and he spoke thus:
"What wish do you seek? I shall grant it to you.
The Prince replied, "As for the wish you have granted, do not later regret it; I shall now request that wish."
The King replied, "As you have said, I shall never regret it; what wish do you seek?
The Prince addressed the King:
"Great King! Today you rule over all within Jambudvīpa with complete freedom;
as for all the unmarried daughters within the lands of Jambudvīpa, let them first enter my household before they are given in marriage."
At that time, the king said, "I shall do as you say.
The king then issued a decree to all the people within his realm, saying:
"Regarding all daughters who have not yet left their homes, first let them go to the Prince Qingjing, and only then shall they be married.
At that time, there was a girl in that city named Sumānā, whose turn it was to go before the King.
At that time, the daughter of the elder Suman was walking among the crowd naked and barefoot,
yet she felt no shame. When the people saw her, they said to one another,
"This is the daughter of the elder, whose fame is heard far and wide."
"How can you walk among people with your body exposed?
How are you any different from a donkey?
The woman replied to the crowd:
"I am not the donkey; it is you all who are the donkeys.
Have you ever seen a woman feel shame upon seeing another woman?"
"All living beings within this city are exclusively women; only Prince Viśuddha is a man!
If I reach the gate of Prince Viśuddha, I shall put on my clothes."
At that time, the people of the city said to one another:
"What this woman has said truly accords with our own thoughts; we are indeed women, not men."
"Only Prince Viśuddha is a man. Today we must perform the duties of men.
