At that time, the people of the city each prepared their weapons of war; donning armor and grasping staves, they went to the presence of the Father King and addressed him, saying:
"I seek two wishes; please grant me leave to state them.
The king replied to him, "What are these two wishes?"
The people said to the king:
"If the King wishes to survive, you must kill the pure Prince;
if the Prince wishes to survive, he must now kill the King."
"We cannot bear to serve the Prince of Purity and thereby disgrace the eternal laws of our kingdom.
At that time, the Father King spoke this verse:
"For the sake of the family, one person is forgotten; For the sake of the village, a family is forgotten."
"For the sake of the state, forget one village; for the sake of oneself, forget the world.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the Father King addressed the people, saying:
"Now is the very time; act according to your own will."

At that time, the people seized Prince Qingjing and bound his two hands. Leading him out of the city, they said to one another, "Let us all strike him to death with tiles and stones; why need only one person kill him?"
"At that time, when Prince Qingjing was about to die, he made this declaration:
'Furthermore, I have made a vow: although the people have seized me and killed me unjustly, my father the King granted me a wish; I now face death and dare not decline it.'"
"In a future life, I shall repay this enmity;
furthermore, may I encounter a true person, an Arhat, and swiftly attain liberation.
At that time, the people took the prince and killed him, then each dispersed.
“O bhikṣus! Do not hold such a view.
As for that King Mahāphala at that time, could he have been anyone else?
He was none other than the teacher Aṅgulimāla here now.”
The courtesan at that time was the teacher’s wife who is now present;
the people at that time were the eighty thousand people who have now died;
and the Prince Viśuddha at that time was the bhikṣu Aṅgulimāla who is now present.
As he was about to die, he made this vow: "I shall now return to take my revenge, and no one shall escape my hand.
Due to these causes and conditions, he committed countless killings. Later, he made another vow, wishing to meet a Buddha; thus, he has now attained liberation and become an Arhat.
"This is its meaning; you should keep it in mind and practice accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the one who is foremost in intelligence and swift wisdom is the bhikṣu Aṅgulimāla."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 31; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 32.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Eight, Part Two:
On Power (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see this Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain?"
The bhikṣus replied, "Indeed, we have seen it.
[The Buddha said,] "You should know that in the distant past, this mountain had another name."
"Do you all also see this Mount Vipula? The bhikṣus replied, "Indeed, we see it."
“You should know this: in the distant past, this mountain had another name, different from what it is now.
Do you see Mount Śvetaśaila?”
The bhikṣus replied, “Indeed, we have seen it. [The Buddha said:
“In the distant past, this mountain had another name, which was not the same as it is now.”
"Do you all see this mountain bearing a heavy load?
The bhikṣus replied, "Indeed, we see it."
“Do you all see this seer, Khadiravaniya? The bhikṣus replied, “Indeed, we see him.”
"In the distant past, this mountain also bore this same name and had no other name.
This is because this Śrīparvata (Sage Mountain) has always been the dwelling place of bodhisattvas with supernatural powers, arhats who have attained the Way, and various sages;
furthermore, pratyekabuddhas also sported within its midst."
I shall now proclaim the names of the pratyekabuddhas; listen attentively!
Reflect upon them well!

There are pratyekabuddhas named Arida and Varida, the Pratyekabuddha of Thorough Investigation, the Pratyekabuddha of Skillful Observation, the Ultimate Pratyekabuddha, the Intelligent Pratyekabuddha, the Stainless Pratyekabuddha, the Pratyekabuddha of Noble Contemplation, the Unextinguished, the Formless, the Victorious, the Most Victorious, the Utterly Great, and the Pratyekabuddha of Utterly Resounding Lightning-Light.
"Monks, when no Pratyekabuddhas or Tathāgatas appear in the world, at that time there are five hundred Pratyekabuddhas dwelling here in this mountain range of the Rishis."
When the Tathāgata was about to descend from the Tuṣita Heaven to be born, the devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens came here in person and announced:
"Proclaim throughout the world that you must purify the Buddha-field; two years hence, the Tathāgata shall appear in the world."
When those Pratyekabuddhas heard the words of the deva and human, they all ascended into the air and spoke this verse:
"When no Buddhas have appeared, The worthy sages dwell in this place;
The self-awakened Pratyekabuddhas Constantly reside within these mountains."
"This is named Ṛṣigiri Mountain, the abode of Pratyekabuddhas;
Ṛṣis and Arhats shall never be absent from it.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddhas immediately incinerated their bodies in mid-air and attained Parinirvāṇa.
The reason for this is that there are no two Buddhas in the world; therefore, he has entered parinirvāṇa.
Just as there can never be two guides among a company of merchants, nor two kings within a single country, so too there cannot be two honored titles within the realm of a single Buddha.

The reason for this is that in the distant past, there was a king in this city of Rājagṛha named Priyarata; he constantly contemplated the suffering of the hells, as well as the suffering of hungry ghosts and animals.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"I now constantly recall the agonizing sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; it is not fitting for me to enter these three evil paths once more."
"Now it is fitting that you completely renounce the sovereign rank of a king, your wife and children, and your attendants; with firm faith, leave the household life to study the Way.

At that time, King Hiteya, weary of this bitter suffering, immediately relinquished the royal throne, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and left the household life to study the Way. In a secluded place, he disciplined himself, contemplating the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) and realizing their impermanence.
That which is called this form, the origin of this form, and the cessation of this form—and likewise feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are all entirely impermanent.
When one contemplates these five aggregates of clinging, all phenomena that are subject to cultivation are, in their entirety, phenomena subject to cessation;
having contemplated these phenomena, one subsequently realizes the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Nandika, having already attained the fruit of the Way, spoke this verse:
"I recall the sufferings of hell And among the five realms of animals;
Having abandoned them, I now study the Way, Walking alone, free from sorrow."
"At that time, this Pratyekabuddha was dwelling on that Mountain of the Rishis.

Bhikshus, you should know that by this means it is understood that this mountain is always inhabited by Bodhisattvas possessing supernatural powers, perfected sages who have attained the Way, and those practicing the way of the rishis; for this reason it is called the Mountain of the Rishis and has no other name."
If the Tathāgata does not appear in the world, the devas constantly come to pay their respects here in this mountain of sages.
This is because within these mountains there are exclusively true persons (ṛṣi), with no others of mixed character.
When Maitreya Buddha descends as an incarnation into the world, the names of these various mountains will each be different; however, this Mountain of the Rishi will have no other name.
Throughout this Bhadrakalpa, the name of this mountain shall likewise remain unchanged.
"You, bhikṣus! You should draw near to this mountain, serve it, and pay it respect; thus you shall increase all your merits. It is even so, bhikṣus!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should cultivate yourselves with single-minded mindfulness.”
How should one practice focused mindfulness? In this regard, O bhikṣu!

When walking, one should know that one is walking; whether moving or stopping, bending or stretching, looking down or looking up, dressing according to the rules, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent—in all these, one should fully know the proper time.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu’s mind is focused and upright, then for that bhikṣu, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen will not arise, and that which has already arisen will be extinguished;
the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen will not arise, and that which has already arisen will be extinguished;
the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen will not arise, and that which has already arisen will be extinguished.
If one focuses one's mindfulness on the discernment of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one will never fall into the evil realms.
"What are the six sense bases that constitute the evil realms?
When the eye perceives these forms—whether beautiful or ugly—one rejoices upon seeing what is beautiful and does not rejoice upon seeing what is ugly; [and so forth for the other senses]."
If one hears sounds with the ear—whether they are pleasant or unpleasant—one rejoices upon hearing what is pleasant and does not rejoice upon hearing what is unpleasant;
the same applies to the nose, mouth, body, and mind.
It is like there being six kinds of creatures whose natures and behaviors differ and whose ways of acting are not the same.
Suppose someone were to take a rope and bind them—taking a dog, a wild fox, a monkey, a sturgeon, a viper, and a bird—and having bound them all together, tied them in one place, and set them free.
At that time, each of the six kinds of insects had its own disposition and behavior.
At that time, the dog intended in its mind to go toward the village;
the wild fox intended in its mind to go toward the cemetery.
The sturgeon intends to go into the water;
the monkey intends to head toward the mountain forests;
the venomous snake intends to enter its hole.
The intention of a flying bird is to soar through the air.
At that time, six kinds of insects each have their own nature and behavior, which do not coincide.
Suppose, furthermore, that someone were to capture these six kinds of insects and bind them together in one place; they would be unable to go east, west, south, or north.
At that time, although the six kinds of worms move about, they do not leave their original locations.
These six internal sense-faculties are likewise: each has its own domain, their functions differ, and what they perceive varies—whether it be beautiful or ugly.
"At that time, monks, bind these six sense-faculties and fix them upon a single point.

Therefore, monks, you should practice with focused diligence and keep the mind from becoming distracted; then, the evil Māra Pāpīyān will never find an opportunity, and all wholesome merits will be fully accomplished."
Thus, monks, you should cultivate the faculty of the eye;
by doing so, you will attain two fruits: either the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) in this very life, or the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"One should contemplate the perception of impermanence and cultivate the perception of impermanence extensively. By contemplating the perception of impermanence and cultivating the perception of impermanence extensively, one will sever sensual craving, craving for form, and craving for the formless; one will completely sever conceit and ignorance."

Why is this? In the distant past, during a long-elapsed eon, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Sunetra (Good Eyes). His countenance was upright and handsome, his face like the color of a peach blossom; his gaze was discerning and clear, his mouth emitted the fragrance of an *utpala* lotus, and his body exuded the scent of sandalwood.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Sunetra, having reached the hour, put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food.
Gradually arriving at the house of the great elder, he stood silently outside the gate.

At that time, the daughter of the elder saw from afar a practitioner standing outside the gate; he was peerlessly handsome, with an extraordinary countenance rarely seen in the world. His mouth emitted the fragrance of an *utpala* lotus, and his body the fragrance of sandalwood. She immediately conceived a desire for him and approached the bhikṣu, saying:
"You are now so handsome, with a face like the color of a peach blossom—rare indeed in this world!"
"Although I am currently a woman, I am nonetheless beautiful and fit for union with you.
Furthermore, my home abounds in rare treasures and my wealth is immeasurable;
yet, it is truly not easy to become a śramaṇa."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha asked, "Sister,
where are you currently attached?"
The daughter of the householder replied:
"I am now truly focused on the beauty of his eyes; furthermore, my mouth emits the fragrance of an *utpala* lotus, and my body the fragrance of sandalwood."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha extended his left hand and, with his right hand, plucked out his eye and placed it in his palm, saying to him:
"That which you love as your eye is this very thing."
Elder sister!
Where have you been today? It is like a festering ulcer, not a single thing in it is worth desiring; yet even within these eyes, impurities leak out.
Elder sister, you should know that the eye is like a bubble on water; it is neither firm nor stable, being illusory and false rather than real, deceiving and deluding the people of the world.
The eye, ear, nose, mouth, body, and mind are all not firm; they are deceptive and untrue.
The mouth is a vessel for saliva, from which impure things issue;
it contains nothing but white bones. The body is a vessel of suffering, subject to decay and extinction, constantly filled with foulness and disturbed by various worms;
it is like a painted jar containing filth within.
Elder sister!
Where have you been today?
Therefore, elder sister!
One should concentrate the mind and contemplate this dharma as illusory, false, and unreal.
Just as when a sister contemplates that the eye and forms are impermanent, all thoughts of attachment and desire naturally vanish.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all impermanent.
Having contemplated this, all desires and intentions will naturally be eliminated;
by contemplating the six sense bases, the notion of desire ceases.
At that time, the elder’s daughter was seized with fear; she immediately stepped forward to prostrate at the feet of the Pratyekabuddha and said to him:
“From this day forward, I shall reform my ways and cultivate virtue, never again giving rise to thoughts of desire.”
"I only pray that you will accept my repentance; thus shall I practice this again and again.
The Pratyekabuddha replied, "Stop!"
"Stop! Great Sister! This is not your fault;
it is due to my own past karma that I have received this form, which causes people to give rise to lustful thoughts upon seeing me."
One should contemplate the eye thoroughly: this eye is not the self, nor does the self belong to it;
it is not created by me, nor is it produced by another; rather, it arises from non-existence and, once arisen, naturally decays.
It belongs neither to the past life, the present life, nor the future life; all are merely the result of the conjunction of causes and conditions.
What is called the causal condition of conjunction means that because this exists, that exists; when this arises, that arises; when this is absent, that is absent; and when this ceases, that ceases.
It is the same for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: they are all entirely empty and quiescent.
Therefore, sister! Do not be attached to the forms of the eye.
By not being attached to forms, you will reach the place of peace and security, where there is no longer any sensual desire.
Thus it is, sister!
"You should train yourself in this way.

At that time, after the Pratyekabuddha had taught the woman the Dharma of the four marks of impermanence, he ascended into the air, manifested the eighteen transformations, and returned to his dwelling.
At that time, that woman contemplated the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as being utterly non-existent; she then went to a secluded place and reflected upon this Dharma.

That woman further contemplated that the six sense bases have no master; she attained the four immeasurable minds and, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.

"Bhikṣus, you should know: if one contemplates the perception of impermanence and extensively disseminates the perception of impermanence, one completely severs craving for desire, form, and the formless realm, and pride and ignorance are entirely eliminated."
"Therefore, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed his charioteer, saying:
“Prepare for me now a chariot adorned with feathers and jewels; I wish to go abroad for sightseeing.
At that time, the man, having received the king’s command, immediately prepared the chariot adorned with feathers and jewels and came forward to address the king:
“The chariot adorned with feathers and jewels has been fully readied; Your Majesty should know that it is now the proper time.”

King Prasenajit then took this man out of the city of Śrāvastī and went to that garden park. There he observed the various trees, all of which were without sound, and there were no people; it was silent, empty, and void.
Having seen this, he immediately recalled the Tathāgata’s teaching on the root of all phenomena.
At that time, the man was behind the king, holding a fan and fanning him. [The king thought:

"In this garden, the fruit trees are entirely silent and there are no people; it is tranquil, empty, and void. I now wish to invite the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, to come and dwell here to transform beings, yet I do not know where the Tathāgata currently resides."
"I wish to go and pay my respects.
The attendant replied, "There is a village of the Śākyas called Ṛṣipatana; the Tathāgata is there, wandering and teaching."
King Prasenajit asked, "How far is this Mṛgadāva from here?
The attendant replied to the king:
“The dwelling place of the Tathāgata is not far from here; it is reckoned to be three *yojanas* by measure of distance.
At that time, King Prasenajit said, “Quickly prepare a carriage adorned with peacock feathers and jewels; I now wish to see the Tathāgata.”
At that time, having received the king’s command, the man immediately prepared the carriage and went before the king, saying:
“The carriage is now yoked; Your Majesty knows the time.”
The king immediately mounted his carriage and proceeded to that village.
At that time, a group of bhikṣus were walking back and forth on an open space; the king then alighted from his carriage and approached the many bhikṣus.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the [Buddha’s] feet and stood to one side.
At that time, the king said to the bhikṣu, “Where is the Tathāgata?”
"I wish to see him.
The many bhikṣus replied, "The World-Honored One is staying in this lecture hall; you may go to see him—do not consider it difficult."
"When the King wishes to depart, he should raise his feet slowly so as not to make a sound.
At that time, King Prasenajit looked back at his attendant; then the attendant thought to himself:
"The King is now meeting with the World-Honored One alone; I should remain here."
At that time, the king went alone to where the World-Honored One was.
Then, with his divine eye, the World-Honored One beheld King Prasenajit standing outside the gate.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and opened the door for the king.
Upon seeing the World-Honored One, the king prostrated himself at his feet and announced his name: "I am King Prasenajit."
Regarding these three self-designations, the World-Honored One said:
"You are now a king; I am now one who has left the household life of the Śākya clan to study the Way."
Then the King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One may prolong his life infinitely, so that gods and humans may attain peace.
The World-Honored One replied:
"May Your Majesty enjoy infinite longevity and govern by means of the Dharma, never by what is contrary to the Dharma.
All who transform others through the Dharma will be reborn in the auspicious realms of the heavens; even after their lives have ended, their fame shall remain imperishable."
What the people of the world transmit says:
"In the past, there was a king who ruled and transformed the realm through the Dharma, never committing an act of injustice.
If there are subjects living within this king's domain who praise his meritorious virtues and remember them without forgetting, the king’s being in the heavens will increase his six kinds of merit."
What are the six? First, celestial lifespan; second, celestial form; third, celestial pleasure; fourth, celestial power; fifth, celestial majesty; and sixth, celestial radiance.
Therefore, Great King, you should govern according to the Dharma and not by what is contrary to the Dharma.
Today, within my body there exists this merit; thus, I am worthy of receiving the respect and prostrations of others.
The King said to the Buddha,
“The Tathāgata’s merit is such that he deserves to receive prostrations.
The World-Honored One replied:
"How is it that you now say the Tathāgata should receive the prostrations of others?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying, "The Tathāgata possesses six meritorious qualities; therefore, he should receive the prostrations of others."

What are the six? The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is exceedingly harmonious and elegant, and is that which the wise practice; this is called the first merit of the Tathāgata, which is worthy of service and worthy of reverence.
"Furthermore, the noble assembly of the Tathāgata is exceedingly harmonious and compliant;
they are perfected in the Dharma, perfected in ethical discipline, perfected in wisdom, perfected in liberation, and perfected in the vision and knowledge of liberation."

What is called the Noble Assembly consists of the four pairs and eight classes; this is the Tathāgata’s noble assembly, worthy of veneration and honor, the great field of merit for the world—this is called the second quality of the Tathāgata.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata has four assemblies of followers who practice all the teachings he has enacted; they do not again cause him disturbance or offense. This is called the third merit of the Tathāgata."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
I see that members of the Kṣatriya caste, Brahmins, householders, and śramaṇas of preeminent talent and renown all come together to deliberate:
'We shall take this discourse and go to question the Tathāgata; if that śramaṇa Gautama does not provide an answer to this discourse, he will be at fault.'"
"If they were indeed able to repay [this kindness], we would surely praise their goodness.
At that time, people of the four castes came to where the World-Honored One was and asked about this discourse; some remained silent.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to them; having heard the Dharma, they no longer asked further questions, much less desired to debate, and all took the Tathāgata as their teacher—this is the fourth merit.
"Furthermore, the sixty-two views deceive and mislead the people of the world; failing to understand the True Dharma, they thereby fall into folly.
However, the Tathāgata is able to eliminate these karmas of false views and cultivate right view. This is called the fifth merit of the Tathāgata."

"Furthermore, if sentient beings have committed evil through body, speech, and mind, yet at the time of their death they recollect the virtues of the Tathāgata, they will leave the three evil destinies and attain rebirth in the heavens;
even those who are the most wicked can thus attain rebirth in the heavens—this is called the sixth virtue of the Tathāgata."
"Any sentient beings who see the Tathāgata will all give rise to a mind of reverence and make offerings to him.
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent!"
Excellent, Great King!
You are indeed able to let out a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata, proclaiming the merits of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, Great King,
you should always direct your mind toward the Tathāgata.
Thus it is, Great King!
"You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to King Prasenajit, causing him to rejoice.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the Great King rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew.
Not long after, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should uphold this Dharma offering, reciting and reflecting upon it well.
Why is this? Because these were spoken by King Prasenajit."
"You all should also extensively expound its meaning to the fourfold assembly. Thus, O bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 11 (11) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of the Kalandakas, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed his ministers, saying:
"Quickly prepare the chariot adorned with feathered jewels; I wish to go and see the World-Honored One!
Thereupon, the ministers, having received the king’s command, immediately prepared the chariot adorned with feathered jewels and came forward to address the king, saying:
"The carriage is prepared; Your Majesty should know that it is time.
Thereupon, the king mounted his precious feathered chariot and proceeded to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation to remain for the ninety-day summer retreat in the city of Rājagṛha."
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the King’s invitation.
Seeing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted his request, the King immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru provided seasonal offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and furniture, and medicines for the sick and infirm.
At that moment, the spirits and deities of the city of Vaiśālī became rampant, and the deaths among the people were beyond counting.
Within a single day, hundreds die; ghosts, spirits, and rākṣasas fill the place, their faces turning yellow, and some die after only three or four days have passed.
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī were struck with fear; they all gathered in one place and deliberated together:
"This great city is exceedingly prosperous, its lands are fertile and abundant, and its wealth and joy are limitless, like the celestial palace where Śakra dwells."
Yet today we are being harmed by these ghosts and spirits; we shall all surely die, and this place will become a desolate wilderness like the mountains and wilds.
Who possesses such divine virtue as to repel this calamity?
At that time, the people said to one another: "We have heard:
'Wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, no various evil spirits are able to harass or approach him.'"
"If the Tathāgata were to come here, these spirits and ghosts would each scatter in all directions.
However, today the World-Honored One is staying here in Rājagṛha and is being supported by Ajātaśatru; I fear he may not come to this place to wander and transform beings."
Or again, some may say:

"The Tathāgata possesses great compassion and takes pity on sentient beings; he surveys all things universally, causing those who have not yet crossed over to cross over, never abandoning any sentient being, just as a mother loves her child."
If someone were to invite the Tathāgata, he would come immediately, and King Ajātaśatru would never be able to detain him.
Who could venture into King Ajātaśatru’s realm and say to the World-Honored One:
"Our city is now beset by this dire distress; we only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and deign to visit!"?
At that time, there was a great elder named Mahāśreṣṭhin who was gathered among that assembly.
Then, the people said to the elder: "We have heard:..."
"Wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, no malevolent spirits can cause him harm.
If the Tathāgata were to come to this place, he would be able to eliminate these calamities."
"You should go to the World-Honored One and report this matter in full, so that this city wall may exist forever.
At that time, the elder remained silent and followed the words of the multitude; he immediately rose from his seat and went home.
Having arrived, he prepared the provisions for the journey and led his attendants to the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The people of the city of Vaiśālī have encountered this calamity; many among the populace have perished. It is estimated that within a single day in that city, there are hundreds of corpses being transported on carts.”
I only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon me with compassion and deliver me, so that others may be selected for safety and enabled to attain the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*).
Furthermore, I have heard:
"Wherever the World-Honored One goes, devas, nāgas, and spirits do not dare to harass or approach."
"I pray that you will deign to visit that city and deliver its people, establishing them in the state of non-action.
The World-Honored One replied,
"I have already accepted the invitation from King Ajātaśatru of Rājagṛha."
"The words of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are without duality; if King Ajātaśatru would grant permission, the Tathāgata would go.
The Great Elder addressed the Buddha, saying, "This matter is extremely difficult;
King Ajātaśatru will never allow the Tathāgata’s messenger to reach that kingdom."
The reason for this is that King Ajātaśatru possesses not even a hair’s breadth of goodness within my realm; throughout the long night, he seeks expedient means, desiring to harm those people.
If King Ajātaśatru were to see me, he would surely seize and kill me, let alone allow me to recount these matters!
If he were to hear that the people of his kingdom have been harmed by ghosts and spirits, he would rejoice immeasurably.
The World-Honored One said:
"Do not harbor fear. Go now to the king's presence and speak these words:
'The Tathāgata’s prediction regarding the former king’s body was never false; his word is without duality.'"
Because you harmed your father, the King, though he was without fault, you shall be reborn in the Avīci Hell for the duration of one kalpa.

However, today you have escaped this transgression; having rectified your offense, you have perfected the faculty of faith within the Dharma of the Tathāgata. By virtue of this root of merit, you shall extinguish this sin so that no remainder remains. When your present life comes to an end, you shall be reborn in the Ball-beating Hell (Kukūla-naraka);
when your life there ends, you shall be reborn above the Four Heavenly Kings (Cāturmahārājika); and when your life there ends, you shall be reborn in the Yāma Heaven.
Having passed away from the Yāma Heaven, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
then, returning again in successive order, they come to the realm of the Four Great Kings.
"Great King, you should know that for twenty kalpas he will not fall into the evil realms, but will always be born among humans.

In his final existence, through firm faith, he will shave off his hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to study the Way, and be known as the Pratyekabuddha named Dūrjaya (Remover of Evil)."
Upon hearing these words, that king will immediately rejoice and leap for joy, unable to contain himself, and he shall also say this to you:
"Whatever essential vow you seek, I shall not go against it."
At that time, the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "I shall now,
sustained by the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual power,
go to that king's abode. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and departed for the king's residence.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru was on a high palace terrace engaged in discussion with his various ministers.
Then, the great elder approached the king’s presence. Seeing him coming from afar, the king said to his ministers, "If this man were to arrive here now, what would you wish to do with him?"
Some said: "We shall take five *varga*s," while others said: [we shall take ten].
"Sever his head! King Ajātaśatru said, "Kill him quickly; you need not see me."
At that time, having heard these words, the elder was filled with extreme fear; he immediately raised his voice and spoke thus:
"I am one sent by the Buddha."
Having heard the Buddha’s voice, the king immediately descended from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and approached the Tathāgata, asking the elder:
"What are the Tathāgata’s instructions?"
The elder replied, “The World-Honored One’s prophecy concerning the former sage-kings is not false; the teachings He utters are ultimately never contradictory.
As the Tathāgata has said:”
"The King seized his father, the King, and killed him; on account of this root of sin, he ought to enter the Avīci Hell and remain there for one kalpa.
However, having immediately repented of his transgression in the presence of the Tathāgata, he shall now be born in the Ball-Beating Hell;
when his life there ends, he shall be reborn among the Four Heavenly Kings."
Passing through successive births, he was born among the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations;

then, returning once more, he was born among the gods of the Four Great Kings. For twenty kalpas, he did not fall into the three evil realms, transmigrating instead between the heavens and the human world.
"In his final incarnation, through firm faith, he will leave the household life to study the Way and appear in the world as a Pratyekabuddha named Duryodhana (Remover of Evil).
Upon hearing these words, the King was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself;
he then addressed the great elder, saying, "What wish do you now seek? I shall grant it to you."
The elder addressed the king, saying,
“Regarding the wish you have requested, may Your Majesty not refuse it. King Ajātaśatru replied:
"Tell me now what boon you seek; I shall not refuse it.
The elder addressed the king:
"The people of the city of Vaiśālī have met with calamity; they are being harmed by spirits and ghosts beyond counting."
"Today, the rākṣasas and spirits are exceedingly violent and cruel.
We only pray that Your Majesty will grant permission for the World-Honored One to go to that world, so that those spirits may each be driven to scatter!"
The reason for this is that we have heard:
"Wherever the Tathāgata goes, devas, nāgas, and spirits cannot find an opportunity to cause harm."
“I only pray that Your Majesty will grant permission for the World-Honored One to travel to that kingdom.
Having heard these words, the king sighed deeply and said to the elder:
“This aspiration is exceedingly great; it is beyond the reach of ordinary people.”
If you were to follow my example and seek cities, villages, national wealth, wives, or children, I would not begrudge them to you.
I do not worry about you; you should instead entreat the World-Honored One for your wishes.
However, I have already granted the requests you made previously, so now I shall comply with your current intent.
At that time, the elder was filled with great joy; he rose from his seat, took his leave, and departed for the place where the World-Honored One was, saying:
"King Ajātaśatru has granted permission for the World-Honored One to travel to his kingdom."
The World-Honored One said, "You may go on ahead; the Tathāgata will know the proper time for himself.
At that moment, the elder prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then withdrew.

At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One, surrounded by his assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, departed from the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove and proceeded toward the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru was atop a high tower, accompanied by a single attendant holding a parasol.
Seeing from afar the World-Honored One heading toward his kingdom, the king sighed and said to those around him:
"We have been deceived by this elder; what use is there for me to live any longer?"
"Therefore, let the Tathāgata depart from the borders of this kingdom.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru took five hundred parasols and went to escort the World-Honored One, fearing that dust might soil his body.
Within the city of Rājagṛha, there were also five hundred precious canopies following behind the Tathāgata.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, knowing what was in the World-Honored One’s mind, again held five hundred precious canopies in the air for fear that dust might soil the Tathāgata’s body;
likewise, the river deities also held five hundred precious canopies in the air.

At that time, the people of the city of Vaiśālī, hearing that the World-Honored One was about to enter the city, again took five hundred precious parasols and went forward to welcome the World-Honored One.
At that time, two thousand five hundred jeweled parasols were suspended in the air.
When the World-Honored One saw these parasols, he immediately smiled.
This is the constant law of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones: whenever a Tathāgata smiles, five-colored rays of light—blue, yellow, white, black, and red—issue forth from his mouth.
The attendant Ānanda, seeing this radiance, reflected thus:
"What is the cause of this?
If the World-Honored One smiles, there must be a reason; the matter cannot be in vain."
At that time, Ānanda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Tathāgata never smiles without cause; this smile must surely have a reason.”
The World-Honored One asked,
"Do you now see these two thousand five hundred jeweled parasols making offerings to the Tathāgata?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"Yes, indeed, I saw him.
The World-Honored One said:
"If the Tathāgata had not left the household life to study the Way, he would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King for two thousand five hundred lifetimes, governing and transforming the people."
"Because the Tathāgata has left the household life to study the Way, he shall no longer accept this precious canopy.

Ānanda, you should know that in the distant past, there was a king named Śubhavyūha who ruled over the kingdom of Mithilā. He governed according to the Dharma and received others with proper propriety; he presided over this land of Jambudvīpa such that there were none who did not obey his commands."

At that time, the king had eighty-four thousand queens and court ladies, all of whom were of the Kṣatriya caste; the principal queen was named Sūryaprabhā, and she likewise had no son to continue the lineage.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"I now rule over this land of Jambudvīpa, yet I have no offspring.
He then prayed to the mountain deities, the tree deities, and the spirits of heaven and earth for the sake of having a son.
Furthermore, before many days had passed, the lady became pregnant.
At that time, Lady Rājyā said to the King:
"Your Majesty, you should know that I have now become aware of my pregnancy; I ought to take care of myself."
After another eight or nine months had passed, a son was born, with a handsome and upright countenance and a face the color of a peach blossom.

Upon seeing him, the lady was filled with extreme joy and went to see the Great King. When the King saw him, he leaped for joy, unable to contain himself; and when the eighty-four thousand ladies-in-waiting saw that a crown prince had been born, they too were each filled with joy.
At that time, the king summoned his ministers, state preceptors, and Daoist masters to examine him and bestow upon him a name to be proclaimed throughout the world.
At that time, the physiognomist came forward and addressed the King, saying:

"The Crown Prince born today is exceedingly handsome and unlike anyone else in the world; there is no one who beholds him who does not feel love and affection for him. He should now be given the name 'Affection' (Piyadassana)."
Once they had finished establishing their respective names, each returned to his own place.
At that time, the king cherished the crown prince so dearly that he never turned his eyes away from him;
he immediately erected for the prince a lecture hall for the three periods of the day, and further filled it with court ladies to provide entertainment for the royal prince.
At that time, the prince thought to himself:
"Among these court ladies, is there anyone who remains forever without departing from this world, nor undergoes change or transformation?"

Yet, when one observes those multitudes, they are all subject to impermanence; there is nothing that remains eternally in the world. All are illusory and false, devoid of reality, causing the various classes of people to become stained by attachment and delight, such that none know how to distance themselves from them.
"What use have I now for these?
I shall renounce them and study the Way.
At that time, Prince Anuruddha, on that very day, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and left the household life to study the Way.
That very night, he severed all fetters and, contemplating that all conditioned phenomena are subject to decay and extinction, he became a Pratyekabuddha.
Having attained enlightenment, he spoke this verse:
“Desire is an impermanent phenomenon; It is subject to change and lacks any fixed reality.”
"Knowing this to be a great affliction, I wander alone without companions.
Having spoken this verse, the Pratyekabuddha immediately flew into the air and circled the city of Mithilā three times.

At that time, the king was on a high terrace together with his court ladies, enjoying themselves in recreation. Seeing the pratyekabuddha circumambulate the city three times, he was filled with such immense joy that he could not contain himself and thought:
"My crown prince now soars through the air like that flying bird."
Furthermore, not knowing that he had become a Pratyekabuddha, [the king] said to him: "Son!
Come down now to this palace hall and enjoy yourself with me."
"At that time, Ānanda!
That Pratyekabuddha immediately descended from the palace roof, desiring to save his parents.
Then the king said to him:"
"Prince! Why today do you wear these garments of a court lady, yet have shaved off your beard and hair, appearing different from other men?
The Pratyekabuddha replied:
"What you have composed now is most extraordinary and elegant; it is not something practiced by ordinary people.
At that time, the king replied, "For what reason do you no longer come to the palace?"
The Pratyekabuddha said,
"From this day forward, I shall no longer practice desire, nor shall I take pleasure in these five sensual desires.
Then the king spoke:
"If you do not take pleasure in these five desires, you may dwell in my rear garden.
At that time, the king himself went to the garden and had dwellings constructed.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha, desiring to deliver his parents, remained in that garden pavilion to receive the king’s offerings; after some time had passed, he entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
The king collected the relics and performed their cremation, and at that site he erected a great shrine.
On another day, the king went to the park to look about and saw that the temple had become dilapidated and ruined.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"This is my son’s shrine, which has now fallen into decay.
At that moment, the king immediately covered the shrine with his own parasol, all because his affection had not yet come to an end.
"Therefore, Ānanda, do not view this as anything other than me. At that time, the King Subhūṣita was none other than my own self.

Because of my son, I once covered the temple with a single parasol; by virtue of this root of merit, I have transmigrated through the realms of gods and humans, becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King hundreds of thousands of times, or serving as Śakra or Brahmā."
At that time, I did not know this was a Pratyekabuddha; had I known it was a Pratyekabuddha, his virtue would have been immeasurable.

Had the Tathāgata not attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path, he would have manifested as a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King another two thousand five hundred times to govern and transform the world.
Because he has attained the Way, these two thousand five hundred canopies now manifest spontaneously.
"Ānanda, it is for this cause and condition that the Tathāgata smiles.
Serving the Buddhas brings about such merit as this, which is beyond measure."
Therefore, Ānanda, you should seek skillful means to make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones!
It is thus.
"Ānanda! You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, leading the assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded toward the city of Vaiśālī and stayed at the city gate, where he spoke this verse:
"Now that I have attained the state of a Tathāgata, the foremost in the world,
by this word of supreme sincerity, may there be no harm in Vaiśālī. Furthermore,
through the Dharma of supreme sincerity, may one attain the realm of Nirvāṇa."
By this word of truth, may there be no harm in Vaiśālī.
Furthermore, by the truth of the Saṅgha, the foremost assembly of noble and holy ones—
by this word of truth, may there be no harm in Vaiśālī.
May bipeds find peace and security, and likewise quadrupeds;
may those traveling on the path be auspicious, and likewise those who come here.
May they find peace by day and by night, with no one to cause them affliction.
"By holding to these words of utmost sincerity, may Vaiśālī be free from calamity.
After the Tathāgata had spoken these words, the rākṣasas and spirits each fled in haste; they no longer remained in their abodes and did not enter the city of Vaiśālī again.
All those who were afflicted by illness were each healed.

At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling by the side of the Monkey Pond. The people of the land served and made offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicines for the sick, according to their respective status, whether noble or humble. Each came in turn to provide meals for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, and they also observed the eightfold precepts without missing the proper times.
At that time, within the city of Vaiśālī, there were six teachers who were traveling there to teach and transform others.
These so-called six teachers were:
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
At that time, the six teachers gathered in one place and spoke thus:
"This śramaṇa Gautama resides in this city of Vaiśālī and is honored by the people, yet we are not honored by the people."
"We should go and debate with him; who will prevail and who will be defeated? Pūraṇa Kāśyapa said:
“Whichever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas do not accept the words of others but resort to skillful means to pose challenges—this is not the dharma of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Yet this śramaṇa Gautama does not accept the words of others but resorts to skillful means to raise difficulties; how can we possibly engage him in debate?”

Ayuan said: "There is no giving and no receiving, nor is there anyone who gives; furthermore, there are no classes of sentient beings in this world or the next, nor is there any retribution for good or evil."
Goyāla said: "On the banks of the Ganges, he slaughtered countless people, piling their flesh into mountains;
yet on the left bank of the Ganges, he performed various meritorious deeds. Because of this, there is no retribution for either good or evil."

Puṣkarasārin said: "Even if one were on the left bank of the Ganges, practicing generosity and observing the precepts, providing for others at all times so that they lack nothing, there would still be no such karmic reward."
Purāṇa Kāśyapa said: "There is no speech, nor is there any response to speech; only silence is bliss. The Nirgrantha said:
“There is speech, and there is also the fruit of speech.
The śramaṇa Gautama is a human being, and I too am a human being; what Gautama knows, we also know.”
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses supernormal powers, and I too possess supernormal powers.
If that śramaṇa manifests one supernormal power, we shall manifest two;
if he manifests two supernormal powers, we shall manifest four."
When he manifests four, I manifest eight;
when he manifests eight, I manifest sixteen;
when he manifests sixteen, I manifest thirty-two. I always cause my manifestations to increase, never yielding to him, so that I am fully able to match his strength.
If they do not accept our doctrine, that is their own fault; once the people have heard this, they will no longer make offerings to them, and we shall receive the offerings instead.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who heard these words and said:
"The six teachers have gathered in one place and produced this fundamental argument:
'The śramaṇa Gautama does not accept debate with others; we shall surely be victorious.'"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Śulani flew into the air and, facing those six teachers, spoke this verse:
"My teacher is peerless, Most honored and unsurpassed;
I am his venerable disciple, Named Śulani."
If you possess any grounds [for debate], then engage me in discussion;
I shall respond to every point, like a lion pouncing upon a deer.
For now, set aside my venerable teacher; originally, there was no Tathāgata at all.
"I, a bhikṣuṇī now, am fully capable of subduing the non-Buddhists.
After this bhikṣuṇī had spoken these words, the six teachers were not even able to look up at her face, much less engage in debate with her.
At that time, the people of the city of Vaiśālī saw from afar the bhikṣuṇī in the midst of the air debating with the six teachers; yet the six teachers were unable to respond to her.
Each person celebrated and rejoiced immeasurably, saying:
"Today the six teachers have been humbled by her."
At that time, the six teachers were filled with extreme sorrow and departed from the city of Vaiśālī, never to enter it again.

When the many bhikṣus heard that the bhikṣuṇī Śulā had prevailed in her debate with the six teachers, they went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and reported these events in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The bhikṣuṇī Śulū possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic authority, and vast wisdom and learning.
For a long night, I have constantly harbored this thought:"
"There is no one else capable of debating with the six teachers, save for the Tathāgata and this bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see any other bhikṣuṇī who is able to subdue the non-Buddhists as this bhikṣuṇī has?"
The bhikṣus replied: “No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus! Among my śrāvakas, the foremost bhikṣuṇī capable of subduing non-Buddhists is the bhikṣuṇī Śulū."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 12 (12) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are six spheres of contact with smoothness. What are the six?
What are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind entrances—these are termed the six entrances (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
When an ordinary person sees a form with the eye, they immediately give rise to a mind of defiled attachment and are unable to relinquish it;
because they see forms and give rise to extreme craving and clinging, they transmigrate through birth and death without a time of liberation.

The six sense-faculties are likewise thus: when they give rise to thoughts of defiled attachment, the mind cannot relinquish them; by means of this, one wanders through saṃsāra without a time of liberation.

"If a noble disciple of the World-Honored One, having seen forms with the eye, does not give rise to defiled attachment and has no defiled mind, he is then able to discern that this eye is a phenomenon of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self."
The six sense-faculties are likewise thus: one does not give rise to a defiled mind, but discerns these six sense-faculties as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
When one contemplates in this way, one immediately attains two fruits: in this very life, one becomes either a non-returner (anāgāmin) or an arhat.

It is just as if there were a person who, being extremely hungry, wished to prepare some grain or barley; by winnowing and cleaning it until it was pure, he would take it and eat it, thereby removing his hunger and thirst.

The noble disciple is also like this: regarding these six sense-faculties, by contemplating them as foul, leaking, and impure, they immediately realize the path and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means to extinguish these six sense-faculties. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya*, Fascicle 32.
Ekottarika Āgama, Scroll Thirty-Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Thirty-Nine: On Equal Dharmas. Chapter Thirty-Nine: On Equal Dharmas.
1. (One) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes seven qualities, he will experience inexhaustible happiness in this present life; and if he wishes to attain the exhaustion of the outflows, he will be able to achieve it.”
What are the seven qualities?

In this regard, a bhikṣu knows the Dharma, knows the meaning, knows the proper time, is further able to know himself, is further able to know contentment, and is further able to know how to enter an assembly and observe those within it; these are called the seven qualities.
“How does a bhikṣu know the Dharma?
In this regard, a bhikṣu knows the Dharma, namely: the sūtras, geyas, verses (gāthās), nidānas, avadānas, vṛttakas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulya-s, adbhuta-dharma-s, upadeśa-s, and vyākaraṇa-s.”
If there is a bhikṣu who does not know the Dharma and does not understand the twelve divisions of the scriptures, he is not a bhikṣu.
Because such a bhikṣu is able to comprehend and understand the Dharma, he is called one who knows the Dharma.
In this way, a bhikṣu understands the Dharma.
How does a bhikṣu understand the meaning?
In this regard, a bhikṣu knows the Tathāgata’s underlying intent, understands the profound meaning, and has no doubts or difficulties.
If there is a bhikṣu who does not understand the definitive meaning (nītārtha), he is not a bhikṣu.
Because a bhikṣu is able to know the profound meaning, he is called one who "understands the meaning."
In this way, a bhikṣu is able to discern the meaning.
"How does a bhikṣu know the appropriate timing? Herein, a bhikṣu knows the proper season:

when it is time to practice insight (vipaśyanā), he practices insight; when it is time to practice tranquility (śamatha), he practices tranquility; when it is time for silence, he knows to remain silent; when it is time for action, he knows to act; when it is time for recitation, he knows to recite; when it is time to teach others, he teaches them; and when it is time to speak, he knows to speak."
If there is a bhikṣu who does not know this—that is, who does not know the proper application of śamatha and vipaśyanā—he is not a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu knows the appropriate timing and does not miss the right occasion, he is said to act in accordance with what is suitable for the situation.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows the appropriate timing.
How does a bhikṣu cultivate himself? In this regard, a bhikṣu is able to know himself:
"I now possess this seeing, hearing, mindfulness, and knowledge; I have such wisdom that in my walking and stopping, I always follow the True Dharma.
If there is a bhikṣu who cannot know for himself what is appropriate regarding his wisdom in his coming and going and his movements, he is not a bhikṣu.

Because that bhikṣu is able to personally cultivate what is appropriate regarding his own conduct and movements, this is called "personally cultivating one's own practice"; this is what is meant by saying a bhikṣu is able to know himself.
"How does a bhikṣu know contentment for himself?

In this regard, a bhikṣu is able to deliberate for himself on what is appropriate regarding sleep, waking, sitting, lying down, walking meditation, and movement; he is able to know contentment in all these matters."
If there were a bhikṣu who could not understand this, he would not be a bhikṣu.
Because a bhikṣu is able to comprehend and realize this, he is called "one who knows contentment."
In this way, a bhikṣu is said to be "contented.
How does a bhikṣu know how to enter a great assembly?

In this regard, a bhikṣu distinguishes the assembly: "This is a group of kṣatriyas; this is a group of brāhmaṇas; this is a group of householders; this is a group of śramaṇas. I shall employ such methods as are appropriate for each of these assemblies, knowing fully when it is proper to speak and when it is proper to remain silent."
If there is a bhikṣu who does not know how to enter the assembly, he is not a bhikṣu.
Because a bhikṣu knows how to enter the great assembly, he is called "one who knows how to enter the assembly."
This is called a bhikṣu who knows how to enter a great assembly.
"How does a bhikṣu know the fundamental dispositions of others?
A bhikṣu should know that there are two kinds of persons."
What are the two? There may be one person who wishes to go to a park to personally visit a bhikṣu;
there may be a second person who does not wish to go there to see that bhikṣu.
"Among those people who wish to go to the grove to personally visit the bhikṣu, this person is the most excellent.
Bhikṣus! Furthermore, there are two other types of persons."
What are these two?
The first person, though he goes to where the bhikṣu is, does not inquire after what is appropriate;
the second person likewise does not go to the monastery to see the bhikṣu.
Among those who go to the monastery, he is the foremost.
"Monks! Furthermore, there are two other types of persons."
What are these two? One person goes to where the bhikṣu is to inquire after his well-being at the appropriate time;
the second person does not go to where the bhikṣu is to inquire after his well-being at the appropriate time.
"Among those who go to the monastery, that person is the most honored and foremost; he stands above all others.
Monks! Furthermore, there are two other kinds of persons."
What are the two? One person goes to where the bhikṣu is and listens to the Dharma with a sincere heart;
the second person does not go to where the bhikṣu is and does not listen to the Dharma with a sincere heart.
"One who listens to the Dharma with a sincere mind is the foremost among such people.
Bhikṣus! Furthermore, there are two other kinds of persons."
What are these two?
There is one person who is able to observe the Dharma, receiving, upholding, reciting, and chanting it;
the second person, however, is unable to receive, uphold, recite, or chant it.
"Among those who receive, uphold, recite, and chant [this], that person is the most preeminent.
Bhikṣus! Furthermore, there are two other types of persons."
What are the two? There is one person who hears the Dharma and understands its meaning;
there is a second person who hears the Dharma but does not understand its meaning.
Among those who hear the Dharma and understand its meaning, such a person is the most honored and foremost.
"Monks! Furthermore, there are two other types of persons."
What are these two? There is one person who hears the Dharma and accomplishes the Dharma;
there is a second person who does not hear the Dharma and does not accomplish the Dharma.
"Among those who have accomplished both the person and the Dharma, this person is foremost.
Monks! Furthermore, there are two other types of persons."
What are these two?
One person, having heard the Dharma, is able to endure and practice it, discerning and upholding the True Dharma;
the second person is unable to endure and practice that Dharma.
Those who are able to practice the Dharma are the most honored and supreme among all these people.
It is just as when there is curd from a cow, from which comes butter, and from which comes ghee; the ghee is the most supreme, and none can equal it.
This is also like that: if there is anyone capable of practicing it, this person is the foremost, with none able to equal them; this is called a bhikṣu observing the faculties of others.
If there are those who do not understand this, they are not bhikṣus.
Among bhikṣus, those who hear the Dharma and discern its meaning are the most excellent.
In this way, a bhikṣu observes the faculties of others.
If a bhikṣu is accomplished in seven qualities, he will experience happiness and non-action in the present life, and he will have no doubt regarding his desire to sever the outflows.
Therefore, bhikkhus, you should seek skillful means to accomplish these seven qualities.
Thus it is, bhikkhus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“The Pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven has a base fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and it is one hundred yojanas high. Its shade covers fifty yojanas to the east, west, south, and north; there, the Trāyastriṃśa devas enjoy themselves for four months.”
"Monks, you should know that there may come a time when the flowers and leaves of that pāṭalī tree wither and fall, lying yellowed upon the ground.
At that time, seeing this auspicious omen, the devas will all feel joy and gladness will arise within them, thinking:
'This tree will soon produce flowers and fruit again.'"
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there may come a time when the flowers and fruits of that tree have all withered and fallen, discarded upon the ground.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven will be even more joyful and will say to one another:
‘This tree will soon turn grey.’”
“Monks, you should know that after a further period of time had passed, that tree turned a grayish color.
At that time, when the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens saw that the tree had turned gray, they were filled with great joy and said to one another:
‘Now that this tree has turned gray, before long its lattice-work will emerge.’”

At that time, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven saw that this pārijāta tree had already produced its network of buds, they knew that before long the stage of the hail-like blossoms would emerge.
Having seen this, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were filled with joy once more, thinking:
"Today this tree has already produced its hail-like blossoms; before long it shall again be in full bloom."
“Bhikṣus, you should know that when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven see this tree gradually blossoming, they each feel great joy, thinking:
‘This tree will soon gradually blossom; before long, it will be covered entirely with flowers.’”
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there may come a time when those trees all bloom at once, and they all feel great joy, thinking:
‘Today these trees have all put forth their flowers.’”
At that time, this fragrance traveled against the wind, such that within a hundred yojanas there was no one who did not smell it.
Then, for four months, the various devas enjoyed themselves among one another; their pleasures were beyond measure.
"It is just so with this: when a noble disciple intends to leave the household life to study the Way, it is like that tree beginning to wither.

Furthermore, when a noble disciple renounces wife and wealth, and out of firm faith leaves the household life to study the Way, shaving off hair and beard, it is like those leaves falling to the ground."

“Bhikṣus, you should know: if a noble disciple is free from thoughts of sensual desire, eliminates unwholesome states, maintains mindfulness and joy, and dwells with a mind focused on the first dhyāna, he resembles that *tāla* tree which has become grey.”

"Furthermore, when the noble disciple has stilled applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and with internal joy and one-pointedness of mind, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied thought and without sustained thought—just as that tree produces a web of vines."

"Furthermore, the noble disciple maintains mindfulness and possesses protection; he personally experiences bliss within his own body, which is that which is rescued by the noble ones. Being fully endowed with protective mindfulness, he dwells in the third dhyāna, just like that tree producing nodes from hail."

"Furthermore, when the noble disciple has brought suffering and pleasure to an end, and being previously free from sorrow, dwells in a state that is neither painful nor pleasant, with pure mindfulness and equanimity, his mind abiding in the fourth dhyāna—this is like that tree gradually blossoming."

"Furthermore, the noble disciple has exhausted all taints (āsrava) and attained the untainted liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, he dwells in joy, knowing according to reality:
'Birth and death have been ended; the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further taking of a womb.'"

Just as those trees were all in full bloom, at that time, the fragrance of the virtuous precepts of the noble disciples pervaded the four quarters, such that there was no one who did not praise them; for four months they enjoyed themselves, dwelling their minds in the four dhyānas and fully accomplishing the foundations of practice.
Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to accomplish the fragrance of virtuous precepts. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of seven matters using the analogy of water; human beings are also like this.”
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One replied: "In what way do those seven things resemble people through the analogy of water?

It is like a person submerged at the bottom of the water; or another who, having briefly emerged from the water, submerges again; or another who, having emerged from the water, looks around; or another who, having raised his head, remains there; or another who walks upon the water; or another who, having emerged from the water, desires to reach the further shore; or another who has already reached the further shore."
"Monks, these are called the seven similes of water that appear in the world.
What kind of person is one who sinks to the bottom of the water and cannot emerge?

In this regard, there may be a person whose body is completely filled with unwholesome states; such a person will pass through kalpas without being able to be cured, and this is called "sinking to the bottom of the water."
"What kind of person is one who emerges from the water and sinks back down?

There may be a person whose faculty of faith gradually thins; although they possess wholesome qualities, these are not firm. They practice wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, but later they again practice unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind. When their body breaks up at the end of life, they are reborn in hell. This is called a person who emerges from the water and sinks back down."
“What kind of person is one who emerges from the water and looks about?

In this regard, there is a certain person who possesses the roots of goodness of faith; however, his conduct of body, speech, and mind does not further increase that dharma, and he remains merely maintaining himself. When his body breaks up at the end of life, he is reborn among the asuras. This is called a person who emerges from the water and looks about.”
"Who is the person who has emerged from the water and stands upon it?

In this regard, there is a certain person who possesses faith and diligence; having severed the three fetters, they do not regress further and will certainly reach the ultimate goal, attaining the unsurpassed path. This is called the person who has emerged from the water and stands upon it."
"Who is that person who desires to cross over the water?

In this regard, there may be a person who possesses the faculty of faith and diligence, who constantly maintains a sense of shame and remorse, who has severed the three fetters, whose lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated, and who, having come to this world, brings an end to suffering. This is called the person who desires to cross over the water."
"Who is the person desiring to reach the further shore?

There is a person who possesses the faculty of faith and diligence, who has severed the five lower fetters, and has become a non-returner (anāgāmin); they attain parinirvāṇa right there and do not return to this world again. This is called the person desiring to reach the further shore."
"Who are those who have reached the further shore?

In this regard, there is a certain person who possesses the faculty of faith and exerts diligence, and who, being possessed of a sense of shame and dread of blame, has exhausted all taints and realized the state of being without outflows;

they find delight in the present life, knowing as it truly is: 'Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further undergoing of conception.'"
"One who attains parinirvāṇa within this realm of nirvana without remainder is called a person who has crossed to the further shore.
This, monks, is what is meant."

I have explained these seven types of people to you through the analogy of water. The practice by which the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, should deliver sentient beings has now been fully implemented.
You should dwell in secluded and quiet places, or beneath trees, and you must practice seated meditation with mindfulness, never giving rise to indolence.
"This is my instruction.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“When a noble wheel-turning monarch rules and transforms a distant land, if he accomplishes seven qualities, he will not be captured by enemies or thieves.”
What are the seven?
That city wall is exceedingly high and steep, well-maintained and orderly; this is called the first quality that the king has first accomplished.
Furthermore, the gates and doors of that city are firm and secure; this is called the second quality by which that city is perfected.
Furthermore, the moat surrounding that city is extremely deep and wide; this is called the third quality by which this city is perfected.
Furthermore, that city has an abundance of various grains and rice, with its granaries and storehouses filled to capacity; this is called the fourth quality by which that city is perfected.
Furthermore, that city abounds in firewood and grass; this is called the fifth quality by which that city is perfected.
Furthermore, that city possesses many weapons and implements of war; this is called the sixth quality by which that city is perfected.

Furthermore, the lord of that city is exceedingly intelligent and highly talented, possessing foreknowledge of human affairs; he applies the whip where it is deserved and administers justice where it is required. This is called the seventh quality by which that city is perfected, such that external enemies cannot come to invade it.
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus!
When the ruler of that city and kingdom accomplishes these seven qualities, outsiders cannot harass him.
In the same way, this bhikṣu, if he accomplishes these seven qualities, the evil Māra Pāpīyān will find no opportunity against him."
What are the seven?
In this regard, monks, one is accomplished in the precepts and fully endowed with dignified conduct; one fears even the transgression of minor rules, let alone those that are major!

This is called a bhikṣu who has accomplished this first dharma; Māra the Evil One finds no opportunity against him, just as that city, being high, broad, and extremely steep, cannot be breached or destroyed.

"Furthermore, bhikṣu! When the eye sees forms, one does not give rise to conceptual attachment nor arouse discursive thoughts; one maintains the faculty of the eye in its full integrity without deficiency or leakage, thus guarding the faculty of the eye.

It is the same for sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental phenomena cognized by the mind: one likewise does not give rise to conceptual attachment, maintains the faculty of the mind in its full integrity without distracted thoughts, and fully guards the faculty of the mind. This is called the second dharma accomplished by a bhikṣu, whereby the evil Māra Pāpīyān finds no opportunity, just as that city’s gates and doors are firmly secured."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

One who is learned and does not forget, who constantly recollects, contemplates, and reflects upon the teachings of the True Dharma, and who fully knows all that was previously experienced—this is called a bhikṣu who has accomplished this third dharma; the evil Māra Pāpīyān cannot find an opportunity against him, just as that city’s outer moat is exceedingly deep and wide."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

There are many skillful means regarding all dharmas that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; they are perfectly pure and lead to the cultivation of the holy life. This is called the fourth dharma accomplished by a bhikṣu, which is like a city wall possessing abundant grain and rice, such that external enemies do not dare to come and invade."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

One contemplates the four dharmas of the higher mind (*catur-adhicitta-dharma*) without omission; this is called the bhikṣu’s accomplishment of this fifth dharma, whereby Māra Pāpīyān finds no opportunity, just as an external foe cannot come to harass a city that has abundant fuel and grass."

"Furthermore, bhikṣu! One who has attained the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) encounters no difficulty in what he undertakes; this is called the bhikṣu’s accomplishment of this sixth dharma, whereby Māra Pāpīyān finds no opportunity, just as in that city where weapons and armor are fully prepared."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

One who is fully able to discern the aggregates (skandhas), the sense bases (āyatanas), and the elements (dhātus), and who likewise discerns the phenomena arising from the twelve links of dependent origination—this is called a bhikṣu who has accomplished these seven dharmas. Māra the Wicked One finds no opportunity against him, just as a ruler of a city-state, wise and highly talented, may either take in or dismiss [those he encounters] as the situation requires."
"Now this bhikṣu is also like this; he fully knows and discriminates the various ailments of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
If a bhikṣu accomplishes these seven dharmas, the evil Māra Pāpīyān will never find an opportunity against him."

Therefore, monks, you should seek the appropriate methods to discern the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) without losing their proper sequence; thus you shall transcend the realm of Māra and not dwell within it.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. (Five) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the seven stations of consciousness;
listen attentively, and reflect upon them well. The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One! At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What are those seven stations of consciousness? They are as follows:
