first, there are sentient beings who possess various kinds of bodies and various perceptions, namely humans and devas.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who possess various kinds of bodies but have a single perception, namely the Brahmakāyika devas when they first appear in the world."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who have a single body with manifold perceptions, namely those of the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
furthermore, there are sentient beings who have a single body with a single perception, namely those of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven;
furthermore, there are sentient beings of infinite space, namely those of the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven.
Furthermore, there are beings who possess infinite consciousness; these are the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
Furthermore, there are beings for whom there is no sphere; these are the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness.
This is what is meant, O bhikṣu!

Regarding the seven stations of consciousness, I have now explained the seven abodes of consciousness; that which the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perform to guide and deliver sentient beings has been accomplished today.
"When dwelling in seclusion beneath a tree, you should skillfully cultivate your practice and not be indolent.
This is my instruction.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Cunda was afflicted by a grave illness; he lay upon his bed and was unable to rise or move about on his own.
At that time, Sundara thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, does not show compassion today; moreover, I have encountered a grave illness, my life will not last long, and medical treatment is unavailable."
Furthermore, I have heard the World-Honored One say:
"As long as there is even one person not yet delivered, I shall never abandon them.
Yet now, I alone am cast aside; what suffering this must be!
At that time, the World-Honored One heard with his divine ear the monk Kundo voicing such grievances.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the monks:
"All of you, assemble and go to the place where the monk Kundo is, and inquire after his illness."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One, accompanied by a great multitude of bhikṣus, gradually arrived at the dwelling of the bhikṣu Kuṇḍadhāna.
At that time, seeing the Tathāgata approaching from afar, Kuṇḍadhāna immediately prostrated himself upon the ground.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying:
"Your illness is now extremely grave; there is no need for you to leave your bed, as I have a seat of my own."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying:
"Is your ailment increasing, decreasing, or neither increasing nor decreasing?
Are you able to endure and receive my instruction?"
At that time, the bhikṣu Sundara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“My illness today is extremely grave; it only increases and does not diminish.
As for the medicinal herbs I have taken, there are none that I have not exhausted.”
The World-Honored One asked,
"Who is it that has been looking after the sick? Kuṇḍadhāna replied:
“May the fellow practitioners of the holy life come to see and attend upon me.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying:
“Are you now capable of explaining the seven factors of enlightenment to me?”
At that time, Samantamukha proclaimed his name three times, saying:
"I am now capable of expounding the Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment before the Tathāgata."
The World-Honored One said:
"If you are able to bear it and speak before the Tathāgata, then speak now.
At that time, Kuṇḍadhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for the seven factors of enlightenment, what are the seven?

They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness as taught by the Tathāgata, the factor of enlightenment of dharma, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity."
“Thus it is, World-Honored One!
That one who possesses these seven factors of awakening refers precisely to this.
When the Venerable Cunda had spoken these words, all his ailments were completely healed, and he was free from all suffering.
At that time, Sundarī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The most excellent among medicines is precisely this Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment.

If one wishes to speak of the most excellent among medicines, it does not exceed these seven factors of enlightenment; by now contemplating these seven factors of enlightenment, all ailments whatsoever are completely healed."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should receive, uphold, contemplate, and recite this Dharma of the seven factors of enlightenment. Do not harbor any doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; then all the ailments of those sentient beings will be completely healed."

The reason for this is that these seven factors of enlightenment are extremely difficult to comprehend; they bring full understanding of all dharmas and illuminate all dharmas, just as excellent medicine cures all manner of ailments, and like ambrosia, one can never have enough of them.
If one does not attain these seven factors of awakening, sentient beings will continue to wander through birth and death. Monks!
You should seek skillful means and cultivate the seven factors of awakening.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7 (Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, seven treasures appear in the world.

They are the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure; these are the seven treasures."
This is called the appearance of the Wheel-Turning Sage King in the world, whereby these seven treasures are then disseminated throughout the world.
"Likewise, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyaṅga) appear in the world."
What are the seven?

They are the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of dharma-discernment, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity; these appear in the world.
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, these seven treasures of the factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga-ratna) likewise appear in the world. Therefore, monks,
you should seek skillful means and cultivate these seven factors of awakening.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, he then selects a choice site to establish a city and citadel, twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from south to north; the land is fertile and abundant, its happiness beyond description."
At that time, the city was surrounded by sevenfold outer walls, with the seven treasures interspersed between them.
As for what are called the seven treasures: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, amber, agate, and musaragalva; these are known as the seven treasures.

Furthermore, there are moats made of the seven precious substances surrounding those sevenfold walls; they are exceedingly deep and wide, difficult for people to cross, and their beds are entirely covered with golden sand.
Moreover, trees made of the seven precious substances grow among them;
these trees possess seven colors: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, and amber.
Furthermore, that city was surrounded by seven layers of gates, all of which were solidly constructed and made of the seven precious substances.

The silver gates were interspersed with gold, the golden gates were inlaid with silver, the crystal gates were inlaid with lapis lazuli, the lapis lazuli gates were inlaid with crystal, and the agate gates were inlaid with amber; it was a place of such exquisite joy that it is truly beyond description.
Furthermore, on the four sides of that city, there are four bathing pools; each pool is one yojana in length and breadth, naturally filled with water, and fashioned from gold, silver, and crystal.
When the water in the silver pond freezes, it becomes silver treasure; when the water in the golden pond freezes, it becomes gold treasure; and the wheel-turning sage king makes use of these.
"At that time, within that city, there were seven kinds of sounds. What are the seven?

They are the sound of conch shells, the sound of drums, the sound of small drums, the sound of bells, the sound of *kettledrums*, the sound of dancing, and the sound of singing; these are called the seven kinds of sounds."
At that time, the people constantly entertained themselves in this manner.
Furthermore, those sentient beings experienced neither cold nor heat, nor hunger nor thirst, nor any illness.

However, while a Wheel-Turning Sage King dwells in the world to transform and guide beings, he accomplishes these seven treasures and the four bases of spiritual power without deficiency, never losing them until the end of his life.
How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King achieve the seven treasures?
They are the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the queen treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure.

Furthermore, he has a thousand sons who are exceedingly valiant and capable of subduing external enemies; yet, throughout this land of Jambudvīpa, he transforms those nations not by means of the sword or the staff.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King achieve the perfection of the wheel-treasure?”
The World-Honored One said:
"At that time, on the fifteenth day at dawn, the Wheel-Turning Sage King had bathed and washed his head; he was seated upon the great palace terrace, surrounded by jade-like women."

At that time, the precious wheel—complete with a thousand spokes—came from the east and appeared before the palace, its radiance brilliant and magnificent, not made by human hands; hovering seven spans above the ground, it gradually approached and came to rest before the king.
Having seen this, the Wheel-Turning Sage King spoke thus:
"I have heard from those of old:

'When a Wheel-Turning King bathes his head and hands on the fifteenth day and sits upon the palace terrace, at that time the Wheel-Jewel naturally appears from the east and comes to rest before the king.'"
"I shall now test this Wheel-Treasure.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King took the Wheel-Treasure in his right hand and spoke these words:
"Now turn according to the Dharma; do not turn by means of what is contrary to the Dharma."
At that time, the precious wheel turned spontaneously and remained suspended in mid-air.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King, together with his fourfold army, likewise remained in the void.
At that time, the wheel-treasure turned toward the eastern direction, and the Wheel-turning Sage King also followed the precious wheel.
Whenever the wheel-treasure came to a halt, the multitude led by the Wheel-turning Sage King likewise remained there with it.

At that time, the minor kings and the various classes of people of the eastern region saw the Wheel-Turning Sage King approaching from afar; they all rose to welcome him and offered him golden bowls filled with broken silver and silver bowls filled with broken gold, saying to the king:
"Welcome, O Sage King!"
"Now this realm is densely populated with people, and its happiness is beyond measure; I pray that Your Majesty shall rule and transform it from within!
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King addressed those people, saying:

"You should govern and transform [the people] by means of the Dharma, not by what is contrary to the Dharma. Furthermore, do not kill, steal, or engage in sexual misconduct; take care not to govern by means of what is contrary to the Dharma."
At that time, the wheel-treasure moved again to the south, the west, and the north, universally pacifying and transforming the people;
it then returned to the king’s seat of governance and came to rest seven cubits above the ground.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
a wheel-turning sage king accomplishes this precious wheel-treasure.
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King come to possess the elephant-treasure?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that on the fifteenth day, the Wheel-Turning Sage King bathes and washes himself in the great hall.”

At that time, the elephant-treasure came from the south; it had six tusks, its coat was exceedingly white, and its seven parts were perfectly proportioned. It was adorned with gold, silver, and precious jewels, and was capable of flying through the void.
At that time, having seen this, the Wheel-Turning Sage King thought to himself:
"This elephant-treasure is now exceedingly exquisite and rare in the world; its nature is gentle and mild, and it does not act with sudden violence. I shall now test this elephant-treasure."
At that time, when the sun was about to rise at dawn, the Wheel-Turning Sage King mounted this elephant-treasure and traveled beyond the four seas to govern and transform the people.
"In this way, a Wheel-Turning Sage King accomplishes the elephant treasure.
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King accomplish the horse treasure?"
The World-Honored One said:

"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, at that time the Horse-Jewel comes from the west; its body hair is intensely blue, and the tail hair has a crimson luster. It moves without swaying and is able to fly through the void without any obstruction."
Having seen this, he was filled with extreme joy and thought:
"This horse-treasure is truly extraordinary; I shall now employ it. Furthermore, its nature is excellent and free from any violent temper; I shall now test this horse-treasure."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King mounted this horse, traversed the four continents to govern and transform the people, and returned to his royal capital.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
a wheel-turning sage king is endowed with the horse-treasure.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Furthermore, by what cause is the jewel-treasure accomplished?
The World-Honored One replied:
“In this regard, bhikṣus!”

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, at that time a precious jewel comes from the east; it has eight facets, with flames of light on its four sides, and measures one foot and six inches in length. Upon seeing it, the Wheel-Turning Sage King thinks to himself:
"This precious jewel is exceedingly sublime and wondrous; I shall now test it."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King assembled the fourfold army at midnight and placed this maṇi jewel atop a high banner; at once, its radiance illuminated the realm for twelve yojanas.
At that time, when the people of the city saw this light, they each said to one another:
"The sun has now risen; we may attend to our household affairs."
At that time, having surveyed the people from atop the palace hall, the Wheel-Turning Sage King returned to his inner chambers.
Then, the Wheel-Turning Sage King took this maṇi jewel and placed it within the palace; both inside and out were entirely illuminated, with no place left unlit.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
a wheel-turning sage king accomplishes this jewel-treasure.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King achieve the possession of the Jewel of the Woman?

The World-Honored One replied, “Bhikṣus, you should know that when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, this Jewel of the Woman naturally manifests. Her countenance is upright and beautiful; her face has the color of a peach blossom. She is neither tall nor short, neither too pale nor too dark. Her nature is gentle and mild; she does not act with violence or rashness. Her breath carries the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and her body exudes the scent of sandalwood.”
He constantly attended upon the noble king at his side, never missing the proper occasion, and always regarded the king’s countenance with a serene and joyful expression.
Thus it was, bhikṣus!
"A Wheel-turning Sage King accomplishes this gem of a woman.
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a Wheel-turning King accomplish the gem of a householder?"
The World-Honored One said:

"In this regard, monks, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, there likewise appears in the world this Householder Jewel. He is neither too tall nor too short; his body is crimson in color; he is highly intelligent and sagacious, with nothing that remains unopened to him; furthermore, he has attained the supernormal power of the divine eye."
At that time, the householder came to the king’s presence and addressed him, saying:
"May the Holy King enjoy infinite longevity!
If Your Majesty requires gold, silver, or precious jewels, I shall provide them all."

At that time, the householder used his divine eye to observe those who possessed treasure stores and those who did not, seeing them all clearly; whatever treasures the king required, he provided and bestowed upon him at all times.

At that time, when the Wheel-Turning Sage King wished to test that householder, he took the householder across the water; before they had reached the opposite shore, he spoke to the householder, saying:
"I now require gold, silver, and precious jewels; provide them for me right now."
The elder replied, "When you have reached the shore, I shall provide for you.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King said:
"I have need of jewels here in this place; I do not need them once we reach the shore.
At that moment, the householder immediately knelt down before him with palms joined toward the water, and instantly the seven treasures surged forth from within the water.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King said to the elder:
"Stop! Stop!"
“Householder, there is no further need for treasures. Thus, monks,
the wheel-turning sage king is endowed with this householder-treasure.
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King achieve the possession of the precious military commander?
The World-Honored One replied:

"Then, monks! When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears in the world, this treasure spontaneously manifests in response to him. Possessing intelligence that surpasses all others, he foreknows the sentiments of men; his physical form is of exquisite beauty, and he approaches the Wheel-Turning Sage King and says to him:
'I pray only that the Sage King may enjoy himself in happiness!'"
"If the Holy King requires a military force, it shall be provided and prepared immediately; the propriety of its advance and retreat shall never miss the proper timing.
At that time, the Jewel of the Military Commander, in accordance with the King's thoughts, mobilized and assembled the troops, keeping them at the King’s side.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King wished to test the Treasure of the Military Commander. He then had this thought:
"Let my military forces assemble right now."
"Immediately, the army was outside the king's gate.
If the Wheel-Turning Sage King wished for the army to stop, it would stop; if he wished for it to advance, it would advance.
In this same way, bhikṣu!"
"A Wheel-turning Sage King accomplishes this treasure of the military commander.
Bhikṣus, you should know that a Wheel-turning Sage King accomplishes these seven treasures.
At that time, that bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King achieve the four bases of psychic power and obtain such excellent benefit?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“In this regard, the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s countenance is upright and handsome, rare in the world and surpassing that of ordinary people; he is like a celestial son whom none can equal. This is called the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s achievement of the first base of psychic power.”

"Furthermore, the Wheel-Turning Sage King was of such transcendent intelligence that there was no matter he had not mastered; he was a hero among men, and at that time, none surpassed this Wheel-Turning Sage King in the abundance of his wisdom."
This is called accomplishing this second supernormal power. "Furthermore, monks!
A Wheel-Turning Sage King is free from disease; his body is robust and strong, whatever he consumes is naturally digested, and he is without the affliction of excrement or urine."
This, monks, is called the third divine power (ṛddhipāda) accomplished by a Wheel-turning Sage King. Furthermore, monks:
The wheel-turning sage king’s life span is exceedingly long, his longevity being incalculable; at that time, the life span of humans does not exceed that of the wheel-turning sage king.
This is what is meant, O bhikṣus!
The wheel-turning sage king accomplishes this fourth basis of psychic power.
Thus it is said, O bhikṣu:
the wheel-turning sage king possesses these four bases of psychic power.
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After a Wheel-Turning Sage King has passed away, where will he be reborn?
The World-Honored One replied:
"After the death of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where he enjoys a lifespan of a thousand years.
This is because the Wheel-Turning Sage King himself refrains from taking life and further teaches others to refrain from taking life;
he himself refrains from stealing and further teaches others to refrain from theft."
They themselves refrain from sexual misconduct and further teach others not to engage in it;
they themselves refrain from false speech and further teach others not to speak falsely;
they themselves practice the ten wholesome dharmas and further teach others to practice these ten wholesome dharmas.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that by virtue of these merits, after the passing of his life, the Wheel-Turning Sage King will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:

“The Wheel-Turning Sage King is truly worthy of longing and admiration; though one might say he is a human being, yet he is not merely a human being. For although he is not actually a deva, he performs the deeds of a deva, enjoys various sublime pleasures, and does not fall into the three evil realms.”
If, through the merit of my diligent observance of the precepts today, I may become a Wheel-Turning Sage King in a future life, would that not be most excellent!
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in that bhikṣu’s mind, addressed him, saying:
"Do not harbor such thoughts in the presence of the Tathāgata."

The reason for this is that although a Wheel-Turning Sage King may possess the seven treasures and the four bases of supernatural power, there is none who can equal him; yet even he cannot avoid the three evil destinies:
the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.

The reason for this is that a Wheel-Turning Sage King does not attain the four dhyānas or the four bases of psychic power, nor does he attain the Four Noble Truths; by virtue of these causes and conditions, he falls back into the three evil realms.
A human body is extremely difficult to obtain; encountering the eight difficulties and seeking liberation from them is exceedingly hard;
being born in a central land is likewise not easy;
and seeking out virtuous and good friends is also not easy.
To encounter a virtuous friend is likewise not easy;
to seek the Way by training in the Dharma of the Tathāgata is likewise difficult to find;
for the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely rare to meet.
The Dharma teachings he expounds are likewise thus: liberation, the Four Noble Truths, and the four types of impermanence are truly impossible to hear;
even a Wheel-Turning Sage King cannot attain ultimate realization regarding these four dharmas.

Monks, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, these seven treasures appear in the world; the Tathāgata’s treasure of the seven factors of enlightenment reaches the ultimate limit and is praised by gods and humans.

“Monk, today you have well cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya); you have attained the end of suffering within this very body. What use have you for these seven treasures of a wheel-turning monarch?

At that time, having heard such instruction from the Tathāgata, that monk dwelt in a secluded place, contemplating the Way and its teachings. Thus, the son of noble family who has shaved off his hair and beard, left the home life to study the Way, and sought to cultivate unsurpassed right practice—knowing according to reality:
“Birth and death are ended; the holy life is established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence.”
At that time, that bhikṣu immediately became an arhat.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Venerable Kumāra-Kāśyapa was staying in the Jyotivana Grove at Śrāvastī.
At that time, Kāśyapa was walking in meditation during the middle of the night.
Then, a deva approached Kāśyapa and, standing in the air, spoke to him, saying:
“Bhikṣus! You should know this:
at night this house has smoke, and during the day it burns with fire.”
The brahmin said to the wise man:
"Now you shall take up a knife and hew at the mountain.
As you hew at the mountain, you will surely see someone carrying a burden."
"You must rescue them!
You must excavate the mountain!
When you excavate the mountain, you will certainly see the mountain."
"You must now leave this mountain!
You must now tunnel through this mountain!
When you tunnel through the mountain, you will certainly see a frog."
"Now you must abandon the frog!
You must now pierce the mountain!
When you pierce the mountain, you will see a mass of flesh."
Having seen the mass of flesh, you must abandon it!
You must now quarry the mountain!
While quarrying the mountain, you will see a yoke.
Having seen the yoke, you shall abandon it!
You must now hew through the mountain!
Having hewn through the mountain, you shall see two paths.
Having seen the two paths, you should abandon them!
You must now cut through the mountain!
Having cut through the mountain, you shall see the tree branches.
"Having seen the tree branch, you must abandon it!
You must now cut into the mountain!
Having cut into the mountain, you will see the dragon."
“Once you have seen the dragon, do not speak with it!
You should take refuge in it and aspire for it to find its proper place.
“Monks! [he said].
You should reflect well upon this meaning;
if you do not understand it, go to the city of Śrāvastī, approach the World-Honored One, and ask about this meaning.
Whatever the Tathāgata may say, reflect upon it well and put it into practice.

The reason for this is that, were it not for the Tathāgata and his disciples who have heard it from me, I do not see anyone—whether a person, a śramaṇa, a brāhmaṇa, Māra, or a deity of Māra—who could understand this meaning.
At that time, Kāśyapa replied to the deva,
"This matter is most excellent! Then,
at dawn, Kāśyapa went to the place where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
For this reason, he reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, Kāśyapa asked the World-Honored One:
"Now I shall inquire into the meaning of the Tathāgata:
To what does that which the deva has spoken point?
For what reason is there smoke at night and fire blazing by day?"
For what reason is one called a *brāhmaṇa*?
For what reason is one called a wise person (*jñānin*)?
Furthermore, as for the statement "one who cleaves the mountain," toward what meaning does that refer?
As for what is called "a knife," that too is not understood.
For what reason is it named "carrying a burden"?
Furthermore, as for what is called "a mountain," what is its meaning?
For what reason is he further called a "frog"?
For what reason is he further called a "mass of flesh"?
For what reason is he further called a "shackle"?
For what reason is it further said that there are two paths?
What is the meaning of the "branches of the tree"?
For what reason is he named "Dragon"?
The World-Honored One said:
"House means the physical body. It is composed of the four great elements and derived matter;
it receives the blood and veins of its parents and gradually grows large. It must always be nourished and fed so that it lacks nothing, yet it is of a nature destined for dispersal."
That which has smoke at night refers to the mental intentions of sentient beings;
that which burns with fire during the day refers to the actions performed by body, speech, and mind.
The Brahmin is the Arhat; the wise man is the seeker (śaikṣa);
and the one who excavates the mountain is the mind of diligent effort (vīrya).
The sword is wisdom; the burden is the five fetters;
and the mountain is pride.
The frog is the mind of anger; the mass of flesh is greed and desire;
the shackle is the five sensual desires.
The two paths are doubt; the tree branches are ignorance;
and the dragon is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"The meaning of what that deva has spoken is thus.
You should now reflect upon it thoroughly; before long, you shall exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).

At that time, Kāśyapa, having received such instruction from the Tathāgata, practiced by himself in a secluded place. This is why sons of noble family shave their hair and beards, leave the household life, and study the Way, desiring to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established;
what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further rebirth in a womb—thus he knows it as it truly is.
At that moment, Kāśyapa became an Arhat.
At that time, Kāśyapa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra also traveled with five hundred bhikṣus to his native place.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had completed the ninety-day summer retreat in Rājagṛha, he gradually wandered through the human world for the sake of teaching and transforming beings, eventually arriving at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in the Jeta Grove within the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, many bhikṣus who had been scattered throughout the human world also came to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus:
"In what places did you spend the summer retreat? The bhikṣus replied:
"In the very place where you have been born, observe the rains retreat.
The Blessed One said:
"Among the bhikṣus in the places where you have been born, those who are able to practice *āraṇyaka* themselves..."
He is able to praise the forest hermitage (āraṇya), personally practices begging for alms, and further teaches others to practice begging for alms at the proper time;
he himself wears robes made of rags from a dust-heap (pāṃsukūla) and further teaches others to wear robes made of rags from a dust-heap;
he personally cultivates contentment and likewise praises the practice of contentment, while personally practicing few desires.
Furthermore, he praised the practice of few desires and delighted in secluded places himself;
he also taught others to dwell in secluded places. He maintained his own conduct and likewise taught others to maintain their conduct.
His own precepts were complete and pure, and he further taught others to cultivate those precepts. His own three...
Having achieved concentration (*samādhi*), they further teach others to practice it; having achieved wisdom (*prajñā*) themselves, they further teach others to practice it;
having achieved liberation (*vimukti*) themselves, they further teach others to practice it;
and having achieved the vision and knowledge of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*) themselves, they further teach others to practice it.
"In this Dharma, his body is capable of teaching and transforming others without ever becoming weary, and he preaches the Dharma without fatigue.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Among these bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is fit to perform the work of teaching and transforming.

He himself practices the *āraṇyaka* (forest-dweller) way of life and also praises the *āraṇyaka* way of life; he himself wears robes made of rags from dust heaps, has few desires and is content, is diligent and courageous, begs for food, and delights in secluded places. He is accomplished in morality, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Furthermore, he teaches others to practice this Dharma; he is himself capable of teaching and transforming others, preaching the Dharma without ever becoming weary."
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the bhikṣus.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the bhikṣus paused for a short while to his left and right, then rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew.
At that time, Śāriputra was not far from the World-Honored One; he sat cross-legged, straightening his body and composing his mind, binding his mindfulness before him.
Then, Śāriputra had this thought: "Now, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra has truly attained a great and wholesome benefit."
The reason for this is that the bhikṣus practicing the holy life praise his virtue, and the Blessed One likewise approves of what they say and does not contradict them.
On what day shall I be able to meet with that person and engage him in conversation?

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, having completed his work of teaching in his native land, gradually traveled among the people to teach them until he arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to him.
Having heard this teaching, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew.
Placing his *niṣīdana* on his right shoulder, he went to the Divyāvasa Garden.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who saw from afar Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra placing his *niṣīdana* on his right shoulder as he arrived at that garden. Having seen him, he immediately went to Śāriputra and said to him:

"The World-Honored One has always praised Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; he has just now gone to the Tathāgata’s presence and heard the Dharma from the Buddha. He is now proceeding to the garden; Venerable Sir, you should know that the time has come."
At that time, having heard the bhikṣu’s words, Śāriputra rose from his seat, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his right shoulder, and went to that grove.
At that time, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was sitting cross-legged beneath a tree, and Śāriputra was likewise seated in contemplation beneath another tree.
Then, Śāriputra rose from his seat and went to where Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was.
Having arrived, they exchanged greetings and sat to one side.
At that time, Śāriputra asked Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra: "How is it, Pūrṇa?"
"Is it because of the World-Honored One that one attains the cultivation of the holy life as his disciple? Pūrṇa replied, "It is so, it is so."
Then Śāriputra asked again: "Furthermore, is it by reason of the World-Honored One that one attains the cultivation of pure precepts?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"No," Śāriputra said, "is it because of the purity of mind toward the Tathāgata that one cultivates the holy life?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied, “No. Śāriputra said:
“Is it for the sake of purifying one’s vision that one may practice the holy life (brahmacarya) under the Tathāgata? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied, “No.”
Śāriputra asked, "How does one become free from hesitation and attain the practice of the holy life?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"No," Śāriputra said, "is it by means of the purity of one's conduct that one attains the cultivation of the holy life?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied, "No. Śāriputra said:
“How is it that within the path, through the purification of wisdom, one attains the cultivation of the holy life?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied, “No.”
Śāriputra asked: "How does one know and see with purity so as to cultivate the holy life?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"No," Śāriputra replied,
"the question I have now asked is whether one may practice the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Tathāgata."
You replied to me again, saying:
"It is so. I asked further:
"By means of wisdom and purity of mind, and through the purity of vision and knowledge of the Path, can one cultivate the holy life?"
You have further said,
"No. How then can you now cultivate the holy life under the Tathāgata?

Pūrṇa replied: "The meaning of the purity of ethical discipline is that it can bring about the purity of the mind; the meaning of the purity of the mind is that it can bring about the purity of view; the meaning of the purity of view is that it can bring about the purity of freedom from doubt; the meaning of the purity of freedom from doubt is that it can bring about the purity of the path of practice; the meaning of the purity of the path of practice is that it can bring about the purity of the Way; the meaning of the purity of the Way is that it can bring about the purity of knowledge and vision; the meaning of the purity of knowledge and vision is that it can bring about the realization of the meaning of Nirvāṇa. This is what is called practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata."
Śāriputra said: "To what does the meaning of what you have just spoken tend?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"I shall now provide a parable to explain this meaning; for the wise understand a meaning through parables, and the wise awaken by themselves.
It is just as if today King Prasenajit were traveling from the city of Śrāvastī to the kingdom of Vṛji, and seven chariots were stationed between the two countries."

At that time, King Prasenajit left the city riding in the first chariot; upon reaching the second chariot, he mounted it and left the first behind. Proceeding a short distance further, he mounted the third chariot and left the second behind. Proceeding a short distance further, he mounted the fourth chariot and left the third behind. Proceeding a short distance further, he mounted the fifth chariot and left the fourth behind. Proceeding yet further, he mounted the sixth chariot and left the fifth behind. Proceeding yet further, he mounted the seventh chariot and left the sixth behind, entering the kingdom of Vajji.
At that time, King Prasenajit arrived at his palace.
Suppose someone were to ask:
"Great King, what kind of vehicle did you ride today to come here to this palace?"
"What would that king say in response? Śāriputra replied:
"If someone were to ask him, he should respond as follows:"

"I departed from the city of Śrāvastī; first I rode the first chariot to the second chariot, then I left the second chariot to ride the third chariot, then I left the third chariot to ride the fourth chariot, then I left the fourth chariot to ride the fifth chariot, then I left the fifth chariot to ride the sixth chariot, then I left the sixth chariot to ride the seventh chariot, and thus arrived at the kingdom of Vārāṇasī."
The reason for this is that it was by means of the preceding carriage reaching the second carriage, through such successive mutual dependence, that one could reach that country.
If anyone should ask about this, you should answer them in this way.
Pūrṇa replied: "The meaning of the purity of ethical discipline is likewise so.

Through the purity of the mind, one attains the purity of vision; through the purity of vision, one attains the purity of the removal of doubt; through the absence of doubt, one attains the purity of the path of practice; through the purity of the path of practice, one attains the purity of the path; through the purity of the path, one attains the purity of knowledge and vision; and through the purity of knowledge and vision, one attains the state of nirvāṇa, wherein one practices the holy life under the Tathāgata."

The reason for this is that the meaning of the purity of precepts is a form of grasping, yet the Tathāgata teaches the removal of grasping; the meaning of the purity of mind is also a form of grasping, yet the Tathāgata teaches the removal of grasping; even the meaning of knowledge and vision is grasping, and the Tathāgata teaches the removal of grasping; and so on, up to nirvāṇa.
Regarding the cultivation of the holy life attained by the Tathāgata:
if it were merely through the purity of precepts that one could cultivate the holy life as attained by the Tathāgata, then even ordinary worldlings would likewise attain parinirvāṇa.

The reason for this is that ordinary worldlings also possess these precepts; however, that which was taught by the World-Honored One leads one to achieve the Way in succession and reach the realm of Nirvana. It is not through the mere purity of the precepts alone that one attains extinction.
It is just as one who wishes to ascend a seven-storied tower must do so step by step.
The meaning of the purity of precepts is likewise:

gradually one reaches the mind; from the mind one reaches vision; from vision one reaches freedom from doubt; from freedom from doubt one reaches pure conduct; from pure conduct one reaches the Path; from the pure Path one reaches knowledge and vision; and from pure knowledge and vision one reaches Nirvana.
At that time, Śāriputra exclaimed: “Excellent! Excellent!”
"Please explain this meaning: what is your name now?
By what title do the bhikṣus who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) address you?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"I am now named Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; my mother’s clan name is Maitrāyaṇī. Śāriputra said, "Excellent!"
Excellent, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Within the Dharma of the noble ones, there is truly no equal; you embrace the nectar of immortality and disseminate it without end. Regarding the profound meaning I have now asked about, you have explained it all.
"Even if all those who practice the holy life were to carry me upon their heads as they wander through the world, they still could not repay my kindness.
Those who come to approach and inquire after my well-being obtain great and wholesome benefit; I too now obtain such wholesome benefit by receiving their instruction."
Pūrṇa replied: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is as you have said. What is your name now?
And what are the names of the bhikṣus?"
Śāriputra replied, “My name is Upatiṣya;
my mother’s name was Śārī, and thus the bhikṣus call me Śāriputra.”
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said:

"I am now debating with a Great Being; previously, I did not know that the Great Lord of Dharma had arrived here. Had I known that the Venerable Śāriputra had come to this place, I would not have been able to provide such eloquent responses in mutual discourse. Yet, when you asked about this profound meaning, I dispatched my answer immediately."

Excellent! Śāriputra, you are the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples; you constantly delight yourself with the ambrosial flavor of the Dharma. Even if all those who practice the holy life were to carry the Venerable Śāriputra upon their heads as they travel through the world from year to year, they still could not repay even a moment’s worth of your kindness.
"Any sentient beings who come to inquire after the Venerable One and draw near to him have gained a great and wholesome benefit; we too have gained a great and wholesome benefit.
At that time, the two sages engaged in this discussion together in that grove.
At that time, the two men each heard what was said and joyfully practiced it. [The following verses summarize the contents:
The Parable of the Equal Dharma and the Day; the Parables of Water and the City Wall;
Consciousness, Mānuṣyaka, and the Two Wheels; Pūrṇa and the Seven Chariots.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume Thirty-three and Volume Thirty-four,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Forty: The Chapter on the Seven Days, Part One of Four. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, after their meal, a great multitude of bhikṣus gathered in the Hall of Universal Assembly and engaged in this discussion:
"This Mount Sumeru is exceedingly vast; it is beyond the reach of all other mountains—how truly marvelous!"
"How extraordinary!
It is so high, vast, and steep.
Yet, before long, it too shall be destroyed and utterly annihilated, leaving nothing behind. Even the great mountains that rely upon Mount Sumeru shall likewise be destroyed."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having heard with his divine ear this discussion among the many bhikṣus, immediately rose from his seat and went to that lecture hall, where he took his place.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What discussion were you having here?
What do you intend to undertake?"
The bhikṣus replied, “These people have gathered here to discuss matters of the Dharma; what they have just discussed was entirely in accordance with the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said:
“Excellent, bhikṣus!
It is precisely appropriate for you who have gone forth to engage in Dharma-discourse, yet you do not abandon noble silence.”
The reason for this is that when bhikṣus assemble in one place, they should perform two tasks. What are these two?
First, you should engage in Dharma-discourse; second, you should maintain the noble silence.
If you discuss these two matters, you will ultimately attain peace and security, and never miss the proper occasion.
"What kind of discourse in accordance with the Dharma were you engaged in just now?
The bhikṣus replied, "Many bhikṣus have gathered in this hall, and we were engaged in such a discussion:"
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!

This Mount Sumeru is exceedingly high and vast; yet this Mount Sumeru, despite being thus, shall before long be destroyed, and the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) on its four sides shall likewise perish."
"Previously, we gathered here to compose this discourse in accordance with the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said:
"Do you wish to hear about the transformation of the destruction and decay of this world?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Now is precisely the right time. We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound it at this moment, so that the minds of all classes of sentient beings may attain liberation.”
The Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Reflect upon this well and keep it in your hearts.
The bhikṣus replied: [So be it.]
"So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"Mount Sumeru is exceedingly vast and great, beyond the reach of all other mountains.
If a bhikṣu wishes to know of Mount Sumeru, it rises eighty-four thousand yojanas above the water, and its depth below the water is likewise eighty-four thousand yojanas."
However, Mount Sumeru is composed of four kinds of jewels:
gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli;
furthermore, it has four corners, which are likewise composed of these same four kinds.
Of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli;
with golden walls and silver gates, silver walls and golden gates, crystal walls and lapis lazuli gates, and lapis lazuli walls and crystal gates.
However, there are five kinds of devas who dwell upon Mount Sumeru, all residing there due to their past karmic conditions.
What are these five?
Namely, within that city of silver, there are the Sūkṣmapādas (Fine-footed) devas who dwell therein.
Within that golden city, the Śirīṣa devas dwell; within the crystal city, the Nandana devas dwell;
and within the lapis lazuli city, the Balavanta devas dwell.
Between the cities of gold and silver, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa dwells, leading incalculable numbers of yakṣas.
Between the cities of gold and crystal, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa resides, leading various nāgas and devas;
between the cities of crystal and lapis lazuli, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka resides.
Between the city of Vaiḍūrya and the city of silver, there dwells the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that beneath Mount Sumeru dwell the asuras."
When the asuras wish to engage in battle with the Trāyastriṃśa devas, they first fight with the Sūkṣmapāda devas;
if they are victorious, they proceed to the Golden City to fight with the Śirīṣa devas;
having defeated the Śirīṣa devas, they proceed to the Crystal City to fight with the Nandana devas.
Having conquered them, he proceeded to the city of Vaiḍūrya;
having conquered those devas as well, he then fought against the Trāyastriṃśa devas.

"Bhikṣus, you should know that the Trāyastriṃśa devas dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. Day and night they are illuminated, their own radiance shining upon one another; it is for this reason that such things occur."

Relying upon Mount Sumeru, the sun and moon circulate. The city of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva) is fifty-one yojanas in length and breadth; the city of the Moon Deity (Candradeva) is thirty-nine yojanas in length and breadth; the largest star is one yojana in length and breadth, and the smallest star is two hundred paces in length and breadth.

The summit of Mount Sumeru measures eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth across the east, west, south, and north. Near the southern side of Mount Sumeru lies the Great Iron Encircling Mountain (Cakravāḍa), eighty-four thousand li in length and eighty thousand li in height.
Furthermore, beyond this mountain, there is Mount Nimindhara which encircles it;
at a distance from Mount Nimindhara, there is another mountain named Khadiraka;
and at a distance from this mountain, there is yet another mountain named Vaiśramaṇa.
Beyond this mountain, there is another mountain named Horse-Head Mountain;
further still, there is a mountain named Vinaya Mountain;
following Vinaya, there is a mountain named Cakravāḍa-Mahācakravāḍa.
"Between the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) there are eight great hells, and each of these hells has sixteen subsidiary hells.
Furthermore, the Iron Ring Mountains provide great benefit to the land of Jambudvīpa; were it not for the Iron Ring Mountains, this region would be perpetually foul-smelling."
Beyond the Cakravāḍa Mountains lies Mount Gandhamādana; on the side of Mount Gandhamādana dwell eighty-four thousand white elephant kings, each possessing six tusks adorned with gold and silver.
Within that Fragrant Mountain there are eighty-four thousand caves where various elephants dwell; these are all constructed of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
The most excellent elephants are those ridden by Śakra Devānām Indra himself, while the lowest are ridden by the Cakravartin King.
Beside Mount Gandhamādana lies Lake Mātā, where *utpala* and *kumuda* lotuses grow; the elephants there dig up the roots to eat.
Beside the waters of Lake Mādhava there is another mountain named Ujjagira; on that mountain grow various kinds of grasses and trees, and birds, beasts, insects, and mollusks all dwell therein.
Relying upon those mountains, there are those who have attained the Way and possess supernatural powers who frequent those regions.
Next, there is another mountain named Paṇḍava; next again, there is a mountain named Gṛdhrakūṭa, which is the place upon which Jambudvīpa rests.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that there may come a time when this world is about to be destroyed; at such a time, the heavens do not send down rain, the sprouts that have been sown no longer grow, and all the small rivers and springs become completely parched.”
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) inevitably return to impermanence and cannot endure for long.
Bhikṣus, you should know that there will come a time when these four great rivers—the Gaṅgā, the Sītā, the Sindhu, and the Vakṣu—will likewise dry up until not a drop remains.
"In this way, bhikṣus!
That which is called 'the hundredfold changes of impermanence' refers precisely to this.
"Bhikṣus! [he continued.]
There may come a time when two suns appear in this world; at that time, all the hundred-grass plants, trees, and woods will wither and fall away. Even so, bhikṣus!
All things are impermanent and subject to change; they cannot endure for long. At that time, all the small waters from the various springs and sources will completely dry up.

Bhikṣus, you should know that when two suns appear, the four great oceans within a range of one hundred yojanas will all dry up, gradually extending to seven hundred yojanas until the water naturally vanishes.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that when three suns appear in the world, the waters of the four great oceans within a thousand yojanas will naturally dry up; gradually, even those within seven thousand yojanas will naturally dry up.”
“Bhikkhus, you should know that when four suns appear in the world, the waters of the four great oceans remain at a depth of one thousand yojanas.
It is thus, bhikkhus!”
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and cannot endure for long.
Monks, you should know that there will come a time when five suns appear in the world.
At that time, the waters of the four great oceans will be reduced to seven hundred *yojanas*, and gradually diminish until they remain at only one hundred *yojanas*."
"Monks, you should know that when five suns appear, at that time the ocean will remain at a depth of one yojana; gradually the water will dry up until nothing remains.
When five suns appear, there will remain only seven feet of water; when five suns appear, the ocean will be completely exhausted with nothing remaining."
"Monks, you should know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and cannot endure for long.

Monks, you should know that there will come a time when six suns appear; at that time, this earth, sixty-eight thousand yojanas in thickness, will all emit smoke, and Mount Sumeru will also gradually melt and crumble away."
When six suns appear, this trichiliocosm will completely melt and disintegrate, just like a potter firing earthenware vessels.
At that time, the trichiliocosm will likewise be thus: fire will burst forth, pervading everywhere without exception.
"Monks, you should know that when six suns appear, the eight great hells will likewise be extinguished and the people there will pass away.

The five classes of devas who dwell upon Mount Sumeru will also pass away; the Trāyastriṃśa devas, the Yāma devas, and so on up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas will also pass away, and their palaces will all become empty."
When six suns appear, at that time Mount Sumeru and the trichiliocosm world-system will all be completely incinerated without remainder.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they cannot endure for long.

Bhikṣus, you should know that there will come a time when seven suns appear. At that time, although this earth is sixty-eight thousand yojanas thick, and including the trichiliocosm, it will all burst into flames."

Furthermore, when seven suns arise, this Mount Sumeru will gradually melt and disintegrate; hundreds of thousands of yojanas will naturally collapse and fall away until nothing remains, and not even a trace of dust or smoke can be seen, let alone ashes!

At that time, the palaces of the gods from the Heaven of the Thirty-three up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations were all ablaze with fire, and these flames reached as far as the Brahma Heaven.

The newly born deva residing in that celestial palace had never before witnessed the conflagration at the end of an eon; seeing this blazing light, he was filled with universal fear, dreading that he would be consumed by the fire.
However, those elder-born devas who had previously witnessed the conflagration at the end of an eon came to console the later-born devas, saying:
"Do not harbor fear; this fire shall never reach this realm."

"Monks, you should know that when the seven suns appear, from this world up to the sixth heaven, and even throughout the trichiliocosm, everything will be reduced to ashes and dust, leaving not even a trace of any physical form."
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they cannot be maintained for long and all end in exhaustion.
At that time, when people’s lives come to an end, they are all reborn in other lands or in the heavens.
Furthermore, if the sentient beings within the hells have exhausted their past karmic offenses, they will be reborn in the heavens or in other buddha-fields;
if those sentient beings in the hells have not yet exhausted their offenses, they will be transferred to other buddha-fields.

"Monks, you should know that when the seven suns arise, there will no longer be the light of the sun and moon, nor the signs of the constellations. At that time, the sun and moon will have already perished, and there will be no further distinction between day and night."
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus:
due to the conditions of karmic retribution, this destruction and ruin comes to pass.

Furthermore, bhikṣus, you should know that when the kalpa is restored and perfected, there may come a time when the fire extinguishes itself, and great clouds arise in the midst of space, gradually raining down."
At that time, this trichiliocosm world-system will be completely filled with water, the water reaching as far as the Brahma-heaven.
Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, this water will gradually come to rest and then vanish of its own accord.
Again, a wind arises named Svalana, which blows this mass of water and gathers it into one place.

At that time, that wind raises a thousand Mount Sumerus, a thousand Mount Kīṭādris, a thousand Mount Nimindhara mountains, a thousand Mount Khadiraka mountains, a thousand Mount Īṣādhara mountains, a thousand Mount Vinataka mountains, a thousand Cakravāḍa mountains, and a thousand Mahācakravāḍa mountains;

it further produces eight thousand hells, and further produces a thousand Aśvamukha mountains, a thousand Gandhamādana mountains, a thousand Pāṇḍava mountains, a thousand Ujjāhaka mountains, a thousand Jambudvīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānīs, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, and a thousand Uttarakurus.
Furthermore, there arise a thousand oceans;

furthermore, there arise a thousand palaces of the Four Great Kings, a thousand [palaces] of the Thirty-three Gods, a thousand Yāma heavens, a thousand Tuṣita heavens, a thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, and a thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that there may come a time when the waters have extinguished the earth and it is born again.
At that time, there will naturally appear on the earth a kind of ‘earth-fat’ (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), which is exceedingly fragrant and delicious, surpassing even nectar.”
If one wishes to know the fragrant essence of that land, it is like sweet grape wine.
Bhikṣus, you should know that there may come a time when the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven say to one another:
"We wish to go to Jambudvīpa to observe the form of that land as it returns to its original state."
The Ābhāsvara deva-son descended to the world and, seeing this earth-fertility upon the ground, took some with his finger, placed it in his mouth, and ate it.

At that time, those devaputras who had consumed much of the earth-fat lost their majestic power and their radiance; their bodies became heavy and grew with flesh and bone, whereby they immediately lost their supernormal power of flight and could no longer soar through the air.

Furthermore, those devaputras who had consumed little of the earth-fat did not find their bodies heavy, nor did they lose their supernormal power of flight, and they were still able to travel through the void by means of flight.
At that time, those sons of heaven who had lost their supernormal powers all cried out together and said to one another:
"Today we have fallen into extreme distress and misfortune; moreover, we have lost our supernormal powers."
They remained in the world and could no longer return to the heavens; they subsequently consumed the fat of this earth.
They gazed at one another’s countenances.
At that time, those sons of heaven who possessed much sensual desire were transformed into women, whereupon they indulged in sexual passion and took pleasure together.
"Monks, this is what is meant:
when the world first came into being, this phenomenon of sexual desire was already present and spread throughout the world; it is an ancient and constant law that women must appear in the world.
Furthermore, this is an ancient law, not something that has arisen only now."
At that time, the other Ābhāsvara devas, seeing this son of heaven falling, all came to rebuke and scold him, saying:
"Why do you practice such impure conduct?"
At that time, sentient beings again had this thought:
"We should employ skillful means; we ought to dwell together so that people do not see us.
Thus, they gradually built houses to cover their bodies.
"Thus it is said, bhikṣus!
It is because of these causes and conditions that there are now houses.
Bhikṣus, you should know that there may come a time when the earth-fat naturally sinks into the ground, and subsequently non-glutinous rice grows, which is exceedingly fresh and pure."
It has no outer bark, is exceedingly fragrant and beautiful, and makes people plump and fair;
if gathered in the morning, it grows by evening, and if gathered in the evening, it grows by morning.
This, monks, is what is called [the *pāricchattaka* tree].
At that time, for the first time, the name "non-glutinous rice" arose. Monks!
There may be a time when the people become indolent and do not strive in their livelihood.
That person then thought to himself:
"Why do I collect this non-glutinous rice every day?
I ought to collect it once every two days."
At that time, those people harvested non-glutinous rice once every two days.
Then, the people became pregnant one after another, and through this, the cycle of rebirth began to increase.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings who said to other sentient beings,
"Let us gather non-glutinous rice together.
At that time, those people replied:
"I have taken provisions for two days' food.
Upon hearing this, the man again had this thought:
"I shall store provisions for four days' food."
Immediately, they prepared provisions for four days' food.
Furthermore, another sentient being said to those beings:
"We should go together outside to gather non-glutinous rice."
The man replied, "I have gathered enough provisions for four days' food.
Upon hearing this, the other man thought to himself:
"I shall prepare provisions for eight days' food.
He immediately prepared a store of food for eight days.
At that time, that non-glutinous rice no longer grew again.
At that time, sentient beings each gave rise to this thought:
"There is a great calamity in the world; now this non-glutinous rice is no longer as it was before, and we must now divide this rice."
Immediately, they began to divide the non-glutinous rice.
At that time, sentient beings again gave rise to this thought:
"I should now hide my own non-glutinous rice, so that I may steal the non-glutinous rice of others."
At that time, those sentient beings began to store up their own non-glutinous rice and then stole the non-glutinous rice of others.
When the owner saw him stealing the non-glutinous rice, he said to that person:
"Why have you taken my non-glutinous rice?"
"Now I forgive your transgression; do not commit it again in the future.
At that time, for the first time in the world, this thought of theft arose.
Then, other sentient beings, hearing these words, likewise conceived the thought within themselves:
"I should now hide this rice I have already harvested and steal the rice of others.
At that time, those beings abandoned their own possessions and took the possessions of others.
When the master saw this, he said to that man,
"Why have you now taken my non-glutinous rice?
However, the man remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, Bhāradvāja immediately joined his hands in a fist and said, "From this day forward, let us no longer encroach upon one another.

At that moment, when the multitude of people heard that living beings were stealing from one another, they gathered together and said to each other, "There is such unrighteousness in the world; everyone is stealing from one another."
"Now I shall establish field-keepers to guard the fields.
Among all sentient beings, whoever is intelligent and of high talent shall be established as the master of the fields.
At that time, he immediately selected a master of the fields and spoke to him, saying:

"You all should know that there exists in the world this unlawful act of theft. You who now guard the fields must employ its rightful price; when people come to take the others' non-glutinous rice, you must immediately punish them for their crime."
At that time, he was immediately established as the lord of the fields.
Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, those who guarded the fields were called the Kṣatriya caste; this was all according to the ancient law, not contrary to the law.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When the Kṣatriya caste first arose, The highest among all lineages,
Men of intelligence and lofty talent, Honored and attended by gods and humans."
"At that time, if there were people who encroached upon the property of others, the kṣatriyas would take them and punish them.
Yet those people did not reform their transgressions and thus committed them again."
At that time, the Kṣatriya lord commanded the manufacture of swords and staves, and having seized that man, he had his head struck off.
At that moment, this first act of killing in the world occurred.
At that time, when the multitude of people heard this decree—"Whoever steals rice shall be executed by the Kṣatriya lord"—they were all filled with fear, their hair standing on end.

Each built a grass hut and sat in meditation therein, cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and unifying their minds. Abandoning their household affairs, wives, children, and daughters-in-law, they remained solitary in their resolve, practicing the holy life.
From that time onward, there arose the names and clans of the Brahmins.
At that moment, these two castes appeared in the world.
"Monks, you should know that at that time, because of theft there was killing; because of killing, there were swords and staves."
At that time, the Kṣatriya ruler addressed the people, saying:
"Whoever among you is upright, handsome, and of high talent shall be appointed to govern these people.
He further addressed them, saying:
"When there were people who committed theft, they were made to punish them for their crimes.
At that time, this Vaiśya caste appeared in the world.
"At that time, many sentient beings will give rise to this thought:
'Today, all classes of sentient beings are killing one another; this is entirely brought about by their karma. We may now come and go and circulate about to sustain our own lives.'"
"At that time, there appeared in the world those of the Śūdra caste.
Then the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"First there were the Kṣatriya caste, Next there were the Brāhmaṇa caste."
The third is the Vaiśya, and next is the Śūdra caste.
These four castes arise from one another in succession;
they have all descended from celestial bodies and are originally of one single color.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, with this mind of killing and stealing, that naturally grown non-glutinous rice no longer existed.
At that time, there were five kinds of grain seeds:
first, root-seeds; second, stem-seeds; third, branch-seeds; fourth, flower-seeds; and fifth, fruit-seeds, as well as other produced seeds. These are called the five kinds of seeds.”
All these have been blown here by the winds from other realms and taken as seeds to sustain themselves.

Thus, monks, when such portents appear in the world, there arise birth, old age, sickness, and death, resulting in the present five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) and the failure to reach the end of suffering; this is called the transformation at the time of the formation and destruction of a kalpa.
I shall speak to you of that which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly practice; I now declare it all to you.

You should delight in dwelling in seclusion and quietude, and you should mindfully practice seated meditation; do not give rise to indolence. If you are not diligent now, repentance later will be of no benefit.
"This is my instruction.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, amidst his ministers, spoke thus:
"This kingdom of Vaiśālī is extremely prosperous and its population is vast; I shall launch an attack and seize that territory."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to the brahmin Bālaki:
"Go now to the place where the World-Honored One is; bearing my name, go to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health, pay him homage, and serve him, saying:
'King Ajātaśatru addresses the World-Honored One thus:'"
"I intend to launch an attack on the kingdom of Vṛji; do you think this is appropriate?
"Whatever the Tathāgata may say, reflect upon it well and come to tell me."
"The reason for this is that the Tathāgata’s speech is never double.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa, having received the king's command, went to where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin said to the Buddha:
“King Ajātaśatru pays homage to the World-Honored One, serves him, and inquires after his well-being; he has further addressed me, saying:
‘I intend to go and attack the great kingdom of Vaiśālī.’”
"Previously, when he came to question the Buddha, was it not permissible?
At that time, that brahmin had covered his head and feet with his robe, wore ivory sandals, and girded his waist with a sharp sword; thus, he was unfit to hear the Dharma being preached.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If the people of Vaiśālī cultivate seven dharmas, they will never be destroyed by external invaders.
What are these seven?

If the people of the kingdom of Vṛji were all gathered in one place and did not disperse, they would not be destroyed by other kingdoms; this is called the first dharma by which one is not defeated by external invaders.
"Furthermore, Ānanda! The people of Vajjī, from the highest to the lowest, live in harmony and accord; thus the people of Vajjī are not captured by outsiders.
This, Ānanda, is called the second quality by which they are not destroyed by foreign invaders."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If the people of Vṛji do not commit adultery with others nor become attached to the beauty of other men's wives, this is called the third factor by which they will not be destroyed by foreign invaders."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If the kingdom of Vṛji does not transmit [its teachings] from here to there, nor transmit them from there to here, this is called the fourth dharma by which it is not destroyed by foreign invaders."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If the people of Vārāṇasī make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and serve and pay homage to those who practice the holy life, this is called the fifth dharma; at such a time, they will not be captured by foreign invaders."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If the people of the kingdom of Vṛji do not covet the wealth and treasures of others, this is called the sixth dharma by which they are not destroyed by foreign invaders."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If the people of the kingdom of Vajji are all of one mind, do not resort to spirit temples, and concentrate their intentions, they will not be destroyed by foreign invaders. This is called the seventh dharma by which they are not destroyed by foreign invaders."
"Ānanda, this is what is meant:
those people of Vṛji who cultivate these seven dharmas will never be destroyed by outsiders.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If even when that person were to accomplish but a single dharma, he would be indestructible, how much more so when he accomplishes seven dharmas?
Cease! Cease!"
“World-Honored One!
State affairs are numerous and pressing; I wish to return to my quarters.
At that time, the brahmin rose from his seat and departed.
Not far from that brahmin, at that time the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now proclaim the seven dharmas of non-retrogression; listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"What are the seven dharmas of non-retrogression?

“Monks, you should know this: if monks assemble in one place and are all harmonious and compliant, honoring one another according to seniority, advancing further toward the higher stages, cultivating various wholesome dharmas without falling back, and not providing an opportunity for Māra to gain an advantage—this is called the first dharma of non-retrogression.”

"Furthermore, when the Saṃgha is harmonious and compliant with its teachings, progressing further upward without regressing and not being destroyed by Māra, this is called the second dharma of non-regression."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

Not being attached to worldly affairs and not cultivating worldly glory, one advances further upward so that Māra or the devas cannot find an opportunity; this is called the third dharma of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!

One does not recite miscellaneous secular texts, but exerts one's mind and will throughout the day, progressing ever upward so that Māra the King finds no opportunity; this is called the fourth dharma of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Diligently practice the Dharma, eliminate drowsiness, and constantly remain vigilant and awake; advancing ever upward, do not allow the evil Māra to find an opportunity. This is called the fifth dharma of non-retrogression."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

One does not study arithmetic, nor does one cause others to practice it; instead, one delights in secluded and quiet places, cultivates that Dharma, and advances further upward, so that the evil Māra finds no opportunity against one."
This is called the sixth dharma of non-retrogression. "Furthermore, bhikṣu!

One gives rise to the perception that all worlds are not to be relished, practices meditative cultivation, endures the teachings of all dharmas, and advances further upward, so that Māra cannot find an opportunity; this is called the seventh dharma of non-retrogression."
"If there are bhikṣus who accomplish these seven dharmas and live in harmony and accord, then Māra shall find no opportunity against them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Having abandoned worldly affairs, And being free from the distractions of discursive thought,"
If one does not practice this, one will likewise not attain samādhi.
Those who can take delight in the Dharma distinguish its meaning;
the bhikṣu who delights in this practice shall attain the concentration of samādhi.
"Therefore, monks, you should seek skillful means to accomplish these seven qualities. Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak of the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); you should reflect upon them well.”
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said: "What are the seven?

First is the latent tendency of sensual desire; second is the latent tendency of ill will; third is the latent tendency of pride; fourth is the latent tendency of ignorance; fifth is the latent tendency of doubt; sixth is the latent tendency of views; and seventh is the latent tendency of the desire realm.
"Monks, this is what is meant:

there are these seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which cause beings to dwell forever in profound darkness, bind their bodies, and cause them to transmigrate through the world without rest, such that they cannot know the root source of birth and death."
It is just like those two oxen, one black and one white, yoked together by a single harness and pulling in tandem, unable to be far apart from one another.

These classes of sentient beings are likewise so; bound and fettered by the latent tendency of greed and the latent tendency of ignorance, they cannot be separated. The remaining five latent tendencies follow along as well, and as these five follow, the seven latent tendencies do so as well.
If ordinary persons are bound by these seven latent tendencies (anuśaya), they transmigrate through birth and death, failing to attain liberation and unable to know the fundamental root of suffering.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that by means of these seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya), there are the three evil destinies:
hell, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;
by means of these seven underlying tendencies, one cannot cross over the domain of Māra the Wicked.”
Furthermore, for these seven messengers, there are seven medicines.
What are the seven? The messenger of sensual desire is treated by the awakening factor of mindfulness.
The messenger of ill will is treated by the awakening factor of dharma;
the messenger of wrong views is treated by the awakening factor of vigor;
the messenger of desire for the world is treated by the awakening factor of joy.
The messenger of pride is treated by the awakening factor of investigation;
the messenger of doubt is treated by the awakening factor of concentration;
the messenger of ignorance is treated by the awakening factor of equanimity.
