"Monks, this is called the seven uses for which the seven factors of enlightenment serve as the remedy.
Monks, you should know that in the past, before I had attained the Buddha-way and was practicing as a bodhisattva, while sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment, this thought arose in me:"
"What are the fetters of sentient beings in the desire realm?
He further reflected:
"These classes of sentient beings transmigrate through birth and death due to the seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya), never attaining liberation."
"I am now likewise bound by these seven latent tendencies (anuśaya) and have not attained liberation.
At that time, he further thought:
"By what means should these seven latent tendencies be treated?"
Again, he reflected further:
"These seven messengers should be treated with the seven factors of awakening; I shall contemplate the seven factors of awakening.

While contemplating the seven factors of awakening, his mind with outflows was exhausted, and he immediately attained liberation. Subsequently, he realized the unsurpassed, right, and true path, remaining in the full lotus posture for seven days as he again contemplated these seven factors of awakening.
Therefore, monks, if you wish to abandon the seven messengers, you should practice mindfulness of the seven factors of enlightenment. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are seven kinds of persons who are worthy of service and worthy of reverence; they are the unsurpassed fields of merit in this world.”
What are the seven kinds of persons? These seven persons are:

first, those who practice loving-kindness; second, those who practice compassion; third, those who practice sympathetic joy; fourth, those who practice equanimity; fifth, those who practice emptiness; sixth, those who practice signlessness; and seventh, those who practice wishlessness.
These are called the seven kinds of persons who are worthy of service and worthy of veneration; they are the unsurpassed field of merit in the world.
Why is this so? Because any sentient being who practices these seven dharmas will obtain their fruit and reward within the present life.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what reason do you not speak of the srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, pratyekabuddha, and Buddha, but instead speak of these seven matters?"
The World-Honored One said:
"The practice of these seven types of persons who cultivate loving-kindness differs from that of those from the stream-enterer up to the Buddha;
although one may make offerings to those from the stream-enterer up to the Buddha, no reward is obtained in the present life."
However, those who make offerings to these seven persons will obtain their reward in the present life.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should diligently apply yourself with vigor to accomplish these seven dharmas.
"In this way, Ānanda,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī by the side of the Monkey Pond, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered Vaiśālī for alms together with Ānanda.
At that moment, there was a great elder in the city of Vaiśālī named Vairaṭṭa, who possessed immeasurable wealth and treasures beyond calculation;
yet he was stingy and greedy, lacking any intention to practice giving, consuming only the merit of his past deeds while creating none anew.
At that time, the householder was in the inner palace with his female attendants, performing music and song for their mutual entertainment.
Then the World-Honored One went to that street and, knowing [the situation], asked Ānanda:
"I hear music and song being performed now; whose house is this?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“This is the house of the elder Vīrāśa.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This householder will pass away seven days from now and shall be reborn in the Tīkṣṇa-rodana (Weeping) Hell.
This is because it is the natural law:
whenever those who have severed their roots of goodness die, they are all reborn in the Tīkṣṇa-rodana Hell."
"Now this householder’s past merit is exhausted, and he creates no new.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
"Is there some cause or condition by which this householder might not pass away for seven days?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There is no cause or condition by which one could avoid meeting death!
The karmic deeds sown in the past have now reached their exhaustion; this cannot be avoided."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Is there some expedient means by which this elder might not be reborn in the Tāpana Hell?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“There is a skillful means by which this elder may be prevented from falling into hell.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
“By what causes and conditions can this elder be prevented from falling into hell?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If this elder were to shave off his hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and leave the household life to study the Path, he would then be able to escape this transgression."
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“I am now able to cause this householder to leave the household life and study the Path.
At that time, having taken leave of the World-Honored One, Ānanda went to the house of that householder and stood outside the gate.
At that time, the elder saw Ānanda approaching from afar; he immediately went out to welcome him and invited him to sit.
Then, Ānanda said to the elder:
"I have just heard this from the One of All-Knowledge, for the Tathāgata has now bestowed this prediction:"
"Seven days from now, your body shall perish and your life shall end, and you will be reborn in the Taidu (Weeping) Hell.
Upon hearing this, the elder was immediately seized with fear; his hair stood on end, and he said to Ānanda, "Is there any cause or condition by which my life might not end within these seven days?"
Ānanda replied, “There is no such cause or condition by which one could avoid death for seven days.
The householder spoke again, saying:
"Is there any cause or condition by which, at the end of my life, I might not be reborn in the Weeping Hell?
Ānanda replied, "The World-Honored One has indeed given this teaching:"
"If the householder were to shave off his hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and leave the home life to study the Way, he would not enter hell.
You should now appropriately leave the home life to study the Way and reach the other shore.
The householder said, "Ānanda, you go on ahead; I shall follow immediately. At that moment, Ānanda departed.
The householder then thought to himself:
"Seven days is still a long time; I should now enjoy myself with the five desires, and only thereafter shall I leave the household life to study the Way."
At that time, Ānanda went again to the householder’s home the following day and said to him:
"One day has already passed; six days remain, so you may now go forth into the religious life."
The elder said, "Ānanda is already ahead; I shall follow immediately.
Nevertheless, the elder still did not depart.
At that time, Ānanda went to the householder’s home on the second day, the third day, and so on, up until the sixth day, and said to the householder:
"It would be well for you to renounce the world now; it will be too late for regrets later."
"If he does not leave the household life and his life ends today, he shall be reborn in the Weeping Hell.
The householder said to Ānanda, "Venerable sir, you go on ahead; I shall follow immediately after."
Ānanda said, "Householder! By what supernormal power did you arrive there today?"
"Did you perhaps send me on ahead?
I simply wish to go together with you at this very moment.
At that time, Ānanda led the elder to where the World-Honored One was; having arrived, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now this householder wishes to leave the household life to study the Way; we only pray that the Tathāgata will shave his hair and beard so that he may study the Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You yourself should now ordain this householder."
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately shaved the elder’s hair and beard, taught him to don the three dharma robes, and set him to study the True Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda instructed the bhikṣu, saying:

"You should practice mindfulness; you should practice mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of generosity, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of renunciation, mindfulness of ānāpāna, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of death. You should practice such dharmas as these."
"Monks, it is said that one who practices these ten recollections shall obtain a great fruit and attain the flavor of the Dharma of the Deathless.
At that time, after Vīrāṣaṇa had practiced this Dharma, he passed away on that very day and was reborn among the Four Great Kings.
At that time, Ānanda immediately performed the cremation of the bhikṣu’s body and returned to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
Then, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The bhikṣu Vīrasiṃha, who passed away earlier, has now reached the end of his life; in what place has he been reborn?”
The World-Honored One replied,
“This bhikṣu has now passed away and been reborn among the Four Great Kings.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Where will he be reborn after passing away from that life? The World-Honored One replied, "After passing away from there, he will be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;

thence, he will successively be reborn in the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. After passing away from those realms, he will return again to be born as far down as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings."
"Ānanda, this is what is meant:

the bhikṣu Vīrasena will circulate seven times among gods and humans, and finally obtaining a human body, he will leave the household life to study the Path and bring an end to the limits of suffering."
The reason for this is that they possess faith in the Tathāgata.

"Ānanda, you should know: this land of Jambudvīpa is twenty-one thousand yojanas from north to south and seven thousand yojanas from east to west. Suppose there were someone who made offerings to all the people of Jambudvīpa; would their merit not be great?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “Very much, very much,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If there are sentient beings who, for as long as it takes to milk a cow, maintain unbroken faith and practice the ten recollections, their merit will be immeasurable; there is no one who can measure it.”
Thus it is, Ānanda! You should seek skillful means and practice the ten recollections. Thus it is, Ānanda!
"One should train in this way.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall now proclaim a most sublime Dharma, excellent in its beginning, middle, and end; its principles are profound, and it fully enables the cultivation of the holy life. This sutra is named ‘The Dharma for Purifying All Outflows’; you should contemplate it well.”
The bhikṣu replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"What is called the dharma for purifying all outflows?"
There are some outflows that are abandoned through insight;
there are some outflows that are abandoned through cultivation;
and there are some outflows that are abandoned through avoidance.
There are some outflows that are severed through enjoyment;
there are some outflows that are severed through deportment;
and there are some outflows that are severed through reflection.
"How are those outflows abandoned through vision?

In this regard, an ordinary person does not behold the noble ones; they do not accord with the Dharma of the Tathāgata; they are unable to uphold the Dharma of the worthy and noble; they do not draw near to spiritual friends, nor do they associate with spiritual friends."
Regarding the Dharma that one hears, they do not discriminate between those dharmas that should be contemplated and those that should not be contemplated.
Consequently, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases;
the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases.
The unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and the arisen taint of ignorance increases.
This is a phenomenon that should not be contemplated, yet one contemplates it.
"What, then, is that phenomenon which should be contemplated, yet this phenomenon is not contemplated?"

What is called "contemplating the Dharma" means: ensuring that the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) which has not yet arisen does not arise, and extinguishing the outflow of sensual desire that has already arisen;
ensuring that the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) which has not yet arisen does not arise, and extinguishing the outflow of existence that has already arisen;
and ensuring that the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) which has not yet arisen does not arise, and extinguishing the outflow of ignorance that has already arisen.
This is called: that which is this dharma which ought to be contemplated but is not contemplated, while that which ought not to be contemplated is instead contemplated;
and that which ought to be contemplated is not contemplated. Consequently, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases;
the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases.
The outflow of ignorance that had not yet arisen arises, and the outflow of ignorance that had already arisen increases.
That person reflects thus:
"How did the distant past come to be?"
"Did I exist in the distant past?
Or again, he reflects:
"Did I not exist in the distant past?"
How can there be a distant past? For whom does a distant past exist?
Furthermore, how can there be a distant future?
"Will I now have a long future?
Or again, they say:
"There will be no long future."
How can there be a long duration in the future?
For whom does this long duration in the future exist?
How can there be such a long duration for these sentient beings?
"From where have these sentient beings come after such a long time?
Where will they be reborn when their lives here end?

As that person gives rise to this inauspicious thought, he immediately develops the six views, successively giving rise to the notion of "otherness"—the view of self, firmly holding to this view; and so on.
There is no view of self, yet one earnestly gives rise to this view;
regarding both the view of self and the view of non-self, one gives rise to a discerning view therein;
furthermore, observing one's own body, one again gives rise to this view:
Not seeing a self within what is self,
one further gives rise to this view:
not seeing non-self within what is non-self, one conceives this view therein.
At that time, that person further gave rise to this wrong view:
"The self is this very world, and it is also the future world; it exists eternally in the world without decaying, nor does it change, nor does it move."
This is called the mass of wrong views.

Wrong view, calamity, affliction, grief, suffering, and distress all arise from this; it cannot be cured, nor can it be abandoned, and thus it increases the root of suffering. Consequently, one does not practice the conduct of a śramaṇa nor the path to nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, monks!
A noble disciple cultivates the Dharma without losing its proper sequence, is well able to protect it, associates with virtuous friends, and is capable of discernment;
he also understands those dharmas that are not to be contemplated."
He is able to know those dharmas that should be contemplated;
he does not contemplate those dharmas that should not be contemplated;
and he contemplates those dharmas that should be contemplated.
"How is it that he does not contemplate those things that should not be contemplated?
In this regard, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) arises where it has not yet arisen, and having arisen, it increases;
the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) arises where it has not yet arisen, and having arisen, it increases."
The unarisen outflow of ignorance arises, and the arisen outflow of ignorance increases.
This is called a phenomenon that should not be contemplated.
"What are those phenomena that should be contemplated, and which he contemplates?"
Thereupon, regarding all phenomena, the outflow of sensual desire that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is extinguished;
the outflow of existence that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is extinguished;
the outflow of ignorance that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is extinguished.
This is what is called "this dharma should be contemplated.
He does not contemplate that which should not be contemplated, but contemplates that which should be contemplated; by contemplating in this way, he extinguishes three dharmas.
What are these three? They are:
attachment to the body, attachment to precepts, and doubt.
If one lacks knowledge and vision, then the conditioned formations leading to further existence (āsrava) increase.
If one sees, hears, recollects, or knows [these things], then one does not increase the conditioned phenomena associated with outflows;
once they have been known and seen, outflows no longer arise.
This is called the outflow that is abandoned through vision.
"What, then, is the outflow that is abandoned through reverence?
In this regard, monks!"

One endures hunger and cold, diligently persevering through wind and rain, mosquitoes and gadflies, harsh words, and insults; even when the body suffers pain and headaches that are extremely distressing and one’s life hangs by a thread, one is able to endure them.
If it were not so, suffering and affliction would arise.
Even if one were able to endure them, such [suffering] would not be produced; this is called the abandonment of these outflows through veneration.
"How is it that he abandons the outflows through cultivation?
In this regard, bhikṣu!

He wears robes with a mind of restraint, not for the sake of vanity or adornment, but merely to support the physical body, to ward off cold and heat, to prevent wind and rain from affecting his person, and to cover the body so that it is not exposed."

Furthermore, maintaining a disciplined mind while begging for food at the proper times, one does not give rise to thoughts of attachment; rather, one seeks only to sustain the physical body so that old ailments may be cured and new ones do not arise.
Guarding all practices without transgression, one dwells in peace throughout the long night, cultivating the holy life and remaining long in the world.

Furthermore, he maintains his mind as he approaches his seat, neither adorning himself with magnificent garments nor ornaments; he desires only to dispel hunger, cold, wind, rain, mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like, merely to sustain his physical form so that he may practice the Way and the Dharma.
Furthermore, one maintains the mind to approach medicine and treatment without giving rise to a mind of attachment;
regarding that medicine, one desires it solely for the purpose of eliminating disease and restoring peace and security to the body.
If one does not associate with them, then the affliction of outflows arises;
if one associates with them, there is no affliction of outflows. This is called "the abandonment of these outflows through association."
"How does one abandon the outflows through detachment?
In this regard, bhikṣu!

One must eliminate distracted thoughts, just as one should avoid—indeed, remain far removed from—an evil elephant, a camel, an ox, a horse, a tiger, a wolf, a dog, a snake, a viper, a deep pit, a precarious precipice, thorny brambles, a steep cliff, and wet mud."

Do not associate with evil companions, nor draw near to wicked people; if you can contemplate this thoroughly and keep it foremost in your mind, then if you do not guard yourself, taints will arise, but if you do protect yourself, taints will not arise.
This is called "the abandonment through distancing oneself from taints."
"How is it that these are abandoned through the enjoyment of the outflows?
In this regard, bhikṣu!

One gives rise to thoughts of desire and does not abandon them; even if thoughts of malice arise, one does not abandon them; and even if thoughts of harm arise, one does not abandon them. If one does not abandon them, then the outflows arise."
One who is able to relinquish [them] can then prevent the arising of outflows (*āsrava*).
This is called "the outflows abandoned through diversion.
What are the outflows abandoned through deportment (*īryāpatha*)?
In this regard, bhikṣus!

When the eye sees forms, one does not give rise to the perception of form, nor does one give rise to a defiled mind; one possesses the faculty of the eye, and without deficiency or leakage, one guards the faculty of the eye.

If one hears sounds with the ear, smells odors with the nose, tastes flavors with the tongue, feels tactile sensations with the body, or cognizes mental phenomena with the mind, one does not give rise to a defiled mind nor give rise to conceptual attachment, thereby guarding the faculty of the mind.
If one does not maintain proper deportment, then outflows arise;
if one maintains proper deportment, then there is no affliction of outflows.
This is called "the severing of these outflows through deportment."
“What are those taints that are to be abandoned through contemplation?

In this regard, bhikkhus, one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on dispassion, relying on fading away, and relying on cessation, seeking the way of escape; one cultivates the awakening factors of dhamma-discrimination, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, relying on dispassion, relying on fading away, and relying on cessation, seeking the way of escape.”
If one does not cultivate this, then the afflictions of outflows arise;
if one is able to cultivate it, then the afflictions of outflows do not arise.
This is called the abandonment of these outflows through contemplation.

"Furthermore, monks! Regarding all the outflows (āsrava) that exist among the monks, those to be abandoned by vision, he abandons them by vision; those to be abandoned by reverence, he abandons them by reverence; those to be abandoned by cultivation, he abandons them by cultivation; those to be abandoned by avoidance, he abandons them by avoidance; those to be abandoned by deportment, he abandons them by deportment; and those to be abandoned by reflection, he abandons them by reflection."
"Monks, this is called being fully endowed with all dignified deportment; one is able to sever the fetters, remove craving, cross over the four floods, and gradually transcend suffering."
This, monks, is called the removal of the phenomena associated with outflows (āsrava).
That which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly practice— compassionate mindfulness toward all beings who possess form— that has now been practiced.
"You should always delight in dwelling in seclusion beneath trees, applying yourselves with diligent vigor and never succumbing to indolence.
If you do not apply yourselves diligently now, it will be of no avail for your regrets later."
"This is my instruction.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 34.
Ekottarika Āgama, Scroll 35, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty;
the remainder of the "Chapter on the Seven Days."
7. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on the banks of the Ajitavatī River together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was in a secluded place and had this thought:
"Is there such a principle as the constant increase of merit?
Or is there no such truth?"
At that time, Kuṇḍadhāna rose from his seat, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side.
Then, Kuṇḍadhāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Just now, while in a secluded and quiet place, I had this thought:
"Is it possible that through the various deeds one performs, there may be the attainment of beneficial merit?"
"I now ask the World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will explain it.
The World-Honored One replied:
"One may increase one's merit.
Guṇamukha addressed the Buddha,
saying, "How does one increase one's merit?"
The World-Honored One said:
"There are seven matters that increase [merit], the blessings of which are immeasurable; furthermore, no one is able to calculate them."
What are the seven?
In this regard, noble sons or noble daughters who establish a monastery where none had previously existed—this merit is incalculable.
"Furthermore, Kuṇḍadhāna!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to provide seats and couches for that monastic community and for the community of bhikṣus, this, Kuṇḍadhāna, is called [the third gift]."
"The second merit is beyond measure. Furthermore, Kūṭadanta!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family gives food to that community of bhikṣus, this, Kūṭadanta, is called..."
The third merit is beyond measure. Furthermore,
Kūṭadanta, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family provides rain-clothing to the community of bhikṣus, this, Kūṭadanta, is called [the third merit].
The merit of the fourth [act] is immeasurable.
"Furthermore, Kuṇḍadhāna!
If a son or daughter of good family should give medicine as an offering to the community of bhikṣus, this is called the fifth merit, which cannot be calculated."
"Furthermore, Kuṇḍadhāna!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family constructs a fine well in the wilderness— this,
Kuṇḍadhāna, is called [a meritorious deed]."
This is the sixth merit, which is beyond measure or calculation.
"Furthermore, Kūṭadanta!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family builds a dwelling near the path so that those who come in the future or have passed by may find a place to stay, this, Kūṭadanta, is called [the sixth merit]."
"The seventh merit is beyond measure and calculation.
This, Kuṇḍadhāna, is called the sevenfold dharma of merit, the blessings of which are immeasurable."

Whether walking or sitting, even if one’s life should come to an end, that merit follows them like a shadow follows the body. That virtue is beyond measure; it cannot be said that there is such-and-such an amount of merit, just as the waters of the great ocean cannot be measured by pints or pecks, nor can it be said that there is such-and-such an amount of water.
These seven merits are likewise thus; their blessings are beyond measure or limit.
Therefore, Kūṭadanta! Sons of good family and daughters of good family should seek skillful means to accomplish these seven merits.
"In this way, Kuṇḍadhāna,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Kuṇḍadhāna rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You all should practice the perception of death and contemplate the perception of death.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu sitting in the assembly addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“I constantly practice and contemplate the perception of death.”
The World-Honored One said:
"How do you contemplate and practice the perception of death?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When contemplating the perception of death, if one intends to remain for seven days and contemplates the seven factors of enlightenment, one will bring great benefit within the Dharma of the Tathāgata and have no regrets after death."
"So it is, World-Honored One! Thus do I contemplate the perception of death.
The World-Honored One said:
"Stop! Stop! Bhikṣu!"
"This is not the practice of the perception of death; this is called the dharma of negligence.
Then another bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am capable of undertaking the practice of the perception of death."
The Blessed One said:
"How do you practice and contemplate the perception of death?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I now have this thought: 'I wish to remain for six days; after contemplating the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, I shall then bring about my passing. In this way, there will be some increase in merit.'"
"Thus one should contemplate the perception of death.
The World-Honored One said: "Stop!
"Stop, bhikṣu!
You too are practicing a way of negligence; this is not the contemplation of the perception of death."
Again, another bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to remain for five days.
Some said four days; others said three days, two days, or one day.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Stop! Stop!”
"Monks! This too is a state of negligence; it is not the contemplation of the perception of death.
At that time, another monk addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am able to endure the practice of the perception of death.
A bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:

"When the time comes, I shall put on my robes, take up my bowl, enter the city of Śrāvastī for alms, and having finished my begging, return from Śrāvastī to my dwelling. Entering a quiet chamber, I shall contemplate the seven factors of enlightenment and bring about the end of my life; this is what is meant by contemplating the perception of death."
The World-Honored One said: "Stop! Stop!"
"Monks! This is not the contemplation and cultivation of the perception of death.
What you, monks, have been saying are all practices of negligence; they are not the method for cultivating the perception of death."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"One who is able to be like the bhikṣu Vakkali—this is what is called 'contemplating the perception of death.'"
That bhikṣu is well able to contemplate the perception of death, becoming weary of and disgusted by this body’s foul impurities.

If a bhikṣu contemplates the perception of death, fixing his attention before him with an unmoving mind, and while mindful of the counting of the incoming and outgoing breaths, contemplates the seven factors of enlightenment therein, he will derive great benefit from the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The reason for this is that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty and quiescent; those that arise and those that cease are all illusory transformations, devoid of any reality.

Therefore, bhikṣus! You should contemplate the perception of death amidst the inhalations and exhalations; thus you shall be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
"In this way, monks, you should know that you must train yourselves thus.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit issued a command to his ministers:
"Quickly prepare the precious feathered chariot; I wish to go to where the World-Honored One is to pay homage and inquire after his well-being.
At that time, the Great King immediately left the city and went to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude as he preached the Dharma.
Then, seven Nirgranthas, seven naked ascetics, seven black Brahmans, and seven naked Brahmins passed by not far from the World-Honored One.
At that time, King Prasenajit saw these people passing by not far from the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Observe these people as they pass by without stopping; they are all few in desire and content with what they have, possessing no household affairs."
In this world today, the Arhat is the most preeminent of all persons. Why is this so?
Because among the multitude, he practices the most extreme asceticism and does not crave gain or offerings.
The World-Honored One said: "Great King!
You have never yet recognized a true person, an Arhat; one does not become an Arhat merely by being naked and exposing the body."
"Great King, you should know that all these are not true practices; you should reflect upon and observe the transformations that have occurred over a long period of time.
Furthermore, you should observe those who are worthy of being associated with and those known as associates, and those who are worthy of being approached and those known as approaches."

The reason for this is that in the distant past, there were seven brahmins who studied together in one place. When they had reached extreme old age and infirmity, they made garments of grass and subsisted on fruits and gourds; having conceived various false views, each of them gave rise to this thought:
"By means of these methods of asceticism we maintain, may we later become great kings, or seek to become Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings."

At that time, there was a celestial teacher named Asita, the grandfather of those brahmins. Knowing what was in the minds of those brahmins, he immediately vanished from the Brahma Heaven and came to where the seven brahmins were.
At that time, the celestial teacher Asita cast off his heavenly raiment and assumed the form of a Brahmin, walking back and forth in the open air.
Then, the seven Brahmacharins saw Asita walking from afar; each harbored resentment and spoke these words:
"Who is this lustful person who walks before us, practitioners of the holy life? We shall now curse him with ashes and extinguish him."
The seven brahmins then cupped water in their hands and sprinkled it upon him, and the brahmins incanted:
"Become ashes and dust this very instant!
Yet, as the brahmins harbored such malice, the Teacher of Devas became even more upright and dignified in countenance.
The reason for this is that loving-kindness can extinguish hatred.
At that time, the seven brahmins thought to themselves:
"Are we not perhaps falling away from our prohibitions and precepts?"
"Just as we were giving rise to anger, that man suddenly became upright and handsome.
At that time, the seven men spoke this verse to the Teacher of Gods:
"Are you a deva, a gandharva, A rākṣasa, or a ghost?"
"What shall his name be at this time? We wish to know it.
At that moment, the master Asita immediately replied with these verses:
"He is not a deva, nor a gandharva; He is not a ghost, nor a rākṣasa spirit."
"The Celestial Master Asita is none other than my present self.
'I now know what is in your mind; therefore, I have descended from the Brahma Heaven.'"

The Brahmā Heaven is extremely remote from here; the body of Śakra, Lord of Devas, is likewise so. Even a Wheel-Turning Sage King cannot be found there, nor can one become Śakra, Brahmā, or a Caturmahārājika king through such ascetic practices.
At that time, the Teacher of Gods, Asita, spoke this verse:
"Though there are various thoughts within the mind, If one’s outward conduct is coarse and fierce,
One must diligently cultivate right view To remain far removed from the evil realms."
"Pure in the conduct of the mind, And likewise in the conduct of speech,
One who stays far removed from evil thoughts Will surely be reborn in the heavens.
At that time, the seven brahmins said to the Teacher of Brahmā:
"Is this truly the Teacher of Heaven? He replied, "It is."
However, O Brahmin, one does not attain birth in the heavens merely by going naked;

nor is it necessarily by practicing such asceticism that one attains birth in the realm of Brahmā; furthermore, it is not by exposing the body and performing various forms of austerity that one attains that place.
Rather, by being able to restrain the mind and prevent it from wavering, one is born in the heavens.
"One cannot be born in that place by means of what you have practiced.
O Great King! Observe this meaning:

one does not become an Arhat merely by being naked. It is not the case that an ordinary person who wishes to know a True Person can do so; rather, it is the True Person who is able to discern the practices of an ordinary person.
Furthermore, ordinary persons are unable to know the conduct of ordinary persons, whereas true persons (āryas) are able to know the conduct of ordinary persons.
But Your Majesty knows this; you should understand through skillful means that this has been so for a long time, not merely from the present.
One should observe it in this way. Thus, Great King,
one should train in it through skillful means.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What the Tathāgata has spoken is most excellent!
It is not something that can be understood by worldly people.”
"However, state affairs are numerous and pressing; I wish to return to my quarters.
The Buddha said to the king, "Your Majesty should know the proper time."
At that time, the king rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and withdrew.
Then, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, the kingdom of the Śākyas, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, after his meal, the World-Honored One departed from the Nyagrodha Garden and went to the village of Vairaṭī, where he sat beneath a tree.
At that moment, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi came out from Kapilavastu and approached the place where the World-Honored One was; he stood before him in silence.
At that time, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi asked the World-Honored One:
"What instructions do you, O Śramaṇa, give?
What is your doctrine?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin, you should know that what I discourse upon cannot be attained by devas, nāgas, or spirits;
nor is it attached to the world, nor does it abide in the world."
"What I have discussed is precisely this.
At that time, the Śākya Yaśoda, having bowed his head and sighed in lamentation, withdrew and departed.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata rose from his seat and returned to his dwelling.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just now, while I was sitting in that grove, a member of the Śākya clan carrying a staff came to me and asked:
'What kind of discourse does the śramaṇa practice?'"
I replied to him: "That which I discourse upon is beyond the reach of gods or men;
it is neither attached to the world, nor does it abide in the world. That which I discourse upon is precisely this."
At that time, having heard these words, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi withdrew and departed.
Then, a certain bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“In what way does one neither cling to the world, yet not dwell apart from the world?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"As for my teaching, it is entirely unattached to the world; as one now attains liberation from desire, the doubts of the Śākyas are severed, and no manifold perceptions remain."
"What I have been discussing is precisely this.
Having spoken these words, the World-Honored One rose and entered his room.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"The meaning of what the Blessed One has briefly discussed—who is capable of expounding this meaning in detail?
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another, "The Blessed One always praises the Venerable Mahākātyāyana; now, it is only Kātyāyana who can explain this meaning."
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus said to Kātyāyana:
"Just now, the Tathāgata briefly explained its meaning; we pray that the Venerable One will expound it in detail, analyzing each point so that all people may attain understanding."
Kātyāyana replied: "It is just as if there were a person in a village who went out from that village seeking a truly real object.
If he saw a great tree, he would cut it down, take its branches and leaves, and depart, leaving the trunk behind."
Yet now you are likewise; having abandoned the Tathāgata, you come to seek the fruit from the branches.

However, that Tathāgata perceives all of this without exception, illuminating the world and serving as a guide for devas and humans. The Tathāgata is the true master of the Dharma, and there will come a time when you shall naturally encounter the Tathāgata’s exposition of this meaning.
Then the bhikṣus replied:
"Although the Tathāgata is the true master of the Dharma and has extensively expounded its meaning,
the World-Honored One has prophesied that you, Venerable Sir, are capable of explaining its meaning in detail."
Kātyāyana replied: "Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well."
"I shall now expound and analyze its meaning.
The bhikṣus replied, "Excellent!"
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately accepted his instruction.
Kātyāyana told them: "Now, that which the Tathāgata has said:"

"What I discourse upon cannot be fathomed by devas, nāgas, or spirits; nor do I cling to the world, nor do I dwell in the world. Yet, I have attained liberation therein, severed all doubts, and am free from further hesitation, unlike the common folk of today who delight in strife and litigation, giving rise to various disordered thoughts."
Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has said:
"I do not give rise to a mind of defiled attachment therein.

This refers to the underlying tendency of sensual desire (*rāgānuśaya*), as well as the underlying tendencies of ill-will, wrong view, worldly desire, pride, doubt, and ignorance. Or, encountering the retribution of suffering from swords and staves, one engages in strife and litigation with others, giving rise to various unwholesome actions, conceiving manifold distracted thoughts, and undertaking unvirtuous conduct.

If the eye sees forms and gives rise to consciousness and perception, these three factors act as mutual causes, resulting in contact (*sparśa*). Because there is contact, there is feeling (*vedanā*); because there is feeling, there is sensation (*saṃjñā*); because there is sensation, there is conceptualization (*saṃskāra*); and because there is conceptualization, one engages in mental weighing, giving rise to various kinds of perceptions and thoughts of attachment.

When the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue tastes flavors, the body contacts what is smooth and fine, and the mind cognizes mental phenomena (*dharma*), consciousness and perception arise. Through the mutual dependence of these three factors, there is contact (*sparśa*); because of contact, there is feeling (*vedanā*); because of feeling, there is sensation (*saṃjñā*); because of sensation, there is ideation (*saṃjñā*); because of ideation, one evaluates; and therein arises various kinds of conceptualizations and thoughts of attachment.

These are the latent tendencies of sensual desire, ill will, wrong views, pride, the worldly desire for existence, ignorance, and doubt; they all give rise to transformations involving swords and staves, manifesting various kinds of transformations beyond measure or calculation.
"If someone were to say:
'There is neither eye nor form, yet there is contact,' this would not be correct."
Furthermore, if it were said:
"There is feeling without contact," this too is not so.
If one were to say,
"There is no sensation, yet there is conceptual attachment," this would not be correct.
Furthermore, suppose someone were to say:
"There is no ear and no sound; no nose and no fragrance; no tongue and no taste; no body and no tactile sensation; no mind and no phenomena; yet there is consciousness."
"In the end, there is no such principle.
Suppose one were to say:
'There is contact and sensation without consciousness.'"
This is not so. Suppose it were said: "There is feeling even without contact."
This is not so. Suppose it were said:
"There is no sensation, yet there is conceptual attachment."
"This is not so. Furthermore, if someone were to say:
'There is the eye and there are forms, and within them consciousness arises.'"
This is necessarily so. If one says:
"Consciousness arises with respect to the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena."
"This matter is certain.
You virtuous ones should know that for this reason, the World-Honored One has said:

'That which I discourse upon cannot be reached by gods, humans, Māras, or those belonging to the realm of Māra; it is neither attached to the world nor does it abide in the world. Furthermore, I have attained liberation from desire, severed all doubt, and am no longer hesitant.'"
"The World-Honored One has briefly explained its meaning based on this occasion.
If you do not understand it in your hearts, go again to the presence of the Tathāgata and ask about this meaning once more."
"If the Tathāgata has anything to say, we shall gladly remember and uphold it.
At that time, having heard what Kātyāyana had said, many bhikṣus neither praised it as good nor rejected it as wrong; they immediately rose from their seats and departed.
They said to one another:
"We should take this matter and go to question the Tathāgata; whatever the World-Honored One may say, we shall respectfully carry it out."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, those many bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

“The bhikṣu Kātyāyana is intelligent and possesses eloquence; he has extensively expounded its meaning. Even if you had come to my presence to ask about this matter, I would have explained it to you in exactly the same way.”
At that time, Ānanda was behind the Tathāgata.
Then, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The meaning and principle of this sutra are exceedingly profound. It is like a person traveling on a road who encounters ambrosia; having taken it and eaten it, it is so extremely fragrant and delicious that one never tires of eating it."
"It is likewise with this: wherever these sons and daughters of good family go, they shall never tire of hearing this Dharma.
He addressed the World-Honored One again:
"What is the name of this sutra, and how should we practice it?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'The Flavor of the Ambrosial Dharma'; you should keep it in mind and practice it accordingly.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Chapter 41: On Not Fearing. *Ekottarika Āgama*, Chapter Forty-one: On Not Fearing. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park of the Śākyas.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then, Mahānāma the Śākya addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have personally received these instructions from the Tathāgata:"

"Any son or daughter of good family who severs the three fetters becomes a srotāpanna; they are called 'non-retrogressive,' destined to realize the fruit of the Way, no longer seeking the teachings of external paths or heterodox schools, nor further examining what others may say."
"Even if that were the case, such a thing would not be so.
If I were to see a fierce bull, horse, or camel, I would immediately become terrified, my hair would stand on end, and I would further think:
'If I were to meet my end today while harboring this fear, where would I be reborn?'"
The World-Honored One told Mahānāman:
"Do not give rise to a heart of fear; even if you should meet your end, you shall not fall into the three evil realms.
Why is this? Because there are now three principles for the cessation [of suffering]."
What are the three?

Suppose one is attached to sensual desire and gives rise to affliction and disturbance, further giving rise to a harmful intent toward others; if one lacks this desire, then one does not give rise to a mind of killing or harm, and does not give rise to suffering and affliction in the present life—those evil and unwholesome states that would otherwise lead to self-harm.
If these are absent, there is no agitation, and consequently, no sorrow or grief.
"Mahānāma, these are the three meanings by which all evil and unwholesome states fall below, while all wholesome states remain above."
It is also like a jar of ghee that has broken in water: at that time, the shards and stones sink to the bottom while the ghee floats on top.
This is likewise; all evil and unwholesome dharmas remain below, while all wholesome dharmas float above.

Mahānāman! You should know that in the past, before I had attained the Way of the Buddha, I practiced asceticism for six years at Uruvilvā. I did not consume delicious foods, and my body became so emaciated that I resembled a man of a hundred years; this was entirely due to my abstaining from food.
Whenever I wished to rise, I would fall back to the ground.
At that time, I further thought:
"If my life were to end here, where would I be reborn?"
At that time, I further thought:
"If my life now comes to an end, I shall certainly not be reborn in the evil realms.
Nevertheless, the underlying principle is that one cannot proceed from pleasure to pleasure; it must be through suffering that one subsequently reaches pleasure.
"At that time, I was again dwelling in a hermitage cave.
At that moment, there were many Nirgrantha ascetics practicing the Way there.
Some of these Nirgranthas pointed their fingers toward the sun while exposing their bodies to practice the Way; others squatted while practicing the Way."
At that time, I went to where they were and said to the Nirgranthas,
"For what reason have you left your seats, raised your hands,
and lifted your feet? Those Nirgranthas replied:
"O Gautama, you should know that in the past my former teacher committed unwholesome deeds; the reason he now endures such suffering is his desire to extinguish those transgressions.
Although he now exposes his body, there is still a sense of shame and humiliation, and through this, he also brings about the extinction of these matters."

"Gotama, you should know that when volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are exhausted, suffering (*duḥkha*) is also exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, volitional formations are also exhausted. When suffering and volitional formations are both exhausted, one then attains *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, I spoke again to the Nirgrantha: "This is not so.

It is not the case that suffering is exhausted because volitional formations are exhausted, nor is it the case that volitional formations are exhausted because suffering is exhausted, such that one would thereby attain *nirvāṇa*."
"However, it is indeed the case that one who exhausts their ascetic practices through present suffering can attain Nirvana;
yet, one cannot proceed from pleasure to pleasure.
The Nirgrantha said:
"King Bimbisāra goes from pleasure to pleasure; what suffering could he possibly have?
At that time, I spoke again to the Nirgrantha:
"How does King Bimbisāra’s pleasure compare to my own pleasure?"
The Nirgrantha replied to me, saying,
"King Bimbisāra’s pleasure is superior to your pleasure.
At that time, I spoke again to the Nirgrantha, saying:
"Can King Bimbisāra enable me to sit cross-legged for seven days and seven nights without my body moving?
Or even for six, five, four, three, two, down to a single day, sitting cross-legged?"
The Nirgrantha replied: "No, Gautama!"
The World-Honored One said:
"I am capable of sitting cross-legged with my body unmoving. How is it, Nigaṇṭha?"
Who is it that experiences happiness?
Is it King Bimbisāra who experiences happiness,
or is it I who experience happiness?
The Nirgrantha said,
"The ascetic Gautama is happy.
[The Buddha replied,] "It is so."
Mahānāma! You should employ this skillful means: know that one cannot go from pleasure to pleasure; one must go from suffering to pleasure.
It is just like this, Mahānāma!
To the left and right of Mahāgrāma there is a great pool of water, one yojana in length and breadth, filled with water.
Suppose, furthermore, that someone were to come and take a single drop of water from it.
"What do you think, Mahānāman!
Which is more: the water [in this ocean], or a single drop of water?"
"Is it the water in the pond that is more?
Mahānāman replied, "The water in the pond is more; it is not that a single drop of water is more."
The World-Honored One said:
"It is just like this.
For the noble disciple whose various sufferings have already been exhausted and will never arise again, that which remains is like a single drop of water."
Among my assembly, even those who follow the lowest path shall, after no more than seven deaths and seven births, reach the end of suffering.
If they further apply themselves with courage and vigor, they will become "house-to-house" practitioners and immediately attain the fruit of the path.
At that time, the World-Honored One further expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to Mahānāman. Having heard the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Mahānāman rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Venerable Nāgapāla was staying in the city of Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, there was a brahmin who was nearly decrepit in age and had been a close friend of the Venerable Nāgapāla since their youth.
At that time, the brahmin went to where Nāgapāla was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. Then the brahman said to Nāgapāla:
"Among those who enjoy pleasures, you are now the most happy."
Nāgabodhi said: "Based on what meaning do you make this statement:
'Among all forms of pleasure, this is the most joyful'?"
The Brahmin replied: "Within seven days, seven sons of mine have died; all were valiant and of high talent, their wisdom beyond compare."
Within the past six days, twelve laborers have passed away; they were capable of their tasks and free from indolence.
Within the past five days, four brothers have passed away; they possessed many arts and skills and were proficient in everything.
Within the past four days, my parents have reached the end of their lives; having reached nearly a hundred years of age, they have departed from me and passed away.
In the past three days alone, two more wives have died; their countenances were so upright and beautiful that they were rare in this world.
Furthermore, there were eight treasuries of precious jewels in the house, which we sought yesterday but could not find their location.
Thus, the suffering I endure today is beyond measure.
However, Venerable One!
Today I am forever free from those afflictions and no longer have any sorrow or anxiety; I find my own delight solely in the Dharma. Having contemplated this meaning, I therefore say:
"Among all forms of pleasure, this is the most supreme happiness!"
At that time, the Venerable Nāgabodhi said to that brahmin:
"Why did you not employ some skillful means to prevent so many people from dying?"
The brahmin replied:

"I too have employed many skillful means, desiring neither death nor the loss of my wealth. Furthermore, I have practiced giving at the proper times, performed various meritorious deeds, made offerings to the devas, supported the elder brahmins, protected the deities, and recited various incantations. I am also able to observe the constellations, compound medicinal herbs, and provide delicious food and drink to those in distress; such things as these are beyond counting."
"Nevertheless, it cannot save his life-force.
At that time, the Venerable Nāgabodhi spoke this verse:
"Medicinal herbs and various incantations, Robes, food, drink, and all necessities—"
Though one gives alms, there is no benefit; it is like embracing the body while practicing asceticism.
Even if one sacrifices to the gods, offering incense, flowers, and ritual bathing—when one calculates the root of these matters, none of them can provide healing.
"Even if one were to give away all manner of things and diligently maintain the holy life,
when these fundamental roots are weighed and compared, there is nothing that can cure them.
At that time, the brahmin asked:
"What dharma should one practice so as to be free from the affliction of such suffering?
At that time, the Venerable Nāgabodhi spoke this verse:
"Affection is rooted in ignorance, Giving rise to all manner of suffering and affliction."
"When that is extinguished without remainder, there shall be no further suffering.
At that time, having heard these words, the brahmin immediately spoke this verse:
"Though old, he is not exceedingly old; his conduct is like that of a disciple."
"I pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and study, so that I may be freed from this calamity.
At that time, the Venerable Nāgabodhi immediately conferred upon him the three robes, granted him the going forth to study, and further addressed him, saying: "Now, O Bhikṣu!"
One should contemplate this body from head to foot: from where do these hair, fur, nails, and teeth come?
From where do the physical form, skin, flesh, marrow, bones, intestines, and stomach all come?
"If one were to depart from here, where would one go?

Therefore, bhikṣus, do not harbor excessive anxiety regarding the sufferings of the world; rather, you should contemplate within this pore and seek the skillful means to realize the Four Noble Truths."
At that time, the Venerable Nāgabodhi spoke this verse:
"Abandon conceptualization and do not grieve excessively; before long, you shall attain the Dharma-eye.
Impermanence moves like lightning; such a great fortune is not easily encountered."
"Contemplate each and every pore, the origin of that which arises and that which ceases;
impermanent processes are like lightning—direct your mind toward Nirvana.
At that time, the elder bhikṣu, having received such instruction, dwelt in a secluded place and contemplated this practice.

For this reason, noble son, those who shave off their hair and beard and, with firm faith, leave the household life to study the Way, do so desiring to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*). They know according to reality: "Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further taking of a womb."
At that time, that bhikṣu became an arhat.
Then, a deva who had been an old acquaintance of that bhikṣu, seeing that he had become an arhat, went to where Nāgabala was and spoke this verse while remaining in mid-air:
"Having attained full ordination, He dwells in that secluded place."
"Having attained the mind of the Way, one is free from attachment, removing the very roots of all original evils.
At that time, that deva again scattered celestial flowers over the Venerable One and immediately vanished into the air, no longer visible.
At that time, those bhikṣus and the devas, having heard what the Venerable Nāgavara had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should contemplate the excellence of the seven points and examine the four dharmas; within this present life, such a person is called a superior man."
"How, bhikkhus, does one contemplate the excellence of the seven stations?
In this regard, bhikkhus..."

With a mind of loving-kindness, he pervades one direction, two directions, three directions, and four directions; likewise for the four intermediate points, the zenith, and the nadir. In this manner, he pervades the entire world with a mind of loving-kindness.
The same applies to the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
With all faculties complete, he measured his food and drink and remained constantly self-awakened.
In this way, bhikṣus, you should contemplate the seven points. "How so, bhikṣus?"
What is the method for examining the four foundations? In this regard, bhikṣu!
One internally contemplates the body to remove sorrow and grief, establishing mindfulness of the body; externally, one again contemplates the body, establishing mindfulness of the body.
Internally and externally, one dwells on the contemplation of the body as a body;
internally, one dwells on the contemplation of feelings as feelings;
externally, one dwells on the contemplation of feelings as feelings.
The application of mindfulness to feelings regarding feelings internally;
the application of mindfulness to the mind regarding the mind internally;
and the application of mindfulness to the mind regarding the mind externally.
Internally observing the mind, one establishes mindfulness of the mind; thus, sorrow and grief are removed, and there is no further suffering or affliction.
Internally observing phenomena, one establishes mindfulness of phenomena;
externally observing phenomena, one establishes mindfulness of phenomena; and both internally and externally observing phenomena, one establishes mindfulness of phenomena.
Thus, bhikṣus, contemplate the excellence of these four dharmas. Furthermore, bhikṣus!
Thus, one who is skilled in these seven points and examines these four dharmas becomes a superior person in this very life. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to accomplish excellence in these seven points and contemplate these four dharmas.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the city of Kapilavastu in the Śākya country, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, those many bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We wish to travel to the northern region to wander and transform beings."
The World-Honored One said:
"Know that now is the time.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Did you take leave of the bhikṣu Śāriputra? The bhikṣus replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Go and take leave of the bhikṣu Śāriputra.”
"The reason for this is that the bhikṣu Śāriputra constantly instructs his fellow practitioners of the holy life in the Dharma, preaching the teachings without ever becoming weary.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the bhikṣus. Having heard the Dharma, the bhikṣus rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew.
At that time, Śāriputra was staying at the Kalandakanivāpa Monastery.
Then, a great number of bhikṣus went to where Śāriputra was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus said to Śāriputra:
"We wish to travel to the human realms of the north to wander and transform beings; we now take our leave of the World-Honored One."

Śāriputra said: "You should know that the people, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas of the northern regions are all intelligent and their wisdom is difficult to equal; furthermore, there are people who delight in coming to test one another."
If someone were to ask you in the future:
"Venerable teachers, what kind of doctrine do you uphold?
should such a question be posed, how would you answer it?
The bhikṣus replied: "If anyone were to come and question us, we would answer him with this principle:
'Form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering.'"
That which is suffering is without self; that which is without self is empty. Because it is empty and without self, it is empty of that [self]; this is what the wise contemplate.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self. In their true nature, they are empty because they are without self and empty; this is what the wise study.
"These five aggregates of clinging are all empty and all quiescent; through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they all return to extinction and cannot endure for long.
The Eightfold Path consists of seven [limbs] leading toward [the goal]; what my Teacher has taught refers precisely to this."
“If kṣatriyas, brahmins, or members of the common people come to question us regarding the Dharma, we shall answer them with this very meaning.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the many bhikṣus:
“You must firmly maintain your minds; do not act rashly.”
At that time, Śāriputra had fully expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the bhikṣus and rose from his seat to depart.
Not long after they had left, Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"How should one practice the eightfold path and the sevenfold dharma?"
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus said to Śāriputra:
“We have come from afar desiring to hear its meaning; we only pray that you will explain it.”
Śāriputra replied: "Listen attentively!
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall now speak."
At that time, the bhikṣu accepted his instruction. Śāriputra told him:
"If one is single-mindedly mindful of right view, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness will not be disturbed."
Regarding "equal cultivation": to be mindful of all phenomena with a single mind is the awakening factor of dharma-discernment (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
regarding "equal speech": physical and mental vigor is the awakening factor of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
regarding "equal action": the arising of all phenomena is the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Equanimity of life means being content with the wealth of the noble ones, relinquishing all household property, settling the physical body, and relying on the awakening factor of mindfulness;
equanimity of skillful means means attaining the four noble truths of the noble ones, exhausting and eliminating all fetters, and relying on the awakening factor of concentration;

equanimity of mindfulness means contemplating the four foundations of mindfulness, seeing that the body has no solidity and is entirely empty and selfless, and relying on the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena.

Regarding "equal samādhi": it is that by which those who have not attained [attainment] attain it, those who have not crossed over cross over, and those who have not realized [realization] cause to realize it.
Suppose someone were to come and ask about this meaning:
"How does one cultivate the Eightfold Path and the Seven Dharmas?"
"You should answer them in this way. Why is that?
Because if there are bhikṣus who cultivate the Eightfold Path and the Seven Dharmas, their minds with outflows will attain liberation."

"I now tell you again: if there be a bhikṣu who practices and contemplates the Eightfold Path and the Seven Dharmas, that bhikṣu will attain two fruits without doubt, reaching the state of Arhatship."
Furthermore, setting this matter aside:
if one cannot do much, yet practices these eight kinds of paths and seven dharmas within a single day, the merit thereof is beyond measure, and one will attain the stage of Anāgāmin or Arhat.
"Therefore, worthy ones, you should seek skillful means; those who practice these eightfold paths and seven dharmas will have no doubt regarding the path to grasping.
At that time, having heard what Śāriputra had said, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
“You are now advanced in years and have lost your youthful vigor; you ought to accept the clothing and food offered by these elders.
Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I am not fit to receive their robes and food; at present, wearing these patched rags and begging for alms as the occasion arises brings me incomparable happiness.”

The reason for this is that in the future there will be bhikṣus whose physical bodies are delicate and soft, yet whose minds are greedy for fine food and clothing; they will thus regress from dhyāna and no longer be able to practice ascetic deeds. Furthermore, they will speak these words:
"In the time of the past Buddhas, the bhikṣus likewise accepted invitations and received food and clothing from others; why should we not follow the example of the sages of ancient times?"

"Because they sit in greed and attachment to clothing and food, they shall then cast off their robes and become white-clad laypeople, causing the holy sages to no longer possess majestic spiritual power, and the fourfold assembly will gradually diminish.
Once the assembly of the holy ones has diminished, the divine temples of the Tathāgata will likewise be destroyed;
because the divine temples of the Tathāgata have been destroyed, the sutras and the Dharma will further decline."
At that time, sentient beings no longer possessed vital radiance; because they lacked this radiance, their lifespans became increasingly short.
At that time, after those beings passed away, they all fell into the three evil destinies.

Just as among the classes of sentient beings today, those who have performed much merit are all born in the heavens, so too in future worlds, those who have committed many sins will all enter the hells.
The World-Honored One said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Kāśyapa has brought great benefit to the world, acting as a virtuous friend and a field of merit for the people.
Kāśyapa, you should know that more than a thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus who regress from meditation and no longer practice the dhūta austerities;
they will neither beg for food nor wear robes of patched rags, but will greedily accept invitations from householders for their clothing and food.

Furthermore, they do not dwell in seclusion beneath trees; rather, they delight in adorning their dwellings. They do not even use excrement or urine as medicine, but instead take only other medicinal herbs that are extremely sweet and delicious.
Or else, they become greedily attached to wealth within those places and, being stingy regarding their dwellings, are constantly engaged in quarreling and strife.
At that time, the donors and patrons were firm in their faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, delighting in the practice of giving and not begrudging their wealth.
When these donors and patrons passed away, they were all reborn in the heavens; however, those bhikṣus who were indolent fell into hell after death.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
All conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent and cannot be maintained for long.

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, you should know that in a future age there will be bhikṣus who shave their hair and beards yet practice the household life; they will have a son in their left arm and a daughter in their right, while holding lutes and flutes as they beg for food in the streets and alleys.
At that time, the donor and patron would receive inexhaustible merit; how much more so for those who today beg for alms with utmost sincerity.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa:
all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and cannot endure for long.

“Kāśyapa, you should know that in a future age, there will be śramaṇas and bhikṣus who shall abandon the eightfold path and the sevenfold dharmas—those very treasures of Dharma that I have accumulated over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas as I do today.”

In the future, there will be bhikṣus who take these as songs and seek alms among the multitude to sustain their own lives; yet even when donors and patrons provide food for such a community of bhikṣus, they still obtain merit—how much more so today, when one would not fail to obtain that merit!
"I now entrust this Dharma to the bhikṣus Kāśyapa and Ānanda.

The reason for this is that I am now old, approaching eighty years of age, and the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa. I now hand over the treasure of the Dharma to these two men; you must recite and uphold it with mindfulness so that it shall not be interrupted, but spread throughout the world."
Whoever obstructs or severs the teachings of the sages falls into the extremes.
Therefore, today I entrust this sutra and its Dharma to you; do not allow it to be lost or neglected.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda rose from their seats, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what reason do you entrust this Dharma of the sutra to these two persons, rather than charging others with it?"
Furthermore, within the assembly of the Tathāgata, there are those of foremost supernatural powers beyond measure; why then do you not entrust [the teachings] to them?
The World-Honored One told Kāśyapa:
“Among gods and humans, I have never seen anyone capable of receiving and upholding this Dharma-treasure who could equal Kāśyapa or Ānanda.”

Furthermore, among the śrāvakas, there are likewise no two who surpass these two; for past Buddhas also had these two individuals who upheld the sūtras and the Dharma, just like the bhikṣus Kāśyapa and Ānanda of the present, who are most exceptionally sublime.
The reason for this is that among the bhikṣus who practiced *dhūta* austerities under the Buddhas of the past, they would remain as long as the Dharma remained, and perish when the Dharma perished.
However, today the bhikṣu Kāśyapa shall remain in the world until Maitreya Buddha appears in the world, after which he will enter parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa now surpasses the assembly of bhikṣus from the past.
Furthermore, how has the bhikṣu Ānanda surpassed the attendants of the past?
In the past, the attendants of the various Buddhas would hear what others said before they could understand;
however, today the bhikṣu Ānanda understands even before the Tathāgata has uttered a word, and he knows all that the Tathāgata does not need to say further.
For this reason, Ānanda Bhikṣu surpasses the attendants of all the Buddhas of the past. Therefore, Kāśyapa! Ānanda!
"I now entrust to you and commit to you this Dharma-treasure; let it not be diminished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; That which arises must necessarily cease."
"Where there is no birth, there is no death; this cessation is the supreme bliss.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 35 and Volume 36.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
42. Chapter on the Eight Difficulties, Part One of Forty-Two. (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Ordinary worldlings do not hear or know the proper seasons for preaching the Dharma.
Bhikṣus, you should know that there are eight seasons when one cannot hear [the Dharma], and during which people are unable to practice.”
What are these eight?

When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he extensively expounds the teachings of the Dharma, leading to nirvāṇa—the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice; yet these sentient beings, remaining within the hells, neither hear nor behold them.
This is called the first objection:
"Furthermore, when a Tathāgata appears in the world and extensively expounds the teachings of the Dharma, these sentient beings remain among the animals, neither hearing nor seeing them."
This is called the second difficulty.
"Furthermore, when a Tathāgata appears in the world and extensively expounds the teachings of the Dharma, these sentient beings, being among the hungry ghosts, neither hear nor see them."
This is called the third difficulty.

"Furthermore, when a Tathāgata appears in the world and extensively expounds the teachings of the Dharma, these sentient beings, being in the Heaven of Longevity (Ābhāsvara), neither hear nor see them."
This is called the fourth difficulty.

Furthermore, when a Tathāgata appears in the world and extensively expounds the teachings of the Dharma, these sentient beings are born in the borderlands, where they slander the noble ones and commit various evil deeds.
This is called the fifth objection.

"Furthermore, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he extensively expounds the teachings of the Dharma so that beings may attain Nirvana; yet these beings are born in a central land, and moreover, their six sense faculties are not fully complete, nor do they distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas."
This is called the sixth difficulty.

"Furthermore, when a Tathāgata appears in the world and extensively expounds the teachings so that one may attain nirvāṇa, there may be sentient beings living in the central lands who, though their six sense faculties are complete and without deficiency, possess minds and consciousnesses of false views:
they hold that there is no person, no giving, and no recipient."
Furthermore, there is no retribution for good or evil;
there is no present life or future life;
nor are there parents.
In the world, there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have attained the state of arhat, having realized it for themselves and dwelling in its bliss.
This is called the seventh difficulty.

"Furthermore, even if a Tathāgata does not appear in the world and does not preach the Dharma to lead beings to Nirvāṇa, yet these beings are born in a central land with their six sense faculties complete, capable of receiving the Dharma, intelligent and of high talent, understanding it upon hearing it, and practicing right view—namely:
that there are things, there is giving, there is a recipient;
and that there are the retributions of good and evil."
"There is this world and the world beyond;
there are in these worlds śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who cultivate right view, realize it, and attain arhatship.
This is called the eighth objection, which is not practiced by those of the holy life.
"Thus it is said, bhikkhus:
there are these eight obstacles where the holy life cannot be practiced.
In this regard, bhikkhus..."
