There is a particular occasion upon which a practitioner of the holy life (brahmacārin) may practice.
What is this one occasion?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world and extensively expounds the Dharma-teaching, leading to the attainment of Nirvāṇa; and when this person is born in a central land, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence, being clear-minded regarding all things, practicing right view, and being able to discern between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; and when there exist in this world and the next world śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who cultivate right view and attain realization as Arhats.
"This is called the practice of a single dharma by a practitioner of the Brahma-faring, which leads to the attainment of Nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"The eight difficulties are not of one kind; They prevent people from attaining the Way."
Now that it has appeared before you, such a moment is difficult to encounter in this world.
You should likewise study the True Dharma and never lose this opportunity;
otherwise, by merely recollecting the past and so forth, you will be reborn in hell.
Thus, having severed desire, one contemplates the True Dharma;
abiding long in the world, there shall be no time of cessation.
Thus, having severed desire, one contemplates the True Dharma.
Forever severing the source of birth and death, may you long remain in this world.
Having obtained this human body, one should discern the true and correct Dharma;
those who fail to attain the fruit will surely wander through the eight difficult states.
Now it is said there are eight difficulties; regarding the essential practice of the Buddha-dharma, even a single difficulty is already severe, like a plank floating upon the great ocean.
Although one may escape this one difficulty, such a principle is indeed possible.
If one is separated from even one of the Four Noble Truths, one is forever separated from the Right Path.
Therefore, one should concentrate the mind and contemplate the subtle principle;
by listening to the True Dharma with utmost sincerity, one shall attain the state of the Unconditioned.
"Therefore, bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means to remain far removed from the eight states of adversity;
do not wish to be born therein. Thus it is, bhikṣus!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are eight great hells.”

What are the eight? First is the Saṃjīva Hell; second is the Kālasūtra Hell; third is the Saṃghāta Hell; fourth is the Raurava Hell; fifth is the Mahāraurava Hell; sixth is the Avīci Hell; seventh is the Tapana Hell; and eighth is the Pratāpana Hell.
"Thus, bhikṣus, are the eight great hells.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra, Samghāta, Raurava, and Mahāraurava, The five heinous crimes lead to Avīci, And the Tapana and Pratāpana hells.
These are called the eight hells; Their interiors are places one cannot endure.
All arise from the root of evil deeds, surrounded by sixteen iron partitions.
Upon that iron prison, it is scorched by fire;
throughout an area of one yojana, the blazing flames are extremely fierce and intense.
The four cities have four gates, and the spaces between them are perfectly level;
furthermore, the cities are made of iron, with iron plates covering them on top.

This arises from the conditions of the karmic retribution for the sins of sentient beings, causing those beings to undergo immeasurable suffering until their flesh and blood are entirely consumed, leaving only bones remaining.
For what reason is it called the Reviving Hell?
Furthermore, the bodies of those sentient beings are rigid and motionless; oppressed by suffering, they cannot shift or turn, for their bodies are devoid of flesh and blood.
At that time, the sentient beings said to one another, "The sentient beings have returned to life! They have returned to life!
And at that moment, those sentient beings indeed returned to life.
For these reasons, it is called the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Black Rope Hell (Kālasūtra)?
It is because the bodies, tendons, and veins of those sentient beings are all transformed into ropes, with which their bodies are sawn; therefore, it is called the Black Rope Hell.
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Hell of Equal Harm?
At that time, those sentient beings gather in one place, and their heads are struck off, yet they immediately grow back again."
For this reason and by these causes and conditions, it is called the Hell of Equal Harm (*Samghāta*).
Furthermore, for what reason and by what causes and conditions is it called the Hell of Weeping and Wailing (*Raurava*)?
It is because those sentient beings have severed the roots of goodness until not even a single hair’s breadth remains.
Within that hell, they undergo immeasurable afflictions; therein they utter cries of resentment and lamentation, their voices never ceasing.
For this reason, it is called the Hell of Weeping and Wailing.
"For what reason is it called the Hell of Great Weeping?
It is because those sentient beings within that hell undergo immeasurable and incalculable suffering;
therein they cry out, beat their breasts, and tear at themselves, wailing in unison."
For these reasons, it is called the Hell of Great Weeping.
Furthermore, for what causes and conditions is it called the Avīci Hell?

It is because sentient beings who kill their parents, destroy a stūpa of the Buddha, cause schism among the Saṃgha, practice perverted and inverted views, and associate with those of such views, become entirely incurable.
For this reason, it is called the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is it called the Jvālā (Flaming) Hell?
Because when beings of various kinds are within that hell, smoke issues from their bodies and they are all melted and scorched; therefore, it is called the Jvālā Hell.
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called the Great Blazing Hell?
Because within that hell, one does not see even the slightest remnant of those who committed sins; this, O bhikṣu, is why it is so named."
For these reasons, they are called the Eight Great Hells.

Each of these hells has sixteen subsidiary hells, which are named: the Utpala Hell, the Padma Hell, the Kumuda Hell, the Puṇḍarīka Hell, the Adbhuta Hell, the Anavasthita Hell, the Mūḍha Hell, the Saṃvarta Hell, the Kṣuradhāra Hell, the Kumbhīpāka Hell, the Vahniśikhā Hell, the Parvata Hell, the Kṣāranadī Hell, the Kaṇṭaka Hell, the Kṣārapurīṣa Hell, the Asipatravana Hell, and the Taptāyoguda Hell.
In this manner, there are sixteen such compartments beyond measure, wherein those sentient beings are made to be born within the hells.

Among them, there are certain sentient beings who destroy right view, slander the true Dharma, and distance themselves from it; after their lives end, they are all reborn in the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
Those sentient beings who take pleasure in killing are born in the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra-naraka*).
Those sentient beings who slaughter oxen, sheep, and various other species are, after their lives end, born in the Hell of Equal Harm (*Samghāta-naraka*).
If there are sentient beings who take what is not given or steal the property of others, they will be born in the Weeping Hell (Rudana-niraya).

If there are sentient beings who constantly delight in lewdness and debauchery, or who further speak falsehoods, after the end of their lives they will be born in the Great Weeping Hell (Mahārudana-niraya).

There are sentient beings who kill their parents, destroy divine temples, cause schisms within the Sangha, slander the sages, and practice inverted and false views; after their lives end, they are reborn in the Avīci Hell.

If there are sentient beings who hear words here and transmit them to that place, or hear them there and transmit them back here, seeking opportunities for others, those people, after their lives end, will be reborn in the Hell of Blazing Heat.

If there are sentient beings who incite strife between one another, who greedily covet the property of others, who give rise to stinginess and malice, and whose minds harbor hesitation, they will, after the end of their lives, be born in the Great Flame Hell.
There are sentient beings who, having committed various mixed karmas, after their lives end, are reborn among the sixteen sub-hells.
At that time, the hell-wardens subject those sentient beings to immeasurable suffering;
they may sever their hands, or sever their feet, or sever both their hands and feet.
Some have their noses cut off, some have their ears severed, and some have both their ears and noses cut off;

some are pressed down with wooden planks, some have grass stuffed into their bellies, some have their hair pulled out and hung up, some have their skin flayed and their flesh cut away, some are split into two parts and then sutured back together, some are dismembered into five pieces, some are roasted over a side-heated fire, some are drenched with molten iron, some are torn apart in five ways, some have their bodies elongated, and some have their heads decapitated with sharp axes—all yet they are immediately restored to life.
Only after they have exhausted their retribution among humans will they be reborn.

At that time, the hell-wardens seize those beings and crush their bodies with great hammers; some they take by the spinal cord and flay them, while others they drive up onto sword-trees and then drive back down.

At that moment, iron-beaked crows come and devour them; they are again seized and bound in five ways so that they cannot move. They are then lifted and cast into large cauldrons of boiling water, where their bodies are struck with iron forks until they are harmed. The wind blows upon their bodies, and they are restored to life as before.

At that time, the hell-wardens further compel sentient beings to ascend mountains of blades and mountains of fire, not allowing them to stop; the suffering they undergo therein is beyond measure, and they must remain until the retribution for the sins committed during their human lives is fully exhausted before they can finally depart.

At that time, the offenders, unable to endure this agony, again sought to enter the Hell of Hot Ashes to undergo immeasurable suffering; emerging from there, they entered the Hell of Inverted Thorns, where the wind blew with incalculable pain; emerging from there again, they entered the Hell of Hot Excrement.
At that time, there are soft and fine insects within the Hell of Boiling Excrement that devour their flesh and bones.
At this point, the sentient beings, unable to endure the suffering and pain, move again to the Hell of Sword Trees, where their bodies are mangled and destroyed, and the agony is unbearable.
At that time, the hell-warden said to those beings,
"From where have you come? Then the sinners replied:
"We ourselves do not know from where we have come," they said.
They asked again,
"Where are you going?"
He replied, "I likewise do not know where I am destined to go.
He asked again:
"What do you seek now? they replied,
"We are suffering greatly from hunger and thirst."

At that time, the hell-wardens place glowing iron balls into the mouths of those offenders; they burn and scorch their bodies until the pain becomes unbearable, yet they must exhaust the full measure of their karmic retribution before their lives finally come to an end.
At that time, the sinner returns once more to pass through as many hells as before, suffering therein for tens of millions of years, and only then does he emerge.
"Bhikṣus, you should know that King Yama then thinks:
'All sentient beings who have committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind must undergo such retribution as this.'"
"Whosoever among sentient beings perform wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind—those of such a kind shall all be born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"The fool is always joyful, Like those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven."
"The wise always harbor fear, as if dwelling in hell.
At that time, the bhikṣu heard King Yama issue this command:

"On what day shall I extinguish the sins committed in the past, so that at the end of this life I may receive a human form, be born in a central land, meet with virtuous friends, have parents who have deep faith in the Buddha-dharma, leave the household life to study the Way within the assembly of the Tathāgata, and in this very life exhaust all outflows to achieve the state of being without outflows?"

I now urge you with earnest exhortation: exert yourself with diligent application to leave behind the eight states of adversity, to be born in a central land, to encounter virtuous friends, and to cultivate the holy life, so that your aspirations may bear fruit and your original vow not be lost.

"Therefore, bhikṣus! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to escape the eight great hells and the sixteen sub-hells, they should seek skillful means and cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path."
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Āmrapālī Grove together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
Gradually, he again wandered and taught among human beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked back toward the city of Vaiśālī and immediately spoke this verse:
"Now I gaze upon Vaiśālī; I shall not behold it again."
"Furthermore, he shall not enter again; from this point on, he must depart.
At that time, the people of the city of Vaiśālī, hearing these verses, were filled with universal sorrow. Following behind the World-Honored One, they each shed tears and said to one another:
"The Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa will take place before long; the world shall lose its light."
The World-Honored One said: "Stop! Stop!"
"O people, do not harbor grief or anxiety. It is simply impossible for that which is destined to perish to remain undestroyed.
Previously, I attained realization through the teaching of the Four Bases; likewise, by means of the fourfold assembly, I have proclaimed this teaching of the Four Bases."
What are the four? All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; this is called the first teaching.
All conditioned phenomena are suffering; this is called the second teaching.
"All conditioned phenomena are without self"—this is called the three dharmas;
"Nirvana is cessation"—this is called the fourth root dharma.
Before long, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
"You all should know that the foundation of the four dharmas is universally taught for the sake of all sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause the people of the city of Vaiśālī to return home, immediately manifested a great chasm; the Tathāgata led the assembly of bhikṣus to the other side, while the people of the kingdom remained on this side.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately cast his own almsbowl into the air and gave it to those people, further addressing them:
"You should make offerings to this bowl with devotion; you should also make offerings to the Dharma Master of Great Talent, so that you may obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night."
At that time, the World-Honored One gave him the bowl and immediately proceeded to the kingdom of Kuśinagara.
At that moment, more than five hundred Mallas of the kingdom of Kuśinagara were gathered in one place, each making this discussion:
"Let us together perform a marvelous deed so that at the time of our death, our fame may spread far and wide, to be passed down by our descendants."
"In the past at Kuśinagara, the power of the Mallas was beyond compare.
After a short while, he again thought:
"What meritorious deed should I now perform?"
At that time, not far from the city of Kuśinagara, there was a large square stone, one hundred and twenty paces long and sixty paces wide.
We should all join together to erect it.
Exhausting all their strength and effort, they sought to set it upright, yet they could not achieve it; it did not even move, let alone be lifted.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where they were and addressed them, saying:
"Young men, what do you intend to accomplish?"
Then the youths said to the Buddha,
“Just now we each made this resolve, wishing to move this rock so that its name might be proclaimed and transmitted through all generations.”
"Since we began our efforts, seven days have already passed, yet we have been unable to move this stone.
The Buddha said to the youths,
"Do you wish for the Tathāgata to set up this stone?"
The youth replied, “Now is precisely the right time; I only pray that the World-Honored One will place this stone.
At that moment, the World-Honored One rubbed the stone with his right hand, lifted it into his left hand, and cast it into the midst of space.
At that time, the stone rose as high as the Brahma-heaven.
At that moment, the Mallas of Kuśinagara did not see the stone and said to the World-Honored One,
"Where has this stone gone now?"
"We all fail to see it together today.
The World-Honored One told them,
"This rock has now reached as far as the Brahma Heaven."
The youth addressed the Buddha, saying,
"When will this rock come down to the surface of Jambudvīpa?
The World-Honored One replied:
"I shall now provide an analogy, for the wise understand through analogies.
Suppose there were a person who went to the Brahma Heaven and took this stone, casting it down toward Jambudvīpa; it would take twelve years to reach.
Yet, moved by the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, it shall return this very moment."
When the Tathāgata had spoken these words, at that very moment the rock returned, and from the midst of the sky there rained down hundreds of varieties of celestial flowers.
At that time, those five hundred or so youths saw the rock approaching from afar; each fled in different directions, no longer remaining in their original places.
The Buddha said to the youths:
"Do not harbor fear; the Tathāgata himself knows the proper time."
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his left hand and reached out from afar to receive that stone, holding it upright in his right hand.
At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and amidst the void, the wondrous devas scattered various kinds of *utpala* lotuses.
At that time, the five hundred youths all marveled at what they had never before experienced, exclaiming:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"

The majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata is truly beyond compare; for this stone, which is now one hundred and twenty paces long and sixty paces wide, he placed it there while holding it with only one hand.
At that time, five hundred youths said to the Buddha, “By what power did the Tathāgata move this stone?
Was it by the power of supernormal feats (*ṛddhi*), or was it by the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) that he placed this stone here?”
The Buddha said to the youth:
"I do not employ the power of supernormal faculties, nor do I employ the power of wisdom; I now employ the power of my parents to rest securely upon this stone."
The youths asked the Buddha, “We do not understand how the Tathāgata employs the power of his parents; what is the nature of that matter?
The World-Honored One replied:
"I shall now provide you with a simile, for the wise understand through parables.
Young man, you should know that the strength of ten camels is not equal to the strength of one ordinary elephant;
furthermore, the strength of ten camels and one ordinary elephant is not equal to the strength of one *kālarāja* elephant."
Furthermore, the combined strength of ten camels and one ordinary elephant, along with the strength of a *kāralaka* elephant, is not equal to the strength of one *gautama* elephant;
even the strength of ten camels, one ordinary elephant, and up to a *gautama* elephant is not equal to the strength of one *vāmana* elephant;
and calculating the strength of these elephants, it is not equal to the strength of one *kaniṣṭha* elephant.
Furthermore, when one calculates the strength of all those elephants, it does not equal the strength of a single *utpala* elephant;
when one calculates the strength of that many elephants, it does not equal the strength of a single *padma* elephant;
and when one calculates and compares the strength of that many elephants, it still does not equal the strength of a single *kumuda* elephant.
Again, when they were calculated and compared, it was still not equal to the strength of one *pundarīka* elephant;
again, when calculated and compared, it was still not equal to the strength of one fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*);
again, when calculated and compared, it was still not equal to the strength of one *mahānagna*.
Again, when they calculated and compared it, it was still not equal to the strength of a single Nārāyaṇa;
again, when they took it up for calculation and comparison, it was still not equal to the strength of a single Cakravartin King;
again, when they took it up for calculation and comparison, it was not equal to the strength of a single Avinivartanīya.
Again, if one were to calculate and compare them, they would not equal the power of a single Bodhisattva in his final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*);
again, if one were to calculate and compare them, they would still not equal the power of a Bodhisattva sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment;
again, if one were to calculate and compare them, they would still not equal the power of a single Tathāgata’s own physical body inherited from his parents.
"I shall now rest upon this stone by the power of my parents.
At that time, the five hundred youths again addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"What is the nature of the Tathāgata’s power of supernormal faculties?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"In the past, I had a disciple named Maudgalyāyana, who was foremost among those possessing supernormal powers.
At that time, he was traveling together with me through the village of Veḷuvana in Vairañjā."
At that time, the land was so impoverished that the people ate one another, and bleached bones filled the roads.
Yet, for those who had left the household life to study, it was difficult to obtain alms; the noble assembly became emaciated, their vital strength utterly exhausted.
Furthermore, among the common folk in the villages, all bore the appearance of hunger and no longer had any means of sustenance.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana came to where I was and addressed me, saying:
"Now this Vairañjā is extremely destitute and famine-stricken; there is nowhere to beg for alms, and the people are so impoverished and exhausted that they have no way left to survive."
I have also personally received these instructions from the Tathāgata:
"Beneath this ground there is natural earth-fat, which is exceedingly fragrant and delicious.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant permission to his disciples to turn this earth-fat upward, so that these people may eat it, and furthermore, so that the noble assembly may be fully sustained in their vital strength.
At that time, I said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Among all the various lands, where would you wish to settle these wriggling insects?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"You should transform one hand to resemble this terrain, and with the other hand turn over this fertile ground, so that the wriggling insects each find their proper place.
At that time, I further addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"What intention do you have in mind that you wish to turn over this ground?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"I could now overturn this terrain just as a strong man might turn over a single leaf without any difficulty.
At that time, I spoke again to Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Stop! Stop! Maudgalyāyana!"
There is no need to turn this ground over.
Why is this? Because when sentient beings see it, they will feel terror and their hair will stand on end; furthermore, the divine temples of the Buddhas would also be destroyed.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant permission for the noble assembly to go to Uttarakuru to beg for alms.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Since there is no one among this great assembly who possesses the power of spiritual transformation (ṛddhi), how shall we go to that place to beg for alms?
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For those who lack the power of spiritual transformation, I shall carry them on my back and proceed to that land."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "Stop! Stop!"
Maudgalyāyana!
Why need the assembly of noble ones go there to beg for alms?
For this reason: in future ages it shall likewise be thus—famine and scarcity will prevail, so that begging for food will be difficult and people will have no healthy complexion.
At that time, the householders and brahmins should say to the bhikṣus:
"Why do you not go to Uttarakuru to beg for alms?

In the past, when the disciples of the Śākya clan possessed great supernormal powers and encountered this famine, they all went together to Uttarakuru to beg for alms and thereby sustained themselves."
"Today, the disciples of Śākyamuni possess no supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), nor do they have the majestic spiritual conduct of a śramaṇa.
Thus he treated the bhikṣus with contempt, causing those elders and householders to harbor universal pride, whereby they incurred immeasurable retribution.
"Maudgalyāyana, you should know that for this reason, it is not appropriate for the entire assembly of bhikṣus to go there to beg for alms.
"Young men, you should know that such is the power of Maudgalyāyana’s supernatural faculties."

Even if one were to employ the power of Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal abilities to traverse the entire trichiliocosm without leaving a single empty space, it would not equal even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a myriad-billionth part of the World-Honored One’s supernormal power; it cannot be compared by any analogy.
“The supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata is of immeasurable virtue.
The youths addressed the Buddha, saying,
“As for the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom (*jñānabala*), what is it?”
The World-Honored One said:

"In the past, I also had a disciple named Śāriputra, who was the foremost among those of wisdom. It was as if there were a great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas in length and breadth, filled with water;
and Mount Sumeru, eighty-four thousand yojanas high, which likewise submerged itself into that water."

Now, the land of Jambudvīpa measures twenty-one thousand yojanas from north to south and seven thousand yojanas from east to west. Suppose we were to take the waters of the four great oceans as ink, the bark of Mount Sumeru as paper, and the vegetation of Jambudvīpa as pens; and suppose all the inhabitants of the three-thousandfold world system were made capable of writing. Even if they were to attempt to transcribe the karmic record of the wisdom of the bhikṣu Śāriputra, you should know, young man, that before the ink of the four great oceans, the pens, and the people themselves have gradually passed away, the wisdom of the bhikṣu Śāriputra could not be exhausted.
Thus it is, young man!
Among my disciples, Śāriputra is the foremost in wisdom; there is none whose wisdom exceeds that of Śāriputra.

Even if one were to imagine this bhikṣu Śāriputra filling the entire trichiliocosm without leaving a single empty space, if one were to compare his wisdom to that of the Tathāgata, it would not be comparable even by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or a hundred millionfold; no analogy can serve as a comparison.
"Such is the nature of the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom.
At that time, the youth again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Is there perhaps another power that surpasses this power?"
The World-Honored One said:
"There is indeed a power that surpasses all other powers. What is it?"
This is what is called the power of impermanence.
This very day, at midnight, between the twin trees, the Tathāgata, drawn by the power of impermanence, shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, all the youths wept together, saying:
"How swift is the Tathāgata’s entry into parinirvāṇa! The world has lost its eyes.
At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī Kuṇḍalakesī—the daughter of the elder Brahmadatta—had this thought:

"I have heard that it will not be long before the World-Honored One attains parinirvāṇa; however, as the days are now exhausted, we should go to where the World-Honored One is to pay our respects and inquire after his well-being."

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī immediately departed from the city of Vaiśālī and went to where the World-Honored One was. From afar she saw the Tathāgata leading the assembly of bhikṣus and five hundred youths directly toward the twin śāla trees.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have heard that the World-Honored One will enter parinirvāṇa before long."
The World-Honored One replied,
"The Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa will take place precisely tonight at midnight.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The reason I have now left the household life to study the Way has not yet fulfilled my original aspiration.
Now that the World-Honored One is about to enter parinirvāṇa, I only pray that you will preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, so that my aspiration may be fulfilled."
The World-Honored One told her:
"You should now contemplate the root source of suffering.
The bhikṣuṇī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed suffering, Blessed One!
It is indeed suffering, Tathāgata!
The Blessed One said:
“What meaning do you perceive that leads you to say it is suffering?
The bhikṣuṇī replied to the Buddha:

“The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of association with the disliked, and the suffering of separation from the beloved.”
To speak briefly, it is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Thus, World-Honored One,
having contemplated this meaning, I say that it is suffering.
At that time, having contemplated the meaning of the teaching, the bhikṣuṇī attained the three types of supernormal knowledge while still seated upon her mat.
Then the bhikṣuṇī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I am unable to behold the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa; I only pray that you will grant me permission to enter parinirvāṇa first.”
At that time, the World-Honored One consented by remaining silent.
Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇī rose from her seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and immediately before the Buddha, she flew into the air and performed the eighteen transformations:

sometimes walking, sometimes sitting, and sometimes pacing back and forth; her body emitted smoke and fire; she leaped up and descended at will without encountering any obstruction; and she emitted water and fire, filling the entire sky.
At that time, after the bhikṣuṇī had performed countless miraculous transformations, she entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
On the very day she attained parinirvāṇa, eighty thousand devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, this bhikṣuṇī Kuntalā is the foremost in the swiftness of wisdom."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Go to the space between the twin trees and spread a seat for the Tathāgata, with its head toward the north. He replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!

Having thus received the Buddha's instruction, he went between the twin trees and prepared a seat for the Tathāgata. Returning to the presence of the World-Honored One, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and addressed him, saying:
"The seat has been prepared; please lie with your head toward the north. You should know that this is the time."
Immediately, the World-Honored One went to that grove of trees and took his seat upon the prepared mat.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"By what cause and condition has the Tathāgata prepared his seat with his head facing north?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, the Buddha-dharma shall flourish in Northern India; for this reason, I have had the seats arranged facing north."
At that time, the World-Honored One sorted his three robes.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata today sort his three robes?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is for the sake of the donors and patrons of future generations that I have distinguished these robes.
Desiring to cause those people to receive their merit, I have thus distinguished the robes."
At that time, in an instant, the World-Honored One emitted five-colored light from his mouth, which illuminated the entire region.
Then Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata today emit five-colored light from his mouth?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"I previously had this thought:
'Before I attained the Way, I dwelt long in hell, swallowing hot iron balls;'"
Some consume grasses and trees to nourish these four great elements;
some become mules, donkeys, camels, elephants, horses, pigs, or sheep;
others become hungry ghosts, nourishing the forms of the four great elements and undergoing the calamity of entering a womb.
"Or they receive celestial blessings, eating natural ambrosia.
Now that I have attained the state of a Tathāgata, I have perfected the body of a Tathāgata through the faculties, powers, and the path of awakening.
For these reasons, five-colored light issued from his mouth.
At that moment, in an instant, a subtle and wondrous light issued from his mouth, surpassing the previous light.
Then Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata again emit a light that excels the former?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"I previously had this thought:
'The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past, have entered parinirvāṇa, and their bequeathed Dharma will not long remain in the world.'"
I further reflected again:
"By what skillful means can my Dharma be made to endure long in the world? The body of a Tathāgata is of adamantine substance;

I wish to crush this body into pieces the size of mustard seeds and distribute them throughout the world. Thus, in future ages, donors who believe and rejoice but do not see the physical form of the Tathāgata may take up the cause of making offerings. By virtue of this merit, they shall be reborn in the families of the four castes, the families of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
By virtue of this merit, one shall be reborn in the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm;

The reason for this is that there are the fruits of the four stages of the śramaṇa, all of which arise from the Eightfold Path of the noble ones. Subhadra!

This was because, among the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, it has always been the case that the foremost disciple who attained realization first entered parinirvāṇa, and the Tathāgata subsequently entered final extinction.

4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Śrāvastī together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the asura Pāhara and the devaputra Muditavatsa arrived unseasonably at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata asked the asuras,
"Do you take great delight in the great ocean?
The asuras replied to the Buddha:
"It is truly pleasant; it is not unpleasant.
The World-Honored One asked:
"What extraordinary phenomena are there within the great ocean that you have seen and take delight in?"
The asura addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Within the great ocean there are eight extraordinary phenomena, wherein all the asuras find delight.”
What are these eight?
In this regard, that the great ocean is exceedingly deep and vast is called the first unprecedented phenomenon.

Furthermore, the great ocean possesses this divine quality: the four great rivers, each with five hundred tributaries, flow into it and lose their original names; this is called the second phenomenon.
"Furthermore, the great ocean is of a single uniform taste; this is called the third quality.
Furthermore, the great ocean receives its tides at the proper time and never misses the appointed season; this is called the fourth extraordinary quality."

"Furthermore, the great ocean is the dwelling place of spirits and deities; there is no sentient being with form that does not exist within the great ocean. This is called the fifth marvelous and unprecedented quality."

"Furthermore, within the great ocean, it can accommodate forms of immense size; forms a hundred yojanas in extent, even up to seven thousand yojanas, without any crowding. This is called the sixth extraordinary quality."
"Furthermore, from within the great ocean emerge various kinds of precious jewels—musāragalva, agate, pearl, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli; this is called the seventh unprecedented phenomenon."
"Furthermore, within the great ocean there is golden sand below, and there is Mount Sumeru, composed of the four precious substances; this is called the eighth unprecedented phenomenon."
"These are called the eight marvelous qualities that cause all the asuras to find delight therein.
At that time, the asuras addressed the World-Honored One:
"What wonders are there within the Dharma of the Tathāgata that cause the bhikṣus, upon seeing them, to find delight therein?"
The Buddha said to the asura:
"There are eight marvelous qualities that cause the bhikṣus to find delight therein.
What are these eight?"
Furthermore, within my Dharma, the precepts are fully perfected and there is no conduct of negligence; this is called the first unprecedented quality.
Having seen this, the bhikṣus take delight therein, just as one delights in the great ocean for its extreme depth and vastness.

"Furthermore, within my Dharma there are four castes; those who become śramaṇas within my Dharma do not retain their former names but instead take other designations. This is just like that ocean, into which the four great rivers all pour and become of one single flavor, such that no other names remain. This is called the second unprecedented quality."
"Furthermore, in my Dharma, the prohibitions and precepts are established such that followers do not transgress their sequence; this is called the third unprecedented quality.

Furthermore, within my Dharma, all share one and the same flavor—namely, the flavor of the Noble Eightfold Path; this is called the fourth unprecedented quality, just as that great ocean has but a single flavor."

"Furthermore, my Dharma is filled with various dharmas, namely the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path. Having seen these, the bhikṣus take delight in them, just as the various deities dwell within that great ocean. This is called the fifth unprecedented quality."
"Furthermore, within my Dharma there are various kinds of precious jewels.

Namely: the jewel of the awakening factor of mindfulness, the jewel of the awakening factor of dharma-discernment, the jewel of the awakening factor of energy, the jewel of the awakening factor of joy, the jewel of the awakening factor of tranquility, the jewel of the awakening factor of concentration, and the jewel of the awakening factor of equanimity. This is called the sixth unprecedented phenomenon."
When the bhikṣus see this, they find delight within it, just as that great ocean produces all kinds of rare treasures.

Furthermore, within my Dharma, there are various classes of sentient beings who shave off their hair and beards, don the three dharma robes, leave the home life to study the Path, and attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder.

However, within my Dharma there is neither increase nor decrease; it is like that great ocean, into which all rivers flow without causing it to increase or decrease. This is called the seventh unprecedented quality, which the bhikṣus, having seen, delight in.

"Furthermore, within my Dharma there is the Vajra-samādhi, the Samādhi of Extinction, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, and the attainment of the Samādhi of Non-arising; there are immeasurable varieties of samādhis such as these. When the bhikṣus behold them, they find delight in them. It is like that great ocean which has golden sand beneath it; this is called the eighth unprecedented quality."
When the bhikṣus see these things, they find delight therein.
Within my Dharma, there are these eight unprecedented qualities, in which the bhikṣus take great pleasure.
At that time, the Asura addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“If there were even a single unprecedented dharma within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, it would surpass those eight unprecedented dharmas of the ocean by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, beyond all comparison; this is what is called the Noble Eightfold Path.”
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
You have spoken these words most excellently.

suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are eight causes and conditions for the great trembling of heaven and earth. What are these eight?

Bhikṣus, you should know that this Jambudvīpa is twenty-one thousand yojanas from south to north, seven thousand yojanas from east to west, sixty-eight thousand yojanas in thickness, with the water layer being eighty-four thousand yojanas thick, the fire layer being eighty-four thousand yojanas thick, and beneath the fire, the wind layer being sixty-eight thousand yojanas thick. At the base of the wind lies the diamond wheel (vajra-maṇḍala), wherein reside all the relics of the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.”
"Monks, you should know that there may be a time when a great wind blows and the fire also moves;
when the fire has moved, the water then moves;
when the water has moved, the earth then moves. This is called the first causal condition by which the great earth shakes violently."

"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva descends from the Tuṣita Heaven and enters his mother’s womb, at that time the earth also shakes greatly; this is called the second cause and condition for the great shaking of the earth."

"Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva descends in spirit and emerges from his mother’s womb, the earth and heavens tremble greatly; this is called the third causal condition that causes the earth to tremble.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva leaves home to study the Way and attains unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment, at that time the earth and heavens tremble greatly; this is called the fourth causal condition that causes the earth to tremble."

"Furthermore, if the Tathāgata enters the realm of nirvana without remainder and attains parinirvāṇa, at that time the heavens and earth shake violently; this is called the fifth cause and condition for the great shaking of the earth."

"Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu of great supernormal power whose mind has attained mastery; he performs countless transformations at will, such as dividing his body into hundreds or thousands of forms and then returning to being one again, flying through the air, passing through stone walls as if they were open space, and leaping up or sinking down with ease. When he contemplates the earth, he has no perception of earth, realizing it to be entirely empty and void. At that time, the earth shakes violently. This is called the sixth cause and condition for the earth shaking violently."

"Furthermore, there are gods of great supernormal power and immeasurable divine virtue who, at the end of their lives there, are reborn again in that same realm. By virtue of their past meritorious conduct, they are fully endowed with all virtues; casting off their original celestial forms, they become Śakra or Brahmā, King of the Gods."
At that time, the earth undergoes a great trembling; this is called the seventh causal condition for the great trembling of the earth.

Furthermore, when the lives of sentient beings have ended and their merit is exhausted, the kings of various lands find no joy in their own realms and engage in mutual warfare; some die of famine and scarcity, while others die by the edge of the sword. At such times, heaven and earth tremble greatly; this is called the eighth causal condition that causes the earth to tremble greatly.
"Thus it is, bhikṣus!
There are eight causes and conditions that cause the earth and heavens to shake violently.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

this Dharma is to be practiced by those who uphold the precepts, not by those who violate them;
it is to be practiced by those established in samādhi, not by those whose minds are distracted.

'Between these two dharmas—precept-keeping and learning—which is the most excellent?'"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse to Anuruddha:
"Is the precept superior, or is hearing superior?
You have now given rise to doubt."
"Since the precepts surpass hearing, why harbor any doubt therein?
Aniruddha, you should know that if a bhikṣu is accomplished in the precepts, he attains concentration;
having attained concentration, he obtains wisdom."
Having attained wisdom, one then attains extensive learning;
having attained extensive learning, one then attains liberation;
having attained liberation, one enters parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder.
"Illuminating this by means of it, the precepts are the most supreme.
At that time, Anuruddha spoke these eight recollections of a great person to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Anuruddha:
“Excellent! Excellent, Aniruddha!”
What you are now contemplating is precisely what a Great Man contemplates:
having few desires and being content; dwelling in a secluded place; and the accomplishment of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and extensive learning.
"Now, Ānanda, you should establish this intention and contemplate the eight thoughts of a great person.
What are these eight?"
This Dharma is practiced by those who possess diligence, not by those who are indolent. Why is this so?

Maitreya Bodhisattva was destined to attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment after thirty kalpas; however, through the power of my diligence, I have surpassed him and attained Buddhahood.

Aniruddha knew that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are of one and the same kind; their precepts, liberation, and wisdom are identical and without difference. They are likewise identical in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They all possess the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, which adorn their bodies, such that one can never tire of beholding them, and none are able to see the crown of their heads—all of these are without distinction.
Only in diligence do we differ; among all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past and the future, I am the most preeminent in diligence. Therefore, Ānanda!
This is the eighth mindfulness of a great person; it is the most supreme, the most honored, the most noble, and beyond compare.
It is just as there is curd from milk, ghee from curd, and clarified butter (sarpis) from ghee; yet among these, clarified butter is the most superior and has no equal.
"This is also like that: the mindfulness of diligence is the most supreme among the eight thoughts of a great man;
truly, there is nothing to compare with it! Therefore, Ānanda!"
One should uphold the eight thoughts of a great man and likewise distinguish their meaning for the fourfold assembly.

If these eight thoughts of a great man were to be disseminated in the world, my disciples would all attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the stage of *anāgāmin*, and the stage of *arhat*.
The reason for this is that my Dharma is practiced by those with few desires, not by those with many desires;
my Dharma is practiced by those who know contentment, not by those who lack satiety;
my Dharma is practiced by those who dwell in seclusion, not by those who remain amidst the crowd.
My Dharma is practiced by those who uphold the precepts, not by those who violate them;
my Dharma is practiced by those who possess meditative concentration, not by those who are distracted;
my Dharma is practiced by those who possess wisdom, not by those who are ignorant.
My Dharma is practiced by those who have heard much, not by those who have heard little;
my Dharma is practiced by those who are diligent, not by those who are indolent.
Therefore, Ānanda! The fourfold assembly should seek skillful means to practice these eight recollections of a great person. Thus it is, Ānanda!
"You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, Āniruddha, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are eight classes of beings; you should know them.”
What are these eight? They are:

the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of śramaṇas, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmās.

"Monks, you should know that from the past until now, when I have entered among the assemblies of kṣatriyas, greeting them, conversing, and engaging in discussion, there has been no one who could equal me; I walk alone without companion, without peer or rival.

I am one who has few desires and is content, whose mindfulness is undisturbed, and who is accomplished in morality, accomplished in samādhi, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, accomplished in learning, and accomplished in diligence."

Furthermore, he recalled that among the assemblies of brahmins, householders, śramaṇas, the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, the hosts of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā kings, he had exchanged greetings, conversed, and engaged in discussion; there he was peerless and without rival, most honored among them, and without equal.
He was one of few desires and contentment, with an undisturbed mind, accomplished in ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, learning, and diligence.
At that time, I shall walk alone without peer among the eight classes of beings, acting as a great canopy for so many sentient beings.
At that time, none of the eight classes of beings will be able to see the crown of my head, nor will they dare to gaze upon my face, let alone engage in debate with me.

The reason for this is that, with the exception of the Tathāgata while he still dwells among us, I do not see anyone within the realms of gods, humans, Māras, or the celestial Māras, nor among the assemblies of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, who is able to accomplish these eight dharmas.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means and practice these eight dharmas. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the householder,
"Is the extensive giving being performed in your home?
The householder replied to the Buddha:

"The poor household gives alms without ceasing day or night at eight locations: within the four city gates, in the great marketplace, in the house, on the road, and to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
"So be it, World-Honored One!

Whatever he may require—whether clothing, I shall bestow clothing; whether food, I shall provide food—I shall never refuse him any of the treasures of this kingdom. I shall provide him with robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for his ailments."
Furthermore, there were devas who came to my presence and, standing in the air, addressed me, saying:
"Distinguishing between the noble and the base, this one maintains the precepts while that one violates them; this one shall obtain merit, while that one shall receive no retribution."

"However, my mind is perfectly impartial, free from the distinction of self and other; I give rise to no thoughts of increase or decrease, but extend a mind of universal equanimity and compassion toward all sentient beings.
There are sentient beings who maintain their forms by relying on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); they survive through food, for without food, life cannot be sustained."
Bestowing bounty upon all sentient beings brings immeasurable retribution; when one receives that fruit of retribution, there is neither increase nor decrease.
The Buddha told the elder:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Householder!
Equal giving brings forth the most supreme merit.
Yet, among the minds of sentient beings, there is further distinction: for example, giving to one who maintains the precepts is superior to giving to one who violates them."
At that time, the deities and celestial beings dwelling in space rejoiced immeasurably and immediately spoke this verse:
“The Buddha has declared that the gift to the Elect is supreme;
Among the ignorant masses there is increase and decrease, But when seeking a field of merit, What surpasses the assembly of the Tathāgata?”
"Now, what the World-Honored One has said is most excellent: 'To give to one who observes the precepts is superior to giving to one who violates them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"I shall now speak to you concerning the assembly of noble sages; reflect upon it well and hold it in your heart."
"Either one gives little and obtains much merit, or one gives much and obtains much merit.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon the meaning of this!"
"How is it that one gives little yet obtains much merit?
How is it that one gives much and obtains much merit?
The Buddha told the householder:

“Those who are practicing for arhatship, those who have attained arhatship; those who are practicing for non-returning, those who have attained non-returning; those who are practicing for once-returning, those who have attained once-returning; those who are practicing for stream-entry, and those who have attained stream-entry.”
"This is what is meant, householder!
Among the noble and holy assembly, one who gives little obtains much merit, and one who gives much also obtains much merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Those who have accomplished the four paths and those who have realized the four fruits—these are called the assembly of noble ones; by giving to them, one obtains vast merit.
In the distant past, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, also had such an assembly of noble ones, no different from what I have today.”
Even when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world in the future, they too shall obtain such a community of noble ones.
Therefore, householder, with a joyful and delighted heart, make offerings to this assembly of noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the elder, establishing him on the stage of non-retrogression.

Having heard the Dharma, the elder experienced immeasurable joy and celebration; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew.
At that time, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If good sons or good daughters bestow gifts of material wealth, they will obtain eight merits."
What are the eight?
First, giving at the appropriate time, not at an inappropriate time;
second, giving what is fresh and pure, not what is foul and turbid.
Third, one personally serves and portions out the food, not delegating it to others;
fourth, one vows to practice giving without a mind of arrogance or self-indulgence;
fifth, one practices giving with liberation, not hoping for any recompense.
Sixth, one practices giving with the aim of attaining cessation, not seeking rebirth in the heavens;
seventh, one gives to seek fertile fields, not barren wasteland;
eighth, one maintains these merits by bestowing them upon sentient beings, rather than for one's own sake.
"In this way, bhikṣus!
A son of good family or a daughter of good family who bestows material gifts obtains eight merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The wise give at the proper time, free from any heart of stinginess or greed;
having performed meritorious deeds, they bestow them all as gifts upon others.
This giving is the most supreme, praised by all the Buddhas."
"One experiences its fruit in the present life, and upon passing away,
one receives celestial blessings. Therefore, bhikṣus,
those who seek such karmic rewards should practice these eight matters."
The retribution for this is immeasurable and beyond calculation; one obtains the treasure of ambrosia and gradually attains parinirvāṇa.
Thus, O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the path leading to niraya and the way toward nirvāṇa; reflect upon it well and do not let it be lost."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “It is so,
World-Honored One!”
The bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“How is it that one follows the path to niraya and turns toward the way of nirvāṇa?”
Wrong view leads to the path of hell; right view leads toward the way to nirvana.
Wrong conduct leads to the path of hell; right conduct leads toward the way to nirvana.
Wrong speech leads to the path of hell; right speech leads toward the way to nirvana.
Wrong action leads to the path of the hells; right action leads to the path of Nirvana.
Wrong livelihood leads to the path of the hells; right livelihood leads to the path of Nirvana.
Wrong means lead to the path of the hells; right means lead to the path of Nirvana.
Wrong mindfulness leads to the path of the hells; right mindfulness leads toward the path to Nirvana.
Wrong concentration leads to the path of the hells; right concentration leads toward the path to Nirvana.
"Monks, this is called the path leading to hell and the way toward nirvāṇa. That which the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, have always been required to teach has now been accomplished!"
"You all delight in dwelling in secluded places, sitting beneath trees or in the open air, contemplating and practicing the wholesome Dharma; do not give rise to indolence or pride.
If you do not practice diligently now, it will be too late for regrets later."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[The sections on] Improper Time, Niraya, the Path, Asuras, Devas, Earthquakes,
the Eight Recollections of a Great Man, the Assembly, Good Men, Giving, and the Path.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 37 and Volume 38.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
43. The Chapter on the Questions of King Ashvakarna Regarding the Eightfold Governance, Part Fourteen, Number One.
(1) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
When it was not the time for humans, the Devaputra Aśvajit went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the Devaputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Just now, this thought arose in me:”
"Can one traverse this world by walking upon the ground?
I now ask the World-Honored One:
can the world be traversed to its end by walking?"
The World-Honored One asked,
"By what principle do you now pose this question?
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, on one occasion, I went to the abode of the Brahmā deity.
At that time, the Brahmā deity saw me coming from afar and said to me:
'Welcome, Devaputra Aśvajit!'"
In this realm of the unconditioned, there is no birth, no aging, no illness, and no death; it has neither end nor beginning, and is likewise free from sorrow, grief, suffering, and affliction.
At that time, I again had this thought:
"Is this the path to nirvana?
For what reason?"
Within nirvana there is no birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction.
Is this the ultimate limit of the world?
"If this were the very limit of the world, would it be possible for the world to be traversed by foot?
The World-Honored One replied,
"What kind of supernormal power do you possess now?"
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Just as a strong man skilled in the art of archery shoots an arrow that travels without obstruction,
so too is the power of my supernormal faculties now such that it is free from all hindrance.”
The World-Honored One said:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.

Suppose there were four men skilled in the art of archery, and each of these four men were to shoot toward one of the four directions. Now, suppose someone were to come along, intending to catch all the arrows from the four directions before they fell to the ground."
"What do you think, Devaputra?
Is this person not exceedingly swift,
being able to cause the arrow not to fall to the ground?"

“Son of Heaven, you should know that before the sun and moon there was a deva named Kṣiprābha (Swift-footed). His coming and going, his advancing and halting, surpassed the swiftness of this man; yet the movement of the palaces of the sun and moon is even swifter than that.”
If one calculates the speed of those human beings, the sons of gods, and the palaces of the sun and moon, it is not as swift as that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
if one calculates the speed of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, it is not as swift as that of the Yāma Heaven.
In this way, the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) possessed by the various devas do not reach one another.
Even if you now possessed such divine merit as those devas, from eon to eon, even unto a hundred eons, you still could not exhaust the realms of the world.
The reason for this is that the realms and regions of the earth are beyond calculation.

"Son of Heaven, you should know that in the distant past, during a long-ago age, I was once a rishi named Ashvakshaya, sharing the same name as yours. My desire and craving were already exhausted; I could fly through the void, meeting with no obstruction."
At that time, my supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) was superior to that of humans; in the mere twinkling of an eye, I was able to withdraw these four arrows so that they did not fall.
Then, possessing such supernormal power, I thought to myself:
"Can I now, by means of this supernormal power, reach the very limits of the world?"
He immediately traversed the world, yet could not exhaust its boundaries.

After his life ended, he advanced in virtue and cultivated his practice until he attained the Way of the Buddha. Sitting beneath the King of Trees, he sat upright in contemplation, reflecting upon the deeds he had performed throughout his past lives:
"Formerly, when I was a seer, even with such spiritual power I could not exhaust the limits of this region; by what kind of supernatural power might I now be able to reach its very extremities?"
At that time, I further thought to myself:
"I must certainly rely upon the noble eightfold path; only then shall I be able to reach the ultimate limit of birth and death."
“What, then, is called the path of the eightfold noble vehicle? It is namely:
right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
"Son of Heaven!
Furthermore, know that this is called the Noble Eightfold Path; by it, one attains the exhaustion of the limits of the world.

All the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who attained the exhaustion of the world, did so entirely by means of this Noble Eightfold Path to reach the ultimate end of the world."
"Even if all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, were to appear in the future, they would likewise attain the ultimate limit through this noble and holy path.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To traverse the world without end, yet to reach its exhaustion—this is the way."
The element of earth is beyond measure, Beyond the reach of supernormal powers.
Ordinary people, following their conceptual minds, Give rise to delusion therein;
Failing to distinguish the true and genuine Dharma, They wander through the five realms of existence.
The Noble Eightfold Path— taking this as one's boat and ship—
is that which all Buddhas have practiced to reach the very limits of the world.
Even the Buddhas of the future, such as Maitreya and his peers, [shall likewise do so].
By likewise employing the eightfold path, one attains the end of the world.
Therefore, the wise person cultivates this path of the noble ones;
practicing it day and night, they reach the state of unconditioned nirvana.

At that time, the devaputra Aśvajit, having heard the Tathāgata’s discourse on the Noble Eightfold Path, immediately attained the purity of the Dharma-eye upon his seat, with all defilements and impurities exhausted.
At that time, the devaputra prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew.
On that very day, the devaputra scattered various kinds of celestial flowers over the Tathāgata and immediately spoke this verse:
"Having wandered through birth and death for a long time, I now wish to cross over this world."
The Noble Eightfold Path, which I neither knew nor saw,
I have now seen through the realization of the Truths; having heard of this Eightfold Path,
I have attained the ultimate limit, the destination reached by all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One approved what that devaputra had said.
Seeing that the Buddha had granted his approval, the devaputra immediately prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now proclaim the noble eightfold precepts of the fast; you should reflect upon them well and practice them with joy!"
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"What is called the Dharma of the Eightfold Precepts of Fasting? It is as follows:"

First, refraining from taking life; second, not taking what is not given; third, refraining from sexual misconduct; fourth, refraining from false speech; fifth, refraining from drinking intoxicants; sixth, refraining from eating at improper times; seventh, refraining from using high or wide beds; eighth, staying far away from performing songs, music, and dances, as well as anointing the body with perfumes and flowers.
"This, bhikṣu, is called the noble and holy eightfold fast-day precept.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does one practice the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast?
The World-Honored One replied: “In this regard, Upāli!”

If a son or daughter of good family, on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the month, goes to a śramaṇa or an elder bhikṣu and declares their own name, maintaining a mind that is as unwavering and immovable as that of an arhat from morning until evening, refraining from inflicting weapons or staves upon living beings, and extending universal compassion to all:
"I now receive the dharma of the fast and shall not transgress it in the slightest; I shall not give rise to the intent to kill, but shall practice the teaching of those True Persons;

I shall not steal, not commit sexual misconduct, not speak falsely, not drink intoxicants, not eat at improper times, not sit upon high or broad seats, and not practice singing, dancing, music, or the anointing of the body with perfumes and flowers."
If there are those possessed of wisdom, they should speak in this manner;
if there are those lacking wisdom, one should instruct them with this very teaching.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu should provide instruction point by point, ensuring that no sequence is lost and that nothing is skipped, and he should further teach them to give rise to vows.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How should one make a vow?
The World-Honored One replied:

"When he makes this vow: 'By means of these eight precepts of the fast, may I not fall into the hells, nor among hungry ghosts or animals; may I not fall into the eight difficult states, nor dwell in border regions, nor fall into places of ruin and calamity; may I not associate with evil companions; may my parents be upright and correct, never practicing false views; may I be born in a central land, hear the sublime Dharma, contemplate it with discernment, and achieve realization in every dharma. By the merit of upholding these fasting precepts, may I gather the goodness of all sentient beings and bestow this merit upon them, causing them to attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path. By the blessing of this vow, may I establish the Three Vehicles and ensure they do not regress midway.'"

Furthermore, one maintains these eight precepts of the fast to study the path of the Buddha, the path of the Pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Arhat; those in all worlds who study the True Dharma also practice this discipline. Even when Maitreya Buddha appears in the world in the future, if they encounter that assembly of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, they shall be granted deliverance at that time.

When Maitreya appears in the world, there will be three assemblies of śrāvakas. At the first assembly, there will be a multitude of nine hundred and sixty million bhikṣus; at the second assembly, nine hundred and forty million bhikṣus; and at the third assembly, nine hundred and twenty million bhikṣus. All of them will be arhats whose outflows are exhausted, and they will likewise have encountered that king, the kingdom, and the teachers who instruct them.
"Give such instructions so that there be no omission.
At that time, Upāli addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"If those sons or daughters of good family observe the eight precepts of the fast but do not make a vow within them, would they not still obtain great merit?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Although they obtain merit, that merit is not worth mentioning.
The reason for this is what I shall now explain."
“In a past age, there was a king named Ratnaśikhin who ruled according to the Dharma without any crookedness, governing this realm of Jambudvīpa.”

At that time, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Ratnagarbha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

That king had a daughter named Muni, whose countenance was exceptionally beautiful and whose face was the color of a peach blossom; all of this was brought about by her having made offerings to various Buddhas in previous lives.

At that time, that Buddha likewise held three assemblies. At the first assembly of śrāvakas, there were one hundred and sixty-eight thousand; at the second assembly, one hundred and sixty thousand; and at the third assembly, one hundred and thirty thousand. All of them were arhats whose outflows were exhausted.
"At that time, that Buddha taught this Dharma to his disciples:
'O Bhikṣus! You should practice seated meditation with mindfulness; do not be indolent.'"
He further sought expedient means, reciting and practicing the sutras and precepts.
That Buddha’s attendant was named Pūrṇa, foremost in extensive learning, just as my disciple Ānanda Bhikṣu is today the most preeminent in extensive learning.
At that time, the bhikṣu Pūrṇamanas addressed the Buddha Ratnagarbha, saying:

"As for those bhikṣus whose faculties are dull and obscured, who do not apply themselves with diligence to the dharma of meditative concentration, nor recite or study it—into which assembly does the World-Honored One intend to place such persons today?"
The Buddha Ratnagarbha replied:
"If there are bhikṣus whose faculties are dull and who are incapable of practicing the dharma of meditation, they should cultivate the three superior human dharmas."
"What are the three? They are:
sitting in meditation, reciting the sutras, and assisting in the communal affairs of the Sangha.
Thus did that Buddha preach such subtle and wondrous Dharma to his disciples.
"At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who likewise was unable to practice the dharma of meditation.
Then, that bhikṣu thought to himself:
'I am now advanced in years and great in age; I can no longer practice the dharma of meditation. I should now seek to cultivate the dharma of providing assistance.'"
At that time, the elder bhikṣu entered the city of Yama and sought out candles and sesame oil, coming daily to make offerings to the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha so that the light would not be interrupted.
At that time, the princess Muni saw this elder bhikṣu begging for alms in the streets and alleys, and she immediately asked him: “Bhikṣu!...”
"What do you seek today?

The bhikṣu replied, "Noble lady, you should know that I am advanced in years and can no longer practice the methods of dhyāna; therefore, I beg for fat and oil to offer as an oblation to the Buddha, so as to continue his venerable radiance."
At that time, having heard the name of the Buddha, the woman was filled with such joy and exultation that she could not contain herself;
she said to the elder bhikṣu: "O Bhikṣu, at this moment!"
"Do not seek alms elsewhere; I shall provide for you myself, and I will even bestow upon you the entire wick of my sesame oil lamp.

At that time, the elder bhikṣu accepted the woman’s offering and came daily to take oil as an offering to the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha. Taking this meritorious karma and dedicating it toward the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, he spoke these words himself:

"I am now advanced in years and moreover dull-witted, lacking the wisdom to practice the methods of dhyāna. By means of this meritorious karma, may I never fall into the evil realms in whatever place I am born, and may I encounter a Holy One in a future age no different from the present Tathāgata Ratnagarbha."
"You shall also encounter a community of noble ones no different from the noble assembly here now;
the teaching of the Dharma shall likewise be no different from that of the present.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that bhikṣu, immediately smiled, and five-colored light issued from his mouth as he addressed him, saying:
"O Bhikṣu! In the future, after incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall become a Buddha, named Dīpaprabha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

At that time, the elder bhikṣu was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, unable to contain himself; his body and mind became firm and steadfast, his resolve never regressed, and his countenance shone with such excellence that it was unlike its usual state.
At that time, the female ascetic saw that the bhikṣu’s countenance was extraordinary and immediately approached him, asking: "Bhikṣu!
Today your countenance is exceedingly sublime and not like your usual appearance; for what reason have you attained this?"
The bhikṣu replied, “O Princess,
you should know that just now the Tathāgata has sprinkled me with the nectar of immortality.
The daughter of the Muni asked:
"How does the Tathāgata bestow the consecration of ambrosia?

The bhikṣu replied, "I have received a prophecy from the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, who said that after innumerable asaṃkhyeya kalpas in the future, I shall attain Buddhahood under the name of Dīpāṅkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; my body and mind are firm and steadfast, and my resolve is irreversible."
"In this way, O Princess,
you have been granted the prediction by that Tathāgata.
The princess asked:
"Did that Buddha perhaps grant me a prediction of enlightenment? The elder bhikṣu replied,
"I too do not know whether he granted you a prediction or not."

At that time, having heard what the bhikṣu said, the princess immediately mounted a carriage adorned with precious feathers and gems, went to where the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the princess addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have now seen that whenever the donor and patron required oil or fat, he constantly provided it for him; yet while the World-Honored One has now conferred a prediction upon that bhikṣu, you alone have not granted me a prophecy."
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha replied, “The merit of generating the aspiration and making a vow is difficult to measure; how much more so, then, the giving of material wealth?
The daughter of the Muni replied:
"If the Tathāgata does not grant me a prediction [of my future enlightenment], I shall take my own life.
The Tathāgata Ratnagarbha replied, "One who,
while dwelling in a female body, seeks to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King will ultimately never attain it."
One who seeks to become Śakra cannot obtain it;
one who seeks to become a Brahmā king cannot attain it;
and one who seeks to become a Māra king cannot attain it either.
"One who seeks to become a Tathāgata is likewise unobtainable.
The girl asked,
"Am I then certainly unable to achieve the unsurpassed path?"
The Buddha Ratnagarbha replied, "She can.
O daughter of the Muni, she shall attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path."
