Nevertheless, Princess, you should know that in the future, after incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, there will be a Buddha appearing in the world who will be your spiritual friend; that Buddha shall grant you the prediction of enlightenment.
At that time, the princess addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it that the recipient is pure while the donor is defiled?
The Buddha Ratnagarbha replied:
"What I have now spoken was with a pure mind and a firm resolve.
Having said this, the princess rose from her seat, prostrated herself at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and then withdrew.

“Upāli, you should know that after incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world. He resided in the great kingdom of Padma, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering one hundred and sixty-eight thousand; the sovereign of the land and the people all came to serve him.”
At that time, there was a king in that country named Tīpayana, who ruled and transformed the realm according to the Dharma, governing this territory of Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the king invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to provide them with a meal.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpamkara dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and entered the city accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus.

At that moment, there was a son of a brahmin named Mikha, whose countenance was exceptionally handsome and who stood out alone among the crowd; he resembled Brahmā in appearance. He had mastered all the scriptural treasuries (piṭakas) without exception, was thoroughly proficient in them, and was fully conversant with all books and incantations. There was nothing regarding astronomy or geography that he did not understand.

At that time, the brahmin saw from afar the Buddha Dīpaṃkara approaching; his countenance was extraordinary and marvelous to the world, his faculties were serene and composed, and his body was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Having seen him, he immediately felt a sense of joy and gladness, and a virtuous mind arose within him:
"As recorded in the scriptures, the appearance of a Tathāgata is extremely rare to encounter."
"They emerge only from time to time, just as the *utpala* flower emerges only at certain times.
I shall now go and test him.
At that moment, the brahmin took five flowers in his hand and went to where the World-Honored One was, thinking once more:
"One who possesses the thirty-two marks is called a Buddha.
He then scattered five-rooted flowers over the Tathāgata and sought to see those thirty-two marks; however, he saw only thirty marks and did not see two. Thereupon, doubt arose within him:
"Now that I observe the World-Honored One, I do not see the broad and long tongue nor the concealed organ like a horse's."
Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"I have heard that there are thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
yet now I do not see two of these marks— are his physical characteristics complete?"
Do you possess the secret organ concealed within a sheath, pure and chaste without lust?
Do you have a broad and long tongue that can lick your ears and cover your face?
Manifest these marks for me, and sever all the knots of my doubt.
"The marks of the horse-hoof and the tongue— I only wish to behold them.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara entered into samādhi and caused that brahmin to see those two marks.
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara again extended his broad and long tongue, licking both ears from left to right and emitting a great radiance, which then re-entered through the crown of his head.
At that moment, the brahmin saw that the Tathāgata was fully endowed with the thirty-two marks. Having seen this, he leaped for joy, unable to contain himself, and spoke these words everywhere:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will look upon me with compassion; I now offer five flowers to the Tathāgata and further offer this very body as an offering to the Holy Honored One."
When he made this vow, those five flowers transformed in mid-air into a precious pavilion, most exquisite and wonderful, with four pillars and four gates.
At that time, having seen the jeweled pavilion, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, and he made this vow:
"In a future age, may I become a Buddha; may my disciples and attendants all be exactly like those of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
At that time, Dīpaṃkara, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that brahmin, immediately smiled.
It is the constant law of the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
whenever the World-Honored One smiles at the time of bestowing a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), five-colored rays of light issue from his mouth, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm.
At that time, the light had already illuminated the trichiliocosm; the sun and moon no longer possessed radiance, and the light returned, entering through the crown of the head.
When the Tathāgata bestows a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), the light enters through the crown of the head;
when he bestows a prediction for a pratyekabuddha, the light issues from the mouth and returns to enter the ears.
If he were to bestow the prediction of becoming a śrāvaka, the light would enter through his shoulders;
if he were to bestow the assurance of rebirth in the heavens, at that time the light would enter through his arms;
if he were to predict rebirth among humans, at that time the light would enter through both his sides.
If he grants the prediction of rebirth as a hungry ghost, at that time the light enters through the armpits;
if he grants the prediction of rebirth as an animal, the light enters through the knees;
if he grants the prediction of rebirth in hell, at that time the light enters through the soles of the feet.

At that time, seeing the light enter through the crown of his head, the brahmin was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately spread his hair upon the ground and spoke thus:
"If the Tathāgata does not grant me a prediction of enlightenment, I shall here and now sever my own life and let my faculties perish."
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the brahmin, immediately addressed him, saying:
"Arise quickly! In a future age, you shall become a Buddha, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s bestowal of the prophecy, the young brahmin was filled with such exuberance that he could not contain himself. Immediately at that spot, he attained the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation and leaped into the air to a height of seven fathoms above the ground, joining his palms toward the Tathāgata Lamp-Light.
“Upāli, do not view this otherwise. At that time, was the elder bhikṣu during the era of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha anyone else?
He was none other than the Tathāgata Dīpapradyota.”
At that time, the princess Muni was none other than myself.

Then the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha established my name as Śākyamuni. Because of these causes and conditions, I now proclaim this Dharma of the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast; you should make vows, for there is no vow that shall not be fulfilled.
The reason for this is that if that woman makes such a vow, she will fulfill her aspiration within that very kalpa. However,
if an elder bhikṣu does not make a vow, he will never attain the path of Buddhahood.
The merit of such vows is beyond measure; it leads to the state of the deathless, the place of total extinction.
Thus, Upāli, you should train yourself in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Upāli rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
Gradually he arrived at the bank of the river.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw a large log being carried away by the current in the river water, and he immediately sat down beneath a tree on the riverbank.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see pieces of wood being carried away by the water?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“Yes, I see it,” he replied.

The World-Honored One said, “Suppose this log were not to stick on this shore, nor stick on the opposite shore; were neither to sink in midstream, nor remain upon the bank; were not seized by humans, nor seized by non-humans; were not turned back by the current, nor was it rotten—then it would surely gradually reach the ocean.”
The reason for this is that the ocean is the source and origin of all rivers.

You bhikṣus are also like this: if you do not cling to this shore, do not cling to the other shore, do not sink in midstream, and do not remain upon the banks; if you are not seized by humans or non-humans, are not turned back by the waters, and do not rot away, then you shall gradually reach the place of nirvāṇa.
The reason for this is that Nirvana has right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration as its foundation.
At that time, there was a cowherd named Nanda who stood leaning on a staff.
Then, having heard from afar what had been said, the cowherd gradually approached the place where the World-Honored One was and stood before him.
At that time, the cowherd addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I now neither cling to this shore, nor am I on the other shore; I am not submerged in the middle, nor am I standing upon the bank. I am not seized by humans, nor am I seized by non-humans; I am not turned back by the water, nor am I putrefying. Gradually, I shall reach the place of Nirvana."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow me to join the ranks of those on the Path and become a śramaṇa.
The World-Honored One told him,
“Only after you have returned the ox to its owner may you then become a śramaṇa.”
The cowherd Nanda replied, "This cow will surely return home of her own accord out of longing for her calf;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to follow in his footsteps."
The World-Honored One told him, "Although these oxen are due to return home, you must still go and deliver them.
At that time, the cowherd immediately accepted his instruction; having gone and delivered the oxen, he returned to the Buddha's presence and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Now that the ox has been returned, we only pray that the World-Honored One will permit us to become śramaṇas.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately granted them permission to become śramaṇas and conferred upon them full ordination.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"What is this shore? What is the other shore?"
What is meant by "sinking in midstream"?
What is meant by "being on the bank"?
And what is meant by "not being seized by others"?
How is it that one is not seized by non-human beings?
How is it that one is not swept away by water?
How is it that one does not decay?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This shore is the body; the other shore is the cessation of the body."
Those who sink in the middle represent sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
Those on the shore represent the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Being seized by others refers to when a son of noble family makes this vow:
"By means of these merits and blessings, may you become a great king or a high minister.
As for those seized by non-human beings, suppose there is a bhikṣu who makes this vow:
"May I be born among the Four Heavenly Kings and practice the holy life; now, by means of these merits, may I be born among the various devas."
This is what is called being seized by non-human beings.
To be turned about by water refers to wrong doubt.
"Rotten" refers to wrong view, wrong resolve, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration; these are what is meant by rottenness.

At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda practiced self-discipline in a secluded place. For this reason, sons of noble family shave off their hair and beards, leave the household life to study the Way, and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*). Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; and there is no further state of existence to be received.
Thereupon, while still seated, he attained arhatship.
At that time, Nanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Devadatta had lost his supernormal powers; nevertheless, Prince Ajātaśatru daily sent five hundred cauldrons of food to provide for him.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having heard that Devadatta had lost his supernormal powers and was being venerated by Ajātaśatru, went together to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, a great many bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"Devadatta possesses immense power; he is now being venerated by King Ajātaśatru, who sends five hundred cauldrons of food every day."
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor such thoughts as to covet the gains and offerings of the bhikṣu Devadatta;
by reason of those very gains, that fool shall bring about his own destruction."
The reason for this is as follows, monks:
Devadatta’s purpose for going forth and training was not fulfilled.

Monks, you should know it is just as if a man were to leave his village, taking a sharp axe in his hand, and go toward a great tree; though his original intention was to take that great tree, when he arrives at the tree, he returns carrying only its branches and leaves.

Now this bhikṣu is also like this: he is greedily attached to gain and offerings; because of these gains and offerings, he praises himself to others and disparages others. Thus, the conduct appropriate for a bhikṣu does not fulfill his aspirations.
Because of those gains and offerings, he does not seek skillful means nor arouse a courageous mind; like that person who sought treasure but failed to find it, he is abandoned by the wise.
"Suppose there is a bhikṣu who, having received offerings and gains, neither praises himself nor disparages others;
yet at times he may say to others of himself:
'I am one who upholds the precepts, while that person is one who violates them. "
"When a bhikṣu’s aspirations are not fulfilled, it is like a person who abandons the root, takes the branches, and returns home; when a wise person sees this, they think:
'Although this person has taken the branches back home, he does not recognize the root.'"
"In this regard, a bhikṣu is also like this: having obtained gain and offerings, he upholds the precepts, cultivates the holy life (brahmacarya), and delights in the practice of samādhi."
With this mind of samādhi, he approaches others and praises himself, saying:
"I have now attained concentration, whereas others have not.
Yet, he does not achieve the dharmas that a bhikṣu ought to practice.
It is just as if there were a person seeking solid wood who, having gone to a great tree and hoping for its fruit, discarded the branches and leaves and took the root instead to carry back.
When a wise person saw this, they would say:
"This person has mistaken the root for the fruit."

Now this bhikṣu is also like this: he gives rise to the pursuit of gain while upholding the precepts, yet he neither praises himself nor disparages others; his cultivation of samādhi is likewise, and he gradually practices wisdom.
Now, wisdom is the foremost among all dharmas.
Yet the bhikṣu Devadatta has ultimately failed to attain wisdom or samādhi within this Dharma, nor is he endowed with the dharma of the precepts.
A certain bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“As for that Devadatta, how is it that he does not understand the Dharma of the Vinaya?
He possesses supernormal powers, has accomplished all practices, and possesses such wisdom.”
"What is meant by not understanding the Dharma of the precepts?
Where there is wisdom, there is samādhi; where there is samādhi, there are the precepts.
The World-Honored One replied:
“The dharma of the precepts is a mundane constant;
the accomplishment of samādhi is also a mundane constant;
the practice of supernatural powers and flight is likewise a mundane constant.”
"The perfection of wisdom—this is the foremost meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Through dhyāna one attains the supernormal powers, Yet reaching the summit does not constitute the ultimate."
Failing to attain the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one falls back into the midst of the five desires.
Wisdom is supreme; it is free from sorrow and has nothing to worry about.
Having long since perfected the attainment of equal vision, one severs existence within birth and death.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that by this means it is evident that Devadatta does not understand the Dharma of the Vinaya, nor does he understand the practices of wisdom and samādhi.”
"You, monks, must not be like Devadatta, greedily attached to gain and offerings.
For such gain and offerings cause one to fall into evil states and prevent one from reaching the happy realms."
If one is attached to gain and offerings, one will cultivate false views and depart from right view;
cultivate false conduct and depart from right conduct;
cultivate false speech and depart from right speech.
They practice wrong action and abandon right action;
they practice wrong livelihood and abandon right livelihood;
they practice wrong means and abandon right means.
They practice wrong mindfulness and abandon right mindfulness;
they practice wrong concentration and abandon right concentration. Therefore, bhikṣus!
Do not give rise to a mind seeking gain; restrain it so that it does not arise.
If a mind seeking gain has already arisen, seek skillful means to extinguish it. Thus, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
As he was preaching this subtle and wondrous Dharma, more than sixty bhikṣus cast off their monastic robes and adopted the conduct of laypeople;
furthermore, more than sixty other bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind, with all defilements and impurities eliminated, obtaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak a parable of a raft; you should contemplate it well and keep it stored within your hearts."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
The bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"What is meant by this parable of the raft?"
If you are captured by bandits while traveling on the road, you should maintain control over your mind and not give rise to ill will;

you should instead cultivate a mind of protection, pervading all directions—immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable. You should hold your mind like the earth: just as this earth receives both the pure and the impure, accepting excrement, urine, filth, and all that is foul without giving rise to thoughts of increase or decrease, nor saying, "This is good" or "This is ugly."
Your current practice should also be like this: even if you are captured by bandits, do not give rise to evil thoughts or a mind of increase and decrease.
Be like earth, water, fire, and wind, which receive both the unpleasant and the pleasant without any mind of increase or decrease;
instead, give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings.
The reason for this is that even the practice of wholesome dharmas may still be abandoned, let alone the habitual indulgence in unwholesome dharmas.
It is like a person who encounters a place of peril and, wishing to cross over that danger to reach a place of safety, runs with all their might in search of security.
He saw that the great river was exceedingly deep and wide, and there was neither boat nor bridge by which one might cross to the other shore;
yet the place where he stood was extremely perilous, while the other shore was free from conditioned activity (*asaṃskṛta*).
"At that time, that person contemplated a plan:

'This river is extremely deep and wide; I should now gather timber and foliage, bind them into a raft to seek a crossing, and by relying upon this raft, I shall be able to go from this shore to the further shore.'"
At that time, the man immediately gathered timber and leaves, bound them together to form a raft, and crossed from this shore to the other shore.
Once he had crossed to the far shore, he thought to himself:
"This raft has been of great benefit to me; by means of this raft, I have escaped from calamity and peril, and from a place of fear, I have reached a state of non-action."
"I shall not abandon this raft now, but will carry it with me wherever I go.
What do you think, bhikṣu?
At whatever place that person arrives, would he be able to take this raft with him?
"Is it that you are unable? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
That person’s wish has now been fulfilled; why would he still carry his raft with him?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Even wholesome dharmas may be relinquished, how much more so unwholesome dharmas.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“In what way should one relinquish even dharmas, let alone non-dharmas?”
"Are we not, indeed, training in the path by means of the Dharma?
The World-Honored One replied:

"By relying on the destruction of conceit, one destroys conceit, arrogance, overweening pride, self-conceit, pride of wrong view, pride within pride, and excessive pride; by means of non-pride, one destroys arrogance, destroys non-pride and right pride, and destroys wrong pride and excessive pride, thereby completely destroying all four types of pride."
In the past, before I had attained the Way of Buddhahood, while sitting beneath the King of Trees, this thought arose in me:
"Within the realm of desire, who is the most noble and powerful that I should subdue?"
"In this realm of desire, neither the devas nor the people have all been subdued.
At that time, I again had this thought:
'I have heard of the evil Māra Pāpīyān; I shall now do battle with him.'"
"Having thus subdued Pāpīyān and all the arrogant and noble devas, there was none who did not submit.
At that time, O Bhikṣus!
I smiled upon my seat, causing the entire realm of Māra Pāpīyān to tremble."
From within the void, the sound of a verse was heard:
"Having renounced the true and pure royal dharma, he has left the household life to study the nectar of immortality.
If he succeeds in fulfilling his vast vows, these three evil realms shall be emptied."
"I shall now assemble my troops and gaze upon the countenance of that śramaṇa;
if he does not heed my plan, I will seize him by the feet and hurl him beyond the sea.
— *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 38.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 39, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 43: The Devaputra Aśvajit, Part Two.
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān, his wrath blazing intensely, addressed the general Siṃha, saying:
"Quickly assemble the fourfold army; I wish to go and attack the śramaṇa!"
Furthermore, I should observe what power and capability he possesses to be able to engage me in combat.
At that time, I reflected once more:
‘If one does not remain silent when contending with an ordinary person, how much less so when facing those who are powerful and noble within the desire realm?’”
"I must indeed contend with them, however little or much. At that time, monks,
I donned the armor of loving-kindness, took up the bow of samādhi and the arrows of wisdom, and awaited that great assembly.
At that time, eighteen billion followers of the evil Māra and his great generals, each with different appearances—such as monkeys and lions—came to where I was.

"At that time, the host of rākṣasas had some with one body and many heads, some with dozens of bodies sharing a single head, some with three necks upon two shoulders and a mouth in the center of the chest,
or some with only one hand; some had two hands, and others had four."
Some held their heads up with both hands while clutching dead snakes in their mouths; some had fire burning upon their heads and flames issuing from their mouths;
some gaped their mouths wide with both hands, intending to devour them;
some stood facing one another with bellies exposed, holding swords and blades in their hands and carrying spears and lances.
Some were holding pestles for pounding grain;
some were carrying mountains, bearing stones, or carrying great trees;
and some had their two feet above with their heads below.
Some rode upon elephants, lions, tigers, wolves, or venomous insects;
some came on foot;
others flew through the air.
At that time, Māra the Evil One, leading such a vast multitude, surrounded the tree of the Way.
Then Māra Pāpīyas stood to my left and said to me:
"Śramaṇa, rise quickly!"
"At that time, monks, I remained silent and did not respond.
This was repeated a second and a third time."
Māra said to me, "Does the śramaṇa not fear me? I replied to him:
"I now hold my mind free from fear. Then Pāpīyas said: "Śramaṇa!
"Do you see my fourfold assembly?
Yet you, all alone, without any vessels, weapons, or blades, with a shaven head and body exposed, wearing these three robes, say:
'I have nothing to fear.'"
At that time, I addressed Pāpīyas and spoke these verses:
“With the armor of benevolence and the bow of samādhi, Holding the arrows of wisdom in hand,
And taking merit and deeds as my host, I shall now destroy your army.”
Then Māra Pāpīyas spoke to me again, saying:
"I have been of great benefit to you, O Śramaṇa.
If you do not follow my words, I shall simply seize you and reduce your form to ashes."
Furthermore, śramaṇa!

Your countenance is handsome and your youth is admirable; you are born of the Kṣatriya lineage of a universal monarch (cakravartin). Arise quickly from this place and enjoy the five pleasures; I shall bring about harmony so that you may become a wheel-turning holy king.
At that time, I replied to Pāpīyas:
"What you have spoken is impermanent and subject to change; it cannot endure for long.
It must also be abandoned and renounced; it is not something I covet."
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān spoke to me again, saying:
"Śramaṇa! What is it that you seek today?"
"What do you aspire to?
At that time, I replied:
"That which I aspire to is a place free from sorrow and fear, peaceful, secure, and tranquil—the city of Nirvana."
"May I lead these sentient beings, who are wandering through birth and death and submerged in the darkness of suffering and affliction, onto the correct path.
Māra replied to me, saying:
"If this śramaṇa does not rise quickly from his seat now, I shall seize your feet and hurl you beyond the surface of the ocean!"
At that time, I replied to Pāpīyān:

"I have personally observed among the heavens and among humanity—whether it be Māras, or the gods of Māra, humans, or non-humans—including you and your fourfold assembly—that none of them can cause even a single hair of mine to move."
The Māra replied to me, saying:
"Śramaṇa! Do you wish to wage war against me today?"
I replied to him, saying,
"I wish to engage in battle.
Māra replied to me, saying:
"Who is your enemy? I replied again, "It is arrogance."
"Overweening pride, self-pride, false pride, pride among prides, and overweening pride.
Mara said to me: "By what means do you extinguish these various forms of pride?"
At that time, I replied:

"Pāpīyan, you should know that there are the samādhi of loving-kindness, the samādhi of compassion, the samādhi of sympathetic joy, the samādhi of equanimity, the samādhi of emptiness, the samādhi of wishlessness, and the samādhi of signlessness. By means of the samādhi of loving-kindness, one accomplishes the samādhi of compassion;
by relying on the samādhi of compassion, one attains the samādhi of sympathetic joy."
By means of the samādhi of joy, one attains the samādhi of protection.
From the samādhi of emptiness, one attains the samādhi of wishlessness;
by means of the samādhi of wishlessness, one attains the samādhi of signlessness.
By the power of these three samādhis, I shall battle with you.
When action is exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, the fetters are exhausted; when the fetters are exhausted, one reaches nirvāṇa.
Then Māra said to me: "Śramaṇa!
Is it possible that a dharma extinguishes a dharma?"
At that time, I replied:
"One may extinguish phenomena by means of phenomena. Māra asked me:
"How does one extinguish phenomena with phenomena?
At that time, I replied:
"One extinguishes wrong view with right view, and extinguishes right view with wrong view."
Right conduct extinguishes wrong conduct, and wrong conduct extinguishes right conduct;
right speech extinguishes wrong speech, and wrong speech extinguishes right speech;
right action extinguishes wrong action, and wrong action extinguishes right action.
Right livelihood extinguishes wrong livelihood, and wrong livelihood extinguishes right livelihood;
right effort extinguishes wrong effort, and wrong effort extinguishes right effort;
right mindfulness extinguishes wrong mindfulness, and wrong mindfulness extinguishes right mindfulness.
"Right concentration extinguishes wrong concentration; wrong concentration extinguishes right concentration.
Then Māra said to me: "O Śramaṇa!"
"Although you have these words today, it will be difficult to overcome me here.
Arise quickly now, lest I hurl you to the far side of the ocean!
At that time, I spoke again to Pāpīyas:
"You performed a meritorious deed, yet with only a single act of giving, you have now become the Māra King of the Desire Realm;
as for the merit I created in the past, it is beyond all calculation."
"What you have just said is indeed very difficult to understand! Pāpīyān replied,
"The merit that has now been performed, you yourself may now bear witness to."
"You claim for yourself that you have created immeasurable merit;
who can testify to this? Then, monks, I extended my right hand, pressed my finger against the earth, and said to Pāpīyan:
"May the earth bear witness to the merit I have created.
When I spoke these words, the Earth Deity emerged from the ground, joined her palms, and said:
"World-Honored One! [I bear witness to this.]"
"I shall bear witness to this.
As soon as the earth deity had finished speaking, Māra Pāpīyān was overcome with grief and distress, and immediately withdrew, ceasing to appear. "O Bhikṣu!"
One should know through this expedient means that even the Dharma is subject to extinction, let alone what is non-Dharma.
For a long night, I have spoken to you the *Ekabuddhopama-sūtra*, yet I have not recorded its text, much less explained its meaning.
The reason for this is that this Dharma is profound and subtle; those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who cultivate this Dharma attain great merit and reach the state of ambrosial non-action.
What is meant by the metaphor of the raft?
It refers to relying on conceit to extinguish conceit; once conceit has been completely extinguished, there are no further thoughts of affliction or mental disturbance.
It is just as when one takes the skin of a wild fox and polishes it thoroughly; even when struck with a clenched fist, it makes no sound and has no hard or resistant parts.
This is also like that: if a bhikṣu’s conceit is exhausted, there is absolutely no increase or decrease.
Therefore, I now tell you all:

"Should you be captured by bandits, do not give rise to evil thoughts; rather, you should pervade all directions with a mind of loving-kindness, like that most supple hide, and thus, throughout the long night, you shall attain the state of the unconditioned."
"In this way, bhikṣus, you should maintain such a reflection.
While this Dharma was being taught, three thousand devaputras in that assembly were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
More than sixty bhikṣus returned their dharma robes and adopted the conduct of laypeople;
more than sixty bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and minds liberated, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha on the banks of the river Gaṅgā, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"It is just as if there were a foolish and deluded cowherd from Magadha, lacking in wisdom, who intended to lead his cattle from this side of the Ganges River to the other side. Without first examining the depths and shallows of either bank, he drove the cattle into the water; he first led across those that were emaciated, and furthermore, the calves were still small and extremely weak in the middle of the stream, so they could not reach the opposite shore."
Furthermore, the ox crossing the middle of the stream is neither fat nor thin, yet it cannot complete the crossing and suffers distress therein.
Next, the one of extreme strength who crosses likewise encounters hardship while in the water.

"Now, the bhikṣus within my assembly are likewise: their minds are dull and dark, lacking the light of wisdom; they cannot distinguish the states of birth and death, nor can they distinguish the bridges and boats of Māra. Desiring to cross the torrent of birth and death, yet failing to practice the dharmas of the prohibitions and precepts, they allow Pāpīyān to gain the advantage over them."
Seeking nirvana through deviant paths and hoping to attain extinction, they ultimately fail to achieve it;
having created their own karmic offenses, they further cause others to fall into the grip of sin.

It is like a wise and highly intelligent cowherd of Magadha who wishes to ferry his cattle from this shore to the other. First, he observes the depth of the water; then, he ferries across the most powerful bulls first, reaching the opposite shore.
Next, he ferries across the middle-aged cattle, which are neither fat nor lean, and they too reach the opposite shore.
Then he ferries across the very weak ones, and they too cross without harm. Finally, the young calves follow behind him and are likewise ferried across safely.

“Monks! The Tathāgata is also like this: he thoroughly examines this world and the world beyond, observes the ocean of birth and death and the paths of Māra, and by means of the Eightfold Noble Path himself crosses over the perils of birth and death.”
Furthermore, by means of this path, one delivers those who have not yet been delivered, just as the lead ox of a team is correctly guided;
when it is corrected, all others follow.

My disciples are also like this: having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained the state of being without outflows, with liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom, they personally realize the truth in this present life and wander freely, delivering others from the realm of Māra to the state of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Just as that powerful bull crosses the Ganges River and reaches the further shore, so too are my śrāvakas:

having severed the five lower fetters, they become non-returners (anāgāmin), attaining parinirvāṇa there and no longer returning to this world, crossing beyond the realm of Māra to reach the state of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Just as that ox in the middle of the stream, being neither fat nor thin, crosses the Ganges River without difficulty or doubt, so too it is with my disciples:

having severed the three fetters, with lust, anger, and delusion attenuated, they become *sakṛdāgāmins* (once-returners); returning to this world once more, they bring an end to the limits of suffering, severing the realm of Māra and reaching the state of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Just as that lean cow led her young calves across the Ganges River, so too are my disciples: having severed the fetters and outflows, they have become stream-enterers (srotāpanna); they are certain to attain liberation, crossing over the realm of Māra and surmounting the perils of birth and death.
Just as that young calf was able to cross over by relying on its mother, so too are my disciples:
upholding faith and adhering to the Dharma, they sever all the fetters of Māra and reach the state of unconditioned nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"That which Māra sought to attain— The ultimate limit of birth and death— The Tathāgata has now fully realized; He manifests the light of wisdom to the world."
That which all Buddhas have realized, the brahmins do not understand;
they still wade along the shore of birth and death, while simultaneously delivering those who have not yet been delivered.
Now these five kinds of people, as well as others beyond counting—
"To cross over the perils of birth and death, one must exhaust the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should concentrate your minds, practice without negligence, and seek skillful means to accomplish the Noble Eightfold Path."
Having relied upon the path of the noble ones, one is then able to cross the ocean of birth and death by oneself.
This is because they are like that foolish cowherd—the non-Buddhist brahmins—who, drowning themselves in the current of birth and death, further cause others to fall into the midst of transgression.
That River Ganges is none other than the ocean of birth and death.
That wise cowherd is the Tathāgata; the crossing over the perils of birth and death is achieved by means of the Noble Eightfold Path.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means to accomplish the Noble Eightfold Path. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Jīvaka-ambavana grove in the city of Rājagṛha together with twelve hundred and fifty disciples. All of them were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who possessed the six supernormal powers with perfect clarity, with the sole exception of the bhikṣu Ānanda.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, when the morning star appeared at midnight, King Ajātaśatru addressed Lady Candraprabhā, saying:
"Today is the fifteenth day; the moon is full and exceedingly clear. What should we do now?"
The lady replied, "Today is the fifteenth day for the recitation of the precepts; we ought to perform music and dance, enjoying ourselves with the five desires.
When the king heard these words, they did not sit well with him.
The King again addressed Prince Udāyī, saying:
"This night is most clear and bright; what should be done?
Prince Udāyī replied to the King:

"Since tonight at midnight is exceptionally clear and bright, you should assemble the fourfold army; as for those external enemies and foreign nations who have not yet submitted, you must go forth to attack and subdue them."
At that time, having heard these words, King Ajātaśatru likewise did not take them to heart.
He spoke again to Prince Abhaya, saying:
"On such a most clear and bright night as this, what should be done?"
Prince Abhaya replied, "Now, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is proficient in all forms of calculation and also knows astronomy and geography; he is revered and looked up to by the multitude."
"You may go there and inquire about this difficult doubt; that person will explain the most sublime principles to you, leaving no room for lingering uncertainty.
When the king heard these words, he still did not find them to his satisfaction.
He further addressed the minister Sunimā, saying:
"This night is exceedingly clear and serene; what should be done?
Sunimā replied to the King:
"Tonight is exceptionally clear and serene; however, Ārya-Ḍhāna is nearby and possesses great erudition. I only wish that Your Majesty would go and consult him regarding what is appropriate."
Having heard these words, the king likewise did not find them to his liking.
He spoke again to the brahmin Vāseṭṭha:
"Now that this midnight is so exceptionally clear and serene, what should be performed?"
The brāhmaṇa replied, “Today, the fifteenth day, is exceptionally clear and bright; however, Goyama is nearby and not far away. I only wish that Your Majesty would go and inquire about its meaning.”
When the king heard these words, he was again dissatisfied with them.
He spoke again to the brahmin Māṭhara:
"Now that it is the middle of the night, most serene and clear, what should be done?"
The brahmin replied, “Great King, you should know that Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is nearby, not far away; I only pray that Your Majesty will go and inquire about his intentions.”
When the king heard these words, they still did not satisfy his mind.
He again addressed Soma, the commander-in-chief of the army, saying:
"Now that it is the middle of the night and extremely clear, what should be done?"
Soma replied, "Pir̥ḍhika is nearby and not far away; he is well-versed in all forms of calculation. You may go and ask him about its meaning.
Having heard these words, the king was still not satisfied with them.
He further addressed his chief minister, saying:
"Today is the fifteenth day, when the sky is exceptionally clear; what should be performed?
The chief minister replied to the king:
"Now there is a Nirgrantha who has extensively studied the various scriptures and is the most eminent among his teachers; I only wish that Your Majesty would go and inquire about their doctrines.
Upon hearing these words, the King was displeased.
He further reflected:
"These people are deluded and ignorant; they cannot distinguish the true from the false and lack skillful means.
At that time, Prince Jīvaka was at the king’s left side, and the king turned to him and said:
"Since it is now the dead of night and the air is exceptionally clear and serene, what should be done?
At that moment, Jīvaka knelt before the king and said to him:

"The Tathāgata is currently nearby, not far from here, staying in the Poor Village Garden with one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples. I only wish that Your Majesty would go and inquire about the meaning of the Dharma."

However, that Tathāgata is clarity and light, free from any doubt or obstruction; he knows the affairs of the three worlds with universal and profound mastery. He shall naturally expound the matter for the King, so that whatever doubts the King possesses will be suddenly and completely resolved through self-awakening.
At that time, having heard Jīvaka’s words, King Ajātaśatru was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; a virtuous mind arose within him, and he immediately praised Jīvaka, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent, Prince! You have spoken these words most eloquently.

The reason for this is that my body and mind are now burning with extreme intensity; furthermore, I have causelessly taken the life of my father, the King. Throughout the long night, I constantly think:
"Who is capable of awakening to the intent of my heart?"
"What Jīvaka has just said accords perfectly with my own thoughts.
How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
Upon hearing the resonance of the Tathāgata’s voice, he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
At that time, the king addressed Jīvaka with these verses:
"Today is most clear and bright, yet my mind has not attained awakening."
Each of you should say: "To whom should we go to inquire about the meaning?
To Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, or to the disciples of Nirgrantha Jñātiputra?
These people are not to be relied upon; they cannot provide any deliverance."
"Today is most clear and bright; the moon is full and free from blemish.
Now I ask Jīvaka: whom should one go to inquire about the meaning [of the Dharma]?
At that time, Jīvaka replied to the king with a verse:
“Having heard your gentle voice, we have been delivered from the makara fish;
we pray only that you will come to the Buddha at once, so that we may dwell forever in the realm of fearlessness.
At that time, the king replied with a verse:
"In the past, the deeds I committed brought no benefit to the Buddha;
I harmed that true son of the Buddha named Piṇḍola.
Now, filled with extreme shame, I have no face to see the World-Honored One."
"How can you now say this, so as to cause me to go and see him?
At that time, Jīvaka again replied to the king in verse:
"The Buddhas have no 'this' or 'that'; all fetters have been forever eliminated."
An impartial mind free from duality— this is the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Even if one were to smear sandalwood paste upon the right hand while holding a blade to sever the left,
the mind would not give rise to increase or decrease.
Just as he pitied Rāhula’s son, taking no second breath for another;
as he held his mind toward Devadatta, making no distinction between enemy and kin—
only I pray that Your Majesty deigns to go and behold the countenance of the Tathāgata.
"You must sever your doubts; do not allow yourself to remain in hesitation.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to Prince Jīvaka:
"Quickly prepare five hundred male elephants, five hundred female elephants, and light five hundred lamps."
Jīvaka replied, “So be it, Great King!
Thereupon, Prince Jīvaka immediately prepared a carriage drawn by a thousand elephants and lit five hundred lamps, then went before the king and said:
"The carriage is prepared; Your Majesty, know that it is time.
At that moment, King Ajātaśatru, leading his retinue, proceeded toward the Lyu-yuan Garden. Midway, he was seized by terror and his hair stood on end;
looking back, he said to Prince Jīvaka, "Could it be that I have been deceived by you?"
"Could it be that you are carrying me away with my enemies?
Jīvaka replied to the king:
"Truly, there is no such possibility; I only pray that Your Majesty will advance a little further, for the Tathāgata is now not far from here."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru’s mind was still filled with fear, and he spoke again to Jīvaka, saying:
"Is it not because you have deluded me? Furthermore, I heard that the Tathāgata was accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty disciples; why do I no longer hear their voices?"
Jīvaka replied, “The disciples of the Tathāgata constantly enter into samādhi and possess no distracted thoughts; I only pray that Your Majesty will proceed a little further.”

King Ajātaśatru immediately descended from his carriage and entered on foot to the front of the lecture hall. Standing there in silence, he observed the assembly of noble ones and, looking back, said to Jīvaka:
"Where is the Tathāgata now?"
At that time, the entire assembly of noble ones entered the Samādhi of Blazing Light, illuminating that lecture hall so that no part remained untouched.
Thereupon, Jīvaka immediately knelt down on his right knee, extended his right hand to point toward the Tathāgata, and said:
"This is the Tathāgata, situated most centrally, like the sun breaking through the clouds."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru said to Jīvaka:
"How extraordinary!
How remarkable!"
"Now this noble assembly’s minds are so concentrated;
by what further cause does this radiance exist?
Jīvaka said to the king:
"It is only because of the power of samādhi that he emits this radiance.
The king spoke again, saying, "As I observe the noble assembly today, they are exceedingly tranquil; may my crown prince Udāyin also become thus tranquil and inactive."
Then, King Ajātaśatru joined his palms and addressed himself, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will deign to look upon me.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Welcome, Great King! Hearing the Tathāgata’s voice, the king was filled with extreme joy that the Tathāgata had addressed him by name.
At that moment, King Ajātaśatru went before the Buddha, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, placed both hands upon the Tathāgata’s feet, and declared:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon me with compassion and accept my repentance.
My father, the King, was innocent, yet I took his life; I only pray that you will accept my repentance so that I may never commit such an act again, reforming my past and cultivating the future.”
The World-Honored One said, "Now is precisely the right time; you should repent at once so that no error remains.
For one who dwells in the world, he who is able to reform his own transgressions is called a superior person."
"Within my Dharma, there is that which is most vast and extensive; you should now perform repentance.
At that time, the king, having paid homage at the feet of the Tathāgata, sat to one side.
Then the king addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to ask a question; if the Tathāgata permits it, I shall venture to ask.
The Buddha said to the king:
"If there be any doubts or difficulties, one should inquire about them at the proper time.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By performing meritorious deeds in the present life, can one receive retribution in the present life as well?"
The Buddha said to the king,
“Since ancient times, have you ever asked anyone about this matter?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, I once asked this same question of another, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa:
'How is it, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa? Is merit performed in the present life received as retribution in the present life?'"
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa replied to me, saying:
"There is no merit and no giving; there is no retribution for good or evil in this world or the next; there are no Arhats or others in the world who have attained perfection."
At that time, when I asked about the retribution for receiving this fruit, he replied, "There is none.
It is just as if someone were asked about the meaning of a melon and replied with the principles regarding a persimmon; so too was it with this Kāśyapa.
At that time, I thought to myself:
"This brahmin does not understand the meaning; regarding the meaning asked by me, a member of a noble royal lineage, he uses skillful means to evade the point and answers me with other matters."
"World-Honored One!
I was then about to cut off his head, as I would not accept his words, and I immediately sent him away.
At that time, I went again to the place of Ajita and asked him about this matter; Ajita replied to me, saying:"
"If one kills sentient beings on the left bank of the Yangtze River, the transgression committed is immeasurable, yet there is neither sin nor the retribution of evil fruits.
At that time, World-Honored One! I—
He further thought:

"I have now asked about the meaning of receiving retribution in the present life, yet this man responds to me with the retribution for killing—just as if someone were to ask about the meaning of a pear and answer with a crabapple."
I immediately left him and went to the place where Gayā-Kāśyapa was, and asked him about this matter.
That man replied to me, saying:
"Though one may perform incalculable meritorious deeds on the right bank of the river, there is no karmic reward for them therein.
At that time, I again thought to myself:
"The meaning of what I have asked has not been explained according to its principle."
Again, he left that place.
He went once more to where Ukkācelaka was and asked about this matter.
That man replied:
"Only one person appears in the world, one person dies, and one person comes and goes, experiencing suffering and joy.
At that time, I again thought:
"The reward in the present life is what I have now asked about, yet he has answered by bringing up birth and death."
Again, I abandoned him and departed.
I went to ask the elder Vairūḍhaka about this same matter.
That man replied to me, saying:
The past has ceased and does not arise again;
the future has not yet arrived and thus does not exist;
the present does not abide, for that which abides is subject to change.
At that time, I again thought to myself:
"The reward in the present life for which I have now inquired has been answered by means of the three periods of time; this is not the correct principle."
He then departed once more.
Arriving at the place where the Nirgranthas were, he asked them about this matter: "How is it, Nirgranthas?"
"Is it possible that by performing meritorious deeds in the present life, one may receive their retribution in the present life? He replied to me:
"There is no cause and no condition for the fetters of sentient beings."
"Furthermore, there is neither cause nor condition, yet sentient beings are attached to fetters and bonds;
there is neither cause nor condition, yet sentient beings are pure.
At that time, I again had this thought:

"These brahmins are indeed deluded and ignorant; they cannot distinguish the true from the false. Like blind men without eyes, they fail to provide any answer to the meaning of what was asked, appearing as if they were merely playing with the lineage of a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
"Having thus sought it, he then abandoned it and departed.
Now, World-Honored One, I ask for the meaning of this:
is it that by performing merit in the present life, one receives the retribution in the present life?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound its meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One said, "Great King!"
I now ask you a question; answer it as you see fit. Great King!
Do you have wine-keepers, cooks, or attendants who guard and protect the property?
The king said to the Buddha, “Indeed, there is. [The Buddha asked:
“If that messenger has labored for a long time, should he not also be granted a reward?”
The King addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I shall appoint them according to their merit so that no resentment arises.
The Buddha told the King:
"By this expedient means, one knows that by performing meritorious deeds in the present life, one receives retribution in the present life.
What do you think, Great King?
Since you occupy a high position and care for the people with propriety, should you not further bestow rewards and gifts upon them?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We share our food together in sweetness, and we would not regret even the loss of our lives.”
The Buddha told the king:

"By this expedient means, you should know that although his former station was extremely lowly, he gradually accumulated merit until he shared in the king's joy. For this reason, by performing meritorious deeds in the present life, one receives the retribution thereof in the present life."
The Buddha said to the king:
"Those men of labor, having served for many years, came and addressed the king, saying:
'Our labors are now complete and are known to Your Majesty; we wish to request from the king whatever our hearts desire.'"
"Would Your Majesty grant it to him?
The King replied to the Buddha:
"I shall comply with his wish and not deny it."
The Buddha told the king:

"That man of diligent service wishes to take leave of you, the king, to shave off his hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to study the Way, and cultivate pure conduct."
"Does Your Majesty grant me leave?
The King addressed the Buddha, saying, "Indeed, I grant it."
The Buddha said to the king:
"Suppose you were to see him with his hair and beard shaven, having left the household life to study the Path, standing by my side; what would you do?"
The king said to the Buddha,
“I shall serve and make offerings to you, and pay homage at the appropriate times.
The Buddha told the king:
"By this expedient means, it is known that one who performs meritorious deeds in the present receives retribution in the present.
Suppose there were a person of diligent effort who maintains the precepts completely and without transgression;
what would the King do to him?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For as long as my life lasts, I shall provide him with robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for sickness and weakness, ensuring that nothing is lacking.”
The Buddha told the king:
"By this expedient means, one knows that by performing merit in this present life, one receives the retribution thereof in this present life.

Furthermore, suppose that person has become a śramaṇa, exhausted all outflows (āsrava), and attained the state of no-outflow (anāsrava); with liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom, having realized it for himself and wandered freely, he has ended birth and death, established the holy life (brahmacarya), accomplished what was to be done, and knows as it truly is that there will be no further existence."
"What does Your Majesty intend to do?
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For as long as I live, I shall serve and provide offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick, ensuring that nothing is lacking."
The Buddha said to the king:
"By this means, you should know that by performing merit in the present life, one receives its retribution in the present life.
Furthermore, even if that person were to exhaust their entire lifespan and attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder, what would you, O King, provide for them?"
The king said to the Buddha:

"I shall build a great divine temple at the crossroads of the four main roads, and furthermore, I shall make offerings of incense and flowers, hang silken streamers, banners, and canopies, and serve and pay homage to it."
"The reason for this is that he possesses a celestial body, not a human body.
The Buddha told the king:
"By this expedient means, you should know that by performing meritorious deeds in the present life, one receives retribution in the present life."
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I now understand through this parable; may the World-Honored One today further expound its meaning.
From this day forward, I shall believe and accept its meaning; I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept me as a disciple!”
I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. Now I again repent:

like one who is foolish and deluded, I caused the harm of taking the life of my father, the King, though he was without fault. I now surrender my own body and life as refuge; I only pray that the World-Honored One will eliminate his transgressions and expound the wondrous Dharma, so that he may dwell in non-action through the long night. As I myself know, regarding the retribution for the sins I have committed, there is no root of goodness whatsoever.
The Buddha told the king:
"There are two kinds of people in the world who die without fault and, in the time it takes to extend or contract one's arm, attain rebirth in the heavens. What are these two?
First, those who do not create the root of evil but cultivate goodness; second, those who commit evil but reform what they have done.
These two types of people, upon the end of their lives, are born in the heavens without any lingering obstruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person commits an extremely evil deed, But repents so that it becomes increasingly slight,
Repenting daily without ceasing, The root of their transgression is forever uprooted."
"Therefore, Great King, you should govern by means of the Dharma and not by what is contrary to the Dharma.
For one who governs by means of the Dharma, at the dissolution of the body after death, will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens."
When he passed away, his reputation spread far and wide, heard throughout the four quarters, and was passed down by later generations:
"In former times there was a king who ruled with the True Dharma, free from any crookedness."
"Because people praise and transmit this, wherever that person is born, their lifespan will increase and their years will be extended, and they shall not suffer an untimely death.
Therefore, Great King, you should give rise to a heart of joy and direct it toward the Triple Gem: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha."
"In this way, Great King,
you should train yourself.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew.
Not long after the king had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If this King Ajātaśatru had not taken the life of his father, the King, he would today have attained the first fruit of śramaṇaship among the four pairs and eight classes of noble ones; he would also have attained the Eightfold Path of the Noble Ones, eliminated the eight cravings, and transcended the eight difficulties. Even so, he has now still obtained great fortune by attaining rootless faith."
Therefore, bhikṣus! A person who has committed an offense should seek skillful means to establish rootless faith.
Among my upāsakas, the one who has attained such rootless faith is Ajātaśatru.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are eight worldly dharmas that revolve in accordance with the world. What are these eight?"
First is gain, second is loss, third is defamation, fourth is praise, fifth is honor, sixth is disparagement, seventh is suffering, and eighth is pleasure.
"Monks, these are the eight things that revolve in accordance with the world. Monks!"
"You should seek skillful means to eliminate these eight things. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The Tathāgata appears in the world and attains the Way of Buddhahood within the world; yet he is not attached to the eight worldly dharmas, even as he moves among them. He is like a lotus flower born from the mud, which is exceedingly fresh and pure, unsullied by dust or water, beloved and respected by the devas, and brings joy to the hearts of all who behold it."

The Tathāgata is likewise in this regard: born from a womb and nurtured therein, he attains the Buddha-body, which—like the precious gem of lapis lazuli or the treasure of pure water—is not defiled by dust or impurities.
The Tathāgata is likewise; though born into the world, he is not defiled or attached by the eight worldly dharmas.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should apply yourselves with diligent effort and cultivate these eight dharmas.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are eight kinds of persons who circulate through birth and death, yet do not abide in birth and death.

What are these eight? They are: those entering the stream and those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry; those entering once-returning and those who have attained the fruit of once-returning; those entering non-returning and those who have attained the fruit of non-returning; and those entering arhatship and those who have attained the fruit of arhatship.”
"Monks, these are the eight kinds of persons who transmigrate through birth and death,
yet do not abide within birth and death. Therefore, monks,"
Seek the skillful means to cross over the perils of birth and death; do not dwell in birth and death.
Thus, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Worldly Dharmas, the Good, and the Eight Persons.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
44. Chapter on the Nine Abodes of Sentient Beings, Chapter Forty-four.
(1) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are nine abodes of sentient beings, which are the places where sentient beings dwell.
What are the nine?
There are some sentient beings who possess various bodies and various perceptions, namely the devas and humans;
there are some sentient beings who possess various bodies but a single perception, namely the Brahmakāyika devas at their initial manifestation;
and there are some sentient beings who possess a single body but various perceptions, namely the Ābhāsvara devas.
There are sentient beings who possess a single body and a single perception, namely the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven (Śubhakṛtsna-deva);
there are sentient beings of infinite space, namely the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana-deva);
and there are sentient beings of infinite consciousness, namely the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (Vijñānānantyāyatana-deva).
There are sentient beings in the Sphere of Nothingness, namely the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness;
there are sentient beings with perception and non-perception, namely the gods of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
All such places of birth are called the nine [abodes].
These, monks, are called the nine abodes of sentient beings, wherein all classes of living creatures have dwelt, do dwell,
and will dwell. Therefore, monks!
"You should seek skillful means to remain free from these nine states. Thus, monks,
you should train yourselves."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now speak of the ninefold virtues of the dedication of merit (dakṣiṇā); you should all reflect upon them well!
I shall now expound their meaning."
At that time, the bhikṣus received the Buddha’s instruction and admonition.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What are those called the nine kinds of virtues of a dedication of merit (dakṣiṇā-praṇidhāna)?"
"Monks, you should know that a donor who is a benefactor accomplishes three qualities;
the gift that is given also accomplishes three qualities;
and the person who receives the gift likewise accomplishes three qualities."
How does that donor and patron accomplish three qualities?
In this regard, the donor and patron accomplishes faith, accomplishes aspiration, and likewise refrains from taking life; this is called the donor and patron accomplishing these three qualities.
How are the objects given accomplished in these three qualities?
In this regard, the object of giving is accomplished in color, accomplished in fragrance, and accomplished in taste; this is called the threefold accomplishment of the object of giving.
What are the three things accomplished by one who receives offerings?
In this regard, the recipient of offerings accomplishes morality, accomplishes wisdom, and accomplishes samādhi; these are called the three dharmas accomplished by the person who receives alms.
In this way, when a *dakṣiṇā* (offering) accomplishes these nine dharmas, it attains a great fruit and reaches the state of the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta-nirodha*).
Now, a donor who wishes to seek merit should seek skillful means and accomplish these nine dharmas.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(3) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is for the sake of accomplishing nine qualities. What are the nine?

A forced countenance, endurance of humiliation, greed, stinginess and attachment, not letting go of thoughts in the mind, forgetfulness, little sleep, concealing lewdness, and lack of reciprocity—these are the nine."
"Monks, it is said that one achieves these nine qualities.
An evil monk likewise achieves nine qualities."
What are the nine? In this regard, they are:

having a forced countenance, enduring humiliation, greediness, stingy attachment, forgetfulness, little sleep, engaging in lewdness while remaining hidden, lacking reciprocity, and being intent on not relinquishing [unwholesome thoughts)—these are the nine.
“What is it for a wicked bhikṣu to have a brazen countenance?
In this regard, a wicked bhikṣu seeks that which should not be sought, thereby contravening the conduct of a śramaṇa.
Such a bhikṣu is said to have a brazen countenance.”
“What is it for an evil bhikṣu to endure humiliation?
In this regard, an evil bhikṣu, in the presence of virtuous and noble bhikṣus, praises himself and disparages others.”
Such a bhikṣu is said to be one who endures humiliation.
"How does a bhikṣu give rise to a covetous mind?
In this regard, when a bhikṣu sees the wealth and possessions of others and gives rise to covetousness toward them, this is called greed."
"What is a bhikṣu’s stinginess and attachment?
In this regard, a bhikṣu does not share with others the robes and bowl he has obtained, but constantly hides and keeps them for himself.
This is called stinginess and attachment."
“What is a bhikṣu who is forgetful?

In this regard, an evil bhikṣu constantly neglects and loses the sublime and wholesome words [of the Dharma], nor does he contemplate skillful means; instead, he discusses matters of state and the methods of warfare.”
In this way, an evil bhikṣu is possessed of this forgetfulness.
How does an evil bhikṣu sleep little?
In this regard, an evil bhikṣu does not contemplate those dharmas that ought to be contemplated; in this way, an evil bhikṣu sleeps little.
"What is it for an evil bhikṣu to conceal his lewdness?
In this regard, an evil bhikṣu acts in secret and does not speak of it to others, thinking:
'I am now engaging in sexual misconduct; let no one know of it.'"
"In this way, a bhikṣu conceals his lewdness.
What is meant by an evil bhikṣu lacking gratitude?
In this regard, an evil bhikṣu lacks a heart of reverence; he does not serve his teachers, elders, or those who are honorable and respected."
Thus, such evil bhikṣus lack gratitude and reciprocity.
"If an evil bhikṣu accomplishes these nine dharmas and does not mindfully abandon them, he will ultimately fail to realize the fruits of the path."
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should resolve to abandon all unwholesome states.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The peacock bird accomplishes nine qualities.”
What are these nine?

In this regard, the peacock bird is handsome in appearance, its voice is clear and resonant, its gait is dignified and orderly, it acts according to the proper time, it knows moderation in eating and drinking, it is constantly mindful of contentment, its mindfulness is not scattered, it sleeps little, and it has few desires and knows how to repay kindness.
"Monks, this is what is called the peacock bird's accomplishment of these nine qualities.
A wise and noble monk likewise accomplishes these nine qualities."
What are the nine?

In this regard, the virtuous bhikṣu is handsome in appearance, possesses a clear and resonant voice, walks with dignified composure, acts according to the proper time, knows moderation in eating and drinking, is constantly mindful of contentment, maintains undistracted mindfulness, sleeps little, and likewise has few desires and knows how to repay kindness.
"What is meant by a virtuous bhikṣu being handsome and dignified in appearance?
It means that in his coming and going, his advancing and retreating, and his every movement and pause, he never fails to maintain proper decorum."
In this way, the virtuous and excellent bhikṣu is handsome and upright in appearance.
How is it that the bhikṣu’s voice is clear and resonant?
In this regard, the bhikṣu skillfully discerns the principles of meaning and never errs or becomes confused.
In this way, the bhikṣu’s voice is clear and resonant.
What is meant by a bhikṣu walking with dignified composure?

Here, a bhikṣu acts according to the proper time and does not lose the sequence; he knows when it is appropriate to recite and recites accordingly, knows when it is appropriate to practice and practices accordingly, knows when it is appropriate to remain silent and remains silent accordingly, and knows when it is appropriate to rise and rises accordingly.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows the proper seasons. How does a bhikṣu act according to the time?
In this regard, a bhikṣu should go when he ought to go, stay when he ought to stay, and listen to the Dharma according to the season.
In this way, a bhikṣu acts with awareness of the proper time.
How does a bhikṣu know moderation in eating?
In this regard, whatever food remains after his own needs, the bhikṣu shares it with others, not begrudging what he possesses.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows moderation in eating.
How does a bhikṣu practice little sleep?

In this regard, during the first watch of the night, the bhikṣu practices wakefulness; he practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without omission or lapse, constantly purifying his mind through walking meditation and lying awake.

Furthermore, during the middle watch of the night, he contemplated the profound; then, at the time of the final watch, he lay on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, contemplating the perception of light, and subsequently rose to walk in meditation (caṅkrama) to purify his mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu has little sleep.
"How does a bhikṣu have few desires and know how to repay kindness?
In this regard, a bhikṣu serves the Three Jewels and reverently honors his teachers and elders."
In this way, a bhikṣu has few desires and knows how to repay kindness.
Thus, a virtuous and excellent bhikṣu accomplishes these nine dharmas.
You should now mindfully practice and uphold these nine dharmas!
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Women bind men by accomplishing nine qualities.
What are these nine? They are:
singing, dancing, performing as an entertainer, playing music, laughing, weeping, constantly seeking opportunities, employing illusory arts, and [appealing with] their complexion and physical form."
Among all such matters, it is only the fetter of sensual pleasure (*kāma-rāga*) that binds a person most urgently; even a hundredfold or a thousandfold [comparison] cannot equal it.
As I observe these principles today, the fetter of sensual pleasure binds a person most urgently, and there is nothing that surpasses it, just as that man bound him with firmness.
Therefore, monks, you should mindfully abandon these nine things. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Bamboo Grove of Ukala together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall now preach to you the sublime Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its meaning is profound, and it consists of the pure practice of the holy life. This sutra is titled 'The Foundation of All Dharmas.'"
"Reflect upon this well," [the Buddha said]. The bhikṣus replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed them, saying:
“What is meant by ‘the root of all dharmas’?

In this regard, bhikṣus, ordinary persons do not perceive the teaching of the noble ones, nor do they uphold the words and teachings of the Tathāgata; they do not draw near to spiritual friends, nor do they receive the instructions of spiritual friends.”
He contemplates this earth and knows it as it truly is: "This is earth; as it is scrutinized, this is earth.

As it truly is earth, so too is it water, so too is it fire, and so too is it wind. These four elements combine to form what is called a "person," which is merely an object of entertainment for the foolish.
The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three know themselves as gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three and take delight in being gods among gods;
the Brahmā gods know themselves as Brahmā gods; the Great Brahmās know themselves as Great Brahmās, with none able to surpass them;
and the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven recognize one another as having come from the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
The Śubhakṛtsna devas know themselves to be Śubhakṛtsna devas;
the Bṛhatphala devas know themselves to be Bṛhatphala devas without confusion;
and the Avṛha devas know themselves to be Avṛha devas.
The gods of the sphere of infinite space know themselves to be gods of the sphere of infinite space;
the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness know themselves to be gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
the gods of the sphere of nothingness know themselves to be gods of the sphere of nothingness.
The gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception know themselves to be gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
those who see know themselves to be seeing;
those who hear know themselves to be hearing.
One who is lustful knows himself as lustful;
one who is wise knows himself as wise;
and those of a certain class know themselves as belonging to that class.
Those who belong to a certain class know themselves as belonging to that class;
those who are fully endowed know themselves as being fully endowed;
and those who have attained nirvāṇa know themselves as having attained nirvāṇa, finding their own delight therein.
The reason for this is that it is not what the wise have taught.

"If a noble disciple goes to visit a sage, receives his Dharma, associates with virtuous friends, and constantly stays close to virtuous friends, he perceives the element of earth with complete clarity; he knows its origin and yet does not cling to earth, nor does he harbor a mind of defilement."
It is likewise with water, fire, and wind.

With regard to humans, devas, Brahmā kings, Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Ākāśānantyāyatana, Vijñānānantyāyatana, Ākiṃcanyāyatana, and Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana—he sees, hears, perceives, and knows them; whether as a single kind or various kinds, even up to nirvāṇa, he does not cling to nirvāṇa, nor does he give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa.
