The reason for this is that it all arises from skillful discernment and skillful observation.

If a bhikṣu is an arhat whose outflows are exhausted, who has accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, brought an end to the root of birth and death, and attained liberation through equanimity, he is able to discern the earth element without giving rise to any conceptual attachment or perception thereof.
It is likewise for the earth element, humans, devas, and Brahmā kings, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Even regarding nirvāṇa, one does not cling to nirvāṇa, nor does one give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa.
The reason for this is that it is all brought about by the destruction of lust, anger, and delusion.

Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is well able to discern the earth element, yet he does not cling to the earth element, nor does he give rise to the perception of the earth element.

The reason for this is that it results from tearing asunder the net of craving. Because of existence there is birth; because of birth there is old age and death. When all these are completely eliminated, the Tathāgata attains supreme perfect enlightenment.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the bhikṣus did not accept his instruction.
This was because Māra Pāpīyas had obstructed their minds.
“This sutra is named ‘The Root of All Dharmas’; I have now fully expounded it.
That which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, ought to practice, I have now fully carried out.”
"You all should mindfully dwell in seclusion beneath trees, sitting in meditation with focused intent and contemplating the sublime meaning.
If you do not do so now, it will be of no avail for later regrets. This is my instruction."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the city of Rājagṛha who had fallen ill; he was so debilitated and emaciated that he lay in his own excrement and urine, unable to rise or move about himself, and no other bhikṣu went to attend to him. Day and night, he invoked the name of the Buddha, saying:
"Why does the World-Honored One alone not take pity on me?"
At that time, the Tathāgata heard with his divine ear that monk lamenting in resentment and crying out for refuge in the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall go together with you all to inspect the various rooms and observe the dwellings."
The bhikṣus replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, proceeded on an inspection tour of the various rooms.
Then, a sick bhikṣu saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar; he immediately wished to rise from his seat, but was unable to move himself.
At that time, the Tathāgata went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him:
"Stop! Stop!"
“Bhikṣu! Do not move;
I have my own sitting mat, which will suffice for you to sit.

At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, knowing the Tathāgata’s thought, vanished from the world of Aśvakarṇa and came to where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what was in the Tathāgata’s mind, immediately came to where the Buddha was.
The Brahmā King likewise knew what was in the Tathāgata’s mind; he vanished from the Brahma realm and came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, knowing what was in the Tathāgata’s mind, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
Then the Buddha said to the sick bhikṣu:
“Are your present sufferings diminishing rather than increasing?”
The bhikṣu replied, “My disciple’s suffering has only increased and not diminished; he finds very little relief.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Where is the attendant now? Who has come to look after him?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that I have encountered this illness, there is no one to look after me.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"In the past, before you were ill, did you ever go to inquire after those who were sick?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha,
“I did not go to inquire after those who were ill.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"You now possess no beneficial gain within the True Dharma.
Why is this? It is entirely because you did not go to visit the sick.
You, bhikṣu, must now..."
Do not harbor fear; you should personally provide offerings so that there is no lack.

Just as I today am peerless and without rival among gods and humans, I am likewise able to look after all who are ill—providing protection to those without protection, serving as eyes for the blind, and rescuing those afflicted by disease.
At that time, the World-Honored One personally removed the impurities and spread out a seat for himself.
Then, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa and Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We ourselves shall attend to this sick bhikṣu; may the Tathāgata no longer trouble himself.”
The Buddha said to the devas:
"Cease for now! The Tathāgata himself shall know the proper time."

As I recall myself in the past, before I had attained the Buddha-way while practicing the bodhisattva path, I sacrificed my own life for the sake of a single pigeon; how much more so today, now that I have attained the Buddha-way, should I abandon this bhikṣu?
Ultimately, there is no such place.
Furthermore, Śakra Devānām Indra did not previously attend to this sick bhikṣu, nor did Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King and Lord of the World Protectors, look after him.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra and King Vaiśravaṇa both remained silent and did not respond.

Then, the Tathāgata took a broom in his hand and removed the filth, prepared a seat, and further washed the monk’s robes; having observed these three matters, he assisted the sick bhikṣu to sit down and bathed him with pure water.
Devas were above, pouring scented water over him.
At that time, having bathed the bhikṣu, the World-Honored One sat back upon his bed and personally offered him food with his own hands.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the bhikṣu had finished eating and had set aside his bowl and utensils, addressed that bhikṣu, saying:
"You should now abandon the sicknesses of the three periods of time."
The reason for this, bhikṣus, you should know, is that birth entails the calamity of dwelling in the womb; because of birth, there is old age.
Now, one who is old has a body that is frail and a vital energy that is exhausted.
Because of old age there is illness.
As for those who are ill, they groan while sitting or lying down; the four hundred and four diseases all arrive at once.
Because of illness there is death.
Now, for those who have died, the physical form and the spirit are separated, each proceeding toward either good or evil.
If one’s transgressions are many, they shall enter hell, where there are mountains of knives and trees of swords, chariots of fire and furnaces of glowing coals, and the swallowing of molten copper;
or they may become animals, driven by others, fed only with fodder and straw, enduring immeasurable suffering.

Furthermore, throughout incalculable and countless kalpas, they take the form of hungry ghosts, their bodies tens of yojanas in height and their throats as thin as needles; molten copper is poured into their mouths, and after passing through countless kalpas, they obtain a human body, only to undergo flogging, whipping, and torture beyond measure.
Furthermore, throughout countless kalpas, one may be born in the heavens, yet still experience the union of affection and the separation from those one loves;
desire remains insatiable, and only upon attaining the path of the noble ones does one finally transcend suffering.
“Now there are nine kinds of persons who are free from suffering and affliction.

What are these nine? They are: one who is a candidate for arhatship, one who has attained arhatship; one who is a candidate for anāgāminship, one who has attained anāgāminship; one who is a candidate for sakṛdāgāminship, one who has attained sakṛdāgāminship; one who is a candidate for srotāpanna-ship, one who has attained srotāpanna-ship; and the person of the spiritual lineage (gotrabhū)—these are the nine.”

"Thus it is said, bhikṣu: The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is extremely difficult to encounter; a human birth is difficult to obtain; being born in a land of the True Dharma is likewise difficult to meet; meeting with a virtuous spiritual friend is also like this; hearing the words of the Dharma teaching is likewise not easily encountered; for dharmas arise from one another only at certain times."

"Monks, you should know that the Tathāgata now exists in the world; having heard the True Dharma with unimpaired faculties, you are capable of hearing that True Dharma. If you do not apply yourselves with earnest diligence now, it will be too late for regrets later."

"This is my instruction. Then, having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching, that bhikṣu gazed intently upon the Honored One’s countenance and, while still seated, attained the threefold knowledge; his outflows were exhausted and his mind was liberated.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
"Have you understood the root cause of illness?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
"Having understood the root cause of illness, I have departed from and transcended this birth, old age, sickness, and death.

All of this is sustained by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata; with the four immeasurable minds, he protects all beings—limitless, boundless, and incalculable—with purity of body, speech, and mind."
At that time, having completed his full exposition of the Dharma, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Quickly strike the ghaṇṭā now; let all the bhikṣus residing in the city of Rājagṛha assemble at the Mahāpariṣad Hall."
At that time, Ānanda, having received the instruction from the Buddha, immediately assembled the bhikṣus at the Hall of Universal Assembly and approached the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣus have gathered; may the World-Honored One know that the time is now right."
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the lecture hall, took his seat, and sat down.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you practice the Way because you fear kings or bandits that you have gone forth from home?"

"Monks! With firm faith, cultivate the unsurpassed holy life, desiring to abandon birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair, and also desiring to be free from the twelve links of dependent origination."
The bhikṣus replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The reason you have gone forth is that you share one teacher and are of one accord, like milk and water; yet, you do not look after one another."
From this day forward, you should look after one another in succession.
If there is a sick bhikṣu who has no disciple, the community shall appoint someone from among its members to act as his caregiver.
The reason for this is that, apart from this, one sees no other way to perform a service more meritorious than attending to the sick;
one who attends to the sick is no different from attending to me.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Should there be one who makes offerings to me, And to all the Buddhas of the past—
The merit of giving to me Is no different from that of nursing the sick."
At that time, having delivered this instruction, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"From this day forward, let the bhikṣus look after one another;
if a bhikṣu knows of [a transgression] yet does not act accordingly, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma and Vinaya."
"This is my instruction.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (Eight) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are nine kinds of persons who are worthy of respect and honor; by making offerings to them, one gains merit.”

What are the nine? They are: one who is progressing toward arhatship, one who has attained arhatship; one who is progressing toward anāgāmin-ship, one who has attained anāgāmin-ship; one who is progressing toward sakṛdāgāmin-ship, one who has attained sakṛdāgāmin-ship; one who is progressing toward srotāpanna-ship, one who has attained srotāpanna-ship; and one who is on the stage of the spiritual lineage—these constitute the nine.
“Monks, these are the nine kinds of persons whom, when one supports, one gains merit that never diminishes.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Prince Pūrṇa approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, Prince Pūrṇa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have heard this before:"
"I have heard that the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka engaged in debate with the brahmin Raudrākṣa, yet this bhikṣu was unable to provide an answer.
I have also heard: 'Among the assembly of the Tathāgata’s disciples, there is none whose faculties are more dull and lacking in wisdom than this bhikṣu.'"
Among the upāsakas of the Tathāgata who dwell at home, there was one from the city of Kapilavastu, a member of the Gautama Śākya clan, whose faculties were dull and whose mind was obstructed.
The Buddha told the prince:
"The bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka possesses the power of supernatural faculties and has attained the state of a superior person; he does not practice the worldly arts of debate."
"Furthermore, Prince, you should know that this bhikṣu possesses most excellent meaning.
At that time, Prince Pūrṇabhadra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Although what the Buddha has said is so, a thought still arises within my mind:"
"How is it that you, possessing such great supernormal power, are unable to engage in debate with those heterodox teachers and followers of other schools?
I now invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, with the sole exception of one person: Cūḍapanthaka.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the invitation.

Having seen that the World-Honored One had accepted, the prince rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then withdrew.
That very night, he prepared various kinds of sweet delicacies and food and drink, spread out fine seats, and announced:
"The time has come; now is precisely the right moment.

At that time, the World-Honored One had the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka hold his almsbowl and follow behind him. Leading the assembly of bhikṣus, with them surrounding him before and behind, he entered the city of Rājagṛha and went to where the prince was; they each took their seats in order.
At that time, the prince addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will personally hand me his bowl; I now wish to serve the Tathāgata my own food with my own hands.
The Buddha said to the prince:
"The bowl is currently with the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, yet he has not brought it at all.
The prince said to the Buddha,
"I pray that the World-Honored One will dispatch a bhikṣu to go and fetch the bowl."
The Buddha said to the prince,
"Go now yourself and fetch the Tathāgata’s bowl.
At that time, the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka manifested five hundred flowering trees, and beneath each tree sat a Cūḍapanthaka bhikṣu.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the prince went to fetch the bowl.
From afar he saw five hundred *cīvaras* beneath the trees, where each had a bhikṣu named Cūḍapanthaka sitting in meditation; they were focused their mindfulness before them without any distraction.
Having seen him, he thought to himself,
"Which one is the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka?
Prince Pūrṇa then returned to the place where the World-Honored One was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When you go into that garden, they will all be the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka;
you will not know which one is the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka.
The Buddha said to the prince:
Returning to the garden, he stood at the very center and snapped his fingers, saying:
"As for the one who is truly the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, I pray that you rise from your seat!"
At that time, Prince Pūrṇabhadra, having received these instructions, went again to the garden and stood in the center, saying:
"If it is indeed the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, let him rise from his seat."
After the prince had spoken these words,
the remaining five hundred transformed bhikṣus naturally vanished, and only the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka remained.
At that time, Prince Pūrṇa, together with the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Then, Prince Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray, World-Honored One!”
"Now I reproach myself for not having believed the Tathāgata’s teaching:
'This bhikṣu possesses supernormal powers and great majesty.
The Buddha said to the prince:
“I accept your confession!
What the Tathāgata has spoken is ultimately without duality.
Furthermore, there are nine types of persons who circulate and come and go within this world.”

What are the nine? First, knowing people's dispositions in advance; second, knowing immediately upon hearing; third, knowing only after observing their physical characteristics; fourth, knowing only after examining the underlying principles; fifth, knowing only after experiencing the flavor; sixth, knowing only after both understanding the meaning and experiencing the flavor; seventh, neither understanding the meaning nor experiencing the flavor; eighth, learning through the power of mental cultivation and supernormal faculties; ninth, having received very little of the teachings.
"These, Prince, are called the nine kinds of persons who appear in the world. Thus it is, Prince."
That person who contemplates signs is the foremost among the eight types of individuals; there is none who surpasses him.
Now, this Bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka has practiced the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and does not study other dharmas; this Bhikṣu constantly uses his supernormal powers to preach the Dharma to others.

I, Ānanda, now observe the signs and immediately know them; I anticipate human intentions and discern what the Tathāgata requires and what he does not require, as well as what the Tathāgata should speak and what he should set aside, making all things clear and distinct. At present, there is no one who surpasses the bhikṣu Ānanda; his extensive study of the meanings of the various sūtras is comprehensive and leaves nothing unmastered.
Furthermore, this bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka is able to transform a single form into many forms, and then merge them back into one again.
This bhikṣu shall later attain parinirvāṇa within the midst of space.
"I do not see any other person who attains parinirvāṇa as does the bhikṣu Ānanda or the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka.
At that time, the Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Among my śrāvakas, there is no one who can transform his physical form, making it large or small, like the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka."

At that time, Prince Pūrṇabhadra personally served the food to the assembly of monks. Having cleared away their bowls, he took a small seat and, standing before the Tathāgata with palms joined, addressed the World-Honored One:

“I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant permission for the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka to come to my home constantly. Whatever robes, miscellaneous items, or requisites for a śramaṇa he may require, let him take them all from my house; I shall provide these necessities for as long as I live.”
The Buddha told the prince: "Prince,
you must now go back and confess to the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, personally entreating him!"
The reason for this is that it is difficult for one who lacks wisdom to distinguish a wise person;
however, it is indeed possible for a wise person to recognize another who possesses wisdom.
At that time, Prince Pūrṇabhadra immediately prostrated toward the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, announced his own name, and sought his forgiveness, saying:
"O Bhikṣu of Great Supernatural Power, I have harbored thoughts of contempt; from this day forward, I shall never dare to offend you again."
"I only pray that you will accept my repentance; henceforth I shall not dare to transgress again.
The bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka replied, "I grant you forgiveness for your transgression.
Do not commit it again in the future, nor do you ever again slander the noble and holy ones."
"Prince, you should know that any sentient being who slanders a noble one will inevitably fall into the three evil destinies and be born within hell.
Thus it is, Prince!"
"You should train yourself in this way.

At that time, the Buddha taught the most sublime Dharma to Prince Manhu, exhorting and inspiring him with joy; immediately upon his seat, the prince attained the realization to recite this prayer of aspiration:
"Sacrifice has fire as its highest; Scriptures and hymns are the most supreme."
Among humans, the king is most honored; among all streams, the ocean is foremost;
among the stars, the moon is first; and for its radiance, the sun is supreme.
Throughout the zenith, nadir, and the four quarters, of all things that possess form—
"Among the devas and the people of the world, the Buddha is the most honored.
Those who wish to seek merit should make offerings to the three types of karmic actions pertaining to the Buddha.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One rose from his seat.
At that time, Prince Pūrṇabhadra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"That which is called a 'good spiritual friend' (kalyāṇamitra) is one who constitutes half of the holy life (brahmacarya); they lead one along the path of goodness until one reaches the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not speak these words:
'One who is called a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is one who constitutes half of the holy life (brahmacarya).'"

The reason for this is that a person who is a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is one who has perfected the holy life (brahmacarya); by engaging in their practice together, one will come to behold the excellent path.
I, too, have attained unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment through spiritual friends;
having realized the fruit of the Way, I have delivered and liberated countless sentient beings, causing them all to be freed from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
By this expedient means, one knows that a person who is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is one who has perfected the holy life (*brahmacarya*). "Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a son or daughter of good family associates with a spiritual friend, their faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) will increase, and they will become fully endowed with the virtues of learning, generosity, and wisdom."
Just as when the moon is about to become full, its radiance gradually increases until it is twice as bright as usual;
so too is it with a son or daughter of good family who draws near to a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra): their faith, learning, mindfulness, generosity, and wisdom all increase.
By this expedient means, one knows that a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is precisely one who has perfected the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
"If I had not associated with a spiritual friend in the past, I would never have been granted a prophecy by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."
Because he associated with and served spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), he was able to receive the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
By this expedient means, one knows that a spiritual friend is precisely one who has perfected the holy life (brahmacarya).

“Ānanda, if there were no virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) in the world, there would be no distinction between the honorable and the lowly; parents, teachers, elders, brothers, and kinsmen would be of the same class as swine and dogs, creating various evil conditions and planting the seeds for the causes of hell.
Because there are virtuous friends, there exist separately parents, teachers, elders, brothers, and kinsmen.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"A virtuous friend is not evil; One who is intimately connected to the Dharma does not seek food.
They lead one along the path of goodness; Such a friend is said to be most venerable."
"Therefore, Ānanda, do not say again:
'A good spiritual friend is half of the holy life.'"
At that time, Ānanda received the instruction from the Buddha; having heard what the Buddha had spoken, he rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (11) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra vanished from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and came to where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What are the thoughts of the devas and human beings?”
"What do you seek? The Buddha told him:
"In the wandering of the world, their natures are not the same; their destinations differ, and their thoughts are manifold."
"O Lord of Devas, you should know that in the past, throughout countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I too gave rise to this thought:
'Where do the minds of devas and the various classes of sentient beings tend toward?'"
"What vow do you seek? From that kalpa until this day, not a single person has been seen whose mind accords with yours.

Śakra Devānām-Indra, you should know that the sentient beings of the world give rise to perverted perceptions: they perceive the impermanent as permanent; they perceive what is without bliss as blissful; they perceive the selfless as having a self; they perceive the impure as pure; they perceive the right path as a deviant path; they perceive evil as merit, and merit as evil. By these means, one knows that among the classes of sentient beings, their faculties are difficult to measure and their temperaments and conducts are each different.

"If all sentient beings were to have only a single perception and no diverse perceptions, then the nine abodes of sentient beings could not be known; it would also be difficult to distinguish the nine abodes of sentient beings, and it would likewise be difficult to clarify where the divine consciousnesses reside. Furthermore, one would not know of the existence of the eight great hells, and the destinies of animals would also be difficult to discern."
They do not perceive the distinct sufferings of hell; they are unaware of the nobility of the four castes, nor do they know the path frequented by the asuras, nor even the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
If they were all to become of one mind, they would be like the devas of Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Because sentient beings possess various kinds of mental conceptions, their thoughts are likewise of various kinds.

For this reason, it is known that there are nine abodes for sentient beings and nine places where spirits dwell; it is likewise known that there are eight great hells and the three evil realms, extending up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
"By these skillful means, one knows that the classes of sentient beings differ in nature and their practices are each distinct.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What the Tathāgata has spoken is most extraordinary and sublime:"

"The nature of sentient beings varies in their conduct, and their thoughts differ; because the conduct of sentient beings is not uniform, there arise disparities such as blue, yellow, white, black, long, and short."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
The affairs of the devas are many; we wish to return to the heavens.
The Buddha said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"It is fitting that you know this is the time.
At that moment, Śakra Devānām Indra rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and withdrew.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Śakra Devānām Indra rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Nine: Restraint, Alms-food, Peacock; Bondage, The Fundamental Disease of the Dharma, Offerings, Paṇḍaka; Holy Life, Various Perceptions.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll Forty.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 41, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 45: The Chapter on the Horse-King. Chapter Forty-Five: The Horse-King.
1. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, there was in that city a brahmin named Mahendriya, who was well-versed in the scriptures and arts of the non-Buddhist sects; he was thoroughly proficient in astronomy and terrestrial sciences, and he possessed a complete understanding of all the worldly methods for social interaction.
That Brahmin woman was named Yì'ài (Manoharā); she was exceedingly intelligent and her countenance was so upright and beautiful as to be rare in the world.
At that time, there was a saying in the Brahmin scriptures:
"There are two kinds of people who appear in the world who are extremely difficult to encounter; indeed, they are not easily met."
"What are these two persons?
They are the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the Cakravartin King.
"When a Cakravartin King appears in the world, seven treasures spontaneously manifest in response."
"I now possess this jewel of a woman, whose countenance is exceptionally beautiful, the foremost among all jade-like maidens.
At present, there is no Wheel-Turning Sage King. Furthermore, I have heard:

'The son of King Śuddhodana, named Siddhārtha, has left the household life to study the Way; he possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics. If he were to remain at home, he would surely become a Wheel-Turning Sage King.'"
"If one leaves the household life to study the Way, they shall attain the Buddha-way.
I should now give this girl to that śramaṇa.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa immediately took the girl to where the World-Honored One was and, approaching the Buddha, said to him:
"I only pray that the Śramaṇa will accept this jade maiden.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa: "Stop!
"Stop! Brahmin! I have no need for such a person who is attached to sensual desires."
Then the brahmin addressed the Buddha again, a second and third time, saying: "Śramaṇa!
Accept this jade maiden; in comparison to all other women in this world, she is peerless."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“I have received your intention; however, I have already left the household life and no longer practice desire.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu standing behind the Tathāgata, holding a fan and fanning the Buddha.
At that time, the elder bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will accept this woman; if the Tathāgata does not require her, please grant her to us for our service."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder bhikṣu:
"You are deluded and foolish to dare to harbor such evil intent before the Tathāgata.
Why have you directed your mind toward this woman?"
Now, for women there are nine unwholesome qualities.

What are these nine? First, women are foul-smelling, filthy, and impure; second, women have harsh speech; third, women lack gratitude and reciprocity; fourth, women are envious; fifth, women are stingy and jealous; sixth, women take great pleasure in wandering about; seventh, women are prone to anger; eighth, women are prone to lying; ninth, women are frivolous in what they say.
"Monks, these are the nine kinds of base and evil conduct found among women.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“Constantly laughing and weeping, appearing friendly though not truly so—seek other skillful means; do not give rise to disordered thoughts.
At that time, the Elder Bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Although women possess these nine kinds of corrupt and evil qualities, today, as I observe this woman, I find her to be without fault.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Are you now a fool, that you do not believe what has been spoken from the divine mouth of the Tathāgata?"
I shall now relate this.
In the distant past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a merchant named Viśvāmitra who, leading five hundred merchants, entered the sea to gather treasures.
However, on the shore of that great ocean there was a dwelling place of rākṣasas who constantly devoured human beings.
At that time, a wind arose in the sea and blew this raft so that it fell into the midst of those rākṣasas.

At that time, the rākṣasī saw the merchants approaching from afar; filled with immeasurable joy, she immediately concealed her rākṣasī form and transformed herself into a woman of incomparable beauty.
She spoke to the merchants, saying: "Welcome, worthy sirs!"
"This jewel-island is no different from those celestial palaces; it abounds in various rare treasures and thousands upon hundreds of kinds of abundant food.
Furthermore, there are many beautiful women who have no husbands, with whom we may enjoy ourselves together."
“Bhikṣus, you should know that among those merchants, the foolish and deluded ones, upon seeing the woman, immediately gave rise to thoughts of attachment and desire for her.”
At that time, the merchant leader Samantabhadra thought to himself:
"This great ocean is a place where no human beings dwell; how could there be a woman living here?"
"This must certainly be a rākṣasa; do not harbor any doubt.
At that time, the merchant leader said to the woman: "Stop!"
"Stop! Sisters! We do not lust after female beauty."
"At that time, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, the Horse King circled in the sky and issued this proclamation:
'Whoever wishes to cross the perils of the great ocean, I am able to carry them across.'"

"Monks, you should know that at that time, the merchant leader climbed a high tree; seeing the horse-king from afar and hearing the sound of his voice, he was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, and went toward where the horse-king was."
Having arrived, he spoke to the horse-king, saying:
"We five hundred merchants were driven by the wind and have now landed here in this most difficult place; we wish to cross the sea, so we pray that you will ferry us across."
At that time, the horse-king said to those merchants:
"All of you come here; I shall carry you across to the edge of the sea.
Then, the Elder Viśāṇa said to the assembly of merchants:
"Now the Horse King is nearby; let us all go to him together to cross over the perils of the sea.
At that time, the multitude replied, "Stop!
"Stop, great lord!
Let us first enjoy ourselves here among one another; as for those who toil with hardship in Jambudvīpa, they do so because they desire to seek a place of happiness."
"Rare curiosities, precious treasures, and even exquisite women are all available here; you may enjoy yourself with the five desires right here.
In the future, we shall gradually gather wealth and goods together, so that we may endure hardships together."
Then, that great caravan leader said to the people: "Stop! Stop!"
"O fool! There are no women here;
how could there be human dwellings within the great ocean?"
The merchants replied: "Stop,
great master!"
"We cannot abandon this place and depart.
At that time, the merchant leader Viśvāmitra spoke these verses:
"We have fallen into this calamity; There is no thought of male or female here."
"These are of the rākṣasa race; they will gradually devour us.
"Even if you do not go with me, each of you must protect yourselves."
"Whatever transgressions I have committed with my body, speech, or mind, may they all be completely forgiven and forgotten;
let them not occupy my thoughts. At that time, the merchants spoke this verse of parting with him:
"Please convey our greetings to those kinsmen of ours in Jambudvīpa."
"Enjoying ourselves here, we cannot return home at this time.
At that moment, the merchant leader replied with a verse:
"You have truly met with calamity; deluded as you are, you refuse to return."
"In this way, before long, they will all be devoured by ghosts.
Having spoken this verse, he departed.
He went to where the horse-king was, prostrated with his head at its feet, and immediately mounted it and rode away.
At that time, when the people saw from afar that their lord had already mounted the horse-king, some among them cried out, while others did not voice their grievances.
Then, the greatest rākṣasa lord spoke this verse to the other rākṣasas:
"Once one has fallen into the mouth of a lion, It is extremely difficult to emerge from it."
"How much more so for those who have entered my island; to wish to leave would truly be difficult.
At that time, the lord of the rākṣasīs immediately transformed himself into the form of a woman, exceedingly beautiful. She then pressed her breast with both hands and said:
"If I do not eat you, I shall never be a rākṣasī."
At that time, the horse-king immediately took up the merchant leader on his back and carried him across to the seashore;
meanwhile, the remaining five hundred merchants all fell into great distress.
"At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled and transformed the people.
At that moment, a rākṣasa followed closely behind the great caravan leader, crying out: 'Ho!'"
"I have lost my husband!
At that moment, the merchant master immediately returned home.
Then, the rākṣasa transformed himself into a man holding a boy and went to King Brahmadatta; approaching the king, he said: [The text continues with the narrative of the rākṣasa’s deception.]
"The world is filled with extreme calamities and portents; it shall all be utterly destroyed.
The King asked him, "What calamities and portents are there in the world that shall all be utterly destroyed?"
The rākṣasī said to the king, "I was abandoned by my husband; I have committed no offense against my lord.
At that time, King Brahmadatta, seeing that this woman was exceedingly exquisite, gave rise to thoughts of desire and said to her:
"Your husband has abandoned you and departed, devoid of any sense of human righteousness.
At that time, King Brahmadatta sent a messenger to summon her husband, saying:
"Did you truly abandon this excellent wife?"
The merchant leader replied,
"This is a rākṣasī, not a woman. The rākṣasī then spoke again to the king:
"This man lacks the virtue of a husband; having abandoned me today, he has further insulted me by calling me a rākṣasī.
The King asked her, "If you truly do not wish for him, I shall take him away."
The merchant leader addressed the king, saying, "This is a rākṣasī; she shall follow Your Majesty’s noble will.
At that time, King Brahmadatta immediately took this woman into his inner palace, receiving her with due care at all times so that no resentment might arise.
At that time, a non-human rākṣasa would seize the king’s food and devour him until only his bones remained, and then it would depart. "O Bhikṣu!
Do not hold such a view."
The merchant leader at that time was the bhikṣu Śāriputra;
the rākṣasī at that time is this woman here;
and King Brahmadatta at that time is the elder bhikṣu here now.
The King of Horses at that time was my own self in this life.
The five hundred merchants were these five hundred bhikṣus.
By this expedient means, one should know that desire is an impure thought; how could it be that one now gives rise to the intention to produce thoughts of attachment?
At that time, the bhikṣu prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I only pray that you will accept my repentance and forgive this grave transgression; from this day forward, I shall never commit it again.”

At that time, having received the instruction of the Tathāgata, that bhikṣu immediately withdrew to a secluded place to discipline himself and practice. For it is for this reason that sons of noble family diligently cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), desiring to practice the unsurpassed holy life.
At that time, that bhikṣu attained arhatship.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, after the Venerable Śāriputra and the Venerable Maudgalyāyana had completed their summer retreat there, they set out on a journey through the human world with five hundred bhikṣus, gradually arriving at the village of Kapilavastu.
At that time, the monks who were traveling and those who were staying each addressed one another, exchanging greetings with loud voices.
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing the loud clamor of the bhikṣus, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"In this garden, whose sound is this? It is so great as to resemble the noise of wood or stone being split."
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have now arrived here with five hundred bhikṣus; it is merely the sound of visiting bhikṣus and long-resident bhikṣus exchanging greetings with one another.”
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Quickly send the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; they need not remain here.
At that time, having received these instructions, Ānanda went at once to where the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were and spoke to them, saying:
"The World-Honored One has given this instruction: 'Depart quickly from here;
you must not remain. Śāriputra replied, 'I shall do as I am instructed.'"
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana immediately departed from that park, leading five hundred bhikṣus along the road.

When the Śākyas heard that the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had been sent by the World-Honored One, they went to where the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were, prostrated themselves at their feet, and said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Where do you intend to go? Śāriputra replied,
"We have been sent by the Tathāgata, each seeking a place of rest."
At that time, the Śākyas said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable ones!
Please attend closely; we shall offer our repentance before the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Śākyas went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
They addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will pardon the transgressions of these bhikṣus who have come from afar; we pray only that the World-Honored One will instruct them at the proper time."

Among them were bhikṣus who had come from afar and were beginners on the Path; having newly entered the Dharma, they had not yet beheld the Honored One’s countenance and thus harbored thoughts of regret and turning back, much like lush seedlings that fail to flourish if they do not encounter moisture.
"Now this bhikṣu is likewise; if he departs without beholding the Tathāgata, I fear he may develop a mind of regret.

At that time, the Brahmā King, knowing what was in the Tathāgata’s mind, vanished from the Brahma Heaven and arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Brahmā Śikhin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will graciously forgive the transgressions committed by this bhikṣu who has come from afar, and instruct him at the proper time!"
Among them, there may be bhikṣus who have not yet reached the ultimate goal and thus harbor thoughts of regret.
Failing to behold the countenance of the Tathāgata, they develop a wavering mind and return to their former occupations.
It is also like a newborn calf that loses its mother at birth; it becomes distressed and refuses to eat.
This case is just the same: if a newly ordained bhikṣu does not get to behold the Tathāgata, he will then distance himself from this True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the exhortation of the Śākya clansmen as well as the "Calf" parable of Brahmā Sahampati.
Then, as the World-Honored One looked about, Ānanda had this thought:
"The Tathāgata has accepted the exhortations of the various people and devas."
At that time, Ānanda went to where the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were and said to them:
"The Tathāgata wishes to meet with the Saṃgha; both devas and humans have all presented this matter to him."
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Each of you should gather up your robes and bowls and go together to where the World-Honored One is; for the Tathāgata has already accepted our repentance."
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, leading five hundred bhikṣus, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the Buddha asked Śāriputra, "I have just now dispatched the community of bhikṣus; what do you think of this? Śāriputra replied:
"Previously, when the Tathāgata sent forth the assembly of monks, I thought to myself:

'The Tathāgata delights in wandering through quiet and secluded places, dwelling alone in non-action; he does not enjoy being in the bustle of crowds. It is for this reason that he has dispatched the noble assembly.'"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"What thoughts did you subsequently give rise to?
At that time, whose burden were the Noble Assembly?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“At that time, World-Honored One,
I again gave rise to this thought:”
"I, too, shall dwell in seclusion and wander alone; I will not remain amidst the bustle of the marketplace.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Do not speak such words, nor give rise to this thought that you shall dwell in a place of seclusion."
"Now, regarding the burden of the noble assembly, is it not dependent upon the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying, "I have dispatched the various members of the Saṃgha; what thoughts do you have on this?"
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
“When the Tathāgata dismissed the assembly of monks, this thought occurred to me:
‘The Tathāgata wishes to dwell alone in the state of non-action; therefore, he has dismissed the noble assembly.’”
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"What further thought did you then conceive?
Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha:
"However, since the Tathāgata has now dispatched the assembly of noble ones, we should return and gather them so that they do not become dispersed.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: "Excellent!"
"Maudgalyāyana!
As you have said, among this assembly, there are only two who stand as preeminent leaders: myself and you alone.

From this day forward, Maudgalyāyana, you shall instruct and admonish the junior bhikṣus, causing them to dwell forever in a state of peace and security throughout the long night, and ensuring that none of them falter midway or fall back into the cycle of birth and death."
If a bhikṣu accomplishes nine qualities, he shall not attain growth in this present life.

What are these nine? Associating with and drawing near to evil friends; constantly delighting in aimless wandering; constantly harboring chronic ailments; being fond of accumulating wealth and goods; being greedily attached to robes and bowls; having much that is empty, dry, false, and distracted, lacking concentration; lacking the light of wisdom; failing to understand the meaning and intent [of the teachings]; and failing to receive instruction according to the proper time.
"Thus it is said, Maudgalyāyana!
If a bhikṣu accomplishes these nine things, he will not attain growth or any beneficial advancement in this present life.
However, if there is a bhikṣu who can accomplish these nine, he will achieve something of accomplishment."

What are these nine? They are: associating with virtuous friends; practicing the True Dharma without engaging in perverse activities; constantly dwelling in solitude rather than delighting in the world of men; having few illnesses and no afflictions; likewise, not accumulating many wealth or treasures; not being greedily attached to robes or alms bowls; practicing diligence with an undistracted mind; understanding the meaning upon hearing it without needing further instruction; and listening to the Dharma at all times without ever feeling weary or satiated.
"Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!
If a bhikṣu accomplishes these nine qualities, he will bring great benefit in this present life.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should mindfully and diligently go to instruct the bhikṣus, so that they may reach the state of the unconditioned throughout the long night [of saṃsāra]."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Always mindfully contemplate self-awakening; Do not cling to what is not the Dharma.
Practice that which accords with right conduct, And you shall cross over the perils of birth and death."
By doing this, one obtains this; by performing this, one reaps this merit.
Sentient beings have wandered for a long time; now they shall sever old age, sickness, and death.
Having accomplished what was to be done, they shall not practice again, nor shall they create further unwholesome deeds.
Such heedless people accomplish tainted actions (*sāsrava-karman*).
But if one possesses a diligent mind that is constantly held foremost in the heart,
and if they mutually instruct and admonish one another, they will become those who have transcended outflows (*anāsrava*).
"Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should instruct the bhikṣus in this way, and they should reflect upon and train themselves accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the most sublime Dharma to the bhikṣus, causing them to give rise to hearts of joy.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, more than sixty bhikṣus among that assembly attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in dependence upon a village, and wholesome qualities diminish while unwholesome qualities increase, that bhikṣu should train himself thus: ‘I am now residing in a village;

unwholesome qualities are increasing and wholesome qualities are gradually declining. My mindfulness is not one-pointed, I have not exhausted the outflows, and I have not reached the state of the unconditioned, the secure place.’”
‘The robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick that I have obtained were acquired only through great hardship.
That bhikṣu should train himself thus:

‘I now dwell in this village where unwholesome dharmas increase and wholesome dharmas perish; it was not for the sake of robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicines that I came to become a śramaṇa!’”
“The wish I sought has not yet borne fruit.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu should depart and dwell far away from villages.

“If there is another bhikṣu who dwells in dependence on a village, and for whom wholesome qualities increase and unwholesome qualities are extinguished, yet the robes, food and drink, and bedding he obtains are acquired only through diligent effort, that bhikṣu should train himself thus:”
"I now dwell in this village; wholesome qualities increase and unwholesome qualities are extinguished, yet the requisites for sustenance that I obtain are acquired only through diligent effort."
"I have not gone forth to study the Way and practice the holy life for the sake of clothing or bedding.
As for the goal I seek through my study of the Way, that dharma shall surely be accomplished; I ought to serve and provide offerings for it as long as my life lasts."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Regarding robes and food and drink, beds, bedding, and places of rest—
one should not harbor thoughts of greedy attachment, nor should one come back to this world."
It was not for the sake of robes that he left the home life to study the Way;
as for the purpose of studying the Way, he shall surely fulfill his aspiration.
The bhikṣu, in accordance with the occasion, dwelt in that village for the rest of his life.
Having attained parinirvāṇa there, he brings his life's foundation to an end.

At that time, if that bhikṣu dwells in a quiet place within a village where he frequents in the human realm, his wholesome dharmas will increase and unwholesome dharmas will naturally perish; that bhikṣu should remain in that village for as long as his life lasts and should not travel far away.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Does the Tathāgata not always say that the four great elements exist by depending on food, and also depend on the dharmas contemplated by the mind?"
All wholesome dharmas arise dependent upon the mind.
Furthermore, that bhikṣu dwells in dependence on a village, exhausting his spirit in the pursuit of food and clothing.
How, then, can he give rise to wholesome dharmas while dwelling in that village without traveling far?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are three kinds [of requisites]: robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the sick.
If a bhikṣu is single-mindedly mindful of these four types of offerings, yet what he desires is not fulfilled, this dependence constitutes suffering."
If one revives the mind of contentment and does not give rise to conceptual attachments, the devas and human beings will rejoice on their behalf.
Furthermore, O Bhikṣu!
You should train yourself in this way.
It is for this reason that I speak this meaning.
Therefore, Ānanda, a bhikṣu should be mindful of having few desires and being content.
Thus, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 4 (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Brāhmaṇa Garden.
At that time, when the hour had come, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village of Bālakalpa to beg for food.
At that moment, the evil Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"Now this śramaṇa wishes to enter the village to beg for food; I shall now employ a stratagem to instruct the men and women so that they will not give him any food."
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyān immediately announced to the people within the kingdom:
"Let no one give food to that śramaṇa Gautama.

Then, when the World-Honored One entered the village to beg for alms, none of the people spoke with the Tathāgata, nor was there anyone who came to attend to or make offerings to him; having failed to obtain any alms, the Tathāgata then departed from the village.
At that time, the evil Māra Pāpīyas went to where the Tathāgata was and asked the Buddha: "Śramaṇa!
Have you failed to obtain alms?"
The World-Honored One said:
"This is the doing of Māra, who has caused me to be unable to eat; you, too, shall soon receive the retribution for this, O Māra!"

Now listen to my words: within this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Krakucchanda Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha and Blessed One.
At that time, he too was dwelling in this village with a retinue of four hundred thousand followers.
Then, the evil Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"I have now sought an opportunity against this śramaṇa, but in the end I shall not succeed."
At that time, Māra again thought to himself:
"I shall now issue a command to the people of the village of Bārāṇasī, causing them not to give food to the śramaṇas."
At that time, the assembly of noble ones put on their robes and took up their alms bowls to enter the village for alms.
Then, those bhikṣus returned from the village without having obtained any food at all.
"At that time, that Buddha addressed the bhikṣus and spoke this sublime Dharma:
'In contemplating food, there are nine matters:
four kinds of human food and five kinds of non-human food.'"
What are the four kinds of food for human beings?

First is edible food (kabaḷīkāra-āhāra); second is contact-food (sparśa-āhāra); third is volition-food (manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra); and fourth is consciousness-food (vijñāna-āhāra). These are called the four kinds of food in the world.
What are these five kinds of food that manifest the supramundane?

First is the food of dhyāna; second is the food of aspiration; third is the food of mindfulness; fourth is the food of the eight liberations; and fifth is the food of joy. These are called the five kinds of food.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

These nine kinds of food are the manifestations of the supramundane; you should together apply yourselves with focused mindfulness to abandon the four kinds of food and seek the skillful means to prepare the five kinds of food.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having received those instructions from the Buddha, the monks disciplined themselves and prepared the five kinds of food.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was unable to find an opportunity. Then, Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"I am currently unable to gain an advantage over this śramaṇa through his skillful means; I shall now seek an opportunity through his eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, and mind."
"I shall now dwell among the villages and instruct the people so that the assembly of śramaṇas may obtain offerings and gain them, thereby increasing their provisions manifold;
I shall cause those bhikṣus to become greedily attached to these offerings, unable to relinquish them even for a moment, and further seek means through the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
“At that time, when it was the appointed hour, that Buddha and his śrāvakas donned their robes, took up their alms bowls, and entered the village to beg for food.

At that time, the people of the brahmin village provided the bhikṣus with clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick and infirm, ensuring they lacked for nothing; everyone came forward, grasping their saṃghāṭī robes, and forcibly offered them material goods.”
At that time, that Buddha taught this Dharma to the assembly of śrāvakas:
"Indeed, gain and offerings cause one to fall into evil realms and prevent one from reaching the state of the unconditioned."
"You, bhikṣus! Do not allow your minds to incline toward attachment and conceptualization regarding gain and offerings; you should instead contemplate their relinquishment.
Any bhikṣu who is attached to gain and offerings will not perfect the fivefold Dharma-body and will not be endowed with the virtue of the precepts."
"Therefore, bhikṣus! As for the mind of gain that has not yet arisen, you should ensure it does not arise;
as for the mind of gain that has already arisen, you must extinguish it immediately."
Thus it is, bhikkhus; you should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas immediately vanished and departed.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should practice a mind of loving-kindness and extensively disseminate this mind of loving-kindness.”
By practicing a mind of loving-kindness, all hearts of anger and malice shall naturally be eliminated.
Why is this so? A bhikṣu should know that in the past there was a ghost who was extremely wicked and violent; he came and sat upon the seat of Śakra Devānām Indra.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were filled with extreme indignation, saying:
"How can this ghost sit upon the bed of our lord?
Just as the gods gave rise to this anger, the ghost suddenly transformed into a person of exquisite beauty, his countenance far surpassing the ordinary.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra was seated in the Hall of Universal Assembly, enjoying himself with his jade maidens.
Then, a certain son of heaven went to where Śakra Devānām Indra was and addressed the Lord of the Devas, saying:

"O Kauśika, you should know that there is now an evil spirit seated upon your honored throne. At this moment, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three are filled with extreme wrath; yet as soon as the gods give rise to their anger, that spirit becomes increasingly handsome, its countenance surpassing that of ordinary beings."
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"This ghost must surely be a divine and wondrous spirit.
Then, Śakra Devānām-indra went to where the ghost was located; not far from him, he announced his own name:
"I am Śakra Devānām Indra, the lord of the devas.
When Śakra Devānām Indra thus declared his name, that evil spirit transformed into a hideous form with an loathsome countenance, and that evil spirit was instantly extinguished.
"Monks! By this means, you should know that one who practices a mind of loving-kindness does not abandon it, and its merit is such as this. Furthermore, monks!"

In the past, for seven years I constantly cultivated a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Throughout seven cycles of cosmic formation and destruction, I did not wander through birth and death. When a kalpa was about to perish, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; when a kalpa was about to form, I was born in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*). At times I became a Brahmā, presiding over the various heavens and governing ten thousand worlds; furthermore, thirty-seven times I manifested as Śakra Devānām Indra, and countless times I manifested as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
"Monks! By this means, you should know that one who practices a mind of loving-kindness possesses such merit as this.

Furthermore, one who practices a mind of loving-kindness, upon the dissolution of the body after death, will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven, remaining free from the three evil realms and departing from the eight difficult conditions."
Furthermore, one who practices loving-kindness is born in a central and righteous land.
Furthermore, one who practices loving-kindness has a handsome and upright countenance, with unimpaired faculties and a complete physical form.

Furthermore, those who practice a mind of loving-kindness personally behold the Tathāgata and serve the Buddhas; they take no pleasure in the household life and desire to leave home to study the Path. They don the three dharma-robes, shave their hair and beards, cultivate the dharma of a śramaṇa, and practice the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya).
“Bhikṣus, you should know that it is just like a diamond: if a person were to take it and eat it, it would never be digested, but would necessarily pass through.

It is the same for one who practices a mind of loving-kindness: if a Tathāgata appears in the world, they will necessarily attain the Way, cultivate the unsurpassed holy life, and—knowing according to reality—realize:
‘Birth and death are exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence.’”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Should the Tathāgata not appear in the world, where would those sons of good family—who do not delight in the household life—turn?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If the Tathāgata does not appear in the world, yet a son of good family takes no pleasure in the household life, shaves his hair and beard, and dwells in a secluded place, disciplining himself through self-cultivation, he will, right there, exhaust all outflows and achieve the state of being without outflows."
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, World-Honored One?
If those people personally cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and the practices of the Three Vehicles, where will they be reborn?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As you have said, I constantly teach the practices of the three vehicles.
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present throughout the three periods of time shall likewise fully teach the Dharma of the three vehicles."

Ānanda, you should know that there will come a time when the appearance and lifespan of sentient beings gradually diminish; their physical forms become emaciated and weak, and they no longer possess majestic power. They will abound in anger, jealousy, hatred, delusion, deceit, and guile, and their conduct will be untruthful.
Furthermore, there may be those of sharp faculties who are quick-tempered, engaging in mutual contention and dispute,
or even harming one another with their fists, tiles, stones, swords, or staves.
At that time, when the various classes of sentient beings grasped blades of grass, they immediately became swords and blades with which they severed one another’s life-faculties.

Among them, those who practiced a mind of loving-kindness were free from anger; yet seeing this calamitous transformation, they all harbored fear and fled together, leaving that evil place. In the midst of the mountains and wilds, their hair and beards were naturally shaved off, and they donned the three dharma-robes. They cultivated the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya), disciplining themselves through self-cultivation until they exhausted the outflows of the mind and attained liberation. Entering the realm of the outflow-free, they each said to one another: "We have already conquered our enemies."
"Ānanda, you should know that he shall be named Most Victorious.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To which division does that person belong?"
"Is he of the Śrāvaka section, the Pratyekabuddha section, or the Buddha section?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"That person’s proper designation is indeed the Pratyekabuddha section."
The reason for this is that these individuals have all accumulated various merits, practiced the roots of manifold goodness, cultivated the pure Four Noble Truths, and discerned all phenomena.
Now, that which constitutes the practice of wholesome dharmas is precisely this mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Why is this so? Because practicing benevolence and exercising loving-kindness, this virtue is vast and great.

In the past, I donned this armor of loving-kindness and benevolence, subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials, sat beneath the King of Trees, and attained the Unsurpassed Way. By this expedient means, I know that loving-kindness is foremost; loving-kindness is the most supreme dharma.
Ānanda, you should know that for this reason it is called "Most Victorious.
The virtue of one who practices a mind of loving-kindness is such as this, beyond all measure and calculation.
You should seek skillful means and cultivate a mind of loving-kindness.
"In this way, Ānanda,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his secluded chamber early in the morning and went to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Your faculties are now pure and your countenance differs from that of ordinary people; in what samādhi are you currently dwelling?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I constantly dwell in the *śūnyatā-samādhi*.”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: “Excellent! Excellent!”
Śāriputra! You are indeed able to roam within the *śūnyatā-samādhi*. Why is this so?

Because among all the *śūnyatā-samādhis*, this is the foremost. When a bhikṣu roams in the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, he reckons that there is no self, person, or life-span, nor does he perceive the existence of sentient beings.
Furthermore, one does not perceive the beginning or end of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); having failed to perceive them, one does not create the root of conditioned phenomena.
Once there are no conditioned phenomena, one no longer undergoes existence (*bhava*).
Having no further existence, one no longer experiences the retribution of suffering or pleasure.
“Śāriputra, you should know that in the past, before I had attained the Way of the Buddha, while sitting beneath the King of Trees, I thought to myself:
‘For what reason do these classes of sentient beings fail to obtain any dharma, such that they wander through birth and death and cannot achieve liberation?’”
At that time, I further thought to myself:
"If there is no emptiness samādhi, one will merely wander through birth and death and fail to attain ultimate liberation."

Although this samādhi of emptiness exists, sentient beings have not yet mastered it; they give rise to thoughts of attachment and conceptualization, and by giving rise to worldly perceptions, they consequently undergo the lot of birth and death.
If one attains this emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi) and has no further aspirations, one then attains the wishlessness samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi).

By attaining the wishlessness samādhi, one does not seek death here or birth there; when all ideations have ceased, that practitioner may further attain the signlessness samādhi (animitta-samādhi) for his enjoyment.
"These classes of sentient beings all wander through birth and death because they do not attain samādhi.
Having thus observed all phenomena, he immediately attained the samādhi of emptiness; having attained the samādhi of emptiness, he then realized anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, having attained the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), I gazed upon the Bodhi tree for seven days and seven nights without once blinking my eyes.
Śāriputra, by this expedient means you should know that among all samādhis, the samādhi of emptiness is the foremost; it is the king of samādhis. This king of samādhis is the samādhi of emptiness.
Therefore, Śāriputra, you should seek skillful means to accomplish the samādhi of emptiness. Thus it is, Śāriputra!
"One should train in this way.
At that time, Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7 (Seven) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a householder in the city of Rājagṛha named Śrīgupta, who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures—gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, and coral—beyond all calculation.
Furthermore, he held the Buddha-dharma in low esteem and served only the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas.
The king and his ministers all knew of this.

At that time, the non-Buddhist brahmins and nirgranthas—both householders and renunciants—began to disparage themselves, saying, "We have a self; we have a personal body. Then the six teachers and their followers all assembled together and deliberated:
"Now the śramaṇa Gautama knows all things and possesses omniscience, yet we receive no offerings while this śramaṇa receives many. We must devise a stratagem so that he shall receive no offerings."
"We shall go to the house of Śrīgupta and instruct that elder to employ expedient means.
At that time, the non-Buddhist ascetics, the Nirgranthas, and those six teachers went to the house of the elder Śrīgupta and said to him:
"O man of great lineage, you should know that you were born from Brahmā; you are a son of Brahmā, one who brings much benefit."
"You should now go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and, out of compassion for us, invite the śramaṇa and his assembly of bhikṣus to a household feast.
Furthermore, order a great fire-pit to be made inside the house and kindle it until the flames blaze intensely; put poison in all the food and invite him to eat."
If the śramaṇa Gautama possesses all-encompassing knowledge and knows the affairs of the three periods of time, he will not accept the invitation;

but if he lacks all-encompassing knowledge, he will surely accept it, and he will lead his disciples so that they are all consumed by fire, while gods and humans attain peace and are free from the harm of fire.

At that time, Śrīgupta remained silent and followed the words of the six teachers; he immediately left the city and went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrating his head at the Buddha’s feet. Holding a mind filled with various poisons, he addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my invitation.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in his mind, accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Then, seeing that the Tathāgata had accepted the invitation through his silence, Śrīgupta rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew.
Then Zhongdao thought to himself:
"What my six teachers have taught is indeed true; yet this śramaṇa does not know what is in my mind, and I shall surely be consumed by a great fire."

At that time, Śrīgupta immediately returned home and ordered a large pit to be dug and a great fire to be lit. He further commanded that various kinds of food and drink be prepared, all of which were mixed with poison. He also constructed a great fiery pit outside the gate and ignited a massive fire; upon this fire, he arranged couches and seats, placing lethal poisons within all the food, and announced:
"The time has come."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the hour had come, donned his robes and took up his bowl. Surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, he proceeded to that house and further instructed the community of bhikṣus:
"None of you shall go before me; nor shall any of you sit before me."
"Furthermore, none shall eat before me.
At that time, the people of the city of Rājagṛha heard that Śrīgupta had prepared a great pit of fire and poisoned food, and invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
The fourfold assembly all wept, saying:
"Could it be that harm will come to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus?
Some even went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray that the World-Honored One does not go to that householder’s home; furthermore, that man has prepared a great pit of fire and also poisoned food.
The Buddha told him:
“Do not harbor fear, people; the Tathāgata can never be harmed by another.”

Even if fire from within Jambudvīpa were to reach as far as the Brahma Heaven, it still could not burn me; how much less so this small fire that seeks to harm the Tathāgata—such a thing is simply impossible.
"The lay follower knows that I have no further intent to harm.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, entered the city of Rājagṛha and arrived at the house of the elder.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"None of you shall enter the householder's home first, nor shall you eat first;
you must wait until the Tathāgata has eaten, and only then may you eat."
At that time, as soon as the World-Honored One placed his foot upon the threshold, the fire pit was spontaneously transformed into a bathing pool, exceedingly cool and refreshing;

it was filled with various flowers, and lotuses also grew there, as large as chariot wheels, with stalks made of the seven treasures, while other lotuses likewise sprang up, where the king of bees sported.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-devarāja, and the four Great Kings, as well as the gandharvas, asuras, yakṣas, spirits, and others, seeing these lotus flowers grow within the fire pit, each offered their congratulations!
With different voices but a single tone, they each declared:
"He is the foremost among the Victorious Ones.
At that time, various heterodox practitioners and followers of diverse schools had gathered at the house of that elder.
At that time, when the upāsakas and upāsikās had witnessed the Tathāgata’s transformations, they leaped for joy with such intensity that they could not contain themselves;
whereas the heretics and followers of other paths, having seen the Tathāgata’s transformations, were filled with profound sorrow and distress.
The various honored deities and heavenly beings in the space above scattered all kinds of named flowers upon the body of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One walked through the air at a height of four inches above the ground and arrived at the house of the elder.
Wherever the Tathāgata raised his foot, lotuses as large as chariot wheels sprang up.
At that time, the World-Honored One turned to the right and addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you, tread upon these lotuses."
Then, all the śrāvakas ascended from atop the lotuses to the house of the elder.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke an ancient parable, saying:

"Throughout my past lives, I have made offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, serving, honoring, and revering them without ever failing in the holy intent. By virtue of this vow of utmost sincerity, may these seats all become firm and stable."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to first touch the seat with their hands and only then sit down; this is my instruction."
At that time, the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus all took their seats; beneath each seat, lotus flowers sprang forth, exceedingly fragrant.
Then, seeing such a miraculous transformation by the Tathāgata, Śrīgupta thought to himself:
"I have been led astray by the heterodox teachers and scholars, losing my conduct as a human being and forever losing the path to the heavens."
My mind was in turmoil, like having drunk a mixture of poisons; I would surely have headed for these three evil realms.
Truly, the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is difficult to encounter.
Having realized this, he immediately shed tears, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me leave to repent my transgressions, so that I may reform the past and cultivate the future.
I am aware of my own faults in having disturbed the Tathāgata.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance, and that I shall not commit such offenses again.”
The Buddha said: "Householder!
