By repenting and abandoning your original intent, you are now able to recognize for yourself that you have offended the Tathāgata."
Within the Dharma of the noble ones, there is great vastness; I grant you permission to reform your errors and abandon them in accordance with the Dharma.
I now accept your repentance; henceforth, do not commit such offenses again.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
At that moment, King Ajātaśatru heard that the householder Śrīgupta had prepared a great pit of fire and food mixed with various poisons, intending to harm the Tathāgata.
Having heard this, his anger flared up, and he addressed his ministers, saying:
"I must utterly destroy all those on the land of Jambudvīpa who bear the same name as this man, Śirigupta."
Furthermore, having recollected the merits of the Tathāgata, Ajātaśatru wept with tears streaming down his face; he removed his celestial crown and addressed his ministers, saying:
"What use have I now for living?"
"If the Tathāgata were to be consumed by fire, the community of bhikṣus would all likewise be burned.
You must come quickly to the house of the elder to behold the Tathāgata."
At that time, Prince Jīvaka addressed King Ajātaśatru: "Great King!
Do not harbor sorrow or anxiety, nor give rise to evil thoughts."
The reason for this is that the Tathāgata can never be harmed by others.
Today, the householder Śrīgupta shall become a disciple of the Tathāgata.
I only pray that Your Majesty will go and witness this transformation.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having been exhorted and instructed by Jīvaka, mounted a great elephant from the Snowy Mountains and immediately proceeded to the house of the householder Śrīgupta; dismounting from the elephant, he entered the interior of Śrīgupta’s residence.
At that time, a great multitude of eighty-four thousand people gathered outside the gate.
Then, King Ajātaśatru, seeing the lotus flower as large as a chariot wheel, was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself, and he spoke these words:
"May the Tathāgata forever triumph over all Māras."
He addressed Prince Jīvaka, saying: "Excellent, Jīvaka!"
"Thus I now believe in such an essential teaching of the Tathāgata.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru saw the light emanating from the Tathāgata’s mouth and also beheld the Tathāgata’s exceptionally sublime countenance; he was filled with such immense joy that he could not contain himself.
At that time, the householder Śrīgupta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The food I have prepared is entirely poisoned; I only pray that the World-Honored One will pause for a moment, for I shall now provide another meal."
"The reason for this is that we must not allow the body of the Tathāgata to undergo any increase or decrease.
The Buddha told the householder:
"The Tathāgata and his disciples can never be harmed by others; however, householder, once your food is prepared, provide it at the appropriate time."
At that time, the elder personally served various kinds of food and drink.
Then, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"In the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, with utmost sincerity, The poison of harm is eliminated without remainder."
The Buddhas have no poison; through the utmost sincerity, the Buddha destroys poison.
Through the utmost sincerity, the Dharma and the Saṅgha destroy poison without remainder.
The Buddhas have no poison; through the utmost sincerity, the Dharma destroys poison.
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are supreme sincerity; they eliminate all poison without remainder.
The Buddhas possess no poison, and the Sangha of supreme sincerity eliminates poison.
Greed, hatred, and delusion—these are the three poisons of the world.
The Tathāgata is forever free from poison; through the Buddha’s utmost sincerity, he destroys poison.
The poisons of desire, lust, and hatred—these are the poisons of the three worlds.
The Dharma of the Tathāgata is without poison; through the Dharma’s utmost sincerity, it destroys poison.
"Desire, lust, and hatred are poisons; there are these three poisons in the world.
The Saṃgha of the Tathāgata is without poison; the Saṃgha of utmost sincerity destroys poison.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, he then ate the food mixed with poison.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"None of you shall eat first; you must wait until the Tathāgata has finished eating before you eat."
At that time, the elder personally served various kinds of food and drink, making offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
Then, seeing that the Tathāgata had finished eating, the elder Śrīgupta removed the bowl and vessel, took another small seat, and sat before the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded a subtle and wondrous discourse to the elder and the assembly of eighty-four thousand people. This discourse consisted of:

a teaching on generosity, a teaching on ethical discipline, and a teaching on rebirth in the heavens; [he spoke of] the impurity of sensual desires, the great calamity of lustful indulgence, and the excellence of the way of renunciation as true happiness.

The Tathāgata, observing the minds of that elder and the eighty-four thousand followers—seeing their minds opened and liberated, free from further defilements—proclaimed for the entire assembly of eighty-four thousand the Dharma constantly taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, extensively analyzing and explaining these practices.

At that time, while still on their seats, all the people had their defilements and impurities completely exhausted and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; it was just as a new cloth easily takes on dye.

At that moment, the commoners were likewise; each, upon their seat, perceived the path, saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma, discerned all phenomena, crossed over all doubts, and attained fearlessness. They no longer served other teachers, but took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and received the five precepts.
At that time, the householder Śrīgupta, knowing for himself that he had attained the path of the stream-enterer, came forward and said to the Buddha:
"It would be better to give poison to the Tathāgata and obtain a great fruit of retribution, than to give nectar to other heterodox teachers and incur further sin."
The reason for this is that I have now invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus with poisoned food, and in this present life I have obtained this verification.
For a long night I was deluded by these non-Buddhists, and thus I gave rise to such a thought toward the Tathāgata; those who serve non-Buddhist heterodox teachers all fall into extreme views.
The Buddha told the householder:
“It is exactly as you have said; there is no difference—it is that all have been deceived by others.
At that time, Śrīgupta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer place my trust in these non-Buddhist heterodox teachers, nor shall I permit the fourfold assembly to provide them with offerings while at home.
The Buddha told the elder:
"Do not speak such words."

The reason for this is that you now constantly make offerings to these various non-Buddhist practitioners and give alms to animals; the merit of such acts is immeasurable, how much more so when it concerns human beings?
If any non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners should ask,
"Whose disciple is Śrīgupta? how would you answer them?
At that time, Śrīgupta rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Brave and liberated, now receiving this human body, he is the seventh rishi and a disciple of Śākyamuni.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, householder!"

"You are indeed able to speak these subtle and wondrous praises. At that time, the World-Honored One again expounded the profound Dharma for the elder, and immediately spoke this verse of praise: "Sacrifice to fire is supreme; The hymns of the *Ṛgveda* are the best. The Brahmin is the highest among men; The cow is the most excellent of quadrupeds. Soma is the king of plants; The sun is the lord of the heavens. The son is the foremost of kinsmen; And the wife is the best of friends. The son is the support of one’s kin; The father is the support of his children. The husband is the support of his wife; And the teacher is the support of the student. The mother is the highest of all women; The father is the greatest of all men.

There is no friend like a son, And no refuge like the Dharma. The Dharma is the supreme refuge; The Dharma is the ultimate reliance. The Dharma protects those who practice it; The Dharma leads one to the heavenly realms."
Among humans, the king is the most honored; among all streams, the ocean is the source;
among stars, the moon is the most bright; and among luminaries, the sun is supreme.
Throughout the zenith, nadir, and the four quarters, among all classes of beings possessing form—
"Among all devas and the world, the Buddha is the foremost;
those who seek to obtain merit should make offerings to the Three Buddhas.
Having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One rose from his seat.
At that time, Śrīgupta and all those assembled who had heard what the Buddha taught rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 41; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 42.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Forty-Six: On Binding and Prohibiting (Kṣepa-pratiṣedha). (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are ten meritorious benefits for which the Tathāgata proclaims the prohibitions and precepts to the bhikṣus.”
What are the ten? They are:
serving the noble assembly with harmony and compliance;
and ensuring the well-being of the noble assembly.
To subdue wicked people;
to ensure that conscientious bhikṣus are not troubled;
and to cause those without faith to establish the root of faith.
It causes those who already possess faith to increase it twofold;
it enables one to exhaust all outflows within this present life;
and it ensures that the maladies of the outflows in future lives are entirely eliminated.
Furthermore, he causes the True Dharma to abide long in the world;
he constantly reflects and contemplates upon what skillful means might cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time.
This, O Bhikṣu, is called...
The Tathāgata has proclaimed the ten qualities of the precepts to the bhikṣus. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to fulfill these precepts and ensure that they are not lost.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are ten qualities of the abodes of the noble ones, wherein the noble ones of the three times always dwell.
What are these ten? In this regard, bhikkhus:”

Having eliminated five matters and accomplished six matters, constantly guarding one matter, he protects the fourfold assembly; observing those who are weak and inferior, he approaches them with impartiality; he is correctly oriented toward the outflow-free state, relying upon bodily conduct, with his mind well-liberated through wisdom.
"What are the five things that have been eliminated by a bhikṣu?
In this regard, a bhikṣu has severed the five fetters.
Thus, these five things have been eliminated."
"How does a bhikṣu accomplish the six matters?
In this regard, a bhikṣu upholds the six weighty dharmas.
In this way, a bhikṣu accomplishes the six matters."
“How does a bhikṣu constantly guard one thing?
In this regard, a bhikṣu constantly guards the mind—whether it be with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—up to the gateway of nirvāṇa.”
In this way, a bhikṣu constantly guards one thing.
How does a bhikṣu protect the fourfold assembly?
In this regard, a bhikṣu accomplishes the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
In this way, one protects and sustains the fourfold assembly.
How does a bhikṣu contemplate what is inferior and weak?
In this regard, the bhikṣu has already exhausted all conditioned phenomena of birth and death.
In this way, a bhikkhu associates with equanimity; herein, the bhikkhu’s three fetters are completely exhausted—this is called a bhikkhu who associates with equanimity.
“How does a bhikkhu rightly incline toward the outflow-free?”
Thereupon, the bhikṣu eliminates conceit.
In this way, the bhikṣu is correctly directed toward the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
"How does a bhikṣu rely upon bodily conduct?
Thus, the bhikṣu has eliminated ignorance.
In this way, the bhikṣu relies upon bodily conduct.
How does the bhikṣu’s mind attain wholesome liberation?
Thereupon, the bhikṣu has utterly exhausted craving.
In this way, the bhikṣu’s mind is well-liberated.
"What is the bhikṣu’s liberation through wisdom?
Thereupon, the bhikṣu contemplates the truth of suffering, the truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path; he knows them as they truly are.
In this way, the bhikṣu is liberated through wisdom.
"Monks, this is called the dwelling place of the ten matters of the noble ones.
In the past, the noble ones also dwelt in this place; they dwelt by dwelling in accordance with the proper way."

Therefore, bhikṣus! Mindfully abandon five things, accomplish six dharmas, guard one dharma, protect the fourfold assembly, observe those who are weak, maintain impartial intimacy, and correctly direct yourself toward the outflow-free state. Relying on bodily conduct, you shall attain liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata has attained the ten powers; knowing himself to be unattached, he can roar the lion's roar amidst the great assembly and turn the unsurpassed Brahma-wheel to deliver sentient beings."

That is to say: "This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form, this is the escape from form. One contemplates feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness: consciousness, the origin of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, and the escape from consciousness. Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, there is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving; with craving as condition, there is clinging; with clinging as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, there is birth; with birth as condition, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair, beyond measure.

Therefore, regarding this body of the five aggregates, there exists this conditioned phenomenon: when this ceases, that ceases; when this is absent, that is absent. With the exhaustion of ignorance, volitional formations are exhausted; with the exhaustion of volitional formations, consciousness is exhausted; with the exhaustion of consciousness, name-and-form are exhausted; with the exhaustion of name-and-form, the six sense bases are exhausted; with the exhaustion of the six sense bases, contact is exhausted; with the exhaustion of contact, feeling is exhausted; with the exhaustion of feeling, craving is exhausted; with the exhaustion of craving, clinging is exhausted; with the exhaustion of clinging, existence is exhausted; with the exhaustion of existence, birth is exhausted; with the exhaustion of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair are all completely eliminated.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that my Dharma is exceedingly vast, boundless and unfathomable; it severs all doubts and establishes one in the security of the True Dharma.

If a son or daughter of good family applies themselves with diligent effort without deficiency—even if their bodies wither away—they shall never abandon the practice of vigor, keeping their minds focused and never forgetting.”

The practice of the Dharma of suffering is extremely difficult; one should delight in dwelling in seclusion, contemplating in stillness, and never abandon the dhūta practices, just as the Tathāgata now dwells in the present, excellently cultivating the holy life (brahmacarya).

Therefore, bhikṣus! When you observe yourselves, contemplate the subtle and wondrous Dharma, and further examine two meanings; practice without negligence so as to bring forth the fruit and reach the state of the extinction of the nectar of immortality.

If one receives from others offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for illness, such labor shall not be in vain; it shall also cause one's parents to obtain their karmic rewards, as one serves, pays homage to, and makes offerings to the Buddhas.
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The Tathāgata has accomplished the ten powers and attained the four fearlessnesses, and is able to roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
What are the ten powers?
In this regard, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is what is possible, and he knows as it truly is what is impossible.”
"Furthermore, in the domain of the Tathāgata, he knows the causes and conditions by which other sentient beings receive their retributions.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows various kinds of elements (*dhātu*), various kinds of bases (*dhāraṇa*), and various kinds of sense-fields (*āyatana*); he knows them as they truly are."
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows various kinds of liberation and immeasurable liberations as they truly are.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows the extent of the wisdom of other sentient beings as it truly is."
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows the thoughts in the minds of other sentient beings as they truly are:
he knows a mind with desire as a mind with desire, and a mind without desire as a mind without desire;
he knows a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, and a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred."
When there is a mind of delusion, one knows there is a mind of delusion; when there is no mind of delusion, one knows there is no mind of delusion.
When there is a mind of craving, one knows there is a mind of craving; when there is no mind of craving, one knows there is no mind of craving.
When there is a mind of grasping, one knows there is a mind of grasping; when there is no mind of grasping, one knows there is no mind of grasping.
With a distracted mind, one knows there is a distracted mind; with an undistracted mind, one knows there is no distracted mind.
With a scattered mind, one knows there is a scattered mind; with an unscattered mind, one knows there is no scattered mind.
With a limited mind, one knows there is a limited mind; with an unlimited mind, one knows there is no limited mind.
When there is a vast mind, one knows there is a vast mind; when there is no vast mind, one knows there is no vast mind.
When there is an immeasurable mind, one knows there is an immeasurable mind; when there is a limited mind, one knows there is a limited mind, knowing them as they truly are.
With a concentrated mind, one knows there is a concentrated mind; with a non-concentrated mind, one knows there is no concentrated mind.
With a liberated mind, one knows there is a liberated mind; with a non-liberated mind, one knows there is no liberated mind.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata fully knows the paths of the minds of all beings as they pass through their destinies—whether for one, two, three, four, five, ten, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred billion, or immeasurable births; through kalpas of formation, kalpas of destruction, or countless kalpas of both formation and destruction. He knows: 'In the past, I was born in that place; my name was such, my surname was such; I ate this kind of food, experienced such suffering and pleasure, and my lifespan was of such length. Dying here, I was born there; dying there, I was born here.'"
He recollects such countless matters of his own past lives.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata knows the destinies of birth and death of sentient beings; with the divine eye, he observes the various classes of beings—their beautiful and ugly forms, their happy and miserable realms—and he fully knows all that they have sown according to their conduct.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who commit evil through body, speech, and mind, slandering the noble ones and performing deeds based on false views; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the hells.

Alternatively, there are sentient beings who perform good through body, speech, and mind, do not slander the noble ones, and constantly practice right view; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in a happy place, in the heavens. This is called the purity of the divine eye, by which one observes the conduct of various classes of sentient beings and the destinations to which they go.
"Furthermore, the Tathāgata has exhausted all taints and attained the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom that are free from taints;
birth and death have come to an end, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows as it truly is that there will be no further existence."

It is said that the Tathāgata possesses these ten powers, which are called "unattached"; having attained the four fearlessnesses, he utters the lion's roar amidst the great assembly and turns the Brahma-wheel.
"How does the Tathāgata attain the four fearlessnesses?
If one were to say that the Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment, yet there exists any sentient being who could claim he does not know [all things], such a case is impossible;
furthermore, if any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should come to revile the Buddha, claiming he has not attained perfect enlightenment, such a case is likewise impossible."
Because such a case does not exist, I have attained peace and security.

"Furthermore, today I have spoken so as to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*). Even if any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, or Māra were to come and say that I have not yet exhausted the outflows, there would be no basis for such a claim;
because there is no such basis, I have attained peace and security."
"Furthermore, regarding the Dharma I have taught, by which the noble ones attain the way of escape and, according to reality, reach the end of suffering:
were any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, or even Māras to come and claim that one has not yet reached the end of suffering, there would be no such possibility;
because there is no such possibility, one attains peace and security."

"Furthermore, regarding what I have taught as the internal phenomena that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies—if any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas should come and wish to declare them otherwise, there is no such possibility."
"Monks, this is called the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses.
Suppose there were followers of other paths and heterodox teachers who said:"
"What powers does that śramaṇa Gautama possess, and what fearlessnesses does he have, such that he claims for himself the title of the Unattached and Most Honorable One?
You should take these ten powers and go to report them to him."
Furthermore, if non-Buddhist heterodox teachers should again say,
"We too have accomplished the ten powers," you bhikṣus should further question them as follows:
"What are your ten powers?
At that time, the non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners were unable to answer, and their confusion only increased.
This was because I have never seen any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who, except for the Tathāgata, could claim for themselves the attainment of the four fearlessnesses.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should seek skillful means to accomplish the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are ten unrighteous things associated with being close to a state.”
What are the ten? In this case, a person conceives a malicious intent toward the state, desiring to kill the king; due to this conspiracy, the king’s life comes to an end.
The people of that realm then think to themselves:
"This śramaṇa and ascetic come and go repeatedly; this must surely be the doing of that śramaṇa.
This is called the first difficulty of a non-dharma relative who harms the state.
"Furthermore, when ministers rebel and are captured by the king, they are all taken and executed.
At that time, the people will think:
'These śramaṇas and practitioners come and go so frequently; this must surely be the doing of those śramaṇas.'"
"This is called the second difficulty of entering a country through unrighteousness.
Furthermore, when the state loses its wealth and treasures,
the keepers of the storehouse will again have this thought:"
"Since I have always guarded these treasures and no other person has entered here, it must be the śramaṇa who has taken them.
This is called the third difficulty for a śramaṇa entering a country in an unrighteous manner.
"Furthermore, the king’s daughter was in the prime of her youth and had not yet been married when she became pregnant.
At that time, the people thought to themselves:
'No one else has come and gone here; this must be the work of the śramaṇa.'"
"This is called the fourth calamity of a kingdom through unrighteous intimacy.
Furthermore, suppose the king suffers from a grave illness and takes another person's medicine.
At that time, the people will again think:"
“‘There is no one else among them; this must surely be the work of the śramaṇa.
This is called the fifth calamity of unrighteousness that harms the state.
‘Furthermore, the king and his ministers each vie with one another in contention, mutually harming each other.’”
At that time, the people thought to themselves:

"These ministers were originally in harmony, yet now they are contending with one another; this cannot have been done by anyone else, but must surely be the work of śramaṇas and Daoist practitioners."
This is called the sixth calamity of a kingdom through unrighteous intimacy with its neighbors.
"Furthermore, when two nations are at war, each vying for victory, the people will think:
'These śramaṇas and practitioners have frequently come within our borders; this must surely be the work of those śramaṇas.'"
This is called the seventh difficulty of unrighteousness that harms the kingdom:
"Furthermore, a king who originally delighted in giving and shared his wealth with the people later becomes stingy and regretful, refusing to practice generosity."
At that time, the people each had this thought:
"Our sovereign was formerly fond of giving, yet now he has become stingy and greedy, lacking any intention to give; this must surely be the work of the śramaṇa."
This is called the eighth calamity of unrighteousness that harms the state:
"Furthermore, a king constantly takes the wealth and property of his subjects in accordance with the True Dharma, yet later takes their wealth and treasures unrighteously."
At that time, the people each conceived this thought:

"Our sovereign originally took the wealth and treasures of the people according to the Dharma; now he again takes the wealth and treasures of the people through unrighteous means. This must surely be the doing of the śramaṇa."
This is called the ninth difficulty: the unrighteousness of being close to the state.
"Furthermore, the people of the land may all contract an epidemic; this is entirely due to past conditions."
At that time, the people each had this thought:
"In the past we were free from illness, but now each of us has fallen sick; with the dead filling the roads, this must surely be caused by the sorcery of these śramaṇas."
"This is called the tenth difficulty of a country having unrighteous relatives.
These, monks, are called the ten difficulties of entering a country with unrighteousness."
Therefore, bhikṣus! Do not again give rise to the thought of associating with states.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If a king fails to accomplish ten qualities, he will not endure for long, and there will be many thieves and bandits.”
What are the ten? At that time, the king is stingy and greedy; for even a minor and trivial matter, he gives rise to anger and fails to consider what is right and reasonable.
If a king possesses this first quality, he shall not endure for long, and his kingdom will abound in thieves and bandits.

"Furthermore, that king is greedily attached to wealth and property and refuses to practice generosity; this is called the second dharma by which a king, having accomplished it, shall not endure for long."

"Furthermore, that king does not accept the admonitions of others; he is violent and cruel toward people and lacks a heart of compassion. This is called the third quality by which one cannot endure for long."

"Furthermore, that king unjustly oppresses his subjects, arbitrarily seizing and imprisoning them within jails from which there is no prospect of release; this is called the fourth condition by which he cannot endure for long."
"Furthermore, if a king possesses the characteristics of unrighteousness and his ministers do not follow correct conduct—these are called the five factors by which he cannot endure for long.
Furthermore, if that king is greedily attached to the beauty of others and abandons his own wife—these are called the six factors by which that king fails to endure for long."
"Furthermore, if a king is fond of and addicted to wine, neglecting his official duties, this is called the seventh quality by which he fails to endure for long.
Furthermore, if a king is fond of and addicted to singing, dancing, and amusements, neglecting his official duties, this is called the eighth quality by which he fails to endure for long."
"Furthermore, if a king constantly suffers from chronic illness and has no days of robust health, this is called the ninth condition by which he cannot endure for long."

"Furthermore, when a king does not trust his loyal and filial ministers, his wings and feathers are few, and he lacks powerful assistants; this is called a king who, having accomplished these ten things, cannot endure for long."

“Now, the community of bhikṣus is likewise; if they accomplish ten dharmas, they do not increase their roots of goodness or merit, and when their bodies perish and their lives end, they enter into hell.”
What are the ten dharmas?
In this regard, a bhikṣu does not uphold the precepts, nor does he possess a mind of reverence; this is called the first dharma accomplished by a bhikṣu, whereby he cannot attain the ultimate goal.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who does not serve the Buddha and does not believe in the true words—this is called the second dharma accomplished by a bhikṣu, by which he cannot abide for long."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who does not serve the Dharma and neglects the various rules of discipline is said to have fulfilled the third condition by which a bhikṣu cannot remain for long."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu serves the noble Saṅgha while constantly maintaining a humble mind and does not trust their reception [of his offerings]. This is called the fourth quality by which a bhikṣu fails to achieve long-term stability."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who is attached to gain and profit, and whose mind does not relinquish them—this is called the fifth quality by which a bhikṣu fails to abide for long."

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu who has not studied much and does not diligently apply himself to recitation, study, and practice—this is called a bhikkhu who, having accomplished six qualities, cannot endure for long."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who does not associate with virtuous friends but constantly associates with evil friends—this is called the seventh dharma by which a bhikṣu cannot endure for long."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who constantly delights in worldly affairs and does not contemplate seated meditation—this is called the eighth factor by which a bhikṣu cannot endure for long.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu who is attached to calculation and arithmetic, turning away from the Path and returning to secular life, and failing to practice the True Dharma—this is called the ninth factor by which a bhikṣu cannot endure for long."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu does not delight in practicing the holy life and is greedily attached to impurity; this is called the tenth quality of a bhikṣu by which he cannot endure for long."
"Monks, it is said that one who accomplishes these ten qualities will certainly fall into the three evil destinies and not be reborn in a favorable realm.
If a king accomplishes ten qualities, he shall dwell long in this world."
What are these ten?

In this regard, the king does not become attached to wealth or possessions, does not give rise to anger, and furthermore, he does not harbor thoughts of malice or resentment over trivial matters. This is called the first dharma, by which he attains long-lasting stability.
"Furthermore, when a king accepts the admonitions of his ministers and does not oppose their words, this is called accomplishing the second dharma, whereby he shall endure for a long time."
"Furthermore, if a king is always fond of practicing generosity and shares his joy with the people, this is called the third [quality].
To acquire things through the Dharma and not through what is contrary to the Dharma—this is called the fourth quality by which he attains long-lasting stability."
"Furthermore, that king does not become attached to the wives of others and constantly protects his own wife; this is called accomplishing the fifth dharma, by which he attains long endurance."
"Furthermore, the king does not drink alcohol, and his mind is not deranged or confused; this is called accomplishing the sixth quality, by which he attains long-lasting stability."
"Furthermore, when a king does not engage in frivolous amusement and subdues external enemies, this is called accomplishing the seventh quality, by which he attains long-lasting stability."
"Furthermore, when a king governs according to the Dharma and never acts with partiality or crookedness, this is called accomplishing the eighth quality, whereby he attains long-lasting stability.

"Furthermore, when a king lives in harmony with his ministers and there is no contention between them, this is called the fulfillment of the ninth quality, by which he attains long-lasting stability."
"Furthermore, when a king is free from illness and possesses great physical vigor, this is called the tenth quality by which he attains long life.
If a king accomplishes these ten qualities, he will attain long life and it shall be impossible for him to be overcome."
“The community of bhikṣus is also like this: if they accomplish ten qualities, they will be reborn in the heavens in the time it takes to bend or extend one’s arm. What are these ten?

Thereupon, a bhikṣu upholds the prohibitive precepts, is fully endowed with the virtue of morality, and does not transgress the True Dharma; this is called a bhikṣu who accomplishes this first dharma, and at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in a good destination, in the heavens.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who possesses a heart of reverence toward the Tathāgata is said to have accomplished this second dharma and shall be reborn in a good destination."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu who complies with the teachings of the Dharma and does not transgress them in the slightest is said to have accomplished the third quality of a bhikṣu, whereby he attains rebirth in a good destination."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu reverently serves the noble Saṃgha with a mind free from indolence; this is called accomplishing the fourth dharma for rebirth in the heavens."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu has few desires and is content, and does not cling to gain and offerings; this is called the fifth dharma of a bhikṣu for being reborn in the heavens."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu does not act according to his own whims but constantly follows the Dharma of the precepts; this is called accomplishing the sixth quality for being reborn in a good realm."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu does not become attached to worldly affairs and always delights in sitting in meditation; this is called accomplishing the seventh dharma, by which one attains rebirth in the heavens."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu delights in secluded places and does not dwell among the populace; this is called accomplishing the eighth dharma, whereby one is born in a favorable realm."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu does not associate with evil friends but always associates with virtuous friends; this is called accomplishing the ninth dharma, by which one attains birth in a good realm."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu constantly cultivates the holy life, remains free from unwholesome dharmas, is learned and studies their meaning, and does not lose the proper sequence.
A bhikṣu who thus accomplishes these ten dharmas will, in the time it takes to bend or extend one's arm, be reborn in a good realm, in the heavens above."
"Monks, this is called unrighteous conduct that leads to hell; you should mindfully abandon it.
As for the ten practices of the true Dharma, you should collectively uphold and cultivate them."
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, when the hour had come, put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
Then, those many bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"We have entered the city to beg for food, yet it is still early; we should go to the followers of other paths and heterodox teachers and engage them in debate."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the various non-Buddhist heterodox teachers were.
When those heterodox teachers saw the śramaṇas coming from afar, they each said to one another:
"Be silent, each of you; do not speak in loud voices, for the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama are now coming this way."
"However, the dharma of śramaṇas praises those who dwell in tranquility, so that people may know our True Dharma is not disturbed by what is disturbed.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to the place where the followers of other paths and heterodox teachings were, exchanged greetings with them, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the non-Buddhists asked the bhikṣus:
"O śramaṇas, does the Śramaṇa Gautama teach this sublime Dharma to his disciples so that all these bhikṣus fully understand all phenomena and sport within them without interference?"
We, too, preach this wondrous Dharma to our disciples and sport therein.
What difference is there between what I have spoken and yours?
What distinction exists?
"The teaching on the precepts of the Dharma is of one kind and without difference.

At that time, having heard what the heterodox followers of other schools had said, the many bhikṣus neither praised it as good nor condemned it as evil; they immediately rose from their seats and each withdrew.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus said to one another:
"We should take up this matter and go to inform the World-Honored One.
Whatever the Tathāgata may say, we shall bear it in mind and practice accordingly."

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, returned to their lodgings, gathered up their robes and bowls, and went to where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads and faces touching them, and stood to one side.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, taking this as their basis, related it all to the Tathāgata.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"After those followers of external paths and heterodox teachings have asked about this matter, you should respond to them with these words: "
"One discourse, one meaning, one exposition; up to ten discourses, ten meanings, ten expositions—when these words are spoken, what is their significance?"

"If you were to take these words and go to question him, that person would be unable to answer them, and those non-Buddhist heterodox teachers would consequently increase in their delusion and confusion.
This is because it is not within the scope of their own domain."

"Therefore, monks, I do not see anyone among the devas, humans, Māras, or the devas of Māra, Śakras, or Brahmā kings who could repay this speech—except for the Tathāgata and his disciples who have heard it from me; these cases are not considered."
One discourse, one meaning, one exposition: although I have spoken this meaning, for what reason have I spoken it?

All sentient beings subsist by means of food; without food, they die. That bhikṣu regards it with equanimity in his weariness of the world, attains liberation with equanimity, observes with equanimity, and discerns its meaning with equanimity, bringing an end to suffering with equanimity—this is a single meaning, not two.
What I have spoken is precisely this: "One meaning, one discourse, one exposition;
up to ten discourses, ten meanings, ten expositions. Although I have spoken these meanings, by what means have I spoken them?
Regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): what is meant by "name" (*nāma*)?
It refers to sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*);
these are called "name. What is meant by "form" (*rūpa*)?
The four great elements and the matter derived from the four great elements—this is what is called "form" (*rūpa*).
It is named "form" because it takes these as its fundamental conditions.
Regarding the two treatises, the two meanings, and the two expositions, I shall now explain them for these reasons.
If a bhikṣu is equally weary of [suffering], equally liberated, equally observes, equally discerns its meaning, and equally reaches the end of suffering.
“The three treatises, the three meanings, and the three expositions—by what cause are these meanings taught?
They refer to the three types of suffering. What are the three?”
They are the painful sensation, the pleasant sensation, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
What is called the pleasant sensation?
It refers to a perception of pleasure within the mind that is not dispersed; this is what is called the pleasant sensation.
What is meant by "affliction"?
It refers to the mind being agitated and unsettled, contemplating various perceptions; this is what is called affliction.
What is meant by "neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation"?

It refers to that which is neither the perception of pain nor the perception of pleasure within the mind; furthermore, it is neither fixed nor distracted, nor does one contemplate what is dharma or non-dharma. It is perpetually and naturally tranquil, with the mind being without mental formation (*avijñapti*); therefore, it is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
These are called the three kinds of feeling.

If a bhikṣu regards them with equanimity and weariness, attains liberation through equanimity, observes them with equanimity, discerns their meaning with equanimity, and brings an end to suffering through equanimity.
What I have called the three treatises, the three meanings, and the three expositions refers precisely to this.
For what reason, then, do you speak again of these four meanings, four treatises, and four expositions?
These are the Four Noble Truths. What are the four?
They are the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
What is the Truth of Suffering?

It refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one desires.
What is called the truth of origination?
It refers to craving that is fundamentally associated with desire; this is what is called the truth of origination.
What is called the truth of the cessation of suffering?
That which is the eternal exhaustion of that craving without remainder, such that it never arises again—this is called the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha-satya*).
What, then, is called the Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha-gāminī-pratipad-satya*)?
What is called the Noble Eightfold Path consists of:
right view, right resolve, right speech, right livelihood, right action, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are known as the eightfold path.

If a bhikṣu is equally weary of [suffering], equally liberated, equally discerns its meaning, equally contemplates it, and equally reaches the end of suffering, these are called the four discourses, the four meanings, and the four expositions.
What I have spoken refers precisely to this:
"The five treatises, the five meanings, and the five expositions—by what cause do I now speak these?"
These are called the five faculties. What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
What is called the faculty of faith?

It refers to the noble disciple who has faith in the path and Dharma of the Tathāgata—that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—who has appeared in the world; this is what is called the faculty of faith.
What is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?

It refers to the application of effort by body, speech, and mind, being untiring and indefatigable, so as to eliminate unwholesome states and increase wholesome ones, maintaining them with a compliant mind; this is called the faculty of diligence.
What is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?

The so-called faculty of mindfulness refers to that which is recited being not forgotten, constantly held in the heart, and maintained through dhāraṇī without loss; it is the never-forgetting of conditioned and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) dharmas—this is what is called the faculty of mindfulness.
What is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?

That which is called the faculty of concentration refers to having no confusion in the mind, no manifold perceptions, and being constantly single-minded and diligent; this is what is called the faculty of samādhi.
What is called the faculty of wisdom?
It refers to knowing suffering, knowing its origin, knowing its cessation, and knowing the path; this is what is called the faculty of wisdom.
These are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Within them, a bhikṣu attains equanimous liberation, equanimously discerns their meaning, and equanimously reaches the end of suffering.
The five treatises, the five meanings, and the five expositions that I have taught refer precisely to this.
"The six treatises, the six meanings, and the six expositions that I have taught—by what cause are they so?
They are what are called the six fundamental dharmas. What are these six?"

Thus, when a bhikṣu constantly practices a mind of loving-kindness through his body—whether staying in a secluded and pure chamber or always remaining single-minded—he becomes worthy of honor and esteem, and remains perpetually in harmony; this is called the first weighty dharma of a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, practicing loving-kindness through speech, being ultimately free from falsehood, and being worthy of respect and honor—this is called the second weighty dharma.
Furthermore, practicing loving-kindness through the mind, not giving rise to hatred or envy, and being worthy of respect and honor—this is called the third weighty dharma.
Furthermore,

if one receives the sustenance of Dharma-gains and gives the remnants remaining in one’s alms bowl to fellow practitioners of the holy life with an impartial mind, this is called the fourth weighty dharma that is worthy of reverence and honor.

Furthermore, to uphold the prohibitive precepts without any transgression or omission is that which is esteemed by the worthy; this is called the fifth weighty dharma, which is worthy of reverence and worthy of esteem.

Furthermore, right view enables the noble ones to attain the way of escape and reach the end of suffering; with an undeluded mind, they practice their conduct together with those who lead the holy life. This is called the sixth dharma that is worthy of reverence and esteem.
At that time, the bhikṣu is equally weary of [suffering], equally liberated, equally discerns its meaning, and equally reaches the end of suffering.
The six treatises, the six meanings, and the six expositions that I have spoken refer precisely to this.
"The Seven Treatises, the Seven Meanings, and the Seven Expositions—by what cause are these spoken?
They refer to the seven stations where consciousness abides. What are the seven?"
There are some sentient beings who possess diverse perceptions and diverse bodies, namely, gods and humans.
There are some sentient beings who possess diverse bodies but a single perception, namely, the Brahmakāyika gods at the time of their first emergence.
There are sentient beings who possess a single perception and a single body; these are the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
There are sentient beings who possess a single body and manifold perceptions; these are the gods of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
There are some sentient beings who are infinite in the sphere of infinite space; these are the devas of the sphere of infinite space.
There are some sentient beings who are infinite in the sphere of infinite consciousness; these are the devas of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There are sentient beings who are immeasurable in the sphere of nothingness; these are the gods of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
There are sentient beings who are immeasurable in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; these are the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
These, monks, are called the seven stations of consciousness. Therein,
a monk attains equanimous liberation, and so on, until he reaches the ultimate end of suffering through equanimity.
The seven treatises, the seven meanings, and the seven expositions—what I have taught refers precisely to these.
As for the eight treatises, the eight meanings, and the eight expositions, for what reason did I teach them?
What are called the eight worldly dharmas revolve according to the world. What are these eight?
Gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure—these are called the eight worldly dharmas that revolve according to the world.
If a bhikṣu attains equanimous liberation therein, he shall even reach the ultimate end of suffering.
These eight discourses, eight meanings, and eight expositions that I have taught refer precisely to this.
"The nine treatises, the nine meanings, and the nine expositions—regarding what I have taught, for what reason was this spoken?
It refers to the so-called nine abodes of sentient beings."
What are the nine?
If there are sentient beings with various kinds of bodies, namely devas and humans.
There are some sentient beings who have diverse bodies but a single perception; this refers to the Brahmakāyika devas when they first emerge.
There are some sentient beings who have a single body and a single perception; this refers to the Ābhāsvara devas.
There are some sentient beings who have a single body but manifold perceptions; these are the so-called Śubhakṛtsna devas.
There are some sentient beings who possess the immeasurable sphere of space; these are the so-called Ākāśānantyāyatana devas.
There are sentient beings whose consciousness is immeasurable, namely the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
There are also sentient beings for whom there is no sphere that is immeasurable, namely the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
There are sentient beings who are immeasurable in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; these are the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Sentient beings without perception and all other such classes of beings constitute the nine abodes of the spirits.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu attains equanimous liberation, even unto the ultimate end of suffering.
These nine discourses, nine meanings, and nine expositions that I have taught refer precisely to this.
"Regarding the ten treatises, the ten meanings, and the ten expositions—by what are they taught? They are known as the ten recollections (*daśa-anusmṛti*):

recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of morality, recollection of generosity, recollection of the devas, recollection of renunciation, recollection of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), recollection of the body, and recollection of death. These are called the ten recollections."
If a bhikṣu attains equanimous liberation, he will even reach the end of suffering.
This is the tenth discourse, the tenth meaning, and the tenth exposition. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"From one to ten.
Bhikkhus, you should know that if followers of other paths and heterodox teachers were to hear these words, they would not even be able to look directly at my face, much less respond to them!"
Any bhikṣu who understands this meaning is the most honored and foremost person in the present life.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī contemplates this meaning for even ten years, they will certainly attain one of two fruits: either arhatship or the state of an anāgāmin.
"Monks! Let alone ten years.
If one contemplates this meaning for even a single year, one will certainly attain two fruits and shall never fall away from them midway."

"Monks! Let alone for one year; if those in the fourfold assembly contemplate this meaning for ten months, or even for a single month, they will certainly achieve one of the two fruits and shall not regress midway."
"Furthermore, let alone one month;
if the fourfold assembly contemplates this meaning for seven days, they will certainly attain two fruits, and there shall be no doubt at all.
At that time, Ānanda was behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan to fan the Buddha.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma is exceedingly profound.”
"In whatever region this Dharma exists, one should know that they have encountered the Tathāgata.
Indeed, World-Honored One!
What is the name of this Dharma, and how should it be practiced?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This sutra is named ‘The Meaning of the Ten Dharmas’; you should bear it in mind and practice accordingly.
At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Those who practice the ten perceptions will exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), realize the fruits, and gradually reach *nirvāṇa*.
What are these ten? They are:

the perception of white bones, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of blood, the perception of being devoured, the perception of permanence and impermanence, the perception of craving for food, the perception of death, and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in.”
"Monks, it is said that one who cultivates these ten perceptions attains the exhaustion of all taints and reaches the realm of Nirvana.
Furthermore, monks!"
Among the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*), the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in (*sarvaloke ’nabhiratisaṃjñā*) is the foremost.

Why is this so? Because those who cultivate the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in and who uphold the Dharma with faith—these two types of persons will certainly transcend their stage and attain realization.
Therefore, bhikṣus! Whether you are under a tree, in a quiet place, or sitting in the open air, you should contemplate these ten perceptions. Therefore, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, that bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Today the Tathāgata has taught the bhikṣus the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*):
'Those who are able to cultivate these will sever all outflows (*āsrava*) and accomplish the practice of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*')."
"O World-Honored One! Like me, I am not capable of practicing this contemplation.
Why is this? Because my lustful mind is excessive, my body and mind are ablaze, and I find no peace."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"You should now abandon the perception of purity and cultivate the perception of impurity;
abandon the perception of permanence and cultivate the perception of impermanence."
Abandoning the perception of self, one contemplates the perception of non-self;
abandoning the perception of the pleasant, one contemplates the perception of the unpleasant.
This is because if a bhikṣu contemplates the perception of purity, the mind of desire will flare up.
If one contemplates the perception of impurity, the mind of desire will cease.
Bhikṣus, you should know that desire is impure, like a heap of excrement;
desire is like a jay bird, full of various clamorous sounds.
Sensual desire is devoid of reciprocity, like a venomous snake;
sensual desire is like an illusion, like snow melting in the sun;
one should contemplate the renunciation of desire as if discarding it in a cemetery.
Desire leads one to self-harm, like a snake harboring venom;
desire breeds insatiable affliction, like drinking salt water;
desire is difficult to satisfy, like the ocean swallowing rivers.
Sensual desire is many and terrifying, like a village of rākṣasas;
sensual desire is like an enemy and should always be kept at a distance.
Sensual desire has little flavor, like a knife smeared with honey.
Sensual desire is not to be craved, like a white bone by the roadside;
sensual desire manifests its outward form like flowers growing in a latrine;
sensual desire is unreal, like a painted vase that contains foul things within while appearing exquisite without.
Sensual desire has no solidity; it is like a mass of foam.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should mindfully distance yourselves from thoughts of sensual desire and contemplate thoughts of impurity.

"Monk, you should now remember the ten perceptions that were practiced under the Buddha Kāśyapa; you should now again contemplate these ten perceptions, and your mind with its outflows will be liberated."
At that time, that bhikṣu wept with such grief that his tears could not be restrained; he immediately prostrated himself before the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O World-Honored One!..."
Having been deluded for a long time, it was only when the Tathāgata himself taught the ten perceptions that I finally sought to distance myself from [evil].
Now I repent of my own accord; henceforth I shall not commit such offenses again!
I only pray that the Tathāgata will accept this grave transgression and grant forgiveness for my shortcomings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“I grant you leave to amend your faults; do not commit them again. Furthermore, when the Tathāgata taught you the ten perceptions, you were unwilling to accept and uphold them.”

At that time, having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, that bhikṣu dwelt in a secluded place, disciplining himself through contemplation. Thus, the son of good family who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and practices the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya) in order to ascend to his aspiration—knows it as it truly is:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further receiving of a womb."
At that time, that bhikṣu became an arhat.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Prohibitions and the Abodes of the Noble Ones; The Two Powers and the Ten Recollections.
The National Preceptor, Unobstructed. Ten Discourses on Contemplation and the Cultivation of Contemplation.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 42, Part 5 (Appendix at the End of the Scroll) (5). Thus have I heard:
At one time.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time,
the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are ten extensive analytical cultivations of mindfulness that completely sever sensual desire, desire for form, desire for the formless, conceit, and ignorance.
What are these ten?

That is to say: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of generosity, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of tranquility and insight, mindfulness of ānāpāna, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of death.

"Monks, it is said that there are sentient beings who, by practicing these ten recollections, completely sever sensual craving, craving for form, and craving for the formless; all ignorance, conceit, and pride are entirely eliminated."
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 43, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 47: On Good and Evil. Chapter Forty-Seven: On Good and Evil.
1 (I) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there are sentient beings who practice ten dharmas, they will be reborn in the heavens;
furthermore, by practicing another ten dharmas, they will be reborn in the evil realms;
and by practicing yet another ten dharmas, they will enter the realm of nirvana."
"What are the ten practices by which one is born into the evil realms?

In this regard, there is a person who kills living beings, steals, commits sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, engages in frivolous speech, uses harsh words, sows discord with double-tongued speech, is jealous, harbors ill will, and gives rise to wrong views—these are called the ten practices."
If there are sentient beings who practice these ten dharmas, they will enter the evil realms.
"How does one practice the ten dharmas to attain rebirth in the heavens?

In this regard, there is a person who does not kill, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, does not engage in frivolous speech or harsh words, does not use double-tongued speech to incite strife between others, and does not harbor envy, malice, or give rise to wrong views.
If there are those who practice these ten dharmas, they will be reborn in the heavens.
"How does one cultivate the ten dharmas to attain nirvana?
They are the so-called ten recollections (daśa-smṛti):"

Mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of ethical discipline, mindfulness of generosity, mindfulness of renunciation, mindfulness of ānāpāna, mindfulness of the body, and mindfulness of death.
This is called practicing ten dharmas to attain nirvāṇa.
Bhikṣus, you should know that those things which lead to rebirth in the heavens or the evil realms should be remembered as things to be abandoned;
as for those ten dharmas that lead to nirvāṇa, you should skillfully cultivate and practice them.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Due to the roots of the ten unwholesome actions, external things decline and waste away; how much more so the internal Dharma!
What are these ten? They are:
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, divisive speech that incites strife between others, envy, malice, and harboring wrong views in one's mind."
Due to the retribution of killing, the lifespan of sentient beings is extremely short;
due to taking what is not given, sentient beings are born into poverty and low status;
due to the retribution of sexual misconduct, the families of sentient beings are not chaste or virtuous.
Due to false speech, the breath of sentient beings becomes foul and unpleasant, resulting in a lack of freshness and purity;
due to frivolous speech, the land becomes uneven;
and as a retribution for divisive speech, thorns and brambles grow upon the earth.
Due to the retribution of harsh speech, there are various kinds of verbal faults;
due to jealousy, crops fail to ripen in abundance;
and due to the retribution of malice and harm, there are many foul and evil things.
Due to the retribution of wrong views, the eight great hells naturally arise.
Because of the retribution for these ten unwholesome actions, all external things undergo decline and exhaustion, let alone internal things.
This is what is meant, bhikṣu:
you should mindfully abandon the ten unwholesome dharmas and practice the ten wholesome dharmas.
Thus it is, bhikṣu!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, King Prasenajit went to the World-Honored One and said:
"The Tathāgata has indeed spoken these words:
'One who gives to me obtains much merit, while others obtain little merit;'"
"Give to my disciples; do not give to others.
If someone were to speak such words, would that not be to disparage the Dharma of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said to the king:
“I have not said this: ‘One should give to me alone, and not to others. Great King!”
You should know that I always say this:

"If a bhikṣu throws the remnants remaining in his alms bowl into the water, even soft-bodied insects that eat them obtain merit; how much more so for one who gives them to another person—how could such a person not obtain merit?"
"However, Great King!
I have this teaching:
'Giving to one who upholds the precepts brings even greater merit than giving to one who violates them.'"
At that time, King Prasenajit came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
Giving to one who upholds the precepts brings merit that is many times greater than giving to one who violates the precepts.”
The King spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“The Nirgranthas came and said to me:
‘The śramaṇa Gautama knows the arts of illusion and is able to turn the minds of worldly people.’”
"World-Honored One!
Is this statement true, or is it not?"
The Buddha said to the king:
"It is so, Great King! It is just as you have just said."
"I possess an illusory art that can transform worldly people.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is this so-called transformative illusory art?"
The Buddha said to the king:
"The transgression of one who takes life is immeasurable, while the merit of one who does not take life is immeasurable;
the transgression of one who takes what is not given is immeasurable, while the merit of one who does not steal is immeasurable."
Those who are licentious and dissolute will receive immeasurable retribution for their sins; those who are not licentious will receive immeasurable blessings.
Those with false views will receive immeasurable retribution for their sins; those with right views will obtain immeasurable blessings.
"What I understand by the dharma of illusion is precisely this.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"If the people of the world, Māra, or the devas of Māra—any sentient beings with form—were to deeply understand this art of illusion, they would obtain great fortune."

From this day forward, I shall no longer permit followers of external paths or heterodox teachings to enter the borders of my kingdom; however, I permit the fourfold assembly to always remain within my palace, where they shall be constantly provided with whatever they require as offerings.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Do not speak such words.
For what reason? Even by giving to the class of animals, one still obtains its merit."
Furthermore, by giving to those who violate the precepts, one likewise obtains merit;
by giving to those who uphold the precepts, the merit is likewise immeasurable;
and by giving to those who follow the path of external sages, one obtains a hundred millionfold merit.
The merit of giving to a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, an arhat, a pratyekabuddha, and a buddha is immeasurable.
Therefore, Great King!
One should resolve to provide for the future and past Buddhas and their śrāvaka disciples.
Thus, Great King, you should train yourself in this way.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, after their meal, a great multitude of bhikṣus gathered together in the Hall of Universal Assembly and discussed various matters among themselves. These discussions concerned clothing and ornaments, food and drink, neighboring kingdoms, bandits and warfare, drinking wine, debauchery, and the five kinds of sensual pleasure, as well as singing, dancing, laughter, and the performance of music.
Such essential matters are beyond calculation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing with his divine ear the various discussions being held by the bhikṣus, went immediately to the Hall of Universal Assembly and asked the bhikṣus:
"Having gathered here, what do you intend to discuss?"
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One,
“We have gathered here together to discuss this trivial matter.
Then, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Stop! Stop! Bhikkhu!"
Do not engage in such discourse.

Why is this? Because this discourse is not meaningful, nor does it lead toward wholesome qualities; one cannot cultivate the holy life through this discourse, nor attain the state of the extinction of nirvana, nor reach the path of equanimity of the śramaṇas.
These are all worldly discourses, not discourses that lead to the true goal.
You have already left the world to cultivate the Path; you should not contemplate discourses concerning failed conduct.
If you wish to discourse at all, you should discourse on the ten matters of meritorious virtue.

What are the ten? They are: if a bhikṣu is diligent; has few desires and is content; possesses a courageous mind; is learned and able to preach the Dharma to others; is fearless and without trepidation; is fully endowed with the precepts; has accomplished samādhi; has accomplished wisdom; has accomplished liberation; and has accomplished the vision and knowledge of liberation.
If you wish to engage in discussion, you should discuss these ten matters.

The reason for this is that they provide moisture to all beings, bring great benefit, allow for the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and lead to the state of cessation and the unconditioned—the essential core of *nirvāṇa*.
Now that you, son of noble family, have left the household life to study the Way, you should contemplate these ten matters.
This discourse is a discourse on the True Dharma; it leads one away from the evil destinies.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus had gathered in the Sahasravarga Lecture Hall and were each engaging in this discussion:
"Currently, grain and rice are extremely scarce in Śrāvastī, making it difficult to obtain food through begging.
Yet the World-Honored One has said:
'The human body exists by depending on food and drink; the four great elements depend upon the mental states of intention; and these dharmas depend upon the root of the wholesome realms.'"
"Today we should appoint people in turn to go begging.

Would it not be excellent if those who go begging were to obtain beautiful and wonderful sights, experience supreme and exquisite touch, and receive clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, pure and without blemish, heard from afar with his divine ear the various discussions arising among the bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded to the Sāla Grove Lecture Hall, sat amidst the assembly, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"For what purpose have you gathered here? What is the subject of your discussion?"
The bhikṣus replied: “We have been discussing this:

‘Now, it is difficult to obtain alms in the city of Śrāvastī; we wish to appoint one person by turn to go on alms-round so that, from time to time, he may obtain fine forms and exquisite garments, as well as clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick.’”
"What we have been discussing is precisely this right discourse.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu who begs for the four requisites of support [is thus supported]:"
Do robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick and weak serve any purpose other than for perceiving forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena?
I constantly instruct that there are two matters regarding the seeking of alms:
those that are to be associated with and those that are not to be associated with.

Even if one obtains robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicine for the sick, if these increase unwholesome qualities and are devoid of wholesome qualities, they are not to be associated with.

If one obtains robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick through begging, and these things increase wholesome qualities while not increasing unwholesome qualities, then such a person may be associated with.
"O bhikṣus, regarding this Dharma, what kind of discourse do you wish to engage in?

That which you are discussing is not a discourse on the True Dharma; you should abandon this teaching and no longer contemplate it, for by means of this you cannot reach the state of rest, cessation, and nirvāṇa."
“Those who wish to debate should debate these ten qualities. What are the ten? They are: a bhikṣu who is diligent;

one who has few desires and is content; one who possesses a courageous mind; one who is learned and able to preach the Dharma to others; one who is fearless and without trepidation; one who is fully endowed with the precepts; one who has accomplished samādhi; one who has accomplished wisdom; one who has accomplished liberation; and one who has accomplished the vision and knowledge of liberation.”
If you wish to engage in discussion, you should discuss these ten matters. Why is this?
Because they provide moisture to all beings, bring great benefit, allow for the cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and lead to the state of cessation—the unconditioned realm of *nirvāṇa*.
This discourse is the meaning of the ascetic life; you should reflect upon it with mindfulness and not let it depart from your mind.
Thus, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus gathered in the Sārvagandhakuṭī Lecture Hall and engaged in this debate:
"Now, alms-food is difficult to obtain in Śrāvastī; it is not a place where bhikṣus can dwell in peace. We should appoint one person to go on a sequential round for alms."
"This begging bhikṣu is able to provide robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick; he lacks for nothing.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who said to the others:
"We cannot endure begging here. Let us each go together to the kingdom of Magadha to beg there; moreover, grain is abundant and cheap, and food and drink are extremely plentiful."
Furthermore, another bhikṣu said:
"It is not appropriate for us to beg for alms in that kingdom.
The reason being that King Ajātaśatru rules there; he practices what is contrary to the Dharma, having murdered his father, the king, and having become a friend to Devadatta."
"For these reasons, it is not appropriate to beg for alms there. Another bhikṣu said:
"In this kingdom of Kośala, the population is flourishing, and there is an abundance of wealth and many treasures; it is fitting to beg for alms in that land."
Furthermore, there were other bhikṣus who spoke thus:
