"It is not fitting for us to beg for alms in that land. Why is this?

King Ajātaśatru rules and governs that land with extreme cruelty and depravity; he possesses no compassion or benevolence. The people are coarse and violent, and they delight in quarreling and litigation."
"For this reason, one should not go there to beg for alms.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu said:

"We should go to the city of Kuśinagara in Vārāṇasī, where King Udayana rules—a land where the Dharma is faithfully upheld and people’s minds do not waver. We should beg for alms in that territory; our wishes will not be thwarted."

At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing with his divine ear that the bhikṣus had each raised this discussion, immediately adjusted his robes, went to where the bhikṣus were, sat in their midst, and asked the bhikṣus:
"For what purpose have you gathered here? What discussion do you wish to hold? What matter are you discussing?"
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“We gathered here and each raised this discussion:

‘Now, in the city of Śrāvastī, grain is extremely expensive and it is difficult to obtain through alms-seeking. We should all go together to the borders of the kingdom of Magadha to seek alms there; moreover, that land abounds in wealth and many treasures, so whatever we seek will be easily obtained.’”
Among them, some bhikṣus said:
"It is not appropriate for us to beg for alms in that country.
Why is this? King Ajātaśatru rules there; he practices what is contrary to the Dharma, having killed his father, the king, and having become a friend of Devadatta."
"For this reason, it is not appropriate to beg for alms there.
Among them, another bhikṣu said:
"Now, the kingdom of Kuruśā is populous, with abundant wealth and many treasures; it is fitting to beg for food in that country."
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who spoke thus:
"It is not appropriate for us to beg for alms there. Why is this?
King Eḷeya rules there; he is a man of fierce cruelty, devoid of compassion and benevolence, and delights in strife and litigation."
"For this reason, it is not appropriate to beg for alms there.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu said:

"We should go to the city of Kuśinagara, Vārāṇasī, where King Udayana rules—a place where the Dharma is faithfully believed and minds are unwavering. It is fitting to beg for alms there; our wishes will not be thwarted."
"What is discussed here refers precisely to this.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not disparage the king’s governance of his realm, nor do you discuss whether the king is superior or inferior."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“When a person performs good or evil, The root of their action has its cause;
Each receives their respective retribution, Which can never be destroyed.”
When a person performs good or evil deeds, their actions have a cause;
by doing good one receives a good retribution, and for evil one receives an evil fruit. "Therefore, bhikṣus!"

Do not give rise to such thoughts or discuss matters of state; for by discussing these things, one cannot reach the place of cessation and nirvana, nor can one attain the Dharma of the true practice of a śramaṇa.
If you wish to engage in such discourse, it is not the correct practice.
You all should study the discourse on the ten matters. What are these ten?

If there is a bhikṣu who is diligent, of few desires and contented, possessed of a courageous mind, learned and able to preach the Dharma to others, fearless and without trepidation, fully endowed with the precepts, accomplished in samādhi, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the vision and knowledge of liberation—if you wish to debate, you should debate on these ten matters.
The reason for this is that it universally moistens all beings, enabling them to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) and reach the state of extinction, which is Nirvana.
You have already left the household life to study the Way and departed from worldly俗事; you should diligently engage in contemplation and never let your resolve waver.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus gathered in the Sāṃkāśya Hall and engaged in this discussion:

"Now King Prasenajit, who presides over the practice of unrighteousness, violates the holy laws and teachings; he has confined the Bhikṣuṇī Kāśyapī—who has attained the path of Arhatship—within his palace for twelve years and has engaged in sexual intercourse with her."

Furthermore, as they do not serve the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, and lack a heart of profound faith directed toward the Arhats, they have no faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Noble Assembly; we ought to distance ourselves from them and not remain in this land.

The reason for this is that when the king practices what is contrary to the Dharma, the king’s ministers also practice what is contrary to the Dharma; because the ministers practice what is contrary to the Dharma, the officials and subordinates around them also practice what is contrary to the Dharma;
and once the officials and subordinates have practiced what is contrary to the Dharma, the common people likewise practice what is contrary to the Dharma.
"I should now seek alms in a distant land rather than remaining in this country.
Furthermore, I may observe the customs and transformations there; having observed those customs and transformations, I shall see points of great distinction."
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing with his divine ear that the bhikṣus were each engaging in this discussion, went to where the bhikṣus were and sat in their midst.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For what discussion have you gathered here?
A great many bhikṣus replied to the World-Honored One:

“We were here discussing King Prasenajit, who practices unrighteousness and violates the holy discipline and teachings; for twelve years he has confined the Bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā within his inner palace, seeking to gratify her with carnal desire.”

Furthermore, those who have attained the Way transcend the three realms; yet Your Majesty does not serve the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, nor do you possess a heart of sincere faith toward the Arhats.
Since you lack this heart, you likewise lack it for the Triple Gem.
"We should travel far away; we need not remain here. Why is this?
When a king practices what is contrary to the Dharma, his ministers and subjects likewise practice evil. Furthermore, one must observe the laws of worldly customs."
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Do not discuss matters of national boundaries; you should instead discipline yourselves, reflect upon and examine within, and engage in analytical discernment."

To say that this treatise does not accord with ultimate truth, nor enables one to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of the unconditioned nirvana of total extinction, is incorrect; rather, one should personally cultivate oneself, ardently practice the Dharma, and take refuge in the Most Honored One.
If a bhikṣu is able to cultivate himself and cause the joy of the Dharma to flourish, such a person is as one born from my own body.
What do you think, bhikṣus?
Being able to kindle oneself and cause the joy of the Dharma to flourish, being without falsehood, and taking refuge in the Most Honored One— thereupon, O bhikṣu!
You should internally contemplate the body, abide in the mindfulness of the body, restrain your own mind, eliminate distracted thoughts, and be free from sorrow.
Externally observing the body, one dwells on the body with mindfulness, restraining the mind, eliminating distracted thoughts, and being free from sorrow and anxiety;
furthermore, observing the body internally and externally, one dwells on the body with mindfulness;
observing feelings internally, observing feelings externally, and observing feelings both internally and externally.
He contemplates the mind internally, contemplates the mind externally, and contemplates the mind both internally and externally;

he contemplates phenomena internally, contemplates phenomena externally, and contemplates phenomena both internally and externally. Through the application of mindfulness to phenomena, he restrains his own mind, eliminates distracted thoughts, and is free from sorrow and anxiety.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
You should be able to kindle your own practice, flourish in the joy of the Dharma, and take refuge in that which is most venerable.
All bhikṣus of the future and the present who can kindle themselves and not lose the root of their practice are truly born from me.
"Therefore, bhikṣus! If you wish to engage in discourse, you should discourse upon ten matters. What are these ten?

What is meant by a bhikṣu who is diligent? He has few desires and is content; he possesses a courageous mind; he is learned and able to preach the Dharma to others; he is fearless and without trepidation; he is fully endowed with the precepts; he has accomplished samādhi, accomplished wisdom, accomplished liberation, and accomplished the vision and knowledge of liberation.
If you wish to engage in discussion, you should discuss these ten matters. Why is this?
Because they provide moisture to all beings, bring great benefit, allow for the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya), and lead to the state of cessation—the unconditioned realm of Nirvana.
This discourse is the meaning of the ascetic life; you should contemplate it with mindfulness and not let it depart from your mind.
In this way, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder in the city of Śrāvastī who built a meditation hut for Rāhula.
Rāhula stayed in that hut for a certain number of days, after which he departed to wander and teach among the people.
At that time, the householder secretly formed this thought:
"I shall go to visit the Venerable Rāhula.
Then, seeing that the Venerable Rāhula’s room was silent and empty, with no one dwelling there, he spoke to the bhikṣus:
“Where is the Venerable Rāhula now? The bhikṣu replied,
“Rāhula is wandering and teaching among the people in the human world.”
The householder replied:
"I only wish that you, venerable sirs, would assign people to dwell in my rooms.
For the World-Honored One has also said:"

"By establishing gardens and orchards, constructing bridges and boats, and providing latrines along the roads as acts of charity, one reaps blessings throughout the long night; through the perfection of the precepts and the Dharma, one will surely be reborn in the heavens after death."
"For this reason, I built a hut for Rāhula.
Now that Rāhula does not take pleasure in my room, I only wish that you, worthy sirs, would assign someone else to dwell in my room."
The bhikṣus replied, "As the householder instructs. Thereupon,
the bhikṣus assigned one bhikṣu in turn to reside in the dwelling.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula thought to himself:
"I have been away from the World-Honored One for a long time; I should now go to inquire after his well-being.
Thereupon, the Venerable Rāhula went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat down to one side.
In a mere moment, he rose from his seat and returned to his room, where he saw another bhikṣu staying inside.
Having seen him, he said to that bhikṣu:
"Who gave me my room to you so that you might stay here?"
The bhikṣu replied, "The Saṃgha has assigned me to dwell in this room by turn. At that time,
Rāhula returned to the World-Honored One and, based on these circumstances, reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
“I do not understand why the Saṃgha has assigned my room to you, Lord, so that you, a practitioner of the Way, must dwell here.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
“Go to the house of the elder and say to him:”
"In the dharmas I practice, is there any transgression of conduct of body, speech, or mind?
Furthermore, is there any transgression of the three of body, the four of speech, or the three of mind?"
"The elder first offered his dwelling to me, and afterwards he gave it to the Noble Assembly.
At that time, Rāhula, having received the Buddha's instruction, went immediately to the elder’s house and said to him:
"Do I not possess the three faults of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind?"
The householder replied,
"I too do not see any fault in Rāhula’s body, speech, or mind.
Rāhula then said to the householder:
"Why have you taken away my dwelling and given it to the noble assembly?
The householder replied, "I saw that the room was empty; therefore, I took it and offered it as a gift to the noble assembly."
At that time, I further thought to myself:
"The Venerable Rāhula surely does not delight in my room.
Therefore, I brought it here to offer as a gift.
At that time, having heard the words of the elder, Rāhula immediately returned to the place where the World-Honored One was and reported these circumstances in detail to the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"Quickly strike the *ghanṭā*; let all the bhikṣus who are in the Jeta Grove Monastery assemble together in the Universal Assembly Hall."
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, summoned the bhikṣus to the Puhui Lecture Hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now speak on the purity of giving; you should reflect upon it well.”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"In what way is it called 'purity of giving'?"
"In this regard, monks!
If someone bestows a gift upon another, and later takes it back to give it to someone else, this is called uneven giving; it is not impartial giving."
Furthermore, if someone seizes the property of another and gives it as an offering to the Noble Assembly,
yet another person then seizes it back from the Noble Assembly and gives it to that other person, this is neither an impartial gift nor a pure gift.
A Wheel-Turning Sage King exercises sovereign mastery over his own realm; likewise, a bhikṣu exercises sovereign mastery even over his own robes and alms bowl.
If, however, one takes another's property and gives it to someone else without that person's consent, this is not an impartial act of giving.
I now tell you, monks: if a donor gives to one person while another recipient does not receive it, this is not an impartial gift.
Furthermore, if that monk should pass away, you must take this room and perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) within the assembly, proclaiming:
"A certain monk has passed away; we now take this room and distribute it among the assembly. To whom shall we assign it?"
In accordance with the instruction of the noble assembly:
"Virtuous ones! Whichever bhikṣu you appoint to remain, all of you should together tolerate him."
"If they do not grant permission, I shall now speak a second and third time, and likewise speak thus.
If the Sangha grants it while even one person does not grant permission, then it is not an impartial gift; it is a defiled and turbid thing."
"Now I return it to Rāhula’s room; he may receive it in purity.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (Nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove near Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, while in a secluded place, gave rise to this thought:
"How can the views of the past, the future, and the present be known?"
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having dressed and taken his bowl, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Kuṇḍadhāna addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"These various views now correspond to one another from beginning to end.
How can these views be extinguished, and how can it be ensured that others do not arise?"
The World-Honored One said:
“In this regard, Kuṇḍadhāna!
That from which these views arise and the place where they are extinguished are all impermanent, suffering, and empty.”
Śrutaviṣaṇa, you should understand this and establish this intention.
There are sixty-two kinds of views; one must fundamentally abide in the ground of the ten wholesome actions and eliminate these views.
What are the ten? In this regard, Kātyāyana!
Others take pleasure in killing living beings; we, however, ought not to kill.
"He is fond of stealing, but I do not steal;
he violates the holy life, but I practice the holy life;
he speaks falsehoods, but I do not speak falsehoods."
"Others practice divisive speech to sow discord between people, frivolous speech, harsh speech, envy, anger, and wrong views; I, however, practice right view.

Kūṭadanta, you should know that it is like one who has fallen into an evil path seeking to encounter the right path, or like one who has fallen into wrong views seeking to reach right view—turning from the crooked toward the straight. This is as impossible as a person who is drowning themselves yet wishing to ferry others across."
If one has not yet attained extinction oneself and wishes to cause others to attain extinction, this is not possible.
It would be as if someone who has not themselves drowned were able to ferry others across; such a principle could not exist.
Now it is likewise: having attained parinirvāṇa oneself, one may also cause others to attain extinction; such a principle is possible.
Therefore, Kuṇḍadhāna, you should reflect: through renouncing killing and not killing, one attains extinction;
through renouncing stealing and not stealing, one attains extinction.
By abstaining from sexual misconduct and not engaging in it, one attains nirvana;
by abstaining from false speech and not engaging in it, one attains nirvana;
by abstaining from frivolous speech and not engaging in it, one attains nirvana.
By abandoning harsh speech, one attains nirvāṇa through the cessation of harsh speech;
by abandoning strife and discord between self and others, one attains nirvāṇa through the cessation of strife and discord between self and others;
by abandoning envy, one attains nirvāṇa through the cessation of envy.
"Free from ill will, one attains nirvana through the cessation of ill will;
free from wrong views, one attains nirvana through the attainment of right view.
Kūṭadanta, you should know that if an ordinary person should give rise to this thought:"
"Is there a self? Is there no self? Is there both a self and no self?"
Is the world eternal?
Is the world non-eternal?
Does the world have a limit?
Is the world infinite?
Is the life-principle identical to the body,
or is the life-principle one thing and the body another?
Does the Tathāgata die?
Does the Tathāgata not die? Is there death?
"Is there no death? Who created this world?
Thus they give rise to various false views.
"Was this world created by Brahmā?
Or was this world established by the Lord of the Earth?
Furthermore, Brahmā [created] these sentient beings, and the Lord of the Earth created this world."
“Sentient beings originally did not exist but now exist; having existed, they then perish.
Such is the thought that arises in ordinary people who lack learning and insight.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“Spontaneously there exists Brahmā; this is the speech of the brahmins.
This view is not true, such as that which they perceive.
I am the Lord who gives birth to the lotus; from within it, Brahmā emerges.”
The earth-lord is born from Brahmā; it is inconsistent that he should be self-born.
The earth-lord belongs to the Kṣatriya caste and is the father and mother of the Brahmins.
How can a son of the Kṣatriyas give rise to the birth of a Brahmin?
Seeking the place of their birth, as the various devas have declared—these are merely words of praise that lead back to the bonds of worldly difficulty.
"Brahmā created human beings; the Lord of the Earth fashioned the world."
Some say it was created by another; who can verify such words?
Deluded by anger and desire, these three factors converge;
the mind finds no autonomy, yet one claims, "I am the most excellent in the world."
The gods created the world, nor was it born from Brahmā;
even if it were Brahmā who created it, would this not be false?
When one investigates its traces, they are found to be manifold; upon careful examination, one speaks of it as empty.
"Their practices are each different, and these practices are not examined for their reality.
Kuṇḍadhāna, you should know that among the various classes of sentient beings, what they perceive differs and their thoughts are each distinct."
All these views are impermanent; whoever harbors such views is subject to the law of impermanence and change.
If others commit killing, we should abstain from killing ourselves;

if others steal, we should distance ourselves from it and not practice such conduct. We must focus our minds and keep them from confusion, reflecting and deliberating so that the views arising from false perspectives—even the ten unwholesome deeds—are all abandoned and distanced, and we do not practice such ways.
If others are angry, we shall practice patience; if others harbor jealousy, we shall abandon it;
if others give rise to arrogance, we shall contemplate abandoning it;
and if others praise themselves and disparage others, we shall neither praise ourselves nor disparage others.
When others have few desires, we should train in having few desires;
when others violate the precepts, we should cultivate those precepts;
when others are indolent, we should practice diligence.
"Others do not practice samādhi; I shall practice samādhi"—thus one should train.
"Others are deluded and ignorant; I shall practice wisdom"—thus one should train.
"One who is able to observe and discern these dharmas will extinguish wrong views, and no others will arise.

At that time, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, Kuṇḍadhāna went to a secluded place where he reflected and deliberated: "For what purpose does a son of good family leave the household life to study the Way, don the three dharma robes, and practice the unsurpassed holy life?
Birth and death are ended; the holy life is established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence to be received—thus he knows it as it truly is."
At that time, Sundarika immediately became an Arhat.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Sundarika rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Sentient beings in the hells undergo the retribution for their offenses for a maximum duration of one kalpa, though some may meet with untimely death in the interim.”
Receiving the retribution of an animal, it lasts for at most one kalpa, though within that period there may be those who die prematurely;
receiving the retribution of a hungry ghost, it lasts for at most one kalpa, though within that period there may be those who die prematurely.
"Monks, you should know that the people of Uttarakuru live for a thousand years, and none die prematurely.
This is because the inhabitants of that land have no attachments; when their lives there come to an end, they are reborn in the higher realms of the heavens, and none fall away."
The people of Pūrvavideha have a lifespan of five hundred years, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the people of Aparagoyānī have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years, yet there are also those who die prematurely;
the people of Jambudvīpa have a maximum lifespan of one hundred years, and many die prematurely.

"Even if the human lifespan were to reach its maximum of one hundred years, and if the population were to consist of those with such a lifespan, their actions would still differ, and their natures and dispositions would each be distinct."
In the first ten years, one is young and small, possessing no discerning knowledge;
in the second ten years, one possesses some knowledge, yet still lacks comprehensive understanding;
in the third ten years, sensual desire blazes forth, and one becomes greedily attached to forms.
In the fortieth year, he mastered various arts and crafts, yet his conduct lacked consistency;
in the fiftieth year, he understood meanings with clarity and never forgot what he had studied;
in the sixtieth year, he became stingy and attached to wealth and property, his mind lacking decisiveness.
Seventieth: being indolent and fond of sleep, with a nature that is sluggish;
eightieth: lacking the vigor of youth and devoid of any splendor or adornment; ninetieth:
afflicted by many ailments and pains, with sagging skin and wrinkled face.
In the tenth decade, the various faculties decline and waste away; the joints of the bones become linked together, and one frequently forgets and errs in thought.
A bhikṣu who understands this knows that even if a person’s lifespan were a hundred years, they would have to undergo such hardships as these.

Suppose a person’s lifespan were one hundred years; they would pass through three hundred winters, summers, springs, and autumns. Calculating their life span in this way, it is truly insufficient to mention.
If a person lives for one hundred years, they would consume thirty-six thousand meals, though during that time there may be occasions when they do not eat:
they do not eat out of anger, they do not eat when food is not given, or they do not eat due to illness.
If one calculates those meals—both those eaten and those not eaten, including the drinking of mother’s milk—to summarize the essential point, there are thirty-six thousand meals.
Bhikṣus! Such is the manner of eating and drinking for a person whose lifespan is limited to a hundred years.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that among the people of Jambudvīpa, there are some whose lifespan is exceedingly long, equal to that of the immeasurable life-span [of the gods].

In the distant past, incalculable eons ago, there was a king named Sarvarogapraśamana (Healer of All Diseases). His lifespan was exceedingly long, his appearance was upright and handsome, and he enjoyed immeasurable bliss.”
At that time, there were no afflictions of illness, old age, or death.
Once, a husband and wife gave birth to a son, who then passed away.
At that moment, the parents took him up in their arms and set him down; they also brought food to give him, yet the child neither drank nor ate, nor did he rise from his seat.
Why is this so? Because their lives have come to an end.
At that time, those parents then had this thought:
"Why is my son so angry today? Why does he refuse to eat or drink, and why does he not speak?
This was because those people had not heard the sound of death.
At that time, his parents thought again:
"Our son has now gone seven days without drinking or eating; we do not know for what reason he remains silent."
"I should now go to inform the Great King, the Physician, of these circumstances so that he may know.
At that time, the parents went to the King's presence and reported these circumstances to him in full detail.
At that time, the Great King thought to himself:
"Today I have heard the sound of death.
The King then said to him:
"You all may take this child to where I am. At that time, the parents immediately took the child in their arms and went to the place where the king was.
Having seen him, the king said to the parents:
"This child has already passed away.
At that time, the parents said to the king,
"In what sense is it called 'passing away'?"

The king said: "This child no longer moves, rises, speaks in response, converses, eats and drinks, or plays; his body remains upright and he does nothing further. Therefore, it is called 'the end of life'."
At that time, the husband and wife again addressed the king, saying:
"How long will such transformations as these continue?
The king told them:
"This child will before long have his body rot and decay; it will swell up and become foul-smelling, until it is no longer fit for anything.
At that time, the parents did not believe the king's words; they took the dead child back home, and before long, the body completely decomposed and became extremely putrid.
At that time, the parents finally believed the king’s words, saying:
"This child will soon have his body swell, and it will all eventually rot away.
Then, the husband and wife again took the swollen infant to the king and said to him:
"Indeed, Great King! We now bring this child to offer as a tribute to Your Majesty.
At that time, the parents did not weep.
The reason for this was that they had not heard the sound of death.
At that time, the Great King flayed their skin to make a great drum, and further commanded the construction of a seven-storied pavilion; he placed the drum upon it and ordered a man:
"You must know this: guard this drum and strike it once every hundred years, never missing the appointed time."
Having received the King’s instruction, they struck it once every hundred years.
At that time, when the people heard the sound of this drum, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to one another:
"What is this sound? Whose voice is it that reaches us here?"
The king told them,
"This is the echo of a dead man's skin.
Having heard this, the sentient beings each gave rise to this thought:
"How marvelous! That we have heard this sound.
"O bhikṣus, who else could that king at that time have been? It was none other than me."
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? The king at that time was none other than myself.
Know from this that in the past, the lifespan in Jambudvīpa was extremely long; whereas now, the people of Jambudvīpa have very short lifespans, and those who pass away are beyond counting.
The reason for this is that because they have committed many acts of killing, their lifespans are extremely short and their physical splendor has faded!
Due to these causes and conditions, such strange transformations occur.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that fifty years on Jambudvīpa constitute one day and night among the Four Great Kings.

Calculating by the number of such days and nights—thirty days making a month, and twelve months making a year—the lifespan of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years, though there may also be those who die prematurely.”
If one calculates that the lifespan among humans is eighteen billion years, it constitutes but a single day and night in the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).

Calculating by the measure of a single day and night there—thirty such days making a month, and twelve months making a year—the maximum lifespan in the Reviving Hell is one thousand such years; furthermore, there are those who die prematurely.

If one calculates the lifespan among humans as thirty-six billion years, then one hundred years among humans constitutes one day and night in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). Calculating by the number of days, months, and years according to that [heavenly] reckoning, the lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is one thousand years; however, within that period, there may be those who die prematurely.

If one calculates the lifespan of humans as thirty-six billion years, that constitutes a single day and night in the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, calculating by the reckoning of those days and months—thirty days making a month and twelve months making a year—their lifespan, measured by those days and nights, is twenty thousand years; calculated by the reckoning of human years, it is one *koṭi*.
In this way, monks, the calculation of this lifespan increases twofold at each stage, with the exception of the Heaven of Non-conception.
The lifespan in the Heaven of Non-conception is eighty-four thousand kalpas; the Śuddhāvāsa deities are excluded, as they do not return to this world.
Therefore, bhikṣus! Do not harbor negligence;
in this very life, you shall bring an end to all outflows.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

In the forty-third fascicle of the *Ekottarika Āgama*, it is stated: "A hundred years shall comprise three hundred winters, summers, and autumns. This means that there are one hundred each for winter, summer, and autumn; therefore, they are said to be three hundred.
The reason "spring" is not mentioned here is that this follows the three seasons of the Western Regions.
These three seasons are cold, hot, and rainy.
Winter corresponds to their cold season, summer to their hot season, and autumn to their rainy season.
However, those three seasons each consist of four months, totaling twelve months for one year.
Now, by using winter, summer, and autumn to correspond to those three seasons, the number of months falls short; this is likely because the translator was not proficient in the local dialect.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 44, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. Chapter 48:
The Ten Unwholesome Actions. Chapter Forty-Eight: The Ten Unwholesome Actions.
1. (I) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there are sentient beings who practice killing and propagate killing, they plant the seeds for the retributions of hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm;
even if they are born among humans, their lifespan will be extremely short.”
The reason for this is that it arises from taking the lives of others.
If there are sentient beings who steal the property of others, they plant the seeds of the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, they will constantly suffer from poverty and destitution, with food insufficient for their mouths and clothing inadequate to cover their bodies.
All this is due to theft; those who plunder and seize the property of others cut off the very life-root of another.
If there are sentient beings who delight in and are addicted to greed and lust, they plant the seeds for the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, their households will not be chaste or virtuous, and they will engage in theft and lewdness.
"If there are sentient beings who speak falsely, they plant the seeds for the sins of hell;
if born among humans, they will be despised by others, their words will not be trusted or accepted, and they will be held in contempt."
The reason for this is that it is all caused by false speech in previous lives.
"If there are sentient beings who engage in double-tongued speech, they plant the seeds of sin for the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, their minds will never be stable, and they will constantly harbor sorrow and anxiety."
The reason for this is that such a person transmits false words from head to head.
"If there are sentient beings who speak coarse words, they plant the seeds of offenses leading to the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, they will be ugly and wretched, and will always delight in reviling and shouting."
The reason for this is that it results from the fact that those people’s speech is neither focused nor upright.
"If there are sentient beings who incite strife between this party and that, they plant the seeds of sin for the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, they will have many enemies and hatreds, and their kin will be scattered."
The reason for this is that it is entirely due to the strife and discord committed in previous lives.
"If there are sentient beings who harbor jealousy, they will plant the seeds for the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, they will lack clothing."
The reason for this is that such a person gives rise to greed and envy.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to harmful intentions, they plant the seeds for the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, they will constantly be full of falsehoods, fail to understand the ultimate truth, and possess a distracted and unstable mind.
The reason for this is that it is all caused by the anger and resentment of previous lives, and a lack of compassion and benevolence.
"If there are sentient beings who practice wrong views, they will plant the seeds for the three evil realms;

even if they are born among humans, they will be in the borderlands rather than the central lands, where they do not behold the meaning of the Dharma of the Three Honored Ones, or else they may be deaf, blind, or mute, with deformed bodies, unable to understand the paths of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas."
The reason for this is that in their previous lives they lacked the faculty of faith, and they likewise did not believe in śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, parents, or brothers.
“Monks, you should know that it is due to the retribution of these ten unwholesome deeds that such calamities and transgressions arise. Therefore, monks,
you should abandon the ten unwholesome deeds and cultivate right view.”
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, on the fifteenth day for the recitation of the precepts, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the bhikṣus before and behind him, proceeded to the Sahasravarga Lecture Hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One observed in silence, while the assembly of noble ones remained tranquil and speechless.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today the entire assembly of noble ones has gathered in the lecture hall; it is so, World-Honored One!"
"I shall preach the prohibitive precepts to the bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not speak.
Then, after a short while, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now is precisely the right time; it is fitting that you should proclaim the prohibitions and precepts, for the first watch of the night is drawing to a close.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not speak.
Then, Ānanda spoke again to the Buddha after a short while:
"When the middle watch of the night is nearly over, the assembly of monks is weary and exhausted; we only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the precepts at this time.
At that moment, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not speak.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha after a short while, saying:
"The latter part of the night is drawing to a close; I only pray that the World-Honored One will, at this opportune time, recite the precepts.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Because there are those who are impure within this assembly, the precepts are not recited.
Now, I authorize the Elder to recite the prohibitory precepts.
If the Elder of the Saṃgha is unable to recite the precepts, I authorize a Vinaya-holder to recite the prohibitory precepts.”
"If there is no one who upholds the Vinaya, then whoever is able to recite the precepts with fluency and mastery shall chant them to deliver the Uposatha.
From this day forward, the Tathāgata will no longer recite the precepts."
"If the Tathāgata were to preach the precepts in the midst of such impurity within the assembly, that person's head would split into seven pieces, no different from a *cūla* fruit.
At that moment, Ānanda was overcome with a mixture of grief and weeping, and he spoke thus:
"The noble Saṃgha has today become truly destitute and forlorn."
"How swiftly does the True Dharma of the Tathāgata depart?
How swiftly do those who are impure emerge?
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought thus:
"Who among this assembly is a person who disparages the Dharma, such that they remain within this assembly and cause the Tathāgata not to proclaim the prohibitory precepts?
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered a state of samādhi and surveyed throughout the hearts of the noble assembly for any flaws or impurities.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana saw the two bhikṣus Aśvajit and Pūrṇamāsa in the midst of the assembly. Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat, went to where those bhikṣus were, and addressed them, saying:
"Rise quickly and leave these seats."
"The Tathāgata has been reviled because of you; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata does not proclaim the prohibitions.
At that time, the two bhikṣus remained silent and said nothing.
Then Maudgalyāyana spoke to them again, a second and a third time:
“Arise quickly, you need not remain here.
At that time, those bhikṣus remained silent and did not respond.
Then Maudgalyāyana went forward, took them by the hand, led them outside the gate, and having closed the door behind him, came before the Buddha and said:
“The impure bhikṣus have already departed outside; indeed, World-Honored One, please now proclaim the prohibitory precepts.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: “Stop!”
"Stop, Maudgalyāyana!
The Tathāgata shall no longer recite the precepts for the bhikṣus."
"What the Tathāgata has spoken contains no duality; let us return to our seats.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now impurity has arisen within this assembly; I am unable to carry out the duties of the *karmadāna*. I only pray that the World-Honored One will appoint another person."
At that time, the World-Honored One silently gave his consent.
Then, Maudgalyāyana prostrated himself at the feet of the World-Honored One and returned to his original seat.
Thereupon, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"When the Tathāgata Vipaśyin appeared in the world, how many were the assembly of noble ones?
After how much time did defilement arise?
And so on, up to: how many were the disciples of Kāśyapa?"
"How is the precept recited?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, appearing in the world."
At that time, there were three assemblies of the noble multitude: in the first assembly, there were one hundred sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus;
in the second assembly, one hundred sixty thousand noble ones;
and in the third assembly, one hundred thousand noble ones—all of whom were arhats.
The lifespan of that Buddha was eighty-four thousand years, and for a hundred years the assembly of noble disciples remained pure. That Buddha constantly used a single verse as his precept:
"Patience is the foremost; The Buddha says non-action is supreme.
One does not become a śramaṇa Merely by shaving one's hair and beard."
"At that time, that Buddha established this single verse as a precept throughout a hundred years; once a flaw or impurity had arisen, he would then establish a precept."
“Furthermore, during the thirty-first kalpa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Pravicaya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, there were likewise three assemblies of the noble ones: in the first assembly, there were one hundred and sixty thousand noble ones;
in the second assembly, there were one hundred and forty thousand noble ones.”
At the third assembly, there were one hundred thousand noble ones.
At that time, for eighty years, that Buddha remained pure and without blemish, and he also spoke this verse:
"If what is seen by the eye is not false, the wise protect it and do not become attached."
"Abandoning all evils, one is wise while in the world.
At that time, for eighty years, that Buddha preached this single verse; later, when defilements arose, he established further precepts.
At that time, it was further questioned: "The Buddha’s lifespan was seventy thousand years.

During that kalpa, there appeared another Buddha in the world named Viśvabhū, who likewise held three assemblies of the noble ones; at the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand noble ones, all of whom were arhats;
at the second assembly, there were eighty thousand arhats."
At the time of the third assembly, seventy thousand arhats had exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
For seventy years, the Tathāgata Viśvabhū was free from any blemish.
At that time, he established a single verse and a half as the precept:
“Neither harming nor censuring, practicing the great precepts,
knowing moderation in food, and likewise regarding one’s seat;
maintaining a single-minded resolve— this is the teaching of all Buddhas.”
"For seventy years, this single verse served as the precept; later, when flaws and impurities arose, further precepts were established.
The Tathāgata Viśvabhū lived for seventy thousand years."
"In this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Krakucchanda Tathāgata, manifesting in the world.
At that time, there were two assemblies of the noble ones: at the first assembly, there were seventy thousand noble ones, all of whom were Arhats;
at the second assembly, there were sixty thousand Arhats."
At that time, for sixty years, that Buddha was free from any blemish or impurity.
At that time, that Buddha established two verses as his prohibitive precepts:
"Just as a bee gathers from flowers, Taking their color, fragrance, and purity, Without harming the flower's essence, So should one enter a village."
Giving flavors as alms to others, the practitioner wanders through the villages.
He does not slander others, nor does he dwell on right and wrong;
he simply observes his own conduct, examining closely what is correct and what is incorrect.
"For sixty years he preached these two verses as his prohibitive precepts; from that time onward, whenever impurities arose, he would establish further prohibitive precepts."
That Buddha’s lifespan was sixty thousand years.
"In this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Kanakamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, there were two assemblies of the holy multitude: at the first assembly, there were six hundred thousand holy ones, all of whom were Arhats;
at the second assembly, there were four hundred thousand holy ones, all of whom were Arhats.
At that time, for forty years, that Buddha was free from any flaw or impurity, and he established a single verse as his precept:
"Maintain your resolve and do not engage in frivolity; You should study the noble and tranquil path.
The wise have no sorrow or anxiety; They constantly extinguish all volitional thoughts."
"For forty years he preached this single verse as his precept; from that time onward, however, there were lapses and impurities, so further precepts were established."
That Buddha’s lifespan was forty thousand years.
During this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa who appeared in the world.
At that time, that Buddha also had two assemblies of holy disciples; at the first assembly, there were four hundred thousand followers.
At the second assembly, there were three hundred thousand followers, all of whom were arhats.
For twenty years, there was no defilement among them, and they constantly took a single verse as their precept:
"Do no evil whatsoever; One should practice what is good."
"By purifying one's own will and mind, this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
For twenty years he preached this single verse as a prohibitive precept; after it was violated, further restrictions were established.
At that time, the lifespan of Kāśyapa Buddha was twenty thousand years.

Now, as I, the Tathāgata, have appeared in the world, there is an assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty noble disciples who, for twelve years, have been free from any blemish. Furthermore, I have established a single verse as the precept:
"Guard the mouth and let the mind be pure; Let the actions of the body also be pure."
"Purify these three tracks of conduct, and practice the path of the seers.

For twelve years, he recited this single verse as a prohibitory precept. As people began to violate the discipline, it was expanded into two hundred and fifty precepts. From this day forward, when the community of monks assembles, they shall announce according to the rule:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Listen all!
Today is the fifteenth day for the recitation of the precepts. If the Sangha consents, the community of monks shall be in harmony.
Having thus announced this by reciting the prohibitory precepts.
If there are bhikṣus who have something to say, they should not speak during the recitation of the precepts; instead, they should all remain silent.
If there is no speech, the precepts should be recited.
Once the introduction to the precepts has been recited, one should further ask:
"Venerable friends, who is not pure?
Thus he asked a second and a third time: "Who is not pure?
Those who were pure remained silent; let it be so held.
However, the lifespan of people today is extremely short; at its maximum, it does not exceed a hundred years.
Therefore, Ānanda, you must receive and uphold this well.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"In the distant past, the lifespan of the various Buddha-Bhagavāns was exceedingly long; those who violated the Vinaya were few, and there were no blemishes. Yet now, the lifespan of the people is short, not exceeding ten years. After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas of the past, how long will their bequeathed Dharma remain in the world?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas of the past, the Dharma did not endure for long.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, for how long shall the True Dharma remain in the world?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“After my parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall remain for a long time.”
After the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, his bequeathed Dharma remained for only seven days. Now, Ānanda,
the disciples of the Tathāgata are few.
Do not hold such a view.
There are countless billions of disciples in the east, and countless billions of disciples in the south. Therefore, Ānanda!
One should establish this thought: the lifespan of me, Śākyamuni Buddha, is exceedingly long.
Why is this so? Although the physical body has entered parinirvāṇa, the Dharma-body remains; such is the meaning.
"You should keep this in mind and practice accordingly.
At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Ānanda bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The Tathāgata’s profound discernment perceives all things; he clearly understands the three periods of time—future, past, and present. He knows the surnames, names, and titles of all past Buddhas, as well as the number of their disciples and bodhisattva attendants. Whether it be one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, or incalculable kalpas, he observes and knows them all.”
Furthermore, he knows the names and surnames of kings, ministers, and the people; he can distinguish these, as well as the various present-day realms, with complete clarity.
In the distant future, when Maitreya appears as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, we wish to hear of his transformations;
how long will his disciples follow him, and for how long will the Buddha-field be prosperous and joyful?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Return to your seat and listen to what I shall say. Pay careful attention to and keep in mind the abundance and joy of the land when Maitreya appears, as well as the number of his disciples."
At that time, Ānanda received the instruction from the Buddha and immediately returned to his seat.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"In the distant future, within this realm, there shall be a city named Kukkutavati, twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from south to north. Its land will be fertile and prosperous, its population dense, and its streets and lanes laid out in orderly rows."
At that time, there was a dragon king in the city named Water-Light (Jala-prabha), who rained down fragrant moisture at night and made the day clear and harmonious.

At that time, in the city of Kukkutavati, there was a rākṣasa ghost named Leaf-Flower (Patra-puṣpa) who acted in accordance with the Dharma and did not violate the true teaching. After the people had fallen asleep, he would remove all filth and impurities, and further sprinkle the ground with fragrant liquid until it was exceedingly pure and fragrant.

"Ānanda, you should know that at that time, the mountains, rivers, stone walls, and cliffs throughout the hundred thousand yojanas of Jambudvīpa in the east, west, south, and north will all spontaneously vanish, and the four great oceans will each occupy their respective quarters."

At that time, Jambudvīpa was exceedingly level, as clear and bright as a mirror. Throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa, grain was abundant and cheap; the population was flourishing and teeming with many precious treasures. The various villages were situated close together, such that the crowing of their roosters reached one another.

At that time, the trees bearing inferior flowers and fruits withered away, and all impurities were naturally extinguished; meanwhile, other trees bearing sweet fruits and possessing exquisite fragrances sprang forth from the earth.

At that time, the seasonal climate was harmonious and the four seasons followed their proper order; among the bodies of human beings, there were no afflictions of the one hundred and eight [defilements].

Greed, anger, and ignorance were not prevalent, and the minds of people were impartial and of a single intent. They greeted one another with joy, addressed each other with kind words, and their speech was uniform without distinction, just like the people of Uttarakuru, and no different from them.
At that time, all the people within Jambudvīpa, whether great or small, were of one voice, without any distinction between them.
When men and women of those times desired to relieve themselves, the earth would naturally open; once their business was finished, the earth would close back up again.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously; it was without husks, exceedingly fragrant and delicious, and its consumption brought no suffering or affliction.
Furthermore, gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and amber were scattered everywhere upon the ground, yet no one took notice of them or gathered them up.
At that time, the people took hold of these jewels in their hands and said to one another:

"In the past, because of these very jewels, people harmed one another, were imprisoned in dungeons, and underwent countless sufferings; yet now these jewels are treated as common as tiles and stones, with no one to guard them."
“At that time, a Dharma King appeared named Śaṅkha, who ruled and transformed the world through the True Dharma, and the seven treasures were perfected.

These so-called seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the precious queen treasure, the military commander treasure, and the treasury guardian treasure. These are called the seven treasures; he governed this land of Jambudvīpa without using the sword or staff, and all naturally submitted.”
Now, Ānanda! Regarding the four treasuries of jewels: the Elāpattra treasure-trove in the kingdom of Gandhāra contains many rare and extraordinary objects beyond measure;
the second, the Pañcāla great treasury in the kingdom of Mithilā, likewise contains many precious gems.
In the third great kingdom of Sūrata, there was a treasure trove containing many rare jewels;

in the fourth, the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a great storehouse with immeasurable and incalculable treasures. These four great treasuries spontaneously appeared, and the respective guardians of each came to inform the king:
"We pray that Your Majesty will bestow these treasures from the storehouses upon the poor!"
At that time, after King Śaṅkha had obtained this treasure, he likewise did not take note of it, for his mind was free from any thought of material wealth.

Then, garments grew spontaneously upon the trees within Jambudvīpa; they were extremely fine and soft. When people took them and wore them, they were no different from the garments that grow spontaneously on the trees for the people of Uttarakuru.

"At that time, that king had a minister named Sūvīra, who had been his companion since childhood. The king held him in great affection and respect; moreover, he was handsome in appearance—neither tall nor short, neither fat nor thin, neither too pale nor too dark, and appearing neither old nor young."

At that time, Bhāradvāja had a wife named Bhāradvājī, who was the most exquisite among celestial women, like the consort of Śakra. Her mouth emitted the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and her body exuded the scent of sandalwood. She was forever free from the eighty-four feminine affectations and possessed no thoughts of illness or distracted conceptualization.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, while in the Tuṣita Heaven, observed that his parents were neither too old nor too young; he then descended from the divine realm to manifest his birth, emerging from the right side of his mother’s womb, no different from my own birth today from the right side, and Maitreya Bodhisattva was likewise so.
The various devas of Tuṣita each proclaimed:
"Maitreya Bodhisattva has already descended into his incarnation.

At that time, Śuddhodana immediately bestowed a name upon his son, calling him Maitreya; he was adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his body resplendent with a golden hue.
At that time, the lifespan of humans was exceedingly long and free from all ailments; everyone lived for eighty-four thousand years, and women did not marry until they were five hundred years old.
At that time, not long after Maitreya had lived as a householder, he would leave the home life to study the Way.
At that time, not far from the city of Kukkuṭa, there will be a tree of enlightenment named Nāgapuṣpa, one yojana in height and five hundred paces in breadth.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva sat beneath that tree and attained the fruit of the unsurpassed path;
at the hour of midnight, Maitreya left the household life, and on that very same night, he realized the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the earth deities each addressed one another, saying:
"Now Maitreya has attained Buddhahood!"
The sound continued until it reached the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings: "Maitreya has already attained the Way of the Buddha!

It proceeded further, reaching through the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, spreading its resonance all the way up to the Brahma Heaven:
"Maitreya has already attained the Way of the Buddha!"

At that time, the Māra named Dharma-Commander, having heard the sound of the Tathāgata’s name being proclaimed, was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; for seven days and seven nights, he neither slept nor rested.
At that time, Māra, leading countless devas and humans of the desire realm, went to the abode of Maitreya Buddha and paid him respectful homage.
The Holy Honored One Maitreya gradually expounded for the devas a subtle and wondrous discourse on the Dharma; that is to say:
the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; [he taught] the perception of the impurity of desire and that the essential means of liberation is sublime.
At that time, Maitreya, seeing that the people had already resolved their minds with joy, extensively analyzed and explained the meaning of the Dharma constantly taught by the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones— the suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path— to all the devas and humans.
At that time, eighty-four thousand devaputras on the seats were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then, the Great General Māra addressed the people of that realm, saying:
"All of you, quickly leave the household life!"
"The reason for this is that Maitreya has today already crossed to the other shore, and he shall likewise lead you all to reach the other shore.

At that time, a householder named Sudhana, living in the city of Kukkutavati, heard the command of the Mara King and also heard the resonance of the Buddha's voice; leading a multitude of eighty-four thousand followers, he went to the place where Maitreya Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, Maitreya gradually expounded for him a subtle discourse on the Dharma; that is to say:

the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven, [explaining that] the perception of the impurity of desire and the excellence of the way of escape are supreme.

At that time, Maitreya, seeing that the minds of the people were opened and their intentions liberated, extensively analyzed the meaning of the Dharma as it is always taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that time, eighty-four thousand people in the assembly were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Then, Sudhana and the eighty-four thousand others immediately stepped forward and said to the Buddha:
"We seek to leave the household life, to cultivate the holy life well, and to fully realize the path of Arhatship."
"At that time, Maitreya’s first assembly will consist of eighty-four thousand arhats.
At that moment, King Śaṅkha, hearing that Maitreya has already attained the path of Buddhahood, will go to the Buddha’s dwelling, desiring to hear the Dharma."
At that time, Maitreya preached the Dharma for him—a teaching that was excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with profound principles and meanings.

Later, on another occasion, the Great King established his crown prince as heir apparent and bestowed precious jewels upon the barber; he then gave various gems to the brahmins and, leading eighty-four thousand sentient beings, went to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek ordination as śramaṇas.
They all attained the fruits of the Path and became arhats.

"At that time, the great elder Śuddhodana, hearing that Maitreya had already attained the path of Buddhahood, led a multitude of eighty-four thousand brahmins to the Buddha's dwelling, seeking to become śramaṇas;
they subsequently attained arhatship."
"Only the one named Brahmayu has severed the three fetters and will certainly reach the end of suffering.
At that time, the Buddha’s mother, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, again led a retinue of eighty-four thousand court ladies to the place where the Buddha was, seeking to become śramaṇas.
At that time, all the women attained arhatship;
only one person, Brahmāvatī, severed the three fetters and became a srotāpanna.

At that moment, when the Kṣatriya wives heard that Maitreya Tathāgata had appeared in the world and attained perfect enlightenment, several tens of millions of them went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads and faces touching the ground, and sat to one side.
Each and every one gave rise to the thought of seeking to become a śramaṇa, leaving the household life to study the Way;
some attained realization by skipping over stages, while others did not attain realization.
At that time, Ānanda!
Those who do not bypass their turn to attain realization are all people who revere the Dharma; they are weary of and loathe all worldly perceptions of the unpleasurable.

At that time, Maitreya shall preach the teachings of the Three Vehicles. Just as among my disciples today, Mahākāśyapa practices the twelve dhūtas and has well-cultivated the pure conduct under past Buddhas, this person will constantly assist Maitreya, exhorting and transforming the populace.
At that time, Kāśyapa sat cross-legged not far from the Tathāgata, straightening his body and composing his mind, fixing his mindfulness before him.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"I am now advanced in years; my age has reached over eighty."
Nevertheless, the Tathāgata now has four great śrāvakas who are capable of traveling abroad to transform others, possessing inexhaustible wisdom and endowed with all virtues.
Who are these four?
These are the bhikṣu Mahākāśyapa, the bhikṣu Kuṇḍopadhānīya, the bhikṣu Piṇḍola-bharadvāja, and the bhikṣu Rāhula.
You four great śrāvakas must not enter parinirvāṇa; you shall only enter parinirvāṇa after my Dharma has completely disappeared.
Mahākāśyapa likewise should not enter parinirvāṇa; he must wait until Maitreya appears in the world.

The reason for this is that all of Maitreya’s converted disciples were originally disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, who attained the exhaustion of outflows through the transformative influence left behind by me.
Within the kingdom of Magadha, in the village of Vitidha, Mahākāśyapa dwelt upon that mountain.

Furthermore, Maitreya Tathāgata, surrounded by a retinue of countless thousands of people, came to this mountain; thereupon, by the grace of the Buddha, the various spirits and deities shall open the gate for him, enabling him to behold Kāśyapa’s meditation cave.
At that time, Maitreya extended his right hand, pointed toward Kāśyapa, and addressed the multitude:
"This is Kāśyapa, a disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha from the distant past!"
"Today, in the present age, the dhūta ascetic practices are foremost.
At that time, when the people saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; hundreds of thousands of beings were cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, there were sentient beings who, upon seeing the body of Kāśyapa, attained arhatship; this was called the first assembly, in which nine hundred and sixty million people all became arhats.
All such persons as these are my disciples.
The reason for this is that it is entirely due to having received my instruction and training.
It is also due to four causal conditions:
Generosity, loving-kindness, benefiting others, and equal benefit.
At that time, Ānanda!
Maitreya Tathāgata shall take up the saṃghāṭī robe of Kāśyapa and wear it.
At that time, Kāśyapa’s body suddenly dispersed like stars.
Then Maitreya took various kinds of incense and flowers to make offerings to Kāśyapa.
This was because all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess a heart of reverence for the True Dharma.
"Maitreya, too, has attained the unsurpassed, true, and correct path through being transformed by the True Dharma received from me.

Ānanda, you should know that during Maitreya Buddha’s second assembly, there will be ninety-four billion people who are all arhats; they, too, are disciples of my bequeathed teaching, and this is the result of their practicing the four kinds of offerings."
Furthermore, at Maitreya’s third assembly, there will be nine hundred and twenty billion people, all of whom will be arhats and likewise my disciples under the bequeathed teaching.
At that time, the surnames and names of these bhikṣus shall all be called "disciples of the Maitreya," just as all the śrāvakas today are called "disciples of Śākyamuni."
At that time, Maitreya was preaching the Dharma to his disciples:

"O bhikṣus, you should contemplate the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is pleasant, the perception of non-self in what is reckoned as self, the perception of emptiness in what is real, the perception of the transformation of form, the perception of bluish discoloration, the perception of bloating, the perception of undigested food, the perception of blood, and the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in."

The reason for this is that, monks, you should know: these ten perceptions were all taught to you by the past Buddha Śākyamuni, so that you might exhaust all outflows and attain liberation of the mind.
"Furthermore, if among this assembly there are disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha who, having practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) in the past, have come to my presence;
or those who, under Śākyamuni Buddha, upheld his Dharma and have come to my presence;
or those who, under Śākyamuni Buddha, made offerings to the Triple Gem and have come to my presence;"
Some have cultivated the roots of goodness for the duration of a finger-snap in the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and have come to this place;
some have practiced the four immeasurable minds in the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and have come here;
and some have received and upheld the five precepts and the three refuges in the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha and have come to my abode.
Some have established divine temples at the site of Śākyamuni Buddha and come to my place;
some have repaired old temples at the site of Śākyamuni Buddha and come to my place;
some have received the Eightfold Precepts of the Fast at the site of Śākyamuni Buddha and come to my place.
Some have come here after making offerings of incense and flowers at the place of Śākyamuni Buddha;
others have come to my presence after hearing the Buddha-dharma there and weeping with tears of sorrow;
still others have come to my presence after listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion at the place of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Furthermore, there are those who have practiced the holy life well throughout their entire lives and come to me;
or those who have come to me by writing, reading, reciting, and chanting;
or those who have come to me by serving and making offerings.
At that time, Maitreya spoke these verses:
"Having increased the virtues of precepts and learning, And the practices of meditation and contemplation,
And having well-cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya), You have come to where I am."
Exhorting others to give, they arouse a joyful mind; practicing the original source of the mind, their thoughts are free from manifold conceptualizations, and all come into my presence.
Some give rise to a mind of equanimity, serving and honoring all Buddhas.
Having partaken of food among the noble assembly, they have all come to my presence.
Some recite the precepts and the sūtras; having skillfully practiced them, they explain them to others.
Being fervent in the fundamental Dharma, they have now come to my presence.
The Śākyas, who are skilled in transformation, Make offerings to the various relics;
Practicing the service of Dharma-offerings, They have now come to my presence.
If there are those who transcribe the sutras And proclaim them upon white silk,
Those who have made offerings to the sutras all come to my presence.
Those who offer silk, brocade, and various articles to divine temples,
and who call out "Namo Buddha," all come to my presence.
Making offerings to the Buddhas of the present and those of the past,
their meditative concentration is perfectly equanimous, without increase or decrease.
Therefore, regarding the Buddha-dharma, one should serve the noble Saṅgha.
"Devoting one's mind single-mindedly to the Three Jewels, one will surely reach the state of non-action.
"Ānanda, you should know that Maitreya Tathāgata will speak this verse among that assembly."

At that time, among the assembly, the devas and humans who contemplated these ten perceptions—eleven *koṭis* of people were cleansed of all dust and defilements, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
“During the thousand years of the Tathāgata Maitreya, the monastic community shall be free from any blemish. At that time, they shall always take a single verse as their prohibitive precept:
‘When mouth and mind do not commit evil, And the body likewise commits no transgression— By eliminating these three modes of action, One shall swiftly escape the abyss of birth and death.’”
"After more than a thousand years have passed, there will be those who violate the precepts, and thus the precepts shall be established once again.
Maitreya Tathāgata’s lifespan shall be eighty-four thousand years; after his parinirvāṇa, his bequeathed Dharma shall remain for eighty-four thousand years."
The reason for this is that at that time, all sentient beings will possess sharp faculties.

Any good man or good woman who wishes to behold Maitreya Buddha, as well as the assembly of śrāvakas from his three great assemblies, the city of Kukkuṭapāda, King Śaṅkha, and the four great treasuries of precious jewels; who wishes to eat naturally grown non-glutinous rice and wear naturally produced garments, and who desires that upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life they be reborn in the heavens—such good men and good women should apply themselves with diligent effort and never give rise to indolence. Furthermore, they should provide offerings and serve the Dharma masters, making offerings of famous flowers, powdered incense, and various other things, ensuring that nothing is neglected.
"In this way, Ānanda,
you should train yourself.
At that time, Ānanda and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 44 and Volume 45.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Forty-Eight: On Unwholesome States (Continued from the preceding chapter). (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus gathered in the Hall of Universal Assembly and each gave rise to this thought:
"How truly marvelous! How truly extraordinary is the Tathāgata now!"

Regarding those who have attained parinirvāṇa in the past, he likewise knows their names, clans, observance of the precepts, and retinues—all clearly and distinctly; he also fully knows their samādhis, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation, as well as the length of their lifespans.
"How is it, worthy ones!
Is it that the Tathāgata, having distinguished the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu) as being utterly pure, knows the names and lineages of those Buddhas and the places from which they arise?"
"Or did these devas come to the Buddha's presence and inform him of this?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having heard with his divine ear the various discussions being raised by the many bhikṣus, went to where the bhikṣus were and sat down in their midst.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"For what discussion have you gathered here?
What Dharma do you wish to speak?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"We gathered here to discuss the essentials of the True Dharma.
Each of us raised this particular discourse:"
"The Tathāgata is truly marvelous!
Truly extraordinary!

He is able to know the names, surnames, and titles of the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, as well as the extent of their wisdom; there is nothing he does not penetrate and master—this is most wonderfully sublime."
"How is it, worthy ones!
Does the Tathāgata, having thoroughly purified the dharma-realm through his discernment, know the names and lineages of those Buddhas and the places from which they emerged?"
"Did these devas come to the Buddha's presence to tell him this?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to hear of the power of the divine wisdom of the Buddhas of the past?"
[What of] their surnames, names, and titles, and the length of their lifespans? The bhikṣus replied:
“Now is precisely the right time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon this meaning.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Reflect upon this well; I shall expound its meaning to you in detail.
At that time, the many bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that ninety-one kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Furthermore, thirty-one kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Again, within those same thirty-one kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named Viśvabhū Tathāgata.
In this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Krakucchanda Tathāgata.
Furthermore, in this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Kanakamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, within this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Kāśyapa.
Again, within this Bhadrakalpa, I have appeared in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Within ninety-one kalpas, there was the Buddha Vipaśyin;
Within thirty-one kalpas, the Tathāgata Śikhin appeared."
Furthermore, within that eon, the Tathāgata Viśvabhū appeared;
today, within this Bhadrakalpa, four Buddhas have likewise appeared in the world.
Kaśyapa of the Koṇāgamana lineage shines upon the world like the sun.
If you wish to know their names, their titles are all as follows:

"Vipaśyin Tathāgata was born of the Kṣatriya caste; Śikhin Tathāgata was also born of the Kṣatriya caste; Viśvabhū Tathāgata was also born of the Kṣatriya caste; Krakucchanda Tathāgata was born of the Brāhmaṇa caste; Kanakamuni Tathāgata was born of the Brāhmaṇa caste; Kāśyapa Tathāgata was born of the Brāhmaṇa caste; and as for me, I am now born of the Kṣatriya caste."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Buddhas who appeared previously were all born from the Kṣatriya caste;
from Kauṇḍinya to Kāśyapa, they arose from the Brāhmaṇa caste.”
Most honored and peerless, I am today the Teacher of gods and men;
my faculties are serene and tranquil, and I am born of the Kṣatriya caste.

"Vipaśyin Tathāgata was of the Gautama clan; Śikhin Tathāgata was also born of the Gautama clan; Viśvabhū was also born of the Gautama clan; Kāśyapa Tathāgata was born of the Kāśyapa clan; Krakucchanda and Kanakamuni were also born of the Kāśyapa clan—just as before, without difference—and I, the present Tathāgata, am of the Gautama clan."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"As the first three Buddhas were born from the Gautama clan,
so the last three up to Kāśyapa were born from the Kāśyapa lineage."
Just as I am now, honored and revered by gods and humans, with my faculties serene and tranquil, born of the Gautama clan—monks, you should know that Vipaśyin Tathāgata was of the Kauṇḍinya clan;

Śikhin Tathāgata was also born of the Kauṇḍinya clan; Viśvabhū Tathāgata was also born of the Kauṇḍinya clan; Krakucchanda Tathāgata was born of the Bharadvāja clan; Kanakamuni Tathāgata was also born of the Bharadvāja clan; Kāśyapa Tathāgata was also born of the Bharadvāja clan; and just as I, the present Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, am born of the Kauṇḍinya clan.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"As for the first three Buddhas, they appeared in Kuśinagara;
