the latter three, up to Kāśyapa, appeared in Vārāṇasī."
"Just as I am now, honored and revered by gods and men, with my faculties serene and tranquil, having emerged from the *kuṇḍinaja* [lotus];

so too did Vipaśyin Tathāgata sit beneath the *pāriyātra* tree and attain the Way of Buddhahood; Śikhin Tathāgata sat beneath the *puṇḍarīka* tree and attained the Way of Buddhahood; Viśvabhū Tathāgata sat beneath the *pāṭala* tree and attained the Way of Buddhahood; Krakucchanda Tathāgata sat beneath the *śirīṣa* tree and attained the Way of Buddhahood; Kanakamuni Tathāgata sat beneath the *udumbara* tree and attained the Way of Buddhahood; Kāśyapa Tathāgata sat beneath the *nyagrodha* tree and attained the fruit of the Way; and as I do today, this Tathāgata sits beneath the *aśvattha* (auspicious) tree and attains the Way of Buddhahood."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The first one attained the Buddha-way beneath the Pāṭalī tree;
Śikhin sat upon the Puṇḍarīka; Viśvabhū sat upon the Pāṭala."
Kakusandha sat at the Śirīṣa tree; Konāgamana descended from the Pāṭali tree;
Kāśyapa [sat] beneath the Nyagrodha tree; and I, the Auspicious One, attained enlightenment.
These seven Buddhas, gods among gods, illuminate the world.
Sitting under various trees through causes and conditions, each has realized the fruit of the Path.

The disciples of Tathāgata Vipaśyin numbered one hundred and sixty-eight thousand; the disciples of Tathāgata Śikhin numbered one hundred and sixty thousand; the disciples of Tathāgata Viśvabhū numbered one hundred thousand; the disciples of Tathāgata Krakucchanda numbered eighty thousand; the disciples of Tathāgata Kanakamuni numbered seventy thousand; the disciples of Tathāgata Kāśyapa numbered sixty thousand; and as for my own disciples today, they number one thousand two hundred and fifty. All of them are Arhats, whose outflows are forever exhausted and who are no longer bound by any fetters.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One hundred thousand, sixty-eight thousand— These were the disciples of Vipaśyin.
One hundred thousand and sixty thousand— These were the assembly of Śikhin’s disciples."
The assembly of one hundred thousand bhikṣus were the disciples of Viśvabhū;
Kakutsunda had an assembly of eighty thousand, and Kanakamuni seventy thousand.
Kāśyapa had an assembly of sixty thousand; all of them were arhats.
I, Śākyamuni, now have one thousand two hundred and fifty [disciples].
All are practitioners of the path of the True Persons, manifesting the teachings of the Dharma;
the number of their remaining disciples who follow the bequeathed Dharma is beyond calculation.
"The attendant of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin was named Mahānāman;
the attendant of the Tathāgata Śikhin was named Sujāta;
the attendant of the Tathāgata Viśvabhū was named Jayasena."
The attendant of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda was named Śrī;
the attendant of the Tathāgata Kanakamuni was named Vīrasena;
the attendant of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa was named Nāyaka.
"My attendant now is named Ānanda.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"The Great Way and Good Awakening, The Victorious Assembly and Auspiciousness."
Vīra was the former guide, and Ānanda was the seventh attendant.
These people made offerings to the Sage; there was never a time when they failed to do so.
They recited and upheld [the teachings], never losing their underlying principles.

“Vipaśyin Tathāgata lived for eighty-four thousand years; Śikhin Tathāgata lived for seventy thousand years; Viśvabhū Tathāgata lived for sixty thousand years; Krakucchanda Tathāgata lived for fifty thousand years; Kanakamuni Tathāgata lived for forty thousand years; Kāśyapa Tathāgata lived for twenty thousand years; whereas my own lifespan today is extremely diminished, such that my maximum lifespan does not exceed one hundred years.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The first Buddha lived for eighty-four thousand years; the next Buddha for seventy thousand years;
Viśvabhū for sixty thousand; and Krakucchanda’s lifespan was fifty thousand.”
"Twelve thousand years was the lifespan of Konāgamana;
Kāśyapa’s lifespan was twenty thousand; and mine alone is one hundred years.
Thus it is, O bhikṣus!"

The Tathāgata perceives and knows the names, surnames, and titles of all Buddhas with complete clarity; he is thoroughly versed in their lineages and origins, and he fully understands their observance of precepts, wisdom, meditative concentration, and liberation.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Tathāgata has also said that he knows all the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who have attained parinirvāṇa;
he also knows all the Buddhas of the future, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who are yet to come.”
"For what reason does the Tathāgata not record the deeds performed by so many Buddhas?
Why now do you speak only of the origins and details of the seven Buddhas? The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Because all things possess causes, conditions, beginnings, and ends, the Tathāgata has spoken of the beginning and end of the seven Buddhas;
the countless Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have likewise spoken of the beginning and end of the seven Buddhas;
and when Maitreya appears in the world in the future, he too shall record the beginning and end of the seven Buddhas."
When the Tathāgata Siṃhahanu appears in the world, he shall likewise record the origins and endings of the seven Buddhas;
when the Buddha Mṛdusvara appears in the world, he shall likewise record the origins and endings of the seven Buddhas;
and when the Buddha Arciṣmat appears in the world, he shall likewise record the names of the seven Buddhas.
When the Buddha Vimala appears in the world, he shall likewise record the beginning and end of Kāśyapa;
when the Buddha Ratnaprabha appears in the world, he shall likewise record the beginning and end of Śākyamuni.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Siṃha, Sūrata, Prabhāsa, Vimala, and Ratnaprabha— In this sequence,
Maitreya and the others Shall all attain the Way of the Buddha.”
Maitreya prophesied Śikhin; Siṃha prophesied Viśvabhū;
Sūrata prophesied Krakucchanda; Arciṣmat prophesied Munī;
Vimala prophesied Kāśyapa; all recounted their former objects of focus.
The three Buddhas born of Jewel Light shall likewise record my name.
All the three Buddhas of the past, as well as those yet to come,
shall all record the seven Buddhas and the origins and endings of their former lives.
"For this reason and by these causes and conditions, the Tathāgata has recorded the names of the seven Buddhas.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?"
"How should this be practiced?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is titled 'The Record of the Buddhas' Names'; you should keep it in mind and practice accordingly."
At that time, Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the householder Siṃha went to where Śāriputra was, prostrated with his head at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, the householder Siṃha said to Śāriputra:
"I pray only that the Venerable One will accept my invitation."
At that time, Śāriputra accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the Venerable One had accepted by his silence, the householder rose from his seat, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew. He then went to Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Revata, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Kātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Upāli, Subhūti, Rāhula, and the novice Cunda; in this manner, he invited five hundred such eminent leaders.
At that time, the elder Siṃha returned and prepared various kinds of most exquisite food and drink, spread out fine seating, and further announced:
"The time has come; there is no true person or arhat who does not oversee this. Now the meal is ready; we only pray that you will deign to visit and grace our humble home."
At that time, the great śrāvakas each donned their three robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to go to the house of the elder.
When the elder saw that the most venerable ones were already seated, he personally served them with his own hands, providing various kinds of food and drink.
Seeing that the assembly of noble ones had finished eating, he served them pure water.
Each person offered him a piece of white cotton cloth, which he accepted while they recited verses of blessing.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra expounded the most sublime Dharma to the elder, after which he rose from his seat and departed.
He returned to his quiet chamber.
At that time, Rāhula went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
Then, the World-Honored One asked:
“From where have you come now? Rāhula replied,
“The householder Siṃha has come today to invite me.”
The Buddha said to him:
"What do you think, Rāhula? Is food excellent?"
Is it not excellent? Is it subtle,
or is it coarse?
Rāhula replied, "The food and drink were most excellent and abundant;
it was from there that I obtained this white cotton cloth."
The Buddha asked Rāhula,
"How many people are there in this assembly of monks?
Who is the senior elder?"
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying,
“My preceptor Śāriputra is the foremost, and there are five hundred disciples of divine virtue.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"Rāhula, what do you think?
Would that householder obtain much merit?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The retribution of merit obtained by that elder is beyond calculation.
The merit of giving to a single arhat is already limitless; how much more so when giving to one who is venerated by great gods, wondrous beings, and humans?”
"Now these five hundred people are all true persons (arhats); how can their merit be measured?

The Buddha told Rāhula: "If one were to take from among this assembly according to the monastic order and invite a single śramaṇa, and having invited him, provide him with offerings—then when one calculates the merit of the person selected from this assembly compared to the merit of the five hundred arhats, it would be a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred million-fold, and beyond any possible analogy."
The reason for this is that those appointed from among the assembly possess merit beyond measure, having attained the state of the extinction of the ambrosia.
Rāhula, you should know it is like a person who makes a vow, saying:
"I must surely drink all the waters of these rivers."
“Would that person be capable of it?
Rāhula replied to the Buddha, “No,
World-Honored One.”
World-Honored One!
The reason for this is that this Jambudvīpa is exceedingly vast.
Within this Jambudvīpa there are four great rivers:
The first is the Gaṅgā, the second is the Sindhu, the third is the Sītā, and the fourth is the Vakṣu.
Each of these rivers has five hundred tributaries.
"However, this person will ultimately be unable to drink all the water; he will merely exhaust his efforts, and the task will never be accomplished.
"That person then says again:
'I have my own skillful means and conditions by which I can drink all the waters until they are exhausted.'"
"How can there be a cause and condition by which one may drink various waters?
At that time, that person then had this thought:
"I shall drink the water of the ocean."
The reason for this is that all streams flow and converge into the ocean.
What do you think, Rāhula?
Would that person be able to drink all those waters?"
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By such a means, one may drink the water until it is exhausted.
This is because all streams flow back to the ocean; for this reason, that person is able to drink the water until it is gone."
The Buddha said to him: “It is so, Rāhula!”
All private offerings are like those flowing streams; they may or may not yield merit. The Sangha, however, is like that great ocean.
This is because when the waters of a flowing river break forth and enter the sea, its original name is extinguished, and there remains only the name "great ocean."
Rāhula! It is just like this: these ten people here have all emerged from the assembly; they would not be accomplished without the assembly. What are the ten?

These are: one who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka), one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna); one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka), one who has attained the fruit of once-returning; one who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-pratipannaka), one who has attained the fruit of non-returning; one who is a candidate for the fruit of arhatship (arhat-pratipannaka), one who has attained the fruit of arhatship; the pratyekabuddha; and the buddha. These ten persons all arise from within the assembly; they do not establish themselves independently.
Rāhula! By this expedient means, you should know that among the multitude, those who differ [in their practice] possess merit that is immeasurable. Therefore, Rāhula!
Good sons and good daughters who wish to seek incalculable merit should make offerings to the noble assembly.
Rāhula, you should know that it is like someone throwing ghee into water: it solidifies and does not spread widely; but if one throws oil into water, it completely fills its surface.
Therefore, Rāhula, you should mindfully provide offerings to the noble Saṅgha of bhikṣus. Thus, Rāhula,
you should train yourself.
At that time, when the householder Siṃha heard the Tathāgata praise the merit of giving to the assembly and not praising any other merit,
he went at another time to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the householder Siṃha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I have just heard the Tathāgata praise the merit of giving to the Saṅgha, but not the merit of inviting individuals. From this day forward, I shall constantly provide offerings to the Noble Assembly."
The Buddha told him:
"I do not speak thus: 'One should make offerings to the noble assembly, but not to others.'"
"If giving even to an animal yields such merit, how much more so for other persons?
However, what I have said concerns the varying degrees of that merit.
This is because the noble assembly of the Tathāgata is worthy of veneration and honor; they are the unsurpassed field of merit in the world."

Now, within this assembly there are those who have entered the four stages of fruition and those who have attained the four fruits, as well as followers of the Śrāvaka-yāna, Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and Buddha-yāna.
Any sons or daughters of good family who wish to attain the path of these three vehicles should seek it from within this assembly.
The reason for this is that the paths of the Three Vehicles all arise from the multitude. Elder!
It is because I contemplate the meaning of these causes and conditions that I have spoken these words.
“Nor should one instruct others that they ought to give to the noble assembly, but not to other people.
At that time, the householder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“It shall be so, according to the Venerable One’s instruction; from this day forward, I shall do as you have commanded.”
"If one performs meritorious deeds, they should all be offered to the assembly of noble ones, without discriminating among individuals when giving.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the elder, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy.
Having heard the Dharma, the elder rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet with his head, and then withdrew.
At that time, the elder Siṃha desired to establish meritorious deeds through giving.
At that time, the devas came and told him:
"This person is one who is heading toward the stage of stream-entry; this person has attained stream-entry. Giving to this one brings great merit; giving to that one brings little merit."
At that time, the deva uttered this verse in praise:
“The Tathāgata praises the gift of discernment; to these virtuous men he gives it.
Giving to them brings great merit, just as a good field produces abundant sprouts.”
At that time, the householder Siṃha remained silent and did not respond.
Then, the deva spoke again to the householder:
"This one is a person who upholds the precepts; this one is a person who violates the precepts."
This one is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry; this one has attained the fruit of stream-entry;
this one is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning; this one has attained the fruit of once-returning;
this one is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning; this one has attained the fruit of non-returning.
"This one is heading toward arhatship; this one has attained arhatship;
this is the vehicle of the śrāvakas; this is the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
this is the Buddha-vehicle; giving to this yields little merit; giving to that yields much merit."
At that time, the householder Siṃha remained silent and did not respond.
Why was this? It was because he was solely mindful of the Tathāgata’s instruction to give without making discriminations.
At that time, on another occasion, the householder Siṃha went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side, saying:
“I recall having invited the noble assembly for a meal, when a deva came and told me:
‘This one is observant of the precepts; this one has violated the precepts;’”
"This person is heading toward the stage of *srotāpanna*, this person has attained *srotāpanna*; thus, even up to the three vehicles, they are all distinguished.
Furthermore, he spoke this verse:
"The Tathāgata praises the gift of discernment, Bestowed upon these virtuous practitioners."
"By giving this, one gains much merit, like sprouts growing in a fertile field.
At that time, I further thought:
"The Tathāgata’s instructions must not be contravened; how could I allow myself to give with a mind of discrimination?"
"In the end, there will be no sense of right or wrong, nor any notion of high or low.
At that time, I again thought to myself:

"I shall give everything to all classes of sentient beings; you may personally maintain the precepts and receive inexhaustible blessings, but if you violate the precepts, you shall suffer the calamity yourself."
"I only pity sentient beings; without food, their lives cannot be sustained.
The Buddha said to the elder, "Excellent!"
Excellent, O Householder!
Your conduct surpasses even the great vows; the mind of a Bodhisattva is ever equal in whatever he bestows.
Householder, you should know that on the day a bodhisattva practices giving, the devas come to inform him:

"Noble son, you should know that this person is one who upholds the precepts and this person is one who violates the precepts; by giving to this one you will obtain much merit, while by giving to that one you will obtain little merit."
At that time, the Bodhisattva never entertains such thoughts as:
"This should be given; this should not be given.
Rather, the Bodhisattva maintains his resolve without judgment of right or wrong, neither saying "this is observance of the precepts" nor saying "this is a violation of the precepts."
"Therefore, householder, you should practice impartial giving; throughout the long night, you shall obtain immeasurable merit.

At that time, the householder Siṃha, recollecting the Tathāgata’s instruction, gazed intently at the World-Honored One with an unwavering mind, and thereupon, while seated, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, the householder Siṃha rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head, and then withdrew.
Not long after the householder had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Because this householder Siṃha recollected his practice of impartial giving and beheld the Tathāgata from head to foot, he attained the pure Dharma-eye while still seated upon his cushion.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my upāsakas, the foremost disciple in equal giving is the elder Siṃha."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was in a secluded spot on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, mending an old robe.

Then, ten thousand Brahmakāyika devas vanished from the Brahma heaven and came to where Śāriputra was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, each surrounding him in attendance, and praised him with this verse:
"We take refuge in the supreme among men; We take refuge in the honored one among men."
"We have not yet attained it; upon what dhyāna do we rely?
At that time, after the ten thousand Brahmakāyika devas had spoken these words, Śāriputra silently assented.
At that time, having seen that Śāriputra had consented by remaining silent, the devas prostrated at his feet and withdrew.
Not long after the devas had departed, Śāriputra entered the Vajra-samādhi.
At that time, there were two spirits: one named Kāla and the other named Upakāla.
Sent by King Vaiśravaṇa to the abode of King Virūḍhaka, they intended to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.

At that time, two ghosts were passing through the sky above. Seeing from afar Śāriputra sitting cross-legged, his mindfulness fixed before him and his mind settled in tranquil concentration, the ghost Kāla said to the other ghost:
"I am now capable of striking this śramaṇa on the head with my fist."
The spirit Upagala said to the second spirit, "Do not harbor such an intention to strike the head of this śramaṇa. Why is this?

This śramaṇa possesses supreme spiritual power and great majesty. This venerable one is named Śāriputra; among the disciples of the World-Honored One, there is none more intelligent or highly talented than him, and he is the foremost among those of wisdom."
"Thus, throughout the long night, you shall suffer immeasurable pain.
At that time, the ghost said a second and third time:
"I am capable of striking this śramaṇa on the head."
The ghost Upagāra replied:
"If you do not follow my words now, you shall remain here; I wish to leave you behind and depart from this place."
The evil spirit asked,
"Are you afraid of this śramaṇa?
Upagāla the spirit replied:

"I am truly afraid of this. If you were to strike this śramaṇa with your hand, this earth would split into two parts; likewise, there would be violent winds and torrential rain, and the earth would tremble. The devas would be startled and agitated; once the earth has trembled, even the Four Great Kings would be struck with terror, and the Four Great Kings, having learned of our situation, would no longer find peace in their abodes."
At that time, the evil spirit said,
"I am now capable of insulting this śramaṇa.
Having heard this, the good spirit abandoned him and departed.
At that time, the evil spirit struck Śāriputra’s head with his hand.

Immediately, heaven and earth shook violently, and fierce winds and torrential rains came rushing from the four directions; the ground split open into two parts, and the evil spirit fell with his entire body into hell.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra arose from samādhi, adjusted his robes, descended from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and went to the Bamboo Grove to the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Is there no illness in your body now? Śāriputra replied:
“I am naturally free from ailment; I suffer only from a headache.
The World-Honored One said, “The Kāla-demon struck your head with his hand.”
If that ghost were to strike Mount Sumeru with his hand, Mount Sumeru would immediately split into two parts.
This is because that ghost possesses great power.
"Now, because this ghost has received the retribution for its offenses, its entire body has entered the Avīci Hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"How extraordinary!
How extraordinary!
The power of the Vajra-samādhi extends even to this.
By the power of this samādhi, one cannot be harmed; even if Mount Sumeru were to strike one’s head, it could never move so much as a single hair on one’s body.
The reason for this is as follows, monks, listen:
In this present Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha named Krakucchanda, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
That Buddha had two great śrāvakas: one named Samajīvī and the other named Mahājñānin.
The bhikṣu Samajīvī was foremost in ṛddhi-powers;
the bhikṣu Mahājñānin was foremost in wisdom, just as today Śāriputra is foremost in wisdom and Maudgalyāyana is foremost in ṛddhi-powers.
At that time, the two bhikṣus, Samāyu and Mahājñāna, both attained the Vajrasamādhi.
On one occasion, while the bhikṣu Samāyu was in a secluded place, he entered the Vajrasamādhi.
At that time, cowherds, shepherds, and wood-gatherers, seeing this bhikṣu sitting in meditation, each said to one another:
"This śramaṇa has met with impermanence today."
At that time, cowherds and wood-gatherers gathered various grasses and wood, piled them over the bhikṣu’s body, set fire to it, and then departed.
"At that time, the bhikṣu Samajīvī arose from samādhi, adjusted his robes, and withdrew.
Then, on that very day, the bhikṣu put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food."
At that time, the wood-gatherers saw this bhikṣu begging for alms in the village and said to one another:
"This bhikṣu died yesterday; we cremated him with fire, yet today he has returned to life. We shall now establish a name for him; let his name be 'Revived' (Punarvasu)."
"If there is a bhikṣu who has attained the vajra-samādhi, he cannot be burned by fire, pierced by a sword, swept away by water, nor can he be harmed or injured by others."
Thus it is, bhikṣu! Such is the majestic power of the Vajra-samādhi.
Now that Śāriputra has attained this samādhi, the bhikṣu Śāriputra frequents two places in great measure:
The emptiness samādhi and the vajra samādhi. Therefore, O bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means and practice the vajra samādhi.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall instruct you so that you may become like the bhikṣu Śāriputra: a bhikṣu of wisdom, of great wisdom, of analytical and vast wisdom, of boundless wisdom, of swift wisdom, of all-pervading wisdom, of sharp wisdom, of profound wisdom, and of decisive wisdom; one who has few desires and is content, who is secluded and courageous, whose mindfulness is undistracted, who is accomplished in ethical discipline, accomplished in meditative concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, liberation, and the vision of the knowledge of liberation; one who is gentle and non-contentious, who discards evil and possesses discernment, who endures all speech, who praises the departure from evil, who constantly reflects on renunciation, who takes pity on all living beings, who kindles the True Dharma, and who never tires of preaching the Dharma to others.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Ten thousand devas and humans, All of them Brahmakāyika,
Have taken refuge in Śāriputra Upon the summit of Vulture Peak."
"I take refuge in the supreme among men; I take refuge in the honored one among men.
I do not now know upon what kind of dhyāna you rely.
Thus, as a disciple-flower, I adorn the Bodhi tree."
"Just as in the Tuṣita Garden of Heaven, its bliss is beyond compare.
"The disciple named Puṣpa was none other than the bhikṣu Śāriputra."
The reason for this is that such a person is able to adorn the Bodhi tree.
The Bodhi tree is none other than the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata is able to provide shelter and protection for all sentient beings.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should be mindful, diligent, courageous, and energetic, just as the bhikṣu Śāriputra was. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 45.
Ekottarika Āgama, Scroll 46, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 49: The Chapter on Tending Cattle. Part Four: The Fourth Section of Analysis.
1. (One) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a cowherd is not accomplished in eleven qualities, his herd will never prosper, nor will he be able to properly protect his cattle.
What are these eleven?

At that time, the cowherd likewise did not distinguish their colors nor understand their characteristics; he failed to groom them when they required it, did not protect their wounds, and did not smoke out the flies at the proper times. He was ignorant of where the fields were fertile and the grass lush, and he knew nothing of safe places to rest. Furthermore, he did not know the locations for crossing rivers, nor did he understand the requirements of the season. When the cows were to eat, he would leave no remainder, consuming everything entirely. Consequently, those great oxen who were fit for work were not properly tended to according to the needs of the time.
"Thus it is, bhikkhus!
If a cowherd is possessed of these eleven qualities, he will ultimately be unable to nourish his cattle or protect their well-being."
“Now, the bhikṣus within this assembly are likewise; they will ultimately be unable to achieve any growth or benefit. What are these eleven?

In this regard, a bhikṣu does not distinguish colors, nor does he understand their characteristics. He fails to scrub and clean [the vessel], fails to protect its sores, fails to release smoke at the proper time, and does not know where the fertile fields and lush grasses lie. He does not know the proper fords, nor does he know places of safety. He lacks knowledge of what is timely, and when eating, he does not know how to leave a remainder. Furthermore, he does not show respect or hospitality toward the elder bhikṣus.”
"What is it for a bhikṣu not to know form?
In this regard, a bhikṣu does not know at all the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
In this way, a bhikṣu does not distinguish that form."
"What is meant by a bhikṣu who does not discern their characteristics?
In this case, a bhikṣu does not know the practice of delusion, nor does he know the practice of wisdom; he does not know them as they truly are."
In this way, a bhikṣu does not discern their characteristics.
"How is it that a bhikṣu should polish and scrub but does not polish and scrub?

In this case, when a bhikṣu sees a form with the eye, he gives rise to the perception of form; various distracted thoughts arise, and furthermore, he does not guard the faculty of the eye. Because he does not skillfully restrain his mindfulness, he creates a multitude of calamities and transgressions, failing to guard the faculty of the eye."

In this way, bhikṣus, if one hears sounds with the ear, smells odors with the nose, tastes flavors with the tongue, feels tactile sensations with the body, or cognizes mental objects with the mind, and gives rise to various distracted thoughts, yet does not guard the faculty of the mind nor rectify one's conduct; [this is called a person who has fallen away from the Dharma.]
In this way, a bhikṣu should scrub and cleanse [the wound], yet he does not scrub and cleanse it.
How does a bhikṣu fail to protect the wound?
In this case, a bhikṣu gives rise to thoughts of desire and does not abandon them, nor does he eliminate those mental impressions.
If one gives rise to thoughts of anger, thoughts of killing, or various other evil and unwholesome thoughts, and never abandons them—
such a bhikṣu does not protect his wound.
"How does a bhikṣu not emit smoke at the improper time?
In this regard, a bhikṣu does not recite the Dharma he has memorized for others at the improper time.
In this way, a bhikṣu does not emit smoke at the improper time."
"What is meant by a bhikṣu not knowing the fertile field and the lush grass?
In this regard, a bhikṣu does not know the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) as they truly are;
thus, a bhikṣu does not know the place of the fertile field and the lush grass."
“What is it for a bhikṣu not to know the place of crossing?
In this regard, a bhikṣu does not distinguish the Noble Eightfold Path; thus, a bhikṣu does not know the place of crossing.”
“What is meant by a bhikṣu who does not know what is cherished?

In this regard, a bhikṣu [is ignorant] regarding the twelve divisions of the scriptures: the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, nidānas, itivṛttakas, vaipulyas, avadānas, jātaka-s, upadeśas, vaipulyas, and adbhuta-dharma-s.”
In this way, a bhikṣu does not know what is dear to him.
What is it for a bhikṣu not to know the proper occasion?
In this case, a bhikṣu goes to the homes of those who are contemptible or to gambling dens.
In this way, a bhikṣu does not know the proper occasion.
How is it that a bhikṣu does not leave any remainder?
In this case, when faithful brahmins or upāsakas come and invite them, yet those bhikṣus are greedily attached to food and drink and do not know moderation.
In this way, a bhikṣu leaves nothing remaining.
What is it for a bhikṣu not to respect the elder bhikṣus of high virtue?
In this case, a bhikṣu does not give rise to a heart of reverence toward those who possess merit; such a bhikṣu transgresses many precepts.
This is called a bhikṣu who does not respect his elders.
If a bhikṣu is possessed of these eleven qualities, he will ultimately be unable to bring much benefit within this Dharma.
"Furthermore, if a cowherd accomplishes eleven qualities, he will be able to protect his cattle, never miss the proper time, and bring about great benefit.
What are these eleven?

Thereupon, the cowherd recognizes their color and distinguishes their characteristics; he brushes them down as required, protects their wounds, and maintains the smoke at the proper times. He knows the locations of fertile fields and lush pastures, and he knows the essential fords for crossing. Cherishing his cattle, he discerns the appropriate timing and understands their temperaments and behaviors. When they graze, he knows how much to leave behind, and he also knows how to protect those fit for service according to the season.
In this way, the cowherd protects and guards his cattle. Likewise, bhikṣus!
If a cowherd is accomplished in these eleven qualities and does not lose the proper seasons, he can never be thwarted or ruined.
“In this way, bhikkhus, if one accomplishes eleven qualities, one will be of great benefit in this very life.
What are these eleven qualities?

Thereupon, the bhikṣu knows form; he knows its characteristics; he knows how to groom it; he knows how to protect the wound; he knows how to produce smoke; he knows the fertile field and the lush grass; he knows what is cherished; he knows how to select the path for travel; he knows the crossing places; he knows moderation in food; and he knows how to respectfully serve the elder bhikṣus, paying them homage at the appropriate times.
“How does a bhikkhu know form? In this regard, a bhikkhu knows the form consisting of the four great elements, and he also knows the form derived from the four great elements.
This is called a bhikkhu who knows form.”
"How does a bhikkhu know the signs?
In this regard, a bhikkhu knows the sign of the ignorant and knows the sign of the wise, knowing them as they truly are.
Thus does a bhikkhu know the signs."
“What is a bhikkhu who knows how to scrub?
In this case, if a thought of sensual desire arises, he recognizes it with mindfulness and abandons it; he does not cultivate it, and thus there is forever no thought of sensual desire.

If thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, or various evil and unwholesome thoughts arise, he recognizes them with mindfulness and abandons them; he does not cultivate them, and thus there is forever no thought of ill will.”
In this way, a bhikṣu knows how to scrub and clean.
How does a bhikṣu know how to protect a wound?

In this regard, when a bhikṣu sees a form with the eye, he does not give rise to the perception of form, nor does he become stained by attachment; he purifies the faculty of the eye, removes sorrow, grief, and unwholesome states, and his mind does not crave or delight therein, thus protecting the faculty of the eye within that state.

In this way, bhikṣus, when the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue perceives tastes, the body perceives tangibles, or the mind cognizes mental objects, one does not give rise to conceptualizations of consciousness, nor does one become stained or attached, thereby purifying the faculty of the mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows how to protect a wound.
How does a bhikṣu know how to produce smoke?
In this regard, a bhikṣu takes the Dharma he has heard and explains it extensively to others.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows how to produce smoke.
How does a bhikṣu know a field of lush grass?
In this regard, a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu who knows the place where the fertile field and lush grass are found.
How does a bhikṣu know what is beloved?
In this regard, when a bhikṣu hears the Dharma-treasure taught by the Tathāgata, his heart immediately feels love and joy for it.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows what is beloved.
"How does a bhikṣu practice by discerning the path?

Herein, a bhikṣu discerns and practices the twelve divisions of the scriptures, namely: sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, nidāna, itivṛttaka, vaipulya, avadāna, jātaka, upadeśa, vaipulya (extensive), and adbhutadharma."
In this way, a bhikṣu knows the practice of discerning the path.
How does a bhikṣu know the crossing-place?
In this regard, a bhikṣu knows the four foundations of mindfulness.
This is called a bhikṣu who knows the crossing-place.
How does a bhikṣu know moderation in food?
In this regard, when faithful brahmins or upāsakas come to invite him, he does not crave food and drink, but is able to exercise self-restraint and contentment.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows contentment.
How does a bhikṣu respectfully serve elder bhikṣus according to the occasion?
In this regard, a bhikṣu constantly directs wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind toward the elder bhikṣus.
In this way, a bhikṣu should respectfully serve elder bhikṣus at the appropriate times. Thus,
if one accomplishes these eleven qualities, one will bring great benefit in this present life.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The cowherd who is heedful gains merit for his master;
In six years, from six cows, he comes to possess sixty.”
Having fulfilled the bhikṣu precepts, he attained mastery over dhyāna;
his six sense faculties were tranquil, and in six years he perfected the six supernormal powers. "It is so."
"Monks! If anyone can abandon these unwholesome qualities and accomplish the subsequent eleven qualities, they will derive great benefit in this present life.
Thus it is, monks!"
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (2) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If a bhikṣu accomplishes eleven qualities, he will certainly be able to achieve growth and progress.”
What are these eleven? In this regard, monks:

one is accomplished in ethical discipline, accomplished in meditative concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the vision and knowledge of liberation; one’s faculties are tranquil; one knows moderation in eating; one constantly practices the shared dharmas and understands their skillful means; one discerns their meaning and does not cling to gain and offerings.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
One who accomplishes these eleven dharmas is capable of nurturing [the path]. Why is this so?
Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) truly consist of these eleven dharmas.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what reason is it that there are exactly eleven dharmas from which there is no escape? What are these eleven?"
"What is called 'araṇya' (wilderness dwelling):

begging for food, sitting in one place, eating at one time, eating only at midday, not choosing specific households for alms, maintaining the three robes, sitting under a tree, sitting in the open air in a secluded place, wearing patched robes, or staying among the tombs."
"Monks, it is said that if a person accomplishes these eleven dharmas, they will be able to reach their destination.
I now tell you again: if there is someone who studies this dharma for eleven years, they will become an Anāgāmin in this very life, and upon changing bodies, they will immediately become an Arhat."
"O bhikṣus! Setting aside eleven years, if one studies this Dharma for nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or even one year, they will attain two fruits:
either that of a non-returner (anāgāmin) or that of an arhat."
Furthermore, setting aside the twelve months, if one can practice this dharma within a single month, that bhikṣu will certainly attain one of two fruits:
either the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin) or arhatship.
The reason for this is that the twelve links of dependent origination all emerge from within eleven dharmas, namely:
birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"I now instruct all bhikṣus that they should be like the bhikṣu Kāśyapa; even if someone were to practice the dharma of austerity, such conduct would be difficult to equal."
The reason for this is that the bhikṣu Kāśyapa has accomplished these eleven dharmas.
You should know that in the past, when the Tathāgatas attained equal and perfect enlightenment, they also accomplished these eleven dharmas of suffering.

Now, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa compassionately regards all sentient beings; whereas if one makes offerings to the past śrāvakas, one will only receive the retribution in a future life, if one makes offerings to Kāśyapa, one receives the retribution in this very life.
Furthermore, were I not to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, it would be through Kāśyapa that I would later achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.
For this reason, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa surpasses all the śrāvakas of the past; those who are able to be like the bhikṣu Kāśyapa possess the highest practice.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(3) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha was surrounded by countless sentient beings, who stood before and behind him as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, Śāriputra was walking in meditation accompanied by a great multitude of bhikṣus.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, Revata, Kātyāyana, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Upāli, Subhūti, Rāhula, and the bhikṣu Ānanda each led a great multitude of bhikṣus, and they took delight in one another’s company.
Devadatta likewise led a great multitude of bhikṣus as he himself practiced walking meditation.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw his disciples endowed with supernormal powers, each leading their own assembly as they practiced walking meditation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The faculties, dispositions, and natures of persons are each similar to one another; the virtuous associate with the virtuous, and the wicked associate with the wicked. It is just as milk corresponds with milk, ghee with ghee, and excrement, urine, and filth correspond with their own kind."

This is also like this: the fundamental natures and the practices of sentient beings correspond to one another individually; those who are good correspond with the good, and those who are evil correspond with the evil.
“Do you see the bhikṣu Śāriputra walking to and fro with the other bhikṣus?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, “Indeed, we do.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All such people as these are men of wisdom.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you see the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana walking for exercise with the bhikṣus?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, “Indeed, we do.”
The Buddha told him,
"These bhikṣus are all masters of supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
He asked again:
"Do you see Kāśyapa leading the bhikṣus as he walks up and down? The bhikṣus replied, "Indeed, we do."
The Buddha told him:
"These noble beings are all practitioners of the eleven dhūta ascetic practices.
He asked again:
"Do you see the bhikṣu Aniruddha? The bhikṣus replied, "Indeed, we see him."
The Buddha told him:
"These worthy men are all foremost in the divine eye.
He asked again:
“Have you seen the bhikṣu Revata? The bhikṣus replied,
“Indeed, we have seen him.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All these people are practitioners who have entered meditative absorption.
He asked again:
“Do you all see the bhikṣu Kātyāyana? The bhikṣus replied, “Indeed, we see him.”
The Buddha told him:
"These noble beings are all people who analyze principles and meanings.
He asked again:
“Do you all see the bhikṣu Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra? The bhikṣus replied, “Indeed, we see him.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These worthy gentlemen are all teachers of the Dharma.
He asked again:
"Do you see Upāli leading the bhikṣus as they walk for exercise? The bhikṣus replied, "Indeed, we do."
The Buddha told him:
"All these people are those who uphold the prohibitive precepts.
He asked again:
“Do you all see the bhikṣu Subhūti? The bhikṣus replied, “Indeed, we see him.”
The Buddha told him:
"These superior men are all foremost in the understanding of emptiness.
He asked again:
“Do you all see the bhikṣu Rāhula? The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, “Indeed, we see him.”
The Buddha told him:
"These worthy gentlemen are all those who are fully endowed with the precepts.
He asked again:
“Do you see the bhikṣu Ānanda? The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, “Indeed, we see him.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These worthy men are all foremost in erudition; they do not forget what they have received.
He asked again:
“Do you see the bhikṣu Devadatta walking for exercise with a group of people? The bhikṣus replied, “Indeed, we do.”
The Buddha told them:
"These people are the leaders of evil; they possess no roots of goodness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Do not associate with evil companions, nor engage in affairs with the foolish;
you should associate with virtuous friends and commune with the wise.
Even if a person is originally without evil, if they draw near to wicked people,"
"In the future, it will surely become a cause for evil, and an ill reputation will spread throughout the world.

At that time, more than thirty disciples of Devadatta, having heard these verses spoken by the World-Honored One, abandoned Devadatta and came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves at his feet, seeking absolution for their grave offense, and further addressed the World-Honored One:

"We were foolish and deluded, failing to distinguish between the true and the false; we abandoned our good spiritual friends and drew near to evil ones. We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us forgiveness and that we shall not commit such offenses again."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“I grant you permission to repent; reform your past ways and cultivate yourself for the future, and do not commit such offenses again.

At that time, Devadatta’s disciples, having received the World-Honored One’s instruction and admonition, dwelt in secluded places, contemplating the sublime meaning, and disciplined themselves in the practice of the Dharma. This is why sons of noble family shave their hair and beards, leave the household life, and study the Way, desiring to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*).
At that time, all the bhikṣus attained arhatship.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that the fundamental natures of sentient beings are all similar to one another: those who are evil associate with the evil, and those who are good associate with the good. The fundamental natures of sentient beings in the past and the future are likewise; they follow according to their kind, just as the pure corresponds with the pure, and the impure corresponds with the impure.”
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in association with purity;
through purity, one leaves behind impurity.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Kuruśravaṇa-dharmacārin together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Śāriputra the Elephant returned his Dharma robes and resumed the conduct of a layperson.
Then Ānanda, having put on his robe and taken up his alms bowl, entered the city to beg for food and gradually arrived at the house of Śāriputra the Elephant.
At that time, Śāriputra the Elephant was leaning against the shoulders of two women. When Ānanda saw this from afar, he immediately conceived feelings of sorrow and displeasure.
Seeing Ānanda, Śāriputra the Elephant felt profound shame and sat down alone.
At that time, Ānanda, having finished his almsround, returned from the city to the place where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Just now, as I entered the city for alms, I gradually made my way to the house of Śāriputra the Elephant. There I saw him being supported on the shoulders of two women; upon seeing this, I felt profound sorrow."
The World-Honored One said:
"Having seen this, what thought has arisen in you?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that Śāriputra was diligent and possessed of great learning; his nature and conduct were gentle and mild, and for a long time he tirelessly taught the Dharma to those practicing the holy life.”
"Why have you now cast aside the dharma robes and taken up the conduct of a layman?
At that time, having seen this, I felt profound sorrow; yet this elephant Śāriputra possesses great supernormal power and immeasurable majesty.
He thought to himself, "I recall that in the past I once saw him debating with Śakra Devānām Indra;
why is it that today he indulges in sensual desires and commits evil?
The World-Honored One said to him:
"So it is, Ānanda! It is as you have said; however, he is not yet an arhat."
Now, an Arhat never again discards the dharma-robes to adopt the conduct of a layperson.
However, Ānanda, do not harbor grief or distress; seven days from now, Śāriputra will come to this place and exhaust all outflows to achieve the practice of the outflow-free state.
"However, this elephant Śāriputra was led by his past karma; thus has he come to this state.
Now that his practice is fully perfected, he shall exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).
At that time, seven days later, the elephant Śāriputra went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
After a short while, he withdrew to sit at the side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Permit me to remain among the ranks of the junior disciples and cultivate the practice of a śramaṇa."
At that time, the bhikṣu Hastiśāriputra immediately attained the status of a śramaṇa and, right there on his seat, realized arhatship.
Thereupon, Hastiśāriputra put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms.
At that time, a certain brahmin conceived this thought:
"These Śākyan scions are present everywhere and pervade all places; moreover, they have brought to an end the incantations and arts we practice."
"I shall now go into the city and speak of this śramaṇa’s faults.
At that time, the brahmin said to the people of the city:
"Do any of you people happen to see the elephant Śāriputra?"
In the past, he claimed for himself to be an Arhat, yet midway he cast off his dharma robes and adopted the conduct of a layman, indulging in the pleasures of the five desires.

Now, having again become a śramaṇa, he begs for food from house to house, feigning integrity and purity; yet he gazes upon women, giving rise to lustful thoughts, and returning to the garden, he dwells on female beauty without letting it depart from his mind, like a weary donkey unable to carry its load, lying there in silence.
"This son of the Śākyas is just like this: he feigns begging for alms while observing the beauty of women and calculating his schemes.
At that time, upon hearing the wicked voice of this brahmin, the elephant Śāriputra conceived this thought:
"This man is utterly foolish; he gives rise to a mind of jealousy."
Seeing others obtain gain and offerings, they give rise to a mind of stinginess and envy;
yet when they themselves obtain gain and offerings, they harbor joy and go to the homes of laypeople to engage in slander.
"I shall now restrain him so that he does no evil, lest this man suffer immeasurable retribution.
At that time, Śāriputra the Elephant flew into the air and addressed the brahmin, saying:
"Blind and lacking skillful means, You have conceived the intent to slander those of pure conduct."
"Having committed harmful deeds for oneself, one shall long endure the sufferings of hell.
At that time, after the elephant Śāriputra had spoken this verse, he withdrew and returned to his own abode.
At that time, the people of the city, having heard the Brahmin’s slander and having also heard the verses spoken by the elephant Śāriputra, each conceived this thought:
"If it were as the Brahmin says, then he would have manifested supernatural powers difficult to equal;
yet we see him instead casting off his dharma-robes and adopting the conduct of a layman."
At that time, a great multitude of people, each leading their companions, went to where the elephant Śāriputra was; they prostrated at his feet and sat down to one side.
Then, the multitude of people asked the elephant Śāriputra:
"Is there any Arhat who has returned to lay life, discarded the dharma-robes, and practices the conduct of a white-clad householder?"
The elephant Śāriputra replied,
"There is no Arhat who would ever cast off the dharma-robes to adopt the conduct of a layperson.
At that time, the people said to the elephant Śāriputra:
“Does an Arhat ever violate the precepts due to past conditions?
Śāriputra the Elephant replied,
“Having attained Arhatship, one never violates the precepts.”
The people spoke again, saying:
"Does one who is still on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) commit a transgression of the precepts due to past conditions?
Śāriputra the Elder replied:
“There is. If a person dwelling on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) violates the prohibitive precepts due to their original conditions.
At that time, the people spoke again:
"Venerable sir, you were previously an Arhat, yet you discarded the dharma-robes to practice the conduct of a layperson, finding pleasure for yourself in the five desires;
now you have again left the household life to study the Way. Since you originally possessed supernormal powers, why is it that they are now like this?"
At that time, Śāriputra the Elephant spoke this verse:
"Those who dwell in worldly meditations Ultimately do not attain liberation;
Failing to reach the track of cessation, They return once more to the practice of the five desires."
"Without fuel, fire does not burn; without roots, branches do not grow;
a barren woman has no womb; and an Arhat does not receive outflows.
At that time, the people asked the elephant-like Śāriputra again:
“Was your venerable predecessor not an Arhat?
Śāriputra the Elephant replied,
“I was not an Arhat before.”

"Householders, you should know that the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) and the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) each have their own distinctions; I shall now explain the eleven types of supernormal powers.

As for the seers possessing the five supernormal powers, once their craving for sensual desire has been exhausted, if they are born in the higher realms, they may again descend back into the realm of desire."

"Those Arhats with the six supernormal powers who are disciples of the Tathāgata have attained the power of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) and shall enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At that time, the people spoke again, saying:
"As we observe what Śāriputra has said, there is no one in the world who, having been an Arhat, would cast off the dharma-robes and adopt the conduct of a white-clad layperson."
Then, the elephant Śāriputra replied: "It is so.
As you have said, there is no arhat who would ever discard the dharma-robes to practice as a layperson."
There are eleven things that an Arhat does not practice. What are these eleven?
An Arhat whose taints are exhausted never discards the dharma-robe to adopt the conduct of a layperson.
An Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never engages in unchaste conduct;
an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never kills living beings;
an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never steals.
An Arhat whose outflows are exhausted leaves no food remaining after he has eaten;
an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never speaks falsely;
an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never associates with or assists a crowd.
An Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never utters harsh words;
an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never harbors doubt;
an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never experiences fear.
An Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never again accepts another teacher, nor does he ever again receive a womb.
Thus it is said, O worthy sirs:
an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted never dwells in the eleventh stage.
At that time, the people said to the Elder Śāriputra:

"Having heard what the Venerable One has spoken, we view the heterodox teachers and their various doctrines as being like empty jars containing nothing at all; yet now, when we examine the internal Dharma, it is like a jar of honey, where there is nothing that is not sweet and delicious—the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is likewise so."
"Now that brahmin shall suffer immeasurable retribution.
At that time, Śāriputra the Elephant flew into the air, sat cross-legged, and spoke this verse:
"Without understanding the essential points of either side, He practiced the arts of the non-Buddhist paths."
"To engage in mutual strife and disorder is something the wise do not practice.
At that time, the people of Kuruṣa addressed the Elder Śāriputra, saying:
"The words you have spoken are exceedingly profound and truly difficult to fathom; it is like a blind man regaining his sight, or a deaf person regaining their hearing."
Now, what the Venerable One has taught is likewise so; you have expounded the Dharma and instruction through countless skillful means.

Today we take refuge in the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. We only pray that the Venerable One will accept us as upāsakas; for as long as life lasts, we shall no longer kill living beings.

At that time, Śāriputra the Elephant preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the multitude, causing them to give rise to hearts of joy; they each rose from their seats, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda heard the brahmin reviling Śāriputra the Elephant, yet he could not even look directly at him, let alone engage him in debate!
He immediately went to where the World-Honored One was and, for these reasons, reported the matter in detail to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"In discussing those who are equal to an Arhat, one should say that Śāriputra is such a person."

The reason for this is that the Elder Śāriputra has now already become an Arhat; what was previously known by the name "Arhat" has been attained today. The five mundane supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are not true practices, for they will inevitably be lost later;
the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), however, are true practices.
The reason for this is that this elephant, Śāriputra, previously possessed five supernormal powers and has now attained six;
you, too, should train until you equal this elephant, Śāriputra.
"This is its meaning; you should reflect upon it and practice accordingly.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 5 (V) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now expound the Dharma of causes and conditions; reflect upon it well and cultivate its practice.”
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“So be it, World-Honored One! Thereupon,
the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said: "What is called the Dharma of Dependent Origination? It is as follows: ignorance conditions volitional formations;

volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—beyond all measure."
In this way, this body composed of the five aggregates is formed. What, then, is called ignorance?
It is said that not knowing suffering, not knowing its origin, not knowing its cessation, and not knowing the path—this is called ignorance.
"What is meant by 'practice'?
There are three kinds of practice. What are the three?
What are called bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations—these are termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
What is meant by "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness.
What are the six? They are namely:
eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness; these are called "consciousness.
What is meant by "name" (nāma)?
That which is called "name" (nāma) consists of sensation, perception, volition, contact, and attention; these are what constitute name.
What is meant by "form" (rūpa)?
It refers to the body composed of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements; this is what is called form.
Because form is distinct and name is distinct, they are called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
What are the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana)?
They are the six internal sense bases.
What are the six? They are the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
What is meant by "contact" (*sparśa*)?
What are called the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-sparśakāya*)? What are the six?
They are the contact of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are what are termed "contacts."
"What is that which constitutes feeling?
It is the three types of feeling. What are the three?
What are called pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—these are termed "feeling" (*vedanā*).
What is termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*)?
It refers to the three bodies of craving.
Craving for sensory desire, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. "What is feeling?
It refers to the four types of feeling."
What are the four? They are the clinging to sensual desire, the clinging to views, the clinging to precepts and observances, and the clinging to a self-concept; these are called the four clingings.
What, then, constitutes their existence?
What is called the three realms of existence? What are the three?
They are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; these are termed "existence."
"What is this that is called 'birth'?
That which is called birth refers to being fully endowed with renunciation, undergoing existence, acquiring the five aggregates, and receiving the sense bases; this is what is meant by birth."
"What is meant by 'aging'?

It refers to those various sentient beings who, in this physical body, have their teeth fallen out and hair turned white; whose vigor and strength are exhausted and depleted; whose faculties have fully matured; whose lifespan daily declines; and who no longer possess their original consciousness—this is called aging."

"What is death? It refers to those various sentient beings who, undergoing successive transformations of form, find their bodies devoid of warmth; they are impermanent and subject to change, their kinsmen are scattered, they cast off the body of the five aggregates, and their life-faculty is severed and destroyed—this is called death."
"Monks, you should know that these are what are called old age, sickness, and death.
These are termed the phenomena of dependent origination; their meaning has been extensively analyzed.
That which all Buddhas and Tathāgatas ought to practice—arousing great compassion—I have now fulfilled."
When you are mindful while sitting in the open air beneath a tree or among the burial mounds, you should practice seated meditation and harbor no fear or anxiety.
If you do not apply yourself with diligence now, it will be of no benefit when you regret it later.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Tathāgata has spoken to the bhikṣus concerning the profound root of dependent origination; yet, as I observe it, I perceive no profound meaning therein.”
The World-Honored One said: "Stop! Stop!"
Ānanda! Do not give rise to such thoughts. Why is this?
The twelve links of dependent origination are exceedingly profound; they are not something that ordinary people can clearly understand.
In the past, before I had awakened to this Dharma of causes and conditions, I wandered through birth and death with no prospect of escape.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
It is not only today that you say these causes and conditions are not very profound; even from days of yore, you have said they were not very profound.

The reason for this is that in a past life, there was a king of the Asuras named Suyama who secretly conceived the thought of seizing the sun and moon; he emerged from the great ocean waters and manifested a body of immense size, such that the sea reached only to his waist.
"At that time, the son of that asura king, named Kunāla, addressed his father, saying:
'I now wish to bathe in the waters of the great ocean.'"
The Asura Suyama replied: "Do not take pleasure in bathing in the waters of the ocean.
For what reason? Because the waters of the ocean are exceedingly deep and vast; one can never endure bathing in the waters of the ocean."
Then, Kuṇāla said, "I now observe that the water reaches only up to the Great King's waist; for what reason do you say it is 'extremely deep'?
At that moment, the Asura King took his son and placed him within the waters of the great ocean.
At that time, the son of the asura could not reach the bottom of the water with his feet and was filled with extreme terror.
Then, Suyāma addressed his son, saying:
"I previously instructed you that the seawater is exceedingly deep, yet you said there would be no suffering."
"Only I am able to bathe in the great ocean; you are not capable of wishing to bathe therein.
At that time, was the Asura Suyama anyone else? [It was none other than myself.]
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? He who was Suyama was none other than my own self.
At that time, the son of the asura was none other than you yourself.
At that time, the waters of the ocean were extremely deep, yet you said there was no suffering;
now you speak again of the profound Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, yet you say once more that there is no such profundity.

There are sentient beings who do not understand the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination; they transmigrate through birth and death with no time of escape, remaining entirely deluded and ignorant of the root of conditioned formations. From this life to future lives, and from future lives back to this life, they remain forever within the five afflictions, making it extremely difficult for them to seek liberation.

When I first attained the Way of Buddhahood, I contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination, subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials, and by eliminating ignorance, I attained the clarity of wisdom; all darkness was forever removed, and there was no longer any dust or defilement. Furthermore, Ānanda!
When these three turnings and twelve proclamations were delivered regarding the root of dependent origination, he immediately attained the path of enlightenment.
By this means, one knows that the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination is extremely profound, and is not something that ordinary people can fully expound.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
You should contemplate this with profound depth, uphold this Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, and practice by contemplating in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the city of Rājagṛha named Śroṇa, who was thoroughly proficient in all arts and sciences; he was well-versed in everything recorded in the scriptures of external paths and heterodox schools, as well as in astronomy and geography, and he further instructed five hundred young brahmin students.

Furthermore, in that city there was a follower of heterodox teachings named Śreṇika, who possessed great knowledge and was held in affection and respect by King Bimbisāra; the king provided him with timely offerings and bestowed upon him whatever requisites a brahmin might require.

At that time, the Tathāgata’s fame spread far and wide; he was the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat. Delivering immeasurable beings, he appeared in the world.
At that time, the brahmin Ciñcā conceived this thought:
"The name of the Tathāgata is extremely difficult to hear; I now wish to go and inquire after his well-being, to draw near to him, and to pay him homage."
At that time, the brahmin Siṅgālaka went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then the brahmin addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “Śramaṇa Gautama!
"What is your clan?
The Buddha told the brahmin,
"My clan is Kṣatriya."
The brahmin asked: "All the brahmins each hold this doctrine:
'Our lineage is the most noble; there is none superior to it.'"
Some said: "His surname is Bai. Others said:
"His surname is Kṛṣṇa.
The brāhmaṇa declared of himself:
"I am born from Brahmā."
"Now, Śramaṇa Gautama! What do you wish to discuss?
The Buddha told him:
“Brahmin, you should know that when it comes to marriage and taking a wife, people invariably seek out families of noble and high status.
However, within my True Dharma, there are no such distinctions of high or low, nor of right or wrong, based on lineage or name.”
The brahmin spoke again, saying:
"How is it, Gautama? Is it that once one's birth is pure, only then does the Dharma attain purity?"
The Buddha asked the brahmin,
"Do you practice the purity of the Dharma for the sake of attaining purity in your place of rebirth?
The brahmin replied again:
"The various brahmins each raised this argument:
'Our lineage is the most noble; there is none superior to us. Or they said:"
"His surname is Bai," some said; others said:
"His surname is Hei."
The brahmin declared of himself:
"I am born from Brahmā.
The Buddha said to the brahmacārin:
"If a Kṣatriya woman marries into a Brāhmaṇa family and gives birth to a son, by whose clan should he be reckoned?
The Brāhmaṇa replied, "He should say he is of the Brāhmaṇa caste."
"The reason for this is that because of the father's form, this son exists.
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"Furthermore, if a brahmin woman marries into a kṣatriya family and gives birth to a son, by whose clan would he belong?"
The brahmin replied, "That man must be of the kṣatriya caste. Why is this so?
It is because of the father’s physical form that this son exists."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Reflect thoroughly upon this, and then respond to me.
What you have just said is inconsistent from beginning to end."
"What do you think, brahmin?
If a donkey were to give birth to a foal after mating with a horse,
should one say it is a horse or a donkey?"
The brahmin replied,
"Such a creature as this should be called a mule.
This is because it obtained this foal through the procreation of a donkey."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Reflect thoroughly, and then reply to me.
What you have just said is inconsistent from beginning to end."
As you previously stated, when a Kṣatriya woman marries into a Brāhmaṇa family and bears a son, he is called of Brāhmaṇa lineage;
yet now, when a donkey pursues a horse and produces a foal, it is called a "donkey-horse."
"Will you not contradict your previous words? Furthermore, brahmin,
if a mare were to give birth to a foal after mating with a donkey, what would you call it?"
The brahmin replied,
"Its name shall be 'Mule'.
The Buddha told him:
"What do you think, brahmin?
Is there any difference between a horse and a donkey, or a donkey and a horse?
Furthermore, if one person says 'a bushel of jewels' and another says 'jewels, a bushel,' is there any difference in the meaning of these two expressions?"
The brahmin replied, "This is one meaning. Why is this so?
Because 'the jewel is one' and 'one is the jewel'—these meanings are not different."
The Buddha said to the brahmin,
"How is it that 'horse and donkey' and 'donkey and horse' do not have the same meaning?
The brahmin replied:
"Now, Śramaṇa Gautama! Although you have spoken these words, the Brahmins themselves claim:
'Our lineage is the most noble; there is none superior to it.'"
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You first praised his mother, and later you extolled his father.

Suppose that both the father and the mother were of the Brahmin caste, and they later gave birth to two sons; at that time, one of them was proficient in many arts and skilled in every field, while the second son knew nothing at all."
At that time, whom do the parents honor and attend to?
Should they honor and attend to one who possesses wisdom,
or should they honor and attend to one who has no knowledge?
The brahmin replied:
“One’s parents ought to show honor and hospitality to those of high virtue and intelligence, not to those who lack wisdom.

This is because this son of mine is there is nothing he does not understand and nothing he is not skilled in; it is precisely this son whom one should honor and entertain, not a son who lacks wisdom.”
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"If those two sons, one of whom was intelligent, were to again set his mind upon the ten unwholesome deeds—killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth;
whereas the other son, who was not intelligent, guarded the actions of his body, speech, and mind, committing not a single transgression against the ten wholesome deeds."
"How should those parents treat him?
The brahmin replied, "Those parents should treat with respect a son who practices the ten wholesome deeds; but why should they treat with respect one who practices unwholesome deeds?"
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
“You first praised his great learning, and afterwards you praised his morality.
What do you think, brahmin?”
Furthermore, suppose there are two sons: one whose father is upright and correct while his mother is not, and another whose father is not upright and correct while his mother is.
If a son’s mother is upright and his father is not, he will be proficient in all matters and possess broad knowledge of the scriptures and arts.
Regarding the second case, where the father is upright but the mother is not: since he has not studied extensively, he merely observes the ten wholesome actions.
Nevertheless, how should his parents treat him with respect?
"Should one respect and honor the mother as pure while regarding the father as impure?
Or should one respect and honor the father as pure while regarding the mother as impure?
The brahmin replied:
"One should honor and attend upon the son of a pure mother.
Why is this? Because he has mastered the scriptures and is proficient in various arts and crafts.
As for the second type of son—the one whose father is pure but whose mother is impure—though he may observe the precepts, he lacks wisdom; what end will he ultimately reach?"
"Where there is hearing, there is precept.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Previously you praised the purity of your father, but did not praise the purity of your mother."
Now, he further praises the purity of the mother, but does not praise the purity of the father;
first he praises the virtue of learning, and later he praises the precepts;
again he praises the exposition of the precepts, and only afterward does he speak of learning.
"How is it, brahmin? Suppose there are two sons of brahmins: among them, one son is learned and widely erudite, and moreover observes the ten wholesome actions;
the second son possesses wisdom, yet practices the ten unwholesome actions."
"How should those parents treat him? The Brahmin replied,
"They should respect the son of the pure father and the impure mother."

The reason for this is that he has extensively studied the various sutras and mastered all technical arts; born of his father Viśuddha-janman, he practices the ten wholesome deeds and commits no transgressions, for he is fully endowed with all the roots of virtue.
The Buddha told him: "At first you spoke of his clan name and then spoke of what he had heard, but did not speak of his clan name;
later you spoke again of his precepts, but did not speak of what he had heard; and later you spoke again of what he had heard, but did not speak of his precepts."
"Now you praise and speak of your parents' hearing and precepts; does this not contradict your previous words?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying: "Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Although such words exist, the brahmins themselves claim:
'Our lineage is the most noble and honorable; there is none superior to it.
The World-Honored One said:
"In all places where there is marriage, one discusses lineage; however, within my Dharma, this principle does not exist.
Have you perhaps heard of those from frontier kingdoms, distant lands, or other outlying regions?"
The brahmin replied,
"Indeed, I have heard that such people exist.
The World-Honored One said:
"The people of that land have two types of clans.
What are these two? First, humans; second, slaves. Furthermore, these two clans are not fixed."
He asked again:
"In what way is it indeterminate?
