The World-Honored One replied:
"Sometimes one is born as a human and later becomes a slave;
sometimes one is born as a slave and later becomes a human.
Nevertheless, all categories of sentient beings are of one and the same nature, without any distinction."
Furthermore, brahmin!
When heaven and earth are destroyed and the world becomes entirely empty,
at that time, the mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, grasses, trees, and all such things are utterly consumed by fire, and human beings likewise reach the end of their lives.
When the heavens and earth were about to form again, there were as yet no limits of days, months, or years.
At that time, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven came to this world.
Then, as the merit of those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven gradually exhausted and they no longer possessed refined radiance, they looked at one another and gave rise to thoughts of desire.
Those with a predominance of desire become women; those with little desire become men.
Through their mutual union, a womb is formed.
By this causal process, the first humans appeared, from whom the four castes were successively born and spread throughout the world.
"By this expedient means, one should know that all people have emerged from the Kṣatriya caste.
At that time, the brahmin addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Stop, Gautama!"
It was as if one who was hunched had been able to straighten up, or one who was blind had gained eyes, or one in darkness had found the light.
The śramaṇa Gautama did likewise for me, teaching the Dharma through countless skillful means.
"I now take refuge in the Śramaṇa Gautama; I only pray that you will preach the Dharma to me and grant me the status of an upāsaka.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa again addressed the World-Honored One:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will accept my invitation and, together with the community of bhikṣus, come to my home."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation through silence, the brahmin rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew.
Returning to his home, he prepared food and drink, spread out various seats, sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground, and spoke aloud:
"The Tathāgata shall sit here."

At that time, the brahmin Śaila, leading five hundred disciples, arrived at the house of the brahmin Keṇiya. Seeing from afar that fine seats had been spread in the house, he asked the brahmin Keṇiya:
"Are you now preparing for the marriage of a son or daughter?"
"Is it because you wish to invite King Bimbisāra of Magadha?
The brahmin Keṇiya replied,
"I am neither inviting King Bimbisāra, nor is there any matter of marriage."
"I now wish to perform a great meritorious deed.
The brahmin Siṅgāla asked: "I pray you will explain your intention;
what kind of meritorious deed do you wish to perform?"
At that time, the brahmin bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, declaring his own name and lineage:
"Śroṇa, you should know that there is one born of the Śākya clan who has left the home life to study the Way, having attained supreme, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"I have now invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; it is for this reason that I have prepared these various seats.
At that time, the brahmin Śaila said to the brahmin Kṛṣṇa: "Do you mean the Buddha?"
He replied, "I am now speaking of the Buddha.
He asked again:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!
Now we have heard the resonance of the Buddha's voice; where, after all, does the Tathāgata abide?"
"I wish to see him.

Chi-ning replied, "He is currently staying in the Bamboo Grove outside the city of Rājagṛha, where he amuses himself with five hundred disciples. If you wish to go and see him, you should know that now is the time."
Then this brahmin, leading five hundred disciples, went to where the Buddha was.
Upon arrival, they exchanged greetings with one another and sat to one side.
At that time, the brahmin Śīla conceived this thought:
“The śramaṇa Gautama is handsome, his body being the color of gold.
Our own scriptures also state this:
‘When a Tathāgata appears in the world, he is truly difficult to encounter, just as the udumbara flower appears only once in a great while.’”
If one is endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, one shall proceed to one of two destinations:
if remaining at home, one shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, possessed of the seven treasures;
if leaving home to study the Way, one will certainly attain the Unsurpassed Way and become a protector of the world within the three realms.
"I now wish to observe the Buddha’s thirty-two marks.

At that time, the brahmin saw only thirty marks and did not perceive two; he was seized by doubt and hesitation, for he did not see the broad and long tongue or the organ concealed within a sheath like that of a horse.
At that time, the brahmin Śroṇa asked in verse:
"I have heard that there are thirty-two marks and signs of a Great Man;
yet now I do not see two of these marks— where, indeed, are they?"
Chaste, with the male organ concealed within the sheath—its marks are exceedingly difficult to describe.
Do you possess a broad and long tongue that can lick your ears and cover your face?
I pray you extend your broad and long tongue so that I may be free from doubt.
"Furthermore, may I behold him, so that forever the net of doubt and entanglement shall be severed.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 46; *Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 47.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Forty-nine: The Chapter on Tending Cattle; now divided into sections.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately protruded his tongue, licking his ears from both left and right, and then withdrew it again.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately entered into samādhi, causing that brahmin to see his horse-hoof concealed organ.
Then, seeing the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, the brahmin leaped for joy, unable to contain himself.
At that time, the brahmin Śroṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am now a brahmin, as are śramaṇas and kṣatriyas;
yet śramaṇas and brahmins all follow the same path, seeking the same liberation."
"Listen, Śramaṇa, do we have the possibility of attaining the same path?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"You hold this view."
The brahmin replied, "I hold this view.
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"You should direct your intention toward a single liberation; that is to say, right view.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying, "If right view is indeed the single liberation, are there further liberations besides it?"
The World-Honored One said:

“Brahmin! There is another way to liberation that attains the realm of Nirvana, and it consists of eight factors, namely: right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
"O Brahmin, this is called the Eightfold Path by which one attains Nirvana.
At that time, the Brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there perhaps any sentient being who knows these eightfold paths?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Not even one in a hundred thousand."
"Brahmin, you should know that countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings understand these eightfold paths.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are there, furthermore, any sentient beings who do not understand these eightfold paths?"
The World-Honored One replied, "There are many such beings who do not understand; they are not alone.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Are there any sentient beings who do not attain this Dharma? The Buddha told him:
“There are such sentient beings who do not attain the Way; such persons are of eleven kinds.”

"What are the eleven? They are: deceit and hypocrisy; harsh speech; being difficult to admonish; lack of gratitude; a nature prone to likes and dislikes; harming one's parents; killing an Arhat; severing the roots of wholesome merit and virtuous deeds; turning toward evil instead; reckoning that there is a self; and giving rise to malicious thoughts toward the Tathāgata. These, O Brahmin, are called [the eleven]."
"Eleven types of persons are unable to attain these eightfold paths.
As he was speaking of these eightfold paths, the dust and defilements of that brahmin were exhausted, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the brahmin Śroṇa said to his five hundred disciples:
"Each of you should recite and practice according to your own preferences; I wish to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) under the Tathāgata."
The disciples replied, "We, too,
wish to leave the household life to study the Path.
At that time, the brahmin and his five hundred disciples each knelt on their right knees and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“May the World-Honored One graciously permit us to leave the household life and study the Path.
The Buddha addressed the brahmins: “Welcome, bhikṣus!”
"Under the Tathāgata, you shall well cultivate the holy life and gradually exhaust the source of suffering.
When the Tathāgata had spoken these words, five hundred brahmins immediately became śramaṇas.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually delivered a subtle discourse to the five hundred [monks]. The discourse was as follows:
a discourse on giving, a discourse on morality, and a discourse on rebirth in heaven; the perception of the impurity of sensual desires and the excellence of renunciation as happiness.

Just as the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always teach the Dharma—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—the World-Honored One then expounded these extensively to all the people.
At that time, the five hundred people were forever freed from all outflows and attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
Then, the brahmin Siṅgālaka spoke again:
"The time has come; I only pray that you will deign to attend."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śroṇa and the other five hundred bhikṣus:
"Each of you should put on your robes and take up your bowls.
Surrounded by these thousand bhikṣus, he went to the city to the residence of the brahmins and sat down upon his seat.
At that time, the brahmin Ciñcā, seeing that five hundred brahmins had all become śramaṇas, spoke to them, saying:
"Excellent! O people, there is no essential path to the Way that surpasses this."
At that time, the bhikṣu Śela spoke this verse for the sake of Kesi:
"Beyond this, there is no further dharma that can surpass this essential teaching;
of such a kind and character, nothing better exists among the virtuous."
At that time, the brahmin Ciñcā addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to wait for a moment!
I shall immediately prepare more food and drink."
The World-Honored One told him, "As for the food and drink you have prepared, simply offer it at the proper time; do not fear that it will be insufficient.
At that moment, the brahmin Ciñcā was filled with immeasurable joy; he personally served the food, making offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished his meal and set aside his utensils, [the man] scattered various kinds of flowers over the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, and approaching the Buddha, he said:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will allow all men and women, both great and small, to seek the status of upāsakas."
At that time, the brahmin’s wife was pregnant. She said to the Buddha, “I am with child, yet I do not know whether it is a boy or a girl.”
"Furthermore, I take refuge in the Tathāgata and request to be accepted as an upāsikā.
At that time, the Tathāgata preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the great assembly, and while seated upon his throne, he spoke these verses:
"How joyful is this karmic reward! Whatever one aspires for shall surely bear fruit."
Gradually reaching a place of peace and security, one shall forever be free from sorrow, calamity, and affliction.
Upon death, one will be born in the heavens; even if all the māras and devas were to intervene, they could not cause one who has performed meritorious deeds to fall into sin.
"He too shall seek skillful means and the wisdom of the noble ones;
he shall bring an end to the root of suffering and forever depart from the eight difficulties.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the brahmin Ciñcā, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I always eat while remaining seated in one posture; thus my body is light and agile, and my physical strength is robust.
You bhikṣus should also eat only once a day, so that your bodies may be light and agile, your physical strength robust, and you may cultivate the holy life.”
At that time, Bhadrapāla addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am not capable of eating but one meal.
The reason for this is that my physical strength is weak and inferior."
The Buddha told him,
"When you arrive at the house of the donor, eat one portion and take the other portion back home.
Bhadrapāla said to the Buddha:
“I am likewise unable to practice this dharma.
The World-Honored One told him,
“I permit you to break your fast and eat throughout the day.”
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I, too, am not capable of practicing this Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not reply.
At that time, as the sun was setting toward dusk, Kālodāyin donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
It was then extremely dark.

Gradually, Udāyin arrived at the house of a certain elder. At that moment, the elder’s wife was pregnant; hearing that a śramaṇa was outside begging for food, she immediately brought out some rice herself and offered it as a gift.
However, Udāyin’s complexion was extremely dark, and at that time, as it was about to rain, lightning flashed everywhere.
When the householder’s wife stepped out and saw that the śramaṇa’s complexion was so very dark, she was immediately struck with terror and cried out,
"This is a ghost!"
He then called out to himself: "Alas!
I see a ghost!"
Immediately, the fetus was injured and the child died shortly thereafter.
At that time, Kāḷodāyin returned to the vihāra, filled with grief and sorrow; sitting down, he reflected within himself, regretting his actions, but it was too late to remedy the harm.
At that time, such an evil report spread throughout the city of Śrāvastī:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, use incantations to cause others' children to fall.
Thereupon, the men and women among them said to one another:
"Now, O śramaṇas! You conduct yourselves without moderation and do not know the proper time for eating; how are you any different from laypeople who wear white robes?
At that time, many bhikṣus heard the various people each discussing this matter.
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, do not know moderation; they come and go without restraint.
Among them, those bhikṣus who maintained the precepts in their entirety also reproached themselves:
“This is truly not fitting for us. To eat without limit and to act without regard for the proper time is indeed our own fault.”
Each taking the other with them, they went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha told a bhikṣu: "Go and summon Kālodāyin to come."
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, that bhikṣu immediately went to summon Udāyin.
Hearing that the Buddha had called for him, Udāyin came at once to the World-Honored One’s presence, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked Udāyin:
"Did you truly enter the city for alms yesterday evening, go to the house of an elder, and cause the elder’s wife to miscarry?"
Udāyin replied to the Buddha,
“So be it, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to Udāyin:
"Why do you not distinguish between different seasons? Furthermore, you enter the city to beg for alms when it is about to rain;
this is not appropriate for you. Rather, you are a son of noble family who has left the household life to study the Way, yet you are greedily attached to food."
At that time, Udāyin rose from his seat and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"From this day forward, I dare not commit such transgressions again; I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Quickly strike the *gandi* and assemble the bhikṣus at the Hall of Universal Assembly.
Having received the Buddha's instruction, Ānanda did as he was told.
He immediately gathered the bhikṣus together in the lecture hall and approached the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣus have assembled, World-Honored One;
may you know that now is the time."
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the lecture hall and sat in the center, addressing the bhikṣus:

"In the distant past, all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, ate while remaining seated in a single posture; the śrāvakas likewise ate while remaining seated in a single posture. Even the Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples who will appear in the future shall also eat while remaining seated in a single posture."
The reason for this is that this is the essential method for practicing the Path; one ought to eat while remaining seated in a single sitting.
If one can eat while remaining seated in a single sitting, the body will become light and agile, and the mind will attain liberation.
Once the mind has attained liberation, one will acquire all roots of goodness.
Having attained the roots of goodness, one then attains samādhi;
having attained samādhi, one knows things as they truly are.
How does one know them as they truly are?
That is to say: knowing the truth of suffering as it truly is;
knowing the truth of the origin of suffering as it truly is;
and knowing the truth of the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
The noble truth of the escape from suffering must be known as it truly is.

You sons of good family have left the household life to study the Way and abandoned the eight worldly concerns, yet you do not know the proper timing; how are you any different from those who are greedy for sensual desires?
"Brahmins have their own distinct Brahmin dharma; non-Buddhists have their own distinct non-Buddhist dharma.
At that time, Upāli addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"The Tathāgatas of the past and all Buddhas of the future all eat while remaining seated in one posture. I only wish that the World-Honored One would likewise observe a fixed time for eating with the bhikṣus."
The World-Honored One said:
"The Tathāgata also possesses this wisdom; however, as for those who have not yet committed an offense, a restriction shall only be established once a fault is actually present before one's eyes."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I eat while remaining seated in one session; you, too, should eat while remaining seated in one session.
Now, you shall eat at midday and must not exceed the proper time."
"You all should also train in the practice of alms-gathering.
How does a bhikṣu train in the practice of alms-gathering?
In this regard, bhikṣus!"
He takes food merely to sustain his life; he feels no joy if he obtains it, nor does he feel any grief if he does not.

When he receives food, he eats with mindful reflection, free from any heart of greedy attachment, desiring only that this body may maintain its form, that old pains may be removed, and that no new ones be created, so that his physical strength remains sufficient.
Thus, bhikṣus, it is called "begging for food. You,
bhikṣus, should eat while remaining seated in one sitting.
“What is it for a bhikṣu to eat in a single sitting?
Once he has risen from his seat, he commits an offense regarding food and should not eat again. Thus it is, bhikṣu!”
This is called eating in a single sitting.
You, bhikṣus, should likewise eat only when you have received food.
How does a bhikṣu eat only when he has received it?
"In this regard, monks!
Once one has obtained food, what further conditioned activity could there be beyond this?
That which has been obtained through eating should not be eaten again."
Thus it is, bhikṣus! You should eat when you have obtained food.

You, bhikṣus, should likewise wear the three robes, sit beneath trees, dwell in secluded and quiet places, practice sitting in the open air as an austerity, wear robes made of patched rags, stay among burial mounds, and wear worn-out, tattered garments.
The reason for this is that I praise those who possess few desires.
I now instruct you all: you should be like the bhikṣu Kāśyapa.
This is because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa personally practiced the eleven dhūta ascetic practices and likewise taught others to practice these essential methods.
I now exhort you all: you should be like the bhikṣu Māṇava.
This is because the bhikṣu Māṇava wears tattered and worn-out robes, and does not wear them as ornaments.
This, monks, is called my instruction; you should mindfully practice it. Thus it is, monks!
"You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, Bhadrapāla did not go to the presence of the World-Honored One for three months.
Then, as the third month drew to a close, Ānanda went to the place where the bhikṣu Bhadrapāla was and addressed him, saying:
“Now all the members of the Sangha are mending their robes.
In this way, the Tathāgata shall wander among the people; if you do not go now, it will be of no avail for you to regret it later.”
At that time, Ānanda led Bhaṭṭipāla to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and further addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”
Please accept my confession; from this day forward, I shall not transgress it again.
Although the Tathāgata has established these prohibitions and precepts, I have not observed them; I only pray that you will grant me your forgiveness.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
At that moment, the Buddha told him:
"I grant you absolution for your transgression; henceforth, do not commit it again."

The reason for this is that I have reflected upon my own countless cycles of birth and death: at times I was born as a donkey, mule, camel, elephant, horse, pig, or sheep, nourishing these four great elements with grass;
at other times I was in the hells, devouring glowing iron balls;
and at other times I was an *preta*, constantly consuming pus and blood.
Some take human form and consume these five grains;
some take celestial form and consume natural nectar.
Throughout incalculable eons, their physical forms and lives have vied with one another, yet from the beginning there has been no satiety.

Upāli, you should know that just as fire never has enough fuel, and just as the waters of the great ocean never have enough to swallow all flowing streams, so too are ordinary people: they are insatiable in their craving for food.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The cycle of birth and death is never severed; It all arises from the cause of craving and desire.
Enmity and hatred increase one's evil, A practice cultivated by the foolish."
"Therefore, Bhaṭṭipāla, you should mindfully practice fewness of desires and contentment; do not give rise to thoughts of greed or engender various distracted thoughts. Thus it is, Upāli!"
"You should train yourself in this way.

At that time, having heard the Tathāgata’s instruction, Bāḍhiputra went to a secluded place and reproached himself: "For what purpose do sons of noble family leave the household life to study the Way? It is to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya):
to know according to reality that birth and death have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
At that time, Bāḍhipāla immediately became an arhat.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the foremost śrāvaka in terms of consuming food and drink is the bhikṣu Kīrtivardhana."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the village of Aṅgīrasa together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All people call you śramaṇas. Suppose they were to ask you: [What is the meaning of this?]"
"Are you śramaṇas? You replied, "We are śramaṇas."

"I now tell you: the conduct of a śramaṇa and the conduct of a brāhmaṇa—these you should mindfully cultivate. Afterwards, you will surely attain the fruit; it shall be exactly as it is, without deviation."
The reason for this is that there are two kinds of śramaṇas:
the śramaṇa who practices and the śramaṇa who makes vows.
What is meant by the "śramaṇa who practices"?

Thereupon, a bhikṣu’s coming and going, his advancing and halting, his looking and gazing, his deportment, his wearing of robes, and his holding of the alms bowl are all entirely in accordance with the Dharma. He is not attached to greed, hatred, or delusion; he merely maintains the precepts with diligence, does not transgress what is contrary to the Dharma, and trains equally in all the precepts. This is called a śramaṇa who practices through training.
“What is meant by a ‘śramaṇa by vow’?

In this regard, there may be a bhikṣu whose deportment, discipline, coming and going, advancing and retreating, walking, appearance, gaze, and movements are all entirely in accordance with the Dharma; who has exhausted all outflows and attained the state of being without outflows; and who, in this very life, has realized through his own body and dwells therein, knowing as it truly is:
‘Birth and death have been ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.’”
This is called a śramaṇa by name; this,
bhikṣus, is called the two kinds of śramaṇas.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“What, then, are called the practices of the śramaṇa-dharma and the practices of the brāhmaṇa-dharma?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Thus, a bhikṣu is moderate in eating and drinking; he practices walking meditation day and night without missing the proper times, cultivating the factors of enlightenment.
How does a bhikṣu have his faculties stilled?

In this regard, when a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he does not give rise to conceptual attachment or various distracting thoughts; therein, his faculty of the eye attains purity, he eliminates all evil thoughts, and he does not dwell upon unwholesome dharmas.

If, when hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tactile sensations with the body, or cognizing mental objects with the mind, one does not give rise to conceptual attachment or various distracted thoughts, then the faculty of the mind attains purity.
In this way, monks, the faculties attain purity.
"How does a monk practice moderation in eating?

Here, a monk eats with due measure for his belly, not seeking physical plumpness or beauty, but desiring only to maintain this body, to remove old pains and prevent new ones from arising, so that he may cultivate the holy life."
It is just as when men or women have sores on their bodies; they apply ointment to the sores at the appropriate time, always desiring that the sores be healed.

This bhikṣu is also like this: he eats in measure according to his belly's capacity. As for using grease to lubricate a cart, it is because one wishes to travel a long distance; likewise, the bhikṣu who eats in measure according to his belly's capacity does so because he wishes to sustain his life.
In this way, a bhikṣu is moderate in eating.
"How does a bhikṣu remain constantly wakeful?
In this regard, a bhikṣu remains constantly wakeful during the first and last watches of the night, contemplating the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."

If one practices walking meditation during the day, one eliminates evil thoughts and all notions of fetters; furthermore, practicing walking meditation during the first and last watches of the night, one eliminates evil fetters and unwholesome thoughts; furthermore, during the middle watch of the night, one lies on the right side with one foot resting upon the other, maintaining only the thought directed toward light; and again during the last watch of the night, one enters and exits through walking meditation, eliminating unwholesome thoughts.
In this way, bhikṣus, you should know the time and remain wakeful. Thus it is, Ānanda!
This is the essential practice of a śramaṇa.
“What, then, is called the essential practice of a brahmin? In this regard, a bhikṣu knows the truth of suffering as it really is;

he knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the way leading to the cessation of suffering as they really are. Thereafter, through the liberation of the mind from the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance, he attains liberation. Having attained liberation, he gains the knowledge of liberation. He realizes as it really is: ‘Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further rebirth in a womb.’”
"This is called the essential practice of a brāhmaṇa.
Ānanda, you should know that this is the meaning of 'essential practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"A śramaṇa is named 'one who has stilled the mind,' for all evils have forever been exhausted;
a brahmin is named 'pure,' for he has removed all distracted thoughts. Therefore, Ānanda!"
One should mindfully practice the conduct of a śramaṇa and the conduct of a brāhmaṇa.
Only when sentient beings practice these various dharmas can they be called śramaṇas.
Furthermore, for what reason is one called a śramaṇa?
Because all fetters (saṃyojana) have been eternally stilled, one is called a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, for what reason is one called a brāhmaṇa?
Because he has completely eliminated the dharmas of ignorance and delusion, he is called a *brahmin*;
he is also called a *kṣatriya*.
Furthermore, for what reason is he called a *kṣatriya*?
Because they have severed lust, anger, and delusion, they are called kṣatriyas;
they are also called "those who have bathed.
For what reason are they called "those who have bathed"?
Because it washes away the twenty-one fetters, it is called "bathing";
it is also called "awakening.
For what reason is it called "awakening"?
Because it awakens to and comprehends both foolish dharmas and wise dharmas, it is called "Awakening" (bodhi).
It is also called "the Other Shore" (pāra).
For what reason is it called "the Other Shore"?
Because one goes from this shore to the other shore, it is called the "other shore. Ānanda!
Only those who are able to practice this Dharma are then called śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
"This is its meaning; you should keep it in mind and practice accordingly.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Garden at Kapilavastu in the Śākya kingdom, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Prince Devadatta went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Devadatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Please grant me permission to enter the path and become a śramaṇa."
The Buddha said to Devadatta,
"It would be well for you to remain at home and practice the giving of alms.
Indeed, to be a śramaṇa is truly not an easy matter."
At that time, Devadatta again addressed the Buddha a second and third time, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Please allow me to stand at the end of the line."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"It is fitting for you to remain at home; it is not fitting for you to leave the household life to practice the conduct of a śramaṇa.
At that time, Devadatta conceived this thought:
"This śramaṇa harbors a mind of jealousy; I should now shave my own head and practice the holy life well.
What use have I for this śramaṇa?
At that time, Devadatta immediately withdrew and returned home; he shaved his own beard and hair, donned the kāṣāya robe, and declared:
“I am a son of the Śākyas.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Surata who practiced the dhūta austerities by begging for food, wore robes made of patched rags, and possessed the five supernormal powers with perfect clarity.
At that time, Devadatta went to where that bhikṣu was, prostrated with his head at the bhikṣu’s feet, and said:
"I only pray that the Venerable One will grant me instruction, so that I may obtain peace and security for a long night."
At that time, the bhikṣu Śuddhodana immediately instructed him in the rules of decorum and etiquette; he contemplated these teachings and abandoned the former for the latter.
At that time, Devadatta followed the instructions of that bhikṣu without any omission.
At that time, the bhikṣu Devadatta said:
"I only pray that the Venerable One will explain the path of supernormal power to me; I am capable of practicing this path."
At that time, the bhikṣu further taught him the way of the supernormal powers (ṛddhi):
"You should now train in the lightness and heaviness of the mind;
having understood the lightness and heaviness of the mind, you should further discern the four great elements (mahābhūta)."
One should discern the lightness and heaviness of earth, water, fire, and wind;
having gained knowledge of the lightness and heaviness of the four great elements, one should then practice the Samādhi of Mastery;
having practiced the Samādhi of Mastery, one should further cultivate the Samādhi of Valor.
Having practiced the *vīrya-samādhi*, one should further practice the *citta-samādhi*;
having practiced the *citta-samādhi*, one should further practice the *sva-śīla-samādhi*;
having practiced the *sva-śīla-samādhi*, before long one will thus accomplish the path of the *ṛddhipāda*.

At that time, having received his teacher’s instruction, Devadatta understood the relative weight of his own mind and mental factors, as well as the relative weight of the four great elements. He cultivated all the samādhis until they were perfected without any loss; before long, he then accomplished the way of supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
In this manner, he performed countless transformations through innumerable skillful means.
At that time, Devadatta’s fame spread far and wide.

Then, by means of his supernormal powers, Devadatta reached as far as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he gathered various kinds of *utpala* and *kumuda* lotuses and presented them to Prince Ajātaśatru, further addressing him thus:
"These flowers come from the Heaven of the Thirty-three; Śakra Devānām-indra has sent them here to present as an offering to the Crown Prince.
At that time, seeing such supernatural power in Devadatta, the Crown Prince made offerings to him according to the occasion and provided him with all his necessities.
The Prince again thought to himself:
"Devadatta’s supernormal powers are exceedingly difficult to equal.
At that time, Devadatta again concealed his form and manifested as a small child, sitting upon the lap of the Prince.
At that time, each of the court ladies had this thought:
"Who is this person? Is he a ghost, or is he a deva?"
Before his speech was finished, he again manifested a transformation body, returning once more to his original form.
At that time, the prince and all the palace attendants exclaimed, "This is Devadatta."
He immediately provided whatever was required and further transmitted these words:
"The name and virtue of Devadatta cannot be fully recorded.
At that time, having heard this, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Devadatta possesses supreme supernormal power (*ṛddhi*); he is able to obtain clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Do not give rise to such thoughts, nor be attached to Devadatta’s gains and offerings, and do not envy his supernormal power. That man shall, by means of this very supernormal power, fall into the three evil realms; the gains and offerings obtained by Devadatta, as well as his supernormal power, shall soon be exhausted.”
"The reason for this is that Devadatta himself shall create his own bodily, verbal, and mental actions.
At that time, he again gave rise to this thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses supernormal powers; I too possess supernormal powers."
"Whatever the śramaṇa Gautama knows, I also know; whatever the śramaṇa Gautama's lineage is noble, mine also is noble.
If the śramaṇa Gautama displays one supernormal power, I shall display two;
if he displays two, I shall display four."
"He has eight, I have sixteen;
he has sixteen, I have thirty-two;
according to the transformations manifested by that śramaṇa, I shall double them again."
At that time, having heard these words from Devadatta, more than five hundred bhikṣus went to Devadatta’s place, as did five hundred bhikṣus who were receiving the prince’s offerings.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana said to one another:
"Let us go together to Devadatta's place and listen to his preaching; what kind of discourse does he speak?"
They then went together to the place where Devadatta was.
At that time, seeing Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana approaching from afar, Devadatta immediately addressed the bhikṣus:
"These two are disciples of Siddhārtha."
He was filled with great joy.
Having arrived, they exchanged greetings and sat to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣus each gave rise to this thought:
"The disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha have now all come toward Devadatta.
At that time, Devadatta said to Śāriputra,
"Are you capable of preaching the Dharma to these bhikṣus?"
"I wish to rest for a short while, yet I am troubled by pain in my back.
At that time, Devadatta lay on his right side with his legs overlapping, and because of his joyful mind, he fell asleep.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, seeing that Devadatta was asleep, immediately used their supernormal powers to take the bhikṣus up and fly away through the air.
At that time, Devadatta awoke; not seeing the bhikṣus, he was filled with extreme rage and uttered these words:
"If I do not take revenge, I shall never truly be called Devadatta."
"This was the first time Devadatta committed one of the five heinous crimes.
As soon as Devadatta gave rise to this thought, he immediately lost his supernormal powers.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Devadatta the bhikṣu possesses such great supernormal powers that he is able to cause a schism in the noble Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“It is not only now that Devadatta has caused a schism in the noble Saṃgha; in past lives as well, he constantly caused schisms in the noble Saṃgha.”
The reason for this is that in the distant past, he likewise destroyed the assembly of noble ones and again gave rise to an evil thought:
"I must seize and kill the śramaṇa Gautama, and become a Buddha within the triple world, uniquely honored and without rival."
At that time, Devadatta said to King Ajātaśatru: "In ancient times, the lifespans of people were extremely long;
nowadays they have become so short. If the Prince, Your Majesty’s son, should suddenly come to his end, then his birth into this world would have been in vain."
"Why do you not seize your father the king and kill him to succeed to the holy throne?
I shall seize the Tathāgata and kill him, and thus I shall become a Buddha.
Would it not be most gratifying to have a new king and a new Buddha?"
At that time, King Ajātaśatru immediately dispatched doorkeepers to seize his father, the king, and confine him in prison; he then established himself as king and governed the people.
At that time, the common people said to one another:
"This child was the son of an enemy even before he was born; therefore, let his name be King Ajātaśatru."
At that time, having seen that King Ajātaśatru had imprisoned his father, the king, Devadatta again formed this thought:
"I must certainly seize the śramaṇa Gautama and kill him."
At that time, the World-Honored One was on a small mountain slope at Vulture Peak.
Then Devadatta arrived at Vulture Peak, took up a large rock thirty cubits long and fifteen cubits wide in his hands, and hurled it at the World-Honored One.

At that time, the mountain deity Kumbhīra, who constantly dwelt on that mountain, saw Devadatta embracing a rock to strike the Buddha; he immediately reached out his hand and caught it, moving it to another place.
At that time, a small fragment of stone shattered and struck the Tathāgata’s foot, immediately drawing blood.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to Devadatta:
"You have now once again conceived the intent to harm the Tathāgata; this is the second of the five crimes of immediate retribution."
At that time, Devadatta again reflected to himself:
"I have still not succeeded in harming this śramaṇa Gautama; I must seek further expedient means."
He departed and went to Ajātaśatru, where he addressed the king, saying:
"You should drink black elephants until they are intoxicated and then have them harm the śramaṇa.
The reason for this is that these elephants are fierce and violent, and will certainly be able to kill this śramaṇa Gautama."
If this śramaṇa were one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom, he would certainly not come into the city tomorrow to beg for alms;
if he does not possess all-encompassing wisdom, and comes into the city to beg for alms tomorrow, he will surely be harmed by this wicked elephant.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru immediately gave strong liquor to the elephant to intoxicate it, and then addressed the people of the kingdom, saying:
"Those who wish for their own peace and would spare their lives, do not come or go within the city again tomorrow."
At that time, when it was time for the meal, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.

The fourfold assembly of men and women, both old and young, having heard that King Ajātaśatru had intoxicated elephants with wine intending to harm the Tathāgata, all went together to where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated themselves at his feet and said to the Buddha:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will not enter the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food!"
"Why is this? King Ajātaśatru has intoxicated an elephant with drink and intends to harm the Tathāgata.
The Buddha told the upāsakas:
"A Truly Enlightened One can never be harmed by another.
At that time, although the World-Honored One heard these words, he nevertheless continued on his way into the city.
At that time, the wicked elephant saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar; his rage blazed forth as he rushed toward the Tathāgata, desiring to harm him.
But when the Buddha saw the elephant coming, he immediately spoke this verse:
"Do not harm the Naga, O elephant! The appearance of a Naga and an elephant is rare."
"Because he did not harm the dragon, he was reborn in a favorable realm.
At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Tathāgata, the elephant immediately stepped forward, knelt on its forelegs, and licked the feet of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the elephant immediately repented its transgressions; with a mind finding no peace, it passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When King Ajātaśatru and Devadatta saw that the elephant had died, they were filled with sorrow and displeasure.
Devadatta said to the king,
"The śramaṇa Gautama has already taken and killed the elephant.
The king replied to him:
"This śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal power and many skills; he must have been able to cast a spell upon this nāga-elephant and kill it.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru spoke again, saying:
"This śramaṇa must be fully endowed with majestic virtue, for he was ultimately not harmed by the wicked elephant."

Devadatta replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama possesses delusive spells that can cause even the non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners to submit and be subdued; how much more so, then, the species of animals?"
At that time, Devadatta again thought to himself:
"I now observe that King Ajātaśatru intends to change his mind and repent.
Then, Devadatta, filled with sorrow and displeasure, departed from the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dharma-dānā saw Devadatta coming from afar and said to him:
"What you have now done is an extreme transgression; it would still be easy to repent now, but I fear it will be difficult later."
When Devadatta heard these words, his anger redoubled, and he immediately replied: "Shaveling woman!
What fault have I committed that it should be easy now and difficult later?"
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied,
"You are now consorting with evil and are creating the root of many unwholesome deeds.
At that moment, Devadatta’s rage blazed like a fierce fire, and he struck the bhikṣuṇī with his hand, killing her.
At that time, having attempted to harm the True Man, Devadatta went to his own quarters and addressed his disciples:
"You should know this: I have now resolved to direct my enmity toward the śramaṇa Gautama."
"However, according to the principles of righteousness, it is improper for an Arhat to give rise to evil intent toward another Arhat; I ought now to offer repentance to him.
At that time, Devadatta, distressed by this sorrow and lack of joy, soon fell gravely ill.
Devadatta told his disciples:
"I do not have the strength to go and see the śramaṇa Gautama!
You should support me and take me to where the śramaṇa is."
At that time, Devadatta smeared his ten fingernails with poison and said to his disciples,
"Carry me to the place where that śramaṇa is."
At that time, the disciples immediately carried him on a litter to where the World-Honored One was.
Then, seeing Devadatta approaching from afar, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Devadatta is coming now; he must surely have a heart of remorse and wishes to come before the Tathāgata to seek repentance for his transgressions."
The Buddha told Ānanda,
“Devadatta shall never reach the presence of the World-Honored One.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha again and yet again, saying:
"Now this Devadatta wishes to come here to seek repentance for his transgressions.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This evil man shall never reach the presence of the Tathāgata; today the life-faculty of this man has already reached its end."
At that time, Devadatta came to where the World-Honored One was and said to his disciples:
"It is not fitting for me to see the Tathāgata while lying down; I should descend from my bed before seeing him."
As soon as Devadatta set foot upon the ground, a great fire and wind arose from within the earth and enveloped Devadatta’s body.

At that moment, Devadatta was consumed by the flames and felt remorse toward the Tathāgata; he intended to cry out "Namo Buddha," but before he could finish, having only managed to utter "Namo," he fell into hell.
At that time, having seen Devadatta enter into hell, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Has Devadatta ended his life today and entered into hell?"
The Buddha told him:
"Devadatta has not attained the ultimate state of extinction.
Now, because Devadatta gave rise to an evil mind toward the body of the Tathāgata, at the dissolution of his body and the end of his life, he shall enter the Avīci Hell."
At that time, Ānanda wept with such sorrow that he could not restrain himself.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Why do you weep so bitterly?”
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“I have not yet exhausted my desire and love; because I am unable to sever desire, I weep with grief.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"As a person creates their own karma, they return to observe its source:
the virtuous receive a virtuous retribution, while the wicked receive their calamity.
When worldly people commit evil deeds, they suffer the pains of hell after death."
Even if one had performed virtuous deeds, one would receive celestial blessings in a future life;
yet he himself invited evil karma and brought about his own descent into hell.
This is not the suffering caused by an enemy of the Buddha—why do you grieve now?
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"After Devadatta’s body has perished and his life ended, where will he be reborn?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Now this Devadatta, with the dissolution of his body at the end of his life, has entered the Avīci Hell.
This is because he committed the five heinous crimes; therefore, he has incurred this retribution."
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha:
“So be it, World-Honored One! It shall be according to the instruction of the Holy Honored One.”

Having committed evil myself, I have entered hell in this very life; it is for this reason that I now weep and shed tears. Because Devadatta disregarded his reputation and lineage, and because he brought shame upon our parents and elders, he has defiled the Śākya clan and destroyed our family’s standing.
However, it would truly be inappropriate for Devadatta to enter hell in his present body.
The reason for this is that our own clan has produced Universal Monarchs (cakravartin), yet Devadatta was born into a royal lineage; he ought not to enter hell in his current physical form.

Devadatta should, in this very life, bring an end to all taints (*āsrava*), achieve the liberation of mind through the outflow-free state (*anāsava-citta-vimukti*) and the liberation by wisdom (*paññā-vimukti*), and within this present body attain the realization of the fruit:
"Birth and death are exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacariya*) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence"—knowing this as it truly is.
Following the path of the True Persons, he shall become an Arhat and enter *parinirvāṇa* in the fruit of Nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
"What a pity that he who maintained this physical manifestation should now enter hell!

When Devadatta was alive, he possessed great majestic power and profound spiritual virtue; he was even able to ascend to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and exercise mastery over transformations. How could such a person as this have entered hell?"
"I do not understand, World-Honored One: how many years has Devadatta spent in hell?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This person has spent one kalpa in hell."
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"There are two kinds of kalpas—the great kalpa and the small kalpa. To which of these kalpas does this person belong?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This person shall pass through a great kalpa.

What is called a 'great kalpa' is precisely this Bhadrakalpa; having exhausted the number of kalpas and completed his course of practice until the end of his life, he will return once more to a human body."
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"Devadatta has completely lost his human faculties, yet he has subsequently attained accomplishment.
This is because the duration of kalpas is vast and long; as for great kalpas, they do not exceed the Bhadrakalpa."
At that time, Ānanda wept all the more bitterly, choking with sobs and feeling distressed; he again addressed the Buddha:
"After Devadatta emerges from the Avīci Hell, where will he be reborn?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Devadatta, having passed away there, shall be reborn above the Four Great Kings.
Ānanda asked again:
“Where will they be reborn after passing away from that life?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“After passing away from there, they will successively be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.”
Ānanda asked again:
"Where will they be reborn after passing away from that life?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Then, having passed away from hell, Devadatta was reborn in a good destination in the heavens. For sixty kalpas he did not fall into the three evil realms, but instead moved between the heavens and the human world. In his final embodiment, he will shave off his hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and with firm faith leave the household life to study the Way, becoming a Pratyekabuddha named Namu."
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is so, World-Honored One!
Devadatta, by reason of his evil retribution, has incurred the punishment of hell."
By performing what merit did he undergo birth and death for sixty kalpas without experiencing suffering or affliction, and later again become a pratyekabuddha named Namu?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The merit of a single thought of good intention for the duration of a finger-snap is difficult to compare; how much more so for Devadatta, who was erudite in antiquity and clear in the present, having studied and recited extensively, maintaining all dharmas in his memory and never forgetting what he had heard."
Considering Devadatta’s past enmity and his intent to kill the Tathāgata,

yet also considering that due to the retribution of past conditions he felt joy toward the Tathāgata, by virtue of these causes and conditions of karmic retribution, he did not fall into the three evil realms for sixty kalpas.
Furthermore, because Devadatta, at the time of his final passing, gave rise to a mind of harmony and joy and uttered the name "Namo," he later became a Pratyekabuddha named Namo.
At that time, Ānanda immediately stepped forward to pay homage to the Buddha and spoke again with earnestness:
"So be it, World-Honored One! I shall do exactly as the Divine One has instructed."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to go into the Avīci Hell to speak of essential practice to Devadatta, and to offer him consolation and congratulations."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "You should know this:
do not again act with such rashness. Concentrate your mind and fix your intention; do not give rise to distracted thoughts. Why is this?
Beings who have committed the most extreme evils are difficult to reform and difficult to bring to maturity; only after that do they fall into the Avīci Hell."
"Furthermore, those sinners do not understand human sounds or the exchange of speech.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now understand the sixty-four tones and can communicate through speech; I shall go to speak to those people using these sounds."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana,
“You should know that now is the time.
At that moment, Ānanda, hearing these words, was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself.

Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and before the Buddha, like a strong man bending and extending his arm, he instantly went to the Avīci Hell.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was in the air above the Avīci Hell, and snapping his fingers to rouse him,
he called out, "Devadatta!
At that moment, Devadatta remained silent and did not respond.
Then the various hell-wardens said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Which Devadatta are you calling now?
The wardens spoke again:

"In this very place, there was also a Devadatta during the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, a Devadatta during the time of Kanakamuni Buddha, and a Devadatta during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha; furthermore, there was a householder Devadatta and a renunciant Devadatta."
"Monk, who now is Devadatta in terms of right livelihood?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"I have now sent for Devadatta, the son of Śākyamuni Buddha’s paternal uncle; I wish to see him.
At that time, the hell-wardens, grasping iron forks or flames in their hands, scorched and roasted his body to awaken him.
At that time, Devadatta’s body was ablaze with flames thirty cubits high, and the wardens of hell said to him:
"You fool, why do you sleep now?"
At that time, Devadatta, oppressed by manifold sufferings, replied to them, saying:
"What instructions do you have for me today?
The wardens spoke again:
"Look now up into the sky.
Following these words, he looked up into the void and saw Mahāmaudgalyāyana sitting cross-legged, seated upon a precious lotus flower like the sun emerging from the clouds.
Having seen this, Devadatta spoke this verse:
"Who is this that manifests celestial light, Like the sun emerging from behind the clouds?
He is like a mass of golden mountains, Forever free from dust and defilement."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana replied with a verse:
"I am the lion of the Śākyas, the last of the Gautama clan;
I am his next disciple, named Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
At that time, Devadatta said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana, for what reason have you deigned to come here?
The sentient beings here have committed immeasurable evils and are difficult to transform."
"Because they did not cultivate roots of goodness, after their lives ended,
they were reborn here. Maudgalyāyana replied,
"I have come here as an envoy of the Buddha, wishing to show compassion for you."
"Uprooting suffering has no fundamental basis.
At that time, Devadatta, hearing the sound of the Buddha’s voice, leaped for joy with such intensity that he could not contain himself, and uttered these words:
"I only pray that the Venerable One will expound this at the proper time: what are the teachings of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One?"
"Furthermore, have you not recorded and taught that the evil realms do not exist?
Maudgalyāyana replied, "Devadatta!"
Do not harbor fear; there is no suffering in the hells that exceeds this place.
That Śākyamuni Buddha, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, takes pity on all wriggling and crawling creatures as a mother loves her child, his mind being without distinction.
He expounded the meaning at the appropriate time, never losing the sequence, nor did he exceed the measure of what was to be taught according to its category.

Now, as recorded by the divine mouth: you originally gave rise to an evil thought, desiring to harm the World-Honored One, and further instructed others to follow suit, making it impossible for them to find a way out.
Due to this causal retribution, you shall enter the Avīci Hell and must pass through one kalpa, with no end in sight.

When his kalpas are exhausted and his life comes to an end after completing his practice, he shall be reborn above the Four Heavenly Kings; successively, he shall be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. For sixty kalpas he shall not fall into the evil realms, but shall circulate between the human and celestial worlds. Finally, receiving a body once more, he shall return to human form, shave off his beard and hair, don the three dharma robes, and with firm faith leave the household life to study the Way. He shall become a Pratyekabuddha, named Namu.
The reason for this is that when you were first dying and your life was about to end, you invoked the name "Namo. Because of this, he has received this title.
Now, that Tathāgata, observing these virtuous words "Namo," has thus proclaimed his name, and he shall act as a Pratyekabuddha for sixty kalpas.
At that time, having heard these words, Devadatta was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; a virtuous mind arose within him, and he spoke again to Maudgalyāyana:

"The teachings spoken by the Tathāgata are certain and beyond doubt. Out of compassion for all living beings, his salvation is immeasurable; through great kindness and great compassion, he transforms both the ignorant and the deluded."
"Even if I were to lie on my right side within the Avīci Hell today for the duration of an eon, my mind would remain focused and upright, never experiencing weariness or fatigue.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana again addressed Devadatta, saying:
"How is it with you now? Has your suffering increased or decreased?"
Devadatta replied: "The pain in my body has only increased and not diminished;
now that I have heard the Tathāgata bestow this name upon me, the pain is slightly lessened, though it is hardly worth mentioning."
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"As for the source of the pain you are currently suffering from,
what kind of thing does it resemble? Devadatta replied:

"A red-hot iron wheel crushes my body until it is destroyed; furthermore, an iron pestle grinds my form to pieces. A black, violent elephant tramples my body, and a mountain of fire comes to press down upon my face. My former *kāṣāya* has transformed into glowing copper plates, burning most fiercely as they are cast upon my body. Such is the nature of this source of suffering."
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"Do you yourself know the original root of your transgressions that have caused you to undergo such suffering?
Shall I now explain each one to you in detail, or do you wish to hear it?"
Devadatta replied: "Indeed. Please speak at this time."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana spoke this verse:
“You once caused dissension within the Saṃgha of bhikṣus at the place of the Most Victorious One;
now, with a red-hot iron pestle, you shall be ground and crushed in your physical form.”
Yet among that great assembly, the foremost of the śrāvakas,
who once sowed discord within the saṃgha of bhikṣus, is now being crushed by a wheel of fire.
You formerly instructed the king to release a rutting elephant and make it drink strong liquor.
Now, with a herd of black elephants, they shall trample upon your body.
Since you formerly hurled a great boulder from afar at the Tathāgata’s feet,
now you shall be requited with a mountain of fire, which shall burn you until nothing remains.
Originally, with your own fist, you killed that bhikṣuṇī;
now you are wrapped in glowing red-hot copper, scorched and unable to stretch it out.
The retribution for one's actions never fails, nor does it remain in emptiness.
Therefore, you should exert yourselves to abandon these roots of all evils.
"What Devadatta originally created was precisely this."
"You should direct your mind single-mindedly toward the Buddha, the Tathāgata; throughout the long night, you shall obtain immeasurable merit.
At that time, Devadatta again addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"I now entrust myself to Maudgalyāyana to prostrate my head at the feet of the World-Honored One."
"May you be light and at ease in your daily activities, and may your movements be healthy and strong.
He also paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana manifested great supernormal power, causing the suffering and pain of the Avīci Hell to cease.
At that time, he further spoke these verses:
"All pay homage to the Buddha, the Teacher of the Śākyas, the most supreme one;
he is able to bestow peace and security, removing all suffering and affliction."

At that time, when the sentient beings in hell had heard these verses spoken by Maudgalyāyana, more than sixty thousand of them exhausted their karma and completed their retribution for sins; they immediately passed away from there and were reborn above the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately withdrew his supernormal powers and returned to his location. Arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
Then, Maudgalyāyana addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Devadatta sends his greetings and pays you infinite respect.”
"May you be at ease in your daily activities and find strength in your movements.
He also inquired after Ānanda’s well-being, speaking thus:
“The Tathāgata has prophesied that I shall become a pratyekabuddha named Namu within sixty kalpas.
Even if I were to lie on my right side within the Avīci Hell, I would never shrink from such toil.”
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Maudgalyāyana, you bring great benefit and provide vast nourishment; out of compassion for the blind masses, you grant peace to devas and humans, leading all Tathāgatas and śrāvakas gradually toward the state of extinction in nirvāṇa.
Therefore, Maudgalyāyana, you should always diligently cultivate and perfect these three dharmas. Why is this?

If Devadatta had practiced the wholesome dharmas of the three actions of body, the four of speech, and the three of mind, that person would never have craved gain and offerings, nor would he have committed the five heinous crimes to enter the Avīci Hell.

The reason for this is that those people who crave gain and offerings may indeed possess a heart of reverence toward the Triple Gem, yet they do not uphold the prohibitive precepts nor are they complete in their conduct of body, speech, and mind; they ought instead to focus their minds on perfecting their conduct of body, speech, and mind.
"In this way, Maudgalyāyana, you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Maudgalyāyana rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there are sentient beings who practice the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī-cetovimukti*), extensively propagate its meaning, and expound it to others, they shall obtain these eleven fruits of retribution."

What are the eleven? One sleeps in peace and awakens in peace; one does not see evil dreams; one is protected by devas and loved by humans; one is not harmed by poison or weapons; and one will ultimately not be invaded or wronged by water, fire, or thieves.
When his body breaks up and his life ends, he will be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
This, monks, is called the ability to practice a mind of loving-kindness, whereby one obtains these eleven blessings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one practices a mind of loving-kindness, And likewise acts without negligence,
All fetters will gradually thin away, And one will increasingly perceive the tracks of the Path."
By being able to practice this loving-kindness, one shall be born in the Brahma Heaven;
swiftly attaining extinction (nirvāṇa), one will forever reach the state of non-action (asaṃskṛta).
With a mind that does not kill and is free from harm, there is likewise no intention for victory or defeat.
"Practicing loving-kindness universally toward all, one never harbors a heart of resentment. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to practice a mind of loving-kindness and widely propagate its meaning."
"In this way, bhikṣus!
You should train yourselves thus.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 47 and Volume 48.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Fifty: Paying Homage to the Triple Gem (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If good men or good women wish to pay homage to a shrine of the Tathāgata, they should perform the homage to the Tathāgata’s shrine by practicing eleven dharmas."
What are these eleven? They are:
giving rise to a courageous mind because of being capable and resilient;
ensuring the mind is not confused by remaining constantly single-minded; and maintaining focused mindfulness through all practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
All thoughts are eternally stilled because he has entered samādhi;
his mind is immeasurable because of his wisdom;
his mind is difficult to fathom because of its form.
The mind is serene and still due to majestic deportment;
the mind does not wander or race because of its renown;
the mind is free from conceptualization because of its physical form.
The Brahma-voice is difficult to equal because its resonance is so supple. O bhikṣus!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to pay homage at a temple of the Tathāgata, they should perform this salutation to the divine temple of the Tathāgata while endowed with these eleven dharmas; thus, throughout the long night, they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If a son or daughter of good family wishes to perform the ritual of prostration, they should contemplate eleven matters before performing the prostration. What are these eleven?
One who possesses pride should eliminate pride; for the True Dharma eliminates the thought of craving toward desires;
for the True Dharma eliminates desire toward desires;
and the True Dharma can sever the deep-flowing current of birth and death.
Indeed, by practicing the true Dharma, one attains the Dharma of equanimity;
this true Dharma severs all evil destinies,
and by seeking this true Dharma, one reaches the excellent destination.
The True Dharma can sever the net of craving;
one who practices the True Dharma proceeds from existence to non-existence;
one who practices the True Dharma possesses a brilliance that illuminates all things.
Now, the True Dharma leads to the realm of Nirvana.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to practice the rites of the Dharma, they should contemplate these eleven dharmas; thereafter, they will obtain immeasurable merit and receive boundless blessings throughout the long night of saṃsāra.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a good son or a good daughter cultivates the practice of paying homage to the Saṃgha, they should first concentrate upon eleven dharmas; only then should they pay homage to the Saṃgha. What are these eleven? "

The assembly of the Tathāgata is accomplished in the True Dharma; the noble assembly of the Tathāgata is harmonious from top to bottom. The Saṅgha of the Tathāgata is accomplished in each and every dharma;

the noble assembly of the Tathāgata is accomplished in ethical discipline, accomplished in meditative concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the vision and knowledge of liberation. The noble assembly of the Tathāgata is able to uphold and protect the Three Jewels;
the noble assembly of the Tathāgata is able to subdue non-Buddhists and those of heterodox learning.
The noble assembly of the Tathāgata is the true friend and field of merit for all sentient beings.
If a son or daughter of good family wishes to pay homage to the Saṃgha, they should contemplate these eleven dharmas; by doing so, they will obtain immeasurable merit throughout the long night.
"In this way, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves.

At that time, the bhikṣus, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, devas, and human beings, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

4. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Pāṭaliputra in the kingdom of Magadha, in the Great Heavenly Garden (Mahādevavana) to the east, together with a great community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, after his meal, the World-Honored One rose and walked in meditation together with Ānanda within a grove of trees.
The Buddha then smiled, and Ānanda thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not smile without cause; why does he smile now?"
"There must surely be a reason; I shall ask him.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and asked the Buddha:
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not smile without cause. Why do you smile now?"
"You must surely have a reason for this; I wish to hear the meaning of your smile.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I shall explain it to you."

In the past, at the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, there was among them a Wheel-Turning Sage King who ruled over the four continents; his name was Mahādeva. He enjoyed long life and freedom from illness, was handsome and valiant, governed by the True Dharma, did not oppress the people, and possessed the seven natural treasures.
What are the seven?

First is the wheel-treasure, second is the elephant-treasure, third is the horse-treasure, fourth is the jewel-treasure, fifth is the woman-treasure, sixth is the householder-treasure, and seventh is the military commander-treasure.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“This Great Heavenly King spent eighty-four thousand years as a youth, eighty-four thousand years as a crown prince, and eighty-four thousand years upon the throne as a holy king.”
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"What is the wheel-treasure?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"On the fifteenth day of the month, when the moon was full, the king bathed himself clean and pure and ascended the eastern tower with his court ladies; looking toward the east, he beheld a golden wheel with a thousand spokes."
A wheel seven *ren* high constitutes one *tāla*;
a *tāla* refers to a solitary, towering tree used as a standard of measurement. It is seven *tālas* high and is made entirely of purple-polished gold.
Having seen the wheel, the king thought to himself:
"This wheel is a fine wheel; I wish to take hold of it.
Having thought this, the wheel immediately came into the king's left hand, and he then lifted it and moved it into his right hand.
The king said to this wheel:
"Subdue all those who do not submit;
seize for me all that is not my territory."
"It is according to the Dharma, not contrary to the Dharma.
Having finished speaking, the wheel returned and stayed suspended in the air, with its rim facing east and its hub facing north.
The king commanded his attendants to assemble the fourfold army.

Having equipped his forces, he immediately led his host and stood in the air upon the wheel; following the wheel as it was drawn toward the east, he traveled until he had traversed the entire eastern boundary;
at dusk, the king and his host would take up residence beneath the wheel.

"The minor kings of the eastern borders have all come to pay their respects; their offerings consist entirely of silver grain placed in golden bowls, and golden grain placed in silver bowls: 'Welcome!'"
"Great King!
This eastern realm—with its lands, treasures, and people—is entirely yours. We pray that you will halt your carriage and remain here; we shall receive and carry out your divine instructions!"
The Great Heavenly King replied to the minor kings, saying:
"If you wish to uphold my teachings, each of you shall return to your own kingdoms and instruct the people in the ten wholesome actions; do not commit acts of injustice or oppression."
Once the instructions were completed, the wheel immediately turned upon the sea and proceeded riding on the clouds.
A path opened naturally in the ocean, one *yojana* wide, and the king, together with his fourfold army, followed the wheel as before to patrol the southern border.

The minor kings of the southern regions also came to pay their respects; all of them filled golden bowls with silver grain and silver bowls with golden grain, presenting them as tribute and saying, "Welcome!"

"O Heavenly King, this southern realm—with its lands, treasures, and people—is entirely yours; we pray that you halt your chariot and dwell here, for we shall receive and carry out your divine mandate!"
Mahādeva replied to the kings:
"If you wish to carry out my command, each of you should return to your own lands and instruct the people in the ten wholesome actions; do not commit acts of injustice or oppression."
Having finished these exhortations, the wheel turned westward to tour the western regions.
After the kings of the western regions had presented their offerings and entreaties, just as in the case of the southern regions, the wheel turned northward again to traverse the northern regions.
The kings of the northern regions also all came to pay their respects, presenting offerings and making entreaties, all according to the previous rites.

After traveling for four days throughout Jambudvīpa and across the four seas, he returned to his original city of Madhyāntarā; he remained suspended in the air before the palace gate at a height of seven tala trees, with the hub facing east, and the king then entered the palace.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Mahādeva obtained the wheel-treasure in this manner.
Ānanda again asked the Buddha:
"How did Mahādeva obtain the precious elephant? The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"On the fifteenth day after that, when the moon was full, Mahādeva bathed himself clean and ascended the eastern tower with his court ladies. Looking toward the east, he saw in the sky a white elephant king named Pūrṇabhadra approaching through the air. Its seven limbs were level and steady; it had six tusks in its mouth, a golden crown upon its head, and golden necklaces. Its body was entwined with strings of pearls, and golden bells hung from its left and right sides."
The elephant possessed divine power and could transform its form at will.
When Mahādeva saw this, he thought to himself:
"Would it be right for me to obtain this elephant?"
"Let it be made to perform some task.
Having finished his thought, the elephant immediately stood in the air before the king. The king then instructed it in five matters.
The king further thought to himself:
"Let us test whether this elephant is capable or not.

On the following day at sunrise, the King mounted the elephant; in a mere moment, he traveled around the four seas and returned to his original location, standing facing east at the eastern side of the palace gate.
"Ānanda! Such is the elephant-treasure obtained by Mahādeva.
Ānanda then asked the Buddha again:
"What was the horse-treasure obtained by Mahādeva like?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"On the fifteenth day after Mahādeva arrived, when the moon was full, he bathed himself in purity and ascended the western tower with his court ladies. Looking toward the west, he saw a dark-blue horse-king named Bālaha—which in the language of Qin means 'black-haired'—whose tail was dark red.
