It came through the air, its body moving without swaying; it wore a golden crown upon its head, necklaces of jewels, and was draped in interlaced strings of pearls with bells hanging on both sides."
The horse possessed divine power and could transform its form at will.
When Mahādeva saw it, he thought to himself:
"It would be well to obtain this mount."

Having finished his reflections, he went before the king. The king, wishing to test him, waited until the next day at sunrise; he then mounted [the horse] and traveled eastward. In a mere moment, he had circled the four seas and returned to his own country, stopping at the west of the palace gate and standing facing west.
"Ānanda! Such is the horse-treasure obtained by Mahādeva.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"What were the precious jewels obtained by Mahādeva?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"On the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month, when the moon was full, Mahādeva bathed himself in purity and, accompanied by his court ladies, ascended the eastern tower. Looking toward the east, he saw a divine jewel. The jewel was sixteen inches long, had eight facets, and was the color of dark blue lapis lazuli; it came through the air at a height of seven *tāla* trees."
Mahādeva saw it and thought to himself,
"Would it not be right to obtain this jewel and behold it?
As soon as he had this thought, he obtained it.

The king wished to test him; at midnight, he assembled the fourfold army, suspended the pearl atop a banner, and went out from the city to travel about. The pearl illuminated the twelve *yojanas* in every direction, so that the soldiers could see one another as clearly as by day. Wherever the light of the pearl reached, the people rose in alarm, all saying, "It is dawn!"
The king immediately returned to the palace and erected the banner within it; inside and out, it was constantly bright, no different from daytime.
Ānanda! Such were the precious jewels obtained by Mahādeva.
Ānanda asked the Buddha,
"What was the nature of the Great King’s Jewel of the Woman?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"When the Great King reached the fifteenth day, at the time when the moon was full, he bathed for purification and ascended the eastern tower accompanied by his court ladies. Looking toward the east, he beheld a Kṣatriya woman-jewel named Manāharī (translated into Chinese as 'Captivating the Heart'), whose beauty was peerless. She was exquisite, refined, and pure; she was neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor slender, neither too pale nor too dark. In winter she was warm, and in summer she was cool. From the pores of her body issued the fragrance of sandalwood, and from her mouth issued the scent of the *utpala* lotus. She was entirely devoid of the wicked manners common to women; her temperament was harmonious, and she anticipated the king's wishes before they were voiced. Arriving through the air, she came directly to the king’s presence."
"Ānanda! Such is the precious jade woman obtained by Mahādeva.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
“What was it like when Mahādeva obtained the *Gṛhapatiratna* (Treasure of the Householder)? The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“On the fifteenth day, when the moon was full, Mahādeva bathed himself clean and pure, took his court ladies, and ascended to the northern pavilion. Looking toward the north, he saw the householder-minister named Arthadatta (translated into Chinese as *Caichuang*, ‘Wealth-Banner’). He was handsome and exquisite, neither tall nor short, neither stout nor thin; his body was golden in color, his hair was deep blue-black, and his eyes were clearly distinguished between white and black. Furthermore, he could perceive the seven treasures hidden beneath the earth: those with owners he protected for them, and those without owners he took and used together with the king. Intelligent and wise, possessing excellent strategic counsel, he came through the air directly before the king and said to him:”
"From this day forward, Your Majesty may take pleasure in yourself; do not grieve any longer. I shall provide you with treasures so that you shall never lack for anything.
The king then tested the minister by embarking on a ship with him alone and entering the sea.
The king said to the treasurer:
"I wish to obtain gold, silver, and treasures.
The treasurer replied to the king:
"When we have returned to the shore, I shall provide you with wealth and treasures.
The king said, "I wish to obtain the treasures from within the water; I do not want those on the shore."

The treasurer then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt on his right knee, and joined his palms in salutation toward the water. Immediately, golden peaks as large as chariot hubs spontaneously emerged from the water, filling the boat in an instant.
The king said, "Stop!
Do not add any more gold; the boat is about to sink."
"Ānanda! Such was the Treasurer of Treasures obtained by Mahādeva.
Ānanda then asked the Buddha again:
"What is this general of the military whom Mahādeva has obtained? The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"When the fifteenth day arrives and the moon is at its full, Mahādeva bathes himself in purity and, accompanied by his court ladies, ascends the southern tower. Looking toward the south, he sees a great general in the southern direction named Bībhatsu—which means 'Fearless' in the local tongue—who is handsome and beautiful. His hair is the color of pearls, and his body is greenish. He is neither tall nor short, neither fat nor thin. His eyes can see through to all things, and he knows the thoughts of others. Skilled in military strategy and tactical maneuvers, he knows the proper time for advancing or retreating. Riding upon the void, he comes directly to the king's location and says to him:"
"May Your Majesty enjoy yourself in pleasure and do not worry about the world; as for the subjugation of the four quarters, your servant shall manage it!
The king, wishing to test him, contemplated at midnight:
"I wish to assemble the fourfold army."
Having finished this thought, the fourfold army assembled completely.
The king thought again:
"I wish to lead them eastward."
The army immediately marched eastward; the king was in the center, the general was at the front, and the four divisions of troops surrounded them.
If the king thought he wished to go forward, he went forward; if the king thought he wished to return, he returned.
"Ānanda! Such is the Jewel of the General-in-Chief obtained by a Great King.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Ānanda.
"Such were the seven treasures obtained by Mahādeva.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"After King Mahādeva had ruled over the world for a very long time, he spoke to his hairdresser and attendant, named Kapphiṇa:"
"If there is anyone with white hair, pull it out and show it to me.
Kapila examined his hair for a long time until he saw a single white strand, whereupon he said to the king,
"That which you previously commanded has now been found."
The king said,
"Bring it here and show me.
Gopaka immediately used golden tweezers to pluck out the white hair and placed it in the king's hand.
The King grasped the white hair and spoke this verse:
“Upon the crown of my head, This destroyer of beauty has grown. My body sends forth this summons:
The time has come to enter the Way.”
The king thought to himself:
"I have already exhausted the five desires of humans; now I shall leave the household life, shave my beard and hair, and don the dharma robes.
He summoned his eldest son, Changsheng, and told him:

"O youth! Gray hairs have already appeared upon my head, and I have grown weary of the five desires of the world. Now I wish to seek that which is desired by the heavens; I now intend to shave off my beard and hair, don the dharma robes, and leave the household life to pursue the Way."
"You should take charge of the administration of the state and establish the eldest as the crown prince;
you must carefully nurture Kapphiṇa and have him watch for the appearance of white hair.
Once white hair has emerged, entrust the kingdom to the crown prince and, like me, go forth from home, shave off your beard and hair, and don the dharma robes."
The king said to the crown prince:
"I now earnestly entrust this noble station to you; you must ensure that this noble station is inherited from generation to generation and that the lineage is not severed.
One who severs the lineage becomes a person of the borderlands."
"If one cuts off wholesome conduct, one will be born in a place where no dharma exists.
Having thus admonished him, the Great Heavenly King entrusted the kingdom to his eldest son, Jīvajīvaka, and provided him with the fields and estates of Kāpiṣṭhala.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"In this city, in this garden, on this spot of ground, King Mahādeva shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and entered the Way.

For eighty-four thousand years at this place, he practiced the four Brahma-vihāras—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and upon the end of his life there, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven."
Seven days after Mahādeva had renounced the household life, the Jewel-Woman (Strīratna) passed away.

After Changsheng had ascended the throne, on the fifteenth day, when the moon was at its full, he took his court ladies up to the eastern pavilion and looked toward the east; there he saw a jade-like woman, as beautiful as before, arriving through the air.
Changsheng returned to wearing the seven treasures.
Having already assumed the administration of the state, Changsheng governed the four quarters of the world.
Changsheng then spoke again to Jieben:
"From this day forward, whenever you are combing my hair and see a white hair, report it to me immediately.
After he had ascended the throne as a Wheel-Turning Sage King for eighty-four thousand years, a white hair grew again, and Jyotipāla informed the King:
"A grey hair has appeared."
The King said,
"Pull it out and place it upon my palm.
Gopāla immediately used golden tweezers to pull it out and set it in the King's hand.
The King grasped the white hair and immediately spoke this verse:
“Upon the crown of my head, This destroyer of beauty has grown. My body sends me forth to summon [the Sage];
The time has come to enter the Way.”
The king thought to himself:
"I have already fully experienced the five desires of humans; now I shall leave the household life, shave my beard and hair, and don the dharma-robes.
He then summoned the crown prince Mukuṭa and addressed him, saying:

"O youth! My hair has already turned white, and I have grown weary of the five worldly desires; I shall now seek celestial desires. I wish to leave the household life to pursue the Way, shaving off my beard and hair and donning the dharma robes."
"You shall take charge of the administration of the kingdom and establish your eldest son as the crown prince;
you must care for Kapphiṇa well and have him watch for white hairs.
Once white hairs appear, entrust the kingdom to the crown prince and, like me, go forth from home, shave off your beard and hair, and don the dharma robes."
The king said to the crown prince:

"I now entrust this position of a holy wheel-turning monarch to you with earnest persistence. You must ensure that this position of a holy wheel-turning monarch is transmitted from generation to generation and that the lineage is not severed;
for one who severs the lineage becomes a person of the borderlands."
"If one severs their wholesome conduct, they will be born in a place where no dharma exists.
Having thus admonished him, King Jyotiṣprabha entrusted the kingdom to his crown prince, Mukuṭa-śikha, and granted him the lands and estates of Kāpota.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“King Jīvaka also, in this very city, in this very garden, on this very spot, shaved off his beard and hair, donned the dharma robes, and entered the Way.

For eighty-four thousand years at this location, he practiced the four Brahma-vihāras—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and upon the end of his life there, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Seven days after Prince Ajātaśatru had gone forth into homelessness, the seven treasures spontaneously vanished.
King Mūrdhaja was filled with sorrow and found no joy."
Seeing that the king was displeased, the ministers asked him,
"Why, O Heavenly King, are you displeased?
The king replied to the ministers:
"It is because they have departed, transformed by the seven treasures!
The ministers said to the king,
"May Your Majesty not grieve over this."
The King said, "How can you not be anxious?
The ministers replied:
"The King, our father, who practices the holy life, is staying nearby in the garden; you may go there to consult him, for he will surely instruct Your Majesty in the method for acquiring treasure.
The king then issued the command:
"Prepare the carriage!"
The ministers then completed the preparation of the carriage and informed the king.
The king, together with his retinue of ministers, mounted a chariot made of the seven precious substances, which was adorned with five insignia:
a jeweled crown, a feathered parasol, a sword, a fan, and jeweled sandals.
Attended by his ministers and retinue on both sides, he proceeded to the garden.

Upon arrival, he descended from his carriage and set aside the five royal insignia; entering the garden gate on foot, he approached his father the king, prostrated himself at the king’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. With palms joined, he addressed him, saying:
"The seven treasures possessed by Your Majesty have now all vanished."

The father first took his seat; hearing what was reported, he looked up and replied, "Young man, according to the law of the noble wheel-turning monarchs, one does not rely upon the possessions of one's father."
"You yourself shall practice the Dharma and uphold it. The King asked again:
"By what Dharma does a Wheel-Turning Sage King transform [his subjects]?"
The father then replied:

"Reverence for the Dharma, honoring the Dharma, mindfulness of the Dharma, nurturing the Dharma, increasing the Dharma, flourishing the Dharma, and upholding the Dharma—one who practices these seven dharmas shall govern as a noble king and will be able to obtain the treasures."
The king asked again:
"What is meant by 'revering the Dharma,' up to and including 'the Great Dharma'?
His father replied:

"One should study the practice of bestowing gifts upon the poor, teaching the people filial piety and the support of their two parents, performing seasonal sacrifices at the four seasons and eight festivals, instructing them in forbearance, and eliminating the practices of lust, envy, and delusion. These seven dharmas constitute the law of a sage-king."
The king immediately accepted the instruction, took his leave with a prostration, and after circumambulating [the teacher] seven times, he led the way back home.

Thereupon, the king followed his father’s command and practiced the seven dharmas, proclaiming them far and near so that all venerated and honored the royal teaching. The king then opened the treasuries to bestow gifts upon the poor and destitute and to provide for the orphaned and the aged; among the people of the four quarters, there were none who did not submit to and uphold these teachings.

Thereupon, on the fifteenth day, at the time when the moon was full, the king bathed himself in purity and ascended the eastern pavilion accompanied by his court ladies. Looking toward the east, he beheld a thousand-spoked wheel of purple-gold, seven *tāla* trees in height and seven *tāla* trees above the ground, coming through the air and halting in mid-space.
The king thought to himself,
"Would it be possible for me to obtain this wheel?
Immediately, the wheel descended into the king's left hand, and he then moved it to his right hand.
The king spoke to this wheel, saying: "Subdue all those who do not submit for me;
seize for me all that is not my territory; act in accordance with the Dharma, and not contrary to the Dharma."

The king then took the wheel in his hand and cast it back into the void; at the eastern side of the palace gate, with its rim facing east and its hub aligned toward the west, it remained suspended in mid-air.

Following the wheel, there appeared in succession a white elephant, then a dark-blue horse, then a divine jewel, then a jade maiden, then a master of the treasury, and finally a general. These seven treasures emerged just as they had for the Great Heavenly King, and the trial was likewise conducted in this manner.

When eighty-four thousand years had passed, the king bestowed the kingdom upon Jiebei, commanded his crown prince, and entrusted him with the affairs of state; he then left the household life to enter the Way, all in accordance with the laws of former kings.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"This King Mukuṭa, in the garden grounds of this city, shaved off his beard and hair, donned the dharma robes, and for eighty-four thousand years cultivated the four Brahma-vihāras—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Thereupon, when his life came to an end, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The lineage of the great prince shall succeed one another, and for eighty-four thousand years the noble seed of the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King shall remain unbroken."

The last of these holy kings was named Ren (in the language of Jin pronounced like *jin* with the second tone), whose appearance was like a red lotus flower. He governed according to the True Dharma; he was intelligent and wise, discerning and possessed of an unfailing memory. His marks numbered thirty-two, and he delighted in practicing generosity, making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, caring for the orphaned and the elderly, and providing relief to the poor.

At the four city gates and in the center of the city, he established treasuries containing gold, silver, various jewels, elephants, horses, chariots, clothing, bedding, medicines for the sick and emaciated, incense, flowers, food, and drink; furthermore, he provided wives to all who were solitary, bestowing various gifts according to the desires of each person.
On the six days of the fast, the King issued a decree that both his inner and outer courts observe the eight precepts;
on these days, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven shall all descend to receive these eight precepts,
and Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven will all praise the people of his kingdom:
"How wonderful! What excellent benefit!
That we have encountered such a Dharma King!
He bestows various gifts, allowing his people to have their desires fulfilled at will, and he is moreover pure in his observance of the precepts and fasts without fail."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked the sons of the gods:
"Would you like to see King Śaṅkha?
They all replied:
"If you wish to see him, you may be sent here.
Śakra-devānām-indra then commanded the celestial maiden Gopikā—Gopikā meaning "Extremely Beautiful" in the language of Jin—to say:
"Go to the city of Mithilā and tell King Daṇḍakin: [message follows]"...
"O Great One! You have attained a most excellent benefit; all the devas here praise your lofty merit and have sent me to inquire after you with great earnestness.
These sons of heaven long to see you; would you deign to come here for a brief while?"
"Having received these instructions, Kuṇḍopadhānī descended; in the time it takes for a person to bend and stretch their arm, she suddenly appeared standing in the air before the king’s palace."

The king was attended by a single court lady and sat upon the palace terrace, reflecting upon the world with the desire that all beings might attain peace and security, free from all suffering and affliction.
Gopikā, who was in mid-air, snapped her fingers to awaken him. The king raised his head and saw the radiance upon the palace roof;
hearing her voice, he said, "I am a servant of Śakra Devendra, and for that reason I have been sent to you, O King.
The king replied, "I do not know what command the Lord of Devas has given."
The goddess replied:

"The Celestial Emperor has sent his greetings with great earnestness; these sons of heaven praise your virtues and have long anticipated meeting you. Might you deign to lower yourself for a brief moment?"
The King silently gave his consent.
The goddess then returned to the Lord of Devas and said:
"I have delivered your command; he has granted that I shall hasten thither."
The Heavenly Emperor immediately commanded his attendants to prepare a carriage drawn by seven-jeweled flying horses and descended to the city of Mithilā to welcome King Aṇeṇya.
Having received these instructions, the attendants harnessed the carriage, and it descended suddenly.
The King met with his ministers at the capital assembly hall when the chariot stopped in mid-air before him.
The charioteer announced:
"The Lord of Devas now sends this chariot to welcome you; the sons of gods stand waiting in solemn dignity. You may board the chariot and no longer look back with lingering attachment."
When the ministers, both high and low, heard that the King was about to depart, they were all filled with displeasure; they rose to their feet, joined their palms, and said:
"After Your Majesty has gone, whom shall we follow for our commands?"
The King replied: "Do not worry, sirs.

After I have departed, my bestowing of favors, observance of fasts and precepts, nurturing of the people, and governance of the state shall be as they were when I was present; I shall return before long."
When the king had finished his instructions, the chariot descended to the ground and the king ascended it.
An attendant asked the king,
"By which road shall we proceed?"
The king asked, "What do these words mean?
The attendant replied:
"Now, there are two paths of conduct: first, the path of evil, and second, the path of goodness.
Those who practice evil travel the path of evil to places of suffering;
those who cultivate goodness traverse the path of goodness to places of bliss."
The King said, "Today I am practicing the Way; I wish for both good and evil to follow me.
When the charioteer heard this, he was awakened after a long time and said:
"Excellent, Great King!
The charioteer then led him between the two paths; beholding both good and evil in their entirety, he proceeded directly to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the various sons of the gods saw the king approaching from afar,
Śakra Devānām Indra said, "Welcome, Great King!
and commanded him to sit together with them.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"The king then took the seat of the Lord of Devas; the king’s appearance, attire, and voice were identical to those of Śakra.
The sons of the gods thought to themselves:"
"Who is Śakra? Who is the king? he thought again.
"A human should blink, yet both do not blink?
Each of them harbors astonishment, having no means to distinguish between them.
Seeing that the devas had doubts, the Lord of Devas thought again:
"I shall detain the king so that he remains here, and only then will I awaken.
Śakra said to the sons of the gods:
"Do you wish for me to detain the king so that he stays here?"
The sons of the gods said,
"We truly wish for him to remain.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, addressed Rṇa:
"Great King! May you remain here; I shall provide for you with the five objects of desire.
It was through these words that the devas finally recognized him.
The King of Men said to the Lord of Devas: "It is so;
you have already bestowed these gifts. May the life-spans of all the sons of heaven be infinite.
Thus did the host and guest exchange their invitations and refusals.
When this had been repeated three times, Śakra said to the king,
"Why do you not stay? The king replied:
"I shall leave the household life to practice the Way; now that I am in the heavens, there is no opportunity to study the Way.
The Lord of Devas said, "Why do you seek to practice the Way?"
The King said, "I have been left with an injunction by my father, the King: when white hair appears, it is the law that I must renounce the world.
Upon hearing this injunction regarding his entry into the Way, Śuddhodana remained silent and did not reply.
While the king was in the heavens, indulging himself in the five desires for a mere moment, it had already been twelve years by worldly reckoning.
As the king was about to depart, he spoke the Dharma of profound discernment to the various devaputras.
The Śākya king issued an order to his attendant:
"You shall escort King Aṇaṅga back to his own country.
Having received these instructions, the attendant immediately prepared the carriage; once it was ready, he addressed the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, please ascend the chariot.

Thereupon, the king took his leave of Śakra and the various devaputras, immediately mounted the chariot, and returned by way of the original path. Upon arriving at the Madhuvana Palace, the attendants and servants returned to the heavens.
After several days had passed, the King again commanded Gopī:
"If you see any white hairs, inform me immediately.
Within a few days, white hairs appeared upon his head; Gopī plucked them out with golden tweezers and placed them in the King's hand.
Having seen this, the King spoke in verse:
“Upon my head has grown this sign of ruin; My body sends me forth to summon [the Sage];
The time has come for me to enter the Way.”
The king thought to himself:
"I have already fully experienced the five desires of humans; now I shall renounce the world, shave my hair and beard, and don the dharma robes.
The king then summoned his crown prince, Sujāti, and said to him:

"My white hair has already appeared; I have grown weary of the five desires of the world. I shall now seek celestial desires; I will shave off my beard and hair, don the dharma robes, and leave the household life to enter the Way."
"Young man!
I now entrust the affairs of state to you; care for Kapila well.
When white hair appears, hand over the kingdom to the crown prince, renounce the world, and enter the path, young man!"
"Now I entrust this noble royal position to you; do not allow the lineage to be severed. One who severs the lineage becomes a person of the borderlands.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"King Rén immediately entrusted the affairs of state to the crown prince and provided him with the lands and estates of Jieben. Then, in the park grounds of this city, he shaved off his beard and hair, donned the dharma robes, and left the household life to practice the Way."
After he had practiced the Path, within seven days, the wheel and the jewel vanished, and the elephant, the horse, the jade lady, the householder, and the general all met with impermanence.

For eighty-four thousand years within the park, the king practiced the four Brahma-vihāras—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and upon the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-heaven.

Thereafter, King Śubhavyūha did not inherit his father’s legacy, and the True Dharma declined and fell into ruin. Consequently, the seven treasures no longer appeared in response to him; as virtuous conduct was not continued, the five degenerations eventually arrived. The people became short-lived, their complexions faded, they lacked strength, were plagued by many illnesses, and were devoid of wisdom. As these five degenerations set in, poverty and destitution increased, leading to mutual entanglement in theft. They went before the king and addressed him, saying: [The text continues with the description of the king's subsequent reign and the eventual appearance of the Maitreya Buddha.]
"This man has committed theft.
The king immediately issued an order for the executioner to carry out the punishment.
When the people heard that the king would invariably execute anyone who committed theft, they all detested this evil and each fashioned a sharp blade.
The sword was first fashioned from this point; from this, the taking of life arose, and thus two evils emerged.
Next, there was the violation of another’s wife;
when the husband disputed it and [the offender] claimed, "It was not I," four evils were thereby established.
Divisive speech and inciting strife constitute the fifth evil;
fighting and mutual abuse constitute the sixth evil;
speaking without sincerity constitutes the seventh evil.
To be jealous of others' harmony is the eighth evil;
to harbor resentment until one's facial expression changes is the ninth evil;
and for the mind to be clouded by doubt and confusion is the tenth evil.
"The ten evils were already complete, and the five degenerations increased.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you wish to know whether the Great Heavenly King who arose at the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa was he?"
That was I. Ānanda! If you wish to know who that King Rin was, who ruled for eighty-four thousand years without any injustice, it was you yourself.

Ānanda, if you wish to know who at that time was the last king named Sujīva—the one who was violent, perverse, and unrighteous, and who severed the lineage of the noble kings—it was Devadatta. Ānanda!
In the past, it was by your merit that you inherited the noble lineage of the Great Heavenly Wheel-Turning Sage King, ensuring its succession remained unbroken.
It is in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to the Dharma. Ānanda!
I am now the unsurpassed Dharma King; I now bequeath the unsurpassed sublime Dharma to you, entrusting it to you with earnest diligence.
"You are a scion of the Śākya clan; do not become a person of the borderlands, and do not perform acts that sever the lineage.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"For what reason would one perform acts that sever the lineage?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“Although King Mahādeva practiced wholesome dharmas, he had not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows or the supramundane state; he had not attained liberation, nor the severance of desire, nor the destruction of two billion fetters. The sixty-two views were not yet eliminated, the three impurities were not yet purified, and he had not attained supernormal powers or the true path of liberation. He did not attain nirvāṇa; the wholesome dharmas practiced by Mahādeva did not exceed rebirth in the Brahma Heaven.”

“Ānanda! My Dharma is ultimately unconditioned; my Dharma reaches the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), surpassing gods and humans. My Dharma is without outflows, free from desire, the crossing over of subsiding, thorough liberation, true śramaṇahood, and the attainment of nirvāṇa.”
Ānanda! I now earnestly entrust this unsurpassed Dharma of the Path to you; do not add to or subtract from my Dharma, and do not act like those of the borderlands!
Ānanda! If there are those who currently practice as śrāvakas, should anyone sever this Dharma, they shall become people of the borderlands.
If one can promote this Dharma, they shall become the eldest son of the Buddha, and their retinue will thereby be perfected.
Ānanda! You should ensure that your followers are well-established; do not act in a way that would lead to the destruction of your clan. Ānanda!
"All the teachings I have expounded from beginning to end, I now entrust entirely to you.
You should study them.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Ānanda rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (Five) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four persons belonging to the great hells. What are the four?
They are the sinner Makhaligosala, the bhikṣu Tiṣya, the sinner Devadatta, and the bhikṣu Kokālika.”
As for the sinner Makarika, fire issues from his body to a height of sixty cubits.
As for the sinner Tiṣya, fire issues from his body to a height of forty cubits.
The sinner Devadatta emitted flames from his body thirty cubits in length.
The sinner Kokālika emitted flames from his body twenty cubits in length.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that Makhalī taught countless sentient beings to practice false views and inverted perceptions, calculating notions of existence and non-existence.
As for the foolish Diśa, he discarded the remnants from the alms bowls of the noble Saṃgha.”
The foolish Devadatta incited strife and discord among the Sangha, killed an Arhat Bhikṣuṇī, and gave rise to harmful intentions toward the Tathāgata.
The sinner Kokālika slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
"Furthermore, monks!
The sinner Makhalī taught countless sentient beings to practice wrong views; when his body broke up and his life ended, he fell into the Hell of Blazing Light."
The sinner Devadatta abandoned those who had committed offenses, cut off the remnants of the noble assembly’s alms-bowls, and at the dissolution of his body after death, fell into the Saṃjīva Hell.
As for the sinner Devadatta, having conceived a murderous intent toward the Tathāgata, at the dissolution of his body after death, he fell into the Avīci Hell.
As for the sinner Kūṭadanta, because he slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, at the dissolution of his body after death, he fell into the Patamdhara hell.
"As for the sinner Makhalin, at that time the hell-wardens will pull out his tongue from its socket and fix it upon his spine.
This is because in the past he taught countless sentient beings to practice false views."

As for the great sinner Diśa, at that time the wardens of hell tore his body apart with their bare hands, poured molten copper into him until it destroyed his heart, and further forced him to swallow glowing iron balls.
The reason for this is that he broke his alms bowl and discarded its remnants.

As for the sinner Devadatta, a wheel of glowing iron shall crush his body; furthermore, his frame shall be ground by iron pestles, and a herd of fierce, evil elephants shall trample upon him. Moreover, a great mountain of glowing iron shall press down upon his face, and his entire body shall be wrapped in sheets of hot copper.
The reason for this is that because he formerly incited strife among the noble assembly and destroyed the harmony of the Saṃgha, an iron wheel has come to crush and sever his head.
Furthermore, because this foolish Devadatta instructed the prince to harm his father, the king, as a result of that karmic retribution, an iron pestle has shattered his body.
Furthermore, that foolish man Devadatta, having intoxicated an elephant to go and harm the Tathāgata, will as a result of that karmic retribution have his body trampled by a herd of elephants.

Furthermore, because that evil man Devadatta climbed to the summit of Vulture Peak Mountain and hurled a stone at the Buddha, as a result of that karmic retribution, a mountain of glowing iron was made to press down upon his face.
However, because that foolish Devadatta killed an Arhat bhikṣuṇī, as a result of that karmic retribution, he was caused to have his body wrapped in sheets of glowing copper and iron.
"Monks, you should know that the sinner Gavāmpati is in that Lotus Hell, where a thousand sets of oxen plow his tongue.
This is because he slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; due to this cause and its karmic retribution, a thousand sets of oxen have been made to ravage his tongue."
"Furthermore, monks!
As for the sinner Makhalin, fire issues from his body, sixty cubits in length.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to this thought: "
"Let me rescue and benefit this person.
He took the waters of the four great oceans—forty cubits high—and poured them over his body; yet that ocean water was instantly consumed, while the flames neither increased nor diminished.
For four days, hot iron leaves were scorched by fire; if someone were to come and sprinkle them with four drops of water, the water would vanish instantly.
This case is just like that.
If someone were to come and drench that person's body with the waters of the four great oceans, wishing to render them inactive, it would ultimately not be possible.
This is because their transgressions are exceedingly deep and grave.

"Furthermore, from the body of that sinner Tiṣya, a fire issues forth forty cubits in length. Even if there were sentient beings who, out of compassion for this man, were to drench his body with the waters of the three great oceans, those ocean waters would instantly evaporate, and the flames would not diminish."
It is like a person who places three drops of water upon a hot griddle; the water immediately evaporates and cannot remain for long.
This case is also like that: even if one were to pour the waters of the three great oceans over the body of Diśā, the water would vanish instantly, while the fire would never increase or decrease.
“The sinner Devadatta emits flames from his body, thirty cubits in length.

If there are sentient beings who give rise to thoughts of affection and desire to cause Devadatta’s body to dwell forever in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and they pour the waters of the two great oceans over his body, the water is exhausted at that very moment, yet the fire never extinguishes.”
It is just as if two drops of water were placed upon a hot griddle; they would ultimately neither increase nor decrease [the heat].

The fool Devadatta is also like this: even if the waters of the two great oceans were poured over his body, the water would vanish instantly, yet the fire would never be extinguished, and Devadatta’s body would suffer such agony.
“Kauṭilya, this sinner emits flames from his body twenty cubits in length.

Even if there were sentient beings who, out of compassion for this man, were to take a great mass of seawater and pour it over his body, that seawater would vanish instantly, and the fire would never be extinguished.”
It is just as a single drop of water placed upon a hot griddle, which is instantly consumed and cannot remain for long;
so too it was with the bhikṣu Kokālika.
Drawn by the retribution of their offenses, they thus undergo these punishments.

Therefore, bhikṣus, it is said that these four kinds of people undergo the most grievous punishment; you should exhaust your efforts to distance yourselves from such calamities and follow the various noble ones who practice the holy life.
"In this way, O virtuous ones, you should train yourselves.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now clearly understand the hells, I also know the path leading to the hells, and I further know the fundamental nature of those sentient beings in hell.”
Furthermore, monks, if sentient beings commit various evil and unwholesome deeds, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life enter into hell, I also know this.
Furthermore, monks!

I also know the animal realm clearly; I know the path leading to the animal realm, and I further know the root of the animal realm. I also fully understand those who commit various evils and are thereby born there.
I now also know the path of the hungry ghosts; those who have committed evil at its very root and are born among the hungry ghosts, I also know them.
I now also know the human realm and the destiny of humans; those sentient beings who have attained a human body, I also know them.
I also know the path leading to the heavens; if there are sentient beings who cultivate the roots of virtue and are reborn in those celestial realms, I also know this.

I also know the path leading to Nirvana; if there are sentient beings whose outflows are exhausted and become outflow-free, attaining liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and realizing the fruit of realization within the present life, I also know this.
“Bhikṣus, you should know: ‘I know the destination of hell; for what reason do I speak these words?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“I now observe the mentalities of sentient beings. That is to say, when this person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they ought to enter hell. Subsequently, I observe that this person has entered hell and undergoes suffering that is bitter and cruel, with countless tortures and interrogations, such that their grief, sorrow, and affliction cannot be fully recorded.”

It is like a great pit of fire, free from dust and smoke; if someone were to come and head straight toward it, and a person with sight were to observe where that person was going, they would surely fall into the fire—it could not possibly be otherwise.
Furthermore, at a later time, one observes that this person has fallen into a pit of fire; the "person" I speak of has likewise fallen into a pit of fire.

Now, when one examines the thoughts and intentions of sentient beings, it is certain they will enter hell without doubt—just as I later observed this person, who was destined to enter hell and undergo suffering so bitter and cruel that it cannot be fully described.
"How is it that this person enters hell?

It is because, when I observe sentient beings heading toward hell who commit various evil deeds and unwholesome karmas, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life they enter into hell, I know all of this."
What I have spoken is precisely this.
"I know the path of animals, and I also know those who go toward the realm of animals; for what fundamental cause and condition do I say this?"
"In this regard, monks!
I observe the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings and see that, upon the dissolution of this body at the end of life, this person is reborn among the animals.
At a later time, I observe this person who has been reborn among the animals, experiencing incalculable sorrow, grief, and suffering."
Why is it that this person falls among the animals?
It is like a village with a large latrine, filled with excrement.

Suppose there were a person who went straight toward that place; a man with sight, seeing this person coming straight toward that place, would know that before long this person will fall directly into the latrine.
Subsequently, he observes that this person has already fallen into a latrine, undergoing unspeakable misery and destitution.
How has this person fallen into a latrine?
I now observe that the various classes of sentient beings are likewise so; at the end of their lives, these people ought to be reborn among the animals.
Furthermore, at times I have observed those already born among the animals, suffering immeasurably.
I now clearly perceive all these animal beings.
What I have spoken refers precisely to this.
"I also know the sentient beings who are hungry ghosts and the path of hungry ghosts; I also know those whose bodies have disintegrated and lives have ended, and who are reborn as hungry ghosts."
If there are sentient beings whose bodies have disintegrated and whose lives have ended, who proceed toward the realm of hungry ghosts, I know them all.
Furthermore, at a later time, I observe these sentient beings as they enter the realm of hungry ghosts and experience painful and pleasant sensations.
Why does this person enter among the hungry ghosts?
It is like a great tree standing beside a large village in a perilous place, its branches and leaves withered and fallen.
Suppose someone were to come and approach this place; a person with sight who observes this individual from afar would have no doubt that they are heading toward the tree.
Later, one might observe this person again, either sitting or lying down, experiencing the retribution of their suffering or happiness.
"How is it that this man has come to sit and lie beneath a tree?

Now, when I observe the various classes of sentient beings, they are likewise: when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will inevitably proceed to the realm of hungry ghosts without doubt, receiving retributions of suffering and joy that cannot be fully described."
"I know the realm of hungry ghosts and the path of hungry ghosts, all clearly and distinctly; that which I have spoken refers precisely to this.

I know the human realm and the path leading to the human realm; I likewise know those who, having performed certain actions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, are reborn among humans."

Thereupon, bhikṣus! I observed the thoughts within the minds of various classes of sentient beings and saw that this person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, would necessarily be reborn among human beings.
Furthermore, at a later time, I observed that this person had been reborn among human beings.
How was it that this person was reborn among human beings?
It was like a great tree standing by the side of a village in a level and open place, providing abundant shade.

If there is a person who comes directly along a single path, one with eyes, having seen them, immediately knows that the direction this person is heading toward will certainly lead them to this tree, without doubt.
At a later time, I again observed this person; having reached this tree, he experienced immeasurable bliss.
How did this person come to reach such a place? It is just like this:
when I observe the thoughts and intentions of sentient beings, it is likewise that upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will certainly be reborn among humans, without a doubt.
Furthermore, at a later time, I observed that this person had been reborn among humans and was experiencing immeasurable happiness.
I know the human realm, and I also know the path leading to the human realm; those who are now born among humans—I know them as well. What I have spoken refers precisely to this.
“I also know the heavens, and I also know the path leading to the heavens; furthermore, I also know those sentient beings who perform various meritorious deeds and are reborn in the heavens.”
For what reason was this said?

I have now observed the thoughts within the minds of various classes of sentient beings and see that this person, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, will surely be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens; subsequently, observing this person’s dissolution of the body at the end of life and their rebirth in a good destination, in the heavens, they will there receive spontaneous blessings and incomparable happiness.
This means that when such a person has been reborn in the heavens, they receive spontaneous blessings there, their happiness being beyond compare.

It is like a fine, lofty, and spacious lecture hall beside a village, adorned with carved and engraved patterns, hung with silken banners and canopies, with fragrant liquid sprinkled upon the ground, and furnished with excellent seats, woolen rugs, fine carpets, embroidered hangings, and sumptuous cushions.

If there is a person who comes directly from a single path, and a man with sight also comes directly from that same single path, the destination toward which this person proceeds will certainly be the High and Vast Hall; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, at a later time, one observes that this person has already arrived at the hall, where he is either sitting or lying down, experiencing incomparable bliss and happiness therein.

It is the same with this: I now observe that when certain classes of sentient beings, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, are reborn in a good destination in the heavens, they experience there an incalculable and sublime joy.
"How does this person, having been born in a good realm among the heavens,
come to know the path to the heavens and the way leading to the celestial realms?
What I have spoken refers precisely to this."
"I now know nirvāṇa, and I also know the path to nirvāṇa; I also know those sentient beings who should attain parinirvāṇa.

There may be sentient beings who exhaust all outflows (āsrava) to become free from outflows, attaining liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, realizing the fruit in this very body while wandering freely to transform others—all of these I fully know."
For what reason was this said? In this regard, monks!

I observed the thoughts in the minds of various classes of sentient beings and saw that this person had exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained the state of being without outflows (*anāsrava*), with liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*) and liberation by wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*); it is for this reason that one says this person has exhausted all outflows and attained the state of being without outflows.
It is just as if there were a great pond not far from a village, its waters exceedingly clear and transparent.

If someone were coming directly along a single path, a person with sight who saw that individual from afar would know for certain that this person would reach the pond’s water without doubt; furthermore, later on, one would observe that the person has indeed reached the pond, bathed and washed themselves, removed all filth and impurities, and is sitting by the side, without quarreling or contending with others.

I now observe the classes of sentient beings and see that they are likewise so: they have exhausted all outflows and attained the state of being without outflows; their minds are liberated and their wisdom is liberated;
birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and name-and-form are known as they truly are.
This is called: "When a person has reached this state, I know the path to nirvāṇa, and I also know all those sentient beings who have attained parinirvāṇa."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses this wisdom, fearlessness, and power, all of which he has fully accomplished.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is immeasurable; the Tathāgata can contemplate the infinite, measureless, and incalculable events of the past, knowing them all completely.
The future and the present, infinite and immeasurable, are all fully distinguished.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should seek skillful means to become fully endowed with the ten powers and the fearlessnesses.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7 (Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"On the Snowy Mountains there is a great, tall, and wide tree that excels in five ways of growth.
What are these five? Its roots are immovable;
its bark is extremely thick; its branches and joints provide distant shade, covering everything without exception; and its leaves are exceedingly lush and flourishing."
"Monks, this is what is meant:
on the Snowy Mountains there is this great tree, which is exceedingly magnificent.
In the same way, a son or daughter of good family who relies upon a noble clan likewise prospers in five ways."
What are the five? They are:
the increase of faith, the increase of ethical discipline, the increase of learning, the increase of generosity, and the increase of wisdom.
These, O bhikṣus, are called [the five].
A faithful son or daughter of good family who relies on a noble household accomplishes these five matters. Therefore, bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to accomplish faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just like a tree on the Snowy Mountains, perfected in five qualities of merit—
its roots, bark, branches, and joints are extensive, and its trunk and leaves are most luxuriant."
A son of noble family endowed with faith accomplishes five meritorious qualities;
through faith, precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom, they are ever further increased.
"In this way, bhikṣus, you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maūraparika lived and associated with the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs likewise took pleasure in associating with him.
When there were people who reviled and censured the bhikṣu Mañjubhadra, at that time the bhikṣuṇīs became extremely filled with anger, sorrowful, and displeased.
Furthermore, if there were someone who reviled the bhikṣuṇīs, at that time the bhikṣu Khaṇḍadravya would also become sorrowful and displeased.
Then, a great multitude of bhikṣus said to the bhikṣu Khaṇḍadravya:
"Why do you now associate so closely with the bhikṣuṇīs?"
"Do the bhikṣuṇīs also associate with you?
Pāpīyān replied, "I now understand the instructions taught by the Tathāgata: for one who commits sexual misconduct, the fault is not even worth mentioning."
The many bhikṣus replied again: "Stop! Stop!"
"O Bhikṣu! Do not speak such words.
Do not slander the teaching of the Tathāgata; for those who slander the teaching of the Tathāgata, the transgression is no small matter."

Furthermore, the World-Honored One has taught through countless skillful means the impurity of sexual misconduct; it is simply impossible that one who practices such conduct could ever be without fault.
You should now abandon this evil view, lest you suffer immeasurable pain throughout the long night of saṃsāra.
Nevertheless, this monk Paṇḍaka continued to associate with them and did not reform his conduct.
At that time, a great number of monks went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"In the city of Śrāvastī there is a monk named Paṇḍaka who associates with various bhikṣuṇīs; likewise, those bhikṣuṇīs also associate with and come and go to the monk Paṇḍaka."

"We went to them to exhort and persuade them to change their conduct; however, those two instead increased [their attachment] even further, did not abandon these perverted views, nor did they accord with the practice of the True Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to where the bhikṣu Khaṇḍadravya is and say:
'The Tathāgata summons you.'"
At that time, the bhikṣu, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, went immediately to where the bhikṣu Bhagnasaṃgha was and said:
"You should know this: the Tathāgata is summoning you."
When the bhikṣus who had broken the group heard those words of the bhikṣu, they immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you have been associating closely with the bhikṣuṇīs?"
That bhikṣu replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"You are a bhikṣu; how can you associate with a bhikṣuṇī?
You are now a son of noble family who has shaved off your hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and with firm faith, gone forth from home to study the Path."
The Bhikṣu Bhagnasaṃgha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
I am a son of noble family who, with firm faith, has left the household life to study the Path.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"This is not your dharma.
Why do you associate with a bhikṣuṇī in such a manner?"
The Bhikṣus of the Broken Group addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We have heard what the Tathāgata has said: that for one who practices sexual misconduct, the fault is truly not worth mentioning.
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus:
"You fool! How can you say that the Tathāgata commits sexual misconduct without fault?
Through countless skillful means, I have spoken of the foulness and impurity of sexual desire; how can you now speak such words?"
"The Tathāgata says that sexual misconduct is without fault"?
You must carefully guard against verbal transgressions, lest you suffer their retribution throughout the long night.
The Buddha said to him:
“Cease for now! I must first question the bhikṣus further.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Have you heard me, along with the bhikṣus, say that sexual misconduct is without fault? The bhikṣus replied,
“Indeed we have, World-Honored One!”
I have never heard the Tathāgata say that sexual desire is without fault.
The reason for this is that the Tathāgata has, through countless skillful means, spoken of the defilement of sexual desire.
Were he to say it is without fault, such a meaning would not be correct.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"O bhikṣus! It is as you have said;
by means of countless expedient means, I have spoken of the filthiness of sexual desire.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

“You should know this: if there are foolish people who practice the teachings of the Dharma—namely, the sūtras, geyas, verses, prophecies, causal narratives, antecedent events, parables, births, vaipulya, wonders, and detailed expositions—even though they recite these teachings, they do not understand their meaning.
Because they do not examine the meaning, they do not accord with the Dharma; thus, regarding that which should be practiced in accordance with the Dharma, they ultimately do not act accordingly.”

Therefore, those who recite this Dharma do so with the desire to compete and contend with others, calculating victory and defeat; nor do they do it for their own benefit or salvation. Once they have recited the Dharma, they then violate its restrictions.

It is just as if there were a person who left a village seeking a venomous snake; upon seeing an extremely large snake, he approached it and stroked its tail with his left hand, whereupon the snake turned its head and bit his hand. Due to the karmic retribution of this cause, he met his end. This case is exactly like that: if there is a foolish person who studies and practices these teachings, weighing and examining all twelve divisions of the scriptures without exception, yet fails to contemplate their true meaning.
The reason for this is that they have not reached the ultimate meaning of the True Dharma.

"In this regard, if there is a son of good family who protects, cherishes, and practices its teachings— the sūtras, geyas, verses, prophecies, causal narratives, introductory accounts, parables, birth stories, vaipulya, marvelous events, discourses, and extensive treatises—
and having recited these teachings, he deeply understands their meaning;..."

By means of the Dharma that explains those profound meanings, one follows its teachings without error or omission. Therefore, those who recite the Dharma do not compete or contend with others out of a desire for victory;
those who study and practice the Dharma do so wishing to personally cultivate and attain realization;
and those who recite the Dharma do so because they have specific aspirations, by which causes and conditions they gradually reach Nirvana.
It is like a person who leaves a village to search for a venomous snake.
Having seen the snake, he takes it by the head with an iron pincer and then seizes it by the neck, preventing it from moving;
even if that venomous snake should turn its tail to strike him, it will ultimately be unable to reach him.
The reason for this, bhikṣus, is that it was because he held [the bull] by the neck!

This son of good family is just like that: he recites and studies until he has mastered everything; he examines its meaning and conforms to its Dharma, never deviating or erring. Gradually, through these causes and conditions, he shall attain nirvāṇa.
The reason for this is that they uphold the True Dharma. Therefore, O bhikṣus!
Those who understand my meaning should mindfully practice it.
"Those who do not understand may come again to question me.
While the Tathāgata is currently present, it will be of no benefit to regret later.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were a bhikṣu among the great assembly who spoke thus:
'I fully understand all the prohibitions and precepts taught by the Tathāgata; as for those who practice sexual misconduct, their transgressions are not even worth mentioning.'"
That bhikṣu should say to this bhikṣu: "Stop! Stop!"
"Do not speak such words!
Do not slander the Tathāgata by uttering these words; the Tathāgata would never speak such a thing.
If this bhikṣu reforms his transgression, that is well.
If he does not reform his conduct, he should be admonished a second and third time.
If he reforms, it is well; if he does not reform, he falls into an offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu conceals such matters and does not allow them to be revealed, all those involved fall into an offense.
"This, monks, is called my precept. At that time, the monks,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-Āsrava went to where the World-Honored One was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin Jāti-Āsrava addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"How many eons have passed?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"The past kalpas are beyond calculation.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
"Is it possible to calculate them?"
The śramaṇa Gautama constantly speaks of the three periods of time.
What are these three?
They are the past, the future, and the present.
“The śramaṇa Gautama also knows the past, future, and present worlds; I only wish that the śramaṇa would expound the meaning of the kalpas.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“If I were to speak of this kalpa, then another kalpa after that, by the time I have entered parinirvāṇa and you have reached the end of your life, you would not know the meaning of the kalpas.”
The reason for this is that the lifespan of people today is short; at most, it does not exceed a hundred years.
To calculate several kalpas within those hundred years, I shall attain parinirvāṇa, and once you have passed away, you will never know the meaning of the duration of such kalpas.

"Brahmin, you should know that the Tathāgata likewise possesses this knowledge; he fully distinguishes the number of kalpas, the length of the life-spans of sentient beings, and their experiences of suffering and pleasure—all of which he knows with complete clarity."
I shall now provide you with an analogy, for the wise gain understanding through analogies.
Just as the number of grains of sand in the Ganges is limitless, immeasurable, and incalculable, so too is the number of past kalpas.
"It is incalculable and beyond measure.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha:
"How many eons will there be in the future?"
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"They are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, without limit or boundary; they cannot be measured or calculated, and exceed the reach of reckoning.
The brahmin asked the Buddha again:
“Is there such a thing as a present eon, or an eon of formation and destruction?
The Buddha told the brahmin:
“There are indeed such eons of formation and destruction, not merely one eon or a hundred eons; it is like a vessel placed on unstable ground, which can never remain steady.”
If one were to abide therein, it would necessarily involve perversion; the same applies to the various regions of all worlds.
There are eons of formation and eons of destruction, and the number of these—how many eons of formation and how many eons of destruction—is likewise impossible to calculate.
The reason for this is that birth and death are long and far-reaching, without any limit.

Sentient beings, covered by the fetters of ignorance, drift and stagnate, passing from this life to the next and from the next life back to this one, suffering affliction throughout the long night; they should therefore feel weary of it and seek to depart from these torments.
"Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself in this way.
At that time, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“O Śramaṇa Gautama! How extraordinary!
How marvelous!”
Knowing the meaning of the kalpas of the past and the future, I now once again take refuge in the Śramaṇa Gautama!
I pray only that the Śramaṇa Gautama will accept me as an upāsaka; for as long as my life lasts, I shall not dare to kill, nor even to drink alcohol.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin Jāti-śroṇa rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Does an eon have a limit?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"Using skillful means, I shall provide an analogy: yet the number of kalpas is inexhaustible. In the distant past, during this present Bhadrakalpa, there appeared a Buddha named Krakucchanda, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, this Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain had another name.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha climbed this Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain; it took them four days and four nights of travel to reach its summit.
Furthermore, monks!
During the time of the Buddha Kanakamuni, this Vulture Peak Mountain had yet another name.
At that time, the people of the city of Rājagṛha traveled as far as the summit of this mountain for three days and three nights.
When the Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world, this Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain had yet another name.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha traveled for two days and two nights until they reached the summit of this mountain.
Just as I, Śākyamuni Buddha, have now appeared in the world, this mountain is named Gṛdhrakūṭa; in a mere moment, I have arrived at its summit.
When Maitreya Tathāgata appears in the world, this mountain shall likewise be named Gṛdhrakūṭa.
This is because the supernatural power of all Buddhas causes this mountain to emerge and remain here.
“Monks! You should know through skillful means that kalpas have their decline and exhaustion, which cannot be calculated.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of kalpas:”
There are great kalpas and small kalpas.
If, within a kalpa, no Buddha appears in the world, yet at that time a pratyekabuddha does appear in the world, this is called a small kalpa.
If a Tathāgata appears in the world during a kalpa, and at that time no pratyekabuddha appears in the world within that kalpa, this is called a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
"Monks! By this means, you should know that the duration of the kalpas is so vast as to be beyond calculation. Therefore, monks!"
"One should remember the meaning of these kalpas.
At that time, another bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*Ekottarika Āgama*, Scroll 48.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 49. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 51: On Impermanence (Anitya-varga). Chapter Fifty-one: On Impermanence.
1. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Monks, how is it? As you have wandered through the cycle of birth and death and undergone suffering and affliction, do the tears you have shed while wailing and weeping therein amount to much?”
"Is the water of the Ganges more?
At that time, the bhikṣus came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"As we contemplate the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught, the tears we have shed while wandering through birth and death exceed the waters of the Ganges."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"O bhikṣus! What you have said is no different from the truth. While you have been in saṃsāra, the tears you have shed exceed the waters of the Ganges.
Why is this so? Within saṃsāra, you have repeatedly experienced the death of your parents; the tears you shed therein are beyond calculation."

Throughout the long night, fathers, elder brothers, sisters, wives, children, and the five types of kinsmen, as well as all those bound by affection, have followed him in mourning and wept with unspeakable sorrow.
For this reason, O Bhikṣu!
"You should cultivate weariness toward birth and death,
and depart from these phenomena. Thus, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves."
When this Dharma was being taught, more than sixty bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Monks, how is it? Is the blood that has flowed from your bodies as you have undergone destruction within the cycle of birth and death more abundant,
or is the water of the Ganges more so?”
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"According to our observation of what the Tathāgata has taught, the blood shed is more than the waters of the Ganges."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Monks! It is as you have said: the blood shed is greater than the waters of the Ganges.

This is because, within the cycle of birth and death, one has been born as an ox, a sheep, a pig, a dog, a deer, a horse, a bird, a beast, or other countless forms, undergoing immeasurable suffering and affliction. This is truly something to be weary of; you should contemplate renouncing it."
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, more than sixty bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and the liberation of mind.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"One should contemplate the perception of impermanence and extensively cultivate the perception of impermanence. By contemplating and extensively cultivating the perception of impermanence, one completely severs sensual craving, craving for form, and craving for the formless; ignorance and conceit are all utterly eliminated."
It is just as when fire burns away grasses and trees until they are forever exhausted with nothing remaining.

Monks, you should know that if one contemplates the perception of impermanence and extensively cultivates the perception of impermanence, one will completely sever all craving and attachment within the three realms.

"In the past, there was a king named Pure Resonance who ruled over Jambudvīpa. He had eighty-four thousand cities and fortresses, eighty-four thousand ministers, and eighty-four thousand palace ladies and maidservants; each of these ladies had four attendants."
At that time, King Ghoṣa had no offspring. Then, the Great King thought to himself:
"I now govern this realm, transforming it through the Dharma without any injustice; yet today I have no heir, and after my passing, my lineage will be extinguished."

At that time, for the sake of obtaining offspring, the king took refuge in the various devas, nāgas, spirits, the sun, the moon, and the stars; he took refuge in Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, mountain deities, tree deities, and even down to the deities of medicinal herbs and fruits, praying for blessings so that he might have progeny.
"At that time, there was a devaputra among the Trāyastriṃśa gods named Subhūti, whose life was about to end; five portents naturally appeared to press upon him."
What are these five?
Furthermore, while the flowers of the other devas never wither, the flower crown of this son of the gods withers of its own accord;
at that time, while the garments of the other devas are free from dust and grime, the garments of this son of the gods become stained with dust and grime.

Furthermore, the bodies of those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three are fragrant and pure, and their radiance shines through everything; yet at that time, the body of this deva-son becomes foul-smelling and cannot be approached.

Moreover, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, celestial maidens are always present, surrounding them before and behind to perform music and song as they indulge in the five desires; yet at that time, when this deva-son’s life is about to end, these maidens disperse.

Furthermore, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three there are natural seats that sink four feet into the ground; when a deva rises from his seat, it rises four feet above the ground, yet when this deva’s life is about to end, he finds no pleasure in his original seat.
These are called the five auspicious omens that spontaneously press upon one.
At that time, because of these auspicious omens, the devaputra Subhūti, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed a certain devaputra, saying:
"Go now to Jambudvīpa and speak to King Vyāghrarāja, saying:"
“Śakra Devānām Indra sends his boundless greetings, inquiring whether Your Majesty’s daily life is light and easy and your movements are healthy and strong.

In Jambudvīpa, there is no person of such virtue as to serve as Your Majesty’s son; however, there is currently a son of heaven in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven named Subhūti. Now, five auspicious omens have spontaneously appeared to press upon him, and he will surely descend in spirit to become Your Majesty’s son.”
"Even so, when you reach the prime of your youth, you must surely leave the household life to study the Way and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya).
The devas replied, "So be it, O Heavenly King;
we shall receive the Heavenly King’s instruction."
"Just as a strong man might flex or extend his arm, he vanished from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and arrived in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, King Sound-Vibration was atop a high tower, accompanied by a single attendant holding a parasol."
At that time, the deva, situated in the air above the pavilion, addressed the king, saying:
"Śakra Devānām Indra sends his boundless greetings; he is in good health and his daily life is comfortable and vigorous."

"In Jambudvīpa, there is no person of virtue who may serve as the King’s consort; however, in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there is a son of heaven named Subhūti. Now five auspicious omens have appeared to urge him on, and he shall descend from his divine abode to become the King’s consort."
"However, when I am in the prime of my youth, I shall certainly leave the household life to study the Way and cultivate the unsurpassed holy life.
When King Sound-Vibration heard these words, he was so filled with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself;

he immediately replied to the deity, "The message you have brought is a most great blessing. If you would deign to descend as a spirit to be my son, I shall never oppose your wish to leave the household life."
At that time, the deva returned to the place where Śakra Devānām-indra was and addressed the Heavenly King, saying:
"King Ghoṣadatta greatly cherishes what I have reported; King Ghoṣadatta said:
'As long as he causes the descent of his spirit, if he wishes to leave the household life, I shall never oppose it.'"
Then Śakra-devānām-indra went to where the devaputra Subhūti was and said to him:
"You should now make a vow to be born into the palace of King Sound-Voice."

The reason for this is that King Śrīghoṣa has no heir, yet he constantly governs and transforms his realm through the True Dharma; you have merit from the past and have performed manifold virtuous deeds, and it is now fitting that you descend in spirit to be born within his palace.
The Devaputra Subhūti said: "Stop! Stop!"
"O Heavenly King!

I do not delight in the wish to be born into the palace of a human king; my intention is to leave the home life and study the Way, for it is extremely difficult to study the Way while remaining in a royal palace.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied:
"Simply make a vow to be born into that royal palace;
I shall protect you and cause you to leave the household life to study the Way.
Bhikṣus, you should know that at that time, the devaputra Subhūti immediately made a solemn vow to be born into the royal palace.
At that time, King Ghoṣadatta united with his chief consort, and she became aware that she was pregnant.
Then the consort said to King Ghoṣadatta:
"Great King, you should know that I have now become aware of being pregnant."

When the king heard this, he leaped for joy and was so overcome with delight that he could not contain himself; he further prepared an exceptionally fine seat and provided food as sweet and delicious as if it were his own royal fare.
At that time, after eight or nine months had passed, the lady gave birth to a son who was exceedingly handsome, with a most extraordinary countenance, such as was rarely seen in the world.

At that time, King Ghoṣadatta summoned the various non-Buddhist ascetics, brahmins, and ministers, commanding them to perform a divination; he then related the entire sequence of events, from beginning to end, in detail to those fortune-tellers.
The brahmins replied:
"May Your Majesty examine this principle!
The Crown Prince born today is extraordinary in this world; in a former life he was a king named Subhūti, and now, following his former title, he is named Subhūti."
When the physiognomists had thus established his clan name and title, they each rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, Prince Subhūti was held in high esteem by the king and was never out of his sight.
At that time, King Ghoṣadatta thought to himself:

"From the past until now, I have had no offspring. For the sake of an heir, I have offered prayers and sacrifices to the various devas so that a son might be born; yet after such a long time, a son is only now born.
Furthermore, as the Lord of Devas prophesied, he is destined to leave the household life to study the Way."
"I must now employ skillful means to ensure that he does not leave home to study the Way.
At that time, King Sound-Vibration established three seasonal palaces for the sake of the crown prince:
a warm palace for the cold season, a cool palace for the hot season, and a palace of moderate climate for seasons that were neither cold nor hot.

He provided four types of residences for the palace women: the first palace had sixty thousand maidens, the second had sixty thousand maidens, the third had sixty thousand maidens, and the fourth had sixty thousand maidens; each had four attendants, and revolving seats were constructed so that the prince might lie upon them.

If Prince Subhūti wished to sport in front, at that time the female attendants would immediately stand before him, and his seat would rotate along with his body; there were sixty thousand female attendants ahead of him, and four personal servants.
If he wished to sport behind, at that time the couch would likewise rotate along with his body.

Furthermore, whenever he desired to enjoy himself with the female attendants, the seat would rotate along with his body, causing Prince Subhūti’s mind to remain intent upon the five desires and not delighting in leaving the household life.
At that time, during the night at the hour of non-humans, Śakra Devānām Indra went to the place where Prince Subhūti was and, standing in mid-air, addressed Prince Subhūti, saying: "Prince!..."
Did you not previously think to yourself:
"When I am at home and in the prime of my youth, I shall leave the household life to study the Way"?
Why is it that today you take pleasure for yourself amidst the five desires?
"Do you no longer wish to leave the household life to study the Way?
Indeed, I too have spoken these words:
