'I urge and encourage the Prince to leave the household life and study the Way.'"
"Now is precisely the right time; had you not left the household life to study the Way, it would have been of no avail for you to regret it later!
Having spoken these words, Śakra Devānām-Indra withdrew and departed.
At that time, Prince Subhūti, while among the palace attendants, had this thought:
"King Ghoṣadatta has already cast for me the net of sensual desire; because of these conditions of the net of sensual desire, I am unable to leave the home life to study the Way."

I shall now sever this net, so as not to be entangled by defilement and turbidity. With firm faith, I shall leave the household life to study the Way; dwelling in a place of emptiness and stillness, I will diligently study the scriptures and teachings, ensuring they are renewed daily.
At that time, Prince Subhūti again had this thought:

"My father the King has these sixty thousand court ladies surrounding him before and behind; I should now examine whether there is any principle by which such a thing could exist forever in the world."
At that time, Prince Subhūti surveyed the entire palace and saw that there was not a single woman who would remain in the world for long.
Then Subhūti thought again: "Why am I now observing external things?"
One should contemplate that this body arises from internal causes and conditions.
Within this present body, are there any such things as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bones, or marrow that can endure in the world for long?
From head to foot, one contemplates the thirty-six impure and loathsome substances.

Thus, upon self-examination, not a single thing is found worthy of desire; there is nothing real, for all is illusory and false rather than true, ultimately returning to emptiness and not remaining long in this world.
At that time, Prince Subhūti again had this thought:
"I shall now sever this net and leave the household life to study the Way.

Then, Subhūti contemplated these five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*): namely, "this form is suffering, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form, and this is the escape from form"; [and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness].
"Suffering, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are suffering; consciousness is its origin, consciousness is its cessation, and consciousness is the escape from it.

At that time, having contemplated this body of the five aggregates—realizing that whatever is subject to arising is subject to passing away—he attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha right there on his seat.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Subhūti, having attained Buddhahood through awakening, spoke this verse:
“I know your origin, O Desire: You arise from conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*).
If I do not conceptualize you, Then you shall no longer exist.”
At that time, having spoken this verse, the Pratyekabuddha flew into the air and departed.
Remaining alone beneath a tree in a certain mountain range, he entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
"At that time, King Ghoṣa addressed his attendant minister, saying:
'Go and observe within the palace of Subhūti; is the prince awake or asleep, and is he at peace?'"
At that time, the minister, having received the king’s command, went immediately to the prince’s palace; however, the doors of the inner chamber where he was sleeping were firmly secured.
The minister then returned to the king’s presence and addressed him, saying:
"The prince is safe and sound whether awake or asleep, and the doors are firmly secured."
Then the king asked him a second and a third time:
"Have you gone to see whether the prince is sleeping well?
At that moment, the minister returned to the palace gate, but the doors were firmly secured.
Again, he went to inform the king:
"The prince remains asleep in the palace, unaware; the gates are firmly secured and remain unopened until this very moment.
Then King Śabdavat again thought to himself:
"When my son, the Prince, was young, he did not even sleep; how much less would he sleep now at this time of youthful vigor?
I should go there myself to see whether my son is well or ill, and whether he might perhaps fall sick."
At that time, King Sound-Vibration went directly to Subhūti’s palace; standing outside the gate, he addressed a man, saying:
"Now, provide a ladder to climb over the wall and enter within to open the door for me."
Having received the king’s command, the man immediately provided a ladder, climbed over the wall, entered the inner quarters, and opened the door for the king.
When the king had entered and surveyed the inner palace, he found the bed empty; he did not see the prince.
Having failed to see him, he addressed the court ladies, saying:
"Where is Prince Subhūti now? The court ladies replied,
"We too do not know where the prince is."
When King Sound-Vibration heard these words, he threw himself upon the ground and only after a long while did he regain consciousness.
At that time, King Sound-Vibration addressed his ministers, saying:
"Even when my son was young, he already conceived such a thought."
"If I grow up, I shall shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and with firm faith, leave the home life to study the Way.
Now, the Prince will surely abandon us to leave the home life and study the Way; each of you must search for the Prince in all four directions to find his whereabouts.
Immediately, the ministers mounted their vehicles and galloped forth, searching everywhere.
At that time, one minister went straight to that mountain; on the way, he thought to himself:
"If Prince Subhūti has left the household life to study the Way, he must surely be studying it here."
At that time, the minister saw from afar Prince Subhūti sitting cross-legged beneath a tree.
The minister then had this thought: "This is Prince Subhūti."
Having observed him closely, he returned to the king's presence and, approaching the king, said:
"Prince Subhūti is currently in the mountains beneath a tree, sitting cross-legged in meditation."

When King Sound-Vibration heard these words, he immediately went to that mountain. From afar, he saw Subhūti sitting cross-legged beneath a tree on the mountain, and he prostrated himself upon the ground, saying:
"In my youth, I made this vow: 'If I reach twenty years of age, I shall leave the household life to study the Way.'"
"Now I shall not be mistaken.
Furthermore, the deva has informed me, saying:
'Your son must surely study the Way.'"
Then King Ghoṣadatta went straight forward and said to Subhūti,
"For what reason do you now forsake me to leave the household life and study the Way?
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha remained silent and did not respond.
The king spoke again, saying:
"Your mother is filled with extreme sorrow and anxiety; she will not eat until she sees you.
You must now depart for the palace."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha neither spoke nor replied, but remained silent.
King Śabdavat then stepped forward and took his hand, yet he did not move.
The king again addressed his ministers, saying:
"The Prince has already passed away this very day. Śakra Devānām Indra previously came to inform me:
'You shall obtain rest; you need only go forth from home to study the Way.'"
"However, the prince has already left the household life to study the Way; now we carry these relics and have come to the borders of your kingdom at the time of the snake festival.
Then, the various deities dwelling in that mountain manifested their upper bodies and said to the king:
"This is a Pratyekabuddha, not a prince."
The method for enshrining the *śarīra* (relics) of snakes is not equal to the method for princes.
Why is this so? Because I am a disciple of the Buddhas of the past, and those Buddhas also possessed this teaching.
There are four persons in the world for whom a stūpa should be erected. What are these four?
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—for him a stūpa should be erected;
A stūpa should be erected for a pratyekabuddha;

likewise, a stūpa should be erected for a disciple of the Tathāgata who is an arhat with out-flows exhausted. Just as when the body of a wheel-turning sage king is cremated, it is the same when the bodies of a Tathāgata or a pratyekabuddha are cremated.
At that time, King Ghoṣa again addressed the devas, saying:
"How should one make offerings to the body of the wheel-turning king Śaśabindu?
The tree deity replied:

They constructed an iron coffin for the Wheel-turning Sage King, filled it with fragrant oil, and bathed the body of the Wheel-turning Sage King therein. They wrapped his body in pure white Kārpāsika cotton cloth, then covered it with painted silken garments, and placed him within the coffin. They sealed it with an iron lid, fastening it with nails at every point, and further wrapped the coffin in a hundred layers of white cotton cloth. Various kinds of mixed incense were piled upon the ground, and the iron coffin was set therein. For seven days and seven nights, they made offerings of flowers and incense, hanging silk streamers, banners, and canopies, and performing music and dance.

After seven days had passed, he again took the king’s body and performed the snake-cremation (sarpa-dāha) to collect the relics; this snake-cremation continued without interruption for another seven days and seven nights, after which a stūpa was erected at the crossroads and further offerings of incense, flowers, banners, and canopies were made in various ways.
Great King, you should know that such is the manner of making offerings to the relics of a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
it is likewise for the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats.
Then King Ghoṣarāja said to those devas:
"By what causes and conditions does one make offerings to the body of a wheel-turning sage king?
By what causes and conditions does one make offerings to the bodies of Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, and arhats?"
The deva replied to the king:
"A Wheel-Turning Sage King governs as a Dharma King; he himself abstains from taking life and further teaches others not to commit killing;
he himself does not take what is not given and further teaches others not to engage in theft."
One does not engage in sexual misconduct oneself and further teaches others not to violate the wives of others;

one does not engage in false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, or divisive speech that incites conflict between parties; nor does one harbor envy, malice, or delusion. With a mind focused and upright, one constantly practices right view and likewise causes others to cultivate that same right view.
"This is why, Great King!
For these reasons and conditions, a stūpa for a Wheel-Turning Sage King should be erected.
The king asked the deva:
"Furthermore, for what reason should a stūpa be erected for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted?
The deva replied to the king:

"An Arhat bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted has ended craving for desire, eliminated hatred and delusion, and has crossed over from existence to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). He is a field of merit (puṇyakṣetra) that brings blessings to the world; for this reason, a stūpa should be erected for an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted."
The King asked again:
"By what causes and conditions should a stūpa be erected for a pratyekabuddha?
The deva replied to the King:

"A Pratyekabuddha awakens by himself without a teacher; his appearance in the world is extremely rare. He attains the fruit of the present life, is liberated from the evil realms, and causes people to be born in the heavens. For these reasons, a stūpa should be erected for a Pratyekabuddha."
The king asked again:
"By what causes and conditions should a stūpa for the Tathāgata be erected?
The deva replied to the king:

“The Tathāgata is fully endowed with the ten powers; these ten powers cannot be attained by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, cannot be reached by Wheel-Turning Kings, and cannot be reached by the multitudes of sentient beings in the world.”
The Tathāgata, possessing the four kinds of fearlessness amidst the great assembly, can roar the lion’s roar and turn the Brahma-wheel.

The Tathāgata delivers those not yet delivered, liberates those not yet liberated, and causes those who have not entered parinirvāṇa to enter parinirvāṇa. To those without protection, he provides shelter; to the blind, he acts as eyes; and for all who are afflicted by disease, he serves as a great King of Physicians. Among gods and worldlings, Māras and the celestial Māras, there are none who do not revere him. He is worthy of honor and esteem; he turns beings away from the evil realms and leads them to the auspicious states.
"Thus it is said, Great King!
For these reasons, a stūpa for the Tathāgata should be erected.
This is what is meant, Great King!"
"For these reasons, from beginning to end, four kinds of persons should erect a stūpa.
At that time, King Ghoṣa said to those devas: "Excellent!"
Excellent, O divine being!
I now accept your instruction; I shall make offerings to these relics as if making offerings to a pratyekabuddha.
At that time, King Ghoṣa said to the people:
"Each of you shall carry the relics of the Pratyekabuddha Subhūti to the borders of my kingdom."
Having heard the king’s command, the ministers laid him upon a golden bed and carried him to the borders of the kingdom.

At that time, King Sound-Vibration (Ghoṣadatta) immediately ordered the construction of an iron coffin, filled it with fragrant oil, and bathed the body of the Pratyekabuddha. He wrapped the body in Kārpāsa cloth, then covered it with fine garments of various colors, and placed it within the iron coffin. He sealed it with an iron lid, fastened it securely with nails at every point, and covered it with a hundred layers of white cotton cloth. Taking various excellent incenses, he placed them around the Pratyekabuddha’s body, and made offerings of incense and flowers for seven days and seven nights.

After seven days had passed, they again made offerings to the relics of the Pratyekabuddha Śunaka for seven days, performing music and dance; they erected a stūpa at a crossroads and subsequently honored it with incense, flowers, silken fabrics, banners, canopies, and musical performances.

“Bhikṣus, you should know that those sentient beings who reverently make offerings to the relics of a pratyekabuddha will, after the end of their lives, be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Furthermore, those sentient beings who contemplate the perception of impermanence will turn away from the three evil realms and be reborn among gods and humans.”
"O bhikṣus! Do not hold such a view.
Who else could that King Sound-Vibration have been at that time?"
I am that very person.
Contemplating the perception of impermanence brings great benefit.
Having now reflected upon this meaning, I tell the bhikṣus: you should contemplate the perception of impermanence and propagate the perception of impermanence.

By contemplating the perception of impermanence, one brings about the total exhaustion and severance of craving for sensual pleasure, craving for form, and craving for the formless; ignorance and conceit are forever eliminated without remainder, just as fire burns up grass, trees, and a magnificent hall with its windows and doors.

Monks! Contemplating the perception of impermanence is also like this: it completely severs craving for sensual desire, craving for form, and craving for the formless, leaving nothing remaining forever.
"Therefore, bhikṣus! You should exert your minds to the utmost and ensure that you do not fall away from this.
When this Dharma was being taught, more than sixty bhikṣus sitting on those seats attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (4) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī does not sever the five corruptions of the mind and does not eliminate the five fetters of the mind, that bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī will, day and night, diminish in wholesome qualities and experience no increase."
What is meant by the five corruptions of the mind that are not severed?

In this regard, bhikṣu, there is a mind of doubt toward the Tathāgata; it is neither liberated nor does it enter into his True Dharma. That person’s mind is not applied to recitation; this is called the bhikṣu whose mental corruption is not severed.

"Furthermore, bhikṣu! If one harbors doubt regarding the True Dharma, one will neither be liberated nor enter into that True Dharma; such a person will not even recite it. This is called the state where the corruption of this person's mind is not severed."

"Furthermore, bhikṣu! If one harbors doubt toward the Saṅgha of noble ones, is not liberated, does not direct the mind toward the harmonious assembly, and furthermore does not abide within the factors of the path (mārgāṅga), this is called the bhikṣu’s defilement of mind being uninterrupted."

"Furthermore, bhikṣu! One who has transgressed the prohibitions and does not repent of his fault—that bhikṣu, having already transgressed the prohibitions, neither reforms nor repents, nor does he apply his mind to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas). This is called the bhikṣu’s corruption of mind being uninterrupted."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! With an unsettled mind, one practices the holy life [thinking]:
'By the merit of this holy life, may I be reborn in the heavens or among the various deities. "
Yet that bhikṣu practices the holy life with such mental activity, so that his mind does not remain focused upon the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas).
Since his mind no longer dwells within the factors of enlightenment, this is called the failure to sever the corruption of the mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu has not severed the five corruptions of the mind.
"How is it that a bhikṣu has not severed the five fetters?
In this regard, bhikṣu!"
Laziness and failure to seek skillful means: when that bhikṣu is already lazy and fails to seek skillful means, this is called the bhikṣu’s mental fetter being unsevered.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! He constantly delights in much frivolity and is greedily attached to sleep.
Because that bhikṣu delights in much frivolity and is greedily attached to sleep, this is called the second mental fetter of that bhikṣu which he has not severed."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! His mind is not settled and is constantly prone to great distraction;
that bhikṣu’s mind is already distracted and unsettled—this is called the third mental fetter of a bhikṣu that has not been severed."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! The doors of the sense faculties are undisciplined;
that bhikṣu, having undisciplined doors of the sense faculties, is said to have not severed the fourth mental fetter.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! One who constantly delights in being in the marketplace and not in a quiet place—this is called the fifth mental fetter that a bhikṣu has not severed.

If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī possesses these five mental corruptions and has not severed these five mental fetters, then throughout their days and nights, wholesome qualities will be cut off and they will experience no increase."

It is just as if there were eight or twelve chicken eggs that were not covered and shaded at the proper times, not turned, and not protected according to the seasons; although those chickens have this thought:
"May my chicks be preserved whole and free from harm."
"However, these chicken eggs will ultimately not remain secure.
The reason for this is that they were not protected according to the proper seasons; consequently, they will later be broken and fail to develop into chicks."

This is also the case here: if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has not severed the five mental fetters and has not removed the five mental corruptions, their wholesome qualities will diminish day and night, and there will be no increase.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has severed the five mental fetters and eliminated the five mental corruptions, their wholesome qualities will increase throughout the day and night, without any diminution."

It is just as if there were eight or twelve chicken eggs, which were protected at the proper time, nurtured at the proper time, and sheltered at the proper time; even though those chickens might have this thought:
"May my chicken eggs not fully develop."
Nevertheless, those chicken eggs naturally reached maturity, remaining peaceful and unconditioned.
This was because they were nurtured according to the seasons, allowing them to attain this state of non-action; consequently, the chicken chicks soon emerged from their shells.

It is the same in this case: if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has severed the five mental corruptions and eliminated the five mental fetters, that bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī will, throughout the long night, experience an increase in wholesome qualities without any diminution.
"Therefore, bhikṣus, whether bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, you should establish a mind free from hesitation and doubt regarding the Buddha, and free from hesitation and doubt regarding the Saṃgha."

Fully endowed with the precepts, his mind is focused and upright without confusion; he harbors no expectations for other dharmas, nor does he practice the holy life with a view toward fortune, thinking:
"By means of this dharma-practice, I shall become a god or a human being, wondrous, noble, and eminent."

"Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who has no doubt or hesitation regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of noble ones, and who has neither violated the precepts nor committed any transgression,"
I now tell you and entrust this to you again: that bhikṣu shall go to one of two places—either rebirth in the heavens or among human beings.
It is like a person in the midst of extreme heat, further afflicted by hunger and thirst, who encounters a place of cool shade and finds cold spring water to drink.
Although that person may have the thought:
"Even though I have encountered cool shade and drunk cold water,
my hunger and thirst are still not severed," yet that person's heat has already been exhausted and their hunger and thirst have already been removed.
It is the same in this case: if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has no doubt or hesitation regarding the Tathāgata, that bhikṣu will go to one of two places:
either rebirth in the heavens or dwelling among human beings.
If monks and nuns would seek skillful means to sever the five corruptions of the mind and eliminate the five fetters of the mind— thus it is, O monks!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (5) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There may be a time when the king’s majesty is not universal and bandits arise in competition;”
As the bandits have already risen up in competition, villages, cities, and all classes of people have been utterly destroyed and perished; some, encountering famine, have met their end.
Those sentient beings who meet their end through famine will all fall into the three evil realms.
Now this diligent bhikṣu is also like this: if his observance of the precepts diminishes, at that time wicked bhikṣus will arise in competition;
once these wicked bhikṣus have arisen in their evil rivalry, the True Dharma will gradually decline and what is not the Dharma will increase;
when what is not the Dharma has increased, the sentient beings therein will all fall into the three evil realms.
"Furthermore, at that time, if the king's majesty extends far and reaches out, the bandits will hide away;
once the king's influence has reached far, the city walls, villages, and the populace will flourish."

Now, this bhikṣu of diligent effort is also like this: if he maintains the precepts in their entirety, then at that time, the bhikṣus who violate the precepts gradually decline, the True Dharma flourishes, and what is not the Dharma declines; those among the multitude there, after the end of their lives, are all reborn in the heavens or among human beings.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should be mindful to fulfill the precepts, the deportment, and the etiquette, ensuring they are not deficient. Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (6) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“It would be better to remain constantly asleep than, while awake, to engage in distracted and discursive thoughts, such that when the body breaks up and life ends, one is reborn in an evil realm.”
It would be better to burn an iron probe with fire and cauterize one’s eyes than to give rise to distracted thoughts upon seeing forms.
A bhikṣu who gives rise to such thoughts is defeated by consciousness;
once a bhikṣu has been defeated by consciousness, he will inevitably head toward the three evil realms.
The hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.
"Why is it that I say this now?
It would be better for that person to sleep than to harbor distracted thoughts while awake."
It would be better to pierce one's ear with a sharp awl than to give rise to distracted thoughts by listening to sounds.
A bhikṣu who gives rise to such thoughts is defeated by consciousness; it would be better for him to remain constantly asleep than to give rise to distracted thoughts while awake.
"It would be better to have one's faculty of the nose destroyed by hot tongs than to give rise to distracted thoughts upon smelling an odor.
A bhikṣu who gives rise to such thoughts is defeated by consciousness;
once defeated by consciousness, he falls into the three evil destinies."
The hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts—
this is precisely what I mean by that.
"It would be better to have one's tongue severed with a sharp sword than to fall into the three evil destinies through malicious speech and coarse language."
The hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.
It would be better to sleep forever than to give rise to distracted thoughts while awake.
It would be better to wrap one's body in hot copper leaves than to engage in sexual intercourse with the daughters of elders, householders, or brahmins.
If one engages in social interaction and converses with them back and forth, one will inevitably fall into the three evil realms:
the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts.
What I have spoken refers precisely to this.
"It would be better to remain perpetually asleep than to awaken with a mind intent on causing schism within the Sangha;
having caused such a schism, one falls into the five heinous crimes, for which even billions of Buddhas can never provide salvation."
Now, one who incites strife and discord among the assembly shall inevitably fall into the sin of being beyond salvation.

Therefore, I now declare that it would be better to remain perpetually asleep than, while awake, to harbor thoughts with the intent to destroy the Noble Sangha and incur the sin of being beyond salvation.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should guard the six sense-faculties so that they do not leak away.
Thus it is, bhikṣus!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (7) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada had four sons who did not serve the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, nor did they take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
At that time, the elder Anāthapiṇḍika said to his four sons:
"Each of you should individually take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha; thus, throughout the long night, you shall obtain immeasurable merit."
The sons said to their father,
"We, your sons, are not capable of taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Noble Sangha. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika replied:
"I now bestow upon each of you one thousand measures of pure gold; follow my instructions and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha.
The sons replied, "We are not capable of taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha ourselves."
The father spoke again, saying:

"I shall grant you an additional two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, or five thousand *liang* of pure gold; you ought to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Noble Ones, so that throughout the long night you may obtain immeasurable merit."
At that time, having heard these words, the sons accepted them in silence.
Then, the sons said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:
"How should we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha?"
The householder Anāthapiṇḍika replied:
"All of you, come with me to the presence of the World-Honored One.
Whatever the World-Honored One may say, you should bear it in mind and practice accordingly."
The sons said to their father:
"Where is the Tathāgata now?
How far is he from here?"
His father replied, “The Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is currently staying nearby in the city of Śrāvastī, residing within my park.
Then Anāthapiṇḍada took his four sons and went to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet and stood to one side.
At that time, the elder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"My four sons have not yet taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha. Only yesterday, I gave each of them five thousand taels of gold, exhorting them to serve the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha. I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma to each of them, so that throughout the long night they may receive immeasurable blessings."
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to the four sons of the elder, exhorting them until they were filled with joy.
Having heard the preaching of the Dharma, the elder’s sons leaped for joy and could not contain themselves; they knelt before him and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“We each take refuge in the World-Honored One, the True Dharma, and the Noble Sangha. From this day forward, we shall no longer kill living beings, nor shall we drink intoxicants.”
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said to the World-Honored One:
“If there were someone who provided goods to hire laborers to serve the Buddha, what would their merit be?”
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"Elder! It is well that you have asked this question; it brings peace to devas and humans that you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this meaning. Reflect upon it well, and I shall explain it for you."
Then the householder accepted the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to him:
“There are four great treasuries.”
What are the four? There is the Elāpattra dragon in Gandhāra; this is called the first treasury, wherein countless precious jewels are piled high within his palace.
Furthermore, there is the great Pañcaka treasury in the kingdom of Mithilā, where precious jewels are accumulated beyond all calculation.
Furthermore, there is a great treasure of Piṅgala in the kingdom of Sūrattha, where precious jewels are accumulated beyond measure.
Moreover, there is a great treasure of Śaṅkha in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, where precious jewels are accumulated beyond measure.

Suppose all the men, women, and children of Jambudvīpa, each taking turns on the fourth day of the fourth month for four years, were to go and take from the storehouse of Elapatra; it would never diminish.
If those of the Varṣadhāra storehouse were each to come and take from it on the fourth day of the fourth month for four years, one would not know it had diminished.
If those of the Piṅgala storehouse were each to take from it on the fourth day of the fourth month for four years, one would not know it had diminished.
"The great treasury of Śaṅkha is in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; those who take from it for four years on the fourth day of the fourth month do not know its contents have diminished.
This is what is meant, O Householder!"
Regarding the four great treasuries of jewels:
if all the men and women, great and small, of Jambudvīpa were each to take from them and embrace their contents for four years, four months, and four days, they would not know any depletion.
"In a future age, there will be a Buddha named Maitreya who shall appear in the world.

At that time, the kingdom shall be named Kikī; it will be the seat of his rule, measuring twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from north to south, where the population will be flourishing and grain will abound."
At the seat of governance of King Kukkuṭa, there is a pond encircling the city seven times, each measuring one yojana in length and breadth, with golden sand at its bottom.

Within it grow *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, appearing externally in the colors of gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli. If the silver water were to freeze, it would transform into silver; if the golden water froze, it would transform into gold; if the lapis lazuli water froze, it would transform into lapis lazuli; and if the crystal water froze, it would transform into crystal.

“Householder, you should know that at that time there were four great city gates: in the silver ponds, the thresholds were made of gold; in the golden ponds, the thresholds were made of silver; in the lapis lazuli ponds, the thresholds were made of crystal; and in the crystal ponds, the thresholds were made of lapis lazuli.”
“Householder, you should know that at that time, bells were suspended all around the city of Kukkuṭa.
At that moment, when the sound of the bells was heard, they all produced the music of the five kinds of instruments.”
At that time, there were always seven kinds of sounds within the city.
What are these seven?

The sound of conch shells, the sound of drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of small drums, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of *bherī* drums, and the sound of singing and dancing—these constitute the seven.

At that time, in the city of Kikuta, natural non-glutinous rice grew spontaneously; each stalk was three inches long, exceedingly fragrant and delicious, surpassing all other flavors. As soon as it was gathered, it grew back immediately, and no place could be found where it had been taken.
At that time, there was a king named Śaṅkha who ruled according to the Dharma and possessed the seven treasures.

"Householder, you should know that at that time, the treasurer was named Subhadra; he was of high virtue and wisdom, foremost in the divine eye, and capable of knowing the locations of all treasure stores."
Treasures that have an owner will be naturally protected; treasures that have no owner shall be offered to the King.
At that time, the four dragon kings—Elāpattra, Pañcika, Piṅgala, and Śaṅkha—who preside over the treasuries of jewels, all went to the repository of the excellent treasure-store and said to him:
"Whatever you may require, we shall provide it to you."
Then the four dragon kings said,
"We only wish to offer you the treasures of the four treasuries so that you may provide for yourself.
Thereupon, the Master of the Good Treasure Canon took the treasures of the four treasuries and presented them to King Śaṅkha upon his precious golden-feathered chariot.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Irāvatī is in Gandhāra; Mucilinda is in Pañcāla; Piṅgala is in Sūlika; Śaṅkha is in Vārāṇasī."
These are four treasuries of jewels, filled with all manner of stores;
they constantly appear at that time through the arrival of merit.
These are offered to that noble king: a chariot with golden, silver, and precious-feathered wheels.
All the deities shall provide protection, and the elder shall receive their blessings.

At that time, there will be a Buddha appearing in the world named Maitreya—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat—who will teach and transform the people.
Householder, you should know this: at that time, was the one who was the Keeper of the Treasury of Good Jewels anyone else?
Do not view it so. Why is this?
The one who was the master of the treasury at that time is none other than the householder yourself now.

At that time, King Śaṅkha, having performed extensive meritorious deeds with his golden chariot, was surrounded by eighty-four thousand ministers as he went to where Maitreya was, to leave the household life and study the Way.

At that time, the Steward likewise performed extensive meritorious deeds and shall also leave the household life to study the Path, reaching the end of suffering; all this is due to the Elder leading his four sons onto the Way, causing them to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Bhikṣus.

By virtue of this merit, he shall not fall into the three evil realms; furthermore, by virtue of this merit, he shall obtain the four great treasuries, and by virtue of this retribution, he shall serve as the Lord of the Treasury for Śaṅkha, whereby in that very life he will reach the end of suffering.
The reason for this is that those who take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha possess immeasurable virtue.
Such is the merit of those who take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Assembly.
Therefore, householder,
you should cultivate loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, seeking skillful means to turn them toward the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha. Thus it is, householder!
"You should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada was filled with such joy and exultation that he could not contain himself.
He rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid homage, and departed; his four sons did likewise.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and his four sons, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was afflicted with a grave illness.
Then, Śāriputra, observing with his pure and stainless divine eye, saw that the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was suffering from a severe ailment. He immediately said to Ānanda:
"Come, let us go together to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika’s residence to inquire after him."
Then Ānanda replied, "Please know that it is time.

At that time, Ānanda took his bowl at the proper hour and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food; proceeding by stages, he arrived at the house of the elder Anāthapiṇḍada and sat down upon a seat.
At that time, Śāriputra, while still on his seat, spoke to the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, saying:
"Does your current illness increase or decrease?
Do you perceive that the pain is gradually subsiding and not becoming more severe?"
The householder replied, "The ailment I now suffer from is extremely debilitating; I perceive only its increase and not its decrease. Śāriputra replied:

"Now, householder, you should recollect the Buddha—him who is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
You should also recollect the Dharma: the Dharma of the Tathāgata is exceedingly profound, worthy of honor and esteem, peerless, and that which is practiced by the noble ones.
You should also recollect the Saṅgha: the community of the Tathāgata is harmonious from top to bottom, free from dispute, and perfected in the Dharma."

The Noble Assembly consists of those accomplished in ethical discipline, accomplished in meditative concentration, accomplished in wisdom, accomplished in liberation, and accomplished in the vision and knowledge of liberation.
What is called the Saṅgha refers to the four pairs and eight ranks; this is known as the noble assembly of the Tathāgata, worthy of honor and reverence, the unsurpassed field of merit in the world.
"Householder!

If one practices the recollection of the Buddha, the recollection of the Dharma, and the recollection of the Sangha of Bhikṣus, their merit is beyond measure; they shall attain the state of ambrosia and the place of cessation."
"If a son or daughter of good family, having brought to mind the Triple Gem—
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha— should fall into the three evil destinies, such a thing shall never happen!"
If those sons or daughters of good family practice mindfulness of the Three Jewels, they will certainly reach a favorable destination among devas or humans.
Thereafter, O Householder!
Consciousness does not arise from form, nor does it arise dependent upon form;
it does not arise from sound, nor does it arise dependent upon sound;
it does not arise from odor, nor does it arise dependent upon odor.
They do not give rise to flavor, nor do they give rise to consciousness by depending on flavor;
they do not give rise to tangibility, nor do they give rise to consciousness by depending on tangibility;
they do not give rise to the mind, nor do they give rise to consciousness by depending on the mind.
Do not give rise to this world or the next world; do not depend on this world or the next world for consciousness to arise.
Do not give rise to craving; do not depend on craving for consciousness to arise.

The reason for this is that conditioned by craving there is feeling; conditioned by feeling there is becoming; and conditioned by becoming there arise birth, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair, beyond all calculation.
This is called the existence of these five aggregates of suffering, wherein there is no self, person, life-span, soul, individual, germ, or any class of material form.
When the eye arises, it does not know its place of origin;
when the eye ceases, it simply ceases, and it does not know its destination.
That the eye comes into being where it previously did not exist, and that once existing it ceases, is entirely due to the convergence of various dharmas and their causal conditions.
That which is called the Dharma of Dependent Origination means that when there is this condition, there is this; when there is not this, then there is not that. That is to say:

with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in incalculable measure.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise: they arise where there was nothing and perish once they have existed; furthermore, one does not know their place of origin, nor their place of departure; all are produced through the causal conditions of the conjunction of various phenomena (*dharmas*).
"This, householder, is called the foremost dharma of the practice of emptiness.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika wept with such profuse tears that he could not stop himself.
At that time, Śāriputra said to Anāthapiṇḍada,
"By what causes and conditions have you become so deeply moved by grief? The elder replied:
"I am not grieved. Why is this?
Because in the past, I have frequently attended upon the Buddha and also revered the elder bhikṣus, yet I never heard such a teaching of profound respect as that which Śāriputra has now proclaimed."
At that time, Ānanda said to Anāthapiṇḍika:
"Householder, you should know that there are two kinds of persons in the world, as taught by the Tathāgata."
What are these two? First, knowing pleasure; second, knowing suffering.
The person who practices for pleasure is the venerable Yaśodharā’s son, the kṣatriya.
The person who practiced asceticism was the bhikṣu Bakkula.
Furthermore, householder,
the bhikṣu Yaśodatta was foremost in the realization of emptiness.
The one liberated through faith is the bhikṣu Vakkali.

Furthermore, householder, there are those who know suffering and those who know happiness; the minds of these two are both liberated, and both are disciples of the Tathāgata with no equal. Because they neither sink nor arise, both diligently receive the Buddha’s teaching without negligence or abandonment; yet, it is only because their minds undergo increase and decrease [in terms of realization].
Among people, there are those who know and those who do not know, as the elder has said:
"Since the past, I have served various Buddhas and honored the elder bhikṣus, yet I have never before heard such a dharma of profound respect as that which Śāriputra has spoken."
The bhikṣu Yaśodatta looked at the ground, and his mind attained liberation;
the bhikṣu Bhadrika gazed at the sword, and immediately his mind attained liberation.
"Therefore, householder, you should become like the bhikṣu Bhāgali.
At that time, Śāriputra extensively expounded the Dharma for him, exhorting him with joy and causing him to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind; he then rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after Śāriputra and Ānanda had departed, in a mere moment, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍika possessed five meritorious qualities by which he surpassed all those other devas.
What are these five?
They are celestial longevity, celestial beauty, celestial pleasure, celestial majestic power, and celestial radiance.
At that time, the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍika had this thought:
"That I have now obtained this celestial body is entirely due to the grace of the Tathāgata.
It is not fitting for me now to indulge myself in the five desires; I should first go to the place of the World-Honored One to prostrate, kneel, and inquire after his well-being."
At that time, the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍika, surrounded by a host of devas before and behind him, took various celestial flowers and scattered them over the body of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.
At that time, the deva stood in mid-air, joined his palms toward the World-Honored One, and spoke this verse:
“This is the realm of Jetavana, Where the hosts of sages find delight;
The domain governed by the Dharma King— One should give rise to a heart of joy.”
At that time, after the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍika had spoken these verses, the Tathāgata signaled his approval by remaining silent.
Then, that devaputra immediately thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata has indeed granted his approval."
He immediately relinquished his supernormal powers and stood to one side.
Then, the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍika addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I am Sudatta, also known as Anāthapiṇḍika, as is well known to all people; I am likewise a disciple of the Tathāgata who has received the holy teachings of the World-Honored One.”
"Now, having reached the end of my life, I have been reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The World-Honored One asked,
"By what merit have you now obtained this celestial body?"
The devaputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "By the power of the World-Honored One, I have obtained this celestial body.

At that time, the devaputra Anāthapiṇḍika again scattered celestial flowers over the body of the Tathāgata, and also scattered them over the bodies of Ānanda and Śāriputra; they then circled the Jetavana Grove seven times and vanished without a trace.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Last night, a son of heaven came to my dwelling and spoke this verse:
'This is the realm of Jetavana, Where the hosts of sages sport and play. "
"In the realm governed by the Dharma King, one should give rise to a heart of joy.
At that time, the deva-son circumambulated the Jeta Grove seven times and then withdrew and departed.
"Ānanda, do you now recognize that devaputra?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This must surely be the elder Anāthapiṇḍika.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is as you have said."
Excellent! You are indeed able to recognize that deva-son by means of the knowledge of the unknown.
This is because he is the deva-son Anāthapiṇḍika.
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“Anāthapiṇḍika! Now that he has been reborn in the heavens, what is his name?”
The World-Honored One replied,
“His name is Anāthapiṇḍika.
The reason for this is that on the very day that deity was born, each of the devas spoke these words:”

"When this devaputra was among humans, he was a disciple of the Tathāgata. He constantly gave universally with an impartial mind, providing for the destitute and relieving the needy. Having performed these meritorious deeds, he now belongs to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; therefore, his name continues to be Ānabhiṣṭi."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There is one who has achieved great merit and wisdom; the bhikṣu Ānanda, though currently at the stage of a learner, possesses wisdom with which none can equal him."
The reason for this is that whatever an Arhat ought to know, Ānanda knows it;
and whatever the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past ought to have studied, Ānanda understands and knows it all clearly.
In the past, there were also such people who understood immediately upon hearing, just as I now know by looking at the bhikṣu Ānanda:
"The Tathāgata requires this;
the Tathāgata does not require this."
"The disciples of the Buddhas of the past entered samādhi before they could know future events; today, however, my disciple Ānanda perceives and understands them immediately."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Among my śrāvakas, there is one who possesses extensive knowledge, is courageous and diligent, whose mindfulness is undisturbed, who is foremost in learning, and who is capable of managing affairs; he is the bhikṣu Ānanda."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had a daughter-in-law named Sujātā, who was beautiful in appearance with a face like the color of a peach blossom. She was the daughter of a minister of King Prasenajit; relying on her family lineage and taking pride in her noble clan, she showed no respect toward her parents-in-law or her husband. Furthermore, she did not serve the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, nor did she venerate the Triple Gem.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the householder addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“Recently I took a wife for my son; she is the daughter of the foremost minister of King Prasenajit. Relying on her family’s noble lineage, she does not serve the Three Jewels or the elders, regardless of their rank. I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma to her, so that she may give rise to joy and her mind may be opened and liberated.”
At that time, the Tathāgata silently granted the householder’s request.
Then, the householder again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation, along with the community of bhikṣus.”
At that time, seeing that the Tathāgata had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, the elder rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed.
Returning to his home, he prepared various kinds of food and drink, spread out fine seats, and then announced:
"The time has come; I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation, for the food and drink are now ready."
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, went to the house of the elder and sat upon the seat.
Then the elder took another small seat and sat before the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the woman Sujātā, saying:
"Daughter of a householder, you should know that there are four things for a wife. What are these four?"
There are wives who are like mothers, wives who are like kin, wives who are like thieves, and wives who are like slaves.
You should now know that a wife who is like a mother attends to her husband at all times, ensuring he lacks for nothing, and serves and honors him.
At that time, the devas will again protect him; neither humans nor non-humans shall find an opportunity to harm him, and upon death, he will be reborn in heaven.
This is what is meant, householder!
"This is what is meant by a wife who resembles a mother.
"How does one have a wife who resembles a kinsman?
In this regard, when a householder’s wife sees her husband, she has no heart of increase or decrease; she shares in his suffering and joy. This is what is meant by a wife who resembles a kinsman."
"How is it that a wife is like a thief?

In this regard, when a woman sees her husband, she conceives anger and harbors malice toward him; she neither serves nor reveres nor pays homage to him, but desires to harm him upon seeing him, her mind being fixed elsewhere."

If a husband does not treat his wife with affection and the wife does not treat her husband with affection, they will not be loved or respected by others; the devas will not protect them, and malevolent spirits will inflict harm upon them. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they will enter hell. Such a person is said to be like a thief.
"What is meant by a woman who is like a maidservant?
In this regard, a virtuous wife observes her husband at all times, enduring his words without ever retorting;
she endures his harshness and maintains a constant heart of compassion. Furthermore, toward the Triple Gem, she gives rise to this thought:"
"Thinking, 'This exists because I exist;

this decays because I decay,' one is protected by the devas for these reasons, and both humans and non-humans will all cherish and care for them. When the body perishes and life ends, they will be reborn in a good destination, in the heavens."
"These, daughter of a householder, are called the four kinds of wives; in which category do you now find yourself?
When that woman had heard these words spoken by the Blessed One, she stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Blessed One, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me leave: I now repent my past ways and cultivate myself for the future, vowing never again to act as I did. From this day forward, I shall constantly practice the rites of propriety, just like a maidservant."
At that time, the woman Sujātā returned to her husband’s place and prostrated herself at his feet, saying:
"I pray only that you will look after me; I shall be like a servant.
Thereupon, the woman Sujātā went again to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught them the Dharma, namely:
discourse on giving, discourse on morality, and discourse on rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desire is an impure perception and sexual lust is a great defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the woman’s mind was opened and her understanding attained, taught her the Dharma that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly preach:

suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Then the World-Honored One explained these to the woman in their entirety, and she immediately attained the purity of the Dharma-eye while still on her seat, just as a new cloth easily takes on dye.
This was likewise so: she discerned all dharmas, thoroughly understood their profound and subtle meaning, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and received the five precepts.
At that time, the woman Sujātā, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
10 (Ten). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
After a short while, he withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Honored One always praises those of noble lineage and high status, yet does not speak of the lowly and base. However, O World-Honored One!"
"He does not praise the noble and honored, nor does he speak of the lowly and base.
He teaches by abiding in the middle, enabling them to leave the household life and study the Way.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You yourselves claim: 'One does not praise the noble and high, nor speak of the lowly and base; by teaching with moderation, one attains the going forth and studies the Path.
Yet today, I likewise do not speak of superior, middling, or inferior, nor of the various modes of rebirth."

The reason for this is that birth is exceedingly bitter and not worth aspiring to or delighting in; it is like that refuse heap, which is already utterly foul even when small, let alone when accumulated in great quantity!

The present state of receiving birth is likewise so: even one life or two lives are already fraught with suffering and difficulty, let alone the beginningless and endless cycle of transmigration—how could such a thing be endured with complacency?

From existence comes birth; from birth comes old age; from old age comes illness; and there are death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. What is there to be craved or delighted in? Thus, the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha) come into being.
Having now contemplated this meaning, I declare:
"If even one birth and two births are still full of suffering and hardship, how much more so could the endless cycle of transmigration from beginning to end be a state to be relished?"
"If, Śāriputra, you should wish to be born, you ought to make a vow to be born into a noble and wealthy family, not into a lowly or humble one. Why is this so, Śāriputra?"
Sentient beings have for a long night been bound by their minds, not bound by noble clans.
Yet I, Śāriputra, am born into a family of great nobility;
I am of the Kṣatriya caste and have emerged as a Wheel-Turning Sage King.

Had I not left the household life to study the Way, I would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; now, having renounced the position of a Wheel-Turning Sage King to leave the household life and study the Way, I have attained the Unsurpassed Way.
Now, one born into a lowly and base family cannot leave the household life to study the Way, but instead falls into the evil destinies.
For this reason, Śāriputra,
you should seek skillful means to subdue the mind.
"In this way, Śāriputra,
you should train yourself.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Śāriputra rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Volume 49 and Volume 50,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 52: The Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī (1) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Sahasravarga Lecture Hall, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma monastery in the city of Vaiśālī, together with a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī heard the bhikṣus say:
"The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa; no more than three months hence, he shall do so between the twin śāla trees in Kuśinagara."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī thought to herself:
"I am not able to bear seeing the Tathāgata pass into parinirvāṇa, nor am I able to bear seeing Ānanda pass into parinirvāṇa; it would be fitting for me to pass into parinirvāṇa first."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that the World-Honored One will before long enter parinirvāṇa; no more than three months hence, he will do so between the twin śāla trees in Kuśinagara."
"I am now unable to bear witnessing the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One and Ānanda; I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to enter Parinirvāṇa first.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent by remaining silent.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"From this day forward, we pray only that the World-Honored One will recite the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs.
The Buddha told her:
"I now authorize the bhikṣuṇīs to recite the prohibitory precepts back to the bhikṣus, so that the prohibitory precepts as they were originally practiced by me shall not be allowed to go astray."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī prostrated herself before the Buddha’s feet and stood before him.
Then, Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha again, saying:

“I shall no longer behold the Tathāgata’s countenance, nor shall I see the Buddhas of the future who do not enter a womb and dwell eternally in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Today, having departed from the holy face, I shall never behold it again.”
Then Mahāprajāpatī circumambulated the Buddha seven times, and likewise circumambulated Ānanda seven times; she then circumambulated the entire assembly of bhikṣus and withdrew.
Returning to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, he addressed them, saying:
"I now wish to enter the realm of unconditioned nirvāṇa.
For this reason, the Tathāgata will soon attain parinirvāṇa; each of you should accordingly follow your own practice."

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Kiṭāsi, Sakhilā, Samā, Padmalañjā, Pāralañjā, Kātyāyanī, Jayā, and five hundred other bhikṣuṇīs went to where the Blessed One was and stood to one side.
At that time, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, with the bhikṣuṇī Khemā as their leader, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We have heard that the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa; we cannot bear to see the World-Honored One and Ānanda enter parinirvāṇa before us."
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will permit us to enter parinirvāṇa first; for it is most appropriate that we attain nirvāṇa now.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently granted his consent.

Then the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, seeing that the World-Honored One had consented by remaining silent, stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then withdrew.
She returned to her own quarters.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī closed the door of the lecture hall, struck the wooden gong, and spread her sitting mat upon the open ground. She then rose into the air, where she sat, lay down, and walked back and forth; at times she emitted flames from her body, with smoke issuing from her lower half and fire from her upper half;
or water issued from her lower half and smoke from her upper half.
His entire body emitted flames, and his entire body emitted smoke;
from his left flank water flowed forth, and from his right flank fire issued;
from his right flank water flowed forth, and from his left flank smoke issued.
First fire issues from the front and water from the back;
first water issues from the front and fire from the back;
his entire body emits fire, and his entire body emits water.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī performed various miraculous transformations, returned to her original seat, sat cross-legged with body erect and mind composed, focused her mindfulness before her, and entered the first dhyāna;
rising from the first dhyāna, she entered the second dhyāna;
rising from the second dhyāna, she entered the third dhyāna.
Emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Arising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness;
arising from the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the cessation of perception and feeling.
From the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one arises and enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one arises and enters the sphere of nothingness;
from the sphere of nothingness, one arises and re-enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Arising from the sphere of consciousness, he enters the sphere of infinite space;
arising from the sphere of infinite space, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
arising from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna.
Rising from the third dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna;
rising from the second dhyāna, he returns to the first dhyāna;
rising from the first dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the second dhyāna, he re-enters the third dhyāna;
emerging from the third dhyāna, he re-enters the fourth dhyāna;
having entered the fourth dhyāna, he attains parinirvāṇa.

At that time, heaven and earth shook violently; the east surged while the west subsided, the west surged while the east subsided, and all four quarters surged while the center subsided. Furthermore, cool breezes arose from the four directions, and the various devas in the sky performed music and dance. The devas of the desire realm wept and wailed with tears falling like the sweet rain sent down by the heavens in the spring month. Divine and wondrous celestial *utpala* flowers were scattered in profusion, as were powdered sandalwood, sprinkled upon [the Buddha].

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Kisāgotamī, Sāgacchā, Samā, Bhaddā Kāpilānī, Kaccānā, and Jayā—these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs led by such as these—each spread out their seats on the open ground and then flew into the air. While in mid-air, they sat, lay down, and walked back and forth, performing the eighteen transformations, and even entering the cessation of perception and feeling, each attaining parinirvāṇa.
At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was a great general named Yaśodatta who, together with five hundred youths, had gathered at the Hall of Universal Assembly to deliver a discourse.

At that time, Yaśodharā and the five hundred youths saw from afar the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs performing the eighteen transformations. Having seen this, they were filled with immeasurable joy and leaped for gladness; each of them joined their palms and turned toward where the nuns were.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Go to the general Yaśodatta and tell him:

'Quickly prepare five hundred couches, five hundred seats, five hundred jars of ghee, five hundred jars of oil, five hundred carriages of flowers, five hundred bundles of incense, and five hundred wagons of firewood.'"
At that time, Ānanda stepped forward and addressed the Buddha,
saying, “I do not know, World-Honored One, what you intend to perform? The Buddha told him:
“Mahāprajāpatī has already entered parinirvāṇa, as have five hundred bhikṣuṇīs; we wish to make offerings to their śarīras.
At that time, Ānanda was overwhelmed by a mixture of grief and weeping, unable to restrain himself:
“How swift was Mahāprajāpatī’s entry into parinirvāṇa!”
At that time, Ānanda wiped away his tears with his hand and went to where the great general Yaśodharā was.
When Yaśodharā saw Ānanda approaching from afar, she rose to meet him, and they all spoke thus: "Welcome, Ānanda!"
"What instructions do you wish to give, and why do you travel at such an unusual hour?
At that time, Ānanda replied, "I am the Buddha’s messenger; I have something to instruct you."
Then the generals all asked together,
"What do you wish to command? Ānanda replied:
The World-Honored One told the General:

"Prepare five hundred beds, five hundred sitting mats, five hundred jars of ghee, five hundred jars of oil, five hundred flower-carts, five hundred bundles of incense, and five hundred carts of firewood; Mahāprajāpatī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs have all entered parinirvāṇa, so let us go to offer worship to their śarīras."
At that time, the Great General was overwhelmed by a mixture of grief and weeping, and spoke thus:
"How swift is the passing into parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī!
And how exceedingly swift is the passing into parinirvāṇa of these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs!"
"Who shall instruct us and teach us how to practice the distribution of alms and offerings?

At that time, General Yaśodatta immediately prepared five hundred beds, five hundred seats, five hundred jars of oil, ghee, and firewood, as well as all the implements for cremation. He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the great general Yaśodatta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The requisites for the offering as instructed by the Tathāgata have now been prepared.
The Buddha told him:
“Now you each take the body of Mahāprajāpatī and the bodies of the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, go from Vaiśālī to a wilderness place; I wish to make offerings to the śarīras there.”
The general Yaśodharā addressed the Buddha, saying,
“So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, the elder went to where Mahāprajāpatī and the others were and said to one person:
"You must now provide a ladder to climb over the wall and enter within; open the door slowly so that it makes no sound.
At that time, the man followed those instructions, entered, and opened the door. He was further instructed to have five hundred people each lift the *śarīra* and place them upon the bed.
At that time, there were two śrāmaṇerīs present: one named Nanda and the other named Upananda.
Then, the two śrāmaṇerīs said to the general, "Stop!
"Stop! General! Do not disturb the teachers."
The general Yaśodatta replied, "Your teachers did not fall into sleep; they have all attained parinirvāṇa.

At that time, the two śrāmaṇeras, hearing that all their teachers had attained parinirvāṇa, were filled with fear. They immediately reflected upon themselves and contemplated how all conditioned phenomena are subject to exhaustion; thereupon, while remaining in their seats, they attained the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers.

At that time, the two śrāmaṇerīs immediately flew up into the air and first went to the midst of the wilderness, where they performed the eighteen transformations: sitting, lying down, and walking; emitting water and fire from their bodies; and manifesting immeasurable miraculous changes. Thereupon, they entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, proceeded to the nunnery of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, Nanda, and Rāhula:
"Lift up the body of Mahāprajāpatī; I shall personally make offerings to her."

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what was in the World-Honored One’s mind, descended from the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Just as a strong man might flex or extend his arm, he arrived at Vaiśālī, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.

Among them, those bhikṣus who had exhausted their outflows all saw Śakra Devānām Indra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; however, those bhikṣus who had not yet exhausted their outflows and still possessed desire, as well as the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who had not yet exhausted their outflows, did not see Śakra Devānām Indra or the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, Brahmā Śikhin, knowing from afar what was in the Tathāgata’s mind, vanished from the Brahma Heaven together with the various Brahmās and came to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.

At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, knowing what was in the mind of the World-Honored One, led the yakṣas and spirits to the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.

At that time, the Heavenly King Dṛḍha-ratha, leading the gandharvas, came from the east to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head and face touching them, and stood to one side.
The Deva-king Virūḍhaka, leading countless kumbhāṇḍas, came from the south to where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
The celestial king Virūpākṣa, leading the various nāga deities, came to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.

Likewise, the devas of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, each knowing what the Tathāgata was contemplating in his mind, came to the World-Honored One, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra and King Vaiśravaṇa came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One does not weary himself; we ourselves shall provide offerings for the śarīra."
The Buddha said to the devas: "Cease! Cease!"
"O Heavenly King!
The Tathāgata himself shall know the proper time.
This is that which the Tathāgata ought to practice; it is not something within the reach of devas, nāgas, or spirits."

The reason for this is that parents give birth to children and provide them with much benefit; their kindness in nurturing is profound. They suckle and embrace them, and one must repay this kindness—it cannot but be repaid.

However, O devas, you should know that for all past Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, their mothers passed into parinirvāṇa first, and only thereafter did those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, themselves make offerings to the *śarīra* relics for ten *yojanas*.

Even if the mothers who gave birth to all future Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, were to pass away first, and only then were those Buddhas to personally make offerings to them, by this expedient means one should know that the Tathāgata ought to make offerings to himself; this is not something that devas, nāgas, or spirits can achieve.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa addressed five hundred spirits, saying:
"Go to the sandalwood grove and bring back fragrant firewood; we shall offer it as an oblation for the snake sacrifice."
Then, having heard the words of the Heavenly King, the five hundred spirits immediately went to the sandalwood forest, gathered sandalwood fuel, and returned to the wilderness.

At that time, the World-Honored One personally lifted one leg of the bier, Nanda lifted one leg, Rāhula lifted one leg, and Ānanda lifted one leg; they flew through the air and proceeded to that cemetery.
There, the fourfold assembly—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—carried five hundred bhikṣuṇī śarīras to the cemetery.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the general Yaśodatta, saying:
"You should now further prepare two couches, two sitting mats, and two loads of firewood for the offering of incense and flowers to the bodies of the two śrāmaṇerīs."
The Great General Yaśodatta addressed the Buddha, saying,
“So be it, World-Honored One! Thereupon,
he immediately prepared the requisites for the offering.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave pieces of sandalwood to each of the devas.
Then, the World-Honored One again addressed the Great General, saying:
"Now you shall each take five hundred śarīras and make offerings to them individually; let the two śrāmaṇeras do the same."
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the great generals each separately took up offerings and immediately brought forth a snake-skin.
Then, the World-Honored One again placed sandalwood upon the body of Mahāprajāpatī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; That which is born must inevitably perish.
By not being born, one does not die; This cessation is the supreme bliss."
At that time, the devas and the people all gathered like clouds at the cemetery;
the assembly of devas and humans numbered ten billion nayutas.
When the Great General had extinguished the fire, he further took up the relics and erected a stūpa.
The Buddha told the general:
"Now take the relics of these five hundred bhikṣuṇīs and erect a stūpa for them; throughout the long night, you shall receive immeasurable merit!"
The reason for this is that there are four types of persons in the world who erect *stūpas*. What are these four?
If one erects a *stūpa* for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; or for a Wheel-turning Sage King (*cakravartin*); or for a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha—one receives immeasurable merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the devas and the people, exhorting them to rejoice.
Then, one hundred million devas and humans were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and the fourfold assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī in the city of Śrāvastī named Bhadrā, who was wandering and teaching among five hundred other bhikṣuṇīs.

Then, while staying in a secluded place, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā sat down cross-legged, focused her mindfulness before her, and recollected countless events from her past lives; she then smiled to herself.

A certain bhikṣuṇī saw the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā laughing from a distance; having seen this, she went to where the bhikṣuṇī was and asked, "Now that the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā is alone beneath the tree and laughing, what could be the reason for it?"
Then, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs went together to the place where the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā was, prostrated themselves at her feet, and said to her:
"For what reason and by what cause are you sitting alone beneath a tree and smiling?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Vadhā addressed five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Just now, beneath this tree, I recalled countless matters of my past lives; I also beheld the bodies I experienced in former times, seeing them all clearly as I died here and was born there."
Then, the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs spoke again, saying:
"We only pray that you will relate the causes and conditions of the past.
