At that time, Bhikṣuṇī Vadhā addressed the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha and Blessed One, who appeared in the world."
At that time, the world was named Bandhumatī, and its population was so vast as to be beyond calculation.
At that time, the Tathāgata traveled through that realm, surrounded before and behind by a multitude of one hundred and sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma for them.
At that time, the name of the Buddha spread far and wide:
"Vipaśyin Buddha is endowed with all the marks of excellence; he is the benevolent field of merit for all people.
At that time, within that realm, there was a youth named Brahmā, whose countenance was upright and handsome, a rarity in the world.
At that time, the young boy walked through the streets and alleys holding a precious parasol in his hand.
At that moment, there was also a householder’s wife, likewise beautiful, walking along this same road; all the people gathered together to gaze upon her.
At that time, the youth thought to himself:
"I am likewise handsome, yet as I hold this precious parasol, no one among the multitude looks at my body; instead, all these people gaze together only upon this woman."
"I must now employ a skillful means to cause people to behold me.

At that time, the youth immediately left the city and went to the place where Vipaśyin Buddha was. Holding precious flowers in his hands, he made offerings for seven days and seven nights, and also made this vow:

"If Vipaśyin Buddha possesses such supernormal powers and such spiritual might as the field of merit for this world and its heavens, by virtue of this merit, may I take birth in a female body in a future age, such that all people who see me will not fail to rejoice and leap with joy."

"At that time, after the youth had made offerings to that Buddha for seven days and seven nights, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven according to the length of his lifespan. There, he took birth in the body of a woman who was exceedingly beautiful, the foremost among jade-like maidens, surpassing the other celestial women in five meritorious qualities."
What are these five?
They are celestial lifespan, celestial form, celestial pleasure, celestial majesty and fortune, and celestial sovereignty.
When the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three saw this, they each said to one another:
"This goddess is exceedingly exquisite; there is no one equal to her.
Among them, some sons of gods spoke thus:
"I should obtain this goddess to be my queen."
They each vied with one another.
Then the Great Heavenly King said:
"Do not quarrel among yourselves; whoever among you can preach the most sublime Dharma, I shall give this heavenly maiden to him as his wife."
At that time, a certain deva spoke this verse:
Whether rising or sitting, Whether waking or sleeping, there is no joy;
Only when I am fast asleep Is there then an absence of desire.
At that time, another son of heaven spoke this verse:
"You now remain thus for the sake of pleasure, Free from thought and perception while asleep;
But I now arouse a desire, Like the beating of a war drum."
At that time, another son of heaven spoke this verse:
"Even if one were to beat the war drums, there would still be a time for rest;
but I wish to rush with such speed that it is like the flow of water, never ceasing."
At that time, another son of heaven spoke this verse:
"As a great log drifting upon the water may yet find a moment's rest,
But my constant longing for desire is like a slaughtered elephant that does not blink."
At that time, the most honored son of heaven among all the devas spoke these verses to the other heavenly beings:
"You all still have leisure, Each able to recite such verses;
But as for me now, I do not know myself— Whether I shall survive or perish."
At that time, the various devas addressed that son of heaven, saying: "Excellent,
O son of heaven!"
"The verses you have spoken are exceedingly pure and subtle.
Today, this goddess has offered them as a tribute to the Heavenly King.
At that time, the goddess immediately entered the palace of the Heavenly King.
"You gods, do not harbor any doubt. For what reason?
Was the youth who at that time offered the precious canopy to the Buddha anyone other than this person?"
Do not hold such a view.
The youth at that time was none other than myself.

Thirty-one kalpas ago, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata Śikhi, who traveled and transformed beings in the world-system of Hayaghoṣa, accompanied by a great assembly of one hundred and sixty thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, that goddess subsequently passed away and was reborn among human beings, receiving a female body that was exceedingly beautiful and rare in the world.
At that time, when the Tathāgata Śikhin arrived at the proper hour, he donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Aśvalāyana to beg for food.
At that moment, the celestial woman, who had been the wife of the elder, offered excellent food and drink to the Tathāgata Śikhin and made this universal vow:

"By the power of these meritorious deeds, may I never fall into the three evil realms in whatever place I am born; may my countenance be upright and handsome, and may I be exceptionally distinguished from other people."

“At that time, after her life had ended, that woman was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There she again took the form of a woman who was exceedingly beautiful, possessing five meritorious qualities by which she excelled all the other devas.”
At that time, was that goddess anyone else?
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this so? That woman was none other than myself.

"In that very kalpa, when the Tathāgata Viśvabhū appeared in the world, at that time the goddess, according to the length of her lifespan, passed away and was reborn among humans; she received a female body, with features so upright and beautiful as to be rare in the world."
Furthermore, she became the wife of a householder and lay devotee.
At that time, the householder’s wife again offered exquisite robes and fine garments to the Tathāgata, making this vow:
"May I obtain a female body in a future life."
After that woman’s life had ended, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven with a countenance so upright and beautiful that she surpassed the other celestial maidens.
At that time, could that woman have been anyone else?
Do not hold such a view.
Why is this? The woman at that time was none other than myself.

After her life ended—having lived out its full span according to its length—she was reborn among humans in the great city of Vārāṇasī as a female servant to the householder Candraprabha; she was coarse and ugly in appearance, such that people loathed the sight of her.
Since the passing of Viśvabhū, no other Buddha has appeared.
At that time, each of the Buddhas was wandering and teaching.
Then, the wife of the householder Candraprabha said to her maidservant:
"You have been traveling abroad seeking a śramaṇa!
If you find one whose countenance is upright and pleasing to my mind, bring him here to my home; I wish to provide him with offerings."
At that time, the maidservant immediately left the house and went outside to search for the śramaṇa.
She encountered him wandering and begging within the city; however, his countenance was coarse and harsh, and his appearance was ugly and wretched.
Then the maidservant said to each of the Buddhas, "The mistress wishes to see you; we pray that you would deign to come to her home.
She then entered and informed the master:
"The śramaṇa has arrived; you may go to meet him.
When the householder’s wife saw the śramaṇa, her heart was not gladdened, and she immediately said to her maidservant:
"Send him back; I will not give alms."
"The reason for this is that his appearance is coarse and shabby.
At that time, the maidservant said to the lady, "If you, my lady,
do not give alms to the śramaṇa, then I shall give away all of my own portion for today's meal as alms."
Then that lady immediately brought forth a portion of food, one *śu* of fine flour.
The maidservant then presented it to the Śramaṇa; having received this food, the Buddha flew into the air and performed the eighteen transformations.
At that time, the householder’s maidservant made another vow:
"By the merit of this, may I never fall into the three evil realms in whatever place I am born; and in a future life, may I become a woman who is exceedingly beautiful."

Then those Pratyekabuddhas, holding their alms bowls in their hands, circumambulated the city three times, while the elder Candraprabha gathered five hundred merchants at the Hall of Universal Assembly.
At that time, the men and women, young and old, within the city saw each of the Buddhas holding their alms bowls and flying through the air.
Having seen this, they said to one another, "Who are these people whose merit is such as this?"
"Have you encountered these various Buddhas and offered them food?
At that time, the elder’s maidservant said to the lady:
"Go out and observe the divine power of the śramaṇa; he flies in the void and performs the eighteen transformations; his divine power is immeasurable."
Then the householder’s wife said to her maidservant:
“If you obtain any merit from this alms-food given to the śramaṇa, give it all to me; I shall give you the price of two days’ worth of food.”
The maidservant replied,
"I am not permitted to give you my portion of merit. The lady said:
“I will give you the price for four days’ worth of food, up to the price for ten days’ worth.
The maidservant replied,
“I am not fit to receive a gift of merit.”
The lady said, "I shall now give you one hundred gold coins.
The maidservant replied:
"I do not need it," [the man] replied. The lady spoke again:
"I will give you two hundred, and even up to a thousand gold coins."
The maidservant replied,
"I do not need it either. The lady said:
"I shall spare your life and ensure you do not remain a slave.
The maidservant replied,
"I have no need to seek to become a free woman."
The lady spoke again: "You shall be the mistress, and I shall be your servant.
The maidservant replied:
"I have no need to seek to become a noble lady.
The noble lady replied,
"I shall now seize you and beat you, mutilate your ears and nose, cut off your hands and feet, and sever your head."
The maidservant replied,
"I can endure such pain as this until the very end, but I will never bestow my merit upon you;
for though our bodies belong to the same master, our hearts and intentions differ."
At that time, the householder’s wife immediately beat her maidservant.
Then, the five hundred merchants each made this reflection:
"This divine being has now come to beg for alms; surely he must be one to whom my family should give."
Then, having sent the people away, the Elder Candraprabha returned home and saw his wife taking a maidservant and whipping her.
He immediately asked her, "For what reason are you whipping this maidservant?"
The maidservant then reported these circumstances in full.
At that time, the elder Candraprabha was so filled with joy and exultation that he could not contain himself; he immediately took his wife as a servant and had the maidservant take her place.
"At that time, there was a king ruling over the city of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta.

When that great king heard that the elder Candraprabha had fed a pratyekabuddha, he was filled with great joy, thinking that he had encountered a true person and bestowed his gifts at the proper time."
King Brahmadatta immediately dispatched a messenger to summon the elder Candraprabha and addressed him, saying:
"Did you truly provide a meal for the seer and true man?
The elder replied to the king:
"I have truly met a Realized One (Tathāgata) and have bestowed food as an act of charity.
At that time, King Brahmadatta immediately granted him rewards and further increased his rank.

The elder’s maidservant, according to the span of her lifespan, passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Her appearance was exceptionally exquisite and rare in the world; she excelled all other devas in five meritorious qualities.
"Sisters, do not hold such a view; the elder’s maidservant at that time was none other than myself.
During this Bhadrakalpa, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Krakucchanda Tathāgata."
At that time, after the life span of those goddesses had ended according to its length, they were reborn among human beings.
At that moment, the Brahmin Yaññadatta was born as a woman.
Then this woman again offered a meal to the Tathāgata and made a vow, seeking to remain in a female body.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where his appearance was so upright and handsome that it surpassed all the celestial maidens.
When his life there ended, he was again reborn among human beings.
"At that time, the Buddha Kanakamuni appeared in the world.
At that moment, that goddess was the daughter of an elder; she again made an offering of golden flowers to the Buddha Kanakamuni, saying:
'By virtue of this merit, may I never fall into the three evil realms in whatever place I am born, and may I obtain a female body in my future life.'"

Then, according to the length of her lifespan, after the end of her life, this woman was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There she was beautiful, surpassing all other celestial maidens, possessing five meritorious qualities that none could equal.
At that time, was the daughter of the elder who made offerings to the Buddha Kanakamuni anyone else?
Do not hold such a view; the daughter of the elder at that time was none other than myself.
Then, that celestial maiden, according to the length of her lifespan, was reborn among humans; she again became the wife of the elder, her countenance exceptionally beautiful and rare in the world.
"At that time, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world.
For seven days and seven nights, the householder’s wife made offerings to Buddha Kāśyapa and made this vow:
'May I obtain a female body in a future life.'"

At that time, the householder’s wife, according to the length of her lifespan, was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven after her death; she possessed five qualities of merit that surpassed those of the other goddesses there.
As for the wife of the elder who made offerings to Kāśyapa Buddha at that time, could she have been anyone else?
Do not hold such a view; the wife of the elder at that time was none other than myself.

"In this Bhadrakalpa, when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, that goddess, after her life there had ended, was reborn in the city of Rājagṛha as the daughter of the Brahmin Kapila; she was of such upright and beautiful countenance that she surpassed all other women."
The Brahmin woman Kapi, holding a statue of purple-gold, went to that woman’s place; though she was as dark as ink, her mind did not crave the five desires.
"Sisters, do not hold such a view. Could this woman’s body be anyone else?
She who was the Brahmin girl at that time was none other than my own self."
"Sisters, you should know that due to the retribution for my merits from former days, I became the wife of this brahmin youth, namely Mahākāśyapa.
Since the Venerable Mahākāśyapa first went forth into homelessness and I only did so on a later day, I recall the female bodies I experienced in the past; it is for this reason that I smile now."
"Shrouded by my own ignorance, I made offerings to six Tathāgatas while seeking to take the form of a woman; for this reason, I smile at what I experienced in the past."

At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus, having heard that the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā recollected events from countless past lives, immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and sat down to one side.
For these reasons, she reported everything in detail to the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among the śrāvakas, have you ever seen a bhikṣuṇī who, like this person, could personally recall such matters from countless past lives?"
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
“I do not see it,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Among my śrāvakas, the foremost disciple who remembers his own past lives through countless world-ages is the bhikṣuṇī Kappilā."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (III) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
After a short while, he withdrew slightly from his seat, came forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is an eon long or short? Is it finite?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The kalpas are extremely long and distant; I shall now provide you with a simile. Listen attentively, for I am about to speak.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know this: suppose there were an iron city one yojana in length and breadth, filled with mustard seeds without any empty space. If someone were to come every hundred years and remove a single mustard seed, even after all those seeds in the iron city had been exhausted, that duration would still not constitute even a single kalpa; it is truly incalculable."

The reason for this is that birth and death are long and far-reaching, without any limit; sentient beings, bound and attached by affection, transmigrate through birth and death, dying here and being born there without end. Within this cycle, I have grown weary of and loathe birth and death.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to escape this notion of attachment.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Ekottarika Āgama, Scroll 50 and Scroll 51.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Fifty-two: The Section on the Parinirvāṇa of Mahāprajāpatī (4). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then, that bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, a kalpa is exceedingly long."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"An eon is extremely remote; it cannot be measured by counting sticks.
I shall now provide you with a simile; reflect upon it well, for I will now speak for your sake."
At that time, those bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said to them:

"Suppose there were a great mountain of rock, one yojana in length and breadth and one yojana in height. Even if someone were to come and brush it once every hundred years with a celestial robe held in their hand, the stone would eventually be worn away; yet the number of kalpas required would be difficult to limit."
The reason for this is that the number of kalpas is vast and long-lasting, without limit.
It is not merely one kalpa or a hundred kalpas.
The reason for this is that birth and death are vast and long-lasting, immeasurable and without limit.

Beings of all kinds are shrouded by ignorance, wandering through birth and death with no time of escape; dying here and being born there without end, I have come to feel weary of and loathing this cycle of birth and death within it.
"In this way, bhikṣus,
you should seek skillful means to escape this notion of craving and attachment.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5 (Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five merits in hearing the Dharma at the appropriate time, such that one never misses the right occasion.

What are these five? One hears the Dharma not yet heard; having heard it, one maintains it; one eliminates doubt; one is free from false views; and one understands the most profound Dharma. These, O bhikṣus, are called [the five merits].”
Hearing the Dharma at the appropriate time possesses these five merits.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should always mindfully listen to the profound Dharma; this is my instruction.
"In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Mahāvana Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, General Siṃha went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the Tathāgata addressed the general, saying:
"A donor, a patron, possesses five merits."
What are these five?

"In this regard, the donor’s fame spreads far and wide: 'In such-and-such a village, there is this excellent donor who relieves the destitute and aids the needy, having no sense of stinginess. This, General Siṃha, is called the first merit resulting from a donor."

"Furthermore, General Siṃha, if a donor or patron enters among the assembly of Kṣatriyas, the assembly of Brahmins, or the assembly of Śramaṇas, they shall be entirely without fear and free from doubt or difficulty. This is what is meant, Siṃha!"
The second merit:

"Furthermore, the donor and *dānapati* is generally loved and cherished by others; they come to revere and look up to him universally, their hearts inseparable from him as a child loves its mother. The donor is likewise thus, being greatly beloved by people."
"Furthermore, Siṃha!

When a donor or benefactor gives a gift, they give rise to a joyful mind; because there is joy, there is gladness, and the nature of their mind becomes firm. At that time, they immediately perceive for themselves both pleasure and pain, and even if they should later feel regret, they know it as it truly is."

"How does one know for oneself, knowing as they truly are the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Generosity is the equipment for all blessings, And through it, one attains the Ultimate Truth."
"One who is able to recollect their giving will immediately give rise to a heart of joy.
Furthermore, Lion Householder!

When a donor, a patron of almsgiving, gives a gift, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where they possess five things that surpass those other devas."
What are the five? First, his countenance is noble and dignified, and he possesses majestic spiritual radiance;
second, he has mastery over all that he desires, such that no undertaking fails to bear fruit.
Third, if the donor or patron is reborn among humans, they will encounter a wealthy and noble family;
fourth, they will possess abundant wealth and many treasures;
fifth, their words will be followed and their instructions heeded.
"Thus it is, Siṃha! A donor who possesses these five merits is led into the good realms.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the general Siṃha was filled with joy and exultation beyond measure; he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my invitation.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, the General Siṃha rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head, and then withdrew. Returning to his home, he prepared various kinds of food and drink, spread out fine seats, and then announced:
"The time has come; now is precisely the right moment. We only pray that the Great Sage will look upon us with compassion.

Then, when the time arrived, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus before and behind him, went to the house of the Great General, where they each sat down in order.
At that time, General Siṃha, having seen the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus seated in order, personally served various kinds of food and drink with his own hands.
While the general was distributing the food, the devas in the midst of the sky addressed him, saying:

"This one is an Arhat; this person is one progressing toward Arhatship. Giving to this one yields great merit; giving to that one yields little merit. This one is an Anāgāmin; this person is one progressing toward Anāgāminship. This one is a Sakṛdāgāmin; this person is one progressing toward the path of Sakṛdāgāminship. This one is a Srotāpanna; this person is one progressing toward the path of Srotāpannaship. This person will undergo seven more births and returns; this person has only one birth remaining. This one upholds faith; this one reveres the Dharma. This one possesses sharp faculties; this one possesses dull faculties. This person is lowly and base; this person is diligent in maintaining the precepts; this person violates the precepts. Giving to this person yields great merit; giving to that person yields little merit."

At that time, having heard the words of the devas, the Great General Siṃha did not take them to heart. Seeing that the Tathāgata had finished eating and had set aside his bowl, he took another small seat and sat before the Tathāgata.
At that time, the General Siṃha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Just now, various devas came to my place and said to me:
'From the Arhats down to those who violate the precepts.'"
They all reported these matters in detail to the Tathāgata.
Although he heard these words, he did not take them to heart, nor did he give rise to this thought:
"I should relinquish this and bestow it upon that, or relinquish that and bestow it upon this."
"Furthermore, I gave rise to this thought:

'I should give to all sentient beings, those with form who exist by means of food and perish without it. Since I personally heard these verses spoken by the Tathāgata, I have constantly kept them in my heart without ever forgetting them."
What is called the verse? It says:
"Generosity should be universal and impartial, Never acting with opposition toward anything;
One will surely encounter sages and worthies, And by means of this, attain liberation."
“‘This, World-Honored One, is what is spoken in this verse.
I have personally heard it from the Tathāgata; I constantly bear it in mind and practice accordingly.”
The Buddha told the General:
"Excellent! This is called the Bodhisattva-mind, which bestows gifts with equanimity."
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they do not give rise to such thoughts as,
"I shall give this to that person, but withhold that.
They always bestow gifts with equanimity, yet they also maintain this thought:
"All sentient beings survive when they have food and perish when they lack it.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, he likewise reflects upon this principle.
He then spoke this verse:
"When a person cultivates their conduct—whether it be evil or good—they themselves receive the retribution for each; once the conduct is performed, it does not diminish."
Just as a person pursues their conduct, they immediately receive its retribution:
by doing good, one obtains good; by committing evil, one receives an evil reward.
Whether it be evil or good, it follows whatever a person has habituated themselves to.
"Just as when one sows the five grains, each yields its own fruit; so too,
General Siṃha, by this analogy you should know that good and evil each have their respective consequences."

The reason for this is that from the initial aspiration until the attainment of enlightenment, the mind remains without increase or decrease; one does not discriminate among people, nor does one regard their status.
Therefore, Siṃha! When you wish to practice giving, always maintain equanimity and do not give rise to thoughts of right or wrong. Thus it is, Siṃha!
"One should train in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke these verses of praise:
"Generosity is beloved by those who rejoice; it is extolled by the multitude."
Wherever one goes, there is no doubt or difficulty, nor is there a mind of envy.
Therefore, when the wise give, they eliminate all evil thoughts;
throughout the long night, they reach the place of goodness, praised by the devas.
At that time, having spoken these words, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and departed.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had taught, Siṃha rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"To what place should a person who practices giving give?
The World-Honored One told the king:
"Give whatever you take pleasure in; give it to them.
The King spoke again to the Buddha:
"To whom should one give so as to obtain great merit?"
The Buddha told the king:
"Regarding what you asked about where one should give, you now ask again about the merit and virtue obtained thereby.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now ask the Tathāgata: To whom should one give so as to obtain its merit?
The Buddha said to the king:
"I shall now ask you in return; answer me according to what pleases you."

"How so? Great King! Suppose a son of the kṣatriya caste or a son of the brāhmaṇa caste were to come—foolish and deluded, possessing no knowledge, with a distracted mind and ever-uncertain—to approach Your Majesty and ask the King:"
"We shall reverently serve the Holy King, providing whatever he requires at all times.
What do you think, Great King?
"Is it necessary for this person to remain by your side?
The King said to the Buddha,
"It is not necessary."
World-Honored One!
The reason for this is that those people lack wisdom and their mental consciousness is unstable; it is because they are incapable of observing external enemies.
The Buddha said to the king, "How so?
Great King!"

If there are members of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa castes who possess many skillful means, who are free from fear and danger, and who are not intimidated, and who are able to repel external enemies, they come before the king and say to him:
"We shall attend upon and serve Your Majesty at all times; we only pray that you will deign to grant us your favor and accept us."
"What do you think,
Great King? Would you accept such a person?"
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
We shall accept this man. Why is this? Because he is capable of guarding against external enemies, being without hesitation or difficulty, and free from fear."
The Buddha told the king:
"Now, it is the same with a bhikṣu: his faculties are complete; he has abandoned five and perfected six, guarding one and subduing four. To give to such a person yields the greatest merit."
The king said to the Buddha,
“How does a bhikṣu abandon five things, establish six, guard one, and subdue four?
The Buddha told the king:
"Thereupon, the bhikṣu abandons the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, drowsiness, restlessness, and doubt; in this way, bhikṣu, he is said to have abandoned the five."
"How does a bhikṣu accomplish the six? Your Majesty should know this:

if a bhikṣu, having seen a form, does not give rise to the perception of form, he guards the faculty of the eye by relying on this; he removes evil and unwholesome thoughts and thus guards the faculty of the eye. Likewise, if his ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind does not give rise to mental consciousness, he guards the faculty of the mind. In this way, a bhikṣu accomplishes the six."
How does a bhikṣu guard one? In this regard, a bhikṣu binds his mindfulness to what is before him; in this way, a bhikṣu guards one.
How does a bhikṣu subdue the four?
Thereupon, the bhikṣu subdues the Māra of the body, the Māra of desire, the Māra of death, and the Māra of the devas; having subdued them all, in this way the bhikṣu has subdued the four.
Thus it is, Great King!
To abandon the five and resort to the six, to protect the one and subdue the four—to bestow gifts upon such a person yields immeasurable merit.
Great King!
"One who is associated with wrong views and extreme views— for such a person, giving a parasol is of no benefit.
At that time, the king said to the Buddha,
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
The merit of giving to such a person is difficult to measure; if even a single quality were perfected by a bhikṣu, his merit would still be difficult to measure, let alone when he possesses more.
What is this one quality?
"This is what is called mindfulness of the body.
The reason for this is that the Nirgranthas constantly calculate bodily actions and mental actions, but do not calculate verbal actions.
The Buddha said to the king:
"The Nirgranthas are deluded and confused; their minds are constantly disordered and their consciousness is unstable. Because such is the nature of their teacher’s doctrine, they utter these words.
The retribution for their bodily actions is indeed insufficient to mention, for it is their mental actions—formless and invisible—that truly matter."
The king said to the Buddha,
“Among these three types of action, which is the most grave:
is it bodily action?”
"Is it verbal conduct?
Or is it mental conduct?
The Buddha said to the king:
"Among these three types of action, mental action is the most weighty; verbal and physical actions are hardly worth mentioning.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what further causes and conditions is it said that mindfulness of the mind is the foremost?"
The Buddha told the king:

"In all that a person does, it first originates in the mind, and only then is it expressed through speech. Once speech has been uttered, one then carries out the physical acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. The faculty of the tongue is unstable and lacks any fixed basis; even when that person’s life has come to an end, the faculties of body and tongue still remain."
"Great King!
For what reason does that person not engage in any activity of body or speech?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Because that person lacked the faculty of mind (manas-indriya), this transformation occurred.
The Buddha told the king:
“By this expedient means, you should know that the faculty of mind is the most important, while the other two are minor.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
If the mind conceives of evil, it immediately acts and immediately manifests; one then undergoes suffering therein, rolling along as if upon a track."
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
If one thinks of goodness within the mind, and acts upon it immediately, one will receive its wholesome retribution, just as a shadow follows a form.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “It is so, Tathāgata!
Those who do evil, performing evil deeds with their bodies, fall into evil destinies in accordance with those actions.”
The Buddha said to the king:
“For what reason do you ask me who it is that, when given a gift, obtains the greatest benefit and merit?
The king replied to the Buddha:
"In the past, I went to the place where the Nirgranthas were and asked a Nirgrantha, saying:
'In what manner should one practice giving?
After hearing my question, the Nirgrantha spoke of other matters instead and did not provide an answer."
At that time, the Nirgrantha said to me:

"The śramaṇa Gautama makes this claim: 'Giving to me brings great merit; others bring no merit. You should give to my disciples and not to others; for any person who gives to my disciples, their merit shall be immeasurable.'"
The Buddha said to the king,
"At that time, how would you have answered him?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At that time, I thought to myself:
'There may indeed be such a principle; the merit of bestowing gifts upon the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
For this reason, I now ask the Buddha:"
"In what place, then, can merit be so immeasurable?
"However, the World-Honored One does not praise himself, nor does he disparage others.
The Buddha told the King:
"I do not say that those who give to me receive great merit while others receive none. However, what I have said today is this:

for one who takes the remnants left in my bowl and gives them to another, the merit is immeasurable. If, with a pure mind, one places [these remnants] in pure water and forms the universal thought that all sentient beings within it may receive boundless blessings, how much more so for those in human form?"
However, Great King!
The merit of giving to one who observes the precepts that I have now described is immeasurable; compared to giving to one who violates the precepts, it is simply beyond words.

"Great King, you should know this: it is like a farmer who properly cultivates his land, removes all impurities and weeds, and sows excellent seeds in that fertile field; from this, he obtains an immeasurable harvest of grain.
It is also like that same farmer who does not cultivate his land, nor does he remove the impurities and weeds before sowing his seeds; what he reaps is truly insufficient to mention."

Now, it is the same with a bhikṣu today: if a bhikṣu abandons five [qualities] to pursue six, guarding one and subduing four, for such a person, the merit of those who bestow gifts upon him is immeasurable;
compared to this, giving to one who holds wrong views is hardly worth mentioning.

It is just as, Great King, when those of the Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa castes have no doubt or hesitation in their minds and are able to subdue external enemies, they should be viewed as being like Arhats; whereas those of the Brāhmaṇa caste whose minds are not concentrated and focused should be viewed as being like people of wrong views.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The merit of giving to one who upholds the precepts is immeasurable.
From this day forward, whenever anyone comes to seek alms, I shall never refuse them.”
Furthermore, if there are those among the fourfold assembly who have any requests, he does not refuse them;
according to the occasion, he provides them with clothing, food and drink, and bedding, and likewise bestows these upon all fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The Buddha told him:
"Do not speak thus. For this reason:
the merit of giving to the class of animals is difficult to measure; how much more so, then, for a human being?"
"However, what I have said today is that the merit of giving to those who uphold the precepts is incalculable, not so for those who violate them.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I now take refuge once again. Yet, World-Honored One, you are so earnest that even when these heterodox teachers and followers of other paths spread slanders against you, and furthermore, you constantly praise and extol them—whereas these heterodox teachers and followers of other paths are greedily attached to gain and offerings, while the Tathāgata does not crave such gain and offerings."
"The affairs of state are many and cumbersome; I wish to return to my quarters.
The Buddha said to the king, "You should know that now is the time."
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having killed the hundred sons of his concubine mother, immediately felt remorse and thought:
"I have created a source of evil that is exceedingly great; what further use is there for this?"
"Because of this royal throne, I have killed these hundred men; who else is capable of removing my sorrow?
King Prasenajit then thought again:
"Only the World-Honored One can remove my grief."
At that time, he further thought:

"It is not fitting for me now to harbor such sorrow and anxiety; I shall go silently to the World-Honored One, yet I shall proceed to the World-Honored One's presence by harnessing the majesty of the King."
Then King Prasenajit addressed his ministers, saying:
"Do you hasten to prepare the precious feathered chariot; according to the former royal custom, I wish to depart from the city of Śrāvastī to approach the Tathāgata."
Having heard the King’s command, the ministers immediately prepared the carriage adorned with peacock-feather jewels and came at once to inform the King, saying:
"The carriage is fully prepared; Your Majesty may know that it is time."

At that time, King Prasenajit immediately mounted a carriage adorned with precious feathers; he struck the bells and beat the drums, suspended silk banners and canopies, and had his attendants all don armor and weapons. Surrounded by his ministers, he departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jetavana. Upon entering the Jetavana monastery on foot, he followed the royal custom of discarding the five insignia of majesty—the parasol, the celestial crown, the fly-whisk, the sword, and the sandals—and laid them all aside.
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, and again rubbed the Tathāgata’s feet with his hands, declaring:

"I now repent my transgressions, reforming my past and cultivating the future. Out of ignorance and delusion, I failed to distinguish between the true and the false; by the power of the king's authority, I killed the hundred sons of my stepmother."
"I now come before you in repentance; I only pray that you will accept me.
The Buddha told the king:
"Excellent, Great King!"
"Return to your original seats; I shall now preach the Dharma.
King Prasenajit immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and returned to his own seat.
The Buddha told the king: "Life is extremely precarious and fragile; even the longest lifespan does not exceed a hundred years, and the time spent is but a small fraction.

One hundred years of human life is calculated as one day and night in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa). Thirty such days and nights constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year. The full lifespan in that Heaven of the Thirty-three is exactly one thousand years, which, when calculated in human terms, is equivalent to one hundred thousand years. Furthermore, this period is but one day and night within the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva)."

Furthermore, calculating thirty such days and nights as one month, and twelve such months as one year, they remain for five thousand such years within the Saṃjīva Hell; their lifespan may last for half an aeon or even a full aeon, according to the deeds committed by each individual, though some may die prematurely—reckoned by human standards as ten billion years.
The wise person constantly reflects upon this and practices it universally; why then would they employ such evil?
The pleasure is slight while the suffering is great, and its calamities are incalculable. Therefore, Great King!
Do not commit sinful deeds for the sake of yourself, your parents, your wife and children, your kingdom, or its people; nor should you create the root of sin for the sake of the king’s person.
It is just as with rock honey, which is sweet at first but bitter afterward; this case is likewise.
Within a short lifespan, why commit evil?

Great King, you should know that there are four great fears that constantly press upon the human body, which can never be restrained, nor can they be suppressed or thwarted by incantations, warfare, or medicinal herbs. Birth, old age, sickness, and death are like four great mountains coming from the four directions, each approaching the others to crush and destroy trees until they are utterly obliterated; these four matters are exactly like this.

Great King, you should know that when birth arrives, it causes one’s parents to experience immeasurable anxiety, sorrow, suffering, and distress; when old age arrives, one no longer possesses youthfulness, the physical form is ruined and decayed, and the limbs gradually grow slack; when illness arrives, even in the prime of life, one no longer has vigor, and as days pass, life becomes ever shorter; and when death arrives, the life-faculty is severed, one is separated from those held dear, and the five aggregates disperse.
"Thus it is said, Great King:
these four great elements all lack self-mastery.
Furthermore, if there is a person who associates with those who take life and partakes in the sources of evil, should they be born among humans, their lifespan will be exceedingly short."
If a person habitually practices stealing, they will be reborn in poverty and destitution in their next life, with clothing that does not cover their body and food that does not fill their mouth.
This occurs because all such conditions result from taking the property of others; thus, even if one is born among humans, they will undergo immeasurable suffering.
If a person commits adultery with another's spouse, when they are later reborn among humans, their wife will not be chaste or virtuous.

If a person speaks falsely, when they are later reborn among humans, their words will not be trusted, and they will be treated with contempt by others; all of this is due to having practiced deception and falsehood in previous lives.

If a person utters harsh words, they will suffer the retribution of hell; if they are reborn among humans, their appearance will be ugly and unattractive—all of which results from the evil speech of previous lives, leading to such a karmic reward.

If a person engages in divisive speech, they will suffer the retribution of the hells; if they are reborn among humans, there will be discord within their family, and they will constantly be subjected to strife and turmoil.
This is because all such occurrences are the karmic retribution for what was created in previous lives.

If a person engages in divisive speech, sowing discord between others, they will suffer the retribution of the hells; if they are reborn among humans, their family will be disharmonious and they will constantly be embroiled in disputes and litigation.
This is because such conditions are entirely brought about by the divisive speech they committed in previous lives.

"If a person delights in hating and envying others, they will undergo the retribution of the hells; even if they are born among humans, they will be detested by others—all of which results from the fundamental actions performed in previous lives."
If a person gives rise to the intent to harm others, they will suffer the retribution of the hells; if they are born among humans, their mind will lack concentration and stability.
This is because it all stems from having given rise to such thoughts in previous lives.

Furthermore, if there are those who practice wrong views and undergo the retribution of the hells, should they later be born among humans, they will be deaf, blind, mute, and loathsome to others to behold.
The reason for this is entirely due to the fundamental actions performed in previous lives.
"It is said, Great King:
because of the retribution for these ten unwholesome deeds, one incurs such calamities and receives immeasurable suffering; how much more so for those external [karmic results]!"
Therefore, Great King, you should transform and govern by means of the Dharma, not by what is contrary to the Dharma; you should govern the people with principle, and never without principle.
Great King!

All those who govern their people with the True Dharma are reborn in the heavens after their lives end; even when Your Majesty’s life has ended, the people will remember you until the end, never forgetting you, as your fame spreads far and wide.
"Great King, you should know that all those who govern and transform the people through what is not the Dharma will, after death, all be born in the hells.
At that time, the wardens of hell bind them with the fivefold bonds;
the suffering they undergo therein is immeasurable—whether by whips, or by binding, or by beating, or by dismembering their limbs, or by taking [their lives]..."
They are roasted by fire, or molten copper is poured over their bodies; their skin is flayed, or grass is driven into their bellies;
their tongues are pulled out, or their bodies are pierced with stakes; they are sawn asunder, or pounded in iron mortars, or crushed by wheels that deform their shapes;
they are forced to run upon mountains of knives and trees of swords, not permitted to rest.
For their respite, they embrace hot copper pillars, or have their eyes gouged out, or have their sense organs of the ears destroyed;
their hands, feet, ears, and noses are severed, yet once severed they grow back again.

They are then lifted by the body and cast into a great cauldron, where their bodies are stirred with iron forks so that their breath cannot rest. Emerging again from the cauldron, they are plucked alive.

Their spinal muscles were used to repair carts; they were then made to enter the Hell of Hot Embers, then the Hell of Hot Excrement, then the Hell of Thorns, then the Hell of Ashes, and then the Hell of the Sword-Tree.
Furthermore, they were forced to lie on their backs and made to eat glowing iron balls, which consumed their intestines.

The five viscera of the stomach are all completely scorched and destroyed; [the molten copper] passes through from below, and then molten copper is poured into their mouths, passing through from below as well, whereby they undergo suffering and affliction therein;
only when their retribution is exhausted do they finally emerge.
Thus it is, Great King!
That sentient beings enter hell is due to such circumstances as these; it is all brought about by the failure to maintain order through the methods of governance in previous lives.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Practicing heedlessness for a hundred years, one subsequently enters hell;
what is there ultimately to crave in this, when the suffering endured is beyond calculation?"
"Great King! Govern by means of the Dharma to sustain yourself, and protect the affairs of state for the sake of your parents, wife and children, servants, and kinsmen.
For this reason, Great King!"
One should always govern and transform others according to the Dharma, and never by what is contrary to the Dharma.

Human life is extremely short; one's stay in this world lasts but a moment. Birth and death are long and far-reaching, fraught with many fears and hardships. When death arrives, one will wail and cry out amidst it, as the joints of the bones separate and the body suffers agonizing pain.
At that time, there will be no one to provide rescue.
Neither parents, wife, children, slaves, servants, kingdom, nor subjects will be able to save them.
Faced with such difficulties, who could bear to take their place?

Only those who practice generosity and uphold the precepts, whose speech is always harmonious and pleasant, who do not wound the hearts of others, who perform manifold meritorious deeds, and who cultivate the roots of all goodness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The wise should practice giving, which is praised by all Buddhas;
therefore, with a pure mind, one should harbor no thoughts of indolence or pride."
Pressed by the force of death, one undergoes extreme suffering and affliction;
having reached those evil realms, there is no time of rest.
If one wishes to return again, one undergoes even greater suffering and affliction.
The sense faculties naturally decay, due to evil that knows no rest.
Even when a physician arrives and gathers all manner of medicinal herbs,
they cannot pervade the entire body, due to evil that knows no rest.
If kinsmen come again to inquire about the origins of their wealth,
yet their ears do not even hear the sound [of his voice], it is because of the unceasing nature of evil.
If he is moved to the ground, the sick person lies upon it.
The form is like the root of a withered tree; because of evil, there is no rest.
If life has already ended, and body, life-force, and consciousness have already separated, the form is like the earth of a wall; because of evil, there is no rest.
"Furthermore, when those corpses are lifted from the grave by their kinsmen, there is nothing they can take with them;
only merit can be relied upon. Therefore, Great King!"
"You should seek skillful means and practice meritorious deeds; if you do not do so now, it will be of no avail for your future regrets.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"By the power of merit, the Tathāgata has subdued the hosts of Māra’s officials."
"Now that he has returned to the power of the Buddha, for this reason his power of merit is supreme.
Therefore, Great King, you should mindfully cultivate merit;
if you have committed evil, you should repent at once and never commit it again."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Though it be the source of extreme evil, If one repents, it gradually becomes thin.
At such a time, within this world, The root is entirely extinguished."
"Therefore, Great King!
Do not, for the sake of yourself, practice evil; do not, for the sake of your parents, wife, children, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, commit evil or habituate yourself to unwholesome conduct."
"In this way, Great King,
you should train yourself.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Neither parents nor brothers, nor any kinsmen, can escape this evil;
all must abandon everything and return to death. Therefore, Great King!"
"From this day forward, you should transform and govern by means of the Dharma,
and not by what is contrary to the Dharma. Thus, Great King, you should train yourself."
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit saw ten things in a dream during the night. Upon awakening, he was overcome with great sorrow and fear, dreading the ruin of his kingdom as well as the loss of himself, his wife, and his sons.

On the following day, the king immediately summoned the high ministers, great officials, wise practitioners, and Brahmins capable of interpreting dreams and omens; they all assembled, and the king then recounted to them the ten matters of his night dream, asking who among them could interpret them.
The brāhmaṇa said,
"I am able to explain it, but I fear that if the King hears it, he will immediately become displeased. The King said:
"Then speak it. The brahmin said, "The king,
the crown prince, and the queen shall perish."
The king said, "What do you say,
sirs! Is it not possible to perform rites of averting and exorcism?"

The Brahmin said: "This matter can be averted through propitiatory rites. One must kill the crown prince, the king’s most esteemed chief consort, her attendants, servants, slaves, and the most honored ministers, using them as offerings to the Heavenly King;
furthermore, all bedding, furniture, and rare treasures should be burned by fire as an offering to the gods."
"In this way, O King, both your person and your kingdom may come to an end, with nothing remaining.
Upon hearing the words of the brahmin, the king was overcome with great sorrow and distress; he withdrew into his chamber of fasting and brooded over these matters.
The king had a queen named Māri; she went to where the king was and asked him, "For what reason do you remain sorrowful and unhappy? Have I, your servant, committed some offense against you?"
The king said, "You have done no wrong against me; simply do not inquire into this matter, for should you hear it, it would cause you grief and fear.
The queen replied to the king:
"I do not dare feel sorrow or fear.
The king said, "There is no need to ask; those who hear it will feel sorrow and fear."

The lady said: "I am half of the King's own body; in times of urgency or distress, he would rather kill me alone so that the King may remain secure and free from fear. I pray that Your Majesty will explain this to me."
The King then explained to his consort:

"Last night I saw ten things in a dream: first, I saw three cauldrons; the two side cauldrons were full while the central cauldron was empty, and the steam from the two side cauldrons mingled with one another but did not enter the empty central cauldron;
second, I dreamed of a horse that ate from both its mouth and its rump."
Third, he dreamed that a great tree blossomed with flowers;
fourth, he dreamed that a small tree bore fruit;
fifth, he dreamed that a man was seeking a rope, whereupon a sheep appeared and began eating the rope.
Sixth, he dreamed that a fox sat upon a golden bed, eating from a golden vessel;
seventh, he dreamed that a great bull turned back to suckle at the udder of its own calf;

eighth, he dreamed that a herd of black oxen came bellowing from the four directions, charging toward one another as if to fight; just as they were about to collide, they vanished, and their whereabouts were unknown.
Ninth, he dreamed that in a great pond, the water was turbid in the center and clear at the four edges;
tenth, he dreamed that the waves of a great mountain stream were flowing a deep crimson.
Having seen these dreams, he immediately awoke in great terror, fearing for the loss of his kingdom as well as his own life, his wife, children, and subjects.
Now, the Duke of Shao, the high ministers, the practitioners of the Way, and the brahmins who were able to interpret dreams were summoned. At that time, one brahmin said:
"One must kill the Prince, the beloved Queen, the high ministers, and the servants and slaves to offer them as a sacrifice to the heavens."
"It is for this reason that I am grieved.
The lady replied, "Great King!"
Do not worry about your dream.
It is like a person who buys gold: by heating it with fire and rubbing it on a stone, its quality—whether good or bad—will naturally be revealed.
Now the Buddha is nearby at the Jetavana Monastery; you may go there to question him. If the Buddha provides an explanation, you may follow what he says.
"How could I have believed the words of this mad and deluded brāhmaṇa, causing myself such grief and distress as to reach this state?

The king, having just now awakened from his joy, immediately summoned his attendants and ministers to quickly prepare the chariots and cavalry. The king mounted a carriage with a high canopy, accompanied by several million riders and attendants, and departed from Śrāvastī for the Jetavana Monastery. Alighting on foot at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Last night I saw ten things in a dream; I pray that the Buddha will take pity on me and explain each matter."
The Buddha told the king:
"Excellent, Great King! That which you have dreamed is a manifestation of auspicious omens for the future world to come."

In future generations, the people will not fear the prohibitive laws; they will all engage in debauchery, coveting wives and children, indulging their passions with lewdness without ever reaching satiety. Driven by jealousy and folly, they will know neither shame nor remorse; those who are pure and chaste will be cast aside, while the sycophantic and the deceitful will bring disorder to the state.

The King dreamed of three cauldrons: the two on the sides were full, while the one in the center was empty. The steam from the two side cauldrons rose and mingled with one another, yet it did not enter the empty cauldron in the center. This signifies that in future generations, people will all lack sufficient means to support their parents and will fall into poverty; those born together will not be close to one another, but instead will become intimate with strangers. The wealthy and noble will associate with one another and exchange gifts.
"The King saw one thing in his dream, and it is precisely for this reason.

In the King's dream, he saw a horse eating from its mouth and also eating from its rump. This signifies that in future generations, the people, ministers, officials, senior administrators, and high dignitaries will receive stipends from the government and yet also consume the resources of the common people. Taxation will never cease; subordinate officials will commit corruption, and the people will find no peace, unable to remain settled in their ancestral lands."
"The King has seen two things in his dream, and it is precisely for this reason.

In the King's dream, he saw a great tree blooming with flowers; in future generations, the people will frequently encounter forced labor, their hearts will burn and their minds be distressed, constantly filled with sorrow and fear, such that by the age of thirty, their hair will turn white."
"The King saw three things in his dream for this very reason.

As for the King's dream of a small tree bearing fruit: in future generations, women will seek marriage even before they have reached the age of fifteen; they will return home carrying their children, yet feel no sense of shame."
"The King’s dream of these four things was precisely for this reason.

In the King’s dream, he saw a man seeking a rope while a sheep followed behind; the sheep ate the rope first. This signifies that in the final age of the world, husbands will go abroad for trade or enter military service, wandering through streets and villages, engaging in social gatherings and jesting with their peers. Meanwhile, their unvirtuous wives will stay at home, committing adultery with men, living together with them, consuming their husbands' wealth, and indulging in their passions and desires as they please. They will have no sense of shame or reproach, and even when their husbands discover this, they will merely follow others’ example by feigning ignorance."
"The King's dream of these five things was precisely for this reason.

That the King dreamed of a fox ascending a golden bed and eating from golden vessels means that in future generations, those who are lowly shall become noble; they shall sit upon golden beds to consume rich delicacies. Those of high birth and great clans shall be reduced to servants and runners; the virtuous shall become slaves, and slaves shall become the virtuous."
The King saw six things in his dream; these are precisely what they refer to.

"In the King’s dream, he saw a great bull returning from its calf to suckle at its milk. This signifies that in future generations, mothers will act as go-betweens for their daughters, bringing other men into their chambers. The mother will stay by the door to receive wealth and provisions, using them to support herself, while the father likewise consents, feigning deafness and ignorance."
The King saw seven things in his dream; these are precisely what they were.

“The King saw in his dream black oxen coming from the four directions in great herds, bellowing and roaring as they rushed toward one another, intending to fight; yet before they could even join, the oxen vanished and their whereabouts were unknown. This shall come to pass for future generations of kings, ministers, officials, and the common people: they shall all fail to fear the Great Prohibitions, becoming greedy and lustful, amassing wealth and hoarding property. From the eldest to the youngest among wives and children, none shall be pure or upright; they shall be lewd, gluttonous, and never know satiety. Driven by jealousy and folly, they shall lack shame and remorse; they shall fail to practice loyalty and filial piety, and through flattery and treachery, they shall bring ruin upon the state. Fearing neither superiors nor inferiors, the rains shall not fall in season, the climate shall be discordant, and violent winds and dust shall arise. Blown sand shall break the trees, and locusts shall devour the crops, causing them to fail to ripen. Because the sovereign and the people act in such a manner, Heaven sends down these portents.”
Furthermore, he manifested clouds rising from all four sides; the sovereign and the people were all filled with joy, each saying, "The clouds have gathered from the four directions;
it will surely rain now. Yet in a mere moment, the clouds dispersed on their own.

He thus manifested this marvel in order to cause the myriad people to reform their conduct, to guard the good and uphold the precepts, to stand in awe of Heaven and Earth, to avoid entering the evil realms, to maintain integrity and self-restraint, to have only one wife, and to possess a compassionate heart free from anger.
The King saw eight things in his dream; these are precisely what they refer to. "In the King's dream, he saw a large pond whose center was turbid while its four edges were clear.

This means that in future generations within Jambudvīpa, ministers will be disloyal and sons will be unfilial; they will not respect their elders, will not believe in the Buddha-dharma, and will not revere those who are learned in the scriptures. Ministers will greedily crave official rewards and sons will greedily crave their fathers' wealth; they will lack gratitude and reciprocity, and will disregard righteousness and principle.

Conversely, people in the borderlands will be loyal and filial, will honor and respect their elders, will have faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, and will provide offerings to those learned in the scriptures, mindful of repaying kindness."
The King saw nine matters in his dream; these are precisely what they refer to.

"In the King's dream, he saw a great river flowing with waves that were perfectly red. This means that in future generations, various emperors and kings shall not grow weary of their own kingdoms, but shall raise armies to fight together, deploying chariot troops and cavalry to attack and invade one another, killing each other until the blood flows perfectly red."
The King saw ten matters in his dream; these were precisely those very things.

They all concern the affairs of people in future generations: if people of future generations can keep their minds fixed on the Buddha-way and serve those who have clearly mastered the scriptures, they will all be reborn in the heavens after death. If, however, they commit foolish deeds and further harm one another, they will enter the three evil realms after death, beyond further description.

The king immediately knelt with his right knee on the ground and, with palms joined, received the Buddha’s instruction. His heart was filled with joy, and he attained concentration and wisdom; his fear vanished entirely. The king then prostrated himself in homage, placing his head at the Buddha’s feet.

Upon returning to the palace, he bestowed further gifts upon the lady and invested her as the principal consort (*mahādevī*). He granted her vast wealth and treasures, instructing her to distribute them to others; consequently, the kingdom became prosperous and joyful.
Furthermore, he confiscated the stipends of all the high ministers, great officials, and *brāhmaṇas*, banished them all from the country, and never again placed them in positions of trust or credit.
All the people resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path; the king and his consort paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
